stories.title: Terrible, dangerous advice from the Ontario premier
stories.summary: Doug Ford was wrong to suggest using weapons against home invaders
stories.author: Marcus Gee
stories.content:
Listen to this article

Learn more about audio

Doug Ford often shoots from the lip. He says some silly things, some rash things – even some sensible things – but seldom does he say something downright dangerous. This Thursday was an exception.

The Ontario premier was answering questions from reporters about home invasions. Toronto has suffered two awful examples of this growing form of crime over the past few weeks. In the first, in the exclusive Bridle Path neighbourhood, the invaders attacked a husband, wife and their two adult daughters, shooting the father and daughters and hitting all four with a hammer. In the second, which happened this week in another prosperous part of town, a talented local musician was shot dead.

Mr. Ford left no doubt about how he would act in such a case. “I’ll tell you one thing: Someone comes through my door with a gun and knife and starts shooting it up, I’ll blow the guy right through the front door,” he said. “You’ll look like Swiss cheese by the time he’s done.”

He said that he himself owns a gun, but for those who don’t, he suggested a knife or a baseball bat. “I encourage people to use whatever tool they have to fight back. Not hide, but fight back.”

That was terrible advice. Police generally recommend avoiding contact and conflict with intruders. If you know someone is in your home, they often say, you should get out if you can, shelter in a safe place if you can’t – and, above all, call 911. If a threatening intruder orders you to surrender some belongings, the sensible thing is to hand them over. Property can be replaced; lives cannot.

Confronting someone who comes into your house to rob you carries enormous risk. You never know what might happen. Even owning a gun – and, thankfully, most of us in Canada don’t – is no guarantee that you will prevail.

The chances that you will be able to find and use a firearm in the confusion of something like a home invasion are small. Mr. Ford said he keeps his gun under lock and key. His ammunition is in a separate place. He admitted that “it takes time” to put gun and ammo together.

You don’t have to look far to see the folly of the blast-away approach that Mr. Ford suggests. Right next door sits the most heavily armed country in the world. Has allowing citizens to keep firearms in their homes with relative ease made the United States a noticeably safer place? Those guns are far more likely to be fired in suicides, domestic altercations or accidents than against some masked bad guy.

Home invasions are a disturbing phenomenon, no question. The invaders often break into a house in search of the key fob for a luxury car. Many carry weapons.

After these last two shockingly violent cases in Toronto, residents are feeling shaken. Could it happen to me? What would I do if it did?

“People are frightened,” Mayor Olivia Chow said. “I have heard it. Neighbours checking their locks. Families lying awake at every sound in the middle of the night… That fear is real. I feel it too, and I am angry.”

But Canadians are not defenceless, either individually or collectively. Rather than arm themselves, individuals can get alarm systems, better locks and other means of reinforcing their homes. If they live in a family or group situation, they can put together a plan for what to do if an invasion happens (even if the probability is low).

As a society, we can toughen laws and improve policing. Police have arrested one suspect in the Bridle Path invasion and say they are closing in on two others. In the Toronto-area region of Peel, police investigating a series of invasions have charged another two men. Federal reforms to bail and sentencing rules enacted earlier this year aim to curb violent crime.

Mr. Ford would like Ottawa to go further and adopt something resembling the “castle” doctrine, a concept that makes it easier for people to use force – in some American states, deadly force – against those who breach their homes. That, too, is bad advice. Our Criminal Code already permits you to use reasonable force against an intruder, especially if you believe your life or the lives of others is in jeopardy.

The question is whether resorting to force is prudent in the moment. Tempting as it May be to grab that baseball bat, the usual answer is no. Far better to stay calm, keep your loved ones safe and call the police.

stories.title: Don’t put too much hope on a Democratic Congress ending Trump’s tariffs
stories.summary: Speculation is rife over the American president’s desire to avoid risking his own party turning against him with a possible vote on repealing the Canadian tariffs.
stories.author: Tracy Moran
stories.content:
Washington, D.C. — With the seating of a new, Democratic-controlled U.S. Congress looming, there’s renewed talk of a possible Canada-U.S. trade deal.

Speculation is rife over the American president’s desire to avoid risking his own party turning against him with a possible vote on repealing the Canadian tariffs. But how much power will the new Congress really have to affect change?

National Post reached out to Bill Reinsch, senior adviser at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, for his thoughts on the likelihood of Congress repealing the tariffs on Canada and on the likelihood of an interim trade deal.

This Q&A has been edited for length and clarity.

In the short run, they shouldn’t be very optimistic because it’ll be very difficult to get a bill across the finish line and have it survive a likely presidential veto. In the long run, I think they’ll be able to raise the public profile of the issue, which was already raised in the election, and they’ll be able to sustain that. I think they May be successful in getting the president to moderate his actions with respect to Canada.

Monday - Saturday Free

NP Posted keeps you updated on the news of the day and the perspectives that define the National Post, while drawing your focus to some of the unexpected stories we like to tell. Delivered straight to your inbox Monday to Friday, with a weekend edition on Saturdays.

The election message was pretty clear that the tariffs in general are not popular, and of all the tariffs, the Canadian ones are probably least popular. The president sometimes reads the tea leaves. He never admits that he reads the tea leaves, and he never admits that he made a mistake, but he does sometimes read them.

First of all, I would expect a deal between now and the end of the year. Second, even if there isn’t one, I would expect no new aggressive actions against Canada, at least no new tariffs, because I don’t think (Trump) wants to have a constant battle with the Congress on this particular issue.

If they pass a bill — that itself will be harder than they think — he’ll veto it. Getting 290 in the House and 67 in the Senate would be very hard. The pressure on Republicans to support the president will be enormous. It always is, regardless of party. You get pressure from your own leadership, and you get pressure from the White House. The White House can dispense goodies. A wavering congressman says, “I have this road project in my district,” and suddenly the government can find funds for road repair. I’ve seen the game played. It pays to be a wavering member in this situation, but the quid pro quo is that the wavering member has to support the president.

But the act of legislating, the hearings, the vote, the debate, puts the Republican members in an awkward position. If they vote with the president, they’re taking an unpopular position that May be harming their district. What you probably will find is Republicans privately and quietly going to the White House and saying, “We need to work something out here. This is just an intolerable situation.” If you don’t get a deal between now and the end of the year, you get a deal early in the year that’s been in part the result of congressional pressure.

That question hasn’t exactly been posed, either in polling or to members of Congress. The problem with tariffs is that everybody likes some of them, and the ones you don’t like vary. If you’re in Pennsylvania, you want to save the steel tariffs. If you’re in the Midwest, you are particularly irritated by agriculture tariffs, because you understand the reciprocity issues.

I wouldn’t say it’s unanimous, but I think there’s a view that the Canadian tariffs in particular are a mistake, that they’ve damaged the bilateral relationship, not irreparably, but for a very long time. That’s a mistake on several levels, not just relating to trade. The best thing to do about it would be to make them go away.

The question that has not been asked of the steel representatives is: ‘Can you live with 50 per cent tariffs on everybody but Canada and Mexico, and then go back, not to Nafta, but to Usmca, and have a zero-tariff situation?’ I don’t know what they’d say about that.

It’s hard to say, because if you have the vote initially to pass it, what happens after that is you see who voted which way. You look at which Republicans voted yes when it initially passes, and then you work to shore that up and make sure they’re going to stick with you, because they’re the ones the pressure is going to come on. Then you look at the ones that stuck with the president initially and figure out why, where they’re from, why this matters.

The first ones to focus on are those with people in their district who are being harmed by the tariffs. You’d have to go district by district, look at the data, and see who’s hurting and what companies are located where. If you’re John Deere, manufacturing tractors, the steel you’re using is a lot more expensive than it used to be. So you look at Nebraska, where there’s John Deere manufacturing in addition to a lot of farmers who don’t like tariffs anyway, and you zero in on that district.

The other place you can look is members of Congress who don’t have any particular stake in this one way or the other and are just supporting the president because they’re Republicans. You try to give them good reasons in this particular case not to support the president. It’s trench warfare, really. The team trying to get the override has to do a lot of vote counting and go one by one.

Nobody at this point has any incentive to part with the president, except the people in border states like Michigan and Maine that are very clearly being affected and where it was obviously an issue in the election.

You can figure out whether the Democrats simply want to make an issue, or whether they want to actually enact something. If you want to put Republicans in an awkward position and force them to vote for an unpopular thing, you do a freestanding bill. With the size of the Democratic majority, I think they probably have the votes to pass that in both bodies. But then you have a veto.

If you really want to accomplish it, you don’t pass it as a separate bill. You tuck it into something that has to pass, a must-pass bill. That’s usually either an appropriation bill, where, if the money isn’t voted on, the agencies have to shut down, or a debt limit extension, which I think there’s going to have to be next year, or the annual defense authorization. If they don’t pass it this year, they could still pass it in January. It’s been (more than 60) years since they haven’t passed one, so a lot of members think we just have to do this, period.

You tuck it in there, and you probably have the votes to do that. Then you put the president in an awkward position, because he wants the rest of the bill and he doesn’t have a line-item veto. He has to veto all or nothing. He might still veto it, but vetoing a big must-pass bill means you’re irritating a whole bunch of other people who May not care about the tariffs but care about everything else in the bill. It’s easier to get an override vote on something like that.

No, I don’t think the debate’s gotten to that point yet. There’s been a number of proposals, some announced and some actually introduced even before the election. Sen. (Ron) Wyden had a bill that would repeal Section 338. It’s not clear to me whether the bill also gets rid of the tariffs. You’d have to repeal it retroactively to do that. They all die at the end of the year, so you have to start over again.

So far the talk has been a bill to do this, a bill to do that. That’s the way it begins, and sometimes you even pass it that way. Then you go back and think, maybe a better route is to make it part of something else. That decision comes later. It also depends on whether something else is actually available. The must-pass bills don’t come up every week.

The things that seem to have the most support are repealing the two provisions of the law he’s been using, Section 122 and Section 338. Just doing that might get a lot of Republicans to support it. Whether it would have any practical effect, I don’t know. Just repealing Section 338 doesn’t automatically mean the tariffs imposed pursuant to it go away. You would have to say that in the bill.

I could see an agreement in which he basically gives back to Canada what he’s taken on a lot of issues, particularly the tariffs, and declares victory because he didn’t give back everything. The more likely outcome is they negotiate a deal in which the tariffs are not fully removed but are mitigated. The Canadians get to a point where they say, “We can live with this,” the Americans agree, and life goes on.

If I were the Canadians, number one, I’d get rid of the ones that are scheduled to go into effect in January — the autos, trucks, and auto parts ones. Bring the steel and aluminum ones down from 50 per cent to some more reasonable level. The Canadians will say zero, but in my experience, when the US says 50 and the Canadians say zero, you can always get to an agreement. There’s some number in between that the two sides can ultimately agree on. It May not be 25. It takes a while, and it’s complicated, but you can get there.

Economists will say that’s a suboptimal outcome, and they’ll be right, but it’ll be what they negotiated. And Trump will say, “I win,” because there are still some tariffs.

Is the auto sector the sticking point?

It is a sticking point. Fundamentally it’s going to be difficult, because Trump wants to move production to the United States, and he doesn’t care if the Canadian automobile industry survives. He doesn’t really seem to understand how supply chains work, particularly in that industry, and how interdependent the three countries have become over the 60 years since the first Canadian (Auto Pact) in ’65. National Post reached out to Bill Reinsch, senior adviser at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, for his thoughts on the likelihood of Congress repealing the tariffs on Canada and on the likelihood of an interim trade deal.
This Q&A has been edited for length and clarity.

In the short run, they shouldn’t be very optimistic because it’ll be very difficult to get a bill across the finish line and have it survive a likely presidential veto. In the long run, I think they’ll be able to raise the public profile of the issue, which was already raised in the election, and they’ll be able to sustain that. The election message was pretty clear that the tariffs in general are not popular, and of all the tariffs, the Canadian ones are probably least popular. The president sometimes reads the tea leaves. He never admits that he reads the tea leaves, and he never admits that he made a mistake, but he does sometimes read them.

First of all, I would expect a deal between now and the end of the year. Second, even if there isn’t one, I would expect no new aggressive actions against Canada, at least no new tariffs, because I don’t think (Trump) wants to have a constant battle with the Congress on this particular issue.

If they pass a bill — that itself will be harder than they think — he’ll veto it. Getting 290 in the House and 67 in the Senate would be very hard. The pressure on Republicans to support the president will be enormous. It always is, regardless of party. You get pressure from your own leadership, and you get pressure from the White House. The White House can dispense goodies. A wavering congressman says, “I have this road project in my district,” and suddenly the government can find funds for road repair. I’ve seen the game played. It pays to be a wavering member in this situation, but the quid pro quo is that the wavering member has to support the president.

But the act of legislating, the hearings, the vote, the debate, puts the Republican members in an awkward position. If they vote with the president, they’re taking an unpopular position that May be harming their district. What you probably will find is Republicans privately and quietly going to the White House and saying, “We need to work something out here. This is just an intolerable situation.” If you don’t get a deal between now and the end of the year, you get a deal early in the year that’s been in part the result of congressional pressure.

That question hasn’t exactly been posed, either in polling or to members of Congress. The problem with tariffs is that everybody likes some of them, and the ones you don’t like vary. If you’re in Pennsylvania, you want to save the steel tariffs. If you’re in the Midwest, you are particularly irritated by agriculture tariffs, because you understand the reciprocity issues.

I wouldn’t say it’s unanimous, but I think there’s a view that the Canadian tariffs in particular are a mistake, that they’ve damaged the bilateral relationship, not irreparably, but for a very long time. That’s a mistake on several levels, not just relating to trade. The best thing to do about it would be to make them go away.

You try to give them good reasons in this particular case not to support the president. It’s trench warfare, really. Nobody at this point has any incentive to part with the president, except the people in border states like Michigan and Maine that are very clearly being affected and where it was obviously an issue in the election.

If you want to put Republicans in an awkward position and force them to vote for an unpopular thing, you do a freestanding bill. With the size of the Democratic majority, I think they probably have the votes to pass that in both bodies. But then you have a veto.

If you really want to accomplish it, you don’t pass it as a separate bill. You tuck it into something that has to pass, a must-pass bill. That’s usually either an appropriation bill, where, if the money isn’t voted on, the agencies have to shut down, or a debt limit extension, which I think there’s going to have to be next year, or the annual defense authorization. If they don’t pass it this year, they could still pass it in January. It’s been (more than 60) years since they haven’t passed one, so a lot of members think we just have to do this, period.

You tuck it in there, and you probably have the votes to do that. Then you put the president in an awkward position, because he wants the rest of the bill and he doesn’t have a line-item veto. He has to veto all or nothing. He might still veto it, but vetoing a big must-pass bill means you’re irritating a whole bunch of other people who May not care about the tariffs but care about everything else in the bill. It’s easier to get an override vote on something like that.

No, I don’t think the debate’s gotten to that point yet. There’s been a number of proposals, some announced and some actually introduced even before the election. Sen. stories.title: Quebec physician burnout jumps to 80%: CMA
stories.summary: The association said one in two physicians screened positive for depression, while reports of suicidal thoughts doubled and now exceed levels recorded during the pandemic.
stories.author: Alessia Simona Maratta
stories.content:
Physician burnout in Quebec has risen sharply over the past year, with new survey data suggesting eight in 10 doctors are experiencing burnout, according to the Canadian Medical Association.

Preliminary results from a CMA physician health survey conducted in Quebec in September found the burnout rate had climbed to 80 per cent from 48 per cent in 2025, with family physicians reporting the highest rates.

The association said one in two physicians screened positive for depression, while reports of suicidal thoughts doubled and now exceed levels recorded during the COVID-19 pandemic.

The CMA said 92 per cent of physicians surveyed reported that the legislation had affected their well-being.

“These numbers are nothing short of shocking, at a time when demand for public health care continues to grow,” said Dr. Jean-Joseph Condé, the Cma’s French-language spokesperson.

Condé said physicians remain committed to providing care but warned that working conditions need to improve. He pointed to reducing administrative burdens, training more doctors and other health-care professionals, expanding team-based care and giving physicians more time with patients as potential solutions.

Despite the rise in burnout, the CMA said physicians’ intentions to reduce their clinical hours or leave medicine remained stable compared with 2025.

CMA president Dr. Bolu Ogunyemi said physician well-being must be addressed as millions of Canadians struggle to access primary care.

“At a time when nearly six million people in Canada don’t have regular access to primary care, we can’t afford to lose more physicians to burnout,” Ogunyemi said.

The association said it will continue working with governments across Canada to monitor physician health and advocate for doctors to be involved in legal reforms affecting their practices and the delivery of patient care.

stories.title: Calgarian with Tourette syndrome interrupted by councillor during budget public hearing
stories.summary: In an interview with Global News, Matthew Riley said the situation has left him hurt and embarrassed, and thinking twice about speaking to Calgary city council again
stories.author: Adam MacVicar
stories.content:
A public hearing at Calgary city hall on the proposed four-year budget went into a lengthy recess Friday afternoon, after a councillor interrupted a presenter who repeatedly used profane language due to tics associated with Tourette syndrome.

Matthew Riley joined the public hearing by phone to voice his concerns about a proposed 15 per cent property tax increase and significant hikes to utility rates.

During his presentation, Riley exhibited a number of tics that included vulgar language and slurs, leading Ward 10 Coun. Andre Chabot to raise a point of privilege during the meeting.

“I don’t care what affliction you May have, inappropriate language is not acceptable in these chambers and if you have to cover your mouth because you have to say something that’s inappropriate, then I would insist that the presenter do so,” Chabot said. “There are children in the audience. I’m sorry, it’s inexcusable.”

Riley told city council he had written to the city clerk’s office to inform staff of his condition, and involuntary tics, and noted he participated by phone rather than instead of in person to prevent disruptions.

When he continued his presentation, Riley accused Chabot of discriminating against him and interfering with his right to participate in the public hearing due to his condition.

“You just primed me, and now anything that comes out of me is going to be worse because of that,” he told council. “You have no idea what it’s like to have Tourettes, sir, you should look into it before you speak.”

Riley attempted to continue his presentation, but his tics included further profane language.

Chabot rose again, and said council has the right “to disqualify someone” from speaking in council chambers.

“I would insist that this person, being as he cannot comply, regardless of his affliction, that he be not allowed to continue,” Chabot argued.

City council recessed the meeting for roughly an hour and councillors could be seen consulting with one another and city lawyers to determine their next steps.

Once the meeting resumed, Calgary Mayor Jeromy Farkas apologized to Riley for the delay in hearing his submission, and noted council has an obligation to “protect the psychological safety” of city staff and the public participating in the hearing.

“We recognize that involuntary expressions associated with a disability are different from deliberately disrespectful language,” Farkas read from a statement. “I have verified that this individual notified the clerks team in advance of this disability and a request for accommodation, and the disability has been confirmed by another member of council.”

“We have an obligation to accommodate to the extent that offering that accommodation does not otherwise cause undue hardship on others,” Farkas added.

The mayor suggested city council move into a closed session to hear Riley’s presentation.

In an interview with Global News, Riley said the situation left him extremely hurt and embarrassed.

“The tics, they’re not a reflection of how I feel about anybody,” he said in a phone interview. “These guys are leading a city and they can’t distinguish between becoming a victim of a man with a disability, who doesn’t mean it, being able to be like ‘okay, he doesn’t mean it. I can hear what he’s saying between the ticks.’ I think that’s awful.”

Riley declined the offer to present behind closed doors, and continued with his presentation in public. A warning was given to those participating in the public hearing before he resumed speaking.

Ward 2 Coun. Jennifer Wyness criticized how city council handled the situation and its offer for Riley to present in a closed session.

“That also removes his right to be heard by his peers and the community,” she told reporters. “For council and our elected officials, we say we want inclusive communities, well this is when the rubber hits the road. You need to take this opportunity to educate Calgarians.”

When asked by reporters about the situation, Chabot said his concern was that the public had not been warned that Riley’s presentation could include offensive language.

“To be forewarned is to be forearmed, essentially. So now we know if there’s a similar condition that happens again in the future, we can advise the public of something that might be disruptive or offensive to individuals,” he said. “I personally don’t have an issue with it, it was more about protecting the interests of the public.”

Riley, who performs stand-up comedy in Calgary and advocates for people with Tourette syndrome, told Global News he plans to seek advice about his next steps.

He told council during the interruption that he would pursue a lawsuit.

Although Riley completed his presentation, he said the pain of the situation has him thinking twice about sharing his thoughts with city council again.

“It’s so hurtful. I don’t know what to do,” he told Global News. “The people who represent me did this to me. I don’t know if I’ll ever be able to go there again.”

stories.title: B.C., Saskatchewan premiers urge conservative unity to Danielle Smith’s fractured UCP
stories.summary: B.C. Premier Lorne Doerkson and Saskatchewn Premier Scott Moe framed the three provinces as a unified economic powerhouse
stories.author: Jesse Snyder
stories.content:
Calgary — The premiers of B.C. and Saskatchewan addressed a large gathering of Alberta Premier Danielle Smith’s supporters on Friday, delivering a message of conservative unity across Western Canada and touting their vision for creating a powerful economic bloc between the three provinces.

Members of Smith’s United Conservative Party are in Calgary this weekend for their annual general meeting, where the premier is attempting to mend the party’s fractured supporter base following the province’s independence referendum. Smith and her supporters have been urging members to remain united ahead of the next general election, warning that a failure to do so threatens to award power to the opposition NDP.

The party invited B.C. Premier Lorne Doerkson and Saskatchewan Premier Scott to attend the AGM, where the pair sought to emphasize the potential economic benefits that the three provinces could reap now that they are all under conservative leadership.

“Today, I believe we have an opportunity to build something more consequential: A partnership — a pipeline,” Doerkson said. “We have concluded a partnership between our provinces that strengthens Western Canada, and in doing so, strengthens Canada itself.” “

Smith, who introduced Doerkson to a mixture of cheers and boos, has been making the same point both to her party base and in public remarks.

“What an incredible time to be a conservative in Western Canada,” she told the crowd during her introduction.

On Friday, Doerkson and Moe both underscored the immense combined natural resource potential between the three provinces, with Doerkson saying B.C. was now “bullish on LNG, natural gas, propane, everything.”

Doerkson’s Conservative Party won the British Columbia legislature with a commanding election win last month, putting B.C., Alberta and Saskatchewan all under the conservative majority rule for the first time in living memory. Doerkson’s election win has transformed the relationship between B.C. and Alberta in particular, erasing previous disagreement between the two provinces on numerous issues including energy policy.

“We love Pacific Link,” Doerkson told the UCP crowd to loud applause, referencing Alberta’s proposed West Coast oil pipeline.

Moe referred to Doerkson and Smith as “very much aligned,” and said that together with Saskatchewan, the three provinces could form an economic powerhouse.

“These three Western provinces are going to drive the national economy for the foreseeable future,” he said.

Doerkson also made a case for keeping conservatives united, reflecting on how his Conservative Party won in B.C. in part because right and centre-right parties joined forces, defeating the incumbent NDP.

“We won because we came together,” he said.

In Alberta, Smith is facing an upheaval from within her own ranks, with the UCP split between strategic-minded members who want to focus on the next election, and some of the party’s most earnest separatists. Smith has sought to restrict separatist sentiments within the UCP in an effort to make it more palatable to mainstream voters, and the party has started requiring constituency presidents to sign declarations that they will abide by the referendum’s result.

In the Oct. 19 referendum, roughly three in four Albertans voted against holding a second referendum that would have proposed seceding from Canada.

B.C. Premier Lorne Doerkson, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith and Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe join hands on stage at the UCP annual general meeting held at the BMO Centre on Friday, Nov. 27, 2026. Dean Pilling/Postmedia

Doerkson in particular made a case for a unified Canada during his address to the UCP members.

“Last month, Albertans asked an enormously important question about the future of this country, and I know that that was a massive challenge,” he said.

“Believe me, we heard you all the way on the Pacific coast. So let me be clear tonight, I am an unabashed Canadian. Canada is the best country in the world. It is worth defending. It is worth building.

Moe warned against the risk of a fractured UCP potentially leading to an NDP government, or as he put it, an “NDP banana republic.” (Banana, Moe said, stands for ‘build absolutely nothing anywhere near anyone.’”

Moe cited the Alberta Ndp’s election win in 2015, which he argued was the “terrible consequence” of vote splitting on the right. Once the UCP brought together the Wildrose Party and Progressive Conservatives, “order was restored to Canada’s most conservative province,” he said.

stories.title: Local politicians tour problem-plagued apartment buildings on Kipps Lane
stories.summary: Renters' advocacy group Acorn provided local politicians with a tour of a group of problem-plagued apartments on Kipps Lane Friday afternoon.
stories.author: Bryan Bicknell
stories.content:
Renters’ advocacy group Acorn provided local politicians with a tour of a group of problem-plagued apartments on Kipps Lane Friday afternoon.

Organizers wanted policy makers to see for themselves the conditions that tenants in the cluster of buildings have been living with.

The organized event was marred by confusion, however, at the outset. London police had been called to deal with trespassing, taking Acorn representatives by surprise.

“Somehow, after five years of being active in this city, London police are confused on that. So thankfully, we were not trespassing, we were not fined,” said Acorn London representative Jordan Smith.

A last-minute decision banished members of the news media to the outside of the building, while London Mayor Josh Morgan and a number of councillors, along with MPP Terence Kernaghan were given an abbreviated tour to witness conditions and hear from tenants.

“The city has issued a number of compliance orders. That’s all done through compliance and bylaw, there’s no political interference in that. Fines have also been levied in some cases. And the city has even moved towards the possibility of emergency procurement when things like the heat are off,” explained Morgan.

The cluster of six buildings had been operated by property manager Sireg until recently, when the company fell into bankruptcy. A court appointed administrator is now in charge.

Smith says the Friday visitors got an eye-full.

“The halls themselves smell like garbage. There’s black mould hanging from the ceiling in several areas. The list goes on, and we didn’t even go inside the units. Again, chronic disrepair which led to systemic neglect,” Smith said.

The tour follows a fatal fire at one of the buildings, 756 Kipps Lane, last week .

In the meantime, those living in the complex have been dealing with a host of problems- from lack of heat to pest infestations.

Tenant Elm Putnam has been living at 758 Kipps Lane for six years and says they can’t wait to move out this weekend.

“We have some security concerns in the building. I don’t know if you noticed on your way in, that front door doesn’t always lock. There’s been a lot of trespassing, people sleeping in the stairwell, some illegal activities, a lot of trash, and sometimes bottles of urine or feces left behind,” she said.

Acorn continues to call on the city to establish a landlord registry to better protect renters.

“What they can do about it has been clear for five plus years. That’s a landlord registration program based on a system of proactive inspections,” Smith said.

content_blocks.text: Renters’ advocacy group Acorn provided local politicians with a tour of a group of problem-plagued apartments on Kipps Lane Friday afternoon.
Organizers wanted policy makers to see for themselves the conditions that tenants in the cluster of buildings have been living with.
The organized event was marred by confusion, however, at the outset. London police had been called to deal with trespassing, taking Acorn representatives by surprise.
“Somehow, after five years of being active in this city, London police are confused on that. So thankfully, we were not trespassing, we were not fined,” said Acorn London representative Jordan Smith.

A last-minute decision banished members of the news media to the outside of the building, while London Mayor Josh Morgan and a number of councillors, along with MPP Terence Kernaghan were given an abbreviated tour to witness conditions and hear from tenants.

“The city has issued a number of compliance orders. That’s all done through compliance and bylaw, there’s no political interference in that. Fines have also been levied in some cases. And the city has even moved towards the possibility of emergency procurement when things like the heat are off,” explained Morgan.
The cluster of six buildings had been operated by property manager Sireg until recently, when the company fell into bankruptcy. A court appointed administrator is now in charge.

stories.title: Alberta government to review access to abortion, health minister says
stories.summary: Adriana LaGrange told members at the Ucp’s annual meeting that Canada’s lack of laws protecting the unborn is a ‘disgrace’
stories.author: Carrie Tait, Matthew Scace
stories.content:
Listen to this article

Learn more about audio

The Alberta government is reviewing access to abortion in the province, one of its four health ministers said at the United Conservative Party’s annual meeting Friday.

Adriana LaGrange, the Minister for Hospital and Surgical Health Services, told UCP members gathered in Calgary that Alberta must make abortion available because Ottawa protects access to the medical procedure. But the minister, who highlighted her religious beliefs when addressing a question abut abortion, said access is under review in Alberta.

“It’s really quite a disgrace that we are the only country in the world that does not have a law in place to protect the unborn,” Ms. LaGrange told the crowd. “But there is a review that is ongoing, and I anticipate getting briefed on that in the very near future, so more to come.”

Ms. LaGrange noted she is a Catholic and spent 26 years as the president or educator with a Red Deer organization that opposes abortion.

“Unfortunately, it is legally protected by the federal government,” she said. “I do think there is lots that can be done, but we do have to make it available.”

The UCP expects roughly 8,000 members in Calgary for its annual meeting this weekend. About 2,000 members were in the room when Ms. LaGrange made her remarks.

The governing UCP shifted to the right under Premier Danielle Smith , although she has resisted pressure to legislate changes to abortion access. The party has avoided opening up the debate, although some of its MLAs openly support restricting access. Ms. LaGrange’s comments, however, are the clearest indication the UCP May be willing to act more aggressively to curb women’s rights.

In Alberta, care is administered by Covenant Health and Alberta Health Services. Covenant, a Catholic provider, does not provide abortions.

Ryan Fournier, a spokesman for Ms. Smith, did not immediately respond to questions about Ms. LaGrange’s statements.

Ms. Smith took the stage late Friday afternoon, to a mix of boos and claps.

“You’re a little quiet tonight,” she told the crowd.

A large proportion of the attendees at the party’s annual meetings have, for years, come from the right flank of the UCP. Members at these conventions vote on policies they want the government to legislate.

At the 2025 meeting, members voted to end public funding for late-term abortions except when there’s “serious risk” to a mother’s health.

Ms. Smith’s government has not passed legislation reflecting this resolution and the topic isn’t on the agenda at this year’s gathering.

Sarah Hoffman, an MLA with the opposition New Democratic Party and a former health minister, said Ms. LaGrange’s comments are about energizing conservative activists.

“We knew that Danielle Smith would be looking for another front in her pointless culture wars,” Ms. Hoffman said in a statement on Friday. “It sounds like she found it in attacking a woman’s right to choose. Alberta’s NDP has always and always will stand with women.”

In 2019, Dan Williams, who is now a UCP minister, tabled a bill designed to protect the conscience rights of Alberta doctors. Mr. Williams, then a backbencher, said the legislation would shield Alberta health care workers from a court ruling in Ontario that determined physicians with religious objections to procedures such as medical assistance in dying and abortion must provide referrals to willing doctors.

The proposed bill did not pass.

Ms. LaGrange, speaking at the annual meeting, said faith fuelled the Ucp’s legislation to limit access to medical assistance in dying , known as Maid.

“I am also of the mind that human life begins at conception and ends at natural death,” she said. “So it is why we took some very significant steps in terms of Maid.”

She added: “We’re going to make sure that no one has access just because they have mental illness.”

This fall, Federal Justice Minister Sean Fraser introduced a bill which would indefinitely exclude Maid for patients whose sole underlying condition is mental illness.

British Columbia’s Supreme Court on Friday ruled that policies of a publicly funded Catholic-run hospital requiring patients to be transferred to another facility for a medically assisted death do not violate the Charter rights of doctors or their patients.

Justice Ronald Skolrood ruled that the hospital’s policies do not stop a patient from accessing Maid, and that doctors who practise medicine at faith-based organizations do so voluntarily, with full knowledge of the facility’s position.

With reports from The Canadian Press

stories.title: Judge in Galloway trial denies request to delay proceedings for accuser’s psychiatric assessment
stories.summary: Proposed adjournment could have significantly delayed verdict in defamation case
stories.author: Mike Hager
stories.content:
The judge hearing Steven Galloway’s defamation trial has sharply denied a request by lawyers for the woman who accused the bestselling author of sexual assault, dismissing a proposed adjournment on the final day of proceedings that could have significantly delayed a verdict in the case.

Lawyers for the woman, known in court as A.B. because of a publication ban on her name, had asked the court for an adjournment until February to give the defence time to obtain a psychiatric assessment of the woman. Her lawyers have said that she has tried to kill herself twice this year.

The trial has been nearly a decade in the making, with testimony wrapping up last week and final submissions finishing Friday.

In dismissing the request for delay, British Columbia Supreme Court Justice Neena Sharma pointed out that judgments take time, especially when she is hearing other, separate matters. She said that while she aims to release her written decision within six months, she can’t promise that she will meet that timeline.

The judge must also decide if A.B. can be held in contempt of court for declining to participate in pretrial discovery months ago. She is now expected to do so in a separate hearing sometime in the coming months.

Mr. Galloway’s lawyers want the judge to view A.B.’s refusal, as well as the woman’s failure to attend any of the court proceedings, in a negative light.

But Arden Beddoes, A.B.’s lead counsel, told the court that his client’s psychiatrist suffered “quite a severe accident” this summer, delaying her ability to assess A.B. and produce an expert report into her mental health for the trial.

Mr. Beddoes asked the judge if all parties could return to court in February to examine the report before it renders a verdict in the defamation case.

The judge appeared surprised by his request, noting that A.B. had not participated meaningfully in the proceedings since 2021, and that her suicidality had been known to the defence for years.

She said A.B.’s former counsel told her in April that his client wanted the claim against her stayed before deciding to ask to be excused from attending a discovery hearing,

“Now I’m being asked, ‘Oh, it’s going to be unfair to her in a fundamental way if you don’t disrupt the running of this trial significantly, so she can go out and get her evidence,’” said Justice Sharma, who later apologized to him for being so “pointed.”

She is scheduled to give her reasons for rejecting the adjournment on Monday afternoon and then will begin crafting her judgment in the defamation lawsuit launched by Mr. Galloway in 2018.

Mr. Galloway sued A.B. and two dozen others for the repetition online that he sexually assaulted her, defamations which he alleges ruined his lucrative career, ended his ability to ever write again and severely damaged his mental health.

Most of those named in the suit settled, leaving only his accuser and her supporters Mandi Gray and Glynnis Kirchmeier. A fourth accused, Dana Kagis, who posted a single statement alleged to be defamatory, has not participated in the legal process.

At the start of the proceedings, A.B. removed her defences of truth and fair comment. But she denies the accusations that she spread lies about Mr. Galloway, with whom she had a two-year relationship from 2011 to 2013.

Mr. Galloway was never charged with a crime but was suspended by the University of British Columbia when the allegations surfaced in November 2015 and created a media maelstrom.

In 2016, a former Supreme Court justice hired by UBC found that, ON a balance of probabilities, it could not be established that he committed sexual assault or assault. She did find that Mr. Galloway had sexually harassed her, with UBC firing him later that year over breach of trust and other misconduct.

Daniel Burnett, lead counsel for Mr. Galloway, told the court that he had already closed his case so the contempt issue might best be dealt with after the trial.

stories.title: Seven teams of architects and builders shortlisted to renovate 24 Sussex
stories.summary: Contenders for work on prime minister’s residence include companies that have led design for Toronto’s Eglinton Crosstown LRT and B.C.’s Audain Art Museum
stories.author: Ian Bailey
stories.content:
Seven teams of architects and builders have made the short list to renovate 24 Sussex Dr., the official residence of Canada’s prime minister.

On Friday, Public Services and Procurement Canada released the list of proponents to work on the house, which fell into such decline that prime ministers have not been able to live there since 2015.

The group includes companies that have led design for Toronto’s Eglinton Crosstown LRT stations, the Audain Art Museum in Whistler, B.C., and the new Ontario Science Centre in Toronto.

On the short list are Amico Design Build Inc. in partnership with Hariri Pontarini Architects; EBC Inc. allied with Diamond Schmitt Architects; Ed Brunet and Associates Canada Inc. with Michael Green Architecture Inc.; and Maple Reinders Constructors Ltd. with Patkau Architects Inc.

The list also includes MARANT Construction Ltd. in partnership with Superkül/Quadrangle Architects Ltd.; QMD-Graebeck with Daoust Lestage; and SAJO-Lundy with ARCHITEM Inc.

Prime Minister Mark Carney in June announced the competition to rebuild the 1860s-era home that has hosted nine prime ministers since Louis St-Laurent moved there in 1951. The winners, chosen by a committee put together by the Royal Architectural Institute of Canada, will be announced by Canada Day in 2027.

“The range of architectural and construction expertise represented speaks to the strength of Canada’s design community,” Mike Brennan, chief executive officer of the institute, said in a statement.

Hariri Pontarini Architects is working on the new Science Centre, and Daoust Lestage served as a design lead for the 19-kilometre Crosstown LRT . Patkau worked on the Audain museum in Whistler.

Adèle Charlebois, marketing director for Superkül/Quadrangle Architects, said in a statement that the rehabilitation of 24 Sussex is one of the most meaningful renewal projects in the country. Her firm’s credits include the Universal Music Canada Creative Campus in Toronto.

“The project will launch a new chapter for this historic property: a welcoming home for prime ministers and their families, a gracious setting for hosting guests from around the world, and an enduring expression of Canadian values ... that will serve generations to come,” she said.

Of the teams, Public Works Minister Joël Lightbound said in a statement that “their expertise brings us one step closer to modernizing 24 Sussex Drive, an important national landmark, in a way that honours its historic character while preparing it for the future.”

Stephen Harper was the last prime minister to live at 24 Sussex Dr. Justin Trudeau, his successor, was unable to move in with his family because of the poor condition of the house.

As a result, he moved into Rideau Cottage on the grounds of Rideau Hall, where the Governor-General lives and works. After Mr. Trudeau’s run as prime minister, Mr. Carney moved into the cottage.

While in power, Mr. Trudeau and his government considered – but did not proceed with – options to renovate the residence, which was eventually gutted by the National Capital Commission. The commission, which manages official residences in the Ottawa region, had furnishings, finishes and other interior components removed to preserve the property.

The Rideau Hall Foundation is working to raise $50-million in public donations for the renovation project. As of Friday, the website for the foundation said $8.4-million has been raised. Mr. Carney has said the government will cover the costs of security for the renovated house.

The Prime Minister has also said he does not expect he will live in the residence.

stories.title: Moe, Doerkson urge unity to Smith's UCP at kickoff for annual meeting
stories.summary: Calgary - Alberta Premier Danielle Smith's counterparts to the east and west have kicked off her party's annual gathering by urging members to stay undivided after last month's separation vote.
stories.author: Jack Farrell The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Calgary - Alberta Premier Danielle Smith’s counterparts to the east and west kicked off her United Conservative Party’s annual gathering Friday by urging rank-and-file members to come together after last month’s separation vote.

Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe and new British Columbia Premier Lorne Doerkson told a few thousand assembled in a Calgary conference centre that if those in the governing party don’t put their differences aside, they risk handing Alberta over to the Opposition NDP in next year’s election.

“For the first time in far too long, we now have Saskatchewan, Alberta, British Columbia, all governed by parties who believe in growing our economies, growing the opportunities for people today and for generations into the future,” Moe said.

“All of that opportunity, all that growth, all the investment, every bit of it disappears the moment we are divided in the West again.”

The weekend convention in Calgary for Smith’s UCP comes nearly six weeks after Albertans voted against holding a second, binding referendum on separation.

About 75 per cent of voters said they want the province to remain in Canada.

After the vote, Smith urged those holding or seeking leadership positions in the UCP to join a new party if they want to keep pushing the independence issue.

She’s also asked that those seeking board positions on the UCP this weekend — as well as the party’s constituency association presidents — sign pledges confirming they will respect the results of the October referendum.

The premier’s ask hasn’t been welcomed by all in the UCP tent, with at least 15 constituency leaders refusing to sign and one high-profile separatist having his membership revoked.

The tension between Smith and some of the party faithful was quickly made evident Friday.

When Smith took the stage for the first time to introduce Moe and Doerkson, she was met with a standing ovation — but there was also a smattering of boos and jeers from some in the crowd.

Smith only provided brief remarks, which were largely limited to introducing Moe and Doerkson to the stage. “What an incredible time to be a conservative in Western Canada and you are in for a treat tonight,” she said.

Both Moe and Doerkson received big cheers and ovations from Smith’s party members.

Doerkson, who rallied a fractured B.C. Conservative party to win a snap election last month, told attendees that the priorities that bring conservatives together are bigger than those than divide them.

“My message from British Columbia tonight is simple: stay united. Let’s work together,” he said.

He also pointed to the importance of interprovincial alliances in order to build large infrastructure projects, and reiterated his support for the potential Pacific Link pipeline to ship Alberta oil to the West Coast.

“We are going to build an incredible legacy if we just work together,” said Doerkson.

Moe and Doerkson, who met with Smith privately earlier in the day, also highlighted that there is plenty of disagreement within their respective caucuses and party membership.

“But when the writ drops, we are one team,” Moe said.

“Before you leave this convention this weekend, and before you head into that election, I would ask you to ask yourself this: would you like to form government?” he said.

“Or would you like to have another accidental NDP government in Alberta?”

Smith said earlier this week that she was hoping that the Ucp’s annual meeting would be a unifying event focused on preparing for the October 2027 election.

The party is selling merchandise at the event, like T-shirts, hats and mugs. The official program says the gear is to make sure members are “campaign ready.”

Members are also to debate resolutions that could affect a wide range of government policy, from land acknowledgments to laws impacting transgender people’s access to washrooms and change rooms.

Adopting separatism as party policy isn’t on the floor for debate, but there will be plenty of attention paid to the election being held for eight provincial board member positions.

It’s being billed as a battle between a slate of Smith supporters and those who have been aligned with or campaigned for the separatist movement.

Smith is set to address party members multiple times on Saturday.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 27, 2026.

— with files from Lisa Johnson

stories.title: Quebec Court of Appeal to rule Monday on oath to the King by legislators
stories.summary: The decision will come a day before the legislature is scheduled to resume parliamentary work.
stories.author: Charlotte Glorieux
stories.content:
Quebec’s Court of Appeal will rule Monday on the provincial government’s bid to allow elected officials to sit in the legislature without swearing allegiance to the King.

The decision will come a day before the legislature is scheduled to resume parliamentary work.

Justice Lori Renée Weitzman heard arguments Friday as the Parti Québécois government seeks to appeal a lower court ruling that suspended a 2022 Quebec law making the oath optional.

Superior Court Justice Ian Demers suspended the law on Monday and ordered his ruling to take immediate effect, even in the event of an appeal.

Demers’ ruling stayed the law pending a decision on its constitutionality.

In his decision, Demers said elected officials would have to swear allegiance to the King before taking office and warned that legislation adopted by members who had not taken the oath would be unconstitutional.

Weitzman will decide whether to allow the government to appeal Demers’ decision and whether to put the lower court ruling on hold pending the appeal. If the court grants permission to appeal, the appeal would be heard Jan. 11.

Michel Déom, a lawyer representing Quebec’s attorney general, argued Friday that Demers made several errors of law, including failing to adequately consider the consequences of disrupting parliamentary work.

University of Ottawa law professor Lawrence David, one of three applicants challenging the constitutionality of the Quebec law, urged the court to reject the government’s requests.

David argued that the constitutional requirement to swear allegiance to the King is unequivocal and warned that laws adopted by elected officials who have not taken the oath would be unconstitutional.

David also expressed concern about political pressure surrounding the case, referring to a letter the premier invited opposition parties to sign reaffirming their opposition to the mandatory oath. He said political manoeuvres should not influence the court’s decision.

Section 128 of the Constitution Act, 1867, requires members of provincial legislatures to swear allegiance to the monarch before taking their seats. But in 2022, Quebec’s legislature unanimously passed a law exempting its members from that requirement.

None of the 127 members of Quebec’s legislature elected in October have sworn allegiance to the King, opting instead to swear allegiance to the people of Quebec.

Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon said Friday the dispute illustrates what he considers to be the shortcomings of the Canadian Constitution. “The Constitution is set in concrete. That’s a problem,” he told reporters in a news conference in Quebec City.

He said the Constitution is dysfunctional in some respects, to the point where a dispute over an oath that was the subject of a unanimously adopted law could paralyze the legislature.

On Wednesday, St-Pierre Plamondon invited opposition parties to sign a joint declaration reaffirming their desire to resume parliamentary work without swearing allegiance to the King.

Ruba Ghazal, Québec solidaire’s parliamentary leader, committed to signing the declaration, but the Quebec Liberals and Conservatives have refused to do so.

Both parties have said they would not defy court orders to sit illegally.

St-Pierre Plamondon said Friday he was “incredibly disappointed and even stunned” by the positions taken by Liberal Leader Charles Milliard and Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime, accusing them of lacking principles and consistency.

The premier said he hoped political pressure would persuade the opposition leaders not to swear allegiance to the King.

St-Pierre Plamondon said Thursday the parliamentary session would begin Dec. 1 as planned, without members taking the oath.

On Friday, he said that “a lot of things could happen on Tuesday.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 27, 2026.

stories.title: Quebec argues ruling requiring oath will cause ‘major disruption’ if MNAs not allowed to sit
stories.summary: Province wants Court of Appeal to permit members to take seats while the case unfolds
stories.author: Maura Forrest
stories.content:
Quebec legislators will have to wait until next week to learn whether a judge will allow them to sit in the National Assembly without taking an oath of allegiance to King Charles III.

On Friday, a lawyer for the Quebec government argued in court that there will be a “major disruption” to the provincial legislature if a Quebec Superior Court ruling declaring elected officials must swear fealty to the Crown is allowed to stand.

The government is seeking leave to appeal the decision and is asking the Court of Appeal of Quebec to allow members of the legislature to sit without taking the oath while the case unfolds.

After the hearing in Montreal on Friday, Justice Lori Renée Weitzman said she would render her decision on Monday, acknowledging the urgency of the matter.

Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon has said his Parti Québécois government will sit in the National Assembly as planned on Tuesday without taking an oath to Canada’s monarch.

The constitutional showdown was triggered early this week, when Justice Ian Demers suspended a 2022 law that had abolished the requirement for members of the National Assembly to swear loyalty to the Crown.

In his decision, Justice Demers wrote that the suspension of the law means that lawmakers will now “be required to take an oath to the King before assuming their duties.”

Lawrence David, an Ottawa lawyer who launched a constitutional challenge of the 2022 law in August, told the appeal court he is “deeply concerned” by the prospect of the government sitting next week “regardless of what this court decides.”

“This court cannot be intimidated by political threats to its judicial independence,” he said Friday.

Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon has said the lower court decision doesn’t explicitly order lawmakers to swear allegiance to the King and there is nothing preventing them from convening in the National Assembly as planned.

The 2022 law was passed with the support of all parties after Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon and his caucus, then in opposition, refused to take the oath and were barred from entering the National Assembly.

But Mr. David argues Quebec has no authority to unilaterally amend the Constitution.

The substance of the case has yet to be heard, but Mr. David filed for an emergency injunction after the October election to force MNAs to take the oath before the legislature reconvened.

Justice Demers sided with Mr. David on Monday. He ruled that if lawmakers did not swear allegiance to the Crown, “all laws passed by the National Assembly would be unconstitutional and would have to be re-enacted,” which he said would cause “paralysis.”

The appeal court ruling next week will determine whether an appeal of that injunction can proceed, and whether MNAs can sit without taking the oath while it does.

Michel Déom, the lawyer for the Quebec government, said Justice Demers should have considered that he was creating “an unprecedented situation that will affect the work of the National Assembly.”

None of the province’s 127 legislators swore allegiance to the King after last month’s election.

Mr. Déom said the judge was wrong to focus on what would happen if the 2022 law were eventually found unconstitutional, instead of the immediate effects of suspending the law.

But Mr. David said the judge accurately concluded the law is “manifestly unconstitutional,” and said the appeal court should not allow lawmakers to convene without taking the oath.

“The fundamental question is this: Why allow systematic constitutional violations by an unlawfully constituted assembly that are certain to occur, instead of preventing them now?” he said.

“Prevention is better than cure.”

Friday’s hearing took place hours after the Supreme Court of Canada largely upheld Quebec’s secularism law, Bill 21, averting a potential constitutional crisis in the province.

stories.title: Alberta court strikes down Onion Lake Cree Nation’s sovereignty act challenge
stories.summary: First Nation didn’t provide evidence the act could be considered unconstitutional, judge rules
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
An Alberta judge has struck down a First Nation’s attempt to get an injunction against the province’s sovereignty act.

Onion Lake Cree Nation had argued the act is unconstitutional because it goes against the Treaty 6 relationship with the Crown. It asked the court to declare that the act infringes on that relationship and isn’t enforceable.

Alberta’s Justice Ministry told court that the First Nation had no reasonable claim for its challenge.

Court of King’s Bench Justice Grant Dunlop sided with the province and struck the claim in a written decision released Thursday.

Justice Dunlop said Onion Lake didn’t provide evidence to show that the potential for the act to be used to violate treaty rights meant it could be considered unconstitutional.

The Alberta Sovereignty within a United Canada Act was Premier Danielle Smith’s flagship first law after she won leadership of her United Conservative Party in 2022.

Ms. Smith said the act was needed to push back against federal encroachment into provincial jurisdiction, but she later conceded it wasn’t needed to make changes and was more symbolic.

Onion Lake Cree Nation, which straddles the Alberta-Saskatchewan boundary just north of Lloydminster, had argued that the act infringes on treaty rights, including traditional ceremonies and guarantees of livelihood and freedom.

Onion Lake said Alberta doesn’t have the power to follow through with the act. But the judge said the First Nation didn’t show how.

“Those parts of the claim are also based on hypothetical facts which makes them not ripe for adjudication,” he wrote in his decision.

Justice Dunlop also said the argument that Alberta failed to consult the First Nation before passing the act was a “hopeless” claim, because consultation isn’t a sole reason to challenge legislation.

Onion Lake also submitted as evidence three executive orders from the government related to the provincial referendum in October.

The key question on the ballot asked Albertans if they want to have a second, binding referendum on separation. About 75 per cent of voters said they want the province to stay in Canada.

The judge said the referendum wasn’t discussed in the First Nation’s claim and was irrelevant.

stories.title: Glendon College rejects proposal to relocate to York University’s main campus
stories.summary: After a 61-8 vote, the bilingual liberal arts school will stay at long-time midtown Toronto location
stories.author: Kelly Grant
stories.content:
Glendon College, York University’s bilingual liberal arts school, will stay put at its long-time home in midtown Toronto after the college’s faculty council rejected a move to York’s huge main campus on the edge of the city.

The Glendon Faculty Council voted 61-8 against a York proposal that would have dissolved Glendon as a stand-alone faculty and would have relocated the university’s bilingual offerings to a dedicated building on the Keele Street campus.

“I think the vote could not be any clearer,” Marco Fiola, the principal of Glendon College, said after secret ballots were tallied on Friday afternoon. “We’ve learned a lot of things during this process. We’ve gathered such an amazing momentum for Glendon. We have to be able to seize that and to move forward in a positive way.”

Friday’s vote spelled the end of one specific idea for reviving York’s bilingual mission, but it’s unlikely to end debates over the future of the Glendon site, or the future of bilingual postsecondary education in Canada’s largest city.

Glendon Campus, a leafy oasis in one of Toronto’s most exclusive neighbourhoods, was the founding site of York University. The land was originally bequeathed to the University of Toronto for educational purposes by a wealthy widow. In the late 1950s, U of T transferred the land to a fledgling York.

Glendon has for decades offered liberal arts courses in either French or English, all while enveloping students in a bilingual atmosphere. Professors, staff, clubs, campus signage and the student newspaper all cater to students in both official languages.

But Glendon’s enrolment has been dwindling. The number of students dropped to 1,419 in 2025-26, down nearly 50 per cent from a peak of 2,770 in 2016-17. Glendon’s accumulated deficit hit $52.4-million at the end of the past academic year.

York as a whole is trying to claw its way out of a deficit , partly caused by the loss of revenue from international students after the federal government restricted student visas beginning in 2024.

The proposal that Glendon Faculty Council rejected on Friday was pitched as a way to revitalize York’s bilingual mandate. The plan, submitted by York’s interim provost Laina Bay-Cheng, argued that more students would be willing to take classes in French at the main campus, where 70 per cent of York’s francophone students are enrolled.

The Glendon Faculty Council – which includes all full-time faculty and a mix of students, staff and contract faculty – disagreed.

Everyone who spoke in person and online at the Friday meeting praised Glendon as a tight-knit community where bilingualism flourished. Speakers switched from French to English with ease. There was no simultaneous translation. Members who voted received an “I voted/J’ai voté” sticker to wear on their shirts.

Natasha Hameed, 20, a member of the faculty council’s student caucus, told the meeting that she wouldn’t have become a fluent French speaker without the chance to regularly converse in the language at Glendon.

She arrived at the campus having only taken core French classes at her high school in Scarborough. Now, she plans to be a French teacher.

“I really encourage everyone to please vote against this proposal for students like myself who would not know what they were doing with their lives if they hadn’t come to a place like this,” Ms. Hameed told the meeting.

Members of the faculty council burst into applause when the results of the vote were announced.

Then, Samuel Nieva, president of the Glendon College Student Union, addressed the room.

“Now that we have showcased that we, as a collective group, do not support this current proposal,” he said, “I want us to ensure that we’re able to build that momentum, and we’re making sure that not only are we just surviving, but we’re here to thrive.”

Yanni Dagonas, deputy spokesman for York, said in a statement Friday that discussions about Glendon’s future had underscored the importance of expanding the university’s bilingual mandate.

“The York community’s focus must now turn to making the most of these opportunities, including finding ways to highlight Glendon and bolster its academic community so that people, programs and ideas thrive on the campus,” he said.

“This is a shared priority across York.”

stories.title: Religious hospitals do not have to provide Maid, B.C. court rules
stories.summary: ‘Within the medical community, and indeed society at large, there is a wide divergence of religious, moral and ethical beliefs concerning Maid,’ the court ruled
stories.author: Sarah Ritchie
stories.content:
Ottawa — British Columbia’s Supreme Court has ruled that faith-based hospitals are not violating the rights of patients by refusing to provide medically assisted deaths.

B.C. Chief Justice Ronald Skolrood wrote in a decision released on Friday that a provincial policy allowing religious hospitals to opt out of providing Maid provides reasonable access to patients by transferring them to other facilities.

“The evidence at trial demonstrated that within the medical community, and indeed society at large, there is a wide divergence of religious, moral and ethical beliefs concerning Maid,” Skolrood wrote.

The case was brought by advocacy group Dying With Dignity Canada and the family of Sam O’Neill, who died in 2023 at age 34 after being diagnosed with cervical cancer.

O’Neill was approved for medical assistance in dying by St. Paul’s Hospital in Vancouver, where she was receiving treatment, but the hospital required her to be transferred to another facility to have the lethal injection.

Her parents, Gaye and Jim O’Neill, testified that she suffered excruciating pain during the transfer and that she had to be sedated en route to the second facility so heavily that she was unable to say a final goodbye to her family.

The plaintiffs argued that what they called “forced transfers” of patients who wish to die by Maid impede their ability to make decisions about their own deaths and subject them to physical and psychological harm. They argued that it violates their rights under Section 7 of the Charter: the right to life, liberty and security of the person.

St. Paul’s Hospital is run by Providence Health Care Society, a Catholic organization that was founded by an order of nuns in 1894. Providence operates 18 health-care facilities in the Vancouver area.

It was one of the defendants in the case, along with the Vancouver Coastal Health Authority and the Province of British Columbia.

At issue was the B.C. Ministry of Health policy that allows faith-based organizations to decline to provide Maid in their facilities.

The defendants successfully argued that transfers of Maid patients are the same as other transfers that happen every day in the health care system.

Providence had also argued that its rights under Section 2 of the Charter protect it from being forced to provide services that “are contrary to deeply and sincerely held beliefs.”

Section 2 guarantees freedom of conscience and religion.

The plaintiffs argued that such a policy violates the Section 2 Charter rights of physicians who provide Maid, along with the rights of patients.

Dr. Jyothi Jayaraman, who quit her job with Providence as a result of its policies, was also a plaintiff.

Skolrood wrote that the evidence did not establish that Maid transfers cause patients “serious and profound” psychological distress, though he noted that “there is no question that the family and friends were profoundly distressed by what they observed.”

Skolrood wrote that patient transfers are a common feature of the health care system and that any risks they pose can be managed. He added the plaintiffs had argued that patients’ rights were only infringed when the transfer happened “because of the institution’s religious objection.”

“However, the reason or motivation for an action is irrelevant” in determining whether rights were violated, he wrote.

Jim O’Neill said Friday he was “hugely disappointed and upset” by the decision.

He said he believes transfers for Maid patients are fundamentally different from other medical transfers because “there is absolutely no benefit to that patient for the transfer.”

Gaye O’Neill pointed out that St. Paul’s, as part of the public health system, gets over 90 per cent of its funding from public funds.

“I struggle with understanding how a hospital with a religion-based administration feels entitled to lord over everyone they invite to receive care because there is a crucifix on the wall,” she said.

In a statement, Providence said it respects the decision.

“We are thankful to the parties, the intervenors and the court for the thoughtful consideration given to this important and complex issue. We are committed to continuing to build on our 130-plus year history of providing compassionate, exceptional and innovative health care to British Columbians,” the statement said.

Dying With Dignity Canada said it has not yet decided whether to appeal the ruling. Its board chair, Daphne Gilbert, told reporters on Friday she remains “committed to this fight.”

“We stand by the legal arguments that were made in court and continue to feel that it is unconstitutional for a health-care facility to make faith-based decisions around care and impose those decisions upon individuals who don’t share the values,” she said.

Sarah Ritchie joined National Post’s politics bureau after four years covering breaking news on Parliament Hill for The Canadian Press, where she worked as a reporter and editor. Before that, she was an anchor and investigative reporter at Global News in Halifax and covered the Nova Scotia legislature for CTV Atlantic.

stories.title: London, Ont., police officer charged with assault in off-duty incident
stories.summary: Investigators say the officer’s name and identifying details will not be released to protect the victim’s privacy.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Police in London, Ont., say one of their own officers has been charged with assault and forcible confinement in an off-duty incident earlier this month.

The force says it referred the investigation to the Strathroy-Caradoc Police Service to ensure impartiality after receiving the initial report, and that led to charges against the officer.

Investigators say the officer’s name and identifying details will not be released to protect the victim’s privacy.

Police say the officer has been reassigned to administrative duties.

They say the matter is also subject to an internal conduct review in accordance with the Community Safety and Policing Act.

The force says in a statement that it takes the allegations seriously.

“As police officers, we are entrusted with significant responsibilities and are held to high standards of conduct, both on and off-duty,” it said.

stories.title: Prosecutors ask for 25-year sentence for Kenneth Law who sold deadly poison for 14 suicides
stories.summary: Law’s lawyer argued his client should get 12 years, partly because he sold a legal chemical for a purpose, suicide, that is the subject of current debate
stories.author: Joseph Brean
stories.content:
Newmarket, Ont. — Ontario prosecutors urged a judge Friday to sentence suicide poison merchant Kenneth Law to 25 years in prison, which would be by far the longest sentence ever for assisting suicide in Canada, and would be in line with Ontario’s original goal of a life sentence for murder.

But in hotly contested arguments before Justice Michelle Fuerst in court in Newmarket, Ont., Law’s lawyer said his client should get less than half that sentence, 12 years, in part because he sold a legal chemical for a purpose, suicide, that is the subject of current mainstream debate over whether and how people should be able to legally access help for it.

“The unresolved debate over assisted dying does not excuse his conduct, but it does help explain how he came to hold his views,” Matthew Gourlay said. Law’s views that people should be able to end their life at will, while misguided, “do echo one side of this ongoing debate,” he said.
