Gourlay encouraged Fuerst to consider the social context of Medical Assistance In Dying in Canada to evaluate what a proportionate sentence for Law might look like. “You have to look at how society deals with, understands and evaluates the act of providing assistance in suicide,” and how that has changed in recent years, Gourlay said.

“Assisting a suicide used to be always wrong, but it isn’t that way any longer,” the defence lawyer said, and he gave an overview of the changing social, legal and moral debate over assisted suicide in Canada, which remains a work in progress before Parliament and the courts.

It is a highly controversial argument, and Gourlay emphasized its limits. Law is not a doctor. He sold poison online to strangers, no questions asked. A dozen of his victims were teenagers. One was 14 years old. About half were in their 20s.

Kenneth Law. Peel Regional Police

He is being sentenced for 14 Canadian victims but is suspected of helping more than 100 people around the word to die.

Asked by the judge if he had anything to say before she sentences him, Law read briefly from a script, in an emotionless tone, saying he was “humbled,” and gave his word that he will never do this again.

“Going through this process has changed me,” he said. He spoke of his regret “that my actions assisted others in ending their lives,” and expressed his intention to “better myself” through rehabilitation programs. He apologized and expressed his remorse and “deepest condolences” to the family members of victims, a few of whom were in the courtroom, and two of whom left before he started speaking.

His lawyer told the court that Law was ideologically committed to the right to die, but he did not counsel, coerce or deceive any victim.

In a secretly recorded phone call with a British journalist who exposed Law, he “does not come across as a monster or mercenary, but a man with a misguided motivation,” Gourlay said. The call, which was played in court earlier this year, makes it clear Law knew his customer wanted his poison in order to kill himself, and that he was aware other customers had been successful in this.

Law should also be given a sort of credit for bearing the stigma of being labelled “Canada’s most prolific serial killer,” a characterization that Gourlay said has no legal basis.

When he was arrested in 2023, Law was charged with two counts of aiding suicide, then 12 more, but those charges were upgraded, first to second-degree murder and ultimately to 14 counts of first-degree murder. Earlier this year on the eve of trial, however, the Crown accepted a plea deal on 14 charges of assisting suicide because a Supreme Court decision in an unrelated case had established that assisting suicide can only be charged as murder if the victim’s free will was overcome.

The unresolved debate over assisted dying does not excuse his conduct, but it does help explain how he came to hold his views

Matthew Gourlay Defence lawyer

Law sold poison, but he was not present at any of the 14 suicides in Ontario that he admitted assisting, or the 79 suicides in Britain that are being considered by the sentencing judge as aggravating factors, with the consent of British authorities who have agreed this Ontario prosecution will be the final word. He also admitted sending 78 packages of poison to Ontario customers, and 330 to the U.K., plus more to other countries.

“In my submission, it was never clear how the Crown could obtain a murder conviction in these circumstances, given Mr. Law had not actually killed any of the victims,” Gourlay said. “He provided a lawful product to people who for diverse and unique reasons chose to end their own lives, tragically. This is a world apart from murder.”

“Mr. Law May be a common denominator but he was not the cause of the troubles that caused them to seek out his products in the first place, and he had no role in their use of them,” Gourlay said. “In short, Mr. Law did not kill anyone.”

“Mr. Law was motivated in substantial part by his ideological commitment to this right to die cause, whatever we May think of that cause. While clearly misguided, Mr. Law wanted to assist individuals who believed they were neglected by the present legal framework. Mr. Law did not get rich from this enterprise, far from it,” Gourlay said.

Gourlay said his client should be sentenced to a total of 12 years. That would represent 13 concurrent terms of nine years for the offences that involved selling poison, plus three years served consecutively for the one offence that involved selling an asphyxiation mask.

Gourlay said the Crown’s suggestion of 25 years would not only be a “de facto life sentence” for the 61-year-old Law, but is “an effort to resurrect on sentencing some semblance of the Crown’s failed homicide prosecution.”

Prosecutor Katie Doherty said a 12-year sentence is “way too low,” given the need to denounce Law’s conduct and deter others. Her 25 year suggestion represents 12.5 years for each of the 14 offences, with one served consecutively.

“These were vulnerable people. What they needed was help, but what they found was Mr. Law and his products for death,” she said.

Doherty urged Fuerst to consider the heightened moral blameworthiness of selling suicide poison to so many people, and of knowing how it was being used. She noted that, long before his arrest in Ontario, British police had contacted Law after finding his products at the scene of a suicide.

“He feigns that he’s surprised and saddened to hear that news from the officer, and he even tells the officer he’s going to stop selling it, but only when he runs out of his inventory,” Doherty said. The vast majority of the 93 deaths being considered at this sentencing occurred after this contact from British police.

She urged the court to reject Law’s claim of an “altruistic” motive. He told a psychologist, for example, it was a “mission of mercy.” The judge cannot be satisfied that this really was his motive, and even if it was, Doherty said that would be an aggravating factor, not a mitigating factor. She dismissed the defence characterization of the profit motive as “modest,” and noted he took in $300,000 over three years, a lot more than he earned in employment.

“If people could pay, he sold it to them,” she said.

Doherty acknowledged that some other single cases of assisting suicide could be much worse or depraved, but she encouraged the judge to still put Law at the highest end of the spectrum of moral blameworthiness because of the scale of his offence.

“We’re not comparing one to one. We’re comparing one to 400,” Doherty said.

She also disagreed with Gourlay’s invocation of the Maid regime. “There’s a debate about assisted dying, but what there’s no debate about is that someone in Mr. Law’s position should be able to serve as judge, jury and executioner in his own scheme.”

Later, that prompted Gourlay to criticize this metaphor because Law did not physically cause the deaths.

He has been in custody for about 3.5 years. His defence asked the judge to credit that at a 2-1 ratio because of harsh conditions in custody, including an assault, triple-bunking, extensive lockdowns and flesh-eating disease that threatened his right leg, which would mean he would be credited for about seven years.

Even the lower defence suggestion of 12 years would be the longest sentence ever in Canada for assisting suicide.

Both sides emphasized the uniqueness of this case, with no parallel jurisprudence to guide sentencing.

“It really is a matter for first impression by this court,” Doherty said.

Many of the prosecutions for assisting suicide that do exist involved compassionate assistance to family members. Others involved depraved malice and emotional coercion.

None involved a vast online international business run through PayPal and Shopify, which in Law’s case also included a marketing scheme that involved posing as a doctor called “Greenberg” on a suicide chatroom in order to identify customers and funnel them to his business, which masqueraded as a culinary supply store because the poison, sodium nitrite, is more commonly used in the curing of meats.

Even the crime is unique, Gourlay observed, as the only offence in the Criminal Code that makes it a crime to help someone do something that itself is not a crime. Suicide itself used to be a crime, and attempted suicide was also a prosecutable crime in Canada until 1972.

Law was born in Hong Kong in 1965, came to Canada aged 6, and became a citizen in 1970. He never married, has no children, no criminal record, and was living in a modest basement apartment in Mississauga, Ont., when he was arrested. He has a younger brother, who is supportive, and a father who is a retired bartender and unaware of this case because of his dementia. Law’s views on the right to die were influenced by seeing his mother suffer the impact of a disabling stroke before she died in 2010.

Law is highly educated and has been employed in various fields, including by Nortel, Export Development Canada, Ontario’s Agriculture Ministry, and as a chef at the Royal York hotel in Toronto.

“He’s not the caricature of an evil doer that has often emerged in the media surrounding this case,” Gourlay said.

Fuerst is expected to deliver her sentence and reasons in the new year.

Joseph Brean has been a national reporter with the Post since 2001, writing general breaking news and more focused coverage of law, science, politics and culture. He also writes longer features, interviews, profiles and obituaries.

Even the crime is unique, Gourlay observed, as the only offence in the Criminal Code that makes it a crime to help someone do something that itself is not a crime. Suicide itself used to be a crime, and attempted suicide was also a prosecutable crime in Canada until 1972.

Law was born in Hong Kong in 1965, came to Canada aged 6, and became a citizen in 1970. He never married, has no children, no criminal record, and was living in a modest basement apartment in Mississauga, Ont., when he was arrested. He has a younger brother, who is supportive, and a father who is a retired bartender and unaware of this case because of his dementia. Law’s views on the right to die were influenced by seeing his mother suffer the impact of a disabling stroke before she died in 2010.
Law is highly educated and has been employed in various fields, including by Nortel, Export Development Canada, Ontario’s Agriculture Ministry, and as a chef at the Royal York hotel in Toronto.
“He’s not the caricature of an evil doer that has often emerged in the media surrounding this case,” Gourlay said.
Fuerst is expected to deliver her sentence and reasons in the new year.

stories.title: Supreme Court’s Bill 21 ruling wards off political crisis in Quebec
stories.summary: Controversial law banning some public sector workers from wearing religious symbols is widely seen by francophones as an expression of the province’s values
stories.author: Eric Andrew-Gee
stories.content:
The Supreme Court’s near-total upholding of Bill 21 , Quebec’s secularism law, has averted a political firestorm in the province amidst renewed constitutional tensions and disputes with Ottawa under a newly-elected sovereigntist government.

The legislation barring some public sector workers from wearing religious symbols is controversial in the rest of Canada and among minority groups, but is widely seen by francophones as an expression of the province’s distinctive values. The Court’s strong support for the use of the notwithstanding clause in this case will reassure many Quebeckers that their legislature can hold sway on important issues within the constraints of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, politicians and lawyers in the province said.

“It’s a victory for Quebec secularism,” said Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon on Friday. “We were worried about the social peace if such a fundamental choice had been literally invalidated by the Supreme Court.”

The Supreme Court judgement avoids what would have been a second potential constitutional crisis in Quebec this week, after a lower court ruled on Monday that the province’s legislators must swear an oath to the King, suspending a 2022 provincial law that abolished that requirement. Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon has said his separatist Parti Québécois plans to sit in the National Assembly as scheduled next week, with a ruling expected Monday on whether elected officials can sit without taking the oath while the case unfolds.

Although it defuses a political bombshell, the survival of Bill 21 was seen as a bitter defeat by some of the religious minorities and civil libertarians who opposed the law in court.

“It’s a dark day for Quebec and Canada,” said Stephen Brown, the Montreal-based CEO of the National Council of Canadian Muslims. “In our country in the 21st century, entire categories of people are now barred from entire sectors of employment, not because of what they have done, but because of who they are.”

English Montreal School Board chair Joe Ortona declared himself “extremely disappointed” by the ruling.

“It’s heartbreaking, gut-wrenching really to know that people can’t exercise their rights because of a law like Bill 21,” he said. “It prevented us from hiring qualified teachers for a completely arbitrary reason, and we’re in a labour shortage when it comes to teachers.”

Other Quebec opponents of the law found silver linings in the decision. Notably, three of seven judges found that large parts of the law should be voided because they violate the Charter’s gender equality protections. Samira Laouni, a hijab-wearing Muslim woman and Laval, Que. resident who has vocally opposed parts of Bill 21, said Friday’s decision produced mixed emotions.

“I’m disappointed by the judgement because it creates a two-tiered citizenship,” she said. “On the other hand, I’m relieved that it was such a close decision; it’s very satisfying that everyone doesn’t think the same.”

The roughly 500-page decision also saw the Court endorse judicial declarations that would allow judges to pronounce future laws inconsistent with the Charter even if they are protected by the notwithstanding clause, which some Quebec advocates saw as a major victory.

“It’s a very strong message about fundamental rights from the Supreme Court,” said Frédéric Bérard, a Montreal lawyer who represented the Fédération autonome de l’enseignement, a grouping of Quebec teachers’ unions. “You can’t violate fundamental rights without having to defend your bill in front of the courts.”

The same provision made Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon describe the ruling as a “setback” for Quebec’s autonomy, because it diminished the force of the notwithstanding clause. He said the possibility of judicial declarations against provincial laws was another reason for Quebec to become independent, an option his Parti Québécois government intends to put to a referendum in the next four years.

“We’ve just witnessed a major reversal for the provinces,” he said. “The only political and judicial solution is to subtract ourselves from a fairly unstable situation.”

Many observers doubt the Supreme Court ruling will help the separatist cause, despite the Premier’s arguments. Quebec Conservative Party leader Éric Duhaime called the decision “a victory for Quebeckers” and “a defeat for the referendum agenda of the PQ, which is often nourished, unfortunately, by defeats for Quebeckers.”

Political analyst Raphaël Melançon, who was a staffer for the governing Coalition Avenir Québec when Bill 21 was passed in 2019, said the judgement was good news for federalists in the province.

“I think it’s an illustration that Canadian federalism works,” he said. “To ordinary Quebeckers who are not nerds about the constitution, what they hear today is that Bill 21 is a done deal. Canada is not intervening in Quebec’s internal affairs.”

The fight over Quebec’s approach to religion in the public sphere will not end with this judgement. The notwithstanding clause shielding most of Bill 21 will have to be renewed in 2029, and the PQ has promised to go further in the meantime by banning students from wearing religious symbols in elementary schools.

Protests around the issue are likely to continue. Students at two Montreal colleges walked out of classes on Thursday to oppose Bill 9, another secularism law passed in April that bans most prayer spaces in public institutions, among other measures.

stories.title: Company denies allegation nurse contract not being renewed over Poilievre photo
stories.summary: The employer of a nurse who Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre says has been told her contract won’t be renewed over a photo with him says the allegations are false.
stories.author: David Baxter
stories.content:
The employer of a nurse who Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre says has been told her contract won’t be renewed over a photo with him says the allegations are false.

Calian Health has issued an email statement after being asked for comment by The Canadian Press on Wednesday when Poilievre raised the issue in the House of Commons.

Poilievre said his parliamentary privilege was being violated when he said a nurse was told she might lose her job after she was photographed speaking with him in the aftermath of the tragic fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright.

The October fire killed five soldiers and left dozens injured during a training exercise at the base, which is in Poilievre’s Alberta riding.

The Calian Health statement says the company has started a “full-scale investigation into the facts and circumstances of the incident” while the nurse remains employed.

Defence Minister David McGuinty said Thursday during a committee appearance he is looking into the matter too, as constituents should always feel free to speak with their MP and vice versa.

— With files from Catherine Morrison

stories.title: Pro-life group challenges constitutionality of London’s graphic flyer bylaw in court
stories.summary: London’s effort to keep graphic images of aborted fetuses from residents’ doorsteps and mailboxes faced a constitutional test Friday, as a local pro-life organization challenged the reach of the city’s graphic flyer bylaw.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
London’s effort to keep graphic images of aborted fetuses from residents’ doorsteps and mailboxes faced a constitutional test Friday, as a local pro-life organization challenged the reach of the city’s graphic flyer bylaw.

The Association for Reformed Political Action (Arpa) says it does not distribute graphic images of aborted fetuses, but the organization argues the bylaw still impacts its door-to-door campaigns.

“The chilling factor that it would have on volunteers like myself,” says Marian Meinen, and Arpa Southwestern Ontario board member. “I have delivered fliers for Arpa before door to door.”

A written submission by Arpa’s lawyers says the bylaw, “is contrary to its stated purpose, a thinly veiled effort to censor local pro-life advocates.”

Council approved the bylaw in May 2022, after receiving numerous complaints about flyers distributed to unsuspecting London homes (by a different pro-life organization) that showed graphic images of aborted fetuses.

The bylaw defines a graphic image as, “an image or photograph showing, or purporting to show, a fetus or any part of a fetus.

It requires flyers with graphic images be to be delivered in sealed envelope that includes a warning on the outside and the name/address of the person responsible for the delivery.

John Sikkema, Arpa’s Director of Law and Policy argued that the definition of graphic material is too broad in scope, impacting the organization’s logo for the We Need a Law campaign (a drawn profile of a living fetus), and the use of ultrasound images in some of its literature.

“Graphic image is defined as really any image of a fetus. How is that then linked to kind of concern about residents health, safety and wellbeing? That’s the connection that it seemed the city had some difficulty establishing,” explains Sikkema.

During the hearing, the three justices repeatedly pressed the city’s lawyer about a hypothetical scenario: Would a prenatal clinic advertising the quality of its ultrasound service have to put its flyer in a sealed envelope labelled as graphic?

Those who pushed for the restrictions worry the court challenge could result in the by-law quashed.

“There’s a real risk to having this bylaw struck down, and we don’t want to give up on the protections that thousands of Londoners fought for,” says Deanna Ronson, a board director with the Abortion Rights Coalition of Canada (Arcc).

Ronson says Arcc urged council to narrow its definition of graphic images long before the court challenge was initiated by Arpa.

“We had tried from the beginning to have that definition quite a bit more narrow because we thought that it would be more likely to be upheld in a legal challenge. The city, unfortunately, did not,” explains Ronson.

She worries striking down the bylaw could trigger a new wave of graphic door-to-door flyers in London neighbourhoods, “If it is struck down, I believe that the city needs to go back to the drawing board, amend that bylaw.”

Meinen has a different perspective on the possibility of the restrictions being lifted, “I’m never concerned where there’s a window of time for freedom of expression. As I said, Arpa does not distribute those images. We feel we can make our point through an ultrasound.”

No one has ever been charged with violating London’s Graphic Flyer Bylaw.

Following Friday’s hearing, no timeline was given for a written decision.

content_blocks.text: London’s effort to keep graphic images of aborted fetuses from residents’ doorsteps and mailboxes faced a constitutional test Friday, as a local pro-life organization challenged the reach of the city’s graphic flyer bylaw.
The Association for Reformed Political Action (Arpa) says it does not distribute graphic images of aborted fetuses, but the organization argues the bylaw still impacts its door-to-door campaigns.
“The chilling factor that it would have on volunteers like myself,” says Marian Meinen, and Arpa Southwestern Ontario board member. “I have delivered fliers for Arpa before door to door.”
A written submission by Arpa’s lawyers says the bylaw, “is contrary to its stated purpose, a thinly veiled effort to censor local pro-life advocates.”

Council approved the bylaw in May 2022, after receiving numerous complaints about flyers distributed to unsuspecting London homes (by a different pro-life organization) that showed graphic images of aborted fetuses.

content_blocks.caption: The Association for Reformed Political Action (ARPA) logo for its We Need A Law campaign (weneedalaw.ca)

content_blocks.text: The bylaw defines a graphic image as, “an image or photograph showing, or purporting to show, a fetus or any part of a fetus.
It requires flyers with graphic images be to be delivered in sealed envelope that includes a warning on the outside and the name/address of the person responsible for the delivery.

John Sikkema, Arpa’s Director of Law and Policy argued that the definition of graphic material is too broad in scope, impacting the organization’s logo for the We Need a Law campaign (a drawn profile of a living fetus), and the use of ultrasound images in some of its literature.

“Graphic image is defined as really any image of a fetus. How is that then linked to kind of concern about residents health, safety and wellbeing? That’s the connection that it seemed the city had some difficulty establishing,” explains Sikkema.

During the hearing, the three justices repeatedly pressed the city’s lawyer about a hypothetical scenario: Would a prenatal clinic advertising the quality of its ultrasound service have to put its flyer in a sealed envelope labelled as graphic?

content_blocks.text: Those who pushed for the restrictions worry the court challenge could result in the by-law quashed.

“There’s a real risk to having this bylaw struck down, and we don’t want to give up on the protections that thousands of Londoners fought for,” says Deanna Ronson, a board director with the Abortion Rights Coalition of Canada (Arcc).
Ronson says Arcc urged council to narrow its definition of graphic images long before the court challenge was initiated by Arpa.

“We had tried from the beginning to have that definition quite a bit more narrow because we thought that it would be more likely to be upheld in a legal challenge. The city, unfortunately, did not,” explains Ronson.

She worries striking down the bylaw could trigger a new wave of graphic door-to-door flyers in London neighbourhoods, “If it is struck down, I believe that the city needs to go back to the drawing board, amend that bylaw.”

Meinen has a different perspective on the possibility of the restrictions being lifted, “I’m never concerned where there’s a window of time for freedom of expression. As I said, Arpa does not distribute those images. We feel we can make our point through an ultrasound.”
No one has ever been charged with violating London’s Graphic Flyer Bylaw.
Following Friday’s hearing, no timeline was given for a written decision.

stories.title: How Edmonton intends to rollback blanket rezoning that allowed for more infill
stories.summary: Permitted residential use, density, building height and minimum parking requirements will largely be reverted back to what they were under the old bylaw.
stories.author: Gates Guarin
stories.content:
City council heard from city administration on how it plans to roll back its current zoning bylaw as part of the province’s directive, intended to halt Edmonton infill amid complaints to the province from residents.

Permitted residential use, density, building height and minimum parking requirements will largely be reverted back to what they were under the old bylaw.

This will vary based on the area in which communities are zoned.

Council voted to hold a public hearing in the new year, which came with apprehension from some councillors.

Councillor Michael Janz called the process a “sham” with a predetermined outcome. Mayor Andrew Knack said public hearings, even in this case, are still useful as it demonstrates the city listening to its residents.

Gates Guarin has the story in the video above.

stories.title: Judge’s ruling that a seized loaded gun couldn’t be used as evidence because of police racism is overturned
stories.summary: The alleged racial bias was based on the judge’s speculation without direct evidence and despite the defendant’s lawyer saying racism was not a factor, appeals court said
stories.author: Adrian Humphreys
stories.content:
Ontario’s court of appeal has overturned a judge’s ruling that said anti-Black racism was behind a police officer’s actions during a traffic stop that found a man illegally driving with a loaded rifle hidden on the back seat of his Jeep.

An appeals court said this week that the alleged racial bias was based on the judge’s own speculation without any direct evidence and despite the defendant’s own lawyer telling her racism was not a factor.

In her 2025 ruling, Justice Renu Mandhane ruled the racial discrimination she had sensed was too egregious to allow prosecutors to use the gun as evidence at the driver’s trial, leading to his acquittal.

Mandhane’s decision, which sparked headlines at the time, came after a pretrial hearing in the Ontario Superior Court of Justice.

A Peel Regional Police officer, Const. Anand Gandhi, was driving his patrol car on a residential street in Brampton, just west of Toronto, ON a Sunday afternoon in 2023 when he passed a red Jeep heading in the opposite direction. An automated licence-plate reader was active in his cruiser and it alerted him that the registered owner of the Jeep had a suspended licence and outstanding drug charges, court heard.

Monday - Saturday Free

NP Posted keeps you updated on the news of the day and the perspectives that define the National Post, while drawing your focus to some of the unexpected stories we like to tell. Delivered straight to your inbox Monday to Friday, with a weekend edition on Saturdays.

Gandhi did a U-turn and pulled the Jeep over.

Behind the wheel of the Jeep was Robert Cameron, described in court as “a middle-aged Black man.” Their interaction was captured on Gandhi’s body-worn camera, although the audio was muted by the officer when he was talking with other officers. The video shows the interaction between the driver and the officer was measured and polite by both men, court heard.

Within a few minutes, the officer confirmed the driver was the owner of the Jeep and he arrested Cameron for driving while suspended, requiring the vehicle to be impounded, court heard. Cameron was handcuffed, patted down and placed in the back of Gandhi’s police car. Cameron was advised of his right to counsel to which he said “No, not right now,” court was told.

The officer asked a second officer, who he called in for backup, to search the Jeep. He told the judge it was an inventory search prior to towing the vehicle for impound, which was police policy to ensure valuable items or existing damage is noted.

The seizure of the firearm was the seed of a poisoned fruit because it was inextricably tainted by the officer’s discriminatory decision to arrest and detain the accused

Justice Renu Mandhane

The second officer found a loaded Beretta CX4 rifle under a cargo mat on the folded down rear seats of the Jeep.

Gandhi told Cameron he was now under arrest for the gun. This time the driver said he would like to call a lawyer. The officer called the man’s lawyer twice for him, but the calls went to voice mail. The officer left a message.

Cameron was charged with possession of an unlicensed firearm and related offences.

Mandhane was the case management judge in the matter, hearing pre-trial motions ahead of a scheduled trial in front of a different judge.

Cameron’s lawyer applied to have the gun and his statements to police excluded from evidence at his pending trail, claiming Charter of Rights violations. He argued handcuffing and placing Cameron in a police car was arbitrary detention and the search of the Jeep was unreasonable.

Cameron’s defence lawyer did not complain of racial bias in his application.

During the lawyer’s cross-examination of the officer, the lawyer asked Gandhi that by the time Cameron was in the back of his police car “you know what Mr. Cameron looks like, right?” Gandhi answered yes. “Did that impact the way you treated him at all?” Gandhi said no.

Mandhane then asked the lawyer if he was advancing racial bias in the case and the lawyer said no, “because it’s clear that the initial stop was entirely lawful and AI-generated,” he said of the licence-plate reader’s automatic alert.

Mandhane then said to the defence lawyer about Gandhi: “If you don’t accept everything he says, then it leads you down another path, which gets you into was this a pretext stop. Are you not going down that path?”

“I don’t think Your Honour has to go here,” the lawyer said.

In her judgment, released April 29, 2025, Mandhane ruled that although there was no direct evidence of racial profiling, the “only available inference” was that the officer arrested and detained Cameron because the officer was biased against Black men, believing them “more prone to criminality and more dangerous than other people,” she said.

“The seizure of the firearm was the seed of a poisoned fruit because it was inextricably tainted by the officer’s discriminatory decision to arrest and detain the accused and, ultimately, to illegally search his Jeep,” Mandhane said in her ruling.

“The short-term gains that flow from racial profiling in terms of police investigations and evidence-gathering cannot overshadow the intergenerational trauma that anti-Black racism in policing causes and the social ills it perpetuates.

“Despite the difficulties of proving it, once it is found, racial profiling cannot be condoned.”

Mandhane added that “racial profiling is a systemic and intractable problem within the Peel Regional Police Service.”

No longer having a loaded gun to use as evidence at trial, the Crown called no evidence, and Cameron was acquitted two weeks later.

The Crown then appealed the acquittal and the judge’s ruling. Prosecutors claimed three errors in the judge’s findings: that the arrest was unlawful, that the search was unreasonable and that Gandhi was racially biased.

Three justices of the Court of Appeal ruled Wednesday that the arrest of Cameron was not tainted by racial bias, but rather Mandhane’s finding of racial bias was tainted by legal mistakes.

The Appeal Court said the officer “could not see the driver of the vehicle before he stopped it, so he did not know the respondent’s race, gender, age, or whether he was the owner of the vehicle.”

“Racial profiling cannot be inferred simply because the officer also learned the individual’s race before an arrest, detention or search. Racial profiling must be proven on a balance of probabilities,” Justice Julie Thorburn wrote on behalf of the three-judge panel.

The Appeal Court did not dismiss the importance of guarding against racial bias, saying: “Racial profiling is a great danger to our society; it reduces individuals to dangerous stereotypes and deeply erodes trust in our institutions that are meant to protect all members of society.”

A new trial for Cameron was ordered to be held before a judge other than Mandhane.

Mandhane has long specialized in social justice and racial equity advocacy. After graduating law school and obtaining a Master of Laws degree she was appointed chief commissioner of the Ontario Human Rights Commission.

“I was often the youngest and the only racialized person at the decision-making table,” she is quoted as saying in a profile published by the Canadian Bar Association. “I practised criminal defence through an equality-rights lens, representing women, both as complainants in sexual assault proceedings, and as accused persons and prisoners. That work brought me into close contact with racialized, Indigenous, and immigrant clients. Working closely with vulnerable communities profoundly shaped how I understand advocacy and justice.”

She was appointed a judge in 2020.

Adrian Humphreys, a founding journalist at National Post in 1998, is a senior national reporter focusing on crime, policing and justice stories, and investigative journalism. He is the author of three non-fiction bestsellers about organized crime, and runs a popular YouTube channel about global gangsters.

stories.title: New St. Thomas Defence Plant will employ 400 by 2028
stories.summary: Plans for a new defence plant in St. Thomas were formally unveiled Friday.
stories.author: Sean Irvine
stories.content:
Plans for a new defence plant in St. Thomas were formally unveiled Friday.

IMT Precision will employ 400 people when it opens in 2028.

The firm, which already employs nearly 500 in Ingersoll, Ont., will operate two factories producing 55-millimetre artillery shells for the Canadian Army.

“The equipment is all dual-use by design so it can support munitions and other complex products like aerospace components”, said IMT CEO Cheryl Hacking, who added the facility will give Canadian Armed Forces flexibility.

Federal Defence Minister David McGuinty cancelled his appearance at the sod-turning.

But in March he confirmed Ottawa will provide over $300 million to the project.

The expenditure is part of a $ 1.4-billion plan to expand domestic ammunition production.

stories.title: The engineering feat at the heart of Canada’s next big Arctic build
stories.summary: The road – about 10 metres wide for traffic in both directions – will traverse low-lying tundra and a maze of lakes, ponds and streams, requiring about 230 bridges and culverts.
stories.author: Jeremy Simes and Be Giant
stories.content:
The deepwater inlet on Nunavut’s northwestern Arctic coast is ringed by treeless tundra, threaded with lakes, ponds and streams and scattered with boulders and the odd hunting cabin.

There is no all-season road in. Everything needed to build one – fuel, steel, heavy equipment and people – would have to arrive by barge in the few ice-free months, or by truck over a road made of ice.

West Kitikmeot Resources Corp (WKR) plans to change that by building an all-season gravel road, a deepwater port and an airfield in a megaproject that would be a first step in connecting Nunavut by road to the rest of the country.

The company says it would also provide Canada with its first deepwater seaport on the Western Arctic coast, bolstering security in the North and making Grays Bay one of Canada’s major economic gateways.

The goal, says Brendan Bell, Wkr’s CEO, is to kickstart copper and zinc mining in the area, spurring development that would ultimately funnel hundreds of millions of dollars into the economy by enabling the movement of critical minerals to international markets.

“There are a number of very high-grade copper and zinc deposits that are landlocked,” Bell says.

“You can’t fly this material out of here – you need infrastructure to get to tidewater.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "You can't fly this material out of here - you need infrastructure to get to tidewater."

Starting close to the Nunavut-Northwest Territories border and stretching 230 kilometres north along several mining deposits, Grays Bay Road and Port (Gbrp) would take an estimated five years to build and cost upward of $1 billion.

The project is currently before the Nunavut Impact Review Board for assessment, and Prime Minister Mark Carney has referred it to the federal major projects office, which could fast-track its construction through the federal regulatory process.

“I think Canada must do it, needs to do it,” Bell says.

The more difficult question is how.

Ed Grozic has been down this road before.

As director of Arctic engineering with Tetra Tech, he worked on the 138-kilometre Inuvik-Tuktoyaktuk Highway (ITH), which his firm helped plan, design and build before it opened in 2017.

“It’s a big deal and a big challenge to complete,” he says of the Gbrp.

It takes what he calls “alignments” – of labour, resources and equipment, but also of the people of Nunavut, governments, landowners, regulators and the environment.

Consider just the resources.

The proposed road needs 15 million cubic metres of rock – enough to build the Great Pyramid of Giza six times over – and nearly all of it has to come from land it is planned to cross.

In total, crews will open up to 40 new quarries along the route, blasting rock into pieces less than a metre across and crushing it into gravel. Blasting would be timed to avoid sensitive periods for wildlife, fish and migratory birds, according to Wkr’s filings with the review board.

Then there’s the route.

The road – about 10 metres wide to carry traffic in both directions – will traverse low-lying tundra and wind through a maze of lakes, ponds and streams, requiring about 230 bridges and culverts.

Those components would need to be prefabricated in the south and brought in by sealift or over a winter road, then installed when the ground and water are frozen.

And there are the workers – they’ll need hundreds of them. With no existing communities along the proposed route, the biggest challenges are likely to be staffing and accommodations.

In the first year, the company plans to set up a temporary work camp with supplies delivered by ship at the Grays Bay port site.

At the coastal end of the project, about a metre of sediment and loose rock will need to be dredged from the ocean floor.

Crews also need to build a harbour breakwater and a boat launch to allow for the transportation of goods during the open-water season, from June to October. Due to sea ice, marine construction season is naturally shorter, says Elliot Holland, Wkr’s chief operating officer.

“We have to account for the force of the ice pushing on the in-water wharf structures.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "We have to account for the force of the ice pushing on the in-water wharf structures."

Once winter arrives, crews would build a temporary airstrip and a pad for a permanent camp, a fuel station, the first quarries and a vital winter road.

Rebuilt each year over ice and snow, the road would connect Jericho Station, a dormant diamond mine site at the south end of the Grays Bay road, to the Tibbitt to Contwoyto Winter Road in the Northwest Territories.

About 1,000 trucks would haul materials and equipment along the route each winter.

Construction would then start at both ends of the route, with crews working towards each other until they meet in the middle. As the road advances, crews would move the camps every three months.

Beneath it all is melting permafrost – ground that’s at or below 0 C and held together by ice. When permafrost thaws, the ground shifts and sinks, buckling roads and tilting buildings; that’s why many homes in the North are built on pilings drilled deep into the ground.

Designed to last 75 years, Grays Bay road needs to remain stable well into the 2100s, in a region warming several times faster than the global average.

WKR plans to use fill-only construction where possible, adding gravel or other materials on top of the existing ground to minimize disruption, rather than using conventional cut-and-fill techniques. As much as possible, the road would be routed on top of stable bedrock.

Where that’s not practical, it would sit on a base of large rocks, preferably non-acid-generating granite. In either case, gravel goes on top.

The road’s embankment would be thicker, with coarse materials such as sand and gravel acting as a blanket. The company says this limits heat seeping into the ground, keeping the permafrost frozen.

Where the ground is most sensitive, the base would be laid in winter.

In the Arctic, says Holland, time is everything.

“If you don’t plan or execute properly, a construction season could definitely be lost,” he says.

“A delay of a month can imply a delay of a year in the Arctic.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "A delay of a month can imply a delay of a year in the Arctic."

There are two precedents for this kind of ambitious road construction in Canada’s Arctic, and both carry hard-won lessons.

The 740-kilometre Dempster Highway, which runs from near Dawson City, Yukon, to Inuvik, N.W.T., opened in 1979 after 20 years of construction.

The project was slowed in part by a funding dispute between Yukon and Ottawa, as well as a shortage of gravel. The ITH faced the same problem decades later: it was built with poorer-quality soil, all that was available in the region, says Grozic.

“The Ith’s road embankment was placed right on the tundra’s surface. That translates to a fair bit of settlement.” To keep embankments level, he says, crews must continually top up the gravel. During Ith’s first spring, muddy, slippery conditions forced the road to close.

Grays Bay has an advantage here: much of its route crosses bedrock, and Grozic expects crews to use higher-quality quarried rock.

On the ITH, most heavy construction happened in winter, often in darkness and at temperatures below -30 C, because the thawed summer ground couldn’t support heavy equipment. Crews placed more than three million cubic metres of fill and installed more than 300 culverts; Grays Bay will need roughly five times as much gravel.

Monitoring has shown that the thickest sections of the Ith’s embankment perform best. Its designers modelled how ground temperatures would change over the road’s lifetime and set the embankment thickness to ensure the permafrost would stay frozen as the Arctic warms.

The Yukon stretch of the Dempster was built entirely on permafrost, and climate-related maintenance costs have risen since the 1990s as thawing ground triggers landslides, washouts and slumping.

Water flowing through culverts carries heat into the frozen ground around them, and the Dempster has seen multiple culvert failures attributed to permafrost thaw – a warning for a road like Grays Bay, with so many water crossings of its own.

It has already taken decades for the idea of a road to get this far.

In 1970, the mining company Texasgulf found a rich zinc and copper deposit at Izok Lake, inland from the Arctic coast. Getting the metal out was the problem.

In 1992, other interested parties asked Ottawa to help pay for a road and port on Bathurst Inlet, to the east of Grays Bay. Brian Mulroney’s government said no.

Versions of plans for an all-season road have surfaced ever since.

An Inuit-backed Bathurst Inlet port and road went before the review board in 2003, then stalled as its estimated cost more than doubled.

In 2012, the mining company MMG proposed a route to Grays Bay, then shelved it the following year over cost.

In 2016, the Kitikmeot Inuit Association, which represents Inuit in the region, partnered with the Nunavut government on the current Gbrp project, but the territory pulled out two years later, saying it couldn’t afford its quarter of the cost.

WKR took over in 2023, with Kitikmeot Inuit Association as a major shareholder, and Calgary-based Atco. invested with a 40 per cent stake. This time, the company expects to raise 25 per cent of its initial funds to get started from the private sector, while the remaining 75 per cent could come from Ottawa.

Bell believes the timing is finally right.

“I feel better than ever before,” he says. “We were toiling away in obscurity before the prime minister was elected and stood up the major projects office.

“This project has real traction now, and we need to take advantage of that.

“I’ve never seen the environment so conducive to getting investments in Arctic infrastructure as I do now.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "I've never seen the environment so conducive to getting investments in Arctic infrastructure as I do now."

Regulatory approvals are still to come.

The Nunavut Impact Review Board received Wkr’s revised impact statement in May, with community meetings scheduled for this fall. Bell says he hopes the board can make a recommendation in early 2027, with a federal decision later that year.

A shortlist of three international construction consortiums has been selected, and WKR plans to choose one in March. It hopes to start construction in 2030, with operations beginning in 2035.

The road before the road is a long one, but its supporters are resolute. Caroline Wawzonek, strategic infrastructure minister for the Northwest Territories, counts herself among them.

“If we’re saying that we want to get to a place where we’re going to actually connect this country and build it into a truly Arctic and northern nation,” Wawzonek says, “then let’s do that.”

content_blocks.text: Once winter arrives, crews would build a temporary airstrip and a pad for a permanent camp, a fuel station, the first quarries and a vital winter road.

Rebuilt each year over ice and snow, the road would connect Jericho Station, a dormant diamond mine site at the south end of the Grays Bay road, to the Tibbitt to Contwoyto Winter Road in the Northwest Territories.
About 1,000 trucks would haul materials and equipment along the route each winter.
Construction would then start at both ends of the route, with crews working towards each other until they meet in the middle. As the road advances, crews would move the camps every three months.

Beneath it all is melting permafrost – ground that’s at or below 0 C and held together by ice. When permafrost thaws, the ground shifts and sinks, buckling roads and tilting buildings; that’s why many homes in the North are built on pilings drilled deep into the ground.
Designed to last 75 years, Grays Bay road needs to remain stable well into the 2100s, in a region warming several times faster than the global average.

content_blocks.alt: A road construction detail schematic for the Grays Bay project in northwestern Nunavut is shown in this handout image.
content_blocks.caption: A road construction detail schematic for the Grays Bay project in northwestern Nunavut is shown in this handout image. Credit: West Kitikmeot Resources Corp.

content_blocks.text: WKR plans to use fill-only construction where possible, adding gravel or other materials on top of the existing ground to minimize disruption, rather than using conventional cut-and-fill techniques. As much as possible, the road would be routed on top of stable bedrock.
Where that’s not practical, it would sit on a base of large rocks, preferably non-acid-generating granite. In either case, gravel goes on top.
The road’s embankment would be thicker, with coarse materials such as sand and gravel acting as a blanket. The company says this limits heat seeping into the ground, keeping the permafrost frozen.
Where the ground is most sensitive, the base would be laid in winter.

content_blocks.alt: Click to play video: 'Climate change threatening Canada’s permafrost'

content_blocks.text: In the Arctic, says Holland, time is everything.
“If you don’t plan or execute properly, a construction season could definitely be lost,” he says.
“A delay of a month can imply a delay of a year in the Arctic.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "A delay of a month can imply a delay of a year in the Arctic."
content_blocks.html: “A delay of a month can imply a delay of a year in the Arctic.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "A delay of a month can imply a delay of a year in the Arctic."

content_blocks.text: There are two precedents for this kind of ambitious road construction in Canada’s Arctic, and both carry hard-won lessons.
The 740-kilometre Dempster Highway, which runs from near Dawson City, Yukon, to Inuvik, N.W.T., opened in 1979 after 20 years of construction.

The project was slowed in part by a funding dispute between Yukon and Ottawa, as well as a shortage of gravel. The ITH faced the same problem decades later: it was built with poorer-quality soil, all that was available in the region, says Grozic.

“The Ith’s road embankment was placed right on the tundra’s surface. That translates to a fair bit of settlement.” To keep embankments level, he says, crews must continually top up the gravel. During Ith’s first spring, muddy, slippery conditions forced the road to close.

content_blocks.alt: This Aug. 12, 2009, photo shows a section of the vital Dempster Highway linking southern Canada with the Northwest Territories after it collapsed because warming temperatures caus…
content_blocks.caption: This Aug. 12, 2009, photo shows a section of the vital Dempster Highway linking southern Canada with the Northwest Territories after it collapsed because warming temperatures caused the permafrost below to thaw. THE CANADIAN PRESS/AP/Rick Bowmer

content_blocks.text: Grays Bay has an advantage here: much of its route crosses bedrock, and Grozic expects crews to use higher-quality quarried rock.

On the ITH, most heavy construction happened in winter, often in darkness and at temperatures below -30 C, because the thawed summer ground couldn’t support heavy equipment. Crews placed more than three million cubic metres of fill and installed more than 300 culverts; Grays Bay will need roughly five times as much gravel.

Monitoring has shown that the thickest sections of the Ith’s embankment perform best. Its designers modelled how ground temperatures would change over the road’s lifetime and set the embankment thickness to ensure the permafrost would stay frozen as the Arctic warms.
The Yukon stretch of the Dempster was built entirely on permafrost, and climate-related maintenance costs have risen since the 1990s as thawing ground triggers landslides, washouts and slumping.

Water flowing through culverts carries heat into the frozen ground around them, and the Dempster has seen multiple culvert failures attributed to permafrost thaw – a warning for a road like Grays Bay, with so many water crossings of its own.

content_blocks.alt: The Grays Bay conceptual port site plan in northwestern Nunavut is shown in this handout image.
content_blocks.caption: The Grays Bay conceptual port site plan in northwestern Nunavut is shown in this handout image. Credit: West Kitikmeot Resources Corp.

content_blocks.text: It has already taken decades for the idea of a road to get this far.
In 1970, the mining company Texasgulf found a rich zinc and copper deposit at Izok Lake, inland from the Arctic coast. Getting the metal out was the problem.
In 1992, other interested parties asked Ottawa to help pay for a road and port on Bathurst Inlet, to the east of Grays Bay. Brian Mulroney’s government said no.
Versions of plans for an all-season road have surfaced ever since.
An Inuit-backed Bathurst Inlet port and road went before the review board in 2003, then stalled as its estimated cost more than doubled.
In 2012, the mining company MMG proposed a route to Grays Bay, then shelved it the following year over cost.

In 2016, the Kitikmeot Inuit Association, which represents Inuit in the region, partnered with the Nunavut government on the current Gbrp project, but the territory pulled out two years later, saying it couldn’t afford its quarter of the cost.

content_blocks.alt: Click to play video: 'Carney announces Mackenzie Valley Highway designated as project of national interest'

content_blocks.text: WKR took over in 2023, with Kitikmeot Inuit Association as a major shareholder, and Calgary-based Atco. invested with a 40 per cent stake. This time, the company expects to raise 25 per cent of its initial funds to get started from the private sector, while the remaining 75 per cent could come from Ottawa.
Bell believes the timing is finally right.
“I feel better than ever before,” he says. “We were toiling away in obscurity before the prime minister was elected and stood up the major projects office.
“This project has real traction now, and we need to take advantage of that.

“I’ve never seen the environment so conducive to getting investments in Arctic infrastructure as I do now.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "I've never seen the environment so conducive to getting investments in Arctic infrastructure as I do now."
content_blocks.html: “I’ve never seen the environment so conducive to getting investments in Arctic infrastructure as I do now.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "I've never seen the environment so conducive to getting investments in Arctic infrastructure as I do now."

content_blocks.text: Regulatory approvals are still to come.

The Nunavut Impact Review Board received Wkr’s revised impact statement in May, with community meetings scheduled for this fall. Bell says he hopes the board can make a recommendation in early 2027, with a federal decision later that year.
A shortlist of three international construction consortiums has been selected, and WKR plans to choose one in March. It hopes to start construction in 2030, with operations beginning in 2035.
The road before the road is a long one, but its supporters are resolute. Caroline Wawzonek, strategic infrastructure minister for the Northwest Territories, counts herself among them.
“If we’re saying that we want to get to a place where we’re going to actually connect this country and build it into a truly Arctic and northern nation,” Wawzonek says, “then let’s do that.”

stories.title: NB Power extends winter disconnection moratorium for vulnerable customers
stories.summary: NB Power has announced that a pilot program, which offered more leniency for vulnerable populations who have difficulty paying their bills, will continue this winter.
stories.author: Rebecca Lau, Johnny James
stories.content:
NB Power has announced that a pilot program launched last year, which offered more leniency for vulnerable populations who have difficulty paying their bills, will continue this winter.

The utility operator said there will be a moratorium on power disconnections from Dec. 1 to March 31, 2027 for eligible customers.

The policy was recommended by the province’s Vulnerable Populations Committee.

“Disconnecting for non-payment is absolutely our last resort. We’re working with our customers,” said Nicole Poirier, NB Power’s vice-president of customer and strategy.

Residents will qualify if they meet one of the following criteria:

are 70 years of age or older

have a confirmed medical requirement for electrically powered equipment and are designated as a priority customer

report an annual household income below $70,000

Poirier said in the first year of the pilot, there were over 8,000 customers that fell into those categories.

“There were about 454 that were considered at risk for disconnection for nonpayment,” she said.

“So we continue to work with those customers and obviously not all of those would have been disconnected. But there were a number that disconnected and we continued to work with them to try and establish arrangements.”

Ability New Brunswick, a non-profit organization, said the moratorium puts stronger language behind the commitment NB Power has previously made.

“They have been working for a long time to make sure that those who are most vulnerable, including those that need power for medical equipment, oxygen equipment, that their power stays on. So we are pleased to see that they are continuing to do that,” said executive director Haley Flaro

As for the greater issue of affordability in the province, advocates say more collaboration between government and agencies is needed.

“There needs to be a better look at energy poverty in New Brunswick, because when people are choosing to pay the power bill or eat, that’s a really big issue,” said Flaro.

Marcel LeBrun, founder of 12 Neighbours — a non-profit that focuses on reducing homelessness and poverty — said daily decisions can become a struggle.

“Every day, you’re making a decision. Today am I putting gas in my car, paying my power bill or buying food? You have to make these trade-offs that are just not reasonable trade-offs,” he said.

Meanwhile, Poirier said a review after the moratorium’s first year found customers continued to struggle with outstanding balances even when the program ended.

“Customers that fell under the criteria of household income below $70,000, they had approximately $2.7 million in total arrears at the time,” she said.

“When I say arrears, it means unpaid balances that can either be 30 days, 60 days, or 90 days or above. So our total arrears for the company is about $27 million for all of our customers.”

Customers protected by the moratorium are still responsible for their electricity bills and are encouraged to continue to make payments throughout the winter, according to NB Power.

Anyone with difficulty paying their bills is encouraged to call NB Power to discuss other assistance options and payment arrangements.

stories.title: Quebec premier announces new review of Churchill Falls energy deal
stories.summary: ST. John's - Quebec’s Parti Québécois government is launching a review of the province’s energy agreement with Newfoundland and Labrador.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
ST. John’s - Quebec’s Parti Québécois government is launching a review of the province’s energy agreement with Newfoundland and Labrador.

Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon says the provincial Finance Department will conduct the review.

He says in a statement posted on social media that it’s important to get independent advice about the funding Quebec will provide to build new infrastructure needed as part of the agreement.

He says the review follows up on a campaign promise to review the terms of the deal.

Newfoundland and Labrador Premier Tony Wakeham says he was informed about the review on Thursday evening.

Wakeham also says in a separate statement on social media that his office has been in touch with the Quebec premier’s office and looks forward to meeting soon.

“As I’ve said previously, it is his duty to do his due diligence,” Wakeham said on social media. “I’m confident that once he has reviewed the deal, he will reach the same conclusion as Newfoundland and Labrador and the Government of Canada, that this is a win-win-win.”

For his part, St-Pierre Plamondon stressed the importance of oversight on public spending as well as the importance of reviewing Hydro-Québec’s assessment of the deal.

“Public money should serve Quebec, and it’s our duty to spend it with rigour and intelligence. This is what this impartial review will allow us to do,” the Quebec premier said.

St-Pierre Plamondon’s Parti Québécois formed a minority government in October after the deal was signed over the summer by the previous Coalition Avenir Québec government.

In August, Newfoundland and Quebec’s Crown-owned utilities signed a sweeping framework deal to build new energy projects and throw out an old contract the Atlantic province said was unfair.

Hydro-Québec was expected to pay more for power, starting in 2027, as part of the deal.

The contract also lays out a partnership between the utilities to upgrade and expand the current Churchill Falls facility and to build a new hydroelectric plant farther down the Churchill River at Gull Island.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 27, 2026.

November 27, 2026 at 5:31 p.m.

The death of a rural B.C. mother while waiting for care outside a locked ER has made international headlines and prompted a GoFundMe page.

“Well mom, you have officially hit international news with The New York Times!,” Courtney McCowan’s daughter, Hailey Schubert, posted on Facebook Thursday. “I know you’d want us all smiling at that one! You’ve hit every major news outlet and I know you’d be proud your story is making changes. I love you so much mom!”

Shubert also expressed her thanks “for the kind words and condolences. I’m slowly making my way through all of the thoughtful messages.”

Courtney McCowan had been sick for several days when a friend drove her to ­hospital last Thursday, reported the Victoria Times-Colonist.

They arrived after 5 p.m., when the Port Hardy ER closes. The next closest ER that would have been open is 40 kilometres away, in Port McNeill, B.C., according to the Times-Colonist.

Her brother, Frank McCowan told the newspaper that he arrived and saw two ­ambulances and two police vehicles. Inside the hospital, his sister was in a trauma room, after paramedics outside were unable to save her.

Chris Hachez, Hailey’s boyfriend wrote on her Facebookon Nov, 25 that McCowan, 48, “was just days away from moving to Victoria on December 1 to be close to Hailey and her mom after 13 years in Port Hardy. It was supposed to be a fresh start, and the whole family was counting down the days.

“Courtney was a loving, caring mom. She was happiest in her garden, she adored animals, and she cheered for the Canucks like every game mattered. Every single night, she and Hailey texted each other good night and ‘I love you.’ Hailey would give anything for one more of those texts.

“Watching the person I love go through this has been heartbreaking. Right now she should be helping her mom unpack boxes. Instead, she is planning a memorial and bringing home her mom’s two cats, who are now a little piece of Courtney we get to keep.”

Hachez pointed to a GoFundMe page that has been set up to help with Courtney’s funeral and memorial, bringing her belongings home, provide care for her cats, and enable time off for the family to grieve.

Hachez posted a similar message about McCowan on the GoFundMe page. Though, he added that paramedics “worked to save her outside the hospital, but she didn’t survive. They left her outside for 39 minutes before letting her in to the hospital. By this point, it was too late. The BC Coroners Service, Island Health and BC Emergency Health Services are all investigating, and the family is still waiting for answers.”

McCowan’s death has illustrated an ongoing problem with ER closures in rural B.C. The province’s new health minister, Ryan Peterson, has keeping rural ERs open amid his new marching orders. This directive was part of the mandate letter he received from Premier Lorne Doerkson on Tuesday.

Port Hardy Hospital’s ER has been closed overnight since January 2023, reports the Times-Colonist.

Stewart Lewis is a writer and editor with National Post. A journalist and lawyer, he has worked in newspapers, radio and TV, and served a legal stint with Global Affairs Canada at the United Nations in New York City.

Doctor says mothers of babies with 'conditions incompatible with life' should be able to access Maid for them

Conservative MP Andrew Lawton speaks during question period in the House of Commons on Thursday, Nov. 26, 2026. Lawton has raised concerns about the ethical challenges of advanced directives for Maid, as review of Bill C-41 continues in parliament. (Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia)

November 27, 2026 at 5:25 p.m.

The admission by a Quebec doctor that he provided Maid to patients who had given an advanced directive to receive it, but were no longer able to consent when they did, is raising alarm bells for Andrew Lawton Conservative MP) for Elgin—St. Thomas—London South.

“Dr. (Alain) Naud admitted to euthanizing dementia patients who don’t know what’s happening to them and cannot contemporaneously consent to Maid, when this practice is illegal in Canada,” Lawton said to National Post in an email Friday. “He acknowledged doing this outside the Criminal Code.”

Lawton is referring to an exchange he had with Laud during a meeting of the House of Commons committee reviewing Bill C-41, the Medical Assistance in Dying Safeguards Act, introduced in parliament on October 27, 2026. The bill aims to provide protection to medical practitioners from Criminal Code prosecution when patients consent to Maid in advance, while they still have decision-making capacity.

Quebec has allowed advance requests since Oct. 30, 2024, but they are not yet legal under federal law, with Bill C-41 pending.

Lawton shared his concerns about Laud’s practice in a X poston Monday

Shocking Testimony A Quebec doctor just admitted in committee to homicide. Equally shocking, Dr. Alain Naud admitted he believes Maid should be available for babies up to one year old. And the Liberal response to this? Lecturing me about "respectfulness." pic.twitter.com/fJ7LBeCtc4 — Andrew Lawton (@AndrewLawton) November 24, 2026

During the exchange with Laud he said: “You’ve admitted to violating the Criminal Code. How are we, as a committee, supposed to expect that safeguards Parliament imposes will work when you are freely discussing not following one of the most important pieces of federal statute in this country?”

Lawton asked whether Laud had provided Maid to a patient who has subsequently refused it. Dr Laud responded: “What Quebec law says, and what’s in C-41, is that there needs to be a clear manifestation of refusal to receive Maid.”

However, Lawton remains concerned about “provinces and doctors … choosing not to follow parameters set out in the Criminal Code. (Laud’s testimony) is proof that existing Maid safeguards aren’t working.”

He argues that “advance requests raise serious medical and ethical questions, so Canadians should be concerned when doctors freely admit to selectively following laws and advocate expansion of Maid to babies with severe health issues.”

His reference to babies refers to his exchange with Laud, when he raised the point about Maid for infants: “I want to ask you about a recommendation you provided to the Special Joint Committee on Medical Assistance in Dying in 2022, do you still believe that the government should allow access to Maid for children zero to one year of age with severe life-threatening conditions?”

And subsequently: “Doctor Naud. Do you still believe that Maid should be available to … quote children zero to one year of age with severe life-threatening conditions, unquote?”

Laud clarified that he is “not talking about children zero to one, but rather babies born with conditions that are incompatible with life. For example, a baby born without a brain. The Netherlands allowed this for many years, and I’ve heard testimonies from mothers in Quebec who went through such hard times. (They) asked to be able to decide that on behalf of the child because they … couldn’t bear to see their baby like that anymore. So these are conditions incompatible with life.”

Bill C-41 is undergoing second reading in the House of Commons as of Nov. 17. It still has to go through committee, third reading, and the Senate before it becomes law.

Meanwhile, Quebec’s law goes further than the national framework and Federal Health Minister Mark Holland has said Ottawa will not challenge Quebec’s law, although the federal government had repeatedly voiced concern about Quebec moving ahead of Criminal Code changes, according to a report by the CBC.

Stewart Lewis is a writer and editor with National Post. A journalist and lawyer, he has worked in newspapers, radio and TV, and served a legal stint with Global Affairs Canada at the United Nations in New York City.

stories.title: Knights player suspended under CHL drug education and anti-doping policy
stories.summary: The Ontario Hockey League announced that a London Knights player and a Niagara IceDogs player have each been suspended following violations of the Canadian Hockey League Drug Education and Anti-Doping Policy.
stories.author: Melanie Kentner
stories.content:
The Ontario Hockey League announced that a London Knights player and a Niagara IceDogs player have each been suspended following violations of the Canadian Hockey League Drug Education and Anti-Doping Policy.

Players Brody Leet of the Knights and Ivan Galiyanov of the IceDogs have each been suspended for eight games, according to a news release on Friday.

Under the policy, each player has been assessed an eight-game suspension for a first violation for use of a prohibited substance.

The league says both violations involved substances classified as recreational drugs and were not related to performance-enhancing substances.

The league says the player well-being resources will be available to both players throughout their suspensions.

stories.title: ‘I was crushed’: N.S. sock drive searches for new funding after 50/50 shutdown
stories.summary: Halifax's so-called Mary Queen of Socks is facing a tough decision after regulators put a stop to her fundraising campaign.
stories.author: Angela Capobianco, Rebecca Lau
stories.content:
Halifax’s so-called Mary Queen of Socks is facing a tough decision after regulators put a stop to her fundraising campaign.

Mary Crosby has been ordered by the Department of Service Nova Scotia to cease her 50/50 draw that raises funds to help shelters provide socks for those in need.

“I was crushed,” she said.

Crosby has been working hard to meet her goal of 25,000 socks collected for shelters across Nova Scotia.

She said it’s to ensure people in the community have clean, warm, and dry pairs of socks on their feet.

“It’s such a good cause, such a needed cause,” she said, adding that the need has grown each year in the community.

Crosby knits some of the socks herself, but the vast majority of the socks are purchased. To help buy them, she has been running a 50/50 draw from her Facebook page ‘Socks for Shelters,’ for the past year and a half.

The money has helped her buy at least 10,000 pairs of socks.

But on Wednesday evening, she said she received devastating news from a compliance officer with the Alcohol, Gaming, Fuel and Tobacco Division of Service Nova Scotia.

She was told to cease operations immediately.

“Now, 10,000 pairs were at least purchased with the 50/50 money. Enough said. If we lose that, that’s a huge, devastating loss to us.”

Susan McKeage, a spokesperson for Service Nova Scotia, said the department appreciates the work Socks for Shelters is doing and understands “how disappointing it can be to learn that a well-intentioned fundraiser May not meet provincial gaming requirements.”

“At the same time, 50/50 draws are regulated gaming activities. Provincial requirements must be in accordance with the federal laws that permit the legalization of gambling in Canada,” the department said in its statement.

“They are in place to ensure lotteries are conducted fairly and transparently and that funds raised are used for their intended community or charitable purpose.”

Organizations that don’t qualify for gaming licences could have other options, including being listed on a charitable lottery licence held by the organization they are helping.

That’s a path Crosby could very well take.

Cherry Laxton, COO of Souls Harbour Rescue Mission, which has accepted tens of thousands of socks from Crosby, says the organization is more than happy to help Crosby if she needs it.

“We would absolutely love to be able to collaborate with her to find some way around this,” said Laxton.

Crosby said she doesn’t know how next year’s Socks for Shelters campaign will work without the 50/50 draw, but she’s optimistic.

She said the province has contacted her and is committed to coming up with a solution with her.

“I was crushed,” she said.
Crosby has been working hard to meet her goal of 25,000 socks collected for shelters across Nova Scotia.
She said it’s to ensure people in the community have clean, warm, and dry pairs of socks on their feet.
“It’s such a good cause, such a needed cause,” she said, adding that the need has grown each year in the community.

Crosby knits some of the socks herself, but the vast majority of the socks are purchased. To help buy them, she has been running a 50/50 draw from her Facebook page ‘Socks for Shelters,’ for the past year and a half.
The money has helped her buy at least 10,000 pairs of socks.
But on Wednesday evening, she said she received devastating news from a compliance officer with the Alcohol, Gaming, Fuel and Tobacco Division of Service Nova Scotia.
She was told to cease operations immediately.
“Now, 10,000 pairs were at least purchased with the 50/50 money. Enough said. If we lose that, that’s a huge, devastating loss to us.”

Susan McKeage, a spokesperson for Service Nova Scotia, said the department appreciates the work Socks for Shelters is doing and understands “how disappointing it can be to learn that a well-intentioned fundraiser May not meet provincial gaming requirements.”

“At the same time, 50/50 draws are regulated gaming activities. Provincial requirements must be in accordance with the federal laws that permit the legalization of gambling in Canada,” the department said in its statement.
“They are in place to ensure lotteries are conducted fairly and transparently and that funds raised are used for their intended community or charitable purpose.”
Organizations that don’t qualify for gaming licences could have other options, including being listed on a charitable lottery licence held by the organization they are helping.
That’s a path Crosby could very well take.
Cherry Laxton, COO of Souls Harbour Rescue Mission, which has accepted tens of thousands of socks from Crosby, says the organization is more than happy to help Crosby if she needs it.
“We would absolutely love to be able to collaborate with her to find some way around this,” said Laxton.
Crosby said she doesn’t know how next year’s Socks for Shelters campaign will work without the 50/50 draw, but she’s optimistic.
She said the province has contacted her and is committed to coming up with a solution with her.
