stories.title: Alberta’s UCP prepares for thousands to attend its annual meeting in Calgary
stories.summary: Vote for control of the party’s board pits Premier Danielle Smith against activists who previously were her supporters
stories.author: Carrie Tait
stories.content:
Alberta’s United Conservative Party expects roughly 8,000 members to converge this weekend in Calgary, where a vote for provincial board seats has morphed into a proxy war over separatism.

The Ucp’s annual meeting kicks off Friday afternoon, with the party’s political enthusiasts bracing for long registration, security and voting lines. While 75 per cent of Albertans who voted in last month’s referendum rejected secession, the debate over independence still dominates UCP politics.

This year’s battle for control of the party’s board pits Premier Danielle Smith against activists who previously were among her most ferocious supporters.

And to successfully block separatists and their sympathizers from positions of power, Ms. Smith needs UCP members who previously felt alienated by her shift to the right to rally behind her and her federalist agenda.

Put it together, and the UCP is preparing for thousands to attend its annual meeting at Calgary’s BMO Centre on the Stampede grounds, according to party spokesman Dave Prisco.

The Ucp’s board consists of 18 voting directors, including the party’s leader. This year, eight spots are up for grabs and candidates campaigning on a pledge to support Ms. Smith have labelled themselves Team Unity. They are, essentially, the anti-separatists.

Brett Wilson, a businessman and philanthropist, plans to vote for this slate of candidates to protect the UCP from secessionists. Independence leaders have openly encouraged UCP members to support like-minded board candidates in order to further their cause within the governing party and work toward deposing Ms. Smith.

“The separatists are trying to do things that are not ethical or democratic,” Mr. Wilson said in an interview this week.

He is agitated by Canada’s equalization system, the federal policy that fuels Alberta’s separation movement, and considers the practice unfair. But he does not believe Alberta’s independence leaders offer a coherent alternative to Confederation, regardless of how much equalization stings.

“These people are not entrepreneurs, not thought leaders. They are not relevant,” he said. “The separation noise gets Alberta nothing.”

Mike Dalke is the Ucp’s constituency association president for Edmonton-Rutherford, a riding held by the New Democratic Party. This weekend, he said, is about the Ucp’s factions coalescing, regardless of who wins seats on the board.

He expects some “fireworks” and “heated conversations,” but save for a few “bad actors” in the separatist ranks, Mr. Dalke thinks the Ucp’s version of unity is within reach.

“It looks like Thanksgiving dinner with your family. Your crazy uncle is gonna have his crazy things. You might have a fight over whatever, whoever gets the last chicken bone.

“But ultimately, you end leaving still as a family.”

And the family members are working toward the same goal: keeping the NDP away from power.

Division is part of the Ucp’s DNA. It formed in 2017, when the Progressive Conservative Association of Alberta merged with the Wildrose Party, in response to the NDP winning Alberta’s 2015 general election.

UCP members put pressure on their inaugural leader, Jason Kenney, into calling a leadership review. He stepped down after winning support from just 51 per cent of voters.

Jenny Walker is a political organizer in the province’s northwest, co-founded Wexit Alberta, and worked for Ms. Smith during her 2022 bid to replace Mr. Kenney. Despite Ms. Walker’s separatist inclinations, she is rallying UCP members to support Team Unity candidates, because she believes the governing party should heed the referendum results.

“We’ve been given one of the clearest mandates in Alberta history,” she said, noting that she will not attend the annual meeting out of fear of being attacked for her politics. “This is actually the unification of the conservative movement.”

Ms. Walker, who said she loves Alberta and Canada, regrets allowing “negativity” to take over the Wexit movement, which she concedes contributed to the cracks in the UCP.

“We created, as conservatives, our own anger machine,” she said. “It is not fuelled by logic. It is all feelings.”

But even if candidates backing the Premier sweep the board, keeping the separatists at bay, the outcome of Saturday’s vote could still stoke turmoil in the party’s executive ranks.

Rob Smith, the president of the provincial board, this week called the Team Unity label a “slap in the face” to candidates who have dedicated hundreds of hours to the UCP cause.

Mr. Smith, who is not related to the Premier, then endorsed people running opposite those under the unity banner. He stumped for two candidates earlier this week and had warm words for two more.

And so, the Ucp’s president, who is not up for re-election this weekend, could be short on allies – and under threat of removal by two-thirds of his fellow board members – if his picks fall short.

“To suggest they are not all for Unity is, honestly, to me, Extremely Offensive!” he wrote on Facebook.

Neither the Premier’s office nor Mr. Smith returned messages seeking comment.

stories.title: A road through Nunavut: The monumental billion-dollar plan to connect Canada’s Arctic
stories.summary: The all-season road would be the first to go across Nunavut, stretching 230 km. from N.W.T. to Grays Bay — where Canada would have its first deepsea port on the Western Arctic.
stories.author: Jeremy Simes and Be Giant
stories.content:
Amanda Dumond lifts the lid of a large freezer chest in Kugluktuk , Nunavut’s westernmost community, where the Arctic Ocean feeds into Coronation Gulf.

The Inuk woman pulls out several bags: there’s a deep-red caribou leg, then a package of the animal’s stomach fat, followed by a hoof and an entire goose.

She gasps when she finds a piece of maktaaq, a traditional food of whale skin and blubber.

“This is the last piece I have,” she says, showing off the fatty, marbled tissue.

Dumond, manager of the hamlet’s hunters and trappers organization, goes hunting with her family every year, taking all-terrain vehicles onto the landscape largely untouched by development.

There are no roads in the surrounding treeless tundra, just an expanse of land stretching to the horizon.

But that could change.

West Kitikmeot Resources Corp., an Inuit-owned and -led company, is planning to build the Grays Bay Road and Port, east of Kugluktuk.

The mega project, which could cost upward of $1 billion, is currently before the Nunavut Impact Review Board for assessment. Prime Minister Mark Carney has referred it to the federal major projects office, which could fast-track its construction by overriding certain federal regulations.

It would be monumental.

The all-season gravel road would be the first to run across the territory, starting at the Nunavut-Northwest Territories boundary and stretching 230 kilometres north along several mining deposits to Grays Bay.

There, Canada would have its first deepsea port on the Western Arctic coast.

It would also be a first step in connecting Nunavut by road to the rest of the country.

The major projects office is also considering a 400-kilometre road called the Arctic Economic Security Corridor, stretching north of Yellowknife to where Grays Bay Road would begin.

Both roads would become part of Canada’s national highway system, and Canadians would be able to drive to Nunavut for the very first time.

The benefits are many, says the company. Besides being able to truck minerals to the port, the project would create jobs, lower housing and food costs, and provide Canada with Arctic security.

But there are worries, too — impacts to caribou herds and marine life.

Dumond says hunting is integral for her family and others in the community. “It’s what I live for. It’s a part of me.”

Kugluktuk Mayor Ryan Nivingalok says he understands the concerns, but his hamlet could benefit from the project.

“As a community leader, you’re looking for the best solution and opportunities to help your people,” Nivingalok says.

“You want to see growth.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "You want to see growth."

The tiny inlet in the frigid Coronation Gulf is surrounded by low-lying tundra with a network of lakes, ponds and streams. Boulders scatter the region, along with the odd hunting cabin.

Kugluktuk, 180 kilometres to the west, is the closest community. It wouldn’t be connected to Grays Bay Road, but residents often take their ATVs out to the area or zip across the water by boat.

In early September, the tundra’s fall colours have set in.

Willows and grasses have turned dark yellow and deep red. Orange lichens and green moss are splotched on exposed bedrock, and ravens make throaty caws in the overcast sky above. The air is cool and fresh.

In Kugluktuk, people bounce on rumbling quads from one point to the next. Some homes are painted in bright yellow, green and blue. Animal furs are draped over porch railings, and some roofs are adorned with caribou or muskox skulls.

Christmas lights are still up from last year on the sides of some homes, in shapes of stars and trees. Each holiday season, residents travel roughly 60 kilometres south to cut down and haul back a tree.

New mothers walk around the hamlet’s two grocery stores carrying babies in pouches on their backs.

After school, children jump on their bikes, climb in the playground and kick balls on the soccer field, squealing with laughter.

Unemployment and poverty in the hamlet of 1,380 is high. Those who have jobs mostly work for mining companies or in public administration.

Groceries are more expensive than in Southern Canada, and many rely on food hampers. Some sell sealskin garments to help make ends meet.

The Grays Bay project would make it easier to get goods to the community and others in the territory, says West Kitikmeot. People currently rely on planes to get products year-round or, in the warmer months, infrequent ships from Montreal.

Simon Kuliktana, a member of Nunavut’s legislative assembly who represents the hamlet, hasn’t thrown his support behind the Grays Bay project. He says he’s speaking with residents and groups before taking a position.

“Our caribou herd is so delicate that it’s a fine line,” Kuliktana says. “We need to ensure that they are around for many centuries to come.”

Nunavut Premier John Main, however, is on board.

“It will bolster Arctic connection into the Arctic Ocean, open mining opportunities and meet Canada’s growing need for responsibly sourced rare earth elements and battery metals, which are essential for clean energy and defence applications,” he says in a statement.

Likewise, the N.W.T. government has thrown its support behind both the Grays Bay and Arctic Economic Security Corridor projects.

Caroline Wawzonek, the territory’s strategic infrastructure minister, says the corridor could cost a lot more, up to $7 billion.

But both projects are tied, she says. And if Canada wants to connect the country and the Arctic, it needs it.

“Let’s do it in a way that involves Indigenous nations so that they are involved from Day 1.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "Let's do it in a way that involves Indigenous nations so that they are involved from Day 1."

The Grays Bay project has been in the works for decades, says Brendan Bell, West Kitikmeot’s CEO.

It has been reimagined several times, Bell says, including changing routes to address concerns about caribou. The port site was selected because the tidewater is naturally deep.

In 2016, the Kitikmeot Inuit Association and Nunavut’s government signed an agreement to partner on the project, but the territory later pulled out.

In 2025, West Kitikmeot took over. The Kitikmeot Inuit Association, which represents Inuit in the region, is a major shareholder of the company. Calgary-based Atco Ltd. also has a 40 per cent stake.

The company expects it will need to raise 25 per cent of funds from the private sector, while the rest could come from Ottawa.

Bell says Canada needs the project.

Back in Kugluktuk, 18-year-old Deagan Miyok plays basketball outside with a friend.

The Grays Bay project is “not bad,” he says.

Others in the community looking for work also say Grays Bay could help them get jobs and put food on the table.

West Kitikmeot promises the port could help communities get goods more reliably, frequently and at a lower cost. It would have an area where supplies could be unloaded, stored and later shipped out to communities by boat.

Bell says he expects non-perishable bulk goods would become cheaper, but items that need to be flown in, such as milk, May not see prices change.

“It really is a vast, wide-open area with lots of room for caribou,” says Bell. “Our largest shareholder is the Inuit people of the region, so we have a mandate in making sure this project facilitates future investments.”

She has been eating what locals call country foods since she was little. She sees the caribou numbers in decline, even without the Grays Bay project.

During a hunting trip this past summer, she says her family harvested only one caribou.

She gasps when she finds a piece of maktaaq, a traditional food of whale skin and blubber.
“This is the last piece I have,” she says, showing off the fatty, marbled tissue.

In early September, the tundra’s fall colours have set in.

Willows and grasses have turned dark yellow and deep red. Orange lichens and green moss are splotched on exposed bedrock, and ravens make throaty caws in the overcast sky above. The air is cool and fresh.

In Kugluktuk, people bounce on rumbling quads from one point to the next. Some homes are painted in bright yellow, green and blue. Animal furs are draped over porch railings, and some roofs are adorned with caribou or muskox skulls.

Christmas lights are still up from last year on the sides of some homes, in shapes of stars and trees. Each holiday season, residents travel roughly 60 kilometres south to cut down and haul back a tree.
New mothers walk around the hamlet’s two grocery stores carrying babies in pouches on their backs.

content_blocks.alt: Children play soccer on an artificial turf field in Kugluktuk, Nvt., on Sept. 8, 2026.
content_blocks.caption: Children play soccer on an artificial turf field in Kugluktuk, Nvt., on Sept. 8, 2026. Pat Kane/Be Giant/THE CANADIAN PRESS

content_blocks.text: After school, children jump on their bikes, climb in the playground and kick balls on the soccer field, squealing with laughter.
Unemployment and poverty in the hamlet of 1,380 is high. Those who have jobs mostly work for mining companies or in public administration.
Groceries are more expensive than in Southern Canada, and many rely on food hampers. Some sell sealskin garments to help make ends meet.

The Grays Bay project would make it easier to get goods to the community and others in the territory, says West Kitikmeot. People currently rely on planes to get products year-round or, in the warmer months, infrequent ships from Montreal.

content_blocks.alt: Click to play video: 'Canada advancing ‘middle power strategy’ with new trade pacts: Anand'

content_blocks.text: Simon Kuliktana, a member of Nunavut’s legislative assembly who represents the hamlet, hasn’t thrown his support behind the Grays Bay project. He says he’s speaking with residents and groups before taking a position.
“Our caribou herd is so delicate that it’s a fine line,” Kuliktana says. “We need to ensure that they are around for many centuries to come.”
Nunavut Premier John Main, however, is on board.

“It will bolster Arctic connection into the Arctic Ocean, open mining opportunities and meet Canada’s growing need for responsibly sourced rare earth elements and battery metals, which are essential for clean energy and defence applications,” he says in a statement.
Likewise, the N.W.T. government has thrown its support behind both the Grays Bay and Arctic Economic Security Corridor projects.
Caroline Wawzonek, the territory’s strategic infrastructure minister, says the corridor could cost a lot more, up to $7 billion.
But both projects are tied, she says. And if Canada wants to connect the country and the Arctic, it needs it.

“Let’s do it in a way that involves Indigenous nations so that they are involved from Day 1.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "Let's do it in a way that involves Indigenous nations so that they are involved from Day 1."
content_blocks.html: “Let’s do it in a way that involves Indigenous nations so that they are involved from Day 1.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "Let's do it in a way that involves Indigenous nations so that they are involved from Day 1."

content_blocks.text: Building the road and port
The Grays Bay project has been in the works for decades, says Brendan Bell, West Kitikmeot’s CEO.
It has been reimagined several times, Bell says, including changing routes to address concerns about caribou. The port site was selected because the tidewater is naturally deep.
In 2016, the Kitikmeot Inuit Association and Nunavut’s government signed an agreement to partner on the project, but the territory later pulled out.
In 2025, West Kitikmeot took over. The Kitikmeot Inuit Association, which represents Inuit in the region, is a major shareholder of the company. Calgary-based Atco Ltd. also has a 40 per cent stake.
The company expects it will need to raise 25 per cent of funds from the private sector, while the rest could come from Ottawa.
Bell says Canada needs the project.
Its goal is to kick-start mining copper and zinc in the area, spurring development that would ultimately funnel hundreds of millions of dollars into the economy.
The project would take five years to build.

content_blocks.alt: A view of the shoreline in Kugluktuk, Nvt., on Sept. 7, 2026. It is the most westerly community in Nunavut and sits on the edge of the Northwest Passage. Residents are split on th…
content_blocks.caption: A view of the shoreline in Kugluktuk, Nvt., on Sept. 7, 2026. It is the most westerly community in Nunavut and sits on the edge of the Northwest Passage. Residents are split on the potential development of the Grays Bay Road and Port Project, which would be located 200 kilometres to the east of the community. Some peo…

content_blocks.text: Several reports from West Kitikmeot detail the massive construction process. The company would hire hundreds of workers, bring equipment in on barges, and build a winter road to bring in more equipment and materials.
Construction on the permanent road would start at the same time from both ends and eventually meet in the middle.
The road has to be gravel, not asphalt or concrete, because of finicky permafrost — ground that’s at or below 0 C and held together by ice.
When it thaws, the ground shifts and can cause roads or structures to distort. That’s why many homes in the North are built on elevated foundations with pilings drilled deep into the ground.
Building a road on permafrost isn’t a new challenge, says Bell.
The 740-kilometre Dempster Highway, cited as Canada’s longest gravel road, stretches from near Dawson City, Yukon, to Inuvik, N.W.T.
“Even if we had the money, I think you probably wouldn’t pave roads in this part of the world,” Bell says.
Arctic sovereignty
Carney has argued the Grays Bay project would also bolster the country’s security.
Ottawa is planning to spend an extra $32 billion on the Armed Forces to beef up operations in the North, and it says the Grays Bay Port could assist the military.
Bell says it could host military ships and submarines. The coast guard, for example, could dock and fuel up.
“We need to send a message to not just our allies that we will do our part, but our adversaries that we’re here, we’re present and will match their intensity in the Arctic.”
The port could also support the coast guard’s search and rescue missions, Bell adds.

content_blocks.alt: Amanda Dumond, manager of the Kugluktuk Hunters and Trappers Organization, points to Grays Bay on a map in Kugluktuk, Nvt., on Sept. 8, 2026.
content_blocks.caption: Amanda Dumond, manager of the Kugluktuk Hunters and Trappers Organization, points to Grays Bay on a map in Kugluktuk, Nvt., on Sept. 8, 2026. Pat Kane/Be Giant/THE CANADIAN PRESS

content_blocks.text: The Forces have various operations in the Arctic.
There’s a training centre in Resolute, Nvt., along with an alert station on Ellesmere Island – the most northern continuously inhabited location in the world.

The Forces also have three other sites in the region that can support fighter jets: Inuvik, Iqaluit and Yellowknife. Ottawa’s $32-billion plan aims to enhance aircraft operations at these locations as well as a base in Newfoundland and Labrador.
Kuliktana, the legislature member for Kugluktuk, says it makes sense to beef up security in the region.

“With declining ice on the Northwest Passage, we have other countries like China and Russia very interested in using the Northwest Passage.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "With declining ice on the Northwest Passage, we have other countries like China and Russia very interested in using the Northwest Passage."
content_blocks.html: “With declining ice on the Northwest Passage, we have other countries like China and Russia very interested in using the Northwest Passage.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "With declining ice on the Northwest Passage, we have other countries like China and Russia very interested in using the Northwest Passage."

content_blocks.text: Improving the economy, housing and food prices
Back in Kugluktuk, 18-year-old Deagan Miyok plays basketball outside with a friend.
The Grays Bay project is “not bad,” he says.
Miyok graduated high school this year and hopes to get a job at a mine.
Others in the community looking for work also say Grays Bay could help them get jobs and put food on the table.

content_blocks.alt: A welcome sign in Kugluktuk, Nvt., on Sept. 8, 2026. Kugluktuk is the most westerly community in Nunavut and sits on the edge of the Northwest Passage. Residents are split on the…
content_blocks.caption: A welcome sign in Kugluktuk, Nvt., on Sept. 8, 2026. Kugluktuk is the most westerly community in Nunavut and sits on the edge of the Northwest Passage. Residents are split on the potential development of the Grays Bay Road and Port Project, which would be located 200 kilometres to the east of the community. Some peopl…

content_blocks.text: West Kitikmeot says it would hire 250 to 400 people for construction on the project over the five years. The port could also support up to 80 permanent employees with West Kitikmeot and other companies.
West Kitikmeot also estimates the project would add about $750 million each year to Nunavut’s economy by 2040.
There would be new businesses, including mines shipping out copper and zinc, and barging companies bringing in food and supplies. The project could also spur tourism and excursion operators.

On the outskirts of Kugluktuk, a new 12-unit housing complex is going up, but there’s no timeline on when it might be finished. An additional 10 modular units were set to arrive on a sealift in late September.
The federal government has said it plans to build 750 housing units in Nunavut by March 2031.
“You have big waiting lists for new people applying for units in town,” Nivingalok says. “There’s still not enough units to go around.”

A dozen people sometimes squeeze into a two-bedroom house in the hamlet, the mayor adds. In many cases, large multi-generational families live together, or singles and couples stay with friends or relatives.
The Grays Bay project could speed up more housing, as infrequent shipments and high costs make it difficult to build homes quickly.

content_blocks.alt: A view of Kugluktuk, Nvt., on Sept. 7, 2026. It is the most westerly community in Nunavut and sits on the edge of the Northwest Passage.
content_blocks.caption: A view of Kugluktuk, Nvt., on Sept. 7, 2026. It is the most westerly community in Nunavut and sits on the edge of the Northwest Passage. Pat Kane/Be Giant/THE CANADIAN PRESS

content_blocks.text: West Kitikmeot promises the port could help communities get goods more reliably, frequently and at a lower cost. It would have an area where supplies could be unloaded, stored and later shipped out to communities by boat.
Bell says the company could also build ice roads — or permanent ones – linking communities to the port, if people support it.
Northeast of Kugluktuk, across the sea, is Cambridge Bay. The community of 1,750 is the centre of government for Nunavut’s Kitikmeot region.
Fred Pederson, the legislature member representing Cambridge Bay, supports the Grays Bay project not only for the jobs it would create, but for getting food and supplies to communities more easily.
In September, Cambridge Bay found itself in a bit of a food crisis.

Grocery store shelves were empty, with fresh vegetables, bread, flour and some frozen goods out of stock for weeks, due to timing issues with the sealift. Residents were panic buying when items became available again.

content_blocks.alt: An employee stocks a refrigerator at the Northern Store in Kugluktuk, Nvt., on Sept. 8, 2026. The cost of food in Nunavut is about two times as high as prices in southern Canada.
content_blocks.caption: An employee stocks a refrigerator at the Northern Store in Kugluktuk, Nvt., on Sept. 8, 2026. The cost of food in Nunavut is about two times as high as prices in southern Canada. Pat Kane/Be Giant/THE CANADIAN PRESS

content_blocks.text: In Kugluktuk, Joey Kunana bags his full cart of groceries at a store checkout. He’s buying toilet paper, eggs, margarine, yogurt cups, frozen pizzas, cereal and canned goods. The trip comes to about $800.
“These prices, it’s like, holy smokes,” he says, adding he pays that amount twice a month to feed his four children. Their mother recently died.
A two-kilogram, family-size jar of peanut butter costs $21. Oranges are $10 per kilogram, and bananas are $4 per kilogram.

Statistics Canada figures show the monthly average price for food items in Nunavut is about double the provincial average. The average in September was $11 for the same jar of peanut butter, $4.50 per kilogram for oranges and $2 per kilogram for bananas.
Asked about the Grays Bay project, Kunana says he’s never heard of it.
West Kitikmeot says in a report that by enhancing supply chains, the Grays Bay project would make store-bought food more accessible.
Bell says he expects non-perishable bulk goods would become cheaper, but items that need to be flown in, such as milk, May not see prices change.

content_blocks.alt: Bagged vegetables at the Northern Store in Kugluktuk, Nvt., on Sept. 8, 2026. The cost of food in Nunavut is about two times as high as prices in southern Canada.
content_blocks.caption: Bagged vegetables at the Northern Store in Kugluktuk, Nvt., on Sept. 8, 2026. The cost of food in Nunavut is about two times as high as prices in southern Canada. Pat Kane/Be Giant/THE CANADIAN PRESS

content_blocks.text: Organizers at the elders centre in Kugluktuk serve lunch three times a week. On the menu one afternoon is bannock and hamburger soup. The room is packed with people talking and joking.
Doris Elatiak, who works at the centre, says many who stop in don’t have much food at home or are out of work.
Some worry about what the Grays Bay project could do to caribou and other animals that are sources of food, she says.
“Most of the elders, they really don’t want it to go ahead.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "Most of the elders, they really don't want it to go ahead."
content_blocks.html: “Most of the elders, they really don’t want it to go ahead.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "Most of the elders, they really don't want it to go ahead."

content_blocks.text: Caribou
Most of Canada’s barren-ground caribou give birth and raise their calves in Nunavut.
Herd populations in the territory’s Western region have sharply fallen over the last few decades.

Figures from the Global Initiative on Ungulate Migration show the Bathurst herd fell from 400,000 animals in the 1980s to fewer than 4,000 in 2025. The Dolphin-Union and Bluenose-East herds have also diminished, although the Beverly herd has increased in recent years.
Researchers and hunters have said warming temperatures, predation and hunting have contributed to declines.

The Dolphin-Union herd, for example, crosses sea ice every spring to give birth on Victoria Island, north of Nunavut’s mainland, before returning in the fall. On weak ice, they can fall into the sea and drown.
Hunters say industrial development has also played a role.
Leah Kadlun started an online petition opposing the Grays Bay project. As of early October, nearly 180 people had signed it.
She says she’s not only concerned about caribou, but also fish, seals, whales and other ocean animals in the region.

“It’s going to affect our water, especially along the Coronation Gulf, if they have a lot of ships, tankers and haulers passing by.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "It's going to affect our water, especially along the Coronation Gulf, if they have a lot of ships, tankers and haulers passing by."
content_blocks.html: “It’s going to affect our water, especially along the Coronation Gulf, if they have a lot of ships, tankers and haulers passing by.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "It's going to affect our water, especially along the Coronation Gulf, if they have a lot of ships, tankers and haulers passing by."

content_blocks.text: Kadlun sits in Kugluktuk’s visitor centre, surrounded by cultural exhibits, artwork and artifacts. The building is in the shape on an ulu knife, a crescent-shaped blade used by Inuit for centuries.

content_blocks.alt: A painting of hunters using bow and arrow to harvest caribou is displayed at the visitor’s centre in Kugluktuk, Nvt., on Sept. 10, 2026.
content_blocks.caption: A painting of hunters using bow and arrow to harvest caribou is displayed at the visitor’s centre in Kugluktuk, Nvt., on Sept. 10, 2026. Pat Kane/Be Giant/THE CANADIAN PRESS

content_blocks.text: On display is a large kayak made with caribou skin. Kadlun says her grandmother taught her how to soften such skins when she was little.
“We don’t have a road in or out, but I’m not complaining,” she says. “Of course we’re going to have problems with housing. We’re going to have problems with food.

“This is how I choose to live, this is what we have. We have our fresh food we get off the land.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "This is how I choose to live, this is what we have. We have our fresh food we get off the land."
content_blocks.html: “This is how I choose to live, this is what we have. We have our fresh food we get off the land.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "This is how I choose to live, this is what we have. We have our fresh food we get off the land."

content_blocks.text: West Kitikmeot says it expects the project won’t change fish populations and that marine habitat is not expected to be significantly affected.
It also doesn’t anticipate significant adverse effects on caribou.
The company plans to reduce disturbances to the animals, including building the road with smaller slopes so the animals can cross easily.

The road, running straight through traditional hunting areas, would give more access points for hunting. But the company says the road would close during times of mass migration, and hunting would be controlled by the Kitikmeot Inuit Association.

“It really is a vast, wide-open area with lots of room for caribou,” says Bell. “Our largest shareholder is the Inuit people of the region, so we have a mandate in making sure this project facilitates future investments.”
In an October 2024 submission to the Nunavut Impact Review Board, the Inuit association said it supports the project but also raised concerns of significant effects to caribou and other wildlife.
The association recently said it’s aware of ongoing discussions and that people can have their voices heard through the review board’s assessment process.
If the Grays Bay project goes ahead, Dumond says she’s not confident the caribou can be properly managed.
She has been eating what locals call country foods since she was little. She sees the caribou numbers in decline, even without the Grays Bay project.
During a hunting trip this past summer, she says her family harvested only one caribou.
“It’s what our people have lived on for thousands of years.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "It's what our people have lived on for thousands of years."

stories.title: Crtc says Bell, Telus, Rogers violated ban on junk fees
stories.summary: The Crtc issued a ruling Friday saying that carriers violated its prohibition on charging a fee for providing and setting up cellphones when signing up for a service plan.
stories.author: Sammy Hudes
stories.content:
Canada’s telecommunications regulator has determined the Big Three providers violated its rules banning so-called junk fees and is ordering the companies to remove those charges by Dec. 27.

The Crtc issued a ruling Friday saying that carriers violated its prohibition on charging a fee for providing and setting up cellphones when signing up for a service plan.

If the companies don’t comply by the new deadline, they could face monetary penalties of up to $10 million while relevant managers could be penalized up to $25,000.

The Crtc launched a review in June, requiring Bell Canada, Telus Corp. and Rogers Communications Inc. to demonstrate certain fees did not contravene its policy.

Bell introduced a $40 device handling fee in May, which applies when customers purchase a device along with their wireless service plan. Then came Telus’ $15 fee for customers switching to a new SIM card, with an additional $10 shipping charge applicable in some cases.

The commission also accused Rogers of charging customers a new $40 device setup fee, a $25 shipping charge and an unspecified SIM card fee. However, Rogers said the shipping and SIM fees were not new, and that the latter is only charged when a customer replaces a lost or damaged SIM, rather than at activation.

The new regulations came into effect June 12, prohibiting activation, modification and cancellation fees to make it easier for customers to switch internet and cellphone plans without having to worry about unexpected costs.

At the time, the Crtc warned each of the companies over their recently introduced fees, saying the charges did not appear to qualify for an exemption to the new policy meant for optional services or equipment customers choose to purchase.

The Crtc said Friday that Bell’s device-handling fee and Telus’ practice of charging a SIM and e-SIM provisioning fee violated its ban.

It also said Rogers was in violation for its practice of charging a setup fee to all customers who purchase a device in store at the same time as activating a new wireless service plan, regardless of whether they request or receive additional services.

However, the commission determined some of the fees in question did comply with the rules. Those include Rogers’ fees “for truly optional services that its customers explicitly choose to purchase,” Rogers’ hardware shipping fee, as well as the SIM replacement fees being charged by Rogers and Telus that are unrelated to activation or modification of wireless plans.

The Crtc encouraged Rogers to consider whether a hardware shipping fee “is truly optional for customers for whom in-store pickup is not a viable option,” such as those with accessibility needs or people living in rural or remote areas.

Sheehan Carter, the Crtc’s acting vice-president of consumer, analytics and strategy, said monetary penalties are on the table if the companies don’t comply with the ruling within 30 days.

“The commission will be watching very closely to make sure they do so, and if they don’t, we’ll be ready to start enforcement action immediately, which could very well include an administrative monetary penalty,” he said.

“Part of our purpose in issuing this decision today … is to give a bit more guidance, a bit more information about how we’re applying the test that we set out in June this year, with the expectation that companies, now that they better understand how the test is applied, will not be charging these types of fees in the future.”

In a statement, Telus said it is reviewing the Crtc decision and considering its next steps.

“Every SIM card and e-SIM comes with real costs associated with providing it to customers, and we believe those costs should be reflected in the price of the product, rather than requiring carriers to provide it free of charge,” said Telus spokesperson Martin Nguyen.

Rogers is also looking into the Crtc’s ruling, said spokesperson Zac Carreiro.

“These charges help recover real costs and we’re pleased the Crtc’s decision on the shipping charge and SIM replacement fee clearly reflect this,” he said in an email.

“We disagree with the commission’s position on the device setup charge, which recovers costs associated with helping customers set-up their device as the Crtc noted, and we’re considering next steps.”

Last month, Rogers chief financial officer Glenn Brandt said the company is taking a hit from the fee ban.

Brandt told analysts during the company’s third-quarter earnings call Rogers is now trying to find new ways to recover some of those costs.

Asked if the Crtc’s decision could prompt telecoms to download more costs onto consumers, Carter said the regulator wants to ensure “consumers are not paying fees that they shouldn’t be paying.”

“In this case, there are certain fees that Rogers is charging that we have deemed are prohibited and others that are not, so it would be a mixed bag for Rogers and we’ll have to see how they react from there.”

Meanwhile, the Crtc issued a separate ruling Friday determining that Bell violated consumer protection measures by locking cellphones for up to 60 days following their purchase.

Bell had argued that practice was necessary to address an increase in crime and fraud. The company noted that devices were automatically unlocked at no charge after 60 days and could be unlocked sooner upon request for free.

But the commission decided the practice went against regulations contained in the Wireless Code and thus violated the Telecommunications Act. The regulations set out that all cellphones provided to customers must be unlocked, meaning they can be used on the networks of any cellphone service provider.

“We simply didn’t receive any evidence that was convincing to the commission that this particular initiative would be the secret remedy, the secret sauce to deal with their fraud issues,” said Carter.

The Crtc said it is of the preliminary view that a $10 million administrative penalty May be appropriate.

Those interested in weighing in on the potential penalty can submit comments by Jan. 15, while Bell has until Jan. 22 to file a response.

Bell spokesperson Ellen Murphy said the company is reviewing both rulings.

“With employee and customer safety at risk, Bell believed we had a responsibility to act against device-related crime and informed the Crtc of our plans before the practice was instituted,” she said in a statement.

“Bell’s safety practice was highly effective at protecting employees and customers from armed robbery, theft and fraud by targeting the underlying economic incentives that drive device-related crime.”

Sheehan Carter, the Crtc’s acting vice-president of consumer, analytics and strategy, said monetary penalties are on the table if the companies don’t comply with the ruling within 30 days.

“The commission will be watching very closely to make sure they do so, and if they don’t, we’ll be ready to start enforcement action immediately, which could very well include an administrative monetary penalty,” he said.

“Part of our purpose in issuing this decision today … is to give a bit more guidance, a bit more information about how we’re applying the test that we set out in June this year, with the expectation that companies, now that they better understand how the test is applied, will not be charging these types of fees in the future.”
In a statement, Telus said it is reviewing the Crtc decision and considering its next steps.

“Every SIM card and e-SIM comes with real costs associated with providing it to customers, and we believe those costs should be reflected in the price of the product, rather than requiring carriers to provide it free of charge,” said Telus spokesperson Martin Nguyen.
Rogers is also looking into the Crtc’s ruling, said spokesperson Zac Carreiro.
“These charges help recover real costs and we’re pleased the Crtc’s decision on the shipping charge and SIM replacement fee clearly reflect this,” he said in an email.

“We disagree with the commission’s position on the device setup charge, which recovers costs associated with helping customers set-up their device as the Crtc noted, and we’re considering next steps.”
Last month, Rogers chief financial officer Glenn Brandt said the company is taking a hit from the fee ban.
Brandt told analysts during the company’s third-quarter earnings call Rogers is now trying to find new ways to recover some of those costs.
Asked if the Crtc’s decision could prompt telecoms to download more costs onto consumers, Carter said the regulator wants to ensure “consumers are not paying fees that they shouldn’t be paying.”

“In this case, there are certain fees that Rogers is charging that we have deemed are prohibited and others that are not, so it would be a mixed bag for Rogers and we’ll have to see how they react from there.”
Meanwhile, the Crtc issued a separate ruling Friday determining that Bell violated consumer protection measures by locking cellphones for up to 60 days following their purchase.

Bell had argued that practice was necessary to address an increase in crime and fraud. The company noted that devices were automatically unlocked at no charge after 60 days and could be unlocked sooner upon request for free.

But the commission decided the practice went against regulations contained in the Wireless Code and thus violated the Telecommunications Act. The regulations set out that all cellphones provided to customers must be unlocked, meaning they can be used on the networks of any cellphone service provider.

“We simply didn’t receive any evidence that was convincing to the commission that this particular initiative would be the secret remedy, the secret sauce to deal with their fraud issues,” said Carter.

Those interested in weighing in on the potential penalty can submit comments by Jan. 15, while Bell has until Jan. 22 to file a response.

“Bell’s safety practice was highly effective at protecting employees and customers from armed robbery, theft and fraud by targeting the underlying economic incentives that drive device-related crime.”

stories.title: Newfoundland's Wakeham only Atlantic premier to react to Supreme Court ruling
stories.summary: Fredericton - Only one of Canada’s Atlantic premiers has reacted to a landmark Supreme Court of Canada ruling about Charter rights.
stories.author: Eli Ridder The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The country’s top court largely upheld Quebec’s Bill 21 banning public servants in positions of authority from wearing religious symbols while on the job.

The historic decision provides more clarity on how provincial governments can use a section of the Constitution that allows legislatures to override Charter rights.

Article continues below

Inside interior designer Nora Voon’s art-filled home

The justices agreed that governments can use the so-called notwithstanding clause of the Constitution pre-emptively as Quebec did for the bill introducing the ban.

Newfoundland and Labrador Premier Tony Wakeham says his province has never used the notwithstanding clause but recognizes the significance of the ruling.

A spokesperson for New Brunswick Premier Susan Holt said she would not comment on the ruling, and representatives for the premiers of Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island did not respond to requests.

Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon hailed the ruling as a “good day for secularism in Quebec” but said legislators will need to read the fine print of the ruling to understand its implications.

Meanwhile, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said the Supreme Court decision confirms the notwithstanding clause is a legitimate and essential part of the Constitution.

Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew in a social media post welcomed the part of the ruling that confirmed courts can still declare when Charter rights are violated by laws like Bill 21.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 27, 2026.

— With files from Erika Morris in Montreal

stories.title: Supreme Court upholds Quebec’s Bill 21 in landmark ruling on Charter of Rights
stories.summary: The fractured top court splits on several big legal questions
stories.author: David Ebner
stories.content:
A fractured Supreme Court of Canada on Friday upheld Quebec’s Bill 21 in a landmark judgment on the province’s secularism law and the limits of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

The top court affirmed the constitutional bargain in the early 1980s that led to the Charter of Rights. At the same time, the court broke new legal ground by allowing judges to rule on alleged Charter rights violations even if governments shield laws with the notwithstanding clause.

The clause is the powerful tool that allows politicians to override many of the rights promised to Canadians in the Charter. It was central to a Liberal-Conservative-NDP political deal in 1981 that solved the debate over how to include the Charter in the Constitution.

Friday’s ruling – delivered in Ottawa from seven Supreme Court judges who divided into multiple camps on different issues – is a victory for the Government of Quebec, in its steadfast defence of secularism in the province.

It is also a win for conservative-led provinces such as Ontario and Alberta that opposed new restrictions on the notwithstanding clause that the federal Liberal government had proposed.

But some challengers who wanted to see Bill 21 struck down celebrated a win on judicial declarations. This new shift means that Canadians can now go to court to have a judge declare that a law shielded by the notwithstanding clause violates the Charter. Such a declaration would be symbolic but politically potent.

The Supreme Court didn’t issue its own declaration on Bill 21, but three judges in dissent concluded that it violates the Charter’s freedom of religion and equality rights.

Friday marks the end of a seven-year legal odyssey but likely also a new beginning for a renewed political debate over the Charter. The Bill 21 case started in 2019 when Quebec passed its secularism law and used the notwithstanding clause. Bill 21 bans many public sector workers in Quebec from wearing religious symbols on the job.

Six of seven Supreme Court judges ruled Quebec had validly used the clause.

“Bill 21 is rooted in Quebec’s legitimate and historical commitment to ensuring the [secularism] of the state in a free and democratic society,” wrote Chief Justice Richard Wagner in the main decision.

The judges ruled 4-3 in favour of allowing judicial declarations, led by Justice Nicholas Kasirer, but by a vote of 4-3 decided against issuing their own, led by Chief Justice Wagner. Both judges are Montrealers with long and deep roots in Quebec.

Opening the door to judicial declarations is a big win, said Frédéric Bérard, counsel for one of the six appellants, the Fédération autonome de l’enseignement, a group of Quebec teachers’ unions.

“We had an 800-kilometre hike to make in bare feet. It’s a good day for democracy,” Mr. Bérard said. “It’s a very strong message about fundamental rights from the Supreme Court. You can’t violate fundamental rights without having to defend your bill in front of the courts.”

Amrit Kaur, a Sikh who wears a turban, graduated in 2019 with an education degree on the day Bill 21 became law. Her teaching career in Quebec ended before it began. She was among the appellants challenging Bill 21 and on Friday she felt the Supreme Court was clear that the law violates rights: “It’s not up for debate any more.”

She also said the fight against Bill 21 shifts back into the political arena from the courts. “The fight for human rights,” Mrs. Kaur said, “continues.”

Others who wanted Bill 21 struck down expressed deep disappointment, starting with the National Council of Canadian Muslims and the Canadian Civil Liberties Association. Both challenged Bill 21 in court the day after it became law in 2019.

Stephen Brown, CEO of the Muslim council, said the Supreme Court’s decision is an “unrestricted licence for every government in the country to pass legislation taking away fundamental freedoms and the legal rights of every community.”

Political reaction poured in on Friday from across Canada.

Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon said the ruling upholding Bill 21 is a “victory for Quebec secularism.”

But he added that judicial declarations would weaken the power of the notwithstanding clause – and therefore weaken Quebec’s autonomy. The separatist-conservative premier called this a setback that, in his view, helps make the case for Quebec independence.

In Manitoba, NDP Premier Wab Kinew saluted the court’s endorsement of judicial declarations, something that Manitoba, the federal government and numerous other groups supported at the Supreme Court during the hearing in March.

He called Quebec’s Bill 21 “legislative racism” and urged Canadians upset with the law being upheld to bring their “outrage” to the superior trial court level of Canada’s justice system to battle governments that use the notwithstanding clause.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, in a social media post, said the Supreme Court confirmed “the notwithstanding clause is a legitimate and essential part of our Constitution,” calling it “a win for provincial rights.”

The federal government had asked the Supreme Court to impose new restrictions on the notwithstanding clause and lost that argument.

Prime Minister Mark Carney, at a news conference in Yellowknife, said his job is to defend “the full application of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms” but said it was too early to consider questions such as amendments to the Constitution.

In the 4-3/4-3 Supreme Court split on declarations – in favour of them but against issuing their own – Chief Justice Wagner for the majority that stood against issuing a declaration said doing so would tread into hypothetical territory and “would substantially diminish the effect” of the notwithstanding clause. He also opposed declarations in general because they are precluded by the notwithstanding clause.

Justices Andromache Karakatsanis and Michelle O’Bonsawin, who supported declarations and made their own, wrote: “This court should not be silent when asked by claimants to acknowledge that [Bill 21] infringes their rights and freedoms. Democratic accountability in Quebec will benefit from informed public discourse.”

The Supreme Court in recent years has been known for split decisions and elongated judgments. This was exemplified on Friday. The seven judges produced four sets of legal reasons. The package ran almost 140,000 words, more than 500 pages.

And while the court upheld Bill 21, it came very close to striking it down on the question of gender equality rights in Section 28 of the Charter (which is separate from Section 15’s equality rights).

The notwithstanding clause does not apply to Section 28/gender equality but the Supreme Court in the end ruled 4-3 that gender equality could not be used to strike down Bill 21. Chief Justice Wagner called Section 28 an interpretive provision that does not create a distinct legal right.

But Justices Sheilah Martin, Karakatsanis and O’Bonsawin concluded that Section 28 was more than interpretative and should serve as the basis for striking down the heart of Bill 21.

Justice Martin declared the law unequally restricts “a woman’s right to respect her faith, freely express herself and to be free from discrimination based on religion and sex.”

stories.title: Judge deciding whether trial of Galloway lawsuit will conclude, or continue in 2027
stories.summary: Vancouver - The judge presiding over the trial of Steven Galloway's defamation lawsuit is set to decide whether it will wrap up on schedule or be put over to next year to deal with a contempt application involving the woman who accused the author of rape.
stories.author: Brenna Owen The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Vancouver - The B.C. Supreme Court trial concluded Friday in author and former professor Steven Galloway’s defamation lawsuit against the woman who accused him of rape, and other defendants, with the judge reserving her decision.

It closes the latest chapter in a more than 10-year odyssey for Galloway and his accuser, a former student with whom the trial heard he had an extramarital affair.

Justice Neena Sharma said as the trial wrapped up that judgments take time, especially when she is hearing other matters, and while she aims to release her written decision within six months, she couldn’t promise she will meet that timeline.

Galloway denies his accuser’s allegations of rape and sexual assault, which rippled through the Canadian literary scene and the University of British Columbia, where he was chair of the creative writing program, after they surfaced in November 2015.

He is suing the woman, known only as A.B., who cannot be named under a publication ban, and three other defendants, over alleged defamatory statements published on social media and elsewhere between 2015 and 2018.

Galloway was never charged, and a retired judge hired by the university found the rape and assault claims against him unsubstantiated.

But Galloway, author of the bestselling novel “The Cellist of Sarajevo,” was fired from his post at the university and he has testified that his career was destroyed.

He told the trial that he could no longer write and now sells boats for a living.

Galloway’s accuser, A.B., did not testify or attend the trial in Vancouver. Her lawyer, Sydney Gomez, said this week her absence was for health reasons.

The court heard midway through the trial that her defence no longer contended her rape and sexual assault claims against Galloway were true, rather that she reported them to the university.

The trial heard Galloway is seeking millions of dollars in damages from A.B. and the other defendants, along with an “explicit” finding by the court that the rape and assault allegations are false, should he win his lawsuit.

The defendants fought the lawsuit all the way to the Supreme Court of Canada, arguing their statements were protected speech.

But in 2024, the high court dismissed their bid to appeal a ruling that allowed it to proceed in a test of laws in B.C., Ontario and Quebec that aim to protect people from so-called Slapp suits, or strategic lawsuits against public participation.

Several people originally named as defendants in the defamation lawsuit settled with Galloway and issued public apologies before the trial began.

Galloway’s lawyer, Daniel Burnett, told the trial his client was once a “star” in the literary world with a bright future that was cut short when the allegations emerged.

Arden Beddoes, a lawyer for A.B., told the trial it was actions by the university, not his client, that led to the destruction of the Galloway’s career.

Beddoes said in his final submissions this week that A.B. could not have foreseen the university’s “unprecedented” move to announce Galloway’s suspension after she shared her allegations with a “relatively small group” of people in late 2015.

Sharma had asked Beddoes about the university’s probe and whether “it had a life of its own” even if she were to find it was “triggered” by A.B.‘s claims.

“Correct,” Beddoes replied.

He said in final submissions that A.B. didn’t seek national attention or publicity for her allegations.

Burnett said Friday the trial heard arguments that the university’s actions, including the public announcement about Galloway’s suspension pending an investigation into “serious allegations,” were the “bigger cause” of the loss of his career.

But Burnett said the school’s actions stemmed from A.B. “initially setting the fire.”

He said A.B.‘s “modus operandi” was to keep her own hands “somewhat clean,” and she was “remarkably good at getting other people to spread her lies.”

Galloway was awarded $167,000 in 2018 by an arbitrator who found the university — which was not a party in the lawsuit — violated his privacy rights and harmed his reputation.

A group of authors, including Margaret Atwood, signed an open letter in November 2016 calling for an investigation into how the university handled Galloway’s case.

A.B.’s former husband testified at the trial, called as a witness by Galloway’s lawyers.

Atwood has recently penned opinion articles supporting Galloway, writing in the Globe and Mail that testimony from A.B.’s ex-husband, saying he was exchanging text messages with A.B. about a hockey game at the time of her alleged 2011 rape in Galloway’s office, was like the “Aha!” moment in a Sherlock Holmes novel.

The conclusion of the trial came moments after Sharma dismissed a last-minute bid by Beddoes to put it over to next year in order to deal with a contempt application involving his client, who the court heard violated a court order compelling her to sit for a discovery examination.

Beddoes said he understood the application was to be dealt with during the trial and he intended to bring evidence related to her risk of suicide in response to it.

The request to extend the trial until an expert report by a psychiatrist was finished drew a sharp response from Sharma, who questioned Beddoes about why he hadn’t raised the issue before or during closing arguments.

“That would have been the point to say, ‘I’m not closing my case, I still have evidence that you need,’” the judge said.

Sharma said there was “a way to look at this as the defence changing its position on a fundamental issue at the close of submissions.”

Beddoes said he didn’t agree that it was a fair characterization.

He said it was his client, not Galloway, who would suffer prejudice if she could not bring evidence about her “suicidality” during the trial.

Sharma said A.B.‘s non-attendance at trial had always been a “huge issue” in the years-long proceedings after Galloway first filed his lawsuit in 2018.

The judge said she hadn’t received first-hand evidence of any kind from A.B. since an affidavit filed in 2021, though her suicide risk was “not a new issue” in the case.

Sharma denied the defence bid to put the case over, saying she would provide her reasons at a hearing on Monday.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 27, 2026.

stories.title: Quebec Court of Appeal to rule Monday about oath to the King by legislators
stories.summary: Montreal - A Quebec Court of Appeal judge says she will rule Monday on whether members of the provincial legislature can resume parliamentary work without swearing allegiance to the King.
stories.author: Charlotte Glorieux The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - Quebec’s Court of Appeal will rule Monday on the provincial government’s bid to allow elected officials to sit in the legislature without swearing allegiance to the King.

The decision will come a day before the legislature is scheduled to resume parliamentary work.

Justice Lori Renée Weitzman heard arguments Friday as the Parti Québécois government seeks to appeal a lower court ruling that suspended a 2022 Quebec law making the oath optional.

Superior Court Justice Ian Demers suspended the law on Monday and ordered his ruling to take immediate effect, even in the event of an appeal.

Demers’ ruling stayed the law pending a decision on its constitutionality.

In his decision, Demers said elected officials would have to swear allegiance to the King before taking office and warned that legislation adopted by members who had not taken the oath would be unconstitutional.

Weitzman will decide whether to allow the government to appeal Demers’ decision and whether to put the lower court ruling on hold pending the appeal. If the court grants permission to appeal, the appeal would be heard Jan. 11.

Michel Déom, a lawyer representing Quebec’s attorney general, argued Friday that Demers made several errors of law, including failing to adequately consider the consequences of disrupting parliamentary work.

University of Ottawa law professor Lawrence David, one of three applicants challenging the constitutionality of the Quebec law, urged the court to reject the government’s requests.

David argued that the constitutional requirement to swear allegiance to the King is unequivocal and warned that laws adopted by elected officials who have not taken the oath would be unconstitutional.

David also expressed concern about political pressure surrounding the case, referring to a letter the premier invited opposition parties to sign reaffirming their opposition to the mandatory oath. He said political manoeuvres should not influence the court’s decision.

Section 128 of the Constitution Act, 1867, requires members of provincial legislatures to swear allegiance to the monarch before taking their seats. But in 2022, Quebec’s legislature unanimously passed a law exempting its members from that requirement.

None of the 127 members of Quebec’s legislature elected in October have sworn allegiance to the King, opting instead to swear allegiance to the people of Quebec.

Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon said Friday the dispute illustrates what he considers to be the shortcomings of the Canadian Constitution. “The Constitution is set in concrete. That’s a problem,” he told reporters in a news conference in Quebec City.

He said the Constitution is dysfunctional in some respects, to the point where a dispute over an oath that was the subject of a unanimously adopted law could paralyze the legislature.

On Wednesday, St-Pierre Plamondon invited opposition parties to sign a joint declaration reaffirming their desire to resume parliamentary work without swearing allegiance to the King.

Ruba Ghazal, Québec solidaire’s parliamentary leader, committed to signing the declaration, but the Quebec Liberals and Conservatives have refused to do so.

Both parties have said they would not defy court orders to sit illegally.

St-Pierre Plamondon said Friday he was “incredibly disappointed and even stunned” by the positions taken by Liberal Leader Charles Milliard and Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime, accusing them of lacking principles and consistency.

The premier said he hoped political pressure would persuade the opposition leaders not to swear allegiance to the King.

St-Pierre Plamondon said Thursday the parliamentary session would begin Dec. 1 as planned, without members taking the oath.

On Friday, he said that “a lot of things could happen on Tuesday.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 27, 2026.

stories.title: Release of Alto’s revised high-speed rail corridor delayed until January
stories.summary: Alto project proposes building around 1,000 kilometres of electrified high-speed rail on new dedicated passenger rail tracks between Quebec City and Toronto
stories.author: Bill Curry
stories.content:
A narrower proposed corridor for a high-speed rail link between Ottawa and Montreal won’t be released until January, according to Alto, the Crown corporation responsible for the project.

In a statement to The Globe and Mail, Alto spokesperson Philippe Archambault said the release of the proposed corridor will be followed by consultations with communities along the route.

Alto had previously said the revised corridor would be released in the fall of 2026.

“Various decisions still need to be made to further refine the corridor, provide residents with as much certainty as possible, and minimize the project’s impacts,” Mr. Archambault said. “We want to ensure that this next phase of consultations takes place under the best possible conditions, rather than within a tight timeline leading up to the holiday season.”

Alto says the consultations will focus on a corridor approximately 500 metres wide on average. Once finalized, the right-of-way required to build the project will be approximately 60 metres wide on average.

Earlier this year, Alto held consultations on a much wider corridor that was about 10 kilometres across.

The Alto project proposes to build about 1,000 kilometres of electrified high-speed rail on new dedicated passenger rail tracks between Quebec City and Toronto. The plan is for construction to start with the link between Ottawa and Montreal.

The current preparation work will lead up to a planned 2029 date when cabinet will make a final decision on whether to go ahead with the project.

The federal government approved new expropriation powers related to the project in a budget bill last year that enacted a new High-Speed Rail Network Act.

On Thursday, Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne released a new budget bill tied to his 2026 budget that includes a further expansion of those powers related to the project.

Some residents along the proposed route between Ottawa and Montreal, particularly farmers, have expressed strong concerns about the consultation process and the potential for expropriations and have called for more transparency related to the project.

Alto has said the project could cost between $60-billion and $90-billion to build.

Parliamentary Budget Officer Annette Ryan released a report in October that said the construction cost could be between $75-billion and $113-billion.

stories.title: QuickQuotes: Politicians and civil society react to court ruling on Quebec's Bill 21
stories.summary: Montreal - The Supreme Court of Canada largely upheld Quebec's secularism law Friday in a landmark decision that clarifies how governments can use a section of the Constitution to override certain rights.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
MONTREAL - The Supreme Court of Canada largely upheld Quebec’s secularism law Friday in a landmark decision that clarifies how governments can use a section of the Constitution to override certain rights.

The country’s highest court confirmed that governments can invoke the so-called notwithstanding clause pre-emptively, before a court has determined whether a law violates the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. The top court also said legislatures can use the notwithstanding clause to override multiple rights at once.

However, the court was divided over whether to declare that Quebec’s secularism law, which bans certain public sector workers from wearing religious symbols on the job, violated Charter rights without striking it down.

Three of the seven justices concluded that the law was incompatible with freedom of religion, freedom of expression and the right to equality.

Here are some quotes from the ruling and reaction from politicians and other stakeholders.

”... A legislative body is not required to show a link or relationship between the law in question and the rights or freedoms it intends to override. More fundamentally, it is not for the courts to substantively review the legitimacy of the legislative policy pursued by the legislative body or the appropriateness of invoking the notwithstanding clause.”

— Supreme Court of Canada Chief Justice Richard Wagner, Justice Malcolm Rowe and Justice Suzanne Côté.

“Notwithstanding anything in this Charter, the rights and freedoms referred to in it are guaranteed equally to male and female persons.”

— Section 28 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms

“Parliament or the legislature of a province may expressly declare in an Act of Parliament or of the legislature, as the case may be, that the Act or a provision thereof shall operate notwithstanding a provision included in section 2 or sections 7 to 15 of this Charter.”

— Section 33 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

“Bill 21 unjustifiably infringes s. 28 of the Charter, which falls outside the scope of the notwithstanding clause in s. 33 of the Charter. Consequently, ss. 6 and 8 of Bill 21 are declared to be of no force or effect pursuant to s. 52(1) of the Constitution Act, 1982. Section 28 is the Charter’s other notwithstanding clause and has both interpretive effects and substantively guarantees sex equality. It affects the interpretation of other rights and freedoms referred to in the Charter and the application of the justification analysis under s. 1. It also guarantees substantive sex equality: legislation cannot have unequal adverse impacts on Charter rights between men and women.”

Supreme Court Justice Andromache Karatkatsanis and Justice Michelle O’Bonsawin in a dissenting opinion.

“We respect the independence of the judiciary, we respect the Constitution. Under the Constitution, there is a notwithstanding clause. The core of the judgment — a judgment I would say my colleagues in justice and elsewhere are studying closely, it’s a 500 page-plus judgment, so making sure they understand all the elements of it. But the core of the judgment is that the use of the notwithstanding clause, for virtually all of the applications of what is called Bill 21, was appropriate.”

“Now what I think is important is that all legislatures, very much including obviously Parliament, do their utmost to respect the rights and liberties of all Canadians, including those in the minority.”

— Prime Minister Mark Carney

“Of course, we were concerned about social peace if such a fundamental decision were overturned by the Supreme Court. So, this is good news and we should celebrate it.”

“It’s a good day for secularism in Quebec, but rules have changed. The rules of the game have just changed without any political discussion with provinces. From now on, the fact of invoking Article 33 doesn’t prevent courts to say what they think about it and they will do so without the participation of provinces.”

— Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon

“It wasn’t the result we were looking for but we do take solace in a lot of the declarations that were made by the court.”

— Joe Ortona, chair of the English Montreal School Board — lead plaintiff in the case.

“Even the Supreme Court of Canada recognizes the relevance and the legitimacy of the Quebec national assembly to invoke the notwithstanding clause.”

— Bloc Québécois Leader Yves-François Blanchet

“Today’s Supreme Court of Canada decision confirms what Alberta has long maintained: the notwithstanding clause is a legitimate and essential part of our Constitution. Alberta was proud to intervene in this case to defend that principle. The notwithstanding clause was included in the Charter so that elected legislatures, accountable to the people they serve, can have the final say on important questions. That’s true for Quebec and it’s true for every province, including Alberta. This ruling is a win for provincial rights and for the democratic balance that holds our federation together. Alberta will continue to defend our constitutional powers and stand up for the right of Albertans to make decisions that reflect their values.”

— Alberta Premier Danielle Smith

“At least now after this decision today, and because of our intervention at the Supreme Court, Canadians who are being discriminated against have a tool. You have a tool that you can use to go to a court and get a ruling, non-binding as it may be, and then you can go out in the next election and say, you know what, this provincial government violated the Constitution, violated our Charter rights otherwise, if it wasn’t for Section 33.”

— Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew

“This fight is not over. Whether it takes a year or a generation, we will put these discriminatory laws on the trash heap of history.”

— Stephen Brown, CEO of the National Council of Canadian Muslims.

paragraphs: MONTREAL - The Supreme Court of Canada largely upheld Quebec’s secularism law Friday in a landmark decision that clarifies how governments can use a section of the Constitution to override certain rights.

The country’s highest court confirmed that governments can invoke the so-called notwithstanding clause pre-emptively, before a court has determined whether a law violates the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. The top court also said legislatures can use the notwithstanding clause to override multiple rights at once.

However, the court was divided over whether to declare that Quebec’s secularism law, which bans certain public sector workers from wearing religious symbols on the job, violated Charter rights without striking it down.
Three of the seven justices concluded that the law was incompatible with freedom of religion, freedom of expression and the right to equality.
Here are some quotes from the ruling and reaction from politicians and other stakeholders.

”... A legislative body is not required to show a link or relationship between the law in question and the rights or freedoms it intends to override. More fundamentally, it is not for the courts to substantively review the legitimacy of the legislative policy pursued by the legislative body or the appropriateness of invoking the notwithstanding clause.”
— Supreme Court of Canada Chief Justice Richard Wagner, Justice Malcolm Rowe and Justice Suzanne Côté.
“Notwithstanding anything in this Charter, the rights and freedoms referred to in it are guaranteed equally to male and female persons.”
— Section 28 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms

“Parliament or the legislature of a province may expressly declare in an Act of Parliament or of the legislature, as the case may be, that the Act or a provision thereof shall operate notwithstanding a provision included in section 2 or sections 7 to 15 of this Charter.”
— Section 33 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

“Bill 21 unjustifiably infringes s. 28 of the Charter, which falls outside the scope of the notwithstanding clause in s. 33 of the Charter. Consequently, ss. 6 and 8 of Bill 21 are declared to be of no force or effect pursuant to s. 52(1) of the Constitution Act, 1982. Section 28 is the Charter’s other notwithstanding clause and has both interpretive effects and substantively guarantees sex equality. It affects the interpretation of other rights and freedoms referred to in the Charter and the application of the justification analysis under s. 1. It also guarantees substantive sex equality: legislation cannot have unequal adverse impacts on Charter rights between men and women.”
Supreme Court Justice Andromache Karatkatsanis and Justice Michelle O’Bonsawin in a dissenting opinion.

“We respect the independence of the judiciary, we respect the Constitution. Under the Constitution, there is a notwithstanding clause. The core of the judgment — a judgment I would say my colleagues in justice and elsewhere are studying closely, it’s a 500 page-plus judgment, so making sure they understand all the elements of it. But the core of the judgment is that the use of the notwithstanding clause, for virtually all of the applications of what is called Bill 21, was appropriate.”

“Now what I think is important is that all legislatures, very much including obviously Parliament, do their utmost to respect the rights and liberties of all Canadians, including those in the minority.”
— Prime Minister Mark Carney
“Of course, we were concerned about social peace if such a fundamental decision were overturned by the Supreme Court. So, this is good news and we should celebrate it.”

“It’s a good day for secularism in Quebec, but rules have changed. The rules of the game have just changed without any political discussion with provinces. From now on, the fact of invoking Article 33 doesn’t prevent courts to say what they think about it and they will do so without the participation of provinces.”
— Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon
“It wasn’t the result we were looking for but we do take solace in a lot of the declarations that were made by the court.”
— Joe Ortona, chair of the English Montreal School Board — lead plaintiff in the case.
“Even the Supreme Court of Canada recognizes the relevance and the legitimacy of the Quebec national assembly to invoke the notwithstanding clause.”
— Bloc Québécois Leader Yves-François Blanchet

“Today’s Supreme Court of Canada decision confirms what Alberta has long maintained: the notwithstanding clause is a legitimate and essential part of our Constitution. Alberta was proud to intervene in this case to defend that principle. The notwithstanding clause was included in the Charter so that elected legislatures, accountable to the people they serve, can have the final say on important questions. That’s true for Quebec and it’s true for every province, including Alberta. This ruling is a win for provincial rights and for the democratic balance that holds our federation together. Alberta will continue to defend our constitutional powers and stand up for the right of Albertans to make decisions that reflect their values.”
— Alberta Premier Danielle Smith

“At least now after this decision today, and because of our intervention at the Supreme Court, Canadians who are being discriminated against have a tool. You have a tool that you can use to go to a court and get a ruling, non-binding as it may be, and then you can go out in the next election and say, you know what, this provincial government violated the Constitution, violated our Charter rights otherwise, if it wasn’t for Section 33.”
