stories.title: Storms slowly relent across U.S. as recovery from Thanksgiving deluge begins
stories.summary: Conditions began to clear up through much of the U.S. on Friday, but the system could take some time to weaken, the National Weather Service said on its website.
stories.author: Rachel Goodman
stories.content:
Heavy rains that flooded communities in the eastern U.S. began to ease on Friday, and crews gradually restored power to hundreds of thousands of customers after a wave of Thanksgiving storms swept across North America.

Severe weather disrupted travel, downed trees and power lines, damaged buildings, and prompted water rescues from New York to Virginia. In New York City, treacherous conditions forced the first postponement of the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day parade in its more than 100-year history.

In other parts of the country, wet snow fell as far south as the Tennessee Valley and freezing rain moved through northern New England. Cold rain fell over the Midwest, Ohio Valley, and Lower Great Lakes, including parts of southern Ontario, where Environment Canada issued freezing rain alerts and warned of wind gusts up to 80 kilometres per hour.

Another storm system in the Northwest brought rain along coastal Oregon on Friday, and more snow was forecast in the Cascade Range, which stretches from southern British Columbia through Washington and Oregon into Northern California. Snow was also forecast in the mountains in Montana and Wyoming.

Conditions began to clear up through much of the U.S. on Friday, but the system could take some time to weaken, the National Weather Service said on its website, which also warned of blustery winds across the east and issued coastal flood warnings through Friday from New Jersey to Virginia.

More than 480,000 homes and businesses lost power on Friday; at the outage’s peak, more than 900,000 were without electricity, the Associated Press reported. In Maryland, nearly 2 million people were told they could resume normal water use after being urged to conserve it during the storm.

More than 1,100 flights were delayed, and at least 116 were cancelled by Friday morning, according to flight tracking service FlightAware.

A fishing pier partially collapsed in Virginia Beach, Virginia, and Avalon, New Jersey residents scrambled to pump out surges of saltwater, bringing some of the most significant tides in the seaside community’s history.

Meanwhile, high tides drove waves that flooded the Pacific coast, disrupting bus and train service across California.

Record tides along the California coast prompted evacuations from Humboldt County in the far north to Ventura County near Los Angeles.

The severe weather came the same week U.S. President Donald Trump approved Florida’s request for a Major Disaster Declaration after historic flooding in October and November.

The $100 million fund will unlock “critical federal recovery resources for residents, businesses, and local governments devastated by the flooding,” according to Florida lawmakers.

“Hundreds of Florida families have lost their homes, cars, and personal belongings and are facing an especially difficult Thanksgiving. The President’s approval of this Major Disaster Declaration is welcome news and will help get our families and small businesses the resources they desperately need to recover and rebuild,” said Rep. Lois Frankel.

— with files from the Associated Press

stories.title: Nova Scotia Sport Hall of Fame reopens after six-year renovation project
stories.summary: The Nova Scotia Sport Hall of Fame has opened its doors to the public for the first time in six years after an extensive renovation project.
stories.author: Mitchell Bailey, Rebecca Lau
stories.content:
The Nova Scotia Sport Hall of Fame has opened its doors to the public for the first time in six years after an extensive renovation project and staff say they’re excited to showcase the province’s rich sporting history again.

“It’s a little surreal, to be honest with you,” said vice-president Shane Mailman, who has been with the hall of fame for three decades.

The rebuild project for the hall of fame, which is located inside Scotiabank Centre in downtown Halifax, came with a $6.5 million price tag.

The organization began renovations after the museum shut down during the pandemic . When rising costs forced delays, Mailman says his team stayed on task.

“For a small staff of four people, there were times where we probably thought we were in over our heads,” he said.

“But we stood, we stuck together the whole time and you know, six years later, we opened our doors again.”

The improvements include a larger exhibition space and an interactive inductee gallery where visitors can search for athletes by name, town, or sport.

“We have a lot more space to put things on display, to have a full-size theatre for presentations and events,” said Katie Tanner, communications manager for the Nova Scotia Sport Hall of Fame.

“And we actually have our artifact collection entirely on site for the first time. So all of our 8,000-plus artifacts are safely stored here.”

One of those artifacts is Sidney Crosby’s infamous dryer, which suffered a few dents from his time shooting a few pucks in the basement of his Cole Harbour home.

The museum also includes a “Where We All Can Play” section, which celebrates the province’s athletic diversity.

“We have our Women on Top of the World exhibit, African Nova Scotians of Excellence, (and) an exhibit honouring the North American Indigenous games being held here in 2023,” said Tanner.

Inductee Mark Smith, a softball legend, says he hopes the museum will inspire the next generation of athletes.

“I would like to think what it says to those young boys and girls is that I too can be recognized in this way if I work hard,” he said.

For first-time visitors like Killian Powers, there was a lot to take in.

“Canadian sport has been shaped by several Nova Scotians. It’s been very cool to learn about that,” said Powers.

The renovation project received funding from all levels of government.

Mailman says he hopes the project will highlight Nova Scotian achievements for years to come.

“Sport has an amazing power to motivate and inspire people, especially the youth of today,” he said.

paragraphs: The Nova Scotia Sport Hall of Fame has opened its doors to the public for the first time in six years after an extensive renovation project and staff say they’re excited to showcase the province’s rich sporting history again.
“It’s a little surreal, to be honest with you,” said vice-president Shane Mailman, who has been with the hall of fame for three decades.
The rebuild project for the hall of fame, which is located inside Scotiabank Centre in downtown Halifax, came with a $6.5 million price tag.
The organization began renovations after the museum shut down during the pandemic . When rising costs forced delays, Mailman says his team stayed on task.
“For a small staff of four people, there were times where we probably thought we were in over our heads,” he said.
“But we stood, we stuck together the whole time and you know, six years later, we opened our doors again.”
The improvements include a larger exhibition space and an interactive inductee gallery where visitors can search for athletes by name, town, or sport.
“We have a lot more space to put things on display, to have a full-size theatre for presentations and events,” said Katie Tanner, communications manager for the Nova Scotia Sport Hall of Fame.
“And we actually have our artifact collection entirely on site for the first time. So all of our 8,000-plus artifacts are safely stored here.”
One of those artifacts is Sidney Crosby’s infamous dryer, which suffered a few dents from his time shooting a few pucks in the basement of his Cole Harbour home.
The museum also includes a “Where We All Can Play” section, which celebrates the province’s athletic diversity.
“We have our Women on Top of the World exhibit, African Nova Scotians of Excellence, (and) an exhibit honouring the North American Indigenous games being held here in 2023,” said Tanner.
Inductee Mark Smith, a softball legend, says he hopes the museum will inspire the next generation of athletes.
“I would like to think what it says to those young boys and girls is that I too can be recognized in this way if I work hard,” he said.
For first-time visitors like Killian Powers, there was a lot to take in.
“Canadian sport has been shaped by several Nova Scotians. It’s been very cool to learn about that,” said Powers.
The renovation project received funding from all levels of government.

“Sport has an amazing power to motivate and inspire people, especially the youth of today,” he said.

“(We’re) very dedicated to young people and showing the sense of possibility — that even though we’re from this small province, that anything is possible because (these athletes have) done it, so the youth can do too.”

stories.title: Pitching in: Ontario couple gives $1-million to help build an animal shelter
stories.summary: Planned facility in Collingwood is expected to open next spring and will be able to house more than 5,000 animals annually
stories.author: Paul Waldie
stories.content:
The organizers: Monika Merz and Michael T. Miller

The gift: $1-million

The cause: A new shelter for the Georgian Triangle Humane Society

Monika Merz and her husband, Michael T. Miller, have been coming to the Collingwood area north of Toronto for years to ski and hike.

During one visit, Ms. Merz came across a pack of feral cats living under a dumpster. When she couldn’t find an animal shelter to take in the animals, she decided to try and help.

She bought a plastic tub, poured in some kibble and placed it under the dumpster. “I don’t know whether the raccoons got it, but at least I felt I was doing something instead of nothing,” she recalled from the couple’s home in Thornbury, Ont., ON Georgian Bay.

She loved animals and almost always had rescue cats at home, even when she lived in Japan working as chief executive of the Asian operations of Toys “R” Us.

The couple have been major donors to the Georgian Triangle Humane Society, and Ms. Merz chaired an annual walkathon, called Walk for Pets, which raised money for the society.

After stepping down from the walkathon – and helping raise $100,000 in total – Ms. Merz joined the society’s board of directors and is currently chair.

A few years ago, the society received a legacy gift and began planning a new 175-square-metre shelter in Collingwood. The charity has raised $14-million so far and needs another $4-million.

The new facility will be able to house more than 5,000 animals annually and perform 6,700 spay-and-neuter surgeries each year. There are also plans for a public vet clinic and programs for young people.

Ms. Merz and Mr. Miller have contributed $1-million to the project, which is expected to open next spring. “We had to do it,” Ms. Merz said of the new building. “We were coming apart at the seams in the current one, and still are.” She added the population of the area served by the society has soared in recent years.

“Our story and the services that we provide are really important to the community,” she said. The new shelter “is going to be a great place for the animals.”

stories.title: Founder wants Freedom Mobile back to build a standalone wireless carrier
stories.summary: Lacavera told Global News he plans to build a standalone wireless operator that is not also competing in the phone and or cable markets.
stories.author: Rachel Morgan, Jacqueline Hansen
stories.content:
Globalive CEO Anthony Lacavera said a Québecor-Telus merger would be a “disaster for Canada,” but it could let him buy back a company he lost more than 10 years ago.

Lacavera, who ran Freedom Mobile — then Wind Mobile — until 2015, told Global News he plans to build a standalone wireless operator that would not compete in the phone or cable markets. By acquiring Freedom, he would be doing just that.

“Canadians need to be able to cut the cord completely and just have a mobile connection for their cell phone, their mobile phone, but also a wireless connection to their home,” he said.

Lacavera said this is how Canada will remain competitive globally as SpaceX takes hold of a wireless-only market in the U.S.

“Whether it’s the Freedom Mobile assets, or the Telus mobility assets, if Bell ends up winning, or I can start again from scratch, I’m perfectly willing to start again from scratch,” he said. “In fact, I’m excited about doing it and offering a new independent choice for Canadians.”

Québecor sent Telus an unsolicited offer earlier this month, a deal worth approximately $31 billion and building off of a private offer made in June. The company said the merger would “serve the public interest.”

Bell Canada’s parent company has also shown interest in Telus.

Both the Competition Bureau and the Canadian Radio-Television and Telecommunications Commission (Crtc) are aware of Québecor’s offer.

It is the responsibility of the Competition Bureau to “review mergers to determine whether they harm competition,” a spokesperson told Global News. “When a Bureau merger investigation determines that a transaction is likely to harm competition, we take appropriate action.”

Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada would also likely review the deal. Industry Minister Mélanie Joly has said the government “will not predetermine the outcomes.”

Earlier this month, Prime Minister Mark Carney said more competition, lower prices and better service would be key to any decision.

Acquiring Telus would leave Canadians with three telecommunications options instead of four. As a result, Québecor could be forced to divest Freedom Mobile, as happened when Rogers and Shaw merged in 2023.

Globalive sold Wind Mobile to Shaw in 2015 for $1.6 billion after several recapitalization attempts. Shaw then renamed the carrier to Freedom Mobile.

“I learned my lesson. It’s very difficult to navigate, bringing a lot of foreign direct investment into Canada,” Lacavera said.

But when Rogers sought to acquire Shaw, Ottawa forced it to divest Freedom Mobile.

At that time, Lacavera made an offer to reacquire Freedom Mobile, but lost to Québecor.

He said he’s confident he can attract Canadian and U.S. capital to acquire Freedom Mobile this time.

Michael Osborne, chair of the Cozen O’Connor Canadian Competition law practice, said that if Globalive proves to be a viable buyer for Freedom Mobile, it could allow the Québecor-Telus merger to go ahead.

But given Globalive’s past forays with Wind Mobile and a previous attempt to buy Freedom, he has his doubts.

“We don’t really know whether or not the Globalive proposal is a sound one that would result in a viable fourth national wireless carrier in the event of a Québecor-Telus merger. But it is interesting, and it’s certainly one that the government’s going to have to look at seriously,” he told Global News.

Global News asked Québecor’s CEO Pierre Karl Péladeau if he would consider divesting Freedom.

“I guess it’s a little bit too early to answer this. We first need to make sure that this transaction will work. If it works, then we’ll be in front of the regulators and we’ll find out,” he said earlier this month.

But Osborne said he’s not fully convinced that Canada can support four national wireless carriers.

He said Freedom Mobile currently holds just under 12 per cent of the market share.

“They’re offering lower prices than the big three. So they’re helping to drive prices down, but that hasn’t resulted in massive increases in market share for them,” Osborne said.

“So the jury’s out.”

stories.title: Five takeaways from the Supreme Court's ruling on Quebec secularism law
stories.summary: Montreal - In a landmark 520-page decision, the Supreme Court upheld most of Quebec's secularism law known as Bill 21.
stories.author: Erika Morris The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - In a landmark 520-page decision, the Supreme Court upheld most of Quebec’s secularism law known as Bill 21.

The law prohibits public officials in positions of authority from wearing religious symbols. The law invokes a section of the Constitution that allows legislatures to override Charter rights and shield the legislation from legal challenges.

The Supreme Court’s historic decision provides more clarity on how governments can use the so-called notwithstanding clause of the Constitution.

Here are five things to know about the historic decision.

The notwithstanding clause of the Constitution allows legislators to override certain Charter rights for up to five years.

The country’s top court confirmed that governments can invoke the clause pre-emptively, before a court has determined whether a law violates the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. The top court also said legislatures can use the notwithstanding clause to override multiple rights at once.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith and Bloc Québécois leader Yves-François Blanchet have celebrated the Supreme Court’s decision.

The ruling May also set a precedent for a similar case out of Saskatchewan in which the province invoked the override clause in legislation restricting the rights of transgender people.

Quebec Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime has said that had the Supreme Court struck down Bill 21, it would have fuelled Quebec’s separatist movement.

Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon had denounced the federal government’s involvement in the legal proceedings as it acted as an intervener.

Following Friday’s ruling, St-Pierre Plamondon said it was a win for secularism in Quebec and for the autonomy of provinces. However, he took issue with a portion of the ruling allowing court justices to give their opinion on laws they can’t strike down due to the use of the override clause.

Bill 21 covers a range of public officials in positions of authority, including members of the province’s national assembly, prohibiting them from wearing religious symbols or face coverings. The seven Supreme Court justices overseeing the case unanimously declared the ban targeting elected officials was violating democratic rights. As a result, this section of the law is overturned.

While the seven Supreme Court justices agreed that Quebec was within its rights to invoke the override clause pre-emptively, they disagreed on aspects of Bill 21’s constitutionality.

Three justices — Michelle O’Bonsawin, Andromache Karakatsanis and Sheilah L. Martin — said the court had the power to strike down Bill 21, despite the use of the notwithstanding clause. They argued the law violates gender equality, which falls under a section of the Charter that governments are not allowed to override.

The three justices also wrote that the law disproportionately targeted Muslim women, keeping them out of the public workforce.

In addition, the seven justices also disagreed on whether to make a declaratory statement about whether Bill 21 violates Charter rights.

Groups representing Canadian Muslims, workers, English-speaking Quebecers, English language school boards, South Asian communities and anti-hate groups have all come out against the Supreme Court’s decision.

They say it is worrying that Canada’s top court upheld a law that discriminates against religious and racialized minorities.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 27, 2026.

Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon had denounced the federal government’s involvement in the legal proceedings as it acted as an intervener.

Following Friday’s ruling, St-Pierre Plamondon said it was a win for secularism in Quebec and for the autonomy of provinces. However, he took issue with a portion of the ruling allowing court justices to give their opinion on laws they can’t strike down due to the use of the override clause.

Bill 21 covers a range of public officials in positions of authority, including members of the province’s national assembly, prohibiting them from wearing religious symbols or face coverings. The seven Supreme Court justices overseeing the case unanimously declared the ban targeting elected officials was violating democratic rights. As a result, this section of the law is overturned.
While the seven Supreme Court justices agreed that Quebec was within its rights to invoke the override clause pre-emptively, they disagreed on aspects of Bill 21’s constitutionality.

Three justices — Michelle O’Bonsawin, Andromache Karakatsanis and Sheilah L. Martin — said the court had the power to strike down Bill 21, despite the use of the notwithstanding clause. They argued the law violates gender equality, which falls under a section of the Charter that governments are not allowed to override.
The three justices also wrote that the law disproportionately targeted Muslim women, keeping them out of the public workforce.
In addition, the seven justices also disagreed on whether to make a declaratory statement about whether Bill 21 violates Charter rights.

Groups representing Canadian Muslims, workers, English-speaking Quebecers, English language school boards, South Asian communities and anti-hate groups have all come out against the Supreme Court’s decision.
They say it is worrying that Canada’s top court upheld a law that discriminates against religious and racialized minorities.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 27, 2026.

stories.title: Predictions of soft shells and tight credit cloud outlook for N.S. lobster season
stories.summary: As the lobster fishery prepares to open Monday, there are indications some lobster fishers in southwestern Nova Scotia are still scrambling to find buyers for their catch.
stories.author: Michael MacDonald
stories.content:
As Canada’s largest and most lucrative lobster fishery prepares to open Monday, there are indications some lobster fishers in southwestern Nova Scotia are still scrambling to find buyers for their catch.

Earlier this month, four organizations representing commercial lobster harvesters sent an urgent letter to federal and provincial fisheries officials saying the economic outlook for the season was looking grim. They said both levels of government should explore the possibility of offering financial relief to affected fishers.

There’s plenty of money at stake.

Lobster was Nova Scotia’s largest seafood export in 2025, generating more than $1.1 billion in revenue, accounting for just over half of the province’s seafood export value, according to provincial figures released Friday.

“We have very serious reservations about the circumstances facing our commercial fishing captains, crew members, their families and the coastal communities whose economic well-being depends so heavily on this fishery,” the industry group said in its letter.

“Our concerns extend well beyond the uncertainty normally associated with the start of a fishing season.”

The problem, they said, is that some lobster buyers and processors have reduced or eliminated their plans to buy lobster this season, forcing some fishing boat captains to find new buyers at the last minute.

Stewart Lamont, managing director of Tangier Lobster Company Ltd., said the financial capacity of on-shore buyers has been diminished by a number of factors during the past two seasons.

Among other things, the quality of the lobsters landed was generally poor. Too many of them had soft shells and a low meat yield, making them less valuable to buyers.

“That has happened two years in a row, from November through March,” said Lamont, who has been shipping live lobsters around the world for 40 years. “Once could be an outlier. Twice begins to look like a trend, and so everybody is very nervous.”

As well, the global affordability crisis has stunted sales of lobster, widely considered a luxury good, Lamont said. As a result, commercial banks have tightened some lines of credit used by Nova Scotia buyers, limiting their financial capacity.

“The collective financial position of the industry has been diminished,” Lamont said.

“Our backers – commercial banks – have not been pleased or impressed by the financial return in the industry over the last three to five years … I’m amazed that the industry has held its model together to the extent it has.”

Nova Scotia’s Fisheries Department issued a statement Friday saying it was aware of harvesters’ concerns about buying capacity.

“We are in active discussions with the federal government and industry to understand their concerns and will continue to monitor them as the season unfolds,” the department said.

Meanwhile, Fisheries and Oceans Canada said that while oversight of buying and processing falls under the purview of the province, the federal government recently announced a fund for supporting buyers and processors.

Kris Vascotto, executive director of the Nova Scotia Seafood Alliance, said that as of Thursday, he was not aware of any fishing boat captains who had no place to sell their lobsters.

“There really are no boats without homes right now,” said Vascotto, whose industry group represents more than 200 land-based seafood buyers and processors. “What was presented in that letter (from the commercial fishing groups) May not reflect the reality of the season.”

In response, Lamont said the situation remains fluid.

“I was told … there remain 100 boats, give or take, who have fishermen without a home for their product,” he said Thursday. “Those fishermen are scrambling.”

Still, Vascotto said there are reasons for the lobster industry to feel optimistic about the coming season.

While he admitted that recent biological testing points to another year of lobsters with soft shells containing little meat, he said increased landings from other lobster fishing areas suggest a better season ahead.

“The shell conditions seem to be in fairly good shape,” Vascotto said. “The meat content and the meat yield seems to be pretty good shape.”

In all, Nova Scotia is expected to ship about 10-million pounds of live lobster during the month of December, he said, adding that almost half is expected to head to the United States and one-third to China. The rest will go to the European Union, Japan and the Indo-Pacific region.

Though tariffs imposed by China were lifted in March, Vascotto said it will take time for Canadian lobster to regain its previous share of the market.

As for the United States, he said Americans are still feeling the pinch from rising prices.

“There’s more concern about buying eggs, milk and bread than a premium product like lobster.”

In Nova Scotia, more than 1,000 boats are expected to drop their traps in Lobster Fishing Areas 33 and 34 on Monday morning. The annual event is known as Dumping Day. But it could be delayed if the weather is rough.

“Fishing has helped shape Nova Scotia for generations, and our lobster fishery is a huge part of who we are,” provincial Fisheries Minister Kent Smith said in a statement.

“To everyone heading out on the water, I wish you a good season and a safe return home.”

stories.title: B.C. court upholds Catholic hospital’s transfer policies for Maid patients
stories.summary: St. Paul Hospital’s policies don’t stop patients from accessing Maid, judge rules
stories.author: Ashley Joannou
stories.content:
The parents of a woman whose care leading up to her death set off a legal challenge over how medically assisted dying is provided in British Columbia say they struggle to understand how her pain was not enough to qualify as a Charter violation.

A B.C. Supreme Court judge said in a ruling released on Friday that policies of a publicly funded Catholic-run hospital requiring patients to be transferred to another facility to be given Maid do not violate the Charter rights of doctors or their patients.

The decision by Justice Ronald Skolrood said the hospital’s policies don’t stop a patient from accessing Maid and that doctors who practice medicine at faith-based organizations do so voluntarily, with full knowledge of the facility’s position.

“A particular physician’s belief in the importance and value of Maid does not give rise to a right to provide Maid services wherever the physician wishes to do so, nor does it permit a physician to compel a facility to make Maid available,” he said.

The legal challenge was filed by the family of 34-year-old Samantha O’Neill, who was denied a medically assisted death at St. Paul’s Hospital in Vancouver in 2023.

She was sedated and transferred to another facility, but never regained consciousness, something that her family said was “traumatic and unbearably cruel.”

The family, advocacy group Dying with Dignity Canada and a Maid provider, argued at the trial earlier this year that requiring a transfer puts patients at increased risk of pain and psychological stress, but the judge ruled that transfers are a routine aspect of health care and the risks are managed.

Skolrood ruled that to suggest Maid transfers are fundamentally different from other transfers “essentially amounts to a claim to the right to demand access to Maid at the time and in the location of the patient’s choice,” which “goes well beyond the established bounds of the Charter.”

O’Neill’s father Jim O’Neill said it appears his evidence of what his daughter experienced during the transfer was dismissed as anecdotal, rather than evidence of harm.

“I was in the vehicle with Sam and witnessed her writhing and moaning in pain and the additional drugs being administered,” he said at a news conference hours after the decision was released.

He said he doesn’t know how what his daughter experienced doesn’t meet “the definition of pain.”

“It’s not a bump in a hallway when you have to be sedated for the rest of your life. And somehow that’s not harm,” he said.

Skolrood said the Charter “is intended to protect individuals from state coercion on matters of conscience.”

“It is not intended to empower individuals to compel the state or other institutional actors to act in a particular manner that accords with that individual’s conscientious beliefs.”

Lawyers for St. Paul’s said the hospital is prohibited by Providence Health Care from offering assisted dying because of a decision by the Archbishop of Vancouver that it is morally wrong under Catholic beliefs.

Lawyers for the plaintiffs said the policy effectively imposes Catholic doctrine on patients, but the judge ruled that allowing faith-based organizations to operate in a manner consistent with their beliefs does not amount to state sponsorship of those beliefs.

“This allegation is similarly not made out on the evidence. Specifically, there is no evidence that any patients, including the patients whose circumstances were in evidence, were compelled to accept or observe Catholic beliefs either generally or as a condition of receiving Maid,” the ruling said.

The patient’s mother Gaye O’Neill told reporters that she was struggling to understand the decision.

“The Catholic administration would like you to turn a blind eye to the fact that forced transfers are not Christian and certainly not humane,” she said, calling them “knowingly harmful.”

“Dying is not the worst thing that happens to people, suffering is.”

A statement from Providence Health Care on Friday said it is thankful for “the thoughtful consideration given to this important and complex issue.”

“We are committed to continuing to build on our 130-plus-year history of providing compassionate, exceptional and innovative health care to British Columbians,” the statement said.

Dr. Jyothi Jayaraman, who is a Maid provider and was also a plaintiff in the case, said the court’s ruling that doctors choose to work at Providence Health Care ignores that some of them need to be there when patients who are qualified for assisted dying are admitted.

“Only the Maid provider who has completed a waiver of final consent with the patient can provide Maid to the patient who has lost capacity,” she said.

“A previously assessed and eligible-for-Maid patient could be admitted to a [Providence Health Care] facility because that is where their care could be optimally provided. And I would not be able to assist them when they needed me the most if I did not have privileges.”

Daphne Gilbert, the board chair for Dying with Dignity Canada, told the news conference that it stands by the arguments that were made in court and it is reviewing the decision before deciding what the next steps might be.

She has previously said the case is likely to end up before the Supreme Court of Canada.

“Forced transfers for Maid are an ongoing issue, not just in British Columbia, but across the country. Of Canada’s 1,087 hospitals, 129 of them are Catholic. Most of those refuse to allow Maid provisions on their premises,” she said on Friday.

“As a country, Canada embraces religious freedom, which means the government doesn’t prefer any one religion over another. And yet religiously affiliated health-care institutions continue to deny access to health-care services because of their religious beliefs.”

“I was in the vehicle with Sam and witnessed her writhing and moaning in pain and the additional drugs being administered,” he said at a news conference hours after the decision was released.
He said he doesn’t know how what his daughter experienced doesn’t meet “the definition of pain.”
“It’s not a bump in a hallway when you have to be sedated for the rest of your life. And somehow that’s not harm,” he said.
Skolrood said the Charter “is intended to protect individuals from state coercion on matters of conscience.”
“It is not intended to empower individuals to compel the state or other institutional actors to act in a particular manner that accords with that individual’s conscientious beliefs.”

Lawyers for St. Paul’s said the hospital is prohibited by Providence Health Care from offering assisted dying because of a decision by the Archbishop of Vancouver that it is morally wrong under Catholic beliefs.

Lawyers for the plaintiffs said the policy effectively imposes Catholic doctrine on patients, but the judge ruled that allowing faith-based organizations to operate in a manner consistent with their beliefs does not amount to state sponsorship of those beliefs.

“This allegation is similarly not made out on the evidence. Specifically, there is no evidence that any patients, including the patients whose circumstances were in evidence, were compelled to accept or observe Catholic beliefs either generally or as a condition of receiving Maid,” the ruling said.
The patient’s mother Gaye O’Neill told reporters that she was struggling to understand the decision.
“The Catholic administration would like you to turn a blind eye to the fact that forced transfers are not Christian and certainly not humane,” she said, calling them “knowingly harmful.”
“Dying is not the worst thing that happens to people, suffering is.”
A statement from Providence Health Care on Friday said it is thankful for “the thoughtful consideration given to this important and complex issue.”
“We are committed to continuing to build on our 130-plus-year history of providing compassionate, exceptional and innovative health care to British Columbians,” the statement said.

Dr. Jyothi Jayaraman, who is a Maid provider and was also a plaintiff in the case, said the court’s ruling that doctors choose to work at Providence Health Care ignores that some of them need to be there when patients who are qualified for assisted dying are admitted.
“Only the Maid provider who has completed a waiver of final consent with the patient can provide Maid to the patient who has lost capacity,” she said.

“A previously assessed and eligible-for-Maid patient could be admitted to a [Providence Health Care] facility because that is where their care could be optimally provided. And I would not be able to assist them when they needed me the most if I did not have privileges.”

Daphne Gilbert, the board chair for Dying with Dignity Canada, told the news conference that it stands by the arguments that were made in court and it is reviewing the decision before deciding what the next steps might be.
She has previously said the case is likely to end up before the Supreme Court of Canada.

“Forced transfers for Maid are an ongoing issue, not just in British Columbia, but across the country. Of Canada’s 1,087 hospitals, 129 of them are Catholic. Most of those refuse to allow Maid provisions on their premises,” she said on Friday.

“As a country, Canada embraces religious freedom, which means the government doesn’t prefer any one religion over another. And yet religiously affiliated health-care institutions continue to deny access to health-care services because of their religious beliefs.”

stories.title: Please put Dirty Dancing: The Musical back in its corner
stories.summary: Retrofitted with a bizarre civil rights subplot, director Lonny Price’s sexless take on the 1987 film is a confounding mess
stories.author: Aisling Murphy
stories.content:
Title: Dirty Dancing: The Musical

Book by: Eleanor Bergstein

Directed by: Lonny Price

Actors: Annalese Starzec, Blake Zelesnikar, Olivia Cece, Bryan Fenkart, Dan Klimko, Lily Kren, Ashley LaLonde, Gina Lamparella

Company: Mirvish Productions

Venue: CAA Ed Mirvish Theatre

City: Toronto

Year: Runs until Jan. 10, 2027

When I was 16, Dirty Dancing: The Musical rolled through my hometown, and a well-meaning friend from my school took me to see it. Almost instantly, I wondered how such rubbish had made it onto the stage of the Baltimore Hippodrome. (In retrospect, I suppose that evening somewhat foreshadowed my career as a theatre critic.)

I was gobsmacked. Why did the leads hardly sing, and why was there no original music? Why wasn’t there a real set? What on earth was Eleanor Bergstein trying to achieve by sloppily paraphrasing the text of her own 1987 screenplay? And, seriously, why was the dancing so bad?

Needless to say, I did not have the time of my life. But for a blissful 11 years, I figured Dirty Dancing would remain in its corner where it belonged – away from anything resembling a commercial theatre – and that the show would fade into a funny relic of my junior year of high school.

But because we live in the worst possible timeline, I am obligated to report that Dirty Dancing: The Musical is back, with most of the same issues as before. Even worse, it’s heading to Broadway in February – but not before stopping in Toronto.

It’s 1963, and social-justice-minded teenager Frances “Baby” Houseman (Annalese Starzec), daughter to a virtuous cardiologist (Bryan Fenkart), is vacationing with her family in the Catskills. (Blame Starzec’s oddly frizzy wig on the August humidity, I guess?)

One day, Baby stumbles across the oft-shirtless dance instructor Johnny Castle (Blake Zelesnikar), whose flirtatious samba skills have earned him an reputation for womanizing. (A complicated one, we later learn.)

Before long, Baby finds herself enmeshed with the resort’s staff, watching Johnny dance and befriending his duet partner Penny (Olivia Cece, Dirty Dancing ’s criminally underused standout).

But Penny, pregnant and not yet ready to be a mother, needs a night off from dancing to get an abortion. Out of options, Johnny turns to Baby to take Penny’s place in an important performance a few days later. (“She’s a natural!” claims Penny, even though we’ve observed little evidence of that – every time we’ve seen Baby dance, it’s been with minimal poise and a facial expression somewhere between surprised and flatulent.)

And so on. Baby and Johnny practice their moves and, surprise, start to fall for one another. Their big show doesn’t go especially well – or, actually, sorry, does it? Bergstein’s script says yes; Darrell Grand Moultrie’s choreography says no. Even when Baby allegedly gets the hang of things halfway through the duet, Starzec doesn’t demonstrate much of a perceptible shift in her dancing.

Save for a bizarre diversion into the burgeoning civil rights movement – complete with a group rendition of We Shall Overcome – Bergstein mostly adheres to the plot of the film. Baby and Johnny dream about the future and learn a thing or two about empathy in the process; Dr. Houseman slowly comes to grips with the idea that his daughter is a person.

But Bergstein’s script, marginally better in its first act than it was a decade ago, completely disintegrates in its back half. Johnny’s assertion that nobody puts Baby in a corner is completely unprompted – at no point in the preceding scene did anyone suggest doing anything of the sort. Why include the line at all, if that’s the case?

Beyond the central pair’s utter lack of chemistry – in the stage version, they don’t even kiss, nor do Starzec and Zelesnikar give the appearance of wanting to – director Lonny Price’s sexless production indulges in choices ranging from peculiar to astonishing. A rehearsal montage sees scenic designer Brett J. Banakis’s set overrun by frightening Baby and Johnny clones; a pivotal scene in the resort’s lake is represented so clumsily that even opening night’s enthusiastic audience only half-succeeded in stifling their laughs.

The whole thing’s soundtracked by sixties standards and favourites from the film – This Magic Moment , Do You Love Me? and, of course, a staggering number of refrains from (I’ve Had) The Time of My Life – most often sung in unison by Price’s ensemble. (The leads, in a strange break from musical theatre tradition, seldom sing by themselves.)

But by the end of Dirty Dancing , it feels as if music supervisor and arranger Joseph Joubert gave up halfway through constructing the musical’s score: A number of the songs’ original recordings are just piped into the theatre as-is.

Some small part of me hoped that, since our last encounter, Dirty Dancing might have experienced a coming-of-age à la Baby. Maybe, I thought to myself, this time would be different. Maybe Dirty Dancing would finally live up to the sizzling reputation of its source material.

But no. Dirty Dancing: The Musical remains a monstrosity of a nostalgia bomb, and in a few short months, it’ll replace the spunky Six at the Lena Horne Theatre in New York. Baby’s best wishes aside, it seems there really is no justice in this world.

Even when Baby allegedly gets the hang of things halfway through the duet, Starzec doesn’t demonstrate much of a perceptible shift in her dancing.

content_blocks.text: Save for a bizarre diversion into the burgeoning civil rights movement – complete with a group rendition of We Shall Overcome – Bergstein mostly adheres to the plot of the film. Baby and Johnny dream about the future and learn a thing or two about empathy in the process; Dr. Houseman slowly comes to grips with the idea that his daughter is a person.

Baby and Johnny dream about the future and learn a thing or two about empathy in the process; Dr. Houseman slowly comes to grips with the idea that his daughter is a person.

content_blocks.text: But Bergstein’s script, marginally better in its first act than it was a decade ago, completely disintegrates in its back half. Johnny’s assertion that nobody puts Baby in a corner is completely unprompted – at no point in the preceding scene did anyone suggest doing anything of the sort. Why include the line at all, if that’s the case?

content_blocks.text: Beyond the central pair’s utter lack of chemistry – in the stage version, they don’t even kiss, nor do Starzec and Zelesnikar give the appearance of wanting to – director Lonny Price’s sexless production indulges in choices ranging from peculiar to astonishing. A rehearsal montage sees scenic designer Brett J. Banakis’s set overrun by frightening Baby and Johnny clones; a pivotal scene in the resort’s lake is represented so clumsily that even opening night’s enthusiastic audience only half-succeeded in stifling their laughs.

content_blocks.text: Some small part of me hoped that, since our last encounter, Dirty Dancing might have experienced a coming-of-age à la Baby. Maybe, I thought to myself, this time would be different. Maybe Dirty Dancing would finally live up to the sizzling reputation of its source material.

content_blocks.text: But no. Dirty Dancing: The Musical remains a monstrosity of a nostalgia bomb, and in a few short months, it’ll replace the spunky Six at the Lena Horne Theatre in New York. Baby’s best wishes aside, it seems there really is no justice in this world.

stories.title: What the future might hold for the Stellantis Brampton auto plant, according to our reporter
stories.summary: Readers asked about Roshel’s plans for the plant, what will happen to the workers and why the federal government is getting involved
stories.author: Globe staff
stories.content:
On Nov. 24, transportation reporter Eric Atkins answered reader questions on the sale of the Stellantis auto plant in Brampton, Ont., the government’s involvement and what could happen next.

Earlier this month, automaker Stellantis said it finalized the sale of its idled factory in Brampton to defence contractor Roshel Inc. for an undisclosed amount.

Stellantis idled the Brampton plant in 2023, laying off about 3,000 workers, with the intent of retooling for the Jeep Compass. But that work was halted after the United States placed 25-per-cent tariffs on Canadian-made cars in early 2025. Later that year, Stellantis said the Jeep would not be built in Brampton, but at an idled plant in Illinois.

Readers asked about Roshel’s plans for the plant, what will happen to the workers there and why the federal government is getting involved. Here are some highlights from the Q&A.

What are Roshel’s plans for the plant and how many jobs will they create? How many of the 3,000 that were laid off are still out of work?

Atkins: Roshel makes armoured vehicles, some built on a Ford rolling chassis, like the ones Ford makes in Oakville. This is called upfitting, where they weld and bolt stuff onto it. As for jobs, that is a question mark.

Roshel say its use of the plant has the “potential” to create more than 2,000 jobs as production increases, and Stellantis workers get first crack at the jobs. It should be said we don’t what the plant will produce and when. Or how much the jobs will pay.

About 2,200 Stellantis workers are still on layoff benefits. A couple hundred took jobs at the Stellantis plant in Windsor.

Are we too focused on what the plant used to do, instead of the plans and employment opportunity from the new owner?

Atkins: Roshel has not released many concrete details, and told me it needs the plant before it can bid on other contracts. It has already bid on the federal government’s $4.9-billion light utility vehicle contract. As for jobs and spillover effects, an auto plant brings more than of those than a low-volume upfitter will.

Is it true that the Stellantis factory in Windsor is not running at full capacity? If so, why does Stellantis require the Brampton factory?

Atkins: Yes, Windsor has had about six weeks of downtime this fall because it doesn’t need all those minivans and muscle cars right now. And Stellantis has been clear it does not need the Brampton factory. That’s why Stellantis sold it.

Stellantis has too much idle capacity and not enough car sales in North America and Europe. The company lost US$26-billion in 2025.

When auto workers are laid off for retooling, who pays their wages?

Atkins: The workers are eligible for Employment Insurance like all of us, and also receive supplemental pay the Unifor union negotiates with the employer for. The EI runs out, like it does for everybody. So the 70 per cent I have written about is from the company. They also miss out on overtime work, so for some their paycheques are less than 70 per cent of their usual ones.

Why do some employers and laid-off workers get special attention and not others? What makes them so special that they get so much coverage and subsidies?

Atkins: Automaking has long been an important part of the Ontario economy so it gets a lot of attention, especially when Trump declares he wants it dead. The plants gets subsidized because they stir up a lot of economic activity elsewhere that are so big that we all notice when things go wrong. Same for steel plants. I know many jobs and smaller companies disappear and don’t get coverage. That’s likely because we don’t know about them or cannot cover it or it is too dispersed.

Why is Industry Minister Mélanie Joly talking of subsidizing Stellantis, a foreign company, to retain a plant that Roshel, a Canadian vehicle maker, wants to purchase? Why not let the market decide the use of the plant?

Atkins: This a big question, and maybe not even really a question. But I’ll start by saying the auto industry relies on subsidies, here and in the U.S. You want a new plant in your county/riding/town? Start with municipal tax breaks and go from there on up. U.S. states lavish billions on automakers, as well.

As for which would employ more people and create more economic benefits, a car plant beats an armoured car plant, experts say, when measuring number of jobs, production volumes and beneficial supply chain impacts.

It’s been many years since I took Econ 101, but I’m pretty sure Trump’s wacky trade policy made most people abandon the usual rules of supply and demand, and instead focus on how to preserve jobs for a time when sanity prevails.

How much money has been released by Canada to Stellantis in a signed agreement?

Atkins: Details of the 2022 funding agreement are confidential but I reported Ottawa wants $831-million back if Stellantis sells the Brampton plant. So that’s a clue. This would be for work in Brampton and at the Windsor assembly plant, and the Nextstar Windsor EV battery plant that Stellantis walked away from.

Why would Minister Joly prepare an “aggressive” package for Stellantis in the hope that it will stop the sale of the Brampton plant, when the government has already sunk millions in the company?

Atkins: A large chunk of that money has been spent (Windsor car plant, Windsor battery plant) and created jobs. And the government very badly wants to save the auto jobs and all the spinoffs.

Lost car plants don’t come back. This is all part of the broader strategy in which Ottawa and the provinces are focused on protecting jobs in industries targeted by Trump and his tariffs.

Why is the government subsidizing a manufacturer of standard uneconomical gas vehicles rather than strategic industries, or EV or hybrid vehicles?

Atkins: The government is subsidizing jobs first and foremost. And the Stellantis plant in Brampton was supposed to build hybrid or electric versions and gas-powered versions of the Jeep Compass.

What is the highest percentage of tariffs that would still allow a viable Ontario auto sector to export to the U.S.?

Atkins: I don’t know and it varies by product and U.S. content (the tariff applies only to the non-U.S. content). The industry says 25 per cent is ruinous long term and 15 per cent is not much better. These companies makes single-digit profit margins, so any tariff quickly destroys that. The auto supply chain was built without tariffs, and needs no tariffs to function as it is meant to. Otherwise, bonne nuit .

This Q&A has been condensed.

stories.title: Special themed holiday trees bring joy to 16 Make-A-Wish kids
stories.summary: Sixteen children and their families received personal-themed holiday trees Thursday as part of the Make-A-Wish...
stories.author: Samantha Luis
stories.content:
Sixteen children and their families received personal-themed holiday trees Thursday as part of the Make-A-Wish ‘Trees of Joy’ event at London’s RBC Place.

As the doors opened, the children and their families paraded into the ballroom to see a room full of trees that had been specially decorated to reflect each of their interests and personalities, with themes ranging from Star Wars to music notes. Each child had a special magic wand to light up their own tree.

Brianne’s reaction to opening a gift (Credit: Sam Luis/ XFM News)

“It means a lot,” said Brianne, 8, who has a liver disorder and whose Tree of Joy was filled with Grinch ornaments. “I never thought it was going to happen but it did.”

Underneath her tree were gifts for both her and her sister, Alison.

Brianne’s favourite part of the tree was the Grinch tree topper, and her favourite gift was a Calico Critters house set, which was one of many toys below the tree.

Like the other children, Brianne had been paired with a sponsor, who donated $10,000 to the event. The Kayser Family Foundation sponsored Brianne’s tree.

‘Tree’s of Joy’ returned for it’s third year. Funds raised through ‘Trees of Joy’ help Make-A-Wish Canada deliver life-changing wish journeys, said Make-A-Wish.

Brianne and Cheryl (Credit: Sam Luis/ XFM News) “

Brianne was diagnosed with a liver disorder when she was 5. Last year, she went on a Make-a-Wish tip that included a visit to Disneyland where even her Grinch sweater became part of the family’s memories.

On Thursday, she giggled as her mom talked about how Stitch, another Disney character, jokingly gave Brianne a hard time for wearing the Grinch shirt.

“Christmas is my favourite,” Brianne said. “Normally school gets cancelled because there’s snow days, all my Grinch things come out, it’s hot chocolate season and it’s really fun because you get to build snow forts.”

The celebration continued with a buffet accommodating different dietary needs and restrictions. Families also had the opportunity to take pictures with Mr. and Mrs. Claus.

Sponsors adding final touch-ups to the trees (Credit: Sam Luis/ XFM News)

For her mom Cheryl, seeing Brianne experience something special after spending so much time in hospitals meant a great deal.

“Sometimes we don’t feel very special when we have to hang out at the hospital a lot. So, just being able to do something fun for our family means a great deal,” said Cheryl.

Make-A-Wish relies on donations and community support rather than government funding.

Despite the support, more than 1,200 children are waiting for their wishes to be granted in Ontario and 3,500 across Canada.

In 2025, 617 children had their wishes granted.

stories.title: Watchdog clears RCMP officer after fatally shooting First Nations man in New Brunswick
stories.summary: Serious Incident Response Team says officer’s use of force was ‘proportionate, necessary and reasonable in the circumstances’
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
New Brunswick’s police watchdog has cleared an RCMP officer of criminality in the shooting death of an Indigenous man earlier this year.

The Serious Incident Response Team issued its findings Friday in the January shooting death of a member of the Neqotkuk First Nation, later identified by the community as Bronson Paul.

The report says a man was shot and killed on Jan. 18 after police responded to a domestic disturbance in the community, also known as the Tobique First Nation.

It says the man kicked down the bathroom door and emerged with two broken pieces of wood with sharp ends.

When the man attacked, one officer deployed a stun gun, which the report says was ineffective.

It says the man charged a second time, then turned and charged at a second officer who fired six shots, hitting the man five times.

The report says the officer’s use of force was “proportionate, necessary and reasonable in the circumstances.”

Neqotkuk Chief Ross Perley said in an interview that the report contains “untruths” including a claim that RCMP did not have an agreement with the First Nation’s leadership to contact its local tribal security when responding to calls.

Perley said the First Nation did have an arrangement in place, and it was not followed.

“There’s several mistakes that were made. At this point we feel that Sirt is a sham,” Perley said in an interview Friday.

stories.title: Holiday classic with a twist returns to the Grand Theatre stage
stories.summary: The holiday season wouldn’t be complete without, “A Christmas Carol”.
stories.author: Nick Paparella
stories.content:
The holiday season wouldn’t be complete without, “A Christmas Carol”.

The latest production at the Grand Theatre in downtown London comes with a unique twist to Charles Dickens classic tale.

This time around it’s a mid-century, carol infused musical that’s bound to please the entire family.

“This is set in 1949, the language is easier to understand because it’s not Victorian English,” says Geoff Armour who plays the part of Ebenezer Scrooge. “My version is more physical and in this adaptation he is younger.”

Julie Lumsden plays the part of Emily Cratchit and she says, “Emily is our version of Bob Cratchit, she’s a war widow trying to raise six children including Tony Tim and is trying to make Christmas magical for these children.”

Armour says he’s excited for the audience to see the stage saying, “The music is wonderful, the set is very colourful because it’s 1949 and the costumes are insane.”

At this time of the year those in the audience are once again asked to think of others with a monetary donation to the London Food Bank at the end of the performance.

“I think that raising money for the London Food Bank is a wonderful extension of the mission statement because theatre is community and the Grand Theatre is stepping up.” says Armour.

A Christmas Carol is on the main stage at the Grand Theatre until December 27 th .

Lumsden adds, “I hope the audience leaves feeling that their hearts are a little bit bigger and full of the Christmas spirit.”

Ottawa — Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre says he will be heading to Washington, D.C., next week to “fight for tariff-free trade.”

Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc told reporters this week that he’s been in discussions with officials from U.S. President Donald Trump’s negotiating team as they try to hash out a trade deal in the face of an ongoing tariff war. He said he expects to continue talks after the American Thanksgiving weekend.

“We’ll continue to try and find a deal that we think is in Canada’s interest,” LeBlanc said after a Liberal caucus meeting on Wednesday.

Poilievre’s office declined to provide any details about the Conservative leader’s trip, including the dates and who he plans to meet with.

This marks the first time the Tory leader has made an official visit to the U.S. capital — though some members of his caucus have met with senior officials in Trump’s administration.

Ontario MP Jamil Jivani led a small delegation of Conservatives to D.C. in April, where they sat down with oil executives and United States Trade Representative Jamieson Greer. Canada’s ambassador to the U.S., Mark Wiseman, was also in the meeting.

Jivani met with his longtime friend, U.S. Vice-President JD Vance, when he first visited Washington in February, a visit that also included a brief conversation with President Trump.

JD Vance and Jamil Jivani in 2019. Jamil Jivani/Instagram

But Poilievredistanced himself from his MPafter Jivani told an American right-wing news outlet that some Canadians were engaging in an anti-American “hissy fit” that was counterproductive to getting a deal with the U.S.

Poilievre later told reporters in Ottawa that Jivani “speaks for himself.”

The Conservative leader has travelled to the United States twice in the last year. His first visit stateside in March included stops in Texas and New York, and last month he travelled to Michigan, the heart of U.S. auto manufacturing.

During those trips, Poilievre made the case in American TV interviews that Canada and the U.S. are stronger when they work together.

stories.title: Off-duty London police officer charged with assault and forcible confinement
stories.summary: A London police officer is facing assault and forcible confinement after an investigation into an off-duty incident earlier this month.
stories.author: Melanie Kentner
stories.content:
A London police officer is facing assault and forcible confinement after an investigation into an off-duty incident earlier this month.

The London Police Service received the initial report and subsequently referred the matter to the Strathroy-Caradoc Police Service to ensure an independent and impartial investigation, in accordance with the conflict-of-interest provisions under the Community Safety and Policing Act, 2019.

The officer was arrested and charged by the Strathroy-Caradoc Police Service with the following offences:

Forcible confinement.

Police say to protect the privacy of the victim and prevent their identification, the name of the officer and further identifying details will not be released at this time.

Following an assessment of the circumstances, the officer has been reassigned to administrative duties and will not be performing frontline policing duties. The officer’s duty status will remain subject to ongoing review as the matter progresses.

The matter will also be subject to an internal conduct investigation, in accordance with the Community Safety and Policing Act.

The London Police Service says it takes these allegations seriously.

“As police officers, we are entrusted with significant responsibilities and are held to high standards of conduct, both on and off duty,” states a news release from police.

“Our commitment to transparency and accountability must be balanced with our responsibility to protect the privacy and well-being of those affected and to respect the integrity and fairness of the judicial process.”

stories.title: Here’s what to know about the Kenneth Law case
stories.summary: Law admitted to running an online business that sold lethal salts and deadly paraphernalia to vulnerable people around the world
stories.author: Globe staff
stories.content:
The sentencing hearing of Kenneth Law resumed in Newmarket, Ont., ON Friday. The case gained global attention when Mr. Law was arrested in 2023 and accused of running an online business selling lethal substances to people at risk of suicide.

He pleaded guilty earlier this year and admitted to playing a role in the deaths of 93 people in Ontario and Britain. The families of some of those people provided victim-impact statements in court in September .

Here’s everything you need to know about the case.

Now 61 years old, Kenneth Law was a resident of Mississauga, Ont., when he admitted to running an online business that sold lethal salts and deadly paraphernalia to vulnerable people around the world. He was arrested in 2023, following a report in the Times of London newspaper, and charged of aiding in the suicides of 14 people in Ontario – charges that were later upgraded to first-degree murder.

He pleaded guilty in May to 14 counts of aiding suicide in Ontario, and the murder charges were dropped. He also admitted to being involved in another 79 deaths in Britain.

On his personal website, Mr. Law states he received an engineering degree from the University of Toronto in 1989 and pursued an MBA at York University seven years later. According to Professional Engineers Ontario, Mr. Law was accredited in 1992, but in 2012 he entered a fee remission program at the professional association. (Duff McCutcheon, a spokesperson for the PEO, said engineers who don’t pay their full fees, such as Mr. Law, “must not practise professional engineering but they can self-identify as licence holders and continue to use the title associated with their licence.”)

By 2020, he was working as a chef at the Fairmont Royal York Hotel and later set up online businesses selling a variety of products that could be used by people seeking to end their lives. A court heard earlier this year that he told clients he had engineered painless suicide methods.

Authorities said he shipped about 1,200 parcels globally to vulnerable young people he met in online suicide forums. He admitted to manufacturing suicide kits, which he sold for as little as $80 apiece between 2021 and 2023, earning around $300,000.

Oct. 14, 2022: A coroner’s report in the United Kingdom looking into the suicide in April of a woman in Surrey lists a postal box in Mississauga, Ont., and the name of one of the websites police linked to Mr. Law.

April 25, 2023: The Times of London publishes an investigation into Mr. Law, reporting on his alleged global online operation.

May 2, 2023: Peel Regional Police announce they have arrested Mr. Law and charged him with two counts of counselling and aiding suicide .

June 16, 2023: Peel Regional Police announce 11 Ontario police forces have formed a major joint operation investigating Mr. Law .

Aug. 25, 2023: Britain’s National Crime Agency says it has identified 232 people in the U.K. who bought products from Canada-based websites allegedly linked to Mr. Law in the two years prior to April 2023, 88 of whom had died.

Aug. 29, 2023: Police announce an additional 12 new charges against Mr. Law of aiding and counselling suicides across Ontario . They allege that in late 2020, Mr. Law started to operate the websites he used to market sodium nitrite and other items that can be used for self-harm.

Dec. 12, 2023: Police announce 14 counts of second-degree murder charges against Mr. Law , in addition to his 14 existing charges of aiding suicide. Mr. Law’s lawyer, Matthew Gourlay, says his client would be pleading not guilty to all charges.

Jan. 26, 2024: Mr. Law’s lawyer confirms that all 14 counts of second-degree murder have been upgraded to first-degree murder, and that the case would proceed by direct indictment, meaning there would be no preliminary inquiry. Mr. Gourlay says Law will plead not guilty to all charges.

October, 2025: Mr. Law’s trial is postponed for a second time, to April 2026, as the Crown and defence await the Supreme Court decision.

April 18, 2026: Mr. Gourlay says a plea deal has been reached with Crown prosecutors, who will drop all 14 murder charges against Mr. Law. Mr. Gourlay says Mr. Law will plead guilty to 14 counts of aiding suicide.

May 28, 2026: The families of people who died in the United Kingdom after allegedly receiving packages from Mr. Law say the country’s National Crime Agency and Crown Prosecution Service have informed them that Mr. Law will not be facing charges there because extradition could be a lengthy process and any sentence imposed in Canada would be similar.

May 29, 2026: Mr. Law enters his guilty pleas in a court in Newmarket, Ont., and signs an agreed statement of facts summarizing the details of the cases of 14 Ontarians whose deaths are linked to his products. The court also hears details about 79 people in the U.K. who died because of products purchased from Law.

Sept. 23, 2026: The first phase of the sentencing hearing came to a close. Prosecutors put 74 victim impact statements on the record. Mr. Law attended these hearings while sitting in a prisoner’s box. He listened to dozens of people denounce him without reacting.

Nov. 27, 2026: Legal arguments begin.

In May, Mr. Law pleaded guilty in an Ontario court to aiding in the suicides of 14 people in Ontario, and also admitted to assisting in 79 other deaths in Britain by shipping toxic substances and suffocation equipment to people seeking to die.

Prior to pleading guilty to the 14 counts of aiding suicide, Mr. Law signed a lengthy agreed statement of facts, which was read aloud in court by prosecutors.

In the agreed facts, Mr. Law admits to shipping hundreds of packages of his products from a Canada Post office near his Mississauga home. Prosecutors named dozens of countries that received shipments but said most went to the United States (431 packages), Britain (330) and Canada (157).

Mr. Law has admitted to aiding in the suicide of at least 93 people in Canada and Britain. Here are some of their stories.

Stephen Mitchell Jr. , from Toronto, died about a month before Law was arrested. He was 21.

He suffered from depression and had stopped taking his medication. He paid US$87.17 via PayPal for a package of poison from Law and was found dead by his brother on March 25, 2023.

His father, Stephen Mitchell Sr., said his son’s death was preventable. When he took the witness box, he addressed Law directly. “You May one day regain your freedom, Mr. Law, but you will never erase the consequences of what you have done,” he. said. “Mr. Law robbed my son of that chance to heal.”

Maria Lopez, from Aurora, Ont., told the court about the immense loss of her lone child, a teenager who was also her best friend and confidante.

Her 18-year-old daughter, Jeshennia Bedoya-Lopez, was found dead in their family home in Aurora on Sept. 10, 2022, after paying Law US$81.48 for a lethal packet of his toxic salt.

The past four years have been incredibly difficult for Lopez and her husband, who are refugees from Colombia awaiting a decision on their immigration status. The couple have worked nights as cleaners in different cities to make ends meet while trying to make sense of their loss.

Tom Parfett , 22, paid Law US$87.09 for his toxic salt on Oct. 11, 2021. Staff at a British hotel found him dead in his room two weeks later.

In the years that followed, his father emerged as the person perhaps most responsible for ensuring that Law was brought to justice. He worked closely with journalist James Beal of The Times of London to expose Law’s activities.

Parfett is not travelling to Canada for the hearings. But he sees the sentencing hearings as the “end of the beginning of the campaigning work to stop online harms and end deaths from suicide.”

There is much work still to be done, he said. Earlier this year, the British government resisted calls for a public inquiry by families of people who died using Mr. Law’s products.

Families have called for a public inquiry into how Mr. Law was able to sell suicide kits around the world for years before being caught, and they repeated those calls during the first phase of hearings in September.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford previously rejected those calls. In September, as the hearings went on, his office confirmed his position hasn’t changed.

“The Premier’s comments in May on a public inquiry stand,” Hannah Jensen, a spokeswoman for the Office of the Premier, said in response to The Globe and Mail when questioned about whether Ford is reconsidering his position.

With reports from Colin Freeze and Mike Hager.

stories.title: ‘Slow down’: police offer winter driving tips
stories.summary: Days after London received its first snowfall of the season, police said motorists should remember to drive ac...
stories.author: Owen Schuller
stories.content:
Days after London received its first snowfall of the season, police said motorists should remember to drive according to weather conditions.

(Credit: London Police Service ON/x.com)

Statistics show crashes often increase during winter weather, and London police said this week that drivers can avoid that trend by taking more care.

“If the roads are slippery and snow covered … slow down and drive appropriately,” said media relations officer Const. Gavin Dell.

Dell said it is important for drivers to carry winter kits with emergency items, such as a blanket, flashlight, first aid kit and food and water. He said they should have those things easily accessible, not in the trunk.

“This is something that some people don’t think of,” Dell said. “Just kind of tie yourself over till emergency services can get to you.”

Dell said having your vehicle up to date is important.

“It is important that your vehicle can handle those (winter) conditions.”

Research done by Canada’s Allstate Snow Smart Campaign found that winter months had the highest collision numbers.

“The data … reveals a clear seasonal trend: the winter months of January, followed by December and then February saw the highest number of collisions,” the report said.

All State said making plans for driving should be a priority.

“Allstate Canada encourages drivers to make winter preparedness a priority,” the report said. “Taking the time to adapt driving habits to the season can help keep everyone safer on the road.”

stories.title: Flood threats, king tides ease in coastal B.C. as cleanup work begins
stories.summary: Environment Canada drops rain and wind warnings, B.C. River Forecast Centre alerts lifted for all but central Vancouver Island
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Nicalena Chidley’s dock was swept away this week as a storm surge, king tides and strong winds pounded it into bits on her oceanfront property on northwestern Vancouver Island.

She lives in the small community of Kyuquot, a remote settlement that has no roads and is accessible only by boat or plane.

With no dock, she’s been stranded since Tuesday.

Video taken by Chidley shows her son in an orange waterproof suit standing on the shoreline, assessing the destruction.

The walkway to the dock is gone, the front section has also disappeared, but two boats, bucking in the strong waves, are still attached to the end of the stranded structure.

Wood debris and other building material are scattered along the waterfront.

“It pulled out our whole platform and our first ramp that goes down to our bigger ramp to our dock. So, we were stranded on the island,” Chidley said, describing the damage.

“It was just incredibly rough in there.”

Her family is one of many cleaning up after days of relentless rain along coastal B.C., made worse by strong winds and king tides that prevented storm surges from washing out.

Environment Canada dropped its rain and wind warnings late Thursday, while alerts from the B.C. River Forecast Centre were lifted Friday for all but central Vancouver Island where a high-streamflow advisory remains posted.

The weather agency has also lifted all coastal flood warnings and statements, which at the peak covered almost the whole B.C. coast.

Residents of Parksville, ON the east coast of Vancouver Island, who live on low-lying or coastal properties were put on evacuation alert earlier this week due to rising water levels. Those have since been rescinded and a spokesman for the city said “minimal cleanup has been identified.”

“The only part from the storm that needs monitoring is waiting for the fields and parks to begin drying up, as there’s a lot of sitting water in those areas,” the statement said.

“There might be some work required to move debris and logs from some beach areas, but that’s done in partnership with [fisheries departments] on the provincial and federal government side of things.”

The weather agency said the storms between Monday and Thursday dropped 734 millimetres of rain on Effingham Island off Western Vancouver Island, which is about 160 kilometres south of Chidley’s home.

Chidley said she has been living in Kyuquot since 1988 – her parents were long-serving lightkeepers on B.C.’s coast, so the area is “in her DNA.” While she has seen storms before, this has “been quite a week.”

The sound of the storm made itself known on Tuesday.

“I was taking a nap and I woke up to a huge thud of water against my window side. Scared the daylights out of me,” said Chidley.

The B.C. River Forecast Centre said the king tides coinciding with the full moon made the coastal flooding situation worse, but that influence was also diminishing.

The District of Squamish, which declared a state of local emergency over high tides and flood risk earlier this week, has asked residents to limit indoor water use until further notice to help manage sewer flows, adding that more rainfall will impact the system.

The district said flood protection measures it took have succeeded in mitigating the effects of localized flooding.

Environment Canada said Squamish received 147 millimetres of rain since Monday, among the highest totals recorded on B.C.’s mainland in the weather event.

Peak winds were recorded in Comox at 89 km/h and Tofino at 82 km/h.

While it’s been a difficult time, Chidley said she has been overwhelmed with the support from people in her tight-knit community.

“I’ve done a lot of crying the last couple of days, everybody’s been pitching in and helping in any way they can. So, that’s fantastic and amazing. I’m very proud of our community on the receiving end instead of being the giving end.”

stories.title: Project to increase Trans Mountain pipeline flows starts up ahead of schedule
stories.summary: A further expansion of 210,000 barrels per day is expected to come into service by the end of 2028, bringing the system's total capacity to 1.19 billion barrels a day.
stories.author: Lauren Krugel
stories.content:
A project to increase the amount of crude that can flow on the Trans Mountain Pipeline using chemical additives has been completed two months ahead of schedule, the Crown corporation said as it released third-quarter results on Friday.

The drag-reducing agent increases the pipeline’s capacity by up to about 10 per cent to 980,000 barrels per day. Trans Mountain carries oil from the Edmonton area to Burnaby, B.C.

A further expansion of 210,000 barrels per day, using new pipeline segments and pump stations, is expected to come into service by the end of 2028, bringing the system’s total capacity to 1.19 billion barrels a day.

During the third quarter, Trans Mountain shipped 840,000 barrels per day on average, up from 777,000 barrels during the same three months of 2025.

About 60 per cent of the throughput during the period went to the Westridge Marine Terminal, from which oil-laden tankers can sail across the Pacific to Asian customers.

The rest went to delivery points in B.C. and Washington state.

Net income for the quarter rose to $132 million from $127 million as revenues increased to $825 million from $765 million.

So far this year, Trans Mountain has paid $1.45 billion to its owner, the federal government, in interest payments, dividends and return of capital distributions. For the quarter, a total of $551 million went to Ottawa.

Ottawa bought the pipeline for $4.5 billion in 2018 after Kinder Morgan Canada walked away from a project to triple the line’s capacity at the time, amid fierce environmental opposition and court challenges.

It ended up costing more than $34 billion by the time it the expanded pipeline started up in May of 2024.

Federal and Trans Mountain officials have said there is no rush to return the pipeline to the private sector. Some Indigenous groups have long expressed interest taking a stake in the pipeline.

Trans Mountain said in its Friday news release that confidential information sessions with potential Indigenous partners began in October.

Meanwhile, Trans Mountain is taking the lead on the development of the Pacific Link pipeline, a new million-barrel-a-day oil pipeline proposed by the Alberta government that would largely follow the same path as Trans Mountain, ending at a port in Delta, B.C.

Pacific Link has been designated a project of national interest, meaning it will be guided through a speedy regulatory process under the federal major projects office.

At least 17 First Nations in Alberta and B.C., one U.S. tribe in Washington state and one individual have filed legal challenges against Pacific Link’s national interest designation, according to a news release Thursday distributed by the St’at’imc Chiefs Council.

The St’at’imc Nation and T’Sou-ke First Nation earlier this month filed a joint application to quash Ottawa’s decision on the pipeline proposal.
