stories.title: B.C. court upholds Catholic hospital transfer policies for Maid patients
stories.summary: Vancouver - British Columbia's Supreme Court has ruled that the policies of a publicly funded Catholic-run hospital requiring patients to be transferred to another facility for a medically assisted death do not violate the Charter rights of doctors or their patients.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Vancouver - The parents of a woman whose care leading up to her death set off a legal challenge over how medically assisted dying is provided in British Columbia say they struggle to understand how her pain was not enough to qualify as a Charter violation.

A B.C. Supreme Court judge said in a ruling released on Friday that policies of a publicly funded Catholic-run hospital requiring patients to be transferred to another facility to be given Maid do not violate the Charter rights of doctors or their patients.

The decision by Justice Ronald Skolrood said the hospital’s policies don’t stop a patient from accessing Maid and that doctors who practice medicine at faith-based organizations do so voluntarily, with full knowledge of the facility’s position.

“A particular physician’s belief in the importance and value of Maid does not give rise to a right to provide Maid services wherever the physician wishes to do so, nor does it permit a physician to compel a facility to make Maid available,” he said.

The legal challenge was filed by the family of 34-year-old Samantha O’Neill, who was denied a medically assisted death at St. Paul’s Hospital in Vancouver in 2023.

She was sedated and transferred to another facility, but never regained consciousness, something that her family said was “traumatic and unbearably cruel.”

The family, advocacy group Dying with Dignity Canada and a Maid provider, argued at the trial earlier this year that requiring a transfer puts patients at increased risk of pain and psychological stress, but the judge ruled that transfers are a routine aspect of health care and the risks are managed.

Skolrood ruled that to suggest Maid transfers are fundamentally different from other transfers “essentially amounts to a claim to the right to demand access to Maid at the time and in the location of the patient’s choice,” which “goes well beyond the established bounds of the Charter.”

O’Neill’s father Jim O’Neill said it appears his evidence of what his daughter experienced during the transfer was dismissed as anecdotal, rather than evidence of harm.

“I was in the vehicle with Sam and witnessed her writhing and moaning in pain and the additional drugs being administered,” he said at a news conference hours after the decision was released.

He said he doesn’t know how what his daughter experienced doesn’t meet “the definition of pain.”

“It’s not a bump in a hallway when you have to be sedated for the rest of your life. And somehow that’s not harm,” he said.

Skolrood said the Charter “is intended to protect individuals from state coercion on matters of conscience.”

“It is not intended to empower individuals to compel the state or other institutional actors to act in a particular manner that accords with that individual’s conscientious beliefs.”

Lawyers for St. Paul’s said the hospital is prohibited by Providence Health Care from offering assisted dying because of a decision by the Archbishop of Vancouver that it is morally wrong under Catholic beliefs.

Lawyers for the plaintiffs said the policy effectively imposes Catholic doctrine on patients, but the judge ruled that allowing faith-based organizations to operate in a manner consistent with their beliefs does not amount to state sponsorship of those beliefs.

“This allegation is similarly not made out on the evidence. Specifically, there is no evidence that any patients, including the patients whose circumstances were in evidence, were compelled to accept or observe Catholic beliefs either generally or as a condition of receiving Maid,” the ruling said.

The patient’s mother Gaye O’Neill told reporters that she was struggling to understand the decision.

“The Catholic administration would like you to turn a blind eye to the fact that forced transfers are not Christian and certainly not humane,” she said, calling them “knowingly harmful.”

“Dying is not the worst thing that happens to people, suffering is.”

A statement from Providence Health Care on Friday said it is thankful for “the thoughtful consideration given to this important and complex issue.”

“We are committed to continuing to build on our 130-plus-year history of providing compassionate, exceptional and innovative health care to British Columbians,” the statement said.

Dr. Jyothi Jayaraman, who is a Maid provider and was also a plaintiff in the case, said the court’s ruling that doctors choose to work at Providence Health Care ignores that some of them need to be there when patients who are qualified for assisted dying are admitted.

“Only the Maid provider who has completed a waiver of final consent with the patient can provide Maid to the patient who has lost capacity,” she said.

“A previously assessed and eligible-for-Maid patient could be admitted to a (Providence Health Care) facility because that is where their care could be optimally provided. And I would not be able to assist them when they needed me the most if I did not have privileges.”

Daphne Gilbert, the board chair for Dying with Dignity Canada, told the news conference that it stands by the arguments that were made in court and it is reviewing the decision before deciding what the next steps might be.

She has previously said the case is likely to end up before the Supreme Court of Canada.

“Forced transfers for Maid are an ongoing issue, not just in British Columbia, but across the country. Of Canada’s 1,087 hospitals, 129 of them are Catholic. Most of those refuse to allow Maid provisions on their premises,” she said on Friday.

“As a country, Canada embraces religious freedom, which means the government doesn’t prefer any one religion over another. And yet religiously affiliated health-care institutions continue to deny access to health-care services because of their religious beliefs.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 27, 2026.

stories.summary: Winnipeg - A First Nation in northern Manitoba has declared a state of emergency over what it says is unsafe drinking water.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
WINNIPEG - A First Nation in northern Manitoba has declared a state of emergency over what it says is unsafe drinking water.

Marcel Colomb First Nation says its drinking water has taken on a sulphur smell this past week, and people have become ill.

A glass of water symbolizing black water, is held by a participant during a media scrum about Bill C-37, the First Nations Clean Water Act, in the in the Foyer of the House of Commons on Parliament Hill in Ottawa, on Friday, Oct. 9, 2026. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Justin Tang

stories.title: ‘Alternative grading’ lets students mark themselves. How does that work?
stories.summary: One professor at Toronto Metropolitan University said it sounded like free cookies for everyone, until he actually tried it
stories.author: Chris Knight
stories.content:
Sean Kheraj remembers thinking that “alternative grading,” a recent buzzword in education, sounded like a terrible idea.

The broad term refers to moving away from points, percentages and letter grades, and toward feedback and proven mastery of what is being taught. It also, controversially, includes self-assessment by students.

“On the surface it looks like students giving their own grades,” Kheraj, the vice-provost, academic at Toronto Metropolitan University told National Post. “It’s like you’re taking the lid off the cookie jar and letting everyone go in there and take as many cookies as they want. And it’s the honour system.”

Kheraj is also a professor of Canadian and environmental history at TMU. He tried alternative grading in one of his courses. “And that’s not really how it plays out in practice,” he said. Keeping the cookie jar analogy, most students were reluctant to take more than their fair share. Some even argued they deserved fewer cookies than he thought they did.

Monday - Saturday Free

“I found that very few students were giving themselves 100, and they are much more honest and more reflective,” Kheraj said. “I even had a student who I was trying to push to give themselves a higher grade because I thought that they had actually contributed a lot more, but they were so much more critical about themselves, and they didn’t feel like they had earned that.

“And so I let them go forward with what they wanted, in part because it wasn’t the entire grade for them.”

Crucially, alternative grading does not allow all scoring to be done by the students. Profs get their say, and work is still evaluated.

It’s also not an approach for every class.

“Obviously, not every type of course is going to be suitable,” said Kheraj. “So, for example, accredited programs with professional licensing that have standardized exams; those are not likely to be suitable for alternative grading methods.” Tmu’s public health inspection licensing course would be an example of that.

TMU has several videos online of professors discussing how alternative grading works for them.

“I did not have any component of my class where I provided a numerical grade on an assessment,” said Alyssa Counsell from the Department of Psychology, adding that this was in a small, graduate-level class where she had already taught the students before. “I would not do this in a 140-person class.”

Feedback took the place of grading. “It really was much more about the learning process and demonstrating that even if you’re struggling through this, struggle is learning.”

And letter grades still show up on students’ transcripts. “At the end of the day, myself and the students are operating within an institution that requires reporting of grades,” said Krystal Nunes of the department of chemistry and biology in another video.

In Counsell’s graduate class, however, students must justify to her the grade they feel they deserve. It’s not an automatic A-plus.

Kehraj says another aspect of alternative grading is to lower the stakes of grading for students.

“A lot of faculty have raised concerns over the last couple of years that students are being driven more and more to being focused on letter grades and GPAs,” he said. “And when students are under pressure and are feeling stressed about grades, it can lead them towards making poor decisions around academic misconduct.”

That includes the use (and misuse) of artificial intelligence. “And so what we can do in terms of relieving the grade pressure on students May also have a positive benefit in encouraging academic integrity.”

Kheraj explained that one course he teaches involves 10 lab sessions. “But students will only be graded on eight. So the students can effectively choose which of the 10 that they want to be graded on, and they May have areas that they feel like they really want to pick up skills or knowledge in, and so they’ll focus on those.”

He added: “It also has this happy side effect of giving students some flexibility. If, for example, that week they’re sick or they’ve got work and they’re unable to attend, that’s not a big deal.”

It’s also a question of semantics as to whether alternative grading is really such a new idea. The website Grading for Growth points out that, in the thousand-year history of Western universities, so-called traditional grading only took hold in the last 130 years or so. In many ways, this is a return to older methods. (Grading for Growth also features an article that spells out “When Not to Use Alternative Grading.”)

“The big takeaway I hope for people is it can be a way to improve how we engage students,” said Kheraj. “Sometimes the grading method can make students either feel a little bit remote from the course, or that it’s kind of a game that you have to beat, and if you can figure your way around the grading method, you can get through the course.

“But alternative grading hopefully has students engage more meaningfully with the content of the course and achieve more meaningful learning outcomes.”

Chris Knight is a long-time reporter/critic/editor at National Post with a special interest in science, space and movies.

stories.title: Ottawa adds Northwest Territories highway to major projects list
stories.summary: Proposed Mackenzie Valley Highway could make deliveries more reliable, open opportunities for resource extraction
stories.author: Brittany Hobson
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney is fast-tracking federal approvals for a proposed 800-kilometre all-season highway in northern Canada that Ottawa says would cut driving distances, unlock more resource development and bolster Arctic security.

During a visit to Yellowknife on Friday, the Prime Minister designated the Mackenzie Valley Highway as a “project of national interest.” The government says this will speed up federal permitting, though the plan still requires an assessment by the Mackenzie Valley environmental impact review board.

The designation “ensures that everyone involved knows where we stand on a major project: communities, Indigenous governments, the territory, and the workers and businesses who will build it,” Mr. Carney said.

Ottawa said in backgrounder documents Friday that the capital cost for construction is expected to be $4.2-billion. The government has already committed to fully fund the highway’s construction and certain maintenance costs, including through funding in Budget 2026 and investments under the government’s Arctic Infrastructure Fund.

The planned route, entirely within the Northwest Territories, would run from Wrigley, at the end of the current all-season highway, to the Dempster Highway south of Inuvik.

Mr. Carney said this new highway would cut more than 1,000 kilometres from the route between military Forward Operating Locations in Yellowknife and Inuvik used by the North American Aerospace Defence Command (Norad), the joint Canada-U.S. command that guards North American skies.

These forward operating locations are northern airfields from which Norad can temporarily deploy fighter jets and support crews. These provide hangars, fuel and accommodations to support fighter squadrons.

Earlier this year, Ottawa earmarked nearly $35-billion to upgrade military installations in the North aimed at defending against threats to North America and asserting territorial sovereignty in the Arctic. These include the Forward Operating Locations in Yellowknife, Inuvik and Iqaluit, as well as the Deployed Operating Base at 5 Wing Goose Bay in Labrador.

“As we bolster our military presence, this highway will facilitate the transport of personnel, equipment, and supplies throughout the Western Arctic,” Mr. Carney said Friday.

Ottawa has set 2032 as a target for completion of this highway, pending environmental assessments. Construction could begin in late 2027 if the plans are approved.

It’s likely Canada will end up counting its spending on the highway construction as part of its Nato pledge to spend 1.5 per cent of gross domestic product annually on security and defence related infrastructure. It’s part of a 5 per cent of GDP target to be reached in the coming years.

David Perry, president of the Canadian Global Affairs Institute, a think tank, said the highway could have an indirect benefit on security in the region and lower costs for supplying the upgrades to forward operating locations or fuel transfers.

However he noted the military has successfully operated these locations for decades without the Mackenzie Valley Highway. “The military does not require the highway’s completion to make them serviceable. But it could help.”

Mr. Carney said the project will provide northern Canadians with reliable transportation in a region where climate change is affecting the duration of ice roads and the water levels for barges.

“The Mackenzie Valley Highway will change that. It will mean more reliable and affordable access to food, fuel, and essentials. More opportunities to visit loved ones, access medical care, and pursue stable, high-paying careers,” he said.

Bob Zimmer, Conservative critic for Arctic affairs and northern economic development, said the federal government has repeatedly promised to support the Mackenzie Valley Highway, yet the start date for construction remains elusive. “This is the sixth time this Liberal government has made an announcement on this project, and the fourth time a member of the Liberal cabinet has flown to Northwest Territories to do so,” he said.

“Every few months brings a new press conference or a new process. People in Wrigley, Tulita, Norman Wells and Fort Good Hope don’t need another announcement. They need shovels in the ground,” the Conservative MP said.

The federal government said the highway would improve transportation access for more than 10,000 people, including approximately 1,900 people in the central Sahtu Region who would gain access to an all-season road connection for the first time. In addition, it would cut the drive between Yellowknife and Inuvik from approximately 38 hours to an estimated 23 hours.

Ottawa also said the project would create 3,000 jobs at peak construction. The highway would also unlock opportunities for local businesses, trade and tourism activity, while supporting new resource exploration and development, the government said.

While Ottawa’s major projects office helps co-ordinate regulatory processes, the federal government is also planning to launch a new Crown corporation in the coming months to manage development and construction of complex major projects.

The Mackenzie Valley Highway would be the initial focus of the new major projects management entity, it said.

It’s likely Canada will end up counting its spending on the highway construction as part of its Nato pledge to spend 1.5 per cent of gross domestic product annually on security and defence related infrastructure. It’s part of a 5 per cent of GDP target to be reached in the coming years.

David Perry, president of the Canadian Global Affairs Institute, a think tank, said the highway could have an indirect benefit on security in the region and lower costs for supplying the upgrades to forward operating locations or fuel transfers.

However he noted the military has successfully operated these locations for decades without the Mackenzie Valley Highway. “The military does not require the highway’s completion to make them serviceable. But it could help.”
Mr. Carney said the project will provide northern Canadians with reliable transportation in a region where climate change is affecting the duration of ice roads and the water levels for barges.

“The Mackenzie Valley Highway will change that. It will mean more reliable and affordable access to food, fuel, and essentials. More opportunities to visit loved ones, access medical care, and pursue stable, high-paying careers,” he said.

Bob Zimmer, Conservative critic for Arctic affairs and northern economic development, said the federal government has repeatedly promised to support the Mackenzie Valley Highway, yet the start date for construction remains elusive. “This is the sixth time this Liberal government has made an announcement on this project, and the fourth time a member of the Liberal cabinet has flown to Northwest Territories to do so,” he said.

“Every few months brings a new press conference or a new process. People in Wrigley, Tulita, Norman Wells and Fort Good Hope don’t need another announcement. They need shovels in the ground,” the Conservative MP said.

The federal government said the highway would improve transportation access for more than 10,000 people, including approximately 1,900 people in the central Sahtu Region who would gain access to an all-season road connection for the first time. In addition, it would cut the drive between Yellowknife and Inuvik from approximately 38 hours to an estimated 23 hours.

Ottawa also said the project would create 3,000 jobs at peak construction. The highway would also unlock opportunities for local businesses, trade and tourism activity, while supporting new resource exploration and development, the government said.

While Ottawa’s major projects office helps co-ordinate regulatory processes, the federal government is also planning to launch a new Crown corporation in the coming months to manage development and construction of complex major projects.
The Mackenzie Valley Highway would be the initial focus of the new major projects management entity, it said.

stories.title: Carney lists N.W.T’s Mackenzie Valley Highway as project of national interest
stories.summary: The proposed 800-kilometre highway would offer year-round access to isolated communities in the North and is expected to open new opportunities in the Arctic.
stories.author: Brittany Hobson
stories.content:
The federal government is prioritizing construction of a critical roadway in the Northwest Territories by designating the Mackenzie Valley Highway as a project of national interest.

The proposed 800-kilometre highway would offer year-round access to isolated communities in the North and is expected to open new opportunities for resource extraction and security in the Arctic.

Once complete, the highway would run the length of the Mackenzie River, north of Wrigley, before connecting with the Dempster Highway, south of Inuvik.

The federal government says this would cut the 28-hour drive from Yellowknife to Inuvik down to 15 hours and make deliveries of food, medicine and construction materials in the region more reliable.

Prime Minister Mark Carney made the announcement Friday in Yellowknife alongside N.W.T. Premier R.J. Simpson. The territorial government is the primary proponent of the project.

Designating a project in the national interest under the Building Canada Act means Ottawa plans to streamline federal regulatory approvals and other reviews needed to get a development moving.

The Mackenzie Valley Highway is the first project in the North named to the major projects list. Ottawa listed the Pacific Link oil pipeline and a planned expansion to the Port of Vancouver as projects of national interest in October.

The federal government said in its budget tabled earlier this month that it would fully cover the costs of construction and some maintenance expenses for the Mackenzie Valley Highway. Ottawa also pledged $405 million toward the project through the Arctic Infrastructure Fund in September.

The federal government put $3.1 billion aside in Budget 2026 for the highway. Ottawa said in backgrounder documents Friday that the capital cost for construction is expected to be $4.2 billion.

Government officials who briefed reporters ahead of the announcement said estimates for the maintenance share of the highway haven’t been finalized.

While the major projects office helps co-ordinate regulatory processes, the federal government is also planning to launch a new Crown corporation in the coming months to manage development and construction of complex major projects.

The Mackenzie Valley Highway would be the initial focus of the new major projects management entity.

On Wednesday, the federal and territorial governments signed a leadership governance understanding for the project with Sahtu Secretariat Incorporated, Gwich’in Tribal Council and Pehdzeh Ki First Nation.

A government news release says the agreement establishes a “collaborative framework for the highway’s governance, planning and long-term direction” with its Indigenous partners in the region.

The project remains subject to a pending impact assessment review by the Mackenzie Valley Environmental Impact Review Board.

If approved, construction could begin in late 2027.

stories.title: Business Cares kicks off annual food drive and is asking for donations
stories.summary: London's Business Cares Food Drive has launched it's annual campaign with donation box's around the city. This...
stories.author: Owen Schuller
stories.content:
London’s Business Cares Food Drive has launched it’s annual campaign with donation box’s around the city.

This is the 27th year for the drive which invites business owners to run company-wide donations. This year’s drive starts as grocery prices continue to rise, and more families struggle to afford groceries.

The Crouch Neighbourhood Resource Centre has seen a 30 percent increase of people using their community cupboard in just the past 6 months, according to Steacy Martin the Executive Director of Crouch.

Food banks have reported they need more people than ever to donate, as more families are relying on banks..

With grocery costs continuing to affect families, Business Cares is looking to provide support to Londoners struggling to afford food through the annual food drive.

“Affordability is a growing challenge across the country,” said Mayor Josh Morgan who was at the Wednesday launch.

“We got to recognize that each and everyone of those items, each and everyone of those dollars, is taking a little bit of stress off of people who need that this time of year and need it all year long,” he said.

Business Cares. Photo Credit: Owen Schuller

“Current demand at the London Food Bank is up two per cent over the same time as last year, which doesn’t sound like a lot, however, this is on top of almost 50 per cent over the past three years,” said Wayne Dunn the Chair of Business Cares Food Drive.

Dunn said they campaign is looking for non perishable items, nutritional items, and female products.

“What we’re really pushing for is that low sodium products, low sugar, penult butter, baby food, baby formula, feminine products, cereals preferably non sugar.”

Dunn said Business Cares has moved more towards nutrition and the shift is going well.

“Business Cares over the last 10 years has really moved into nutrition, and I think we’ve done a really good job on it,” he said.

When it comes to donations, Dunn said going through their website and going to grocery stores is the best way to donate.

“They go online “BusinessCares.CA”, they can go in to any grocery store in the city of London this coming Saturday and Sunday.”

Business Cares Food Drive is hosting more events throughout the next few weeks that can be found here: Events – Business Cares Food Drive.

The final event they host is The Morning of Celebration, which takes place at the Western Fair Agriplex on Dec. 18.

stories.title: Montreal light-rail trains evacuated overnight on Champlain Bridge
stories.summary: Two Montreal light-rail trains were evacuated in the middle of the night after coming to a stop on the Champlain Bridge.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Two Montreal light-rail trains were evacuated in the middle of the night after coming to a stop on the Champlain Bridge.

According to the company that operates the Réseau express métropolitain, or REM, the stoppage was due to an issue with the wires that supply electricity to the trains.

Pulsar says a total of 14 passengers were safely escorted away.

The company did not immediately specify the cause of the problem with the wires or whether it was related to weather conditions.

Environment Canada had forecast two to ten millimetres of freezing rain for Friday in the Montreal area.

The latest stoppage comes days after Pulsar released a new plan to improve the Rem’s winter performance after a number of service disruptions in recent years.

stories.title: Seven teams chosen for 24 Sussex Drive design competition
stories.summary: The federal government says seven teams have been selected to take part in a design competition to restore the prime minister’s official residence at 24 Sussex Drive in Ottawa. The 35-room mansion was built over 1867 and 1868 as a private residence. It was expropriated in 1949 to become the official residence of the prime […]
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Catherine Morrison, The Canadian Press

Posted November 27, 2026 1:46 pm.

Last Updated November 27, 2026 1:59 pm.

The federal government says seven teams have been selected to take part in a design competition to restore the prime minister’s official residence at 24 Sussex Drive in Ottawa.

The 35-room mansion was built over 1867 and 1868 as a private residence.

It was expropriated in 1949 to become the official residence of the prime minister, though it has been vacant since 2015.

A Public Services and Procurement Canada news release says the next phase of the competition will be launched in January 2027 and will task the teams with developing “bold and innovative” designs for the property.

It says their proposals will help shape a modern, sustainable, secure and functional official residence that meets the needs of future prime ministers and their families.

The department says the successful design team is expected to be chosen and announced by Canada Day next year.

stories.title: Project to boost Trans Mountain pipeline flows starts up ahead of schedule
stories.summary: New chemical additives increase pipeline’s capacity by about 10%
stories.author: Lauren Krugel
stories.content:
A project to increase the amount of crude that can flow on the Trans Mountain Pipeline using chemical additives has been completed two months ahead of schedule, the Crown corporation said as it released third-quarter results on Friday.

The drag-reducing agent increases the pipeline’s capacity by up to about 10 per cent to 980,000 barrels per day. Trans Mountain carries oil from the Edmonton area to Burnaby, B.C.

“We started moving more volume in October and basically are full here in November and expect to be full in December,” Trans Mountain CEO Mark Maki said in an interview.

When Trans Mountain sought bids from customers this summer to ship more of their oil on the line, demand was 5½ times what was being offered.

A further expansion of 210,000 barrels per day, using new pipeline segments and pump stations, is expected to come into service by the end of 2028, bringing the system’s total capacity to 1.19 million barrels a day.

During the third quarter, Trans Mountain shipped 840,000 barrels per day on average, up from 777,000 barrels during the same three months of 2025. About 60 per cent of the throughput during the period went to the Westridge Marine Terminal, with most of the oil-laden tankers sailing across the Pacific to Asian customers, Maki said. The rest went to delivery points in B.C. and Washington State via pipeline.

Net income for the quarter rose to $132-million from $127-million as revenues increased to $825-million from $765-million.

So far this year, Trans Mountain has paid $1.45-billion to its owner, the federal government, in interest payments, dividends and return of capital distributions. For the quarter, a total of $551-million went to Ottawa.

Ottawa bought the pipeline for $4.5-billion in 2018 after Kinder Morgan Canada walked away from a project to triple the line’s capacity at the time, amid fierce environmental opposition and court challenges. It ended up costing more than $34-billion by the time the expanded pipeline started up in May of 2024.

Federal and Trans Mountain officials have said there is no rush to return the pipeline to the private sector. Some Indigenous groups have long expressed interest taking a stake in the pipeline.

Trans Mountain said in its Friday news release that confidential information sessions with potential Indigenous partners began in October. Meetings have been held in Edmonton, Kamloops, Victoria and Vancouver and were well attended, Maki said.

As for when a deal might be announced, “it’ll take a while,” he added.

“There’s lots of nations and lots of considerations that they have to think through.”

Meanwhile, Trans Mountain is taking the lead on the development of the Pacific Link pipeline, a new million-barrel-a-day oil pipeline proposed by the Alberta government that would largely follow the same path as Trans Mountain, ending at a port in Delta, B.C.

Pacific Link has been designated a project of national interest, meaning it’s being guided through a streamlined regulatory process under the federal major projects office.

Before the major projects office was set up last year, a regulatory application for a project the scale of the Trans Mountain expansion completed a few years ago would have been gargantuan – filling binders lining the entire length of a boardroom table, Maki said.

“What I expect the application for the next project to be is much skinnier, so it’s changed a lot,” he said.

The changes to the process have been welcomed among those working on new projects under the new regime, but it has taken a “mindset shift,” Maki added.

“Perfection was probably the aiming point for that first filing. Here, the expectation is, it’s got to be good. And then there’ll be the expectation of some updating, refinements, changes which are effectively in process.”

At least 17 First Nations in Alberta and B.C., one U.S. tribe in Washington State and one individual have filed legal challenges against Pacific Link’s national interest designation, according to a news release Thursday distributed by the St’at’imc Chiefs Council. The St’at’imc Nation and T’Sou-ke First Nation earlier this month filed a joint application to quash Ottawa’s decision on the pipeline proposal.

In an interview earlier this week, federal Natural Resources Minister Tim Hodgson said the major projects office and Canada Energy Regulator will be holding comprehensive consultations on the project.

“I am confident we will find a path forward,” he said. “Will there be hiccups and bumps along the way? Sure, maybe. But I am confident that we can find a win-win by working together.”

Editor’s note: An earlier version of this story incorrectly stated the total daily capacity of the Trans Mountain pipeline with its upcoming expansion. It is 1.19 million barrels.

stories.title: Ottawa lists Mackenzie Valley Highway as project of national interest
stories.summary: The prime minister's announcement with Northwest Territories Premier R.J. Simpson has been billed as one that would "connect and transform Canada’s North."
stories.author: Brittany Hobson The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Yellowknife - The federal government on Friday prioritized construction of a critical road in the Northwest Territories by designating the Mackenzie Valley Highway as a project of national interest.

The proposed 800-kilometre highway would offer year-round access to isolated communities in the North and is expected to open new opportunities for resource extraction and security in the Arctic.

Once complete, it would run the length of the Mackenzie River, north of Wrigley, before connecting with the Dempster Highway, south of Inuvik.

Ottawa said this would reduce the road distance between Yellowknife and Inuvik by 1,300 kilometres, cutting a 38-hour drive to 23 hours, and making deliveries of food, medicine and construction materials in the region more reliable.

The project is 70 years in the making, Prime Minister Mark Carney told a news conference in Yellowknife.

“Generations of northerners have waited for this moment. I have myself,” said Carney, who was born in the territory town of Fort Smith.

“These roads will open the way to better lives, more opportunities and a stronger more sovereign Canada.

“It is beyond time, beyond time to connect the North.”

Previous federal and territorial governments have supported construction of the highway. Various iterations of the proposed road have been studied since 1958.

Ottawa said more than 10,000 people, or roughly 22 per cent of the territory’s population across 12 communities, would benefit from improved transportation access. That includes the 1,900 in the Sahtu region, who would gain access to an all-season road for the first time.

The major projects office estimates about 3,000 workers would be employed at the peak of construction.

The federal government put $3.1 billion aside in Budget 2026 for the highway. Ottawa said in background documents on Friday that the capital cost for construction is expected to be $4.2 billion.

Government officials who briefed reporters ahead of the announcement said estimates for the maintenance share of the highway haven’t been finalized.

The territorial government is the primary proponent of the Mackenzie Valley Highway project.

N.W.T. Premier R.J. Simpson, standing with Carney at the announcement, said the highway is key to unlocking mineral and petroleum resources and providing economic opportunities.

He said everyone in territory who is able and willing to work on the project will get the opportunity.

“Construction of the Mackenzie Valley Highway alone will take more workers than we have in the territory, so we know we’ll need support from our southern neighbours,” Simpson said.

Designating a project in the national interest under the Building Canada Act means Ottawa plans to streamline federal regulatory approvals and other reviews needed to get a development moving.

The Mackenzie Valley Highway is the first project in the North named to the major projects list. Ottawa listed the Pacific Link oil pipeline and a planned expansion to the Port of Vancouver as projects of national interest in October.

The federal government said in its budget tabled earlier this month that it would fully cover the costs of construction and some maintenance expenses for the Mackenzie Valley Highway. Ottawa also pledged $405 million toward the project through the Arctic Infrastructure Fund in September.

While the major projects office helps co-ordinate regulatory processes, the federal government is also planning to launch a new Crown corporation in the coming months to manage development and construction of complex major projects.

The government said the Mackenzie Valley Highway would be the initial focus of the new major projects management entity.

The highway remains subject to treaty-based environmental assessment and regulatory processes.

If approved, construction of the Mackenzie Valley Highway could begin in late 2027.

On Wednesday, the federal and territorial governments signed a leadership governance understanding for the project with Sahtu Secretariat Inc., Gwich’in Tribal Council and Pehdzeh Ki First Nation.

A government news release said the agreement establishes a “collaborative framework for the highway’s governance, planning and long-term direction” with its Indigenous partners in the region.

The road would connect to several communities, including Fort Good Hope on the east bank of the Mackenzie River. It’s accessible by the river in the summer and by air year-round.

“I’m just really happy today that this has finally been announced. We’ve got some things to look forward to,” Chief Shawn Grandjambe said after the announcement.

He said the highway would provide financial relief to residents who face high costs of shipping in food and other goods. They would have the option of driving south for shopping.

Grandjambe and other northern leaders have said they’re concerned about increased access to drugs and alcohol.

“It’s there already. Right now, we just got to try and figure a way of how we can control the flow of it coming in,” said Grandjambe.

Bob Zimmer, federal Conservative critic for Arctic affairs and the Canadian Northern Economic Development Agency, said northern communities don’t need more announcements.

“They need shovels in the ground,” he said in a statement. “Northerners have heard plenty of promises but they are still waiting for a road.”

Mackenzie Valley Highway is part of what Ottawa has dubbed the “Northern Resilience Projects.”

The Grays Bay project would see a 230-kilometre all-season road run from the Northwest Territories-Nunavut boundary and stop at the Arctic coast, where there would be a port.

The Arctic Economic and Security Corridor is a proposed 400-kilometre, all-season road that would stretch north of Yellowknife and connect to Grays Bay road.

And the Taltson Hydro Expansion Project would double the hydro capacity in the Northwest Territories.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 27, 2026.

— With files from Craig Lord in Ottawa

Note to readers:This is a corrected story. A previous version said the Mackenzie Valley Highway would cut the 28-hour drive from Yellowknife to Inuvik down to 15 hours. It also said the Whitehorse Power Centres project was deemed in the national interest.

“I’m just really happy today that this has finally been announced. We’ve got some things to look forward to,” Chief Shawn Grandjambe said after the announcement.
He said the highway would provide financial relief to residents who face high costs of shipping in food and other goods. They would have the option of driving south for shopping.
Grandjambe and other northern leaders have said they’re concerned about increased access to drugs and alcohol.
“It’s there already. Right now, we just got to try and figure a way of how we can control the flow of it coming in,” said Grandjambe.
Bob Zimmer, federal Conservative critic for Arctic affairs and the Canadian Northern Economic Development Agency, said northern communities don’t need more announcements.
“They need shovels in the ground,” he said in a statement. “Northerners have heard plenty of promises but they are still waiting for a road.”
Mackenzie Valley Highway is part of what Ottawa has dubbed the “Northern Resilience Projects.”
The Grays Bay project would see a 230-kilometre all-season road run from the Northwest Territories-Nunavut boundary and stop at the Arctic coast, where there would be a port.
The Arctic Economic and Security Corridor is a proposed 400-kilometre, all-season road that would stretch north of Yellowknife and connect to Grays Bay road.
And the Taltson Hydro Expansion Project would double the hydro capacity in the Northwest Territories.

stories.title: Buy Canadian movement challenged during the holiday season and Black Friday
stories.summary: It's Black Friday, and many small businesses in Canada that have been benefiting from the Buy Canadian movement say this time of year is one of the most challenging financially.
stories.author: Ariel Rabinovitch
stories.content:
Black Friday unofficially kicks off the holiday shopping season, but many small businesses in Canada that have benefited from the Buy Canadian movement say this time of year is one of the most financially challenging.

According to two survey reports released this week, small businesses face cost pressures from higher gas prices and newly imposed U.S. tariffs, and even if the Buy Canadian movement keeps its momentum through the holiday shopping season, it’s not guaranteed to boost small businesses.

Half of 92 small businesses surveyed last month by Merchant Growth, a small business financer, said they expect higher holiday sales this year, and only six per cent expect a decline, down from 25 per cent in 2025.

But the holiday rush demands cash up front — for inventory, extra staff, decorations and more — and 24 per cent of small businesses say they can’t cover it.

“Small businesses have faced three to four years of challenge, rising prices, many of them didn’t raise prices for the first couple of years, and that caused their own financial cushion to get eroded,” says Hash Aboulhosn, chief growth officer at Merchant Growth.

“Now they’re presented with the present moment really coming at it from a position of weakness, unfortunately, rather than one of strength.”

The deeper pockets of big box stores and online retailers also make it hard for small businesses during the holidays, with about a fifth (21 per cent) citing this as a barrier.

A total of 1,675 small business owners participated in a Canadian Federation of Independent Business (Cfib) study last month and said they were concerned about cost pressures, including from newly imposed tariffs, trade uncertainty and consumer spending.

Thirty-two per cent said they expect the holidays to turn out positive or profitable, while nearly six in 10 anticipate flat or weak results.

Nearly three quarters (73 per cent) said they were concerned about how consumers faced with cost pressures could impact their holiday sales.

But many consumers are willing to pay more for Canadian-made goods, according to a survey by PricewaterhouseCoopers released last month.

Nearly three out of four (72 per cent) of participants in that survey said they were seeking alternatives to U.S.-made goods, with more than half (54 per cent) saying they will be willing to pay more for goods made in Canada. This is despite budget pressures, which have meant Canadians plan to spend 11 per cent less on holiday shopping overall, it added.

“There’s a lot of positive sentiment around buying Canadian for consumers to help businesses in their community, but at the same time, small businesses are not necessarily seeing the outcome of that in their data,” says Aboulhosn.

Consumers feeling compelled to support local Canadian businesses amid the trade war with the U.S. May face a difficult choice between the value offered by larger retailers, including American ones, and paying more to support local.

That May be an especially tough decision for many as higher gas prices and inflation have been eating into household budgets, forcing many to cut back and look for deals wherever they can.

For businesses that are struggling with higher costs but also want to meet consumers where they are, Aboulhosn says it May be about finding a compromise.

“Canadians certainly indicated an intention and a desire to buy Canadian, and while it hasn’t necessarily shown up in a big way, certainly the sentiment is there,” he says.

“Switching buyer and buying patterns takes mental effort and it involves higher costs, and so I encourage businesses to meet their clients halfway.”

– with a file from Global News’ Uday Rana

stories.title: Costco’s return policy pushed a Toronto rug supplier to the brink, lawsuit alleges
stories.summary: A Toronto rug manufacturer is suing Costco Wholesale Canada Ltd. over a return policy it says has put its entire business in jeopardy.
stories.author: Tara Deschamps
stories.content:
A Toronto rug manufacturer is suing Costco Wholesale Canada Ltd. over a return policy it says has put its entire business in jeopardy.

The lawsuit filed in an Ontario court in May paints Amskor Corp. as a humble manufacturer whose 2017 arrangement to supply the U.S. retail giant with area rugs quickly morphed into a more stable, high-volume partnership.

But almost a decade later, Amskor is alleging it had to close two distribution centres and cut staff because the specifics of Costco’s supplier agreements and return program have become so untenable.

“They preach that they are really loyal to their vendors and everything and we really, truly believed it, but our experience tells us that it’s really nothing more than marketing,” said Saeid Korhani, a third-generation carpet salesman who’s been in the industry for 44 years.

He runs Amskor, a roughly 20-year-old business which sells products under the CAM Living label.

The company is suing Costco for breach of contract, negligent misrepresentation and unjust enrichment. It is asking for about $9 million in damages.

The allegations have yet to be tested in court.

Costco and its lawyers did not respond to requests for comment and have not filed a statement of defence, which would lay out its rebuttals to Amskor’s claims.

Instead, according to legal documents provided by Korhani, the retailer has asked for the case to be sent to arbitration rather than heard by the courts. According to the documents, Costco said Amskor “improperly” launched the lawsuit because both sides previously “contractually agreed” to use arbitration for disagreements stemming from their contract.

The Canadian Press was not able to confirm whether Costco had filed the motion with the court.

The lawsuit sheds light on how one supplier feels squeezed by Costco’s return policy, which consumers praise as one of the most generous in Canada.

The return policy listed on Costco’s website broadly says, “we guarantee your satisfaction on every product we sell and will refund your purchase price.” There are exceptions for certain electronics, as well as diamonds, gold bars, cigarettes, event tickets and select other products. It does not specify time limitations or other terms for many products.

On web forums and social media, customers report examples of the retailer taking back half-eaten food, years-old stained furniture, used batteries and even fresh-cut flowers weeks after they were purchased.

When products are returned, Amskor alleges that Costco charges suppliers by subtracting the value of returns from payments owed. The retailer then chooses — often without suppliers knowing — whether to restock, discount or dispose of the products brought back, the company’s statement of claim said.

Amskor’s brush with Costco’s return policy began in 2017, when the business headquartered in Toronto’s north end started supplying the U.S. retail giant with carpets and area rugs.

Within a year, the two sides were working to ramp up their relationship into a year-round affair, where Amskor would supply two sizes of shag rugs — thick carpets versatile enough to accent most areas of a home.

The smaller of the two sizes would sell for up to $289 elsewhere and the larger for about $500, but Korhani said Costco “negotiated very hard” to offer them for $99 and $199, respectively. (Years into the agreement, Costco agreed to pandemic- and shipping-related cost increases.)

Amskor alleges in the court documents that Costco wanted to position the rugs as a loss leader — an item offered at a price below its market cost to attract customers and boost sales of other merchandise.

Amskor said the only way its Turkey production facilities could offer a program pricing rugs at or near cost was if Costco was selling a high volume of carpets — and not processing a high number of returns.

Amskor alleges Costco led it to believe that returns would remain within “a defined and commercially manageable range” of about four to five per cent and requested Amskor open a west coast distribution centre in Vancouver to support the expanded business the partnership would bring in.

While Amskor would have preferred to sell its rugs at a higher price, Korhani agreed to Costco’s demands in 2019 because the retailer’s customer base is so big, it felt “exciting” to land the company’s business and expose Amskor to an even broader audience, he said in an interview. He said he was also enticed because the retailer dangled possible opportunities to periodically carry additional Amskor products in the future.

Throughout their interactions, Amskor alleges Costco didn’t disclose the specifics of its return program the carpetmaker now sees as “limitless.”

Amskor claims it shouldered the cost of any returns without knowing whether Costco choose to restock, resell, discount or salvage the items brought back.

In the first years of supplying Costco, Amskor said it operated with the expectation that returns would amount to about four and five per cent of gross sales annually. The supplier alleges Costco led it to believe returns would remain within that kind of “manageable” range.

Korhani says that with little insight into returns, Amskor asked Costco in June 2022 to send it any returned rugs. Korhani says he wanted to resell them himself rather than let Costco flip them to customers or liquidators. Costco was not responsive to this request, Amskor’s statement of claim said.

By 2023, Amskor alleges the number of rugs being brought back was increasing. In 2024, it reached 20 per cent at times and it peaked at 28 per cent last year, according to the claim.

Korhani, whose business was now shouldering millions in costs for far more returns than it anticipated, couldn’t understand the rise because there were no changes to Amskor’s manufacturing or materials.

“We don’t cut corners,” he said.

“They preach that they are really loyal to their vendors and everything and we really, truly believed it, but our experience tells us that it’s really nothing more than marketing,” said Saeid Korhani, a third-generation carpet salesman who’s been in the industry for 44 years.
He runs Amskor, a roughly 20-year-old business which sells products under the CAM Living label.
The company is suing Costco for breach of contract, negligent misrepresentation and unjust enrichment. It is asking for about $9 million in damages.
The allegations have yet to be tested in court.
Costco and its lawyers did not respond to requests for comment and have not filed a statement of defence, which would lay out its rebuttals to Amskor’s claims.

Instead, according to legal documents provided by Korhani, the retailer has asked for the case to be sent to arbitration rather than heard by the courts. According to the documents, Costco said Amskor “improperly” launched the lawsuit because both sides previously “contractually agreed” to use arbitration for disagreements stemming from their contract.
The Canadian Press was not able to confirm whether Costco had filed the motion with the court.
The lawsuit sheds light on how one supplier feels squeezed by Costco’s return policy, which consumers praise as one of the most generous in Canada.

The return policy listed on Costco’s website broadly says, “we guarantee your satisfaction on every product we sell and will refund your purchase price.” There are exceptions for certain electronics, as well as diamonds, gold bars, cigarettes, event tickets and select other products. It does not specify time limitations or other terms for many products.

On web forums and social media, customers report examples of the retailer taking back half-eaten food, years-old stained furniture, used batteries and even fresh-cut flowers weeks after they were purchased.

When products are returned, Amskor alleges that Costco charges suppliers by subtracting the value of returns from payments owed. The retailer then chooses — often without suppliers knowing — whether to restock, discount or dispose of the products brought back, the company’s statement of claim said.
Amskor’s brush with Costco’s return policy began in 2017, when the business headquartered in Toronto’s north end started supplying the U.S. retail giant with carpets and area rugs.

Within a year, the two sides were working to ramp up their relationship into a year-round affair, where Amskor would supply two sizes of shag rugs — thick carpets versatile enough to accent most areas of a home.

The smaller of the two sizes would sell for up to $289 elsewhere and the larger for about $500, but Korhani said Costco “negotiated very hard” to offer them for $99 and $199, respectively. (Years into the agreement, Costco agreed to pandemic- and shipping-related cost increases.)

Amskor alleges in the court documents that Costco wanted to position the rugs as a loss leader — an item offered at a price below its market cost to attract customers and boost sales of other merchandise.

Amskor said the only way its Turkey production facilities could offer a program pricing rugs at or near cost was if Costco was selling a high volume of carpets — and not processing a high number of returns.

Amskor alleges Costco led it to believe that returns would remain within “a defined and commercially manageable range” of about four to five per cent and requested Amskor open a west coast distribution centre in Vancouver to support the expanded business the partnership would bring in.

Throughout their interactions, Amskor alleges Costco didn’t disclose the specifics of its return program the carpetmaker now sees as “limitless.”
Amskor claims it shouldered the cost of any returns without knowing whether Costco choose to restock, resell, discount or salvage the items brought back.

In the first years of supplying Costco, Amskor said it operated with the expectation that returns would amount to about four and five per cent of gross sales annually. The supplier alleges Costco led it to believe returns would remain within that kind of “manageable” range.

By 2023, Amskor alleges the number of rugs being brought back was increasing. In 2024, it reached 20 per cent at times and it peaked at 28 per cent last year, according to the claim.

Korhani, whose business was now shouldering millions in costs for far more returns than it anticipated, couldn’t understand the rise because there were no changes to Amskor’s manufacturing or materials.

He said he couldn’t afford to offer those rates to everyone because the deal he agreed to with Costco had already cut so deeply into his margins and profits.

“Once production is disrupted, looms idled or workforce lost, those losses cannot be readily restored,” Amskor’s statement of claim said.
Eventually, Korhani says he had to face reality. Amskor closed its Vancouver distribution centre in February and Oakville, Ont., facility in June, laying off roughly 50 workers in the process.
Korhani was reluctant to file a lawsuit but felt he had no other choice.
“We tried everything and we knew once we filed a lawsuit, we will lose (Costco) forever and that’s a hard decision that we had to make,” Korhani said.
“But otherwise, our business would be closed down, shut down by our financing team, because how much bleeding can you take every year?”

stories.title: Four people, company fined $4.9m in B.C. 'pump-and-dump' securities scheme
stories.summary: Vancouver - Four people and a company have been fined a combined $4.9 million and banned from British Columbia's investment market over what the British Columbia's Security Commission alleges was a "pump-and-dump" scheme.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Vancouver - Four people and a company have been fined a combined $4.9 million and banned from British Columbia’s investment market over what the British Columbia’s Security Commission alleges was a “pump-and-dump” scheme.

A commission panel has found that Core Capital Partners and four people linked to the company participated in conduct that artificially inflated the share prices of two publicly traded companies.

stories.author: Globe Staff
stories.content:
The Globe and Mail is celebrating the launch of The Globe 100 for 2026 - our definitive list of the year’s best reads. Join The Globe’s Judith Pereira and Kasia Mychajlowycz for an evening filled with engaging conversations with some of the most exciting voices in current Canadian literature—multi-award-nominated Emily St. John Mandel and international bestselling Shari Lapena.

stories.title: Ontario calls for changes to self-defence laws after Toronto home invasions
stories.summary: Request was made by Ontario’s Attorney-General Doug Downey and Solicitor-General Michael Kerzner
stories.author: Kathryn Mannie
stories.content:
The Ontario government has called on Ottawa to amend federal law to give Canadians stronger legal protections to confront attackers in their homes after a spate of violent home invasions in Toronto.

The request was made by Ontario’s Attorney-General Doug Downey and Solicitor-General Michael Kerzner in a letter to the federal justice and public safety ministers , asking for more clarity on when people can resort to self-defence to fend off attackers on their property.

They asked that the Criminal Code of Canada be changed to explicitly guarantee that residents do not need to first retreat from their home before relying on self-defence to confront a home invader.

They also called for the Criminal Code to include a list of considerations to help determine if self-defence was reasonable during a home invasion, including whether children were in the home, if someone forced their way in and the time the residents had to respond to the situation.

The requests come after a 39-year-old musician was killed in a home invasion in an affluent Toronto neighbourhood, not long after a family of four was injured in another home invasion in the wealthy Bridle Path area of the city.

Federal law already allows Canadians to – when reasonable – defend themselves from attacks and threats of force and to defend their property.

Mr. Downey and Mr. Kerzner wrote that the changes they’re calling for will “provide greater certainty about how those protections apply during a home invasion.” Premier Doug Ford called them “common-sense changes” that would protect people who defend their homes from criminals.

In a statement to The Canadian Press, a spokesperson for Justice Minister Sean Fraser reaffirmed the right to self-defence already exists and said the federal government has introduced stricter laws to keep violent offenders in prison longer under the Bail and Sentencing Reform Act, which came into force this July.

Joannie Fogue wrote in an e-mail that Ottawa is committed to keeping Canadians safe, but provincial governments are responsible for key parts of the justice system, including policing.

“As threats evolve, our government will keep working with law enforcement and provinces, move with urgency to strengthen Canada’s laws, and keep Canadians safe,” Ms. Fogue wrote.

Mr. Downey and Mr. Kerzner have also asked that Ottawa work with provinces and territories to lay out best practices around claims of self-defence in home-invasion cases.

Asked about Ontario’s requests, Prime Minister Mark Carney pointed to the recently introduced tougher bail and sentencing standards for violent crimes.

“What needs to happen is that those changes move quickly through the system ... so that they are fully applied,” he said Friday at a news conference in Yellowknife.

“We have just made arguably the tightest, the most significant tightening of the Criminal Code in many years, in decades. So we need that to settle first,” he said.

After the fatal Toronto home invasion, Mr. Ford drew headlines and criticism from opposition leaders by encouraging people to use any means necessary to defend their families , including using weapons such as guns, knives and baseball bats.

The Premier also called on the federal government on Thursday to strengthen bail laws and increase mandatory jail time for violent offenders.

Toronto police say there have been 111 home invasions in the city so far this year, up from 93 last year. In 2024 the city saw 149 home invasions.

stories.title: An explainer on the notwithstanding clause and how governments have used it
stories.summary: Montreal - The Supreme Court of Canada largely upheld Quebec's secularism law Friday in a landmark decision that clarifies how governments can use the notwithstanding clause to override certain Charter rights.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
MONTREAL - The Supreme Court of Canada largely upheld Quebec’s secularism law Friday in a landmark decision that clarifies how governments can use the notwithstanding clause to override certain Charter rights.

The country’s highest court confirmed that governments can invoke the clause pre-emptively, before a court has determined whether a law violates the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. The top court also said legislatures can use the notwithstanding clause to override multiple rights at once.

However, the court was divided over whether to declare that Quebec’s secularism law, which bans certain public sector workers from wearing religious symbols on the job, violated Charter rights without striking it down.

Three of the seven justices concluded that the law was incompatible with freedom of religion, freedom of expression and the right to equality.

Here is a look at the notwithstanding clause, which has been increasingly used by provincial governments in recent years:

The notwithstanding clause — or Section 33 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms — gives provincial legislatures or Parliament the ability, through the passage of a law, to override certain Charter protections for up to five years.

The clause in its current form came about as a tool to bring provinces onside with then-prime minister Pierre Trudeau’s signature constitutional project. With Charter negotiations ramping up in the early 1980s, Trudeau didn’t see the need for the clause, but provinces such as Alberta and Saskatchewan wanted an out should they disagree with a decision of the courts. In the end, Trudeau reluctantly agreed.

ITS STRUCTURE

The clause only applies to certain sections of the Charter, including those protecting freedom of religion, freedom of expression, legal rights and most equality rights.

It cannot be used to override gender equality, democratic rights, mobility rights or language rights, including minority-language education rights.

The clause also can’t be used for more than five years at a time, although governments can renew it for additional five-year periods. The time limit is intended to give the public an opportunity to challenge a government’s decision to use the clause in a general election before it can be renewed.

While historically used rarely, the notwithstanding clause has been increasingly invoked by provincial governments in recent years. The federal government has never used it.

Quebec, the only provincial government to oppose the 1982 constitutional agreement, passed legislation that year invoking the clause in every new law until 1985.

In 1986, Saskatchewan used the clause to protect back-to-work legislation, and Quebec used it again in 1988 to protect legislation requiring French-only commercial signs.

Alberta attempted to use the clause in 2000 to limit marriage to a man and a woman, but the definition of marriage falls under federal jurisdiction.

RECENT NOTABLE USES

Quebec pre-emptively invoked the notwithstanding clause in 2019 to shield its secularism law, known as Bill 21, and again in 2022 to protect its French-language law reform, known as Bill 96.

Ontario invoked the clause in 2021 to restore restrictions on third-party election advertising and in 2022 to prevent education workers from striking.

The latter legislation was subsequently repealed.

Saskatchewan used the clause in 2023 to require parental consent for students under 16 who want to change their names or pronouns at school.

In October 2025, Alberta invoked the clause to order some 51,000 striking teachers back to work. It invoked the clause again that December to shield three laws restricting the rights of transgender people.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 27, 2026.

—with files from Erika Morris in Montreal

stories.title: Ukraine urges countries to follow Canada’s lead in barring Russian athletes
stories.summary: Ukraine's sports minister wants other countries to follow Canada's lead in blocking Russian teams from international hockey tournaments.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By The Canadian Press

Posted November 27, 2026 1:04 pm.

Last Updated November 27, 2026 2:13 pm.

Ukraine’s sports minister wants other countries to follow Canada’s lead in blocking Russian teams from international hockey tournaments.

Matviy Bidnyi, in an op-ed published Friday by the Ukrainian news agency RBC-Ukraine, credited diplomatic efforts by Ukrainian government officials for Canada’s decision to bar Russian players from next month’s world junior hockey championship in Edmonton and Red Deer, Alta.

“Canada, one of our most consistent partners since the first days of the full-scale invasion, has shown how this works in practice,” Bidnyi wrote in Ukrainian.

Bidnyi said Canada’s position forced the International Ice Hockey Federation to proceed with the tournament without Russia despite a Court of Arbitration for Sport ruling ordering the reinstatement of Russian teams to five international championships, starting with the world juniors.

“One of my priorities is to extend this mechanism to all hockey competitions and establish it as a systematic approach in partner countries,” Bidnyi wrote.

Bidnyi argued that decisions by international sports arbitration bodies should not supersede the national security and sanctions policies of individual countries. He is pushing for a unified European Union policy restricting Russian participation in international sport.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said earlier this month that Russian players would not be permitted to compete in Canada as long as Russia’s war in Ukraine continues. Ottawa subsequently clarified that Russian players would be barred from the world juniors even if they held valid Canadian visas.

The Iihf announced Wednesday it would challenge the Oct. 30 CAS ruling ordering the reinstatement of Russian teams to five international championships, citing concerns about the impartiality of two of the three arbitrators and their potential links to Russia.

Russia and Belarus have been barred from international hockey since Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, and several European federations have vowed to boycott games if Russia is allowed to compete.

Major sponsors, including Czech automaker Skoda and German workwear company Strauss, have also warned they could withdraw their support for next May’s men’s world championship in Germany if Russia competes.

Bidnyi said Russia’s return to international sport is a Kremlin priority personally overseen by Russian President Vladimir Putin and warned against relying solely on international sports institutions to maintain restrictions.

He said more than 18 EU countries have introduced their own restrictions on Russian participation in sports competitions or supported initiatives restricting funding or the use of Russian symbols.

Seven Russian figure skaters missed a Grand Prix event in Finland last week after the Finnish government barred Russian athletes from entering the country.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 27, 2026.

stories.title: Calgary driver who killed pedestrian, then tried to avoid detection, avoids jail
stories.summary: A conditional sentence 'best engages Parliament’s imperative to reduce incarceration while furthering restorative justice objectives,' said the judge
stories.author: Chris Lambie
stories.content:
A motorist who struck and killed a Calgary pedestrian with his van, fled the scene, then tried to avoid detection by replacing damaged parts on his Dodge Caravan has avoided jail but is now subject to a 579-day conditional sentence that includes performing community service.

Rajnesh Kumar, 48, pleaded guilty in the Alberta Court of Justice to failing to stop after the accident that killed Brandy Hillman on July 21, 2023, around 1:20 a.m.

“Mr. Kumar’s is one of those most agonizing sentencing decisions that must balance the community’s condemnation of a crime committed by an offender with an unblemished past when the case is aggravated by the unimaginable trauma and grief visited on friends and family of the victim whose death he caused,” Justice Anne Brown wrote in the Nov. 23 decision.

The court heard Hillman, 39, was wearing dark clothing, pushing a shopping cart containing personal belongings and was in the northbound lanes with her back to traffic when Kumar hit her.

“She had fentanyl, morphine and other drugs in her system, and was observed to be in a stupor shortly before being hit by Mr. Kumar’s van,” the judge said.

Hillman was thrown approximately 20 metres and the contents of the shopping cart were strewn about the north lanes.

Kumar steered left and avoided Hillman’s body “but did not stop, carrying on several blocks before stopping briefly at a 7-11 store where he purchased cigarettes,” said the decision.

“Over the next two days, Mr. Kumar made a series of repairs and purchases of vehicle parts to mask the damage to his Dodge Caravan caused by the striking of Ms. Hillman.”

Hillman was “deeply loved by many, including two sisters who filed victim impact statements describing their profound grief,” said the decision.

One of Hillman’s sisters wrote “she loved everything and everyone. Her smile and laugh… could light up the darkest of days.”

According to Hillman’s other sister, “Brandy was a beautiful, giant-hearted, kind soul.”

Police found surveillance video from the 7-11 showing Kumar buying cigarettes after the fatal accident and obtained his cellular phone records “documenting repairs to, and purchases of parts for, his van.”

Police arrested Kumar on July 27, 2023, interviewed him, then released the Canadian-Fijian dual citizen without charges.

They arrested Kumar again nearly four months later, ON Dec. 20, 2023, interviewed him again, then charged him.

“His bail hearing could not be accommodated until January 3, 2024. Detained over Christmas, he lost his employment,” said the decision.

Kumar was released on bail conditions that included a driving prohibition “with exceptions for driving himself to and from work and his children to and from school,” said the decision.

Kumar spoke directly to Hillman’s family in court.

“I understand that no words I speak today can undo what has happened or bring the deceased back to her family. I recognize the profound pain, grief and suffering that her death has caused, and I am truly sorry,” he said.

“I know that an apology cannot replace the person you have lost, erase your grief, or make things right. Nevertheless, I want you to know that I carry a profound sense of sorrow for your loss and that my thoughts and prayers are with you.”

The Crown argued Kumar should get between nine and 12 months behind bars. It “strenuously” opposed the imposition of a conditional sentence order (CSO) due to Kumar’s “deliberate efforts to avoid detection by replacing parts on his vehicle.”

Kumar’s lawyer argued for a 20-month conditional sentence, given his guilty plea, lack of criminal record, “genuine remorse,” support from his family, employer and community, and collateral consequence of losing his job after being held in custody for two weeks without a bail hearing.

Kumar, who born and raised in Fiji, emigrated to Canada at the age of 29. He’s worked as a cook, shipper/receiver and forklift operator.

His current employer described Kumar as “reliable, honest and dedicated.”

The author of his pre-sentence report described Kumar as “cooperative and polite,” a man who “accepted responsibility” and “did not attempt to minimize, justify, or rationalize his actions.”

The arrest on Thursday came the same day a report was released that found 'deeply troubling' antisemitism on Canadian university campuses

The Johnston Clock Tower on the University of Guelph's main campus is shown in this Google Maps image. (Google Maps)

Courtney Greenberg

November 27, 2026 at 12:33 p.m.

A man was arrested Thursday after antisemitic graffiti was discovered more than once on the University of Guelph campus, according to police.

There were “numerous incidents of graffiti” reported on the university’s campus, police said in a news release, between Oct. 9 and Nov. 12. The graffiti included anti-Israel messages on university property.

Working together, Guelph police and the university’s campus safety office identified a suspect. A 26-year-old man was charged with mischief under $5,000.

Police did not say if he was a student at the University of Guelph.

In a previous news release, police said since the initial incidents on campus, hate-related graffiti was found in other parts of the city on metal bollards, electrical boxes, a bench, cross walk pole and an abandoned building.

Police said Thursday that they are still investigating instances of graffiti in the the downtown area.

The arrest came on the same day that a report, called the Campus Antisemitism and Student Experiences, was released that found “deeply troubling levels of antisemitism and anti-Jewish attitudes” on Canadian university campuses.

In June, Jewish advocacy group StandWithUs Canada said the Chabad Pop Up of Guelph had been vandalized with anti-Israel graffiti.

For the second time in a month, the Chabad of Guelph was vandalized with anti-Israel graffiti. Look no further for proof that antizionism is a cover for antisemitism. Can an anti-Israel activist explain what a Jewish space has anything to do with Israeli government policy? The… pic.twitter.com/afIfihJvGM — StandWithUs Canada (@StandWithUsCA) June 9, 2026

“Can an anti-Israel activist explain what a Jewish space has anything to do with Israeli government policy? The answer: it isn’t about Israel. It’s an excuse to target Jews,” it said in a post on X.

Courtney Greenberg is a Toronto-based journalist covering breaking news, with a focus on antisemitism in Canada. In 2026, she was a Postmedia Fellow with the Investigative Journalism Bureau, where she worked on in-depth investigations into women’s health and the justice system.
