stories.title: Hoopp names Shrirang Apte as chief investment officer as Wissell announces retirement
stories.summary: Leadership change comes as pension plan evolves how it builds its investment portfolio
stories.author: James Bradshaw
stories.content:
Healthcare of Ontario Pension Plan has named Shrirang Apte as its next chief investment officer and announced that current CIO Michael Wissell plans to retire in January.

Mr. Wissell, 62, has been CIO since 2021 at Hoopp, the $132-billion pension plan that invests on behalf of more than 504,000 members in Ontario’s health care sector. Over that span, the plan’s assets have increased from $77-billion, and it is fully funded with $1.09 in assets for each dollar it expects to pay in pensions.

Mr. Apte is currently a senior managing director and Hoopp’s head of global capital markets. He will start as CIO on Jan. 4, and Mr. Wissell’s last day will be Jan. 15.

“Michael has been a thoughtful and trusted leader whose judgment, experience and commitment to our members have had a lasting impact on Hoopp,” chief executive officer Annesley Wallace said in a statement.

Since Ms. Wallace took over last year , Hoopp has rolled out key structural changes to how it builds its investment portfolio. One is that the plan is shifting toward a “total portfolio approach” – a popular investing philosophy among large pension funds that relies less on rigid targets to divide money between asset classes.

Another is the way Hoopp uses artificial intelligence to analyze the vast troves of data the pension plan collects. That data includes proprietary information from its relationships with financial powerhouses, such as asset managers Blackstone Inc. and BlackRock Inc., hedge funds Citadel Securities LLC and Millennium Management LLC, and banks JPMorgan Chase & Co. and Toronto-Dominion Bank.

“Nobody has more access to information than a Maple Eight pension plan,” Mr. Wissell said in an interview on Friday, referring to the informal group of Canada’s eight largest pension funds. “The hidden reality is we never could read it all, we could never consume it all ... But in an AI world, we’re starting to be able to.”

Those two changes in the way Hoopp invests, which are expected to happen over several years, “are best managed by somebody who can see them from the beginning to the end, and that’s why I think now is the right time to hand the reins to Shrirang,” he said.

Mr. Apte joined Hoopp in 2006 and spent much of his earlier career at the plan in its credit division, overseeing strategies such as derivatives and fixed income.

He is “a very good builder of portfolios” who has delivered strong results for the plan’s capital markets division, Mr. Wissell said. He added that Mr. Apte understands that in this kind of role, “you have to be simultaneously super confident and humble at the same time, and he brings those characteristics.”

In 2025, Hoopp earned a 7.7-per-cent return in a turbulent year when many pension plans were marking down the value of some of their privately owned assets. Mr. Wissell said he is optimistic about the plan’s prospects in an environment where interest rates are higher and some assets are trading at attractive prices. A period of rock-bottom rates were challenging for pension funds that have long-term liabilities that are sometimes indexed to inflation.

“This is absolutely one of the few times I’ve been wholly optimistic because the cost of capital is high, and we’re a big pool of capital deploying it at really good rates of return, every dollar that’s going out the door,” he said.

stories.title: Breakout Canadian artist Brat Star sings about Aritzia sweaters, Lululemon and Canada Goose
stories.summary: ‘I feel like brands are kind of like modern gods,’ the musician says
stories.author: Erica Commisso
stories.content:
On Aritzia Sweater , independent artist Brat Star sings about how her soul is “on fleek” (as in flawless or on point), being tired of clout chasers and feeling “anxious and unstable” but keeping it real.

It’s a song about sticking to who you are and leaning into the things and people you love. And the singer-songwriter gives shape to these themes – comfort, authenticity, affection and familiarity – with the image of an Aritzia cashmere sweater, a clothing item that’s a cult classic for a certain segment of the Canadian population.

Born in the suburbs of Montreal and based in Toronto, the 34-year-old Brat Star – who keeps her legal name under wraps – sings about the everyday items around her, many of which are Canadian. Brands such as Canada Goose, Arc’teryx, Lululemon and, of course, Aritzia all show up as characters in her alt-pop music. Her debut album, Southern Ontario Gothic , which has been described as a love letter to Toronto, dropped in late October to a flurry of media attention and a conversation in Interview Magazine with one of the artist’s personal heroes, singer Clairo.

On the record, Brat Star sings about familiar clothing items – such as Hoka sneakers – as if they are animate, giving them distinct characteristics and personalities.

“I grew up in a working class family in an affluent neighbourhood in Montreal,” said the singer, “so I grew up obsessed with designer names. I would see the rich people wearing Chanel, Dior, whatever, and it always felt so inaccessible. I was always interested in thinking about what it represented.”

She started thinking about how we invest brands and icons with so much meaning.

“I feel like brands are kind of like modern gods, or almost a form of spirituality in this day and age because they’re so immense, powerful, amorphous and made powerful by narrative.”

Aritzia Sweater and other references to Canadian fashion are her way of reclaiming that narrative.

“I’m able to use narrative to give things meaning, so I was like, ‘What do I want to make meaningful?’” the artist said. “For me, that was just the stuff around me, and what I have around me are my dirty sneakers. What I have around me is my Aritzia sweater, my Lululemon ... I wanted to validate where I’m from.”

The brands she references in her music exemplify what it means to be Canadian, she added, because they’re all articulated around function, quality and authenticity.

“It’s not about pizzazz. It’s more stuff to wear that will last a long time.”

To illustrate how fashion can tell a story, Brat Star pointed to her friend Nina Cooren’s label, the Montreal-based Nina Bow.

“I really relate to her ethos. She presents each piece of clothing with a whole narrative world, and she works in an anti-season of fashion. She’ll go piece-by-piece and work on her own time, which I also think is so cool.”

The singer uses her own personal uniform as a way to communicate with audiences, too. This winter, she’ll reach for her turquoise Arc’teryx shell, which she calls a “superhero item” because it’s technically powerful and makes her feel strong and safe. As for the rest of her wardrobe, she makes her allegiance clear.

“I have three colours: blood red, white and black. It’s the Canadian colours, and I throw in the black because I’m not afraid of darkness. I’m not afraid of going through the dark to re-emerge in the light.”

stories.title: Western’s iHEAL program reaches 200 women experiencing intimate partner violence
stories.summary: The iHEAL program developed by Western University researchers supports women experiencing intimate partner violence.
stories.author: Keri Ferguson
stories.content:
More than 200 women experiencing intimate partner violence (IPV) have received support from local public health nurses through a model of care developed by researchers at Western University.

Eight registered nurses with the Middlesex-London Health Unit (MLHU) and Southwestern Public Health (Swph) began providing tailored, individualized care to women last year, by offering the Intervention for Health Enhancement and Living (iHEAL) program.

The evidence-based iHEAL is the only program of its kind to integrate health care and IPV response. It focuses on strengthening women’s health and safety, while helping them build the knowledge, skills, resources and connections they need for long-term healing and self-sufficiency.

“We always tie it back to the health and well-being of the woman, which is a unique entry point, because most services focus more on safety and immediate basic needs,” said Marilyn Ford-Gilboe, a professor in the Arthur Labatt Family School of Nursing in Western’s Faculty of Health Sciences, who led the development of iHEAL in partnership with researchers at the University of British Columbia and University of New Brunswick.

Short-term funding from Ontario’s Ministry of Children, Community and Social Services, through the National Action Plan to End Gender-Based Violence, allowed iHEAL to expand. The Western team and its collaborators investigated whether iHEAL could be successfully integrated into local community services with similar benefits for women shown in earlier studies. The researchers have evaluated the success of iHEAL as it has rolled out across the region by interviewing nurses, organizational leaders, community organizations and women who have completed the program.

The program was developed to address the widespread issue of IPV, which affects more than 40 per cent of women in Canada.

Statistics Canada data shows the rate of police-reported IPV rose for the eighth consecutive year and was 15 per cent higher in 2025 compared to 2018 – sobering statistics as Canada marks 16 Days of Activism Against Gender-based Violence.

“This problem is not going away,” said Ford-Gilboe, who has studied IPV for the past 30 years, with a focus on long-term impacts on women’s health and how poorer health affects women’s safety, economic stability, parenting and quality of life.

iHEAL provides coordinated, wrap-around care, extending existing services and community responses to violence, while reducing strain on the system.

“IPV affects many different parts of women’s lives. It’s not a single-issue problem,” Ford-Gilboe said.

Marilyn Ford-Gilboe

The program takes a broad view of what is needed to improve women’s health, safety and well-being, with nurses supporting each woman to identify her own priorities and set goals to address them.

Key to the program are partnerships between the research team, public health units and community organizations that help connect women to iHEAL and support their access to other services and supports.

Results are showing both strong demand for the program and positive outcomes for women including better physical and mental health, increased confidence in managing daily life and health issues, and focusing more on goals for the future, including returning to work or school.

Across both health units, 95 community partnerships have been established. The program reached near capacity within six months, with 80 per cent of the women who start the program completing it, and 100 per cent reporting it fit their needs.

Community partners have reported that the longer-term, health-focused support offered by iHEAL nurses is unique and fills a critical gap in supports for women experiencing IPV.

“We’ve spent years developing, piloting, refining this program and building the evidence behind it. To get to this point, where what we’ve discovered can be embedded into services in ways that benefit women, is so gratifying,” Ford-Gilboe said.

Specially trained registered nurses deliver the program, which they promote through presentations to community organizations and groups. Community partners, friends or family members May direct women to the program, or women sometimes reach out on their own after seeing posters on iHEAL at childcare centres, churches or libraries.

Once connected, nurses meet with each woman weekly or every two weeks for six to seven months. They talk by phone, online or in person, in a place where the woman feels safe. Participants choose what to focus on, whether that’s health, safety, relationships, social connections, personal growth or access to basic resources. Nurses help the women overcome barriers on the path to achieving those goals, such as getting to appointments, finding safe spaces for their children or arranging interpreters. They also support women to learn about and access other services when needed, including violence services, housing providers, or health care.

### “I came into the program feeling pretty desperate and not sure I could continue with my life, and I left with a five-year plan.” – Testimonial, past iHEAL client

As one of five MLHU public health nurses working within the iHEAL program, Leanne Field has helped her clients manage their physical and mental health, addressing issues including chronic pain, anxiety, depression and lack of sleep. She’s also seen an impact that goes beyond improved health symptoms.

“It’s been incredibly rewarding to see women increase their confidence and self-efficacy and to see their resilience, strengths and skills emerge,” Field said. She has also seen women find new housing and improve relationships with their children or other family members.

Field also appreciated the ongoing support of Ford-Gilboe’s team, which provided training and ensured organizational policies, including those associated with safety, were in place to support the program. The researchers also facilitated a community of practice, offering nurses ongoing support and an opportunity to share their knowledge and experiences.

Evaluation of the program showed high satisfaction from Registered Nurses involved.

“It was really helpful to connect with other nurses, the research team and experts in the field and to gain a solid foundation of knowledge and education going into this work,” Field said. “We also share what we learn from our clients, what the struggles are and what’s most helpful to them.”

With the short-term funding, Southwestern Public Health was able to offer the program to women in rural communities for the first time.

Laura Anguish, program manager of the healthy growth and development team, said community partners responded positively to the program.

“We worked alongside them to complement their work, rather than duplicating services,” she said. “The beauty of the iHEAL is its woman-led philosophy. That means following what the woman wants. Public health nurses are well-trained to pivot and continue to help if priorities change.”

Anguish said rural women experiencing IPV face a unique set of challenges including transportation, isolation and long wait lists for services.

Swph public health nurse Emily Robertson said privacy concerns can also prevent a woman from seeking support.

“In small communities, everyone knows everyone, so we spend a great deal of time and care arranging safe, discreet places to meet,” she said. “Meeting at the library May work for one woman, but it’s not feasible for another, so we meet in many places to safeguard our clients.”

Robertson said she’s been able to watch women transform.

“They start to feel hopeful again. They recognize possibilities for their future and the lives beyond trauma and violence.”

As the short-term initiative wraps up, Ford-Gilboe and the nurses noted the ongoing need for IPV support that also addresses women’s health and well-being.

### “When you only have one option in town, and for whatever reason things have not worked out there, people give up. iHEAL is different enough that women are more open to trying it. Without it, more people will fall through the cracks.” – Testimonial, iHEAL community partner

The specialized expertise of nurses who have offered iHEAL will live on in their work.

“My iHEAL education and knowledge will be a major benefit going forward in all aspects of my job, because IPV is everywhere,” Field added.

She uses the iHEAL app,developed by Ford-Gilboe and her team, to support women between visits and after they completed the program.

The free, private and secure app lets women assess their risk of serious violence, build a safety plan and find resources they can save for later. Field also shares it as a training tool with other nurses, who regularly interact with women and families experiencing IPV.

Robertson added that public awareness and community-led responses are critical to helping women find a path forward.

“I don’t think people really realize the prevalence of IPV in our communities,” Robertson said. “It’s happening everywhere. We need evidence-based interventions like iHEAL to confront intimate partner violence, to advocate for people who May not feel safe, heard or valued and to sustain long-term healing beyond crisis.”

Call or text 988 for free, bilingual mental health support

Use the free, bilingual iHEAL app

To access confidential violence services, call the Ontario Assaulted Women’s Helpline 1-866-863-0511

For services in French, call Fem’aide (Ligne de soutien pour femmes violentées), 1-877-336-2433

Anguish said rural women experiencing IPV face a unique set of challenges including transportation, isolation and long wait lists for services.

“In small communities, everyone knows everyone, so we spend a great deal of time and care arranging safe, discreet places to meet,” she said. “Meeting at the library May work for one woman, but it’s not feasible for another, so we meet in many places to safeguard our clients.”
Robertson said she’s been able to watch women transform.

content_blocks.text: More than 200 women experiencing intimate partner violence (IPV) have received support from local public health nurses through a model of care developed by researchers at Western University.

Eight registered nurses with the Middlesex-London Health Unit (MLHU) and Southwestern Public Health (Swph) began providing tailored, individualized care to women last year, by offering the Intervention for Health Enhancement and Living (iHEAL) program.

The evidence-based iHEAL is the only program of its kind to integrate health care and IPV response. It focuses on strengthening women’s health and safety, while helping them build the knowledge, skills, resources and connections they need for long-term healing and self-sufficiency.

“We always tie it back to the health and well-being of the woman, which is a unique entry point, because most services focus more on safety and immediate basic needs,” said Marilyn Ford-Gilboe, a professor in the Arthur Labatt Family School of Nursing in Western’s Faculty of Health Sciences, who led the development of iHEAL in partnership with researchers at the University of British Columbia and University of New Brunswick.

Short-term funding from Ontario’s Ministry of Children, Community and Social Services, through the National Action Plan to End Gender-Based Violence, allowed iHEAL to expand. The Western team and its collaborators investigated whether iHEAL could be successfully integrated into local community services with similar benefits for women shown in earlier studies. The researchers have evaluated the success of iHEAL as it has rolled out across the region by interviewing nurses, organizational leaders, community organizations and women who have completed the program.
The program was developed to address the widespread issue of IPV, which affects more than 40 per cent of women in Canada.

Statistics Canada data shows the rate of police-reported IPV rose for the eighth consecutive year and was 15 per cent higher in 2025 compared to 2018 – sobering statistics as Canada marks 16 Days of Activism Against Gender-based Violence.

“This problem is not going away,” said Ford-Gilboe, who has studied IPV for the past 30 years, with a focus on long-term impacts on women’s health and how poorer health affects women’s safety, economic stability, parenting and quality of life.

“IPV affects many different parts of women’s lives. It’s not a single-issue problem,” Ford-Gilboe said.
Marilyn Ford-Gilboe
The program takes a broad view of what is needed to improve women’s health, safety and well-being, with nurses supporting each woman to identify her own priorities and set goals to address them.

Key to the program are partnerships between the research team, public health units and community organizations that help connect women to iHEAL and support their access to other services and supports.

Results are showing both strong demand for the program and positive outcomes for women including better physical and mental health, increased confidence in managing daily life and health issues, and focusing more on goals for the future, including returning to work or school.

Across both health units, 95 community partnerships have been established. The program reached near capacity within six months, with 80 per cent of the women who start the program completing it, and 100 per cent reporting it fit their needs.
Community partners have reported that the longer-term, health-focused support offered by iHEAL nurses is unique and fills a critical gap in supports for women experiencing IPV.

“We’ve spent years developing, piloting, refining this program and building the evidence behind it. To get to this point, where what we’ve discovered can be embedded into services in ways that benefit women, is so gratifying,” Ford-Gilboe said.

Specially trained registered nurses deliver the program, which they promote through presentations to community organizations and groups. stories.title: Immigration minister defends levels plan amid heavy criticism
stories.summary: Facing heavy criticism from the Conservatives, Canada’s immigration minister defended her government’s immigration levels plan during a committee meeting Thursday afternoon.
stories.author: Katie Griffin
stories.content:
Ottawa - Facing heavy criticism from the Conservatives, Canada’s immigration minister defended her government’s immigration levels plan during a committee meeting Thursday afternoon.

“We have a strong, responsible plan that provides stable, durable and predictable numbers that is right for Canada at this time,” Lena Metlege Diab told the Standing Committee on Citizenship and Immigration.

The updated plan unveiled earlier this month includes admitting 380,000 permanent residents each year for the next three years in addition to granting permanent residency to up to 282,000 people who are already in Canada.

The Conservatives have accused the Liberal government of pushing immigration to unsustainable levels and put forward a motion this week that sought to reject the government’s plan to add upwards of 662,000 permanent residents next year. That motion was defeated on Wednesday in a vote that fell along party lines.

“Only eight per cent want higher [immigration levels]. How come you’re not listening to them?” Conservative immigration critic Michelle Rempel Garner asked Diab, citing a poll.

“I have listened extensively for the last 18 months. I know where we were, I’ve been a minister of immigration a decade ago, I know where we are today. This level plan is what Canadians are looking for, it’s what our communities are looking for from coast-to-coast,” Diab answered.

“What you are doing right now is creating a generational cohesion issue in this country and you’re telling me everything’s OK?” Rempel Garner put to Diab. “Will you promise to push back on the prime minister because I know it’s him telling you to do this and say that this is wrong?”

The Conservatives have argued the permanent resident target would put more pressure on the housing market and services like health care.

“So what you’re saying is that you did a lot of consultations then to make sure there are enough hospital beds in the provinces to accommodate your plan?” Conservative MP Brad Redekopp asked Diab.

“Thirty-three per cent of specialists in clinical and laboratory medicine and surgery are immigrants and we have a lot of people that are here on temporary status, so this will help a lot of our Canadians that are here to use and make sure we maintain the people that we need,” she replied.

Some immigration experts warn the one-time measures will only capture a small amount of the backlog when it comes to those who applied for permanent residency on humanitarian and compassionate grounds.

‘The immigration plan is an economic plan’

Conservative MP Grant Jackson pressed Diab on whether the business lobby asked “for more immigration because young Canadians are lazy and did you agree with them? Is that why you’re bringing in more immigrants?”

Diab said the government wants to retain the people that are here and that “the vast majority are people that are feeding us, caring for us, that are helping us heal and that are building our homes.”

“Minister, there are 424,000 young Canadians that are unemployed today. Do you not think they are capable of caring for us and building homes?” Jackson asked.

“The government has a lot of investments for young people,” Diab said. “We are here to work with young Canadians and frankly all Canadians.”

When asked by Bloc Quebecois MP Alexis Brunelle-Duceppe why the government put immigration targets in the budget, Diab responded that “it’s very much linked with our economy, and with our budget and with our future. The immigration plan is an economic plan.”

Diab said as of July 2026, temporary residents made up 6.7 per cent of the population and said their plan would reduce the number to 5.5 per cent or less by the end of 2027.

In September, Prime Minister Mark Carney told The New York Times that Canada will eventually resume a “controlled increase” in its population once the immigration system remains fully under control, but he did not provide specifics.

Weeks later, Carney insisted his government will “not budge” from its goal of keeping national immigration levels sustainable.

Last year, the Carney government lowered and stabilized permanent resident admissions in response to significant increases in immigration in the early 2020s under former prime minister Justin Trudeau that led to pressures on housing and social services.

stories.title: Prosecutors demand 25-year sentence for Kenneth Law after he admitted to aiding suicides
stories.summary: Canadian shipped 1,200 poison packages between 2020 and 2023 around the world
stories.author: Colin Freeze
stories.content:
Kenneth Law apologized in court to the families of dozens of suicidal young people who died after consuming poisons he sold to them online.

The 61-year-old, who has admitted he shipped 1,200 poison packages to aid in suicide, spoke in an emotionless tone at a Superior Court sentencing hearing Friday, ahead of a ruling scheduled for Feb. 26.

“The fact that my actions assisted others in ending their lives is something that I deeply regret,” Mr. Law said reading from a piece of paper in Newmarket, Ont.

“For families of the victims, words will never replace the loss of their loved ones,” Mr. Law said. “I convey my deepest condolences. I remain remorseful and sorry.”

Mr. Law, who worked as a chef before starting his online business, vowed to never again start a similar business and expressed hope that he will one day leave prison and be a “contributing member of society.”

Earlier Friday, prosecutors asked the court to sentence Mr. Law to 25 years in prison for selling deadly substances online that contributed to the deaths of dozens of suicidal people in Canada and Britain.

“Our position is that a 25-year sentence is fit,” Crown attorney Katie Doherty told Superior Court Justice Michelle Fuerst.

“It’s unprecedented, there’s simply no case like this,” Ms. Doherty said.

Mr. Law admitted in court to being directly involved in at least 93 deaths in Canada and Britain as he shipped poison packages from his online business to addresses around the world between 2020 and 2023.

“Ninety-three deaths. The worst possible outcome. Human life lost 93 separate times,” Ms. Doherty said. She told the court that half of the victims were in their 20s, and 12 more were teenagers, including one who was just 14 years old.

Mr. Law pleaded guilty earlier this year to 14 criminal counts of aiding in the suicide of 14 Ontarians. As part of this plea deal, prosecutors agreed to drop murder charges he was facing in these same cases.

Mr. Law has also admitted in court to aiding in the suicides of an additional 79 people in Britain, though these deaths were not charged as a crimes.

Outside the jurisdictions of Ontario and Britain, no crimes have ever been charged against Mr. Law for any suicides from his products.

The court heard testimony from victims’ families in September.

At the sentencing hearing, prosecutors told the court that Mr. Law’s actions have scarred entire families for decades to come.

Crown attorneys cast Mr. Law’s conduct as egregious because he made about $300,000 from his sales. They also said he has admitted to using an online alias to recommend his products in forums frequented by young suicidal people.

Prosecutors say he was motivated by money and was recklessly indifferent to the vulnerable mindsets of his clients. “The only thing Mr. Law has done to determine who to sell to is to demand $80 to $90 up front,” Ms. Doherty said.

But Mr. Law’s defence lawyers dispute many of the Crown’s characterizations. They argue the court must reject prosecutors’ demands to impose the equivalent of a life sentence on Mr. Law.

“Mr. Law is not the mercenary predator he has sometimes been portrayed as,” defence lawyer Matthew Gourlay told the court. “He has shown remorse and insight.”

The Toronto lawyer argued that his client should only get a 12-year sentence.

The defence lawyer told the court Mr. Law sold industrial chemicals that were not themselves illegal. He added that Mr. Law has no prior criminal record. In addition, he said, Mr. Law’s blameworthiness is tempered by circumstances indicating that he operated on a “misguided” belief that he was helping people.

Mr. Gourlay said the court heard no evidence that Mr. Law ever made anyone consume any lethal substance.

The defence lawyer urged the court to consider how Mr. Law’s crimes occurred in an era where suicide is being destigmatized through medical assistance in dying legislation.

“My friend characterized Mr. Law’s views on this whole fraught subject as irrelevant because he was, and I quote, ‘not entitled to set himself up as ‘judge, jury and executioner,’” Mr. Gourlay said. “Of course, he wasn’t ‘the executioner’ in any of these cases. His view was quite the contrary. That other individuals ought to have the choice, through themselves.”

Under Canadian law, aiding suicide is a crime punishable by up to 14 years in prison and guilty pleas ensure some leniency at sentencing.

For these reasons, the Crown said, Mr. Law should face 12.5 years on each of the 14 deaths he has admitted to aiding in Ontario. While most of these sentences would be served at the same time, the Crown is asking that one of those counts be stacked – or served consecutively – for a total of 25 years.

Since Mr. Law was arrested in May 2023 and never granted bail, he has spent 3½ years in custody awaiting trial.

His lawyers say Mr. Law should get credit for his time in detention and have seven years taken off of his eventual sentence.

Editor’s note: A previous version of the photo caption accompanying this article stated that Jeshennia Bedoya Lopez was Maria Lopez’s sister. She was her daughter.

Prosecutors say he was motivated by money and was recklessly indifferent to the vulnerable mindsets of his clients. “The only thing Mr. Law has done to determine who to sell to is to demand $80 to $90 up front,” Ms. Doherty said.
But Mr. Law’s defence lawyers dispute many of the Crown’s characterizations. They argue the court must reject prosecutors’ demands to impose the equivalent of a life sentence on Mr. Law.
“Mr. Law is not the mercenary predator he has sometimes been portrayed as,” defence lawyer Matthew Gourlay told the court. “He has shown remorse and insight.”
The Toronto lawyer argued that his client should only get a 12-year sentence.

The defence lawyer told the court Mr. Law sold industrial chemicals that were not themselves illegal. He added that Mr. Law has no prior criminal record. In addition, he said, Mr. Law’s blameworthiness is tempered by circumstances indicating that he operated on a “misguided” belief that he was helping people.
Mr. Gourlay said the court heard no evidence that Mr. Law ever made anyone consume any lethal substance.
The defence lawyer urged the court to consider how Mr. Law’s crimes occurred in an era where suicide is being destigmatized through medical assistance in dying legislation.

“My friend characterized Mr. Law’s views on this whole fraught subject as irrelevant because he was, and I quote, ‘not entitled to set himself up as ‘judge, jury and executioner,’” Mr. Gourlay said. “Of course, he wasn’t ‘the executioner’ in any of these cases. His view was quite the contrary. That other individuals ought to have the choice, through themselves.”
Under Canadian law, aiding suicide is a crime punishable by up to 14 years in prison and guilty pleas ensure some leniency at sentencing.

For these reasons, the Crown said, Mr. Law should face 12.5 years on each of the 14 deaths he has admitted to aiding in Ontario. While most of these sentences would be served at the same time, the Crown is asking that one of those counts be stacked – or served consecutively – for a total of 25 years.
Since Mr. Law was arrested in May 2023 and never granted bail, he has spent 3½ years in custody awaiting trial.
His lawyers say Mr. Law should get credit for his time in detention and have seven years taken off of his eventual sentence.

stories.title: Michael Douglas encourages Jews to ‘speak up’ in face of antisemitism
stories.summary: Actor tells Toronto fundraiser for Ben- Gurion University that Masar Badil's anti-Israel conference is 'deplorable'
stories.author: Dave Gordon
stories.content:
Toronto – Actor Michael Douglas, one of comparatively few A-list Hollywood celebrities speaking out against antisemitism and in support of Israel, told a Toronto audience he did not think “it’s any heroic gesture.”

Instead, he suggested it was simply necessary in a world growing less friendly to Jews and Israel.

“It’s important more than ever that we speak up,” he said last Sunday, at the BGU Canada Toronto’s BGU Strong Gala in front of more than 1,400 attendees.

Douglas, who has a long relationship with Toronto and spoke of owning property in the city, criticized an anti-Israel group’s planned event in the city this weekend that will openly celebrate and seek to build on Hamas’s October 7 terror attack on Israel.

Actor Michael Douglas (L), speaking onstage to Canadian sports journalist Elliotte Friedman at BGU Canada Toronto’s BGU Strong Gala in front of more than 1,400 attendees on Nov. 22, 2026.

Masar Badil — the Palestinian Alternative Revolutionary Path Movement — was recently labelled a terror entity by the Canadian government, but said it will proceed with the conference, even as Toronto police suggested they’d be monitoring for terror activity.

“It’s deplorable,” Douglas said of the conference.

In the 45-minute onstage conversation with Canadian sports journalist Elliotte Friedman, the two-time Oscar-winner reflected on his decades-long career as an actor and producer – which includes leads in film hits including Wall Street and Fatal Attraction – his Jewish heritage, and his family life.

Douglas, whose Bermudian mother was raised in the Church of England, said he more fully embraced his Jewish identity shortly after his actor father Kirk’s near-death helicopter crash in 1991 that killed two people, including an 18-year-old.

The tragedy prompted Kirk Douglas, the son of Russian Jewish parents, to wonder why he survived and the young man did not. Kirk began to reflect more on his spirituality, and found mentorship with Los Angeles-based Rabbi David Wolpe, and “all of a sudden he just changed,” according to his son.

Michael Douglas, who noted Judaism grew to more fully embrace children of non-Jewish mothers like himself during his lifetime, soon found his father’s journey was having an effect on him.

“As a result, I began feeling those feelings strongly. And my kids decided they wanted a bar-mitzvah,” said the 82-year-old actor.

“I love the tribe … I’m very proud to call myself a Jew.”

In 2015, Douglas accepted the $1-million Genesis Prize in Jerusalem and announced that the money would support outreach to intermarried families. Often referred to as “the Jewish Nobel Prize,” it was established in 2013 to honour individuals — primarily of Jewish heritage — for professional achievement, contributions to humanity and commitment to Jewish values and the State of Israel.

That same year, Douglas spoke out in a Los Angeles Times oped against Jew-hatred after his then-14-year-old son Dylan was verbally abused while wearing a Star of David.

In April 2024, he said on Pbs’s Finding Your Roots: “I feel more of a spiritual, religious connection to Judaism than I ever had before.”

Through the show he learned that his grandfather, Harry Demsky (born Girsh Danilovich), came to America in the early 1900s. In June 2024, Douglas visited Israel, including Kibbutz Be’eri, the Nova festival memorial and other sites attacked by Hamas, meeting hostage families and President Isaac Herzog.

At the Toronto event, Douglas told stories from his long movie career, including his friendship with Danny DeVito, his pursuit of the much-younger Catherine Zeta-Jones, now his wife, and the audience factors that led filmmakers to change the ending of Fatal Attraction. He appeared delighted at the best-seller status of his new autobiography, One Helluva Ride.

Douglas also apologized to Canadians for President Donald Trump, noting that he himself was a fan of Prime Minister Mark Carney. That prompted much murmuring in the crowd, seemingly split on Carney’s decision that Canada would recognize a Palestinian state following the Hamas attacks and subsequent Gaza war.

Earlier the same evening, British best-selling author and political pundit Douglas Murray spoke in conversation with National Post editor-in-chief Rob Roberts. Murray noted that while in Toronto about two years ago he watched “a pro-Palestinian, anti-Israel protest” and that “nobody at those protests ever carries a Canadian flag. You know, they carry their Palestinian flags and sometimes their Iranian revolutionary government flags, but they’re never proud of Canada.

“And, you know, the flip side of that is so obvious, which is that any synagogue in this country or any pro-Israel protest in this country, people are always proudly singing Hatikva and O Canada.”

He summarized the distinction as “a fight between people who loved life and the people who worshiped death.”

According to organizers, the event raised over $2.2 million in support of The Lior Project at Ben- Gurion University of the Negev. Established in memory of BGU student Lior Tkach who was murdered on October 7, 2023, The Lior Project harnesses AI-driven medical research to help ICU physicians make life-saving decisions.

stories.title: Woman, 90, fined in B.C. Interior city for driving while scrolling Facebook
stories.summary: Nelson - Police in British Columbia are urging drivers to resist using cellphones while driving after a 90-year-old woman was caught scrolling on Facebook behind the wheel.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
NELSON - Police in British Columbia are urging drivers to resist using cellphones while driving after a 90-year-old woman was caught scrolling on Facebook behind the wheel.

Nov. 27, 2026

Darren Calabrese[](https://www.thestar.com/news/canada/british-columbia/woman-90-fined-in-b-c-interior-city-for-driving-while-scrolling-facebook/article_fbc41941-f2eb-5fc6-84eb-cf609d9d6158.html)

By The Canadian Press

The BC Highway Patrol says in a statement that the unusual case happened on Nov. 16 at around 10 a.m. in the Kootenays city of Nelson.

Police say a patrolling officer driving through the city “went nose-to-nose” with another vehicle, close enough that he could see the elderly woman holding a cellphone in her hand.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Inside interior designer Nora Voon’s art-filled home

The highway patrol says the woman was checking her social media feed on the popular platform while driving.

She was fined $368 for the violation, and officers say she otherwise had functional awareness and the ability to drive

Police say the case is a reminder to drivers of the lure of mobile device use while driving despite its dangers and are urging motorists to put their phones out of reach when operating a vehicle.

“These powerful little devices are massively distracting, and that’s why people keep using them right in front of our officers,” BC Highway Patrol spokesman Sgt. Michael McLaughlin says in a statement.

“This woman lived 60 years of her life before cell phones existed, but she got sucked into checking Facebook while driving. If she can’t resist, maybe you can’t either.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 27, 2026.

stories.title: Allstate disrupted as website and app outage enters 5th day
stories.summary: According to the outage tracking website Downdetector, customers started reporting problems accessing the insurance website and app on Monday.
stories.author: Rachel Morgan
stories.content:
A multiday outage at Allstate insurance has left some customers unable to make claims, renew policies or request roadside assistance.

According to the outage tracking website Downdetector, about 150 customers in the U.S. were still experiencing difficulties accessing Allstate’s online services as of 10:17 a.m. Eastern time.

On Friday morning, the company’s roadside assistance website displayed an error message.

Customers started reporting problems accessing the insurance website and app on Monday.

In a statement Wednesday, the insurer said some of its services had been restricted.

“Some access has been restricted over the last 48 hours, but we continue to be available for customers and respond to and settle claims,” it said.

The company said customers that are unable to make a payment due to the disruption will not lose coverage or be charged late fees.

Allstate said customers can still reach them through multiple channels including over the phone or in person at local offices.

The insurer has not said publicly what has caused the disruption. Global News reached out for more information but did not receive an immediate response.

Earlier this month, Allstate CEO Tom Wilson said the company is planning to launch AI-powered sales assisted by a personal agentic assistant by early 2027.

Three people were injured, one of them seriously, when a vehicle was used to break into and rob a Toronto jewelry store, police say.

Toronto Police Services reported a robbery at Yonge Street and Briar Hill Avenue, just north of Yonge and Eglinton, at 4:34 p.m. Thursday. Police said there were “reports of vehicle into a jewelry store,” adding: “Suspects in the store stole merchandise before fleeing in another vehicle.”

Robbery: Yonge St & Briar Hill Ave 4:34 pm – reports of vehicle into a jewelry store – suspects in the store stole merchandise before fleeing in another vehicle – unknown injuries – ongoing investigation#GO2498162 ^sc pic.twitter.com/MxuKIYGKP9 — Toronto Police Operations (@TPSOperations) November 26, 2026

A short while later they provided an update that two patients were being transported to the hospital with non-life-threatening injuries, and one with serious injuries.

The store, Pinto Gold, has been in business since 1995 and describes itself as”the best and most reputable gold buyer and dealer of cash for gold Toronto has to offer.” It specializes in high-end watches such as Rolex.

Images from the scene show a damaged TTC shelter as well as shards of glass scattered across the sidewalk.

Police told National Post Friday that the three injured people were all in the store at the time of the robbery, and that they were a female in her 50s, a male in his 40s and a male in his 60s. The female sustained minor injuries, the younger male non-life-threatening injuries, and the older male serious but non-life-threatening injuries.

Police also said that there were between five and seven suspects, all male and all wearing black clothing.

Truck smashed a bus shelter and the front of a business at Yonge & Briar Hill in what police say was a jewellery store robbery. Paramedics treated three people, two went to hospital. Police say suspects fled in another vehicle pic.twitter.com/EuCk3k3MsS — Melissa Duggan (@meldug) November 26, 2026

The robbery comes shortly after two recent violent home invasions rocked the city within the past month. In the affluent Bridle Path neighbourhood, suspects broke into a house on Oct. 29 and attacked two members of the family with a hammer before fleeing.

On Wednesday there was another home invasion at a home near Casa Loma where the homeowner’s son, Michael Eckert, 39, was fatally shot.

The recent spike in crime has garnered strong reaction from Ontario Premier Doug Ford, who said if someone tried breaking into his home he would fight back.

The Ontario premier said he is a legal gun owner “and I would use it in a heartbeat if someone came in with a gun, ready to shoot up my house, my family.” He added, during a scrum with reporters at Queen’s Park on Thursday: “Like I said, I’ll blow the guy right through the front door.”

At an unrelated event on Thursday, Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow said she is working with all levels of the government to put an end to crime as the city sees a spike in home invasions.

Chow said: “People are frightened. I have heard it. Neighbours checking their locks. Families lying awake at every sound in the middle of the night.”

She added: “That fear is real. I feel it too, and I am angry.”

stories.title: Criminal lawyer shares how to legally defend yourself during a home invasion
stories.summary: Ontario Premier Doug Ford’s response to a spate of home invasions this month that left one person dead and another family injured May have some residents asking what their rights are when confronted by an armed robber.
stories.author: Devika Desai
stories.content:
Ontario Premier Doug Ford’s response to a spate of home invasions this month that left one person dead and another family injured May have some residents asking what their rights are when confronted by an armed robber.

On Thursday, Ford revealed that he is a legal gun owner and said he would not hesitate to use the weapon on someone who invaded his home and threatened his family.

“I’ll blow the guy right through the front door,” he told reporters at Queen’s Park .

The premier’s comments come a day after police confirmed that one or more suspects broke into a home in Toronto’s Casa Loma neighbourhood and shot one of the residents.

The homicide follows just weeks after another home invasion in Toronto’s Bridle Path neighbourhood where three residents were shot and a fourth was a struck by a hammer.

Ontario’s attorney general and solicitor general are now asking the federal government to amend the Criminal Code to “strengthen and clarify the legal protections available to homeowners confronted with a home invasion.”

Toronto criminal lawyer Joseph Neuberger says Canadians have “robust rights under the Criminal Code to defend themselves, their family, their friends in their home, as well as their property.”

However, they must be able to prove a “reasonable and proportional” use of force against a threat, he told CTV’s Your Morning on Friday.

A resident, for example, could use force to “repel or possible kill the individuals” if confronted in a home invasion by armed individuals, where they feel they’re “under imminent risk of grievous bodily harm,” he said.

Residents who are lawful gun owners can use their firearms to defend themselves, but must “have some certainty” that there is a risk to their and their family’s lives.

“It’s a bit of a delicate balance in Canada,” he said “It’s different than the United States.”

Reasonable use of force and firearms

Canadians have the right to “not retreat,” Neuberger said, which means, residents can stay to protect themselves.

The circumstances of the confrontation May dictate whether a person’s use of force to respond was reasonable or not.

For instance, if a threatening, but unarmed, individual invades a home and orders residents to give them things, responding with a firearm is “unreasonable,” he said.

“If it’s clear they’ve come into the home, they’re brandishing firearms, it’s more than one individual and you feel at that point that you’re at risk, that can be reasonable force,” he added.

Neuberger added that the best way to respond is to try to find a secure place with the family and call 911, without engaging the individuals.

“But if you’re caught in these circumstances, then you can use reasonable force,” he said.

The change in local police messaging on how to protect oneself from a home invasion suggests that police might be “frustrated,” Neuberger said.

In 2024, a Toronto police officer suggested that homeowners leave their car keys near the front door to avoid invaders coming into the house and threatening families.

This week, police suggested that victims “follow their gut” and call 911 first.

“We do have a rise of home invasions in Toronto,” Neuberger said. “I feel that the police are underfunded. In my opinion, we need more officers trained and on the streets and patrolling.”

He added that criminals are less likely to invade homes when there are police cars patrolling the area. “It’s clear that we need a much more significant presence,” he said.

Some residents have turned to courses to get their own firearm licences, Neuberger added.

“I think the police are saying, do what you think is reasonable to protect yourself and your family because we’re having deaths occur or serious injuries. And I think a part of it (comes from) some level of frustration.”

“I think the police are saying, do what you think is reasonable to protect yourself and your family because we’re having deaths occur or serious injuries. And I think a part of it (comes from) some level of frustration.”

stories.title: Ottawa rejects call to relieve Canadian automakers of greenhouse gas rules
stories.summary: Environment Minister defended tailpipe emissions rules and carbon taxes after hearing from Premier Ford, Unifor leader
stories.author: Eric Atkins
stories.content:
The federal government has rejected a call by Ontario Premier Doug Ford and Unifor national president Lana Payne to relieve automakers in Canada of tailpipe emissions rules and carbon taxes.

Mr. Ford and Ms. Payne on Thursday issued a joint letter urging Ottawa to spare the companies from greenhouse-gas regulations, arguing they cost jobs and make Ontario a less desirable place to manufacture at a time automakers face U.S. tariffs on exports.

Federal Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin fired back in a social media post, saying it is “misleading” to claim the carbon tax hurts manufacturers, when it adds just “several dollars” to the cost of making a car. She defended the tailpipe emissions rules, which require all car companies to buy offsets if their fleets exceed a pollution threshold, as presenting “no distinct cost” for Ontario manufacturers.

The rules “apply to every new vehicle sold in Canada, whether it was built here or abroad,” Ms. Dabrusin said. The rules do not apply to Canadian-made cars that are exported, she said, which covers about 90 per cent of the products of Ontario’s assembly plants, including those of Stellantis NV. STLA-N

Stellantis held talks this week and last with officials from governments in Ottawa and Ontario and the Unifor union over the future of its assembly plant in Brampton, Ont. Stellantis has sold the plant to armoured car maker Roshel Inc. after idling the factory for almost three years. Government and union leaders are trying to stop the sale before it becomes final by the end of the year.

Mr. Ford emerged from a Stellantis meeting last week to say the automaker needs breaks on the greenhouse gas regulations, which he said are costing it $300-million a year.

LouAnn Gosselin, a spokeswoman for Stellantis, declined to comment on the emissions policies. She said the company remains in talks with the union and governments over the future of the Brampton plant, and has resumed collective bargain talks with Unifor.

Under the tailpipe emissions plan unveiled by Ottawa this year, auto companies whose fleets exceed the emissions limits must buy carbon offsets from those who comply. The sales are private and the prices are confidential. Tesla is the biggest seller of credits in Canada, given its fleet is all electric.

The aim of the program is to slow climate change by encouraging car companies to increase the number of electric and low-emissions vehicles for sale. By 2035, 75 per cent of new vehicle sales should be electric, the government said when it announced the program.

This is lower than the 100 per cent required in the program that it replaced, which placed ever-increasing quotas on the number of new low-emissions vehicles for sale. The car industry fought to get rid of that system, and is not happy about the new one, either.

Brian Kingston, head of the Canadian Vehicle Manufacturers’ Association, which represents Stellantis, Ford and General Motors, said the credit system is the most costly regulation for car companies.

Still, Ms. Dabrusin said in her post that the future of cars is increasingly electric, and the system helps Canadians save money on gas. She pointed to aid the government has provided automakers, including a $2.5-billion fund Ottawa and Ontario announced together.

“We are consulting with the auto industry and remain ready to further support its competitiveness and protect manufacturing in Ontario,” Ms. Dabrusin said.

Stellantis has also benefited from government help, receiving millions of dollars since 2022 to retool plants in Brampton and Windsor, Ont., as well as the Nextstar battery plant in Windsor.

The federal industrial carbon tax also works on a credit system. Companies that pollute more than their industry benchmark must either buy credits from other companies or pay $95 a tonne to a government fund administered by the province. They can get their money back to invest in plant upgrades that reduce their carbon emissions.

Etienne Rainville, a vice-president of Clean Prosperity, a non-profit group that advocates for climate policies, said scrapping the carbon pricing will do little to help Stellantis, he said, given the carmaker is likely exempt from it during the retooling.

“It’s a modest cost when they’re operating,” he said. “It’s almost no cost at all when they’re not operating.”

Industry Minister Mélanie Joly has threatened Stellantis with a lawsuit over what she said are broken commitments that the company made when it received government aid. She said it must repay the money received if the sale of the Brampton plant is finalized. The Globe and Mail has reported that amount is $831-million. Stellantis has offered $24-million, the amount it said it received for work on the Brampton plant.

stories.title: Canada extends Ebola travel rules for 90 days as outbreak rages on
stories.summary: The measures have been extended to Feb. 25, 2027.
stories.author: Hannah Alberga The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - Canada is extending its travel and immigration restrictions related to the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo for 90 more days.

The government says the measures remain in place to reduce the risk of Ebola disease entering and spreading in Canada.

The move comes as the World Health Organization announced its updated guidance today, recommending countries “identify and assess travellers” who May have been exposed to the disease.

The agency stopped short of calling for a blanket ban, but says it’s deeply concerned that the outbreak has surpassed 12,000 cases, including more than 5,900 deaths.

People from Uganda, South Sudan and the Democratic Republic of Congo have been barred from travelling to Canada since May.

There have been no cases reported in South Sudan, and an outbreak in Uganda was declared over in August after 20 people got sick. In October, the outbreak spread to Kenya and Nigeria.

The Canadian travel restrictions were set to expire on Friday at midnight but have been extended to Feb. 25, 2027.

Immigration documents, including valid visas and travel authorizations, remain suspended for people from all three countries.

That includes people who have been granted permanent residency but are not in Canada.

A mandatory self-isolation period of 21 days will stay in place for anyone entering the country who has recently been in the Democratic Republic of Congo, Uganda and South Sudan.

Foreign nationals who have been in the DRC in the last 21 days will not be allowed to board a flight to Canada.

Those who have been in South Sudan or Uganda in that time can enter the country, but will have to quarantine.

The WHO has previously said blanket travel restrictions are based on fear rather than science.

Efforts to contain the outbreak have been hampered by insecurity in the region. WHO says it has verified at least 94 attacks on health-care workers, patients and facilities in the DRC over the past six months.

An emergency committee reporting on the outbreak is calling for faster clinical trials of candidate vaccines and treatments, and says it’s important to engage communities to promote clear and transparent information on how the trials are planned and implemented.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 27, 2026.

stories.title: What are your legal rights to defend yourself in a home invasion?
stories.summary: Ontario Premier Doug Ford’s response to a spate of home invasions this month that left one person dead and another family injured May have some residents asking what their rights are when confronted by an armed robber.
stories.author: Devika Desai
stories.content:
Ontario Premier Doug Ford’s response to a spate of home invasions this month that left one person dead and another family injured May have some residents asking what their rights are when confronted by an armed robber.

On Thursday, Ford revealed that he is a legal gun owner and said he would not hesitate to use the weapon on someone who invaded his home and threatened his family.

“I’ll blow the guy right through the front door,” he told reporters at Queen’s Park .

The premier’s comments come a day after police confirmed that one or more suspects broke into a home in Toronto’s Casa Loma neighbourhood and shot one of the residents.

The homicide follows just weeks after another home invasion in Toronto’s Bridle Path neighbourhood where three residents were shot and a fourth was a struck by a hammer.

Ontario’s attorney general and solicitor general are now asking the federal government to amend the Criminal Code to “strengthen and clarify the legal protections available to homeowners confronted with a home invasion.”

Toronto criminal lawyer Joseph Neuberger says Canadians have “robust rights under the Criminal Code to defend themselves, their family, their friends in their home, as well as their property.”

However, they must be able to prove a “reasonable and proportional” use of force against a threat, he told CTV’s Your Morning on Friday.

A resident, for example, could use force to “repel or possible kill the individuals” if confronted in a home invasion by armed individuals, where they feel they’re “under imminent risk of grievous bodily harm,” he said.

Residents who are lawful gun owners can use their firearms to defend themselves, but must “have some certainty” that there is a risk to their and their family’s lives.

“It’s a bit of a delicate balance in Canada,” he said “It’s different than the United States.”

Reasonable use of force and firearms

Canadians have the right to “not retreat,” Neuberger said, which means, residents can stay to protect themselves.

The circumstances of the confrontation May dictate whether a person’s use of force to respond was reasonable or not.

For instance, if a threatening, but unarmed, individual invades a home and orders residents to give them things, responding with a firearm is “unreasonable,” he said.

stories.title: Home invasion in Hamilton neighbourhood leaves owner in hospital
stories.summary: Officers first responded to the residence on Stoney Creek Mountain when the homeowner heard glass breaking on the main floor of their home early Friday
stories.author: Sadeen Mohsen
stories.content:
Hamilton police say they are investigating a home invasion in a quiet neighbourhood on Stoney Creek Mountain.

Officers first responded to the residence at 5:12 a.m. when the homeowner heard glass breaking on the main floor of their home early Friday.

Police say at least three people broke into the residence and began causing damage to the property.

When the homeowner tried to intervene, they were assaulted by one of the suspects.

Investigators say the suspects fled the home and were seen travelling in a dark sedan, northbound on Centennial Parkway.

They say the homeowner was transported to hospital with non-life-threatening injuries.

Police say the investigation remains ongoing and are asking anyone with information to come forward.

The incident comes two days after a violent home invasion in Toronto’s Casa Loma neighbourhood that left a beloved local musician dead.

stories.title: European author Giuliano da Empoli explores Silicon Valley's pursuit of power
stories.summary: Montreal - When a former political adviser enters the inner circle of one of the world's most powerful and secretive technology entrepreneurs, he discovers that the rules of political power have changed.
stories.author: Charlotte Glorieux The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - When a former political adviser enters the inner circle of one of the world’s most powerful and secretive technology entrepreneurs, he discovers that the rules of political power have changed.

It’s the premise of European novelist Giuliano da Empoli’s latest novel, “Le Fondateur” or “The Founder,” which draws inspiration from American billionaire Peter Thiel and his data analytics company, Palantir Technologies.

But the dystopia depicted by the author of “The Wizard of the Kremlin” is not set in some distant future.

“Each of us increasingly feels that we’re losing control over our lives, our professions, our futures,” da Empoli said.

In an interview with The Canadian Press ahead of his appearance at the Salon du livre de Montréal, da Empoli warned that technology giants are acquiring political power and seeking to reshape human existence — a transformation he believes democracies such as Canada can still resist.

Da Empoli drew inspiration from Thiel and Palantir, fascinated by how much power they wield while being less familiar to the public than tech giants such as Google or Meta.

Palantir, which received early funding from the Cia’s investment arm, helps governments, police agencies, and businesses manage and analyze large amounts of data. It has faced criticism for its work on software supporting the Trump administration’s deportation efforts.

Da Empoli argues that when governments depend on private companies to organize and analyze sensitive information, they risk losing control over some of their most important functions.

“It’s an immense power that today touches the very heart of state sovereignty,” he said, pointing to military operations, border control and intelligence.

For da Empoli, the ambitions of Silicon Valley’s most powerful figures are reflected in the novel’s title. He said technology entrepreneurs increasingly call themselves founders — a term that evokes the founding fathers of the United States.

“They are founding not simply companies, but a new human condition whose parameters they will have chosen and whose rules they will have established,” he said.

At the heart of that transformation, he argues, is the replacement of human autonomy — including people’s choices, mistakes and weaknesses — by algorithms and machines.

“The human being is always an obstacle, something they need to free themselves from as much as possible,” he said.

Yet through fiction, da Empoli also wanted to expose the vulnerabilities of the men behind these technologies. “The main character is someone who is at once immensely powerful and completely powerless,” he said.

“He’s capable of designing instruments that will govern the world, and at the same time, he’s incapable of speaking to the woman he loves.”

By exploring that contradiction, da Empoli hopes to challenge the sense of powerlessness that technology giants can inspire. “We’re not dealing with gods, we’re dealing with men,” he said. “We shouldn’t let ourselves be too intimidated, either.”

Da Empoli sees Canada and Europe as facing a common challenge: resisting what he calls an “alliance of predators” between political figures such as U.S. President Donald Trump and technology executives.

While describing Europe’s response as one of humiliation, he praised Canadian leaders for their pushing back despite their country’s economic dependence on the United States.

“I think it’s always good to start from a position of courage, because if you don’t, you’ve already lost,” he said.

Digital sovereignty

Ottawa has responded to Trump’s trade offensive with retaliatory tariffs and efforts to reduce its reliance on the U.S. economy.

But Canada’s ability to resist pressure from technology companies is also being tested.

Manon Paquet, associate director of policy at McGill University’s Centre for Media, Technology and Democracy, pointed to Meta’s decision to block Canadian news on Facebook and Instagram in response to the federal Online News Act.

She said Canada’s willingness to regulate technology giants sets it apart from the United States, but protecting its digital sovereignty requires sustained efforts.

“Political leaders and the public administration must also show courage and firmness in resisting pressure, whether it comes from industry or foreign governments,” she said.

David Grondin, a communications professor at Université de Montréal who studies digital surveillance, said Canada has been reluctant to exercise its legislative powers against technology giants, citing Ottawa’s decision to abandon its digital services tax in June 2025.

He described technology giants as “quasi-states” capable of circumventing national regulations. “Ultimately, it is the very idea of democratic sovereignty that is threatened,” he said in an email.

Hope for the future

For da Empoli, reclaiming control begins with recognizing that technological progress is a matter of political choice rather than an inevitability.

“We’re not dealing with a weather phenomenon. It rains, the sun shines, and we accept it,” he said. “Technology doesn’t work that way.”

He praised Montreal artificial intelligence researcher Yoshua Bengio, founder of the Quebec AI research institute Mila and co-recipient of the 2018 Turing Award, for his work on AI governance and safety.

Despite the darkness of his novel, da Empoli hopes to shake readers out of their passivity and encourage them to reclaim control over the technologies shaping their lives. “I wouldn’t write this book if I were disillusioned or radically pessimistic,” he said.

For the author, the question is not whether to embrace technology, but who should shape its future. “We would like all of this to be governed by people who love humanity and who love life,” he said.

The novel is published in French by Gallimard.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 27, 2026.

stories.title: Study shows path to more resilient future for Canada’s forests
stories.summary: New study finds genetic clues to lodgepole pine trees ability to resist mountain pine beetle attacks and outbreaks.
stories.author: Jeff Renaud
stories.content:
Mountain pine beetles have killed millions of lodgepole pines across Western North America since the 1990s, but some trees have proved more resilient than others. New research suggests part of the difference is genetic and that the resistance can be passed from one generation of trees to the next.

The discovery could help researchers and the forestry industry identify and grow trees better equipped to withstand future beetle outbreaks, offering a new way to build resilience into Canada’s forests.

David Coltman (Submitted)

In a study published in Molecular Ecology, a research team including Western University biologist David Coltmanfound survival during an extreme mountain pine beetle outbreak has a substantial genetic component. Researchers estimate nearly half of the variation in survival among the offspring studied was attributable to inherited genetic differences.

In other words, the surviving trees May have passed on more than seeds. They May also have shared the genetic traits that helped them withstand the outbreak, giving their offspring a better chance of resisting future attacks.

“These trees show genetic variation for resistance to attack, and we can now use that knowledge to build better trees,” said Coltman, professor and chair of Western’s department of biology and co-author of the study. “We can identify seed sources from trees with greater natural resistance and incorporate them into reforestation. That gives us a way to breed trees better equipped to withstand future beetle attacks.”

The mountain pine beetle is native to Western North America, but its most recent population explosion has been unprecedented in scale. Since the late 1990s, the outbreak has affected more than 27 million hectares of forest across Canada, the United States and northern Mexico.

Protective pitch tube formed by a tree’s resin defence. (Submitted)

“When a mountain pine beetle bores into a tree, the tree responds by producing resin. It’s both a chemical defence and a physical one,” said Coltman. “The resin can push the beetle back out, trap it and potentially kill it. It forms a little tube around the point of attack, almost like a tree scab.”

Under normal conditions, mountain pine beetles play a role in forest renewal, typically attacking older or weakened trees. But warmer winters, forest-management practices and fire suppression, which can change the age and structure of forests, have created conditions that allow beetle populations to grow beyond their normal limits and overwhelm even healthy pines.

To understand why some trees survived, Coltman and his collaborators took advantage of an unusual feature of lodgepole pines. Their cones can remain attached to branches for years, even after a tree dies.

Researchers collected cones from trees that survived the outbreak and those killed by beetles, then planted the seeds and grew the young trees under the same conditions. Cones from surviving trees were collected near the ends of branches, where seeds were likely to have been fertilized by other surviving trees. Cones from dead trees provided seeds from trees that had succumbed to the outbreak.

Supported in part by Genome Canada, the research team analyzed the DNA of 418 young trees, examining more than 14,000 genetic markers to look for differences between the offspring of trees that survived the outbreak and those that did not.

The results showed that genetic differences accounted for nearly half of the variation in survival among the young trees. This suggests that much of the ability to withstand a beetle attack can be passed from parent trees to their offspring.

The findings also suggest the beetle outbreak itself has changed the genetic makeup of surviving lodgepole pine tree populations. Researchers found evidence of reduced genetic diversity at most of the sampled sites, alongside genetic signatures associated with survival.

Mountain pine beetle (Submitted)

Those genetic differences May help explain why some trees are better equipped to defend themselves against an attack. But even strong natural defences have limits.

When beetle populations grow large enough, as has happened across North America, the insects can overwhelm even healthy trees through mass attack. They also introduce a fungus that helps them colonize the tree and contributes to its death. The fungus causes the blue staining sometimes found in beetle-killed pine timber.

This new research could eventually help forestry companies select seed sources and breed trees with a better chance of surviving future outbreaks. The research team was able to use genetic information to predict survival profiles across regions with lodgepole pines, finding higher predicted levels of survival in areas where the beetle has historically been present.

But there are complications. Coltman says existing research shows trees investing more energy in defence May grow more slowly, creating a potential trade-off between resistance and timber production. Nor is there a guarantee that genetic characteristics associated with surviving an extreme beetle outbreak will protect trees against other threats. Coltman and his collaborators found their genetic predictions did not translate reliably to survival patterns from beetle attacks in areas with lower beetle population pressure.

Regardless, Coltman sees considerable potential for how forestry companies can utilize these findings as the industry is accustomed to thinking far beyond the next planting season.

“Foresters have always thought on this kind of timescale,” said Coltman. “They’re planning what the forest inventory will look like 20, 50 or even 100 years from now. The trees being planted today May not be harvested for generations, so the decisions we make about which trees to grow and which genetic traits to favour can have a lasting impact.”

stories.title: Corus reports $59.4-million loss as revenue falls in fourth quarter
stories.summary: Result represents best year-over-year quarterly performance since 2023
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Corus Entertainment Inc. CJR-B-T reported a net loss attributable to shareholders of $59.4-million in its latest quarter as the company behind Global Television saw its revenue fall 11 per cent compared with a year ago.

The television and radio broadcaster says the loss amounted to 30 cents per diluted share for the quarter ended Aug. 31. The result compared with a loss of $277 million or $1.39 per diluted share for the same quarter last year.

Chief executive John Gossling says the results reflected significant improvement in advertising revenue trends and the best quarterly performance year-over-year since the second quarter of fiscal 2023.

On an adjusted basis, Corus says it lost 20 cents per share in its latest quarter compared with an adjusted loss of 36 cents per share a year earlier.

Revenue for what was the company’s fourth quarter totalled $206.8-million, down from $232-million a year earlier.

The company says it will receive $36-million as part of Ottawa’s funding support of Canadian local news sectors announced during the federal budget.

Corus says the amount will be reflected in its fiscal first quarter of 2027.
