stories.title: Bill 21 live updates: Supreme Court of Canada to deliver landmark ruling on Quebec secularism law today
stories.summary: Challenge to secularism law tests provinces’ powers to use Charter’s notwithstanding clause; decision expected at 9:45 a.m. ET
stories.author: Globe Staff
stories.content:
The Supreme Court’s Bill 21 decision defines the limits of your Charter rights, and not just for people in Quebec. The consequential ruling upheld the province’s secularism law as well as the Charter’s notwithstanding clause, paving the way for other provincial governments to use it to shield their own laws from Charter challenges.

But as justice reporter David Ebner explains, it will likely take legal experts years to untangle the full implications of the lengthy ruling.

When Canada’s premiers convene in Toronto next month, there is expected to be quite a bit of tension in the room because of their clashing opinions on the Bill 21 ruling, says Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew.

“We disagree significantly,” he told The Globe and Mail in Winnipeg on Friday.

That includes disagreements with his friend, Ontario Premier Doug Ford, who has not yet commented on the Supreme Court’s decision, though he has previously issued strong support toward usage of the notwithstanding clause, Kinew added.

“Doug, I get along with him; other premiers, whatever. But if you in the Prairie provinces have to target gay people in order to get elected, quit. Give it up. We don’t need you in public,” Kinew said, speaking directly to his fellow provincial leaders, in reference to Alberta and Saskatchewan’s use of the notwithstanding clause on legislation related to gender and sexuality.

“If you in Quebec have to target Muslims and Sikhs in order to win office, get out of here.”

As an Anishinaabe man, Kinew said he “grew up with racism,” which is why the issue of Bill 21 feels personal to him.

“And so, if I see somebody who’s rich and powerful pick on the one trans kid in an entire region of their province, yeah, I’m going to say something. If I see somebody who’s rich and powerful, who is trying to make the working class vote against their economic self-interest by picking on Muslims, yeah, I’m going to say something about it.”

Federal NDP Leader Avi Lewis criticized the decision to uphold Bill 21, which he said “affirms the right of provincial governments to override fundamental freedoms without any guardrails.”

“From Alberta and Saskatchewan to Ontario and Quebec, conservative premiers are sweeping aside the rights of workers, trans kids, and minorities to distract from their inability to solve the real crises we face, first and foremost the cost of living,” he wrote in a statement on X on Friday . “And they’re preemptively using the notwithstanding clause to get away with it.”

Lewis reiterated his condemnation of the Quebec secularism law and urged Canadians to take this issue to the ballot box now that legal options have been exhausted.

“We need to elect progressive governments across the country who will not abuse their authority to violate the fundamental freedoms we cherish,” he wrote.

Kerri Froc, an associate professor at the University of New Brunswick’s Faculty of Law who focuses on women’s constitutional rights, said Canada’s top court had set a worrying precedent in refusing to limit the powers of provinces as long as they invoke the unusual constitutional provision.

“The Supreme Court has sent a clear message it’s not going to step in when the rights of vulnerable minorities are trampled on in these cases, so perhaps this needs to move to the political sphere,” Froc said.

The Quebec Liberals are welcoming the Supreme Court’s confirmation that the decision of whether to invoke the notwithstanding clause rests solely with Quebec, the Official Opposition said in a statement Friday .

“Quebec has the right to invoke the exemption clause, and we will not hesitate to do so as a preventive measure if it proves necessary to defend our democratic choices and our shared values,” Liberal Leader Charles Milliard wrote.

“In Quebec, the secular nature of the state and the promotion and protection of the French language are shared values,” he said. “For too long, they have been used as arguments to divide us. It is time for this to stop.”

The Liberals reiterated their position that the ban on religious symbols should be limited to public servants with “coercive authority,” such as judges and police officers.

“Once again, the Quebec Liberal Party’s approach is both reasonable and responsible, and aims to maintain social stability while limiting infringements on fundamental rights and freedom,” wrote Milliard.

Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew says the Supreme Court’s allowance for non-binding judicial rulings on government usage of the notwithstanding clause should serve as an important new tool for voters in Quebec and other provinces.

He urged Canadians who, like him, disagreed with Friday’s decision to bring their “outrage” at the superior court level by requesting rulings in the future when they believe their Charter rights are being denied by what he called “discriminatory” laws in Alberta, Saskatchewan and Quebec.

Decisions on those rulings will give the “voting public knowledge, which is power,” on how exactly their province is unjustifiably infringing on their Charter rights, Kinew told The Globe at an unrelated RCMP event in Winnipeg. “And then, hopefully, you, the good people of Canada, will vote governments like that out of office,” he said.

“Bill 21, let’s just be honest here — this was designed to discriminate against Muslims primarily, but also Sikhs and other religious minorities,” he said.

“The Canada that I want to live in should have an RCMP officer free to wear a turban. Should have a school teacher, if she chooses to wear a hijab, to be able to do so. A Hutterite woman should be able to wear a head covering. You should be able to wear a cross if you so choose. And yes, your Premier,” he added, speaking about himself as Canada’s first First Nations premier, “should be able to have long hair. These are all cultural symbols that would be banned by Bill 21, which I think is legislative racism.”

Conservative Senator Salma Ataullahjan, who also is chair of Senate Human Rights Committee, wrote on X that Friday is a “sad day for Canada” following the decision to uphold Bill 21.

“If the Supreme Court has ruled that the legislation as currently written allows governments to create laws that violate citizens’ Charter rights, then the federal government has a responsibility to initiate a constitutional amendment,” she wrote. “We cannot allow for the undermining of fundamental freedoms guaranteed by our Charter.”

B.C. Premier Lorne Doerkson says his recently sworn-in Conservative government “welcomes today’s Supreme Court decision upholding the availability of the notwithstanding clause,” a provision he said is “at the heart of Canadian federalism.”

In a statement posted to X on Friday , he also expressed his disagreement with Quebec’s Bill 21 and acknowledged the concerns many in British Columbia have about the ban on religious symbols for public servants.

“Freedom of religion is fundamental in this country, and it is not government’s place to tell a teacher, or anyone else who serves the public that they cannot wear a turban, a hijab, a kippah or a cross to work,” Doerkson said in the post.

“Our government was elected to protect the freedoms of British Columbians, and that is what I will always do.”

- The Canadian Press

The case was brought forward by the English Montreal School Board, which argued Bill 21 also infringed on minority language rights.

“This result is very disappointing for many people today,” said Joe Ortona, chair of the school board, speaking to journalists after the ruling.

But, he added, it was encouraging to see a split vote on whether the law could have been abolished under the guarantee of gender equality.

He promised to continue to lobby the government to amend or abolish the law.

Nevien Waly worries she’ll never get to teach in Quebec schools after the Supreme Court of Canada upheld the province’s law banning public servants in positions of authority from wearing religious symbols while on the job.

The law applies to public school teachers, police officers, government lawyers and other officials.

It also applies to Waly, who wears a hijab.

Speaking moments after the court released its ruling, Waly explained how she left her career as an accountant and started studying education in 2019, right before Bill 21 was adopted. Now that the court decision is out, the 45-year-old said she feels sad and disappointed.

The law has even prevented her from volunteering at the schools of her four children.

“When there was no final decision, there was always a glimpse of hope that things could change around, and now it’s kind of set in stone, so it’s just kind of like a mourning period,” she said.

– David Ebner and Eric Andrew-Gee

Among the more voluble and eloquent lawyers on the Bill 21 case is Frédéric Bérard, counsel for the Fédération autonome de l’enseignement, a group of Quebec teachers’ unions. On the last day of the hearing in March he cited the French writer Albert Camus and his well-known observation that democracy is not the law for the majority but for the protection of minorities. The Bill 21 case is at its heart about “respecting fundamental rights,” Bérard said in the courtroom.

In an interview Friday, Bérard said four judges found Bill 21 unconstitutional, even as the court as a whole upheld the law. He was especially happy the court endorsed judicial declarations.

“We won, for the most part,” he said. “We had an 800-kilometre hike to make in bare feet. It’s a good day for democracy.”

He added: “It’s a very strong message about fundamental rights from the Supreme Court. You can’t violate fundamental rights without having to defend your bill in front of the courts.”

The head of the National Council of Canadian Muslims says the federal government has no choice but to protect the rights of minority Canadians given Friday’s Supreme Court ruling.

During a news conference on Parliament Hill shortly after the ruling on Bill 21 and the notwithstanding clause, Stephen Brown, CEO of the council, called for the federal government to bring provinces into talks on limiting the use of the notwithstanding clause.

“Is it realistic that it’s going to happen tomorrow? No,” Brown said.

But he added that, although a difficult task, the Charter can be changed. “Our elected officials were elected to do the difficult job of running this country. And the core of that means protecting Canadian citizens and protecting Quebeckers,” he said. “Saying that it’s difficult, I’m sorry, is not a good enough reason to remain in inaction.”

He suggested that Ottawa use the federal power of disallowance to prevent provinces from using the notwithstanding clause. Disallowance is a rarely used power that allows the federal government to kill a provincial law by requesting the Governor-General to do so.

Anaïs Bussières McNicoll, the director of the fundamental freedoms program at the Canadian Civil Liberties Association, said at the same news conference that her organization has been pushing for limits on the notwithstanding clause, and would continue that effort at all levels of government in Canada.

“I also do believe that Quebeckers and Canadians should take away from the judgment today that they are all vulnerable to government abuse, and this is something that they should not readily accept,” she said.

“I think it’s collectively our job to reinstore the political cost that was supposed to be tied to any invocation of the notwithstanding clause.”

Good day. I’m Matthew Scace, a reporter with The Globe’s Alberta bureau in Calgary.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, who has deployed the notwithstanding clause to shield four of her government’s laws from Charter challenges, celebrated the Supreme Court’s decision.

Smith’s government sided with Quebec as an intervenor in the case. She reiterated her long-held belief that elected officials, not judges, should have the final word on important issues.

“This ruling is a win for provincial rights and for the democratic balance that holds our federation together,” she wrote on social media.

Smith used the notwithstanding clause in October 2025 when she forced teachers to end a strike of more than three weeks that put more than 750,000 students out of classrooms. The clause forced teachers to accept an agreement nearly 90 per cent of them rejected in a vote.

Three weeks later, she used it to shield a trio of sweeping bills affecting transgender and gender-diverse youth.

Those bills limited gender-affirming treatment, banned transgender participation in women’s and girls’ sports divisions, and required parental consent for name and pronoun changes in school. All three bills were facing lawsuits.

– Konrad Yakabuski

The Carney government took a very cautious approach in its intervention before the court on Bill 21, no doubt so as to avoid ruffling political feathers in Quebec. The judgment spares Carney from a constitutional crisis that would have resulted from an invalidation of Bill 21.

The federal government’s call for a limit on the repetitive use of the notwithstanding clause was rejected by the court, sticking to a strict reading of Section 33, which does not impose explicit limits on its use. The court did hand Ottawa a victory on allowing lower courts to issue declaratory judgments specifying which rights have been violated by laws that are shielded by Section 33, without invalidating those laws.

Federal Justice Minister Sean Fraser says the government is carefully reviewing the Supreme Court decision on Bill 21 and the notwithstanding clause.

“We respect the independence of the Court,” Fraser said in a statement issued by his office.

Fraser, also the Attorney General, added that the court confirmed Canadians have the right to know when their Charter rights have been unjustifiably infringed when the notwithstanding clause has been invoked.

“This is an important part of ensuring transparency, accountability and a healthy democracy,” he said.

“Our government is unwavering in its commitment to upholding the Constitution and the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, protecting the rights and freedoms of Canadians, and respecting the jurisdiction of provinces as well as the independence of the Court.”

Fraser’s office said he would not otherwise be commenting on today’s development and the statement stands as his response until further notice.

Bloc Québécois Leader Yves-François Blanchet says the court ruling is an “important victory” for Quebec.

“The Supreme Court of Canada recognizes the relevance and legitimacy of the National Assembly of Quebec’s use of the notwithstanding clause,” he told reporters in Ottawa.

“We acknowledge that we are in a position to move forward with the preservation of elements that profoundly define what makes Quebec society distinct.”

But Blanchet criticized the federal government, which had intervened to propose restrictions on the use of the notwithstanding clause.

“They will say to us, ‘Here is proof that Canada works,’” he said, referring to the ruling. “My friends, you did everything to ensure that it would not work.”

Adam Dodek, a law professor and a former law dean at the University of Ottawa, said the deep divisions among the judges means it is “not a great day for the Supreme Court.”

He questioned the court’s push to get the Bill 21 decision out by the end of November, after the hearing in March. In a case of this magnitude, the court would normally have taken more time but the end of November marked the last point at which Justice Sheilah Martin could participate in judgments after retiring from the top court in May.

“This case was too important for the court to rush it out under deadline,” Dodek said. “They should have taken more time to attempt to find consensus on at least some issues. The case should force the court to undertake a serious rethink about how to manage mega-cases of this size.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney has weighed in on the Bill 21 decision, saying he respects “the independence of the judiciary” and the Constitution.

“The core of the judgment is that the use of the notwithstanding clause for virtually all of the applications of what is called Bill 21 was appropriate,” he told the CBC in an interview during a visit to the Yukon.

He added it’s important that all provinces and the federal government “do their utmost to respect the rights and liberties of all Canadians, including those in the minority.”

Hi, I’m Temur Durrani, The Globe’s national correspondent in Winnipeg. I’ve been covering Manitoba and Prairie affairs since late 2023.

Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew, who has been a vocal critic of Quebec’s Bill 21 and other provincial governments’ usage of the Charter’s notwithstanding clause, just issued a statement supporting the Supreme Court’s ruling.

Manitoba was one of the intervenors in this case, presenting arguments on how Bill 21 affects constitutional law, democracy and provincial statutes.

Kinew praised the top court for allowing non-binding judicial rulings, which would allow superior court judges to declare that a law protected by the notwithstanding clause violates the Charter, even while that law is allowed to be enacted.

“Manitoba intervened to make this point and I am glad we won it,” Kinew said.

He also mentioned that Manitoba, where Kinew’s New Democrats have been in power since 2023, has passed recent legislation requiring any future provincial government seeking to invoke the notwithstanding clause to first obtain a non-binding court ruling.

“If voters know their government is violating Charter rights they can hold them accountable in the next election,” Kinew said.

The Premier is expected to issue further comments later this afternoon.

Hello, I’m Konrad Yakabuski, a Globe and Mail columnist based in Montreal.

The Supreme Court of Canada has handed down a complex judgment that will be studied by jurists for decades. Though the tensions among the seven justices who heard the appeal on Bill 21 are evident in the 520-page ruling, Chief Justice Richard Wagner successfully squared the circle of accommodating Quebec’s distinctness. That has been the hallmark of previous rulings by the top court. In doing so, the court clearly (if not explicitly) showed it remains sensitive to the political implications of its decisions.

Quebec Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime says the decision is a victory for Quebeckers and secularism in the province, and will do little to foster separatist sentiment.

“This is certainly a defeat, I believe, for the Parti Québécois’s referendum agenda, which, unfortunately, often feeds on Quebec’s failures to keep the flame of the referendum alive,” he told reporters in Quebec City.

The PQ formed a minority government last month with a promise to hold a third referendum on independence.

Amrit Kaur, a Sikh woman who wears a turban, graduated with an education degree in 2019 on the day Bill 21 became law. Her career teaching in Quebec ended before it began. She has for years been among the challengers in court against Bill 21 and was one of the appellants at the Supreme Court.

On Friday morning, Kaur said in an interview with The Globe that despite Bill 21 being upheld, she considers the declaration by three of the judges that the law violates the Charter to be a victory. She also said the fight against Bill 21 will continue in grassroots political work in Quebec, just as opposition to the law began in the late 2010s.

“The fight for human rights continues,” she said.

She emphasized the fact that four of the judges made it clear on Friday that Bill 21 is discriminatory, even as it remains in force.

“It’s not up for debate anymore,” she said, referring to some politicians and commentators who previously argued Bill 21 did not in fact explicitly discriminate against her and other minority women.

At an ongoing news conference on Parliament Hill, the Canadian Civil Liberties Association has expressed its concern with the Supreme Court ruling.

“We are deeply disappointed that the Supreme Court has allowed Bill 21 to remain in force,” said Howard Sapers, the association’s executive director.

He said today’s ruling raises questions about government accountability and the use of the notwithstanding clause.

“These legal proceedings have come to an end,” he said.

“But the broader struggle for equality and religious freedom is far from over.”

Hello, It’s Ian Bailey from the Ottawa bureau of The Globe and Mail.

On Parliament Hill, the CEO of the National Council of Canadian Muslims denounced the Supreme Court ruling.

“The decision is an unrestricted licence for every government in the country to pass legislation taking away fundamental freedoms and the legal rights of every community,” said Stephen Brown, adding that he hopes legislators will show restraint.

Brown called on the federal government to show leadership by bringing the provinces together to establish limits on the use of the notwithstanding clause.

I’m Eric Andrew-Gee, a reporter in The Globe and Mail’s Quebec bureau. I’ll be covering the political and social fallout of the Supreme Court ruling in the province today.

The upholding of Bill 21 will likely avert a political firestorm in Quebec, where the law is popular and widely seen as an expression of the province’s distinctive secularist values. The Court’s strong support for the use of the notwithstanding clause in this case will also reassure many Quebeckers that their legislature can hold sway on important issues within the constraints of the Charter.

This result should avoid a second constitutional crisis in Quebec after a lower court ruling this week that the province’s legislators must swear an oath to the King, suspending a 2022 provincial law that abolished that requirement. A hearing on the appeal filed by the separatist Parti Québécois government to the temporary injunction will be held Friday, while Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon has said his party plans to sit in the National Assembly as scheduled next week.

Although it defuses a possible political bombshell, the survival of Bill 21 will likely fuel protests in Quebec by groups representing religious minorities and civil liberties. The student union of the University of Montreal has organized a rally on campus for noon on Friday against “the systemic violence done to Muslim women,” regardless of the Court’s decision.

Hundreds of college students in Quebec had already walked out of classes on Thursday to oppose restrictions on religious practice in public institutions, including postsecondary schools, through the province’s Bill 9, another secularism law.

Reactions to the decision are starting to trickle in from Quebec, where the Coalition Avenir Québec is celebrating a “victory” for the law it passed in 2019. “We are pleased to note that the law has been upheld and maintained by the Court,” interim CAQ Leader Mathieu Lévesque said in a statement.

The CAQ passed Bill 21 under the leadership of former premier François Legault, but was wiped off the map in last month’s provincial election.

Meanwhile, the English Montreal School Board, one of the groups that challenged the law, said it is “deeply disappointed to have lost its appeal by the narrowest of margins.” The board pointed out that three of the seven judges argued the law should be struck down based on the gender equality section of the Charter.

One other big issue in the case was Section 28 of the Charter: gender equality.

Bill 21 prohibits many public servants in Quebec, including teachers and police, from wearing religious symbols, such as a hijab or a cross, ON the job. While the law applies to all people, critics have long argued it specifically aimed at minority women such as Muslims.

The court ruled 4-3 that the Charter’s gender equality section could not be used to strike down Bill 21. Chief Justice Richard Wagner called Section 28 an interpretive provision only that does not create a distinct legal right.

But Justices Sheilah Martin, Andromache Karakatsanis and Michelle O’Bonsawin all argued that Section 28 was more than interpretative and should serve as the basis for striking down the heart of Bill 21, the ban on religious symbols.

Justice Martin, who grew up in Montreal and was appointed to the court in 2017 from Calgary, delivered a tour-de-force judgment, writing for herself alone, in her last ruling of her eight-plus years on the Supreme Court. She retired in May and is allowed to sign judgements on cases on which she sat until the end of this month.

On gender equality, and striking down Bill 21, Justice Martin declared Bill 21 unequally restricts “a women’s right to respect her faith, freely express herself and to be free from discrimination based on religion and sex.”

Divisions were clear at the Supreme Court hearing on Bill 21 in March and the current court for years has been noted for its tendency to split rather than come together.

Chief Justice Richard Wagner, in his statements and questions in the courtroom in March, suggested he would take a tempered view on any restrictions on the notwithstanding clause, and Justices Malcolm Rowe and Suzanne Côté echoed this. The three judges joined together on Friday to write the keystone ruling of the four judgments.

Justice Nicholas Kasirer on the second of four days asked extensively about judicial declarations. Justices Sheilah Martin, Andromache Karakatsanis and Michelle O’Bonsawin didn’t ask a single question over the entire four days. These four judges on Friday put out alternative views on various legal issues and won the day, 4-3, ON whether courts can issue declarations even if the notwithstanding clause is used.

While the Supreme Court didn’t make its own judicial declaration on Bill 21, voting 4-3 against such a move, Justice Nicholas Kasirer in dissent declared that Bill 21 violates Section 2 of the Charter, which includes freedom of religion, and Section 15, equality rights.

Justices Andromache Karakatsanis and Michelle O’Bonsawin, agreeing in dissent with Justice Kasirer, wrote: “This court should not be silent when asked by claimants to acknowledge that [Bill 21] infringes their rights and freedoms. Democratic accountability in Quebec will benefit from informed public discourse.”

Chief Justice Richard Wagner, for the majority that stood against issuing a declaration, said doing so would tread into hypothetical territory and “would substantially diminish the effect” of the notwithstanding clause.

The Supreme Court’s ruling is an obvious win for Quebec and other conservative-led provinces that argued judges of the top court should not impose any new restrictions on the notwithstanding clause, as the federal Liberal government and others at the hearing in March had proposed.

But the narrow endorsement of judicial declarations – an idea opposed by conservative-led provinces but supported by many others including Ottawa – will make it easier for citizens to take on governments that use the notwithstanding clause.

The Supreme Court of Canada on Friday morning upheld Quebec’s Bill 21 in its landmark judgment on the province’s secularism law and the limits of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms – but fractured on other key questions.

Six justices from the top court ruled Quebec had validly deployed the Charter’s notwithstanding clause when the province passed the law in 2019. The controversial clause allows legislators to override numerous protections promised to Canadians in the Charter, such as freedom of religion and equality rights.

“Bill 21,” wrote Chief Justice Richard Wagner, “is rooted in Quebec’s legitimate and historical commitment to ensuring the [secularism] of the state in a free and democratic society.”

But the judges also broke new legal ground on Friday, by endorsing the ability of the courts to issue judicial declarations on laws protected by the notwithstanding clause. This means a judge could declare Bill 21 violates the Charter – even as the law is allowed to stand.

The Supreme Court did not issue its own declaration on whether Bill 21 violates the Charter.

Seven judges split into four camps.

Judicial declarations garnered a 4-3 endorsement from the Supreme Court, led by Justice Nicholas Kasirer. The Chief Justice dissented on this issue. Both men are Montrealers with deep roots in Quebec.

The court decided not to issue its own declaration on Bill 21, by a count of 4-3 – led by Chief Justice Wagner.

The sprawling package of judgments runs to almost 140,000 words – roughly the same as a 500-page book. It is a mash of legal opinions on the fundamental question of how Canada operates as a federation. The Supreme Court in recent years has been known for its internal divisions, exemplified on Friday. The four judgments run to a truly epic length, from a court that often produces elongated judgments.

In November 1981, five weeks after the Supreme Court ruled that the federal government, by convention, had to garner substantial support among the provinces to patriate the Constitution from Britain, a final federal-provincial meeting in Ottawa began to disintegrate on the third day. “Can you give us more time?” whispered justice minister Jean Chrétien to Pierre Trudeau.

Later, in a small kitchen at the old conference centre near Parliament Hill, Chrétien and counterparts from NDP Saskatchewan and Progressive Conservative Ontario struck a deal. The Charter would include a notwithstanding clause that could override numerous rights.

This unlocked the 1982 patriation of the Constitution and the enactment of the Charter in the Constitution. Since Confederation in 1867, Canada’s founding document had resided at Westminster in London as the British North America Act.

For much of the past 44 years, political leaders rarely deployed the notwithstanding clause. Quebec’s Bill 21 in 2019 stands as a demarcation. Alberta used it in four laws a year ago, one to end a teachers strike and three to restrict the choices of transgender youth. The federal government, Conservative or Liberal, has never used the clause.

At the heart of the Bill 21 case are two questions, both revolving around the notwithstanding clause and the Charter promises it can override, such as freedom of religion in Section 2 and equality rights in Section 15.

The first question is whether there should be new limits on political use of the clause, as the federal Liberal government and some appellants and intervenors proposed. None of the provinces, from conservative to NDP, supported this argument.

The Supreme Court has only once issued a significant ruling on the clause, in the 1988 Ford case. The precedent endorsed governments’ mostly unfettered right to use the notwithstanding override power as they like, in a case about French-language commercial signage in Quebec.

This is the second big question is around judicial declarations.

Ottawa, along with numerous appellants and intervenors, support the idea of judicial declarations. This would allow superior trial court judges to declare that a law insulated by the notwithstanding clause violates the Charter, even as the law is allowed to continue to operate.

An endorsement of judicial declarations from the Supreme Court would make it easier for citizens to take on governments that use the notwithstanding clause.

Hi, I’m Maura Forrest, and I cover Quebec politics from Montreal. As we wait for the Supreme Court ruling on Bill 21 this morning, here’s a recap of what Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon had to say about the pending decision on Thursday.

St-Pierre Plamondon said the case is about “preserving the choices of Quebec’s democracy” and the province’s ability to make decisions that “differ from the rest of Canada.”

A decision by the Supreme Court to limit the power of legislatures to “make their own democratic decisions will trigger, of course, a very strong reaction among all provinces,” he added.

The Quebec Premier said if the Supreme Court issues a ruling with the effect of “centralizing power even more,” it will prompt “very heated” discussions at an upcoming meeting of Canada’s premiers in Toronto.

Quebec’s secularism law, Bill 21, prohibits many public sector workers, including teachers and police, from wearing religious symbols, such as a hijab or a cross, ON the job.

Quebec shielded the law from being struck down by the courts with Section 33 of the Charter, the notwithstanding clause. But an array of groups and affected citizens – including female Muslim, Sikh and Catholic teachers – launched court challenges. Critics of Bill 21 view the law as squarely aimed at minority women in a province with long and deep Catholic roots.

In April 2021, the Quebec Superior Court upheld Bill 21 after a 33-day trial. Justice Marc-André Blanchard observed that the law forced “a cruel consequence that dehumanizes the people targeted” but could not be struck down for Charter violations because it was protected by the notwithstanding clause.

The Quebec Court of Appeal, for the same reason, upheld the law in February 2024.

Nine months later, the Supreme Court agreed to hear six appeals, to be decided Friday. In March the court held four days of hearings, among the longest in its history. It included a record 38 outside intervenor groups.

Hi – David Ebner here, The Globe’s justice reporter since late 2024 (and at The Globe for the past quarter century in a variety of roles from business and the editorial board to sports features).

I’ve immersed myself in the Bill 21 case at the Supreme Court over the past two years, and was in Ottawa in March when the case was heard over four days in the old courtroom.

On Friday morning, I am in the lockup ahead of the decision – the court, like the federal government on budgets, is giving journalists and lawyers time to understand the judgment ahead of its official release at 9:45 a.m. Ottawa time. Among the stories about the case I’ve written that I think can add some depth to Canadians’ understanding of everything going is my profile of Chief Justice Richard Wagner from July .

Judges of the country’s top court will answer essential questions about how Canada operates as a federation in their landmark ruling on six appeals of Bill 21.

The judgment revolves around the limits of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms and governments’ ability to use the notwithstanding clause, the powerful tool that legislators can invoke to override many of the protections promised to Canadians in the Charter.

In 2019, Quebec enacted Bill 21, a law to promote secularism. It prohibits public sector workers, including teachers, from wearing religious symbols such as a hijab on the job.

Quebec shielded the law from court challenges with the Charter’s notwithstanding clause. That allows governments to override many Charter rights.

Challengers to Bill 21 insist it violates freedom of religion and the right to equality but the law was twice upheld in the lower courts in Quebec because of the notwithstanding clause.

At the heart of the case is the balance between government powers and Canadians’ rights.

Quebec insists the top court take a hands-off approach and respect the generally unfettered power of elected governments to use the notwithstanding clause.

Challengers want the law struck down and the top court to impose new limits on the clause. Minority rights are under attack, they say, such as those of Muslim women who wear a hijab and can’t be teachers in Quebec.

Back in late March, The Globe’s justice reporter, David Ebner, attended the four-day Supreme Court hearing. At the time, he shared his thoughts on the landmark case, its potential precedent-setting magnitude and the major implications for the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

Watch his recap of the hearing below.

The Supreme Court of Canada will deliver its landmark ruling in the Quebec secularism case on Friday.

The country’s top court said the ruling will be issued at 9:45 a.m. ET.

The hotly political case is rooted in foundational questions about Canada’s Constitution and the limits of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Seven judges of the top court heard the appeal over four days in March , one of the longest hearings in the history of the Supreme Court.

The decision is the biggest in the court’s recent history and one of the most important Charter rulings ever. The Supreme Court’s judgment is in part a reckoning with the political compromises of the early 1980s that helped achieve the patriation of the Constitution from Britain in 1982 and the inclusion of the Charter in the Constitution.

At issue in the Quebec secularism case at the Supreme Court is the province’s Bill 21 . Passed in 2019, the law prohibits many public-sector workers in the province, including teachers and police officers, from wearing religious symbols (such as a hijab or a cross) on the job. The provincial government shielded Bill 21 from court challenges with Section 33 of the Charter, the notwithstanding clause, which allows legislatures to override many of the rights in the Charter.

Quebec’s goal is secularism but some people believe Bill 21 violates freedom of religion and is a state attack on minorities.

The notwithstanding clause requires renewal every five years and Quebec did so in 2024. Bill 21 was also twice upheld by the lower courts in Quebec, in 2021 and 2024, both times because of the notwithstanding clause.
paragraphs: The Supreme Court’s Bill 21 decision defines the limits of your Charter rights, and not just for people in Quebec. The consequential ruling upheld the province’s secularism law as well as the Charter’s notwithstanding clause, paving the way for other provincial governments to use it to shield their own laws from Charter challenges.
But as justice reporter David Ebner explains, it will likely take legal experts years to untangle the full implications of the lengthy ruling.

When Canada’s premiers convene in Toronto next month, there is expected to be quite a bit of tension in the room because of their clashing opinions on the Bill 21 ruling, says Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew.
“We disagree significantly,” he told The Globe and Mail in Winnipeg on Friday.

That includes disagreements with his friend, Ontario Premier Doug Ford, who has not yet commented on the Supreme Court’s decision, though he has previously issued strong support toward usage of the notwithstanding clause, Kinew added.

“Doug, I get along with him; other premiers, whatever. But if you in the Prairie provinces have to target gay people in order to get elected, quit. Give it up. We don’t need you in public,” Kinew said, speaking directly to his fellow provincial leaders, in reference to Alberta and Saskatchewan’s use of the notwithstanding clause on legislation related to gender and sexuality.
“If you in Quebec have to target Muslims and Sikhs in order to win office, get out of here.”
As an Anishinaabe man, Kinew said he “grew up with racism,” which is why the issue of Bill 21 feels personal to him.

“And so, if I see somebody who’s rich and powerful pick on the one trans kid in an entire region of their province, yeah, I’m going to say something. If I see somebody who’s rich and powerful, who is trying to make the working class vote against their economic self-interest by picking on Muslims, yeah, I’m going to say something about it.”
Federal NDP Leader Avi Lewis criticized the decision to uphold Bill 21, which he said “affirms the right of provincial governments to override fundamental freedoms without any guardrails.”

“From Alberta and Saskatchewan to Ontario and Quebec, conservative premiers are sweeping aside the rights of workers, trans kids, and minorities to distract from their inability to solve the real crises we face, first and foremost the cost of living,” he wrote in a statement on X on Friday . “And they’re preemptively using the notwithstanding clause to get away with it.”
Lewis reiterated his condemnation of the Quebec secularism law and urged Canadians to take this issue to the ballot box now that legal options have been exhausted.
“We need to elect progressive governments across the country who will not abuse their authority to violate the fundamental freedoms we cherish,” he wrote.

Kerri Froc, an associate professor at the University of New Brunswick’s Faculty of Law who focuses on women’s constitutional rights, said Canada’s top court had set a worrying precedent in refusing to limit the powers of provinces as long as they invoke the unusual constitutional provision.

“The Supreme Court has sent a clear message it’s not going to step in when the rights of vulnerable minorities are trampled on in these cases, so perhaps this needs to move to the political sphere,” Froc said.

The Quebec Liberals are welcoming the Supreme Court’s confirmation that the decision of whether to invoke the notwithstanding clause rests solely with Quebec, the Official Opposition said in a statement Friday .

“Quebec has the right to invoke the exemption clause, and we will not hesitate to do so as a preventive measure if it proves necessary to defend our democratic choices and our shared values,” Liberal Leader Charles Milliard wrote.

“In Quebec, the secular nature of the state and the promotion and protection of the French language are shared values,” he said. “For too long, they have been used as arguments to divide us. It is time for this to stop.”
The Liberals reiterated their position that the ban on religious symbols should be limited to public servants with “coercive authority,” such as judges and police officers.

“Once again, the Quebec Liberal Party’s approach is both reasonable and responsible, and aims to maintain social stability while limiting infringements on fundamental rights and freedom,” wrote Milliard.

Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew says the Supreme Court’s allowance for non-binding judicial rulings on government usage of the notwithstanding clause should serve as an important new tool for voters in Quebec and other provinces.

He urged Canadians who, like him, disagreed with Friday’s decision to bring their “outrage” at the superior court level by requesting rulings in the future when they believe their Charter rights are being denied by what he called “discriminatory” laws in Alberta, Saskatchewan and Quebec.

Decisions on those rulings will give the “voting public knowledge, which is power,” on how exactly their province is unjustifiably infringing on their Charter rights, Kinew told The Globe at an unrelated RCMP event in Winnipeg. “And then, hopefully, you, the good people of Canada, will vote governments like that out of office,” he said.
“Bill 21, let’s just be honest here — this was designed to discriminate against Muslims primarily, but also Sikhs and other religious minorities,” he said.

“The Canada that I want to live in should have an RCMP officer free to wear a turban. Should have a school teacher, if she chooses to wear a hijab, to be able to do so. A Hutterite woman should be able to wear a head covering. You should be able to wear a cross if you so choose. And yes, your Premier,” he added, speaking about himself as Canada’s first First Nations premier, “should be able to have long hair. These are all cultural symbols that would be banned by Bill 21, which I think is legislative racism.”
Conservative Senator Salma Ataullahjan, who also is chair of Senate Human Rights Committee, wrote on X that Friday is a “sad day for Canada” following the decision to uphold Bill 21.

“If the Supreme Court has ruled that the legislation as currently written allows governments to create laws that violate citizens’ Charter rights, then the federal government has a responsibility to initiate a constitutional amendment,” she wrote. “We cannot allow for the undermining of fundamental freedoms guaranteed by our Charter.”

B.C. Premier Lorne Doerkson says his recently sworn-in Conservative government “welcomes today’s Supreme Court decision upholding the availability of the notwithstanding clause,” a provision he said is “at the heart of Canadian federalism.”

In a statement posted to X on Friday , he also expressed his disagreement with Quebec’s Bill 21 and acknowledged the concerns many in British Columbia have about the ban on religious symbols for public servants.

“Freedom of religion is fundamental in this country, and it is not government’s place to tell a teacher, or anyone else who serves the public that they cannot wear a turban, a hijab, a kippah or a cross to work,” Doerkson said in the post.
“Our government was elected to protect the freedoms of British Columbians, and that is what I will always do.”

“This result is very disappointing for many people today,” said Joe Ortona, chair of the school board, speaking to journalists after the ruling.
But, he added, it was encouraging to see a split vote on whether the law could have been abolished under the guarantee of gender equality.
He promised to continue to lobby the government to amend or abolish the law.

The law applies to public school teachers, police officers, government lawyers and other officials.
It also applies to Waly, who wears a hijab.

Speaking moments after the court released its ruling, Waly explained how she left her career as an accountant and started studying education in 2019, right before Bill 21 was adopted. Now that the court decision is out, the 45-year-old said she feels sad and disappointed.
The law has even prevented her from volunteering at the schools of her four children.
“When there was no final decision, there was always a glimpse of hope that things could change around, and now it’s kind of set in stone, so it’s just kind of like a mourning period,” she said.
– David Ebner and Eric Andrew-Gee

Among the more voluble and eloquent lawyers on the Bill 21 case is Frédéric Bérard, counsel for the Fédération autonome de l’enseignement, a group of Quebec teachers’ unions. On the last day of the hearing in March he cited the French writer Albert Camus and his well-known observation that democracy is not the law for the majority but for the protection of minorities. The Bill 21 case is at its heart about “respecting fundamental rights,” Bérard said in the courtroom.
In an interview Friday, Bérard said four judges found Bill 21 unconstitutional, even as the court as a whole upheld the law. He was especially happy the court endorsed judicial declarations.
“We won, for the most part,” he said. “We had an 800-kilometre hike to make in bare feet. It’s a good day for democracy.”
He added: “It’s a very strong message about fundamental rights from the Supreme Court. You can’t violate fundamental rights without having to defend your bill in front of the courts.”
The head of the National Council of Canadian Muslims says the federal government has no choice but to protect the rights of minority Canadians given Friday’s Supreme Court ruling.

During a news conference on Parliament Hill shortly after the ruling on Bill 21 and the notwithstanding clause, Stephen Brown, CEO of the council, called for the federal government to bring provinces into talks on limiting the use of the notwithstanding clause.
“Is it realistic that it’s going to happen tomorrow? No,” Brown said.

But he added that, although a difficult task, the Charter can be changed. “Our elected officials were elected to do the difficult job of running this country. And the core of that means protecting Canadian citizens and protecting Quebeckers,” he said. “Saying that it’s difficult, I’m sorry, is not a good enough reason to remain in inaction.”

He suggested that Ottawa use the federal power of disallowance to prevent provinces from using the notwithstanding clause. Disallowance is a rarely used power that allows the federal government to kill a provincial law by requesting the Governor-General to do so.

Anaïs Bussières McNicoll, the director of the fundamental freedoms program at the Canadian Civil Liberties Association, said at the same news conference that her organization has been pushing for limits on the notwithstanding clause, and would continue that effort at all levels of government in Canada.

“I also do believe that Quebeckers and Canadians should take away from the judgment today that they are all vulnerable to government abuse, and this is something that they should not readily accept,” she said.
“I think it’s collectively our job to reinstore the political cost that was supposed to be tied to any invocation of the notwithstanding clause.”
Good day. I’m Matthew Scace, a reporter with The Globe’s Alberta bureau in Calgary.
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, who has deployed the notwithstanding clause to shield four of her government’s laws from Charter challenges, celebrated the Supreme Court’s decision.
Smith’s government sided with Quebec as an intervenor in the case. She reiterated her long-held belief that elected officials, not judges, should have the final word on important issues.
“This ruling is a win for provincial rights and for the democratic balance that holds our federation together,” she wrote on social media.

Smith used the notwithstanding clause in October 2025 when she forced teachers to end a strike of more than three weeks that put more than 750,000 students out of classrooms. The clause forced teachers to accept an agreement nearly 90 per cent of them rejected in a vote.
Three weeks later, she used it to shield a trio of sweeping bills affecting transgender and gender-diverse youth.

Those bills limited gender-affirming treatment, banned transgender participation in women’s and girls’ sports divisions, and required parental consent for name and pronoun changes in school. All three bills were facing lawsuits.
– Konrad Yakabuski

The Carney government took a very cautious approach in its intervention before the court on Bill 21, no doubt so as to avoid ruffling political feathers in Quebec. The judgment spares Carney from a constitutional crisis that would have resulted from an invalidation of Bill 21.

The federal government’s call for a limit on the repetitive use of the notwithstanding clause was rejected by the court, sticking to a strict reading of Section 33, which does not impose explicit limits on its use. The court did hand Ottawa a victory on allowing lower courts to issue declaratory judgments specifying which rights have been violated by laws that are shielded by Section 33, without invalidating those laws.
Federal Justice Minister Sean Fraser says the government is carefully reviewing the Supreme Court decision on Bill 21 and the notwithstanding clause.
“We respect the independence of the Court,” Fraser said in a statement issued by his office.

Fraser, also the Attorney General, added that the court confirmed Canadians have the right to know when their Charter rights have been unjustifiably infringed when the notwithstanding clause has been invoked.
“This is an important part of ensuring transparency, accountability and a healthy democracy,” he said.

“Our government is unwavering in its commitment to upholding the Constitution and the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, protecting the rights and freedoms of Canadians, and respecting the jurisdiction of provinces as well as the independence of the Court.”
Fraser’s office said he would not otherwise be commenting on today’s development and the statement stands as his response until further notice.
Bloc Québécois Leader Yves-François Blanchet says the court ruling is an “important victory” for Quebec.
“The Supreme Court of Canada recognizes the relevance and legitimacy of the National Assembly of Quebec’s use of the notwithstanding clause,” he told reporters in Ottawa.
“We acknowledge that we are in a position to move forward with the preservation of elements that profoundly define what makes Quebec society distinct.”
But Blanchet criticized the federal government, which had intervened to propose restrictions on the use of the notwithstanding clause.
“They will say to us, ‘Here is proof that Canada works,’” he said, referring to the ruling. “My friends, you did everything to ensure that it would not work.”
Adam Dodek, a law professor and a former law dean at the University of Ottawa, said the deep divisions among the judges means it is “not a great day for the Supreme Court.”

He questioned the court’s push to get the Bill 21 decision out by the end of November, after the hearing in March. In a case of this magnitude, the court would normally have taken more time but the end of November marked the last point at which Justice Sheilah Martin could participate in judgments after retiring from the top court in May.

“This case was too important for the court to rush it out under deadline,” Dodek said. “They should have taken more time to attempt to find consensus on at least some issues. The case should force the court to undertake a serious rethink about how to manage mega-cases of this size.”
Prime Minister Mark Carney has weighed in on the Bill 21 decision, saying he respects “the independence of the judiciary” and the Constitution.

“The core of the judgment is that the use of the notwithstanding clause for virtually all of the applications of what is called Bill 21 was appropriate,” he told the CBC in an interview during a visit to the Yukon.
He added it’s important that all provinces and the federal government “do their utmost to respect the rights and liberties of all Canadians, including those in the minority.”
Hi, I’m Temur Durrani, The Globe’s national correspondent in Winnipeg. I’ve been covering Manitoba and Prairie affairs since late 2023.

Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew, who has been a vocal critic of Quebec’s Bill 21 and other provincial governments’ usage of the Charter’s notwithstanding clause, just issued a statement supporting the Supreme Court’s ruling.
Manitoba was one of the intervenors in this case, presenting arguments on how Bill 21 affects constitutional law, democracy and provincial statutes.

Kinew praised the top court for allowing non-binding judicial rulings, which would allow superior court judges to declare that a law protected by the notwithstanding clause violates the Charter, even while that law is allowed to be enacted.
“Manitoba intervened to make this point and I am glad we won it,” Kinew said.

He also mentioned that Manitoba, where Kinew’s New Democrats have been in power since 2023, has passed recent legislation requiring any future provincial government seeking to invoke the notwithstanding clause to first obtain a non-binding court ruling.
“If voters know their government is violating Charter rights they can hold them accountable in the next election,” Kinew said.
The Premier is expected to issue further comments later this afternoon.
Hello, I’m Konrad Yakabuski, a Globe and Mail columnist based in Montreal.

The Supreme Court of Canada has handed down a complex judgment that will be studied by jurists for decades. Though the tensions among the seven justices who heard the appeal on Bill 21 are evident in the 520-page ruling, Chief Justice Richard Wagner successfully squared the circle of accommodating Quebec’s distinctness. That has been the hallmark of previous rulings by the top court. In doing so, the court clearly (if not explicitly) showed it remains sensitive to the political implications of its decisions.
Quebec Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime says the decision is a victory for Quebeckers and secularism in the province, and will do little to foster separatist sentiment.

“This is certainly a defeat, I believe, for the Parti Québécois’s referendum agenda, which, unfortunately, often feeds on Quebec’s failures to keep the flame of the referendum alive,” he told reporters in Quebec City.
The PQ formed a minority government last month with a promise to hold a third referendum on independence.

Amrit Kaur, a Sikh woman who wears a turban, graduated with an education degree in 2019 on the day Bill 21 became law. Her career teaching in Quebec ended before it began. She has for years been among the challengers in court against Bill 21 and was one of the appellants at the Supreme Court.

On Friday morning, Kaur said in an interview with The Globe that despite Bill 21 being upheld, she considers the declaration by three of the judges that the law violates the Charter to be a victory. She also said the fight against Bill 21 will continue in grassroots political work in Quebec, just as opposition to the law began in the late 2010s.
“The fight for human rights continues,” she said.
She emphasized the fact that four of the judges made it clear on Friday that Bill 21 is discriminatory, even as it remains in force.
“It’s not up for debate anymore,” she said, referring to some politicians and commentators who previously argued Bill 21 did not in fact explicitly discriminate against her and other minority women.
At an ongoing news conference on Parliament Hill, the Canadian Civil Liberties Association has expressed its concern with the Supreme Court ruling.
“We are deeply disappointed that the Supreme Court has allowed Bill 21 to remain in force,” said Howard Sapers, the association’s executive director.
He said today’s ruling raises questions about government accountability and the use of the notwithstanding clause.
“These legal proceedings have come to an end,” he said.
“But the broader struggle for equality and religious freedom is far from over.”
Hello, It’s Ian Bailey from the Ottawa bureau of The Globe and Mail.
On Parliament Hill, the CEO of the National Council of Canadian Muslims denounced the Supreme Court ruling.

“The decision is an unrestricted licence for every government in the country to pass legislation taking away fundamental freedoms and the legal rights of every community,” said Stephen Brown, adding that he hopes legislators will show restraint.
Brown called on the federal government to show leadership by bringing the provinces together to establish limits on the use of the notwithstanding clause.
I’m Eric Andrew-Gee, a reporter in The Globe and Mail’s Quebec bureau. I’ll be covering the political and social fallout of the Supreme Court ruling in the province today.

The upholding of Bill 21 will likely avert a political firestorm in Quebec, where the law is popular and widely seen as an expression of the province’s distinctive secularist values. The Court’s strong support for the use of the notwithstanding clause in this case will also reassure many Quebeckers that their legislature can hold sway on important issues within the constraints of the Charter.

This result should avoid a second constitutional crisis in Quebec after a lower court ruling this week that the province’s legislators must swear an oath to the King, suspending a 2022 provincial law that abolished that requirement. A hearing on the appeal filed by the separatist Parti Québécois government to the temporary injunction will be held Friday, while Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon has said his party plans to sit in the National Assembly as scheduled next week.

Although it defuses a possible political bombshell, the survival of Bill 21 will likely fuel protests in Quebec by groups representing religious minorities and civil liberties. The student union of the University of Montreal has organized a rally on campus for noon on Friday against “the systemic violence done to Muslim women,” regardless of the Court’s decision.

Hundreds of college students in Quebec had already walked out of classes on Thursday to oppose restrictions on religious practice in public institutions, including postsecondary schools, through the province’s Bill 9, another secularism law.

Reactions to the decision are starting to trickle in from Quebec, where the Coalition Avenir Québec is celebrating a “victory” for the law it passed in 2019. “We are pleased to note that the law has been upheld and maintained by the Court,” interim CAQ Leader Mathieu Lévesque said in a statement.
The CAQ passed Bill 21 under the leadership of former premier François Legault, but was wiped off the map in last month’s provincial election.

Meanwhile, the English Montreal School Board, one of the groups that challenged the law, said it is “deeply disappointed to have lost its appeal by the narrowest of margins.” The board pointed out that three of the seven judges argued the law should be struck down based on the gender equality section of the Charter.
One other big issue in the case was Section 28 of the Charter: gender equality.

Bill 21 prohibits many public servants in Quebec, including teachers and police, from wearing religious symbols, such as a hijab or a cross, ON the job. While the law applies to all people, critics have long argued it specifically aimed at minority women such as Muslims.

The court ruled 4-3 that the Charter’s gender equality section could not be used to strike down Bill 21. Chief Justice Richard Wagner called Section 28 an interpretive provision only that does not create a distinct legal right.

But Justices Sheilah Martin, Andromache Karakatsanis and Michelle O’Bonsawin all argued that Section 28 was more than interpretative and should serve as the basis for striking down the heart of Bill 21, the ban on religious symbols.

Justice Martin, who grew up in Montreal and was appointed to the court in 2017 from Calgary, delivered a tour-de-force judgment, writing for herself alone, in her last ruling of her eight-plus years on the Supreme Court. She retired in May and is allowed to sign judgements on cases on which she sat until the end of this month.

On gender equality, and striking down Bill 21, Justice Martin declared Bill 21 unequally restricts “a women’s right to respect her faith, freely express herself and to be free from discrimination based on religion and sex.”
Divisions were clear at the Supreme Court hearing on Bill 21 in March and the current court for years has been noted for its tendency to split rather than come together.

Chief Justice Richard Wagner, in his statements and questions in the courtroom in March, suggested he would take a tempered view on any restrictions on the notwithstanding clause, and Justices Malcolm Rowe and Suzanne Côté echoed this. The three judges joined together on Friday to write the keystone ruling of the four judgments.

Justice Nicholas Kasirer on the second of four days asked extensively about judicial declarations. Justices Sheilah Martin, Andromache Karakatsanis and Michelle O’Bonsawin didn’t ask a single question over the entire four days. These four judges on Friday put out alternative views on various legal issues and won the day, 4-3, ON whether courts can issue declarations even if the notwithstanding clause is used.

While the Supreme Court didn’t make its own judicial declaration on Bill 21, voting 4-3 against such a move, Justice Nicholas Kasirer in dissent declared that Bill 21 violates Section 2 of the Charter, which includes freedom of religion, and Section 15, equality rights.

Justices Andromache Karakatsanis and Michelle O’Bonsawin, agreeing in dissent with Justice Kasirer, wrote: “This court should not be silent when asked by claimants to acknowledge that [Bill 21] infringes their rights and freedoms. Democratic accountability in Quebec will benefit from informed public discourse.”

Chief Justice Richard Wagner, for the majority that stood against issuing a declaration, said doing so would tread into hypothetical territory and “would substantially diminish the effect” of the notwithstanding clause.

The Supreme Court’s ruling is an obvious win for Quebec and other conservative-led provinces that argued judges of the top court should not impose any new restrictions on the notwithstanding clause, as the federal Liberal government and others at the hearing in March had proposed.

But the narrow endorsement of judicial declarations – an idea opposed by conservative-led provinces but supported by many others including Ottawa – will make it easier for citizens to take on governments that use the notwithstanding clause.

The Supreme Court of Canada on Friday morning upheld Quebec’s Bill 21 in its landmark judgment on the province’s secularism law and the limits of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms – but fractured on other key questions.

Six justices from the top court ruled Quebec had validly deployed the Charter’s notwithstanding clause when the province passed the law in 2019. The controversial clause allows legislators to override numerous protections promised to Canadians in the Charter, such as freedom of religion and equality rights.
“Bill 21,” wrote Chief Justice Richard Wagner, “is rooted in Quebec’s legitimate and historical commitment to ensuring the [secularism] of the state in a free and democratic society.”

But the judges also broke new legal ground on Friday, by endorsing the ability of the courts to issue judicial declarations on laws protected by the notwithstanding clause. This means a judge could declare Bill 21 violates the Charter – even as the law is allowed to stand.
The Supreme Court did not issue its own declaration on whether Bill 21 violates the Charter.
Seven judges split into four camps.

Judicial declarations garnered a 4-3 endorsement from the Supreme Court, led by Justice Nicholas Kasirer. The Chief Justice dissented on this issue. Both men are Montrealers with deep roots in Quebec.
The court decided not to issue its own declaration on Bill 21, by a count of 4-3 – led by Chief Justice Wagner.

The sprawling package of judgments runs to almost 140,000 words – roughly the same as a 500-page book. It is a mash of legal opinions on the fundamental question of how Canada operates as a federation. The Supreme Court in recent years has been known for its internal divisions, exemplified on Friday. The four judgments run to a truly epic length, from a court that often produces elongated judgments.

In November 1981, five weeks after the Supreme Court ruled that the federal government, by convention, had to garner substantial support among the provinces to patriate the Constitution from Britain, a final federal-provincial meeting in Ottawa began to disintegrate on the third day. “Can you give us more time?” whispered justice minister Jean Chrétien to Pierre Trudeau.

Later, in a small kitchen at the old conference centre near Parliament Hill, Chrétien and counterparts from NDP Saskatchewan and Progressive Conservative Ontario struck a deal. The Charter would include a notwithstanding clause that could override numerous rights.

This unlocked the 1982 patriation of the Constitution and the enactment of the Charter in the Constitution. Since Confederation in 1867, Canada’s founding document had resided at Westminster in London as the British North America Act.

For much of the past 44 years, political leaders rarely deployed the notwithstanding clause. Quebec’s Bill 21 in 2019 stands as a demarcation. Alberta used it in four laws a year ago, one to end a teachers strike and three to restrict the choices of transgender youth. The federal government, Conservative or Liberal, has never used the clause.

At the heart of the Bill 21 case are two questions, both revolving around the notwithstanding clause and the Charter promises it can override, such as freedom of religion in Section 2 and equality rights in Section 15.

The first question is whether there should be new limits on political use of the clause, as the federal Liberal government and some appellants and intervenors proposed. None of the provinces, from conservative to NDP, supported this argument.

The Supreme Court has only once issued a significant ruling on the clause, in the 1988 Ford case. The precedent endorsed governments’ mostly unfettered right to use the notwithstanding override power as they like, in a case about French-language commercial signage in Quebec.
This is the second big question is around judicial declarations.

Ottawa, along with numerous appellants and intervenors, support the idea of judicial declarations. This would allow superior trial court judges to declare that a law insulated by the notwithstanding clause violates the Charter, even as the law is allowed to continue to operate.
An endorsement of judicial declarations from the Supreme Court would make it easier for citizens to take on governments that use the notwithstanding clause.

Hi, I’m Maura Forrest, and I cover Quebec politics from Montreal. As we wait for the Supreme Court ruling on Bill 21 this morning, here’s a recap of what Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon had to say about the pending decision on Thursday.
St-Pierre Plamondon said the case is about “preserving the choices of Quebec’s democracy” and the province’s ability to make decisions that “differ from the rest of Canada.”
A decision by the Supreme Court to limit the power of legislatures to “make their own democratic decisions will trigger, of course, a very strong reaction among all provinces,” he added.

The Quebec Premier said if the Supreme Court issues a ruling with the effect of “centralizing power even more,” it will prompt “very heated” discussions at an upcoming meeting of Canada’s premiers in Toronto.
Quebec’s secularism law, Bill 21, prohibits many public sector workers, including teachers and police, from wearing religious symbols, such as a hijab or a cross, ON the job.

Quebec shielded the law from being struck down by the courts with Section 33 of the Charter, the notwithstanding clause. But an array of groups and affected citizens – including female Muslim, Sikh and Catholic teachers – launched court challenges. Critics of Bill 21 view the law as squarely aimed at minority women in a province with long and deep Catholic roots.

In April 2021, the Quebec Superior Court upheld Bill 21 after a 33-day trial. Justice Marc-André Blanchard observed that the law forced “a cruel consequence that dehumanizes the people targeted” but could not be struck down for Charter violations because it was protected by the notwithstanding clause.
The Quebec Court of Appeal, for the same reason, upheld the law in February 2024.

Nine months later, the Supreme Court agreed to hear six appeals, to be decided Friday. In March the court held four days of hearings, among the longest in its history. It included a record 38 outside intervenor groups.
Hi – David Ebner here, The Globe’s justice reporter since late 2024 (and at The Globe for the past quarter century in a variety of roles from business and the editorial board to sports features).
I’ve immersed myself in the Bill 21 case at the Supreme Court over the past two years, and was in Ottawa in March when the case was heard over four days in the old courtroom.

On Friday morning, I am in the lockup ahead of the decision – the court, like the federal government on budgets, is giving journalists and lawyers time to understand the judgment ahead of its official release at 9:45 a.m. Ottawa time. Among the stories about the case I’ve written that I think can add some depth to Canadians’ understanding of everything going is my profile of Chief Justice Richard Wagner from July .
Judges of the country’s top court will answer essential questions about how Canada operates as a federation in their landmark ruling on six appeals of Bill 21.

The judgment revolves around the limits of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms and governments’ ability to use the notwithstanding clause, the powerful tool that legislators can invoke to override many of the protections promised to Canadians in the Charter.
In 2019, Quebec enacted Bill 21, a law to promote secularism. It prohibits public sector workers, including teachers, from wearing religious symbols such as a hijab on the job.
Quebec shielded the law from court challenges with the Charter’s notwithstanding clause. That allows governments to override many Charter rights.
Challengers to Bill 21 insist it violates freedom of religion and the right to equality but the law was twice upheld in the lower courts in Quebec because of the notwithstanding clause.
At the heart of the case is the balance between government powers and Canadians’ rights.
Quebec insists the top court take a hands-off approach and respect the generally unfettered power of elected governments to use the notwithstanding clause.

Challengers want the law struck down and the top court to impose new limits on the clause. Minority rights are under attack, they say, such as those of Muslim women who wear a hijab and can’t be teachers in Quebec.

Back in late March, The Globe’s justice reporter, David Ebner, attended the four-day Supreme Court hearing. At the time, he shared his thoughts on the landmark case, its potential precedent-setting magnitude and the major implications for the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
Watch his recap of the hearing below.
The Supreme Court of Canada will deliver its landmark ruling in the Quebec secularism case on Friday.
The country’s top court said the ruling will be issued at 9:45 a.m. ET.

The hotly political case is rooted in foundational questions about Canada’s Constitution and the limits of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Seven judges of the top court heard the appeal over four days in March , one of the longest hearings in the history of the Supreme Court.

The decision is the biggest in the court’s recent history and one of the most important Charter rulings ever. The Supreme Court’s judgment is in part a reckoning with the political compromises of the early 1980s that helped achieve the patriation of the Constitution from Britain in 1982 and the inclusion of the Charter in the Constitution.

At issue in the Quebec secularism case at the Supreme Court is the province’s Bill 21 . Passed in 2019, the law prohibits many public-sector workers in the province, including teachers and police officers, from wearing religious symbols (such as a hijab or a cross) on the job. The provincial government shielded Bill 21 from court challenges with Section 33 of the Charter, the notwithstanding clause, which allows legislatures to override many of the rights in the Charter.
Quebec’s goal is secularism but some people believe Bill 21 violates freedom of religion and is a state attack on minorities.

The notwithstanding clause requires renewal every five years and Quebec did so in 2024. Bill 21 was also twice upheld by the lower courts in Quebec, in 2021 and 2024, both times because of the notwithstanding clause.

content_blocks.text: The history of the notwithstanding clause
content_blocks.html: The history of the notwithstanding clause

content_blocks.text: In November 1981, five weeks after the Supreme Court ruled that the federal government, by convention, had to garner substantial support among the provinces to patriate the Constitution from Britain, a final federal-provincial meeting in Ottawa began to disintegrate on the third day. “Can you give us more time?” whispered justice minister Jean Chrétien to Pierre Trudeau.
