stories.title: Ontario’s mortgage squeeze, banning AI listing photos and the Home of the Week: Canadian real estate news for the week of Nov. 27
stories.summary: Plus, the gamble facing homeowners right now
stories.author: Moira Wyton
stories.content:
This week: Rate of Ontarians falling behind on their mortgages jumps, and the gamble facing homeowners that 100 years of price data can help with. Plus, the province trying to ban AI-generated listing photos, and one property worth a look.

Buying a home is often considered a way to get ahead, but more and more homeowners in Ontario are falling behind. Nearly one in every 300 households in Ontario haven’t been able to pay their mortgages for three or more months, nearly triple the prepandemic rate, according to a recent TD Bank report . That’s a 30-per-cent jump in the past year, a different analysis by credit-rating agency Equifax shows , and experts say delinquency rates are expected to keep rising in 2027.

As Salmaan Farooqui reports, Ontario’s 0.34 per cent delinquency rate puts it near levels not seen since the 2008 financial crisis, when mortgage arrears peaked at 0.43 per cent. Rising interest rates are hitting homeowners across Canada, but the delinquency problem is concentrated in Ontario and B.C., where mortgage balances are higher and leave little wiggle room.

However, unlike in B.C., Ontario’s arrears growth rate hasn’t slowed. Why? More people in cities such as Hamilton, Windsor and Oshawa are losing their jobs thanks to U.S. tariffs, making it harder for them to pay their mortgage, says TD economist and report author Maria Solvieva. “Ontario is one of the weakest economies in Canada currently with pressure coming from U.S. tariffs, and it is seeing a higher unemployment rate,” she told Salmaan. “There is a combination of income shock and payment shock from higher interest rates.” Read the full story .

Wondering whether to list your home or hold out for a recovery? You might wish you had a crystal ball. This year has added uncertainty on top of uncertainty for homeowners, but a look back at the past 100 years of Canadian home prices May help you make a decision.

The chances of a significant recovery next year are slim , but as Hanif Bayat writes, historical data suggests the long-term picture could be brighter. If the market follows the pattern of years past in the decade after the 2022 peak, prices will be at least 13 per cent and more likely up to 20 per cent above today’s levels by 2032.

But, of course, history is not guaranteed to repeat itself. It might be the time to sell if you’re trying to upgrade (to take advantage of lower prices) or even if you’re trying to downsize (borrowing costs are high and recovery isn’t assured). However as Hanif explains, the answer is more complicated for older sellers. Read his analysis on the numbers to consider before you decide your next move.

Have you ever fallen in love with a home from the photos online, only to find out in person that it was too good to be true? Artificial intelligence-generated listing photos are on the rise and duping buyers, as we’ve reported before , and now Manitoba is trying to crack down on the bait-and-switch.

But many in the industry are skeptical Premier Wab Kinew’s NDP government can put the genie back in the bottle. Misleading images have been an issue since before AI came on the scene, and as Shane Dingman reports, major real estate bodies across Canada have conflicting messaging about what is permitted, or if it has to be disclosed.

In Manitoba, the province’s Real Estate Services Act already has rules against misleading images, but some realtors risk it anyway to remove clutter, clear power lines or even cover up major issues such as a hole in the floor. “If they are making $100,000 commission, do you think they give a crap about the $450 fine and slap on the wrist?” Mitchell Fain, a high-end real estate photographer in Toronto, told Shane. Read more about why AI use is splitting the real estate industry .

Artificial Christmas trees have become a rockin’ option for avoiding holiday messes and spills, but they’re not such a gift for the environment. As Matthew Hague writes, most are made of plastic, aren’t biodegradable and will end up sitting in landfills. You’d have to keep an artificial tree for at least 20 years to make the carbon footprint the same as getting a real one.

But while real trees are better for the environment, experts say cutting your holiday waste this season doesn’t necessarily mean chopping down your own tree. From arbours made of recycled pop bottles to paper and wood options made to last, here are six eco-friendly artificial Christmas trees to light up for years to come.

4761 9th Line, New Tecumseth, Ont. – Full gallery here

Though they seem like oil and water, this modernist home and its country surroundings bring out the best in each other. The all-white, cube-like structure , built in 1992 by a former architect, stands out in Simcoe County, north of Toronto. But its current owner has leaned into the contrast to elevate the design to hold its own next to – and enhance – the natural beauty of the setting.

Throughout the four-bedroom, three-bathroom home, minimalist white walls and oversized, commercial-grade windows serve as a canvas for the forests and open skies outside. The split-level design offers a plethora of different views to these bursts of colour, and features such as dark accent walls and the kitchen’s anchoring black quartz island up the drama.

Equipped with unusual features like geothermal heating and cooling and concrete and steel construction, the home was easy to renovate because it is essentially an empty shell that doesn’t need internal supports. But while owner Anna Davydov focused on bringing the interiors into this century for her family, she says the outdoors has been the greatest gift. The privacy, pool and skating pond make this an all-season oasis. “You don’t need to go anywhere else,” Davydov says.

What do you think is the asking price for the property?

a. $2,350,000 b. $2,550,000 c. $2,750,000 d. $2,950,000 c. The asking price is $2,750,000.

stories.title: One person dead after stabbing on TTC bus, Toronto police say
stories.summary: Toronto police said officers were called to Eglinton and Falmouth avenues at 10:04 p.m. for reports of someone stabbed on a TTC bus.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
One person is dead after being stabbed while on a TTC bus Thursday night, Toronto police say.

Police said officers were called to Eglinton and Falmouth avenues at 10:04 p.m. Nov. 26 for reports of someone stabbed on a bus.

Paramedics took one person to hospital with life-threatening injuries. A male victim was later pronounced dead at hospital.

He’s been identified as 34-year-old Toronto resident Jordan Berry.

He is Toronto’s 38th homicide victim of the year.

Police said one suspect fled on foot.

Toronto resident Nicholas Crawford, 40, is wanted for second-degree murder. He is described as standing 5’8-5’9,” has a medium build and is clean-shaven.

He was wearing a black hoodie, black pants, black shoes, and walking with a white pit bull-type dog.

The homicide squad is investigating.

TTC CEO Mandeep S. Lali offered his condolences to the victim and their loved ones in a statement.

“Our operator is receiving the Ttc’s full support as well. Safety of our customers and employees is paramount and the cornerstone of all we do,” he said.

“We are, as always, providing our full cooperation, including statements and video, to police as they investigate. ”

ATU Local 113, which represents TTC workers, thanked first responders who attended the scene.

“Everyone should be able to ride the TTC and go to work without fear of violence,” it said in part in a statement.

“We will continue to press the TTC and the City to make transit safer for riders and workers.”

Anyone with information is asked to contact police.

stories.title: A modern Ontario home in a vibrant natural setting
stories.summary: The home’s sleek interiors are accented by oversized window serving as a canvas for the trees
stories.author: Shane Dingman
stories.content:
4761 9th Line, New Tecumseth, Ont.

Asking price: $2,750,000

Land Size: 450.3 by 590.3 feet

Annual Property Taxes: $9,083

As long as humans have been writing down our experience of the world, we have been drawn to contrasts. And for just as long, humans have realized that contrasts are often not zero-sum; that things in conflict and in tension can highlight the differences but also enhance our appreciation of each aspect.

North of Toronto, in the southern part of Simcoe County, is a rural area with farmers’ fields and thick stands of trees between the towns of New Tecumseth and Bradford West Gwillimbury. At this time of year, the trees have mostly turned or lost their leaves, but the thick mixed woods provide a lush contrast to the modernist cubelike structure tucked away from view at 4761 9th Line.

Clad all in white, the three-storey home feels like a commercial office building in the middle of the woods, with a three-car garage at grade and the entrance off to the right. There are banks of windows covering the entire front of the house on the second and third storeys, and once inside, there are more windows on all sides looking into the forest.

For Anna Davydov, the last decade of ownership has been about bringing the interior of the home, built in 1992, up to a design standard that matched and enhanced her enjoyment of the rural setting.

“Everything was white walls, very minimalist; the finishes were all original,” she said. “There was a green tile throughout, and a very old carpet on the second floor.”

Dated colour schemes couldn’t hide the bones of the building, though, which are all made of steel. The builder was an architect, according to listing agent and long-time friend Leon Klaiman, and the home has features that are uncommon in today’s construction, let alone in 1992. Some of those features include geothermal heating and cooling, commercial-grade windows, as well as concrete and steel construction.

When Ms. Davydov bought the home, the interior space was chopped up into separate rooms, but the house is essentially a steel shell with no internal supports needed, which created opportunities for dramatic spaces once renovations began.

Inside the house reveals that it’s not a cube, so much as a split-level layer cake of curated spaces. Travelling from the minimalist white foyer up the first flight of stairs (white steel with white oak treads), you enter the ground-level living room that extends beyond the main volume of the house into the rear yard.

From this room, with its massive entertainment-centre wall that appears to float above the floor, you can walk out to the pool deck through the wall of windows facing the back lot (three acres’ worth). Turning back toward the front of the house, the space opens up with a loft from the kitchen a half-floor above, and the stairs continue to climb upward.

This area and the kitchen were the first to be renovated – a process Ms. Davydov led by choosing materials and finishes and letting her contractor connect them together. The white walls were kept for the most part, but the cool modernist interiors have bursts of colour and nature, with each oversized window serving as a canvas for the trees beyond.

The dining room occupies about half the space at the front of the house, and a wall wrapped in glass-walled wine storage separates it from the kitchen beyond.

The kitchen is anchored by a large island – black millwork with a black quartz slab that waterfalls to the floor – with bar seating. The pantry storage is white, with a huge double-door fridge-freezer in the centre of the working space. Windows on all sides flood in light (there are automated blinds to help maintain the home’s temperature in the blazing sun), and a set of patio doors at the back connect to a raised deck that walks down to a long (also modernist) covered cabana and outdoor kitchen space next to the pool on the decking below.

The upper two levels have bathrooms recently updated with inspiration from a spa Ms. Davydov had visited.

“For the walls, I wanted a textured tile to look like stone; some things I had to wait for, but I generally got what I wanted,” she said. The result is a luxuriously dark and intimate space with brass trim and backlit oval mirrors.

The bedrooms are on the top floor, with the primary suite occupying the rooms facing the back lot and the children’s rooms facing the front. The primary bedroom faces a wall of windows looking out over the rear yard, accessed by passing through the dressing room/bathroom off the stairs.

All the rooms have balconies, though Ms. Davydov says the family prefers to lounge on the pool deck rather than on these elevated spaces.

Ms. Davydov grew up in more modest surroundings, apartments and the like, as Mr. Klaiman said. This large home has given her young family all it could ask for as she continued to build her employment agency business. But for all the focus on the interiors, the outdoors has been the greatest gift.

“The privacy is really an oasis; you don’t need to go anywhere else,” she said, and not just to the pool deck in the summer, but to the nearby pond to play hockey and skate in the winter. There are people nearby, but you don’t ever need to see them. “We just met my next-door neighbour last year,” she said.

stories.title: Buyers time a Kitsilano home purchase as prices slide
stories.summary: Front half of duplex would have been priced closer to the $1.8 million mark when the young family first started looking
stories.author: Kerry Gold
stories.content:
2727 W. 14 th Ave., Vancouver

Asking price: $1.65-million (August 2026)

Selling price: $1.616-million (August 2026)

Taxes: $6,462.46 (2026)

Days on the market: 8

Buyer’s agent: Dennis Sepulveda, Stilhavn Real Estate Services

This five-year-old front half of a duplex in Kitsilano was in new condition, bright, with an open-concept living area and desirable features, such as oak floors, radiant heat and a landscaped setting. The two-bedroom, 2½-bathroom home has a gas fireplace, heat pump and air conditioning, a 484-square-foot crawl space and one-car garage. The two-level unit is within walking distance of shops, restaurants, schools and transit, in the popular west side neighbourhood.

The owner had built the duplex and lived in the back unit, while renting out the front unit. The buyers’ agent, Dennis Sepulveda, had been helping his clients look for a year. The young family wanted a west side location, but west-side prices were too high, so they refocused their search on the east side of the city. After missing out on several properties on the east side, they found that west side prices had dropped enough that they could return to their original plan, Mr. Sepulveda said. As soon as the Kitsilano unit came on the market, they went in with a strong offer.

“I said, ‘Let’s give them a respectable offer; they would be silly to refuse,’” and they got it. They are absolutely thrilled.”

The sale completed Nov. 18.

Mr. Sepulveda estimates that the half duplex would have been priced closer to the $1.8-million mark when his clients first began looking a year ago. The assessed value is $1.823-million.

He doesn’t expect prices to go back up any time soon.

“I think we are going to go sideways for the next year. Maybe the next couple of years would be my prediction.”

stories.title: Community bond gives investors opportunity to buy into affordable housing
stories.summary: Vancouver non-profit launches Together for Homes Community Bond to raise more than $3-million
stories.author: Kerry Gold
stories.content:
A long-established B.C. non-profit housing society is launching one of the province’s first community bonds to help pay for affordable housing on Vancouver’s Commercial Drive.

Entre Nous Femmes Housing Society, a 42-year-old organization founded by three single mothers, launched the Together for Homes Community Bond last week. The target is to raise more than $3-million toward the development of the 15-storey tower at 800 Commercial Dr., ON a triangular-shaped parking lot north of Venables Street, owned by the City of Vancouver. Entre Nous Femmes chief executive officer Lilian Chau said the project will consist of 107 units and 4,000 square feet of community space. The plan is to start construction early in the new year.

“We wanted a project that really has a really clear path to repayment for investors as our first bond,” Ms. Chau said. “Hopefully other groups can then learn from our example.”

Community bonds typically act as short-term bridge financing alongside grants and conventional loans. Annual interest will be paid from cash reserves generated from the society’s 15 Metro Vancouver properties. Once the building is complete, a lower-rate long-term mortgage will be arranged to repay the principal owed to investors. While community bonds are commonly used to build housing in Ontario, Quebec, Manitoba and Nova Scotia, the model only arrived in B.C. in recent years, when a Kamloops non-profit launched a community bond to help fund a six-storey co-op.

The move toward community bonds is partly born out of necessity, as government funding for new affordable housing has tightened. The 2026 provincial budget abruptly pulled back on the Community Housing Fund, which left several projects in limbo.

“It’s another opportunity for affordable housing, especially in our province, which has now seen really a shrinking of any public dollars and it’s getting much harder for us to build more affordable housing,” Ms. Chau said. “And we are one of the most expensive places to be constructing as well, so there are lots of challenges. But we do see this as an alternative tool so that we can lessen our reliance just on government funding.”

The minimum investment for the Entre Nous Femmes project is $1,500 and terms range from two to four years, with interest rates of 2.5 to 4 per cent paid each year. Investors from across Canada can sign up on the society’s website. Twenty per cent of units will be for those residents on income assistance, 50 per cent will be based on income and 30 per cent will be on the low end of the market. A rent-geared-to-income three-bedroom unit, for example, would rent for around $1,500, Ms. Chau said. She predicts around 250 residents will occupy the building.

Lindsay Harris is the co-founder and executive director of Propolis Cooperative Housing Society, which was the first non-profit in B.C. to use a community bond to build non-market housing. The Tranquille Hive is a 53-unit below-market housing co-op in Kamloops, scheduled for occupancy next year. The grassroots group raised $1.1-million, offering bonds with 2.5 to 3.5-per-cent interest on three-year terms. Being the first of its type in the province, there was a learning curve: it took 21 months to raise the money. They got help from a credit union and some community foundations who made large investments.

“If you’re a new start-up co-op, you don’t have existing capital or assets or a track record of delivering housing, and it’s going to be incredibly hard to get access to financing. And so, we really wanted to find a way of harnessing support from the community,” Ms. Harris said.

“I think that the length of our campaign was probably a little bit longer than the campaigns that have been done out east, where community bonds are a little bit more recognized.

“People from the community really did step forward to support us. We just needed to allow the time to educate people about what community bonds were and what we were trying to accomplish with them.”

Ms. Harris said they repaid their 101 community investors, with interest, earlier this year.

“Really the benefit for most of our investors was knowing that that money was having such a significant impact in the community,” Ms. Harris said. “It’s not just the interest rate of return that they get, it’s knowing that they are tangibly supporting something meaningful.”

But if housing groups are to tap into community bonds on a wider scale, they will need government to make policy changes to incentivize investors, says Suzanne Faiza, Montreal-based policy and research manager for Tapestry Community Capital, which is the administrator for both B.C. community bonds.

“The most common investments are between that range of $1,000 to $5,000, and those folks cannot put their community bonds right now into TFSAs or their RRSPs. And it’s been a really common request. We’ve seen kind of the light go out of investors’ eyes when that comes up,” said Ms. Faiza.

“That’s a policy change that I am lobbying the federal government on right now.”

Ms. Faiza is working on other policy proposals, such as a national tax credit on investments in co-operatives and non-profits, and an allowance for investors to deduct 75 per cent of losses on community capital investments.

Community bonds are not risk-free, and investors are encouraged to read the fine print and learn about the organization behind the project, Tapestry co-founder and co-executive director Ryan Collins-Swartz said.

The national non-profit has helped raise about $170-million across four provinces and funded 50 or so projects in renewable energy, non-market housing and various social endeavours, including independent schools and food and agriculture projects. The community bonds they’ve administered have been funded by 5,000 investors – a number that should easily grow, but will depend on education and awareness, Mr. Collins-Swartz said.

“Our big-picture mission is that every Canadian can invest locally within their own community, and whether it’s climate change or a lack of housing affordability, we need to address the financialization and investment that’s behind these industries and move money out of harmful industries and into something positive, community-controlled – in this case, non-market housing.

“I think most Canadians, if they knew about this type of opportunity, they would want to direct some portion of their investments locally into something with a positive impact. And with Canadians holding about $4-trillion in household wealth, if just a small percentage of those investments could be redirected into these community-led projects, we’d see a really strong impact.”

Ms. Chau said she’s invested her children’s savings into the community bond for 800 Commercial Dr. She hopes that even 1 per cent of the $4-trillion or so that Canadians invest in personal investment products is diverted toward community bonds to build affordable housing.

stories.title: District of Squamish asks residents to limit indoor water use after wet B.C. weather
stories.summary: The rain and wind warnings have been dropped across British Columbia's coast, but flooding is still a risk as other communities manage the aftermath.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
The rain and wind warnings have been dropped across British Columbia’s coast, but flooding is still a risk as other communities manage the aftermath.

The District of Squamish, which declared a state of local emergency over high tides and flood risk earlier this week, asks residents to limit indoor water use until further notice to help manage sewer flows.

The district says it still expects more rainfall that will impact the sewer system when combined with peak busy periods.

It says there were reports of localized flooding throughout town but that tidal water peaked Thursday and flood protection measures have made a significant difference.

Much of the province’s coastal region was drenched with heavy rain and strong winds and when combined with king tides, led to flooding in low-lying areas and along the coast.

A flood warning from the B.C. River Forecast Centre remains in place for central Vancouver Island, while the lower flood watches and high streamflow advisories are upgraded for the rest of Vancouver Island and much of the south coast.

In the Regional District of Nanaimo, where multiple properties were ordered evacuated this week, officials say they are closing the French Creek Estuary Nature Preserve and French Creek Community Park due to the severe conditions.

stories.title: How Carney is staking out foreign policy through hockey
stories.summary: The Big Story discusses what Carney's decision says about his approach to foreign policy, and what it means for international competition going forward.
stories.author: Patricia D'Cunha
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney is refusing to follow a court ruling that could lead the way for Russia’s return to international sports. But with the World Juniors coming up in December, and the International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) standing by Carney, it’s raising questions about what happens when sports meets foreign policy.

Host Devang Desai speaks with Aaron Ettinger, associate professor of political science at Carleton University, about Carney’s decision, what it says about his approach to foreign policy, and what it means for international competition going forward.

stories.title: Premiers await Supreme Court ruling on Quebec’s secularism law
stories.summary: Premiers across Canada are expected to be keeping a close eye on the Supreme Court Friday morning as it releases a ruling on the constitutionality of Quebec's secularism law.
stories.author: Erika Morris
stories.content:
Premiers across Canada are expected to be keeping a close eye on the Supreme Court Friday morning as it releases a ruling on the constitutionality of Quebec’s secularism law.

The historic decision could change how provinces are allowed to act when adopting laws that could override Charter rights.

The case stems from a Quebec law known as Bill 21, which bans public servants in positions of authority from wearing religious symbols while on the job.

The legislature pre-emptively invoked a section of the Constitution to shield the law from legal challenges based on Charter rights to freedom of conscience and religion and equality rights.

Since it passed in 2019, Quebec, Ontario, Saskatchewan and Alberta have all invoked the same section of the Constitution to shield some other laws from legal challenges.

These include laws restricting the rights of transgender people in Alberta and Saskatchewan, back-to-work orders in Alberta and Ontario, and Quebec’s language-law reform.

At a news conference in Quebec City on Thursday, Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon said that Section 33 of the Constitution, also known as the notwithstanding clause, is an essential and democratically accepted tool for legislators.

He added that “if the Supreme Court goes forward to centralize power even more and putting provinces in a situation where they cannot have their own say,” the reaction from premiers will be “very heated.”

stories.title: Kenneth Law sentencing hearing set to resume
stories.summary: Ontario man sold potentially deadly substances online to people who then used those products to take their own lives
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Prosecutors asked the court on Friday to sentence Kenneth Law to 25 years in prison for selling deadly substances online that contributed to the deaths of dozens of suicidal people in Canada and Britain.

Sentencing hearings in Mr. Law’s case resumed in court in Newmarket, Ont., with lawyers’ arguments. The court heard testimony from victims’ families in September.

“Our position is that a 25-year sentence is fit,” Crown attorney Katie Doherty told Superior Court Justice Michelle Fuerst.

“It’s unprecedented, there’s simply no case like this,” Ms. Doherty told the court. She added “there’s no case even remotely similar” to his under Canadian law.

Prosecutors reminded the court that Mr. Law ran an online business from his Mississauga home that contributed to enormous amounts of death and grief. He has admitted in court to being directly involved in at least 93 deaths in Canada and Britain as he shipped 1,200 poison packages around the world between 2020 and 2023.

“Ninety-three deaths. The worst possible outcome. Human life lost 93 separate times,” Ms. Doherty said. She told the court that half of the overall victims were in their 20s, and that 12 more were teenagers including one who was just 14 years old.

Mr. Law pleaded guilty earlier this year to 14 criminal counts of aiding in the suicide of 14 Ontarians. As part of this plea deal, prosecutors agreed to drop murder charges he was facing in these same cases.

Mr. Law has also admitted in court to aiding in the suicides of an additional 79 people in Britain, though these deaths were not charged as a crimes.

Outside the jurisdictions of Ontario and Britain, no crimes have ever been charged against Mr. Law for any suicides from his products.

Prosecutors told the court that Mr. Law’s actions have scarred entire families for decades to come after the suicide deaths of his victims. The families “will live with the consequences of what happened,” Ms. Doherty said.

Crown attorneys cast Mr. Law’s conduct as egregious because he made about $300,000 selling poisons. They also said he has admitted to using an online alias to recommend his own death-causing products in online forums frequented by young suicidal people.

Prosecutors say he was motivated by money and was recklessly indifferent to the vulnerable mindsets of his clients. “The only thing Mr. Law has done to determine who to sell to is to demand $80-$90 up front,” Ms. Doherty said.

But Mr. Law’s defence lawyers are disputing many of the Crown’s characterizations. In addition, they are arguing that the court must reject what they say are prosecutors’ demands to impose the equivalent of a life sentence on the 61-year-old man.

“Mr. Law is not the mercenary predator he has sometimes been portrayed as,” defence lawyer Matthew Gourlay told the court. “He has shown remorse and insight.”

The Toronto lawyer, who has pleaded Mr. Law’s case for the past three years, argued that his client should only get a 12-year sentence.

The defence lawyer told the court Mr. Law sold industrial chemicals that were not themselves illegal. He added that Mr. Law has no prior criminal record. In addition, he said, Mr. Law’s blameworthiness is tempered by circumstances indicating that he operated on a “misguided” belief that he was helping people.

“Mr. Law did not get rich from this enterprise; far from it,” Mr. Gourlay said. He said the court has heard no evidence that Mr. Law ever made anyone consume any lethal substance. “He did not try to push substances on any uncertain, reluctant, or wavering individual.”

The defence lawyer said the court needs to consider how Mr. Law’s crimes occurred in an era where suicide is being destigmatized through medical assistance in dying (Maid) legislation. Mr. Gourlay told Justice Fuerst this does not excuse Mr. Law’s admitted crimes, but it does yield important context.

“My friend characterized Mr. Law’s views on this whole fraught subject as irrelevant because he was, and I quote, ‘not entitled to set himself up as ‘judge, jury and executioner,’” Mr. Gourlay said. “Of course, he wasn’t ‘the executioner’ in any of these cases. His view was quite the contrary. That other individuals ought to have the choice, through themselves.”

Under Canadian law, aiding suicide is a crime punishable by up to 14 years in prison and guilty pleas ensure some leniency at sentencing.

For these reasons, the Crown said, Mr. Law should face 12.5 years on each of the 14 deaths he has admitted to aiding in Ontario. While most of these sentences would be served at the same time, the Crown is asking that one of those counts be stacked – or served consecutively – for a total of 25 years.

Since Mr. Law was arrested in May 2023 and never granted bail, he has spent 3½ years in custody awaiting trial. Defence lawyers have told the court Mr. Law should get credit for the time he’s spent in detention.

The sentencing hearing is continuing.

stories.title: What we sow before birth
stories.summary: It’s time we realized that there can be no world peace without peaceful pregnancy and birth
stories.author: Dr. Thomas Verny
stories.content:
Thomas R. Verny is a clinical psychiatrist, academic, award-winning author, poet and public speaker. He is the author of eight books, including the global bestseller The Secret Life of the Unborn Child and The Embodied Mind: Understanding the Mysteries of Cellular Memory, Consciousness and Our Bodies .

In my previous column I described how hundreds of millions of children around the world suffer from deprivation and abuse. The umbrella term for such harmful experiences is adversity.

Often, adversity will affect human development even before birth, and in many cases even before conception.

Conditions a child was exposed to in utero have enduring consequences not only for individuals, but also for society. While much depends on genes, experiencing adversity at a time when all our cells and tissues are rapidly developing tends to exert a gravitational pull on our bodies and minds long after we have taken our first breath.

In Why Zebras Don’t Get Ulcers , author Robert M. Sapolsky, professor of biology and neurology at Stanford University, explains that, unlike zebras, humans can activate their stress responses simply by worrying about past or future events. This is an important point if the person doing the worrying is also pregnant.

Stress activates the sympathetic nervous system, popularly referred to as the fight-or-flight system, resulting in an outpouring of adrenalin and cortisol and the suppression of the parasympathetic system, or the rest and restore system. This works very well for the average non-pregnant person. Within seconds, the heart beats faster, blood pressure rises, breathing quickens and blood is redirected from the inner organs toward the muscles of the arms and legs. Glucose is released into the bloodstream, providing the energy needed to fight or flee.

One of the organs from which blood is siphoned off is the uterus which means that, in the case of a pregnant woman, her unborn child is temporarily receiving less than optimum amounts of nutrients. Simultaneously, the increase in stress hormones in the mother is partially passed through the placenta to the fetus. Problems arise when stress becomes chronic and these systems remain switched on.

Research on the relationship between stress and congenital malformations and later development of cancer, type 2 diabetes, cardiac conditions, the immune system and premature aging are solid and persuasive. They can fill a book. So, here I shall only focus on the impact of stress on the brain and personality of a child that was exposed to it in the prenatal period.

A study from the Medical University of Vienna concluded that in utero exposure to maternal distress leads to structural and functional aberrations in the limbic system, prefrontal cortex and insula.

These alterations increase the risk for developing a neuropsychiatric illness in adulthood. [1] Neuropsychiatric illness is a broad term for disorders that affect the brain and produce disturbances in thinking, feeling and acting. Examples include “internalizing behaviours” − psych-speech for depression, Adhd, schizophrenia, anxiety and bipolar disorder.

In a recent paper, Dr. Irene Tung, an associate professor of psychology at California State University, synthesized 55 longitudinal studies and found a small but statistically significant association between prenatal distress and later development of aggression, hyperactivity and impulsivity, collectively referred to as “externalizing behaviours.” [2]

One needs to distinguish ordinary worries during pregnancy from sustained psychological distress. Anxiety and stress frequently coexist. Often a mother who was stressed and anxious while pregnant May continue to experience those feelings after giving birth. [3] Acute or persistent maternal anxiety activates the same hormonal processes as stress does, leading to similar alterations in brain physiology. [4, 5]

During embryonic development, the cerebral cortex is occupied by newborn neurons that originate at the very bottom, next to the fluid-filled ventricles. Radial glial cells span the entire thickness of the developing brain. Their long, vertical processes or fibres act as “ladders” extending from the deep ventricular zone, one of the principal birthplaces of new neurons, up to the outer surface of the brain. The very youngest neurons migrate a short distance up these radial glial cell fibres to form the deepest layers of the cortex. Neurons born later in development climb up the exact same radial glial tracks, past their siblings, gradually reaching the upper layers. [6]

Toxic substances such as alcohol, nicotine and cannabis, as well as many infections, interfere with the above-described brain development. [7] Some disrupt the migration of neurons, causing them to take up residence in the wrong place. Others can block the formation of synapses between neurons or, at sufficiently high concentration, cause neuronal death.

Depending on genetic susceptibility, the substance, the amount and the stage of pregnancy at which exposure occurs, a child May be born with barely detectable changes to the brain or a profoundly miswired one. [8, 9] This is hard science. Simple, straightforward and sobering.

According to Adriana P. C. Hermans, a researcher at Erasmus University Medical Center in Rotterdam, one in five pregnant women will experience depression. [10]

A large Canadian study that involved more than 1.2 million pregnancies in Ontario found that 8.1 per cent of women experienced depression, 10.5 per cent experienced anxiety and 15.8 per cent experienced at least one mental health condition during pregnancy. The risk was significantly greater among women living in economically disadvantaged neighbourhoods. [11]

An important qualification: The Ontario study identified depression based on health records, whereas Ms. Hermans’s statistics relied on the presence of depressive symptoms, which are considerably more common than clinically diagnosed depression.

A review of American studies published between 2010 and 2020 found that women who experienced depression during pregnancy had 46 per cent higher odds of giving birth prematurely and 90 per cent higher odds of having a baby with low birth weight. The more severe a woman’s depressive symptoms are during pregnancy, the greater her risk of giving birth prematurely. [12]

This is consequential because premature birth and low birth weight contribute to above-average emotional problems later in life. [13]

The strongest recent evidence linking maternal prenatal depression with children’s later emotional, behavioural and cognitive development comes from a 2026 European study involving 76,514 children. It concluded that the offspring of mothers diagnosed with prenatal depression had higher rates of internalizing and externalizing behaviours, Adhd and autism spectrum disorder symptoms than a control group. Importantly, associations were largely independent of pre-pregnancy depression. [10]

In view of these findings, women need to know that depression in pregnancy is common, might affect the child she is carrying, and can be treated.

The devastating Dutch Hunger Winter of 1944–45 provided researchers with an unusual opportunity to study the long-term consequences of prenatal starvation. A 1996 study by Ezra Susser found that women exposed to famine around the time of conception or during early gestation had children who were at twice the risk of developing schizophrenia in both sexes. [14]

Fourteen years later, in 2010, a Dutch research team led by Susanne de Rooij, studying survivors of the same Dutch Hunger Winter, found that people exposed to severe maternal undernutrition during early pregnancy performed significantly worse on a test of selective attention at ages 56–59. [15] Together, these studies suggest that prenatal starvation can affect both mental health and cognitive functioning later in life.

Prenatal maternal undernutrition also increases risks for hypertension, diabetes and cardiovascular disease. Some of the body’s “memories” of early undernutrition become translated into pathology and thereby increase susceptibility to disease later in life. [16]

Shifting focus now to poverty, a research paper from Washington University in 2022 found that children of mothers who prenatally experienced severe poverty and social disadvantage had, ON average, smaller brain volumes and less developed cortical folding at birth than a control group. [17]

These differences May have implications for subsequent learning, memory, attention and emotional development. Regrettably, the researchers have not, as of now, established the children’s subsequent developmental outcomes, though I believe this is a work in progress. Despite that limitation, what is noteworthy about this study is that differences in brain development associated with poverty were evident at birth, before postnatal deprivation could have confounded the findings.

The authors of the Washington study confirmed that social disadvantage and psychosocial stress were correlated. Frequently, hunger and poverty coexist but they are not the same. Hunger is a relatively specific biological state. Poverty is a social and economic condition with multiple pathways through which it May affect prenatal development.

In 2024, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) published a study involving nearly 48,000 women who had recently given birth. Of these, 5.4 per cent reported experiencing intimate partner violence during pregnancy. Among the women who reported abuse, 96 per cent experienced emotional abuse, 28 per cent physical abuse and 19 per cent sexual abuse. Many suffered more than one form of abuse. Since domestic abuse is frequently concealed, these figures probably underestimate its actual prevalence.

All types were associated with delayed or no prenatal care, depression during pregnancy, cigarette smoking, alcohol, marijuana or illicit substance use during pregnancy and having an infant with low birth weight. [18]

A study by Dr. Megan Steele-Baser, with the division of violence prevention at the CDC, of 182 mothers aged 18-34 links abuse of pregnant women to giving birth to children at increased psychological risks. These children often present in the first year of life with symptoms that include nightmares, startling easily, being bothered by loud noises and bright lights, avoiding physical contact and having trouble experiencing enjoyment. [19]

The prenatal environment can influence our lifelong vulnerability to illness, our responses to stress and aspects of our emotional and cognitive development. The evidence is stronger for effects on brain development and mental health than for lasting changes in personality.

Be mindful of the fact that when we are navigating the seas of human psychology, we must not run aground on the shoals of simplistic determinism. Not every negative prenatal exposure has enduring consequences, and the effects depend on timing, intensity, duration, individual susceptibility and, of course, postnatal love and care or absence thereof. Here we are dealing in probabilities, not certainties. It’s more like quantum mechanics than Newtonian physics.

One other point: Prenatal adversity studies have sometimes been communicated or interpreted in ways that inadvertently make mothers and sometimes fathers feel responsible and guilty for every health problem their child develops, especially if the pregnancy or birth was a difficult one. Many of the most serious sources of prenatal adversity − war, poverty, violence, displacement and environmental contamination − are circumstances over which a parent has little control. We need to remember that parents do the best they can under prevailing conditions.

Unless we, as individuals and society, endeavour to eliminate all chemical, physical and emotional toxins from the amniotic universe of unborn humans and provide a healthy environment with appropriate prenatal medical care for all, we will continue to raise children with serious potential for ill health, self-harm and violence.

It is high time we realized that as we do to our children so they will do to us. There can be no world peace without peaceful pregnancy and birth.

content_blocks.caption: The Globe and Mail

content_blocks.text: In my previous column I described how hundreds of millions of children around the world suffer from deprivation and abuse. The umbrella term for such harmful experiences is adversity.
content_blocks.html: In my previous column I described how hundreds of millions of children around the world suffer from deprivation and abuse. The umbrella term for such harmful experiences is adversity.

content_blocks.text: Often, adversity will affect human development even before birth, and in many cases even before conception.
content_blocks.html: Often, adversity will affect human development even before birth, and in many cases even before conception.

content_blocks.text: Conditions a child was exposed to in utero have enduring consequences not only for individuals, but also for society. While much depends on genes, experiencing adversity at a time when all our cells and tissues are rapidly developing tends to exert a gravitational pull on our bodies and minds long after we have taken our first breath.

content_blocks.text: Prenatal stress
content_blocks.html: Prenatal stress

content_blocks.text: In Why Zebras Don’t Get Ulcers , author Robert M. Sapolsky, professor of biology and neurology at Stanford University, explains that, unlike zebras, humans can activate their stress responses simply by worrying about past or future events. This is an important point if the person doing the worrying is also pregnant.
content_blocks.html: In Why Zebras Don’t Get Ulcers, author Robert M. Sapolsky, professor of biology and neurology at Stanford University, explains that, unlike zebras, humans can activate their stress responses simply by worrying about past or future events. This is an important point if the person doing the worrying is also pregnant.

content_blocks.text: Stress activates the sympathetic nervous system, popularly referred to as the fight-or-flight system, resulting in an outpouring of adrenalin and cortisol and the suppression of the parasympathetic system, or the rest and restore system. This works very well for the average non-pregnant person. Within seconds, the heart beats faster, blood pressure rises, breathing quickens and blood is redirected from the inner organs toward the muscles of the arms and legs. Glucose is released into the bloodstream, providing the energy needed to fight or flee.

content_blocks.text: One of the organs from which blood is siphoned off is the uterus which means that, in the case of a pregnant woman, her unborn child is temporarily receiving less than optimum amounts of nutrients. Simultaneously, the increase in stress hormones in the mother is partially passed through the placenta to the fetus. Problems arise when stress becomes chronic and these systems remain switched on.

content_blocks.text: Research on the relationship between stress and congenital malformations and later development of cancer, type 2 diabetes, cardiac conditions, the immune system and premature aging are solid and persuasive. They can fill a book. So, here I shall only focus on the impact of stress on the brain and personality of a child that was exposed to it in the prenatal period.

content_blocks.text: A study from the Medical University of Vienna concluded that in utero exposure to maternal distress leads to structural and functional aberrations in the limbic system, prefrontal cortex and insula.

content_blocks.text: These alterations increase the risk for developing a neuropsychiatric illness in adulthood. [1] Neuropsychiatric illness is a broad term for disorders that affect the brain and produce disturbances in thinking, feeling and acting. Examples include “internalizing behaviours” − psych-speech for depression, Adhd, schizophrenia, anxiety and bipolar disorder.

content_blocks.text: In a recent paper, Dr. Irene Tung, an associate professor of psychology at California State University, synthesized 55 longitudinal studies and found a small but statistically significant association between prenatal distress and later development of aggression, hyperactivity and impulsivity, collectively referred to as “externalizing behaviours.” [2]

content_blocks.text: One needs to distinguish ordinary worries during pregnancy from sustained psychological distress. Anxiety and stress frequently coexist. Often a mother who was stressed and anxious while pregnant May continue to experience those feelings after giving birth. [3] Acute or persistent maternal anxiety activates the same hormonal processes as stress does, leading to similar alterations in brain physiology. [4, 5]

content_blocks.text: Toxins
content_blocks.html: Toxins

content_blocks.text: During embryonic development, the cerebral cortex is occupied by newborn neurons that originate at the very bottom, next to the fluid-filled ventricles. Radial glial cells span the entire thickness of the developing brain. Their long, vertical processes or fibres act as “ladders” extending from the deep ventricular zone, one of the principal birthplaces of new neurons, up to the outer surface of the brain. The very youngest neurons migrate a short distance up these radial glial cell fibres to form the deepest layers of the cortex. Neurons born later in development climb up the exact same radial glial tracks, past their siblings, gradually reaching the upper layers. [6]

content_blocks.text: Toxic substances such as alcohol, nicotine and cannabis, as well as many infections, interfere with the above-described brain development. [7] Some disrupt the migration of neurons, causing them to take up residence in the wrong place. Others can block the formation of synapses between neurons or, at sufficiently high concentration, cause neuronal death.

content_blocks.text: Depression
content_blocks.html: Depression

content_blocks.text: According to Adriana P. C. Hermans, a researcher at Erasmus University Medical Center in Rotterdam, one in five pregnant women will experience depression. [10]
content_blocks.html: According to Adriana P. C. Hermans, a researcher at Erasmus University Medical Center in Rotterdam, one in five pregnant women will experience depression. [10]

content_blocks.text: A large Canadian study that involved more than 1.2 million pregnancies in Ontario found that 8.1 per cent of women experienced depression, 10.5 per cent experienced anxiety and 15.8 per cent experienced at least one mental health condition during pregnancy. The risk was significantly greater among women living in economically disadvantaged neighbourhoods. [11]

content_blocks.text: An important qualification: The Ontario study identified depression based on health records, whereas Ms. Hermans’s statistics relied on the presence of depressive symptoms, which are considerably more common than clinically diagnosed depression.

content_blocks.text: A review of American studies published between 2010 and 2020 found that women who experienced depression during pregnancy had 46 per cent higher odds of giving birth prematurely and 90 per cent higher odds of having a baby with low birth weight. The more severe a woman’s depressive symptoms are during pregnancy, the greater her risk of giving birth prematurely. [12]

content_blocks.text: The strongest recent evidence linking maternal prenatal depression with children’s later emotional, behavioural and cognitive development comes from a 2026 European study involving 76,514 children. It concluded that the offspring of mothers diagnosed with prenatal depression had higher rates of internalizing and externalizing behaviours, Adhd and autism spectrum disorder symptoms than a control group. Importantly, associations were largely independent of pre-pregnancy depression. [10]

content_blocks.text: In view of these findings, women need to know that depression in pregnancy is common, might affect the child she is carrying, and can be treated.

content_blocks.text: Hunger and poverty
content_blocks.html: Hunger and poverty

content_blocks.text: The devastating Dutch Hunger Winter of 1944–45 provided researchers with an unusual opportunity to study the long-term consequences of prenatal starvation. A 1996 study by Ezra Susser found that women exposed to famine around the time of conception or during early gestation had children who were at twice the risk of developing schizophrenia in both sexes. [14]
content_blocks.html: The devastating Dutch Hunger Winter of 1944–45 provided researchers with an unusual opportunity to study the long-term consequences of prenatal starvation. A 1996 study by Ezra Susser found that women exposed to famine around the time of conception or during early gestation had children who were at twice the risk of developing schizophrenia in both sexes. [14]

content_blocks.text: Fourteen years later, in 2010, a Dutch research team led by Susanne de Rooij, studying survivors of the same Dutch Hunger Winter, found that people exposed to severe maternal undernutrition during early pregnancy performed significantly worse on a test of selective attention at ages 56–59. [15] Together, these studies suggest that prenatal starvation can affect both mental health and cognitive functioning later in life.

[15] Together, these studies suggest that prenatal starvation can affect both mental health and cognitive functioning later in life.

content_blocks.text: Prenatal maternal undernutrition also increases risks for hypertension, diabetes and cardiovascular disease. Some of the body’s “memories” of early undernutrition become translated into pathology and thereby increase susceptibility to disease later in life. [16]

content_blocks.text: Shifting focus now to poverty, a research paper from Washington University in 2022 found that children of mothers who prenatally experienced severe poverty and social disadvantage had, ON average, smaller brain volumes and less developed cortical folding at birth than a control group. [17]

[17]

content_blocks.text: These differences May have implications for subsequent learning, memory, attention and emotional development. Regrettably, the researchers have not, as of now, established the children’s subsequent developmental outcomes, though I believe this is a work in progress. Despite that limitation, what is noteworthy about this study is that differences in brain development associated with poverty were evident at birth, before postnatal deprivation could have confounded the findings.

content_blocks.text: The authors of the Washington study confirmed that social disadvantage and psychosocial stress were correlated. Frequently, hunger and poverty coexist but they are not the same. Hunger is a relatively specific biological state. Poverty is a social and economic condition with multiple pathways through which it May affect prenatal development.

content_blocks.text: Domestic violence
content_blocks.html: Domestic violence

content_blocks.text: In 2024, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) published a study involving nearly 48,000 women who had recently given birth. Of these, 5.4 per cent reported experiencing intimate partner violence during pregnancy. Among the women who reported abuse, 96 per cent experienced emotional abuse, 28 per cent physical abuse and 19 per cent sexual abuse. Many suffered more than one form of abuse. Since domestic abuse is frequently concealed, these figures probably underestimate its actual prevalence.

content_blocks.text: A study by Dr. Megan Steele-Baser, with the division of violence prevention at the CDC, of 182 mothers aged 18-34 links abuse of pregnant women to giving birth to children at increased psychological risks. These children often present in the first year of life with symptoms that include nightmares, startling easily, being bothered by loud noises and bright lights, avoiding physical contact and having trouble experiencing enjoyment. [19]

content_blocks.text: Closing thoughts
content_blocks.html: Closing thoughts

content_blocks.text: The prenatal environment can influence our lifelong vulnerability to illness, our responses to stress and aspects of our emotional and cognitive development. The evidence is stronger for effects on brain development and mental health than for lasting changes in personality.
content_blocks.html: The prenatal environment can influence our lifelong vulnerability to illness, our responses to stress and aspects of our emotional and cognitive development. The evidence is stronger for effects on brain development and mental health than for lasting changes in personality.

content_blocks.text: Be mindful of the fact that when we are navigating the seas of human psychology, we must not run aground on the shoals of simplistic determinism. Not every negative prenatal exposure has enduring consequences, and the effects depend on timing, intensity, duration, individual susceptibility and, of course, postnatal love and care or absence thereof. Here we are dealing in probabilities, not certainties. It’s more like quantum mechanics than Newtonian physics.

Not every negative prenatal exposure has enduring consequences, and the effects depend on timing, intensity, duration, individual susceptibility and, of course, postnatal love and care or absence thereof. Here we are dealing in probabilities, not certainties. It’s more like quantum mechanics than Newtonian physics.

content_blocks.text: One other point: Prenatal adversity studies have sometimes been communicated or interpreted in ways that inadvertently make mothers and sometimes fathers feel responsible and guilty for every health problem their child develops, especially if the pregnancy or birth was a difficult one. Many of the most serious sources of prenatal adversity − war, poverty, violence, displacement and environmental contamination − are circumstances over which a parent has little control. We need to remember that parents do the best they can under prevailing conditions.

content_blocks.text: Unless we, as individuals and society, endeavour to eliminate all chemical, physical and emotional toxins from the amniotic universe of unborn humans and provide a healthy environment with appropriate prenatal medical care for all, we will continue to raise children with serious potential for ill health, self-harm and violence.

stories.title: All eyes on Danielle Smith as she addresses UCP members at consequential annual meeting
stories.summary: Separatists in the party will be parsing the Alberta premier's every word as she tries to push her unity message
stories.author: Jesse Snyder
stories.content:
When Alberta Premier Danielle Smith takes the stage at the annual United Conservative Party meeting this weekend, party members will be parsing her every word.

Coming off of Alberta’s Oct. 19 independence referendum, Smith has been working to win over the separatist segments of her party and emphasizing a message of conservative unity ahead of next year’s general election.

But the message hasn’t landed with some key separatist supporters within the party, who say they expect more of a hard-nosed posture toward Ottawa from a premier who they were instrumental in helping get elected. They will be waiting to see how Smith looks to appease her pro-independence base as thousands of party members gather in Calgary to discuss the Ucp’s top priorities.

“After this weekend, the line will be set in the sand,” said Mitch Sylvestre, co-founder of Stay Free Alberta, the organization that led the petition to hold a secession vote.

“We’re going to get a real feel for what’s going on here right away,” he said. “This weekend is going to be a pivotal weekend for the UCP.”

Political parties’ annual general meetings are typically dull affairs, often receiving little media attention or interest from anyone outside of the party faithful.

Yet a fracturing within the UCP following the referendum has made this particular AGM one of significant political consequence. More than 8,000 UCP members are expected to attend to hear from the premier and be given the chance to question her directly. Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe and newly minted B.C. Premier Lorne Doerkson will also be among the guest speakers.

Smith and the UCP leadership have sought to suppress separatist priorities since the referendum. In late October, the party started requiring all board candidates and constituency association candidates to sign a declaration that they will abide by the results of the referendum vote. It also ejected Jeff Rath, a particularly outspoken and often volatile separatist, from the party. In November, 15 UCP constituency association heads said they had refused to sign the document, according to the CBC.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith speaks at last year’s UCP annual general meeting in Edmonton on Nov. 29, 2025. Shaughn Butts/Postmedia

Alberta’s separatist movement has lost momentum ever since the referendum, which saw roughly three-quarters of Albertans voting in favour of staying in Canada. And separation itself isn’t expected to be an official topic of conversation at the annual general meeting, but observers expect that Smith will emphasize policies that will animate the more right-wing segments of the party.

Richard Sigurdson, a political science professor at University of Calgary, said Smith is likely to play up recent policies on various cultural issues as a way to reinvigorate her base. Those include efforts to outlaw diversity, equity and inclusion hiring in the public sector, or the UCP government’s recent motion aimed at protecting religious expression. (The motion was in response to Ottawa’s new hate speech laws, which removed some exemptions for speech that is based on religious texts.)

Sigurdson, for his part, said the separatist elements of the party are not likely to overtake the agenda of the UCP, whose members will likely be largely focused on beating the NDP in the next election.

“Observers from outside of Alberta are expecting there’s going to be some kind of battle royale with the UCP over separatism at this meeting, and I don’t see that as being likely at all.”

Given that the referendum result was firmly in support of staying in Canada, he said Smith will have a strong platform from which to address the party.

“I think she’s really got the cards right now going forward and focusing on unity and moving forward to the next general election,” he said. “There will be some contrary people that will be elected, there will be some provincial constituency organizations that are still going to snipe and complain that she’s not doing enough. But I think at the end of the day, she’s going to carry the vote on most of the positions that are available.”

Sylvestre, who also serves as the head of the Ucp’s Bonnyville–Cold Lake constituency association, said Smith could make progress with her base by pushing for similar policies as separatist parties in Quebec, like introducing a provincial police force or working to get more provincial control over immigration.

Most of all, a push to establish an autonomous provincial pension plan separate from the Canada Pension Plan would show that Smith is hearing their concerns, he said.

He said there was “absolutely no question” that the party is now looking to shift from the type of grassroots supporters who helped get Smith elected, particularly when it comes to the declaration that the UCP is asking party presidents to sign. (Sylvestre is among those who has refused to sign it).

Sylvestre also warned that, by ignoring those grassroots supporters, Smith runs the risk of losing support in the general election. Many of those who were most supportive of separation will simply not partake in the next election, which will give the NDP a higher proportion of the vote. That, he said, is partly what caused the UCP to lose a recent byelection in Calgary, in which the party lost a seat it had long held.

“It happened in Calgary-Shaw, and I’m telling you, it’s going to happen all over the province. And as a consequence to that, she’s gambling. I don’t think there’s any reason for her to take this gamble. There’s no reason for her to alienate these people. I just don’t get it.”

stories.title: As B.C. prepares to end education savings grant, residents seek extension
stories.summary: New research shows grants in savings accounts can finance postsecondary enrolment at a lower public cost
stories.author: Andrew Galbraith
stories.content:
Some British Columbia residents are calling for the extension of a provincial grant for postsecondary education after the previous NDP government announced its discontinuation, citing weak adoption and the potential for cost savings.

The cancellation of the British Columbia Training and Education Savings Grant (Bctesg), introduced in 2015, would leave only Quebec offering a provincial-level postsecondary education grant. The Québec Education Savings Incentive, or Qesi, pays a refundable tax credit of up to $300 a year to a child’s Resp, up to a maximum of $3,600.

B.C. is set to end its program in April 2028. Alberta ended a similar program in 2015, and Saskatchewan stopped payments under the Saskatchewan Advantage Grant for Education Savings in 2018.

But Jacky Ip, a certified financial planner, said he questioned the reasoning behind the end of the B.C. grant, which offers eligible children a one-time $1,200 deposit in their Registered Education Savings Plan accounts. Some research suggests that certain savings grants can be an effective and cost-efficient way to promote savings and postsecondary education.

Mr. Ip said the problem was not with the program, but with poor government communication around it. “How can you quash a grant like this without the education and awareness?”

He hopes that a petition submitted to his MLA will encourage the new Conservative government to consider extending the grant.

The B.C. Ministry of Education and Child Care had not responded to The Globe and Mail’s questions as of Thursday evening.

In announcing the end of the program in its 2026 budget, the B.C. government said less than 50 per cent of eligible children had applied for the Bctesg, and that it expected the move to save $30-million annually from 2028.

Governments in both Alberta and Saskatchewan also highlighted potential cost savings when they ended their programs. But a paper published last month by researchers at the University of Montreal and McGill University focused on the federal Canada Learning Bond (CLB) program found that delivering aid through savings accounts can finance postsecondary enrolment at a lower cost for governments.

The CLB program provides up to $2,000 in Resp grants for eligible children from low-income families. The federal government also offers the Canada Education Savings Grant (Cesg), which matches 20 per cent of annual contributions to an Resp, up to $500 a year, to a $7,200 maximum, with additional grants for low- and middle-income families.

The researchers’ analysis found that the CLB encouraged parents to open accounts and contribute their own money. Researchers William Arbour, Laëtitia Renée and Fernando Saltiel found CLB recipients accumulate $1,470 in additional parental savings by age 17. Parents were also more likely to save for older siblings who were ineligible for the CLB grant.

“The evidence on the CLB suggests that non-matching grants paid into RESPs can raise both Resp savings and postsecondary enrolment, with effects that were larger than I expected,” Dr. Renée said in an e-mail.

She cautioned that her findings May not directly apply to a program like the Bctesg. Unlike the CLB, which is designed for low-income families, the Bctesg is available to all B.C.-resident children with a valid social insurance number and a parent or guardian who is also a B.C. resident. Applications are valid between a child’s sixth birthday and the day before they turn nine.

Dr. Renée said grants such as the Bctesg depend on families having an Resp account. “Higher-income families are much more likely to open one, so this creates inequalities in access to grants,” she said. At the same time, governments should carry out “rigorous evaluation” before ending such programs, she said.

“If the concern is cost or reaching the families who need it most, one option would be to means-test the grant rather than drop it altogether,” she said.

Reuben Ford, a Vancouver-based research director at the non-profit Social Research and Demonstration Corporation, said it was too early in the life of the program to properly assess the grant’s effectiveness.

The Bctesg was initially offered at a time when other programs, including the CLB, were also suffering from weak adoption, he said. “The key thing, of course, was that the federal government has responded to that.”

Starting in April 2028, the federal government will automatically open an Resp to deposit the CLB to address low participation.

Whether or not his petition succeeds in pressing the government to extend the B.C. program, Mr. Ip says he encourages his clients with eligible children to apply while they can.

“There’s a physical deadline of 2028 for people to apply for their Bctesg, and more than half of the eligible families aren’t doing it, and it’s free money,” he said.

stories.title: Ontario’s bad bet on online gambling ads
stories.summary: The province belatedly contemplates restrictions on rampant advertising for digital betting
stories.author: The Editorial Board
stories.content:
Ontario Premier Doug Ford can’t believe how many gambling ads he is seeing. They’re “out of control,” he said this week, and his government will look at reining them in. As it happens, he won’t have to look too hard to find the culprit.

It was Mr. Ford’s own government that legalized online gambling in the province, four years ago. It is his government’s online gambling agency that oversees it, and rakes in hundreds of millions of dollars annually. It was his government that voted against an attempt earlier this year to ban gambling ads.

The fact is that Mr. Ford’s government has stood by while gambling became a serious problem in the province. Restricting ads would be a good start, but more must be done to reduce gambling itself by adjusting age thresholds, requiring gamblers to set financial and time limits, which are currently optional , and improving supports for problem gamblers.

That’s not Mr. Ford’s goal – the problem for him is just the number of ads – but it should be.

Many people can place bets, absorb their losses and face no further ill effects. For a minority of people, though, easy access to gambling can open the door to disaster.

Research for Ontario’s own agency, iGaming Ontario, showed higher-than-expected levels of problem gambling even before legalization. That finding led officials to bury the data, which was supposed to form the baseline for analysis of legalization’s impact, according to an investigation by the Toronto Star.

However, other research has begun to emerge, and to paint a worrying picture.

A study published in the American Journal of Preventive Medicine showed that emergency room visits for gambling disorders, which often coincide with mental health and addiction issues, doubled after the province legalized online gambling in 2022.

Coroner’s data analyzed by the CBC showed that gambling-related suicides tripled after online betting was legalized.

According to research by the Alberta Gambling Research Institute, the number of problem gamblers in Ontario has nearly tripled since 2018. They still account for only 0.8 per cent of the population but the rise is equivalent to an additional 57,500 problem gamblers. A further 2.4 per cent of Ontarians were at-risk gamblers.

Is the prevalence of gambling ads part of the problem? There can be little doubt that they are having an effect.

Research led by Toronto Metropolitan University found that 77 per cent of men under 30 reported seeing gambling ads on a weekly basis, and 60 per cent said that their gambling was influenced by the ads. The same research showed that counter-ads promoting responsible gambling are losing the battle, with 60 per cent of young men saying these ads had “little to no impact on reducing their betting habits.”

And while there are rules about making gambling ads so that they don’t appeal specifically to children, that cannot prevent young people from seeing them. Research by Toronto’s Centre for Addiction and Mental Health found that one-quarter of students in grades 7 through 12 reported seeing online gambling ads every day. These people are too young to gamble legally but they are the market of the future.

A key problem with gambling ads is that online gambling allows impulsive betting. This is unlike alcohol or tobacco, in which an urge to buy sparked by an ad is not followed by immediate consumption of cigarettes or booze. Someone who sees a gambling ad can go directly to an online casino or sports book to place a bet.

Reducing the prevalence of gambling ads would be a public health – and social – victory.

Parliament is making a step in that direction with Bill S-211 , which seeks to restrict sports gambling ads specifically. That’s a start. But as the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health says in its submission on the subject, the government should consider broadening the approach given that traditional betting options such as slots “account for most of the total amount wagered online.”

Online gambling has been lucrative, which makes it perhaps understandable that Mr. Ford shows little interest in reducing gambling itself. Instead, he focuses on the ads. And, reminiscent of the ersatz outrage of that French police captain in the movie Casablanca , Mr. Ford is shocked to find out what has been going on.

stories.title: ‘Demolition by inaction’: City staff suggest council block demolition of long-vacant heritage building
stories.summary: The latest application to demolish the historic Fraser House Hotel in Downtown London, Ont. is renewing debate about when heritage buildings should be demolished, and when they should be incorporated into new developments.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
The latest application to demolish the historic Fraser House Hotel in Downtown London, Ont. is renewing debate about when heritage buildings should be demolished, and when they should be incorporated into new developments.

Constructed in 1892, the A-ranked heritage building at 183 King St. (between Richmond and Clarence) is the subject of a demolition request by owner Southside Construction Management that cites deteriorating structural integrity.

There are multiple broken/missing windows on the upper floors, bricks along the rear of the building are disintegrating, and wood rot has hollowed out some exterior architectural features.

According to an engineer’s report submitted by Southside, the most recent estimate to shore up the front façade and underpin the existing north foundation wall is more than $2 million.

However, city staff recommend that council refuse to grant the demolition permit.

The recommendation is based on the findings of an independent engineer who reviewed the developer’s submission on behalf of city hall.

The report to the Planning and Environment Committee (PEC) suggests little has materially changed since council refused Southside’s previous demolition request in 2015.

It reads, “Since then, there does not appear to have been maintenance or repairs to the building on the property, resulting in ‘demolition by inaction’ as described by engineering consultant Read Jones Christoffersen.”

It concludes, “The independent review of the information submitted determined that the building, as presented within the engineering reviews, did not appear to pose an elevated or imminent risk that required its demolition.”

Downtown Coun. David Ferreira says he cannot support the demolition request as it currently stands.

“I’d like to see redevelopment in our downtown, and clearly I would like to see it incorporate our heritage assets,” Ferreira told CTV News. “The way this report stands on its own, it is just a demolition and there is no redevelopment.”

“I haven’t necessarily seen too much investment into the building in the last decade, or so, but we’re here now and we need to ask, what can we do moving forward?” he added.

Located in the corner of an almost 1.1-acre parking lot owned by Southside, the developer’s Heritage Impact Assessment does not include plans to rebuild on the property.

“I’m worried, what if council were to approve a demolition? Considering (real estate) market conditions, how long would this be sitting empty with no [redevelopment] application? How long would it be a surface level parking lot?” Ferreira asked.

In their report, city staff suggest a potential path forward, conserve much of the building by incorporating it into a larger mixed-use redevelopment.

“There could be a referral [to a later date] at the committee meeting [to] come back with an application,” Ferreira explained. “Right now, things are up in the air. I’ll have to see how the discussion goes at the planning committee.”

Ferreira worries that approving demolition without a redevelopment application could leave another gap in the downtown.

Despite his concerns, Ferreira acknowledges Southside’s contributions to housing in London.

“They’ve contributed significantly to the city with nonprofit and community housing. I’m really appreciative of that, and I’ve had conversations with the applicant about this application,” he said.

A representative from Southside Group declined to comment to CTV News before the application is considered at the PEC meeting on Dec. 1.
