stories.title: Supreme Court of Canada to issue ruling on Quebec secularism law Bill 21
stories.summary: The Supreme Court of Canada is expected to release its decision regarding Quebec’s secularism law on Friday morning. The country’s highest court will determine whether the province’s use of the notwithstanding clause to pass Bill 21 — which bans public officials in positions of authority from wearing religious symbols on the job — was constitutional. […]
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
The Supreme Court of Canada has upheld most portions of Quebec’s secularism law, delivering a major victory to the provincial government in a decision that will reverberate across the country.

Canada’s highest court, in its 532-page decision released Friday morning, ruled Quebec’s use of the notwithstanding clause to pass Bill 21 was in large part constitutional.

The legislation bans public officials in positions of authority, like teachers, police officers and judges, from wearing religious symbols on the job. It also requires anyone providing or receiving a government service to have their face uncovered.

“In short, Bill 21 is rooted in Quebec’s legitimate and historical commitment to ensuring the laicity of the state in a free and democratic society,” wrote Chief Justice Richard Wagner in the opening paragraphs of the judgment.

The seven Supreme Court justices, however, did strike down Section 8 of the law, which required elected members of the National Assembly to sit with their faces uncovered.

The overall ruling offers governments significant clarity into how they can use the Constitution’s notwithstanding clause — known as Section 33 — to temporarily shield controversial legislation from legal challenges. Saskatchewan, Alberta and Ontario have also invoked Section 33 in recent years on laws affecting transgender youth, back-to-work legislation, third-party political advertising, and others.

Read: Bill 21 ruling: Victory for secularism but setback for , says Quebec premier

“Today, Quebec’s secularism is affirmed, as the court has confirmed what we already knew. Yet, this remains significant: it concerns the ability of the National Assembly and the parliaments of other provinces to invoke the notwithstanding clause,” said Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon.

“This is undeniably a victory for secularism. Furthermore, it provides a degree of short-term legal stability for the Government of Quebec. Naturally, there were concerns regarding social peace should such a fundamental policy choice be effectively struck down by the Supreme Court. So, this is good news. It is something to be welcomed.”

The Quebec premier, however, also described it as a setback for provincial autonomy. That’s because the ruling, he says, allows the Court to weigh in on the constitutionality of a law, even when that law is protected by the notwithstanding clause. The courts will, in effect, be delivering “hypothetical judgments,” he says, which invites “highly visible legal activism by certain groups and the federal government.”

Quebec pre-emptively invoked the Charter override clause when it adopted Bill 21 in 2019. It quickly encountered a constitutional challenge, with civil liberties groups arguing the legislation is discriminatory, especially against Muslim women wearing hijabs.

Friday’s ruling says Quebec correctly applied a section of the Constitution that allows governments to override Charter rights.

Former Quebec Premier François Legault, who was in power when the legislation was adopted, celebrated the decision on social media. “Because that’s how we live in Quebec!” Legault wrote. “Very proud of this legacy!”

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, speaking to reporters from Yellowknife, said he respects the “Supreme Court’s clarification of the application of the Constitution, including the notwithstanding clause.”

“There’s a number of aspects to that decision and some complexities to it, and those far more expert than I are studying those complexities and assessing the implications,” Carney said.

Carney added Ottawa will not be using the notwithstanding clause.

“The Government of Canada, my job as prime minister, the job of the Government of Canada, this government, is to defend the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, the full application of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. I would remind that the benefit of constitutionally protected rights is most important for minorities, those most vulnerable in our society.”

The Supreme Court of Canada was divided over whether to declare that Bill 21 violated Charter rights.

Two of the seven justices determined the legislation is incompatible with freedom of religion, but not so incompatible as to be invalid since the notwithstanding clause must be renewed every five years.

“It treats visible religious minorities as less worthy of full participation in Quebec society, influences their life choices and mobility, and creates professional barriers for them by preventing qualified individuals from being hired, promoted or transferred within public sector workplaces,” they wrote.

The same two justices — and a third — also declared the law violated gender equality and has a disproportionate effect on Muslim women.

However the other four justices determined the section protecting gender equality in the Canadian Charter could not be used to strike down Bill 21. The majority also determined that the override clause prevents the court from ruling on the inconsistency of Bill 21 with Charter rights.

The Canadian Muslim Forum called the ruling profoundly disappointing, describing it as a setback for religious freedom and women’s rights.

“The implications of this ruling extend beyond those directly affected today,” the group wrote in a statement. “It raises serious concerns about the protection of fundamental rights and the scope of government authority to restrict religious expression in ways that May affect citizens’ equality, freedoms, and access to professional opportunities.

“A society committed to equality and democracy must protect the rights of all its citizens, not make access to employment and public opportunities conditional upon abandoning deeply held beliefs.”

Friday’s ruling can be considered a victory for the province’s new Parti Québécois government as well as the federal Bloc Québécois, two ardent supporters of Bill 21.

Bloc Leader Yves-François Blanchet took umbrage with the fact some of the justices pronounced themselves on whether the law violated Charter rights.

“It remains perfectly legitimate for individuals to hold their own personal opinions,” Blanchet told reporters. “However, it must be noted that the role of a judge is to interpret the law, not to express ideological preferences.

“This is a prime example of an attempt to pervert the judicial process and turn it into a biased ideological vehicle. Thankfully, that is not what happened.”

The Bloc and PQ have been critical of the federal government’s opposition to Bill 21. Ottawa, which had intervening status in the challenge to the Quebec law, argued the repeated use of the notwithstanding clause amounts to “indirectly amending the Constitution.”

Canada’s Justice Department spent approximately $3.45 million in connection with the legal challenge to Bill 21.

Blanchet says the ruling — combined with Canada’s legal challenge to the law — could stoke separatist sentiment in the province.

“While certainly not the court’s intention, I interpret the judgment as saying to the people of Quebec: your distinctiveness is known, recognized, and legitimate,” the Bloc leader said. “You have the right to reflect on this and pursue it to its ultimate conclusion, which would, in fact, be the sovereignty of Quebec.”

Since the ruling will have repercussions across the country, Canadian premiers reacted to the Supreme Court’s decision.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith called it a “win for provincial rights and for the democratic balance that holds our federation together.”

Alberta, which was an intervener in the Bill 21 case, invoked the notwithstanding clause in two separate instances last year covering four laws.

In October 2025, the province used it to end a teachers’ strike by imposing back-to-work legislation and a new collective agreement. Two months later, Alberta invoked Section 33 again related to laws affecting transgender individuals — covering the use of pronouns in school, youth gender-affirming care and in amateur female sports.

“Alberta was proud to intervene in this case to defend that principle,” Smith said in a statement.

“The notwithstanding clause was included in the Charter so that elected legislatures, accountable to the people they serve, can have the final say on important questions. That’s true for Quebec and it’s true for every province, including Alberta.

“Alberta will continue to defend our constitutional powers and stand up for the right of Albertans to make decisions that reflect their values.”

While British Columbia Premier Lorne Doerkson welcomed the Supreme Court’s decision, saying the notwithstanding clause is at the “heart of Canadian federalism,” he acknowledged Bill 21 is concerning to “many people of faith here in British Columbia.”

“Freedom of religion is fundamental in this country, and it is not government’s place to tell a teacher, or anyone else who serves the public that they cannot wear a turban, a hijab, a kippah or a cross to work,” Doerkson wrote on X. “Our government was elected to protect the freedoms of British Columbians, and that is what I will always do.”

In Manitoba, Premier Wab Kinew celebrated that certain justices pronounced themselves on whether Quebec’s law violated Charter rights.

“The Supreme Court of Canada ruled today courts CAN say if rights are violated by laws like Bill 21 with non-binding rulings,” Kinew wrote on X. “Manitoba intervened to make this point and I am glad we won it.

“Section 33 stands, but we now have a tool to get out the vote so democracy prevails over legislated discrimination.”

Kinew said his government would never use the notwithstanding clause.

The legal challenge was led by the English Montreal School Board (Emsb), specifically regarding sections 23 and 28 of the Charter — on minority language education rights and gender equality.

“Even though I know that this result is very disappointing for a lot of people today, the sun comes up tomorrow,” said Emsb Chair Joe Ortona moments after the decision. “We have a minority government in Quebec, and the notwithstanding clause needs to be renewed every five years, and that’s going to come again in 2029.

“This isn’t the end of the road, this is the end of the legal road. The advocacy and the lobbying to the MNAs and keeping this as one of the questions on the ballot at every provincial election stays. We respect the decision of the court, but the advocacy continues.”

Ortona says the Emsb’s seven-year legal challenge cost the school board upwards of $1 million.

“But quite frankly, we stood for vulnerable and marginalized people,” he said. “And I think we taught a good lesson to our students that everybody matters and we fought the good fight. And you can’t put a price tag on that.”

The Supreme Court heard the case over four days last March in what was one of the longest hearings in its history. Sixty-one parties participated in the case, including 51 interveners, which the court says is a record number.

One of those interveners was the Task Force on Linguistic Policy, an advocacy group that campaigns for minority language rights.

“It’s very disappointing that we didn’t get the judgment we were hoping for,” said Geoffrey Chambers, the task force’s vice-president. “The fact that a substantial portion of the court actually dissented shows that it’s a very complicated matter. I mean obviously this is a final judgment and we’re not saying that it’s gonna get relitigated, but it’s not a judgment that is going to resonate across the country as the absolutely clear solution to this question because there’s a substantial amount of very well argued dissent from serious legal minds, Supreme Court justices.”

–With files from The Canadian Press

stories.title: Business Brief: Will Canada seize the Montney opportunity?
stories.summary: Inside the vast natural gas play spanning the B.C.-Alberta border
stories.author: Tim Kiladze
stories.content:
Good morning. For the past 18 months, oil has dominated the domestic conversation about natural resources. Ottawa proposed a new pipeline, and crude prices have soared because of the Iran war. Yet globally, natural gas is just as intriguing – and lucky for Canada, we’re home to one of the world’s hottest gas plays. Today, we’re taking you inside the Montney. But first:

Telecom: Anthony Lacavera, a founder of what is now Freedom Mobile, tried to buy back the wireless carrier in 2008. Now, the proposed takeover of Telus by the carrier’s current owner, Quebecor, has inspired him to try again .

Trade: Ottawa is clamping down on cheap canned-vegetable imports that Canada’s trade tribunal says are flooding the market and outcompeting domestic processors.

Tech: Ottawa begins rolling out $700-million in AI compute funding under new sector-based approach, starting with companies in health and life sciences.

Hi, I’m Tim Kiladze, a business reporter and columnist with The Globe, and I recently travelled to the heart of the Montney Formation, which straddles the British Columbia-Alberta border, to understand why the natural gas play is so hot right now .

It’s a bit of a mind trip for anyone who has followed oil and gas for some time. Two decades ago, the Montney was all the rage because new drilling techniques had unlocked the gas trapped in its tight rock.

The problem: The same technology was deployed in the U.S., and Americans were able to tap vast reserves that once seemed inaccessible. In no time, Canada’s top export market for natural gas became its biggest competitor, and investors got burned.

It was a particularly bruising period for Encana Corp., which used to be Canada’s most valuable company. In 2008, management went all-in on natural gas and hived off the company’s oil sands assets, only for natural gas prices to tank once North American supply surged.

So it can be disorienting to hear people talk up the Montney again. Yet, the potential is very real. The Montney has hundreds of trillions of cubic feet of gas, making it one of the world’s largest gas plays, and the region has barely been developed. Its gas is also quite affordable to produce.

What really changes things this time around is LNG, or liquefied natural gas. Canada’s first large LNG export facility is now up and running, and a major expansion was just greenlit. The lead backer of that project, Shell, is so gung-ho on the Montney that it swooped in this spring and bought Calgary’s Arc Resources for $19-billion.

It’s fuelled a rush in the region, and there have been even more acquisitions this fall.

For some, the hope is that more LNG plants will sprout up, which will enable more Canadian gas to hit the open sea. The second it leaves Canada, natural gas becomes 10 to 15 times more valuable, because countries that import LNG have to pay global prices. And those prices shot up after 20 per cent of the world’s LNG supply got trapped in the Strait of Hormuz in March.

Data centres have also changed the Montney equation. Canada is keen on achieving data sovereignty when it comes to AI, and Alberta has opened its arms to developers of these facilities. However, the province has stipulated that new projects must not drain the existing electricity grid, so developers are looking to build natural gas plants to power their facilities. That gas will largely come from the Montney.

Is it possible this all ends badly again? Absolutely. Geopolitics are hard to predict, and the U.S. is building LNG export facilities like crazy, which steals some of Canada’s shine.

Yet, the potential is also undeniable, and it supports Ottawa’s recent thesis. Amid the trade war with the United States, Prime Minister Mark Carney is telling anyone who will listen that Canada has what the world wants. When it comes to the Montney, it’s absolutely true.

Over the past century, nominal home prices in Canada have risen by an average of 5.8 per cent a year. A look at 100 years of Canadian home prices may offer some guidance for homeowners wondering whether to list now or wait for a recovery.

I’ll tell you one thing: someone comes through my door with a gun and a knife and starts shooting it up – I’ll blow the guy right through the front door, you’ll look like Swiss cheese by the time he’s done. — Ontario Premier Doug Ford

In the wake of a recent string of Toronto home invasions , Ontario’s Doug Ford said he would use his (legally owned) gun to protect his family.

Chips: Jensen Huang survived his scandal, but China’s remote access to Nvidia’s advanced computer chips didn’t.

Calls: Ontario and Unifor say Ottawa should exempt Canadian automakers from tailpipe-emissions rules and other greenhouse-gas regulations.

Global markets rallied with ​a U.S. holiday lull giving some respite from the AI ‌jitters that have weighed heavily on markets this month.

Wall Street futures were in positive territory ahead of a shortened trading session, while TSX futures followed sentiment higher.

Overseas, the pan-European STOXX 600 was up 0.8 per cent in morning trading. Britain’s FTSE 100 rose 0.61 per cent, Germany’s DAX gained 0.51 per cent and France’s CAC 40 advanced 0.1 per cent.

In Asia, Japan’s Nikkei closed 2.11 per cent higher, while Hong Kong’s Hang Seng also gained 2.11 per cent.

The Canadian dollar traded at 70.21 U.S. cents.

stories.title: Grays Bay at a glance: Promises and pitfalls of the Nunavut road and port project
stories.summary: Kugluktuk - The proposed Grays Bay Road and Port Project would be built in northwestern Nunavut at a cost of more than $1 billion. The federal government has referred it to the major projects office, which could fast-track its development.
stories.author: Jeremy Simes, Be Giant and The Canadian Press The Canadian Press
stories.content:
KUGLUKTUK - The proposed Grays Bay Road and Port Project would be built in northwestern Nunavut at a cost of more than $1 billion. The federal government has referred it to the major projects office, which could fast-track its development.

Here are some details:

The year-round, 230-kilometre gravel road would run from the Northwest Territories boundary up to Grays Bay, where the country’s first deepsea port could ship out critical minerals from the area and accommodate the Canadian military. It would take about five years to build.

West Kitikmeot Resources Corp. would construct the road and port and aims for 75 per cent in federal government funding. The Kitikmeot Inuit Association, which represents Inuit in the region, is a major shareholder of the company; Calgary-based Atco Ltd. has a 40 per cent stake.

Economic boom

West Kitikmeot says the project would add $750 million per year to Nunavut’s economy by 2040. The company says the goal of the project is to spur mining development of copper and zinc. Three major mineral exploration sites sit along or near the route: two owned by MMG Ltd. and one by Glencore.

Caribou herds in the region have collapsed, with researchers and local residents blaming predation, disease, overhunting and warming temperatures. Hunters say they worry the project could devastate herds further, as Grays Bay Road would cut through habitat and provide hunters with more access points.

The company plans on hiring 250 to 400 people during construction. About 80 potential employees could work at the port and three at a road station. Up to 20 would be hired directly by the company during operations. New mines, shipping companies and tourism operators may also start up.

There’s a housing shortage in Nunavut and across the North. Building supplies could brought in, stored at the port and shipped to area communities, making it easier to get homes built.

The North has the highest food prices in Canada. More reliable, frequent shipments of food would make non-perishable bulk goods cheaper.

Arctic security

The port is seen as a strategic asset for Arctic sovereignty, with the capacity to host the military and coast guard vessels.

Bigger corridor planned

The Arctic Economic Security Corridor has also been referred to the major projects office. The 400-kilometre road would stretch north of Yellowknife and connect to Grays Bay Road. If both roads are built, they would become part of the national highway system.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 27, 2026.

stories.title: Rain sticks around London before weekend improvement
stories.summary: Another day of rain in the Forest City.
stories.author: Fiona Robertson
stories.content:
Another day of rain in the Forest City. “The winds easing off though, not quite as gusty through the afternoon as they were yesterday,” admitted CTV London Meteorologist Julie Atchison. “Periods of rain expected to continue past noon hour and the temperature hovering between 3 and 4 degrees.” Conditions continue to improve as we inch closer to the weekend.

“Saturday looks good. A mix of sun and cloud and five degrees,” added Atchison. “The chance for showers on Sunday returns but we will have some rain develop Sunday night.” A chance for showers lingers into Monday, and daytime highs will take a bit of a dip.

Here’s a look at the rest of the forecast Friday: Periods of rain. Wind northeast 20 km/h becoming light early in the morning. High plus 5. UV index 1 or low. Friday night: Periods of rain ending overnight then cloudy with 30 per cent chance of showers.

Wind west 20 km/h gusting to 40. Low plus 2. Saturday: A mix of sun and cloud with 30 per cent chance of showers. High plus 5. Sunday: Cloudy with 40 per cent chance of showers. High plus 5. Monday: Cloudy with 40 per cent chance of showers.

High plus 3. Tuesday: Cloudy. High plus 1.

stories.title: Living amid Vancouver’s homelessness crisis made me a Nimby. Here’s how I changed my mind
stories.summary: As addiction and despair consumed my neighbourhood, I confess that it hardened my heart. Understanding was my way through
stories.author: Arno Kopecky
stories.content:
Arno Kopecky is a Vancouver-based journalist and author.

There were no shelters when we moved into our home on the north end of Commercial Drive, Vancouver’s bohemian strip, 10 years ago – though there was plenty of grit. The Downtown Eastside, Canada’s most infamous open-air drug market, is two kilometres away, and our little alleyway has long been on the edge of that ecosystem. But over the past decade we’ve watched the Dtes grow in size and severity, engulfing our neighbourhood and our lives.

It started with the first shelter – the one across our alley, which opened five years ago – and then soon afterward, a second shelter opened a block away. Small groups of people – young and old, brown and white, male and female – began huddling up and down the block, sharing pipes or flaps of blackened tinfoil day and night. Many were contorted, or displayed terrible open wounds. Fentanyl had replaced heroin by this time, and their regular overdoses drew the sirens of first responders at all hours.

This landscape defies comprehension. Yet many Canadians are all too familiar with it – not only because they’ve seen footage of the Downtown Eastside, but because homelessness and drug addiction have taken root in their communities too. According to annual nationwide point-in-time counts, the number of Canadians without a home has doubled since 2018, from 29,000 to 58,000 (though this is almost certainly an undercount, as such surveys capture a single-night snapshot). Most of those Canadians sleep in shelters like the one behind my house, but the proportion that’s sleeping rough, either on the streets or in encampments, has also doubled, and comprised almost a third of all homeless people counted in 2024. The past decade has also seen an explosion of addiction to fentanyl and even deadlier analogues; between 2016 and 2026, more than 57,000 Canadians died of opioid overdose. This is now the leading cause of death for young men and women aged 20 to 40.

After years of broad neglect, this crisis has finally earned a serious response from our federal government. Ottawa’s latest budget committed almost $30-billion to a plan that Prime Minister Mark Carney says will end homelessness in 10 years. It promises to boost the Canada Housing Benefit, to build more supportive and transitional homes, to integrate support with health care, social services and addictions programs. A great deal of that money will flow through local community agencies that are already on the ground.

Homelessness experts across the country have expressed cautious optimism about the plan; it appears comprehensive and ambitious and right-minded. It wisely calls on provinces and cities to partner with Ottawa, so that all three levels of government work in tandem, and on that front, the city of Winnipeg and the province of Manitoba were the first to opt in.

But to succeed, there’s another constituency that will have to co-operate: Canadians who May not be thrilled about the prospect of mental-health facilities and supportive housing popping up next door to where they live, because they’ve seen what they can do to their daily lives.

Canadians, I’m loath to confess, like me.

Because here’s the thing: Watching a humanitarian disaster surround my home did not elicit a purely compassionate response in me. I had empathy, yes, but there was also horror and revulsion. When human feces started showing up on our doorstep, when bodies that could either be unconscious or dead became a regular feature of the landscape, when screams and sirens became the backdrop to our dinner conversations, I’m embarrassed to admit that my immediate reaction was not to say Yes, we must support this. Instead I was flooded by a sentiment I think many Canadians quietly share, no matter how progressive their politics: Make it go away.

And so, for a little while, I became something I’ve long detested: A Nimby.

Not that I was particularly good at it. I went to a city council public hearing to oppose a 22-storey apartment proposed for next door; that’s three times the maximum height allowed by my neighbourhood’s zoning rules, yet it was permitted because the developer proposed including a handful of social-housing units and a mental-health drop-in centre. Ten minutes after my speech, city council approved it unanimously. Then, I harangued public officials about how it felt like the new shelters were drawing the Downtown Eastside’s worst elements our way, only to have new management take over our back-alley shelter and make things worse, by removing the limits to drug consumption and intoxication that had previously been in place.

Everything I opposed marched unstoppably forward. But at the same time, it also felt like I was failing the test of my own convictions. I support caring for society’s neediest citizens, just as I support urban densification. But when confronted with the application of these principles next door, ON an intense scale, I was appalled. What did that say about me?

I needed to understand how Canada, one of the world’s most prosperous countries, got to this place – and how I got to this place, too.

“You’ll always have the people who say, ‘we’re all for supportive housing, as long as it’s on Mars,’” Micheal Vonn told me when I reached her by phone this summer. She was teasing me – I’d just confessed to her my conversion to Nimby-hood – but she was also voicing a real conundrum she deals with every day.

Ms. Vonn is the CEO of PHS (formerly the Portland Hotel Society), a non-profit that provides long-term supportive housing to more than 1,500 people in the Downtown Eastside, plus a slew of overnight shelters, health care centres and much else. PHS is one of the oldest and biggest outfits of its kind, with an operating budget north of $85-million a year, mostly from municipal and provincial grants.

Ms. Vonn’s organization illustrates how governments of every stripe and jurisdiction have managed the Downtown Eastside for decades: by outsourcing it. There are no city-run shelters, or clinics, or job-placement programs in the Dtes; there’s no government agency keeping tabs on the population. As a result, for all its shocking visibility, the area’s issues remain mostly unquantified. Nobody knows exactly how many people live there, what proportion of them use hard drugs, what the collective cost of emergency room visits and first responders and policing May be, or just how much money taxpayers are spending on organizations like PHS.

The dozens of charities and non-profits who operate here do collect their own data, but it ends at their doorstep. This patchwork of essential-service providers cares for a demographic no one else will touch, from offering wound care, laundry and storage, to soup kitchens, dentistry and subsidized dwellings of every shape and size. The result is a bewildering warren of buildings, beds and offices through which some of Canada’s most impaired citizens shuffle every day.

This is what critics on both the left and the right deride as the “non-profit industrial complex,” or Npic. Opponents on the right argue that mission creep has turned non-profits into political-advocacy vehicles rather than providers of grassroots aid, and that many organizations are exploiting a crisis to milk taxpayers. Opponents on the left, meanwhile, argue that the Npic maintains the status quo and quells the upheaval needed to make serious change; as one academic paper put it , “Vancouver’s Npic allows the government and the wealthy to shirk responsibility for deepening health and social inequities.”

Ms. Vonn doesn’t disagree with that statement – responsibility is dumped onto these organizations. But she vehemently disputes the corollary: that non-profits like hers, serving people the rest of society refuses to engage with, are exacerbating the problem. “We are the housing of last resort,” she told me. “When you have a 71-year-old with a brain injury who yells abuse, who is incontinent and in a wheelchair, staying in an ordinary shelter, what you have is a recipe for chaos. And what you’re seeing is all of these system gaps devolve down to the very last thing that can possibly catch it, which is us. And we are not resourced for that.”

Indeed, Ms. Vonn’s organization has been completely overwhelmed by the Downtown Eastside’s last decade of metastatic growth. Not only has fentanyl supplanted heroin, but a new generation of harder drugs is now replacing fentanyl; scores of young people are developing brain damage and becoming permanent wards of the state, only without any direct state support.

On top of all that, Ms. Vonn told me, a fresh wave of retired seniors whose sole affliction is not being able to afford rent is starting to compete for the finite bed space, too. “It’s beyond comprehension to try to keep up,” Ms. Vonn said.

Ms. Vonn argues that organizations like hers, with boots on the ground and years of experience, are best placed to handle the crisis, but they need more money and some policy control. “We have total responsibility for the people we serve, but we have no power,” she said. “We don’t control the funding and we don’t control the model.” Others feel the non-profits are too dug-in already, and that what’s needed is for government to take back the reins and run its own programs. Some level of state involvement is clearly required, as Ms. Vonn acknowledges, for even the best-run non-profits can’t control what happens on the street.

This all made good sense. But what about the street-level chaos that such organizations attract? When I suggested that the public might not support a build-out of new shelters and mental-health centres unless organizations like PHS could control it – or at least manage it – Ms. Vonn actually agreed. “Yes, you want whoever is working in there to work effectively with all the partners, to be appropriately resourced, and have all the appropriate tools to be able to manage that,” she said.

Investing in those tools won’t just help organizations like hers reduce the chaos that surrounds their buildings, she added. It would also alleviate the strain on other public systems at the breaking point – in particular, our hospitals and jails, which is where homeless people with mental health and addiction crises tend to wind up when society gives up on them.

That’s the problem with ignoring the problem, as Ms. Vonn reminded me: “It doesn’t just go away.”

At the heart of the Nimby mindset is something of a universal human desire: to live in peace . Of course that’s what the people disturbing my peace want, too; they’re desperate for it. Yet a significant portion of them seem unable to stop attracting unwanted attention; they shout, they steal, they overdose, over and over again. This raises a core knotty question for anyone with good intentions: How do you help people who won’t help themselves?

“Now you’re getting into philosophical questions around free will and agency, and where it begins and ends,” said Nicole Luongo, a policy analyst with the Canadian Drug Policy Coalition.

Ms. Luongo was a co-author of a 2023 paper critiquing the non-profit industrial complex. I called her in late August, and found myself in an hour-long conversation with a deeply intelligent and thoughtful academic, over the course of which she shared that she, too, had spent years living on the Downtown Eastside.

She’d been one of the people I’m trying to understand. “[I was] ranting and raving, incoherent, covered in weeks’ and months’ worth of body fluids,” she told me.

Ms. Luongo’s story wasn’t typical, she said – she’s white, and grew up in a comfortable middle-class household. But she was born, as she said, “a little different.” She developed an eating disorder in childhood, among other behavioural challenges that overwhelmed her family. She wound up in a hospital psych ward in her teens; soon after she was released, she left home and lived in a shelter. That’s when her substance use began in earnest.

“I spent a lot of years in the thick of it, cycling through involuntary care, homeless shelters and detox,” she said.

As we spoke, I kept looking out my window at the shelter behind my house. There was a group of three people smoking from glass pipes just outside the entrance; one was in a wheelchair, and the other two were slumped beside her on the ground. Soon all three were unconscious. I told Ms. Luongo that I struggled to imagine a future for them.

“We don’t know what someone’s capable of until some things radically change in their world,” she replied.

I asked: What changed in hers?

Ms. Luongo had both a long and a short answer to that question. The former was a “not necessarily replicable” cycle of addiction-treatment centres, academe, and relapse: “My master’s degree was basically a two-year bender,” she said. “Don’t ask me how I pulled it off.” She went to Oxford next to begin a PhD, “got about five days in, went on yet another bender, was institutionalized again, got expelled.” That was in 2017; she’s now been sober for eight years.

The short answer: “I think what has done it is to get really angry. Not at myself. At the policy-makers. Then I found some spaces where I feel I belong, and I have a purpose.”

Ms. Luongo came back to this point at the end of our conversation. We’d covered a vast policy terrain, full of intractable crises with contradictory solutions, but in the end it was a personal story for her. “I just have to return to the idea that folks need meaning and purpose,” she said. “And to have their basic needs met. More and more, across the country and the world, that is not happening.”

That’s her primary concern, she said: “the material precarity that is increasing across the country.”

Climate change is the issue I write most about, and I can’t help but feel there’s a parallel in how we talk about homelessness. When it comes to the climate crisis, the consequences of rising greenhouse gases are so extreme – unprecedented floods, forest fires, heat waves, intense storms – that they tend to suck up all the attention. Of course we must respond to the emergencies, but until we do something about those carbon emissions, the disasters will keep outpacing our solutions.

By the same token, we must help the 20,000 people sleeping rough across this country on any given night. But if we ignore the forces that unhoused them in the first place, tens of thousands more might pour into the streets by the time Mr. Carney’s $30-billion have been spent. The disaster will outpace our solutions.

So what’s the equivalent of emissions in this crisis? Ms. Luongo named it, as did Ms. Vonn and others I spoke to: Canadians’ financial precarity. They weren’t just talking about the current stretch of higher inflation, either: They meant an economic system that feels designed to concentrate ever more wealth in ever fewer hands.

The wealth gap in Canada is higher today than it’s ever been, with the richest 1 per cent holding almost as much wealth as the bottom 80 per cent. Inequality keeps growing. In this context, it’s little wonder that people of all ages are ending up on the streets. Yet the notion of taxing that wealth or redistributing it in any way appears to be political kryptonite.

That’s what I’d like to see our leaders address. I’m not at all sure they’re prepared to.

But for those of us who aren’t running the country, we can still focus closer to home.

As it turned out, the officials my neighbours and I complained to were listening, after all. When summer turned to fall, conditions in my neighbourhood began improving. The shelter hired more supervisors, who cracked down on the open consumption of fentanyl and related hijinks. There’s much less shouting. Police patrols have ticked up. I haven’t seen an overdose in weeks. The return of calm has made it easier to support the shelter, and to look at this problem square in the face. That’s the only way we as a society can overcome it.

Speaking to experts like Ms. Vonn and Ms. Luongo also helped me appreciate the heroic efforts already under way to address this pressing crisis. Gently, and with more patience than I May have deserved, they put my own tribulations in perspective.

Understanding – the shortest path to empathy I know – helped cure me of being Nimby. But so too did a little peace and quiet.

Small groups of people – young and old, brown and white, male and female – began huddling up and down the block, sharing pipes or flaps of blackened tinfoil day and night. Many were contorted, or displayed terrible open wounds. Fentanyl had replaced heroin by this time, and their regular overdoses drew the sirens of first responders at all hours.

This landscape defies comprehension. Yet many Canadians are all too familiar with it – not only because they’ve seen footage of the Downtown Eastside, but because homelessness and drug addiction have taken root in their communities too. According to annual nationwide point-in-time counts, the number of Canadians without a home has doubled since 2018, from 29,000 to 58,000 (though this is almost certainly an undercount, as such surveys capture a single-night snapshot). Most of those Canadians sleep in shelters like the one behind my house, but the proportion that’s sleeping rough, either on the streets or in encampments, has also doubled, and comprised almost a third of all homeless people counted in 2024. The past decade has also seen an explosion of addiction to fentanyl and even deadlier analogues; between 2016 and 2026, more than 57,000 Canadians died of opioid overdose. This is now the leading cause of death for young men and women aged 20 to 40.

After years of broad neglect, this crisis has finally earned a serious response from our federal government. Ottawa’s latest budget committed almost $30-billion to a plan that Prime Minister Mark Carney says will end homelessness in 10 years. It promises to boost the Canada Housing Benefit, to build more supportive and transitional homes, to integrate support with health care, social services and addictions programs. A great deal of that money will flow through local community agencies that are already on the ground.

Homelessness experts across the country have expressed cautious optimism about the plan; it appears comprehensive and ambitious and right-minded. It wisely calls on provinces and cities to partner with Ottawa, so that all three levels of government work in tandem, and on that front, the city of Winnipeg and the province of Manitoba were the first to opt in.

But to succeed, there’s another constituency that will have to co-operate: Canadians who May not be thrilled about the prospect of mental-health facilities and supportive housing popping up next door to where they live, because they’ve seen what they can do to their daily lives.
Canadians, I’m loath to confess, like me.

Because here’s the thing: Watching a humanitarian disaster surround my home did not elicit a purely compassionate response in me. I had empathy, yes, but there was also horror and revulsion. When human feces started showing up on our doorstep, when bodies that could either be unconscious or dead became a regular feature of the landscape, when screams and sirens became the backdrop to our dinner conversations, I’m embarrassed to admit that my immediate reaction was not to say Yes, we must support this. Instead I was flooded by a sentiment I think many Canadians quietly share, no matter how progressive their politics: Make it go away.
And so, for a little while, I became something I’ve long detested: A Nimby.

Not that I was particularly good at it. I went to a city council public hearing to oppose a 22-storey apartment proposed for next door; that’s three times the maximum height allowed by my neighbourhood’s zoning rules, yet it was permitted because the developer proposed including a handful of social-housing units and a mental-health drop-in centre. Ten minutes after my speech, city council approved it unanimously. Then, I harangued public officials about how it felt like the new shelters were drawing the Downtown Eastside’s worst elements our way, only to have new management take over our back-alley shelter and make things worse, by removing the limits to drug consumption and intoxication that had previously been in place.

Everything I opposed marched unstoppably forward. But at the same time, it also felt like I was failing the test of my own convictions. I support caring for society’s neediest citizens, just as I support urban densification. But when confronted with the application of these principles next door, ON an intense scale, I was appalled. What did that say about me?
I needed to understand how Canada, one of the world’s most prosperous countries, got to this place – and how I got to this place, too.

“You’ll always have the people who say, ‘we’re all for supportive housing, as long as it’s on Mars,’” Micheal Vonn told me when I reached her by phone this summer. She was teasing me – I’d just confessed to her my conversion to Nimby-hood – but she was also voicing a real conundrum she deals with every day.

Ms. Vonn is the CEO of PHS (formerly the Portland Hotel Society), a non-profit that provides long-term supportive housing to more than 1,500 people in the Downtown Eastside, plus a slew of overnight shelters, health care centres and much else. PHS is one of the oldest and biggest outfits of its kind, with an operating budget north of $85-million a year, mostly from municipal and provincial grants.

Ms. Vonn’s organization illustrates how governments of every stripe and jurisdiction have managed the Downtown Eastside for decades: by outsourcing it. There are no city-run shelters, or clinics, or job-placement programs in the Dtes; there’s no government agency keeping tabs on the population. As a result, for all its shocking visibility, the area’s issues remain mostly unquantified. Nobody knows exactly how many people live there, what proportion of them use hard drugs, what the collective cost of emergency room visits and first responders and policing May be, or just how much money taxpayers are spending on organizations like PHS.

The dozens of charities and non-profits who operate here do collect their own data, but it ends at their doorstep. This patchwork of essential-service providers cares for a demographic no one else will touch, from offering wound care, laundry and storage, to soup kitchens, dentistry and subsidized dwellings of every shape and size. The result is a bewildering warren of buildings, beds and offices through which some of Canada’s most impaired citizens shuffle every day.

This is what critics on both the left and the right deride as the “non-profit industrial complex,” or Npic. Opponents on the right argue that mission creep has turned non-profits into political-advocacy vehicles rather than providers of grassroots aid, and that many organizations are exploiting a crisis to milk taxpayers. Opponents on the left, meanwhile, argue that the Npic maintains the status quo and quells the upheaval needed to make serious change; as one academic paper put it , “Vancouver’s Npic allows the government and the wealthy to shirk responsibility for deepening health and social inequities.”

Ms. Vonn doesn’t disagree with that statement – responsibility is dumped onto these organizations. But she vehemently disputes the corollary: that non-profits like hers, serving people the rest of society refuses to engage with, are exacerbating the problem. “We are the housing of last resort,” she told me. “When you have a 71-year-old with a brain injury who yells abuse, who is incontinent and in a wheelchair, staying in an ordinary shelter, what you have is a recipe for chaos. And what you’re seeing is all of these system gaps devolve down to the very last thing that can possibly catch it, which is us. And we are not resourced for that.”

Indeed, Ms. Vonn’s organization has been completely overwhelmed by the Downtown Eastside’s last decade of metastatic growth. Not only has fentanyl supplanted heroin, but a new generation of harder drugs is now replacing fentanyl; scores of young people are developing brain damage and becoming permanent wards of the state, only without any direct state support.

On top of all that, Ms. Vonn told me, a fresh wave of retired seniors whose sole affliction is not being able to afford rent is starting to compete for the finite bed space, too. “It’s beyond comprehension to try to keep up,” Ms. Vonn said.

Ms. Vonn argues that organizations like hers, with boots on the ground and years of experience, are best placed to handle the crisis, but they need more money and some policy control. “We have total responsibility for the people we serve, but we have no power,” she said. “We don’t control the funding and we don’t control the model.” Others feel the non-profits are too dug-in already, and that what’s needed is for government to take back the reins and run its own programs. Some level of state involvement is clearly required, as Ms. Vonn acknowledges, for even the best-run non-profits can’t control what happens on the street.

This all made good sense. But what about the street-level chaos that such organizations attract? When I suggested that the public might not support a build-out of new shelters and mental-health centres unless organizations like PHS could control it – or at least manage it – Ms. Vonn actually agreed. “Yes, you want whoever is working in there to work effectively with all the partners, to be appropriately resourced, and have all the appropriate tools to be able to manage that,” she said.

Investing in those tools won’t just help organizations like hers reduce the chaos that surrounds their buildings, she added. It would also alleviate the strain on other public systems at the breaking point – in particular, our hospitals and jails, which is where homeless people with mental health and addiction crises tend to wind up when society gives up on them.
That’s the problem with ignoring the problem, as Ms. Vonn reminded me: “It doesn’t just go away.”

At the heart of the Nimby mindset is something of a universal human desire: to live in peace . Of course that’s what the people disturbing my peace want, too; they’re desperate for it. Yet a significant portion of them seem unable to stop attracting unwanted attention; they shout, they steal, they overdose, over and over again. This raises a core knotty question for anyone with good intentions: How do you help people who won’t help themselves?
“Now you’re getting into philosophical questions around free will and agency, and where it begins and ends,” said Nicole Luongo, a policy analyst with the Canadian Drug Policy Coalition.

Ms. Luongo was a co-author of a 2023 paper critiquing the non-profit industrial complex. I called her in late August, and found myself in an hour-long conversation with a deeply intelligent and thoughtful academic, over the course of which she shared that she, too, had spent years living on the Downtown Eastside.
She’d been one of the people I’m trying to understand. “[I was] ranting and raving, incoherent, covered in weeks’ and months’ worth of body fluids,” she told me.

Ms. Luongo’s story wasn’t typical, she said – she’s white, and grew up in a comfortable middle-class household. But she was born, as she said, “a little different.” She developed an eating disorder in childhood, among other behavioural challenges that overwhelmed her family. She wound up in a hospital psych ward in her teens; soon after she was released, she left home and lived in a shelter. That’s when her substance use began in earnest.
“I spent a lot of years in the thick of it, cycling through involuntary care, homeless shelters and detox,” she said.

As we spoke, I kept looking out my window at the shelter behind my house. There was a group of three people smoking from glass pipes just outside the entrance; one was in a wheelchair, and the other two were slumped beside her on the ground. Soon all three were unconscious. I told Ms. Luongo that I struggled to imagine a future for them.
“We don’t know what someone’s capable of until some things radically change in their world,” she replied.
I asked: What changed in hers?

Ms. Luongo had both a long and a short answer to that question. The former was a “not necessarily replicable” cycle of addiction-treatment centres, academe, and relapse: “My master’s degree was basically a two-year bender,” she said. “Don’t ask me how I pulled it off.” She went to Oxford next to begin a PhD, “got about five days in, went on yet another bender, was institutionalized again, got expelled.” That was in 2017; she’s now been sober for eight years.
The short answer: “I think what has done it is to get really angry. Not at myself. At the policy-makers. Then I found some spaces where I feel I belong, and I have a purpose.”

Ms. Luongo came back to this point at the end of our conversation. We’d covered a vast policy terrain, full of intractable crises with contradictory solutions, but in the end it was a personal story for her. “I just have to return to the idea that folks need meaning and purpose,” she said. “And to have their basic needs met. More and more, across the country and the world, that is not happening.”
That’s her primary concern, she said: “the material precarity that is increasing across the country.”

Climate change is the issue I write most about, and I can’t help but feel there’s a parallel in how we talk about homelessness. When it comes to the climate crisis, the consequences of rising greenhouse gases are so extreme – unprecedented floods, forest fires, heat waves, intense storms – that they tend to suck up all the attention. Of course we must respond to the emergencies, but until we do something about those carbon emissions, the disasters will keep outpacing our solutions.

By the same token, we must help the 20,000 people sleeping rough across this country on any given night. But if we ignore the forces that unhoused them in the first place, tens of thousands more might pour into the streets by the time Mr. Carney’s $30-billion have been spent. The disaster will outpace our solutions.

So what’s the equivalent of emissions in this crisis? Ms. Luongo named it, as did Ms. Vonn and others I spoke to: Canadians’ financial precarity. They weren’t just talking about the current stretch of higher inflation, either: They meant an economic system that feels designed to concentrate ever more wealth in ever fewer hands.

The wealth gap in Canada is higher today than it’s ever been, with the richest 1 per cent holding almost as much wealth as the bottom 80 per cent. Inequality keeps growing. In this context, it’s little wonder that people of all ages are ending up on the streets. Yet the notion of taxing that wealth or redistributing it in any way appears to be political kryptonite.
That’s what I’d like to see our leaders address. I’m not at all sure they’re prepared to.
But for those of us who aren’t running the country, we can still focus closer to home.

As it turned out, the officials my neighbours and I complained to were listening, after all. When summer turned to fall, conditions in my neighbourhood began improving. The shelter hired more supervisors, who cracked down on the open consumption of fentanyl and related hijinks. There’s much less shouting. Police patrols have ticked up. I haven’t seen an overdose in weeks. The return of calm has made it easier to support the shelter, and to look at this problem square in the face. That’s the only way we as a society can overcome it.

Speaking to experts like Ms. Vonn and Ms. Luongo also helped me appreciate the heroic efforts already under way to address this pressing crisis. Gently, and with more patience than I May have deserved, they put my own tribulations in perspective.
Understanding – the shortest path to empathy I know – helped cure me of being Nimby. But so too did a little peace and quiet.

This raises a core knotty question for anyone with good intentions: How do you help people who won’t help themselves?

content_blocks.text: Climate change is the issue I write most about, and I can’t help but feel there’s a parallel in how we talk about homelessness. When it comes to the climate crisis, the consequences of rising greenhouse gases are so extreme – unprecedented floods, forest fires, heat waves, intense storms – that they tend to suck up all the attention. Of course we must respond to the emergencies, but until we do something about those carbon emissions, the disasters will keep outpacing our solutions.

content_blocks.text: As it turned out, the officials my neighbours and I complained to were listening, after all. When summer turned to fall, conditions in my neighbourhood began improving. stories.title: More Canadians are struggling to pay their mortgage
stories.summary: The number of households behind on payments by more than 90 days has increased over 30 per cent
stories.author: The Decibel Staff, Sherrill Sutherland, Salmaan Farooqui
stories.content:
A growing number of Canadians are falling behind on their mortgage payments. According to a report from Equifax Canada, the number of Canadian households more than 90 days behind on mortgage payments has reached a 13-year high . Ontario, which is faring worse than other parts of the country, is nearing levels last seen during the 2008 financial crisis. Meanwhile, though housing prices have softened across the country, the increasing cost of mortgages are eroding housing affordability .

Salmaan Farooqui is the Globe’s housing and mortgages reporter. He explains what’s going on with mortgages and what it signals about the overall health of the Canadian economy.

stories.title: This Christmas, don’t let driving get in the way of your drinking. Stay home
stories.summary: Andrew Clark has tried to change behaviour with the ‘don’t drink and drive’ message, so this year he is changing tactics with a ‘if-you-can’t-beat ’em-join ’em’ approach
stories.author: Andrew Clark
stories.content:
Do not drink and drive.

Even if it is Christmas. Even if it’s during the weeks leading up to Christmas. Even if it during the weeks following Christmas and leading up to New Year’s.

In fact, don’t do it anytime.

That’s really all the explanation that should be required when it comes to impaired driving. It’s not complicated. It’s not a mystery. It’s a well-known reality, time-tested given, an unimpeachable correctness, an unequivocal statement of fact, a truth universally acknowledged, a stubborn actuality.

Don’t drink and drive. Period. Don’t do any narcotics or mind-altering substances, be they prescription or non-prescription, and drive.

Yet, people continue to astonish. Imbued with the Christmas spirit and inspired by Saint Paul’s “ O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?” they have a few too many festive cocktails and get behind the wheel hoping to discover firsthand if there really is such as thing as eternal life.

It’s a depressing reality I’ve grappled with over the years. No matter how obvious and deadly the dangers, drivers keep doing it. As I type, law enforcement agencies across the country are launching their annual “Reduce Impaired Driving Everywhere” (Ride) holiday campaigns.

New York Yankee great Yoga Berra put it best: “It’s like déjà vu all over again.” To some, it seems, impaired driving is a holiday tradition like trimming the tree, roasting a turkey or, in the case of a 25-year-old from Brampton, Ont., crashing your vehicle into a hydro pole and getting charged with driving impaired, dangerous operation and failure or refusal to comply with demand.

Then there’s the 47-year-old woman in Sault Saint Marie, Ont. who was charged with impaired driving and dangerous operation after police say the vehicle she was driving on November 21 “exited the intersection when it was not safe to do so and struck another vehicle before driving away.” She left the scene, but police retrieved a license plate and identified her vehicle.

A 30-year-old woman in Tweed Ont., faces charges of operation while impaired after police found the pick-up she was driving heavily damaged and rolled onto its side on November 23. These aren’t the greatest impaired driving hits; they’re just a few of the latest. None of the charges have been proven in court.

Thus far in 2026, according to the Ontario Provincial Police , “35 people have died in alcohol- or drug-related collisions, and more than 9,300 motorists have been charged with impaired driving.” The Alberta RCMP says impaired driving incidents have increased by 15 per cent since 2022. They are up 16 per cent in York Region .

In the past, I’ve tried to appeal to the better angels of our nature and encouraged readers to simply forgo alcohol and drugs when driving. Go out, socialize, have a good time and take a cab, public transit or get a sober person to drive them home. This doesn’t seem to be working.

So, it’s time to take a different “if-you-can’t-beat ’em-join ’em” approach. If it were a public service campaign, it would be along the lines of “This Christmas, don’t let driving get in the way of your drinking. Stay home.”

That’s my pitch. Dump the shame. Own your drinking. A lot of impaired driving is caused by people who have convinced themselves it’s okay to drive to a party or bar because they are not going to get drunk. Then they get drunk (that’s what alcohol can do) and drive. I’m saying, forget that. Own it. You are going to get drunk. Fine. Stay home and do that or walk somewhere or have a “friend” drive you.

If someone calls you and invites you to a Christmas Eve party, simply say, “I’d love to but that would interfere with my drinking.” Put yourself, well – your drinking – first.

Besides, if you go to a party or holiday event and get so impaired that you think drunk driving is an appropriate action, how much fun have you really had? Odds are you won’t even remember the evening clearly (if at all). If you are that drunk, you’ll probably turn sour at some point and get in quarrels. Save yourself the time, trouble and potential criminal charges and stay home. Sit down with your alcohol and get ready to watch that hockey game or movie you’ve been dying to see, then down the booze, pass out and come to just as the third period is ending or the credits are rolling. No one gets hurt. Problem solved.

In an ideal world, you might consider reducing or stopping your alcohol consumption all together. Many recommend this course of action. While I’ve met a few people who’ve stopped drinking alcohol who admit to missing it occasionally, I’ve never met anyone who completely regrets quitting.

But why overreach? I am trying to stay in the zone of harm reduction. This Christmas season (every Christmas season) if you are going to drink, go ahead and drink, just don’t drink and drive.

content_blocks.text: Besides, if you go to a party or holiday event and get so impaired that you think drunk driving is an appropriate action, how much fun have you really had? Odds are you won’t even remember the evening clearly (if at all). If you are that drunk, you’ll probably turn sour at some point and get in quarrels. Save yourself the time, trouble and potential criminal charges and stay home. Sit down with your alcohol and get ready to watch that hockey game or movie you’ve been dying to see, then down the booze, pass out and come to just as the third period is ending or the credits are rolling. No one gets hurt. Problem solved.

stories.title: This Ontario hospital locks patients up alone as a ‘first resort,’ ex-Waypoint psychotherapist warns
stories.summary: Isolation was the 'go-to approach to patient management' at Waypoint Centre for Mental Health Care, said ex-staff psychotherapist Sarah Butterworth.
stories.author: Jacques Gallant
stories.content:
The former lead behavioural support specialist at Waypoint Centre for Mental Health Care says she was looking to improve the lives of those detained in the hospital when she outlined her concerns in a 2022 affidavit filed as part of a proposed class-action lawsuit brought by patients: the hospital used seclusion as “an intervention of first resort,” patients were routinely isolated for non-violent and even trivial incidents because it was the “go-to approach to patient management,” and she was instructed to withhold information about seclusion from an independent oversight body.

In a recent interview, Butterworth, a psychotherapist who worked at the hospital from 2015 to 2021, said she was prepared for Waypoint to make it personal.

“And that is exactly what happened.”

In a responding affidavit filed by Waypoint, then-vice-president of clinical services Rob Desroches first dismissed Butterworth’s expertise. “I do not agree with any of Ms. Butterworth’s opinions regarding the alleged improper use of seclusion and use of restraints at Waypoint,” Desroches wrote in his 2022 affidavit, saying he deferred to the “clinical judgment of trained psychiatrists” for why a patient needed to be secluded.

Camelott Hamblett, who has been locked in isolation at Waypoint for two decades, watched Monday’s hearing for eight hours without issue.

“I note that Ms. Butterworth is not, to my knowledge, a psychiatrist,” he wrote.

He then spent several more paragraphs detailing her “complicated employment record and relationship with Waypoint,” including details from her employment and personal life that she says weren’t relevant to the issues and were an effort to discredit her character.

Like at any psychiatric hospital, psychiatrists — who are medical doctors — are ultimately in charge of Waypoint patients’ treatment. A psychiatrist also decides whether or not a patient should remain secluded. But as the Star has previously reported, that decision doesn’t happen after an in-person assessment. Patients’ day-to-day interactions are usually with other staff, including nurses and psychotherapists.

Butterworth chooses to focus on what she said really matters: helping the seriously mentally ill patients who have been locked up alone for years in their rooms at Waypoint.

“At the end of the day, I was focused on supporting the patients and seeing that policies and procedures needed to be changed,” she told the Star, contending that Waypoint was communicating that she shouldn’t be listened to at all.

Butterworth is not the first ex-Waypoint staffer to ring alarms about seclusion. Her concerns echo forensic psychiatrist Dr. John Bradford, who briefly worked at Waypoint and warned the Ford government in 2018 about the hospital's "horrific" practices . Ministry of Health bureaucrats spoke briefly with Desroches at Waypoint by phone about Bradford's concerns and decided to take no further action.

Psychiatrist Dr. John Bradford warned the province in 2018 about “horrific conditions" at Waypoint Centre for Mental Health Care.

Butterworth’s two affidavits do, however, offer the most detailed inside account of how Waypoint staff handle the daily decisions to keep patients locked up alone in their rooms. While she hasn’t worked at the hospital in the last five years, families of patients and their lawyers continue to express many of the same concerns.

The courts refused to certify the proposed class-action lawsuit from Toronto firm Rochon Genova, finding that seclusion is an individualized decision and the patients would have to bring individual claims. The firm is exploring other avenues of pursuing the lawsuit.

In a statement noting the dismissal of the case, Waypoint reiterated that it only uses seclusion as an option of last resort.

“We will not comment on testimony or evidence presented during the proceedings.”

What Sarah Butterworth saw at Waypoint

“At Waypoint, seclusion is always at an all-time high,” Butterworth wrote in an August 2022 affidavit.

The hospital has always refused to divulge the number of secluded patients. Butterworth said she was “personally aware” of multiple Waypoint patients being secluded for years without meaningful social contact — at any given time, about half of the patients just in her 20-bed unit were in seclusion.

“Several of my patients had been in seclusion for a decade or longer,” she wrote in 2022.

She ended up leaving Waypoint in part because “the pervasive use of seclusion and restraints significantly interfered” with the ability of many of her patients to benefit from treatment.

“Seclusion and restraints are frequently used even when a patient is not physically aggressive and is not attempting to become physically aggressive,” Butterworth said in her affidavit. “Their use continues far longer than necessary.”

Butterworth said she personally witnessed patients being secluded for refusing to listen to staff, verbally acting out and banging on their door, all of which she said would be contrary to Waypoint’s policies and training. No attempts were made to use less restrictive options, she said.

Patients would also be secluded more often if they refused to take their medication, she said, and some would be kept in seclusion based on their illness and past incidents, rather than current risk.

She said it became obvious that the “excessive and prolonged use” of seclusion and restraints was “significantly” worsening patients’ illnesses and preventing them from benefiting from therapy.

“Waypoint patients often fall into a vicious cycle of being secluded for acting out due to their illness, becoming more ill because of their prolonged detention in seclusion, and then acting out more, resulting in continued, extended seclusion,” she said.

“This is a very difficult cycle to break.”

Butterworth wasn’t able to reveal the full extent of the use of seclusion at Waypoint because patient-confidentiality requirements prevented her from sharing identifying information about any patients.

Among other things, the Star’s investigation has revealed how warnings about Waypoint’s use of seclusion go back as far as the 1980s. Leading experts have described the hospital’s practice as “egregious,” “abusive,” unlike anything seen in other North American hospitals, and akin to torture .

Staff told to keep seclusion out of records, Butterworth says

Butterworth described feeling shocked when she first arrived at Waypoint and saw so many patients in seclusion. She had also been left with the impression during her training that working with the most severely ill patients was going to be scary. She told the Star she was “petrified” until she spent a day on her unit interacting with the patients, developing trust and realizing when and when not to approach.

“Working in those environments, you do have to be cognizant of your surroundings, but I was going onto the unit eight months pregnant and realized it wasn’t as scary as what they had told me,” she said.

“They’re just human beings. Many of them with psychosis, many with behavioural issues, but at the core, they’re human beings, and they don’t want to remain in a room. They want more for themselves.”

Butterworth was not only worried about patients being in seclusion, but about staff inaccurately documenting just how long the patients were being kept locked up. She said she brought her concerns to a number of senior leaders during her employment, including Desroches, himself a registered nurse who began his career at Waypoint in 1992 as a staff nurse; then-chief nursing executive Linda Adams; and then-CEO Carol Lambie. But to no avail.

According to her affidavit, senior leaders took steps “to prevent staff from accurately logging the use and duration of seclusion and restraints” after news broke in 2020 about the proposed class-action lawsuit being filed. She said staff were told to keep the word “seclusion” out of patients’ behaviour management plans.

The hospital did eventually change its policies mandating that seclusion be used less often; the policies also included a requirement that patients be told what they needed to do to get out of seclusion.

“Unfortunately, these changes only occurred on paper,” Butterworth said in her affidavit, as staff continued to breach the policies and there was “no meaningful leadership or oversight” to ensure the polices were being followed.

‘There was only so much I could do to make changes’

Patients who have been found not criminally responsible or unfit to stand trial fall under the jurisdiction of the independent Ontario Review Board (ORB) , which annually reviews their cases to determine whether they should remain detained or released with conditions. The board also has a duty to inquire into the patient’s treatment and living conditions.

The patients under the board’s jurisdiction are known as forensic patients, and represent the bulk of the people kept in long-term seclusion at Waypoint.

Butterworth had been including information showing how long patients had been secluded over the previous year in the reports that the hospital has to provide to the ORB ahead of each patient’s hearing. The information came in the form of graphs showing how many times the patient was being offered seclusion relief and a shower, along with their behaviours.

Jake Gordon has been transferred closer to family just weeks after the Star published footage of his life kept locked in isolation at Waypoint Centre.

The ORB appreciated the graphs, and Butterworth was even instructed by management to train the other behavioural support specialists on including those graphs as well.

But then around 2020, a manager told Butterworth to stop including the graphs because it would put Waypoint “in a bad light,” in that they would show there wasn’t always behaviour that warranted the use of seclusion.

She said in her affidavit that anything she tried to include in a report to the ORB that was “classed as a ‘hot topic’ — one likely to be questioned at the annual ORB hearing” would result in an email from Waypoint management directing that the information be removed.

“On some occasions, this information was removed from my reports after I submitted them and I was then informed that it would be ‘contentious’ in the ORB environment,” she said in her affidavit.

Given that the ORB has such a crucial oversight role, Butterworth told the Star she was dismayed at what she was being asked to do by management.

“Morally and based on my values, it went against everything that I wanted to present as a clinician,” she said. “However, I’m a single person there, and there was only so much I could do to make changes.”

In a second affidavit in 2023 responding to Desroches, Butterworth said she had hoped that all parties “would stick to the important issues with respect”: how seclusion and restraint were being used at Waypoint. That’s all she ever wanted to focus on, she said.

“I am supporting this case because these patients do not have a voice inside Waypoint that will come forward to support them,” she said in the second affidavit.

To the Star, Butterworth said she hopes the renewed focus on the institution finally leads to meaningful and long-lasting change.

“I hope that the organization is going to look at how often seclusion is getting utilized and hire staff to actually decrease it, instead of just having staff that are utilized as security guards,” she said.

“I’m hopeful that Waypoint will focus on rehabilitation going forward.”

content_blocks.text: The hospital has always refused to divulge the number of secluded patients. stories.title: Quebec doctors increasingly burnt out, depressed one year after controversial law, survey finds
stories.summary: Nearly 20% of participating physicians reported having suicidal thoughts, Canadian Medical Association says
stories.author: Tu Thanh Ha
stories.content:
A new survey by the Canadian Medical Association says that nearly 20 per cent of participating Quebec doctors reported having suicidal thoughts and 80 per cent felt burnt out.

Nearly half of the respondents also reported signs of depression.

The rates for burnout and suicidal ideation were higher than those in a similar survey conducted in 2021, the second year of the COVID-19 pandemic.

The new survey released on Friday was collected following months of turmoil in Quebec, triggered by a provincial law commonly known as Bill 2, which originally proposed tying doctors’ remuneration to performance targets.

The province eventually removed the contentious parts of the law that tied performance to remuneration. However, 68 per cent of those surveyed said that Bill 2’s impact remains unresolved.

“The sheer increase in burnout as well as other variables, including depressive and anxiety symptoms and distress – it’s surprising and problematic. Especially since these numbers are even worse than during the height of the pandemic,” CMA president Bolu Ogunyemi said.

Dr. Ogunyemi also noted that one in 10 of those surveyed said they would likely leave Quebec to practice elsewhere.

The Quebec survey follows the latest iteration of the National Physician Health Survey commissioned every four years by the CMA, a national organization that represents doctors and medical learners.

Because of the controversy created by Bill 2, the association decided to canvass Quebec members a year after the 2025 national survey .

The online survey was conducted for the CMA by Ipsos, the same firm that produced last year’s national survey. A link was provided to Quebec members and 1,151 responded between Aug. 25 and Sept. 21. The survey has a margin of error of 2.9 percentage points, 19 times out of 20.

Opinion: Quebec cracks down on doctors – but will imposing a contract improve patient care?

Another CMA spokesperson, Jean-Joseph Condé, a family doctor in Val-d’Or, Que., said that even before Bill 2, Quebec physicians were already burdened by heavy workloads and special requirements that aren’t widely mandated elsewhere in Canada.

In their first years of practice, Quebec family doctors have to work compulsory shifts in short-staffed hospitals and other public facilities, and territorial staffing plans determine how many general practitioners work in a region.

“Compared to other provinces, Quebec is the province where the practice of medicine is the most regimented by laws,” Dr. Condé said.

In October 2025, the government of then Quebec premier François Legault invoked closure to pass Bill 2 , which linked doctors’ remuneration more closely to the number of patients they enroll and to other performance targets, while also threatening heavy fines for those who opposed the proposed changes.

“Bill 2 was putting the blame on physicians for the shortcomings of the system and the lack of access to care,” Dr. Condé said.

In the backlash to the bill, hundreds of Quebec physicians started applying to be able to work in Ontario.

Even after the government backtracked, Dr. Condé said Quebec physicians remain distraught because they are overworked, burdened with paperwork and left with a shortage of resources, such as family team nurses, and surgical nurses and respiratory therapists to support operating rooms.

The 80-per-cent burnout rate in the latest survey is a marked jump from previous data – up from 48 per cent in 2025 and 60 per cent in 2021.

While the CMA reported a 37-per-cent rate of depression among Quebec doctors in 2025, this year, 48 per cent of respondents screened positive for depression.

The rate of suicidal ideation had doubled to 18 from 9 per cent last year.

On Sept. 18, as the survey was being conducted, an open letter signed by more than 1,500 physicians asked for a public inquiry after five suicides by Quebec doctors in five months.

Coroner Géhane Kamel has since been assigned to investigate the five deaths.

The new Parti Québécois government of Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon has not made specific promises about physicians’ pay or working conditions, but wants to increase the number of doctors by enlarging medical school cohorts.
