stories.title: Carney travels to Yellowknife for announcement on 'major' initiative
stories.summary: Whitehorse - Prime Minister Mark Carney is to continue his swing through the North with a stop in Yellowknife this afternoon for an announcement on a "major new initiative."
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Yellowknife - The federal government on Friday prioritized construction of a critical road in the Northwest Territories by designating the Mackenzie Valley Highway as a project of national interest.

The proposed 800-kilometre highway would offer year-round access to isolated communities in the North and is expected to open new opportunities for resource extraction and security in the Arctic.

Once complete, it would run the length of the Mackenzie River, north of Wrigley, before connecting with the Dempster Highway, south of Inuvik.

Ottawa said this would reduce the road distance between Yellowknife and Inuvik by 1,300 kilometres, cutting a 38-hour drive to 23 hours, and making deliveries of food, medicine and construction materials in the region more reliable.

The project is 70 years in the making, Prime Minister Mark Carney told a news conference in Yellowknife.

“Generations of northerners have waited for this moment. I have myself,” said Carney, who was born in the territory town of Fort Smith.

“These roads will open the way to better lives, more opportunities and a stronger more sovereign Canada.

“It is beyond time, beyond time to connect the North.”

Previous federal and territorial governments have supported construction of the highway. Various iterations of the proposed road have been studied since 1958.

Ottawa said more than 10,000 people, or roughly 22 per cent of the territory’s population across 12 communities, would benefit from improved transportation access. That includes the 1,900 in the Sahtu region, who would gain access to an all-season road for the first time.

The major projects office estimates about 3,000 workers would be employed at the peak of construction.

The federal government put $3.1 billion aside in Budget 2026 for the highway. Ottawa said in background documents on Friday that the capital cost for construction is expected to be $4.2 billion.

Government officials who briefed reporters ahead of the announcement said estimates for the maintenance share of the highway haven’t been finalized.

The territorial government is the primary proponent of the Mackenzie Valley Highway project.

N.W.T. Premier R.J. Simpson, standing with Carney at the announcement, said the highway is key to unlocking mineral and petroleum resources and providing economic opportunities.

He said everyone in territory who is able and willing to work on the project will get the opportunity.

“Construction of the Mackenzie Valley Highway alone will take more workers than we have in the territory, so we know we’ll need support from our southern neighbours,” Simpson said.

Designating a project in the national interest under the Building Canada Act means Ottawa plans to streamline federal regulatory approvals and other reviews needed to get a development moving.

The Mackenzie Valley Highway is the first project in the North named to the major projects list. Ottawa listed the Pacific Link oil pipeline and a planned expansion to the Port of Vancouver as projects of national interest in October.

The federal government said in its budget tabled earlier this month that it would fully cover the costs of construction and some maintenance expenses for the Mackenzie Valley Highway. Ottawa also pledged $405 million toward the project through the Arctic Infrastructure Fund in September.

While the major projects office helps co-ordinate regulatory processes, the federal government is also planning to launch a new Crown corporation in the coming months to manage development and construction of complex major projects.

The government said the Mackenzie Valley Highway would be the initial focus of the new major projects management entity.

The highway remains subject to treaty-based environmental assessment and regulatory processes.

If approved, construction of the Mackenzie Valley Highway could begin in late 2027.

On Wednesday, the federal and territorial governments signed a leadership governance understanding for the project with Sahtu Secretariat Inc., Gwich’in Tribal Council and Pehdzeh Ki First Nation.

A government news release said the agreement establishes a “collaborative framework for the highway’s governance, planning and long-term direction” with its Indigenous partners in the region.

The road would connect to several communities, including Fort Good Hope on the east bank of the Mackenzie River. It’s accessible by the river in the summer and by air year-round.

“I’m just really happy today that this has finally been announced. We’ve got some things to look forward to,” Chief Shawn Grandjambe said after the announcement.

He said the highway would provide financial relief to residents who face high costs of shipping in food and other goods. They would have the option of driving south for shopping.

Grandjambe and other northern leaders have said they’re concerned about increased access to drugs and alcohol.

“It’s there already. Right now, we just got to try and figure a way of how we can control the flow of it coming in,” said Grandjambe.

Bob Zimmer, federal Conservative critic for Arctic affairs and the Canadian Northern Economic Development Agency, said northern communities don’t need more announcements.

“They need shovels in the ground,” he said in a statement. “Northerners have heard plenty of promises but they are still waiting for a road.”

Mackenzie Valley Highway is part of what Ottawa has dubbed the “Northern Resilience Projects.”

The Grays Bay project would see a 230-kilometre all-season road run from the Northwest Territories-Nunavut boundary and stop at the Arctic coast, where there would be a port.

The Arctic Economic and Security Corridor is a proposed 400-kilometre, all-season road that would stretch north of Yellowknife and connect to Grays Bay road.

And the Taltson Hydro Expansion Project would double the hydro capacity in the Northwest Territories.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 27, 2026.

— With files from Craig Lord in Ottawa

Note to readers:This is a corrected story. A previous version said the Mackenzie Valley Highway would cut the 28-hour drive from Yellowknife to Inuvik down to 15 hours. It also said the Whitehorse Power Centres project was deemed in the national interest.

paragraphs: Yellowknife — The federal government on Friday prioritized construction of a critical road in the Northwest Territories by designating the Mackenzie Valley Highway as a project of national interest.
The proposed 800-kilometre highway would offer year-round access to isolated communities in the North and is expected to open new opportunities for resource extraction and security in the Arctic.
Once complete, it would run the length of the Mackenzie River, north of Wrigley, before connecting with the Dempster Highway, south of Inuvik.

Ottawa said this would reduce the road distance between Yellowknife and Inuvik by 1,300 kilometres, cutting a 38-hour drive to 23 hours, and making deliveries of food, medicine and construction materials in the region more reliable.
The project is 70 years in the making, Prime Minister Mark Carney told a news conference in Yellowknife.
“Generations of northerners have waited for this moment. I have myself,” said Carney, who was born in the territory town of Fort Smith.
“These roads will open the way to better lives, more opportunities and a stronger more sovereign Canada.
“It is beyond time, beyond time to connect the North.”
Previous federal and territorial governments have supported construction of the highway. Various iterations of the proposed road have been studied since 1958.

Ottawa said more than 10,000 people, or roughly 22 per cent of the territory’s population across 12 communities, would benefit from improved transportation access. That includes the 1,900 in the Sahtu region, who would gain access to an all-season road for the first time.
The major projects office estimates about 3,000 workers would be employed at the peak of construction.
The federal government put $3.1 billion aside in Budget 2026 for the highway. Ottawa said in background documents on Friday that the capital cost for construction is expected to be $4.2 billion.
Government officials who briefed reporters ahead of the announcement said estimates for the maintenance share of the highway haven’t been finalized.
The territorial government is the primary proponent of the Mackenzie Valley Highway project.
N.W.T. Premier R.J. Simpson, standing with Carney at the announcement, said the highway is key to unlocking mineral and petroleum resources and providing economic opportunities.
He said everyone in territory who is able and willing to work on the project will get the opportunity.
“Construction of the Mackenzie Valley Highway alone will take more workers than we have in the territory, so we know we’ll need support from our southern neighbours,” Simpson said.
Designating a project in the national interest under the Building Canada Act means Ottawa plans to streamline federal regulatory approvals and other reviews needed to get a development moving.

The Mackenzie Valley Highway is the first project in the North named to the major projects list. Ottawa listed the Pacific Link oil pipeline and a planned expansion to the Port of Vancouver as projects of national interest in October.

The federal government said in its budget tabled earlier this month that it would fully cover the costs of construction and some maintenance expenses for the Mackenzie Valley Highway. Ottawa also pledged $405 million toward the project through the Arctic Infrastructure Fund in September.

While the major projects office helps co-ordinate regulatory processes, the federal government is also planning to launch a new Crown corporation in the coming months to manage development and construction of complex major projects.
The government said the Mackenzie Valley Highway would be the initial focus of the new major projects management entity.
The highway remains subject to treaty-based environmental assessment and regulatory processes.
If approved, construction of the Mackenzie Valley Highway could begin in late 2027.
On Wednesday, the federal and territorial governments signed a leadership governance understanding for the project with Sahtu Secretariat Inc., Gwich’in Tribal Council and Pehdzeh Ki First Nation.
A government news release said the agreement establishes a “collaborative framework for the highway’s governance, planning and long-term direction” with its Indigenous partners in the region.
The road would connect to several communities, including Fort Good Hope on the east bank of the Mackenzie River. It’s accessible by the river in the summer and by air year-round.
“I’m just really happy today that this has finally been announced. We’ve got some things to look forward to,” Chief Shawn Grandjambe said after the announcement.
He said the highway would provide financial relief to residents who face high costs of shipping in food and other goods. They would have the option of driving south for shopping.
Grandjambe and other northern leaders have said they’re concerned about increased access to drugs and alcohol.
“It’s there already. Right now, we just got to try and figure a way of how we can control the flow of it coming in,” said Grandjambe.
Bob Zimmer, federal Conservative critic for Arctic affairs and the Canadian Northern Economic Development Agency, said northern communities don’t need more announcements.
“They need shovels in the ground,” he said in a statement. “Northerners have heard plenty of promises but they are still waiting for a road.”

The Grays Bay project would see a 230-kilometre all-season road run from the Northwest Territories-Nunavut boundary and stop at the Arctic coast, where there would be a port.
The Arctic Economic and Security Corridor is a proposed 400-kilometre, all-season road that would stretch north of Yellowknife and connect to Grays Bay road.
And the Taltson Hydro Expansion Project would double the hydro capacity in the Northwest Territories.

stories.title: Supreme Court ruling on Quebec's secularism law expected Friday morning
stories.summary: Montreal - Premiers across Canada are expected to be keeping a close eye on the Supreme Court this morning as it releases a ruling on the constitutionality of Quebec's secularism law.
stories.author: Erika Morris The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - Nevien Waly worries she’ll never get to teach in Quebec schools after the Supreme Court of Canada upheld the province’s law banning public servants in positions of authority from wearing religious symbols while on the job.

In a landmark 520-page decision, the top court upheld most of the Quebec secularism law known as Bill 21, except for a section that banned members of the legislature from wearing religious symbols.

The law applies to public school teachers, police officers, government lawyers and other officials.

It also applies to Waly, who wears a hijab.

Speaking to The Canadian Press moments after the court released its ruling, Waly explained how she left her career as an accountant and started studying education in 2019, right before Bill 21 was adopted. Now that the court decision is out, the 45-year-old said she feels sad and disappointed.

She said the law has even prevented her from volunteering at the schools of her four children.

“When there was no final decision, there was always a glimpse of hope that things could change around, and now it’s kind of set in stone, so it’s just kind of like a mourning period,” she said in an interview.

The Supreme Court’s historic decision provides more clarity on how governments can use a section of the Constitution that allows legislatures to override Charter rights. The justices agreed that governments can use the so-called notwithstanding clause of the Constitution pre-emptively as Quebec did when it introduced Bill 21.

They also said the Constitution allows a legislature to override multiple Charter rights at the same time by pre-emptively using the notwithstanding clause.

“Similarly, a legislative body is not required to show a link or relationship between the law in question and the rights or freedoms it intends to override,” wrote Chief Justice Wagner, and Justices Malcolm Rowe and Suzanne Côté in the ruling. “More fundamentally, it is not for the courts to substantively review the legitimacy of the legislative policy pursued by the legislative body or the appropriateness of invoking the notwithstanding clause.”

It’s a victory for the Quebec government, with Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon having promised to expand secularism laws to schoolchildren.

At a news conference in Quebec City on Friday afternoon, he said it is a “good day for secularism in Quebec” but that legislators will need to read the fine print of the ruling to understand its implications.

St-Pierre Plamondon has also denounced the federal government’s involvement in the legal challenge. Ottawa participated as an intervener and asked the court to set limits around how provincial governments can override the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

Prime Minister Mark Carney reacted to the ruling in a radio interview, saying his government respects the independence of the court and the provisions in the Constitution.

He added it’s important for all legislators to respect the rights and liberties of all Canadians, including minority rights.

While the court unanimously determined that the override clause was used correctly, justices were divided over whether to declare that Bill 21 violated Charter rights, without overturning it.

While the majority did not address whether the law violated rights, three of the seven justices overseeing the Bill 21 case wrote in the ruling that the Quebec secularism law is incompatible with freedom of religion, freedom of expression and the right to equality.

The majority ruled it can issue a non-binding declaratory judgment on the inconsistencies of such laws with Charter rights, but the majority also declined to do so in the case of Bill 21.

Justices Michelle O’Bonsawin and Andromache Karakatsanis wrote that “there can be no serious question that Bill 21 violates freedom of religion.”

“It treats visible religious minorities as less worthy of full participation in Quebec society, influences their life choices and mobility, and creates professional barriers for them by preventing qualified individuals from being hired, promoted or transferred within public sector workplaces,” they wrote.

They also wrote that Bill 21 is not so incompatible with freedom of religion or human dignity as to be invalid because the notwithstanding clause must be renewed every five years.

Three justices — O’Bonsawin, Karakatsanis and Sheilah L. Martin — also argued that court had the power to strike down Bill 21, despite the use of the notwithstanding clause, since the law violates gender equality, which falls under a section of the Charter that governments are not allowed to override.

The three justices noted in their dissenting opinion that Bill 21 has a disproportionate effect on Muslim women.

“The attorney general of Quebec chose not to address whether any breaches related to Bill 21 could be justified in a free and democratic society,” they wrote.

However, Wagner, Rowe, Côté and Nicholas Kasirer determined that the section protecting gender equality in the Canadian Charter could not be used to strike down Bill 21.

St-Pierre Plamondon said that the court’s decision to allow declaratory statements in rulings is “a setback” for provincial autonomy as it “weakens” the notwithstanding clause. Justices will thereby be allowed to give their opinion on cases involving the override clause in non-binding judgments, he said.

The Supreme Court heard the case over four days last March in what was one of the longest hearings in its history. Sixty-one parties participated in the case, including 51 interveners, which the court says is a record number.

The case was brought forward by the English Montreal School Board, which argued the law also infringed on minority language rights.

“This result is very disappointing for many people today,” said Joe Ortona, chair of the school board, speaking to journalists after the ruling.

But, he added, it was encouraging to see a split vote on whether the law could have been abolished under the guarantee to gender equality.

He promised to continue to lobby the government to amend or abolish the law.

The CEO of the National Council of Canadian Muslims said the decision provides an “unrestricted licence” for governments in Canada to pass legislation that strip away the fundamental freedoms and legal rights of every Canadian.

“Your freedom of expression. Your freedom of religion. Your right to equality. Your right to a fair trial,” Stephen Brown said Friday on Parliament Hill.

He said if rights can be violated when governments find it politically convenient to do so, those rights do not exist.

“This fight is not over. Whether it takes a year or a generation, we will put these discriminatory laws on the trash heap of history.”

Since Bill 21 passed in 2019, Quebec, Ontario, Saskatchewan and Alberta have all invoked the notwithstanding clause pre-emptively to shield some of their own laws from legal challenges.

These include laws restricting the rights of transgender people in Alberta and Saskatchewan, back-to-work orders in Alberta and Ontario, and Quebec’s language-law reform.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said that the ruling confirms the notwithstanding clause is a legitimate and essential part of the Constitution.

“Alberta was proud to intervene in this case to defend that principle,” Smith said in a statement posted on social media. “The notwithstanding clause was included in the Charter so that elected legislatures, accountable to the people they serve, can have the final say on important questions. That’s true for Quebec and it’s true for every province, including Alberta.”

— with files from Anja Karadeglija and Alessia Passafiume in Ottawa

The justices agreed that governments can use the so-called notwithstanding clause of the Constitution pre-emptively as Quebec did when it introduced Bill 21.

content_blocks.text: St-Pierre Plamondon has also denounced the federal government’s involvement in the legal challenge. Ottawa participated as an intervener and asked the court to set limits around how provincial governments can override the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

content_blocks.text: While the majority did not address whether the law violated rights, three of the seven justices overseeing the Bill 21 case wrote in the ruling that the Quebec secularism law is incompatible with freedom of religion, freedom of expression and the right to equality.

stories.title: A timeline of key events in the case of Kenneth Law, who admitted to aiding suicides
stories.summary: A sentencing hearing is expected to resume Friday for Kenneth Law, an Ontario man who sold lethal substances online to people who later used them to take their own lives.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A sentencing hearing concluded Friday for Kenneth Law, an Ontario man who sold lethal substances online to people who later used them to take their own lives.

Law, a former chef, has pleaded guilty to 14 counts of aiding suicide in the province. Court heard earlier this year that he ran several websites that were used to sell sodium nitrite and other items that can be used for self-harm, shipping them to people in more than 40 countries.

Here is a timeline of key events in the case:

Oct. 14, 2022: A coroner’s report in the United Kingdom looking into the April death by suicide of a woman in Surrey lists a postal box in Mississauga, Ont., and the name of one of the websites police linked to Law.

March 31, 2023: Peel Regional Police investigate the circumstances of a local sudden death where the person is believed to have consumed a chemical substance. It’s the first of two deaths police would later link to Law and the allegations against him.

April 25, 2023: The Times of London publishes an investigation into Law, reporting on his alleged global online operation.

May 2, 2023: Peel Regional Police announce they have arrested Law and charged him with two counts of counselling and aiding suicide.

May 10, 2023: Several other police forces in Canada, including those in Toronto and Durham Region, say they are reviewing sudden deaths in light of the allegations against Law.

June 16, 2023: Peel Regional Police announce 11 Ontario police forces have formed a major joint operation investigating Law.

Aug. 25, 2023: Britain’s National Crime Agency says it has identified 232 people in the U.K. who bought products from Canada-based websites allegedly linked to Law in the two years before April, 88 of whom had died.

Aug. 29, 2023: Police announce an additional 12 new charges against Law of aiding and counselling suicides across Ontario. They allege Law started to operate the websites he used to market sodium nitrite and other items that can be used for self-harm in late 2020.

Sept. 12, 2023: Montreal police announce they are also investigating allegations against Law, suspecting he May have sent kits containing sodium nitrite to addresses in Montreal.

Dec. 12, 2023: Police announce 14 counts of second-degree murder charges against Law, in addition to his 14 existing charges of aiding suicide, for a total of 28 charges. Law’s lawyer, Matthew Gourlay, says his client would be pleading not guilty to all charges.

Jan. 26, 2024: Law’s lawyer confirms that all 14 counts of second-degree murder had been upgraded to first-degree murder, and that the case would proceed by direct indictment, meaning there would be no preliminary inquiry. Gourlay says Law would plead not guilty to all charges.

July 23, 2024: A New Zealand coroner says four people who died by suicide in that country had ordered items online from a business associated with Law, including two university students, a 21-year-old woman and a 40-year old man. The coroner noted that Law’s activities were outside the jurisdiction of the New Zealand courts.

October 2024: Lawyers for Law file a motion for leave to intervene after prosecutors asked the Supreme Court of Canada to urgently review a recent Ontario ruling in a separate case that could undermine the murder charges against him. That ruling suggested a person May only be liable for murder if they provided a person who died by suicide with the lethal substance and “overbore the victim’s free will in choosing suicide.”

October 2025: Law’s trial is pushed back for a second time, to April 2026, as the Crown and defence await the Supreme Court decision.

Dec. 5, 2025: The Supreme Court of Canada declines to “conclusively resolve” the legal issue regarding whether murder charges can be laid against people who aid in suicides.

April 18, 2026: Gourlay says a plea deal has been reached with Crown prosecutors, who will drop all 14 murder charges against Law. Gourlay says Law would plead guilty to 14 counts of aiding suicide.

May 28, 2026: The families of people who died in the United Kingdom after allegedly receiving packages from Law say the country’s National Crime Agency and Crown Prosecution Service have informed them that Law will not be facing charges there because extradition could be a lengthy process and any sentence imposed in Canada would be similar.

May 29, 2026: Law enters his guilty pleas in a Newmarket, Ont., court as an agreed statement of facts outlines the last moments of 14 Ontarians whose deaths were linked to him. The court also hears details about 79 people in the U.K. who died because of products purchased from Law, as the National Crime Agency says in a press release that will be included as part of Law’s sentencing in Canada.

Sept. 23, 2026: Friends and relatives of those who died after consuming products purchased from Law tell the court about the last impact of his crimes as his sentencing hearing begins.

Nov. 27, 2026: Law apologizes to victims’ families during sentencing hearing as prosecutors ask the court to impose a 25-year sentence and the defence proposes 12 years.

Feb. 26, 2027: Law is expected to be sentenced.

If you or someone you know is thinking about suicide, support is available 24/7 by calling or texting 988, Canada’s national suicide prevention helpline.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 27, 2026.

stories.title: Sentencing hearing to continue for Kenneth Law, who admitted to aiding suicide
stories.summary: A sentencing hearing is set to continue today for an Ontario man who sold potentially deadly substances online to people who then used those products to take their own lives.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
An Ontario man who sold potentially deadly products online to people who used them to take their own lives apologized in court to the families of his victims on Friday, denouncing his past actions as “categorically wrong” and vowing to never repeat them in the future.

“The fact that my actions assisted others in ending their lives is something I deeply regret,” Kenneth Law said from the prisoner’s box in a Newmarket, Ont., courtroom.

“To the families of the victims, words can never replace the loss of your loved ones. I convey my deepest condolences. I remain remorseful. I’m sorry.”

Law, who pleaded guilty earlier this year to 14 counts of aiding suicide in the deaths of 14 people in Ontario, said going through the legal process changed him and he is committed to continuing his rehabilitation behind bars.

He made his brief comments after lawyers for the Crown and defence spent the day laying out what they believe would be an appropriate sentence in the case that has captured international attention.

The former chef has been linked to dozens of deaths worldwide, including 79 in the United Kingdom that are being considered as part of the sentencing process.

Scores of grieving family members and friends told the court about the lasting impact of Law’s crimes over two days in September as his sentencing hearing got underway. Some delivered the message in person, while others did so by video or in written statements read by prosecutors.

Law’s reasons for selling his wares over nearly 2 1/2 years were a focal point Friday as the lawyers made their pitch to the court.

Money was his motivation, prosecutors argued in asking for a 25-year sentence.

Law’s lawyers, meanwhile, argued the 61-year-old was not a “mercenary predator” but rather a misguided man committed to his belief in the right to die and whose actions did not warrant a “de facto life sentence.”

Both sides noted the unique nature of the case and the resulting lack of meaningful jurisprudence as they made their arguments.

“No case such as this has come before this court, and hopefully it never will again,” said Crown attorney Katie Doherty. “Part of ensuring that that happens is to denounce and deter the offender’s conduct with a sentence that is fit and proportionate in all the circumstances.”

The scale of Law’s operations should be counted as an aggravating factor, as should the fact that his actions “actually caused death,” she argued.

Ninety-three people died because they used the products purchased from Law, including 12 teenagers, she said.

“These were vulnerable people ... What they needed was help, but what they found was Mr. Law and his products for death,” Doherty said.

Law’s actions run contrary to his claim of an altruistic purpose, the prosecutor argued. The only factor that determined whom he sold to was whether they paid upfront, she said.

“If people could pay, he sold it to them. There’s no discussion or inquiries or anything going on whereby Mr. Law would have any ability to appreciate the circumstances of the individual he was dealing with,” she said.

Law’s guilty plea, which spared grieving families a lengthy trial, and his lack of a prior criminal record count as mitigating factors, she said.

The maximum sentence for aiding suicide is 14 years and Doherty argued Law should face 12 1/2 years for each count, with two to be served back to back and the rest at the same time.

After subtracting credit for the time Law has spent in custody since his arrest in May 2023, he would be left with 19 years and 7 1/2 months to serve.

Defence lawyer Matthew Gourlay argued that while Law sold the victims the tools they used to end their lives, he was not “the cause of the struggles and hardships that caused all of these victims to seek out his products in the first place,” nor did he play a role in their decision to use the products in the way they did.

“In short, Mr. Law did not kill anyone,” he said.

Law’s views on the right to die were shaped by his experience of his late mother’s health struggles after she had strokes that left her bedridden, he told the court.

His actions and sentence should also be considered in the context of the ongoing, unresolved debate in Canadian society over assisted dying, Gourlay argued.

“To be very clear, the context in no way justifies Mr. Law’s choice to act outside of lawful bounds,” he said.

“But in my submission, you do need to look at that social context in order to evaluate what a proportionate sentence for Mr. Law might look like, and you have to do that especially because of the relative dearth of meaningful sentencing jurisprudence in this area.”

Though misguided, Law “genuinely believed he was helping people whom the system had failed,” argued defence lawyer Stephanie DiGiuseppe.

A psychological assessment found he saw himself as supporting others’ autonomy, not as promoting suicide, she said.

The sentence proposed by the Crown would “far exceed” any sentence known to have been imposed for this offence in Canada, DiGiuseppe said. The defence’s proposal would also represent the longest sentence imposed for it, she said.

The defence argued an appropriate sentence under the circumstances would be 12 years — nine for the cases involving sodium nitrite and three for those involving other equipment, to be served one after the other — minus credit for the time Law has already served.

He should also receive enhanced credit for his time in detention due to the particularly harsh conditions he faced, which included lockdowns, triple bunking and “a life-threatening case” of flesh-eating disease he contracted at the Maplehurst Correctional Complex, Gourlay argued.

Law’s plea deal in May came soon after he was set to stand trial on the aiding suicide charges and another 14 counts of first-degree murder related to the same victims. Prosecutors are expected to withdraw the murder charges after Law is sentenced.

An agreed statement of fact presented after his plea said Law ran several websites that were used to sell sodium nitrite and other products that can be used for self-harm. He shipped products to people in more than 40 countries, knowing his customers were likely to use them for suicide, the document said.

Law also went on a forum where people talked about using certain substances to take their own life, at times leaving comments and referring people to his websites, it said.

Law is expected to be sentenced in February.

If you or someone you know is thinking about suicide, support is available 24/7 by calling or texting 988, Canada’s national suicide prevention helpline.

stories.title: Supreme Court to deliver historic ruling on Quebec’s Bill 21
stories.summary: The Supreme Court of Canada will deliver a landmark decision this morning that could shape constitutional debates with provinces for years to come
stories.author: Catherine Lévesque
stories.content:
Ottawa — The Supreme Court of Canada will deliver a landmark decision this morning that could shape constitutional debates with provinces for years to come.

At 9:45 a.m. ET on Friday, Canadians will finally know the extent to which Quebec could override constitutional rights by pre-emptively invoking the notwithstanding clause in adopting its controversial Bill 21.

The Supreme Court justices heard the case over four days in March, making it one of the longest hearings in the court’s history, with a record number of roughly 60 parties and intervenors, including six attorneys general.

Since 2019, Quebec’s Bill 21 prohibits public sector workers in positions of authority, such as judges, police officers, teachers and prison guards, from wearing religious symbols at work and requires them to perform their duties with their faces uncovered.

Monday - Saturday Free

NP Posted keeps you updated on the news of the day and the perspectives that define the National Post, while drawing your focus to some of the unexpected stories we like to tell. Delivered straight to your inbox Monday to Friday, with a weekend edition on Saturdays.

A major part of the controversy around the law was Quebec’s decision to invoke section 33 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, known as the notwithstanding clause.

The clause allows a government to override certain Charter rights for up to five years, at which point the use of the power must be reviewed. It’s been invoked increasingly by Alberta, Quebec and Ontario in recent years to shield their laws from court challenges.

Quebec’s Bill 21 as well as the invocation of section 33 were quickly challenged in court, where it was upheld twice before landing at the Supreme Court.

The highest court of the country is expected to deliver decisions on a multitude of issues surrounding the law, but one of the main conclusions of their ruling could be whether there are limits on the use of the notwithstanding clause by provinces.

Quebec, Ontario and Alberta argued there should be no limits, while the federal government said there should be some given its repeated use by provinces.

To maintain an odd-numbered bench, Justice Mary Moreau — the most junior judge on the court — was also absent.

stories.title: Rabies is on the rise in Ontario. Here’s what experts want you to know to keep you and your pet safe
stories.summary: Over the past few years in Ontario, confirmed cases of rabies have been on the rise. Statistics posted by the ...
stories.author: Curtis Stokman
stories.content:
Over the past few years in Ontario, confirmed cases of rabies have been on the rise. Statistics posted by the province show that 121 cases of rabies were confirmed in 2025, with 91 the year prior and 65 in 2023, and with the risk the disease poses experts are sharing their knowledge to help people understand it and stay safe.

The reasons for this increase are multifaceted. Registered veterinary technician (RVT) and manager of the St. Marys Veterinary Clinic Trish Brennan attributes the rise in rabies cases in part due to lapsing programs by the provincial government during the COVID pandemic.

“I do think some of their programs got put on hold,” said Brennan. “That obviously gives us a lapse in protection, and here we are.”

As an RVT, Brennan believes that the increase in rabies cases represents an “increase for cause of concern” regarding pets such as dogs and cats. She also states that out of over 4,000 clients serviced by the clinic, 80 per cent of them are up to date on the rabies vaccine.

“We are doing a much better job of reaching out to clients to make sure that our animals are up to date,” said Brennan.

Brennan also said that the rabies vaccine is 99 per cent effective in protecting against rabies.

Pets and people are not the only animals that can carry rabies. Statistics on confirmed rabies cases show that most of the animals who were found carrying the disease were bats.

Brian Salt, the head of the Salthaven Wildlife Rehabilitation and Education Centre, says that this is because bats congregate in large groups compared to other, more solitary animals that typically carry rabies such as raccoons, skunks and foxes.

“It [rabies] spreads like wildfire,” Salt said. “If one [bat] had rabies, there’s a good chance a whole bunch are gonna get it.”

At the same time, Salt said that even with rabies cases increasing, coming across a rabid animal is uncommon. Out of between 30 and 50 bats that Salthaven receives each year, he said only two per cent of them typically test positive for rabies, and that all of the bats that come into the centre are vaccinated.

A big brown bat at Salthaven. Bats are responsible for most confirmed cases in Ontario, but rabies among them is still uncommon. Photo by: Salthaven Wildlife Rehabilitation and Education Centre

Salt also emphasized that he believes bats are a good animal to have around, especially for controlling insect populations.

“They save farmers literally billions of dollars every year in North America because they eat these insects that destroy crops,” said Salt.

Like Brennan, Salt also mentioned programs that the Ontario Ministry of Natural Resources has done and is doing to attempt to control rabies. He specifically mentioned one program that involves dropping bait containing the rabies vaccine out of aircraft into areas where rabies was a concern.

“It worked,” said Salt, citing a rabies outbreak in 2015 where 449 confirmed cases were found on the Niagara Peninsula. “In five years they had pretty much controlled it down to zero.”

Both Brennan and Salt advise that if people find an animal they believe May have rabies, it should be reported to the Ontario Ministry of Natural Resources and the Canadian Food Inspection Agency so the animal can be captured and tested.

Ultimately, both say that the best way to keep pets and people safe from rabies is to keep pets indoors and make sure they are vaccinated.

“It also helps to protect you,” said Brennan.

stories.title: Kelowna hospital among longest waits for CT scans, new data reveals
stories.summary: One in 10 people waited longer than 607 days for a routine CT scan.
stories.author: Klaudia Van Emmerik
stories.content:
A Kelowna woman waiting for a CT scan earlier this year says she was surprised when her doctor suggested travelling outside of the Okanagan to get medical imaging.

“My doctor basically looked at me and said, “The wait times here in Kelowna are so long. Would you be willing to go to Salmon Arm to get it done, and I was like, I guess so. Even though it was a long drive,” said Suzanne Summers-Gill.

Not wanting to wait to determine whether she had a serious health issue, Summers-Gill made the more than 200-kilometre round trip and got her CT scan within a couple of weeks.

While she was pleased to have the option, she expressed concern about having to travel that far.

“It’s inconvenient for sure. I mean, it’s my gas, my expense, right?,” she said. “So I don’t know. I think that the system definitely needs some work for sure, and we shouldn’t have to do things like that.”

Her experience comes as new data obtained by Health Data BC through Freedom of Information requests reveals lengthy waits for medical imaging at Kelowna General Hospital (KGH).

The analysis, based on scans in 2025, shows KGH had the longest median waits in B.C. for both routine and urgent CT scans.

For routine scans, the median wait was 210 days, more than three times the provincial target of 60 days.

One in 10 people waited longer than 607 days for a routine CT scan.

For urgent CT scans, the median wait was 76 days, compared with the seven-day target.

One in 10 patients waited longer than 245 days.

Median wait times represent the mid-point, meaning half of patients waited longer than those figures.

While MRI waits at KGH were not as lengthy as CT waits, the data shows they also exceeded recommended targets.

The median wait for a routine MRI was 160 days compared with a provincial target of 60 days.

One in 10 patients waited more than 322 days for a routine MRI.

For urgent MRI scans, the median wait was 27 days, nearly four times the recommended seven-day benchmark.

One in 10 patients waited longer than 78 days for an urgent MRI.

“I just wonder why, like why is there such a long wait,” said Summers-Gill.

Interior Health did not provide any answers Thursday.

B.C.’s new Health minister says the ministry plans a comprehensive review of the system including access to medical imaging.

“We don’t have a solution today because we need to listen to our workers and what that looks like,” said health minister Ryan Peterson. “You need better throughput through the system and we do need to invest in imaging, whether it’s MRI, CT scans.”

Peterson said as soon as there is a plan, it will be communicated to the public at large.

stories.title: A $13,000 dinner tab and a secret CEO salary: Inside the allegations roiling Ontario’s dental association
stories.summary: A $13,000 Ritz-Carlton tab, secret CEO salary, and board firings spark human rights complaints and revolt at the Ontario Dental Association.
stories.author: Shree Paradkar
stories.content:
It’s been said that in all of those 159 years, the association had never fired a board director — until two years ago. Since then, it has happened twice.

The tumult has cracked open a window into an organization riven with infighting and facing allegations of unaccountable and lavish spending, discrimination, and intolerance of dissent from within its ranks.

One of the fired directors, Laurie Houston, as well as two other senior ODA members, have filed complaints to the Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario (HRTO) and called for external oversight of the ODA. Houston also wants an audit of board expenses.

The once-uncontroversial group now has an anonymous collective of members-turned-online agitators dogging it with questions about how it spends the millions it collects in membership dues every year.

In its responses to the HRTO complaints, and in emails to the Star, the ODA denied the allegations. “With approximately 12,000 members, disagreements and differences of opinion are inevitable,” the association’s president Janet Leith told the Star. The concerns “do not define the work of the ODA.”

What is the ODA?

The association is a non-profit created to promote ethical and clinical standards for practitioners, offer continuing education programs and raise public awareness of oral hygiene. It does this through advocacy, including government lobbying.

But more than 10 members who spoke to the Star say the discord has been a major distraction from the ODA’s focus on better serving patients. And they worry about more distractions to come.

The ODA board recently ratified the association’s next president: A dentist with a history of complaints and cautions from the professional regulator.

Why Ritz dinner put out this senior ODA member

Board member Laurie Houston’s concerns about the ODA’s finances mounted when she attended an event at the Ritz-Carlton that she says flowed with unlimited booze.

It was 2024, and the board’s expenditures had already climbed $200,000 over budget for that year, according to her complaint to the HRTO. She asked the ODA for a more detailed accounting of how members’ dues were being spent.

Houston was promised cost breakdowns but never got them, she alleged in her HRTO complaint. Then, a fellow board member allegedly told her she was “attacking” the governing body. Houston declined to comment to the Star, saying she feared legal repercussions from the ODA.

Months later, dentists would learn that the dinner attended by about 30 people cost $13,000, according to a former board member who was at the meeting. The ODA’s Leith told the Star the dinner was a “year-end appreciation event” in recognition of volunteers (directors), staff and others and that the board has since “reduced the cost of these events.”

The board, composed of 15 volunteer dentists, has within it three committees focused respectively on finance, human resources and governance. Each is staffed with five board members. The CEO, who is hired by the board, advises it and runs the organization.

Questions swirl around CEO pay and transparency

It’s not just the Ritz dinner tab that came under scrutiny at the ODA, which takes in about $25 million a year, mostly from member fees.

According to another of the three complaints to the HRTO, the ODA has not been transparent about the salary of CEO Frank Bevilacqua.

In June 2025 Engage ODA, the anonymous group of members, alleged on its website that Bevilacqua makes $426,000.

“The Prime Minister of Canada’s salary is $406,200, and Premier Doug Ford makes $208,974. How could one justify his pay raise?” the post said.

After the figure surfaced, board member Nafisa Ahmad alleged she requested to see a copy of Bevilacqua’s employment contract but was denied access.

The document was available to chairs of the human resources committee but otherwise confidential, the ODA explained in records before the HRTO.

Bevilacqua cannot comment on his compensation, the ODA told the Star.

The ODA leadership launched an investigation to find the source of this leak, and an internal email shows past president of Durham Dental Society Austin Saldanha was a suspect. The board president at the time said Saldanha allegedly communicated to other members that he was in possession of the information and intended to go public with it.

When contacted by the Star about the letter, Saldanha said he did plan to release the figure, but didn’t since Engage ODA posted it. “I just posted the link to the article.” The ODA told the Star it has an obligation to investigate when confidential information is shared without authorization.

The November 2025 email notifying Saldanha of the probe into the leak did not dispute the salary amount.

Anil Kishen’s resignation as dean is voluntary, “reflects his acceptance of the university’s sanction,” school’s VP said.

The association told the Star the amount was incorrect and that the Engage ODA website is often inaccurate, misleading or lacking context, and reflects the views of a minority of members.

But it would not say if Bevilacqua, who has been in the corner office since 2016, gets more or less than $426,000.

Waji Khan, a dental surgeon and ODA member for 29 years, said financial transparency is reasonable to expect. “Isn’t transparency something we ask all levels of government and society?”

ODA president Leith told the Star that the association’s balance sheets are audited by a third-party accounting firm, and it is accountable to its members for how its funds are managed.

But association member Fares Sbaiti doesn’t agree and said the lack of transparency makes him question the leadership’s motives. “Got nothing to hide? Open the books.”

Why was board director Laurie Houston fired?

Houston was fired in December 2024, the first dismissal of a director in the organization’s history, she told the HRTO. She alleges it was punishment for fulfilling her fiduciary duty to seek transparency from the board.

“There seems to be a general culture of fear in this organization, making it difficult for individuals to speak truth to power,” Houston told the HRTO in her complaint, adding that there was “no concrete evidence” to warrant her removal and that the ODA failed to consider lesser punishments such as a reprimand. She also said she was banned for life from being a volunteer for the ODA. The ODA denies this.

The association told the Star it did not fire Houston for asking questions. It told the tribunal her ouster was a governance decision and that her “harsh, overly critical and negative dealings with others” factored into it.

According to a confidential memo by the then-ODA board president, Houston violated board confidentiality when she consulted with past directors about changing its charter. She had also allegedly undermined a board rule when she told university students that the ODA would not be funding lunch-and-learn sessions for them. Houston was voted out by a council of 100 members.

The firing shocked some members — and triggered more complaints.

One of those was from pediatric dentist Deborah Lin, who had heard the association paid $600,000 in legal and other fees to sack Houston after she had questioned the association’s spending.

After Lin raised this concern with the ODA, the association removed her from a committee that worked with the province to improve the terms of provincial dental programs such as Healthy Smiles Ontario, Lin alleged in her HRTO complaint.

The ODA denied spending anywhere near that much on the Houston ouster, though it did not provide details to the Star.

Lin was removed from the committee in the middle of a negotiation with the province and replaced by a male dentist with significantly less experience, she alleged to the HRTO — an allegation that the ODA denied. She asked the tribunal to reinstate her.

All three HRTO complainants allege sexism at the ODA.

In her claim, Houston recounted when several female board members and one male board member excused themselves from a 2023 team-building axe-throwing exercise, and another board member allegedly casually commented that his male colleague “must have a vagina.”

In the third complaint to the HRTO, Nafisa Ahmad, the ODA’s first visibly Muslim woman elected as an ODA director, accused the ODA of having “a toxic, gender-biased operational culture designed to suppress dissent and isolate female leadership.”

The association told the Star it takes allegations of misconduct seriously. “Several of the matters referred to in your questions … either were or are currently being addressed through established processes.” It said it was “regrettable” that the complainants refused attempts to discuss and resolve concerns.

Mediation in Lin’s case failed, and mediation in Ahmad’s case has not yet been scheduled. Mediation in the Houston case is set to begin next month. All three complainants are also seeking monetary compensation for what they alleged they suffered.

Lin and Ahmad declined to comment for this story.

Why was Jonathan Mayer removed?

In 2026, the internal turmoil seemed to spill out of the confines of the ODA’s Yorkville office. Unlike Houston’s case, the ouster of the second director was not what the board wanted.

In February, the board began receiving numerous complaints about vice-president Jonathan Mayer’s social media posts on the Israel-Palestine crisis and other issues. An online petition demanded his removal, citing reputational damage to the ODA. The organization appointed a third-party task force to investigate the issue in March.

The investigators concluded that some of Mayer’s posts could be perceived as “divisive,” “inflammatory” and “stigmatizing towards identifiable communities.”

Mayer declined to comment for this story. He told the task force that his posts were not hate speech and were meant to reflect his personal views, not those of the ODA.

The task force did not recommend removal, noting that would be a “truly extraordinary” step to be reserved for dealing with a director who had committed the “worst offence.” It instead recommended reconciliation, including Mayer issuing an apology.

The ODA released the investigators’ report online and in the same note, announced the board had ratified Mayer as president-elect, with his one-year term scheduled to start next year. That decision sparked a flurry of questions from members to the board: Why had it ratified Mayer before the remedial steps had been taken? Why wasn’t Houston also afforded an independent investigation?

In Mayer’s case, “the board did not have internal expertise to evaluate the matter appropriately” and sought independent input, Leith told the Star.

The ODA published an apology from Mayer, in which he acknowledged his posts were offensive, but some members felt it was performative, coming after being compelled by the task force. A council of ODA members requested a special meeting in June to move a motion to remove Mayer from the board. At that meeting, leaders including Leith repeatedly told the councillors that a reprimand was an alternative to removal.

After a contentious two-and-a-half hours of discussions, Mayer was ousted. The position of president-elect was now vacant.

New president’s record draws member outrage

If some members felt that the association had finally started to emerge from a quagmire of infighting and dysfunction, they would soon be disappointed.

Three months later, the ODA board voted to install Edward Busvek, a recurring subject of investigations by the Royal College of Dental Surgeons of Ontario (RCDSO), the provincial dentist watchdog.

Between 2021 and 2023, the RCDSO investigated six complaints against Busvek, issued three cautions and ordered him to take remedial programs. It found concerns with his lack of compliance with the College, which hindered its ability to investigate him, ordered him to be truthful on patient chart notes, and observed clinical deficiencies.

Of the remedial programs Busvek was required to take, one was titled: “Establishing and maintaining appropriate boundaries in the dentist/patient relationship.”

The College would not tell the Star what boundaries it was referring to, and the ODA did not say if, at any point, it was aware of those details.

Busvek told the Star he took the trust of his patients and members seriously and said the complaints did not involve allegations of sexual misconduct. “There was a situation where I acted with the best intentions to assist a patient in a difficult personal matter. I cannot elaborate due to my duty to protect patient privacy,” he said.

The anonymous online group Engage ODA was outraged. They posted a mock report card of Busvek’s adherence to several core competencies, including “ethics” and “cooperation with college,” and beside each, in bright red all-capital letters, wrote: “FAIL.”

Busvek is due to start his one-year term on June 1.

content_blocks.text: Why was board director Laurie Houston fired?

content_blocks.text: Houston was fired in December 2024, the first dismissal of a director in the organization’s history, she told the HRTO. She alleges it was punishment for fulfilling her fiduciary duty to seek transparency from the board.

content_blocks.text: “There seems to be a general culture of fear in this organization, making it difficult for individuals to speak truth to power,” Houston told the HRTO in her complaint, adding that there was “no concrete evidence” to warrant her removal and that the ODA failed to consider lesser punishments such as a reprimand. She also said she was banned for life from being a volunteer for the ODA. The ODA denies this.

stories.title: Queen’s Bridge rehabilitation nearing completion
stories.summary: Five-day closure coming up as crews continue work toward the bridge’s spring 2027 reopening.Work on the
stories.content:
Work on the Queen’s Bridge Rehabilitation project is progressing, with crews moving into the next stage of bridge deck construction.

Since construction began in spring 2026, crews have competed work on the north side of the bridge and are continuing rehabilitation work on the south side, while keeping at least one lane open to traffic.

The next major step is pouring the new concrete bridge deck. Once complete, the north side of the bridge will reopen to traffic, and the south side will remain closed to complete the remaining rehabilitation work.

Work will continue through the winter as weather conditions allow.

The bridge is expected to fully reopen to traffic in spring 2027.

Queen’s Bridge, which carries Queens Avenue over the Thames River, will be fully closed to vehicle traffic from Wednesday, December 2, to Monday, December 7, while crews pour the new concrete bridge deck.

The upcoming closure is necessary to allow for proper curing of the concrete deck.

The closure will affect people travelling out of downtown, including those visiting over the weekend of December 5 and 6. Drivers should plan an alternate route and allow extra time.

Pedestrians will maintain full access across the bridge throughout the closure.

LTC buses will detour around the work area. Visit the London Transit Commission website for the latest bus schedules and detour information.

Remaining work on the Queens Avenue Bridge includes completing the concrete walls and road connections, waterproofing the bridge deck, and paving the road surface.

Crews are also working to replace the staircases connecting Queens Avenue to the Thames Valley Parkway, restore the pathway beneath the bridge and repair the riverbank along the east side of the Thames River to help prevent erosion.

This work is expected to be completed in spring 2027.

Want to keep up with construction in your neighbourhood? Visit the Queen’s Bridge Rehabilitation project page on the City's Get Involved website and click Follow button at the top of the page, just below the project title.

You'll receive email updates about construction progress, upcoming work, and closures.

Friday, November 27, 2026

This winter, local service providers will offer more places for people experiencing homelessness to warm up, rest and stay overnight through the 2026/27 Winter Response.

From December 1, 2026, to March 31, 2027, local service providers will operate 238 seasonal spaces each night as part of London’s Winter Response, including 121 overnight warming spaces, 97 emergency shelter beds and 20 resting and respite spaces.

An additional 29 spaces will be open at some of the participating organizations’ existing shelter sites when the temperature reaches minus 15°C or colder or the wind chill reaches minus 20°C or colder.

Participating organizations include:

London Cares

Ark Aid Street Mission

My Sisters’ Place

Atlohsa Family Healing Services

The Salvation Army

Mission Services of London

Youth Opportunities Unlimited

In addition, 419 year-round emergency shelter beds, respite beds and transitional housing spaces will continue to offer support for people experiencing homelessness throughout the winter months.

Together, year-round shelters, respite programs, transitional housing and seasonal services will provide 657 overnight spaces this winter and 686 during extreme cold conditions.

Throughout the winter, outreach teams will connect with people experiencing unsheltered homelessness, encourage them to come indoors and help them access available spaces.

For more details related to the 2026/27 Winter Response, visit the City’s winter spaces and supports webpage: london.ca/WinterSpaces

“Every Londoner deserves a safe, warm place to call home. That remains our goal, but we have a responsibility to protect those who are most vulnerable this winter,” says Mayor Josh Morgan. “I’m grateful to our community partners and the federal government for working alongside us to meet that immediate need to accompany investments for the long-term that we’ve seen in the recent budget. We’ve established and funded our winter response plan, but next we must build on those cross-government partnerships. Our focus needs to not only be helping people out of homelessness, but to prevent them from experiencing it in the first place. London has the will and expertise to make that happen, and we’re ready to work closely with all other levels of government to achieve it.”

“Our 2026/27 Winter Response is a life-saving service for people experiencing homelessness in our community,” says Kevin Dickins, Deputy City Manager of Social and Health Development at the City of London. “On the coldest nights of the year, it provides more than warmth—it offers safety, dignity and a place where people know they will be welcomed and cared for. I’m grateful to the local agencies and frontline teams who will be there night after night to welcome people in and help them get the support they need.”

Homelessness in London

London continues to experience a homelessness crisis, driven by a shortage of affordable housing, insufficient income supports and unmet healthcare needs. The 2026/27 Winter Response provides immediate support while the City and its partners work to expand access to supportive, transitional and deeply affordable housing. This work is ongoing, and we remain committed to improving outcomes for Londoners experiencing homelessness.

Through service agreements with the City of London, local agencies deliver emergency shelter, drop-in programs, outreach and housing supports. They also operate the seasonal spaces available this winter. The approved budget for the 2026/27 Winter Response is $5,784,775, including $3,632,500 in municipal funding and $2,152,275 from the Government of Canada’s Unsheltered Homelessness and Encampments Initiative.

The City will continue to work with federal and provincial partners to increase the supply of deeply affordable and attainable housing in London.

Friday, November 27, 2026
This winter, local service providers will offer more places for people experiencing homelessness to warm up, rest and stay overnight through the 2026/27 Winter Response.

From December 1, 2026, to March 31, 2027, local service providers will operate 238 seasonal spaces each night as part of London’s Winter Response, including 121 overnight warming spaces, 97 emergency shelter beds and 20 resting and respite spaces.

An additional 29 spaces will be open at some of the participating organizations’ existing shelter sites when the temperature reaches minus 15°C or colder or the wind chill reaches minus 20°C or colder.
Participating organizations include:
London Cares
Ark Aid Street Mission
My Sisters’ Place
Atlohsa Family Healing Services
The Salvation Army
Mission Services of London
Youth Opportunities Unlimited
In addition, 419 year-round emergency shelter beds, respite beds and transitional housing spaces will continue to offer support for people experiencing homelessness throughout the winter months.
Together, year-round shelters, respite programs, transitional housing and seasonal services will provide 657 overnight spaces this winter and 686 during extreme cold conditions.
Throughout the winter, outreach teams will connect with people experiencing unsheltered homelessness, encourage them to come indoors and help them access available spaces.
For more details related to the 2026/27 Winter Response, visit the City’s winter spaces and supports webpage: london.ca/WinterSpaces

“Every Londoner deserves a safe, warm place to call home. That remains our goal, but we have a responsibility to protect those who are most vulnerable this winter,” says Mayor Josh Morgan. “I’m grateful to our community partners and the federal government for working alongside us to meet that immediate need to accompany investments for the long-term that we’ve seen in the recent budget. We’ve established and funded our winter response plan, but next we must build on those cross-government partnerships. Our focus needs to not only be helping people out of homelessness, but to prevent them from experiencing it in the first place. London has the will and expertise to make that happen, and we’re ready to work closely with all other levels of government to achieve it.”

“Our 2026/27 Winter Response is a life-saving service for people experiencing homelessness in our community,” says Kevin Dickins, Deputy City Manager of Social and Health Development at the City of London. “On the coldest nights of the year, it provides more than warmth—it offers safety, dignity and a place where people know they will be welcomed and cared for. I’m grateful to the local agencies and frontline teams who will be there night after night to welcome people in and help them get the support they need.”
Homelessness in London

London continues to experience a homelessness crisis, driven by a shortage of affordable housing, insufficient income supports and unmet healthcare needs. The 2026/27 Winter Response provides immediate support while the City and its partners work to expand access to supportive, transitional and deeply affordable housing. This work is ongoing, and we remain committed to improving outcomes for Londoners experiencing homelessness.

Through service agreements with the City of London, local agencies deliver emergency shelter, drop-in programs, outreach and housing supports. They also operate the seasonal spaces available this winter. The approved budget for the 2026/27 Winter Response is $5,784,775, including $3,632,500 in municipal funding and $2,152,275 from the Government of Canada’s Unsheltered Homelessness and Encampments Initiative.
The City will continue to work with federal and provincial partners to increase the supply of deeply affordable and attainable housing in London.

stories.title: Ontario’s public health agency warned Ford government of increasing gambling harms, internal documents show
stories.summary: has for several months advised Doug Ford’s government that it needs to take action to reduce the growing harms of “rapidly increasing participation” in online gambling, according to internal government records shared with the Star.
stories.author: Brendan Kennedy
stories.content:
Ontario’s public health agency has for several months advised Doug Ford’s government that it needs to take action to reduce the growing harms of “rapidly increasing participation” in online gambling, according to internal government records shared with the Star.

Public Health Ontario provided evidence of increasing health harms and made a series of specific recommendations — including implementing more restrictions on advertising, prohibiting features that encourage continuous betting and increasing protections for youth.

At one point, the agency’s president personally emailed the province’s chief medical officer to make the case for swift action.

“Our strong advice is that we need the government to take action on these recommendations to start mitigating the public health harms that are growing as a result of rapidly increasing participation in online gambling, including sports betting,” Public Health Ontario president and CEO Dr. Michael Sherar wrote to Dr. Kieran Moore on May 6.

The disclosure comes as the province is facing increased scrutiny and criticism for what its critics charge is insufficient oversight of its online gambling market, which launched in April 2022.

Ontario’s online gambling agency commissioned research to track problem gambling rates, then quietly shelved it. Here’s what investigative reporter Brendan Kennedy uncovered through a years-long freedom of information pursuit.

Speaking to reporters in Milton on Friday, Tourism, Culture and Gaming Minister Zee Hamid said the flood of online gambling advertising has the province’s attention.

“We’re very concerned about the rise in problematic gambling and gambling addiction,” Hamid said.

He said he could not reveal specifics, but the government is eyeing a clampdown on gambling ads and will make an announcement “probably in the New Year.”

The internal briefing notes and presentations to government officials were obtained by an advocacy group, the Campaign to Ban Ads for Gambling, in response to a freedom of information request. They were subsequently provided to the Star and other media outlets.

Ontarians wagered $82.7 billion on regulated gambling websites in the 2024-25 fiscal year, according to iGaming Ontario’s most recent annual report. Preliminary data shows those numbers have risen since then.

The bulk of the revenue generated from those wagers — 80 per cent — went to the private gambling companies, while the province pocketed $574 million.

There is also mounting evidence of increased costs to public health. Recent academic research has found ER visits for gambling disorders have doubled since iGaming Ontario launched. Data from the provincial coroner also shows an apparent rise in suicides linked to gambling, and calls to the province’s problem gambling helpline have surged.

Recent Star investigations have revealed that iGaming Ontario, the provincial agency in charge of online gambling, secretly shelved a study it had commissioned intended to track rates of problem gambling in the province.

The briefing material from Public Health Ontario notes the particular health risks associated with gambling online, describing it as the “largest risk factor for developing a gambling disorder,” and pointing to research that shows heightened risk for hospitalization and suicide.

“Signals of increased problem gambling are unique to online gambling, particularly among young men and male adolescents.”

An April presentation the agency made to government officials, including the deputy minister of health, urged the province to “intervene now.”

“Ontario led the country in initiating regulated online gaming, it can also lead in supporting a healthy market and population,” reads one of the slides.

IGaming Ontario vowed to share data to reduce problem gambling. More than 4 years later, it still hasn’t done it and problem gambling’s on the rise.

Specifically, the agency recommended reinvesting gambling revenues into prevention and surveillance programs; implementing product design controls that would restrict “rapid play cycles,” continuous play and in-game inducements; and mandating “balanced marketing” with evidence-based messages to “normalize safer play.”

Regarding advertising, the agency points to what other jurisdictions have done to limit advertising, such as the UK’s so-called “whistle-to-whistle” ban, which prohibits advertising during live sporting events before 9 p.m.

Earlier this week, Premier Ford said gambling ads were “out of control,” though his government has thus far resisted opposition attempts to pass legislation that would curb them.

Asked Friday why the Progressive Conservative government voted against a Liberal private member’s bill to ban all online gambling ads, Hamid said an outright ban could push gamblers to unregulated “grey market” websites and that a more “thoughtful, methodical” approach was necessary.

The internal records show that Public Health Ontario recommends the government shift from a “responsible gambling” approach to mitigating harm, in which the “burden” is on the individual, to a more public-health-focused approach, which would require stricter advertising controls and regulations for operators.

The agency also pointed to the fact that there is currently no surveillance system for monitoring problem gambling. A Star investigation found the Ontario government has yet to follow through on a nearly five-year old promise to require gambling companies to share anonymized player data with independent researchers, which would be studied to recommend the most effective ways of preventing harm.

“Ontario currently has insufficient data to monitor the prevalence and harms of online gambling, exposure to advertising, and the effectiveness of any public health measures to reduce the risk of problem gambling,” one slide reads, calling on the government to improve data collection and collaboration across different government agencies.

The agency also encourages the government to track ad volumes and design features that prolong play.

“Report trends and impacts publicly to build trust,” one slide reads.

With files from Robert Benzie.

Friday, November 27, 2026

Dundas Street will be closed between Clarence Street and Wellington Street downtown from Monday, November 30 to Wednesday, December 2 while crews repair a maintenance hole at the Dundas and Clarence intersection.

A map showing the temporary closure on Dundas Street between Clarence Street and Wellington Road, with signed detour route.

A signed detour will direct drivers around the closure. Drivers should follow posted signs and directions.

Traffic will be detoured along King Street and Queens Avenue.

Sidewalks will be closed during this work.Businesses will remain open and accessible during repairs.

For more information about construction projects in London, visit theRenew London map.

stories.title: LPS officer charged following off-duty incident
stories.summary: London, ON (November 27, 2026) – A London Police Service (LPS) officer is facing criminal charges following an investigation into an off-duty incident earlier this month.
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
LONDON, ON (November 27, 2026)– A London Police Service (LPS) officer is facing criminal charges following an investigation into an off-duty incident earlier this month.

The London Police Service received the initial report and subsequently referred the matter to the Strathroy-Caradoc Police Service to ensure an independent and impartial investigation, in accordance with the conflict-of-interest provisions under the Community Safety and Policing Act, 2019.

The officer was arrested and charged by the Strathroy-Caradoc Police Service with the following offences:

Assault; and

Forcible confinement.

To protect the privacy of the victim and prevent their identification, the name of the officer and further identifying details will not be released at this time.

Following an assessment of the circumstances, the officer has been reassigned to administrative duties and will not be performing frontline policing duties. The officer’s duty status will remain subject to ongoing review as the matter progresses.

The matter will also be subject to an internal conduct investigation in accordance with the Community Safety and Policing Act, 2019.

The London Police Service takes these allegations seriously. As police officers, we are entrusted with significant responsibilities and are held to high standards of conduct, both on and off duty.

Our commitment to transparency and accountability must be balanced with our responsibility to protect the privacy and well-being of those affected and to respect the integrity and fairness of the judicial process.

All media inquiries regarding the investigation or the charges should be directed to the Strathroy-Caradoc Police Service.

London Police Service 601 Dundas Street London, Ontario N6B 1X1

stories.title: Whitehorse Power Centres deemed project of national interest
stories.summary: First phase of the project would add 15 megawatts of power by 2027
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The federal government has named the Whitehorse Power Centres as a project of national interest.

Prime Minister Mark Carney announced the move Thursday at a meeting in Whitehorse with Yukon Premier Currie Dixon.

Carney says the move is part of his government’s plan to provide reliable and affordable power to the Yukon and ensure economic and energy security in the north.

The first phase of the project would add 15 megawatts of power by 2028, with future phases increasing to around 150 megawatts.

A news release from the Prime Minister’s Office says the major projects office will help Yukon assess necessary upgrades to accommodate stress on its power grids as a result of the project.

It says the office will also look at opportunities for Indigenous partners to participate in the energy sector, including through potential equity ownership.

Carney said he planned to discuss the topic with Indigenous leaders in Whitehorse on Thursday.

Editor’s note: An earlier version of this Canadian Press story stated an incorrect year for the first phase of the project. This has been updated.
