stories.title: York University’s Glendon College to vote on the future of its bilingual location
stories.summary: Enrolment is down nearly 50 per cent from a peak in 2016-17
stories.author: Kelly Grant
stories.content:
When it came time for Samuel Nieva to pick a university, maintaining the French language skills he worked hard to master in elementary and high school was a top priority.

So he felt fortunate to find a bilingual haven not far from his home in Pickering, Ont., at York University’s Glendon Campus, a small liberal arts college tucked into one of the poshest neighbourhoods in Toronto.

At Glendon, Mr. Nieva was able to pursue a double major with economics courses taught in English and history courses taught in French. He also had plenty of opportunities to practise his French in casual conversations with classmates, professors and campus staff.

“I’ve met a lot of people who said they studied French in high school, but then once they graduated, they weren’t able to continue their French, so they lost their language,” Mr. Nieva said. “I chose Glendon for that reason.”

Mr. Nieva, now 22 and the president of the Glendon College Student Union, wants the same choice to be available to future students. That is why he and his organization, along with some professors and Glendon alumni, are fighting a York University proposal to move Glendon’s bilingual academics and activities to the sprawling main Keele Street campus on the outskirts of the city.

The Glendon Faculty Council is scheduled to vote on the plan Friday. Their choice hinges on a question that matters beyond the bucolic setting of the Glendon campus: What is the best way for a major university in an anglophone province to carry out a bilingual mandate?

If they reject the proposal, their decision will be final.

York’s proposal , which was submitted to Glendon Faculty Council in September by interim provost Laina Bay-Cheng, pitches the move to a dedicated building at Keele as a means of revitalizing York’s bilingual academic offerings and activities.

As it stands, enrolment at Glendon has been declining. The student head count fell to 1,419 in 2025-26, down nearly 50 per cent from a peak of 2,770 in 2016-17. Glendon’s accumulated deficit hit $52.4-million at the end of the last academic year, a heavy burden for a university trying to claw its way out of the red by 2028-29.

The written proposal argues that more students would be willing to take classes in French at the main campus, which has many more program offerings and is easier to access by public transit than Glendon. An estimated 70 per cent of York’s francophone students are already in Keele-based programs.

“This transition would allow for meaningful growth and new possibilities: the development of bilingual pathways in a wider range of academic programs; the expansion of students’ postgraduate prospects; and granting over 52,000 students at Keele Campus access to French-language courses, services and community,” the proposal says.

Critics of the move counter that students are less likely to improve or maintain their French in a sea of English at Keele. They say students are better off staying in a small bilingual pond at Glendon. More than 2,800 people have signed a petition opposing the move.

Glendon provides “a really wonderful academic ecosystem,” said Imola Ilyes, a contract philosophy instructor at the college. Glendon’s classes are small and welcoming, she said. The library, café and administrative offices offer services in both official languages.

“I think that bilingual part of the ecosystem is super important, and that would be completely lost if these changes went ahead,” she added.

Jérémie Séror, a professor in the University of Ottawa’s Official Languages and Bilingualism Institute, agreed that students are more likely to use their French at an avowedly bilingual campus such as Glendon.

“The advantage of creating an environment that really celebrates it and makes it normal to use French, hear French, see French, is that it does encourage the language to be used in this real, natural way – which is what we know is the key for a language to be vital and preserved,” he said.

People involved in a campaign to preserve Glendon say enrolment at the campus has declined because York hasn’t adequately marketed the bilingual liberal arts college.

“I think recruitment is probably the key issue,” said Marcia Macaulay, a linguistics professor who has taught at Glendon for 35 years. “Students almost unanimously say that they sort of inadvertently discovered Glendon. Nobody was coming and promoting it.”

That isn’t the case, according to Yanni Dagonas, deputy spokesman for York.

“There has been a concerted effort in recent years to boost visibility and enrolment through dedicated, campus-specific marketing and integration of Glendon programs across advertising,” he said by e-mail.

Another concern that Prof. Macaulay and other Glendon supporters raised was that York’s motive for shifting the bilingual mandate to Keele could be to redevelop part of the Glendon site, which sits on a valuable swath of greenery near elite private schools and clubs on Bayview Avenue.

“I think they fully intend to redevelop in some way,” Prof. Macaulay said, adding that York recently commissioned a preliminary land use study of the Glendon site that has not been released in full.

Prof. Macaulay has filed a freedom of information request to obtain it.

Mr. Dagonas, the university’s deputy spokesman, said York has “no intention of ceasing academic activities at the Glendon site and is committed to maintaining an ongoing academic presence there.”

If the Glendon Faculty Council – which includes Glendon’s principal and associate principals, all full-time faculty and a mix of students, staff and contract faculty – votes in favour of the proposal, then new academic uses for the campus will be explored, Mr. Dagonas said.

“Decisions about the use of Glendon Campus lands are a separate matter and are not driving any academic proposal,” he said.

The written proposal argues that more students would be willing to take classes in French at the main campus, which has many more program offerings and is easier to access by public transit than Glendon. An estimated 70 per cent of York’s francophone students are already in Keele-based programs.

“This transition would allow for meaningful growth and new possibilities: the development of bilingual pathways in a wider range of academic programs; the expansion of students’ postgraduate prospects; and granting over 52,000 students at Keele Campus access to French-language courses, services and community,” the proposal says.

Critics of the move counter that students are less likely to improve or maintain their French in a sea of English at Keele. They say students are better off staying in a small bilingual pond at Glendon. More than 2,800 people have signed a petition opposing the move.

Glendon provides “a really wonderful academic ecosystem,” said Imola Ilyes, a contract philosophy instructor at the college. Glendon’s classes are small and welcoming, she said. The library, café and administrative offices offer services in both official languages.
“I think that bilingual part of the ecosystem is super important, and that would be completely lost if these changes went ahead,” she added.

Jérémie Séror, a professor in the University of Ottawa’s Official Languages and Bilingualism Institute, agreed that students are more likely to use their French at an avowedly bilingual campus such as Glendon.

“The advantage of creating an environment that really celebrates it and makes it normal to use French, hear French, see French, is that it does encourage the language to be used in this real, natural way – which is what we know is the key for a language to be vital and preserved,” he said.
People involved in a campaign to preserve Glendon say enrolment at the campus has declined because York hasn’t adequately marketed the bilingual liberal arts college.

“I think recruitment is probably the key issue,” said Marcia Macaulay, a linguistics professor who has taught at Glendon for 35 years. “Students almost unanimously say that they sort of inadvertently discovered Glendon. Nobody was coming and promoting it.”
That isn’t the case, according to Yanni Dagonas, deputy spokesman for York.

“There has been a concerted effort in recent years to boost visibility and enrolment through dedicated, campus-specific marketing and integration of Glendon programs across advertising,” he said by e-mail.

Another concern that Prof. Macaulay and other Glendon supporters raised was that York’s motive for shifting the bilingual mandate to Keele could be to redevelop part of the Glendon site, which sits on a valuable swath of greenery near elite private schools and clubs on Bayview Avenue.
“I think they fully intend to redevelop in some way,” Prof. Macaulay said, adding that York recently commissioned a preliminary land use study of the Glendon site that has not been released in full.
Prof. Macaulay has filed a freedom of information request to obtain it.
Mr. Dagonas, the university’s deputy spokesman, said York has “no intention of ceasing academic activities at the Glendon site and is committed to maintaining an ongoing academic presence there.”

If the Glendon Faculty Council – which includes Glendon’s principal and associate principals, all full-time faculty and a mix of students, staff and contract faculty – votes in favour of the proposal, then new academic uses for the campus will be explored, Mr. Dagonas said.
“Decisions about the use of Glendon Campus lands are a separate matter and are not driving any academic proposal,” he said.

stories.title: Ottawa deems Whitehorse Power Centres project of national interest
stories.summary: Whitehorse - The federal government has named the Whitehorse Power Centres as a project of national interest.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney announced the move Thursday at a meeting in Whitehorse with Yukon Premier Currie Dixon.

Carney says the move is part of his government’s plan to provide reliable and affordable power to the Yukon and ensure economic and energy security in the north.

Article continues below

Inside interior designer Nora Voon’s art-filled home

The first phase of the project would add 15 megawatts of power by 2027, with future phases increasing to around 150 megawatts.

A news release from the Prime Minister’s Office says the major projects office will help Yukon assess necessary upgrades to accommodate stress on its power grids as a result of the project.

It says the office will also look at opportunities for Indigenous partners to participate in the energy sector, including through potential equity ownership.

Carney said he planned to discuss the topic with Indigenous leaders in Whitehorse on Thursday.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Defendants in Galloway case deny social media posts were made with malice
stories.summary: Women did not set out to harm the bestselling author’s reputation, they say in final submissions
stories.author: Mike Hager
stories.content:
Two women being sued for defamation by Steven Galloway for repeating the allegation he sexually assaulted a former student both said in their final submissions Thursday that they did not post the statements on social media out of malice for the bestselling author.

The lawyer for Mandi Gray, who is on medical leave from her position as an assistant professor of criminology at Trent University because of the proceedings, told the British Columbia Supreme Court that her client regretted defaming Mr. Galloway on social media, but she posted from a genuine desire to contribute “fair comment” to the public discussion about campus sexual violence.

And Glynnis Kirchmeier told the court the lone count of defamation against her should be thrown out on the basis that Mr. Galloway’s legal team cut the social media post in question in half to strip it of necessary context. Ms. Kirchmeier, a former University of British Columbia history graduate student, is now in law school and representing herself at trial.

Ms. Kirchmeier and Dr. Gray’s lawyer argued that even if Justice Neena Sharma finds they defamed the bestselling author, he does not deserve the massive award he is seeking from them and his accuser, known as A.B. because of a publication ban on her identity.

A fourth defendant, a woman named Dana Kagis who allegedly posted a single defamatory statement on social media, did not participate in the weeks-long trial. Nor did A.B., whose lawyers have said has tried to kill herself twice this year because of the stress of the legal process.

Earlier this week, Mr. Galloway’s counsel told court their client deserves a rare award of special damages solely against A.B. amounting to $4.9-million. They are also asking she pay at least $2.5-million in general, aggravated and punitive damages, which – if granted – would total $7.4-million.

Mr. Galloway is also seeking general, aggravated and punitive damages in the form of at least $250,000 from Dr. Gray, at least $80,000 from Ms. Kirchmeier and $30,000 from Ms. Kagis.

Mr. Galloway’s team alleges Dr. Gray is the person who most aggressively promoted A.B.’s alleged defamations and kept them alive “from the very start and through every stage.”

Vanshika Dhawan, Dr. Gray’s lawyer, argued that if her client is found liable, her conduct does not rise to the level of a six-figure award for damages and – because there is not enough evidence she acted out of malice – she should not pay anything more than general damages.

Ms. Dhawan argued that Dr. Gray posted on social media a handful of times in reaction to the initial suspension of Mr. Galloway in November 2015 and, a year later, to the UBC Accountable open letter signed by a number of high-profile authors calling on the school to open a new investigation into his firing.

That pales in contrast with similar defamation awards, Ms. Dhawan told the court, which penalized aggressive internet campaigns that were much more widespread and “heavy-handed” than her client’s public comments about the author.

She said Dr. Gray’s threat of a “boycott” of Penguin Random House, Mr. Galloway’s publisher, over its public statement of support after his suspension never amounted to much at all.

Plus, Ms. Dhawan said, her client’s e-mail to the publisher was never alleged to be defamatory, noting her message urged the company to respect Ubc’s investigation before weighing in. She noted that her client’s e-mail includes a sentence saying, “I am not jumping to any conclusions about what May or May not have happened in the case of Steven Galloway.”

Mr. Galloway was never charged with a crime but he was suspended by UBC when the allegations surfaced in November 2015, creating a media maelstrom and a civil war in Canadian literature that forced many to pick his or his accuser’s side.

In 2016, Mary Ellen Boyd, a former provincial Supreme Court justice hired by UBC, found that, ON a balance of probabilities, it could not be established that he committed sexual assault or assault. Ms. Boyd did find that he had sexually harassed A.B., with UBC firing him later that year over breach of trust and other misconduct.

Near the end of the day, Daniel Burnett, lead counsel for Mr. Galloway, was given an opportunity to respond to the final submissions from the two defendants and that of A.B. earlier this week.

Mr. Burnett challenged A.B.’s core contention that she was only following the university’s reporting protocols when she shared her allegations in November 2015 with professors and other graduate students.

Her legal team says she never commented publicly and only shared this sensitive information with fewer than 10 people, which kicked off a process she could not foresee or control that ultimately did the majority of the damage to Mr. Galloway’s mental health and lucrative writing career.

But Mr. Burnett told the court the evidence shows A.B. was helping a former classmate find more allegations even before UBC started its formal process of investigating Mr. Galloway’s sexual misconduct.

He and his co-counsel Daniel Coles are scheduled to continue their response to the final arguments of the defendants on Friday, which is expected to be the last day of the trial.

stories.title: Public Health Ontario warned province about online gambling risks in April, document shows
stories.summary: Province has seen sharp growth in betting since it opened to private operators in April 2022
stories.author: Simon Houpt
stories.content:
Public Health Ontario urged the Ford government last spring to intervene in the province’s growing online gambling market to ensure the harms associated with the activity didn’t undercut its development, an internal document from the health agency shows.

Ontario has seen sharp growth in online gambling since it became the first province to open to private operators in April 2022. As the number of gamblers has risen, so too has the amount wagered – to more than $10-billion a month – and the concern.

Michael Sherar, the president and chief executive of PHO, the arms-length provincial agency, offered a series of recommendations to Deborah Richardson, the deputy minister of health, for what he told colleagues was aimed at “harm mitigation in the context of the rapid rise in online gambling including sports betting, particularly in young males.”

A slide deck in a virtual presentation Mr. Sherar gave to the deputy minister in late April noted that “the greatest proportion of gambling harms are in those who do not meet the criteria for a disorder” and that the government should treat the potential harms as a matter of public health rather than the responsibility of individual players.

The slide deck was included in a package of briefing notes and other public-service communications released under a freedom-of-information request by the advocacy group Ban Ads for Gambling, which seeks to have all advertisements for online gambling banned in Canada. The organization shared the information with media outlets on Thursday.

Bruce Kidd, a former Olympian who co-founded the organization, said that, while the government’s release of information did not answer many of the questions his organization had asked, such as the number of underage gamblers, “what they did release is highly damning. It suggests that, at the senior civil service level and probably the political level they knew or ought to have known that their strategy of radical expansion of gambling and the radical presentation of gambling ads was harmful.”

In a slide titled “Options to Protect a Healthy Online Gambling Market,” the presentation outlined a number of areas through which the government could tackle problematic gambling.

Among its recommendations, it suggested building an integrated surveillance system to track player participation along with risk factors and harms across populations. It also suggested prioritizing youth education by adding digital gambling, advertising literacy and the role of gaming influencers to the province’s curriculum.

The presentation also suggested the Alcohol and Gaming Commission of Ontario, which regulates the sector, should strengthen its oversight of sports-betting advertising and promotion, including by introducing limits on inducements and bonuses, advertising frequency, and promotional practices that are associated with increased gambling harms. Some online gambling companies have reportedly targeted players with promotions that they should have known were experiencing harm.

In October, iGaming Ontario, which oversees online gambling in the province, reported there were a record 1.47 million active accounts, with $10.7-billion wagered on online casino games, poker and sports betting in the month. About 8 per cent of that total, or $450-million, was kept by the companies. (They remit 20 per cent of that as a tax to the province.) The figures do not include gambling done through the provincially owned OLG.

But that explosive growth has provoked a public backlash.

Mr. Kidd noted that even Ontario Premier Doug Ford this week criticized the volume of ads for online gambling, telling reporters at Queen’s Park the promotions are “out of control.”

In a statement e-mailed to The Globe, Scott Clark, a spokesperson for Zee Hamid, Minister of Tourism, Culture and Gaming, noted that the government has invested more than $400-million in public education and problem gambling awareness campaigns.

“We recognize there is more that needs to be done to strengthen Ontario’s iGaming market and protect players across the province. That is why, in response to concerns from families … we will bring forward changes in the new year to further strengthen online gaming regulations and crack down on operators taking advantage of players.”

stories.title: Was Paul Bernardo involved in the disappearance of Elizabeth Bain? Dateline Canada digs into new evidence
stories.summary: A Dateline Canada exclusive has revealed new information possibly linking Paul Bernardo to Elizabeth Bain’s unsolved disappearance.
stories.author: Michael Talbot
stories.content:
By Michael Talbot

Posted November 26, 2026 9:59 pm.

EDITOR’S NOTE: This article contains details concerning violent sexual crimes and murder.

Paul Bernardo’s ex-girlfriend introduced him to Elizabeth Bain and an eyewitness later described an attack along Highway 401 in Scarborough on the night she vanished involving a woman and man matching the descriptions of Bain and Bernardo in a vehicle believed to be Elizabeth’s.

Those startling revelations were part of an exclusive Dateline Canada report into the unsolved murder mystery that aired on Citytv on Thursday night.

Bain, a 22-year-old University of Toronto student disappeared after driving to the Scarborough campus to check a tennis schedule on June 19, 1990. Her blood-stained car was found three days later a few blocks away, but her remains have never been found.

Bernardo’s ex-girlfriend’s account was among several revelations during the two-hour Dateline Canada special that pointed towards the notorious schoolgirl sex killer’s possible involvement in the case.

The ex-girlfriend’s identity is legally protected, and her voice was altered during the Dateline Canada report, where she’s refereed to as Janine Godsoe.

Godsoe claims she saw Bain, who she knew and considered a friend, at a gas station just two weeks before she disappeared on June 19, 1990.

They chatted briefly before Godsoe left for a vacation.

When Godsoe returned from her trip and learned that Bain was missing and presumed dead, she immediately feared that her violent ex-boyfriend, Bernardo, was somehow involved and went to police.

By this time, however, investigators had zeroed in on Bain’s boyfriend, Robert Baltovich, as their prime suspect. In 1992, Batlovich would be convicted of her murder and sentenced to life, only to later be exonerated in a retrial.

On the day she went missing, Baltovich told investigators he spotted Bain’s empty vehicle parked in a secluded section of Colonel Danforth Park — the same area that Godsoe said Bernardo frequently took her.

The Dateline Canada special aired audio segments of Godsoe being interviewed by private investigator, Brian King, who has spent the last three decades probing the mystery of Bain’s disappearance.

“He (Bernardo) had these strange things where you know, he would only take you to certain places. It’s kind of like a pattern, I guess,” Godsoe told King.

“Would this be a place (Colonel Danforth Park) that you would have gone with him (Bernardo) on occasion to be intimate?

“Yes,” Godsoe replied.

According to Godsoe, Bernardo frequently beat her.

King shared a police report detailing one such incident.

“He grabbed her and threw her in the car, every time he stopped at a red light, he hit her in the head and face and smashed her head against the window. He punched her in the back leaving a handprint through her heavy clothes. He pulled out clumps of her hair. En route he told her I’m going to f****n take you somewhere and kill you.”

King later called her a “very credible witness.”

When asked why these reports didn’t put the focus of the police probe more clearly on an alternative suspect, journalist Paula Todd, who covered Bernardo’s terrifying spree as the Scarborough Rapist, told Dateline Canada: “You have to consider the possibility that Robert Baltovich was going to be their suspect, and all of this very inconvenient evidence was just going to be ignored.”

The attack described by Godsoe in the police report bore eerie similarities to another attack in a vehicle described by a witness, with the suspect and victim matching the descriptions of Bernardo and Bain.

A man named Keith Nobrega approached King after Baltovich’s first trial. He told King in an audio statement that he was driving on Highway 401 at around 7:30 p.m., on June 19, 1990 -– the night of Bain’s disappearance — when he witnessed a blond man attacking a woman in a car that closely matched the description of Bain’s Toyota Tercel.

Nobrega said he noticed the car in his rearview, racing up behind him.

“In my rearview mirror, I saw a Toyota, a small Tercel, come right up to the back of my car,” he recalled.

“The number plate caught my eye, but I had remembered it was 394 BNC.”

Bain’s licence plate was a very close, 397 CNB.

He went on to describe a large man and a small woman who resembled Bain violently fighting.

“He was like punching at her and she was hitting at him. And I said, ‘holy smoke a big guy like that beating up on a little girl.’ ”

“She had her hands up to the window and she was screaming, because her mouth was wide open, and her face and her eyes (were) in (a) real sort of horror.”

Nobrega went to police, who seemed focused on the suspect’s hair colour.

“He (the detective) says ‘now what colour is this guy’s hair?’ I remember telling him … ‘it was like blondish.’ ”

“He suddenly railroaded me into thinking it would be black,” he recalled.

But Nobrega was emphatic in his account to police, describing a large blond man who looked nothing like the slim, dark-haired Baltovich.

Police said they couldn’t reach Nobrega again to follow up, but Nobrega said they weren’t interested in what he had to say.

King told Dateline Canada he believed police “didn’t pursue anything he (Nobrega) said, because it did not fit the theory” that Baltovich was responsible.

King argued that the two similar incidents in vehicles raised obvious suspicions that should’ve been more fully probed.

“When you put the two together it gives you a sense of potentially the person that was responsible for Elizabeth Bain’s abduction,” he told Dateline Canada.

King said others came forward saying Elizabeth was seen in the company of a blond man in the days leading up to her disappearance.

At one point a witness said she saw a man who matched a composite sketch of the Scarborough Rapist on the Scarborough UofT campus the same day Bain disappeared.

Todd also openly questioned why a potential suspect with blond hair wasn’t more fervently investigated.

“People were pulling on the police saying ‘I saw, perhaps, Elizabeth Bain with a blonde haired man,’ so many people were trying to get the attention of the police and nothing,” she said.

“Add to that the ex-girlfriend who went to police early on who said all of these places that Elizabeth Bain was, that’s where my ex-boyfriend (Bernardo) used to take me.”

Bernardo would only be identified as the Scarborough Rapist in early February, 1993, when a lab secured a DNA match from a victim.

But it was during his spree that Bain vanished.

Dateline Canada said police initially didn’t draw a connection, believing the culprit behind the slew of sexual assaults didn’t murder his victims.

In his first televised interview in decades, Baltovich told Dateline Canada he followed news of the Scarborough Rapist arrest from his jail cell.

“I was reading a lot of coverage of his trial in The Globe and Mail and I was starting to note interesting little coincidences like Bernardo was living in Scarborough at the time Liz went missing,” he said, along with “the fact that he was indeed known to have blond hair.”

Todd said: “People were asking, ‘hey we know now who was the Scarborough Rapist and right in the middle of the exact time frame Elizabeth Bain disappears? Do you think we should look at that?’ ”

In 2007, Toronto police detectives travelled to Kingston Penitentiary, where Bernardo was serving life in prison for the murders of Leslie Mahaffy, Kristen French and the manslaughter of Karla Homolka’s sister, Tammie Homolka.

During that visit, Bernardo was asked about his possible involvement in Bain’s disappearance.

The convicted killer gave rambling, elusive answers, but ultimately denied killing Bain.

When asked if he had ever met her, he said he couldn’t remember.

But his ex-girlfriend did.

She described introducing Bain to Bernardo in an interview with King that was aired by Dateline Canada.

“I remember a church play that I was in, like a Christmas play, and I remember Paul came down to see it. And we were coming out of the church, and I remember Elizabeth passing by and I introduced him.”

Bernardo remains behind bars, while Homolka is now free. She served 12 years after being convicted on two counts of manslaughter in the so-called ‘Death with the Devil’ that saw her testify against her former husband.

Homolka was released from prison in 2005.

Bernardo was given an indeterminate life sentence with a dangerous offender designation. He has applied for parole several times since 2018, but has been denied.

Neither responded to Dateline Canada’s questions about Bain’s disappearance.

Back in 2005, while Baltovich was awaiting his second trial, Dateline Canada revealed that a man named Robert Jones came forward to Quebec police with new information he says was gleaned from a 2002 conversation he had with Homolka while she was serving time at Ste-Anne-des-Plaines, in Quebec, where he volunteered.

Dateline Canada aired portions of Jones’ police interview on Thursday night.

“I told her I said ‘Karla, I know who you are, I know what you’ve done, you killed three people’ and she looked at me and said no we killed five people,’ ” Jones told officers.

“I have nothing against Karla,” he added. “It’s just that this is information that I know, and it should be shared.”

Jones said he was compelled to come forward after reading about Baltovich’s appeal.

“I was overwhelmed to a point because that’s information that could set maybe an innocent man free,” he added.

When asked if Homolka shared the names of any additional alleged victims, Jones recalled the name “Dion.” Months later he would contact police and say he was mistaken, and the name was Elizabeth Bain.

Weeks before she was due to be released, police confronted Homolka about Jones’ claims.

Detective : “And Jones said ‘How many people did you kill? So, we killed five people, did you say that?”

Homolka : “Never. He’s crazy.”

Homolka : “I never speak about what I did, ever, unless I have to with my case management team or my psychologist. But even then, it’s like pulling teeth for me to speak about it.”

When asked her if she believed Bernardo had been involved in the death of Bain, Homolka remarked: “I don’t believe that he had anything to do with Elizabeth Bain’s murder. I don’t believe that.”

Jones has since passed away, and the Toronto Police Service (TPS) declined to comment on his past recollection of a conversation with Homolka.

Dateline Canada did reach out to TPS, which provided this statement:

“ We understand how devastating the disappearance of Elizabeth Bain was, and continues to be, for her family, loved ones, and all those who have spent decades seeking answers. Like her family, we want to see the person responsible for this crime held accountable. We want to be clear that investigators interviewed both Paul Bernardo and Karla Homolka as part of the investigation into Elizabeth Bain’s case. After thoroughly examining the information available to them, investigators found no direct evidence linking either individual to her disappearance. While we understand the public interest in exploring all possible avenues, it is important that investigative conclusions be guided by clear, direct evidence. If anyone has information that could help police locate Elizabeth’s remains and bring her home to her family, please contact police. “

Today, Baltovich continues to seek answers to Bain’s disappearance, working with both King and a former police officer, to sift through boxes of evidence released through disclosure.

His conviction was tossed on appeal after it was discovered that several eye witnesses were hypnotized before giving statements, in some cases adding damning details only after they’d already seen images of Baltovich and Bain’s vehicle.

“When I saw him following me home yesterday, I felt like killing myself,” Bain wrote in one entry, noting a “cold ugly streak inside him,” in another.

When a detective asked Baltovich: “Have you ever thought about killing her (Bain)?

He replied: “Yes.”

Decades later, he tried to explain why he said that.

“I guess the problem is I made a comment during that interview that I know that the Crown absolutely loved,” he admitted.

“I wanted the police to understand that, yes, at the time that I first met her and I was very romantically attracted to her, when she disclosed that she had a boyfriend, I was absolutely furious with her. King said the circumstantial evidence and his own remarks made Baltovich “low hanging fruit” for police.

“The police were going to get a conviction one way or the other and the only suspect they had is Robert Baltovich,” he said. “In my mind, this is a clear case of tunnel vision by the police officers.”

Baltovich agrees.

“I think what it really boils down to … is that the police made a decision, very, very early on in the investigation that I was the one, and they went and they did everything and anything they could to point things in my direction.”

Baltovich’s retrial lasted just half-an-hour before he was found not guilty after the Crown failed to produce any witnesses or submit any evidence.

While relieved, Baltovich told Dateline Canada he was looking forward to watching his lawyers dismantle the case against him while presenting evidence pointing to a potential alternate suspect.

“I’ve been out of prison for 26 years but that whole time I’ve never lost hope that we might find out what happened to Liz, I almost feel like it’s a sense of duty,” Baltovich said.

For friends and loved ones of Bain, there’s still no closure after all these years.

“She was a stunning woman and she was very kind and she would listen to you carefully when you spoke to her,” her childhood friend Lisa Wallner told Dateline Canada.

Bain dreamed of becoming a social worker and worked at group home for adults with developmental disabilities.

Co-worker and friend, Sherri Rutten remembers her as popular, hard-working, and always on time.

“When Elizabeth never showed up to work, all of our stomachs just fell,” she recalled. “There has to be a reason for somebody, so responsible, to just disappear. It was crazy to me.”

“Elizabeth deserves to be in peace,” she said.

“She deserves the truth.“

Paul Bernardo’s ex-girlfriend introduced him to Elizabeth Bain and an eyewitness later described an attack along Highway 401 in Scarborough on the night she vanished involving a woman and man matching the descriptions of Bain and Bernardo in a vehicle believed to be Elizabeth’s.
Those startling revelations were part of an exclusive Dateline Canada report into the unsolved murder mystery that aired on Citytv on Thursday night.

Bain, a 22-year-old University of Toronto student disappeared after driving to the Scarborough campus to check a tennis schedule on June 19, 1990. Her blood-stained car was found three days later a few blocks away, but her remains have never been found.

Bernardo’s ex-girlfriend’s account was among several revelations during the two-hour Dateline Canada special that pointed towards the notorious schoolgirl sex killer’s possible involvement in the case.
The ex-girlfriend’s identity is legally protected, and her voice was altered during the Dateline Canada report, where she’s refereed to as Janine Godsoe.
Godsoe claims she saw Bain, who she knew and considered a friend, at a gas station just two weeks before she disappeared on June 19, 1990.
They chatted briefly before Godsoe left for a vacation.
When Godsoe returned from her trip and learned that Bain was missing and presumed dead, she immediately feared that her violent ex-boyfriend, Bernardo, was somehow involved and went to police.

By this time, however, investigators had zeroed in on Bain’s boyfriend, Robert Baltovich, as their prime suspect. In 1992, Batlovich would be convicted of her murder and sentenced to life, only to later be exonerated in a retrial.

On the day she went missing, Baltovich told investigators he spotted Bain’s empty vehicle parked in a secluded section of Colonel Danforth Park — the same area that Godsoe said Bernardo frequently took her.
The Dateline Canada special aired audio segments of Godsoe being interviewed by private investigator, Brian King, who has spent the last three decades probing the mystery of Bain’s disappearance.
“He (Bernardo) had these strange things where you know, he would only take you to certain places. It’s kind of like a pattern, I guess,” Godsoe told King.
“Would this be a place (Colonel Danforth Park) that you would have gone with him (Bernardo) on occasion to be intimate?
“Yes,” Godsoe replied.
According to Godsoe, Bernardo frequently beat her.
King shared a police report detailing one such incident.

“He grabbed her and threw her in the car, every time he stopped at a red light, he hit her in the head and face and smashed her head against the window. He punched her in the back leaving a handprint through her heavy clothes. He pulled out clumps of her hair. En route he told her I’m going to f****n take you somewhere and kill you.”
King later called her a “very credible witness.”

When asked why these reports didn’t put the focus of the police probe more clearly on an alternative suspect, journalist Paula Todd, who covered Bernardo’s terrifying spree as the Scarborough Rapist, told Dateline Canada: “You have to consider the possibility that Robert Baltovich was going to be their suspect, and all of this very inconvenient evidence was just going to be ignored.”

The attack described by Godsoe in the police report bore eerie similarities to another attack in a vehicle described by a witness, with the suspect and victim matching the descriptions of Bernardo and Bain.

A man named Keith Nobrega approached King after Baltovich’s first trial. He told King in an audio statement that he was driving on Highway 401 at around 7:30 p.m., on June 19, 1990 -– the night of Bain’s disappearance — when he witnessed a blond man attacking a woman in a car that closely matched the description of Bain’s Toyota Tercel.
Nobrega said he noticed the car in his rearview, racing up behind him.
“In my rearview mirror, I saw a Toyota, a small Tercel, come right up to the back of my car,” he recalled.
“The number plate caught my eye, but I had remembered it was 394 BNC.”
Bain’s licence plate was a very close, 397 CNB.
He went on to describe a large man and a small woman who resembled Bain violently fighting.
“He was like punching at her and she was hitting at him. And I said, ‘holy smoke a big guy like that beating up on a little girl.’ ”
“She had her hands up to the window and she was screaming, because her mouth was wide open, and her face and her eyes (were) in (a) real sort of horror.”
Nobrega went to police, who seemed focused on the suspect’s hair colour.
“He (the detective) says ‘now what colour is this guy’s hair?’ I remember telling him … ‘it was like blondish.’ ”
“He suddenly railroaded me into thinking it would be black,” he recalled.
But Nobrega was emphatic in his account to police, describing a large blond man who looked nothing like the slim, dark-haired Baltovich.
Police said they couldn’t reach Nobrega again to follow up, but Nobrega said they weren’t interested in what he had to say.
King told Dateline Canada he believed police “didn’t pursue anything he (Nobrega) said, because it did not fit the theory” that Baltovich was responsible.
King argued that the two similar incidents in vehicles raised obvious suspicions that should’ve been more fully probed.
“When you put the two together it gives you a sense of potentially the person that was responsible for Elizabeth Bain’s abduction,” he told Dateline Canada.
King said others came forward saying Elizabeth was seen in the company of a blond man in the days leading up to her disappearance.
At one point a witness said she saw a man who matched a composite sketch of the Scarborough Rapist on the Scarborough UofT campus the same day Bain disappeared.
Todd also openly questioned why a potential suspect with blond hair wasn’t more fervently investigated.
“People were pulling on the police saying ‘I saw, perhaps, Elizabeth Bain with a blonde haired man,’ so many people were trying to get the attention of the police and nothing,” she said.
“Add to that the ex-girlfriend who went to police early on who said all of these places that Elizabeth Bain was, that’s where my ex-boyfriend (Bernardo) used to take me.”
Bernardo would only be identified as the Scarborough Rapist in early February, 1993, when a lab secured a DNA match from a victim.
But it was during his spree that Bain vanished.
Dateline Canada said police initially didn’t draw a connection, believing the culprit behind the slew of sexual assaults didn’t murder his victims.
In his first televised interview in decades, Baltovich told Dateline Canada he followed news of the Scarborough Rapist arrest from his jail cell.

“I was reading a lot of coverage of his trial in The Globe and Mail and I was starting to note interesting little coincidences like Bernardo was living in Scarborough at the time Liz went missing,” he said, along with “the fact that he was indeed known to have blond hair.”
Todd said: “People were asking, ‘hey we know now who was the Scarborough Rapist and right in the middle of the exact time frame Elizabeth Bain disappears? Do you think we should look at that?’ ”

During that visit, Bernardo was asked about his possible involvement in Bain’s disappearance.
The convicted killer gave rambling, elusive answers, but ultimately denied killing Bain.
When asked if he had ever met her, he said he couldn’t remember.
But his ex-girlfriend did.
She described introducing Bain to Bernardo in an interview with King that was aired by Dateline Canada.

“I remember a church play that I was in, like a Christmas play, and I remember Paul came down to see it. And we were coming out of the church, and I remember Elizabeth passing by and I introduced him.”

Homolka was released from prison in 2005.
Bernardo was given an indeterminate life sentence with a dangerous offender designation. He has applied for parole several times since 2018, but has been denied.
Neither responded to Dateline Canada’s questions about Bain’s disappearance.

“I was overwhelmed to a point because that’s information that could set maybe an innocent man free,” he added.

stories.title: Multiple soldiers remain in critical condition as health officials detail CFB Wainwright response
stories.summary: Health officials say 19 soldiers injured from the CFB Wainwright fire remain in Alberta hospitals and seven of them in critical condition, as of Tuesday.
stories.author: Kathy Le
stories.content:
Calgary — More than five weeks after a fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta killed five soldiers and injured dozens more, health officials say 19 remain in hospital in the province, seven of them in critical condition as of Tuesday.

“The immediate emergency response is over now. But for many of those affected, the journey is far from over,” Michael Suddes, interim chief operating officer for Alberta Health Services’ Edmonton corridor, said Thursday.=

Health officials revealed the extent of the demands placed on Alberta’s health-care system following the Oct. 17 fire, which prompted a provincewide emergency response and brought in specialized medical personnel from across the country.

Among the hardest hit was the University of Alberta Hospital in Edmonton, where most of the critically injured soldiers are being treated.

“Within a very short time, we admitted 20 critically ill patients to the intensive care unit, which meant that we were at five times our specialized burn critical care capacity,” said Dr. Josh Wong, interim medical director of the Edmonton Firefighters’ Burn Treatment Unit.

The unit, which typically has four intensive care beds and four high-intensity beds for patients transitioning out of intensive care, was already treating 15 other burn patients.

Specialized medical personnel from Ontario, Manitoba and the Canadian Armed Forces were also brought in to assist.

Just 2 ½ weeks before the fire, burn specialists from across Canada had gathered for a tabletop exercise to discuss how the country would respond to a mass casualty event.

The exercise was held in early October through the Canadian Burn Association.

That collaboration extended beyond providing additional medical personnel.

“We even had one of the surgeons come from Toronto to help us with repatriating the ones that would go back to the Ontario burn centres,” Wong said.

“That support was tremendous.”

Within Alberta, an emergency co-ordination centre was established to oversee the response, with health officials monitoring hospital capacity and mobilizing resources.

Thirty emergency transport units, including 22 ground units, six fixed-wing aircraft and two helicopters, were mobilized to transfer patients from Wainwright.

The injured were taken to the University of Alberta Hospital and Royal Alexandra Hospital in Edmonton, the Foothills Medical Centre in Calgary and the Red Deer Regional Hospital Centre.

While some soldiers have been discharged and others transferred closer to home, Wong said patients with severe burns can require multiple surgeries, extensive rehabilitation and ongoing medical support for months or even years.

Families have also been warned that the emotional challenges of surviving such traumatic injuries May become more pronounced over time.

“The psychological impact actually comes on stronger as they recover and become more aware later on as well,” Wong said.

Health officials are also mindful of the toll the tragedy could take on those working on the front lines.

For the first three weeks following the fire, full-time psychological support was available on site for staff at the University of Alberta Hospital.

Wong said the effects of treating so many severely injured patients could emerge in the weeks and months ahead, as the initial adrenaline subsides.

Suddes said it is too early to identify specific areas for improvement.

For now, Dr. Sayeh Zielke, interim CEO of Acute Care Alberta, said the focus remains on the patients who continue to require treatment.

“For us, it very much feels like a marathon, and we are right in the middle of it,” she said.

stories.title: Vet tranquilizer detected amid spike in Regina overdoses, Saskatchewan health officials warn
stories.summary: The ministry says the substance involved is unknown and May have been sold as fentanyl, methamphetamine, cocaine or other substances.
stories.author: Alessia Simona Maratta
stories.content:
Saskatchewan health officials are warning of an elevated risk of overdose in Regina after a veterinary tranquilizer was detected in the local drug supply amid a spike in overdoses.

Regina Fire and Protective Services and the Regina Overdose Outreach Team reported 28 overdoses over two days, including 16 on Nov. 22 and another 12 on Nov. 23.

The Saskatchewan Ministry of Health says the number of overdoses is elevated compared with daily averages and medical intervention was required in most cases, including transportation to hospital.

The ministry says those figures do not include overdoses responded to by other agencies during the same period.

Officials suspect the overdoses May be linked to medetomidine and/or xylazine in the local drug supply, with one test coming back positive for medetomidine.

Both drugs are veterinary tranquilizers that May have been added to other substances, including fentanyl or methamphetamine.

The ministry says the substance involved is unknown and May have been sold as fentanyl, methamphetamine, cocaine or other substances.

Naloxone was administered in the reported overdoses with varying results. While naloxone can counter the effects of opioids, it does not reverse the effects of other substances such as medetomidine.

Health officials are still recommending naloxone be administered in all suspected overdoses, including when it is unclear which drug caused the overdose, noting it will not harm someone experiencing an overdose.

The overdose alert remains in effect until Dec. 3.

stories.title: Kraft Dinner protest targets Montreal mayor over historic property tax hike
stories.summary: A protest involving Kraft Dinner took aim at Montreal Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada amid backlash over the city’s historic property tax hike.
stories.author: Alessia Simona Maratta, Elizabeth Zogalis
stories.content:
Montrealers armed with pots, portable stoves and Kraft Dinner gathered outside city hall Thursday to protest a historic residential property tax increase and mock the mayor’s controversial remarks about the financial choices facing the city.

Dubbed “Soraya Dinner,” the demonstration took aim at Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada’s comparison of municipal budget decisions to choosing Kraft Dinner over filet mignon.

The remarks came as Montrealers face an average 9.8 per cent residential property tax increase under the city’s proposed 2027 budget, amounting to an additional $515 a year for the average homeowner.

Martinez Ferrada made the comments during a recent interview with Quatre95 , an Urbania platform focused on personal finance, after being asked how her administration intends to increase city revenues.

“It’s just like when you’re putting together your personal budget: If you know you’re going to have less money next year, well, you have to make some choices,” she said.

“Let’s be honest, maybe sometimes we’ll eat a little more Kraft Dinner because we can’t afford filet mignon.”

The comparison quickly drew backlash, prompting Martinez Ferrada to acknowledge Wednesday that the analogy was ill-judged.

“Let’s be honest, it was pretty tactless,” she said in a short social media post.

“What I meant was that when a city makes choices, it’s the same as when you make personal choices,” Martinez Ferrada said. “In this instance, the city has to choose between paying for new parks or filling potholes, and I’m going to choose filling potholes.”

But demonstrators on Thursday said the mayor’s clarification did little to ease their concerns about the affordability of the proposed budget.

“The mayor is talking about fighting homelessness, but she’s also fuelling it with this tax hike,” one protester told Global News.

Protest organizer Raul Garate pointed to concerns about how rising costs could affect renters. “There is a study that said that if there is a rent hike of six per cent, that means that 30,000 people will be more precarious because of that,” Garate said, referring to an analysis by Runwithit Synthetics for Centraide of Greater Montreal that found a six per cent rent increase could push more than 30,000 people into financial precarity, including more than 16,000 into extreme precarity. Others at the demonstration raised concerns about spending on policing.

“We’re investing in the over-surveillance of the population, investing in Flock cameras (AI-powered licence-plate readers), while regular working people are being told to eat Kraft Dinner,” activist Lyn Lee told Global News.

Montreal’s proposed 2027 budget allocates nearly $1 billion to police operations, excluding purchases of body cameras, vehicles and communications equipment.

The budget also includes $40 million for police body cameras and the hiring of 52 additional STM constables.

Global News reached out to the mayor’s office for comment following the backlash but was told Martinez Ferrada was too busy.

The controversy has also inspired an online take on the city’s finances. A Montreal developer created KDGate.CA, an interactive website that presents major budget items and compares spending with the previous year using the format of a Kraft Dinner nutrition facts label.

Global News also reached out to Kraft Canada for comment but did not receive a response before deadline.

The budget will be presented to city council Tuesday.

stories.title: Doerkson arrives in Calgary with sights set on energy sector investments
stories.summary: Visit marks B.C. Premier’s first out-of-province trip since taking office
stories.author: Andrea Woo
stories.content:
B.C. Premier Lorne Doerkson is in Calgary for his first out-of-province trip since taking office, a visit that includes meetings with oil and gas representatives and fellow Western Canadian conservative premiers, as well as an address to Alberta’s United Conservative Party.

The newly sworn-in Premier said he is aiming to meet with the leaders of 15 to 20 energy companies to discuss the Pacific Link pipeline and other potential investments in his province’s energy sector.

“We’re looking for any opportunity that we might be able to capitalize on in British Columbia,” Mr. Doerkson said in an interview on Thursday.

“We’ve had some great upticks recently. We’ve obviously had the federal government announce an expansion of Woodfibre [LNG]. We’re obviously very bullish on natural gas and excited to meet these folks.”

He will also meet with Alberta Premier Danielle Smith and Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe.

“I do think there’s obviously an opportunity to chat with the premiers about a bit more willingness on our part in British Columbia to do what we can to help each other and work forward,” Mr. Doerkson said.

Their meeting will take place one week after the B.C. Conservative cabinet was sworn in following a landslide victory in October’s provincial election and puts the three Western premiers in a position to etch out a shared agenda.

Alberta’s UCP extended invitations to both Mr. Doerkson and Mr. Moe to speak at its annual general meeting this weekend to celebrate the three conservative governments with its members, particularly those fired up about B.C.’s first Conservative government in nearly a century, said Dave Prisco, the party’s director of communications.

“With our three provinces pulling in the same direction, there’s no limit to what we can do together, from getting our resources to market to creating good jobs and making life more affordable across the West,” Mr. Prisco said in an e-mail.

“Premier Danielle Smith has a great relationship with both premiers and is excited to work closely with them.”

Drew Lumbard, executive director of communications for Mr. Moe’s office, confirmed that the Premier will be attending but declined to provide further comment.

Mr. Doerkson declined to comment on what message he planned to deliver in his remarks during the opening ceremony of the UCP annual meeting, which runs Friday through Sunday at BMO Centre.

Mr. Doerkson and Ms. Smith had signalled early that they intended to establish a co-operative relationship.

In a news conference a day after the Oct. 24 election, Mr. Doerkson said his first calls would be to Prime Minister Mark Carney and Ms. Smith to get the Pacific Link pipeline working group moving. Ms. Smith, in return, said the two provinces shared strong economic ties and common interests, and that she looked forward to working with the new B.C. Premier.

The overtures mark a potential reset in relations between the two provinces, which have long clashed over energy and environmental policy. Disagreements have included then-B.C. premier John Horgan’s opposition to the Trans Mountain pipeline expansion and then-Alberta premier Rachel Notley’s retaliatory ban on B.C. wine sales.

More recently, B.C.’s David Eby and Ms. Smith traded barbs over the Alberta Premier’s proposal for a new pipeline to B.C.’s north coast, which would have required repealing a federal tanker ban in the region. Mr. Eby derided the plan as “fictional,” arguing that it had no proponent, no route and no funding.

Asked how he would reconcile competing interests between the two provinces, Mr. Doerkson said his government would always place B.C.’s interests first.

“But I’m obviously very willing and open to conversation with anybody that wants to help British Columbia, so that conversation is wide open,” he said.

Duane Bratt, a political-science professor at Mount Royal University, noted that many Alberta conservatives worked on Mr. Doerkson’s campaign and that there is “clear ideological alignment” between the B.C. Conservatives and the UCP.

“There was ideological alignment between Notley and Horgan, but not on pipelines,” Prof. Bratt said. “Same thing with [premiers] Christy Clark and Alison Redford. But this is different. Doerkson and Smith are on the same page. The challenge for building the pipeline will be Indigenous groups in both provinces – not the B.C. government.”

Kathryn Harrison, a political-science professor at the University of British Columbia, said how far right the B.C. Conservatives land on the political spectrum remains an open question, with implications for its relationship with Alberta.

The resignation of former leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay, the departure of some of the party’s most conservative members and the return of former CentreBC defectors could suggest a revival of the broad coalition that once made up the now-defunct BC Liberal Party, she said.

“If so, I’d expect there would still be a gap between the B.C. and Alberta governments,” Prof. Harrison said. “And that could create challenges for Mr. Doerkson if he signals too much alignment with Danielle Smith’s Alberta Conservatives.”

Alberta’s separatist movement is expected to loom over the gathering, one month after 75 per cent of Albertans rejected separation in a referendum.

On Saturday, The Globe and Mail reported that UCP members remain divided on the issue despite Ms. Smith’s decree that officials within her organization must abandon the quest for secession. Many of the movement’s leaders are prominent players in the UCP and believe that most party members want the organization to continue pushing for separation.

Mr. Doerkson said he is “certainly not a separatist” but would not cast judgment on others.

“I’m here to build relationships with Alberta and other people that want to build British Columbia,” he said.

The overtures mark a potential reset in relations between the two provinces, which have long clashed over energy and environmental policy. Disagreements have included then-B.C. premier John Horgan’s opposition to the Trans Mountain pipeline expansion and then-Alberta premier Rachel Notley’s retaliatory ban on B.C. wine sales.

More recently, B.C.’s David Eby and Ms. Smith traded barbs over the Alberta Premier’s proposal for a new pipeline to B.C.’s north coast, which would have required repealing a federal tanker ban in the region. Mr. Eby derided the plan as “fictional,” arguing that it had no proponent, no route and no funding.
Asked how he would reconcile competing interests between the two provinces, Mr. Doerkson said his government would always place B.C.’s interests first.
“But I’m obviously very willing and open to conversation with anybody that wants to help British Columbia, so that conversation is wide open,” he said.

Duane Bratt, a political-science professor at Mount Royal University, noted that many Alberta conservatives worked on Mr. Doerkson’s campaign and that there is “clear ideological alignment” between the B.C. Conservatives and the UCP.

“There was ideological alignment between Notley and Horgan, but not on pipelines,” Prof. Bratt said. “Same thing with [premiers] Christy Clark and Alison Redford. But this is different. Doerkson and Smith are on the same page. The challenge for building the pipeline will be Indigenous groups in both provinces – not the B.C. government.”

Kathryn Harrison, a political-science professor at the University of British Columbia, said how far right the B.C. Conservatives land on the political spectrum remains an open question, with implications for its relationship with Alberta.

The resignation of former leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay, the departure of some of the party’s most conservative members and the return of former CentreBC defectors could suggest a revival of the broad coalition that once made up the now-defunct BC Liberal Party, she said.

“If so, I’d expect there would still be a gap between the B.C. and Alberta governments,” Prof. Harrison said. “And that could create challenges for Mr. Doerkson if he signals too much alignment with Danielle Smith’s Alberta Conservatives.”
Alberta’s separatist movement is expected to loom over the gathering, one month after 75 per cent of Albertans rejected separation in a referendum.

On Saturday, The Globe and Mail reported that UCP members remain divided on the issue despite Ms. Smith’s decree that officials within her organization must abandon the quest for secession. Many of the movement’s leaders are prominent players in the UCP and believe that most party members want the organization to continue pushing for separation.
Mr. Doerkson said he is “certainly not a separatist” but would not cast judgment on others.
“I’m here to build relationships with Alberta and other people that want to build British Columbia,” he said.

stories.title: ‘I just existed as a Jewish and Israeli student’: Antisemitism unchecked on campuses, report finds
stories.summary: The report surveyed students who do not identify as Jewish about how aware they are of antisemitism, ON campus and online, and how they see it.
stories.author: Heather Wright
stories.content:
Toronto – Hadar Zaidman, a fourth-year communications student at Toronto Metropolitan University, said she grew up learning about antisemitism but had never experienced it herself. That changed three years ago.

“I think that everything kind of happened at once,” Zaidman said.

In the first few months after the Oct. 7 attacks, Zaidman said she lost 99 per cent of her friends.

“I didn’t even, like, post anything political. I just existed as a Jewish and Israeli student. And that was enough to deter people from wanting to be associated with me.”

Her experience reflects the findings of a government-commissioned report released Thursday, which concludes that antisemitism on Canadian university campuses is pervasive and unchecked.

The latest part of the Campus Antisemitism and Student Experiences (Case) project surveyed students who do not identify as Jewish about how aware they are of antisemitism, ON campus and online, and how they see it.

According to the report , 54 per cent of those students did not consider boycotting Jewish-owned businesses or demonstrating outside Jewish houses of worship to protest Israel to be antisemitic. Seventeen per cent agreed that Israel’s military actions in Gaza justify negative attitudes toward Jewish people in Canada.

Thirty-nine per cent agreed that saying the Holocaust is a myth or exaggerated is not antisemitic.

“A lot of the classical elements of what constitute antisemitism are considered not to be antisemitic, and this is wrong,” said Marc Miller, the federal minister of culture and identity.

“These findings are profoundly disturbing,” Simon Wolle, B’nai Brith Canada’s chief executive officer, said in a statement. “They suggest that some of the most historically dangerous expressions of antisemitism are being dismissed and/or accepted within the very institutions entrusted with educating Canada’s next generation.”

The survey follows an earlier Case report released in August that asked Jewish students about their own experiences on campus. In that survey, 96 per cent of respondents said they had experienced or witnessed antisemitism.

TMU student Coby Sadeh said he has been followed on campus and spat at.

“I was at a peaceful protest holding up signs for the release of the hostages,” he recalls. “It was a silent protest, and someone came up to me and spat on me while I was holding up the release-the-hostage signs.”

Both Sadeh and Zaidman say far too often Jews are being blamed for the decisions made by the Israeli government.

“That logic doesn’t translate with any other community, which is when it becomes antisemitism and not just anti-Israel sentiment,” Zaidman said. “Because you can be an Israeli and be against what the Israeli government is doing, just like you can be Canadian and not like what your government is doing.”

The report includes 12 recommendations, among them that universities adopt institutional neutrality, do more to protect Jewish students on campus and better define academic freedom, including developing a code of professional ethics for professors and teachers.

There are also calls for people who are not Jewish to do more and speak up, with many in the Jewish community saying they cannot fight antisemitism alone.

stories.title: Controversial flag on London home draws concern from neighbours and Jewish community
stories.summary: A quiet crescent in northeast London is suddenly a hot spot for political provocation.
stories.author: Bryan Bicknell
stories.content:
A quiet crescent in northeast London is suddenly a hot spot for political provocation.

The front yard of a home in the Stoneybrook neighbourhood has been decorated with several signs and flags with pro-Palestinian messaging, including ‘From THE River TO THE SEA,’ ‘Free Palestine,’ and ‘Nothing Justifies Genocide.’

But another one in particular has created a stir. It’s a flag that hangs on the home with the message ‘F**K Israel.’ There is a Star of David in the middle of the flag with what looks like a large splotch of blood over it.

Eric Robinson, an area resident and the program director at Jewish London, says the message is intimidating.

“I welcome all Canadians to express their political opinions. I never have a problem with that. What we do have an issue with, is one of the flags in particular incites hate against the Jewish people. It seems to suggest violence with the red, splattered blood there. And that goes back to a long history of violence against Jews and blood libels,” Robinson exclaimed, while standing in front of the home in question.

He says no fewer than three Jewish families live on the small street.

But the homeowner, Eve Lebiedowski, is making no apologies.

“It is currently the state of Isreal that is committing a genocide. And I feel it is incumbent upon myself and all other people with conscience to do whatever they can,” Lebiedowski said.

“I’m not saying it against Jewish people. I’m saying it against the state,” she added.

Ward 4 Coun. Tom Cull says he’s fielded several concerns from constituents about the ‘F**K Israel’ flag. He’s waiting to hear from London’s bylaw department to see if any violations are being committed.

When asked if he would like it taken down, he said he would be interested in having a conversation with the homeowner.

“Instances of anti-Semitism and Islamophobia have grown significantly. And I’m not sure that the text or the symbol helps in that regard. I think it turns the temperature up and doesn’t create a circumstance where we can bridge divides,” said Cull.

London Police Acting Insp. Michelle Romano says no crime is being committed by the public display in the front of the home.

“Our hate crime investigators have reviewed this and spoken to the homeowner in regards to this. And it does not meet the definition of a hate crime. We classify this as a hate-incident. This is on private property and is believed to be a political statement only. And that does not meet the definition of a hate-crime,” explained Romano.

CTV News spoke with several neighbours on the street of the home in question. Many expressed that they were upset or offended by the signage, particularly the ‘F**K Israel’ flag. None wanted to appear on camera, saying they feared retribution from the homeowner.

Not all feel that way, however. Other neighbours CTV news spoke with defended what they say is the homeowner’s right to display the symbols on her own property.

“No, I don’t think that I’m inciting any type of hate. What I’m showing to whomever sees these things is that the position is, and must remain on the right side of history,” stated Lebiedowski.

Robinson is asking that the flag be taken down.

“For anyone living here, Jewish or not, having someone suggest violence in the symbols that they choose to fly is very concerning, and it’s not the Canadian way. I just hope they think better of it,” he said.

stories.title: Funding future for Calgary’s Foothills Fieldhouse questioned during budget talks
stories.summary: A lack of funding commitments from other orders of government has some Calgary city councillors considering reallocating funding for the Foothills Fieldhouse to other priorities.
stories.author: Adam MacVicar
stories.content:
It’s been on the books for nearly a decade but proposed spending on Calgary’s planned Foothills Fieldhouse is being questioned as city council prepares to deliberate its four-year budget.

The project, which is slated for the site of the former Burns Stadium near the University of Calgary and McMahon Stadium, intends to include spaces for field sports, courts and a 200-metre indoor track with space for spectators.

The City of Calgary previously allocated $109 million into a reserve fund for the project, and the proposed four-year budget earmarks an additional $70 million towards the fieldhouse.

However, the city hasn’t been able to secure funding from the province or federal government, despite repeated requests for $180 million each.

Since the proposed 2027-30 budget was publicly released earlier this month, a number of city councillors have suggested using the funding elsewhere.

“It’s going to be very difficult for council to continue to sit on these funds after 10 years being idle without any provincial or federal funding,” Calgary mayor Jeromy Farkas told reporters. “But that’s not to say that we can go it alone either. The ask to the province is if not the fieldhouse, then what?”

The budget proposes $284 million for recreation projects across the city, but only funds four of 17 projects prioritized in the first phase of the city’s GamePLAN strategy .

Those projects include the fieldhouse, the Forest Lawn recreation facility replacement, as well as Kingsland and Belmont athletic parks.

“If you did pull that lever back, there’s several other facilities that could be funded,” Ward 12 Coun. Mike Jamieson said. “There’s an argument there that there’s a greater good in pulling that and moving it. There’s an argument that a lot of us are considering right now.”

As city council continues to hear from Calgarians during a public hearing on the proposed budget, a number of speakers have noted support for the fieldhouse project as part of a push for more recreation spaces.

Dale Schoenthaler, a track and field coach in Calgary for the last 30 years, said local track teams need to travel to Edmonton and Saskatoon during the indoor season as those cities have fieldhouses that can accommodate track.

According to Schoenthaler, Calgary’s lack of a fieldhouse with track amenities has forced teams to be creative when it comes to practices too.

“One of the big things now is (The MNP Centre) has resurfaced their track and now we’re not allowed to wear track spikes, so that’s taking away one more major thing for our training,” he said.

Schoenthaler noted the city misses out on hosting at least five major track meets annually due to its facilities, and said a reallocation of funding for the Foothills Fieldhouse would be detrimental to years of advocacy efforts.

“It would be a huge issue for us,” he said, “I don’t know where we would begin again, to start all over.”

Jasmine Mian, who formerly represented Ward 3 on the previous city council, also spoke in favour of the funding.

Mian urged city council to wait until after the provincial election before making any decisions around the Foothills Fieldhouse funding.

“These are the types of projects that really get funded in an election, you’re not going to get a provincial government giving you $100 million for a project like that mid-cycle,” she told council. “I’ll be back here next year if the city doesn’t get any traction from the provincial government, telling you reallocate it to other recreation priorities.”

Back in 2023, the Foothills Fieldhouse was estimated to cost $380 million, but that cost is likely to be around $500 million, according to Ward 5 Coun. Raj Dhaliwal.

Dhaliwal, who chairs the Foothills Multisport Fieldhouse committee, said making changes to the project’s funding is “insanity,” and would send a poor signal to provincial and federal governments.

“We shouldn’t even be talking about it right now,” he told reporters. “I think it should be where it is right now, which is demonstrating to other levels of government that we are committed, that we are fully in.”

The Foothills Fieldhouse was listed in 2019 as one of four major city projects at the time along with the BMO Centre Expansion, the Werklund Centre transformation, and the new event centre.

It is the only one of those projects not completed or under construction.

“I’ve heard we’ve never been closer to provincial funding for a fieldhouse,” Farkas said. “I’ve heard that this year, I’ve heard it last year, I’ve heard it the year before that. I heard it in my final year as a city councillor, at this point we’ve really got to shoot or get off the ice.”

stories.title: Antisemitism pervasive, unchecked on Canadian campuses: report
stories.summary: The report surveyed students who do not identify as Jewish about how aware they are of antisemitism, ON campus and online, and how they see it.
stories.author: Heather Wright
stories.content:
Toronto – Hadar Zaidman, a fourth-year communications student at Toronto Metropolitan University, said she grew up learning about antisemitism but had never experienced it herself. That changed three years ago.

“I think that everything kind of happened at once,” Zaidman said.

In the first few months after the Oct. 7 attacks, Zaidman said she lost 99 per cent of her friends.

“I didn’t even, like, post anything political. I just existed as a Jewish and Israeli student. And that was enough to deter people from wanting to be associated with me.”

Her experience reflects the findings of a government-commissioned report released Thursday, which concludes that antisemitism on Canadian university campuses is pervasive and unchecked.

The latest part of the Campus Antisemitism and Student Experiences (Case) project surveyed students who do not identify as Jewish about how aware they are of antisemitism, ON campus and online, and how they see it.

According to the report , 54 per cent of those students did not consider boycotting Jewish-owned businesses or demonstrating outside Jewish houses of worship to protest Israel to be antisemitic. Seventeen per cent agreed that Israel’s military actions in Gaza justify negative attitudes toward Jewish people in Canada.

Thirty-nine per cent agreed that saying the Holocaust is a myth or exaggerated is not antisemitic.

“A lot of the classical elements of what constitute antisemitism are considered not to be antisemitic, and this is wrong,” said Marc Miller, the federal minister of culture and identity.

“These findings are profoundly disturbing,” Simon Wolle, B’nai Brith Canada’s chief executive officer, said in a statement. “They suggest that some of the most historically dangerous expressions of antisemitism are being dismissed and/or accepted within the very institutions entrusted with educating Canada’s next generation.”

The survey follows an earlier Case report released in August that asked Jewish students about their own experiences on campus. In that survey, 96 per cent of respondents said they had experienced or witnessed antisemitism.

TMU student Coby Sadeh said he has been followed on campus and spat at.

“I was at a peaceful protest holding up signs for the release of the hostages,” he recalls. “It was a silent protest, and someone came up to me and spat on me while I was holding up the release-the-hostage signs.”

Both Sadeh and Zaidman say far too often Jews are being blamed for the decisions made by the Israeli government.

“That logic doesn’t translate with any other community, which is when it becomes antisemitism and not just anti-Israel sentiment,” Zaidman said. “Because you can be an Israeli and be against what the Israeli government is doing, just like you can be Canadian and not like what your government is doing.”

The report includes 12 recommendations, among them that universities adopt institutional neutrality, do more to protect Jewish students on campus and better define academic freedom, including developing a code of professional ethics for professors and teachers.

There are also calls for people who are not Jewish to do more and speak up, with many in the Jewish community saying they cannot fight antisemitism alone.
