content_blocks.text: Her experience reflects the findings of a government-commissioned report released Thursday, which concludes that antisemitism on Canadian university campuses is pervasive and unchecked.

The latest part of the Campus Antisemitism and Student Experiences (Case) project surveyed students who do not identify as Jewish about how aware they are of antisemitism, ON campus and online, and how they see it.

According to the report , 54 per cent of those students did not consider boycotting Jewish-owned businesses or demonstrating outside Jewish houses of worship to protest Israel to be antisemitic. Seventeen per cent agreed that Israel’s military actions in Gaza justify negative attitudes toward Jewish people in Canada.
Thirty-nine per cent agreed that saying the Holocaust is a myth or exaggerated is not antisemitic.
“A lot of the classical elements of what constitute antisemitism are considered not to be antisemitic, and this is wrong,” said Marc Miller, the federal minister of culture and identity.

“These findings are profoundly disturbing,” Simon Wolle, B’nai Brith Canada’s chief executive officer, said in a statement. “They suggest that some of the most historically dangerous expressions of antisemitism are being dismissed and/or accepted within the very institutions entrusted with educating Canada’s next generation.”

The survey follows an earlier Case report released in August that asked Jewish students about their own experiences on campus. In that survey, 96 per cent of respondents said they had experienced or witnessed antisemitism.
TMU student Coby Sadeh said he has been followed on campus and spat at.

“I was at a peaceful protest holding up signs for the release of the hostages,” he recalls. “It was a silent protest, and someone came up to me and spat on me while I was holding up the release-the-hostage signs.”

content_blocks.alt: TMU
content_blocks.caption: Students make their way around the renamed Toronto Metropolitan University (TMU), formerly known as Ryerson University in Toronto on Wednesday, April 26, 2023. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Nathan Denette

content_blocks.text: Both Sadeh and Zaidman say far too often Jews are being blamed for the decisions made by the Israeli government.

“That logic doesn’t translate with any other community, which is when it becomes antisemitism and not just anti-Israel sentiment,” Zaidman said. “Because you can be an Israeli and be against what the Israeli government is doing, just like you can be Canadian and not like what your government is doing.”

The report includes 12 recommendations, among them that universities adopt institutional neutrality, do more to protect Jewish students on campus and better define academic freedom, including developing a code of professional ethics for professors and teachers.
There are also calls for people who are not Jewish to do more and speak up, with many in the Jewish community saying they cannot fight antisemitism alone.

November 26, 2026 at 7:50 p.m.

Ottawa — A former member of Ontario’s Maid death review committee told parliamentarians Thursday that the assisted deaths of two Ontario patients appear to have been in violation of Canada’s Criminal Code and should have been referred to police.

During her two years on the oversight committee, “many cases were actually published that I think really test the limits of the law,” said Ramona Coelho, who is a family doctor in London, Ont.

In her appearance before a Commons committee Thursday, she described two unpublished cases.

One involved a woman with a history of severe mental illness, she said.

“She had Dying with Dignity and a reporter involved in her Maid journey, which I am concerned about could be coercive influences to go forward with Maid,” Coelho told the justice and human rights committee reviewing Bill C-41, a new piece of legislation that would extend the prohibition of Maid for mental illness alone indefinitely.

“When we looked at the case, the neurologist said there was no physical diagnosis. She only had mental illness,” Coelho told the committee.

The post-mortem listed no abnormalities, she said. The death review committee was also told the woman had undergone a single Maid assessment. The law requires two assessments from two independent doctors or nurse practitioners.

“I think that’s a clear violation of Maid eligibility,” said Coelho, an adjunct research professor in Western University’s department of family medicine.

A second case “that still haunts” her involved a man in his 30s “who was not considered to have capacity to do any of his treatment decisions,” Coelho said.

Dr. Ramona Coelho in Edmonton on March 18, 2026. Shaughn Butts/Postmedia

A family member was consulted “for everything, even when he could take over-the-counter medications.”

The same family member told the clinical team they were concerned he wouldn’t be eligible for Maid. “They were disappointed,” she said.

After several hospital meetings, but no change in his health status, “all of a sudden he became eligible for Maid,” Coelho said.

She said it was documented in nursing notes that the family member had asked that he not be told that he could change his mind.

In his health history, he had reported several years earlier that the family member had been abusing him, she said. Coelho described the case as a “conspiracy to end his life.”

“I consider that to be a gross violation” of the Criminal Code.

She said that, to her knowledge, the cases had not been referred to police.

She said the cases were not published in reports from the death review committee “and I think it’s because they were frankly illegal,” she said.

“But that is my speculation.”

The justice and human rights committee passed a motion to request documents related to the two cases from the Office of the Chief Coroner.

As of last December, the coroner’s office had referred 13 practitioners to their licensing colleges over concerns identified in death review investigations since Maid was legalized in 2016.

The office can refer cases to police if a referral is necessary. “However, to ensure the integrity of any investigation, information cannot be shared regarding the notification or investigation,” the coroner’s office said in an email to National Post last December.

stories.title: Advisory council to issue antisemitism report as Jewish groups call out campus hate
stories.summary: The government launched the equity and inclusion council in June after scrapping the role of federal envoy on antisemitism and another one touching on Islamophobia.
stories.author: Dylan Robertson
stories.content:
The federal government’s new equity council will publish its first report in December with a focus on anti-Jewish hate, along with a government response, Heritage Minister Marc Miller said.

“The report, that is very summary in nature, will be released in the next week or two,” Miller said Thursday. “These are recommendations that have been formulated to me. In full transparency, I want the public to be able to benefit from those.”

The government launched the equity and inclusion council in June after scrapping the role of federal envoy on antisemitism and another one touching on Islamophobia. Miller has argued the change could help various communities experiencing hate to work together.

Jewish organization B’nai Brith Canada said earlier this month that the council has “done nothing” since June, even as dozens of antisemitic incidents have taken place. That included a shooting outside a synagogue in Belleville, Ont., ON Yom Kippur in September. A police officer hired to stand guard outside the synagogue was seriously injured, and the attacker was killed.

The council has made antisemitism its priority focus while also pledging to undertake work affecting other communities, such as Islamophobia and anti-Lgbtq+ discrimination.

Miller said the council’s next focus won’t be a pivot away from anti-Jewish hate but will take a closer look at other issues, including ensuring prosecutors understand matters affecting places of worship.

“There are many intersections, particularly when it comes to campus hate, where groups are targeted. There are intersections as to how government institutions deal with bigotry within our own institutions,” he said.

“There is also the importance of the leadership role that the federal government plays, in the complex web that is our federation in making sure that we are doing our job.”

Miller was speaking at a Thursday news conference where his department released a government-funded study about how non-Jewish post-secondary students understand antisemitism.

The report found two-thirds of non-Jewish students surveyed believe it is not antisemitic to call for Israel to cease to exist as a state. It found 17 per cent of respondents agreed that Israel’s military actions in Gaza justify negative attitudes toward Jewish people in Canada.

Authors of the report say the online survey shows troubling beliefs that seek to hold Canadian Jews accountable for the actions of the Israeli government.

Jewish groups argue campuses are going beyond legitimate criticism of Israel by allowing hateful beliefs to spread across colleges and universities and failing to enforce their codes of conduct.

“The survey includes several troubling revelations that see far too many students unable to recognize classic antisemitic stereotypes as they are,” said Jack Jedwab, head of the Association for Canadian Studies.

Thursday’s study follows an August report that surveyed Jewish students across Canada who reported frequent antisemitic comments. That survey was criticized by Jewish groups who are skeptical of the Israeli government and military — they argued it recruited student respondents through groups aligned with Israel.

Unlike the August report, Thursday’s report did not provide the entire list of questions asked to students.

The respondents in Thursday’s report attributed most incidents of antisemitism — such as Nazi salutes or comments that seek to minimize the Holocaust — to fellow students rather than instructors.

A slight majority of non-Jewish students told the online survey that it’s not antisemitic to boycott Jewish-owned businesses.

Jedwab did not confirm if the survey differentiated between boycotting a business because it is owned by Jewish people and boycotting those who explicitly fundraise for Israeli soldiers or promote land sales in the occupied Palestinian territories.

Some pro-Palestinian groups argue they target protests at institutions in Canada that explicitly support the Israeli state. But some acts of vandalism and threats have targeted institutions and businesses across Canada with no apparent links to the Israeli government or security forces.

The Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs and some Hillel campus groups said in a joint statement that tropes and conspiracies can spur physical attacks.

“This report reveals a significant gap in how antisemitism is experienced by Jewish students and understood by the general student population,” the groups wrote. “This gap is especially concerning as Canadian security agencies have warned about the growing threat of radicalization and violent extremism, particularly among young Canadians.”

stories.title: Thames Valley Family Health Team workers warn of possible strike amid stalled contract talks
stories.summary: Workers with the Thames Valley Family Health Team (Tvfht) took part in information pickets Thursday, calling for a fair deal as contract negotiations remain stalled.
stories.author: Reta Ismail
stories.content:
The pickets were held at five locations across the region, including London, Middlesex, Woodstock, St. Thomas, and Strathroy.

Represented by Opseu Local 176, the employees are seeking their first collective agreement with the publicly funded primary-care organization. Negotiations began in the spring, but the two sides have yet to reach a deal.

Andrea Hunt, vice-president of Opseu Local 176, says workers are frustrated with the lack of progress.

“We don’t want to do more with less. We’re tired and we’re here for our patients, and we want to serve them as best as we can,” Hunt said during Thursday’s rally.

The union says management has proposed a one per cent wage increase over three years. It is also raising concerns about workload, burnout, and proposed changes to breaks and time off.

Opseu says members delivered a strong strike mandate in a vote last week, with 92 per cent participating and 93 per cent of those voting in favour of job action.

“We are the largest family health organization across Ontario, and we service a lot of patients,” Hunt said.

The organization serves more than 162,000 patients through 19 clinical sites across London, Middlesex, Elgin, and Oxford counties.

Executive Director Mike McMahon says the organization recognizes the importance of its employees and remains committed to reaching a collective agreement.

Tvfht recently received approximately $20 million in provincial funding to help expand access to primary care. The union has questioned why that investment has not translated into a stronger wage offer.

McMahon says the funding is specifically intended to connect more people with primary-care providers.

“Expansion resources are not available for us to sit down and use those resources to settle a collective agreement. Expansion resources are so that more people across Thames Valley can experience having a primary-care provider,” McMahon said.

He says the organization wants employees to feel valued, noting that their working conditions are closely tied to the quality of care patients receive.

“Satisfied employees, employees that feel valued are in health care the best service providers for the patients in our communities,” McMahon said.

Hunt says workers want to return to the bargaining table and avoid job action, warning that a strike could have far-reaching consequences.

“The disruption that this May cause to patients is going to be astronomical,” she said.

stories.title: Supreme Court set to rule on Quebec secularism law in landmark Charter case
stories.summary: The Supreme Court is set to rule on Quebec’s secularism law in a landmark case that could reshape how governments use the notwithstanding clause.
stories.author: Alessia Simona Maratta
stories.content:
The Supreme Court of Canada is set to hand down a highly anticipated ruling Friday on Quebec’s controversial secularism law, a decision that could change how provinces use the Constitution’s notwithstanding clause and override charter rights.

At the heart of the case is Bill 21 , a provincial law adopted on June 16, 2019, by the Coalition Avenir Québec government led by then-premier François Legault.

The government invoked closure to pass the legislation, which also pre-emptively invoked the notwithstanding clause. The use of the notwithstanding clause shielded the law from challenges based on charter rights to freedom of conscience and religion and equality rights.

The law, designed to enforce state secularism, bars public sector workers in positions of authority from wearing religious symbols on the job, including hijabs, kippahs and turbans. The law also requires people offering and receiving government services to have their faces uncovered while doing so.

But Friday’s ruling could have implications beyond the province of Quebec.

The country’s top court has been asked to consider whether there are limits on governments’ use of Section 33 of the Constitution, known as the notwithstanding clause, which allows legislatures to override certain Charter rights.

Since 2019, Quebec, Ontario, Saskatchewan and Alberta have invoked the clause to shield controversial legislation from legal challenges, including laws restricting the rights of transgender people in Alberta and Saskatchewan and Quebec’s language-law reforms.

Some legal observers say Friday’s decision could be studied by law students for generations, while others see it as a potential stepping stone toward lasting change rather than the final word.

The law applies to public school teachers, police officers, government lawyers and other officials. A grandfather clause exempts those who were already employed before the bill was tabled, provided they do not change jobs.

Bill 21 has faced sharp opposition since its introduction, with critics arguing it disproportionately targets racialized religious minorities, particularly Muslim women who wear the hijab, by forcing them to choose between some public sector jobs, like teaching, and their religious beliefs.

Former premier Legault defended the legislation as a “moderate” way to settle Quebec’s long-running debate over secularism and religious accommodation.

His government later extended the ban on religious symbols to everyone who interacts with children in public daycares, elementary schools and high schools, including volunteers.

The law has been challenged by teachers, religious and civil liberties groups and the English Montreal School Board (Emsb), which argued it violates constitutional rights and exceeds Quebec’s legislative authority.

Lower courts upheld most provisions of the law, but the Supreme Court was also asked to determine whether Quebec properly used the notwithstanding clause, whether there are limits on its use and whether a court can still declare that Bill 21 violates Charter rights.

The Supreme Court heard the case over four days last March in what was one of the longest hearings in its history. 61 parties participated in the case, including 51 interveners, which the court says is a record number.

The federal government participated as an intervener and asked the court to impose limits on how provincial governments can override the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Quebec’s newly elected premier and Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon recently vowed to defend the province’s secularism laws. He also pledged to extend the ban on religious symbols to schoolchildren .

–with files from The Canadian Press

stories.title: Ford says gambling ads are ‘out of control,’ but his government is resisting calls for a quick ban
stories.summary: Days after Premier Doug Ford said online gambling ads are "out of control" and need to be curbed, his government is resisting a push to ban them by the end of the year.
stories.author: Rob Ferguson
stories.content:
Days after Premier Doug Ford said online gambling ads are “out of control” and need to be curbed, his government is resisting a push to ban them by the end of the year.

Opposition parties pressed his government Thursday to pass a ban before the legislature rises for its Christmas break, insisting action is urgent because of a rise in emergency room visits from distraught problem gamblers as well as increased suicides, bankruptcies and help hotline calls.

stories.title: Make-A-Wish Canada’s Trees of Joy illuminate London with holiday magic for local children
stories.summary: The Make-A-Wish Canada Foundation brought an early wave of holiday magic to London, Ont. Thursday morning, holding a "Trees of Joy" celebration at RBC Place.
stories.author: Gerry Dewan
stories.content:
The Make-A-Wish Canada Foundation brought an early wave of holiday magic to London, Ont. Thursday morning, holding a “Trees of Joy” celebration at RBC Place.

The annual event transformed the venue into a festive wonderland, dedicated to bringing hope and joy to local children facing critical illnesses.

Now in its third year, Trees of Joy saw 16 local wish children and their families parade into the RBC Place ballroom just after 10 a.m. They were greeted by a dazzling display of 16 custom-decorated trees.

Each tree was meticulously crafted by local businesses and community agencies, reflecting the unique passions, interests, and personalities of the child it was designed for. Complementing the festive trees was a collection of presents, thoughtfully chosen to match each child’s personalized theme.

Among the wish children celebrated was 14-year-old Emma Moon, who has been navigating a challenging health journey for over three and a half years.

Emma was diagnosed with acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), a condition initially resistant to treatment, which necessitated a life-altering bone marrow transplant.

The procedure required Emma and her mother, Amy Moon, to spend three months at Toronto’s Sick Kids Hospital. Emma continues to receive ongoing treatment.

Amy Moon shared with CTV News that the support extending beyond medical treatment has been invaluable to Emma’s recovery and overall well-being.

“Now she’s, you know, really herself,” Amy Moon stated. “And so to be able to think about what she likes and to have people really see that and create something for her is incredibly special.”

Bonnie Shepherd of Make-A-Wish Canada emphasized the profound impact of these wishes on the children and their families.

“That’s why we say wishes are medicine, because it really does bring them something that is theirs and that they can really look forward to it as well,” Shepherd explained. “So the partners in this room are helping us raise money that will grant even more kids wishes going forward.”

The custom trees, which ranged from musical themes to pop culture inspirations like the Grinch, are later delivered to the wish families’ homes, extending the spirit of the season and the joy of their unique celebrations.

Make-A-Wish Canada is currently working to fulfill the wishes of over 3,500 eligible children across the country, with approximately 1,200 children in Ontario still waiting for their wish to be granted.

Funds raised through initiatives like Trees of Joy directly support these life-changing wish journeys, providing crucial hope, strength, and encouragement.

stories.title: Summerland woman’s stolen family coin collection rebuilt by content creator
stories.summary: When Marcia Kozak evacuated Summerland during the Bald range wildfire, she took some of the most important things she could with her, her cat and her late mother’s coin collection.
stories.author: Cohan Sassaman
stories.content:
When Marcia Kozak evacuated Summerland during the Bald Range wildfire, she took some of the most important things she could with her: her cat and her late mother’s coin collection.

She ended up living out of her vehicle in Penticton and Kelowna during the evacuation. While she was away from it, someone broke in and stole the collection.

The coins were worth an estimated $10,000, but for Kozak, they were worth far more. The collection had been passed down from her mother and carried years of family memories.

“The coin collection meant family time, being together, sitting there with my mom and my niece and myself across the old kitchen table that we had, and just spending time together,” Kozak said.

Thousands of kilometres away in Florida, coin collector and content creator who goes by International Stacker heard about Kozak’s story. He keeps his identity private because of security concerns related to travelling and dealing with valuable gold and silver. He says keeping his name and personal information out of the public eye helps protect himself and his collection.

As a collector himself, he believed there was a way he could help.

He reached out to his online community, asking fellow collectors if they would donate coins from their own collections to help recreate Kozak’s lost family heirloom.

“We knew we could never replace her mother’s coins, you know, the mental imagery and the emotions tied to that,” International Stacker said. “But we wanted to try to help restore her faith in humanity.”

More than 100 people responded with coins. Others contributed money so International Stacker could search for specific pieces to recreate the collection.

The search took him across the United States and into Canada, where he visited coin conventions, markets and dealers looking for rare and matching pieces.

After more than a month of travelling and searching, International Stacker arrived in Summerland with a rebuilt collection containing more than 300 coins, matching the collection Kozak lost, with additional pieces added.

He also presented Kozak with $4,000 in leftover donations from his subscribers.

“When we gave her that cash, and I just literally saw like thousands of pounds lift off her shoulder when she said she wasn’t sure how she was going to pay the next heat bill or the rent,” International Stacker said.

International Stacker says the effort grew far beyond the original group of collectors. More than 70,000 people ultimately helped in some way by donating coins or money, or sharing Kozak’s story.

For Kozak, the response was about more than replacing the coins.

“It’s overwhelming. I was almost crying during it because it was just such an incredible journey that I managed to get into. And I just couldn’t believe how loving people were,” she said.

Kozak added that when she first heard from International Stacker, she considered how he might be a scammer and almost didn’t reply.

The original collection has never been recovered.

But Kozak says she never plans to sell the new collection. While it isn’t the collection her mother originally gave her, she says she now feels connected to it in a different way, because each coin represents the strangers who came together to help her, while still reminding her of her mother and the collection she lost.

“Seventy thousand people, you’ve healed my heart and I restored my faith in humanity again,” Kozak said.

“When a bunch of strangers on the internet come together, you’d be surprised how much of a change you can make in somebody’s life,” International stacker added.

paragraphs: When Marcia Kozak evacuated Summerland during the Bald Range wildfire, she took some of the most important things she could with her: her cat and her late mother’s coin collection.
She ended up living out of her vehicle in Penticton and Kelowna during the evacuation. While she was away from it, someone broke in and stole the collection.
The coins were worth an estimated $10,000, but for Kozak, they were worth far more. The collection had been passed down from her mother and carried years of family memories.
“The coin collection meant family time, being together, sitting there with my mom and my niece and myself across the old kitchen table that we had, and just spending time together,” Kozak said.

Thousands of kilometres away in Florida, coin collector and content creator who goes by International Stacker heard about Kozak’s story. He keeps his identity private because of security concerns related to travelling and dealing with valuable gold and silver. He says keeping his name and personal information out of the public eye helps protect himself and his collection.
As a collector himself, he believed there was a way he could help.
He reached out to his online community, asking fellow collectors if they would donate coins from their own collections to help recreate Kozak’s lost family heirloom.

“We knew we could never replace her mother’s coins, you know, the mental imagery and the emotions tied to that,” International Stacker said. “But we wanted to try to help restore her faith in humanity.”
More than 100 people responded with coins. Others contributed money so International Stacker could search for specific pieces to recreate the collection.
The search took him across the United States and into Canada, where he visited coin conventions, markets and dealers looking for rare and matching pieces.

After more than a month of travelling and searching, International Stacker arrived in Summerland with a rebuilt collection containing more than 300 coins, matching the collection Kozak lost, with additional pieces added.
He also presented Kozak with $4,000 in leftover donations from his subscribers.

“When we gave her that cash, and I just literally saw like thousands of pounds lift off her shoulder when she said she wasn’t sure how she was going to pay the next heat bill or the rent,” International Stacker said.
International Stacker says the effort grew far beyond the original group of collectors. More than 70,000 people ultimately helped in some way by donating coins or money, or sharing Kozak’s story.
For Kozak, the response was about more than replacing the coins.
“It’s overwhelming. I was almost crying during it because it was just such an incredible journey that I managed to get into. And I just couldn’t believe how loving people were,” she said.
Kozak added that when she first heard from International Stacker, she considered how he might be a scammer and almost didn’t reply.
The original collection has never been recovered.

But Kozak says she never plans to sell the new collection. While it isn’t the collection her mother originally gave her, she says she now feels connected to it in a different way, because each coin represents the strangers who came together to help her, while still reminding her of her mother and the collection she lost.
“Seventy thousand people, you’ve healed my heart and I restored my faith in humanity again,” Kozak said.
“When a bunch of strangers on the internet come together, you’d be surprised how much of a change you can make in somebody’s life,” International stacker added.

For Kozak, what started as a devastating loss has become a new family heirloom carrying the memory of her mother, while also carrying the story of the people from around the world who helped bring it back.

stories.title: Meteor enters the sky over London, Ont. at 90 times the speed of sound
stories.summary: A green trail of light seen over the skies of London and southwestern Ontario Wednesday evening was a meteor moving at 90 times the speed of sound.
stories.author: Sean Irvine
stories.content:
A green trail of light seen over the skies of London and southwestern Ontario Wednesday evening was a meteor moving at 90 times the speed of sound.

It was caught by multiple cameras, including one monitoring a downtown London freight train.

At 7:40 p.m. Wednesday, a flare of green light appeared in the night sky above the train, followed by a cosmic trail.

In another case, Londoner Scott Dawe was heading to a friend’s home in the city’s east end when his vehicle dashcam caught a green flash.

“And all of a sudden, in the top right of my windshield, it was just a bright light. And I saw it, and I was like, are there fireworks? Is there something like crashing down?” Dawe recalled.

Scientific cameras in the Southwestern Ontario Meteor Network also recorded the inbound object, later determined to be a large meteor.

“We think it was roughly basketball sized. And moving at those speeds, of course, it’s bright. It was sort of comparable to the moon in the sky in terms of brightness last night,” said Peter Brown, a physics and astronomy professor at Western University.

Using cameras and other data, researchers determined the meteor was part of the Taurid meteor shower that occurs annually between September and December.

Debris comes from the comet Encke .

Brown said a piece of that debris was setting its sights on the Forest City, “It came in almost right over London, moving down towards Detroit.”

The meteor continued along a path over southwestern Ontario before it burned up well above Michigan.

It is believed no fragments impacted the earth.

Still, Brown conceded it made for quite a show, “One or two bright meteors over North America any given night. So, it’s unusual for it to happen so close to London.”

Dawe said he was thrilled to have witnessed a celestial treat millions of years in the making that vanished in seconds, “As quickly as I saw it, it was done. And I was just, you know, blown away by the sight of it!”

stories.title: Restoring the bison population May be possible, ‘groundbreaking’ study finds
stories.summary: A University of Saskatchewan-led paper researched the genetics of modern bison and compared it to the DNA structure of ancient bison.
stories.author: Tavi Dhillon
stories.content:
A University of Saskatchewan-led study May be the blueprint for genetically restoring the once-plentiful population of American bison in North America.

The paleogenomic research was done by the Bison Integrated Genome (BIG) project. It compared the complete DNA set, or genomes, of 115 ancient, 200 to 20,000-year-old wood and plain bison, to 45 modern ones.

“We’ve made huge progress in understanding bison biology,” Gregg Adams, one of the principal investigators with BIG, said. Adams is also a retired professor from the University of Saskatchewan’s Western College of Veterinary Medicine.

“We need to know what a pure plains bison is and what a pure wood bison is before we messed with the mix. We thought if we get ancient DNA, we could get the gold standard of what they were and what they had evolved to over thousands and thousands of years. And then we’d know how we can get back to that.”

In the paper, dozens of researchers found the most glaring difference of the genetic makeup of a modern American bison, when compared to the ancient animals, is the high degree of fragmentation between herds. Prior to the industrial revolution, bison travelled as a “monstrous, roaming herd across North America,” Adams said.

The various herds interacted and interbred during those journeys, creating genetic diversity, he added.

Bison were once populous in the Great Plains of North America, which spans into parts of Canada’s Prairie provinces and territories. That population of approximately 30 million began to dwindle in the 19th century as European settlers hunted the animals for their hides, meat or as sport until only hundreds remained.

“Despite this decline, genetic diversity remained stable, although subsequent drift and isolation led to the high degree of structure in bison herds today,” according to the study.

That “subsequent drift” was partly the result of the introduction of roads and railways, Adams said.

“There’s no way for those bison herds to move and so, they have become disconnected. And when they’re disconnected, by definition, they’re in isolation,” he added. “That isolation will eventually cause the demise of a small population.”

Another consequence of that drift was the structural change in the ancestry of all modern wood bison, who now carry plains bison ancestry.

This occurred during the 1920 translocation of plain bison from northern Montana in the United States to a park in Wainwright, Alta., to Wood Buffalo National Park, located in northern Alberta and the southern Northwest Territories, when the animals bred with one another, Adams said.

“That caused two serious, serious problems in conserving the bison. One is that resulted in the immediate start of hybridization between plains bison and wood bison,” Adams added. “The second, terrible, thing was it resulted in the introduction of cattle diseases.”

Ultimately, the study concluded that as a result of their near extinction, there was a widespread loss of genetic diversity among the American bison – though, it noted that that loss was not the result of interbreeding with cattle.

“Restoring gene flow across herds managed as a metapopulation could more closely mirror past population structure, while ensuring the maintenance of diversity and preventing the fixation of cattle alleles,” the study said.

Allele fixation occurs when a specific gene is present in every single animal in a herd.

In news release, the University of Saskatchewan said this research can be used to inform project partners, including the Toronto Zoo and Parks Canada. By bettering understandings of bison genetics, researchers can help to mitigate related challenges by introducing more genetic diversity to herds and decreasing the risk of disease transmission.

“We got really what I think is a blueprint of what bison were before we messed it up. And that’s amazing,” Adams told Global News.

He said now researchers can take the sperm and eggs of modern bison and determine “which herds are missing which genes or which herds are hybrid. And make a strategic decision.”

“Every time I think about it, I get goosebumps. It really is groundbreaking,” Adams continued. “We are really in a position where we can do something. We can make an impact.”

Adams said the research can be used to help inform research models for other at-risk species.

stories.title: McGuinty investigating after Poilievre said nurse’s job threatened over photo
stories.summary: Poilievre said his privilege as a MP was breached when a nurse was told she might lose her job after she was photographed speaking with him at the Wainwright base.
stories.author: Catherine Morrison
stories.content:
Defence Minister David McGuinty says he has been working to resolve a situation involving a government contractor and a nurse after Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said her job was threatened over a photo with him at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright last month.

“I happen to agree with Mr. Poilievre that constituents should always feel free and MPs should always be able to speak to their constituents,” McGuinty said when asked about the matter at a House of Commons committee on Thursday.

Poilievre rose on a point of privilege in the House of Commons Wednesday. He said his privilege as a member of Parliament was breached when a nurse was told she might lose her job after she was photographed speaking with him in the aftermath of the tragic fire at the Wainwright base.

Poilievre’s Alberta riding includes Wainwright, about two hours southeast of Edmonton. He spent several days in the area after a fire suddenly overtook a training area on the base on Oct. 17, killing five soldiers and injuring dozens of others.

Poilievre said he met with the nurse, Maureen Carpenter, who works at both the Wainwright hospital and on contract with Calian Health. He said she talked to him about her experiences after the fire, when she helped triage and treat badly burned patients.

Thirty-nine people were injured in the fire, 19 of them critically.

Poilievre told the House on Wednesday that the “implicit message was that her contract would no longer have any chance of renewal, something that she had taken for granted before that point.

“Other work opportunities which were also expected to follow have since vanished.

“Simply put, it appears she is losing her chance to continue her work at CFB Wainwright because she met with her local MP.” Poilievre said the situation affects his ability to do his job.

“If the people cannot speak to us, we cannot speak for them,” he said. “By threatening and imposing consequences on Maureen for speaking with me, the government’s contractor Calian is effectively interfering with my duties as member of Parliament for Battle River—Crowfoot.”

Poilievre said he contacted McGuinty after hearing about the situation but “the problems have only gotten worse” since then.

Speaking at the House of Commons national defence committee Thursday, McGuinty said he spoke to Poilievre about three hours after the Opposition leader had his conversation with Carpenter. He said the government has since looked into the issue and he has provided Poilievre with an update.

McGuinty said he has not spoken to Carpenter. He said that as a third-party to the contract, he has no legal standing to address it but he has spoken twice to Carpenter’s brother, including last weekend.

He also said he asked his deputy minister to raise the issue with Calian.

“I’ve been on this file, ON this issue, because I’m very concerned,” said McGuinty. “It’s not right that a member of Parliament should not be able to speak to a constituent. And I don’t know any more detail than that. I don’t know what’s going on inside the company, but I’m hoping this can come to a successful outcome.”

The Canadian Press has reached out to Calian Health for comment but has yet to receive a response.

Kevin Lamoureux, Liberal MP and parliamentary secretary to the leader of the government in the House of Commons, said Wednesday the government has been and will continue to be there for members of the Canadian Armed Forces.

“I find it very upsetting to hear the comments with regards to Maureen,” he said. “We recognize the sacrifices and the emotions and the service that was provided by health care professionals, by first responders.

“I appreciate the member raising it, and I will report back, Mr. Speaker, once we’ve had the opportunity to look a little bit deeper into the situation.”

Deputy Speaker Tom Kmiec, who was presiding over the House Wednesday as Poilievre made his point of privilege, said Speaker Francis Scarpaleggia would return to make a complete ruling.

Bloc Québécois MP Gabriel Ste-Marie said his party would also look into the issue and get back to the House “soon.”

stories.title: Talent agency’s internal fight over Olympians Sarah Nurse, Penny Oleksiak sparks lawsuit
stories.summary: The company is suing a former top employee it says plotted to start a competing agency. The alleged evidence: An AI meeting summary
stories.author: Michael McKiernan
stories.content:
A Toronto talent agency is suing a former top employee after a disputed AI summary of an internal meeting escalated into a fight over the management of some of Canada’s biggest Olympic stars, including Sarah Nurse and Penny Oleksiak.

In a statement of claim filed with the Ontario Superior Court of Justice, Dulcedo Inc. says that it placed Phoebe Balshin, a team lead in its sports division, ON paid leave after discovering the auto-generated meeting notes, alleging they are evidence she was planning to start a competing agency while still employed by the firm.

Regardless of what the AI summary indicated, Balshin told the company that she had no intention of setting up a competing business and had not taken any action – or even investigated the steps necessary – to open her own shop.

With no sign of her suspension being lifted, Balshin resigned soon after and Dulcedo has now launched a legal action, accusing her of misusing its confidential information to solicit clients to follow her out of the company. Among the sports stars Balshin managed at Dulcedo were Nurse, a Team Canada hockey forward, record-setting swimmer Oleksiak and trailblazing hockey coach Jessica Campbell.

Dulcedo alleges that all three terminated their management agreements with the company within weeks of Balshin’s May 2026 resignation amid an internal investigation into her conduct.

“Balshin’s actions and Dulcedo clients subsequently terminating their agreements with Dulcedo strongly evidence that these clients left because of Balshin soliciting and inducing those clients to do so,” Dulcedo alleges in its claim.

The company is seeking an unspecified amount of damages from Balshin, alleging that she violated provisions in her contract barring her from soliciting business from Dulcedo customers within 12 months of her departure.

“As a result of Balshin breaching her legal obligations, Dulcedo has incurred significant financial losses arising from the departure of talent managed by Balshin, the loss of management revenue and business opportunities, and the diversion or threatened diversion of clients and brand partnerships,” the claim continues.

None of the allegations have been proven in court and neither Balshin nor any of the athletes mentioned in Dulcedo’s statement of claim responded to requests for comment. A spokesperson for Dulcedo declined to comment.

Following her hiring in 2023, Dulcedo says that Balshin was responsible for managing a variety of prominent athletes. In _The Athletic’s_2024 profile of Nurse, Balshin explained some of the day-to-day tasks and broader strategic vision that are required when managing a high-level sports figure with an entire roster of major sponsors.

“When I first came on, a big conversation was: Sarah works with so many brands, but what is her brand? Who is she? What is her mission and vision?” Balshin told the sports journalism site. “So we basically built out a five-year plan with her to take us through Milan (the 2026 Olympics).”

“Our goal is to get her neck and neck with the best,” Balshin added, referencing Nurse’s appearance in an Adidas Super Bowl commercial alongside athletes including NFL star Patrick Mahomes and soccer icon Lionel Messi.

According to Dulcedo’s claim, Balshin was promoted to team lead of its sports division in August 2025. However, the claim says the relationship soured in March 2026, following a routine weekly meeting between Balshin, a sports division colleague and Dulcedo executive Benjamin Carter.

In its claim, the company says that once Carter had left the meeting, Balshin “openly discussed” with her remaining colleague plans “to leave within six months and start her own competing business.”

“Balshin proposed that they begin identifying athletes that would leave with her competing business and specifically referenced opportunities for Nurse. She proposed that they be strategic about current conversations and contract signings with athletes, implying that Balshin’s new competing business would impact business opportunities between Dulcedo and its clients,” the claim reads.

The company says it discovered the comments weeks later in auto-generated meeting notes that it uses for all “huddle meetings” and placed Balshin on a paid leave of absence on March 31, pending investigation.

According to Dulcedo’s account of a meeting with investigators six weeks later, Balshin initially denied having discussions about starting her own business.

“After being confronted with the notes from the March 2, 2026 Huddle Meeting, Balshin said she did not recall the Huddle Meeting but that irrespective of comments she made, she regretted the comments, and she had no intention of setting up a competing business and took no steps to set up a competing business,” the claim continues.

On May 19, less than a week after the investigation meeting, Balshin resigned, according to Dulcedo’s claim.

Balshin announced her departure at the time on LinkedIn, writing that she “can’t wait to share what’s next!” The post remains Balshin’s most recent on the networking site and she has not provided any further employment or representation updates on the site.

Nurse provided Dulcedo with notice of termination under her management agreement on May 29, while Oleksiak, Canada’s most decorated female Olympian of all time with seven medals, provided her notice of termination on June 8. She is currently serving a two-year suspension after missing three drug tests, but told the CBC last year that she aims to add to her record medal total at the next summer games in Los Angeles in 2028 once she’s cleared to compete.

Campbell’s notice of termination followed on July 6. As a hockey player, she was part of the Team Canada squad that won the 4 Nations Cup in 2014, and is now an NHL executive. In 2024, Campbell became the NHL’s first female assistant coach with an on-bench role at the Seattle Kraken and is currently the manager of player development at the New Jersey Devils.

In contrast to non-compete clauses, which are generally prohibited in Ontario, Nadia Zaman, an employment lawyer with Toronto firm Rudner Law, explains that the narrower class of non-solicitation clauses are typically designed to restrict the ability of departing employees to draw away their employer’s clients, co-workers or independent contractors.

“But that does not mean that every non-solicitation clause is enforceable,” said Zaman, who has no involvement in the Dulcedo case and was speaking generally.

The timing of any departures is just one factor that a judge will consider when determining whether solicitation occurred in a case such as this one, she adds, noting that any decision will ultimately depend on a full assessment of the precise language in the employment agreement and the details of any contacts or correspondence between the parties.

Regardless of the outcome in the Dulcedo case, Zaman said it offers an important reminder to parties on both sides of working relationships.

“For employers, it is critical that before they even hire the employee, they enter into proper employment agreements to protect themselves,” she said. “For an employee in a client-facing role, they also need to approach their departure carefully in terms of not only what happens after they leave, but also what happens before they leave the company.”

stories.title: Conservatives call on Diana Fox Carney to testify to Parliament about ocean envoy role
stories.summary: The Conservatives say Canadians should know more about Fox Carney’s priorities
stories.author: Dylan Robertson
stories.content:
Diana Fox Carney’s role as Canada’s Ocean Envoy is to promote an international conference on the seas that Canada is hosting next spring and to secure commitments from governments and “other partners,” according to a letter setting out her mandate obtained by The Globe and Mail.

The letter comes as Conservatives press for Ms. Fox Carney, the Prime Minister’s wife, to answer questions about the job before Parliament.

Liberal MPs have repeatedly blocked motions to call her before the House fisheries committee, and on Thursday, Conservatives brought a similar motion to the House environment committee, which was also blocked.

Conservative MPs Clifford Small and Connie Cody have also filed written questions in the House about her appointment.

The two-page letter, dated Sept. 16, the day her appointment was announced , said Ms. Fox Carney will serve “as an independent steward and champion” of the 12th Our Ocean Conference in Halifax “in an advisory, convening, and ambassadorial capacity,” wrote Paul MacKinnon, deputy minister of Fisheries and Oceans.

The position is “voluntary, non-remunerated, and time-limited, extending through the planning and delivery” of the conference.

The letter does not say to whom Ms. Fox Carney reports, and it sets aside no budget for her role, including for travel. It mentions support only from a departmental planning committee, not from the Prime Minister’s Office. The fall federal budget includes $8-million over two years for Fisheries and Oceans Canada to host the conference.

Before her appointment, Ms. Fox Carney “expressed interest in serving as Chair” of the conference, according to a briefing note prepared for the department’s deputy minister and released to The Globe through access to information.

The note says she had “personally expressed interest in ocean conservation financing,” as well as announcements related to the Arctic and the High Seas Treaty, and that “in her role as Chair, she could also advance strategic outcomes related to these interests.”

The commitments that Ms. Fox Carney is looking for are voluntary pledges from governments, companies and non-profit groups.

Since 2014, the Our Ocean Conference has generated 3,270 such commitments, ranging from new marine protected areas to funding for ocean protection, worth a combined US$176.7-billion, according to the World Resources Institute, which serves as the conference secretariat.

Canada has made 100 commitments worth US$4.2-billion since 2014, said John Lyons, a communications manager at WRI.

The briefing note, which is undated but was written in the weeks before her appointment, shows that the Prime Minister’s Office was involved early. Ms. Fox Carney and PMO staff met on Aug. 6 with the WRI, six weeks ahead of when she was named, according to the note.

Since a trip to Halifax in October, Ms. Fox Carney has travelled to Iqaluit, where she was part of federal Arctic conservation announcements , and to the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, as part of Canada’s official delegation .

The briefing note had listed COP31 among international meetings where she could promote the conference. It is less clear whether federal announcements in the Arctic fall within a mandate limited to “conference-related activities.”

“The government has highlighted that this is an unpaid position, but it’s not ceremonial,” Conservative MP Branden Leslie told reporters before Question Period on Thursday. “If you’re going to be travelling abroad and speaking on behalf of Canadians, you have to be answerable to Canadians.”

Conservatives have also questioned what role she has in the federal government’s $1.2-billion ocean-protection funding, announced two weeks after her appointment. In Question Period on Thursday, Fisheries Minister Joanne Thompson said the envoy “does not manage the $1.2-billion in ocean funding.”

“The $1.2-billion in ocean funding is my responsibility.”

The Ethics Commissioner’s office told The Globe in October that an unpaid ministerial appointee without an order-in-council generally “would not be considered a public office holder” under the Conflict of Interest Act.

Instead, the letter requires her to follow the department’s Values and Ethics Code, which governs public servants. It does not say how that code applies to a volunteer or who enforces it.

Under the Lobbying Act, a person appointed to an office by a minister counts as a public office holder, Manon Dion, communications manager for the Office of the Commissioner of Lobbying, told The Globe in October.

But lobbyists must report their oral and arranged communications only with “designated” public office holders, and determining whether a position is of comparable rank requires “careful analysis of all relevant facts,” she said.

stories.title: ‘Why have they not been doing this all along?’ Expert on Microsoft’s Code Red
stories.summary: Expert Evan Light said the question is not whether Microsoft will set a precedent by calling a "code red", but rather “why have they not been doing this all along?”
stories.author: Rachel Morgan
stories.content:
Microsoft’s “code red” is “good PR,” a cybersecurity expert says, but the outage that left millions without email for 24 hours should never have happened.

“It ultimately makes for better management of technology on the backend, but whether that will improve things for the long term, I don’t know, I kind of doubt it,” Evan Light, a University of Toronto coordinator of Critical Information Policy Studies, told Global News.

Light said the question is not whether Microsoft will set a precedent for other companies to follow suit and go all hands on deck on cybersecurity, but rather “why have they not been doing this all along?”

In a statement to Global News, a Microsoft spokesperson said the declaration was made to “quickly implement lessons learned” from the outage.

“Our customers and partners depend on our services, and we owe it to them to not only fix problems when they occur, but to do everything we can to keep them from happening again,” they said.

But when technology fails, it’s the users and consumers who face the consequences.

The Microsoft outage affected 70 countries , taking governments, hospitals, businesses, and airlines offline. The total number of people affected was not clear, but in January in its year end results, Microsoft said it had more than 450 million paid commercial subscriptions to its 365 services.

Just a day later, thousands of people across North America were stranded in airports when the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration ordered a ground stop after losing communication signals. As a result, FlightAware reported that nearly 15,000 flights were cancelled over one weekend.

Both Microsoft and the FAA said the disruptions were not related to artificial intelligence or a cyberattack. But those threats have also been ramping up.

Staples Canada said a “security incident” involving its print website between Nov. 1 and 5 saw a third party gain access to customer data.

Bell Canada said it was targeted by a cyberattack on Nov. 17 when a threat actor gained access to internal systems.

When asked whether Canadians should be concerned about the pace of these breaches, Light said the federal government should be providing information on what to do if certain services go dark.

Earlier this month, Public Services Canada reminded the public to keep three days’ worth of food and water, as well as other supplies, ON hand in case of an emergency. But Light said information on how to safeguard personal information and how to communicate when cell service or email is down should also be provided to the public.

He added that many Canadians aren’t even aware of how much of their personal information is out there.

Everything you do online leaves a trail of data, from browser searches to accepting cookies and signing up to new websites or apps.

“Yet they’re seen as legally binding,” he added.

“These aren’t things that are easily understood or that are legislated to be understood. They’re just there to click through and absolve a company of actual responsibility.”

Light said there are industry standards for how personal information is managed, and if done properly, a breach “really shouldn’t be possible.”

But he said broader regulation for all companies could come from the federal government.

Canadian privacy laws require companies to follow 10 principles, including openness, accountability and consent, when collecting, using and safeguarding personal information.

Light said these principles are treated as best practices and aren’t always strictly enforced.

So should companies be held to a higher standard when it comes to protecting users’ personal information? Light said yes, in theory, but doubts it’ll happen.

“Given the level of monopolization and the lack of alternatives – it’s not like my place of work, University of Toronto, can tomorrow decide, you know what, we’re going to ditch Microsoft for email and scheduling and messaging because they screwed up last week and we don’t trust them anymore. It’s a much more complicated process than that,” he said.

stories.title: 50th anniversary of The Last Waltz concert Review: Massey Hall celebrates The Band’s legendary 1976 farewell concert
stories.summary: An impressive roster of mostly Canadian talent performed songs that reflected a collaborative, historically significant era of the Band and Bob Dylan
stories.author: Brad Wheeler
stories.content:
Martin Scorsese’s film The Last Waltz documents the Band’s “farewell concert appearance” at San Francisco’s Winterland Ballroom on Nov. 25, 1976, which was U.S. Thanksgiving Day. After Robbie Robertson, Richard Manuel and Rick Danko struggle to rehearse Old-Time Religion , Robertson smiles and tries to get high.

But the joint isn’t lit – he doesn’t get a hit. “Aw, it’s not like it used to be,” he says after the sloppy version of the gospel hymn. The Band’s spark was gone, which is why Robertson pulled the group off the road in the first place.

In a broader sense, “it’s not like it used to be” speaks to the Band’s raison d’être . Look at the sepia-tone photo by Elliott Landy from their 1968 debut album, Music from Big Pink. The five musicians − four Canadians and one from Arkansas − are dressed in a stylized way, as if they might rob a train or drink lemonade with young Anna Lee.

Surveying the modern musical landscape, the Band got back to what once was. The Old-Time Religion scene in The Last Waltz leads into a performance of The Night They Drove Old Dixie Down.

“Like my father before me I will work the land…”

At Massey Hall on Wednesday, the 50th anniversary of The Last Waltz concert was commemorated with a benefit concert for the music-education charity MusiCounts. An impressive roster of mostly Canadian talent performed songs that generally reflected a collaborative, historically significant era of the Band and Bob Dylan, roughly 1965 to 1976.

A mostly full house heard everything from a dramatic version of Dylan’s Highway 61 Revisited by July Talk’s Peter Dreimanis and Leah Fay Goldstein (who worked the siren whistle like a champ) to the bluegrass harmony of Evangeline by Georgia Harmer and a pair of sweet-singing accompanists. Rapper Cadence Weapon, who covered Million Dollar Bash from The Basement Tapes album by Dylan and the Band, rocked a funky, period-perfect winter coat.

All of the guest artists were backed by a strong house band led by Aaron Goldstein and featuring, among others, hired-gun guitarist Nichol Robertson and Hammond organ player Robin Hatch. The Northern Soul Horns were essential in general and specifically effective in adding a country-soul aesthetic to Basia Bulat’s take on Neil Young’s Helpless , ON which Tamara Lindeman handled Joni Mitchell’s high and breathy harmony. (Lindeman returned later for a beautiful take on Mitchell’s Coyote .)

For context, the fruitful partnership of Dylan and the Band – originally known as the Hawks – began in September, 1965, at rehearsals held at Toronto’s Friar’s Tavern, right around the corner from Massey Hall (where they performed two months later on the controversial Dylan’s “goes electric” tour). By the time they reunited for an arena tour that brought them to Maple Leaf Gardens in 1974, the Hawks were the Band.

Fun fact: Neil Young’s U.S. Thanksgiving Day in 1976 started with the second of two concerts at Atlanta’s Fox Theatre. It belatedly began at 1 a.m. and finished hours later. At some point afterward he hopped on an airplane to cross the continent for his Last Waltz appearance.

Why is that worth mentioning? Toronto balladeer Justin Rutledge played two shows on Wednesday. After an early-evening set at the Cameron House, he headed to Massey Hall for a feel-good run-through of the Band’s Up on Cripple Creek . Rutledge and the two back-up singers nailed the “loddle-loddle-loddle-whoo” parts.

It was a highlight, as were Tears of Rage (by Tony Dekker and Colleen Brown), Don’t Do It (by Jeremie Albino), It Makes No Difference (by Joel Plaskett), Forever Young (by Thunder Queens) and The Weight (by Shakura S’Aida).

The set list was remarkable for what it represented: A stunning period of musical output that stands the test of time. Beyond Dylan and the Band, the decade covering the late 1960s and early 1970s is arguably rock music’s best. Fifty years later, the genre is not like it used to be.

For the concert finale, all the artists convened for a stage-crowding rendition of I Shall Be Released , an evocative expression of freedom.

This article will likely be my final concert review. Next month, I’m moving on from music journalism to obituaries writing. The change is my choice, but Harry Styles, the ghost of Prince and you too May might see it as a sign of the times. They say everything can be replaced, but full-time newspaper rock critics are a thing of the past.

Twenty years ago, I reviewed a Last Waltz 30th-anniversary concert at Toronto’s Glenn Gould Studio. Singer-songwriter Tom Wilson was there, and he was at Massey Hall on Wednesday, sharing a microphone with his son. Wilson, old enough to shop with a seniors’ discount, represented the old guard at the concert. I suppose I did as well.

Loddle-loddle-loddle-whoo.

QUÉBEC - Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon says the parliamentary session will begin Dec. 1 as planned, without swearing the oath to the King.

Nov. 26, 2026

New subscriber benefit!

Copied to clipboard

A gifted article has been claimed.

Out of gifts for the month

Unfortunately you've used all of your gifts this month. Your counter will reset on the first day of next month.

Jacques Boissinot/The Canadian Press[](https://www.thestar.com/news/canada/quebec/quebec-premier-says-parliamentary-session-will-go-ahead-without-oath-to-the-king/article_1c6837d7-8e38-52bc-b5f1-e5c82b2e81aa.html)

By The Canadian Press

The premier says there is too much work to do at the legislature to wait until legal procedures conclude to begin the session.

None of Quebec’s officials elected in the Oct. 5 election have sworn their allegiance to King Charles.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Inside interior designer Nora Voon’s art-filled home

The province passed a law making it optional for members of the legislature to swear their allegiance to the British monarch in 2022.

But lawyer Lawrence David challenged the law in Superior Court last summer, arguing Quebec has exceeded its constitutional powers.

Quebec Superior Court Justice Ian Demers temporarily reinstated the oath requirement until the constitutional challenge can be heard on its merits.

The Parti Québécois government is challenging the court ruling, and the Quebec Court of Appeal will hear the case Friday afternoon.

St-Pierre Plamondon denounced the Quebec Liberals and Conservatives, who both said they would not defy court orders and sit illegally after he asked them to sign a declaration refusing the oath.

“It isn’t Mr. Lawrence Whatever from the University of Ottawa who is going to stop me from dedicating myself to the public service and Quebecers,” St-Pierre Plamondon said at a news conference in Quebec City on Thursday.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 26, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Business Cares Food Drive launches 2026 campaign, aims to broaden impact amidst rising demand
stories.summary: The annual Business Cares Food Drive officially launched Thursday morning, kicking off its 2026 campaign with a renewed focus on expanding its reach and impact to meet escalating community needs.
stories.author: Gerry Dewan
stories.content:
The annual Business Cares Food Drive officially launched Thursday morning, kicking off its 2026 campaign with a renewed focus on expanding its reach and impact to meet escalating community needs. Business leaders gathered at the RBC Place London Convention Centre for the campaign’s kick-off event.

Addressing the attendees, London District Construction Association Board Member Scott Massé shared his perspective on the season’s spirit.

“Nothing makes me feel more Christmas spirit than being out here trying to help other people that are in need,” he said.

The campaign, which runs from Thursday, Nov. 26, through Dec. 18, aims to collect vital food and financial donations for the London and Area Food Bank.

Organizers acknowledge that businesses are currently navigating their own economic challenges, but Business Cares Chair Wayne Dunn expressed confidence in the community’s enduring generosity.

“The need remains high,” Dunn noted, “but I’m confident people will continue to give.”

Current demands on the food bank have reportedly increased by another two per cent over the past year.

A significant enhancement for this year’s campaign is the expansion of the popular Grocery Weekend initiative.

“We’re piloting Grocery Weekend. We’re at eight extra stores tomorrow [Friday, Nov. 27],” Dunn explained. “We’ve never done Friday before. And that’s going to give us probably the equivalent of four big stores over the course of a weekend. And that in itself will all of a sudden take care of a lot of the downfall that we’re missing.”

This expanded effort complements the broader collection drive, which will see volunteers stationed at 45 grocery stores across the London area on Nov. 28 and 29.

Beyond these direct collection efforts, Business Cares is partnering with various community events throughout the holiday season.

These include initiatives like Tampon Tuesday, Golfers Care, Kids Care Skate, Nonprofits Care, and collaborations with the London Knights and the Grand Theatre’s production of “A Christmas Carol,” running from Nov. 24 to Dec. 27.

The community’s generosity proved instrumental last year, with Business Cares successfully delivering 695,000 pounds of food to the London and Area Food Bank in December 2025.

Individuals and businesses looking to contribute to the 2026 campaign have several options. Organizing food donation drives within businesses or networks is encouraged throughout the Nov. 26 to Dec. 18 period.

Non-perishable food items can be dropped off at several locations: the J-AAR Agriplex Expo Warehouse (preferred, enter off Rectory St.), the LDA Office (331 Aberdeen Dr., contact Emilee at 519-453-5322 to arrange between Nov. 23-Dec. 16), any Finch Auto Dealerships (Nov. 27-Dec. 16), or the Talbot Centre (465 Richmond St., Dec. 1-16). Specific drop-off dates for non-perishable food are Dec. 15, 16, or 17 at the J-AAR Agriplex.

For businesses unable to transport donations, Business Cares will arrange food pickups from their premises. Alternatively, cash donations are welcomed.

Organizers urge the public to register on their website , and to follow their social media channels on Facebook and Instagram for campaign updates.

“We would appreciate your help by talking with other businesses or colleagues to partner with Business Cares this Holiday Season,” a statement from the organization reads.

The campaign, which runs from Thursday, Nov. 26, through Dec. 18, aims to collect vital food and financial donations for the London and Area Food Bank.
Organizers acknowledge that businesses are currently navigating their own economic challenges, but Business Cares Chair Wayne Dunn expressed confidence in the community’s enduring generosity.
“The need remains high,” Dunn noted, “but I’m confident people will continue to give.”
Current demands on the food bank have reportedly increased by another two per cent over the past year.
A significant enhancement for this year’s campaign is the expansion of the popular Grocery Weekend initiative.

“We’re piloting Grocery Weekend. We’re at eight extra stores tomorrow [Friday, Nov. 27],” Dunn explained. “We’ve never done Friday before. And that’s going to give us probably the equivalent of four big stores over the course of a weekend. And that in itself will all of a sudden take care of a lot of the downfall that we’re missing.”
This expanded effort complements the broader collection drive, which will see volunteers stationed at 45 grocery stores across the London area on Nov. 28 and 29.
Beyond these direct collection efforts, Business Cares is partnering with various community events throughout the holiday season.

These include initiatives like Tampon Tuesday, Golfers Care, Kids Care Skate, Nonprofits Care, and collaborations with the London Knights and the Grand Theatre’s production of “A Christmas Carol,” running from Nov. 24 to Dec. 27.
The community’s generosity proved instrumental last year, with Business Cares successfully delivering 695,000 pounds of food to the London and Area Food Bank in December 2025.

Individuals and businesses looking to contribute to the 2026 campaign have several options. Organizing food donation drives within businesses or networks is encouraged throughout the Nov. 26 to Dec. 18 period.

Non-perishable food items can be dropped off at several locations: the J-AAR Agriplex Expo Warehouse (preferred, enter off Rectory St.), the LDA Office (331 Aberdeen Dr., contact Emilee at 519-453-5322 to arrange between Nov. 23-Dec. 16), any Finch Auto Dealerships (Nov. 27-Dec. 16), or the Talbot Centre (465 Richmond St., Dec. 1-16). Specific drop-off dates for non-perishable food are Dec. 15, 16, or 17 at the J-AAR Agriplex.
For businesses unable to transport donations, Business Cares will arrange food pickups from their premises. Alternatively, cash donations are welcomed.
Organizers urge the public to register on their website , and to follow their social media channels on Facebook and Instagram for campaign updates.
“We would appreciate your help by talking with other businesses or colleagues to partner with Business Cares this Holiday Season,” a statement from the organization reads.

stories.title: Guitarist killed in home invasion mourned by Toronto music scene
stories.summary: Michael Eckert remembered as a warm, engaging person and a talented, versatile artist
stories.author: Kaitlyn McGrath
stories.content:
Michael Eckert, a Toronto pedal steel guitarist who was fatally shot during an overnight home invasion, is being remembered as a warm and engaging person and a talented, versatile artist who made an indelible mark on the city’s music scene.

“You can see the outpouring of grief in our community,” said Ori Dagan, a Toronto jazz musician and producer. “It’s really quite remarkable to see how many people he touched.”

Police say Eckert was shot after a confrontation with a suspect inside a midtown residence. He was pronounced dead in hospital on Wednesday. He was 39.

Eckert was a celebrated musician whose talents were in demand across Toronto’s diverse music scene.

Less than two weeks ago, Eckert performed with Canadian country-rock band Blue Rodeo at the Grey Cup pre-game show in Calgary. The band called Eckert “an absolute wizard on his instrument.”

Blue Rodeo bassist Bazil Donovan had known Eckert for about five years.

“He took chances that nobody else might take or he tried to go beyond what the instrument normally was,” said Donovan.

During a Jim Cuddy Band performance on Wednesday in Meaford, Ont., Cuddy paid tribute to the Toronto musician.

“I couldn’t stop thinking about him the whole night we were playing,” Donovan said.

Dagan said he first met Eckert when they were both students at Humber College about 20 years ago and continued to run into each other while performing locally. Dagan said despite Eckert’s “blow-your-mind” talent playing a technically difficult instrument, he was humble and down to earth, with zero ego or attitude.

“Everybody loved him,” Dagan said, adding every time he ran into him, he gave “the most generous hug.”

Eckert was “someone who you just feel completely at ease with,” said Justin Gray, a Toronto-based music producer and engineer.

“He was always a really positive energy in the room and a certain gravity where it’s like, if he’s there, I think people are just drawn to him,” said Gray, who also knew Eckert since they were students at Humber.

Derek Downham, a Toronto-based music producer and Eckert’s longtime friend, called the pedal steel guitar one of the most difficult instruments to play, but Eckert had “impeccable dexterity, impeccable pitch and impeccable rhythm.”

“I can’t express how deep of a hole he leaves in the Toronto music scene,” he said.

Ryan Granville-Martin, a Toronto-based musician, said he remembers Eckert for his stage presence.

“He always had this big grin on his face,” said Granville-Martin, a drummer who performed with Eckert as recently as two months ago. “He would make eye contact with you when you were playing. He was really listening. He’s just the exact kind of player that you want to make music with.”

Ken Kelley, a guitarist and Eckert’s friend of 16 years, lives in Owen Sound, Ont., but travelled to Toronto after hearing the news. Seeing the police officers and caution tape in front of a home he called a place of refuge for him and others was devastating, he said.

“Where he died, I drank coffee,” he said, adding that the house was a gathering place for other musicians to practice.

“It’s been very traumatic to see that home that we’ve all spent so much time in.”

Toronto police say they are seeking at least one suspect in the shooting that happened shortly after 2:30 a.m. They are asking anyone with information about the case to come forward.
