stories.title: Canadians’ debt rising ahead of 2027 mortgage renewal wave, says TransUnion
stories.summary: With a wave of mortgage renewals expected in 2027, a new report shows Canadians are carrying more debt than ever — and non-mortgage debt is accelerating fast.
stories.author: Ariel Rabinovitch
stories.content:
With a wave of mortgage renewals expected in 2027, a new report shows Canadians are carrying more debt than ever — and non-mortgage debt is accelerating fast.

TransUnion released its third-quarter credit industry insights report on Wednesday, saying that “financial pressures are beginning to build for some homeowners, particularly as higher borrowing costs and larger mortgage balances continue to affect household budgets.”

It adds: “some homeowners were finding it more difficult to absorb higher housing costs.”

The report shows that Canada’s total outstanding credit debt topped a record $2.66 trillion in the third quarter of this year, up 3.8 percent from a year earlier, with mortgage debt making up nearly three-quarters (74 per cent) of that total.

Non-mortgage debt, which includes credit cards, lines of credit, auto and personal loans, posted the fastest increase of 3.6 percent year-over-year compared to strictly mortgage debt.

On average, Canadians each owed $136,024 across all credit products, up 2.9 per cent compared to last year.

For non-mortgage debt, each Canadian consumer owed $28,083 on average, up 3.63 per cent year-over-year.

Consumers in B.C. and Ontario saw non-mortgage credit climb the fastest among the provinces and territories, with an average balance of $30,492 in B.C., up 3.87 per cent, and $29,197 in Ontario, up 3.2 per cent.

TransUnion says there were 32.8 million credit-active consumers in the third quarter, up 1.1 per cent overall. That growth was also concentrated at both the highest and lowest end of the credit score spectrum.

For example, TransUnion says the number of consumers categorized as Super Prime, meaning they typically have the highest credit scores and lowest risk, was up four per cent year over year. Meanwhile, Prime, which is considered the median category, fell 3.7 per cent, and the number of Subprime borrowers increased 1.5 per cent.

This pattern reflects the so-called “K”-shaped economy, where higher-income households are becoming more financially empowered as lower-income households lose spending power.

Although rising debt levels May not be a big issue for all households, TransUnion says for many these figures suggest there is a “challenging backdrop.”

“In some provinces, balances have grown amid relatively strong economic and credit conditions, while in others, debt has increased against a more challenging backdrop for households,” said Matt Fabian, senior director of financial services research and consulting at TransUnion Canada in the report.

“Understanding how debt levels, borrowing behaviors, and local economic conditions interact with affordability, and repayment trends will be increasingly important for assessing regional credit trends.”

TransUnion says mortgage delinquency risk is also high amid rising debt levels and household pressures.

A separate report from Equifax earlier this week showed the national 90-plus day mortgage delinquency rate — defined as missed payments three months in a row — reached 0.32 per cent, the highest since the credit agency started tracking the metric in 2013. That’s up 31.1 per cent year-over-year, mainly pushed higher by missed mortgage payments in Ontario and British Columbia.

In July, August and September, 36,797 Canadians filed for insolvencies, according to the Canadian Association of Insolvency and Restructuring Professionals (Cairp). A consumer insolvency is a measure that indicates how many Canadians filed for relief under the Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act.

Many Canadian households will renew their mortgages in 2027 and face a major financial challenge as economists expect interest rates to rise in the months ahead.

Households that took out mortgages during or shortly after the pandemic May have had comparably lower interest rates. Plus, home prices have fallen from the post-pandemic peak, when interest rates were historically lower.

TransUnion says this will result in a higher loan-to-value ratio than when borrowers first purchased a home.

In other words, many homeowners will owe a larger share of their home’s current value than when they first bought it, leaving them with less equity. Less equity means less financial leverage when it’s time to renew a mortgage.

Interest rates are also rising because of volatility in global bond markets and the Bank of Canada raising its key policy rate to bring inflation under control.

TransUnion says it believes most households will still be able to make their mortgage payments on time in 2027, but it won’t be easy for many.

“Mortgage delinquency rates remained low, and most homeowners continued to make their payments on time. However, some borrowers could need to adjust household spending or reallocate other financial obligations to manage higher mortgage payments at renewal,” the report said.

– with files from Global News’ Uday Rana and The Canadian Press

“In some provinces, balances have grown amid relatively strong economic and credit conditions, while in others, debt has increased against a more challenging backdrop for households,” said Matt Fabian, senior director of financial services research and consulting at TransUnion Canada in the report.

“Understanding how debt levels, borrowing behaviors, and local economic conditions interact with affordability, and repayment trends will be increasingly important for assessing regional credit trends.”
TransUnion says mortgage delinquency risk is also high amid rising debt levels and household pressures.

A separate report from Equifax earlier this week showed the national 90-plus day mortgage delinquency rate — defined as missed payments three months in a row — reached 0.32 per cent, the highest since the credit agency started tracking the metric in 2013. That’s up 31.1 per cent year-over-year, mainly pushed higher by missed mortgage payments in Ontario and British Columbia.

content_blocks.text: What could happen next year?
Many Canadian households will renew their mortgages in 2027 and face a major financial challenge as economists expect interest rates to rise in the months ahead.

Households that took out mortgages during or shortly after the pandemic May have had comparably lower interest rates. Plus, home prices have fallen from the post-pandemic peak, when interest rates were historically lower.
TransUnion says this will result in a higher loan-to-value ratio than when borrowers first purchased a home.

In other words, many homeowners will owe a larger share of their home’s current value than when they first bought it, leaving them with less equity. Less equity means less financial leverage when it’s time to renew a mortgage.
Interest rates are also rising because of volatility in global bond markets and the Bank of Canada raising its key policy rate to bring inflation under control.

“Mortgage delinquency rates remained low, and most homeowners continued to make their payments on time. However, some borrowers could need to adjust household spending or reallocate other financial obligations to manage higher mortgage payments at renewal,” the report said.

stories.title: Ford says he would use his own gun to fight back against intruder
stories.summary: Premier encourages residents to defend themselves after violent Toronto home invasions, says to protect his family, he would ‘blow the guy right through the front door’
stories.author: Laura Stone
stories.content:
Ontario Premier Doug Ford says he owns a gun and encouraged homeowners to use weapons to protect themselves in the wake of a deadly home invasion in Toronto that has stoked fears about an increase in violent break-ins.

The killing of an accomplished Toronto musician in his home in an affluent neighbourhood has also sharpened calls from police and politicians, including Mr. Ford and opposition MPs on Parliament Hill, for amendments to the Criminal Code to deter home invasions.

In an impromptu 10-minute scrum with reporters at the Ontario legislature on Thursday, Mr. Ford spoke about two recent violent incidents in the city, including the death Wednesday of renowned pedal--steel guitarist Michael Eckert, who was killed during a break-in at his home in midtown Toronto.

Another violent break-in took place in the affluent Bridle Path neighbourhood on Oct. 29. A man and his two adult daughters sustained gunshot wounds while the mother was injured with a hammer.

Mr. Ford said in such cases people should be able to use weapons – be it a gun, knife or another instrument – to protect themselves if their home is invaded.

“I encourage people to use whatever tool they have to fight back, not hide, but fight back,” he said.

“I’ll tell you one thing: someone comes through my door with a gun and a knife and starts shooting it up – I’ll blow the guy right through the front door,” adding that the perpetrator will look like “Swiss cheese.”

Mr. Ford confirmed to reporters that he owns a gun and that the ammunition is in a locked case separate from the weapon.

“I do own a gun. I am a legal gun owner. And I would use it in a heartbeat if someone came in with a gun ready to shoot up my house, my family.”

Mr. Eckert, 39, was shot during a confrontation with an unknown number of assailants who allegedly broke into his Poplar Plains Road home around 2:40 a.m. Wednesday. He was rushed to hospital, where he was pronounced dead.

Detective Sergeant Alan Bartlett at the Toronto Police Service has said he had no information to suggest the family was targeted.

Toronto Police released an image late Wednesday of a dark Honda they said was a suspect vehicle, but by Thursday evening had not released additional information about the investigation.

Responding to questions from The Globe and Mail on Thursday, Toronto Police Chief Myron Demkiw said the homicide demonstrates the need for tougher federal legislation to deter home invasions.

“Yesterday, a man lost his life in his own home,” Chief Demkiw said in an e-mail. “That is the devastating reality of the violence we are seeing, and it underscores the urgency of these reforms.”

Crime statistics show that homicides have dramatically declined to near-record lows in and around Toronto. However, police say the city has had 119 home invasions in 2026, up 35 per cent from the same time last year.

In October, Michael Guglielmin, a Conservative Vaughan MP, introduced a private member’s bill in Parliament that seeks to change the Criminal Code so that home invasions are singled out as a stand-alone offence that can be punished by a potential life sentence.

Conservative MP Melissa Lantsman raised the issue in Parliament on Thursday, criticizing the government for failing to act on private members’ bills aimed at tackling rising home invasions.

Mr. Ford last month made public a letter to Prime Minister Mark Carney, in which he urged similar changes. During Thursday’s scrum, he said that Ontario’s home invasion problem is “out of control.”

A senior federal government source said there are no plans to amend the Criminal Code with respect to home invasions but that the government is open to suggestions to changes, including those proposed in private members’ bills.

The Globe is not identifying the source because they were not authorized to speak publicly on the matter.

In a statement Thursday, Jeanne Joannie Fogue Mgamgne, a spokesperson for Justice Minister Sean Fraser, noted that Canadians already have the right to defend themselves in their homes and touted new crime laws passed by the Liberal government.

“We know there is always more work to do. As threats evolve, our government will keep working with law enforcement, move with urgency to strengthen Canada’s laws, and keep Canadians safe,” she said.

Mr. Eckert, an accomplished guitarist, played a kickoff show for the Grey Cup in Calgary earlier this month with members of Blue Rodeo.

A fixture in city music venues for more than a decade, he was a musician’s musician, according to those who knew him; just as comfortable accompanying soprano Measha Brueggergosman-Lee or playing with his experimental group, Neon Eagle.

“Michael was an incredibly humble guy who would always let his music do the talking,” Ms. Brueggergosman-Lee told The Globe. “No agent, but always on tour. No manager, but in great demand. No career plan, but always the standard to which everyone was aspiring.”

Mr. Ford told reporters that he is directing his Attorney-General and Solicitor-General to find ways to prevent such attacks.

However, critics warn that the Premier’s rhetoric about weapons could put people in danger.

Ontario NDP Leader Marit Stiles says that “there are things that the Premier of Ontario certainly, surely, can do, rather than just tell everybody, ‘Hey, you’re on your own. It’s the Wild West. Go buy a gun.’”

Catherine Latimer, executive director of advocacy group John Howard Society, said that “you can always count on Doug Ford for a ‘stand your ground’ kind of response.”

“For a lot of people who don’t own guns and who are reluctant to swing a baseball bat at somebody’s head, it’s not a good solution,” she said in an interview. “We need much better answers if there is an upswing in home invasions.”

Mr. Ford has previously spoken out about such violence. In March of this year, Mr. Ford celebrated a Vaughan homeowner who was not criminally charged after he shot a 24-year-old man trying to break in.

“The person was defending his family, he was a legal gun owner, stored properly – congratulations. I’m glad you shot the guy,” he said at the time.

On Thursday, Mr. Ford told reporters, “I’ve always had a saying: I’d rather be judged by 12 than carried by six. Protect your family at all costs.”

With reports from Patrick White and Mercedes Stephenson

stories.title: Man from Ontario gets 4.5 years for meth smuggling at Vancouver International Airport
stories.summary: Vancouver - An Ontario man has been sentenced to more than four years in prison after getting caught at Vancouver International Airport with a "significant amount" of methamphetamine in his luggage.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Vancouver - An Ontario man has been sentenced to more than four years in prison after getting caught at Vancouver International Airport with a “significant amount” of methamphetamine in his luggage.

Mounties say in a release that the investigation began on Aug. 29, 2024, when officials from the Canada Border Services Agency stopped the man before he was to board a flight to New Zealand.

stories.title: Report reveals ‘deeply troubling levels of antisemitism, anti-Jewish attitudes’ on Canadian university campuses
stories.summary: Nearly half of the non-Jewish students surveyed said it was not antisemitic to boycott Jewish-owned businesses
stories.author: Courtney Greenberg
stories.content:
Jewish advocacy groups and allies are pushing the federal government to take action after a report published Thursday revealed “deeply troubling levels of antisemitism and anti-Jewish attitudes” on Canadian university campuses.

The report, entitled Campus Antisemitism and Student Experiences (Case) II, surveyed 755 non-Jewish students across the country to gain insight into how they felt. It found that nearly 40 per cent said it was not antisemitic to call the Holocaust a myth or to say that it was exaggerated.

More than half said it was not antisemitic to say that “Jews have too much influence on the economy” and 45 per cent said it was not antisemitic to boycott Jewish-owned businesses “because they are Jewish-owned.”

Just over 20 per cent of students said they had personally heard or seen antisemitic comments or actions on or around campus over the past year. Among those students, 14 per cent attributed such incidents to professors, instructors or teaching assistants, and 11 per cent to administrators or staff.

The Network of Engaged Canadian Academics — an organization of Canadian faculty members using academic freedom, research, and intellectual pluralism to counter antisemitism — held a conference on Parliament Hill to discuss the report on Thursday.

Queen’s University student and advocate Mokshi Asnora, who is not Jewish and was not among the students surveyed in the report, joined the meeting online to speak about her frustration with the lack of support for Jewish students.

She said she has heard countless anti-Jewish statements in lecture halls and club settings over the years.

Two weeks after October 7, she said anti-Israel fliers appeared on campus. The following semester, she said, the Queen’s University branch of Solidarity for Palestinian Human Rights hosted a speaker who had denied the Holocaust.

She said she found these incidents, and others, “troubling” to witness.

University administrators have caved to intimidation rather than unequivocally condemning antisemitism, said Asnora. She called on universities to intervene, rather than backing down “at the first sign of backlash.”

Following the report’s publication, the CEO for Jewish advocacy group B’nai Brith Canada Simon Wolle called its findings disturbing.

“They suggest that some of the most historically dangerous expressions of antisemitism are being dismissed and/or accepted within the very institutions entrusted with educating Canada’s next generation,” he said.

It should be a wake-up call for university leaders and Canadian society, he added.

When deeply rooted antisemitic stereotypes are permeating through Canadian campuses, we have a serious problem. The newly released Campus Antisemitism and Student Experiences (Case II) report reveals that some of the most historically dangerous expressions of Jew-hatred are… pic.twitter.com/ZPhoa59J6z — B'nai Brith Canada (@bnaibrithcanada) November 26, 2026

B’nai Brith Canada’s Director of Research and Advocacy Richard Robertson said that while criticism of the Israeli government’s policies is legitimate, “there is no justification for the targeting of Jewish students or the broader Jewish community because of their perceived connection to a foreign state.”

The Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs released a joint statement along with Hillel organizations from Ontario, Montreal, British Columbia, Ottawa, Atlantic Canada, Edmonton, Calgary and StandWithUs Canada.

“Governments and university administrations must follow through on their commitments, including enforcing their own rules and ensuring meaningful accountability for institutions that fail to protect students, faculty and staff,” it said.

Minister of Canadian Identity and Culture Marc Miller attended the conference on Thursday. He said the federal government has a role in making sure that Jews can feel safe on campus and that institutions are held to account.

I think it's a recognition that we're all failing Canadian Jews, in particular students

“This is not a finger-pointing operation. I think it’s a recognition that we’re all failing Canadian Jews, in particular students,” said Miller.

The first part of the Case report was released in August. It was commissioned by the Government of Canada and produced by the Association for Canadian Studies and the Metropolis Institute. It focused on the experiences of 900 Jewish students.

It revealed that 96 per cent of Jewish students surveyed said they had experienced at least one instance of antisemitism over the previous year.

The second report, also commissioned by the Canadian government and ACS, focused on the broader student population that did not identify as Jewish.

It surveyed students between Dec. 9 and 21, 2025 who responded through a self-administered online questionnaire.

The findings aligned with an external review published in August 2026 for Toronto Metropolitan University, which found “that incidents on that campus reflected an increasingly hostile campus climate devoid of decisive institutional action.”

University campuses in Canada became a hotbed of antisemitism following October 7, when Hamas terrorists killed 1,200 people in Israel in 2023.

Students who were protesting Israel’s military response soon set up encampments on campuses across Canada and around the world, calling for universities to severe ties with the Middle Eastern country.

Many of the encampments devolved into places where antisemitism went unchecked, isolating Jewish students and disrupting university life.

Jewish groups are now urging the government to take the findings of the second Case report seriously.

“No Canadian should have to choose between expressing their Jewish identity and feeling safe,” said Wolle.

“No student should be held collectively responsible for the actions of a foreign state. And no university should tolerate an environment in which antisemitism becomes an accepted feature of campus life.”

Courtney Greenberg is a Toronto-based journalist covering breaking news, with a focus on antisemitism in Canada. In 2026, she was a Postmedia Fellow with the Investigative Journalism Bureau, where she worked on in-depth investigations into women’s health and the justice system.

stories.title: London police investigate ‘cash-for-card’ fraud ring targeting public
stories.summary: Members of the London Police Service (LPS) Financial Crime Unit are warning the public about a cash-for-card fraud.
stories.author: Melanie Kentner
stories.content:
Members of the London Police Service (LPS) Financial Crime Unit are warning the public about a cash-for-card fraud.

Police want residents to remain vigilant while using debit and credit cards as officers are investigating a series of frauds involving individuals asking for assistance paying for taxis, rideshares or food deliveries.

In the reported incidents, suspects approached victims and claimed they were unable to pay using cash, Apple Pay or their own bank card. Victims were offered cash in exchange for using their debit card to complete a transaction on a portable payment terminal located inside or near a vehicle.

Police say during the transactions, suspects distracted the victims and obtained their PINs. In some instances, victims’ debit cards were also switched with other cards without their knowledge.

The stolen debit cards and PINs were then used to make unauthorized cash withdrawals and purchases.

Investigators believe the incidents are connected. Suspects were associated with several vehicles, including white and grey Hyundai Elantras.

Suspect descriptions

There are multiple suspects involved in the investigations, both male and female, believed to be between the ages of 18 – 20 years of age. Investigators are sharing images of three of the reported male suspects in the hopes that members of the public can assist in identifying them.

Tips to protect yourself

The London Police Service reminds members of the public to:

Be cautious if a stranger asks you to use your debit or credit card to pay for a taxi, rideshare or food delivery in exchange for cash;

Never allow another person to handle your debit or credit card during a transaction;

Shield the keypad when entering your PIN;

Keep your card in sight and ensure the card returned to you is yours;

Do not feel pressured to complete a transaction because someone claims to need urgent assistance;

Regularly review your bank and credit card activity and immediately report suspicious transactions to your financial institution; and

If you believe your card has been stolen or switched, contact your financial institution immediately to have the card blocked.

Investigators are asking anyone with information about these incidents, or who can identify any of the individuals or vehicles pictured, to contact the London Police Service at 519-661-5670.

stories.title: Supreme Court of Canada to hear challenge of law central to Ontario land dispute
stories.summary: Ottawa - The Supreme Court of Canada has agreed to hear a developer's constitutional challenge of an Ontario law at the heart of a dispute over land in a protected area known as the provincial Greenbelt.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
OTTAWA - The Supreme Court of Canada has agreed to hear a developer’s constitutional challenge of an Ontario law at the heart of a dispute over land in a protected area known as the provincial Greenbelt.

Nov. 26, 2026

NSD/[](https://www.thestar.com/news/ontario/supreme-court-of-canada-to-hear-challenge-of-law-central-to-ontario-land-dispute/article_8a6b7807-9262-5c9d-9e3a-9f0f4500fc87.html)

By The Canadian Press

An Ontario regulation included land owned by Minotar Holdings Inc. in Markham, Ont., in the Greenbelt, preventing commercial development.

A provincial ministry told the firm the land was included through a mistake that would be fixed during a 10-year review, but this was not done.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Inside interior designer Nora Voon’s art-filled home

In 2017, Minotar initiated court action against the government alleging negligence, misrepresentation and misfeasance in public office, and seeking both damages and a declaration the lands were wrongfully included in the Greenbelt.

The parties reached a settlement in 2022 that removed most of the land from the Greenbelt and gave Minotar the right to take “any steps available” if the land was later restored to the protected area.

The next year, Ontario’s Progressive Conservative government enacted legislation that returned Minotar’s land and 14 other parcels to the Greenbelt and shielded the Crown from liability.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 26, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Thorough review ongoing in cause of fatal crash outside Delta, B.C., mall: police
stories.summary: Delta - It's been almost two months since a truck drove into a crowd of people at a mall in Delta, B.C., ON the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation, but police say they are still trying to find out what happened through an objective investigation.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Delta - It’s been almost two months since a truck drove into a crowd of people at a mall in Delta, B.C., ON the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation, but police say they are still trying to find out what happened through an objective investigation.

Two women were killed immediately, while another woman died later and a fourth injured person has been released from hospital.

stories.title: Two Ontario Maid cases should have been referred to police, former oversight committee member says
stories.summary: Ramona Coelho, a physician and university professor, said the cases ‘really test the limits’ of Canada’s law
stories.author: Kristy Kirkup, Nancy Macdonald
stories.content:
A family physician and former member of Ontario’s Maid oversight regime told a parliamentary committee Thursday that she is aware of two cases of medically assisted death she believes should have been referred to police.

Ramona Coelho, an adjunct professor at Western University’s Department of Family Medicine, said the cases “really test the limits” of Canada’s Maid law, and that she and two colleagues reached out to Ontario’s chief coroner with the hopes the incidents would be referred to law enforcement or the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario.

The justice committee is currently examining Bill C-41, legislation that would open the door for people diagnosed with a “capacity-limiting disease,” such as Alzheimer’s, to indicate when they would want to receive Maid in the future, under circumstances when they have lost the ability to consent.

Dr. Coelho told the committee Canada’s existing Maid safeguards are already inadequate and the regime should not be further expanded.

One of the concerning deaths, she said, was of a woman with a severe history of mental illness but no physical medical diagnosis. Dr. Coelho said the death review committee was informed the patient received only one Maid assessment, despite the Criminal Code requiring assessments from at least two independent clinicians, either a physician or a nurse practitioner.

“I think that is a clear violation of the Maid eligibility,” she said.

Dr. Coelho, who was part of Ontario’s Maid Death Review Committee (Mdrc) until March of this year, described the other case as one that “still haunts” her.

She said the patient, a man in his 30s, was considered incapable of making decisions about his treatment. Instead, a family member was consulted for all health decisions, including when he could take over-the-counter medication.

She alleges that this family member expressed disappointment to the patient’s medical team that the man could not receive Maid, and that the patient had made a complaint of abuse against the family member.

The patient later became eligible for Maid, she said, despite no changes to his medical condition.

Dr. Coelho said it was documented in nurses’ notes that a family member had asked health care providers not to tell the patient he could change his mind about receiving Maid.

“If the Liberal government decides to go through with this bill as is, I will be devastated because you guys know now and should have known what is happening with Maid in Canada,” she testified.

Dr. Coelho said that after meeting with Ontario’s Chief Coroner Dirk Huyer and urging him to report the cases to police, she and two other committee members with concerns about Maid practice were told not to reapply to a renewed Mdrc.

In an e-mailed statement, Dr. Huyer said his office would not reveal whether either case spoken about by Dr. Coelho had been referred to police in order to protect the integrity of any potential investigation.

He said the coroner’s office has an established process for escalating concerns identified during Maid death reviews, ranging from informal feedback to referrals to external organizations, including regulatory colleges and police.

Later Thursday, the justice committee passed a motion requesting the production of documents referenced in Dr. Coelho’s testimony from the Office of the Chief Coroner of Ontario.

In the statement, Dr. Huyer said his office would produce the records requested by the parliamentary committee if legally compelled and if privacy protections could be satisfied.

Dr. Coelho also told the parliamentary committee that neither case was subsequently examined in an Mdrc report, despite the committee’s practice of reviewing and publishing cases that challenged “the limits of the law.”

Dr. Coelho told the committee she believes the cases were not published because they were not legal.

The Mdrc reviews a small number of cases involving difficult legislative, clinical or social circumstances to understand the deaths, generate discussion and identify opportunities to improve Maid practice.

Its reports have provided a layer of public scrutiny over the administration of Maid in Ontario, and have generated public debate and criticism from some Maid practitioners.

Laura Zilke, a spokeswoman for the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario, declined to provide information on whether the college received concerns about the cases from the coroner’s office, citing confidentiality constraints.

“If the College receives information relating to the provision of Maid, from the Office of the Chief Coroner or any other source, we assess it as we would any other concern about care or treatment provided by a doctor,” Ms. Zilke said in a statement.

The location of the deaths of the two patients was not made public during the hearing Thursday, so it is not clear which police force May have been contacted about the deaths.

Along with opening up advanced requests, Bill C-41 would also indefinitely pause Maid for patients whose sole underlying condition is mental illness. It was tabled this fall by Justice Minister Sean Fraser.

Mr. Fraser said in October that while the bill would remove the criminal prohibition on health care providers administering Maid to patients who make advanced requests, provinces and territories will have the authority to decide whether or not to offer the option.

When Maid became legal in Canada a decade ago, it was only for patients whose deaths are reasonably foreseeable. In 2021, the law was updated after a legal battle in Quebec led Parliament to establish “Track 2,” which allows patients to qualify if chronic diseases or disabilities are causing intolerable suffering.

Dr. Coelho mentioned in her testimony that the United Nations Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities previously recommended that Ottawa should repeal Maid for anyone without a terminal illness and that it should not permit advance requests.

“I have sympathy for those who want this option. But public policy must protect everyone it affects,” she said.

In a report last year, the UN committee said “inequality and discrimination cause and compound ‘suffering’ for persons with disabilities,” and that inadequate social supports can lead them to disproportionately seek advance requests.

The justice committee also heard on Thursday from former Conservative cabinet minister Lisa Raitt, who called for advance requests to be separated from Mr. Fraser’s bill so the issue can be studied separately.

Ms. Raitt’s husband, Bruce Wood, was diagnosed with early onset Alzheimer’s disease when he was 56.

stories.title: Toronto cybersecurity firm 1Password says hacker stole customer names, e-mail addresses
stories.summary: Company says customer password information was not accessed in attack
stories.author: Vanmala Subramaniam
stories.content:
Toronto-based cybersecurity company 1Password Inc. said Wednesday that it was the target of hackers who gained access to customer names and e-mail addresses, but did not manage to steal customer passwords.

In a public statement on Wednesday, the company said an attacker gained access to its back-end services and was able to download some customer names and e-mail addresses. However, its customer vault – where passwords are stored – remained secure.

The hacker was able to break into 1Password’s internal systems through an employee’s corporate GitHub account, a software-making tool owned by Microsoft, the statement said. 1Password became aware of the breach on Nov. 19.

The company did not immediately respond to The Globe’s request for comment on how many people were affected, or how customers were notified.

1Password is the latest victim in a series of hacks and data breaches that have taken place in recent months across the corporate world, including at Canadian law firms and consulting companies.

1Password is one of the largest and most popular password and credential managers, servicing millions of customers worldwide and more than 200,000 businesses. The company has been on a growth streak in the past year, fuelled by AI adoption, as companies look to secure internal AI agents using 1Password’s new AI security tools. Its annual recurring revenue, as of October this year, surpassed US$500-million, a 90-per-cent increase compared with the year prior.

Earlier this year, the company introduced a new tool called 1Password for Agents, which essentially allows a personal AI agent to access websites without exposing a user’s password to the agent.

The Wednesday statement on 1Password’s website states that users should be cautious about potential phishing attempts in the form of “unexpected e-mails about 1Password, such as invitations or account recovery requests that you did not initiate.” The company also said it has brought in independent cybersecurity experts to better understand what happened and how to prevent another breach.

Cybersecurity experts have long warned that AI tools are making it easier for bad actors to carry out hacks, and businesses should dedicate additional resources to beefing up their internal security practices. This month alone, two prominent Canadian brands – Staples and Bell – were involved in cybersecurity incidents, with third parties gaining access to customer data, such as names and e-mail addresses.

This is the first known incident in which 1Password has become the target of a direct data breach of its own customers’ data. In 2023, it was involved in a cyberincident related to San Francisco-based Okta, another security platform, where 1Password’s employee data was exposed because of a hack of Okta.

LastPass, a Boston-based password manager and competitor to 1Password has experienced major data breaches. In 2022, LastPass user passwords were exposed, and in another incident this year, LastPass customer data contained in Salesforce’s systems was compromised.

stories.summary: The court ordered Flair to pay for replacement items the plaintiff had to buy during her vacation, as well as baggage fees and court costs

‘It’s a weird thing when you get a letter telling you that you shouldn’t trust you.’ — Dave Carrol, who is running as an independent in a Dec. 7 Ontario byelection

Navigate

The court ordered Flair to pay for replacement items the plaintiff had to buy during her vacation, as well as baggage fees and court costs

A Flair Airlines jet. A court has ruled that the airline must pay a passenger for replacement items that she boughtwhen her bag was lost. (Photo courtesy of Flair Airlines)

November 26, 2026 at 3:03 p.m.

A wronged airline passenger has prevailed in a court dispute with Flair Airlines over delayed baggage compensation and ordered to pay $848.82.

Yin Lam Ma took her case against Flair before the B.C. civil tribunal, which oversees small court claims. Flair acknowledged that it temporarily lost her baggage while she was travelling from Vancouver to Calgary and offered to reimburse her baggage fees but it refused to pay for essential items, such as undergarments, clothing and cosmetics, that she had to buy while waiting for the luggage to be returned.

For her five-day vacation, Ma claimed $88.20 for baggage fees and $582.33 for the other expenses.

Flair contended in court that its tariff — a legal document that sets out the terms and conditions for plane tickets — reflects that the airline is not liable for expenses related to delays of “less than 21 days from the originally scheduled arrival” of a passenger’s luggage.

“It does not matter what Flair’s tariff’s says,” airline passengers rights advocate Gábor Lukács told National Post in an email. “The laws prevail, and Flair cannot avoid liability for baggage.”

Indeed, the court upheld the governing law and Ma prevailed. The law governing such disputes in Canada is set out in the Air Passenger Protection Regulations, which extend the baggage liability rules under the international Montreal Convention rules to domestic flights.

The story behind the dispute arose from a flight that Ma took to Calgary with one checked bag for a five-day vacation on June 24, 2024.

She subsequently reported the missing bag missing to Flair, then bought clothing and other items for her stay.

She testified that Flair advised her on June 30 that her luggage had been located and could be delivered to her home address. Then on July 8, Flair advised her the baggage was available at Vancouver International Airport. She picked it up on July 9.

In mid-July, Ma emailed Flair the receipts for the clothing and other items, requesting reimbursement. Flair refused to pay.

Ma argued that the Appr rules applied to her flight.

Flair disagreed and contended in court that it refers to its “Knowledge Base” when assessing passenger claims. But the airline did “not identify any legal authority” in court, noted civil tribunal member Deanna Rivers in her Nov. 17 decision.

Rivers wrote that “Appr section 23(2) addresses compensation when an airline returns delayed baggage within 21 days, as happened here. In these circumstances, section 23(2) requires Flair to compensate Ms. Ma … the amount the airline would have been required to pay for delayed baggage if Ms. Ma’s flight had been international.

“When baggage does not arrive on the same flight as the passenger, the airline must compensate the passenger for lost baggage and incidental expenses. At the time of Ms. Ma’s flight, the maximum compensation was … about $2,300,” Rivers wrote.

For almost 20 years, says Lukács, much of his advocacy before the Canadian Transportation Agency, the government agency that oversees airline passenger disputes (unless passengers go to court), “were about airline tariffs that excluded liability when the Montreal Convention said that liability cannot be excluded. Sadly, (this case) is nothing new and the CTA doesn’t do much to fight this.”

Rivers prefaced her decision by saying she would only find that “reasonably necessary and essential purchases are compensable in the circumstances.” The court decision sets out that Ma purchased several items, including a cellphone dashmount, personal care products, dental care items, cosmetics and undergarments, slippers, clothing and a jacket, for a total of $582.33.

“At the time Ma made these purchases,” Rivers wrote, “she did not know when Flair would return her baggage. She says she drove a rental vehicle from Calgary to Banff to visit the glaciers. In these circumstances, I find that each purchase was reasonable and not excessive. The receipts support the amounts claimed.”

On top of the reimbursement for these items and the baggage fee, Rivers ordered Flair to pay pre-judgment interest of $53.29. Ma was also entitled to court costs of $125.

Stewart Lewis is a writer and editor with National Post. A journalist and lawyer, he has worked in newspapers, radio and TV, and served a legal stint with Global Affairs Canada at the United Nations in New York City.

stories.title: Schulich Dentistry students earn national research awards
stories.summary: Student research spans regenerative dentistry, dental imaging, biomaterials and the links between social conditions and children’s health
stories.author: Special to Western News
stories.content:
From regenerating damaged dental tissues to understanding how social conditions affect children’s health, Schulich Dentistry students have earned national recognition for research exploring new approaches to oral health.

Schulich Dentistry students account for 25 per cent of this year’s recipients of awards jointly sponsored by the Canadian Association for Dental Research(Cadr) and the Network for Canadian Oral Health Research (Ncohr). Five students received 2026 Cadr-Ncohr Student Research Awards this month, which recognize outstanding student research and support recipients in presenting their work at national and international conferences.

“This recognition represents the growing strength and breadth of research at Schulich Dentistry,” said Dr. Noha Gomaa, professor in oral medicine and dental public health and the associate director for research at Schulich Dentistry.

### “I’m incredibly proud of our students and excited to see their work being showcased on national and international stages.” – Dr. Noha Gomaa, Schulich Dentistry professor and associate director for research

Among the recipients is third-year dental student Eric Mun, who ranked among the top two applicants nationally and will represent Canada at the International Hatton Competition in Melbourne, Australia, in June 2027. His research could help lay the groundwork for regenerating damaged tissues inside the teeth.

Dental pulp, the soft tissue inside a tooth containing nerves and blood vessels, helps keep the tooth alive and healthy. For children and adolescents, when the pulp dies before a tooth’s roots have fully formed, root development stops, leaving the tooth weaker and more vulnerable to fracture and eventual loss.

“Current treatments do not reliably restore natural pulp tissue or allow root development to continue,” explained Mun. “One of the major challenges in regenerative endodontics is creating an environment that encourages stem cells to form tissue resembling natural dental pulp.”

Eric Mun’s research could help lay the groundwork for regenerating damaged tissues inside the teeth. (Megan Morris/Schulich Medicine & Dentistry)

Under the supervision of Dr. Georgia Nikoloudaki, Mun is developing a biomaterial coating made from bovine dental pulp. The researchers remove the original cells while preserving the extracellular matrix – the natural environment that supports cells and sends biological signals that influence how they grow and behave.

By growing dental stem cells on the coating in the laboratory, the researchers can study how these natural components influence stem cell behaviour, with the longer-term goal of developing materials that could support tissue regeneration.

The research is still at an early stage, but could eventually inform treatments that help young patients preserve their natural teeth.

Mun is looking forward to sharing this work and connecting with researchers from around the world at the upcoming competition.

“It is an honour to represent Canada at an international conference. I am especially excited to share the high-quality research that is being conducted at our school,” he said. “I am looking forward to meeting researchers from around the world and learning about the different areas of research being explored in dentistry globally.”

The other four recipients represent research spanning dental imaging, biomaterials and the relationships between social conditions and children’s health:

Marie Le, a DDS/PhD candidate supervised by Dr. Gürkan Ünsal and Aaron Fenster, is investigating the feasibility of a head-mounted 3D ultrasound system to standardize imaging of the temporomandibular joint, which connects the jaw to the skull.

Rafaela Passos De Souza, a PhD candidate supervised by Dr. Sheila Butler, is studying how nanoparticle-modified (PEO) coatings enhance titanium bioactivity in simulated body fluid.

Luis Limo, a PhD candidate, supervised by Dr. Noha Gomaa, is investigating connections between socioeconomic disadvantage, biological aging, and child oral and developmental health.

Sandra Zivkovic, DDS Class of 2028, supervised by Dr. Noha Gomaa, is examining how parental stress and children’s dental caries are amplified by family socioeconomic disadvantage.

stories.title: Freezing rain warnings and Special Weather Statements issued for parts of southwestern Ontario
stories.summary: Environment Canada has issued Special Weather Statements for parts of southwestern Ontario due to gusty northeasterly winds and significant rain expected.
stories.author: Melanie Kentner
stories.content:
Environment Canada has issued Special Weather Statements and freezing rain warnings for parts of southwestern Ontario due to gusty northeasterly winds and significant rain expected.

Northeast winds gusting up to 80 km/h and rainfall amounts of 30 to 50 millimetres are possible beginning Thursday afternoon and diminishing overnight.

Freezing rain warnings in effect for:

Southern Wellington

Special Weather Statements in effect for:

St. Thomas - Aylmer - Eastern Elgin County

Rodney - Shedden - Western Elgin County

Woodstock - Tillsonburg - Oxford County

Simcoe - Delhi - Norfolk

The forecaster says rain and strong northeasterly winds are expected to develop as a low pressure system approaches the area.

Loose objects May be tossed. Utility outages are possible. Water will likely pool in low-lying areas.

stories.title: Slain guitarist Michael Eckert mourned by Toronto music scene: 'Everybody loved him'
stories.summary: Toronto - Michael Eckert, a Toronto pedal steel guitarist who was fatally shot during an overnight home invasion, is being remembered as a warm and engaging person and a talented, versatile artist who made an indelible mark on the city's music scene.
stories.author: Kaitlyn McGrath The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - Michael Eckert, a Toronto pedal steel guitarist who was fatally shot during an overnight home invasion, is being remembered as a warm and engaging person and a talented, versatile artist who made an indelible mark on the city’s music scene.

“You can see the outpouring of grief in our community,” said Ori Dagan, a Toronto jazz musician and producer. “It’s really quite remarkable to see how many people he touched.”

Police say Eckert was shot after a confrontation with a suspect inside a midtown residence. He was pronounced dead in hospital on Wednesday. He was 39.

Eckert was a celebrated musician whose talents were in demand across Toronto’s diverse music scene.

Less than two weeks ago, Eckert performed with Canadian country-rock band Blue Rodeo at the Grey Cup pre-game show in Calgary. The band called Eckert “an absolute wizard on his instrument.”

Blue Rodeo bassist Bazil Donovan had known Eckert for about five years.

“He took chances that nobody else might take or he tried to go beyond what the instrument normally was,” said Donovan.

During a Jim Cuddy Band performance on Wednesday in Meaford, Ont., Cuddy paid tribute to the Toronto musician.

“I couldn’t stop thinking about him the whole night we were playing,” Donovan said.

Dagan said he first met Eckert when they were both students at Humber College about 20 years ago and continued to run into each other while performing locally. Dagan said despite Eckert’s “blow-your-mind” talent playing a technically difficult instrument, he was humble and down to earth, with zero ego or attitude.

“Everybody loved him,” Dagan said, adding every time he ran into him, he gave “the most generous hug.”

Eckert was “someone who you just feel completely at ease with,” said Justin Gray, a Toronto-based music producer and engineer.

“He was always a really positive energy in the room and a certain gravity where it’s like, if he’s there, I think people are just drawn to him,” said Gray, who also knew Eckert since they were students at Humber.

Derek Downham, a Toronto-based music producer and Eckert’s longtime friend, called the pedal steel guitar one of the most difficult instruments to play, but Eckert had “impeccable dexterity, impeccable pitch and impeccable rhythm.”

“I can’t express how deep of a hole he leaves in the Toronto music scene,” he said.

Ryan Granville-Martin, a Toronto-based musician, said he remembers Eckert for his stage presence.

“He always had this big grin on his face,” said Granville-Martin, a drummer who performed with Eckert as recently as two months ago. “He would make eye contact with you when you were playing. He was really listening. He’s just the exact kind of player that you want to make music with.”

Ken Kelley, a guitarist and Eckert’s friend of 16 years, lives in Owen Sound, Ont., but travelled to Toronto after hearing the news. Seeing the police officers and caution tape in front of a home he called a place of refuge for him and others was devastating, he said.

“Where he died, I drank coffee,” he said, adding that the house was a gathering place for other musicians to practice.

“It’s been very traumatic to see that home that we’ve all spent so much time in.”

Toronto police say they are seeking at least one suspect in the shooting that happened shortly after 2:30 a.m. They are asking anyone with information about the case to come forward.

— With files from Sadeen Mohsen in Toronto

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 26, 2026.

stories.title: Defendant in Galloway defamation lawsuit played 'limited' role, lawyer tells trial
stories.summary: Vancouver - The lawyer for a defendant in Steven Galloway's defamation lawsuit says her client was not an "aggressive supporter" of the woman who accused the author and former University of B.C. professor of rape and sexual assault.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Vancouver - The lawyer for a defendant in Steven Galloway’s defamation lawsuit said Thursday that her client was not an “aggressive supporter” of the woman who accused the author and former University of B.C. professor of rape and sexual assault.

Rather, Vanshika Dhawan told the B.C. Supreme Court trial that her client Mandi Gray played a “relatively limited” role in the public fallout from the unproven claims.

Galloway denies the accusations and is suing his accuser, a woman whose name is covered by a publication ban, and three other defendants, over alleged defamatory statements published on social media and elsewhere between 2015 and 2018.

Galloway’s lawyer, Daniel Burnett, told the trial this week that there was “no person who did more to keep the defamatory message alive” than Gray.

That’s a mischaracterization, Dhawan said, and Gray’s “participation in the public discourse, though perhaps impulsive and regrettable,” was not personal or targeted.

Gray defended two allegedly defamatory statements as fair comment, while she did not contest three others during the trial.

Dhawan told the court that Gray’s actions were those of “somebody driven by a sense of justice for complainants” in sexual assault cases, including Galloway’s accuser, a woman known as A.B., whose allegations Gray “honestly believed.”

The rape and assault claims against Galloway were found unsubstantiated by retired judge Mary Ellen Boyd, who was hired by the university to investigate.

But Galloway, author of the bestselling novel “The Cellist of Sarajevo,” was fired from his post as chair of creative writing and has told the judge his career was destroyed.

The court has heard he is seeking millions of dollars in damages from A.B. and other defendants.

Dhawan said Gray was asking the court to consider damages “proportionate to her responsibility” among others whose actions caused Galloway harm.

The potential damages from Gray do not rise to a six-figure sum, she said.

She noted Gray testified earlier in the trial that she regretted some of her social media posts about Galloway and has deleted them.

“Regret is not an apology,” Justice Neena Sharma said.

Dhawan said a lack of apology does not necessarily mean a lack of remorse.

The lawyer also said her client’s statements were not malicious or reckless in nature. She said Gray had an “honest belief” in A.B.‘s account.

Dhawan concluded her final submissions on Thursday.

A.B.‘s lawyer Sydney Gomez said in closing submissions that her client didn’t attend the trial for health reasons, and her legal defence no longer contended her claims against Galloway were true, rather that she reported them to the university.

Galloway’s lawyers told the court this week they were asking for an “explicit” finding that the rape and assault allegations are false, should he win his lawsuit.

Burnett began his reply to the defendants’ arguments on Thursday.

He said A.B. had said she told fewer than 10 people about her allegations against Galloway, each in confidence, but that assertion was “not accurate.”

Burnett pointed to testimony from multiple witnesses earlier in the trial who told the court they did not recall A.B. requesting confidentiality.

The court has heard members of the creative writing department had convened a meeting about the allegations against Galloway and Burnett pointed on Thursday to evidence from two witnesses, including one whose affidavit became evidence after his death, who indicated “there was nothing said about confidentiality.”

The spread of a “deadly serious” allegation against Galloway had a “devastating effect” that an “unhinged” campaign would not, Burnett said.

“To say something about somebody who is in the public eye is to invite it to go viral,” he told the court.

Another defendant, Glynnis Kirchmeier, a former graduate student who is representing herself, also made her final submissions to the court on Thursday.

Galloway’s claim against her concerns a single post on Twitter in 2018 and she said it alone would not convince a reasonable reader that he was a rapist.

Kirchmeier told the court the motivation behind her statement was not to defame Galloway. Rather, she said it was to express her disapproval of what she described as his “efforts to control” a story about him published in the Walrus in 2016.

Kirchmeier has also argued Galloway’s claim against her was improperly pleaded, saying it’s an excerpt from a full sentence in which she wrote “raping/sexually harassing a student” as part of her commentary on the Walrus story.

The slash was meant to convey “and/or,” she said, and ending the claim at the word “raping” while excluding “sexually harassing” changes the meaning of the phrase.

“While it is true slashes can indicate duality instead of alternatives, this is a possibility, I submit, not a dominant meaning,” Kirchmeier said.

She said leaving out “a student” would mean she was accusing Galloway of “raping an undetermined number of people, a much graver defamation.”

In his earlier testimony, Galloway recalled becoming nauseated by the tweet and wondering “why is this person I’ve never met calling me a rapist?”

Kirchmeier said the tweet was one of some 7,000 in which she “almost exclusively” wrote about institutional mishandling of sexual misconduct complaints.

She acknowledged she has not apologized for the tweet at issue.

Galloway and his wife had testified about emotional harms relating to statements repeating the allegations against him, but Kirchmeier told the court on Thursday those harms were already playing out prior to her tweet in 2018.

Kirchmeier also said there was a “total lack of causation” between her tweet and the loss of Galloway’s writing career.

Several people originally named as defendants in the lawsuit settled with Galloway and issued public apologies before the trial began.

The trial is expected to conclude on Friday.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 26, 2026.

— With files from Darryl Greer

stories.title: Student athletes – how they juggle both education and athletics
stories.summary: With exam season approaching, many students are spending nights prepping for the biggest tests of the first se...
stories.author: Ryan Baynton
stories.content:
With exam season approaching, many students are spending nights prepping for the biggest tests of the first semester. But some need to find time during those same nights to practice for their college teams.

Balancing education and athletic expectations can be difficult for some student athletes. Time management is tough enough as a post-secondary student learning to navigate college courses and studies, even before factoring daily practices and games.

Cam Andree pitches in semi final game 2 against St.Clair 2026 -Photo credit Michael Barfoot

“It’s definitely trickier than I’d like it to be but if you just put the work in and get going to classes, even if you have games, it’s not that bad,” said student athlete Cam Andree. “It’s just when you fall behind and don’t do the work it catches up to you quick.”

Alongside needing to balance both the athletics and education, the bar is set high on every level, from weight rooms to expectations around school and student leadership, according to fitness and wellness program co-ordinator Tabitha Liston.

“I think the expectation for the athletes is that they are training seriously and that they are being the best role models for other students.”

Sleep is vital for success when juggling both aspects, Andree said.

“Make sure you’re getting a good nights rest.. everyday is going to be busy for a student athlete so it’s important that you rest,” Andree said.

First semester exams begin December 14.

stories.title: Injured Wainwright soldiers face long mental recovery, doctor says
stories.summary: Nineteen soldiers are being treated in provincial hospitals, with seven listed in critical condition, Acute Care Alberta says
stories.author: Daniela Germano
stories.content:
Soldiers being treated in hospital for burns from a deadly fire at an Alberta military base have a long psychological recovery ahead of them, says an Edmonton surgeon treating some of the injured.

Dr. Josh Wong, the interim medical director of the Edmonton Firefighters Burn Treatment Unit at the University of Alberta Hospital, says recovering from such severe burns can take months or years.

“For patients who experience severe burns, recovery is often a long and challenging journey. Their care doesn’t end when they leave the ICU or even the hospital,” Wong said Thursday at a news conference at the hospital.

“Many will require ongoing treatment and rehabilitation.”

Wong, who is a plastic and reconstructive surgeon specializing in burn cases, said the mental impact from even small burns can become more intense over time.

“I have mentioned to the families that the psychological effect actually comes up stronger as they recover and become more aware later on as well,” he said.

The Armed Forces had said that a windstorm on Oct. 17 pushed flames from a grass fire onto troops in a training exercise at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, southeast of Edmonton.

Prime Minister Mark Carney called the fire one of the worst tragedies for the Armed Forces on home soil during peacetime.

Four were killed in the fire. They have been identified as: Pte. Shaun Farrell, 23, of Prince Albert, Sask.; Pte. Aidan Goulding, 23, of North Vancouver, B.C.; Pte. Hayden Lykkemark, 19, of Langley, B.C.; and Sgt. Morgan Wong, 26, of Edmonton.

A fifth soldier, Pte. William Douglas Dal Bianco, died of his injured earlier this month while in an Ontario hospital.

About three dozen soldiers were initially injured.

Acute Care Alberta said 19 were still being cared for in provincial hospitals, with seven listed in critical condition.

The military said Saturday that two others remained in hospitals in British Columbia and Ontario, where they were transferred to be closer to their families.

Michael Suddes, interim chief operating officer for the Alberta Health Services’ Edmonton area, said officials could not provide specifics about the recovering soldiers due to patient confidentiality.

“But there is a spectrum,” he said. “Several patients, while they May be in critical condition, several (other) patients have already been discharged home.”

Alberta health officials say burned soldiers injured during a deadly fire at military base southeast of Edmonton will have a long psychological recovery ahead of them. The Canadian Press

Dr. Sayeh Zielke, interim chief executive officer of Acute Care Alberta, said the fire put a huge stress on the province’s health-care system.

“We passed it,” she said. “We were able to manage the capacity and co-ordinate the response to provide the care, not only for the injured soldiers, but also the rest of our version that needed care.”

Zielke said health-care providers are still in the thick of treating the injured soldiers, but soon there will be a debriefing process to see if improvements can be made.

“We’re trying to do our best by every single day. So for us, it very much feels like a marathon,” she said.

“There’s always lessons to be learned, and we can always do better and aim for perfection.”

Wong said patients with severe burns require complex, intensive treatment that involves multiple procedures and surgeries, extensive rehabilitation, psychological support and ongoing follow-up care.

He said the Wainwright fire presented an extraordinary challenge for his team, who admitted 20 critically injured patients in a short period of time – about five times the specialized burn critical care capacity.

He added that there were already 15 other burn patients in care at the time.

“Our teams moved quickly to mobilize the physicians, the nurses, other health-care professionals with specialized training and experience needed to provide this level of care,” Wong said.

He also recognized that many health-care workers May start to feel the effects of their hard work and trauma they have witnessed, and his team is preparing for that.

“When you’re in the midst of all the work and the adrenalin rushing and trying to help these patients, that’s where our focus is going to,” he said.

“But we know very well that as the weeks and the months go on, there will be some effects, there will be some fatigue, there’ll be some psychological effects of these injuries.”

stories.title: Middlesex County welcomes 2026 to 2030 County Council and Sue Clarke as next Warden
stories.summary: Middlesex County officially welcomed the 2026 to 2030 County Council during today's Inaugural Meeting, with newly elected and returning members taking their Oath of Office and formally beginning a new term of service.
stories.content:
MIDDLESEX COUNTY, ON – Middlesex County officially welcomed the 2026 to 2030 County Council during today's Inaugural Meeting, with newly elected and returning members taking their Oath of Office and formally beginning a new term of service.

Following the swearing-in ceremony, Council's first order of business was electing the Warden. Council elected Sue Clarke, Mayor of Adelaide Metcalfe, as the Warden of Middlesex County for the 2026 to 2027 term.

Warden Clarke brings a proven record of public service and community leadership to the role, having served Adelaide Metcalfe since 2018, including four years as a Councillor and serving as Mayor since 2022. This is Warden Clarke’s second term as Warden after holding the position for the 2025 to 2026 term.

"I am honoured by the confidence Council has once again placed in me and grateful for the opportunity to continue serving as Warden. As I look around the horseshoe, I am excited to see both familiar faces bringing valuable experience and new faces bringing fresh perspectives. Together, we can build strong relationships, work collaboratively on our priorities, and continue moving Middlesex County forward,” said Warden Clarke.

As outlined in Middlesex County's Procedural By-Law, the Deputy Warden will be most immediate past Warden serving on County Council. For the 2026 to 2027 term, Councillor Brian Ropp will be Deputy Warden.

The ceremony was attended by members of County Council, local municipal representatives, community leaders, family members, and guests.

County Council for the 2026 to 2030 term:

Adelaide Metcalfe Mayor Sue Clarke

Lucan-Biddulph Mayor Dave Manders

Middlesex Centre Mayor John Brennan Deputy Mayor Sue Cates

North Middlesex Mayor Brian Ropp

Southwest Middlesex Mayor Mike Sholdice

Strathroy Caradoc Mayor Colin Grantham Deputy Mayor Mike McGuire

Thames Centre Mayor Michelle Smibert Deputy Mayor Ed Lee

Middlesex County is an innovative, well-run organization offering high-value programs and services to the best community in which to live, visit, and do business in Southwestern Ontario. The County serves a vibrant, growing community of 89,000 people and offers a great place to call home, offering exceptional lifestyle, a wide variety of local attractions, and wonderful sense of community.

stories.title: Alberta projects $8.5-billion surplus as global turmoil drives up oil prices
stories.summary: Province remains reluctant to increase spending despite an $18-billion improvement in its fiscal outlook since February
stories.author: Matthew Scace
stories.content:
The Alberta government says it’s on track to post an $8.5-billion surplus as the oil-rich province continues to reap financial benefits from global turmoil, adding billions more to its coffers than it projected even a few months ago.

The province’s new estimate, unveiled at the second-quarter update on Thursday, means Alberta could end the fiscal year with about $18-billion more in the bank than expected when it delivered the 2026-27 budget in February predicting a $9.4-billion deficit.

Alberta’s financial boon is almost fully owed to high oil prices spurred by the war between the U.S. and Iran that has snarled supply chains and sent oil prices higher than $100 per barrel. The province has also escaped much of the damage inflicted by the trade war between Canada and the U.S., which has pushed neighbouring provinces deep into the red.

The provincial government is hesitant to increase spending in case oil prices drop, Alberta Finance Minister Jason Nixon told reporters in Edmonton.

“One lesson we can take away from the past several months is that we cannot take today’s conditions for granted,” Mr. Nixon said.

“Oil prices can change. They will change.”

The substantial financial cushion will help the province pay for one-time infrastructure projects that have yet to be announced, Mr. Nixon said, while several billions will be tucked away in the rainy-day fund created to wean Alberta off its reliance on oil revenues.

The province’s strong fiscal position will also give Premier Danielle Smith’s government financial firepower going into the upcoming election, scheduled for next October.

Mr. Nixon did not announce new affordability measures, but pointed to Alberta’s low-tax environment compared to its provincial counterparts when asked what steps the United Conservative government might take to ease concerns over the cost of living.

The province’s rapidly evolving financial picture underscores Alberta’s unique sensitivity to oil prices, with every $1 shift in the price of West Texas Intermediate representing a $680-million swing in the provincial purse. Since the February budget, the province’s oil-price projections have increased $23, to $83.50 a barrel.

In total, non-renewable resource revenues are now expected to hit $28.6-billion, a figure that would mark a provincial record, government officials said.

The government’s new estimates are a dramatic increase from the $2-billion projected surplus Mr. Nixon announced in late-August during its first-quarter update.

Mr. Nixon said the government is approaching the windfall with caution. The latest update shows the province has added about $600-million in spending to its budget since February, a small portion of the record $86-billion it plans to spend this year.

Without high oil prices rescuing the province’s books, the deficit would have broken a law implemented by Ms. Smith’s own government that aimed to control spending.

“There will be a cliff coming on WTI. At some point, it’s going to come,” Mr. Nixon said. “The two things that we do not know ... is when that is, and second, how steep that is.”

Alberta’s rosy financial picture is a stark contrast to other provinces. Ontario most recently upped its expected deficit to $16.9-billion, a roughly $3-billion increase from its initial expectations, pointing to tariffs and oil prices as the primary culprit.

To the west, British Columbia’s most recent fiscal outlook projected a $13.8-billion deficit – its largest shortfall since at least 1991. Newly elected B.C. Premier Lorne Doerkson has ordered an independent panel to examine the province’s books and has committed to “restoring fiscal discipline.”

In Alberta, Mr. Nixon said the province was drawing up parameters to make sure the surplus is spent properly. He did not say what those measures would entail.

But he said the province will likely make a “multibillion-dollar contribution” by fiscal year end to the Heritage Savings Trust Fund. Ms. Smith has committed to building it up to $250-billion by 2050 to limit oil prices’ influence on government coffers. The fund is currently valued at $36-billion.

With a report from Andrea Woo

Emmanuel Macron leans into the picture with Katy Perry and Justin Trudeau. The pop star shared the photo on Instagram this week. (Instagram)

November 26, 2026 at 1:52 p.m.

Former prime minister Justin Trudeau continues to lead a busy out-of-Canada life, with a recent visit to Oxford University following a romantic trip with girlfriend Katy Perry aboard the Orient Express.

Trudeau was at the British university this week for a conversation with Professor Ngaire Woods, founding Dean of the Blavatnik School of Government, a global public policy graduate school and research department within Oxford’s social sciences division.

Local news site Oxford Mail said Trudeau was in the city on Tuesday for an event at the Inamori Forum, the central, open atrium at the heart of the Blavatnik School.

Katy Perry and Justin Trudeau at Venice’s Marco Polo Airport on Nov. 23, 2026 in Venice, Italy. Stefano Mazzola / Getty Images

Earlier this month it was announced that Trudeau had joined the Blavatnik School as a distinguished fellow and a member of the World Leaders Circle, described by the university as a network of former heads of government “whose experience and insight shape the Blavatnik School’s work to improve governance around the world.”

The group includes former New Zealand prime minister Jacinda Ardern and former U.K. prime minister Rishi Sunak.

“In the decade that I was Prime Minister, the world went through profound change both geopolitically and technologically, which fundamentally reshaped our world,” Trudeau said Nov. 6 on accepting the appointment.

He added: “I look forward to contributing my experience, exchanging perspectives with fellow leaders, and engaging with the next generation of government and policy leaders as we consider how governments can respond to change and build a more hopeful, inclusive and prosperous future for everyone.”

National Post has reached out to Oxford for more details on his recent appearance.

Trudeau’s speaking engagements this year have included appearances at Queens University in Charlotte, N.C.; the Impact CEE (Central and Eastern Europe) conference in Poznan, Poland in May; and the World Travel and Tourism Council (Wttc) Global Summit last month in Malta.

Trudeau’s most recent stop at Oxford came after a week-long getaway with Perry, the pop star he’s been officially dating for about a year now. Rumours of their relationship started to spread after they were spotted together in Montreal in July 2025.

The couple began their vacation Nov. 17 in Spain, where Trudeau appeared as a speaker at the Metafuturo conference, an annual event to discuss global and societal challenges. They were spotted in Paris two days later, photographed leaving the Ritz hotel in the French capital.

Next up, a trip from Paris to Venice aboard the famed Orient Express. (The original service ended in 2009 but the name lives on in a series of luxury rail routes across Europe.) Perry shared a photo of herself in a bathtub aboard the train, and another with Trudeau, this one photobombed by French president Emmanuel Macron.

Paparazzi and social media posts then captured them in Venice, dining out and playing card games before taking a water taxi for the city’s Marco Polo Airport on Nov. 23.
