stories.title: Quebec government will sit without taking oath to King, Premier says
stories.summary: Province has appealed court ruling that declares legislators must swear allegiance to the monarch
stories.author: Maura Forrest
stories.content:
The Quebec Premier says his government will sit in the National Assembly next week, despite a court ruling that declares legislators must take an oath of allegiance to King Charles III.

Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon said Thursday that the Quebec Superior Court decision does not prevent the provincial legislature from opening as planned on Dec. 1, though none of Quebec’s 127 elected members have sworn fealty to the Crown.

“We’ll be at the Salon Bleu next Tuesday, and we won’t take an oath to the King of England,” Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon told reporters in Quebec City, referring to the assembly chamber.

“It’s absolutely absurd to think we should be forced to do that just to carry out our duties.”

The court ruling, released Monday , has been met with exasperation in Quebec, where members of the National Assembly decided unanimously nearly four years ago that the oath to Canada’s monarch no longer applies.

It has thrown Quebec politics into disarray just as the Supreme Court of Canada is set to weigh in on another constitutional battle with major implications for the province. On Friday, the top court will issue its ruling on Bill 21 , Quebec’s law banning religious symbols for certain public servants.

Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon, who led the sovereigntist Parti Québécois to form a minority government last month with a promise to hold an independence referendum, said both disputes are about “preserving the choices of Quebec’s democracy.”

A decision by the Supreme Court to limit the power of legislatures to “make their own democratic decisions will trigger, of course, a very strong reaction among all provinces,” he added.

In Monday’s ruling, a Quebec Superior Court judge suspended a 2022 law that had abolished the requirement for members of the National Assembly to swear loyalty to the Crown.

In the decision, Justice Ian Demers wrote that the suspension of the law means that lawmakers will now “be required to take an oath to the King before assuming their duties.”

The government has appealed that ruling and has asked the court to allow legislators to sit without taking the oath while the case proceeds. A hearing is scheduled for Friday afternoon.

But Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon said the court decision doesn’t explicitly order lawmakers to swear allegiance to the King.

“At the moment, there is nothing preventing us from sitting without being forced to humiliate ourselves and commit perjury as our first act in the National Assembly,” he said.

The Premier also accused opposition leaders of a “lack of consistency and loyalty” for refusing to sign a declaration stating their commitment to sit in the provincial legislature next week without taking an oath to the King.

“It speaks to them and their principles – or rather, their lack of principles,” Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon said Thursday.

Liberal Leader Charles Milliard and Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime have said they want the National Assembly to open as planned next week, but are awaiting the outcome of the appeal court hearing. They have not ruled out the possibility of swearing allegiance to avoid a delay.

On Wednesday, Mr. Duhaime raised doubts about the legality of sitting in apparent contravention of a court ruling.

The 2022 law was passed with the support of all parties after Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon and his caucus, then in opposition, refused to take the oath and were barred from entering the National Assembly.

Lawrence David, a lawyer who teaches at the University of Ottawa, launched a legal challenge in August, arguing Quebec has no authority to unilaterally amend the Constitution.

The substance of the case has yet to be heard, but Mr. David filed for an emergency injunction after the October election to force MNAs to take the oath before the legislature reconvened.

Justice Demers sided with Mr. David on Monday, ruling that if lawmakers did not swear allegiance to the Crown, “all laws passed by the National Assembly would be unconstitutional and would have to be re-enacted.”

The legal battle has prompted debate in Quebec this week, some of it tinged with frustration at the challenge to a unanimously adopted law that the federal government has shown no desire to fight. A column in La Presse dubbed it “a needless and ridiculous crisis.”

Other commentary has taken aim at Mr. David, and Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon also had words for the Ottawa lawyer on Thursday. “It is not Mr. Lawrence Whatever from the University of Ottawa who will stop me from dedicating myself to public service and to the people of Quebec,” he said.

Mr. David told The Globe and Mail in text messages that he has received “repeated hate mail and threats” over his role in the case. “This is unbecoming of a mature democracy, even if robust debate is one of its component parts,” he said.

Meanwhile, legislators have been firing shots at each other on social media, with one newly elected Conservative sharing a compilation of clips of current PQ MNAs swearing the oath to Queen Elizabeth II in years past.

“You see, it’s not that hard to pledge allegiance,” Marcos Archambault wrote on X. “It’s time to get to work!”

stories.title: More consultations planned on proposal to replace Ontario bar exam with course
stories.summary: Toronto - A proposal to replace the Ontario bar exam with a mandatory skills-based course remains up in the air more than a year after it was introduced, with the province's legal regulator promising to carry out more consultations before making a decision.
stories.author: Paola Loriggio The Canadian Press

Toronto - A proposal to replace the Ontario bar exam with a mandatory skills-based course remains up in the air more than a year after it was introduced, with the province’s legal regulator promising to carry out more consultations before making a decision.

In a new report, the professional development and competence committee of the Law Society of Ontario, the body that regulates and licenses the province’s lawyers and paralegals, says it plans to present a modernized lawyer licensing assessment model for approval by the end of 2027.

stories.title: $25 million nicotine seizure across southern Ontario: Cbsa
stories.summary: More than $350,000 worth of nicotine has been seized at Blue Water Bridge. This is part of a broader $25 million seizure from U.S. commercial shipments carried out across southern Ontario in a four-day period.
stories.author: Kate Otterbein
stories.content:
More than $350,000 worth of nicotine has been seized at Blue Water Bridge. This is part of a broader $25 million seizure from U.S. commercial shipments carried out across southern Ontario in a four-day period.

On Nov. 7, Canada Border Services Agency officers seized 463 kilograms of nicotine vapes and pouches, worth $355,250.

Officers also seized 268,388 kilograms of nicotine pouches from Queenston Bridge and 9,270 kilograms from Ambassador Bridge.

“The seizure of more than $25 million worth of illicit nicotine products by the Cbsa in Southern Ontario in November has helped combat organized crime and strengthened the security of our border,” said Gary Anandasangaree, minister of Public Safety.

“By stopping the illegal movement of contraband across our borders, we are protecting Canadian communities and safeguarding public safety.”

Seizures took place from Nov. 7 to Nov. 10.

“These significant seizures are a direct result of the vigilance, expertise, and dedication of our border services officers across the southern Ontario region,” saif Michael Prosia, regional director general of the southern Ontario Region Cbsa.

stories.title: Alberta expecting $18B budget turnaround propelled by oil royalties
stories.summary: Edmonton - Alberta's government says the oil-rich province is on track to reach record-high resource revenues this year.
stories.author: Lisa Johnson The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Edmonton - Alberta’s government says the oil-rich province is on track to reach record-high resource revenues this year.

Its second quarterly update of the year, released Thursday, predicts an $8.5-billion surplus — a wild swing from the $9.4-billion deficit originally expected for 2026-27.

Alberta’s finances are tethered to global energy prices, which surged earlier this year after the conflict between the United States and Iran began.

In February, the province was predicting West Texas Intermediate – the North American benchmark oil price — would average US$60.50 a barrel this year.

It’s now forecasting that price to be US$83.50 per barrel, driven by disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, a vital shipping lane at the mouth of the Persian Gulf.

Finance Minister Jason Nixon said global energy prices can change quickly, so the United Conservative Party government still needs to exercise caution and be disciplined in its spending.

“That means resisting the temptation to treat a sudden increase in resource revenue as permanent,” he said.

In the 2022-23 fiscal year, the province took in a record $25 billion in resource revenues, but the province expects to break that with almost $29 billion this year.

Nixon noted that between July and September, the WTI price was pushed as high as US$106 per barrel and as low as US$68.50 per barrel.

With every dollar increase in the average price, Alberta’s treasury stands to gain $680 million.

The latest outlook frees up $3.9 billion in surplus cash the government plans to spend before the end of the fiscal year. By law, at least half must go to the Heritage Saving Trust Fund, which is now expected to reach $36 billion by March.

The government’s goal is to see the rainy day fund’s net assets reach $250 billion by 2050, so the province can get off what’s long been characterized as a roller-coaster of royalty revenue.

Nixon said the money will also go toward one-time infrastructure spending on things such as roadway construction, but specifics won’t be decided until the province has more actual budget numbers.

“I do hear one thing and one thing all the time, which is concerns about roads. So we’ll start with that,” he said.

Despite the expected windfall, overall spending this year is only going up by $646 million.

Nixon said headlines don’t always match kitchen-table concerns, and he acknowledged the pressure Albertans are under due to inflation and the cost of living.

However, he said the government is focused on maintaining existing affordability programs, including the province’s comparably low tax rates.

Nixon didn’t announce any new rebates or relief Thursday, but said cabinet would consider targeted ways to help.

In October, high gas prices that had battered consumers for months pushed the government to cut the gas tax for at least three months, saving most drivers 13 cents per litre.

That replaced a $100 fuel tax rebate program that began in July, but the application process was criticized as invasive and onerous.

On Thursday, the Canadian Automobile Association pegged the national average price of regular gas at $1.42 per litre. The gas price tracking website GasBuddy estimated Alberta’s average to be $1.23 per litre — the lowest in the country.

Nixon said low gas prices are lowering the inflation rate and the cost of other commodities, including groceries.

Opposition NDP finance critic Court Ellingson told reporters that the UCP government has been given the gift of higher oil prices, but Albertans aren’t feeling it.

“They’re feeling that the costs of living are exceeding wage growth,” he said.

“Albertans can’t afford to buy groceries. Albertans can’t afford to pay their rent.”

He pointed to the Ndp’s affordability proposals. They include increasing the minimum wage predictably to $18 per hour from the current $15 per hour then tying it to inflation.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 26, 2026.

stories.title: ‘Don’t do it’: expert urges young people to avoid using nicotine
stories.summary: Nicotine can be highly addictive with risks such as strokes and affects to your brain development, according t...
stories.author: Torey Joseph Legarrie
stories.content:
Nicotine can be highly addictive with risks such as strokes and affects to your brain development, according to Rob Cunningham, Senior policy analyst at the Canadian Cancer Society. He urges young people to avoid tobacco and nicotine products.

He said that the best advice he has is to never start smoking nicotine.

“Don’t do it. Don’t do it.”

He warned that smoking can negatively affect both health and finances and that some young people who experiment don’t think they’ll ever become addicted, only to find themselves struggling with dependence years later.

Rob Cunningham, senior policy analyst at Canadian Cancer Society (tbnewswatch.com)

He said the brain is particularly vulnerable to nicotine’s addictive effects, and the risks associated with nicotine addiction are especially concerning for younger people cause their brains are still developing.

“Nicotine is highly addictive. The brain is a central part where addiction occurs.”

While vaping is considered less harmful than smoking, Cunningham stressed that vaping is not-risk-free and that using both products can undermine the benefits of quitting smoking.

“Health Canada has said that vaping is less harmful than smoking. They’ve not said that for dual use.”

He said that the progression of getting youth to stop using nicotine is going backwards.

“We’ve made such great progress in reducing youth smoking. We’re having a new generation becoming addicted to nicotine.”

For people deciding to quit nicotine, Cunningham said motivation, support and accessible resources can help.

The Middlesex-Health-Unit provides treatments like counselling and treatments to those who would like to quit, and there is a toll-free number and website listed on cigarette cartons.

“Support can help people stay smoke-free and reinforce the decision to quit.”

stories.summary: NEW Westminster - The family of a British Columbia woman found dead more than five years ago has filed a civil lawsuit against her husband, asking the B.C. Supreme Court to declare that he killed her.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The family of a British Columbia woman found dead more than five years ago has filed a civil lawsuit against her husband, asking the B.C. Supreme Court to declare that he killed her.

Trina Hunt’s burned body was found in March 2021 near Hope, B.C., two months after the 48-year-old was reported missing.

stories.title: Former North Perth mayor passes away
stories.summary: Todd Kasenberg, former mayor of North Perth, has passed away.
stories.author: Kate Otterbein
stories.content:
Todd Kasenberg, former mayor of North Perth, has passed away.

Mayor Doug Kellum confirmed the news.

“It is with great sadness that we share the passing of former Mayor Todd Kasenberg, a dedicated public servant and passionate advocate for our community,” Kellum said in a statement.

“We extend our sincere condolences to Todd’s family, friends, and all who knew him.”

Kasenberg was elected as mayor in 2018. He served two terms on county council until 2026. He also served as the manager of community development for United Way Perth Huron.

“Todd brought a thoughtful approach to his time on County Council and was exceedingly proud of the North Perth community he represented,” said Sue Orr, Perth County warden.

“He was a diligent advocate, often joining staff at a variety of delegation meetings with provincial ministries over the course of his tenure. He was particularly committed to advancing the issue of affordable housing and ensuring Perth County was a place where everyone could thrive.”

Flags at municipal buildings have been lowered to half-mast.

stories.title: Used-car prices are falling — here’s what’s driving the decline
stories.summary: Used cars May be getting more affordable in Canada, recent reports show, while potential buyers May be holding back amid ongoing cost-of-living challenges.
stories.author: Ariel Rabinovitch
stories.content:
Used cars May be getting more affordable in Canada, recent reports show, while potential buyers May be holding back amid cost-of-living challenges, higher gas prices, and rising inflation and borrowing costs.

Reports show that although comparable used vehicles are getting cheaper, consumers aren’t feeling much relief amid weaker transactions and higher financing costs.

A new report released Wednesday from Clutch , a Canadian used-car buying platform, shows the average price for all used vehicles in Canada in October was $33,920, down 0.3 per cent from a year earlier.

But when doing an apples-to-apples comparison of individual vehicles by model year and mileage, the average price is two per cent less, or about $630, and 11 out of 12 of the top-selling used vehicles in Canada cost comparably less than a year ago.

In some cases, vehicles were thousands of dollars cheaper.

For example, a used Nissan Rogue cost about $2,600 less last month than one of the same age and mileage a year earlier, while the GMC Sierra 1500 and Chevrolet Silverado 1500 saw declines of around $2,200 and $1,900 respectively.

Clutch says one of the main reasons for these comparable price drops is an increase in supply that’s been happening for several months as demand has remained relatively stable.

“After the pandemic, you saw a lot of production come back online, and a lot of those cars are now coming to market in the used market,” says Clutch CEO Dan Park.

About a quarter of all used Nissan Rogues sold on Clutch so far this year were a 2023 model year, about double the rate from last year, Park says.

But just because some of these used vehicles May be comparably cheaper to buy doesn’t necessarily mean most Canadians can afford them or are ready to buy.

AutoTrader released its Q3 price index on Nov. 10, which included the results of a survey conducted in September.

Among nearly 1,200 Canadian participants, roughly half (48 per cent) said they were postponing the purchase or lease of a vehicle.

However, about two-thirds (65 per cent) said they still planned to buy within 12 months.

Another report from Carfax, released last month, showed used vehicle inventory levels increased to 228,788 in August. This is the highest level recorded since the start of the year, and up nearly 19 per cent compared to July.

At the same time, the number of used vehicle transactions in August fell nearly seven per cent month-over-month, and 6.6 per cent compared to a year earlier.

Carfax said this signals “softer demand as affordability challenges and economic uncertainty weigh on Canadian consumers.”

Financing a vehicle, whether used or new, is also getting more expensive as the Bank of Canada raises borrowing rates.

According to the Clutch report, the hike in October means a vehicle loan of $29,500 over a six-year term could cost about $255 more. That increase is poised to double as early as next month i f the central bank hikes rates another 0.25 percentage points, which many economists now expect.

That rate hike could be coming as financing a vehicle is already getting more expensive in Canada, according to AutoTrader.

Used vehicle monthly payments are currently averaging $638, up 1.8 per cent from last year, AutoTrader added.

Despite economic uncertainty and affordability pressures, the numbers show that, at least for now, the used car market is stabilizing, Park says.

“Things are certainly more expensive. Thankfully, you’ve seen fuel prices come down, which is making car ownership a little bit more affordable for those that have gas-powered vehicles,” he adds.

“I think what you’re seeing is stability and we’ve seen stability in prices over the last 18 months and the stability in price certainly helps allow people to make a more confident decision .”

Things could change with the trade war, and how tariffs could result in higher prices for new vehicles in Canada.

Higher prices for newer vehicles could result in more demand for comparably cheaper options on the used market.

“Given the relative stability of both the new- and used vehicle markets, there hasn’t been a material change in vehicle prices. As seen during the pandemic and last year’s tariff period, shifts in the new-car market tend to affect used vehicle prices more rapidly and significantly,” AutoTrader said in its report.

“If trade uncertainty persists, which seems to be the case at the time of writing, used vehicle prices could face some pressure closer to the tariff deadline in January.”

stories.title: Carney in Saskatchewan to campaign for long-shot byelection win
stories.summary: Yorkton - Prime Minister Mark Carney is in Yorkton, Sask., to help the Liberals campaign for a byelection in a riding his party has never won in its nearly 60 years of existence.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Yorkton - Prime Minister Mark Carney campaigned Thursday in Yorkton, Sask., for a byelection in a riding his party has never won in its nearly 60 years of existence.

The byelection in Yorkton—Melville is one of six which will be decided on Dec. 7. Carney made a stop in the Saskatchewan city just ahead of advance voting, which begins Friday.

The prime minister also met with Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe in Regina.

Saskatchewan has been something of a political desert for the federal Liberals for several decades. Carney, who is 61, was just three years old the last time Yorkton welcomed a sitting Liberal prime minister. Pierre Trudeau campaigned there as prime minister during the 1968 election.

That previous visit by a prime minister wasn’t quite as long ago as Carney thought, however — he told a crowd of about 200 people at the Owl’s Nest restaurant that he was the first to visit the city since 1910.

Yorkton, a city of about 16,000 people in southeastern Saskatchewan, is the largest city in Yorkton—Melville, a mostly rural riding that shares a border with Manitoba.

Cathay Wagantall resigned the seat in August after having held the riding for the Conservatives since 2015. In 2025, she won with nearly 80 per cent of the vote and had the ninth highest margin of victory of any of the 343 ridings across Canada.

Yorkton-area farmer Nelson Pohl won a nomination contest to run in the riding for the Conservatives. The Liberals are challenging him with Aaron Kienle, the mayor of Yorkton.

Conservative MP Kevin Waugh told reporters in Ottawa Thursday that the Liberals have “only worked Yorkton” and have no shot at winning.

“I was in rural Saskatchewan. They are nowhere to be seen,” he said, suggesting the party doesn’t have enough volunteers. “The riding’s a little bigger than Yorkton.”

Yorkton accounts for about one-fifth of the riding’s population.

Carney expressed some optimism Thursday when asked if he felt Kienle could overcome Conservative dominance in Saskatchewan. While he said the party was lucky to have Kienle carry its banner in the byelection, he was also aware of the odds of winning.

“I looked at the results of the last election here. The percentages were just a little off in terms of the votes for the Liberal party,” he said.

The Liberals earned less than 15 per cent of the vote in Yorkton—Melville in 2025.

The Conservative, Canadian Alliance and Reform parties have collectively held Yorkton—Melville for three decades, winning every election there since 1993 — all but one of them with more than 50 per cent of the vote.

In 2025, Buckley Belanger became the first Liberal to win a seat in the province since 2015, when the party also won just one seat. In 2019 and 2021, the party was shut out of the province entirely.

Polling aggregator 338Canada suggests the Liberals’ overall popularity May be shifting some seats in Regina and Saskatoon in their direction — but not Yorkton—Melville.

Dan Arnold, chief strategy officer at Pollara Strategic Insights, said even though it’s unlikely the Liberals will win Yorkton, Carney’s visit might help the party in other Saskatchewan ridings in future elections.

Arnold, who oversaw the Liberals’ research program during their 2015, 2019 and 2021 election campaigns, said former prime minister Justin Trudeau would visit every riding during byelections, even if he had no hope of winning.

“I think this is more a symbol to the rest of the province,” he said. “And ultimately, if they got a good result there and increased the vote share from the last election, that would also be a signal that in non-traditional markets, there’s some openness to the party.”

Yorkton—Melville is one of two seats the Conservatives won in 2025 which are being contested again in the December byelections.

The other, Brantford—Brant South in Ontario, May be a lot harder for the Conservatives to hold after leader Pierre Poilievre opted against a nomination contest there.

Poilievre chose instead to appoint Brantford, Ont., Mayor Kevin Davis as the Conservative candidate, which prompted some blowback from local conservatives. Dave Carrol, a pastor and longtime Conservative, had already spent months campaigning for a nomination contest that never happened.

Carrol is now running as an Independent, a decision which adds intrigue to the byelection since it could draw votes away from the Conservatives, who were already expected to face a tough challenge from the Liberals.

Joy O’Donnell, a financial planner and the local chamber of commerce president, is running for the Liberals.

Poilievre has been to the riding multiple times to campaign and there are signs the Conservatives are concerned about Carrol’s potential to draw away votes. Social media posts suggest Conservative volunteers have been handing out flyers in the riding claiming Carrol would join the Liberals if he were to win.

Sarah Fischer, a spokesperson for the Conservative Party of Canada, told The Canadian Press volunteers and members of the Conservative campaign distribute authorized literature in accordance with the Canada Elections Act.

“The lit piece in question is accurate and highlights a local candidate liking a social media comment that encouraged him to cross the floor to the Liberals,” she said in an email. “It was authorized by the Conservative party and contained the required ‘authorized by’ line. All rules were followed and the information is accurate.”

Arnold said the Brantford—Brant South riding is important to the Conservatives. He compared it to the Toronto-St. Paul’s riding, which had been held by the Liberals for decades before it was won by Conservative candidate Don Stewart in 2024.

“When Trudeau lost St. Paul’s, it was a longtime Liberal stronghold and that created a series of chain events and spirals that ultimately ended his leadership of the party,” he said.

“If I was advising (Poilievre), I’d say, ‘Yes, spend a lot of time there.’”

Poilievre said Wednesday voters have a clear choice before them.

“You vote Liberal for more soft on crime, you vote Conservative to fight against crime. You vote Liberal for more out-of-control mass migration, you vote Conservative to get immigration under control,” said Poilievre.

Arnold said a Conservative loss in Brantford—Brant South would embolden Conservatives who want Poilievre to quit the leadership.

“It would give them a right to add on to weak polling numbers, weak fundraising numbers, weak byelection results. You start to build a pretty strong case against him in that case,” he said.

When asked Wednesday about the party’s chances in the byelections, Conservative MP Ben Lobb said he doesn’t think anybody knows how the vote in Brantford—Brant South will go.

“I think it’s close,” he said. “Really, ON that one, it’s whoever gets out the vote.”

Lobb said Conservatives are focused on victory and are not talking about “what-ifs.”

Three of the six byelections are being held in Quebec: Laurier—Ste-Marie and Rosemont—La Petite-Patrie, both in Montreal, and St-Hyacinthe—Bagot—Acton in the Montérégie region of southwestern Quebec. The sixth byelection is in Scarborough North in Toronto.

Polls suggest the Liberals are sitting at close to 50 per cent support in Quebec, which could give them an edge in all three contests there. The Toronto seat is considered a Liberal stronghold.

Since the 2025 election, 13 of 343 members of Parliament have decided to step down and seven byelections have been held.

The Liberals have won six of those byelections — five in seats they already held and one a pickup from the Conservatives in Chicoutimi—Le Fjord in Quebec.

The Conservatives won one in Alberta in 2025, when Poilievre had to run to find a seat in the House after losing his long-held Ottawa-area seat in the 2025 general election.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 26, 2026.

— With files from Ian Bickis in Yorkton, Sask., and Catherine Morrison and Nick Murray in Ottawa

When asked Wednesday about the party’s chances in the byelections, Conservative MP Ben Lobb said he doesn’t think anybody knows how the vote in Brantford—Brant South will go.
“I think it’s close,” he said. “Really, ON that one, it’s whoever gets out the vote.”
Lobb said Conservatives are focused on victory and are not talking about “what-ifs.”

Three of the six byelections are being held in Quebec: Laurier—Ste-Marie and Rosemont—La Petite-Patrie, both in Montreal, and St-Hyacinthe—Bagot—Acton in the Montérégie region of southwestern Quebec. The sixth byelection is in Scarborough North in Toronto.
Polls suggest the Liberals are sitting at close to 50 per cent support in Quebec, which could give them an edge in all three contests there. The Toronto seat is considered a Liberal stronghold.
Since the 2025 election, 13 of 343 members of Parliament have decided to step down and seven byelections have been held.
The Liberals have won six of those byelections — five in seats they already held and one a pickup from the Conservatives in Chicoutimi—Le Fjord in Quebec.
The Conservatives won one in Alberta in 2025, when Poilievre had to run to find a seat in the House after losing his long-held Ottawa-area seat in the 2025 general election.

stories.title: Canadian dollar edges lower as investors await key GDP data
stories.summary: The ​loonie was trading 0.2 per cent lower at 1.4242 per US dollar
stories.author: Fergal Smith
stories.content:
The Canadian dollar weakened against its ​US counterpart on Thursday but ‌the move was limited as investors turned attention to domestic GDP data that could guide expectations for Bank of Canada interest rate ⁠hikes.

The ​loonie was trading 0.2 per cent lower at 1.4242 per US dollar, or 70.21 US cents, giving back some of the gains made over the previous two days after the ​Bank of Canada said it May need ‌to respond forcefully to tackle supply shocks.

Investors see a roughly 80-per-cent chance the central bank will tighten next month, swap market data showed.

“We remain sceptical that a December hike is ‌warranted, with ​CPI-trim at 1.8 per cent ‌and three consecutive monthly employment declines, so Monday’s Q3 GDP ​and next Friday’s November jobs report remain ⁠the real test of BoC pricing,” strategists at Monex ⁠Europe said in a note.

Economists say Canada’s economy likely ​slowed in the third quarter after posting second-quarter annualized growth of 3.3 per cent.

Equity markets globally notched gains as the U.S. Thanksgiving holiday appeared to offer a welcome break from AI jitters and after the latest ⁠salvo of U.S. tariffs looked less damaging than first feared.

“Trade remains a background risk after Canada was spared from a new U.S. tariff package, albeit with issues around steel, aluminium, and autos still unresolved,” the Monex Europe strategists said.

⁠The price of oil, one of ​Canada’s major exports, rose after Yemen’s Houthis said they hit ⁠Saudi Arabia’s largest oil refinery and Iran said mines struck ships in the ‌Strait of Hormuz, reviving concerns about supply disruption. U.S. crude oil futures were ​trading 1.1 per cent higher at $84.63 a barrel.

Canadian government bond yields moved lower across the curve. The 10-year was down 3.3 basis points at 3.636 per cent, moving closer ​to the bottom of its range in recent months.

stories.title: Independent candidate surprised to receive flyer warning him he would join Carney’s Liberals
stories.summary: 'It's a weird thing when you get a letter telling you that you shouldn't trust you,' said Dave Carrol, an independent candidate in Brantford—Brant South.
stories.author: Sarah Ritchie
stories.content:
Ottawa — Dave Carrol returned home from a recent day of door-knocking in Brantford—Brant South to find two notices in his mailbox marked “important voting information.”

He opened them and read a pair of identical warnings, underlined and in bold font: “A vote for Dave Carrol is a vote for the Liberals.”

“It’s a weird thing when you get a letter telling you that you shouldn’t trust you,” he said with a bemused chuckle.

But his amusement was short-lived.

“The truth is that it’s not ridiculous, and it’s not OK, and it’s not how we should be doing things,” he said.

Carrol is running as an independent candidate in a byelection that will end with a vote on Dec. 7.

It’s a tightly contested seat, and the race itself has already featured “twists and turns” he couldn’t have anticipated a couple of months ago.

As a longtime volunteer for local Conservatives and the former president of the Conservative electoral district association, Carrol helped run campaigns for former Tory MPs Phil McColeman and Larry Brock.

Before resigning his seat in the House of Commons this fall, Brock recorded a video offering Carrol his full endorsement and telling voters, “Dave is poised — he’s well-poised — to take over. I hand over the baton to him to take over and be your strong voice in Brantford—Brant South.”

But he never had the chance to offer his name as a Conservative candidate.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre held a rally in Brantford on Sept. 20 where he announced from the stage that the party’s banner would be carried in the byelection by outgoing mayor Kevin Davis. Poilievre used his prerogative as leader to skip the nomination contest and install a candidate of his choosing.

Carrol said he was never given an explanation.

Polls at the time suggested the riding was a dead heat between the Conservatives and the Liberals, buoyed by Prime Minister Mark Carney’s popularity. The chattering classes in Ottawa were already discussing what a potential Tory loss could mean for Poilievre’s job security.

Seven MPs have left the official Opposition benches since the 2025 election. Between November 2025 and April 2026, four MPs crossed the floor to join Carney’s government in a slow trickle of morale-busting rumours that helped hand the Liberals a majority.

Quebec MP Richard Martel accepted Carney’s appointment to the Senate over the summer. Brock and Cathay Wagantall both resigned, while Scott Aitchison announced plans to do the same later this fall.

Brock, who was seated behind Poilievre at the rally that day, appeared visibly shocked at the announcement. McColeman marched off the stage, later telling reporters he was upset with the decision. He, too, had endorsed Carrol.

For his part, Carrol thought long and hard about what to do next. He said a conversation with Bobbi Ann Brady, who’s been an independent member of Ontario’s legislature since 2022, helped convince him it was feasible to run without the backing of a major party.

“She’s able to function with any different party. She’s able to cut through all of the different partisan fighting,” he said.

It was an encouraging message from a former colleague — and a self-described fan of Carney’s — that provided the alleged evidence of his intention to cross the floor. The letter that landed in Carrol’s mailbox includes a printed screenshot of a comment on his Facebook page that reads, in part, “I certainly wish you well in your political career, but not too much success. If you win maybe I can convince you to cross the floor.”

It ends with a laughing emoji, and the screenshot highlights that Carrol “liked” the post.

Carrol is emphatic that he will not join the Liberals, should he win on Dec. 7. He simply meant to show his appreciation for the endorsement.

“In the next two-and-a-half years between now and the next federal election, we’re either going to have an unpopular Conservative representative, or a Liberal representative that is going to be at the back of the House, or you can have an Independent that goes, ‘Here’s what our needs are. I’m going to go match up resource with local needs,’” he said.

The calls and text messages from friends and neighbours started coming in shortly after Carrol opened the letter in his own mailbox. People who had his signs on their lawns were receiving the same note.

“I saw that you might be supporting Dave Carrol in this federal byelection for Brantford,” it said.

“We can’t elect someone that will break our trust and become a Liberal.”

The unsigned note ends with, “I am voting Conservative, and I hope you will too.”

Carrol doesn’t know for sure who’s spreading the messages. He has his suspicions.

He opened them and read a pair of identical warnings, underlined and in bold font: “A vote for Dave Carrol is a vote for the Liberals.”
“It’s a weird thing when you get a letter telling you that you shouldn’t trust you,” he said with a bemused chuckle.
But his amusement was short-lived.
“The truth is that it’s not ridiculous, and it’s not OK, and it’s not how we should be doing things,” he said.
Carrol is running as an independent candidate in a byelection that will end with a vote on Dec. 7.
It’s a tightly contested seat, and the race itself has already featured “twists and turns” he couldn’t have anticipated a couple of months ago.

As a longtime volunteer for local Conservatives and the former president of the Conservative electoral district association, Carrol helped run campaigns for former Tory MPs Phil McColeman and Larry Brock.

Poilievre used his prerogative as leader to skip the nomination contest and install a candidate of his choosing.
Carrol said he was never given an explanation.

Polls at the time suggested the riding was a dead heat between the Conservatives and the Liberals, buoyed by Prime Minister Mark Carney’s popularity. The chattering classes in Ottawa were already discussing what a potential Tory loss could mean for Poilievre’s job security.

The unsigned note ends with, “I am voting Conservative, and I hope you will too.”
Carrol doesn’t know for sure who’s spreading the messages. He has his suspicions.
“The day before these pieces of mail wound up in my mailbox, an email to Conservative supporters went out that had very similar language,” he said.

A spokesperson for the Conservative party later confirmed the party has authorized literature that “is accurate and highlights a local candidate liking a social media comment that encouraged him to cross the floor to the Liberals.”

stories.title: Community of crafters seeks 900 handmade quilts for children in foster care
stories.summary: Carefully planning each block — just as if their creations were hugs — a group of crafters near St. John’s are working to create or collect 900 quilts across Newfoundland and Labrador: one for each child in foster care in the province.
stories.author: Garrett Barry
stories.content:
Mount Pearl, N.L. - A group of crafters near St. John’s are working to create or collect 900 quilts across Newfoundland and Labrador: one for each child in foster care in the province.

About 100 have been counted so far among the Cabot Quilters’ Guild, who are aiming to collect all the quilts by April 2027. This initiative is part of the group’s regular outreach efforts, though this is the first year they’ve picked donations for foster children in the province.

“As quilters, we look at our quilts as hugs. It’s comfort,” said Heather Blagdon, a quilter with the group.

“This is a hug from a stranger that belongs to them forever. And so no matter where they go, they will bring that comfort with them.”

The donations will be intended for children, not foster parents. A personalized name tag will be sewn onto every quilt, so that children in foster care have something that’s uniquely their own.

“For a child entering foster care, to know that someone thought about me, someone knew that I was going to have this difficult day, unfortunately, but they decided to do this for me to help bring a smile to my face on a really tough day — There’s no dollar value or no amount that can be put on that,” said Kelli Hodder, the executive director of Foster Families Newfoundland and Labrador.

Her group provides supports to parents who are fostering or considering it — something the province dearly needs.

‘A hug from a stranger’

Hodder says one of her organization’s programs gives a full book bag to children as they enter foster care, with teddy bears and art supplies — and she’s seen how a simple act of kindness can make, “quite a difference.”

“Now to be able to give them their own beautiful quilt that they can have with them forever, and they’ll probably treasure forever, that’s just incredible.”

Foster Families Newfoundland and Labrador will distribute the quilts collected as part of this crafting drive.

The effort is also partly a memorial for two former members of the Cabot Quilters’ Guild, who both died in recent years. Both Bev McFadyen and Lorraine Dyke were presidents of the guild, as well as first cousins.

“Children had a special place in their heart,” said Michelle Whelan, another guild member. “When you look at all these quilts and that we’re doing this project for foster care — I’m sure if Bev and Lorraine were here, they’d be so happy.”

The group hosts regular quilting meetups where they work on projects and share tips. A three-day quilting retreat was held this week, giving members a perfect chance to ramp up their efforts towards this year’s lofty goal.

“I think there’s no shortage of enthusiasm,” said Whelan. “We’re happy to have other guilds and other people from across Newfoundland and Labrador help us with our project.”

Some donations have come in from out-of-province too, like a quilt from Nova Scotia. Each is made with children particularly in mind.

“Sometimes when we’re anxious or sad, we need something to touch,” explained Blagdon, demonstrating the binding on her quilt. “So I intentionally chose to do something called big stitch binding so that the child can sit there and they can just rub along this if they wish.”

“This spoke of sunshine and bright colours and happiness, and that’s what I wanted to pass along to another child.”

stories.title: Costs to host Canada’s Investment Summit surpassed $8.1-million
stories.summary: Agency tasked with attracting foreign capital incurred most of the cost for the two-day event
stories.author: Craig Lord
stories.content:
Newly disclosed figures show the cost of hosting Canada’s first-ever national investment summit earlier this year topped $8.1-million.

Prime Minister Mark Carney gathered scores of international investors and global business leaders in downtown Toronto in September for the inaugural Investment Summit .

The two-day event was designed to show Canada is open for business and to promote a list of shovel-ready projects to prospective investors.

Major Canadian banks, corporations and institutional investors used the summit as a backdrop to announce financing and capital project plans, but it will likely be months before Ottawa sees whether the event led to meaningful foreign investment.

Conservative House leader Andrew Scheer requested a breakdown of costs to host the summit and the government’s response was tabled in the House of Commons on Monday.

Most of the summit costs were incurred by Invest in Canada, the agency responsible for attracting foreign investment to the country, with a small portion handled by the Privy Council Office.

Roughly $1.4-million of those costs have already been settled but nearly $6.7-million in expected payments have yet to be doled out.

Among those outstanding costs is the $132,935 sum for a gala dinner at the Art Gallery of Ontario, where attendees dined on smoked Arctic char, bison short rib and roasted pear – all sourced within Canada.

There’s also a $6.5-million line item in the pending costs for “estimated remaining costs associated with event production.”

A spokesperson for Invest in Canada said in a statement issued to The Canadian Press that those figures relate to a range of expenses.

“These included production management, audiovisual and technical production, staging and sets, event personnel, venue-related requirements, equipment, transportation, creative services and other event-delivery costs,” the spokesperson said.

Ottawa awarded almost $1.9-million in contracts as part of the event, including money for design direction, hotel spaces, an opening prayer and an Indigenous drumming performance.

The Four Seasons Hotel in Toronto – the primary site for the summit’s programming – received a sole-source contract valued at more than $1-million for the event.

The Art Gallery of Ontario and the Royal Ontario Museum each received sole-sourced contracts of roughly $100,000 for hosting receptions related to the summit.

stories.title: Parts of Ontario under freezing rain special advisory
stories.summary: Environment Canada issued several freezing rain advisories across Ontario early Thursday morning. It says a low pressure system will move into the region around midnight.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Environment Canada issued several freezing rain advisories across Ontario early Thursday morning.

The agency says several hours of freezing will bring two to five millimetres of ice-build up, with possible utility outages.

It says a low pressure system will move into the region around midnight.

The affected areas include areas such as Ottawa, Perth, Petawawa, Guelph and Kitchener.

In southwestern Ontario, for areas such as Owen Sound, the agency warns of wind gusts up to 60 kilometres per hour during the onset of freezing rain.

It says this raises the risk of broken tree branches.

Environment Canada says the weight of the ice could cause property or tree damage and there is risk of injury due to slippery roads and walkways.

The agency also says that less ice-build up is expected in some parts of the province as the temperature May rise above the freezing mark.

stories.title: Evacuation orders, alerts issued on Vancouver Island amid rising flood risks
stories.summary: Much of coastal B.C. and Haida Gwaii have faced flood, wind and rainfall warnings as rain and strong gusts coincide with the year’s highest tides
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The head of the British Columbia River Forecast Centre says much of Vancouver Island and the province’s south coast have passed the peak of flooding after days of drenching rain that led to evacuations, though central Vancouver Island is still “in the thick of it.”

Dave Campbell said that many waterways are running high but as the rainfall lets up, the coastal region should improve.

However, he said Thursday that it will take time for the waters to be safe enough for flood watches and warnings to come down.

“It’s still high, so we’re going wait a little bit for the rivers to come down before we drop those advisories.”

The centre issued a flood warning on Thursday for central Vancouver Island, meaning river levels had either crested the banks or would do so imminently and that flooding along the rivers would result.

“I think we’re really kind of in the thick of it for the central Island part, and then the rest of the Island [and] south coast, I think, we are past the worst of it now,” Mr. Campbell said in an interview.

Since Monday, much of coastal B.C., including Vancouver Island and Haida Gwaii, has been pummelled with rain and wind, coinciding with the year’s highest tides.

Environment Canada figures show 469 millimetres of rain fell at the Effingham Island station off the west coast of Vancouver Island in just over two days this week, however other areas received between 100 and 250 millimetres of rain.

Rain and wind warnings issued by Environment Canada for the South Coast were lifted on Thursday but coastal flood warnings remained in place for much of Vancouver Island.

Mr. Campbell said waterways in the central region will take more time to return to normal.

“It just takes longer to drain off the landscape, and so we haven’t seen the peak on those river flows yet,” he said

A flood watch remained in place on Thursday for eastern Vancouver Island, while a high streamflow advisory covered the remaining parts of Vancouver Island and the south coast.

The City of Courtenay on eastern Vancouver Island declared a state of local emergency and issued an evacuation order for several properties in low-lying areas, including the Maple Pool campground, while evacuation alerts are in effect for other properties near the Puntledge River.

The declaration, signed by Mayor Manno Theos, says rain, river swell and high tides pose an existing or imminent threat to people and property in the community.

Courtenay’s evacuation order says flood levels pose immediate danger to life and health and people should leave the area immediately.

To the south, the Regional District of Nanaimo issued an evacuation order for some properties along the Nanaimo River in the community of Cedar, with residents told to leave immediately.

The River Forecast Centre said significant snow fell in mountain areas this week and it’s now melting rapidly at lower elevations, flowing into swollen waterways.

The latest low-pressure system also brought warm temperatures that set new daily records in a number of communities, including in Abbotsford where the 14.5 degrees reported broke an old record of 13.9 degrees set on Nov. 25, 1962.

Prince George broke a record by almost three degrees that was set on the same day in 1954.

Elsewhere in the province, Environment Canada issued snowfall warnings for multiple highways through mountain passes, including the Okanagan Connector from Merritt to Kelowna and the Coquihalla Highway from Hope to Merritt, as well as Highway 3 from the Paulson Summit to the Kootenay Pass.

As much as 25 centimetres of snow could be arriving by Thursday night, with the forecaster warning that mountain weather can change suddenly and become hazardous.

A rainfall warning was also issued for the Sea to Sky Highway from Squamish to Whistler on Thursday.

The Transportation Ministry has advised drivers to check conditions before travelling through coastal areas due to the risk of flooding.

stories.title: Motorcycle and scooter-style e-bikes on Ontario roads to soon face stiffer rules
stories.summary: Drivers of motorcycle-style and motor scooter e-bikes in Ontario will soon have to get a licence, registration and insurance to operate the vehicles on roads in the province.
stories.author: Allison Jones
stories.content:
Drivers of motorcycle-style and motor scooter e-bikes in Ontario will soon have to get a driver’s licence, registration and insurance in order to operate the vehicles on roads in the province.

Transportation Minister Prabmeet Sarkaria announced Thursday that as of May 1, e-bikes will be defined as having a bicycle-style frame, fully operable pedals and a maximum motor-assisted speed of 32 kilometres per hour.

Anything above that would be subject to the licence, registration and insurance rules, and would not be allowed in bike lanes, he said.

“We’ve all seen them: high-powered e-bikes travelling through our neighbourhoods that look and operate more like motorcycles than bicycles,” he said at a press conference.

“Some are capable of travelling at dangerous speeds; other have pedals that barely function, or have been modified to get around existing rules, yet they’re being marketed and operated as e-bikes without the licensing, registration, or insurance required for motorcycle, and that’s putting pedestrians, cyclists, and other drivers at risk across Ontario.”

Penalties include fines of up to $2,500 and vehicle impoundment.

Toronto police chief Supt. Mandeep Mann said there have been hundreds of reported collisions involving e-bikes.

“These figures reinforce the importance of clear rules, education, and enforcement, and retailers also have a responsibility to provide accurate information about the vehicles they sell,” he said.

“A vehicle is not a legal e-bike simply because it is available for sale, it’s marketed as an e-bike or it has pedals attached to it.”

The government says riders should check with their local municipality for any additional e-bike rules that May apply.

stories.title: Prosecutor appeals electronic monitoring order for Canadian in Belgian espionage case
stories.summary: Ottawa - The Belgian federal prosecutor's office says it has appealed a decision that would allow a Canadian facing espionage allegations to remain in detention under electronic monitoring — not behind bars.
stories.author: Jim Bronskill The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - The Belgian federal prosecutor’s office says it has appealed a decision that would allow a Canadian facing espionage allegations to remain in detention under electronic monitoring — not behind bars.

The prosecutor’s office says this means the suspect will stay in custody pending the outcome of the appeal, which is to be heard early next month.

stories.title: ‘Quilts as hugs’: Quilters searching for 900 creations, one for each of N.L.’s foster children
stories.summary: Carefully planning each block — just as if their creations were hugs — a group of crafters near St. John’s are working to create or collect 900 quilts across Newfoundland and Labrador: one for each child in foster care in the province.
stories.author: Garrett Barry
stories.content:
Mount Pearl, N.L. - A group of crafters near St. John’s are working to create or collect 900 quilts across Newfoundland and Labrador: one for each child in foster care in the province.

About 100 have been counted so far among the Cabot Quilters’ Guild, who are aiming to collect all the quilts by April 2027. This initiative is part of the group’s regular outreach efforts, though this is the first year they’ve picked donations for foster children in the province.

“As quilters, we look at our quilts as hugs. It’s comfort,” said Heather Blagdon, a quilter with the group.

“This is a hug from a stranger that belongs to them forever. And so no matter where they go, they will bring that comfort with them.”

The donations will be intended for children, not foster parents. A personalized name tag will be sewn onto every quilt, so that children in foster care have something that’s uniquely their own.

“For a child entering foster care, to know that someone thought about me, someone knew that I was going to have this difficult day, unfortunately, but they decided to do this for me to help bring a smile to my face on a really tough day — There’s no dollar value or no amount that can be put on that,” said Kelli Hodder, the executive director of Foster Families Newfoundland and Labrador.

Her group provides supports to parents who are fostering or considering it — something the province dearly needs.

‘A hug from a stranger’

Hodder says one of her organization’s programs gives a full book bag to children as they enter foster care, with teddy bears and art supplies — and she’s seen how a simple act of kindness can make, “quite a difference.”

“Now to be able to give them their own beautiful quilt that they can have with them forever, and they’ll probably treasure forever, that’s just incredible.”

Foster Families Newfoundland and Labrador will distribute the quilts collected as part of this crafting drive.

The effort is also partly a memorial for two former members of the Cabot Quilters’ Guild, who both died in recent years. Both Bev McFadyen and Lorraine Dyke were presidents of the guild, as well as first cousins.

“Children had a special place in their heart,” said Michelle Whelan, another guild member. “When you look at all these quilts and that we’re doing this project for foster care — I’m sure if Bev and Lorraine were here, they’d be so happy.”

The group hosts regular quilting meetups where they work on projects and share tips. A three-day quilting retreat was held this week, giving members a perfect chance to ramp up their efforts towards this year’s lofty goal.

“I think there’s no shortage of enthusiasm,” said Whelan. “We’re happy to have other guilds and other people from across Newfoundland and Labrador help us with our project.”

Some donations have come in from out-of-province too, like a quilt from Nova Scotia. Each is made with children particularly in mind.

“Sometimes when we’re anxious or sad, we need something to touch,” explained Blagdon, demonstrating the binding on her quilt. “So I intentionally chose to do something called big stitch binding so that the child can sit there and they can just rub along this if they wish.”

“This spoke of sunshine and bright colours and happiness, and that’s what I wanted to pass along to another child.”

“For a child entering foster care, to know that someone thought about me, someone knew that I was going to have this difficult day, unfortunately, but they decided to do this for me to help bring a smile to my face on a really tough day — There’s no dollar value or no amount that can be put on that,” said Kelli Hodder, the executive director of Foster Families Newfoundland and Labrador.
Her group provides supports to parents who are fostering or considering it — something the province dearly needs.
‘A hug from a stranger’

Hodder says one of her organization’s programs gives a full book bag to children as they enter foster care, with teddy bears and art supplies — and she’s seen how a simple act of kindness can make, “quite a difference.”
“Now to be able to give them their own beautiful quilt that they can have with them forever, and they’ll probably treasure forever, that’s just incredible.”
Foster Families Newfoundland and Labrador will distribute the quilts collected as part of this crafting drive.

The effort is also partly a memorial for two former members of the Cabot Quilters’ Guild, who both died in recent years. Both Bev McFadyen and Lorraine Dyke were presidents of the guild, as well as first cousins.

“Children had a special place in their heart,” said Michelle Whelan, another guild member. “When you look at all these quilts and that we’re doing this project for foster care — I’m sure if Bev and Lorraine were here, they’d be so happy.”

The group hosts regular quilting meetups where they work on projects and share tips. A three-day quilting retreat was held this week, giving members a perfect chance to ramp up their efforts towards this year’s lofty goal.
“I think there’s no shortage of enthusiasm,” said Whelan. “We’re happy to have other guilds and other people from across Newfoundland and Labrador help us with our project.”
Some donations have come in from out-of-province too, like a quilt from Nova Scotia. Each is made with children particularly in mind.

“Sometimes when we’re anxious or sad, we need something to touch,” explained Blagdon, demonstrating the binding on her quilt. “So I intentionally chose to do something called big stitch binding so that the child can sit there and they can just rub along this if they wish.”
“This spoke of sunshine and bright colours and happiness, and that’s what I wanted to pass along to another child.”

stories.title: New Brunswick community plans to expropriate land from owner that closed mill
stories.summary: A small New Brunswick community says it plans to expropriate land around a recently closed pulp mill as it looks towards its future.
stories.author: Eli Ridder
stories.content:
A small New Brunswick community says it plans to expropriate land around a recently closed pulp mill as it looks towards its future.

It comes after AV Group NB Inc., an affiliate of the India-based Aditya Birla Group, announced in September that AV Nackawic Mill would be idled due to market conditions.

Tim Fox, mayor of the Nackawic-Millville Rural Community, says the municipality wants to secure 77 acres of property around the mill for industrial uses.

Fox says the community never reached an agreement on price after spending about two years negotiating with AV Group NB to buy the land.

But after the company put all of its local real estate up for sale, Fox says Nackawic-Millville wanted to ensure the land around the idled mill wasn’t purchased by a third party.

Fox says the municipality plans to serve the landowner with a formal notice of intent in the coming days, at which point the company can choose to object and trigger a hearing process.

A spokesperson for AV Group NB says the company has not yet received a formal notice of action from Nackawic-Millville and so would not be commenting.

stories.title: Huron County paramedics avert strike with tentative agreement
stories.summary: A tentative agreement between Huron County and its paramedics has averted a potential strike.
stories.author: CTVNewsLondon.ca Staff
stories.content:
A tentative agreement between Huron County and its paramedics has averted a potential strike.

Union officials say that the agreement was made in the wake of two days of negotiations, which took place on Monday and Tuesday.

Officials say 110 of 112 paramedics in the county had voted in favour of strike action if the two sides were unable to come to an agreement.

Paramedics in the county had been working without an agreement since Jan. 1.

The president of Cupe Local 4513 Paramedics’ Union said that Huron County paramedics had only seen wage increases of $6 in the past decade.

stories.title: Ford, Unifor call for Canadian automakers to be exempt from GHG penalties
stories.summary: Ontario Premier Doug Ford and Unifor National President Lana Payne said greenhouse gas emissions regulations pose “significant costs” for the Canadian auto sector.
stories.author: Rachel Morgan
stories.content:
Ontario Premier Doug Ford and Unifor are calling on the federal government to scrap greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions penalties for domestic auto manufacturers.

GHG emissions regulations pose “significant costs” for the sector that is already threatened by U.S. tariffs, said both Ford and Unifor National President Lana Payne in a statement Thursday.

“Over the coming years, these penalties will force companies that build in Canada to pay out billions in non-compliance costs, mostly paid as credits to automakers who build no vehicles in Canada. These additional costs are an ‘own goal’ that are helping President Trump achieve his objective of putting every single Canadian autoworker out of a job,” they said.

The demand comes as Stellantis announced it has signed a deal to sell its idled Brampton plant to defence contractor Roshel. The federal and provincial governments are in talks with Unifor and the automaker to revive it.

Following a closed-door meeting last week, Ford said he had “ more insight ” into Stellantis’ operations.

“To keep the Brampton facility just open and warm — not production — is costing the clients about $135 million a year,” Ford told reporters following the meeting.

“This is one of the things that is in our control – to take away what is a major problem for the auto industry at the moment,” Payne said.

Ford and Payne said in their statement an exemption for automakers “must come with a firm commitment that automotive production will be preserved in Canada, including a full reversal of the sale of the Stellantis Brampton Assembly Plant.”

“At a time of unprecedented uncertainty and trade disruption, governments should be doing everything in their power to support autoworkers and automakers while making Canada the most competitive and attractive place in the G7 to invest in auto production and create good union autoworker jobs,” they said.

The federal government did not immediately respond to Global News’ request to comment on the demands.

The federal government served Stellantis with a notice of default on its 2022 funding agreement earlier this month, saying the sale of the Brampton plant breached agreed upon conditions of up to $529 million in funding that was provided to retool Stellantis facilities in Brampton and Windsor.

“If they go ahead and sell the plant, well then they will face legal recourses from the Government of Canada of hundreds of millions of dollars,” Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said.

stories.title: 3 in 4 Canadians can’t see their family doctor within a day, report finds
stories.summary: The Canadian Institute for Health Information released its annual report on the state of primary care in Canada for 2026 on Thursday.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
While most Canadians have access to a primary care physician or a health practitioner, they struggle to get an appointment on short notice, a new report says.

The Canadian Institute for Health Information released its annual report on the state of primary care in Canada on Thursday.

More than eight in 10 adults (83 per cent) and nine in 10 children (89 per cent) had a primary health care provider in 2025.

This means there are around six million Canadians without access to a source of regular, ongoing care.

Among those who do have doctors, timely access to family doctors is where the gap lies.

Only around a quarter (26 per cent) of Canadian adults and four in 10 (41 per cent) of children received either same-day or next-day appointments when they last needed it, the Cihi report added.

However, most Canadians (68 per cent of adults and 69 per cent of children and youth) were satisfied with how long they waited for care when they needed it.

Four in five (80 per cent of adults and 82 per cent of children and youth) also said their primary care provider treated them with respect regarding their culture and identity.

An area where gaps showed up was hospital visits, with 329 hospitalisations per 100,000 Canadians under 75 for conditions that can often be effectively managed through the primary care system.

While this level remains below pre-pandemic hospitalisation levels, Cihi noted they have been rising steadily since 2021.

Access to a primary care physician can differ depending on who is seeking it, the report shows.

Low-income Canadians were less likely (78 per cent in adults, 87 per cent for children) to have a primary health care provider, especially when compared to high-income Canadians (84 per cent in adults, 93 per cent for children).

Canadians living in lower-income neighbourhoods also had more hospital stays for conditions that could have been managed with effective primary care at 535 stays per 100,000 people compared to 192 for those living in the highest-income neighbourhoods.

Racialised groups also saw lower access, with both Black (66 per cent) and Latin American (68 per cent) adults less likely to have a primary health care provider compared to those who identified as white (86 per cent).

Access to care for Canadians drops off for those between the ages of 18 and 34, before picking up after 35.

This is because many young adults lose access to care when they transition from childhood to adulthood.

“Moving from pediatric to adult care or relocating for school or work can mean needing to find a new provider, often amid long wait-lists. Younger adults — who are generally healthier — May also be less motivated to find a regular provider,” the report said.

stories.title: Tracey DeWare appointed New Brunswick chief justice, prime minister says
stories.summary: Tracey DeWare replaces former chief justice Marc Richard, who chose to take on a reduced workload in August.
stories.author: Eli Ridder
stories.content:
Tracey DeWare replaces former chief justice Marc Richard, who chose to take on a reduced workload in August.

A description from the Prime Minister’s Office says DeWare was first appointed to the family division of the Court of King’s Bench of New Brunswick in 2012.

The PMO says she has served as the top judge at the province’s Court of King’s Bench since 2019.

Prior to her time as a judge, DeWare was a partner at Stewart McKelvey, where her practice focused on insurance, personal injury, and medical malpractice.

DeWare, who is fluently bilingual, graduated from the University of New Brunswick’s Faculty of Law in 1994.

stories.title: CTV News brings Canadian stories to Canada’s sovereign social platform
stories.summary: CTV News has launched an official channel on Gander, a new Canadian social media platform developed and operated in Canada.
stories.author: Corey Bellamy
stories.content:
Toronto - CTV News has launched an official channel on Gander, a new Canadian social media platform developed and operated in Canada. The move expands access to Canadian journalism at a time when some global technology platforms have restricted news content in Canada. Expanding access to news With the launch, Gander users can follow CTV News content directly through the platform and access stories published on CTVNews.CA.

“The addition of CTV News to Gander strengthens our commitment to making our Canadian-focused original reporting and storytelling available to consumers of all ages where, when and how they want it,” said Richard Gray, Vice-President, CTV News. “That the platform is also fully Canadian in nature makes this an even stronger fit for us.”

“Canada needs strong, independent journalism, and journalists need places where their work can reach real people and spark meaningful conversations,” said Ben Waldman, founder and CEO of Gander Social. “We built Gander News to help Canadians discover quality reporting, better understand the world around them, and engage in thoughtful dialogue.”

Waldman said the company is pleased to welcome CTV News to the platform and expand access to news content for Canadians online. How does it work? Gander is a social media platform hosted in Canada, available in both English and French, which allows users to share text posts, photos, links, image galleries and short-form videos.

The platform uses a chronological feed, displaying content in the order it is published rather than surfacing posts through a personalized algorithm. According to the company, users can create free accounts to browse content and follow organizations, public figures and other users. To publish posts, comment or participate in certain community features, users are required to complete a verification process intended to confirm they are real individuals.

Gander says it was built using the AT Protocol, an open social networking technology that supports interoperability between participating platforms. The company says its infrastructure is located in Canada and operates under Canadian laws and privacy regulations. You can find out more about Gander and follow CTV News here.

stories.title: Ontario to require licences for drivers of motorcycle-style e-bikes
stories.summary: They will also need registration and insurance in order to operate the vehicles on roads in the province
stories.author: Allison Jones
stories.content:
Drivers of motorcycle-style and motor scooter e-bikes in Ontario will soon have to get a driver’s licence, registration and insurance in order to operate the vehicles on roads in the province.

Transportation Minister Prabmeet Sarkaria announced Thursday that as of May 1, e-bikes will be defined as having a bicycle-style frame, fully operable pedals and a maximum motor-assisted speed of 32 kilometres an hour.

Anything above that would be subject to the licence, registration and insurance rules, and would not be allowed in bike lanes, he said.

“We’ve all seen them: high-powered e-bikes travelling through our neighbourhoods that look and operate more like motorcycles than bicycles,” he said at a press conference.

“Some are capable of travelling at dangerous speeds; other have pedals that barely function, or have been modified to get around existing rules, yet they’re being marketed and operated as e-bikes without the licensing, registration, or insurance required for motorcycle, and that’s putting pedestrians, cyclists, and other drivers at risk across Ontario.”

Penalties include fines of up to $2,500 and vehicle impoundment.

Toronto police chief Supt. Mandeep Mann said there have been hundreds of reported collisions involving e-bikes.

“These figures reinforce the importance of clear rules, education, and enforcement, and retailers also have a responsibility to provide accurate information about the vehicles they sell,” he said.

“A vehicle is not a legal e-bike simply because it is available for sale, it’s marketed as an e-bike or it has pedals attached to it.”

The government said riders should check with their local municipality for any additional e-bike rules that May apply.

Mayors across Ontario welcomed the new rules and noted the need for better safety measures as more people ride e-bikes. Mississauga Mayor Alvin Tedjo said residents of his city have been calling for such measures.

“As our city grows and the way people get around continues to evolve, our safety measures need to keep up,” he said in a social media post.

Aurora Mayor Tom Mrakas said the government’s decision to strengthen e-bike regulations is “a step in the right direction for road safety.”

“Clear rules make it easier for riders to know what’s expected and for police to enforce them consistently,” he said in a statement.

The new rules come as communities have seen an increase in injuries and deaths involving people riding e-bikes and e-scooters.

Toronto’s St. Michael’s Hospital has said that the number of people injured in incidents involving e-bikes and e-scooters has been rising every year at its trauma centre – and across Canada. It said the injuries can range from broken bones to traumatic brain and spinal cord injuries.

The Canadian Paediatric Surveillance Program said in an August report that 10 children died from using these devices in 2025, including six in Ontario.

Toronto police regularly issue warnings about unsafe e-bike use and say they have handed out hundreds of tickets during e-bike and e-scooter traffic safety blitzes.

Some cities in Ontario, such as Brampton and Mississauga, are part of an e-scooter pilot program that allows riders ages 16 and older to ride electric devices at speeds up to 24 km/h. Toronto, however, has banned e-scooters on public roads, sidewalks and park pathways, though many ignore the bylaw and e-scooters are still sold in the city.

Dr. April Kam, head of pediatric emergency medicine at Hamilton Health Sciences’ McMaster Children’s Hospital, said riding e-bikes and e-scooters comes with risks of injuries, especially for children, including broken bones, traumatic head injuries and brain bleeds.

“Because of the speed involved, because e-bikes and e-scooters just go a lot faster, of course, because they’re motorized ... when the velocity of these e-scooters and/or e-bikes hit an impact, then the injuries are more severe,” she said in an interview.

“We definitely have seen an increase in these injuries, not just at our hospital but across the country.”

Kam said the new regulations are “definitely an important first step” but more should be done to ensure the rules are enforced.

“We need to enforce the existing age regulations and restrictions, like helmet requirements, speed limits, all those things need to be enforced,” she said. “We need similar attention towards e-scooters as well, and increase (efforts) with our road infrastructure and education for the public.”

Kam acknowledged it will take time until the rules and enforcement are more uniform across the province.

“It’s hard because, initially, a lot of these motorized vehicles were marketed as toys, kind of fancy toys, right?” she said.

“People think, ‘Oh this is fun. I want my kids to have fun,’ and they don’t realize ... the implication of it, just like most people don’t think they’ll have a motor vehicle collision.”

The Accessibility for Ontarians with Disabilities Act Alliance said Thursday it is also calling on the Ford government to impose similar restrictions on e-scooters.

It said e-scooters are “a silent menace” endangering the safety of pedestrians, people with disabilities, seniors and others, “and far too often they are illegally ridden in Ontario without effective law enforcement.”
