stories.title: Mother of Jamal Francique tells inquest anti-Black racism played role in son's death
stories.summary: The mother of a man who was fatally shot by police during an attempted arrest in Mississauga, Ont., told a coroner's inquest today she believes anti-Black racism played a role in her son's death.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The mother of a man who was fatally shot by police during an attempted arrest in Mississauga, Ont., nearly seven years ago told a coroner’s inquest Thursday she believes anti-Black racism played a role in her son’s death.

Jamal Francique’s mother, Ann-Marie White, said she believes Peel regional police saw her son for the colour of his skin rather than “as a human being who is deserving of dignity, care, and protection.”

Officers who testified throughout the inquest were able to recall details of their training on use of force and firearms but not on anti-Black racism, leaving her to wonder whether there was “genuine effort” to recognize bias and how it can affect the way people are treated, she said.

“I also remained deeply troubled by the approximately 25 minutes that passed before medical assistance was rendered to my beautiful son. Taking together these circumstances reinforced my belief that anti-Black racism played a big role in what happened to my child,” she said.

White, who was the final witness at the two-week long inquest, said that to this day, she doesn’t understand why police resorted to such an “elaborate and botched plan” to arrest her son on Jan. 7, 2020, ON the basis of unconfirmed allegations.

The inquest has heard police secretly surveilled Francique for days before moving to arrest him, after receiving a tip through Crime Stoppers that he was trafficking drugs and had a gun.

Officers did not find anything to corroborate those allegations but decided to instead arrest him for an alleged breach of his bail conditions, which included house arrest with exceptions for medical emergencies or appointments and other specific situations.

White learned after her son’s death that he had left the home that evening because his paternal grandfather had a medical crisis, which was one of the permitted exceptions, she testified.

Francique did not get to say goodbye to his grandfather, who died shortly after the 28-year-old was laid to rest, she said.

White, who was one of her son’s sureties, said she did not observe nor was she aware of any violations of his bail conditions. Police did not come to their home to check on compliance or contact her regarding any concerns about his bail, she said.

Several officers have testified it was necessary to arrest Francique on the alleged bail violation because of the possibility that he was armed, pointing to the tip as well as the fact that he was released on a firearms charge related to an alleged incident in Guelph, Ont.

A team of plainclothes officers in unmarked cars set up in the townhouse complex where Francique lived with his mother and stepfather, the inquest heard.

The plan was to arrest Francique after he left his home but before he got to his car, the officers said. However, the inquest heard they were not prepared for how quickly Francique moved, and the officer tasked with blocking his car was late.

Francique got into his car and reversed out of the parking spot despite a device installed to deflate his tire, the inquest heard. As he made another manoeuvre to drive away, an officer on foot shot at the car four times, with one bullet hitting Francique in the head, jurors heard.

The officer who opened fire testified this week that he acted out of “fight-or-flight” instinct when he saw the car accelerate directly toward him. Milan Ivkovic testified he couldn’t remember when he took out his gun and didn’t make a conscious decision to shoot in the direction of where a driver would be.

Francique’s car swerved sharply and crashed into a nearby garage, the inquest heard. He did not receive medical care until at least 20 minutes later, after tactical officers arrived at the scene and removed him from the car.

One of the tactical officers said he found a satchel in the car and believed based on its weight that it contained a gun. Const. Marc Charlebois said he later opened the satchel and saw a gun inside.

White said she believes the plainclothes officers did not identify themselves clearly during the operation. Had they done so, she believes her son would have complied, she said.

“I believe my son May have panicked. He was ambushed before, and having been shot previously in Peel by yet another unknown assailant, which the Peel police has yet to apprehend ...I believe that my son would have attempted to drive away,” she said.

Francique was shot by an unknown person in October 2017, leaving him with ongoing physical and psychological health issues that required regular appointments, she said. He had significant nerve damage in his left arm and couldn’t use that hand, she said.

Near the end of her testimony, one of the jurors asked White what recommendations she would like to see come out of the inquest process.

“Just the whole approach that they took for my child,” she answered.

“There were so many options that they had. You know, pick up the phone, give the sureties a call, knock the door ... I felt like they just perceived my son as a career criminal, you know, and it was just the skin he was in that took his life,” she said.

“For me, the best option would have been just ringing the doorbell ... Taking those approaches will definitely save lives out here in Peel, Black lives specifically.”

Under questioning from one of the lawyers, White also said she would support a recommendation that coroner’s inquests be carried out in a more timely manner.

Coroner’s inquests don’t assign legal responsibility, but jurors May make recommendations meant to prevent similar deaths.

Inquest counsel and most of the parties, including Francique’s mother, father and partner, presented their proposed recommendations Thursday, for a total of 40. The jury is not required to adopt them.

Many of the proposed recommendations were aimed at Peel police. The force opposed at least a dozen of them, which their lawyer argued were not feasible, not supported by evidence or overlapped with existing efforts.

The force proposed one recommendation of its own, regarding the timing of coroner’s inquests.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 26, 2026.

By The Canadian Press

Investigators say they believe five home invasions between May 29 and June 2 were carried out by the same group of three to four suspects.

They allege the suspects would forcibly enter homes in the early morning hours and demand vehicle keys from residents.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Inside interior designer Nora Voon’s art-filled home

Several vehicles, including BMW and Mercedes models, were stolen during the home invasions, but police say none of the victims were injured.

Police say the investigation dubbed Project Twilight led to the arrests of a 22-year-old man and a 20-year-old woman on June 8, when officers found two illegal loaded firearms, ammunitions and fentanyl.

Police say they believe the man was connected to other alleged crimes, including two tow truck arsons in Brampton.

They say they also found a large collection of child sexual abuse and exploitation evidence and recovered three stolen luxury vehicles valued at $400,000.

stories.title: Motorcycle-style e-bikes on Ontario roads to soon face stiffer rules
stories.summary: Toronto - Drivers of motorcycle-style e-bikes in Ontario will soon have to get a driver's licence, registration and insurance in order to operate the vehicles on roads in the province.
stories.author: Allison Jones The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - Drivers of motorcycle-style and motor scooter e-bikes in Ontario will soon have to get a driver’s licence, registration and insurance in order to operate the vehicles on roads in the province.

Transportation Minister Prabmeet Sarkaria announced Thursday that as of May 1, e-bikes will be defined as having a bicycle-style frame, fully operable pedals and a maximum motor-assisted speed of 32 kilometres per hour.

Anything above that would be subject to the licence, registration and insurance rules, and would not be allowed in bike lanes, he said.

“We’ve all seen them: high-powered e-bikes travelling through our neighbourhoods that look and operate more like motorcycles than bicycles,” he said at a press conference.

“Some are capable of travelling at dangerous speeds; other have pedals that barely function, or have been modified to get around existing rules, yet they’re being marketed and operated as e-bikes without the licensing, registration, or insurance required for motorcycle, and that’s putting pedestrians, cyclists, and other drivers at risk across Ontario.”

Penalties include fines of up to $2,500 and vehicle impoundment.

Toronto police chief Supt. Mandeep Mann said there have been hundreds of reported collisions involving e-bikes.

“These figures reinforce the importance of clear rules, education, and enforcement, and retailers also have a responsibility to provide accurate information about the vehicles they sell,” he said.

“A vehicle is not a legal e-bike simply because it is available for sale, it’s marketed as an e-bike or it has pedals attached to it.”

The government said riders should check with their local municipality for any additional e-bike rules that May apply.

Mayors across Ontario welcomed the new rules and noted the need for better safety measures as more people ride e-bikes. Mississauga Mayor Alvin Tedjo said residents of his city have been calling for such measures.

“As our city grows and the way people get around continues to evolve, our safety measures need to keep up,” he said in a social media post.

Aurora Mayor Tom Mrakas said the government’s decision to strengthen e-bike regulations is “a step in the right direction for road safety.”

“Clear rules make it easier for riders to know what’s expected and for police to enforce them consistently,” he said in a statement.

The new rules come as communities have seen an increase in injuries and deaths involving people riding e-bikes and e-scooters.

Toronto’s St. Michael’s Hospital has said that the number of people injured in incidents involving e-bikes and e-scooters has been rising every year at its trauma centre – and across Canada. It said the injuries can range from broken bones to traumatic brain and spinal cord injuries.

The Canadian Paediatric Surveillance Program said in an August report that 10 children died from using these devices in 2025, including six in Ontario.

Toronto police regularly issue warnings about unsafe e-bike use and say they have handed out hundreds of tickets during e-bike and e-scooter traffic safety blitzes.

Some cities in Ontario, such as Brampton and Mississauga, are part of an e-scooter pilot program that allows riders ages 16 and older to ride electric devices at speeds up to 24 km/h. Toronto, however, has banned e-scooters on public roads, sidewalks and park pathways, though many ignore the bylaw and e-scooters are still sold in the city.

Dr. April Kam, head of pediatric emergency medicine at Hamilton Health Sciences’ McMaster Children’s Hospital, said riding e-bikes and e-scooters comes with risks of injuries, especially for children, including broken bones, traumatic head injuries and brain bleeds.

“Because of the speed involved, because e-bikes and e-scooters just go a lot faster, of course, because they’re motorized ... when the velocity of these e-scooters and/or e-bikes hit an impact, then the injuries are more severe,” she said in an interview.

“We definitely have seen an increase in these injuries, not just at our hospital but across the country.”

Kam said the new regulations are “definitely an important first step” but more should be done to ensure the rules are enforced.

“We need to enforce the existing age regulations and restrictions, like helmet requirements, speed limits, all those things need to be enforced,” she said. “We need similar attention towards e-scooters as well, and increase (efforts) with our road infrastructure and education for the public.”

Kam acknowledged it will take time until the rules and enforcement are more uniform across the province.

“It’s hard because, initially, a lot of these motorized vehicles were marketed as toys, kind of fancy toys, right?” she said.

“People think, ‘Oh this is fun. I want my kids to have fun,’ and they don’t realize ... the implication of it, just like most people don’t think they’ll have a motor vehicle collision.”

The Accessibility for Ontarians with Disabilities Act Alliance said Thursday it is also calling on the Ford government to impose similar restrictions on e-scooters.

It said e-scooters are “a silent menace” endangering the safety of pedestrians, people with disabilities, seniors and others, “and far too often they are illegally ridden in Ontario without effective law enforcement.”

stories.title: On Stellantis, does the government even know what it’s doing?
stories.summary: The response to the Brampton, Ont., plant being sold was a surplus of tactics and a shortage of strategy. That is troubling
stories.author: Stephen Beatty
stories.content:
Stephen Beatty was the former vice-president of corporate at Toyota Canada.

A former politician recently told me that, in his view, the only thing a government can’t do in the middle of a crisis is nothing. That would seem to explain the frenzied chaos of statements coming from the federal government in the wake of news that automaker Stellantis has sold its plant in Brampton, Ont., to Canadian armoured car manufacturer, Roshel.

Facing a crisis, the government responded with a surplus of tactics and a shortage of strategy. That is troubling.

Consider the sequence of events.

On Nov. 12, Mélanie Joly, the federal Industry Minister, told Canadians she intended to sue Stellantis to recover subsidies paid out and committed to the automaker for, among other things, retooling of its Brampton and Windsor plants.

On Nov. 13, she said she had an aggressive, new offer to Stellantis to take back Brampton and keep the plant open.

On Nov. 14, Prime Minister Mark Carney said that a viable auto sector was a red line in any trade talks with the United States and that Canada would not sign a deal with Washington that did not preserve the Canadian industry.

And on Nov. 16, Mr. Carney said Canada might turn to Chinese automakers if an acceptable deal is not struck with the United States.

The net effect of all this is a whole lot of chaos and nothing concrete achieved.

At the heart of this dispute is whether the company is in breach of its contractual undertakings. A heavily redacted version of that contract has circulated in media and industry circles showing that Stellantis committed to maintaining production and employment at Brampton and Windsor (among other things) as a funding condition. The contract dates back to 2022 and was subsequently amended in 2023.

That amendment contains language that would hold Stellantis in breach if it closes Brampton for reasons other than modernizing its technology, a new model launch or factors beyond the reasonable control of the company that would have rendered the continued operation of the plant commercially unfeasible. The latter was precisely what happened.

Since the agreement was signed, the auto industry has incurred massive losses on its electric vehicle programs. Those programs, guided by federal policy in both Canada and the United States, were subsequently rolled back or delayed.

Stellantis recorded a US$26.3-billion loss in 2025, largely driven by unusual charges and write-downs as it was forced to scale back its electrification plans. Add the more obvious example of a factor beyond the company’s control in the form of Trump tariffs and what more do you need to demonstrate that the plan was not commercially feasible?

The Jeep Compass was the vehicle originally slated for Brampton. The Compass is an entry level product with thin margins and stagnant demand. Canada wanted it to be offered as an EV, further challenging its viability in the current market.

One can argue that Stellantis should have assigned a different, more attractive, product to Brampton. It is not clear that one exists. The Stellantis product lineup is being rebuilt. However, those new vehicle launches lie in the future, and tariffs prevent any transfer of current production from the U.S. to Canada.

In fact, a single year’s tariff savings from not operating the plant, not exporting Compass, would allow Stellantis to repay all of the federal contributions received to date.

Making the Stellantis news more complicated is the suggestion from the company that it might lease back a section of the plant to assemble complete knock down (CKD) vehicles from China. CKD production involves final assembly of vehicles from parts imported from abroad. The value added in Canada would primarily be just the labour. Mr. Carney has said this type of assembly work for Chinese vehicles will not be allowed.

Ironically, as has been agreed to by Mr. Carney, Canada will allow finished Chinese vehicles to be imported with low tariffs and no Canadian content.

That’s what troubles me most. Ottawa likely would not have opposed a CKD project that involved final assembly of parts and components from the U.S. After all, that is largely what happened in Oshawa in 2018 when truck bodies were brought by rail from the U.S. to Oshawa for final assembly.

So, what is really at play here?

Is this a game of chicken using the threat of Chinese cars to extract more favourable trade terms from the White House? Did the proposed Roshel deal upset government plans to have GM manufacture military vehicles in the idled Cami plant in Ingersoll, Ont., by creating competition in Brampton? Or is this just a flustered government flailing? Time will tell.

stories.title: Nato intern suspected of spying to remain in jail in Belgium after appeal
stories.summary: A Canadian Nato intern arrested in Belgium on suspicion of espionage will remain in jail pending an appeal against a court order to free her and place her under electronic monitoring, prosecutors said on Thursday.
stories.author: Reuters Staff
stories.content:
A Canadian Nato intern arrested in Belgium on suspicion of espionage will remain in jail pending an appeal against a court order to free her and place her under electronic monitoring, prosecutors said on Thursday.

At the time of her ⁠arrest in July, prosecutors said the woman worked at ​Nato’s military headquarters near the city of Mons and ​was a Canadian national of Chinese origin suspected of espionage on behalf of a third country.

The federal prosecutor’s office said it had launched the appeal against the court ruling made on Tuesday. A court is due to examine the appeal in early December and then rule on whether to maintain the pre-trial detention, it added.

Sources familiar with the investigation have told Reuters the ‌suspect, identified as Claire Z, was a woman in her 30s and that investigators suspect the activity was linked to China.

The woman has not responded to messages sent to social media ​accounts believed ​to belong ⁠to her. Her lawyer did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The ​Chinese embassy in Brussels has not responded ​to ⁠an emailed request for comment.

Nato’s Supreme Headquarters Allied Powers Europe alerted Belgian intelligence services after staff observed behavior ⁠that ​raised concerns, the prosecutor’s office said at the time.

A Shape spokesperson previously ​said there was no indication the case had affected Nato’s operational ​readiness, command structure or ongoing missions.

Reporting by Andrew Gray, Charlotte Van Campenhout and Inti Landauro; Editing by Andrew Heavens

stories.title: Was Elizabeth Bain one of Bernardo and Homolka’s victims?
stories.summary: The Big Story speaks with Diana Swain, contributing correspondent for Dateline Canada, about the state of the Elizabeth Bain case.
stories.author: Patricia D'Cunha
stories.content:
Who killed Elizabeth Bain? It’s one of Toronto’s most enduring unsolved murder cases, a mystery that has haunted the city for decades.

In 1992, Bain’s boyfriend, Robert Baltovich, was convicted of her murder. But after years of appeals, his conviction was overturned, and he was later acquitted at a retrial. Elizabeth Bain’s killer has never been identified.

In this exclusive interview, host Caryn Ceolin speaks with Diana Swain, contributing correspondent for Dateline Canada , about the state of the Bain case, what her investigation uncovered, and how it may be connected to Canada’s most notorious serial killers.

The Dateline Canada two-hour special airs tonight at 8 p.m. on Citytv and Citytv+.

stories.title: Premier Ford, Unifor leader call on Ottawa to scrap greenhouse gas rules for Canadian automakers
stories.summary: Statement follows politicians’ attempts to reverse the sale of the Stellantis assembly plant in Brampton, Ont., to armoured-car maker Roshel
stories.author: Laura Stone, Eric Atkins
stories.content:
Ontario Premier Doug Ford and Unifor national president Lana Payne are calling on the federal government to exempt Canadian automakers from tailpipe emissions rules and other greenhouse gas regulations, arguing they threaten the viability of operations in this country.

The unusual joint statement from the Progressive Conservative Premier and the union leader was issued as federal and provincial politicians are attempting to reverse the sale of the Stellantis assembly plant in Brampton, Ont., to armoured-car maker Roshel Inc.

In the statement, Mr. Ford and Ms. Payne say Canada’s environmental regulations are hurting the domestic auto sector, calling them an “own goal” that helps U.S. President Donald Trump achieve his aim of seeing every Canadian auto worker out of a job.

“In response to President Trump’s direct attacks on Canadian auto workers, the federal government must address the significant costs that its own greenhouse gas emission regulations impose on domestic auto manufacturers that, along with U.S. tariffs, threaten the jobs of Canadian auto workers and the viability of Canadian automaker operations,” the statement says.

“Together, we are calling on the federal government to exempt non-compliance penalties for passenger automobile greenhouse gas emission regulations for Canadian automakers.”

Polluters in Canada face a web of regulations and taxes aimed at reducing the emissions that cause climate change. The leaders are seeking breaks for automakers on the carbon tax and tailpipe emissions rules.

Canada’s tailpipe emissions system requires companies whose cars don’t meet federal emissions standards to buy credits from those whose automobiles do. It is designed to encourage the sale of low-emissions vehicles and to make it expensive to sell gas guzzlers.

Stellantis’s most popular vehicles in Canada include Ram trucks and Jeeps.

In the letter, Mr. Ford and Ms. Payne say the system rewards companies that do not manufacture in Canada.

The two leaders said the penalties will force companies that build in Canada to pay out billions in non-compliance costs, adding that an exemption for Canadian automakers must come with “a firm commitment that automotive production will be preserved in Canada, including a full reversal of the sale of the Stellantis Brampton Assembly Plant.”

Hannah Jensen, a spokeswoman for Mr. Ford, said the non-compliance regulations are costing Stellantis $300-million a year. Stellantis declined to comment.

On Wednesday, officials from Stellantis, the federal and Ontario governments and Unifor met in Toronto and agreed to continue discussions another day.

A spokesperson for federal Industry Minister Mélanie Joly did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Brian Kingston, head of the Canadian Vehicle Manufacturers’ Association, which represents Stellantis, Ford and General Motors, said the tailpipe rules can be costly for car companies.

There are a variety of ways car companies can make their overall fleets more efficient, he explained, including using lighter materials, installing smaller engines or offering fewer trucks for sale.

“But at the end of the day, if you can’t meet it with your fleets, you have to purchase credits,” he said. “If you can’t purchase credits, you have to restrict sales. So it’s a quite impactful regulation that can have real cost consequences on manufacturers.”

The credit sales are private and prices are not disclosed. Tesla is the main seller in Canada, followed by Honda and Toyota, Mr. Kingston said.

Joanna Kyriazis, director of policy and strategy at Clean Energy Canada, a think tank at Simon Fraser University, said Canada is already offering many incentives to retain auto manufacturing, including billions of dollars in grants and subsidies, plus tariff remissions for manufacturing here.

“If the idea is that it costs too much to produce vehicles in Canada, then removing a policy that applies to the vehicles sold in Canada is not helping Stellantis’s Brampton plant that only sells 10 per cent of its vehicles here,” she said. “It’s actually disproportionately going to help Stellantis’s American plants that sell more of its vehicles into the Canadian market.”

Vic Fedeli, Ontario’s Minister of Economic Development, told reporters on Thursday that giving Stellantis a break on tailpipe emissions would help defray some of the expense of keeping the Brampton plant warm.

The emissions costs “don’t make us competitive with the United States,” Mr. Fedeli said. “They’re costs that Canadian companies, Canadian manufacturers bear that are not available in the States. We’re not aligned with the cost structure in the United States, and it makes it very difficult for companies to be here.”

Stellantis announced it had sold the plant, which employed about 3,000 people when it was idled in 2023, to Brampton-based Roshel earlier this month. Government and union officials are trying to reverse the transaction and save the auto workers’ jobs.

Ms. Joly has said Stellantis must repay the government “hundreds of millions” of dollars if it sells the plant, referring to aid the government has given the company since 2022 for work on car plants in Brampton and Windsor, Ont., plus the NextStar Energy EV battery plant in Windsor.

The Globe and Mail has reported the exact amount the government wants Stellantis to return is $831-million. The automaker has offered to pay $24-million, the amount it said it received for work on the Brampton plant. Ms. Joly has said she is prepared to offer Stellantis an “aggressive package” to reverse the plant’s sale.

Speaking to reporters in Ottawa on Thursday, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre called the government’s tailpipe emissions rules a “backdoor” electric vehicle mandate. He said the regulations benefit American-made Teslas while putting Canadian vehicle manufacturing under water.

stories.title: Blue Rodeo honours ‘great Toronto musician’ killed in midtown home invasion
stories.summary: A Toronto musician killed in a home invasion was an “absolute wizard” the pedal steel guitar, iconic Canadian band Blue Rodeo says.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
A Toronto musician killed in a home invasion was an “absolute wizard” the pedal steel guitar, band Blue Rodeo says.

Michael Eckert, 39, died Wednesday after being shot during an invasion at his home near Poplar Plains Road and St. Clair Avenue West.

Ten days before the incident, Eckert performed at the Grey Cup pre-game show in Calgary with Blue Rodeo.

The legendary Canadian band was one of several paying tribute to Eckert, whose death has been “especially painful” for them.

“We are deeply shocked and saddened by the sudden loss of the great Toronto musician Michael Eckert,” Blue Rodeo said in a social media post.

“He was a kind, supportive and sweet person who was loved by so many in our music community and music fans across Canada. He was an absolute wizard on his instrument, deeply accomplished and fearlessly adventurous.”

Friends tell Global News Eckert was known for his improvisational talents and creativity on the pedal steel guitar, dobro and guitar.

“The world lost a good one in tragedy last night. Eckert understood the fabric of this world more than most; you could see it in his eyes, and in the depths of his music,” local band The Honeyrunners said on social media.

Det.-Sgt. Alan Bartlett told reporters a suspect or suspects forced their way into a home around 2:30 a.m. Wednesday. A resident was confronted and a weapon was fired.

Four residents were inside at the time, but no one else was hurt during the altercation. Bartlett said police are looking for at least one suspect but didn’t provide a description.

Bartlett added it was a “relatively brief period” from the time the invasion occurred to when gunshots were heard.

“I understand and recognize how deeply troubling this must be, not only to the residents in that community, but to the residents of the City of Toronto as a whole,” Bartlett said.

“It is the Toronto Police Service’s solemn commitment that we will do everything that we can do. We will work diligently to locate, identify, apprehend and bring those responsible for this to justice.”

Police said a suspect vehicle has been identified, describing it as a four-door sedan – possibly a dark Honda with dark winter metal rims. An image of the vehicle was released.

Eckert is Toronto’s 37 th homicide victim of the year.

“It’s always sad when we lose someone in our community, but a senseless, tragic loss of this sort is especially painful,” Blue Rodeo said.

“Our hearts go out his family and the people who played with him and loved him.”

stories.title: Canada expected to bar diplomats in high-risk missions from dating apps, relationships with locals
stories.summary: The new rules are expected to be tailored specifically to high-threat postings in countries with a 'hostile intelligence service' such as China and Russia.
stories.author: Christopher Nardi
stories.content:
Ottawa — Global Affairs Canada plans on barring diplomats in high-risk postings like China and Russia from entering a relationship with locals in their host country or even use dating apps, National Post has learned.

The new policy has been in the works since at least the beginning of the year and is “fairly sketched out,” but has not yet been officially published, according to three diplomatic sources who have been briefed on its contents.

National Post is not identifying the sources as they were not authorized to discuss the policy publicly.

The new rules, part of a new non-fraternization policy, are expected to be tailored specifically to high-threat postings in countries with a “hostile intelligence service” such as China and Russia, said the sources.

Canadian diplomats are already subject to a host of measures impacting their personal lives and relationships, such as getting approval for someone to move in with them abroad or a security vetting of their partner before cohabiting or getting married.

Monday - Saturday Free

NP Posted keeps you updated on the news of the day and the perspectives that define the National Post, while drawing your focus to some of the unexpected stories we like to tell. Delivered straight to your inbox Monday to Friday, with a weekend edition on Saturdays.

But the new policy is expected to go a step further by barring impacted diplomats from entering into relationships with foreign nationals from their host countries. But it should allow them to engage romantically with people from other countries, said one senior diplomatic source.

Diplomats from affected missions are also expected to be banned from using dating apps, which are seen by the department as a potential gold mine of personal information that can be exploited by foreign intelligence.

“If I could put it into the old Cold War analogy: ‘sleep Nato’,” said the senior diplomat in reference to the advice given to Western diplomats stationed in Eastern Europe and the Soviet Union in the 1980s to only fraternize with Nato allies.

The change underscores the increasingly hostile landscape for Canadian diplomats and the lengths to which some foreign intelligence services will go to compromise Canada’s foreign service officers.

Concerns about foreign states’ use of age-old “honey trap” schemes have come to the fore as the U.S. reckons with the Jenson Huang scandal. The Nvidia CEO has been embroiled in controversy since admitting his extramarital affair with Alice Huang, whom U.S. intelligence services believe May have fed information to China’s intelligence services.

The new expected policy also illustrates Canada’s concerns with China’s intelligence collection efforts, even as Prime Minister Mark Carney ramps up efforts to develop a new, closer “strategic relationship” with the Asian economic behemoth.

All three diplomatic sources confirmed that most foreign service officers in Canada’s Chinese and Russian missions had been advised this summer of the upcoming policy, though they were not told when it would be officially implemented.

Two of them noted that the policy is proving to be controversial with Canada-based staff in affected missions, with many worrying about the impact on their personal lives during a four-year deployment. The likely ban on the use of dating apps is of particular concern for many single foreign service officers.

“It’s all very vague, no one really knows what’s going on,” said a second source.

Asked about the draft policy, Global Affairs Canada did not deny its existence, nor did it say why it had yet to be published.

“Global Affairs Canada has existing policies and practices in place for personnel serving at all missions abroad, and the Department regularly reassesses these measures. Should changes be required, they would be communicated to missions and personnel as appropriate and in due course,” GAC spokesperson Rachael Dolan said in an email.

All three sources agreed that a non-fraternization policy is a complex thing to develop because of the impact on diplomats’ personal lives. But, two of them said, the department must reckon with the reality that certain countries’ security apparatus exert extreme leverage over their people.

“Why hasn’t it come out? It’s complicated, where you’ve got that mix between the personal and the professional and trying to get it right, not to overstep, but also not underdo it and end up not going as far as actually is necessary,” said the first source.

“The issue is that you can meet a person who’s absolutely decent and it’s true love, etc. The problem is not that person. The problem is the system that they are in, and that you have coercive systems that will take advantage of it,” they added.

They also added that Canada is a laggard compared to its Five Eyes allies when it comes to having a non-fraternization policy for diplomats in high-risk postings.

“We are definitely behind. Australia, New Zealand and the U.S. definitely have them,” particularly for their Chinese missions, said the source.

Alison LeClaire, Canada’s ambassador to Russia until her retirement from the foreign service in 2023, said that the policy makes sense but questioned how enforceable it would be.

“I can certainly see situations where it could be helpful. It’s not about controlling people’s lives, it’s about keeping them safe,” said LeClaire. “But I can’t say that while I was there, I felt that that was a gap.”

She said she was never briefed on such a policy during her tenure in Moscow.

In a separate interview, Senator Peter Boehm — a retired diplomat and top GAC executive until 2018 — said such a policy wouldn’t be a requirement for foreign service officers to be chaste while deployed, but rather to be smart about whom they mingle with abroad.

“Even ‘sleep Nato’… was not an invitation or an instruction to be celibate,” Boehm said with a laugh. “All major countries that have, shall we say, more sophisticated career foreign ministries, they have something like this.”

Christopher Nardi is a senior parliamentary reporter in Ottawa. He has worked in both French and English media, speaks Italian and writes about politics, national security, justice and how things work (or don't) in government. Reach him on Signal: ChrisNardi.01 cnardi@postmedia.com

stories.title: Toronto police ID suspect vehicle in home invasion shooting that killed musician
stories.summary: They are looking for a four-door sedan, possibly a dark Honda with dark winter metal rims
stories.author: Sadeen Mohsen
stories.content:
Police have released a description of a suspect vehicle after the fatal shooting of a 39-year-old musician occurred during an overnight home invasion in an affluent Toronto neighbourhood.

Toronto police say they are looking for a four-door sedan, possibly a dark Honda with dark winter metal rims.

No suspect description has been released yet.

Officers first responded to reports before 2:40 a.m. of a man who had been shot after responding to a home invasion in the area of St. Clair Avenue West and Poplar Plains Road on Wednesday.

They say the victim, later identified as Michael Eckert, was taken to hospital, where he died.

Toronto police are asking anyone with information about the case to come forward.

Investigators previously said this latest home invasion occurred while four residents were inside the house but no one else was injured.

Several online tributes say Eckert was a respected local musician, including Canadian rock band Blue Rodeo, who described him as a “kind, supportive and sweet person who was loved by so many in our music community” and “an absolute wizard on his instrument.”

The shooting comes less than a month after a violent home invasion in the Bridle Path neighbourhood , another affluent part of the city, where a family of four was attacked by masked intruders.

stories.title: Council endorsed homelessness strategy restructures to focus on implementation as crisis worsens in London
stories.summary: London’s cornerstone homelessness strategy recently underwent a quiet makeover, including a new name and organizational structure, as it shifts its focus towards implementation.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
London’s cornerstone homelessness strategy recently underwent a quiet makeover, including a new name and organizational structure, as it shifts its focus towards implementation.

In 2023, council endorsed the Health and Homelessness Whole of Community System Response, including its initial plan to open up to 15 low-barrier 24/7 hubs and 600 highly supportive housing units.

Now, the title of a progress report reveals that the organization has been rebranded as London’s Health and Homelessness Partnership.

The community-led organization emerged from a sector-wide summit on homelessness in late 2022.

“Now, [we have] clusters that represent all the different key stakeholders, and then we have leads and delegates who sit at the leadership table, who bring information back and forth,” explained Jodi Younger, chair of the Health and Homelessness Partnership.

Lynette Lewis, regional director of Indwell, says the changes reflect a shift in focus towards taking action on previously developed strategies from the Whole of Community System Response.

“It’s similar in that there’s the opportunity for many voices to be heard and different sectors to be represented at the table,” Lewis explained.

“It’s different in that we’ve moved from high-level strategizing to working groups and implementation.”

For more than two years, the Whole of Community System Response was the centrepiece of city hall’s lobbying efforts for homelessness funding from the provincial and federal governments.

Two municipally funded hubs opened, a youth hub operated by Youth Opportunities Unlimited and an Indigenous hub led by Atlohsa Family Healing Services.

They inspired the provincial Hart hub system.

London Mayor Josh Morgan supports the new organizational model.

“We don’t need a big, broad coalition of many people in the room, at the same time. We need a focused approach that actually achieves results through the implementation phase and the very important advocacy phases,” said Morgan.

The partnership’s annual progress report highlights the ability of supportive housing to improve individual outcomes and reduce pressure on local healthcare and emergency services.

“We continue to see, as we did in last year’s report, that highly supportive housing and 24/7 hubs are really important lifelines for people,” explained Kelly Barnes, one of the evaluation report’s authors.

As of September, London had 169 completed highly supportive housing units.

In total, there are 422 units in development, planned, or completed.

At Indwell’s Thompson Road building, visits to emergency departments among 26 residents fell from 111 to 26.

At House of Hope, the evaluation found 97 per cent fewer emergency department visits and 84 per cent fewer police interactions among participants at the 18-month follow-up, compared with the six months before they moved in.

Combined, both hubs have served more than 1,000 people and have transitioned 84 people into housing.

However, London’s homelessness crisis continues to grow.

In the first six months of 2026, the coroner recorded 26 deaths among homeless Londoners compared with 16 over the same period in 2025.

“We know how to get people off the streets. We know how to get them help. You know how to get them housed. What we don’t have is the capacity to do it in the numbers that meet the challenge that homelessness is,” Morgan emphasized.

According to the city’s dashboard, September (2,388) and October (2,534) set new highs for unique clients accessing homeless services.

“I think there’s a lot of reasons why we see fluctuations in this kind of data,” explained Younger.

“If you look at the data over time, it’s always [an up and down] trajectory, So, I don’t think it’s surprising to see fluctuations.”

The Community and Protective Services (Caps) Committee will consider the evaluation report on Monday.

stories.title: Western named top university for Academic All-Canadians for second consecutive year
stories.summary: Western leads Canada for the second year in a row, with 564 Mustangs named U Sports Academic All-Canadians in 2025-26.
stories.author: Special to Western News
stories.content:
Nearly half of all Western Mustangs student-athletes earned recognition for academic achievement in the 2025-26 academic year, with 565 named Scholar Athletes. It also led Western to itssecond year in a row ranked No. 1 in Canada for U Sports Academic All-Canadians.

Both distinctions use the same requirements: Western Scholar Athletes and U Sports Academic All-Canadians must achieve an academic average of 80 per cent or higher while competing in varsity athletics. Western’s total number of Scholar Athletes – which represents 46.5 per cent of all Mustangs – includes all varsity athletes who earned the academic recognition, including those under the national U Sports umbrella and sports that operate in other leagues.

“Western is proud of its exceptional student-athletes who match their dedication and talent in sports with their commitment to academic excellence,” said President Alan Shepard. “The same qualities that drive success in sport – preparation, resilience, leadership, teamwork and accountability – also drive success in their studies. Congratulations to everyone receiving the Academic All-Canadian designation this year.”

Western Mustangs student-athletes who received averages of 80 per cent or higher are named Scholar Athletes in honour of their academic and athletic success. In the 2025-26 season, 46.5 per cent of Western Mustangs earned the distinction. (Brandon VandeCaveye)

Their accomplishments reflect the dedication required to balance academic success with the demands of training, competition and representing Western, said Christine Stapleton, director of sports and recreation.

“Being recognized as a Scholar Athlete requires an extraordinary level of commitment,” she said. “Our student-athletes are balancing rigorous academic programs alongside training, competition, travel and countless other demands throughout the year. To have 565 Mustangs achieve this distinction while helping Western remain the national leader is a remarkable accomplishment. Their pursuit of excellence reflects the very best of what it means to be a Mustang.”

The 565 Scholar Athletes reflect the strength of Western’s student-athlete community across campus, representing faculties, schools and affiliated university colleges from every corner of the university.

Western has consistently ranked among Canada’s top two universities for U Sports Academic All-Canadians over the past decade, and its continued national leadership highlights a strong culture of academic achievement among Mustangs student-athletes, said John Doerksen, vice-provost (students).

“The success of our student-athletes speaks to the incredible partnership that exists across the Western community,” said Doerksen. “Faculty members, academic advisors, coaches, staff and teammates all play an important role in supporting student-athletes throughout their journeys. These students have demonstrated an exceptional commitment to their academics while competing at the highest level of university sport, and we are proud to celebrate their achievement.”

Together, the Faculties of Health Sciences, Social Science and Science accounted for more than half of Western’s Scholar Athletes during the 2025-26 year. Academic achievement was also strong across a range of disciplines. More than 56 per cent of student-athletes in health sciences earned Scholar Athlete recognition, while more than 62 per cent of student-athletes in the Ivey School of Business achieved the distinction.

stories.title: Toronto police identify suspect vehicle in Casa Loma fatal shooting
stories.summary: Toronto - Police have released a description of a suspect vehicle after the fatal shooting of a 39-year-old musician occurred during an overnight home invasion in an affluent Toronto neighbourhood.
stories.author: Sadeen Mohsen The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - Ontario Premier Doug Ford said Thursday he wants to see legal changes to address a spate of home invasions, and in the meantime he advised people to protect their families by any means necessary.

Ford, who has police protection, said he owns a gun and wouldn’t hesitate to use it on someone trying to break into his home, advising people without guns to use knives or baseball bats to protect themselves and their children.

“I encourage people to use whatever tool they have to fight back, not hide, but fight back,” he said Thursday after question period.

“I’ll tell you one thing: (if) someone comes through my door with a gun and knife and starts shooting it up, I’ll blow the guy right through the front door. He’ll look like Swiss cheese by the time he’s done.”

The premier was reacting to the fatal shooting of a 39-year-old musician during an overnight home invasion in an affluent Toronto neighbourhood on Wednesday, which came not long after a violent home invasion in the wealthy Bridle Path area of the city left a family of four injured.

NDP Leader Marit Stiles said Ford should be looking for ways to ensure people feel safe in their own homes, not telling them to arm themselves in order to protect their families.

“Doug Ford, he’s really good at writing letters and coming out with outrageous statements, but the truth is that he can control some things in the province of Ontario,” she said.

“For example, we have absolutely overloaded courts right now in the province of Ontario. We are letting the bad guys out too soon because of these packed courts, and he can do something about that and refuses to take responsibility. He has the power as the premier of Ontario to be able to protect Ontarians, and instead he’s saying, ‘You’re all on your own. Protect yourselves.’ That is unacceptable.”

Green Party Leader Mike Schreiner said he trusts police.

“I would call 911 and make sure my family is safe and allow the police to do their job,” he said. “I think it’s incredibly dangerous to suggest to people that they should be shooting other people.”

It’s not the first time Ford has advocated for a violent approach to crime.

At an unrelated press conference in June of last year he told a story about masked men who had tried to steal a vehicle overnight from Ford’s home, with the premier saying that if they came back he would “take care” of them better than the police.

At the same press conference he said a man charged by York regional police for allegedly shooting a gun in the air during an attempted vehicle theft deserved a medal.

A few months later, the premier spoke about threatening to beat up a Home Depot shoplifter.

Earlier this year, he said a York Region resident who shot and injured an alleged home invader “should have shot him a couple more times.”

“Congratulations,” he said. “I’m glad you shot the guy.”

Ford said Thursday that he is directing his attorney general and solicitor general to look at legal changes that could bring the province “right up to the edge” of so-called castle law.

Ford has previously mused about introducing the castle doctrine, laws in some U.S. states that allow people to use reasonable force, sometimes including lethal force, to protect themselves in their homes.

Attorney General Doug Downey said there are already rules around self defence, but that they will examine whether the line is in the right spot.

Ford also called on the federal government to strengthen bail laws and increase mandatory jail time for violent offenders, which federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre echoed.

“This unfortunately has become an all-too-common story,” he said in Ottawa. “Canadians are literally afraid to go to sleep at night.”

Toronto police said Thursday there have been 111 home invasions in the city so far this year, a 29 per cent increase from the same time period last year. Spokesperson Stephanie Sayer said the number is lower than what was reported after the violent home invasion in the Bridle Path neighbourhood last month because some of the incidents have since been reclassified and are no longer being investigated as home invasions.

Police also announced Thursday that the suspect vehicle they are looking for in the shooting of 39-year-old Michael Eckert is a four-door sedan, possibly a dark Honda with dark winter metal rims.

Eckert was remembered in tributes as a respected musician. Canadian rock band Blue Rodeo described him as a “kind, supportive and sweet person who was loved by so many in our music community” and “an absolute wizard on his instrument.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 26, 2026.

— With files from Nick Murray in Ottawa

stories.title: Upscale Mount Pleasant East semi with an elevator gets an offer at full price
stories.summary: Mount pleasant east
stories.author: Sydnia Yu
stories.content:
5 Thurloe Ave., Toronto

Asking price: $3,295,000 (October 2026)

Selling price: $3,295,000 (October 2026)

Previous selling price: $2,895,000 (2017)

Taxes: $13,842 (2026)

Days on the market: 15

Listing agents: Mary Jo Vradis and Meray Mansour, Sage Real Estate Ltd.

About 10 years ago, Shram Homes built six semi-detached houses about a block west of Mount Pleasant Road, near June Rowlands Park. An original owner of one model, encompassing 3,354 square feet of living space across four levels, aimed to find a buyer, knowing that a neighbour sold their home for about $3.37-million in April. Agent Mary Jo Vradis advised her client to list with an asking price of $3,295,000, adjusting for declining property values this fall.

“It is the biggest unit,” Ms. Vradis said. “But we were aware the market was not the same as it was in April, and listed it $75,000 lower.”

The tactic worked, with three visitors arranging second showings of the home, designed by Richard Wengle Architects and Robin Nadel Design. One buyer paid the full price on Halloween, about two weeks after its launch.

“They all have elevators and about 3,000 square feet,” Ms. Vradis said. “They’re very sought-after properties.

“Looking at the structure and all the details, they built it like a bunker. You don’t see stuff built like that.”

This three-bedroom house has up to 10-foot ceilings, heated flooring in the laundry room, four full bathrooms and a fourth bedroom in the basement. Down the hall, there is access to two parking spots and two storage lockers in a common garage.

The living room has a gas fireplace and an exit to a brick patio on the 24-by-125-foot lot.

A powder room and dining area are close to a kitchen with an island and Miele appliances.

Monthly parcel of tied land fees are $730.

“The whole property is maintenance-free,” Ms. Vradis said. “There isn’t a big yard, irrigation is built in and an association maintains the property.

“It’s also very walkable, in an upper-end neighbourhood.”

stories.title: Alberta health officials to give update on soldiers injured in CFB Wainwright fire
stories.summary: The military has said a windstorm on Oct. 17 pushed flames from a grass fire onto troops in a training exercise at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, southeast of Edmonton.
stories.author: Daniela Germano
stories.content:
Alberta health officials are expected to provide an update Thursday on the recovery of soldiers injured during a deadly fire at a military base.

The military has said a windstorm on Oct. 17 pushed flames from a grass fire onto troops in a training exercise at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, southeast of Edmonton.

Four were killed in the fire, and a fifth died of injuries earlier this month while in an Ontario hospital.

About three dozen soldiers were injured, with many suffering from serious burns.

Acute Care Alberta says, as of Tuesday, there were 20 still being cared for in provincial hospitals, with seven listed in critical condition.

The military said Saturday that two others remained in hospitals in British Columbia and Ontario, where they were transferred to be closer to family.

An additional soldier was released from hospital on Friday.

Three investigations are looking into what happened on the base. Prime Minister Mark Carney has called the fire one of the worst tragedies for the Armed Forces on home soil during peacetime.

stories.title: Ontario golf course worker who punched manager in a ‘blind rage’ ordered to pay him $45,000
stories.summary: 'He was, in my view, itching for a confrontation,' said the judge
stories.author: Chris Lambie
stories.content:
An Ontario golf course worker who punched a manager nearly half his size over missing a contest at an end-of-summer tournament has been ordered to pay him $45,000.

Andrew Shaw, then general manager of Tarandowah Golf Course in Springfield, Ont., was running the last tournament of the summer on Sept. 11, 2021, when Paul Hopkins, who worked part-time at the course and was playing in the 60-person event, was one of the last players to come off the links.

“As part of the golf events, the participants arrange a betting contest called Calcutta where the players can bet on the performance of other players,” Justice Spencer Nicholson wrote in a recent decision from the Ontario Superior Court of Justice.

“The game of Calcutta had started before Mr. Hopkins finished his round of golf, effectively excluding him.”

Hopkins, six feet tall and weighing 235 pounds, “admits that he became upset that he could not participate,” said Nicholson’s Nov. 23 decision.

Shaw is about five foot seven and weighed 147 pounds at the time.

The 55-year-old was sitting in his office when he heard Hopkins, then 51, shouting through the closed door.

“He opened his door and saw Mr. Hopkins standing outside his office, screaming at him about allowing the game of Calcutta to begin in his absence.”

Shaw advised Hopkins he hadn’t organized the Calcutta game. He told Hopkins to calm down, adding if he didn’t he would lose his job.

“Mr. Shaw deposes that it was at that point that Mr. Hopkins struck the left side of his jaw with his fist. He fell backwards onto his desk and then onto the ground, twisting his right knee. He blacked out. His first memory was being seated in a chair with another employee holding ice onto his face.”

Shaw sued Hopkins for battery. Hopkins argued unsuccessfully that he acted in self-defence.

“I do not accept that Mr. Hopkins felt physically threatened. Instead, I find that Mr. Hopkins became even angrier when Mr. Shaw threatened his job and punched him as a result. Punching your superior at work because of a threat towards your job security is clearly an excessive use of force,” the judge said.

Shaw thought Hopkins was drunk when he started yelling about the Calcutta. “He was very combative, loud, confrontational and his eyes were red.”

Hopkins said he had one drink before he teed off at 10:20 a.m., and that he didn’t bring any alcohol on the course.

“He testified that to the best of his knowledge there were no servers on the course during the round,” said the judge.

“Mr. Shaw, ON the other hand, testified that there were servers on the course during the tournament, which strikes me as likely.”

A trio of golfers walk towards the first tee box at Tarandowah Golfers Club in Springfield, Ont. QMI Agency / Craig Glover

Hopkins “denied being intoxicated,” but stated he’s a diabetic and can appear that way when his blood sugar is low. “He indicates that he did not eat during the day.”

Hopkins admitted on cross-examination that he’d bought two additional beers when he teed off and another two after the 9th hole.

The judge found that Hopkins misled the court about his alcohol consumption that day, which “seriously undermines his credibility.”

“Mr. Hopkins makes it seem like he peacefully strolled towards Mr. Shaw’s office to get an explanation with respect to Calcutta,” said the judge, who noted the exchange was captured on surveillance video.

“This was again entirely misleading given the video. Mr. Hopkins was irate from the moment he entered the bar area and bee-lined for the office. He was, in my view, itching for a confrontation.”

Nicholson found Hopkins’ behaviour throughout was aggressive.

“Whether or not he was drunk, or suffering from low blood sugar, it is clear that he was in a blind rage.”

Shaw, now 60, started managing a golf club in the Turks and Caicos this past February.

He complained of “headaches, sensitivity to light and sound, problems with his concentration and memory and changes to his behaviour” after Hopkins’ punch.

He feels anxious and experiences “trauma symptoms,” said the decision. “He deposes that he sought treatment from a psychotherapist for these emotional difficulties in the spring of 2022. His low back and neck pain has also continued.”

Shaw “was let go from Tarandowah in December of 2022, which he attributed to his inability to do his regular, in person hours and effectively perform management tasks,” said the decision.

He was diagnosed with “a mild traumatic brain injury with persistent post-concussion symptoms,” said the decision, which notes he has post-traumatic stress disorder and ongoing bilateral tinnitus, along with neck and back injuries.

The judge found Shaw “has exaggerated the extent of his symptoms and his damages,” which his lawyer pegged at somewhere between $175,000 and $200,000.

“Respectfully, I think that range to be entirely inconsistent with Mr. Shaw’s circumstances and a significant overreach,” Nicholson said.

The judge didn’t accept that Shaw “sustained significant physical injuries as a result of this incident, including to his brain.” But Nicholson accepted that Hopkins’ punch “aggravated his chronic back complaints.”

The judge also accepted that Shaw “has ongoing emotional distress as a result of the incident,” that caused him “shame and embarrassment, especially in light of the reaction that the incident drew at his place of employment.”

Nicholson awarded Shaw $40,000 for general damages, including aggravated damages.

“This considers that Mr. Shaw’s physical injuries were not particularly serious, nor did they have a significant impact on Mr. Shaw’s activities of daily living,” said the judge.

He also awarded Shaw $5,000 for future psychological counseling. “Mr. Hopkins’ conduct was clearly reprehensible and inexcusable.”

Chris Lambie is Atlantic bureau chief for National Post. He has worked for news organizations from Newfoundland to the Northwest Territories and is a three-time National Newspaper Award nominee, with a win for local reporting.

Hopkins, six feet tall and weighing 235 pounds, “admits that he became upset that he could not participate,” said Nicholson’s Nov. 23 decision.
Shaw is about five foot seven and weighed 147 pounds at the time.
The 55-year-old was sitting in his office when he heard Hopkins, then 51, shouting through the closed door.
“He opened his door and saw Mr. Hopkins standing outside his office, screaming at him about allowing the game of Calcutta to begin in his absence.”
Shaw advised Hopkins he hadn’t organized the Calcutta game. He told Hopkins to calm down, adding if he didn’t he would lose his job.

“Mr. Shaw deposes that it was at that point that Mr. Hopkins struck the left side of his jaw with his fist. He fell backwards onto his desk and then onto the ground, twisting his right knee. He blacked out. His first memory was being seated in a chair with another employee holding ice onto his face.”

“I do not accept that Mr. Hopkins felt physically threatened. Instead, I find that Mr. Hopkins became even angrier when Mr. Shaw threatened his job and punched him as a result. Hopkins said he had one drink before he teed off at 10:20 a.m., and that he didn’t bring any alcohol on the course.
“He testified that to the best of his knowledge there were no servers on the course during the round,” said the judge.

Hopkins “denied being intoxicated,” but stated he’s a diabetic and can appear that way when his blood sugar is low. “He indicates that he did not eat during the day.”
Hopkins admitted on cross-examination that he’d bought two additional beers when he teed off and another two after the 9th hole.
The judge found that Hopkins misled the court about his alcohol consumption that day, which “seriously undermines his credibility.”

“Mr. Hopkins makes it seem like he peacefully strolled towards Mr. Shaw’s office to get an explanation with respect to Calcutta,” said the judge, who noted the exchange was captured on surveillance video.
“This was again entirely misleading given the video. Mr. Hopkins was irate from the moment he entered the bar area and bee-lined for the office. He was, in my view, itching for a confrontation.”
Nicholson found Hopkins’ behaviour throughout was aggressive.
“Whether or not he was drunk, or suffering from low blood sugar, it is clear that he was in a blind rage.”
Shaw, now 60, started managing a golf club in the Turks and Caicos this past February.
He complained of “headaches, sensitivity to light and sound, problems with his concentration and memory and changes to his behaviour” after Hopkins’ punch.

He feels anxious and experiences “trauma symptoms,” said the decision. “He deposes that he sought treatment from a psychotherapist for these emotional difficulties in the spring of 2022. His low back and neck pain has also continued.”
Shaw “was let go from Tarandowah in December of 2022, which he attributed to his inability to do his regular, in person hours and effectively perform management tasks,” said the decision.

He was diagnosed with “a mild traumatic brain injury with persistent post-concussion symptoms,” said the decision, which notes he has post-traumatic stress disorder and ongoing bilateral tinnitus, along with neck and back injuries.
The judge found Shaw “has exaggerated the extent of his symptoms and his damages,” which his lawyer pegged at somewhere between $175,000 and $200,000.
“Respectfully, I think that range to be entirely inconsistent with Mr. Shaw’s circumstances and a significant overreach,” Nicholson said.

The judge didn’t accept that Shaw “sustained significant physical injuries as a result of this incident, including to his brain.” But Nicholson accepted that Hopkins’ punch “aggravated his chronic back complaints.”

The judge also accepted that Shaw “has ongoing emotional distress as a result of the incident,” that caused him “shame and embarrassment, especially in light of the reaction that the incident drew at his place of employment.”
Nicholson awarded Shaw $40,000 for general damages, including aggravated damages.
“This considers that Mr. Shaw’s physical injuries were not particularly serious, nor did they have a significant impact on Mr. Shaw’s activities of daily living,” said the judge.
He also awarded Shaw $5,000 for future psychological counseling. “Mr. Hopkins’ conduct was clearly reprehensible and inexcusable.”

stories.title: Ontario kept funding career college with massive Osap growth despite early warning, letter shows
stories.summary: Canadian College of Business, Science and Technology was not among six schools cut off this spring despite reporting the fastest growth
stories.author: Allison Jones
stories.content:
A career college with student financial aid usage that grew thousands of per cent in a few years was not among those the minister cut off this spring, and a letter newly obtained by The Canadian Press shows he was specifically warned about the school more than a year earlier.

Career Colleges Ontario flagged in a January 2025 letter to the ministry that the association was concerned about unusually high growth in Ontario Student Assistance Program usage at 10 campuses.

The names of most of the schools were redacted when a copy of the letter was filed in court this year, but an unredacted copy obtained by The Canadian Press shows that the Canadian College of Business, Science and Technology topped that list.

“As an association that represents career colleges in Ontario, we are concerned about how schools with increases exceeding 2,000 per cent in submissions, such as Ccbst … with a 2,696.26 per cent increase, are accommodating these students effectively while upholding educational standards,” executive director Kate Bartz wrote.

That growth of nearly 2,700 per cent was over two years, and it further exploded at that campus to nearly 6,000 per cent over three years, according to data obtained through a freedom-of-information request by The Canadian Press.

The school’s other three campuses in the Greater Toronto Area were also on Career Colleges Ontario’s list, but the Canadian College of Business, Science and Technology was not among six schools the government cut off from Osap eligibility in May.

Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn is defending the fact that Osap kept flowing to the school until last month by saying the data the ministry was receiving was evolving.

“I think ultimately, we’re running multiple investigations at the same time, and that would be one of the ones that we are investigating, and once that threshold is met, that’s when we act, as we have earlier this year,” Quinn said, referring to both removing six schools from eligibility in May and a sector-wide pause on Osap he enacted early last month.

Liberal critic Tyler Watt said the minister’s explanations don’t make sense.

“You either didn’t catch it or you knew and chose to do nothing about it, so which one is it?” he said. “If this (school) was the top of the list, wouldn’t that be your No. 1 priority to investigate?”

NDP critic Peggy Sattler said she questions the strength of the ministry’s investigations.

“We have heard no answers from the government as to how this was allowed to happen,” she said. “Any actions that the government took were far too delayed to try to protect the integrity of the Osap program.”

Quinn has said that preliminary findings of a Kpmg audit into career colleges and Osap are so troubling that he has referred the matter to the Ontario Provincial Police. He has not named any specific schools associated with that police referral.

The Canadian College of Business, Science and Technology has not responded to multiple requests for comment.

In May, the province ended Osap eligibility at six campuses, the same schools that the federal government had flagged concerns about a year prior. The number of students receiving Osap increased between about 650 per cent and 1,375 per cent from 2021-22 to 2024-25 at those schools.

At the Canadian College of Business, Science and Technology, the data shows an overall increase of 3,000 per cent during that time, and at one of its four campuses it was nearly 6,000 per cent.

The students at four campuses in total in 2024-25 accounted for about $151-million in provincial grants.

stories.title: Why you might start seeing police officers at some Lcbo outlets
stories.summary: The Liquor Control Board of Ontario is putting police officers in some locations across the province to target stores where booze bandits are running off with bags of expensive spirits.
stories.author: Adrian Ghobrial
stories.content:
Toronto- The Liquor Control Board of Ontario is putting police officers in some locations across the province to target stores where booze bandits are running off with bags of expensive spirits.

“We know there is a lot of repeat crime so we’re aware those operations exist,” said Lcbo media relations director Sebastian Skamski.

Ontario’s government-run liquor stores say they’re using internal data to help them locate the most vulnerable locations.

“We’re very aware of the role of organized crime in theft at the Lcbo, these are very sophisticated operations where they act in tandem to coordinate and target stores,” Skamski added.

Dubbed “Operation Secure Stores,” the Lcbo said it will be hiring 40 paid duty officers to patrol roughly 40 separate liquor stores across Ontario in an anti-theft blitz to curb crime and promote safety in stores.

In other stores, the Lcbo said it will add “double guarding” to allow guards to better screen who is coming in and out of a store while looking for repeat offenders. In a news release , the Lcbo said it will “deploy more members of our covert security taskforce,” made up of security guards in plain clothing, who have more training and are permitted by the Lcbo to make arrests inside a store.

However, the Lcbo has roughly 690 stores provincewide, and some crime experts say the Lcbo’s move to deploy plainclothes officers is more about optics and making customers feel safer than reducing the number of brazen robberies.

“The criminals are going to move on, they’re going to move onto softer targets, in often cases further outside big city limits,” said former homicide detective and CTV News crime specialist Mark Mendelson.

Skamski disagrees, telling CTV News that many of the “2,000 arrests made last year linked to Lcbo liquor store thefts didn’t just take place where there were police officers stationed.”

“Our staff, guards and employees were able to help local low law enforcement make arrests and bring justice and that’s what we’re going to continue to do.”

However, one security guard company executive, speaking on condition of anonymity, believed the Lcbo will remain vulnerable because they don’t have the budget to curb robberies at their locations.

The Lcbo’s internal data shows that 70 per cent of thefts are linked to organized crime. “This isn’t the Hells Angels or the mafia, this is a group of four or five criminals working together to hit up liquor stores,” said Mendelson.

Thousands of dollars worth of expensive liquor is selling on the black market.

“They’re going for the high-end stuff. They’re not stealing bottles of Baby Duck,” he said.

It’s not just a problem in Ontario; robberies have plagued liquor stores across the country. In Manitoba, you must show identification to enter most liquor store locations. It’s a move Mendelson would welcome in Ontario.

“Anything would help, we have to think outside of the box and come up with a sustainable plan to bring an end to this crime that’s flooding the black market with thousands in stolen booze.”

For now, the Lcbo said they’re committed to reducing crime inside their locations, while keeping staff and customers safe.

content_blocks.text: In other stores, the Lcbo said it will add “double guarding” to allow guards to better screen who is coming in and out of a store while looking for repeat offenders. In a news release , the Lcbo said it will “deploy more members of our covert security taskforce,” made up of security guards in plain clothing, who have more training and are permitted by the Lcbo to make arrests inside a store.

However, the Lcbo has roughly 690 stores provincewide, and some crime experts say the Lcbo’s move to deploy plainclothes officers is more about optics and making customers feel safer than reducing the number of brazen robberies.

“The criminals are going to move on, they’re going to move onto softer targets, in often cases further outside big city limits,” said former homicide detective and CTV News crime specialist Mark Mendelson.
Skamski disagrees, telling CTV News that many of the “2,000 arrests made last year linked to Lcbo liquor store thefts didn’t just take place where there were police officers stationed.”
“Our staff, guards and employees were able to help local low law enforcement make arrests and bring justice and that’s what we’re going to continue to do.”

content_blocks.alt: LCBO
content_blocks.caption: A person walks past an LCBO in Ottawa, Thursday March 19, 2020. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Adrian Wyld

content_blocks.text: However, one security guard company executive, speaking on condition of anonymity, believed the Lcbo will remain vulnerable because they don’t have the budget to curb robberies at their locations.

The Lcbo’s internal data shows that 70 per cent of thefts are linked to organized crime. “This isn’t the Hells Angels or the mafia, this is a group of four or five criminals working together to hit up liquor stores,” said Mendelson.
Thousands of dollars worth of expensive liquor is selling on the black market.
“They’re going for the high-end stuff. They’re not stealing bottles of Baby Duck,” he said.

It’s not just a problem in Ontario; robberies have plagued liquor stores across the country. In Manitoba, you must show identification to enter most liquor store locations. It’s a move Mendelson would welcome in Ontario.
“Anything would help, we have to think outside of the box and come up with a sustainable plan to bring an end to this crime that’s flooding the black market with thousands in stolen booze.”
For now, the Lcbo said they’re committed to reducing crime inside their locations, while keeping staff and customers safe.

stories.title: 20 per cent of nine-year-olds aren’t reading to expectations, and they aren’t catching up as teenagers: report
stories.summary: One in five Grade 10 students is at a merely ‘functional’ level of literacy, meaning they can't read enough to succeed in education or the workplace
stories.author: Joseph Brean
stories.content:
Child literacy in Canada is low and falling, with as many as one child in five failing to meet expected levels around age 9, with similar results at age 15, according to provincial reporting and an authoritative international report.

“It’s been a consistent pattern over time,” said Robert Savage, professor of educational psychology at the University at Buffalo, and until earlier this year dean of education at York University in Toronto. He has studied literacy policy in Canada for more than 25 years, and says there is a clear link between a child’s literacy around Grade 3 and their reading ability in the early years of high school.

“We need to do a better job of helping the lowest performing 20 per cent,” he said in an interview.

One in five students in Grade 10 is at a level of literacy so low it is described as merely “functional,” meaning they can read and critique to some degree, but not enough to succeed in education or the workplace. Savage describes this as struggling to read “in ways that will impact their life,” and the numbers are broadly consistent across Canada, a little better in Alberta, Ontario and British Columbia, a little worse in New Brunswick.
