These numbers are from theProgramme for International Student Assessment, released in September and conducted on behalf of the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development, which offers some of the most accurate Canadian measurements of child literacy.

It continues to show the decline in literacy made worse by the pandemic, but it also shows overall levels of child literacy in Canada are declining in both absolute and relative terms. As Savage put it, recalling a provocative recent headline about the international numbers, a typical 15-year-old today is reading like a 13-year-old might have a few years ago.

The snapshot of this literacy crisis comes amid a broad shift in educational strategies slowly taking hold in education ministries across Canada, but often failing to find expression at the classroom level, some critics argue. One new think tank report, for example, describes the “stranglehold that ineffective teaching pedagogies” have over education faculties and teachers’ unions, reflecting an “ideological capture” that resists science-informed best practices.

Canadian literacy education remains stuck between two teaching paradigms, with literacy numbers still moving in the wrong direction. Postmedia/File

The shift is an evidence-based move away from the once faddish notion of “balanced literacy,” in which children are encouraged to anticipate or guess what words are going to come next from contextual cues, to immerse themselves in texts, and to learn to read much as they previously learned to speak, by passively absorbing the language around them and trying to join in.

“People got swept away with the movement,” Savage said. It was a romantic notion that children would recognize whole words without analyzing their structural components. It imagined children would be immersed in a “whole language” approach, in which they would be exposed to books and literary culture, “but not actually given the skills to read them.”

“There was an optimistic hope that because it works for oral language it will work for print,” Savage said. “It doesn’t work like that.”

Instead, the current shift is toward a more structured approach that emphasizes sounding out letters in combination, and following a closely managed curriculum of learning to decode how graphemes (the smallest units of written language) relate to their corresponding phonemes (the smallest units of spoken language).

A key insight is that learning to read is not like learning to speak, a misapprehension that Savage said has inspired some failed literacy strategies.

“There has been, and to an extent still is, a lot of confusion about how literacy operates,” Savage said.

Reading sits within an ability to use language effectively, Savage said, but children do not acquire it the same way they acquire spoken language. If a person, especially a young person, is immersed in a spoken language environment, such as their home, “it’s quite hard not to pick up a language,” Savage said. Our brains are well prepared to process language input, and children will learn the language spoken around them.

“Reading is something that was invented, and as an invention, we can’t assume that children will pick it up by magic, by immersion alone,” Savage said. “Unfortunately that’s not how it works, because it’s an invented and artificial system.”

Teaching literacy requires early instruction in the alphabet, he said, and maximized success requires significant cognitive activity. That means direct, careful instruction, sustained over time, and where children are struggling, continued intervention until they have managed each progressive step.

This is not to say reading should be learned by rote through drills, Savage said, and there is a danger in overemphasizing the morphology of words at the expense of the exciting cultures of language. But in order to appreciate either of those, children first need to learn the systematic patterns in written language that represent words.

“Children need to be taught that skill, and an awareness that we can reconfigure a spoken word into its constituents,” Savage said.

“What I’m seeing in school boards is a movement towards actually trying to deliver this,” Savage said, but this is only a fairly recent shift.

In Ontario, for example, a 2022 report by the Ontario Human Rights Commission (Ohrc) that was first called to examine reading disabilities instead found a sweeping literacy problem, with one third of students graduating schools without attaining the level of literacy that the Organization of Economic Co-operation and Development regards as necessary to function in the modern economy.

That prompted Ontario to revamp its curriculum in 2023 to emphasize the more structured approach based on phonics.

National reporting on the problem is patchy and inconsistent, partly because education is a provincial mandate. But direct provincial reporting gives provincial level glimpses. In British Columbia, in Grade 4, 30 per cent of students are not on track toward literacy standards. It also shows that about 40 per cent are still in the “emerging” category by Grade 7, and a similar proportion have improved to be “on track.”

In Manitoba, just 45 per cent of students were meeting literacy expectations.

New Brunswick reports an especially dire situation, with “inconsistent” measurement and “insufficient” monitoring of children’s literacy achievement, according to provincial Auditor General Paul Martin. His report this summer showed that in the past three years “no provincial literacy assessment target was met, with achievement results falling short of targets from 7.8% to 34.4%. We found that some provincial literacy targets are not currently assessed, and that achievement gaps are not always driving timely, targeted intervention. Furthermore, not all literacy programs and student-level supports are consistently evaluated to determine their effectiveness.”

“For literacy to improve, Canadian provinces need to prioritize evidence-based teaching strategies for reading, use a knowledge-rich curriculum, apply science-of-learning principles, and implement early and rigorous reading interventions,” says a new report. Adobe Stock

More than half of New Brunswick anglophone students reading below their level were not receiving specialized interventions, the report found. Early intervention is a key factor because improvement becomes more difficult as children grow up.

But teachers are often not doing these early interventions because this new science of literacy is a “powerful but largely unused tool in the school toolbox,” according to a new report for the Aristotle Foundation for Public Policy, a think tank, by David Livingstone, a retired professor and author of books on education and civics, with David Hunt and Pio Tran.

The report, which surveys current literature on the problem, emphasizes that learning to read must happen in a curriculum that also teaches a variety of knowledge because prior knowledge has a greater impact on comprehension than simple reading ability, and because students with a strong background of knowledge are better equipped to absorb more.

“Therefore, teachers must be equipped and trained to effectively utilize a knowledge-rich curriculum, or else efforts to improve literacy will be futile. One of the problems in Canada is that many provincial education ministries, education faculties, teachers’ unions, and school boards promote pedagogies such as discovery learning or inquiry-based learning, which place far less emphasis on content acquisition,” it read.

The report describes this as “ideological capture,” a structural obstacle to change that reflects the “stranglehold that ineffective teaching pedagogies, such as discovery learning, have over the faculties of education and the teachers’ unions that influence the teachers in the classroom.”

The report cites the work of Jamie Metsala, professor of education at Mount Saint Vincent University in Halifax, who was a key consultant on the Ohrc report. She has published research showing that morphological awareness — a knowledge of morphemes, root words, prefixes, suffixes and other structural aspects of words — was the “strongest oral language predictor of reading comprehension.”

The report describes Metsala’s concern that many teachers are unaware of this, not taught it in their own professional education, and so teaching practice is not keeping up with the best teaching theory.

It also cites research this year by George Georgiou, director of the University of Alberta’s Reading Research Lab, jointly with Savage and others and funded by the Max Bell Foundation, that tracked the impact of a large systematic program to improve phonological and morphological awareness among 1,000 Grade 2 students across five provinces.

More than half showed a tripled rate of progress after five months, and 80 per cent showed an improvement equal to what would have otherwise been expected in 18 months, according to a UofA press release.

Savage said they have data from this research, and they are still reviewing it, but an “eyeball” of the numbers shows robust improvements in reading, and knock-on effects on reading comprehension, which should provide guidance to schools.

The issue has attracted popular and cultural support. The late Dolly Parton, for example, famously a lifelong literacy advocate in tribute to her father who could not read, created the Imagination Library in 1995, which sends free books in the mail, often with government support. This year, P.E.I. announced it would cut its funding, but abruptly backtracked and maintained the program.

Heather Reisman, the founder and CEO of Indigo Books, has called for a national literacy strategy partly on the grounds that functional illiteracy among young adults is a drag on the economy.

A report by the large accounting firm Deloitte in November 2020, for example, estimated that every one per cent increase in adult literacy would boost GDP by $67-billion, and that the best way to boost adult literacy is to boost child literacy.

That warning came in the early days of the pandemic, which reinforced the negative effects on literacy of digital technology, while also throwing up new psychological and pedagogical obstacles to regular reading instruction.

More than five years later, however, Canadian literacy education remains stuck between two teaching paradigms, with literacy numbers still moving in the wrong direction.

Joseph Brean has been a national reporter with the Post since 2001, writing general breaking news and more focused coverage of law, science, politics and culture. He also writes longer features, interviews, profiles and obituaries.

More than five years later, however, Canadian literacy education remains stuck between two teaching paradigms, with literacy numbers still moving in the wrong direction.

stories.title: Accused at murder trial testifies he never meant to set his best friend on fire
stories.summary: As he took the stand at his murder trial testifying in his own defence, Bradley Joudrey, 36, broke down and sobbed several times as he recalled how his best friend, 29-year-old Jonathan Graham, died after being set on fire in the early morning hours of July 12, 2022.
stories.author: Nick Paparella
stories.content:
As he took the stand at his murder trial testifying in his own defence, Bradley Joudrey, 36, broke down and sobbed several times as he recalled how his best friend, 29-year-old Jonathan Graham, died after being set on fire in the early morning hours of July 12, 2022.

Joudrey said he was upset with Graham because after a night of drinking the pair got into a fight at an after-hours hangout in east London.

“We had arguments but never fist fights ... I was upset and embarrassed because I was the one who got punched and I was kicked out,” he said.

“I was really pissed off. I said I was going to burn his car.”

Joudrey told the court he left the gathering in anger to go siphon gasoline into a plastic pop bottle from his ATV and he wanted to meet up with Graham saying, “I grabbed the Pepsi bottle, I grabbed a beer and drove away.”

The accused said after several calls and text messages, he eventually met up with Graham at a strip plaza with a convenience store located at Admiral Drive and Trafalgar Street.

When he saw the Graham’s white Jeep parked at the side of the store, “My plan was to set the car on fire when he was in the store.”

Joudrey said as he walked up to the vehicle with the gas in a bottle, a lighter, and a piece of paper, “I figured nobody’s in it … I run up to the Jeep and I’m throwing it in and at that point I realized he’s in the vehicle and he gets out and says ‘what the f**k?”’

“That’s when I said, ‘I was here to Iight your vehicle on fire’ and that’s when I lit the piece of paper on fire and he caught fire.”

Through tears, Joudrey said, “I never physically wanted to hurt Jonathan.”

He would race away from the scene and crash his Dodge Journey saying, “I just set my best friend on fire, I was worried. I take off, I’m super panicked.”

He would be arrested by London Police when he eventually returned to the crash site minutes later to retrieve his identification and cellphone.

Graham would be rushed to hospital where he would die from thermal injuries.

Joudrey, who called himself a functioning alcoholic, would be charged with first-degree murder and has pled not guilty.

Later under cross-examination from Crown Attorney Marcia Hilliard, Joudrey was questioned about his intentions on the night his best friend was set on fire.

The Crown asked, “You were planning to kill Jon in his car?”

Joudrey responded, “No, I never meant to kill Jon.”

Joudrey said he quickly ran to his own vehicle once Graham was set on fire and Hilliard asked, “You sat in your car a couple of seconds and watched Jon burn?”

He replied, “No, I disagree.”

Asked why he never called 911 to help his friend the accused said, “Because I was selfish, I worried about going to jail. I regret everything.”

The trial is now adjourned until Dec. 2 when the Crown and the defence are expected to give closing arguments in the case.

stories.title: London’s Homes for Heroes welcomes first veterans Friday
stories.summary: London’s new home for at-risk and homeless veterans has officially opened on a greenspace near Parkwood Hospital.
stories.author: Sean Irvine
stories.content:
London’s new home for at-risk and homeless veterans has officially opened on a greenspace near Parkwood Hospital.

Built for $6 million, Homes for Heroes will offer living quarters and support programs for 25 veterans from across the region.

The site includes a resource centre and open spaces for reflection. It will welcome its first veteran on Friday.

Governments, local military organizations, service clubs, and the public contributed to the project.

The largest donation of $4 million came from an anonymous donor.

Homes for Heroes organizers have long called the facility a “game changer” for those who served, with President and CEO Brad Field adding, “The true measure of this village will not be the homes we open today, but the lives that will be changed within them for years to come.”

“Today is more than a grand opening. It’s a promise that we will continue to stand beside those who once stood for us,” he said.

London mayor Josh Morgan acknowledged the role of community support, adding, “When a veteran walks onto this site and can close the door and say, ‘I’m home’, take pride in knowing you had something to do with that.”

“And Homes for Heroes is a star, it is a star!” exclaimed General (Retd) Walter Natynczyk, who added, “because it’s here where our veterans can get on the path to well-being.”

Each unit in the facility is fronted by a plaque telling a personal story of sacrifice or of battles Canadians have served in.

stories.title: Elizabeth Bain’s disappearance and Robert Baltovich’s wrongful conviction: The timeline
stories.summary: June 19, 1990 Twenty-two-year-old Elizabeth Bain leaves home to check a schedule at the U. of T.’s Scarborough campus. When she doesn’t return, her worried mother calls police. June 22-24, 1990 Fears grow after the missing woman’s car is discovered at an auto body shop not far from her home. A large bloodstain is ominously found in […]
stories.author: Michael Talbot
stories.content:
By News Staff

Posted November 26, 2026 6:00 am.

Last Updated November 26, 2026 6:01 am.

Twenty-two-year-old Elizabeth Bain leaves home to check a schedule at the U. of T.’s Scarborough campus. When she doesn’t return, her worried mother calls police.

Fears grow after the missing woman’s car is discovered at an auto body shop not far from her home. A large bloodstain is ominously found in the backseat, but there’s no sign of Bain. Cops immediately turn to her boyfriend, 24-year-old Robert Baltovich. He’s questioned by detectives for hours, but some of his responses arouse their suspicions. There are massive searches for the absent woman during most of that summer, but her body is never found. Police conclude she’s been murdered.

A heartbreaking public appeal is issued by the Bain family, asking for any clues to Elizabeth’s whereabouts. Included in the plaintive plea: a message to her suspected killer to at least let them know where her body can be found. The request goes unanswered.

Police zero in on Baltovich as the main suspect in the crime. They search his home and his car, and are seen leaving the area with numerous pieces of potential evidence.

Robert Baltovich is arrested and charged with first-degree murder in Bain’s disappearance, despite the fact police don’t have the body. It’s been exactly five months since she walked out the door of her house, never to return.

The accused boyfriend’s first trial starts, with more than 100 witnesses taking the stand. The Crown drops the charge to second-degree murder, painting Baltovich as a spurned lover who became murderously angry when Bain tried to end their relationship. Baltovich continues to insist he’s innocent, offering a not guilty plea. His lawyers claim there’s significant evidence someone else may have committed the crime, introducing witness testimony about a blond man seen near her before she vanished. It comes at the same time the so-called “Scarborough Rapist” is on the prowl, and will later lead to speculation that Paul Bernardo could be a viable suspect.

Baltovich is found guilty of second-degree murder and receives a life sentence.

Baltovich hires a new attorney and files an appeal. Legal documents cite a number of suspect issues with the trial, including the judge’s address to the jury and the fact that some witnesses were hypnotized to aid their memory recall.

Paul Bernardo is arrested and accused of being the Scarborough Rapist, among other crimes. When Baltovich’s lawyer hears about the arrest, he hires a private investigator to probe the suspect’s background. The P.I. claims to have found evidence that may tie Bernardo to Bain.

Baltovich’s appeal is filed with the Ontario Court of Appeal. Although it doesn’t name Bernardo, it does contain references to the Scarborough Rapist as one of the main reasons the verdict may be in doubt. The court is supposed to hear the case in February of the following year, but it gets put off with no timetable for resumption. Baltovich remains in jail, still swearing his innocence.

The Assocation in Defence of the Wrongly Convicted takes up the case, filing its own documents with the Court of Appeal. For the first time, Paul Bernardo is directly named in a legal brief as a possible main suspect. The group demands Baltovich be released while the appeal is considered. He’s been behind bars for eight years.

The court agrees to review the case and frees Baltovich pending the appeal. A judge appears to agree with at least one major contention from the appeal – calling the conviction wholly ‘circumstantial’ and admitting it needs a second look.

After endless delays and more than a decade after his guilty verdict, The Ontario Court of Appeal finally reviews the Baltovich case.

The Ontario Court of Appeal sets aside the Baltovich conviction and orders a new trial. The court agrees there were significant errors made in the first case, but refuses to acquit the accused outright, opting to let another jury decide.

The Attorney General’s office confirms it intends to retry Baltovich on the murder of Bain. Once again, they’re pinning second-degree murder charges on him.

Toronto Police secretly travel to Kingston to interview Bernardo on the Bain murder. He denies any involvement.

In a case already fraught with so many delays came yet another one. On the day jury selection was set to start in a new trial, the judge who was going to hear it was appointed to a new court – and the proceedings have been stopped.

The long awaited resumption is set to begin with jury selection underway. The actual trial may not start until mid-April.

Jury finds Robert Baltovich not guilty of second-degree murder in Bain’s death minutes into the retrial.

Attorney General Chris Bentley confirms he won’t call an inquiry into the case because it won’t help the administration of justice.

Dateline Canada ‘s two-hour exclusive is set to reveal new information pointing to the possible involvement of Paul Bernardo in Bain’s disappearance.

By Michael Talbot

Posted November 26, 2026 6:00 am.

Last Updated November 26, 2026 6:01 am.

Who killed Elizabeth Bain?

It’s a question that’s haunted her loved ones and perplexed authorities for more than 25 years after the 22-year-old University of Toronto student vanished near the school’s Scarborough campus on June 19, 1990, and was never seen again.

Her former boyfriend, Robert Baltovich, was initially convicted of second-degree murder in her death. He was released on bail pending an appeal after spending eight years behind bars and was later found not guilty in a retrial.

During his appeal in September 2004, Baltovich’s lawyers pointed at convicted sex killer Paul Bernardo as possibly being involved in Bain’s death — something Bernardo would deny in a 2007 interview with Toronto police detectives.

Now, a Dateline Canada investigation claims to have uncovered previously unreported evidence that could shed light on the enduring murder mystery and a possible connection to Canada’s most notorious sex killer.

Dateline Canada premieres Thursday, November 26 at 8 p.m. ET/PT on Citytv and Citytv+.

Bain left home on June 19, 1990 to check a schedule at UofT’s Scarborough campus. When she didn’t return, her worried mother called police. Days later her blood-stained vehicle was discovered a few blocks away, but she was nowhere to be found.

It didn’t take long for investigators to zero in on her-then boyfriend, Baltovich, who was 24-years-old at the time.

Baltovich was questioned for hours while extensive searches for the missing woman took place.

When she wasn’t found, police declared the case a homicide.

By late July, Baltovich was considered the prime suspect in the case and police searched his home and car.

Four months later, on November 19, 1990, Baltovich was arrested and charged with first-degree murder.

The Bain murder trial got underway in February, 1992, with more than 100 witnesses taking the stand. The Crown downgraded Baltovich’s charge to second-degree murder, painting a theory that he killed Bain in a jealous fit when she tried to break off their relationship.

Baltovich vehemently denied it, pleading not guilty.

His lawyers introduced an alternate suspect narrative, introducing witness testimony about a blond man seen near her before she vanished — matching early descriptions of the so-called “Scarborough Rapist” who was later determined to be Paul Bernardo.

On March 31, 1992, Baltovich was found guilty of second-degree murder and received a life sentence.

Just months after he was sentenced, Baltovich hired a new lawyer and filed the appeal that would ultimately lead to his exoneration.

The Ontario Court of Appeal, citing numerous errors in his first trial, ultimately set aside his conviction and ordered a new trial, which took place in 2008.

A jury found Baltovich not guilty just minutes into the start of the retrial after Crown prosecutors said they wouldn’t be presenting any evidence or calling any witnesses.

The abrupt end to the retrial meant Baltovich’s lawyer, James Lockyer, didn’t have the chance to present his Bernardo theory.

Speaking to reporters outside the courthouse afterwards, Lockyer said he believed Bernardo “probably committed the crime” but conceded that it couldn’t be proven beyond a reasonable doubt.

“It’s an unbelievable relief,” Baltovich said outside court after being found not guilty.

“It’s an 18-year nightmare and in half an hour, it’s over. I’m just glad it’s over. No more bail. No more conviction. No more charges. I get to live the rest of my life free.”

Baltovich filed a civil lawsuit against the Attorney General for Ontario, the Toronto Police Services Board, two TPS detectives and two of his former trial defence lawyers, seeking $13 million in compensation for his wrongful conviction.

The resolution of that lawsuit has not been publicly disclosed.

Attorney General Chris Bentley later confirmed he wouldn’t call an inquiry into the case because it wouldn’t help the administration of justice.

Between Baltovich’s appeal and his ultimate acquittal in 2008, two Toronto police detectives travelled to Kingston Penitentiary to interview Bernardo and question him about his possible involvement in the Bain murder.

The interview, which was videotaped, was later released to the public.

Bernardo, who is serving life for sexually assaulting and murdering school girls Leslie Mahaffy and Kristen French, seemed annoyed when the detectives ask if he will take a polygraph.

Twelve minutes into the interview, one of the detectives asks Bernardo: “Did you kill Elizabeth Bain on June the 19th, 1990?”

“Well, that’s a loaded question,” the arrogant killer replies. “I mean are we going to go back and go through the time sequence of what happened in my life? I could just give a yes or no answer, but there’s a lot of issues about that.”

“The answer to that is ‘no,’” he finally says. “But the 800-pound gorilla is in the room. That’s a life-25 sentence. It really comes down to credibility … But the answer is no to that question.”

When the detectives try to jog his memory about what he was doing around the time of Bain’s disappearance, Bernardo fails to give a definitive answer.

“See what happens when you lock a guy up for 15 years in a windowless cell? Memory gets fuzzy.”

When one of the detectives asks if he ever met Bain, Bernardo replies “I don’t remember,” before saying he only heard about Bain’s case after he was already in jail.

The Dateline Canada two-hour special airs Thursday, Nov. 26 at 8 p.m. on Citytv and Citytv+.

With files from The Canadian Press

stories.author: Michael Talbot
stories.content:
Despite denying any involvement, notorious Canadian sex killer and ‘Scarborough Rapist’ Paul Bernardo has long been considered a potential person of interest in the disappearance and presumed murder of Elizabeth Bain.

Now, 36 years after Bain vanished, a Dateline Canada exclusive is set to reveal startling new information possibly linking Bernardo to the case.

The two-hour Dateline Canada special, which airs Thursday night on Citytv and Citytv+ at 8 p.m., includes a never-before-televised eyewitness account of an apparent assault along Highway 401 in Scarborough involving a woman and man matching the descriptions of Bain and Bernardo, in a vehicle believed to Bain’s.

When detectives travelled to Kingston Penitentiary in 2007 to grill Bernardo about the case, he replied “I don’t remember” when asked if he ever met Bain.

The Dateline Canada investigation includes an account from an ex-girlfriend of Bernardo’s who claims she introduced him to Elizabeth.

Dateline Canada also uncovered information that police were told in 2005 about an alleged jail-house confession from Karla Homolka, indicating the couple was responsible for additional killings beyond their three known victims.

Both Homolka and Bernardo have denied involvement and neither has faced charges connected to Bain.

Instead, Bain’s then-boyfriend, Robert Baltovich, was originally convicted of second-degree murder in her death. Baltovich later appealed the conviction and was found not guilty in a 2008 re-trial.

During the two-hour special, Baltovich takes part in his first sit-down television interview in almost 20 years, telling Dateline Canada’s Contributing Correspondent, Diana Swain, that he’s hopeful justice will be served for Elizabeth.

“I’ve been out of prison for 26 years, but that whole time, I’ve never lost hope that we might find out what happened to Liz.”

Dateline Canada premieres Thursday, November 26 at 8 p.m. ET/PT on Citytv and Citytv+.

stories.title: Strong storm system to bring heavy rain, powerful winds to southwestern Ontario
stories.summary: You’ll want to grab an umbrella before you head out the door this morning, some active weather is moving into the region this afternoon.
stories.author: Fiona Robertson
stories.content:
You’ll want to grab an umbrella before you head out the door this morning, some active weather is moving into the region this afternoon. “Periods of rain expected, general rainfall amounts in London close to about 20 to 30 millimeters,” said CTV London Meteorologist Julie Atchison.

“This is a significant system that’s moving up the east coast, bringing strong gusty winds.” Atchison says we could see wind gusts upwards of 80 km/h close to the Lake Erie shoreline. “Now there is the potential for some mixed precipitation as well.

Even the risk of freezing rain in and around Kitchener, Waterloo, Mount Forest,” added Atchison. “You can see possibility of a bit of a rain snow mix, but this is going to be a soaker across southern Ontario.” This weather system will linger in the area, with rain dominating the seven-day forecast.

Here’s a look at the rest of the forecast Thursday: Becoming cloudy in the morning then rain at times heavy. Amount 10 to 20 mm. Wind east 30 km/h gusting to 50 becoming northeast 50 gusting to 70 early in the afternoon.

High plus 5. UV index 2 or low. Thursday night: Rain at times heavy. Amount 10 to 20 mm. Wind east 40 km/h gusting to 60 diminishing to 20 gusting to 40 in the evening then becoming light before morning. Low plus 3. Friday: Periods of rain or snow.

High 6. Saturday: Cloudy with 30 per cent chance of showers. High 7. Sunday: Cloudy with 40 per cent chance of rain. High 9. Monday: Cloudy with 40 per cent chance of showers. High 7.

stories.title: Locked in: How many Canadians who bought at peak housing prices can’t afford to move?
stories.summary: Could collective immobility be creating an overlooked bottleneck in the housing market?
stories.author: Stewart Blair and Michael Buzzeli
stories.content:
A recent convergence of housing-market pressures has left some Canadian homeowners who bought at peak housing prices unable to move. Could their collective immobility be creating an overlooked bottleneck in Canada’s housing market?

Consider those who purchased during the 2020–2022 housing boom. Using actual property transactions from that period across three Ontario housing markets, we modelled 2,502 hypothetical outcomes to assess whether those buyers could sell today and purchase another home.

In nearly 60 per cent of the scenarios, after accounting for current property values, selling costs and the down payment required for another home, the numbers simply didn’t add up. Many would exhaust their available housing equity and need more money to move.

That’s because those who bought in this time frame did so at record-high prices and historically low interest rates. Today’s reality is quite different: declining property values, higher borrowing costs and a less forgiving economy.

We May not yet know how many homeowners are effectively stuck in place. However, more than one million residential properties changed hands through Canada’s multiple listing service between 2020, when the market was heating up, and 2022, when prices were highest. Since the peak, the Canadian Real Estate Association’s composite Home Price Index has fallen by about 23 per cent.

If the price retractions weren’t concerning enough, let’s not forget the mortgage-renewal wave that followed. For many borrowers, renewal meant a considerably less pleasant financial reality. The Bank of Canada estimated that 60 per cent of outstanding mortgages would renew in 2025 and 2026. Average monthly payments were expected to increase by about 10 per cent and 6 per cent, respectively, compared with December 2024.

So far, the renewal wave appears to have been weathered reasonably well. For those who purchased at record prices, have we mistaken a delayed impact for no impact at all?

While we were all riding the renewal wave, a worrying picture was emerging elsewhere in the economy: consumer debt rose 4.6 per cent from a year earlier to $2.64-trillion, mortgage arrears are rising in Ontario and Statistics Canada’s shelter index has climbed nearly 31 per cent since January 2020. Surely some homeowners are taking on additional debt, drawing down savings or liquidating investments – simply to keep up with their housing costs.

Put yourself in their shoes for a moment. How much could you afford to lose just to move?

For some homeowners, the dilemma is even sharper: they can no longer afford to stay, yet they cannot afford to move.

How does this fit into the broader market? Consider the unsold homes in your neighbourhood. We often assume sellers are simply unwilling to accept market realities. But what if the prices they need to move are higher than the prices buyers are willing to pay?

Simply put, housing markets depend on movement. Renters become buyers, apartment owners move to townhomes, growing families seek more space and older homeowners downsize.

When one household can’t move, others in the chain are affected. If a significant enough share of homeowners can’t move, what begins as an individual constraint could snowball into a substantial, market-wide bottleneck.

Let us pose another sobering thought: If prospective buyers cannot sell their current properties, who will buy the homes we’re so focused on building and incentivizing?

Housing researchers have long studied the lock-in effect: conditions that discourage or prevent homeowners from moving, such as transaction costs and land transfer taxes. Our concept, Practical Equity Lock-In, builds on this research by examining whether homeowners retain sufficient equity, after accounting for changing property values and typical transaction costs, to finance their next purchase.

Our 60 per cent finding is not a national estimate. Our model focuses on available housing equity, a common source of funds for moving and buying another home. We excluded additional financial burdens, such as second mortgages, consumer debt and mortgage penalties. Conversely, we also didn’t account for other household resources, such as savings, investments or the bank of Mom and Dad, that might help cover a shortfall.

Given the considerable public investment in housing, we hope policymakers will consider this issue. Perhaps it’s time to stop assuming we can simply build or incentivize our way out of every housing problem.

Understanding why some homeowners can’t afford to move might be a good place to start.

Stewart Blair, MBA, is a PhD student, graduate fellow at Western’s Centre for Urban Policy and Local Governance, and real estate broker. Michael Buzzelli, PhD, is an associate professor and former director of Western’s Centre for Urban Policy and Local Governance.

stories.title: A 10-hour meeting, a heated point of order — and a Niagara Falls CAO fired with strong-mayor powers by morning
stories.summary: After a pointed council debate about the scope of strong-mayor powers, Niagara Falls Mayor Lori Lococo used those same powers to terminate chief administrative officer Jason Burgess a little more than a week into her leadership.
stories.author: Ray Spiteri
stories.content:
A pointed question about mayoral authority — and a contested point of order — set a contentious tone early in what became a marathon first session for Niagara Falls city council’s new term.

By the following morning, the debate had moved well beyond the council chamber: Mayor Lori Lococo had used those same strong-mayor powers to terminate the city’s chief administrative officer.

Under new business near the end of a 10-hour and 19-minute meeting — it began with an in-camera session after 2 p.m., opened to the public just after 4:30 p.m., returned behind closed doors at about 11:20 p.m. and went back to the open session before adjourning at 12:26 a.m. — Coun. Mona Patel put Lococo on the spot over strong-mayor powers.

“Since Niagara Falls was granted strong-mayor powers in 2023, you have raised concerns about this power on several occasions,” said Patel, noting mayors across Ontario have taken varying approaches, with some delegating powers back to council.

Niagara Falls Coun. Mona Patel

Patel said the issue had been generating buzz among residents, particularly in the wake of a controversial move by Fort Erie’s newly elected mayor, Tom Insinna, who less than 48 hours after taking office used his strong-mayor powers to dismiss the town’s chief administrative officer, Chris McQueen, without cause — bypassing council entirely.

“Now that we’re beginning a new term, I think both residents of Niagara Falls and council would appreciate some clarity on where you stand,” said Patel. “Do you intend to formally delegate the powers that can legally be delegated back to council?”

Before Lococo could respond, Coun. Joyce Morocco jumped in.

“I’m going to call a point of order,” said Morocco. “I think that there’s going to be a lot of situations where the mayors now that have the ability to have the mayors’ power …”

Patel cut in sharply: “Point of order. My question was to the mayor.”

Morocco pushed back. The two councillors began speaking over each other, prompting Lococo to intervene.

“Councillors …” the mayor said, trying to restore order.

Morocco stood firm, saying she was raising a point of order. Patel was equally insistent: “I had the floor, I asked the question to the mayor.”

Morocco’s argument was one of fairness to Lococo, not procedure.

“I think you’re putting the mayor on the spot,” she said, “because how can the mayor now actually address that when there’s so many things that we’re just beginning to know.”

Trying to settle the room, Lococo said: “Please stop. I will address Coun. Patel.”

The mayor said her recent research, particularly in light of the Fort Erie situation, had led her to conclude that strong-mayor powers cannot simply be set aside wholesale.

In some instances, she said, Premier Doug Ford’s government has removed traditional mayoral authorities, effectively requiring mayors to use strong-mayor powers in their place — leaving no room for delegation.

“Step No. 2, being inclusive,” continued Lococo, referencing the Fort Erie situation as a cautionary tale. “To my understanding there was no discussion — they just used strong-mayor powers.”

Lococo said her preference would be for discussion to precede any use of those powers — but acknowledged that in certain mandated situations, the mayor’s hand is effectively forced.

“It’s going to depend on a case-by-case basis, and it will depend on having discussion, what others think and where we go from there,” she said.

The mayor said strong-mayor powers remain widely misunderstood — including, she suggested, among some heads of council now holding them.

“There’s a lot of people talking to legal about it. Strong-mayor powers have completely changed.”

Patel accepted the answer graciously.

“I appreciate the answer. Thank you very much.”

Hours later, the mayor’s position became clear in action.

Mayor Lori Lococo confirmed she used Ontario’s strong-mayor powers to terminate the city’s top

The city confirmed Wednesday that Lococo had terminated CAO Jason Burgess — a little more than a week after taking the oath of office.

Erik Nickel, general manager of municipal works and chief engineer, has been appointed acting CAO.

Patel — the same councillor who hours earlier had pressed Lococo on strong-mayor powers — responded publicly Wednesday, raising questions about the financial cost to taxpayers.

“How much will taxpayers across Niagara Falls ultimately be paying in severance packages alone? With affordability front and centre throughout the municipal election, and municipalities looking for ways to reduce spending and keep property tax increases manageable, these are questions worth asking,” she wrote on Facebook.

“It appears we now have our answer” on where Lococo stands on strong-mayor powers.

Strong-mayor powers were introduced through the Strong Mayors, Building Homes Act of 2022 and have since expanded to 216 municipalities, including Niagara Falls in 2023. The powers give mayors significant unilateral authority — including the ability to hire and dismiss CAOs — without requiring council approval.
paragraphs: A pointed question about mayoral authority — and a contested point of order — set a contentious tone early in what became a marathon first session for Niagara Falls city council’s new term.
By the following morning, the debate had moved well beyond the council chamber: Mayor Lori Lococo had used those same strong-mayor powers to terminate the city’s chief administrative officer.

Under new business near the end of a 10-hour and 19-minute meeting — it began with an in-camera session after 2 p.m., opened to the public just after 4:30 p.m., returned behind closed doors at about 11:20 p.m. and went back to the open session before adjourning at 12:26 a.m. — Coun. Mona Patel put Lococo on the spot over strong-mayor powers.

“Since Niagara Falls was granted strong-mayor powers in 2023, you have raised concerns about this power on several occasions,” said Patel, noting mayors across Ontario have taken varying approaches, with some delegating powers back to council.
Niagara Falls Coun. Mona Patel

Patel said the issue had been generating buzz among residents, particularly in the wake of a controversial move by Fort Erie’s newly elected mayor, Tom Insinna, who less than 48 hours after taking office used his strong-mayor powers to dismiss the town’s chief administrative officer, Chris McQueen, without cause — bypassing council entirely.

“Now that we’re beginning a new term, I think both residents of Niagara Falls and council would appreciate some clarity on where you stand,” said Patel. “Do you intend to formally delegate the powers that can legally be delegated back to council?”
Before Lococo could respond, Coun. Joyce Morocco jumped in.
“I’m going to call a point of order,” said Morocco. “I think that there’s going to be a lot of situations where the mayors now that have the ability to have the mayors’ power …”
Patel cut in sharply: “Point of order. My question was to the mayor.”
Morocco pushed back. The two councillors began speaking over each other, prompting Lococo to intervene.
“Councillors …” the mayor said, trying to restore order.
Morocco stood firm, saying she was raising a point of order. Patel was equally insistent: “I had the floor, I asked the question to the mayor.”
Morocco’s argument was one of fairness to Lococo, not procedure.
“I think you’re putting the mayor on the spot,” she said, “because how can the mayor now actually address that when there’s so many things that we’re just beginning to know.”
Trying to settle the room, Lococo said: “Please stop. I will address Coun. Patel.”
The mayor said her recent research, particularly in light of the Fort Erie situation, had led her to conclude that strong-mayor powers cannot simply be set aside wholesale.

In some instances, she said, Premier Doug Ford’s government has removed traditional mayoral authorities, effectively requiring mayors to use strong-mayor powers in their place — leaving no room for delegation.
“Step No. 2, being inclusive,” continued Lococo, referencing the Fort Erie situation as a cautionary tale. “To my understanding there was no discussion — they just used strong-mayor powers.”
Lococo said her preference would be for discussion to precede any use of those powers — but acknowledged that in certain mandated situations, the mayor’s hand is effectively forced.
“It’s going to depend on a case-by-case basis, and it will depend on having discussion, what others think and where we go from there,” she said.
The mayor said strong-mayor powers remain widely misunderstood — including, she suggested, among some heads of council now holding them.
“There’s a lot of people talking to legal about it. Strong-mayor powers have completely changed.”
Patel accepted the answer graciously.
“I appreciate the answer. Thank you very much.”
Hours later, the mayor’s position became clear in action.
Mayor Lori Lococo confirmed she used Ontario’s strong-mayor powers to terminate the city’s top
The city confirmed Wednesday that Lococo had terminated CAO Jason Burgess — a little more than a week after taking the oath of office.
Erik Nickel, general manager of municipal works and chief engineer, has been appointed acting CAO.
Patel — the same councillor who hours earlier had pressed Lococo on strong-mayor powers — responded publicly Wednesday, raising questions about the financial cost to taxpayers.

“How much will taxpayers across Niagara Falls ultimately be paying in severance packages alone? With affordability front and centre throughout the municipal election, and municipalities looking for ways to reduce spending and keep property tax increases manageable, these are questions worth asking,” she wrote on Facebook.
“It appears we now have our answer” on where Lococo stands on strong-mayor powers.

Strong-mayor powers were introduced through the Strong Mayors, Building Homes Act of 2022 and have since expanded to 216 municipalities, including Niagara Falls in 2023. The powers give mayors significant unilateral authority — including the ability to hire and dismiss CAOs — without requiring council approval.

stories.title: Shooting at the auto shop: how Canada is tackling India’s extortion gangs
stories.summary: Documents obtained by Global News give a rare inside look at an investigation into an extortion scheme.
stories.author: Stewart Bell
stories.content:
On October 10, 2025, India’s Lawrence Bishnoi gang began shaking down a prominent South Asian businessmen and community member in Surrey, B.C.

Over WhatsApp, the gang threatened the owner of Star Autobody Ltd., sprayed his office with bullets, and then fired a dozen more rounds at his house.

A year later, three of the gang members responsible for the shooting have been arrested and deported, and a fourth is wanted on a Canada-wide warrant.

Records on the case obtained by Global News reveal how police and immigration officers are tackling the Indian extortion gangs preying on South Asian Canadians.

The documents, released by the Immigration and Refugee Board, show how Surrey police used hi-tech tools to catch the suspects as they fled the scene of the shooting.

They also disclose how the Canada Border Services Agency successfully expelled the suspected getaway driver, even as he claimed he could not remember what he did.

The shooting, part of an attempt to extort money from Star Autobody, was one of dozens like it in Surrey last year.

But a flurry of law enforcement action appears to be having an impact on the Bishnoi gang and its affiliates across Canada.

In Surrey, extortions have been dropping for the past six months. While in January, 10 extortion shootings were reported, none have occurred since the start of October, police said.

“We remain encouraged by the decline and reduction in reported extortions and extortion-related shots fired,” said Surrey Police Service Sgt. Lindsey Houghton.

“But we know the work is far from done,” the police spokesperson said, adding, “we know that we can’t take our foot off the gas, so to speak.”

Police in Edmonton and Calgary also confirmed that extortion-related incidents were trending downwards in both cities.

“We have seen a decrease in the frequency of these occurrences, which is a promising sign that our investigative and enforcement efforts are working,” said a Calgary police spokesperson.

All three police departments have been working with the Canada Border Services Agency, which said it had removed more than 100 suspects identified through extortion investigations.

A U.S. crackdown on the Bishnoi gang in July resulted in the arrests of two dozen members in California, Canada and Europe.

It also saw a million dollar reward offered for Goldy Brar , the gang’s lieutenant, who is on the run and atop Canada’s most wanted list .

The Bishnoi gang is made up of “young Indian males … who have been issued either a work or study permit ,” according to the documents.

At deportation hearings for Indian extortion suspects that Global News has observed this year, all had come to Canada on student visas.

Instead of going to class, however, they imported Indian organized crime to Canadian cities with large South Asian populations, notably Surrey, Edmonton, Calgary and Brampton.

Murders, threats, shootings and arsons have all been tied to Bishnoi, which recruits through the glorification of the gangster lifestyle on social media.

The gang is also suspected of working for the Indian government , notably to assassinate a prominent B.C. Sikh temple leader, Hardeep Singh Nijjar, in 2023.

But the gang’s main focus has been extorting businesses owned by Sikh-Canadians in B.C., Alberta and Ontario.

By August 2025, extortions were soaring and the gang was so emboldened it allegedly sent a letter to police threatening to shoot their stations unless they backed off.

“We will rule in Canada,” according to a copy obtained by Global News that said all businesses would soon have to pay protection money.

Two months later, a gunman opened fire on Surrey’s Star Autobody . Police initially said they had found “no established ties to any extortion investigations.”

But then the owner received an extortion threat by phone, followed by another on Oct. 25, according to the investigation documents.

And then the gang went after his family.

The suspected getaway driver, Palwinder Singh, entered Canada in January 2024 with a study permit for a teaching assistant diploma at Portage College in Alberta.

Within months, however, he had dropped and agreed to accompany his roommate, Manavdeep Singh, ON a road trip to B.C. with two others.

According to Palwinder, it was just a holiday to see “waterfalls.” But the Bishnoi gang is known to use gunmen from out of province for its extortion shootings.

From Edmonton, the four suspects drove 1,100 kilometres to Surrey, where their plot went awry when police pulled them for speeding and impounded their Dodge Durrango .

Then on Oct. 29, a witness contacted Surrey police to report that he had overheard four men discussing a shooting. He only caught one of their names: Palwinder.

At about 2 a.m. the next morning, a car drove past the home of Star Autobody owner’s while a passenger stuck a handgun out the window and shot up the residence.

Police said several people were inside the house at the time. A suspected Bishnoi gang leader claimed responsibility in a social media post.

But the gunmen didn’t get far.

An automatic licence plate reader captured their brown Kia Spectra fleeing the scene. Surrey police found the vehicle nearby and conducted a roadside stop.

The two men inside, Manavdeep Singh and Akashdeep Singh, were arrested. A balaclava and bullets matching those used in the shooting were found in the car.

A third suspect fled the car into bushes but was later identified as Arshdeep Singh. Police then went to the basement suite where the suspects were staying.

As police watched, two men left the building and drove off in a Hyundai Elantra. Police pulled them over and arrested Arshdeep Singh and Palwinder Singh.

A box of ammunition matching the brand and calibre used in the extortion shooting was found in their vehicle, according to the documents.

On Arshdeep’s phone, police found a video of the shooting, while Cctv showed Palwinder and the other suspects leaving their accommodations shortly before the attack.

Palwinder was not charged and disappeared. Immigration authorities issued a warrant for his arrest in May, and he was picked up in Saskatoon in June 2026.

When Palwinder’s deportation hearing got underway on July 3, two of his alleged accomplices, Arshdeep and Manavdeep, had already been removed from Canada.

In his testimony, Palwinder had little to say about the shooting, claiming he did not remember that night because he was intoxicated.

“We had weed, we were drunk,” he said.

The Cbsa argued that Palwinder was a member of a criminal organization and that the shooting was “linked to the Lawrence Bishnoi gang.”

Palwinder maintained there was no proof he was involved, only what he called assumptions. But then he waved a white flag.

“I want to go back to my country,” he said, “so please just send me back.”

He had just one request, he added. “I don’t want my pictures posted anywhere or any of my information shared with anyone.”

The Immigration and Refugee Board ruled that Palwinder was a member of the Bishnoi gang and ordered his deportation.

On Sept. 14, the Cbsa announced that Palwinder was “linked to an extortion-related shooting” and had been deported.

His photo was included in the news release.

Stewart.Bell@globalnews.CA

content_blocks.text: “But we know the work is far from done,” the police spokesperson said, adding, “we know that we can’t take our foot off the gas, so to speak.”
Police in Edmonton and Calgary also confirmed that extortion-related incidents were trending downwards in both cities.
“We have seen a decrease in the frequency of these occurrences, which is a promising sign that our investigative and enforcement efforts are working,” said a Calgary police spokesperson.
All three police departments have been working with the Canada Border Services Agency, which said it had removed more than 100 suspects identified through extortion investigations.

content_blocks.text: A U.S. crackdown on the Bishnoi gang in July resulted in the arrests of two dozen members in California, Canada and Europe.
It also saw a million dollar reward offered for Goldy Brar , the gang’s lieutenant, who is on the run and atop Canada’s most wanted list .
content_blocks.html: It also saw a million dollar reward offered for Goldy Brar, the gang’s lieutenant, who is on the run and atop Canada’s most wanted list.

content_blocks.text: ‘No one can stop us’
The Bishnoi gang is made up of “young Indian males … who have been issued either a work or study permit ,” according to the documents.
content_blocks.html: The Bishnoi gang is made up of “young Indian males … who have been issued either a work or study permit,” according to the documents.

content_blocks.text: At deportation hearings for Indian extortion suspects that Global News has observed this year, all had come to Canada on student visas.
Instead of going to class, however, they imported Indian organized crime to Canadian cities with large South Asian populations, notably Surrey, Edmonton, Calgary and Brampton.
Murders, threats, shootings and arsons have all been tied to Bishnoi, which recruits through the glorification of the gangster lifestyle on social media.
The gang is also suspected of working for the Indian government , notably to assassinate a prominent B.C. Sikh temple leader, Hardeep Singh Nijjar, in 2023.
content_blocks.html: The gang is also suspected of working for the Indian government, notably to assassinate a prominent B.C. Sikh temple leader, Hardeep Singh Nijjar, in 2023.

content_blocks.text: But the gang’s main focus has been extorting businesses owned by Sikh-Canadians in B.C., Alberta and Ontario.
By August 2025, extortions were soaring and the gang was so emboldened it allegedly sent a letter to police threatening to shoot their stations unless they backed off.
“We will rule in Canada,” according to a copy obtained by Global News that said all businesses would soon have to pay protection money.
Two months later, a gunman opened fire on Surrey’s Star Autobody . Police initially said they had found “no established ties to any extortion investigations.”
content_blocks.html: Two months later, a gunman opened fire on Surrey’s Star Autobody. Police initially said they had found “no established ties to any extortion investigations.”

content_blocks.text: But then the owner received an extortion threat by phone, followed by another on Oct. 25, according to the investigation documents.
And then the gang went after his family.
The 'getaway driver'
content_blocks.html: The 'getaway driver'

content_blocks.text: The suspected getaway driver, Palwinder Singh, entered Canada in January 2024 with a study permit for a teaching assistant diploma at Portage College in Alberta.
Within months, however, he had dropped and agreed to accompany his roommate, Manavdeep Singh, ON a road trip to B.C. with two others.
According to Palwinder, it was just a holiday to see “waterfalls.” But the Bishnoi gang is known to use gunmen from out of province for its extortion shootings.
From Edmonton, the four suspects drove 1,100 kilometres to Surrey, where their plot went awry when police pulled them for speeding and impounded their Dodge Durrango .
Then on Oct. 29, a witness contacted Surrey police to report that he had overheard four men discussing a shooting. He only caught one of their names: Palwinder.
At about 2 a.m. the next morning, a car drove past the home of Star Autobody owner’s while a passenger stuck a handgun out the window and shot up the residence.
Police said several people were inside the house at the time. A suspected Bishnoi gang leader claimed responsibility in a social media post.
content_blocks.html: Police said several people were inside the house at the time. A suspected Bishnoi gang leader claimed responsibility in a social media post.

content_blocks.text: But the gunmen didn’t get far.
An automatic licence plate reader captured their brown Kia Spectra fleeing the scene. Surrey police found the vehicle nearby and conducted a roadside stop.
The two men inside, Manavdeep Singh and Akashdeep Singh, were arrested. A balaclava and bullets matching those used in the shooting were found in the car.
A third suspect fled the car into bushes but was later identified as Arshdeep Singh. Police then went to the basement suite where the suspects were staying.
As police watched, two men left the building and drove off in a Hyundai Elantra. Police pulled them over and arrested Arshdeep Singh and Palwinder Singh.
A box of ammunition matching the brand and calibre used in the extortion shooting was found in their vehicle, according to the documents.
On Arshdeep’s phone, police found a video of the shooting, while Cctv showed Palwinder and the other suspects leaving their accommodations shortly before the attack.
Palwinder was not charged and disappeared. Immigration authorities issued a warrant for his arrest in May, and he was picked up in Saskatoon in June 2026.
Deported

content_blocks.text: When Palwinder’s deportation hearing got underway on July 3, two of his alleged accomplices, Arshdeep and Manavdeep, had already been removed from Canada.
In his testimony, Palwinder had little to say about the shooting, claiming he did not remember that night because he was intoxicated.
“We had weed, we were drunk,” he said.
The Cbsa argued that Palwinder was a member of a criminal organization and that the shooting was “linked to the Lawrence Bishnoi gang.”
Palwinder maintained there was no proof he was involved, only what he called assumptions. But then he waved a white flag.
“I want to go back to my country,” he said, “so please just send me back.”
He had just one request, he added. “I don’t want my pictures posted anywhere or any of my information shared with anyone.”
The Immigration and Refugee Board ruled that Palwinder was a member of the Bishnoi gang and ordered his deportation.
On Sept. 14, the Cbsa announced that Palwinder was “linked to an extortion-related shooting” and had been deported.

stories.title: Police officers to be deployed at Lcbo outlets in effort to curb liquor store robberies
stories.summary: The Liquor Control Board of Ontario is putting police officers in some locations across the province to target stores where booze bandits are running off with bags of expensive spirits.
stories.author: Adrian Ghobrial
stories.content:
Toronto- The Liquor Control Board of Ontario is putting police officers in some locations across the province to target stores where booze bandits are running off with bags of expensive spirits.

“We know there is a lot of repeat crime so we’re aware those operations exist,” said Lcbo media relations director Sebastian Skamski.

Ontario’s government-run liquor stores say they’re using internal data to help them locate the most vulnerable locations.

“We’re very aware of the role of organized crime in theft at the Lcbo, these are very sophisticated operations where they act in tandem to coordinate and target stores,” Skamski added.

Dubbed “Operation Secure Stores,” the Lcbo said it will be hiring 40 paid duty officers to patrol roughly 40 separate liquor stores across Ontario in an anti-theft blitz to curb crime and promote safety in stores.

In other stores, the Lcbo said it will add “double guarding” to allow guards to better screen who is coming in and out of a store while looking for repeat offenders. In a news release , the Lcbo said it will “deploy more members of our covert security taskforce,” made up of security guards in plain clothing, who have more training and are permitted by the Lcbo to make arrests inside a store.

However, the Lcbo has roughly 690 stores provincewide, and some crime experts say the Lcbo’s move to deploy plainclothes officers is more about optics and making customers feel safer than reducing the number of brazen robberies.

“The criminals are going to move on, they’re going to move onto softer targets, in often cases further outside big city limits,” said former homicide detective and CTV News crime specialist Mark Mendelson.

Skamski disagrees, telling CTV News that many of the “2,000 arrests made last year linked to Lcbo liquor store thefts didn’t just take place where there were police officers stationed.”

“Our staff, guards and employees were able to help local low law enforcement make arrests and bring justice and that’s what we’re going to continue to do.”

However, one security guard company executive, speaking on condition of anonymity, believed the Lcbo will remain vulnerable because they don’t have the budget to curb robberies at their locations.

The Lcbo’s internal data shows that 70 per cent of thefts are linked to organized crime. “This isn’t the Hells Angels or the mafia, this is a group of four or five criminals working together to hit up liquor stores,” said Mendelson.

Thousands of dollars worth of expensive liquor is selling on the black market.

“They’re going for the high-end stuff. They’re not stealing bottles of Baby Duck,” he said.

It’s not just a problem in Ontario; robberies have plagued liquor stores across the country. In Manitoba, you must show identification to enter most liquor store locations. It’s a move Mendelson would welcome in Ontario.

“Anything would help, we have to think outside of the box and come up with a sustainable plan to bring an end to this crime that’s flooding the black market with thousands in stolen booze.”

For now, the Lcbo said they’re committed to reducing crime inside their locations, while keeping staff and customers safe.

stories.title: The historic stakes in Friday’s landmark Supreme Court ruling on the Charter and Quebec’s Bill 21
stories.summary: A step-by-step guide to a ruling that will consider the limits of political power and the Charter at a turbulent time in Canadian history
stories.author: David Ebner
stories.content:
On Friday at 9:45 a.m. in Ottawa, the Supreme Court of Canada delivers a historic judgment at a roiling moment of political division and economic discord.

Judges of the country’s top court will answer essential questions about how Canada operates as a federation in their landmark ruling on six appeals of Bill 21, the secularism law Quebec passed in 2019. The judgment revolves around the limits of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms and governments’ ability to use the notwithstanding clause, the powerful tool that legislators can invoke to override many of the protections promised to Canadians in the Charter.

The ruling will reckon with the political compromises of the early 1980s that led to the enactment of the Charter, the entrenched contemporary divide between liberal and conservative views of the Charter, and what some people see as government attacks on minority groups.

In the Bill 21 case, there are clear echoes of two landmark judgments of the past, Patriation in 1981 and Secession in 1998, said Wade Wright, a law professor at the University of Western Ontario and co-author of the widely cited reference book Constitutional Law of Canada . Like Patriation and Secession, Bill 21 requires the Supreme Court to balance fundamental legal questions against politically sensitive puzzles. The role of the Charter, of legislators and of the courts are all once more in play.

“The Supreme Court,” said Prof. Wright, “must interpret the Constitution while being sensitive to, but not unduly influenced by, these political implications.”

When the Supreme Court weighs in on Quebec’s secularism law, it will be from a new home at the West Memorial Building in Ottawa. The courthouse across the street, which held public hearings on Bill 21 in March, is undergoing renovations. Justin Tang/The Canadian Press

Quebec’s secularism law, Bill 21, prohibits many public sector workers, including teachers and police, from wearing religious symbols, such as a hijab or a cross, on the job.

Quebec shielded the law from being struck down by the courts with Section 33 of the Charter, the notwithstanding clause. But an array of groups and affected citizens – including female Muslim, Sikh and Catholic teachers – launched court challenges. Critics of Bill 21 view the law as squarely aimed at minority women in a province with long and deep Catholic roots.

In April 2021, the Quebec Superior Court upheld Bill 21 after a 33-day trial. Justice Marc-André Blanchard observed that the law forced “a cruel consequence that dehumanizes the people targeted” but could not be struck down for Charter violations because it was protected by the notwithstanding clause.

The Quebec Court of Appeal, for the same reason, upheld the law in February 2024.

Nine months later, the Supreme Court agreed to hear six appeals, to be decided Friday. In March the court held four days of hearings, among the longest in its history. It included a record 38 outside intervenor groups.

The so-called Gang of Eight, sitting for breakfast in 1981, were instrumental in getting the notwithstanding clause we have today. These premiers played hardball with the Pierre Trudeau government on a plan to patriate the Constitution. Peter Bregg and Andy CLark/The Canadian Press

In November 1981, five weeks after the Supreme Court ruled that the federal government, by convention, had to garner substantial support among the provinces to patriate the Constitution from Britain, a final federal-provincial meeting in Ottawa began to disintegrate on the third day. “Can you give us more time?” whispered justice minister Jean Chrétien to Pierre Trudeau.

Later, in a small kitchen at the old conference centre near Parliament Hill, Mr. Chrétien and counterparts from NDP Saskatchewan and Progressive Conservative Ontario struck a deal. The Charter would include a notwithstanding clause that could override numerous rights.

This unlocked the 1982 patriation of the Constitution and the enactment of the Charter in the Constitution. Since Confederation in 1867, Canada’s founding document had resided at Westminster in London as the British North America Act.

For much of the past 44 years, political leaders rarely deployed the notwithstanding clause. Quebec’s Bill 21 in 2019 stands as a demarcation. Alberta used it in four laws a year ago, one to end a teachers strike and three to restrict the choices of transgender youth. The federal government, Conservative or Liberal, has never used the clause.

On the first day of the Supreme Court hearing in March, one lawyer for an appellant seeking to strike down Bill 21 warned of the dangers of a “mini-Trump” in Canada wielding the clause.

On the hearing’s last day, Chief Justice Richard Wagner sounded skeptical of such arguments: “I don’t think that this case will be disposed of by extremist or catastrophic scenarios.”

There are many. The six appellants all want the judges to strike down Bill 21 and presented a long list of arguments.

Several of those focused on Section 23 of the Charter, protecting minority language education, and Section 28 on gender equality. Neither can be overridden by the notwithstanding clause and appellants argued these sections protected people affected by Bill 21.

At the heart of the Bill 21 case are two questions, both revolving around the notwithstanding clause and the Charter promises it can override, such as freedom of religion in Section 2 and equality rights in Section 15.

The first question is whether there should be new limits on political use of the clause, as the federal Liberal government and some appellants and intervenors proposed. None of the provinces, from conservative to NDP, supported this argument.

The Supreme Court has only once issued a significant ruling on the clause, in the 1988 Ford case. The precedent endorsed governments’ mostly unfettered right to use the notwithstanding override power as they like, in a case about French-language commercial signage in Quebec.

In March, conservative-led provinces, starting with Quebec, repeatedly cited that precedent in the courtroom as the reason why today’s judges should not heed calls for change. But many others argued the Ford ruling did not definitively settle every legal debate.

Alberta’s October referendum asked voters about constitutional reform, the courts and other issues besides independence. It’s one of the provinces opposed to an overhaul of the notwithstanding clause, which it has used in some recent legislation. Leah Hennel/The Globe and Mail; Ahmed Zakot/Reuters

This is the second big question. Ottawa, along with numerous appellants and intervenors, support the idea of judicial declarations. This would allow superior trial court judges to declare that a law insulated by the notwithstanding clause violates the Charter, even as the law is allowed to continue to operate.

An endorsement of judicial declarations from the Supreme Court would make it easier for citizens to take on governments that use the notwithstanding clause.

In laws protected by the clause, the long-standing presumption has been that judges cannot issue declarations, as they can and do in some other cases.

Quebec, Ontario, Alberta and Saskatchewan argued the notwithstanding clause precludes judges from making declarations, while B.C. – under the previous NDP government – and Manitoba supported judges being able to issue them.

The concept of judicial declarations took off in 2019, a month before Bill 21 became law, in a short essay entitled “the faulty received wisdom around the notwithstanding clause” in Policy Options, the online magazine of the Institute for Research on Public Policy. Academic journal work followed.

Supreme Court Justice Nicholas Kasirer, on the March hearing’s second day, when Quebec detailed its arguments, asked a dozen questions about declarations and cited the 2019 essay and related work.

Top provincial courts have split on this question. The Quebec Court of Appeal in its 2024 Bill 21 judgment rejected judicial declarations, saying the notwithstanding clause means judges “can no longer engage” in allegations of rights violations.

Last year, however, the Saskatchewan Court of Appeal ruled in favour of the idea. That case, UR Pride, stems from Saskatchewan’s 2023 law on transgender youth, personal pronouns and parental rights in which the government invoked the notwithstanding clause.

Judicial declarations were a primary issue in the UR Pride case at the Saskatchewan appeal court. The Supreme Court has scheduled a hearing on UR Pride this coming March but the issue may be fully settled in Friday’s Bill 21 judgment.

Eric Mendelsohn, a Montreal lawyer and one of the three authors of the 2019 Policy Options essay, has long thought about judicial declarations, going back to his time as a clerk for former chief justice Beverley McLachlin in the early 2000s.

In the centuries-long history of constitutional law, he described the 44-year-old Charter as “brand new.” He said if the Supreme Court rejects judicial declarations, it would open a dangerous avenue where governments could routinely use the notwithstanding clause to override Canadians’ rights with no recourse in the courts.

“The stakes,” said Mr. Mendelsohn, “are enormous.”

Significant – but not widespread.

Amrit Kaur, one of the appellants at the Supreme Court, grew up in Quebec and graduated with an education degree on the day Bill 21 became law. She is Sikh and wears a turban. Her planned teaching career in Quebec ended before it began.

“It’s about standing up to oppression,” Ms. Kaur told The Globe in March before the Bill 21 hearing of the seven-year legal odyssey.

In Alberta, where the province’s use of the notwithstanding clause faces court challenges, Kimberly Large worries about her teenage trans daughter. “It feels like the government doesn’t want us here, doesn’t want trans kids to live,” Ms. Large told The Globe in March.

The Bill 21 ruling lands at a delicate moment in Canadian history. The country is under a sustained economic assault from a capricious U.S. President and Prime Minister Mark Carney is working to get provinces on board with an ambitious agenda of industrial development.

The Prime Minister’s key provincial partners are sometimes foes, such as conservative governments in Alberta and Ontario – and, as of October, British Columbia. And Quebec in October elected a separatist-conservative minority government.

Niki Sharma, a B.C. NDP opposition MLA who was attorney-general from late 2022 until this fall, called the notwithstanding clause “a problematic tool.”

“What it’s saying to your citizens is: ‘We’re going to block your Charter rights,’” Ms. Sharma said, adding that: “What is the guarantee of a Charter right if it can be so easily punted aside through the legislature?”

The clause has become a symbol of political power among conservatives and at times a literal invocation of provincial political autonomy.

Quebec, most of all, insists its political soul is at stake. When the Supreme Court agreed to hear the Bill 21 case in early 2025, Quebec’s justice minster said it was essential and vital for the province of Quebec “to make its own choices.”

Last year, when the federal government in September filed its legal argument calling for restrictions on the notwithstanding clause, Ottawa asserted that the repeated override of rights effectively eliminates those rights.

This sparked umbrage among conservative-led provinces. A letter dispatched to Mr. Carney declared that Ottawa’s position threatened national unity. Five premiers demanded the Prime Minister “withdraw [the] written legal argument immediately.” The federal Liberals did not accede.

Bronwyn Eyre, senior counsel at the Canadian Constitution Foundation, said Ottawa’s move politicized the notwithstanding clause that had multi-partisan support in 1981.

“There is an ideological political aspect to this,” Ms. Eyre said, who was attorney-general for the conservative Saskatchewan Party government when it used the notwithstanding clause on the 2023 transgender law.

In September 1981, with patriation and the Charter in peril, the Supreme Court understood the stakes. The court planned its first television broadcast of a judgment, after the provinces had challenged the federal government’s patriation plan. Could Ottawa act alone? Did Ottawa need provincial backing?

The broadcast failed. Walking into the courtroom one of the judges unknowingly kicked out an audio connection. The mishap rendered Chief Justice Bora Laskin’s reading inaudible to viewers.

The judgment also seemed contradictory. The court said yes to both key questions, that Ottawa could legally act alone and by convention needed provincial backing, with two mixes of nine judges in 7-2 and 6-3 camps.

Yet the ruling delivered clarity that helped propel the federal-provincial political deal five weeks later that led to patriation and the Charter.

In August 1998, a Supreme Court riven by internal discord delivered a judgment on the rules around Quebec’s potential separation from Canada. This time there was no TV broadcast and the result was far clearer, 9-0, signed by “The Court.”

Like Patriation, the judges in the Secession judgment helped defuse a political bomb. They stepped beyond a cautious reading of black-letter law and into something more akin to a conjuring of Canada’s fundamental character: compromise and co-operation, when we are at our most divided.

Bill 21 may be much the same but the outcome, with myriad legal and political issues entwined in Canada’s past and present, is difficult to guess.

Prof. Wright, the co-author of Constitutional Law of Canada , feels reluctant to venture a forecast but said he is skeptical that the court would impose substantive restrictions on the notwithstanding clause. But after watching the hearing he is unsure which way the court might go on judicial declarations.

“I’m sure the court will make a concerted effort to reach a unanimous decision,” Prof. Wright said, “but that could be hard for it to achieve.”
