In April 2021, the Quebec Superior Court upheld Bill 21 after a 33-day trial. Justice Marc-André Blanchard observed that the law forced “a cruel consequence that dehumanizes the people targeted” but could not be struck down for Charter violations because it was protected by the notwithstanding clause.
The Quebec Court of Appeal, for the same reason, upheld the law in February 2024.

Nine months later, the Supreme Court agreed to hear six appeals, to be decided Friday. In March the court held four days of hearings, among the longest in its history. It included a record 38 outside intervenor groups.

The so-called Gang of Eight, sitting for breakfast in 1981, were instrumental in getting the notwithstanding clause we have today. These premiers played hardball with the Pierre Trudeau government on a plan to patriate the Constitution. Peter Bregg and Andy CLark/The Canadian Press

In November 1981, five weeks after the Supreme Court ruled that the federal government, by convention, had to garner substantial support among the provinces to patriate the Constitution from Britain, a final federal-provincial meeting in Ottawa began to disintegrate on the third day. “Can you give us more time?” whispered justice minister Jean Chrétien to Pierre Trudeau.

Later, in a small kitchen at the old conference centre near Parliament Hill, Mr. Chrétien and counterparts from NDP Saskatchewan and Progressive Conservative Ontario struck a deal. The Charter would include a notwithstanding clause that could override numerous rights.

This unlocked the 1982 patriation of the Constitution and the enactment of the Charter in the Constitution. Since Confederation in 1867, Canada’s founding document had resided at Westminster in London as the British North America Act.

For much of the past 44 years, political leaders rarely deployed the notwithstanding clause. Quebec’s Bill 21 in 2019 stands as a demarcation. Alberta used it in four laws a year ago, one to end a teachers strike and three to restrict the choices of transgender youth. The federal government, Conservative or Liberal, has never used the clause.
On the first day of the Supreme Court hearing in March, one lawyer for an appellant seeking to strike down Bill 21 warned of the dangers of a “mini-Trump” in Canada wielding the clause.
On the hearing’s last day, Chief Justice Richard Wagner sounded skeptical of such arguments: “I don’t think that this case will be disposed of by extremist or catastrophic scenarios.”
There are many. The six appellants all want the judges to strike down Bill 21 and presented a long list of arguments.

Several of those focused on Section 23 of the Charter, protecting minority language education, and Section 28 on gender equality. Neither can be overridden by the notwithstanding clause and appellants argued these sections protected people affected by Bill 21.

At the heart of the Bill 21 case are two questions, both revolving around the notwithstanding clause and the Charter promises it can override, such as freedom of religion in Section 2 and equality rights in Section 15.

The first question is whether there should be new limits on political use of the clause, as the federal Liberal government and some appellants and intervenors proposed. None of the provinces, from conservative to NDP, supported this argument.

The Supreme Court has only once issued a significant ruling on the clause, in the 1988 Ford case. The precedent endorsed governments’ mostly unfettered right to use the notwithstanding override power as they like, in a case about French-language commercial signage in Quebec.

In March, conservative-led provinces, starting with Quebec, repeatedly cited that precedent in the courtroom as the reason why today’s judges should not heed calls for change. But many others argued the Ford ruling did not definitively settle every legal debate.

Alberta’s October referendum asked voters about constitutional reform, the courts and other issues besides independence. It’s one of the provinces opposed to an overhaul of the notwithstanding clause, which it has used in some recent legislation. Leah Hennel/The Globe and Mail; Ahmed Zakot/Reuters

This is the second big question. Ottawa, along with numerous appellants and intervenors, support the idea of judicial declarations. This would allow superior trial court judges to declare that a law insulated by the notwithstanding clause violates the Charter, even as the law is allowed to continue to operate.
An endorsement of judicial declarations from the Supreme Court would make it easier for citizens to take on governments that use the notwithstanding clause.
In laws protected by the clause, the long-standing presumption has been that judges cannot issue declarations, as they can and do in some other cases.

Quebec, Ontario, Alberta and Saskatchewan argued the notwithstanding clause precludes judges from making declarations, while B.C. – under the previous NDP government – and Manitoba supported judges being able to issue them.

The concept of judicial declarations took off in 2019, a month before Bill 21 became law, in a short essay entitled “the faulty received wisdom around the notwithstanding clause” in Policy Options, the online magazine of the Institute for Research on Public Policy. Academic journal work followed.
Supreme Court Justice Nicholas Kasirer, on the March hearing’s second day, when Quebec detailed its arguments, asked a dozen questions about declarations and cited the 2019 essay and related work.

Top provincial courts have split on this question. The Quebec Court of Appeal in its 2024 Bill 21 judgment rejected judicial declarations, saying the notwithstanding clause means judges “can no longer engage” in allegations of rights violations.

Last year, however, the Saskatchewan Court of Appeal ruled in favour of the idea. That case, UR Pride, stems from Saskatchewan’s 2023 law on transgender youth, personal pronouns and parental rights in which the government invoked the notwithstanding clause.

Judicial declarations were a primary issue in the UR Pride case at the Saskatchewan appeal court. The Supreme Court has scheduled a hearing on UR Pride this coming March but the issue may be fully settled in Friday’s Bill 21 judgment.

Eric Mendelsohn, a Montreal lawyer and one of the three authors of the 2019 Policy Options essay, has long thought about judicial declarations, going back to his time as a clerk for former chief justice Beverley McLachlin in the early 2000s.

In the centuries-long history of constitutional law, he described the 44-year-old Charter as “brand new.” He said if the Supreme Court rejects judicial declarations, it would open a dangerous avenue where governments could routinely use the notwithstanding clause to override Canadians’ rights with no recourse in the courts.
“The stakes,” said Mr. Mendelsohn, “are enormous.”
Significant – but not widespread.

Amrit Kaur, one of the appellants at the Supreme Court, grew up in Quebec and graduated with an education degree on the day Bill 21 became law. She is Sikh and wears a turban. Her planned teaching career in Quebec ended before it began.
“It’s about standing up to oppression,” Ms. Kaur told The Globe in March before the Bill 21 hearing of the seven-year legal odyssey.

In Alberta, where the province’s use of the notwithstanding clause faces court challenges, Kimberly Large worries about her teenage trans daughter. “It feels like the government doesn’t want us here, doesn’t want trans kids to live,” Ms. Large told The Globe in March.

The Bill 21 ruling lands at a delicate moment in Canadian history. The country is under a sustained economic assault from a capricious U.S. President and Prime Minister Mark Carney is working to get provinces on board with an ambitious agenda of industrial development.

The Prime Minister’s key provincial partners are sometimes foes, such as conservative governments in Alberta and Ontario – and, as of October, British Columbia. And Quebec in October elected a separatist-conservative minority government.
Niki Sharma, a B.C. NDP opposition MLA who was attorney-general from late 2022 until this fall, called the notwithstanding clause “a problematic tool.”

“What it’s saying to your citizens is: ‘We’re going to block your Charter rights,’” Ms. Sharma said, adding that: “What is the guarantee of a Charter right if it can be so easily punted aside through the legislature?”
The clause has become a symbol of political power among conservatives and at times a literal invocation of provincial political autonomy.

Quebec, most of all, insists its political soul is at stake. When the Supreme Court agreed to hear the Bill 21 case in early 2025, Quebec’s justice minster said it was essential and vital for the province of Quebec “to make its own choices.”

Last year, when the federal government in September filed its legal argument calling for restrictions on the notwithstanding clause, Ottawa asserted that the repeated override of rights effectively eliminates those rights.

This sparked umbrage among conservative-led provinces. A letter dispatched to Mr. Carney declared that Ottawa’s position threatened national unity. Five premiers demanded the Prime Minister “withdraw [the] written legal argument immediately.” The federal Liberals did not accede.
Bronwyn Eyre, senior counsel at the Canadian Constitution Foundation, said Ottawa’s move politicized the notwithstanding clause that had multi-partisan support in 1981.

“There is an ideological political aspect to this,” Ms. Eyre said, who was attorney-general for the conservative Saskatchewan Party government when it used the notwithstanding clause on the 2023 transgender law.

In September 1981, with patriation and the Charter in peril, the Supreme Court understood the stakes. The court planned its first television broadcast of a judgment, after the provinces had challenged the federal government’s patriation plan. Could Ottawa act alone? Did Ottawa need provincial backing?
The broadcast failed. Walking into the courtroom one of the judges unknowingly kicked out an audio connection. The mishap rendered Chief Justice Bora Laskin’s reading inaudible to viewers.

The judgment also seemed contradictory. The court said yes to both key questions, that Ottawa could legally act alone and by convention needed provincial backing, with two mixes of nine judges in 7-2 and 6-3 camps.
Yet the ruling delivered clarity that helped propel the federal-provincial political deal five weeks later that led to patriation and the Charter.

In August 1998, a Supreme Court riven by internal discord delivered a judgment on the rules around Quebec’s potential separation from Canada. This time there was no TV broadcast and the result was far clearer, 9-0, signed by “The Court.”

Like Patriation, the judges in the Secession judgment helped defuse a political bomb. They stepped beyond a cautious reading of black-letter law and into something more akin to a conjuring of Canada’s fundamental character: compromise and co-operation, when we are at our most divided.
Bill 21 may be much the same but the outcome, with myriad legal and political issues entwined in Canada’s past and present, is difficult to guess.

Prof. Wright, the co-author of Constitutional Law of Canada , feels reluctant to venture a forecast but said he is skeptical that the court would impose substantive restrictions on the notwithstanding clause. But after watching the hearing he is unsure which way the court might go on judicial declarations.
“I’m sure the court will make a concerted effort to reach a unanimous decision,” Prof. Wright said, “but that could be hard for it to achieve.”

stories.title: Quebec braces for Supreme Court decision on Bill 21
stories.summary: The judgment, which could restrict the use of the notwithstanding clause, has the potential to upend the province’s politics and strain national unity
stories.author: Eric Andrew-Gee
stories.content:
Quebec has its eyes on the Supreme Court of Canada this week in anticipation of Friday’s ruling on Bill 21 , the province’s law banning religious symbols for certain public servants.

The judgment, which could restrict the use of the Charter of Rights and Freedom’s notwithstanding clause and expose the legislation to being overturned in the courts, has the potential to upend the province’s politics and strain national unity.

If the Supreme Court produces a bombshell decision, the shrapnel will hit Quebec the hardest. The minority Parti Québécois government could use any reproach to fuel support for independence. That’s an outcome that the sovereigntist movement has been seeking since the law passed in 2019, with the notwithstanding clause as a shield.

“They’re hoping that this ruling will be controversial,” said former Liberal premier Jean Charest at an event in Toronto on Tuesday.

Such a decision would take place at a moment of constitutional turmoil in the province, after a court ruling on Monday required Quebec legislators to swear allegiance to the King, suspending a 2022 law replacing the age-old requirement with an oath to the Quebec people. The government is appealing and seeking a way to move ahead with next week’s scheduled sitting of the National Assembly, a first since the Oct. 5 election that brought the PQ to power.

Controversy about the Supreme Court’s ruling on Bill 21 risks further embroiling the province in constitutional arguments at a time when bread-and-butter issues are seen as a priority by most Quebeckers.

Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon was elected – albeit with only 28 per cent of the popular vote, a record low – promising to focus on pragmatic governance amid a cost-of-living surge and trade war before embarking on an independence referendum years down the road.

Instead, his first weeks in office have been consumed with federal-provincial disputes about largely symbolic matters, such as whether Quebec would be allowed to publicly address the Canada-EU summit in Montreal, and the appropriate site of a first meeting between Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon and Prime Minister Mark Carney.

Even so, the PQ government would likely welcome a decision limiting the use of the notwithstanding clause or even invalidating parts of Bill 21.

Influential separatist commentators such as Richard Martineau have been openly “praying” for the Supreme Court to rule Bill 21 unconstitutional this week. “It would clarify things,” he wrote in his popular Journal de Montréal column Wednesday.

Such a ruling would be deeply unpopular in Quebec, where the law has broad support and state secularism is a cherished value, likely converting many soft nationalists to the separatist cause, said Jean-Christophe Jasmin, Quebec director of the Christian think tank Cardus.

“A lot of nationalists have come to the conclusion that the best way to preserve the Quebec nation is within the Canadian constitutional order. It is a safe place for the Quebec nation to flourish,” said Mr. Jasmin. “A very restrictive decision would give ammunition to the separatist nationalists.”

Although many religious minorities would cheer the defeat of Bill 21, some devout Quebeckers dread the possible backlash such a result could produce.

Mr. Jasmin pointed to the legislation defunding religious schools in the wake of alleged Islamic influence at a Montreal public school, and restrictions on public prayer after concerns about the religiosity of some street protests against the war in Gaza.

Bill 21 was just the beginning of a suite of secularism legislation by the conservative, nationalist Coalition Avenir Québec, which was ousted in October’s election. In the spring, the CAQ extended the ban on religious symbols to public daycare workers, banned most prayer spaces in public institutions such as universities, and forbade those institutions from only offering halal or kosher food.

The government invoked the notwithstanding clause to shield that law, Bill 9, from judicial review as well, although it was sharply criticized by religious and civil-liberties groups.

The new PQ government is promising to go further still, barring elementary-school students from wearing religious symbols.

If such legislation is widely seen as infringing on religious freedom in the rest of Canada, it is a natural outgrowth of Quebec’s hostility to religious authority after centuries of vesting enormous power in the Catholic Church.

“It shows how deep the two solitudes still are today,” said Mr. Jasmin.

On Friday, the Supreme Court could bring those solitudes into renewed conflict.

With reports from Laura Stone

2019, June 16: Quebec’s conservative Coalition Avenir Québec passes Bill 21, its secularism law that invokes the notwithstanding clause in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms to prevent courts from striking it down.

2019, June 17: The first of several legal challenges is filed, by teacher Ichrak Nourel Hak, the National Council of Canadian Muslims and the Canadian Civil Liberties Association.

2021, April 20: Quebec Superior Court upholds most of Bill 21, because it was shielded from being struck down by the notwithstanding clause, but exempts English-language school boards. Justice Marc-André Blanchard, after a 33-day trial, offers an observation in his judgment that the choice of affected people between their beliefs and their livelihoods is “a cruel consequence that dehumanizes the people targeted.”

2024, Feb. 29: The Quebec Court of Appeal unanimously upholds Bill 21, after several appeals of the 2021 Quebec Superior Court judgment. The appeal court also overturns the English-language school boards exemption.

2024, May 7: The Coalition Avenir Québec government officially renews the notwithstanding clause in Bill 21, at the five-year mark as required by the Charter.

2025, Jan. 23: The Supreme Court of Canada agrees to hear six appeals of the 2024 Quebec appeal court ruling.

2025, Sept. 17: The federal government, an intervener at the Supreme Court, files its legal arguments and calls for new restrictions on governments’ use of the notwithstanding clause.

2025, Oct. 7: Five conservative premiers dispatch a letter to Prime Minister Mark Carney, asserting that Ottawa’s legal filing threatens national unity and demanding that it be withdrawn.

2026, Feb. 16: The Supreme Court, in an unexpected move a month before the Bill 21 hearing, asks the main parties to file written arguments on whether Bill 21 infringes on the Charter’s freedom of religion, a potential factor in the court’s deliberations.

2026, March 23-26: The Supreme Court holds four days of hearings on Bill 21, among the longest in the court’s history.

2026, Nov. 27: Decision day. The Supreme Court releases its ruling at 9:45 a.m. Ottawa time.

stories.title: Winter is coming: A DIY guide to changing your tires
stories.summary: If you have an hour and a torque wrench, it’s easy to handle the seasonal changeover yourself. Mark Richardson explains how to do it safely
stories.author: Mark Richardson
stories.content:
If you’re one of the three-quarters of Canadian drivers who swap tires between hot and cold seasons, well, it’s that time. The temperature is routinely dropping into single digits, which is when summer and all-season tires become less flexible and less effective. Tire manufacturers recommend using winter tires when the temperature consistently drops below 7 C.

Swapping tires is a simple procedure. If the tires are already mounted on rims, it’s not expensive – service shops usually charge $50 to $100 for changing over the four wheels. If the tires are not already on rims, that cost will likely double because it’s more time-consuming and requires special equipment. It’s also quick and easy, as any race fan will witness watching pit stops. At this time of year, though, shops often get backed up with tire-change appointments until well after the first snowstorm.

Fortunately, it’s something you can do yourself, as I’ve done twice a year for the past couple of decades. It takes me about an hour, and that’s at a leisurely pace.

The only piece of specialized equipment you need is a torque wrench. A basic model costs around $50 new, while a more robust wrench runs $100 or more. Don’t be tempted to buy a used torque wrench from a stranger; if the wrench is not routinely unwound after use to release the pressure from the internal spring, it can become inaccurate.

First, make sure the wheels and tires you’re going to install are in good condition. Check that the tread depth is enough to last the season. The legal minimum in Canada for light vehicles is 1.5 millimetres, but winter tires need deeper tread to cut through snow, and manufacturers recommend a minimum of four millimetres. There will be built-in wear bars – rubber indicators in the tread that should not be flush with the outer surface of the tire.

Clean the wheels before installing them by wiping off any accumulated dirt and brake dust. It’s much simpler to do this with the wheel off the car and, if last season’s buildup is still there, it won’t disappear on its own.

Make sure your vehicle is parked on a flat surface, away from traffic. If you must park on a slope, chock the wheels with two-by-fours or something similar to prevent the vehicle from rolling downhill.

Optional: Turn on some music. Use a mobile speaker or your vehicle’s sound system rather than isolating yourself with headphones.

When the new wheels and the vehicle are ready, put a jack into place to raise the vehicle one wheel at a time. A pump jack is best and easiest for this, but you can also use the small emergency jack that should be supplied with your vehicle if it carries a spare tire. There are reinforced places along the frame that are safe jacking points, and the owner’s manual will identify them if they’re not obvious.

Before jacking up the vehicle, while the wheel is on the ground and fixed in place, loosen the lug nuts. They should be very tight, and if the wheel is already raised, the nuts won’t loosen because the wheel will rotate.

Jack up the wheel so it is clear of the ground by about a hand’s width, then loosen and remove all the lug nuts. You May need a solid metal tube of some kind to slip over the wrench handle to add extra leverage – the longer your wrench, the greater the force you can apply.

Remove the wheel and, before you forget, mark its location on the vehicle with chalk or marker on the inside of the tire: LR for left rear, RF for right front, and so on. While there’s no wheel in place, wipe and clean the exposed axle that the new wheel will slip onto.

Place the new wheel onto the axle so the lug studs go through the holes on the wheel rim, then spin a nut onto the topmost stud so the wheel is held loosely in place. Wheels are fairly heavy, and you May want to have a friend help you lift them into place.

Make sure to use the correct nuts – most wheels use conical nuts that have an angled taper to fit in a recessed seat, but many others use standard flat nuts and washers. The wheels you’ve removed May use different nuts from the ones you’re installing, and they’re not interchangeable. European brands usually bolt in from the outside, which can be a little more awkward.

Jiggle the wheel into place and finger-tighten the nuts so the wheel is flush with the mounts. This is the point where you can mess up if the wheel is not quite straight or if something is blocking one of the lug studs. When you’re satisfied the wheel is properly in place, tighten the nuts with your wrench in a star pattern: if there are five nuts, for example, tighten nut 1, then nut 3, then nut 5, nut 2, nut 4, and repeat. This ensures the wheel is pulled evenly onto the axle.

When all the lug nuts are reasonably tight, lower the car and remove the jack. Now tighten the nuts with your torque wrench to the manufacturer’s specification – this will be in the owner’s manual, but it is also easily found online.

Repeat for the other three wheels.

Make sure to rotate the wheels during installation. A tire that was at the left front last season, for example, should typically move to the right rear for the new season so all four wear evenly. High-performance and directional tires, however, May need a different pattern. If you’re unsure, Google it or check here . Bridgestone Blizzaks, for example, are directional tires and must rotate in a specific direction. They cannot be swapped to the other side of the vehicle, where they would be backwards. Don’t ask me how I know this.

Once all four new wheels are installed, go around again with your torque wrench to ensure the nuts are properly tightened, and double-check the tires’ air pressures. After a few days, or about 100 kilometres of driving, recheck the tightness of the nuts, and then loosen the setting on your torque wrench to take the pressure off its spring.

Finally, clean the removed wheels to prepare them for storage. Many service centres and dealerships offer off-season storage for a fee if you don’t have a dry place to keep them. And pat yourself on the back – your tires, at least, are ready for the winter. Now it’s time to find an empty parking lot on a snowy morning to practise your skid control.

Jeff McKague is the president of Event Matrix, which conducts independent tire testing for a major retailer. He’s changed thousands of tires over the years and shares several tips for improving the basic process:

Add some extra height to change two wheels at once

“We use one jack and just jack it up high. If you jack up the front higher, the majority of the weight is there from the engine and you can get both the front and rear wheels off the ground. But chock the other wheels on the ground and put a jack stand underneath just in case the pump jack fails. And never, ever get underneath the vehicle if you’re just changing the wheels – you don’t need to.”

When loosening the lug nuts, pull the wrench handle up instead of pushing it down

“If you’re pushing down, when [the tension] does suddenly crack, you might slip off it and down to the ground. It’s safer to pull up.”

Use a metal scouring pad to clean the axle mounting points and the inside of the wheel before installation

“That will scrape off any excess rust or debris that’s in there, and just make sure there’s nothing rough to get in the way.”

If you’re using an impact gun for the initial tightening, loosen the nuts when you’re done and then re-torque them with a manual torque wrench

“You can over-torque it with the impact gun and the wrench won’t tell you that. So back it off and then retighten it to the correct spec, just to be sure.”

When storing the old tires, ensure they’re fully inflated

“They won’t deform when they’re properly inflated. And also, in the spring, if one of them is not as inflated as the others, you can see you might have a problem and deal with it before you put them on.”

stories.title: Over-the-counter hearing aids are coming to Ontario. Here’s how they can help — and how they're limited
stories.summary: Selling aids without a prescription or a visit to an audiologist could help some people get quicker, cheaper treatment.
stories.author: Kerry Gillespie
stories.content:
Adele Ostfield still remembers the awe she felt when she first got hearing aids: the tap-tap of her fingers on a keyboard, the whoosh of water in the sink that “sounded like Niagara Falls.”

“Because hearing loss is so gradual, you don’t realize what you’re not hearing anymore,” she said.

Now 77, she’s a hearing advocate among her friends, and that role is getting easier as greater awareness of the broader health risks helps combat the stigma of hearing aids.

Hearing loss goes well beyond just missing sounds or needing to turn up the volume on the TV. Untreated hearing loss is linked to increased risks of falls, social isolation, memory loss and dementia, yet many Ontarians wait a decade or more to get help.

“For my age group, dementia is the boogieman,” Ostfield said. “Being able to hear better — that’s almost a fringe benefit. You really don’t want to develop dementia when you get older, so you’ve got to do something about your hearing. When I say that, that sometimes pushes people to action.”

In October, Ontario announced plans to offer “more choice and convenience” in hearing aids by changing regulations so they can be sold without a prescription or a visit to an audiologist. They are not available yet, but the government has included a regulation-making provision in an omnibus budget bill that is likely to pass by Dec. 10, when the legislature breaks for the holidays.

Experts say over-the-counter sales are a good way to get hearing aids to some people more cheaply and at younger ages, but warn the devices — which can be as simple as Apple AirPods with the hearing aid feature enabled — aren’t suited to everyone. They also won’t help those who need traditional hearing aids and can’t afford them. The impact of hearing loss, and how much of it goes untreated, is something that experts say needs far more attention given the ties to so many serious health risks.

Baycrest audiologist Sylvia Ciechanowski said research shows people wait 10 years on average after they first notice signs of hearing loss before seeking help.

According to Statistics Canada data, nearly one-quarter of Canadians over age 15 with a hearing disability did not having a hearing aid. That’s some 370,000 Canadians, and the majority of them cited cost as the biggest barrier.

Sylvia Ciechanowski, an audiologist at Baycrest in Toronto, said research shows people wait an average of 10 years after they first notice signs of hearing loss before seeking help. And she often sees people who have waited 20 to 30 years.

Ontario’s assistive devices program pays a maximum of $1,000 for a pair of hearing aids, but that’s well below the current cost of prescribed devices. Those generally range from $3,000 to $7,000, compared to over-the-counter devices that in the States sell for $200 to $2,000 (U.S.), she said.

The provincial funding program for hearing aids will not apply to over-the-counter devices, and when asked by the Star, the government did not explain why the devices have been excluded.

Over-the-counter devices are designed for adults with mild to moderate hearing loss and no medical conditions, but they are not suitable for people with more severe or asymmetrical hearing loss. They’re also not a good option for people who are not technically savvy and will need a lot of support to adjust them, Ciechanowski said.

Hearing loss is the greatest preventable risk factor for dementia — and the earlier it’s treated, the better your prospects, experts say.

To her, one of the biggest upsides of over-the-counter devices is the potential to reach younger people and earlier in their hearing loss. That’s vital given that “the longer we wait with untreated hearing loss the higher chance we have of developing cognitive changes.”

According to studies, the average age of people in the U.S. who use over-the-counter devices is 58, compared to 73 for traditional hearing aids, she said.

The links between hearing loss and memory loss and dementia are still being researched but experts say multiple mechanisms May play a role, including areas of the brain tied to memory shrinking with reduced sound stimulus, the taxing mental effort of straining to hear, leaving fewer cognitive resources for memory, and the social isolation brought on people avoiding outings and gatherings because of their hearing loss.

Baycrest already has a program to fit and test over-the-counter devices that people have purchased elsewhere, and Ciechanowski hopes that once Health Canada-approved devices are being sold in Ontario, more hearing professionals will offer similar services.

Cost is not the only barrier that keeps people from addressing hearing loss.

Adele Ostfield’s hearing aids.

“Oftentimes people feel like (hearing aids) make them look old. They’re afraid that they’ll be judged ... I’ve even heard people say ‘people May think that I’m not as intelligent.’ There’s this constant, ‘I want something invisible so no one will be able to tell that I have one,’” Ciechanowski said.

“In my dreams, I would love for people to think of hearing aids like glasses. I have vision loss, I wear glasses; I have hearing loss, I should wear a hearing aid.”

The first person in North America to get a new kind of cochlear implant, at SickKids, describes how it’s helping her.

Dr. Samir Sinha, a geriatrician and clinician scientist at Sinai Health and the University Health Network in Toronto, said Ontario needs to do more to raise awareness that hearing loss is a significant public health issue.

“People just assume that hearing loss is kind of a natural thing that happens, that we lose our hearing increasingly as we age, and there’s really nothing you can do about it,” he said, adding that more needs to be done to overcome that attitude.

“When you do have hearing loss it increases the risk for falls, which if you ask older people what’s the number one thing they fear the most — it’s often fear of falling. And what’s the other thing that my older patients really fear the most? It’s developing dementia.”

Sinha had a stark demonstration of the power of making that connection with his father, a retired physician. When his mom raised concerns that his dad was starting to experience memory loss, Sinha suspected it might be related to a decline in hearing.

“I forwarded this scientific article that basically showed him that untreated hearing loss significantly increases your risk of developing dementia and, my God, he was down at the Costco (getting hearing aids) right away,” Sinha said.

Ostfield has been wearing hearing aids since her mid-30s, but in her age cohort these days, half the people she’s in regular contact with have them, leading to many conversations about background noise, “the bane of those with hearing aids.” Of the rest, she figures most need them and “maybe 10 per cent truly don’t.”

She hopes Ontario’s move helps get hearing aids into more ears, more affordably. “As more people wear them, the stigma will go down.”

stories.title: Why a Supreme Court ruling on a secularism law could reverberate across Canadian politics
stories.summary: The Supreme Court of Canada is set to release a decision Friday that could ignite a powder keg under federal-provincial relations.
stories.author: Stephanie Taylor
stories.content:
Ottawa— The Supreme Court of Canada is set to release a decision Friday that could ignite a powder keg under federal-provincial relations.

The case concerns Bill 21, a controversial Quebec law that bans the wearing of religious symbols by certain public sector workers.

But the issue of national significance in the case is the tool Quebec used to pass the law: Section 33 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, the so-called notwithstanding clause , which governments can use to override certain Charter rights for renewable periods of five years.

Any move by the court to impose limits on the use of the notwithstanding clause, or provide guidance on its use, would mark a first since the Constitution Act, 1982, and could touch off a political firestorm for Prime Minister Mark Carney ‘s government.

A ruling perceived as limiting Quebec’s ability to legislate within the federation would likely be fiercely opposed by Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon and his Parti Québécois government, potentially setting the stage for Quebec to defy Canada’s top court.

In Alberta and Saskatchewan, where governments have used the notwithstanding clause to restrict children’s use of preferred pronouns in schools, any new limits could inflame concerns over the centralization of power in Ottawa and its institutions at the expense of provincial legislatures.

Then comes the ruling’s potential impact on debates over minority rights, gender equality and religious freedom.

Here’s a look at what’s at stake:

Dozens of intervenors and parties presented arguments in the case through written submissions and over three days in oral arguments this past spring , including five other provincial governments and the federal government.

“The question is whether they will maintain (the clause) essentially roughly as was agreed in 1982, or whether they will impose some new restraint on it that people haven’t seen before,” said Dwight Newman, an expert in constitutional law who teaches at the University of Saskatchewan.

“That’s a pretty major question, just in terms of our approach to the Constitution.”

Carney has built his entire prime ministership around regard for the rule of law and institutions, Susan Delacourt writes.

The notwithstanding clause was created as a compromise to satisfy provincial governments that balked at the notion of the courts, not legislatures, having the ultimate say in what the rights of Canadians would be.

Provinces such as Ontario, Alberta and Saskatchewan, all of which have used the clause pre-emptively before their laws were challenged in court, have urged the Supreme Court to protect that override power.

They warn that placing limits on the notwithstanding clause risks upending the deal that saw the provinces sign on to the Constitution in the first place.

“Simply put,” said the submission from Alberta’s attorney general, “there would have been no Charter” without the notwithstanding clause.

Saskatchewan pushed back against claims that using the notwithstanding clause tramples on Canadians’ rights, arguing that it “enables legislatures to open certain social and moral questions to public debate, outside of the courtroom.”

It maintains that “certain matters are, by their very nature, non-justiciable,” and that “heightened democratic scrutiny” was already baked into the provision, as use of the override must be publicly declared — and expires after five years if it is not proactively renewed.

Ontario rejected criticism of its pre-emptive use of the notwithstanding clause, warning the imposition of limits would “sterilize” it.

“If new requirements are desirable, the proper way to add them is through constitutional amendment, not judicial interpretation,” its submission said.

For Eric Freeman, acting legal director for Egale Canada, which has been against use of the clause for laws affecting those who identify as Lgbtq, a win would be recognition by the court that some “guardrails” are needed.

“A guardrail will at least help to provide assurances that provincial governments and the federal Parliament can’t use the notwithstanding clause in ways that are totally inconsistent with the very idea of Charter and Constitutional rights,” Freeman told the Star.

While the clause May remain intact, Freeman would like conditions imposed on its use “to make sure that it can’t be used in particularly egregious ways.”

Failing that, critics would at the very least like to see courts offer “declaratory relief”— a formal recognition that rights have indeed been violated, albeit legally – when the notwithstanding clause has been invoked. They believe such recognition would serve to better inform the public.

Canadian Civil Liberties Association director Harini Sivalingam acknowledges that in this case, such recognition would amount to a “hollow victory” because nothing about the law would be changed.

But Sivalingam also believes a declaration by the court that rights have been infringed carries power, in that it could raise awareness ahead of the next election, which the five-year limit on notwithstanding clause overrides is meant to capture.

“The idea of the declaration is that maybe it could have some influence in the public electorate in knowing that, ‘Hey, your government is enacting these laws that are violating rights — what could be next?’

“It could be your right to protest. It could be your right to have an abortion.”

Once Friday’s ruling comes down, the prime minister will no longer be able to say that it’s inappropriate for him to comment on the Quebec law because a challenge to it is before the court.

Whether Carney believes the secularism law is an unjustifiable violation of individuals’ rights remains unclear. The Bloc has called on him to clearly state his position.

Whatever he eventually says will be heard far and wide in Quebec, where public opinion polling has suggested he enjoys considerable popularity, and where three of six byelections he has called for Dec.7 will be held.

With files from Tonda MacCharles

stories.title: Ontario was warned about career college with skyrocketing Osap growth, letter shows
stories.summary: Toronto - A career college with student financial aid usage that grew thousands of per cent in a few years was not among those the minister cut off this spring, and a letter newly obtained by The Canadian Press shows he was specifically warned about the school more than a year earlier.
stories.author: Allison Jones The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - A career college with student financial aid usage that government data shows grew thousands of per cent in a few years was not among those the minister cut off this spring, and a letter newly obtained by The Canadian Press shows he was specifically warned about the school more than a year earlier.

The college itself strongly denies any wrongdoing.

Career Colleges Ontario flagged in a January 2025 letter to the ministry that the association was concerned about unusually high growth in Ontario Student Assistance Program usage at 10 campuses.

The names of most of the schools were redacted when a copy of the letter was filed in court this year, but an unredacted copy obtained by The Canadian Press shows that the Canadian College of Business, Science and Technology topped that list.

“As an association that represents career colleges in Ontario, we are concerned about how schools with increases exceeding 2,000 per cent in submissions, such as Ccbst … with a 2,696.26 per cent increase, are accommodating these students effectively while upholding educational standards,” executive director Kate Bartz wrote.

That growth of nearly 2,700 per cent was over two years.

Government data obtained by The Canadian Press through a freedom-of-information request shows that in 2021-22 there were 74 students accessing Osap, and in 2024-25 there were 4,481 students — an increase of nearly 6,000 per cent.

A statement from a lawyer for the Canadian College of Business, Science and Technology says it did not experience anywhere near a 6,000 per cent increase at any of its campuses and suggested that number comes from “what is at best an inability or failure to understand the financial information that is contained in government records.”

Allan Dick wrote that the college’s records indicate enrolment increases of less than 1,900 per cent.

“Insinuations that Ccbst has been involved in fraudulent wrongdoing are not just categorically and simply denied,” he wrote. “They are false. And the very premise that these insinuations are based on is false.”

Dick said the college has provided auditors Kpmg, who Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn has tasked with a system-wide audit, with detailed explanations for its growth. It was well-placed to deliver online programming at the start of the COVID-19 pandemic due to technology advances it had implemented, and one campus was relocated and it attracted many more students, he wrote.

“The college was aware of allegations of improper conduct in the industry and how such conduct was allegedly being undertaken,” Dick wrote.

“The college never participated in these activities. It made all efforts in real time and in response to the available information to ensure its enrolling students were legitimate, attended their classes, did their assignments and fulfilled their placement obligations in order to graduate.”

The school’s other three campuses in the Greater Toronto Area were also on Career Colleges Ontario’s list, but the Canadian College of Business, Science and Technology was not among six schools the government cut off from Osap eligibility in May.

Quinn is defending the fact that Osap kept flowing to the school until last month by saying the data the ministry was receiving was evolving.

“I think ultimately, we’re running multiple investigations at the same time, and that would be one of the ones that we are investigating, and once that threshold is met, that’s when we act, as we have earlier this year,” Quinn said, referring to both removing six schools from eligibility in May and a sector-wide pause on Osap he enacted early last month.

He said Monday that once data showed “they were worse than what we initially thought, that’s when we put a pause,” referring to when he stopped Osap payments to all private post-secondary institutions last month.

Liberal critic Tyler Watt said the minister’s explanations don’t make sense.

“You either didn’t catch it or you knew and chose to do nothing about it, so which one is it?” he said. “If this (school) was the top of the list, wouldn’t that be your No. 1 priority to investigate?”

NDP critic Peggy Sattler said she questions the strength of the ministry’s investigations.

“We have heard no answers from the government as to how this was allowed to happen,” she said. “Any actions that the government took were far too delayed to try to protect the integrity of the Osap program.”

Dick said there is a simple explanation for why the minister did not lump Canadian College of Business, Science and Technology in with the six schools it cut off from Osap in May.

“Ccbst never had the ministry put the brakes on its programs because it never engaged in any improper conduct,” he wrote. “Any suggestion that the ministry was lax in its assessment of the college through its usual audit processes is simply unfounded.”

Quinn has said that preliminary findings of a Kpmg audit into career colleges and Osap are so troubling that he has referred the matter to the Ontario Provincial Police. He has not named any specific schools associated with that police referral.

The Canadian College of Business, Science and Technology had previously not responded to multiple requests for comment.

In May, the province ended Osap eligibility at six campuses, the same schools that the federal government had flagged concerns about a year prior. The number of students receiving Osap increased between about 650 per cent and 1,375 per cent from 2021-22 to 2024-25 at those schools.

The students at four campuses in total in 2024-25 accounted for about $151 million in provincial grants, according to the data.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 26, 2026.

stories.title: Who’ll pay for overruns on the Darlington small modular reactor? – and other unanswered questions
stories.summary: Nuclear projects are notorious for suffering cost overruns and taking longer than promised, often with consequences for consumers
stories.author: Matthew McClearn
stories.content:
Just months into construction, Canada’s most ambitious nuclear project in four decades has already suffered serious setbacks.

Construction of a new nuclear power plant officially began in April when the foundation for its first reactor building was set in place. Located in Clarington, Ont., Ontario Power Generation’s Darlington New Nuclear Project (Dnnp) contemplates building four small modular reactors (SMRs) known as Bwrx-300s, a model that has never been built before. The project’s overall budget was $20.9-billion, $7.7-billion of which was for the first unit. But on Nov. 10, OPG announced that it no longer expects that first reactor to meet its approved budget, nor will it enter service by October 2030 as promised.

Nuclear projects are notorious for suffering massive cost overruns and taking far longer than promised, often with significant consequences for consumers. Here’s what to know about the Dnnp’s setbacks, and what past failed nuclear projects reveal about what might happen next.

OPG is offering few details, however the original budget already included significant contingencies and escalations intended to cushion setbacks. The utility said it launched “a comprehensive assessment” to determine a new schedule and budget, expected to be completed by mid-2027.

OPG did not respond to queries from The Globe and Mail about which aspects of the project are behind schedule. An analysis of OPG disclosures by The Globe suggests key project milestones have already been missed by months.

For example, OPG was to have completed assembly of a tunnel-boring machine by February 2026. But that was achieved sometime during the three months ended Sept. 30.

Opg’s deadline for drilling the station’s marine intake was Oct. 31. However, as of Nov. 10, OPG reports show it had not yet even commenced tunnel boring; it expected to do so by the end of this year.

How much those and other delays set back the project as a whole isn’t apparent, but there are hints. The timing of Opg’s original plan – reflected in its Dec. 2025 rate application to the Ontario Energy Board, covering 2027 through 2031 – indicated the first unit would begin generating electricity in October 2030. In a Nov. 10 report, the OPG notified the Ontario Energy Board that it would remove the Dnnp entirely from the application, suggesting startup will be not before 2031, making it at least 14 months late. However, that is not definitive: The same document elsewhere contemplated the possibility Unit 1 might enter service earlier.

In financial statements published Nov. 10, OPG attributed the overruns to GE Vernova Hitachi Nuclear Energy’s “ongoing engineering” work. That, in turn, “has impacts on construction execution and supply chain performance.”

GE Vernova Hitachi is responsible for designing the Bwrx-300 reactor at the plant’s heart, as well as procuring major components and providing engineering and support. OPG began construction without a detailed set of plans.

Such reasoning has spelled disaster for countless nuclear projects, particularly those involving “first-of-a-kind” reactors such as the Bwrx-300. Much project management literature counsels proponents to not rush to begin construction, because problem-solving and delays cost a lot less during the planning phase.

Consider this: Opg’s financial statements indicate it’s spending roughly $100-million a month on the Dnnp. Earlier this year, it reported having as many as 1,500 workers on site on a typical day.

“You don’t want to have 1,500 people just sitting around,” said Koroush Shirvan, an associate professor of nuclear engineering at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

“Because that’s going to eat through your budget and contingency very, very fast.”

It was. In past interviews with The Globe, OPG officials said that the facility’s design would be sufficiently advanced that “first-of-a-kind” risks would be eliminated before construction began. In May 2025, Ontario’s government reported that “OPG has completed their engineering and design work for the first SMR” and developed a “‘high-confidence’ budget and schedule.”

When The Globe asked in May about the status of the Bwrx-300’s detailed design, OPG replied that “standard plant design was substantially completed in December 2025 as planned.”

However, experts told The Globe that “standard plant design” is very different from “detailed” design. The latter includes three-dimensional representations of every pipe, cable and duct, exact weld specifications and a whole lot more. That’s what’s required to actually build a nuclear power plant. It’s unclear what detailed design work has been completed and what remains outstanding.

France’s Flamanville-3, completed a dozen years behind schedule and massively over budget, offers a good example. A report by Jean-Martin Folz, former head of French automaker Peugeot, found that the plant’s construction began without a complete set of validated plans. The result was that the design continuously changed during construction, and lots of work had to be redone. Flamanville-3 blew its budget many times over.

In Burke County, Georgia, two units at the Alvin W. Vogtle plant, the U.S.’s largest nuclear station, began construction in 2009; they were the first to feature Westinghouse’s AP1000 reactor. The U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission licensed the AP1000’s design prior to completion, but the missing elements led to myriad problems during construction and huge cost overruns. Similar problems occurred with two nearly identical AP1000s in South Carolina, V.C. Summer Units 2 and 3, which were abandoned in 2017 after billions of dollars had been spent.

“These lessons have been repeated over and over and over again,” Dr. Shirvan said.

The financial fallout from Vogtle and V.C. Summer led to the bankruptcy of Westinghouse, the main contractor and reactor designer on both projects.

The Dnnp is being executed under what’s referred to as a “integrated product delivery model,” under which OPG, GE Vernova Hitachi, architect-engineer AtkinsRéalis Group Inc. Atrl-T and construction company Aecon Group Inc. ARE-T share risks. A portion of their fees can be withheld if certain objectives aren’t met. A senior OPG executive told reporters in 2025 that if the Dnnp went late or over budget, “all of us – the partners and OPG – will have to share the risk of that overrun.”

However, in a statement to The Globe, AtkinsRéalis spokesperson Daniela Pizzuto wrote that the overruns would not have a material financial impact on her company because “our risk is capped.”

Vogtle and V.C. Summer demonstrate how, even when private companies were contractually obligated to deliver a nuclear power plant under a fixed-price contract, the public ended up paying dearly. Georgia Power raised residential electricity rates significantly to cover Vogtle’s construction costs and overruns. South Carolina’s utility, Santee Cooper, owed US$3.6-billion for the unfinished V.C. Summer units, which its customers pay for on their monthly bills despite never receiving a single kilowatt hour.

Opinion: The cost of Ontario’s nuclear plan spirals. When will the province get serious?

“Contracts don’t fix problems, they fix blame,” said James Little, a member of South Carolina’s Governor’s Nuclear Advisory Council, in April at a hearing at which the potential restart of construction at V.C. Summer was discussed.

“Relying on contracts to manage risk, it’s a false hope.”

The Ontario Energy Board sets the rates OPG can charge for electricity generated by its nuclear power plants, and is mandated to provide information to consumers. “We will never lose sight of the individual rate payers, the consumers, the people of Ontario,” the regulator asserts on its web site.

The Globe requested an interview with the OEB to explore how consumers might be exposed to the Dnnp overruns. Spokesperson Tom Miller denied the request and said such questions should be directed to OPG.

With the extent of the overruns unclear, it’s difficult to gauge Opg’s ability to adapt and respond. The utility reported that construction will continue. It did not answer questions about how it has adjusted its on-site work plans in response to incomplete engineering work. Aecon, the constructor, declined an interview request, as did GE Vernova Hitachi.

Critics of Ontario’s nuclear-focused electricity strategy were quick to pounce on the Dnnp’s troubles; the Ontario Clean Air Alliance demanded its cancellation.

“The most head shaking part of this risky project is that Ontario willingly chose to be a guinea pig for an unproven American (GE-Hitachi) nuclear technology,” director Angela Bischoff wrote in a statement.

“While other jurisdictions stood back and said ‘after you,’ Ontario rushed forward and recklessly committed to a design that has not been built anywhere in the world.”

The provincial and federal governments have shown no indications they are reconsidering their commitments – and some observers say they shouldn’t.

Chris Gadomski, a nuclear analyst at BloombergNEF, said first-of-a-kind nuclear projects are exceptionally difficult to deliver, invariably suffer delays and are painfully expensive. It was “disheartening,” he added, that Dnnp proponents hadn’t learned from Vogtle and V.C. Summer.

But, following missteps during construction of the first unit, “the question to be asking is: Will OPG and General Electric Hitachi learn from their mistakes and get the second, third and fourth one right?” he said.

“It would be a shame if they stopped after one…the worst thing they could possibly do is stop the project.”

content_blocks.text: Opg’s deadline for drilling the station’s marine intake was Oct. 31. However, as of Nov. 10, OPG reports show it had not yet even commenced tunnel boring; it expected to do so by the end of this year.

content_blocks.text: How much those and other delays set back the project as a whole isn’t apparent, but there are hints. The timing of Opg’s original plan – reflected in its Dec. 2025 rate application to the Ontario Energy Board, covering 2027 through 2031 – indicated the first unit would begin generating electricity in October 2030. In a Nov. 10 report, the OPG notified the Ontario Energy Board that it would remove the Dnnp entirely from the application, suggesting startup will be not before 2031, making it at least 14 months late. However, that is not definitive: The same document elsewhere contemplated the possibility Unit 1 might enter service earlier.

content_blocks.text: What caused the overruns?
content_blocks.html: What caused the overruns?

content_blocks.text: In financial statements published Nov. 10, OPG attributed the overruns to GE Vernova Hitachi Nuclear Energy’s “ongoing engineering” work. That, in turn, “has impacts on construction execution and supply chain performance.”
content_blocks.html: In financial statements published Nov. 10, OPG attributed the overruns to GE Vernova Hitachi Nuclear Energy’s “ongoing engineering” work. That, in turn, “has impacts on construction execution and supply chain performance.”

content_blocks.text: GE Vernova Hitachi is responsible for designing the Bwrx-300 reactor at the plant’s heart, as well as procuring major components and providing engineering and support. OPG began construction without a detailed set of plans.
content_blocks.html: GE Vernova Hitachi is responsible for designing the BWRX-300 reactor at the plant’s heart, as well as procuring major components and providing engineering and support. OPG began construction without a detailed set of plans.

content_blocks.text: Why does that matter? Can’t OPG work on other parts of the project while GE Vernova Hitachi’s engineers catch up?

content_blocks.text: Such reasoning has spelled disaster for countless nuclear projects, particularly those involving “first-of-a-kind” reactors such as the Bwrx-300. Much project management literature counsels proponents to not rush to begin construction, because problem-solving and delays cost a lot less during the planning phase.

content_blocks.text: Consider this: Opg’s financial statements indicate it’s spending roughly $100-million a month on the Dnnp. Earlier this year, it reported having as many as 1,500 workers on site on a typical day.

content_blocks.text: However, experts told The Globe that “standard plant design” is very different from “detailed” design. The latter includes three-dimensional representations of every pipe, cable and duct, exact weld specifications and a whole lot more. That’s what’s required to actually build a nuclear power plant. It’s unclear what detailed design work has been completed and what remains outstanding.

content_blocks.text: What happened to other nuclear plants that began construction without detailed plans?
content_blocks.html: What happened to other nuclear plants that began construction without detailed plans?

content_blocks.text: France’s Flamanville-3, completed a dozen years behind schedule and massively over budget, offers a good example. A report by Jean-Martin Folz, former head of French automaker Peugeot, found that the plant’s construction began without a complete set of validated plans. The result was that the design continuously changed during construction, and lots of work had to be redone. Flamanville-3 blew its budget many times over.

content_blocks.text: In Burke County, Georgia, two units at the Alvin W. Vogtle plant, the U.S.’s largest nuclear station, began construction in 2009; they were the first to feature Westinghouse’s AP1000 reactor. Similar problems occurred with two nearly identical AP1000s in South Carolina, V.C. Summer Units 2 and 3, which were abandoned in 2017 after billions of dollars had been spent.

content_blocks.html: Who’ll pay for the DNNP overruns?

content_blocks.text: The Dnnp is being executed under what’s referred to as a “integrated product delivery model,” under which OPG, GE Vernova Hitachi, architect-engineer AtkinsRéalis Group Inc. Atrl-T and construction company Aecon Group Inc. ARE-T share risks. A portion of their fees can be withheld if certain objectives aren’t met. A senior OPG executive told reporters in 2025 that if the Dnnp went late or over budget, “all of us – the partners and OPG – will have to share the risk of that overrun.”

content_blocks.text: Vogtle and V.C. Summer demonstrate how, even when private companies were contractually obligated to deliver a nuclear power plant under a fixed-price contract, the public ended up paying dearly. South Carolina’s utility, Santee Cooper, owed US$3.6-billion for the unfinished V.C. Summer units, which its customers pay for on their monthly bills despite never receiving a single kilowatt hour.

stories.title: Weather station records 469 millimetres of rain in latest B.C. soaking
stories.summary: Ucluelet - Environment Canada says 469 millimetres of rain fell at a weather station west of Vancouver Island in just over two days as British Columbia continues to get drenched by wet weather.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The head of the British Columbia River Forecast Centre says much of Vancouver Island and the province’s south coast have passed the peak of flooding after days of drenching rain that led to evacuations, though central Vancouver Island is still “in the thick of it.”

Dave Campbell said that many waterways are running high but as the rainfall lets up, the coastal region should improve.

However, he said Thursday that it will take time for the waters to be safe enough for flood watches and warnings to come down.

“It’s still high, so we’re going wait a little bit for the rivers to come down before we drop those advisories.”

The centre issued a flood warning on Thursday for central Vancouver Island, meaning river levels had either crested the banks or would do so imminently and that flooding along the rivers would result.

“I think we’re really kind of in the thick of it for the central Island part, and then the rest of the Island (and) south coast, I think, we are past the worst of it now,” Campbell said in an interview.

Since Monday, much of coastal B.C., including Vancouver Island and Haida Gwaii, has been pummeled with rain and wind, coinciding with the year’s highest tides.

Environment Canada figures show 469 millimetres of rain fell at the Effingham Island station off the west coast of Vancouver Island in just over two days this week, however other areas received between 250 and 100 millimetres of rain.

Rain and wind warnings issued by Environment Canada for the South Coast lifted on Thursday but coastal flood warnings remained in place for much of Vancouver Island.

Campbell said waterways in the central region will take more time to return to normal.

“It just takes longer to drain off the landscape, and so we haven’t seen the peak on those river flows yet,” he said

A flood watch remained in place on Thursday for eastern Vancouver Island, while a high streamflow advisory covered the remaining parts of Vancouver Island and the south coast.

The City of Courtenay on eastern Vancouver Island declared a state of local emergency and issued an evacuation order for several properties in low-lying areas, including the Maple Pool campground, while evacuation alerts are in effect for other properties near the Puntledge River.

The declaration, signed by Mayor Manno Theos, says rain, river swell and high tides pose an existing or imminent threat to people and property in the community.

Courtenay’s evacuation order says flood levels pose immediate danger to life and health and people should leave the area immediately.

To the south, the Regional District of Nanaimo issued an evacuation order for some properties along the Nanaimo River in the community of Cedar, with residents told to leave immediately.

The River Forecast Centre said significant snow fell in mountain areas this week and it’s now melting rapidly at lower elevations, flowing into swollen waterways.

The latest low-pressure system also brought warm temperatures that set new daily records in a number of communities, including in Abbotsford where the 14.5 degrees reported broke an old record of 13.9 degrees set on Nov. 25, 1962.

Prince George broke a record by almost three degrees that was set on the same day in 1954.

Elsewhere in the province, Environment Canada issued snowfall warnings for multiple highways through mountain passes, including the Okanagan Connector from Merritt to Kelowna and the Coquihalla Highway from Hope to Merritt, as well as Highway 3 from the Paulson Summit to the Kootenay Pass.

As much as 25 centimetres of snow could be arriving by Thursday night, with the forecaster warning that mountain weather can change suddenly and become hazardous.

A rainfall warning was also issued for the Sea to Sky Highway from Squamish to Whistler on Thursday.

The Transportation Ministry has advised drivers to check conditions before travelling through coastal areas due to the risk of flooding.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 26, 2026

stories.title: Smith hopes to leave separatism behind as UCP meets after divisive referendum
stories.summary: Edmonton - Alberta's governing United Conservative Party is gathering this weekend for the first time since an independence referendum divided the province, opened internal party cracks and led to a high-profile member's expulsion.
stories.author: Lisa Johnson The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Edmonton - Alberta’s governing United Conservative Party is gathering this weekend for the first time since an independence referendum divided the province, opened internal party cracks and led to a high-profile member’s expulsion.

Premier Danielle Smith says she hopes to leave the issue of separatism in the rear-view mirror and have her UCP regroup to win next year’s provincial election.

But prominent separatist leader Mitch Sylvestre says Smith May need to quell frustration from disappointed members of the independence movement.

More than 7,000 UCP members are registered to attend its annual general meeting Friday through Sunday in Calgary. They are set to vote on policy, a board of directors, and hear from Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe and newly elected British Columbia Premier Lorne Doerkson.

Smith has said spokespeople for the party must accept the results of the Oct. 19 referendum. About 75 per cent of voters said they want the province to stay in Canada and not to hold a second, binding referendum on leaving the country.

“We think it’s really important from a credibility point of view,” the premier said Tuesday.

“I hope at the end of that, we emerge united. Because the whole preparation for this (annual general meeting) is prepping for the next election.”

That includes developing a party platform to put to voters for the general election, set for Oct. 18, 2027.

It has been a challenge for conservative movements to find unanimous agreement, Smith added.

“We can either focus on the things that drive us apart, or we can focus on the things that draw us together,” she said.

Party officials sent a letter last month to board candidates, and later to constituency presidents, asking them to make a pro-Canada pledge.

After at least 15 dozen refused to sign, calling it an affront to their freedom of expression, Smith said that she hoped to speak with them directly to persuade them otherwise.

Sylvestre said Wednesday he believes the number of holdouts is significantly higher. And he said he hasn’t spoken directly with the premier since constituency presidents were asked to sign the pledge.

“This weekend is going to be a very interesting weekend,” he said.

He added that it’s difficult to gauge how large a contingent of independence supporters will attend or how they might react to the premier.

“I think that people are frustrated. I don’t have any idea what’s going to happen.”

The party, long dedicated to empowering grassroots members, stripped separatist leader Jeffrey Rath of his membership last month, citing code of conduct issues — a decision Smith has said she supports.

Rath served as a lawyer for the group that collected roughly 300,000 signatures on a petition calling for a binding separation referendum.

The ouster means Rath can’t attend this weekend. At the meeting last year, when he went to the mic and asked the crowd who supported independence, he was met with roaring applause.

Sylvestre, who spearheaded the separatist petition, is the constituency association president for Bonnyville-Cold Lake-St. Paul, and he signed the letter opposing the Ucp’s code of conduct.

He said Rath was ejected to prevent a repeat of that public show of support.

“They want the independence movement out of the party, and that’s what they’re trying to do.”

He said much of the battle ahead will be pushing for Smith’s government to make good on other promises she has made to her supporters.

Sylvester said he believes one example is taking steps to pull out of the Canada Pension Plan in favour of a provincial fund in order to unite the party.

Smith previously shut the idea down, saying it doesn’t have popular support in Alberta.

Members of the separatist movement have also criticized Smith for publicly endorsing to remain in Confederation and not offering a binding referendum on the issue.

“If they’d done what they said they were going to do, then we wouldn’t even be having this conversation,” Sylvestre said.

On Saturday, members are to vote for the party’s board of directors, a ballot Sylvestre said is “massively important.”

“The party board actually is supposed to represent the membership. That’s its job,” he said. “We’re seeing that the government is not representing its members very well right now.”

When candidates spoke to members at a virtual town hall last weekend, the issue of party unity dominated and many anchored their pitches to the goal of defeating the Opposition NDP.

Vince Byfield, a candidate a board vice-president position, said the referendum “cost us members on both sides.”

He’s challenging incumbent Patrick Malkin, the deputy chief of staff in Smith’s office. Malkin is part of a slate of candidates dubbed “Team Unity,” believed by some to be Smith’s set of preferred candidates.

While several candidates emphasized bridging divides, candidate Rob Anders, a former Conservative member of Parliament, said the board ought to push back on governments that go “offside” of the membership.

Members are also to debate resolutions that could affect a wide range of government policy, from land acknowledgments to laws impacting transgender people’s access to washrooms and change rooms.

Adopting separatism as party policy isn’t on the floor for debate.

Policy resolutions approved at these meetings are not binding on the government, but many have been adopted by Smith and passed into law.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 26, 2026.

stories.title: Long mental recovery for soldiers burned in CFB Wainwright fire: doctor
stories.summary: Soldiers still being treated in hospital for burns from a deadly fire at an Alberta military base have a long psychological recovery ahead of them.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Soldiers being treated in hospital for burns from a deadly fire at an Alberta military base have a long psychological recovery ahead of them, says an Edmonton surgeon treating some of the injured.

Dr. Josh Wong, the interim medical director of the Edmonton Firefighters Burn Treatment Unit at the University of Alberta Hospital, says recovering from such severe burns can take months or years.

“For patients who experience severe burns, recovery is often a long and challenging journey. Their care doesn’t end when they leave the ICU or even the hospital,” Wong said Thursday at a news conference at the hospital.

“Many will require ongoing treatment and rehabilitation.”

Wong, who is a plastic and reconstructive surgeon specializing in burn cases, said the mental impact from even small burns can become more intense over time.

“I have mentioned to the families that the psychological effect actually comes up stronger as they recover and become more aware later on as well,” he said.

The Armed Forces had said that a windstorm on Oct. 17 pushed flames from a grass fire onto troops in a training exercise at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, southeast of Edmonton.

Prime Minister Mark Carney called the fire one of the worst tragedies for the Armed Forces on home soil during peacetime.

Four were killed in the fire. They have been identified as: Pte. Shaun Farrell, 23, of Prince Albert, Sask.; Pte. Aidan Goulding, 23, of North Vancouver, B.C.; Pte. Hayden Lykkemark, 19, of Langley, B.C.; and Sgt. Morgan Wong, 26, of Edmonton.

A fifth soldier, Pte. William Douglas Dal Bianco, died of his injured earlier this month while in an Ontario hospital.

About three dozen soldiers were initially injured.

Acute Care Alberta said 19 were still being cared for in provincial hospitals, with seven listed in critical condition.

The military said Saturday that two others remained in hospitals in British Columbia and Ontario, where they were transferred to be closer to their families.

Michael Suddes, interim chief operating officer for the Alberta Health Services’ Edmonton area, said officials could not provide specifics about the recovering soldiers due to patient confidentiality.

“But there is a spectrum,” he said. “Several patients, while they May be in critical condition, several (other) patients have already been discharged home.”

Dr. Sayeh Zielke, interim chief executive officer of Acute Care Alberta, said the fire put a huge stress on the province’s health-care system.

“We passed it,” she said. “We were able to manage the capacity and co-ordinate the response to provide the care, not only for the injured soldiers, but also the rest of our version that needed care.”

Zielke said health-care providers are still in the thick of treating the injured soldiers, but soon there will be a debriefing process to see if improvements can be made.

“We’re trying to do our best by every single day. So for us, it very much feels like a marathon,” she said.

“There’s always lessons to be learned, and we can always do better and aim for perfection.”

Wong said patients with severe burns require complex, intensive treatment that involves multiple procedures and surgeries, extensive rehabilitation, psychological support and ongoing followup care.

He said the Wainwright fire presented an extraordinary challenge for his team, who admitted 20 critically injured patients in a short period of time — about five times the specialized burn critical care capacity.

He added that there were already 15 other burn patients in care at the time.

“Our teams moved quickly to mobilize the physicians, the nurses, other health-care professionals with specialized training and experience needed to provide this level of care,” Wong said.

He also recognized that many health-care workers May start to feel the effects of their hard work and trauma they have witnessed, and his team is preparing for that.

“When you’re in the midst of all the work and the adrenalin rushing and trying to help these patients, that’s where our focus is going to,” he said.

“But we know very well that as the weeks and the months go on, there will be some effects, there will be some fatigue, there’ll be some psychological effects of these injuries.”
