stories.title: Low-income, Black and Latin American people less likely to have a family doctor: report
stories.summary: Toronto - A new report by the Canadian Institute for Health Information says people with low incomes and people who are Black or Latin American are less likely to have a primary-care provider.
stories.author: Nicole Ireland The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - A new report by the Canadian Institute for Health Information says people with low incomes and people who are Black or Latin American are less likely to have a primary-care provider.

About six million people in Canada — including both adults and children — don’t have a family doctor or nurse practitioner, leaving them “without a source of regular, ongoing care,” the report released Thursday said.

Access to a primary-care provider isn’t equal across the population, it said, noting 87 per cent of adults with the highest incomes in Canada have one, compared to 78 per cent of people with the lowest incomes.

Data analyzed by the institute showed that people living in the lowest-income neighbourhoods are almost three times more likely to have a hospital stay for something that might have been managed with good primary care than people in the highest-income communities.

Possible reasons for the disparity include the fact that low-income jobs often don’t have the flexibility for employees to take time off work to go to doctors’ appointments, difficulty getting child care and inability to pay for medications, the report suggested.

“We’ve designed our system to be 9 to 5, Monday to Friday. We’ve designed our system so that it’s actually really hard to navigate a lot of the time,” said Dr. Tara Kiran, a family physician and researcher at St. Michael’s Hospital and the University of Toronto.

“We’ve also not done a really good job (of) always telling people what the benefits of having ongoing primary care is, compared to, like, just going to a walk-in clinic or an emergency department,” said Kiran, whose own research has produced similar findings to the institute’s.

The report said only 66 per cent of Black adults and 68 per cent of Latin American adults have a primary-care provider compared to 86 per cent of white adults.

“Some racialized Canadians report having their health concerns dismissed or not taken seriously because of their race, skin colour or where they come from,” the report said.

“Some May also face language barriers, experience cultural differences or be newcomers navigating an unfamiliar health system. These experiences can make it harder to communicate with providers and build trust, affecting the care they receive and, ultimately, their health.”

Dr. Mojola Omole, president of the Black Physicians’ Association of Ontario, said many Black people live in high-density neighbourhoods where there May not be enough family doctors or nurse practitioners to serve the population.

“Most people are more likely to seek care when it’s closer to home, when it’s closer to their work,” Omole said.

“When we don’t have a high concentration of health-care providers in those high-needs neighbourhood(s), it makes it more challenging to access care. And when you do access care, you’re accessing emergency care, not primary care.”

Both Omole and Kiran said systemic racism plays a role in hesitancy to see a primary-care provider, even if one is available.

“I think one factor that we underestimate in Canada is just how much racism and discrimination there is in the system,” Kiran said, noting that her research team has gone out into communities to consult with Black and Indigenous people.

“We heard about how often, you know, they would go to a (clinical) practice or to another part of the health-care system expecting to be discriminated against,” she said.

“We also heard that one of the things that actually helps them to access care and helps them to feel safe is when actually the workforce is more reflective of the community.”

There are fewer Black and Indigenous physicians per capita than there should be in Canada, Kiran said.

Omole said part of the Black Physicians’ Association of Ontario’s mandate is to increase the number of Black doctors in practice.

“The more you see of people who look like you and have positive experience(s), the more you’re like, ‘Oh, OK, this is changing. This is not what I was expecting, you know, that I had an experience 10 years ago, 12 years ago. Or this is not my parents’ experience,’” she said.

“The more that we have Black physicians — and especially having Black primary-care physicians — the better it is that we’re changing the perception and the legacy of health care in Canada.”

The report noted that data on First Nations, Inuit and Métis people’s experiences were not available, but “Cihi acknowledges that they can face greater barriers to accessing primary care, including challenges finding a regular provider, long travel distances and a lack of culturally appropriate care.”

It also found that access to family doctors or nurse practitioners varied between provinces.

Only 66 per cent of adults in Prince Edward Island have a primary-care provider, compared to 89 per cent of adults in Ontario, the report said.

The institute used its hospitalization databases, survey data from Statistics Canada, and provincial and territorial data to calculate the primary-care findings in the report.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 26, 2026.

stories.title: Adults in lowest-income neighbourhoods more likely to be hospitalized for manageable conditions, study says
stories.summary: Men, young adults and racialized groups are less likely to have access to a primary care doctor
stories.author: Kristy Kirkup
stories.content:
People living in Canada’s lowest-income neighbourhoods were nearly three times more likely to be hospitalized for conditions that could have been managed in a primary health care setting than those residing in the country’s highest-income communities, according to a new study.

Research released Thursday from the Canadian Institute for Health Information found only 78 per cent of adults in living in areas with the lowest 20 per cent of household incomes had a primary health care provider.

That compares with 87 per cent of adults living in areas with the country’s top 20 per cent of household incomes.

Cihi said these disparities had an impact on hospital usage: Individuals from the lowest-income neighbourhoods had 535 hospitalizations for every 100,000 residents in 2025 for conditions that might have been managed with appropriate primary care. In comparison, those in the highest-income areas had 192 hospitalizations per 100,000 in 2025.

Conditions that respond to primary care on an outpatient basis, but can result in hospitalization, include angina, asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, diabetes, congestive heart failure, epilepsy and high blood pressure, the study said.

Men, younger adults age 18 to 34, and people with the lowest incomes faced greater challenges accessing primary care, the study said.

Certain racialized groups, including Black and Hispanic adults, are also less likely to have a primary health care provider, according to Statistics Canada data cited by Cihi.

“Gaps in primary care can mean that health problems are not identified in time, ongoing conditions become harder to manage and people May not get the care they need,” the study said.

“The effects can also spill into the rest of health care systems – including greater use of emergency departments, more hospitalizations and poorer health outcomes, including higher mortality rates.”

The study’s findings underscore how patients’ health is affected when they face challenges accessing family health care providers. Health experts say demand for such providers is growing while Canada’s population ages.

Tara Kiran, who practises family medicine at the St. Michael’s Hospital Academic Family Health Team in Toronto, said primary care is a “foundation of the health care system.”

“A key ingredient is that ongoing relationship with a family doctor who really knows you well and can help take care of you as a whole person,” Dr. Kiran said.

Cihi’s study said the next few years will be important to understanding whether efforts by provinces and territories to improve health care access reach those who encounter the greatest barriers.

Cihi said, however, that most Canadians reported having positive experiences when they can access primary care.

More than two in three Canadian adults, or 68 per cent, reported being satisfied with how long they waited for care when it was needed.

“This suggests that many felt their wait time was appropriate for their health concern,” the study said.

Four in five Canadians said their primary care provider treated them with respect with regard to their culture and identity.

Those without a regular provider navigate uncertainty at the outset of their care journey, the study added, such finding a walk-in clinic, deciding whether or how long to wait for an appointment, or opting to delay care.

Although the study notes most Canadians – 83 per cent of adults and 89 per cent of children and youth – have access to a primary health care provider, it said only 26 per cent of adults and 41 per cent of children and youth received same-day or next-day appointments when needed.

Cihi said its findings also reinforce why it matters where individuals live. The study found primary care access and experiences varied across provinces, territories and communities.

paragraphs: People living in Canada’s lowest-income neighbourhoods were nearly three times more likely to be hospitalized for conditions that could have been managed in a primary health care setting than those residing in the country’s highest-income communities, according to a new study.

Research released Thursday from the Canadian Institute for Health Information found only 78 per cent of adults in living in areas with the lowest 20 per cent of household incomes had a primary health care provider.
That compares with 87 per cent of adults living in areas with the country’s top 20 per cent of household incomes.

Cihi said these disparities had an impact on hospital usage: Individuals from the lowest-income neighbourhoods had 535 hospitalizations for every 100,000 residents in 2025 for conditions that might have been managed with appropriate primary care. In comparison, those in the highest-income areas had 192 hospitalizations per 100,000 in 2025.

Conditions that respond to primary care on an outpatient basis, but can result in hospitalization, include angina, asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, diabetes, congestive heart failure, epilepsy and high blood pressure, the study said.
Men, younger adults age 18 to 34, and people with the lowest incomes faced greater challenges accessing primary care, the study said.
Certain racialized groups, including Black and Hispanic adults, are also less likely to have a primary health care provider, according to Statistics Canada data cited by Cihi.
“Gaps in primary care can mean that health problems are not identified in time, ongoing conditions become harder to manage and people May not get the care they need,” the study said.
“The effects can also spill into the rest of health care systems – including greater use of emergency departments, more hospitalizations and poorer health outcomes, including higher mortality rates.”

The study’s findings underscore how patients’ health is affected when they face challenges accessing family health care providers. Health experts say demand for such providers is growing while Canada’s population ages.
Tara Kiran, who practises family medicine at the St. Michael’s Hospital Academic Family Health Team in Toronto, said primary care is a “foundation of the health care system.”
“A key ingredient is that ongoing relationship with a family doctor who really knows you well and can help take care of you as a whole person,” Dr. Kiran said.
Cihi’s study said the next few years will be important to understanding whether efforts by provinces and territories to improve health care access reach those who encounter the greatest barriers.
Cihi said, however, that most Canadians reported having positive experiences when they can access primary care.
More than two in three Canadian adults, or 68 per cent, reported being satisfied with how long they waited for care when it was needed.
“This suggests that many felt their wait time was appropriate for their health concern,” the study said.
Four in five Canadians said their primary care provider treated them with respect with regard to their culture and identity.

Those without a regular provider navigate uncertainty at the outset of their care journey, the study added, such finding a walk-in clinic, deciding whether or how long to wait for an appointment, or opting to delay care.

stories.title: Molly’s story: From patient to provider to patient again
stories.summary: November 26, 2026
stories.content:
Molly Bokkers, Registered Practical Nurse, in the Post Partum Care Unit at LHSC

November 26, 2026

A 13-year-old is a new teenager, someone who is soon entering high school, and is just starting to curate their taste in music, finding out what they love to do, and spending time with their friends.

But when Molly Bokkers was 13 years old, she was going through more than just the transition from grade eight to high school, she was diagnosed with Hodgkins Lymphoma and had to begin treatment right away.

Bokkers went through her initial treatment, and when she had her one-year check-up appointment, she found out she had relapsed - the cancer that was previously localized, had moved to her chest. The second time, she went through more intensive treatment with radiation, chemotherapy, and an inpatient stay.

"The first diagnosis feels like bad luck, but the second one hit harder because I felt like the situation had solidified into something bigger that I had to deal with," Bokkers shares.

Bokkers grew up in Stratford, so her first experience with London was coming to the Paediatric Medical Day Unit (PMDU) at London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC) for treatment. The staff were critical to her positive experience and inspired her to want to help others as a nurse.

"My goal was always to work at LHSC, and that dream came true in 2015 when I started my career as a registered practical nurse in the Sub Acute Medicine Unit at University Hospital," Bokkers says. "But the start of my career had to be paused because my cancer came back in 2016."

She also found out she was pregnant and was renewed with fight and vigor to bring this new life into the world.

Bokkers was monitored throughout her pregnancy and her condition remained stable until she gave birth. She started treatment after she had delivered her daughter who is now 8 years old and thriving

This time, Bokkers was receiving care in the adult cancer centre and had a whole new team supporting her care – but found a familiar face in one nurse.

"There was one nurse who was a part of my care team when I had cancer as a teenager who happened to transfer to adult cancer care and she ended up as part of my care team again. It was so helpful to have a familiar face as I was going through this cancer battle again," Bokkers explains. "She would always go above and beyond with small gestures that meant the world to me and made a big difference in my inpatient experience."

The next step in Bokkers' treatment was getting a stem cell transplant. Since a person effectively has no immune system following a stem cell transplant, she was in isolation for 17 days as her immune system rebuilt. This was a hard time for her and her family, especially since her daughter was not able to see her other than through FaceTime calls during this time.

"At first, I was worried that the care experience was going to be so different without the specific resources within Children's Hospital, I had been a paeds patient for over 10 years and was used to stickers, Ollie the clown and art therapy but my nurse on the first day in adult oncology brought in a balloon that said, 'you’re doing a good job' and hung it on the end of my bed on the first day after my transplant. I still have that balloon," shares Bokkers.

Bokkers shares that she loves being a postpartum nurse and while she personally does not want to work in oncology because that feels too close to her treatment experience, the teams of people she interacted with are just the kindest, smartest, and sweetest people. "I felt so loved and cared for. It was really special," she says.

Bokkers is finally cancer free after her fourth round of treatment and has been back to work in the Post Partum Care Unit since 2024.

"When me and my husband would drive past Victoria Hospital we would say to each other – there's new life there, there are babies being born - as a recognition that the hospital is also a happy place. While some of people's worst days happen here, people also experience some of their best days," Bokkers says. "I feel privileged to care for people in their hardest, happiest, and most vulnerable times and support both paediatric and adult patients as they embark on a new phase of their life as parents."

Even though Bokkers continues being a patient with regular check-up appointments for her condition, she is happy to focus on being a provider right now, taking what she learned as a patient and bringing those experiences into her own patient care practices.

"I recognize that little things make a big difference like actively listening and bringing warm blankets. I remember as a patient that I loved warm blankets because they felt like a warm hug, truly making me feel relaxed and cared for. I try to make my patients feel as cared for as I felt by my care teams when I was a patient," Bokkers shares.

Bokkers continues, noting that she feels that being able to go back to work has felt like a miracle. "I’ve always wanted to be a nurse, while my journey has been hard, I am grateful for the empathy I have after having been a patient, and grateful to all the nurses, doctors and other members of LHSC who made my cancer treatments easier by being so kind and compassionate."

stories.title: Financial crime unit investigation
stories.summary: London, ON (November 26, 2026) – Members of the London Police Service (LPS) Financial Crime Unit are warning the public to remain vigilant while using debit and credit cards as officers are investigating a series of frauds involving individuals asking for assistance paying for taxis, rideshares or food deliveries.
stories.author: London Police Service
paragraphs: London, ON (November 26, 2026) – Members of the London Police Service (LPS) Financial Crime Unit are warning the public to remain vigilant while using debit and credit cards as officers are investigating a series of frauds involving individuals asking for assistance paying for taxis, rideshares or food deliveries.

In the reported incidents, suspects approached victims and claimed they were unable to pay using cash, Apple Pay or their own bank card. Victims were offered cash in exchange for using their debit card to complete a transaction on a portable payment terminal located inside or near a vehicle.
During the transactions, suspects distracted the victims and obtained their PINs. In some instances, victims’ debit cards were also switched with other cards without their knowledge.
The stolen debit cards and PINs were then used to make unauthorized cash withdrawals and purchases.
Investigators believe the incidents are connected. Suspects were associated with several vehicles, including white and grey Hyundai Elantras.

There are multiple suspects involved in the investigations, both male and female, believed to be between the ages of 18 – 20 years of age. Investigators are sharing images of three of the reported suspect males in the hopes that members of the public can assist in identifying them.
How to protect yourself
The London Police Service reminds members of the public to:
Be cautious if a stranger asks you to use your debit or credit card to pay for a taxi, rideshare or food delivery in exchange for cash;
Never allow another person to handle your debit or credit card during a transaction;
Shield the keypad when entering your PIN;
Keep your card in sight and ensure the card returned to you is yours;
Do not feel pressured to complete a transaction because someone claims to need urgent assistance;
Regularly review your bank and credit card activity and immediately report suspicious transactions to your financial institution; and
If you believe your card has been stolen or switched, contact your financial institution immediately to have the card blocked.
Investigators are asking anyone with information about these incidents, or who can identify any of the individuals or vehicles pictured, to contact the London Police Service at 519-661-5670.

Thursday, November 26, 2026

Gore Road will be closed between Hamilton Road and Clarke Road starting Friday, November 27 to facilitate private site servicing for a property located near Hamilton Road. The work is expected to be completed by Tuesday, December 1.

During this time, a signed detour will be in place redirecting traffic around the closure using Hamilton Road, Clarke Road and Gore Road nearby.

Transit riders are advised to visit the LTC website for service updates and detours and the most up-to-date information.

Access to properties and businesses in the area will be maintained during the closure. Sidewalks will be closed to pedestrians.

For more information on construction impacts in London, view the Renew London map.

stories.title: London Knights earn road win, spoil Otters’ teddy bear toss
stories.summary: Kane Barch broke a 0-0 tie midway through the third period, helping the London Knights defeat the Erie Otters 2-0 in Pennsylvania Wednesday night.
stories.author: Carlyle Fiset
stories.content:
Kane Barch broke a 0-0 tie midway through the third period, helping the London Knights defeat the Erie Otters 2-0 in Pennsylvania Wednesday night.

Goaltender Arvin Jaswal stopped all 24 shots he faced, earning his first win and shutout since joining London this season.

For his efforts, Jaswal was named the game’s first star, while Barch took home second star honours. Evan Van Gorp scored an empty net goal to secure the win, earning the game’s third star recognition.

For London, the win is just their second in their last eight games. They next play Friday night at Canada Life Place against the Niagara Ice Dogs.

stories.title: Galloway has not proven that accusations have taken a toll on his writing, defence argues
stories.summary: Lawyers for the author’s accuser say claims of psychological injury rely only on assertions from Galloway and his wife
stories.author: Mike Hager
stories.content:
Lawyers for the former University of British Columbia student who accused Steven Galloway of sexual assault told a judge Wednesday that the bestselling author’s claim that the allegations ruined his ability to ever write again required more proof.

Lawyers for the woman, known in court as A.B. due to a publication ban on her name, wrapped their final submissions in defence of their client who is the major target of Mr. Galloway’s defamation suit.

Mr. Galloway’s legal team, who said he deserves one of the biggest defamation awards in Canadian history, concluded their arguments earlier this week. The trial continues Thursday with more closing arguments.

On Wednesday, A.B.’s lawyer Sydney Gomez told B.C. Supreme Court Justice Neena Sharma that Mr. Galloway’s claims of psychological injury so severe that he cannot write rely solely on assertions from the author and his wife Katie Wagner. Both testified earlier in the trial.

Ms. Gomez argued the court requires more evidence of such harm – such as medical records or the opinion of an expert – to justify Mr. Galloway’s claim to a rare award of special damages. Mr. Galloway is seeking $4.9-million in special damages based largely on future earnings from books he argues he can no longer write.

But Justice Sharma questioned what a psychiatrist or another mental health clinician could say about the plight of such a writer.

“It’s not a mental thing – his loss of the creative spark to write and the desire to put his work out there into the public – is it?” the justice asked defence counsel.

Justice Sharma then asked what type of expert would be sufficient.

“You would have to find a writer and say to them, ‘Imagine you were falsely accused of rape and then there was a national controversy about you. Do you think you could write again?’ You [Ms. Gomez] would stand up and say to me ‘You can’t take that evidence,’” Justice Sharma said.

Ms. Gomez argued that the law says if a plaintiff doesn’t offer expert or similar evidence then they run the risk of not meeting the burden of proof.

“In this case, because of the substantial sum that rests on his own assertion that he will never write again – that should be borne in mind when the court is assessing has he met his burden,” she said.

At the start of the defamation trial, Mr. Galloway and his wife both spoke to how the author of the 2008 international bestseller The Cellist of Sarajevo didn’t even dream of writing again after the allegations created the long-simmering scandal in November 2015.

Ms. Wagner testified her husband’s mental health was brutally impacted and the former chair of Ubc’s creative writing department didn’t even read any more, only listening to audiobooks about history.

Court has previously heard that one expert’s report found the author’s lost income to date and future earnings up to the age of 70 amounted to an estimated $7.1-million, while another pegged that figure at $11.7-million.

A.B.’s lawyers disputed these figures Wednesday, arguing the larger estimate is based off a faulty comparison with the earning potential of bestselling novelist and Governor-General’s Award winner Miriam Toews and the publishing expert used an unrealistic timeline for how often Mr. Galloway would publish new novels.

Mr. Galloway was never charged with a crime but was suspended by UBC when the allegations surfaced in November 2015, creating a media maelstrom.

In 2016, Mary Ellen Boyd, a former Supreme Court justice hired by UBC, found that, ON a balance of probabilities, it could not be established that he committed sexual assault or assault. Ms. Boyd did find that he had sexually harassed A.B., with UBC firing him later that year over breach of trust and other misconduct.

In 2018, Mr. Galloway launched the defamation case against A.B. and two dozen others for repeating the allegations online.

Most of them settled, leaving only his accuser standing trial alongside her supporters Mandi Gray and Glynnis Kirchmeier, and Dana Kagis, who posted a single defamatory statement and has not participated in the legal process.

Mr. Galloway’s lawyers want a judgment of millions of dollars in damages against A.B. for embarking upon what they say was a strategic campaign to leverage criminal accusations of sexual assault and to spread these far and wide through a cast of collaborators.

Mr. Galloway’s counsel told court Tuesday their client deserves a rare award of special damages solely against A.B. amounting to $4.9-million. They are also asking she pay at least $2.5-million in general, aggravated and punitive damages, which – if granted – would total $7.4-million.

The plaintiff is also seeking general, aggravated and punitive damages in the form of at least $250,000 from Dr. Gray, at least $80,000 from Ms. Kirchmeier and $30,000 from Ms. Kagis.

A.B.’s lawyers argued their client did not act maliciously, unlike defendants in other major defamation cases who were found to have engaged in protracted campaigns to sully the reputation of someone else, often by posting on social media or disseminating their libel through mainstream news outlets.

Arden Beddoes, lead counsel for A.B., argued she only ever shared the alleged defamatory statements with fewer than 10 professors, family members and friends, followed the university’s process for reporting alleged misconduct and refrained from posting anything about it on social media or doing traditional media interviews.

Plus, he argued, she specifically held a 2018 art show – which Mr. Galloway also alleges defamed him – in a faraway metropolis where she felt it would make less of an impact on that city’s art scene.

“They’re not the sort of facts that indicate that our client is trying to broadcast this as far as possible and sink the plaintiff’s reputation as much as she possibly can,” he said. “If she was trying to do that, she’d be in front of the [Vancouver] art gallery, a block away.”

The trial continues with closing arguments from the lawyer for Dr. Gray and Ms. Kirchmeier, a law student who is representing herself.

Lawyers for the woman, known in court as A.B. due to a publication ban on her name, wrapped their final submissions in defence of their client who is the major target of Mr. Galloway’s defamation suit.

Mr. Galloway’s legal team, who said he deserves one of the biggest defamation awards in Canadian history, concluded their arguments earlier this week. The trial continues Thursday with more closing arguments.

On Wednesday, A.B.’s lawyer Sydney Gomez told B.C. Supreme Court Justice Neena Sharma that Mr. Galloway’s claims of psychological injury so severe that he cannot write rely solely on assertions from the author and his wife Katie Wagner. Both testified earlier in the trial.

Ms. Gomez argued the court requires more evidence of such harm – such as medical records or the opinion of an expert – to justify Mr. Galloway’s claim to a rare award of special damages. Mr. Galloway is seeking $4.9-million in special damages based largely on future earnings from books he argues he can no longer write.
But Justice Sharma questioned what a psychiatrist or another mental health clinician could say about the plight of such a writer.
“It’s not a mental thing – his loss of the creative spark to write and the desire to put his work out there into the public – is it?” the justice asked defence counsel.
Justice Sharma then asked what type of expert would be sufficient.

“You would have to find a writer and say to them, ‘Imagine you were falsely accused of rape and then there was a national controversy about you. Do you think you could write again?’ You [Ms. Gomez] would stand up and say to me ‘You can’t take that evidence,’” Justice Sharma said.
Ms. Gomez argued that the law says if a plaintiff doesn’t offer expert or similar evidence then they run the risk of not meeting the burden of proof.

“In this case, because of the substantial sum that rests on his own assertion that he will never write again – that should be borne in mind when the court is assessing has he met his burden,” she said.

At the start of the defamation trial, Mr. Galloway and his wife both spoke to how the author of the 2008 international bestseller The Cellist of Sarajevo didn’t even dream of writing again after the allegations created the long-simmering scandal in November 2015.
Ms. Wagner testified her husband’s mental health was brutally impacted and the former chair of Ubc’s creative writing department didn’t even read any more, only listening to audiobooks about history.

Court has previously heard that one expert’s report found the author’s lost income to date and future earnings up to the age of 70 amounted to an estimated $7.1-million, while another pegged that figure at $11.7-million.

A.B.’s lawyers disputed these figures Wednesday, arguing the larger estimate is based off a faulty comparison with the earning potential of bestselling novelist and Governor-General’s Award winner Miriam Toews and the publishing expert used an unrealistic timeline for how often Mr. Galloway would publish new novels.
Mr. Galloway was never charged with a crime but was suspended by UBC when the allegations surfaced in November 2015, creating a media maelstrom.

In 2016, Mary Ellen Boyd, a former Supreme Court justice hired by UBC, found that, ON a balance of probabilities, it could not be established that he committed sexual assault or assault. Ms. Boyd did find that he had sexually harassed A.B., with UBC firing him later that year over breach of trust and other misconduct.
In 2018, Mr. Galloway launched the defamation case against A.B. and two dozen others for repeating the allegations online.

Most of them settled, leaving only his accuser standing trial alongside her supporters Mandi Gray and Glynnis Kirchmeier, and Dana Kagis, who posted a single defamatory statement and has not participated in the legal process.

Mr. Galloway’s lawyers want a judgment of millions of dollars in damages against A.B. for embarking upon what they say was a strategic campaign to leverage criminal accusations of sexual assault and to spread these far and wide through a cast of collaborators.

Mr. Galloway’s counsel told court Tuesday their client deserves a rare award of special damages solely against A.B. amounting to $4.9-million. They are also asking she pay at least $2.5-million in general, aggravated and punitive damages, which – if granted – would total $7.4-million.
The plaintiff is also seeking general, aggravated and punitive damages in the form of at least $250,000 from Dr. Gray, at least $80,000 from Ms. Kirchmeier and $30,000 from Ms. Kagis.

A.B.’s lawyers argued their client did not act maliciously, unlike defendants in other major defamation cases who were found to have engaged in protracted campaigns to sully the reputation of someone else, often by posting on social media or disseminating their libel through mainstream news outlets.

Arden Beddoes, lead counsel for A.B., argued she only ever shared the alleged defamatory statements with fewer than 10 professors, family members and friends, followed the university’s process for reporting alleged misconduct and refrained from posting anything about it on social media or doing traditional media interviews.
Plus, he argued, she specifically held a 2018 art show – which Mr. Galloway also alleges defamed him – in a faraway metropolis where she felt it would make less of an impact on that city’s art scene.

“They’re not the sort of facts that indicate that our client is trying to broadcast this as far as possible and sink the plaintiff’s reputation as much as she possibly can,” he said. “If she was trying to do that, she’d be in front of the [Vancouver] art gallery, a block away.”
The trial continues with closing arguments from the lawyer for Dr. Gray and Ms. Kirchmeier, a law student who is representing herself.

stories.title: Montreal mayor apologizes for Kraft Dinner comment amid tax hike backlash
stories.summary: A Kraft Dinner analogy from Montreal’s mayor is fuelling backlash as residents face a nearly 10 per cent property tax hike and growing affordability pressures.
stories.author: Alessia Simona Maratta, Elizabeth Zogalis
stories.content:
Montreal Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada is walking back comments comparing the city’s financial choices to eating Kraft Dinner instead of filet mignon, calling the analogy “tactless” after it drew criticism amid an ongoing affordability crisis.

“Let’s be honest, it was pretty tactless,” Martinez Ferrada said in a short social media post Wednesday.

“What I meant was that when a city makes choices, it’s the same as when you make personal choices,” she said. “In this instance, the city has to choose between paying for new parks or filling potholes, and I’m going to choose filling potholes.”

The clarification came after remarks Martinez Ferrada made during a recent interview with Quatre95, an Urbania platform focused on personal finance.

Asked how she intends to increase the city’s revenue, the mayor said she would go through each department to determine where savings could be found.

“It’s just like when you’re putting together your personal budget: If you know you’re going to have less money next year, well, you have to make some choices,” she said.

“Let’s be honest, maybe sometimes we’ll eat a little more Kraft Dinner because we can’t afford filet mignon,” she said.

The comparison quickly drew criticism as Montrealers face a 9.8 per cent average residential property tax increase under the city’s proposed 2027 budget, amounting to an additional $515 per household.

The official opposition at city hall, Projet Montréal, also seized on the remarks.

Organizations working with people experiencing food insecurity say the mayor’s analogy does not reflect the choices many Montrealers are already being forced to make.

“What we see on a daily basis is people struggling to put food on the table,” said Suzanne Scarrow, director general of the West Island Mission. “They are already making choices between this and that.”

Food banks are also seeing a shift in the people seeking assistance, including more people with jobs or other sources of income.

“We’re really seeing an uptick in people, especially people who are employed or who have other sources of income, still not being able to meet their needs,” said Sosena Tilahun, philanthropy lead at the NDG Depot.

Tilahun said food insecurity is an issue of affordability rather than people failing to make smart financial choices.

“It’s not the reality that folks are facing. It’s not an issue where it comes to smarter decisions, it’s an issue when it comes to how much money you have to be able to make those decisions,” she said.

Scarrow said the city should speak with organizations that work directly with people experiencing poverty and homelessness as it considers the impact of its decisions.

“The city needs to sit down and potentially talk to senior leaders in organizations that deal with homelessness and deal with poverty and figure out what the relief looks like,” she said.

With the holidays approaching, Tilahun also urged people donating to food banks to consider the quality and nutritional value of what they give.

“Generally when you’re giving I would recommend to give the same quality that you would like to receive,” she said.

A protest called “Soraya Dinner” is planned for Thursday at 1 p.m. outside city hall. A digital flyer for the event invites participants to bring pots, portable stoves and ingredients.

stories.title: Ukrainians in Canada wait for permanent residency as calls grow for more pathways
stories.summary: The Ukrainian-Canadian Congress in B.C. is urging Ottawa to create additional pathways for permanent residency for those who don't have Canadian family connections.
stories.author: Klaudia Van Emmerik
stories.content:
Alina Bohomolova and her 16-year-old son Dima are grateful to call Canada home, at least for now.

“It’s safe for us, for me and my son,” Bohomolova said.

The pair escaped war-torn Ukraine and came to the Okanagan in 2023.

They are among the hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians who came to Canada under the Canada-Ukraine Authorization for Emergency Travel (Cuaet) program after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

But many who remain in Canada are still waiting for permanent residency years after applying.

“It’s stressful for me. We are thinking about this every day,” Bohomolova said. “It’s hard to make plans if I don’t know if I will be able to stay.”

Despite the uncertainty, the West Kelowna single mom has built her own cleaning business while her son has settled into school, taken on a part-time job and joined a local soccer club.

Now the family has reason for hope.

The federal government plans to fast-track nearly 19,000 permanent residency applications from Ukrainians under the family reunification pathway.

Bohomolova qualifies because her father is a Canadian citizen.

“I hope we have answers soon,” she said. “It’s my dream.”

But the announcement does not address the situation facing many other Ukrainians, who don’t qualify through family reunification.

While the exact number is unknown, federal immigration figures indicate roughly 300,000 Ukrainians arrived in Canada under the Cuaet program. Roughly half are still believed to be in the country.

The Ukrainian-Canadian Congress in B.C. is urging Ottawa to create additional pathways for permanent residency for those who don’t have Canadian family connections.

“The only way to get a permanent residency is going through the humanitarian program, which May take up to 10 years, ” said Iryna Shyroka, president of the Ukrainian-Canadian Congress, B.C. Provincial Council. “This is very unsettling.”

Shyroka added that Ukrainians have been contributing members of society since arriving in Canada.

“For the last five years, the Ukrainians, displaced people, have contributed into the Canadian society economics. You know, by paying taxes, working, opening their own businesses,” Shyroka said.

Advocacy work continues, with Shyroka hoping that in addition to extending Cuaet visas, a permanent solution is found.

“Russia is still shelling Ukrainian cities, destroying houses, killing people, and that’s the problem. Ukrainians in Canada they have nowhere to come back to…they are trying to find any ways in Canada to stay here permanently,” Shyroka said.

Global News requested information from Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada on whether it plans to create additional permanent residency pathways, but it did not respond by publication time.

For Bohomolova, the hope is that her permanent residency application will be approved sometime in 2027.

“Thank you to Canadian people and Canadian Government for taking a chance on Ukrainians,” Bohomolova said.

The federal government plans to fast-track nearly 19,000 permanent residency applications from Ukrainians under the family reunification pathway.
Bohomolova qualifies because her father is a Canadian citizen.

The Ukrainian-Canadian Congress in B.C. is urging Ottawa to create additional pathways for permanent residency for those who don’t have Canadian family connections.

“The only way to get a permanent residency is going through the humanitarian program, which May take up to 10 years, ” said Iryna Shyroka, president of the Ukrainian-Canadian Congress, B.C. Provincial Council. “This is very unsettling.”
Shyroka added that Ukrainians have been contributing members of society since arriving in Canada.
“For the last five years, the Ukrainians, displaced people, have contributed into the Canadian society economics. You know, by paying taxes, working, opening their own businesses,” Shyroka said.
Advocacy work continues, with Shyroka hoping that in addition to extending Cuaet visas, a permanent solution is found.

“Russia is still shelling Ukrainian cities, destroying houses, killing people, and that’s the problem. Ukrainians in Canada they have nowhere to come back to…they are trying to find any ways in Canada to stay here permanently,” Shyroka said.
Global News requested information from Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada on whether it plans to create additional permanent residency pathways, but it did not respond by publication time.
For Bohomolova, the hope is that her permanent residency application will be approved sometime in 2027.
“Thank you to Canadian people and Canadian Government for taking a chance on Ukrainians,” Bohomolova said.

stories.title: Pierre Poilievre says Alberta nurse May lose job after photo with him in Wainwright
stories.summary: Pierre Poilievre said a nurse working on contract at the CFB Wainwright has been told she might lose her job after she was photographed speaking with him after the tragedy.
stories.author: Catherine Morrison
stories.content:
Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said a nurse working on contract at the CFB Wainwright has been told she might lose her job after she was photographed speaking with him in the aftermath of the tragedy.

Five soldiers were killed and dozens injured in a fire that suddenly overtook a training area on the central Alberta military base on Oct. 17.

Poilievre’s new Alberta riding includes Wainwright, about two hours southeast of Edmonton, and he spent several days in the area following the fire, including meeting with first responders who aided the victims.

Poilievre rose on a point of privilege in the House of Commons Wednesday insisting his privilege as a member of Parliament has been breached over the incident.

He said he met with a nurse, Maureen Carpenter, who works both at the Wainwright hospital and on contract with Calian Health, who talked to him with permission about her experience following the fire, when she helped treat and triage badly burned patients.

Thirty-nine people were injured in the fire, 19 of them critically.

Poilievre said it has since been “intimated” to her that because she was photographed with him that her Calian contract won’t be renewed.

“The implicit message was that her contract would no longer have any chance of renewal, something that she had taken for granted before that point,” he said. “Other work opportunities which were also expected to follow have since vanished.”

“Simply put, it appears she is losing her chance to continue her work at CFB Wainwright because she met with her local MP.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "Simply put, it appears she is losing her chance to continue her work at CFB Wainwright because she met with her local MP."

Poilievre said the situation means he can’t properly do his job.

“If the people cannot speak to us, we cannot speak for them,” he said. “By threatening and imposing consequences on Maureen for speaking with me, the government’s contractor Calian is effectively interfering with my duties as member of Parliament for Battle River—Crowfoot.”

Poilievre said the nurse has appealed the reprimands and asked for an apology but that her actions have been met with “nothing but silence.”

Poilievre said he contacted National Defence Minister David McGuinty after hearing about the situation but that since then “the problems have only gotten worse.”

“I truly tried to resolve this quietly. It was certainly not my intention to ever have this rise to the floor of the House of Commons,” said Poilievre.

“I believed in sharing it with the minister and with Maureen’s family doing the same with his office that this would be resolved by now, but it has now been a month.”

The Canadian Press has reached out to Ottawa-based Calian Health and McGuinty’s office for comment but has yet to receive a response.

Kevin Lamoureux, Liberal MP and parliamentary secretary to the leader of the government in the House of Commons, said the government has and will continue to be there for members of the Canadian Armed Forces.

“I find it very upsetting to hear the comments with regards to Maureen,” he said. “We recognize the sacrifices and the emotions and the service that was provided by health care professionals, by first responders.”

“I appreciate the member raising it, and I will report back, Mr. Speaker, once we’ve had the opportunity to look a little bit deeper into the situation.”

Deputy Speaker Tom Kmiec, who was presiding over the House Wednesday during Poilievre’s point of privilege, said Speaker Francis Scarpaleggia would return to make a complete ruling.

Bloc Québécois MP Gabriel Ste-Marie said his party would also look into the issue and get back to the House “soon.”

stories.title: Bird advocates press case against Pelee Island tower
stories.summary: Margaret Atwood and other opponents are calling for a federal environmental assessment of the project, which would sit in the path of migrating songbirds
stories.author: Ivan Semeniuk
stories.content:
Flanked by board members of the Pelee Island Bird Observatory, Margaret Atwood was unequivocal on Wednesday in her opposition to a 182-metre-tall radio tower that a U.S. company aims to build directly in the path of migrating songbirds.

“It’s a horrible idea,” said the celebrated author during an online press briefing organized by the observatory, which she co-founded more than 20 years ago. “Everywhere that I’ve travelled recently, people know about this and have said, ‘Can you stop it?’”

Stopping the tower’s construction on the 40-square-kilometre Lake Erie isle in Southwestern Ontario is precisely what the observatory’s board and its supporters say they have in mind.

The organization has called for a federal environmental assessment of the project for which it marshalled more than 27,000 letters of support ahead of a deadline for public comment last week.

Those objecting to the tower include residents, scientists and the Caldwell First Nation, which considers Pelee Island as part of its traditional territory. At the briefing, Chief Nikki van Oirschot said the First Nation had yet to be contacted by the municipality or the proponent of the project, Chicago-based DRW NX Co.

The company plans to erect a tower on Pelee Island as early as next spring. The tower’s purpose would be to facilitate line-of-site microwave transmission of stock trading data en route to financial communication hubs in New Jersey. This would provide Drw’s clients with an advantage – measured in milliseconds – over those who depend on information moving through fibre-optic cables.

The island’s township council quietly approved the tower last year, though many of the island’s residents say they only became aware of it recently.

Many details have not been disclosed, including the rent the township will receive for leasing public land for the project.

What is clear is that the proposed height of the tower would be immense – equivalent to the north building of Toronto’s TD Centre, which has 46 floors. Its design – including 16 support cables, or guy wires – would pose a hazard at altitudes that are common for migrating songbirds, which typically move at night. The presence of lights on the tower would be an additional problem because they can confuse birds and cause them to circle the structure.

“Estimates suggest that communication towers in Canada and the United States alone kill about 6.8 million birds per year,” said Dan Mennill, an ornithologist and professor at the University of Windsor who participated in the Wednesday briefing.

Dr. Mennill added that his own work suggests the concentration of migrating birds above Pelee Island is about three times that in neighbouring locations.

Alice Boyle, a researcher at the University of Western Ontario in London, Ont., who was not a participant in the briefing, said it would be hard to overstate how important Pelee Island is as the neck of a geographic funnel that a large fraction of North America’s birds pass through on their way to and from Canada each year.

“I can’t believe that the interests of a few people with no benefit to Canada are taking precedence over such an important biological, cultural and economic thing,” she said.

In a statement, Drw’s chief marketing and communications officer, Caroline Vasquez, said the company shares “the community’s commitment to protecting migratory birds and the island’s environment.” She added that DRW would also voluntarily install “best-in-class bird collision mitigation technologies” on the tower.

However, an environment study commissioned by DRW did not consider the effect of bird collisions and site visits conducted for the study did not take place during spring or fall migration.

Critics of the project have also noted that the location of the tower would affect critical habitat for some of the island’s rare and threatened reptiles, including the blue racer, a snake species that occurs nowhere else in Canada.

The bird observatory board has filed a freedom of information request to access details of the township’s dealings with DRW and this week sent additional follow-up questions on the matter. The group has also asked for the tower to be on the agenda when a newly elected township council holds its first public meeting next month.

“This is the wrong place for this tower. Our regulatory systems should have recognized that before this project reached this point, and we still have an opportunity to get it right,” said Deborah Egan, who chairs the observatory board.

A key question will be whether three new members of the five-person council will be less supportive of the project than their predecessors.

Rebecca Kandola, who heads the Pelee Island Property Owners Association, said that she is in the process of surveying owners to learn more about their views.

A high number don’t support the tower, she said, and did not learn about it until after the township’s letter of concurrence, the document which allows DRW to proceed.

She said that some owners are in favour of the tower because of the revenue it could generate. There are also worries that a tower could simply be placed on private land if the council reverses its decision.

Many residents have expressed their desire to see an island-wide policy for towers, something that the previous council voted down twice.

Meanwhile the federal government must decide by Jan. 19 if it will require its own assessment before the project can proceed.

During the Wednesday briefing, Ms. Atwood – who is also a property owner on the island – said that she and the observatory board would continue to advocate for a rethink of the DRW tower before construction begins.

“We will keep going and we will see what happens, and I hope that what happens will be the right thing,” she said.

stories.title: London Abused Women’s Centre collecting holiday donations to support women and children
stories.summary: From ‘Gift Guides’ to social media ‘Influencer Store Fronts’, the options of what to buy your loved ones for the holidays seem endless, but that isn’t the case for everyone.
stories.author: Lauren Stallone
stories.content:
From ‘Gift Guides’ to social media ‘Influencer Store Fronts’, the options of what to buy your loved ones for the holidays seem endless, but that isn’t the case for everyone.

“There are a lot of people in our community that are less fortunate,” said Jennifer Dunn, executive director of the London Abused Women’s Centre (Lawc).

“There are people that are living below the poverty line.”

According to the Canadian Women’s Foundation, 10 per cent of women in our country live on low incomes. Those who face barriers are at a higher risk of poverty including racialized women, those with disabilities, and single mothers.

“When women come to our centre they’re probably going through what could be the most difficult time in their lives,” said Dunn.

“The last thing on their mind is providing for Christmas.”

Dunn said every year they collect donations to create a “Holiday Room”.

Last year the program supported 76 women and 103 children.

“It’s essentially a set up like a store, where women can go in and pick out a gift for themselves and for their children,” said Dunn.

“Sometimes the children will even pick out gifts for their moms.”

Dunn said donations from the community are essential.

“Typically, donations of new, unwrapped toys and gifts for women who are accessing our services,” said Dunn.

Jane Piper, a peer-support worker at Lawc knows how hard the holidays can be.

“I am a survivor myself; I have lived experience, it’s been many years but when i was going through the darkest times that I experienced the holidays were really difficult,” said Piper.

“I would have loved to have something like this to access and just feel cared for.”

The call for donations comes on the International Day for the Elimination of Violence Against Women and the first day of the 16 days of activism.

“For the next 16 days, we will continue to raise awareness of gender-based violence,” said Dunn.

“As well as violence against women.”

The full holiday wish list can be found on Amazon .

stories.title: Ontario teacher who wore oversized prosthetic breasts awarded $20,000 in discrimination case
stories.summary: A letter sent to families ahead of Kerry Lemieux’s return to school violated his right to protection from discrimination based on gender identity and gender expression, arbitrator ruled
stories.author: Sharon Kirkey
stories.content:
An Ontario teacher who identifies as “gender fluid” and who wore oversized prosthetic breasts to class, garnering worldwide media attention, has been awarded $20,000 by an arbitrator who ruled the school board effectively outed him.

A letter sent to families ahead of Kerry Lemieux’s return to school violated his right to protection from discrimination based on gender identity and gender expression under the Ontario Human Rights Code, arbitrator Mike Hart wrote in a labour arbitration decision dated Nov. 19.

Protests and bomb scares broke out after the letter was reported by the media.

While it didn’t expressly name Lemieux, it was “blatantly obvious” who the board was referring to, Hart wrote.

Lemieux self-identifies as gender fluid and first began to present as a female in the spring of 2022, Hart wrote.

He’d been employed full-time at the Hamilton-Wentworth District School Board since 2007. He took an unpaid leave for the 2022-23 school year, working part time at a high school in the Halton District School Board.

It was while working for the Halton board that Lemieux began presenting as female “in the professional sphere,” Hart wrote. “He went by a female name and wore women’s clothing,” Hart wrote. (The decision uses male pronouns.)

Lemieux was teaching at an Oakville high school in late 2022 when images of the teacher wearing large prosthetic breasts with protruding nipples and a blonde wig during a shop class went viral on social media.

His “gender identity, style of dress and body attracted worldwide media attention that was overwhelmingly negative in nature,” the arbitrator said.

The high school began receiving bomb threats. In February 2023, Lemieux was placed on paid leave.

In May of that year, he began applying for job postings, but decided “after much reflection” to return to his old school board presenting as a male and “hoping that he would be able to avoid future unwanted attention and public scrutiny,” Hart wrote.

Lemieux feared the bomb threats wouldn’t stop “unless he ceased to present as a woman” and hoped the new school year “would be a fresh start and a return to a quiet, private life.”

“This, regrettably, was not to be,” Hart wrote. After media were tipped the teacher would be returning to classes in September 2023, the school began receiving “troubling messages” and “hateful emails.”

A school crisis response team was set up and “the Team” met weekly throughout the summer developing “pre-emptive” safety measures, including designated entry and exit locations, locked exterior doors and advance notice of parents or visitors on site.

Days before the new school year began, the school board sent a letter to families cautioning them.

“We are writing to you today because we anticipate the school year your child is attending this year …. May receive some level of public attention, and we want to communicate what this means for you, your children and our school.”

It goes on to say that an “experienced educator” who would be teaching at the school “was recently the subject of public attention, pertaining to their gender expression” at a school in a different community.

Lemieux had earlier told school officials that he didn’t believe the board owed the community an explanation, Hart said. He’s had “no allegations or convictions of any type of wrongdoing, hasn’t faced any type of discipline and hasn’t been reprimanded or investigated by the Ontario College of Teachers,” Hart said.

While Hart found it “entirely appropriate” for the board to communicate with families about the new security measures, “What is less clear to me is why the Board felt it necessary to identify (Lemieux) in the way it did,” he said in his decision.

The usual approach in such circumstances “is to simply say that, for reasons of privacy and confidentiality, information as to specifically why these security measures are required at this specific time can’t be shared.”

Hart said it would be “unthinkable” if the situation involved an abusive spouse of a school staff member.

The board had hoped the letter to parents would help “turn down the volume” and that the controversy would eventually fall out of the news cycle.

“As it turned out, nothing could be further from the truth,” Hart wrote.

His ‘gender identity, style of dress and body attracted worldwide media attention that was overwhelmingly negative in nature’

When school resumed in September 2023, Lemieux faced reporters outside the school and at his condominium, including reporters from the New York Post and the U.S. edition of the Daily Mail, a U.K. publication. There were protests in front of the school and people in the school parking trying to take pictures of him. He was targeted by bomb threats. The school received bomb threats that spread to other schools within the board — “upwards of 20” that September connected to Lemieux, Hart wrote.

Hart said “there can be no doubt” the letter to families made Lemieux identifiable to anyone who had been following the story.

This “outing” and the naming of the school where he would be teaching, amounted to a violation of Lemieux’s right to protection against discrimination on the basis of gender identity and gender expression under the Ontario Human Rights Code, the arbitrator wrote in awarding $20,000 in general damages for “the additional media and public scrutiny and response” to which Lemieux was exposed.

The code isn’t restricted to extending human rights protection to transgender persons, “but extends further to all persons who don’t conform to gender stereotypes,” Hart wrote.

“This includes a person like the Grievor who self-identifies and who lives out his self-identification as gender fluid.”

The letter to parents also “materially increased the risk to his safety,” in violation of the province’s Occupational Health and Safety Act, Hart wrote.

Lemieux’s union, the Ontario Secondary School Teachers’ Federation, filed the grievance on his behalf, seeking $75,000 in damages.

Sharon Kirkey is a national reporter with National Post focusing on health and science stories. She is also a three-time National Newspaper Awards nominee, with a win for beat reporting.

Hart said it would be “unthinkable” if the situation involved an abusive spouse of a school staff member.
The board had hoped the letter to parents would help “turn down the volume” and that the controversy would eventually fall out of the news cycle.
“As it turned out, nothing could be further from the truth,” Hart wrote.
His ‘gender identity, style of dress and body attracted worldwide media attention that was overwhelmingly negative in nature’

When school resumed in September 2023, Lemieux faced reporters outside the school and at his condominium, including reporters from the New York Post and the U.S. edition of the Daily Mail, a U.K. publication. There were protests in front of the school and people in the school parking trying to take pictures of him. He was targeted by bomb threats. The school received bomb threats that spread to other schools within the board — “upwards of 20” that September connected to Lemieux, Hart wrote.
Hart said “there can be no doubt” the letter to families made Lemieux identifiable to anyone who had been following the story.

This “outing” and the naming of the school where he would be teaching, amounted to a violation of Lemieux’s right to protection against discrimination on the basis of gender identity and gender expression under the Ontario Human Rights Code, the arbitrator wrote in awarding $20,000 in general damages for “the additional media and public scrutiny and response” to which Lemieux was exposed.
The code isn’t restricted to extending human rights protection to transgender persons, “but extends further to all persons who don’t conform to gender stereotypes,” Hart wrote.
“This includes a person like the Grievor who self-identifies and who lives out his self-identification as gender fluid.”
The letter to parents also “materially increased the risk to his safety,” in violation of the province’s Occupational Health and Safety Act, Hart wrote.
Lemieux’s union, the Ontario Secondary School Teachers’ Federation, filed the grievance on his behalf, seeking $75,000 in damages.

Premier Lorne Doerskon speaks after he and his cabinet were sworn in Friday, Nov. 20, 2026. (Darren Stone / Victoria Times Colonist)

November 25, 2026 at 6:38 p.m.

B.C.s new provincial cabinet ministers have received their marching orders in mandate letters from Premier Lorne Doerkson.

The new Conservative government aims to make the province more affordable, as well as cut the deficit and health-care wait times. Meanwhile, it plans to end the “safe supply” approach to drug abuse, provide protection against coercion in making Maid decisions, and follow through on a campaign promise to ensure O Canada is sung every day in B.C. schools.

It will also repeal the Ndp’s controversial Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act (Dripa) and key environmental legislation.

Doerkson’s cabinet was sworn in at the end of last week. The mandate letters are formal expressions of several of the promises that the Conservatives made during the recent election campaign.

“British Columbians voted for change, and our government is getting to work delivering it,” Doerkson said in a statement that accompanied the release of the mandate letters on Tuesday. “These mandate letters make clear what British Columbians expect each minister to accomplish.

Here are some of the mandate letter highlights for key cabinet portfolios.

This mandate letteris where the intention to repeal Dripa (Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act) and section 8.1 of the Interpretation Act is announced.

As previously commented on extensively by National Post, adoption of Dripa by Ottawa and the B.C. government was followed by the controversial B.C. Supreme Court decision, Cowichan Tribes v. Canada, involving private lands in Richmond, B.C. The court declared government and City of Richmond land titles “defective and invalid” and Indigenous claims to be superior.

The mandate letter also promises the introduction of a new Property Rights Defence Act, aimed at protecting private property rights and upholding the validity of B.C.’s land title system. Added is a plan to repeal the previous government’s Crown litigation directives concerning Aboriginal title and property rights.

The Doerkson government plans to introduce legislation to repeal CleanBC and associated regulatory requirements, as well as reform the environmental assessment process to ensure that assessments finish on time while protecting the public interest, environment and safety.

The zero-emission vehicle sales quota will also be ended to “restore the ability of British Columbians to choose the vehicle that best meets their family and work needs.”

The public safety minister has been directed to work with the ministers of health and social development “to end the ‘safe supply’ approach to drug use.” The minister has also been directed to “expand drug courts” and “stop forcing drug-friendly facilities on communities.”

The government aims to “stop the revolving door for repeat and violent offenders” by establishing “a dedicated repeat-offender court stream.” It’s looking to add to policing capacity, with 250 more police recruits, 500 more RCMP officers, 30 sheriffs and 150 civilian staff over five years.

As previously reported by National Post, Doerkson wants his new education minister to “restore daily singing of O Canada” every day in B.C. schools. He also wants the restoration of letter grades for Grades 4–9, supervised provincial exams, the return of shop classes and expansion of apprenticeships.

Frequent closures of rural emergency rooms have been an issue in B.C. The Conservative government aims to ensure they and maternity wards stay open “backed by flexible staffing” and a $50 million Rural Health Emergency Fund.

It is also looking to expand long-term, palliative, and respite care and help seniors age at home. The ministry has been directed to “strengthen safeguards against coercion in Maid decisions and protect patient choice.”

The finance minister is to “immediately appoint an independent panel to review the province’s true fiscal position and report its findings publicly, as well as bring government staffing “back in line with the population it serves … while ensuring frontline workers are protected.”

Stewart Lewis is a writer and editor with National Post. A journalist and lawyer, he has worked in newspapers, radio and TV, and served a legal stint with Global Affairs Canada at the United Nations in New York City.

'She orchestrated lies to support the lies, and she knew she was doing it.' — Steven Galloway’s lawyer, referring to the author’s accuser

Navigate

David suggested it is highly unlikely that MNAs will be able to take their seats on Dec. 1 as expected.

Lawrence David, constitutional litigator and founder and president of the Public Interest Litigation Institute, holds a press conference on Parliament Hill on Nov. 25, 2026. (Blair Gable / Postmedia)

Catherine Lévesque

November 25, 2026 at 6:36 p.m.

Ottawa — Constitutional lawyer Lawrence David said he wishes he didn’t have to take it upon himself to force Quebec legislators to respect the Canadian Constitution and force them to take an oath to King Charles III.

But if not him, then who?

“Unfortunately, it’s a path where, if one stays passive and permissive, like the Government of Canada, what does that breed? Additional encroachments, additional abuses, additional excesses,” he told National Post on Wednesday.

David has become the Parti Québécois government’s nemesis ever since he and his organization, the Public Interest Litigation Institute, successfully managed to suspend a 2022 law voted by Quebec’s national assembly to make the oath to the King optional.

The decision made public by the Quebec Superior Court on Monday has thrown the governing party into chaos as they are expected to bring back the legislature next week.

Quebec Minister of Justice Marie-Claude Sarrazin expressed surprise that the opposition to the 2022 law was coming from a resident outside her province.

“Before a constitutional law professor from Ontario asked a court to break the Quebec consensus, no one was complaining about it,” she told reporters in Quebec City.

David, who was born and raised in Montreal but now works as a professor at the University of Ottawa’s faculty of law, is not worried about playing into the PQ government’s hands by sparking a constitutional crisis that could promote the idea of independence.

David said there is no point in tiptoeing around the issues when there is what he called “widespread, systematic, unacceptable attacks on the integrity of the judicial system.”

“At the end of the day, the rule of law has to prevail, and also, we have gotten at a point where the abuses are so severe, flagrant, and frankly embarrassing that it would be a mockery to our entire system for no one to do anything,” he said.

“But I wish I didn’t have to take on these things myself,” he added.

Bloc Québécois Leader Yves-François Blanchet thinks the University of Ottawa professor is being deliberately provocative because he is enjoying the spotlight.

“He has just discovered that he could be a TV star,” said Blanchet.

The federal government has decided to stay far away from the issue.

Sarrazin noted that Ottawa did not say a peep about Quebec’s attempt to unilaterally change the Constitution when it happened four years ago, nor did the attorney general of Canada participate in the judicial hearings that led to the suspension of the law.

That trend continued this week with federal ministers doing their best to keep quiet about the oath to the King.

“In my view, this is an issue that began in Quebec, and that will have to be resolved in Quebec,” said Gatineau MP and Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon.

Joël Lightbound, who is the prime minister’s Quebec lieutenant, said the matter was before the courts and that he would be following future developments with interest.

“Like many Quebecers, my hope is that the national assembly will be able to sit.”

All 127 MNAs have sworn an oath to the “people of Quebec” but, now that the law that allowed them to do that has been suspended by the courts, they would have to be sworn-in again, with an allegiance to the King, for them to sit next Tuesday as planned.

Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon and his government have already made it clear it is out of the question for them to do that. So, his government reached out to the Quebec Court of Appeal to attempt to reverse the suspension of the law.

On Wednesday, St-Pierre Plamondon sent a letter to the other party leaders in Quebec asking them to co-sign a declaration of intent to start the legislature as planned.

But two opposition parties — the Quebec Liberals and the Quebec Conservatives — said they could not sign the letter as they are not willing to defy an order of the court.

“We won’t be getting involved in a circus,” Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime said.

The cause will be heard at the Quebec Court of Appeal on Friday, with provincial attorneys seeking to reverse the immediate suspension of the 2022 law as ordered by the Quebec Superior Court so that the MNAs will be able to take their seats legally.

In parallel, the Quebec Liberals are attempting to gain clarity from the outgoing president of the national assembly, Nathalie Roy, ON whether the will of the legislature as expressed by the 2022 law supersedes the court order on the oath to the King.

But given that permission to appeal isn’t automatic and that Roy would be reversing her own decision taken four years ago on the matter, David suggested on Wednesday it is highly unlikely that MNAs will be able to take their seats on Dec. 1 as expected.

That would leave St-Pierre Plamondon with the choice of defying the court order or further postponing the return of the legislature.

Catherine Lévesque covers federal-Quebec relations for National Post. She joined the parliamentary bureau in Ottawa in 2022, after a decade spent in French media in Montreal, Quebec City and Ottawa.

“Before a constitutional law professor from Ontario asked a court to break the Quebec consensus, no one was complaining about it,” she told reporters in Quebec City.

David, who was born and raised in Montreal but now works as a professor at the University of Ottawa’s faculty of law, is not worried about playing into the PQ government’s hands by sparking a constitutional crisis that could promote the idea of independence.
David said there is no point in tiptoeing around the issues when there is what he called “widespread, systematic, unacceptable attacks on the integrity of the judicial system.”

“At the end of the day, the rule of law has to prevail, and also, we have gotten at a point where the abuses are so severe, flagrant, and frankly embarrassing that it would be a mockery to our entire system for no one to do anything,” he said.
“But I wish I didn’t have to take on these things myself,” he added.
Bloc Québécois Leader Yves-François Blanchet thinks the University of Ottawa professor is being deliberately provocative because he is enjoying the spotlight.
“He has just discovered that he could be a TV star,” said Blanchet.
The federal government has decided to stay far away from the issue.

Sarrazin noted that Ottawa did not say a peep about Quebec’s attempt to unilaterally change the Constitution when it happened four years ago, nor did the attorney general of Canada participate in the judicial hearings that led to the suspension of the law.
That trend continued this week with federal ministers doing their best to keep quiet about the oath to the King.
“In my view, this is an issue that began in Quebec, and that will have to be resolved in Quebec,” said Gatineau MP and Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon.
Joël Lightbound, who is the prime minister’s Quebec lieutenant, said the matter was before the courts and that he would be following future developments with interest.
“Like many Quebecers, my hope is that the national assembly will be able to sit.”

All 127 MNAs have sworn an oath to the “people of Quebec” but, now that the law that allowed them to do that has been suspended by the courts, they would have to be sworn-in again, with an allegiance to the King, for them to sit next Tuesday as planned.

Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon and his government have already made it clear it is out of the question for them to do that. So, his government reached out to the Quebec Court of Appeal to attempt to reverse the suspension of the law.
On Wednesday, St-Pierre Plamondon sent a letter to the other party leaders in Quebec asking them to co-sign a declaration of intent to start the legislature as planned.
But two opposition parties — the Quebec Liberals and the Quebec Conservatives — said they could not sign the letter as they are not willing to defy an order of the court.
“We won’t be getting involved in a circus,” Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime said.

The cause will be heard at the Quebec Court of Appeal on Friday, with provincial attorneys seeking to reverse the immediate suspension of the 2022 law as ordered by the Quebec Superior Court so that the MNAs will be able to take their seats legally.

In parallel, the Quebec Liberals are attempting to gain clarity from the outgoing president of the national assembly, Nathalie Roy, ON whether the will of the legislature as expressed by the 2022 law supersedes the court order on the oath to the King.

But given that permission to appeal isn’t automatic and that Roy would be reversing her own decision taken four years ago on the matter, David suggested on Wednesday it is highly unlikely that MNAs will be able to take their seats on Dec. 1 as expected.
That would leave St-Pierre Plamondon with the choice of defying the court order or further postponing the return of the legislature.
Catherine Lévesque covers federal-Quebec relations for National Post. She joined the parliamentary bureau in Ottawa in 2022, after a decade spent in French media in Montreal, Quebec City and Ottawa.
