stories.title: London mayor pledges city support as province considers suspending property tax exemption for affordable housing
stories.summary: London Mayor Josh Morgan pledged the city will take steps to safeguard affordable housing initiatives, vowing to ensure property tax breaks remain in place for crucial projects despite a proposed provincial change that could suspend such exemptions starting in 2027.
stories.author: Gerry Dewan
stories.content:
London Mayor Josh Morgan pledged the city will take steps to safeguard affordable housing initiatives, vowing to ensure property tax breaks remain in place for crucial projects despite a proposed provincial change that could suspend such exemptions starting in 2027.

The move has ignited widespread concern among non-profit housing developers across Ontario, who fear the suspension could halt the creation of much-needed affordable units and financially jeopardize their operations.

The provincial government, as part of its Fall Economic Statement delivered in late October, introduced an amendment to the Assessment Act. The change proposed in Bill 143, the “Plan to Protect Ontario Act (Budget Measures), 2026 (No. 2),” would suspend a vital property tax exemption for not-for-profit rental housing projects applying for it from 2027 onwards.

For organizations like Residenza Affordable Housing, the tax exemption is critical to their mission. Roger Caranci, President of Residenza, whose group is currently building its third affordable housing project, Residenza Victoria, at the corner of Colbourne and South Street, explained the direct impact.

“Monies that we save on paying property taxes goes right back into the building in terms of keeping the rents lower and helping leverage any equities that we have within those buildings to build another project,” Caranci stated.

He emphasized that his organization is “100 per cent volunteer.”

Caranci further warned that even a temporary financial strain would be devastating.

“The province has said, ‘well, you guys pay taxes for a year and we’ll figure this out.’ Well, even a year would be detrimental to our expenses, to our books. We wouldn’t be able to afford it,” he said, adding that having to pay property taxes would likely stall or cancel many projects.

Residenza Affordable Housing is among 24 not-for-profit agencies that have collectively voiced their opposition to the provincial proposal through a letter submitted by the law firm Cohen Highley LLP. Katelyn Schoffer, a lawyer with Cohen Highley specializing in multi-residential housing law, cautioned that the proposed change could have “widespread” consequences.

“The result is we are going to see a stoppage in the development of affordable housing in Ontario,” Schoffer noted.

She highlighted that property taxes can represent “approximately one-third of an affordable housing provider’s operating costs,” making the loss of an exemption financially devastating for organizations operating on narrow margins. While projects already granted the exemption are grandfathered, many currently in development, with contracts signed and preliminary work underway, face significant risk.

Mayor Josh Morgan underscored the importance of these developments, citing projects like the Doorways to Dreams development on Dundas Street, which aims to provide housing for refugees and new Canadians.

“Stability and predictability are key in any business venture,” Morgan stated.

“Uncertainty is what puts you on your heels.”

He asserted that the city “will ensure the property tax break remains in place” for such initiatives, recognizing the ongoing need for affordable options for thousands of Londoners struggling with homelessness or on the verge of it.

However, Morgan also expressed a preference for a unified provincial approach. He believes the most effective strategy is for the province to coordinate rules around property tax relief rather than having a hodgepodge that comes with every municipality creating their own solutions.

The Ministry of Finance, in a statement from Senior Media Relations Advisor Scott Blodgett, described the proposed change as a “temporary pause on the implications of court decisions” designed to allow for consultations with affordable housing providers and municipalities.

The ministry confirmed that properties already exempt would maintain their status during this pause and suggested providers explore “other tax relief options through their municipality,” also referencing an existing “Affordable Rental Housing Subclass” that offers municipalities the option to reduce property taxes by up to 35 percent.

The bill has passed its second reading and is currently before the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs, leaving a limited window for potential amendments.

stories.title: Stage diva Dawn Greenhalgh was the brash matriarch of a Canadian theatrical dynasty
stories.summary: She was detained with her family in a Japanese camp during the Second World War, and when she saw a play mounted by fellow inmates, ‘theatre became like a religion’ to her
stories.author: Brad Wheeler
stories.content:
Dawn Greenhalgh’s parents were British subjects living well in Shanghai in the 1930s. The father of the future actor was a civil engineer who helped maintain the cosmopolitan city’s waterworks. The family wasn’t wealthy but they belonged to clubs, and with membership (and British citizenship) came privileges.

When life handed them lemons, they made gin and tonics.

Things began to go sour when Japanese forces invaded China in 1937. The situation worsened after the invasion of Pearl Harbor four years later. Japanese authorities looted China and controlled Shanghai, going door to door to earmark expensive possessions to be confiscated in the name of Emperor Hirohito.

Young Ms. Greenhalgh was cheeky. When the Japanese made it to her house, the child defiantly played the patriotic anthem There’ll Always Be an England on the piano as they entered the home.

“Though worlds May change and go awry …"

Her world went drastically awry when the family was held in a Japanese internment camp in a former university dormitory outside Shanghai for three years. In 1944, the adult inmates mounted a play, The Challenge . The performance changed her life.

“Theatre became like a religion to me,” she told The Globe and Mail in 2002.

Ms. Greenhalgh, a powerhouse stage diva and brash matriarch of a Canadian theatrical dynasty, died in her long-time home in Toronto on Nov. 6, surrounded by her family. The lifelong smoker was 93.

“She died of old age,” said Megan Follows, one of four actor-children born to Ms. Greenhalgh and the late thespian Ted Follows .

Ms. Greenhalgh was one of the few surviving performers from the Stratford Festival’s inaugural season, having joined the company in 1953 as a 19-year-old ingénue from the High School of Montreal. She played a Lady at the Court of France in All’s Well That Ends Well , a Tyrone Guthrie-directed production that featured Alec Guinness as the King of France.

Unsatisfied with small roles, she left after two seasons but would return for six others. In 1958, she married festival actor Mr. Follows in Stratford, Ont. He proposed to her over the phone while she was working in New York.

“We got a lot of publicity, Stratford marriage and all of that,” she said in Richard Ouzounian’s book Stratford Gold . “And I remember Jason Robards gave me for a wedding present his script of Long Day’s Journey into Night .”

At Stratford, she played such characters as Charmian in Antony and Cleopatra in 1967, Natalia Petrovna in A Month in the Country in 1973, Béline in The Imaginary Invalid, the Princess of France in Love’s Labour’s Lost and Dionyza in Pericles , all in 1974; and Heloise in Heloise and Abelard in 1978.

“As an extraordinary artist she could be both charming and unsettling,” former Stratford Festival artistic director Antoni Cimolino said in a statement. “It was a pleasure to hear her perspective on plays and productions as it was informed by a lifetime of wide experience, a sparkling intellect and an independent, free-thinking mind.”

While the parents thrived on stage as acting partners in Stratford, Halifax (as founding members of Neptune Theatre) and elsewhere, their tumultuous marriage received less than stellar reviews. Their arguments earned them the nickname “The Fighting Follows.”

“On stage they got along like a house on fire,” their son Laurence Follows said. “But the minute they had to work in a matrimonial situation, that’s when it broke down.”

The marriage made in Stratford lasted until 1979 and produced the acting, writing and directing Follows children Samantha, Laurence, Edwina and Megan, the latter known for her titular role in the 1985 Canadian television miniseries Anne of Green Gables and its two sequels.

Ms. Greenhalgh was known to enjoy gin and vermouth with her olives. “I think drinking emboldened her when she was younger,” Laurence said. “She had to move into an adult world fast.”

After the divorce, she was taken to an Alcoholics Anonymous meeting by a famous (and anonymous) fellow actor. Ms. Greenhalgh, who thrived portraying complex, powerful characters but always had the capacity to show vulnerability, never took another drink, according to Laurence.

“It saved her life,” Megan said. “We got a lot out of her sober.”

Early in her career she did live radio. Among her many small-screen credits were Canadian television series Slings & Arrows, Strange Paradise , the animated Babar (voicing Queen Celeste ) and, with her daughter, Anne of Green Gables . She appeared in Sophia Coppola’s The Virgin Suicides and David Cronenberg’s 2014 satirical black comedy Maps to the Stars .

In the 2002 Globe profile, Ms. Greenhalgh was described as a husky-voiced entertainer who had a look in her eyes that suggested she “had seen more than her fair share of life.” What her eyes implied, her life drama confirmed. And although there isn’t a film based on her years in China, Steven Spielberg’s 1987 war drama Empire of the Sun wasn’t far off.

Hazel Dawn Greenhalgh was born in Shanghai on Sept. 25, 1933, the day an extermination campaign began against communists in China’s Jiangxi province. She and her brother were the offspring of British subjects who spent little time in England. Laurence Greenhalgh was born in India; homemaker Elizabeth Greenhalgh (née Birchby) was from Shanghai.

Their daughter seemingly inherited a wicked sense of humour from her father, who was tasked to cook meals for 1,500 inmates after Shanghai fell to the Japanese. He called the rotten protein he was given “Italian meat” because it shared the red, white and green colours of the Italian flag.

After the Second World War, the family moved to England but soon returned to Shanghai. The father worked for the Sassoons, the global merchants known as the Rothschilds of the East. Calamity struck again when Chinese communists took over Shanghai in 1949. The teenaged Ms. Greenhalgh was sent to Hong Kong somewhere around that time.

“I got out just before the city went up in flames, carrying 20 pounds of luggage, mostly Fats Waller records,” she told The Globe in 1970.

The plan was for her to move on to England. Not allowed to supply her with money, her parents instead outfitted her with a leopard-skin coat that she was to sell once she made it to the land of fish, chips and corner kicks.

She never sold the coat, never even made it to England. The teenager worked as a secretary for six months and hung out in Hong Kong with the mostly American aviators of the former Flying Tigers group who formed years earlier to oppose the Japanese invasion of China. Then the headstrong kid headed to Hollywood.

She made it there with the help of the famous Chinese-Canadian pilot Albert Mah. He was older by a decade; the two had a fiery but platonic relationship. After living in Los Angeles and San Francisco, she needed to leave the U.S. and formally re-enter because of immigration protocol. The idea was to do so from Montreal, but she instantly took a liking to the city and stayed instead.

High School of Montreal principal Grace Gardner arranged for the fascinating Ms. Greenhalgh to be sponsored by Imperial Order Daughters of the Empire so she could complete her schooling. There she founded and edited the school newspaper, The Medium. The school had a theatrical tradition – the great actors Christopher Plummer and Norma Shearer attended the place.

She played Gertrude opposite Richard Easton’s Hamlet at the school and was recommended to Tyrone Guthrie, the theatre legend (and second-cousin of film star Tyrone Power) brought in from England to be the Stratford Festival’s founding artistic director.

According to Ms. Greenhalgh, Mr. Guthrie hired her on the strength of her pipes alone.

“He said, ‘Right, you’ve got a great voice.’”

In the 1950s, she toured with the Canadian Players, formed by Stratford’s Tom Patterson and Douglas Campbell to produce plays across the country in the festival’s off-season. Her future husband, Mr. Follows, was in that troupe. Ms. Greenhalgh said he was the one actor she always felt totally safe with on stage. “Even if the scenery fell down, I knew it would be okay. He was always so well prepared that he could rescue any mishaps.”

As part of a pioneering generation of actors in Canadian theatre and live television, the immigrant Ms. Greenhalgh was committed to the country. “It was important for her to be a part of that voice,” Megan said. “She absolutely loved Canada.”

Ms. Greenhalgh brought her parents to Toronto in the 1950s. They came with nothing. The mother found work as a seamstress at Simpsons department store; the father worked in a waterworks facility.

Ms. Greenhalgh kept the leopard-skin coat they had given her. “In her mind, it kept her parents wrapped around her when she wore it, I think,” Megan said. In the 1960s, Ms. Greenhalgh had it tailored to a more contemporary fashion.

Among the family collaborations was the Theatre Calgary production of Tennessee Williams’s The Glass Menagerie in 1989. Ms. Greenhalgh played the problematic mother, Amanda Wingfield; her real-life daughter Samantha played the daughter, Laura; Daniel MacIvor played the son, Tom.

At the time, Mr. MacIvor was a young playwright and serious actor who felt he was in a semi-playful contest with the veteran Ms. Greenhalgh for the play’s spotlight attention.

“I’m sitting on stage at the table trying to be Tom,” he told The Globe. “Dawn would walk up with her back to the audience and make a comment like, ‘Dead house.’ There was a competition happening and she was messing with me. She had a glint in her eye, but it was a little intimidating.”

A 2001 mounting of Noël Coward’s Hay Fever at the Gravenhurst Opera House in Ontario’s cottage country was produced by her son, directed by her ex-husband and featured the whole clan (including a couple of in-laws) on stage.

Another family reunion at the Gravenhurst Opera House, 2002’s The Originals , was about the Straw Hat Players, Canada’s first professional theatre company. Both Ms. Greenhalgh and Mr. Follows performed in that troupe. In The Originals , Megan’s 10-year-old daughter played her grandmother as a young girl.

“Canada doesn’t have many theatrical dynasties, but the Follows family is certainly to Canadian theatre what the Redgraves are to the British stage,” The Globe’s Ray Conlogue wrote .

The nana to six grandchildren and two step-grandchildren did not remarry and never officially retired. Though she had issues with short-term memory, Ms. Greenhalgh had a recurring role in the 2022 Apple TV+ disaster medical series Five Days at Memorial and acted in the 2025 indie comedy-drama Stealing the Sky , directed by Megan.

She leaves her four children and extended family, along with a disintegrating leopard-skin jacket and a legacy as an intense presence and an indomitable, unshockable survivor.

“My mother always performed like her life depended on it, with an ability to transform into a greater self,” Megan said. “It was not something she could ever do halfway.”

You can find more obituaries from The Globe and Mail here .

To submit a memory about someone we have recently profiled on the Obituaries page, e-mail us at obit@globeandmail.com .

The teenager worked as a secretary for six months and hung out in Hong Kong with the mostly American aviators of the former Flying Tigers group who formed years earlier to oppose the Japanese invasion of China. Then the headstrong kid headed to Hollywood.

She made it there with the help of the famous Chinese-Canadian pilot Albert Mah. He was older by a decade; the two had a fiery but platonic relationship. After living in Los Angeles and San Francisco, she needed to leave the U.S. and formally re-enter because of immigration protocol. The idea was to do so from Montreal, but she instantly took a liking to the city and stayed instead.

High School of Montreal principal Grace Gardner arranged for the fascinating Ms. Greenhalgh to be sponsored by Imperial Order Daughters of the Empire so she could complete her schooling. There she founded and edited the school newspaper, The Medium. The school had a theatrical tradition – the great actors Christopher Plummer and Norma Shearer attended the place.

She played Gertrude opposite Richard Easton’s Hamlet at the school and was recommended to Tyrone Guthrie, the theatre legend (and second-cousin of film star Tyrone Power) brought in from England to be the Stratford Festival’s founding artistic director.
According to Ms. Greenhalgh, Mr. Guthrie hired her on the strength of her pipes alone.
“He said, ‘Right, you’ve got a great voice.’”

In the 1950s, she toured with the Canadian Players, formed by Stratford’s Tom Patterson and Douglas Campbell to produce plays across the country in the festival’s off-season. Her future husband, Mr. Follows, was in that troupe. Ms. Greenhalgh said he was the one actor she always felt totally safe with on stage. “Even if the scenery fell down, I knew it would be okay. He was always so well prepared that he could rescue any mishaps.”

As part of a pioneering generation of actors in Canadian theatre and live television, the immigrant Ms. Greenhalgh was committed to the country. “It was important for her to be a part of that voice,” Megan said. “She absolutely loved Canada.”
Ms. Greenhalgh brought her parents to Toronto in the 1950s. They came with nothing. The mother found work as a seamstress at Simpsons department store; the father worked in a waterworks facility.

Ms. Greenhalgh kept the leopard-skin coat they had given her. “In her mind, it kept her parents wrapped around her when she wore it, I think,” Megan said. In the 1960s, Ms. Greenhalgh had it tailored to a more contemporary fashion.

Among the family collaborations was the Theatre Calgary production of Tennessee Williams’s The Glass Menagerie in 1989. Ms. Greenhalgh played the problematic mother, Amanda Wingfield; her real-life daughter Samantha played the daughter, Laura; Daniel MacIvor played the son, Tom.
At the time, Mr. MacIvor was a young playwright and serious actor who felt he was in a semi-playful contest with the veteran Ms. Greenhalgh for the play’s spotlight attention.

“I’m sitting on stage at the table trying to be Tom,” he told The Globe. “Dawn would walk up with her back to the audience and make a comment like, ‘Dead house.’ There was a competition happening and she was messing with me. She had a glint in her eye, but it was a little intimidating.”

A 2001 mounting of Noël Coward’s Hay Fever at the Gravenhurst Opera House in Ontario’s cottage country was produced by her son, directed by her ex-husband and featured the whole clan (including a couple of in-laws) on stage.

Another family reunion at the Gravenhurst Opera House, 2002’s The Originals , was about the Straw Hat Players, Canada’s first professional theatre company. Both Ms. Greenhalgh and Mr. Follows performed in that troupe. In The Originals , Megan’s 10-year-old daughter played her grandmother as a young girl.
“Canada doesn’t have many theatrical dynasties, but the Follows family is certainly to Canadian theatre what the Redgraves are to the British stage,” The Globe’s Ray Conlogue wrote .

The nana to six grandchildren and two step-grandchildren did not remarry and never officially retired. Though she had issues with short-term memory, Ms. Greenhalgh had a recurring role in the 2022 Apple TV+ disaster medical series Five Days at Memorial and acted in the 2025 indie comedy-drama Stealing the Sky , directed by Megan.
She leaves her four children and extended family, along with a disintegrating leopard-skin jacket and a legacy as an intense presence and an indomitable, unshockable survivor.
“My mother always performed like her life depended on it, with an ability to transform into a greater self,” Megan said. “It was not something she could ever do halfway.”

stories.title: Cold-plunge campaign aims to raise awareness for men’s mental health
stories.summary: Jake Uberti has endured a long road to recovery following multiple concussions while playing hockey at a high level.
stories.author: Paul Hollingsworth
stories.content:
Halifax - For the month of November, 24-year-old Jake Uberti is bringing together a group of men and women to participate in the “Daily Dip,” a social media campaign to support men’s mental health.

View this post on Instagram

The Movember global health movement began in November 2003. Male participants often grow moustaches during the month to raise money and awareness for men’s health. However, Uberti’s challenge takes a different approach to the well known Movember movement.

Uberti started the Daily Dip three years ago when he was recovering from one of his concussions and would often jump in the water alone.

His concussions were so severe, at one point, Uberti was forced to mostly stay indoors and suspend any physical activity for several months.

“I was told that the cold-water exposure would help me feel normal,” Uberti said. “This is now for anyone who is struggling or going through a hard period at a time in life so they know they can try again the next day and always do what is good for you.”

Uberti has endured a long road to recovery following multiple concussions while playing hockey at a high level.

“It was lonely having the concussions,” said the 24-year-old from Vaughn, Ont., who saw his playing career at Saint Mary’s University cut short, which had a harmful impact on his mental health. “It was hard to wake up every day and not want to do anything that day.”

Uberti is now healthy and has pushed forward in life.

Mental-health lessons

He said he is also armed with valuable life lessons and he has honed some helpful self-care coping mechanisms.

“I learned that not every day is going to be a good one, but I also learned that I needed to try again for the people around me,” Uberti said.

With that in mind, he launched the “Daily Dip.”

View this post on Instagram

The Movember global health movement began in November 2003. Male participants often grow moustaches during the month to raise money and awareness for men’s health. However, Uberti’s challenge takes a different approach to the well known Movember movement.
Uberti started the Daily Dip three years ago when he was recovering from one of his concussions and would often jump in the water alone.
His concussions were so severe, at one point, Uberti was forced to mostly stay indoors and suspend any physical activity for several months.

“I was told that the cold-water exposure would help me feel normal,” Uberti said. “This is now for anyone who is struggling or going through a hard period at a time in life so they know they can try again the next day and always do what is good for you.”
Uberti has endured a long road to recovery following multiple concussions while playing hockey at a high level.

“It was lonely having the concussions,” said the 24-year-old from Vaughn, Ont., who saw his playing career at Saint Mary’s University cut short, which had a harmful impact on his mental health. “It was hard to wake up every day and not want to do anything that day.”
Uberti is now healthy and has pushed forward in life.

He said he is also armed with valuable life lessons and he has honed some helpful self-care coping mechanisms.

stories.title: B.C. court rules against supplement makers in class action over false labelling
stories.summary: Vancouver - Lawyers representing plaintiffs in a class-action suit involving a falsely labelled health supplement say they have received a favourable ruling from the Supreme Court of British Columbia.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Vancouver - Lawyers representing plaintiffs in a class-action suit involving a falsely labelled health supplement say they have received a favourable ruling from the Supreme Court of British Columbia.

CFM Lawyers, one of two firms representing the plaintiffs, says the court has found products labelled as glucosamine sulphate made by Jamieson Laboratories, WN Pharmaceuticals and Natural Factors Nutritional Products did not contain the chemical compound.

stories.title: Girl’s family frustrated with Icbc, access to care, after she was hit by car
stories.summary: Makenna suffered a severe brain injury in May after a car hit her and a boy while they were on an e-scooter crossing the street at Hastings and Hythe Avenue in Burnaby.
stories.author: Amy Judd, Grace Ke
stories.content:
Frustrated with Icbc’s no-fault insurance, a Burnaby mother is speaking out, saying it’s preventing her daughter from getting the proper care she needs and leaving their family in financial hardship.

Ten-year-old Makenna suffered a severe brain injury in May after a car hit her and an 11-year-old boy while they were on an e-scooter crossing the street at Hastings and Hythe Avenue in Burnaby.

The case is still under investigation.

Icbc’s Enhanced Care model will provide rehabilitation, including occupational therapy and physiotherapy.

But Makenna’s mother says her daughter also needs around-the-clock care.

She gets the maximum personal care assistance level of $11,872 a month but her mother, a single parent, told Global News that’s barely enough to cover the cost of her daughter’s care.

“I’m not working because now I’m the caretaker,” Kaia Haley said.

“I also have to maintain a life for my eight-year-old son who still needs to go to school and his activities and all this. Then I have to also drive to (occupational therapy and physical therapy).”

Haley said she also has to administer all the medications at bedtime, while making sure her son keeps up with school.

She has also set up a GoFundMe to help cover costs .

2:16 Tsawwassen crash victim battles Icbc

Icbc also pays for modifications to the family home, but the family is frustrated that nothing has been done so far and Makenna has recently returned home after a lengthy hospital and rehabilitation stay.

Icbc says a change in occupational therapists required a review of the proposed modifications and as Makenna’s function has improved, some of her care needs have changed. They are moving forward as quickly as possible.

stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Prince George - A salmon hatchery under construction in northern British Columbia has received approval for a roughly $11-million expansion to include infrastructure dedicated to sockeye conservation.

The Fisheries Department says in a statement that the Upper Fraser River Salmon Conservation Hatchery project was previously planned to help chinook Pacific salmon without the newly announced expansion.

stories.title: U.S. prosecution opposes release of alleged co-conspirator in B.C. mass shooting
stories.summary: Seattle - U.S federal prosecutors say the accused co-conspirator in the mass shooting in Tumbler Ridge, B.C., prioritized her loyalty to the killer over the lives of innocent children and she shouldn’t be released before trial.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The accused co-conspirator in the mass shooting in Tumbler Ridge, B.C., prioritized her loyalty to the killer over the lives of innocent children and she shouldn’t be released before trial, U.S federal prosecutors say.

James Bryant, who uses female pronouns and goes by the name Melody, pleaded not guilty to conspiracy to murder persons in a foreign country in a Seattle court in October. She was ordered to be kept in custody until the trial next year, but her lawyers have made an application for her release.

The criminal complaint against Bryant, 30, alleges she colluded with 18-year-old shooter Jesse Van Rootselaar online and attempted to set up a livestream of the murders.

Van Rootselaar killed eight people last February, including five students and an educational assistant at the local secondary school, before fatally shooting herself as police closed in.

In a 33-page filing to court last week, Bryant’s lawyers argued she would not pose a threat to society and claimed the nearly 74,000 texts exchanged between her and the shooter were misconstrued by the government as it argued for her detention.

In response to the motion, prosecutors filed documents in Seattle on Wednesday saying the defence has attempted to minimize Bryant’s role and she would pose a “serious danger to the community” if released.

“Up until the last moment, Bryant could have changed course and put a stop to this horrific crime,” the document says.

“But Bryant chose not to intercede. Instead, Bryant moved forward with the agreement to assist Van Rootselaar in committing the murders.”

The document says the evidence overwhelmingly shows she knew that Van Rootselaar planned to commit mass murder and took “multiple, concrete steps to further” that plot, including providing monetary support and tactical advice, and agreeing to record a livestream of the attack, while assuring the shooter she would not “snitch” to authorities.

Bryant’s lawyers argued in their motion that the conversations she had with Van Rootselaar are protected by the U.S. First Amendment right to free speech because Van Rootselaar had made it clear she had no immediate intention to commit an act of violence.

Bryant’s lawyers also claimed that six months before the attack, the plan the two discussed over the Discord platform was “fantasy” because Van Rootselaar did not have access to guns. It cited the RCMP seizing — and later returning — one of the guns Van Rootselaar would use in the attack.

The prosecution called that a “bogus claim.”

“It was clear to Bryant from the outset that Van Rootselaar had firearms, ammunition, and the other means to commit the attack,” the response says, as it pointed to a conversation as early as August 2025 in which the pair discussed Van Rootselaar being careful with a loaded firearm.

“Bryant knew this was no fantasy,” it says.

Prosecutors argue that the characterization by Bryant’s defence lawyers that Van Rootselaar would have committed the attack regardless of the livestream was not supported by the evidence.

It says the pair had discussed its importance on several occasions, with Van Rootselaar “insisting that an essential part of the plot was for the murders to be livestreamed, recorded and broadcast over the internet for the world to view.”

Bryant, it says, assisted in testing the livestream equipment on multiple occasions, and tried to record the broadcast on the day of the attack.

The livestream only lasted about 20 seconds due to “technical issues” and Bryant was the only one to view the feed before it cut out, but the document says “the livestream’s failure was despite Bryant’s best efforts to make it happen.”

Bryant’s motion for release claims she did not understand “when violence was imminent” that day because Van Rootselaar “had been talking about killing people nearly every day for at least six months,” and Bryant was able to dissuade her from acting on at least three occasions.

The prosecution says it’s a “preposterous claim,” pointing to Discord chat logs of their conversations during the attack on Feb. 10 and to an interview with Homeland Security Investigations special agents two days after the killings where Bryant admitted to knowing the attack was ongoing. She confirmed Van Rootselaar told her she had killed her mother and brother at their home.

It says Bryant told agents that she believed Van Rootselaar was going to hurt someone, described watching the livestream and seeing Van Rootselaar in the car with the guns, and that she was struggling to start the car.

“And what did Bryant do at that moment? Bryant helped Van Rootselaar figure out how to start the car.”

“During this entire conversation, Bryant knew full well that ‘violence was imminent’ and chose to further it,” the document says.

The prosecution calls for the motion to be dismissed and asks the judge not to revoke the detention order.

“A defendant whose character allows them to help plan a mass shooting, and then sits back and literally tries to watch as schoolchildren are murdered instead of ‘snitching’ on the killer, is a danger to the community and should be detained pending trial,” it says.

The defence application asks the court to order release of Bryant with conditions, “which May include home confinement, mental health treatment if an assessment determines it is appropriate, and restrictions on her use of digital devices.”

But prosecutors say there is “no combination of conditions that would reasonably ensure Bryant’s presence at future court proceedings or the safety of the community.”

It says her future online behaviour should be a “primary concern” for the court. It says she lives in a home with two other people and while authorities can monitor devices belonging to Bryant, the defendant would also have “easy access to several unmonitored devices” that belong to her roommates.

It says the court should have additional concerns about Bryant’s own character, pointing to a conversation with Van Rootselaar on Jan. 25, where she discussed the desire to engage in violence, specifically a stabbing.

The conversation quotes Bryant as saying she wanted to get a gun for self-defence but called it “less fun than digging a knife into flesh.”

“I just feel like there’s something to enjoy about how direct you are in their maiming. Warm blood getting on your hands. Any movement being agony,” Bryant wrote.

The trial on the charges against Bryant is scheduled for December 2027.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 25, 2026.

stories.title: Lcbo to deploy paid duty cops in over 40 stores to bolster anti-theft efforts
stories.summary: Existing measures led to more than 2,000 arrests last year, alcohol seller says
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The Liquor Control Board of Ontario says it’s partnering with local police forces across the province to place paid duty cops in more than 40 stores to deter theft.

The Lcbo says additional guards and members of its security task force will also be deployed as part of the anti-theft campaign, the latter of which will focus on targeting organized crime groups the alcohol seller estimates are behind about 70 per cent of theft-related losses.

The provincial Crown agency says it’s a target for criminal activity as one of Ontario’s largest retailers.

It says existing anti-theft measures led to more than 2,000 arrests last year.

The enhanced security measures will roll out in “high-risk areas” and some of the busiest and most frequently targeted stores.

Al Almeida, the agency’s senior director for resource protection, says the campaign uses data analysis to identify where additional security is needed most.

The Lcbo says it will also work with police forces to strengthen information sharing across jurisdictions and will roll out mandatory refresher training for security guards.

stories.title: ‘Henry didn’t have to die,’ grieving Regina parents say after landlords charged
stories.summary: "The wheels of justice take a long time," the family of a Regina boy who died of carbon monoxide poisoning said after their apartment building's owners were charged with breaches.
stories.author: Tavi Dhillon
stories.content:
The family of Henry Losco, a boy who died of carbon monoxide poisoning, says their grief remains, but they are hopeful it is a step towards justice after regulatory charges were laid against their former apartment building owner.

Henry Losco, 11, died after the deadly chemical leaked from the boiler inside his downtown Regina apartment building last December.

Marina Hills and Sergio Losco, the boy’s parents, told Global News that the upcoming court hearing is a long time coming.

“The wheels of justice take a long time, and we really didn’t know how long it was going to take,” Marina said. “We’ve now embarked on this path of accountability and as much as it pains us, we’re ready for it.”

“We believe, very strongly, that this was senseless and that Henry didn’t have to die.”

Last week, the City of Regina confirmed to Global News that D.R. Andersons Holdings Inc., the owner of the apartment building where Marina and Sergio’s 11-year-old son died, is facing regulatory charges related to fire safety and construction code from the city.

The case will be heard in bylaw court on Dec. 9.

Global News reached out to D.R. Andersons Holding Inc. for comment. None was received at the time of publication.

Henry’s parents told Global News they were informed that the regulatory charges were laid last Thursday.

“It felt like the wind was knocked out of me because it just all came down to what we knew was possibly coming but didn’t know for sure,” Marina said.

Marina added that she knew it was time for her and her husband to advocate for safer carbon monoxide measures in Saskatchewan as soon as her son’s death was confirmed.

“I said, ‘We have to do something about this. We need accountability. We need justice. And we need to stop this from happening,” Marina recalled. “So, we started our advocacy because that was the only thing we were able to do.”

“And that gave us something to live for, leaning on each other and keeping each other strong. It didn’t feel like strength. It felt like we were just surviving. We were in shock for quite a while.”

She and her husband said they intend to be at the bylaw court when the case is presented in two weeks’ time.

“We know that it’s just the first hearing, and that there will not be many answers from that.

“But maybe we will be able to know what the actual violations are. And those violations are just the base. It’s (also) what was already missing; that was the safety procedures that were not in place,” Sergio said.

“We are confident this is a first step in the right direction for justice for Henry and for accountability.”

Marina said she hopes no family will have to experience what hers has in the past 11 months.

“Children can’t be dying in their beds anymore. No family should have to go through losing their children. No family. Ours was torn apart,” she said.

“These people took away mom and dad. And now we’re Sergio and Marina. We aren’t going to get the future that we were hoping for, and we certainly don’t want anyone else to have to go through what we’re going through and what we will have to be going through for the rest of our lives.”

Henry’s family is also pursuing the apartment building owners, as well as other entities, in a civil suit . Those allegations have not been tested in the courts.

stories.summary: Notice about key ingredient in drugs such as Ozempic and Wegovy follows similar warnings from other health regulators
stories.author: Chris Hannay
stories.content:
Health Canada is warning of a very rare risk of vision loss for patients who take semaglutide, the key ingredient in the blockbuster diabetes and weight loss drugs Ozempic and Wegovy.

The Canadian regulator’s notice , published Wednesday, follows similar warnings from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration and the European Medicines Agency .

Health Canada said it will work with semaglutide manufacturers to update the Canadian product monographs – the official information about the drugs – to include a “very rare” risk of non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (Naion), which can cause sudden, painless and permanent vision loss.

The main global manufacturer of semaglutide is Denmark’s Novo Nordisk. Generic versions became available in Canada this year, made primarily by Apotex and India’s Dr. Reddy’s Laboratories Ltd.

Health Canada said it made its determination by reviewing information from a manufacturer and a foreign regulator; reviewing 23 cases of patients taking semaglutide who developed Naion; and 10 scientific studies.

“Although it is not fully understood how semaglutide May contribute to Naion, it is thought that a rapid drop in blood sugar levels following the use of semaglutide May cause swelling of the optic nerve and reduce its blood supply, especially in individuals with other risk factors,” the Health Canada warning said.

Health Canada recommends patients who take semaglutide to seek urgent assessment from an ophthalmologist if they experience sudden vision loss or worsening of the eyes and to stop taking the drug if Naion is confirmed.

Nina Ahuja, president of the Canadian Ophthalmological Society, said the risk of vision loss is rare, but it is important for patients to be aware of it.

“We don’t want people to stop taking their medication out of fear, but to have a conversation with their prescribing physician about their individual risk factors and the benefits of continuing treatment,” Dr. Ahuja said in an e-mail.

Ozempic has been by far the best-selling drug in Canada in recent years. About $1.5-billion of Ozempic was sold in Canada in the first six months of 2026, plus $455-million of Wegovy, both made by Novo Nordisk, according to aggregated prescription data collected by Iqvia Canada, an analytics company. (All prices include pharmacy markup and dispensing fees.) Novo Nordisk has said more than a million Canadians take semaglutide.

Semaglutide has been sold in Canada since 2018. The drug was initially approved to treat type 2 diabetes, and it has since been approved for a variety of conditions, such as weight management and certain kidney and liver diseases.

Novo Nordisk said patient safety is a top priority for the company. “Novo remains confident in the benefit-risk profile of our GLP-1 medicines, when prescribed as indicated,” spokesperson Kate Hanna said in an e-mail.

Semaglutide is part of a class of drugs called glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists. Health Canada said it is currently assessing whether there is a similar risk for other GLP-1 drugs as well.

stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - The Liquor Control Board of Ontario says it’s partnering with local police forces across the province to place paid duty cops in more than 40 stores to deter theft.

The Lcbo says additional guards and members of its security task force will also be deployed as part of the anti-theft campaign, the latter of which will focus on targeting organized crime groups the alcohol seller estimates are behind about 70 per cent of theft-related losses.

stories.title: Bruce Power ‘fish kill’ charges withdrawn, but will be refiled
stories.summary: Bruce Power’s first court appearance on federal charges related to a massive 2025 fish kill wasn’t much of a court appearance at all.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
Bruce Power’s first court appearance on federal charges related to a massive 2025 fish kill wasn’t much of a court appearance at all. Crown prosecutors had to withdraw the charges against Bruce Power because they were filed in the wrong court.

The charges are for allegedly killing as many as 5 million fish during a February 2025 incident will be refiled in a Walkerton court, ON Dec. 9. In late October, Bruce Power was charged after millions of fish were killed inside the company’s underwater infrastructure.

That warm water attracts fish, specifically Gizzard Shad. During the 2025 incident, nearly 8 million fish were hovering near this warm water exchange pipe and entered a recirculation duct through a gate that is only open in the winter to keep frazil ice from forming and clogging up Bruce Power’s pumps.

Frazil ice is a collection of loose, sub-millimetre to millimetre-sized ice crystals that form in turbulent, supercooled open water and is notorious for blocking water intakes for hydropower plants and nuclear facilities.

Bruce Power had to temporarily shut down one of their nuclear reactors as a result of the large amount of dead fish clogging their underwater equipment. “The 2025 event occurred during a rare convergence of environmental conditions, including prolonged cold weather, and an unusually large presence of Gizzard Shad following several warm years.

The last time this convergence of factors occurred was in the late 1970s,” the company said. Bruce Power’s next court appearance will be Dec. 9 in Walkerton.

stories.title: Jamie Heffer elected Huron County warden
stories.summary: The mayor of the Municipality of Morris-Turnberry is the warden of Huron County again.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
The mayor of the Municipality of Morris-Turnberry is the warden of Huron County again.

Heffer held the warden’s job for the past two years, and will serve as Warden for 2027 and 2028. He was selected as warden by his fellow councillors this week.

“It is an honour to be re-elected as Warden of Huron County,” said Heffer.

“As warden, I look forward to working together to advance the priorities of our communities and continue building a strong future for Huron County.”

Heffer has been Morris-Turnberry’s Mayor since 2018. He raises sheep and beef on his family’s farm near Wingham.

His brother, Paul Heffer, is a current councillor and former mayor for the nearby Township of North Huron.

stories.title: Public gives feedback on battery storage project near Port Elgin
stories.summary: 18 residents opposed to a 29-acre battery energy storage project near Port Elgin, Ont. got to share their concerns with the company and Saugeen Shores council this week.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
18 residents opposed to a 29-acre battery energy storage project near Port Elgin, Ont. got to share their concerns with the company and Saugeen Shores council this week.

Opponents had concerns about safety of the proposed facility, the loss of farmland, and what would happen in case of a fire at the industrial complex.

The proposed project would entail 344 lithium iron phosphate battery containers pulling electricity from the grid during times of overproduction and low demand, storing that energy, and then putting it back on the grid when demand is high.

It’s one of 29 such projects either in operation, or in development in Ontario.

Opponents, including the National Farmer’s Union, suggested 320 acres of farmland is lost to development in Ontario each day. Projects like this make that situation worse for incremental energy gains, opponents say.

The project proponent, Neoen Canada, says the project is important to balance out Ontario’s energy system, specifically using power from wind turbines, that typically churn at night when demand is low. They believe the site, located two concessions south of Port Elgin, is suitable and took years to finalize.

“It’s a comprehensive process. We consider a lot of constraints, and we are really convinced that the site that we have selected with the Saugeen Ojibway Nation and is a good site for that project,” said Neoen Provincial Director, Benoit Pinot de Villechenon.

The project is endorsed by the Saugeen Ojibway Nation but is awaiting zoning amendment approvals from Saugeen Shores council and Bruce County council. The decisions won’t come until early next year.

If those approvals are ultimately granted, Neoen says construction could begin late next year, and the 20-year project would be operational by the end of 2028.
paragraphs: 18 residents opposed to a 29-acre battery energy storage project near Port Elgin, Ont. got to share their concerns with the company and Saugeen Shores council this week.
Opponents had concerns about safety of the proposed facility, the loss of farmland, and what would happen in case of a fire at the industrial complex.

The proposed project would entail 344 lithium iron phosphate battery containers pulling electricity from the grid during times of overproduction and low demand, storing that energy, and then putting it back on the grid when demand is high.
It’s one of 29 such projects either in operation, or in development in Ontario.

Opponents, including the National Farmer’s Union, suggested 320 acres of farmland is lost to development in Ontario each day. Projects like this make that situation worse for incremental energy gains, opponents say.

The project proponent, Neoen Canada, says the project is important to balance out Ontario’s energy system, specifically using power from wind turbines, that typically churn at night when demand is low. They believe the site, located two concessions south of Port Elgin, is suitable and took years to finalize.

“It’s a comprehensive process. We consider a lot of constraints, and we are really convinced that the site that we have selected with the Saugeen Ojibway Nation and is a good site for that project,” said Neoen Provincial Director, Benoit Pinot de Villechenon.
The project is endorsed by the Saugeen Ojibway Nation but is awaiting zoning amendment approvals from Saugeen Shores council and Bruce County council. The decisions won’t come until early next year.
If those approvals are ultimately granted, Neoen says construction could begin late next year, and the 20-year project would be operational by the end of 2028.

stories.title: Driver charged in August fatal crash
stories.summary: A driver has been charged in a fatal Central Elgin crash dating back to August.
stories.author: Kate Otterbein
stories.content:
A driver has been charged in a fatal Central Elgin crash dating back to August.

On Nov. 19, police charged a 61-year-old London resident with careless driving causing death and three counts of careless driving causing bodily harm in relation.

On the evening of Aug. 20, emergency services were called to the incident involving two SUVs and a pickup truck at the intersection of Fairview Road and John Wise Line.

Two adults and three children were taken to the hospital with life-threatening injuries. A nine-year-old child from London was pronounced dead at hospital.

One adult and two children from the pickup truck were taken to hospital with serious, but non-life-threatening injuries.

Two other adults were not hurt.

stories.title: Sports Notes: Mustangs leave for Vanier Cup, Ofsaa high school previews, Brier medallist curling in St. Thomas, Ont.
stories.summary: The Western Mustangs have arrived in Quebec City, and preparations are underway for the 61st Vanier Cup game Saturday.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
The Western Mustangs have arrived in Quebec City, and preparations are underway for the 61st Vanier Cup game Saturday.

“Littered around those practices are a lot of meetings, a lot of meals, a lot of rest for the guys in the hotel as they prepare for 12 p.m. on Saturday,” said Michael Faulds, Mustangs head coach.

Similarly to Super Bowl week, the hype around the National Championship game can be chaotic. Faulds has been there in 2008 as a Mustangs player and as Wilfrid Laurier head coach in 2024.

“I tell them, ‘Let me be the travel coordinator and let me kind of organize them,’” added Faulds.

“I’ll make sure the practice plans are set so that our coordinators, our coaches, and our players can just execute. Sure, there’s a little bit of travel built-in in there, but when we’re in a meeting room, when we’re on the practice field, it’s just Western football. The least distractions that our players and coaches have, the better our chances are on Saturday.”

Western will be facing the defending Vanier Cup champion Montreal Carabins.

“It’s going to be underdog mentality,” said Faulds.

“We’re playing the Vanier Cup champions from last season, and we’ve got a lot of respect for coach Marco (Iadeluca). Pepe Gonzalez, their starting quarterback, is back again this week, his first game back being last week in the Uteck Bowl against B.C. and he did quite well. Our guys have a great game plan and with a good week of practice there’s a lot of excitement.”

To get ready, the Mustangs held one last practice on the snowy turf at Alumni Stadium Tuesday before getting set to leave.

“The Mitchell Bowl on Saturday was unseasonable with 17 C and sunny,” said Faulds.

“We knew winter was going to come at some point and sure enough, heading to Quebec City, we know there could be snow, there could be sleet, there’s going to be wind. Having some snow for practice actually sets us up and prepares us a little bit more.”

Ofsaa football, volleyball, and basketball wrap up Fall sports season

On the hardwood, the Saunders Sabres (AAA), Stratford St. Mikes Warriors (AA), and Ecole-Monseigneur Bruyere Pantheres (A) will compete in girls’ basketball.

The Sabres will head to Barrie, Ont. as the number three seed.

“We’ve played together for a number of years now,” said Sabres forward Izzy Gordon.

“A lot of us have been a core group building up since I was in Grade 9. We have good experience and we’ve just played well all year together. We’ve grown all year and I think we’re ready.”

Shooting guard Aliyah Serbouti believes they have the mindset to come home with the gold.

“We’ve been working hard for a number of days since September,” said Serbouti.

“The first time we walked into the gym, it was definitely the main goal.”

Saunders students will be able to cheer them on during their opener Thursday at 1:30 p.m. against Sir Edmund Campion. The game will be livestreamed on YouTube in the school’s auditorium.

“That’s amazing and I think it really shows our school spirit,” said Gordon.

“I do think we should have been a little bit higher, but it is what it is,” said Oaks’ head coach Jamie Neilson.

“The one thing that I will say I like our scheduled start times and I’m very, very happy with the situation that we’re sitting in. I wish the number in front of us was a little bit lower than nine, but that’s just a number, and it’s up to us to go and show that we should have been seeded higher.”

“We are led by Sam Moore, who won Mr. Volleyball in Tvra,” said Neilson.

“He’s the only player that signed in Tvra right now as he’s going to York next year and York is a big eastern powerhouse. For them to show interest in him, shows what type of player he is.”

Neilson first went to Ofsaa back in 2005 and won gold in the tournament which was held in Chatham. With his career winding down, he’s hoping he can bookend his Ofsaa experience with another gold in the Crow city.

The South Lions (AA) and St. Marys District Collegiate and Vocational Institute (A) are also headed to Ofsaa.

CCH Crusaders and South Lions both ranked first heading into Ofsaa football bowls

London has been widely regarded as the football capital of Ontario and this year that moniker is well earned.

South will take on Holy Cross from Peterborough (number two) in the Western Bowl on Friday at 2 p.m. at Richardson Stadium in Kingston.

The Crusaders will face Huron Heights (number two) in the Western Bowl on Monday at 5 p.m. at the same venue.

“They’re a good program and they have been for a long time,” said Kurowski.

“I think what they’ve done in Canadian high school, football’s really grown a lot and it’s being felt by our student athletes,” said Kurowski.

“The game is really grown, and CFC (Canada Football Chat) has done a great job with the national rankings, as has Ontario High School Football with Ontario rankings.”

This matchup wasn’t decided until mid-November. CCH crushed Oakridge 37-3 in the Wossaa AAA final last Friday at 1Password Park in St. Thomas to advance.

The Crusaders will be looking for a bowl victory for the third consecutive year.

“This is a really special group of guys in our fifth year and for our fourth-year players who are graduating,” said Kurowski.

“These seniors have had a heck of a run here at Catholic Central, and it’d be a great way to send them off Monday night.”

18-time Brier competitor among Canadian Club curlers in St. Thomas

The best club curlers in Canada are competing for a national championship in St. Thomas this week.

One of the favourites on the men’s side is James Grattan of New Brunswick, who is no stranger representing his province on the big stage.

Here he gets to compete with his best friends from his home club.

“I think that’s been the most enjoyable part of it for me, because I play with these guys in leagues back home, and they’re the ones that are usually supporting me when I’m off doing my thing over the last few years,” said Grattan.

“It’s nice to be able to represent like a home club, like you have a pinpoint group of people that you’re representing out here,” said Grattan.

“We’ve been hearing lots and lots from all those folks back home. And it’s been great so far.”

He’s been to St. Thomas before for a bonspiel, so he’s familiar with the city, restaurants, and areas around the rink so that has helped him settle in.

The St. Thomas Curling Club recently underwent a $1 million renovation. It allows them to host major tournaments.

“St. Thomas and Elgin [County] have just been unbelievable,” said Peter Inch, tournament coordinator and past president of the club.

“The players can’t say enough about the shopping, the hotels, the curling, the ice. It’s really been fantastic.”

The club has pulled out its extra bleachers, and the lobby has been packed for the matches.

The finals will be played on Saturday.

stories.title: London man facing child sexual abuse charge
stories.summary: London police say a 27-year-old man was arrested earlier this week by members of the LPS Internet Child Exploitation (ICE) Unit in relation to making of Child Sexual Abuse and Exploitation Material (Csaem).
stories.author: Melanie Kentner
stories.content:
London police say a 27-year-old man was arrested earlier this week by members of the LPS Internet Child Exploitation (ICE) Unit in relation to making of Child Sexual Abuse and Exploitation Material (Csaem).

Officers launched an investigation on Monday, after the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (Ncmec) made them aware of information involving a London man.

A search warrant was executed the same day at a residence near Dundas Street and Clarke Road.

A man suspect was arrested, and police seized electronic devices. Officers say evidence of Child Sexual Abuse and Exploitation Material (Csaem) was located.

As a result of the investigation, a London man has been charged with one count of possess child sexual abuse and exploitation material.

The accused was scheduled to appear in London court Wednesday, in relation to the charge.

Anyone with information in relation to this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670.

stories.title: Liberals, Carney defend ‘brutal’ pace of committee work on major projects bill
stories.summary: The committee reviewing Bill C-39 spent more than 100 hours debating it over seven days before wrapping up on Monday.
stories.author: Nick Murray
stories.content:
Federal Liberals, including Prime Minister Mark Carney, are defending the speed at which their major projects bill passed through a House of Commons committee — a process one opposition MP called “inhumane.”

The committee reviewing Bill C-39 spent more than 100 hours debating it over seven days before wrapping up on Monday. The Liberals used their majority to accept only minor amendments to the sweeping bill, which is meant to fast-track approvals for major projects, cut their review times and create zones of “national interest” to pre-approve certain types of projects.

It also proposes major changes to collective bargaining, including the use of more federal mediation to get deals done and repair relationships between unions and businesses.

Opposition MPs said they aren’t taking issue with the long hours — which they acknowledged are part of the job — they argued a longer period of debate with some breaks would have allowed them to provide better oversight.

MPs, staff and witnesses often sat in committee until close to midnight over the seven days they spent reviewing the bill. The committee logged back-to-back 15-hour days on Saturday and Sunday.

“It was really excessive. I would say it was on the line of being inhumane,” Bloc Québécois MP Gabriel Ste-Marie said in French.

“After 15 hours, we’re aren’t as effective anymore to find the right words to get our point across.”

“I would have preferred for there to be breaks because … what goes on actually in the committee, there’s hours of prep,” Conservative MP Phil Lawrence told The Canadian Press on Wednesday.

“So it’s nice to be able to, after a couple of hours, go back to your office review it, and you see what changes have been made, and you can have a little bit more substance.

“Give us at least the evening to review, to change, to sub-amend. Because that reflection time can often make the bill better. It also gives time for the witnesses, the officials, to recap and recover.”

On Tuesday, Manitoba Conservative MP Branden Leslie called the committee process “pretty brutal.”

“I mean, I’ll be very frank, this is our job. But the witnesses that had to sit at the end of that table and take questions for hours and hours on end, yeah, it was pretty brutal on them, as well as all the support staff,” he said.

“My entire time in Parliament, and I have been here over seven years, I’ve never seen anything like this,” said NDP MP Heather McPherson.

“Nobody’s at their best after 15-hour days, ON and on and on … Nobody is doing the work that we need to be able to do. It’s impossible.”

Committee chair James Maloney defended the long hours spent reviewing the bill, although he also acknowledged he’d never seen that happen before.

“Everybody was on board with it. The longer it went, the longer it would have gone. And once you get a little momentum in the committee, it’s good to keep going,” said Maloney, who also serves as the Liberal caucus chair.

“I was tasked with chairing the committee and I decided on the schedule in consultation with all the members, I might add. So there’s no surprise to anyone, if they’re being candid about it. It was my decision.”

While Ste-Marie denied the claim that MPs were consulted on the schedule, he also said Maloney was a “gentleman” throughout the process.

“I don’t think it was his choice to have those hours. I’m convinced that it was an order from the government to have those hours. I have a lot of respect for Mr. Maloney,” Ste-Marie said in French.

“The message was clear: ‘We’re going to fatigue you, we’re going to burn you out, and we’re going to come out ahead, regardless if we respect the staff who are there.’ It’s disrespectful of the democratic process.”

Carney has described the bill as his government’s most consequential piece of economic legislation.

When asked if the pace at which the committee reviewed the bill was excessive, Carney replied, “Absolutely not.”

“I think it’s a mistake to count days as opposed to hours spent on the actual clause-by-clause review,” he told reporters.

“I want to salute all members of the committee, obviously members of the government caucus, but all members of the committee for the time they put in.

“They didn’t get to spend quality time with their family on the weekend, at various events. Some people came in, missed birthdays and other things, in order to move forward.”

The Senate has started its review on the bill, even though it has yet to pass third and final reading in the House of Commons.

The Senate committee has begun hearing from a list witnesses which already exceeds the number of witnesses who presented to the House committee.

stories.title: Workers at Manitoba disability support non-profit vote for strike mandate: Mgeu
stories.summary: Employees represented by the Mgeu at Manitoba Possible voted in favour of a strike mandate after contract talks with its employer stalled.
stories.author: Tavi Dhillon
stories.content:
Employees with a disability support non-profit in Manitoba have voted in favour of a strike mandate after negotiations reached an impasse, according to the workers’ union.

The Manitoba Government and General Employees’ Union (Mgeu) Local 626 has 132 members working at Manitoba Possible, a non-profit offering programs for people with disabilities. Those programs include support services for people who use wheelchairs, clients who are deaf and hard of hearing, along with older adults.

Manitoba Possible employees have been bargaining with management since May and voted in favour of a strike mandate, meaning they are willing to strike if called upon by the union, Nov. 6, according to an Mgeu news release.

Roles such as American Sign Language (ASL) instructors, wheelchair service technicians and rehabilitation counsellors are among the roles represented by the union.

“These workers are amongst some of the lowest paid for what they do,” Kyle Ross, president of the Mgeu, told Global News, reiterating an argument made by Premier Wab Kinew when he spoke with 680 Cjob last Thursday.

The premier was speaking with the station about determining who does, and does not, receive provincial funds.

“We have so many asks for the provincial treasure, and (it’s) really good stuff. Disability support workers need a raise,” Kinew said on Cjob last week.

The Mgeu president said that the premier’s comments on wages do not reflect the offers being presented by Manitoba Possible.

“The offer doesn’t really respect what’s happening out there in a greater environment. The cost of living has skyrocketed over the last couple of years, and if wages don’t keep up, it just really makes it much harder for workers to work these positions,” Ross said.

“Our goal is to avoid a strike at all costs. We’re going to work really hard with the employer to try because we know the valued service they provide to Manitobans, but until then we have to keep it on the table.”

Speaking with reporters at the unveiling of a new Manitoba Possible facility in Winnipeg, its CEO, Lindsey Cooke, said the organization is committed to reaching a deal that will ensure all parties are satisfied.

“Manitoba Possible cares deeply about fair pay for our staff. At the same time, we’re obligated to ensure the continuity of disability services that people rely on here,” she said.

“We think both of those things can be done, so, we’re dedicated to moving forward in finding a fair and sustainable collective agreement.”

In an emailed statement to Global News sent after the news conference, Cooke added that the offer on the table is “within the market range identified by the union’s committee.”

The Manitoba government said it hopes both parties can reach an agreement “that works for everyone.”

“We respect the collective bargaining process and believe the best agreements are reached at the bargaining table. We hope both sides can continue working together to reach a fair deal that works for everyone,” a provincial spokesperson said in an emailed statement to Global News.

On Wednesday, the disability support nonprofit revealed its new space in Winnipeg that it said met the more than 400 recommendations the organization received from disabled Manitobans.

The facility, located at 1680 Notre Dame Avenue, has a fully accessible community kitchen and accessible washrooms, as well as tactile navigation paths, hearing loop technology and mechanical lifts.

“Accessibility isn’t just a policy or building code. It’s the difference between someone feeling included or feeling like an afterthought,” Janelle-Marie Emond, an ambassador with Manitoba Possible, told reporters.

Her favourite part of the site is the accessible bathrooms, which include a self-rising toilet that was brought in from Europe, Emond added. She said the facility will allow Manitobans with disabilities to feel they “can do anything.”

“Nobody should be able to stop living their life just because they have a disability, just because they use a different device,” the ambassador said.

The site cost approximately $4.8 million, with $3.8 million of those funds coming from donors.

stories.title: Pause on Cape Breton AI data centre needed, new Nova Scotia Liberal leader says
stories.summary: Nova Scotia's new Liberal leader is demanding stronger regulation around a planned AI data centre in Cape Breton and is calling for the premier to put the project on hold.
stories.author: Rebecca Lau, Mitchell Bailey
stories.content:
Nova Scotia’s new Liberal leader is demanding stronger regulation around a planned AI data centre in Cape Breton and is calling for the premier to put the project on hold.

Becky Druhan won the leadership race over the weekend and held her first news conference Wednesday, telling reporters regulations are needed to ensure communities, power bills and the environment are protected.

“Announcing a big project is one thing. Making sure it’s a good deal for Nova Scotians is another,” she said.

“Nova Scotians need assurances that utility bills will not subsidize private developments, that taxpayers won’t be exposed to unnecessary financial risk and that companies will pay for the infrastructure that their projects require.”

2:11 Growing pushback against planned AI data centre in Nova Scotia

EverWind has committed $10 billion in private investment for the 420-megawatt data centre at its existing Point Tupper site near Port Hawkesbury, N.S., and AI development company Anthropic has signed a long-term lease to use it.

Druhan said her party is proposing a bill that would regulate data centres in the province.

“The Data Centre Water and Ratepayer Protection Act provides for protections around water use, protections to ensure that power rates will not go up and that Nova Scotians will not bear the added cost of infrastructure associated with power,” she said.

Protests against the project have taken place across the province since it was announced a month ago .

The provincial NDP has also been critical of the project, with leader Claudia Chender calling for emergency debate in the legislature on the topic.

Acadia University political science professor Alex Marland said it’s clear the data centre has become a hot-button issue.

“If you can be seen as a politician who is standing up against the March of AI, you’ll probably get a lot of currency compared to if you’re somebody who’s seen as promoting it,” said Marland.

A representative for EverWind told Global News last week the project is moving ahead as planned. The company recently signed an agreement with Nova Scotia Power, pledging ratepayers won’t shoulder the burden of the data centre’s energy demand.

2:22 EverWind representative says data centre proposal in Cape Breton moving ahead as planned

Druhan, who left the governing Progressive Conservatives in 2025, served as an independent MLA until joining the Liberals this past spring.

In a statement, Premier Tim Houston responded to Druhan’s comments about data centres, saying it was “interesting.”

“It is interesting to see the Provincial Liberals at odds with Mark Carney’s Federal Liberals on the issue of data centres,” Houston wrote.

“We can both protect our environment and grow our economy. The Mark Carney Liberals recognize that and have been supporting this project every step of the way.”

In June, the prime minister and AI Minister Evan Solomon unveiled Canada’s new AI strategy, which includes proposals for the building of large-scale data centres and a plan to ramp up use across industry, government and individuals.

“Artificial intelligence, the defining technology of our era, is here,” Carney said at the time.

But Druhan said it’s up to the province to enshrine those commitments in law.

“Fundamentally, what we need are laws and regulations that protect Nova Scotians, and then the agreements can fit within those,” said Druhan.

stories.title: Trump hasn’t raised Pentagon’s defence complaints, Carney says
stories.summary: Canada making ‘historic investments’ in military and getting armed forces members the pay they deserve, Prime Minister says
stories.author: Craig Lord
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney says the Pentagon’s recent complaints about Canada’s defence spending have not come up in his conversations with U.S. President Donald Trump.

On Monday, the Pentagon released what it called a “fact sheet” claiming Canada’s defence spending has limited its ability to contribute to the protection of North America.

Asked about those complaints on his way into the Liberal caucus meeting on Wednesday, Carney said Trump hasn’t brought up those concerns with him.

“I can assure you that in my discussions with the president the United States, we’re focused on conflict resolution around the world and he has not raised issues such as has been reported recently,” Carney said.

The prime minister said Canada is taking responsibility for its own defence. He said Canada is on the front lines in Europe through Operation Reassurance in Latvia and is engaging with Nato partners to secure the Arctic and the Far North.

Carney also said Canada is making “historic investments” in its military and getting members of the armed forces the pay they deserve.

Under U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, the Trump administration has taken symbolic steps to upend the long-standing bilateral defence relationship between Canada and the United States.

Hegseth last week issued a classified memo imposing restrictions on military co-operation with Canada on think-tanks and socializing.

Defence Minister David McGuinty said Tuesday he can’t “divine” the thinking behind the Pentagon’s recent criticism of Canada’s defence spending.

“The amount of co-operation that we are pursuing together under Norad has not changed. What we are doing together at Nato has not changed,” McGuinty told reporters in Ottawa. “Our military-to-military co-operation has not changed.”

Stephen Fuhr, secretary of state for defence procurement, suggested Wednesday that the Pentagon’s “briefing books haven’t been updated recently.” He cited Canada hitting Nato’s two per cent spending target earlier this year and its plans to buy new submarines, radar units and aircraft.

“Our readiness has been not where we want it to be, and we all acknowledge that, but we’re making great progress and changing it. We’re buying new capabilities, we’re moving faster, more people are joining the Canadian Forces,” he told reporters before the caucus meeting Wednesday.

“If we were to react to every single thing that came out of the United States, we’d have a headache. I don’t think they either know or appreciate how fast we’re moving.”

A senior U.S. Department of Defense official said Hegseth’s memo was intended to ensure a unified objective during engagements with Canada. It does not affect military operations.

The Trump administration official briefed a small group of Canadian journalists Monday on background in order to speak more candidly about Canada-U.S. relations.

The official, who said the Pentagon is looking for Canada to commit to a realistic approach focused on military efficiency, cited the F-35 review.

The Liberal government has yet to reach a decision on its full order of F-35 fighter jets from Lockheed Martin – which Pentagon officials have cited as a source of frustration. Canada has committed to buy 16 of the aircraft, but the decision on the remainder of the planned 88-aircraft order has been the subject of a political review for more than a year.

On Wednesday, Fuhr rejected the idea that the Pentagon was putting pressure on Ottawa to purchase the jets.

He said Canada is still buying military equipment from the United States but is also diversifying into other markets and spending more of its defence dollars at home.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre told reporters after question period on Wednesday that Hegseth should not dictate how Canada spends its defence dollars.

But he also took issue with how the Liberals have been doling out defence spending and claimed the government is lining the pockets of lobbyists and corporations rather than helping military personnel.

'She orchestrated lies to support the lies, and she knew she was doing it.' — Steven Galloway’s lawyer, referring to the author’s accuser

The immigration levels plan, released this month, sets aside 380,000 spaces for new permanent residents in each of the next three years.

Conservative Party of Canada leader Pierre Poilievre speaks during question period in the House of Commons on Parliament Hill on Nov. 24, 2026. (Blair Gable / Postmedia)

November 25, 2026 at 4:09 p.m.

Ottawa — Prime Minister Mark Carney’s declaration on Wednesday that the federal government “has taken back control of immigration” was met with an incredulous shout of “What?” from somewhere across the aisle.

Carney and Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre traded barbs during question period before the House of Commons voted on a Tory motion calling on MPs to reject the latest immigration levels plan.

The Conservatives say the plan includes a record increase to permanent immigration. The government maintains that it’s helping people who are already in Canada transition from temporary to permanent status.

“Only a Liberal would claim that undercounting the number of people who are already here by 300,000 means taking back control of the system,” Poilievre said during one of his questions to the prime minister.
