Carney responded in kind.

“Only the Conservative Party of Canada would have in their platform: ‘We will create pathways to permanence for those already living and working in Canada,’” he said, as those on the Liberal benches beside him jeered.

“That is what this government is doing. We are listening to the Conservative Party of Canada, Mr. Speaker.”

Carney did quote from a Conservative election platform, but the line appears in the version put forward by former leader Erin O’Toole in 2021.

Poilievre’s platform featured no such pledge, though the 2026 Conservative policy statement does include a call to “examine ways to facilitate the transition of foreign workers from temporary to permanent status.”

Starting in 2024, the Liberals capped the number of temporary student and work visas and lowered the number of spaces set aside for permanent residents after then-prime minister Justin Trudeau acknowledged his government had failed to “turn off the tap” of newcomers entering the country post-pandemic.

The annual immigration levels plan, released earlier this month, sets aside 380,000 spaces for new permanent residents in each of the next three years. It also includes a plan to transition up to 200,000 people who are already in Canada to permanent status.

The Liberals say half of those spaces will be divvied up among provinces seeking skilled workers, subject to negotiation with the provinces, while the other half includes people who came from Ukraine and Hong Kong via humanitarian programs, or people looking to reunite with family.

The Conservatives argue Ottawa should slow immigration until services like health care and education can keep up, and until shortages of housing and employment are dealt with.

Thursday’s question period also featured a softball question from floor-crosser Marilyn Gladu, a former Conservative, to Immigration Minister Lena Diab.

The Tories’ non-binding motion was defeated, with Conservative and Bloc Québécois MPs voting in favour.

Diab is set to appear at the House immigration committee on Thursday to answer questions about the levels plan.

Sarah Ritchie joined National Post’s politics bureau after four years covering breaking news on Parliament Hill for The Canadian Press, where she worked as a reporter and editor. Before that, she was an anchor and investigative reporter at Global News in Halifax and covered the Nova Scotia legislature for CTV Atlantic.

stories.title: Oxford County elects Ingersoll Mayor Brian Petrie as Warden
stories.summary: Petrie was elected Wednesday in a 6-4 vote, defeating Woodstock Mayor Jerry Acchione.
stories.author: Bryan Bicknell
stories.content:
Oxford County Council elects Ingersoll Mayor Brian Petrie as warden while work begins on budget

Oxford County Council has elected Ingersoll Mayor Brian Petrie to serve as the county’s 137th warden.

Petrie assumes the role from former Zorra Township Mayor Marcus Ryan, who did not run for office in last month’s municipal election.

Petrie was selected by his council colleagues Wednesday in a vote of 6-4 over Woodstock Mayor Jerry Acchione.

Petrie says councillors are hitting the ground running.

“There’s no downtime. We have to make some big decisions,” said the new warden.

Those big decisions include the next county budget. At its inaugural meeting the new council also got its first look at the draft 2027 budget. The proposed budget puts forward a tax levy of $111.8 million, or a 6.6 per cent tax increase over 2026 on the county portion of municipal tax bills. That averages out to $103 more for a single-family detached home.

“Just getting the documents. Hard to get the drivers and seeing what’s driving that increase,” Petrie said.

“So, that’s where we’re going to have to get into whether it’s justified and what level of service and where the direction to go. And that’s really up to the 10 councillors around the table to decide that. That’s where the discussions will happen about, okay, where do we want to see that number go.”

Oxford’s overall operating budget of $297.8 million covers programs like affordable housing, support for vulnerable and unhoused people, children’s services, water and wastewater, paramedic services, long-term care at Woodingford Lodge, waste management, road safety, community planning and development, provincial offences administration, county library, and more.

Meanwhile, $153.4 has been budgeted for capital expenditures, including infrastructure, such as roads, bridges, water, and wastewater.

Also at Wednesday’s meeting, Tillsonburg mayor Deb Gilvesy was tapped for deputy warden, which is now a two-year term, up from one year.

As for the proposed tax increase, she says council has its work cut out.

“The economy is slowing, housing starts are very, very slow. And we have to recognize that as a council. We have to really put forward some fiscal restraint and think about what we’re passing on to our ratepayers, who many of them are struggling,” she said.

A number of budget sessions are set for next month, with the final budget set for approval Jan. 13, 2027.

stories.title: Conservative motion to block Ottawa's plan to add more permanent residents defeated
stories.summary: A Conservative motion to block the government’s plan to add upwards of 662,000 permanent residents next year was defeated today in a vote that fell along party lines.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — A Conservative motion to block the government’s plan to add upwards of 662,000 permanent residents next year was defeated today in a vote that fell along party lines.

The Bloc Québécois voted with the Conservatives, while the NDP and Green MP Elizabeth May joined the Liberals in opposing the motion.

The Conservatives argue the government’s permanent resident target would put more pressure on the housing market, health services and other social infrastructure.

The government says most of the people expected to receive permanent residency are already living and working in Canada.

The immigration plan tabled earlier this month looks to admit 380,000 permanent residents, and about half of those admissions are expected to be people currently in Canada.

Another 282,000 additional permanent residents are to be approved through a variety of “one-time” measures, and immigration officials say the vast majority of those people have lived here for years.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 25, 20206.

David Baxter, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Canadian auto sector moving away from U.S. imports, new report shows
stories.summary: The data analysis showed that light vehicle imports from the United States have accounted for 40 per cent of Canada's total thus far in 2026 when measured by dollars.
stories.author: Sammy Hudes
stories.content:
A new report suggests the Canadian auto sector is starting to pivot away from U.S. imports toward other global markets amid the ongoing trade war.

The data analysis from DesRosiers Automotive Consultants showed that light vehicle imports from the United States have accounted for 40 per cent of Canada’s total thus far in 2026 when measured by dollars.

That result is down from 49.1 per cent of Canada’s light vehicle imports in 2024. Meanwhile, most other markets saw their shares rise from two years ago.

The proportion of Canada’s light vehicle imports from Mexico increased from 16.7 per cent in 2024 to 20.5 per cent so far this year, while Japan saw an increase to 12.9 per cent from 10.7 per cent in 2024. Imports from South Korea have risen from 10.4 to 12.5 per cent, and the combined European markets saw a bump from 9.8 to 11.1 per cent.

Aside from Canada’s southern neighbour, China was the only market behind its 2024 share at 2.6 per cent thus far in 2026, down from 2.9 per cent.

The overall shift is notable given that not all manufacturers are affected by Canada’s counter-tariffs, which exclude some of the highest volume players, the report said.

DesRosiers managing partner Andrew King said certain manufacturers affected by the tariff situation “have moved rapidly to seek other sourcing where possible and to continue to provide Canadians with vehicles at the best possible price.”

“What the U.S. lost in share was captured readily by the other major light vehicle exporters, with the trade war helping to diversify Canada’s sourcing in this space,” he said in a statement.

Vehicles made in Canada are tariffed by the United States at 25 per cent, minus their American content, while auto and truck parts that comply with the Canada-United States-Mexico agreement on trade are exempt.

In August, President Donald Trump threatened to hike tariffs on all vehicles, auto parts and steel from Canada to 50 per cent on Jan. 1. Canada maintains import duties of 25 per cent on U.S. autos that are not compliant with Cusma. Ottawa allows automakers to import a quota of vehicles made in the United States tariff-free, based in part on their level of automotive assembly in Canada.

Automotive analyst Daniel Ross said the figures show manufacturers are “fighting … to keep prices from climbing.”

“I think it’s directly related to trade policy and the trade war at hand,” said Ross, senior manager of auto industry insights at Canadian Black Book.

“A lot of manufacturers are finding their way to decrease dependency for the Canadian market based off of what’s happening in the U.S. So the narrative is, ultimately, where else can we get these? Where is it easier? Where can we work with?”

Prime Minister Mark Carney said in recent weeks that trade talks with the U.S. are making progress, but Ottawa won’t accept a deal that doesn’t allow for a viable auto sector. That came three months after Canada pulled out of trade talks with the U.S. due to last-minute demands from Washington that included a hit to Canada’s auto sector.

Whether automakers continue to shift imports to non-U.S. markets will depend on how trade negotiations progress, said Ross.

“If it were not to move (in a positive) direction, then I think we could continue to see that climb of market share for Mexico, for Japan specifically,” he said.

“Whether or not that’s the best way forward, it’s a better way forward than having our skin in the game with a U.S. marketplace that’s highly volatile for the last few years.”

stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon is reaching out to opposition leaders in the province’s legislature about pursuing a battle over the oath to the King.

The premier is asking his political rivals to sign a letter he posted on Facebook reaffirming their desire to resume their work in the legislature on Dec. 1, without swearing the oath to the British monarch.

stories.title: Man on Canada’s most-wanted list arrested at London, Ont. motel
stories.summary: Ayoub Mohammed was arrested Tuesday afternoon, after the London Police Service was contacted by police in Québec
stories.author: Reta Ismail
stories.content:
Police in London, Ont., have arrested a 19-year-old man wanted in connection with a homicide in Quebec.

Ayoub Mohammed was arrested Tuesday afternoon, after the London Police Service was contacted by the Sûreté du Québec for assistance in locating a suspect wanted on a Canada-wide warrant.

London police said investigators located Mohammed at a motel on Dundas Street with assistance from the service’s Emergency Response Unit and other police units.

“We were able to contain and safely arrest the male,” said Jennifer Noel, a detective inspector with the London Police Service’s Criminal Investigation Division.

Quebec provincial police said Mohammed was the fourth most-wanted suspect featured on the Bolo (Be On The Lookout) Program, which amplifies police appeals for public assistance.

Investigators say information from the public helped lead them to Mohammed’s location in London.

Noel said the arrest is an example of interjurisdictional police work, noting police services are frequently called upon to assist other jurisdictions in locating and arresting wanted individuals.

Mohammed is expected to appear by video in Valleyfield, Que., court Wednesday to face a charge of second-degree murder in connection with the death of Jordan Gagné.

Gagné was killed in Salaberry-de-Valleyfield on Sept. 4.

stories.title: Musician killed during violent home invasion in midtown Toronto
stories.summary: Death of Michael Eckert heightens fear among residents after second such incident in an affluent neighbourhood this month
stories.author: Jill Mahoney, Patrick White
stories.content:
An accomplished musician was killed during a break-in at his home in midtown Toronto early Wednesday, the second violent home invasion in the city’s affluent neighbourhoods in less than a month.

The fatal attack has heightened fear among residents, especially in wealthy areas where homeowners fed up with an increase in break-ins have gone so far as to hire their own private security guards.

“When the public feels vulnerable, they’re not going to wait for the police or anybody else to protect their family,” said City Councillor Josh Matlow, who represents the ward where Wednesday’s home invasion happened. “Those who have the means are more and more taking things into their own hands, and that’s not a burden they should have to bear, and it’s a very sad reflection on where a lot of people are at right now.”

Michael Eckert, a noted pedal steel guitarist, was killed in the home invasion.

Mr. Eckert played a solo with members of Blue Rodeo during the kick-off show for the Grey Cup earlier this month in Calgary. He was nominated for the Canadian Country Music Association’s steel guitar player of the year award in 2025 and 2023.

Police say Mr. Eckert, 39, was shot during a confrontation after an unknown number of assailants broke into his Poplar Plains Road home around 2:40 a.m. He was rushed to hospital, where he was pronounced dead.

“I understand and recognize how deeply troubling this must be, not only to the residents in that community, but to the residents of the city of Toronto as a whole,” Detective Sergeant Alan Bartlett told reporters. “It is the Toronto Police Service’s solemn commitment that we will do everything we can do and work diligently to locate, identify, apprehend and bring those responsible for this to justice.”

Though the investigation is in its early stages, Det. Sgt. Bartlett said he doesn’t believe the family was targeted. Four people were in the home at the time. None of the other residents were injured.

Mr. Eckert was shot shortly after his home was broken into, he said. “It was a relatively brief period … It’s not my understanding this was a protracted interaction.”

Investigators are poring over surveillance video to determine how many suspects were involved and whether they used a getaway vehicle, said Det. Sgt. Bartlett, who is part of the homicide and missing persons unit.

The attack happened at a home on a leafy residential street in a well-off midtown neighbourhood near Casa Loma and the intersection of St. Clair Avenue West and Avenue Road.

The home invasion occurred less than a month after a violent break-in in the city’s exclusive Bridle Path neighbourhood.

In the Oct. 29 attack, police say three masked gunmen stormed into a house and demanded money or other valuables shortly after 3 a.m.

A man and his two adult daughters sustained gunshot wounds while the mother was injured with a hammer. All four victims survived ; two were said to have “life-altering” injuries.

Home invasions are up across the city, according to Toronto Police data.

So far this year, 233 home invasions have been reported to police, compared to 170 at this time last year and 212 at this time in 2024.

However, home invasions have spiked since 2022 and 2023, when the figure at this time of year was 82 and 84, respectively.

With a report from Stephanie Chambers

stories.title: N.S. RCMP recovered cockpit voice recorder of downed Ontario air ambulance
stories.summary: The RCMP say their underwater recovery team in Nova Scotia played a key role in recovering evidence from an Ontario air ambulance that went down off the coast of Massachusetts.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
By Staff The Canadian Press

Posted November 25, 2026 3:12 pm

The RCMP say their underwater recovery team in Nova Scotia played a key role in recovering evidence from an Ontario air ambulance that went down off the coast of Massachusetts last month.

The Mounties say their team worked with the Canadian Coast Guard and the Transportation Safety Board to find the cockpit voice recorder from the aircraft.

The Transportation Safety Board first announced locating the recorder and the upper third of the aircraft cockpit on Nov. 2.

The safety board said the evidence would be transferred to its engineering laboratory in Ottawa as part of its ongoing investigation.

The air ambulance was carrying six people, including four Canadian crew members, when it went missing in early October .

The remaining passengers were later identified as a 66-year-old woman and her 41-year-old son from Bermuda.

The Gulfstream G100 jet belonged to Hamilton-based medical evacuation company Latitude Air Ambulance.

The aircraft was en route to Boston when it lost contact with air-traffic-control prompting a United States Coast Guard search that ended after 66 hours.

The United States Coast Guard said in early October that debris from the plane was recovered 32 kilometres off Nantucket.

stories.title: Bank of Canada expected to hike interest rate next month, economists say
stories.summary: The Bank of Canada is expected to deliver its next rate decision on Dec. 9, its last and final of 2026 after raising it 0.25 per cent in October.
stories.author: Sean Previl, Jacqueline Hansen
stories.content:
Some Canadians could see their finances tighten more as economists say they expect the Bank of Canada to increase its key interest rate again next month.

The prediction comes after they say the central bank’s governor, Tiff Macklem, warned Tuesday that cost pressures are building on businesses.

“We thought that there might be an opening where the Bank of Canada could delay the next interest rate increase into early next year,” said Sal Guatieri, BMO Capital Markets senior economist.

“But that seemed to just go out the window with the governor basically just confirming that the bank is still quite concerned about energy costs pass-through to the broader measures of inflation.”

Guatieri said Canadians could see at least a 0.25 basis point increase, bringing the key interest rate to 2.75 per cent.

During his speech at the Economic Club of Canada, Macklem spoke of ongoing economic “shocks” and said that while oil prices and refinery margins have dropped, inflation is expected to persist.

He also predicted a “second-round effect of the oil shock” will add to that in the new year.

Guatieri added that with the governor still describing the economy as “resilient,” and its goal to get inflation under control, another hike is likely needed.

The Bank of Canada is expected to deliver its next rate decision on Dec. 9 — its last of 2026.

It announced a rate hike of 0.25 basis points on Oct. 28, bringing the policy rate to 2.5 per cent – the first time it had raised the rate in more than three years.

At the time, Macklem said the decision was an effort to prevent higher energy prices from spreading to the prices of other goods and services. It was also seen as a response to pressure the bank faced due to the Iran war and other geopolitical conflicts resulting in higher prices for oil and gas.

1:45 Variable mortgage rates rise following interest rate increase by the Bank of Canada

Macklem said Tuesday that when disruptions, such as to oil markets, push prices up without slowing economic growth, it can cause higher prices for households.

When this happens, along with worse job prospects, the central bank has to weigh the risk of ongoing inflation with the possibility of weakening the economy with further interest rate changes.

“The best contribution monetary policy can make to the well-being of Canadians is to keep inflation low, stable and predictable,” said Macklem.

Though he stressed the economy was showing resilience, Cibc Chief Economist Avery Shenfeld said they’ve seen it weaken.

“That still leaves us now thinking that he wants to raise interest rates sooner than later rather than wait and see another month or two,” Shenfeld said.

With the potential for businesses that have shouldered the increased costs of transportation and production for some time to start passing those higher costs down to consumers, the bank is likely to take action again.

According to Shenfeld though, December might be where the rate hikes stop – at least for now.

But it will rely on energy prices to continue to cool.

“We don’t expect this inflation outburst to last too long, and we don’t expect to see a lot of interest rate hikes either,” he said. “We expect that December hike to be the last one we’ll see for quite a while.”

Even if a rate hike is expected in an effort to battle back persistent inflation, Guatieri cautions the Bank of Canada from doing so.

He said if the economy is weaker than expected, there’s a softer labour market and if unemployment continues to rise, interest rate hikes could have a heavier affect. That stands more true if a trade deal — even an interim one — isn’t reached with the U.S. and more tariffs come into effect in January.

“It could end up being premature and who knows, the bank May end up having to reverse these rate increases if the economy softens through the next year,” Guatieri said.

stories.title: Telecom consumer group needed to push back against ‘gouging’, advocates say
stories.summary: A consumer advocacy group is pushing for a new telecommunications consumer organization (TCO) in Canada to protect against what it calls "gouging and abuse."
stories.author: Ariel Rabinovitch
stories.content:
As Québecor looks to acquire Telus, with Bell also reportedly in the mix , a consumer advocacy group is pushing for a new telecommunications consumer organization (TCO) in Canada to protect against what it calls “gouging and abuse by Canada’s big telecom companies.”

Democracy Watch, a Canadian non-profit group that advocates on democratic reform, government accountability and corporate responsibility, said Monday in a statement that, if formed, a TCO would offer Canadians free assistance with shopping around, filing complaints, pursuing lawsuits and representing consumers in regulatory and policy-making processes.

Québecor said on Nov. 16 it had sent an enhanced unsolicited offer to acquire Telus in a merger deal valued at approximately $31 billion, which Telus confirmed it received. The proposed merger is expected to face scrutiny from regulators because of the perceived risk that it could lead to less choice in the telecommunications space and potentially higher prices for consumers.

The Competition Bureau also confirmed to Global News last week it was “aware” of the proposed merger.

1:53 Potential mega-merger: Why Quebecor wants to buy Telus for $31B

Democracy Watch said a TCO needs to be created in Canada regardless of whether the Quebecor-Telus merger is approved, and it must be facilitated by the large telecom players — Rogers, Bell, Telus and Québecor, by inviting its customers to join.

“To really stop ongoing gouging and abuse by Canada’s big telecom companies the federal government must create a national, consumer-run telecom watchdog group that will empower and provide free help to consumers with shopping around, complaining and suing to get good, fairly priced service from the companies,” said Duff Conacher, co-founder of Democracy Watch and the Corporate Responsibility Coalition in a release.

“Requiring the companies to facilitate the creation of a consumer-run telecom watchdog group is [the] most low-cost, effective thing to do to empower and educate consumers, give them a place to call that will give them free, effective help when they are gouged or abused, and ensure telecom companies serve everyone fairly and well at fair prices.”

This also comes after Prime Minister Mark Carney suggested on Nov. 18 when speaking to reporters that when there are fewer market players, depending on the circumstances, oligopolies like with the Canadian telecom sector can help improve competition, but did not elaborate.

Conacher tells Global News in a statement that there are some merits to Carney’s theory.

“My guess is that he meant that if there are high costs to operating as a business in any sector, then three big companies that can afford to pay all of those costs and still make a profit can, as a result, afford to compete with each other on prices for their products and/or services,” said Conacher.

“I don’t think his comment makes any sense for the telecom industry in Canada.”

1:44 Crtc launches inquiry into fees from Rogers, Bell, and Telus

Moshe Lander, an economics professor at Concordia University, said in an earlier interview with Global News that if the proposed merger goes through, and there are three main players instead of four, that could, in theory, help lower costs for consumers.

He explains that it comes down to cost savings for the combined company by growing market share while also gaining access to more infrastructure, including fibre optics and cell towers.

“If they [Québecor and Telus] were allowed to merge together, then you really only need one network that you would have to maintain. And so because you would get all of the customers combined, then given that the infrastructure network could be shared out across more consumers, that would lower your average cost,” says Lander.

“Assuming then you pass some of that cost saving onto your customers, you could deliver lower prices. I just don’t think that’s what’s going to happen here, and if we look at the Rogers tie-up with Shaw, it’s not like it’s led to lower prices for Rogers users or for Shaw users.”

In order to create a TCO, Democracy Watch says the federal government would first need to pass a law requiring telecom companies to send membership invitations to customers via email or regular mail, and once established, members could elect leaders.

Such an organization would require funding, which Democracy Watch estimates each member could pay an annual average membership fee of $30. This estimate, it says, was based on similar U.S. models.

Democracy Watch says, if created, it expects about five per cent of telecom consumers would sign up and contribute membership fees to fund an approximately $30 million annual budget.

The group says a TCO will seek to educate consumers through price surveys, public forums, shopping guides and other publications. It will also hire economists, experts, organizers and lawyers to represent consumers as needed.

stories.title: Canadians with cannabis possession records can apply for pardon through new online portal
stories.summary: The Parole Board of Canada has approved pardons for 944 cannabis possession convictions
stories.author: Stewart Lewis
stories.content:
The Parole Board of Canada has approved pardons for 944 cannabis possession convictions since mid-2019, according to spokesperson Andrea Fournier.

That number is likely to increase with the recent Parole Board launch of an online portal to apply for criminal record pardons , including for possession of cannabis for personal use.

“For eligible individuals, obtaining a … cannabis record (pardon) can help remove barriers to employment, education, volunteering and housing,” the Parole Board says in the news release accompanying the launch.

The 944 pardons followed from new legislation that enabled “a streamlined application process for simple possession,” Fournier told National Post in an email on Wednesday.

“Between August 1, 2019 … and November 20, 2026, the PBC has received 1,476 applications for cannabis record (pardons),” she said, adding that 526 applications were returned because “the individual was either not eligible for the streamlined application process or their documentation was incomplete.”

The #PBCServicePortal is a safe and convenient way to apply online for a record suspension (pardon) or a cannabis record suspension. 🔗 https://t.co/cNH4x8IQpL 2/2 — Parole Board of Canada (@PBC_CLCC_en) November 19, 2026

The federal government legalized possession of up to 30 grams of legal cannabis on Oct. 17, 2018. It followed the legalization for medical cannabis , two decades earlier.

Potential pardon applicants can check on their eligibility on the federal government website.

It says a person can apply for a cannabis record pardon if they “were convicted in Canada as an adult of simple possession of cannabis … Simple possession is a charge for possession of a controlled substance, in this case cannabis, for personal use (i.e., with no intent to traffic).”

Individuals who are neither Canadian citizens or residents can also apply if they have “a record of conviction(s) for simple possession of cannabis in Canada.”

The new portal enables applicants to start an application and return later to complete it. Supporting documents can be uploaded, such as: the conviction record, court documents, police record checks and identification.

Applicants can then track their application’s progress online.

“By simplifying the application process, the PBC Service Portal helps people benefit from programs that can support their successful reintegration, while maintaining the integrity of the … cannabis record (pardon) processes and supporting public safety,” states the parole board new release.

stories.title: Health Canada warns of rare vision loss risk with Ozempic and other semaglutide drugs
stories.summary: Toronto — Health Canada has issued a warning about a "very rare" risk of vision loss with Ozempic, Wegovy and other semaglutide drugs.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Nicole Ireland, The Canadian Press

Posted November 25, 2026 2:48 pm.

Last Updated November 26, 2026 8:22 am.

Toronto — Health Canada has issued a warning about a “very rare” risk of vision loss with Ozempic, Wegovy and other semaglutide drugs.

In the warning issued Wednesday, the department said it has completed a safety review “that found a possible link between prescription semaglutide drugs and the risk of non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy.”

The eye condition, also known as Naion, “causes sudden painless vision loss or vision changes due to reduced blood flow to the optic nerve.”

Health Canada said it is working with semaglutide manufacturers to include warnings about the condition in their product monographs.

Patients taking the diabetes and weight loss drugs should talk to their health-care provider about the potential risks before taking them, the warning said.

Anyone currently taking semaglutide should get urgent medical attention if they experience blurring, cloudiness, rapidly worsening sight or sudden vision loss.

Health Canada said its safety review focused on semaglutide drugs, but it is also assessing the risk with all other GLP-1 drugs.

Earlier in November, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration announced manufacturers of all GLP-1 medications — including tirzepatide drugs Mounjaro and Zepbound — must add a warning about Naion to their product labels.

Non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy is the most common type of damage to the optic nerve in adults over 50, Health Canada’s summary of its review said.

People with diabetes, high blood pressure and high cholesterol are at increased risk for the condition.

The link between semaglutide and Naion “is not fully understood,” the summary said, but a rapid drop in blood sugar levels after using the medication “May cause swelling of the optic nerve and reduce its blood supply, especially in individuals with other risk factors.”

It’s not known how long it takes symptoms of the condition to develop, the summary said.

In an email on Wednesday, the Canadian Association of Optometrists said it has been aware of the rare risk of Naion “for some time.”

“If you’re starting a GLP-1 medication and haven’t had an eye exam in the last year, it’s a good idea to get your eyes checked. It’s also important to let your optometrist know that you’re taking the medication,” said Dr. Allison Scott, the association’s president.

“Anyone experiencing sudden vision loss should seek immediate eye care. An optometrist can assess the issue and, where necessary, facilitate an urgent referral to an ophthalmologist,” she said.

Novo Nordisk, the manufacturer of Ozempic, Rybelsus and Wegovy semaglutide medications, said Health Canada has previously communicated with GLP-1 manufacturers about Naion and the company identifies the condition in its product monographs.

“Patient safety is a top priority for Novo, and we take all reports of adverse events very seriously,” said Kate Hanna, spokesperson for Novo Nordisk, in an emailed statement on Wednesday.

“Novo remains confident in the benefit-risk profile of our GLP-1 medicines, when prescribed as indicated,” she said.

“We recognize that adverse events can have a profound impact on patients and their families. We continue to monitor the safety of our medicines, review new research and work with health authorities around the world.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 25, 2026.

stories.title: Why Canada’s psychiatrists are issuing a caution on Ottawa’s new Maid bill
stories.summary: Last month, Justice Minister Sean Fraser announced that Canada will deny access to medical assistance in dying for people who are seeking it on the basis of mental illness alone.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
A body representing Canada’s psychiatrists are issuing a note of caution over the federal government’s proposed law for medical assistance in dying (Maid).

Last month, Justice Minister Sean Fraser announced that Canada will not extend Maid for people who are seeking it on the basis of mental illness alone.

Currently, the law excludes Maid for people seeking it on the grounds of mental illness as a sole criteria, but that rule is set to expire in March 2027.

Bill C-41, the Medical Assistance in Dying Safeguard Act, maintains that exclusion “on an indeterminate basis,” Fraser said.

The Canadian Psychiatric Association (CPA) said the law runs the risk of furthering harmful assumptions about people struggling with mental illness.

“It is important to not reinforce potentially discriminatory assumptions about people with mental disorders or their decision-making capacity,” the body said in a statement.

However, the CPA added that it was not taking a position on the legality or morality of Maid, or weigh in on whether it should be available on the sole basis of a mental disorder.

Receive the latest medical news and health information delivered to you every Sunday.

Officials cited “difficulty in assessing an individual’s decision-making capacity when seeking Maid on the basis of a mental illness” as a reason for preventing the expansion of Canada’s Maid laws for mental illness.

Whether or not a person is able to make an informed decision about their care is already subject to “rigorous, individualized assessments” assessment, CPA said.

Healthcare professionals are required to ascertain “whether their decision is voluntary, stable and consistent with their values, and whether all reasonable treatment options have been explored.”

These safeguards apply equally to physical and mental illnesses, CPA said.

“This means that the presence of mental disorder alone is not used as a proxy for incapacity or vulnerability, with a focus on ensuring that autonomy and equality rights are protected,” it added.

Acknowledging the “complex and difficult” nature of the Maid debate, CPA said it “remains committed to advancing access to high-quality, evidence-based care for people with mental disorders.”

6:05 Canada announces changes to Maid

The federal bill restricts advance directive on Maid only to people who are:

at least 18 years of age

eligible to receive government-funded health services

able to make their own decisions about Maid

diagnosed with a “serious and incurable illness or disease prior to making the advance request that is expected to lead to a permanent loss of capacity to consent” to Maid.

Advocacy group Dying With Dignity Canada said it was disappointed by the federal government’s decision to exclude mental illness from the scope of the law.

“It is stigmatizing and unconstitutional and Dying With Dignity Canada continues to be dismayed in any action that prevents all Canadians from equal access to apply for Maid,” Helen Long, the group’s CEO said.

stories.title: Struggling Kensington Capital names new CEO
stories.summary: Company founder to step down after asset manager suffers worst-ever monthly loss
stories.author: Jameson Berkow
stories.content:
After three decades running Kensington Capital, Tom Kennedy is stepping down, leaving the struggling asset manager in the hands of former pension-fund executives.

Toronto-based Kensington announced Wednesday that Mr. Kennedy, who founded the company in 1996, will transition from chief executive officer to vice-chairman as of April 1, 2027. Saar Pikar, who joined Kensington in July as president, will then assume the CEO role.

Mr. Pikar was most recently head of venture capital and growth-equity investments at Ontario Municipal Employees Retirement System. Bo Cenanovic, a former Ontario Teachers’ Pension Plan and PSG Equity executive who also joined Kensington in July to be head of the firm’s private-equity division, will replace Mr. Pikar as president.

Last week, Kensington reported the worst-ever monthly loss for its billion-dollar private-equity fund. The fund halted redemptions in late 2025, preventing investors from cashing out their holdings, and it has since lost nearly 20 per cent of its value. In September alone, the fund declined by 13 per cent.

At the time, Mr. Pikar pledged to sell off and write down bad investments in order to repay debt. In a statement on Wednesday, he expressed confidence in the turnaround plan.

“I am honoured to be appointed CEO for Kensington at a crucial time for the company as we navigate unprecedented and rapidly evolving market conditions,” he said.

Alfred Chuang, Kensington’s chief financial officer for the past five years, who is also a former Omers executive, left the company on Tuesday to pursue other opportunities, the company announced separately on Wednesday. According to his LinkedIn profile , Mr. Chuang has joined Verilum Financial as managing director.

Kensington’s recent challenges are reflective of the broader difficulties facing private-equity funds over all, as many of them borrowed money when interest rates were low in order to invest more aggressively. But when rates started to rise in 2022, firms such as Kensington found the higher interest payments increasingly difficult to manage.

While most private-equity funds require investors to lock in their money for at least five years, Kensington’s original pitch was for a fund that promised regular opportunities to cash out. Circumstances forced Kensington to renege on that promise, though Mr. Pikar said last week “we took our medicine” in September and the fund was now “poised to do some really good things.”

In a statement, Mr. Kennedy said he was “a strong believer in the value that leadership renewal brings to organizations as they evolve and grow,” adding Mr. Pikar and Mr. Cenanovic are “the right individuals to shape the future direction [of] the firm.”

AGF Management Ltd. AGF-B-T , a global investment company with roughly $77-billion in assets under management, purchased a majority stake in Kensington in 2024.

stories.title: Exceptional access to cancer drugs not a simple issue, minister says amid outcry
stories.summary: Toronto - A question has been swirling in Ontario's legislature: what happens when terminal cancer patients are told there is nothing more the medical system in the province can do for them, but promising treatments exist that are just out of reach?
stories.author: Allison Jones The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - A question has been swirling in Ontario’s legislature: what happens when terminal cancer patients are told there is nothing more the medical system in the province can do for them, but promising treatments exist that are just out of reach?

Several people with metastatic cancer, previously unknown to each other, have come together to battle for access to drugs either not approved or funded here. They are appealing to the courts to overturn Ontario Health Insurance Plan decisions, and to the politicians in charge on a basic human level.

The patients themselves and opposition critics say the answer to the central question should be an easy one. If there is a medication that can save them, the public system they have contributed to for much of their lives should be able to figure out a way to fund it.

It is unfortunately not that simple, Ontario Health Minister Sylvia Jones suggests.

Jones has come under fire for amending regulations to clarify that out-of-country drug treatments will only be publicly funded in very narrow circumstances, a move that followed a win in court by one of the cancer patients.

The minister sat down recently with The Canadian Press to discuss the issue in greater detail, as the values and processes underpinning Ontario’s publicly funded health system are confronted with heartbreaking personal stories.

“I think it is fair to say that we all have individuals in our lives who have chased that cure, chased that option, and so I completely understand why they are researching, advocating, trying to find what is out there that is available to them,” Jones said in the interview.

“It is not lost on me. Like I said, I’ve spoken to many families. I can absolutely appreciate why they’re doing it. I guess, I also have a role as the minister of health to make sure that the system continues to be welcoming, encouraging, and available to all Ontario residents.”

The reason for the policy to not fund drug treatments out of country — unless they are already funded here but temporarily unavailable — Jones said, is in part to ensure drug manufacturers can’t circumvent Health Canada’s processes.

After Health Canada’s approval of a drug, there is a clinical assessment by experts that asks questions such as, “Is it for pediatric patients? Is it for seniors? Is it for the entire population?’” she said.

“There are times when people request exceptional access for drugs, primarily, that have been tested and gone through clinical trials for a specific age group, but it hasn’t been tested for another age group,” Jones said.

“Until the pharmaceuticals do that, I don’t think it is government’s role to say, ‘Go ahead and try that. I don’t know if it’s going to work.’ I don’t think that’s our role, and I don’t think it ever should be.”

In the case of Alex Shved, a 37-year-old father of two with Stage 4 melanoma, the tumour-infiltrating lymphocyte therapy his oncologist has recommended is available in the United States at an approximate cost of US$600,000. It has been approved by Health Canada, but the conclusion of the subsequent review and price negotiation process for public funding will likely come too late for Shved.

Ontario has the Funding Accelerated for Specific Treatments program, which speeds up approvals for certain cancer medicines and does contemplate funding in the interim period between Health Canada approval and provincial price negotiations. TIL therapy isn’t part of it.

Shved bristles at Jones’ characterization, which he sees as an implication that patients are asking for fringe treatments, when even the health experts consulted by the government bureaucrats who denied his out-of-country funding supported TIL therapy for him.

“This isn’t about patients reading Facebook posts and wanting to try some experimental drug no one has heard of,” he said.

“These therapies are standard of care in more developed health-care systems and most of the time Canadian doctors are familiar with them.”

In 31-year-old Sabrina Apitz-Grossman’s case, a drug that could treat the rare form of cancer in her knee has been approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, but the manufacturer has said it has no plans to apply for approval in Canada.

As cancer treatments become more personalized, targeted to specific gene mutations of specific types of cancer, Apitz-Grossman said there should be a different way of assessing cases such as hers, where the Canadian market May be too small for companies to bother applying.

“I feel like we all want the same thing, which is we want people to receive treatment, and we want there to be strong options at Princess Margaret (Hospital) and clinical trials,” she said this week after attending question period.

“We want the Fast program to keep operating. That is amazing. But we also probably want a safety net for when those things don’t catch your circumstances.”

Jones said it is “very seldom” that drug companies decline to apply in Canada due to the relatively small market compared to the United States.

“It is very appealing for a drug manufacturer to have their product on Ohip drug formulary,” she said.

She suggested that since a lot of the new, highly targeted therapies are very expensive, those companies should be motivated to go through the process for public funding in Ontario, even if the market is small, because patients are unlikely to be able to afford the drugs out of pocket.

The current system is already well-equipped to deal with precision oncology, Jones said.

“What I worry about is by some nuance in government policy, we actually discourage, or say we actually don’t need to list in Canada because we can get through in a different way,” she said.

“I want all Ontario cancer patients, all Ontario patients to benefit. We shouldn’t need to be looking at expanding an out-of-country process when we have everything here.”

But if we had everything here, the out-of-country program wouldn’t need to exist, Shved said, and he and Apitz-Grossman and others would be receiving potentially life-saving drug therapies here.

“She is just saying, ‘Wait two to three years until the paperwork is signed so we can physically give you the drug here,’ whereas the (out-of-country) program asks, ‘How about we send the most needy patients to get the drug somewhere else in the meantime?’”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 25, 2026.

stories.title: Quebec Premier invites provincial party leaders to sign declaration refusing oath to King
stories.summary: Opening of legislative session is uncertain after judge suspended law abolishing the requirement
stories.author: Maura Forrest
stories.content:
The Quebec government says a court decision declaring that legislators must swear allegiance to King Charles III does not prevent members of the National Assembly from sitting without taking the oath.

Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon on Wednesday sent a declaration to opposition leaders that he invited them to sign, which stated they’re ready to return to the provincial legislature next week despite having sworn loyalty only to the Quebec people.

But rival party leaders and constitutional experts have raised doubts about any plan to open the National Assembly in apparent contravention of a court ruling.

On Monday, a Quebec Superior Court judge suspended a 2022 law that had abolished the requirement to take an oath of loyalty to the Crown.

Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon has said he cannot swear fealty to Canada’s monarch. His government has appealed the decision and has asked the court to allow members of the National Assembly to sit while the appeal is under way.

Separately, the Premier has also said he is committed to “abolishing the monarchy” in Quebec by eliminating the office of Lieutenant-Governor, the King’s official representative in the province.

On Wednesday, Deputy Premier Catherine Gentilcore announced that all parties had reached an agreement to ask Lieutenant-Governor Manon Jeannotte not to attend the opening of the National Assembly. Instead, she will be asked to submit a written address that will be tabled in the legislature.

The National Assembly is set to open Dec. 1 for the first time since the Parti Québécois formed a minority government last month. However, none of the 127 elected members have sworn allegiance to the King.

Ms. Gentilcore said there’s “absolutely nothing” that prevents the legislature from sitting.

“What we want right now is to reach out to the other parties so that we can all agree that, no matter what happens, we will meet as scheduled on Tuesday,” she told reporters in Quebec City.

Justice Minister Marie-Claude Sarrazin said the court decision does not explicitly order MNAs to swear allegiance to the King. “Nor is there any order to sit or not to sit,” she said.

In the decision, however, Justice Ian Demers wrote that the suspension of the 2022 law means that lawmakers will now “be required to take an oath to the King before assuming their duties.”

On Wednesday, Quebec Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime called on the Premier to share any legal opinions that support the conclusion that MNAs can sit without swearing allegiance to the King.

“Is it legal?” he asked. “What we want is to ensure that Parliament not only resumes its work, but that it does so in full compliance with the law.”

Neither Mr. Duhaime nor Quebec Liberal Leader Charles Milliard have ruled out the possibility of taking an oath to the Crown if it prevents a delay to the legislative session.

Mr. Milliard accused the PQ of “putting the cart before the horse” while the government’s appeal is pending. A hearing is scheduled for Friday afternoon, though it’s unclear how quickly the court could decide whether to allow legislators to sit as the case unfolds.

Patrick Taillon, a professor of constitutional law at Laval University, said the government’s position presents a scenario of “high constitutional tension.”

“On the one hand, the separation of powers and parliamentary privilege clearly prevent the courts from intervening to stop members of the legislature from convening,” he said in an e-mail.

“On the other hand, nothing prevents the courts from suspending or invalidating laws” passed by legislators who haven’t sworn the oath.

Ms. Sarrazin suggested on Wednesday that the Speaker of the National Assembly could choose to allow legislators to sit despite the court ruling.

But Karine Millaire, a professor of constitutional law at the University of Montreal, said that would be a surprising decision. “In my opinion, it violates the Constitution.”

The Lieutenant-Governor might also decline to give royal assent to laws passed by a legislature in such circumstances, she added.

The office of Speaker Nathalie Roy declined to comment on the matter.

The 2022 law was passed unanimously after Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon and his caucus, then in opposition, refused to take the oath and were barred from entering the National Assembly.

Ottawa lawyer Lawrence David launched a legal challenge of the law in August, arguing Quebec has no authority to unilaterally amend the Constitution.

The substance of the case has yet to be heard, but Mr. David filed for an emergency injunction after the October election to force MNAs to take the oath before the National Assembly reconvened.

Justice Demers sided with Mr. David on Monday, ruling that if lawmakers did not swear allegiance to the Crown, “all laws passed by the National Assembly would be unconstitutional and would have to be re-enacted.”

At a news conference in Ottawa on Wednesday, Mr. David accused the Quebec Premier of “demagoguery” for suggesting legislators can sit without taking the oath.

He also chided the federal government for staying quiet on the matter, accusing it of permitting “clear violations of the Constitution.” He said Ottawa could have referred the issue directly to the Supreme Court of Canada .

stories.title: Rain, gusty winds and possible wintry mix in forecast for southern Ontario
stories.summary: A cold start to the day Wednesday, but temperatures recover this afternoon thanks to the sunshine.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
After a stretch of sunshine and above-freezing temperatures, a more active weather pattern is set to arrive across southern Ontario heading into Thursday and Friday.

CTV News London meteorologist Julie Atchison says Wednesday’s clear skies and mild temperatures are the result of a high-pressure system that will soon move out, making way for a low-pressure system developing over the Carolinas.

“Lots of sunshine. A beautiful day in southern Ontario,” Atchison said Wednesday afternoon, noting temperatures ranged from near zero to as high as 7 C across the region.

According to Atchison, the approaching system will track up the eastern seaboard, pushing significant moisture northward and bringing rainfall into the London area Thursday afternoon.

“We will see all of this rain wrapping back around towards the eastern Great Lakes,” she said.

Rainfall totals of 10 to 15 millimetres are possible in the London region, along with gusty winds as the storm moves through.

As colder air wraps into the system Thursday night, conditions could become more complicated. Atchison said temperatures are expected to fall, creating the potential for some snow to mix with the rain. Areas northeast of Toronto could also see a risk of freezing rain by Friday.

A rain-snow mix remains possible across much of southern Ontario on Friday before the system exits to the east by Saturday.

Overnight temperatures are expected to hover between -1 C and 1 C over the next several days.

Looking ahead to the weekend, Saturday is expected to be mainly cloudy, while Sunday carries a slight chance of showers. Temperatures are forecast to remain mild, climbing to between 7 C and 9 C.

“Mixed precipitation is expected on Friday,” Atchison said, adding residents should be prepared for changing conditions as the system moves through the region.

stories.title: LHSC files $2M lawsuit over alleged deficient window work at Victoria Hospital
stories.summary: The latest allegations from LHSC supervisor David Musyj reveal that windows on two towers at Victoria hospital were determined substandard and prone to leaks.
stories.author: CTVNewsLondon.ca Staff
stories.content:
London health sciences centre is seeking two-million dollars in a new lawsuit alleging deficient and incomplete work.

The allegations follow separate ongoing litigation against former employees and firms alleging mismanagement and system failures.

The latest allegations from LHSC supervisor David Musyj reveal that windows on two towers at Victoria hospital were determined substandard and prone to leaks.

The hospital is seeking $2-million dollars in damages in its lawsuit against BH Contractors, Matter Architectural Studio and the hospital’s former vice-president of facilities, Dipesh Patel.

According to a release, the hospital contends the work completed “did not meet the project requirements.”

Its claim also states that only slightly more than 50 per cent of the invoiced work was completed or deficient.

Meanwhile, after the discoveries were made, the hospital contends more windows in building 14 were found to be residential grade, not the commercial windows specified in an initial contract.

Musyj contends all windows remain safe, and said legal proceedings are moving forward as separate cases, relating to allegations of mismanagement and incomplete work proceed through the courts.

“We’re at what is called the discovery phase, where we exchange affidavits and documents as well as have examinations for discoveries. And were cooperating with the police investigation and when the police ask us for information or service for orders of production orders, we comply with that of course,” Musyj said while s peaking at a community update meeting on Nov. 18.

LHSC is also seeking more than $50 million in damages from several former employees, including Patel, along with BH Contractors, GBI Construction, and contractor Paresh Soni.

The claim accuses the group of manipulating procurement processes, inflating invoices, and awarding contracts to companies with secret ties — actions that LHSC says amount to civil fraud and breach of fiduciary duty.

In another claim, former CEO Jackie Schleifer Taylor is among the executives accused of ignoring a 2022 report that flagged potential fraud and failing to notify auditors or the board of directors.

None of the allegations have been tested in court.

Meanwhile, in its is release Wednesday, LHSC announced it has launched lawsuits against insurance companies for coverage related to the claims it believes it is entitled to.

'She orchestrated lies to support the lies, and she knew she was doing it.' — Steven Galloway’s lawyer, referring to the author’s accuser

Navigate

Canada is one of just a handful of countries with universal healthcare that does not use some mix of styles

An ambulance arrives at the Foothills Hospital in Calgary on Feb. 25, 2026. (Darren Makowichuk/Postmedia)

November 25, 2026 at 12:55 p.m.

A new report from the Fraser Institute is calling on Canada to explore private and for-profit hospitals as well as the traditional government-run institutions, arguing that most advanced countries are already using a mix of styles and getting good value for money.

The report, “Evaluating the Arguments Against For-Profit Health Care,” was written by Steven Globerman, a Senior Fellow at the Fraser Institute and a former professor at Simon Fraser University, York University and elsewhere.

It notes that of 19 countries with universal healthcare that report hospital beds as private or government-run, only four — Canada, Denmark, Finland and Iceland — do not use some mix of styles. A host of others, including Australia, Ireland, Japan and Switzerland, make use of both.

One country on the list, the Netherlands, relies entirely on private hospitals, an indication that there is no single system at play in the world.

“The Netherlands is an outlier in having no government-run hospitals,” Nadeem Esmail, the Fraser Institute’s director of health policy, told National Post. “The hospitals are all private not-for-profits. These are entities that are allowed to go out of business if they fail to serve patients in a timely fashion and if they fail to attract patients to their facility.”

He added: “Hospitals in the Netherlands are paid on the basis of the care they provide. They’re not given budgets the way we do here in Canada. It’s a very interesting approach.”

Esmail also pointed to Sweden’s Capio St. Goran Hospital in Stockholm as an example where publicly funded, privately delivered healthcare can improve the system. Dating back to the 13th century, it became the country’s first privatized hospital in 1999. (Sweden briefly banned further privatizations in 2004 before reversing that law three years later.)

“Today, that hospital is 28 per cent less expensive than the national average in terms of cost per procedure,” said Esmail. “It ranks at the very top in comparisons of hospital performance and hospital quality, and it has one of Sweden’s busiest emergency rooms. This is a beacon hospital showing what is possible, and by its existence and through the pressure it creates, it brings other hospitals in the area up.”

The Fraser Institute report points to broader studies that suggest that for-profit hospitals provide “spillover efficiency benefits” to non-profits in the same geographical region. U.S. data found that heart-attack patients received similar levels of care in both types of hospitals, but that costs were 2.4 per cent lower in government hospitals when there were for-profit hospitals nearby.

“Empirical evidence does not support the argument that for-profit hospitals have worse outcomes, and in fact it suggests that for-profit hospitals are more efficient, and that their presence will actually lead to improved efficiency of non-profit and government hospitals,” Esmail said.

“So I think, as Canadians are looking for answers, this is one solution. It’s a solution that has worked in Sweden and that is deployed in 100 per cent of the top performing universal access healthcare systems. I think that’s where the pressure will come from; Canadians’ desire for change, because the healthcare system right now simply isn’t working for them.”

As to why Canada is so slow to change, Esmail blamed institutional inertia, as well as “defenders of the status quo.”

“I think in some cases these are vested interests who benefit from the current structure and who would see their stranglehold on the healthcare system weakened by the introduction of private competition, and so they’re potentially arguing for their position and veiling it as a defence of the Canadian patient,” he said. “When we know in reality, for-profit competitive providers will make the Medicare experience better for patients and for the taxpayers who fund their care.”

Esmail was co-author of another recent report, “Comparing Performance of Universal Health Care Countries,” which found that, of 32 high-income countries offering universal healthcare, Canada ranks among the highest for spending but falls consistently at the bottom of the list when it comes to results.

Globerman in the newest report notes that it is an uphill battle to suggest a change in the current system.

“It is difficult to even broach the issue of whether the performance of Canada’s health-care system would improve if economic incentives were more heavily relied upon to guide resource-allocation decisions, and bureaucratic guidance and direction played a less important role in decision-making,” he writes.

“Advocates of allowing profits to drive health-care decision-making are often dismissed out-of-hand as promoting ‘American-Style’ healthcare, which is typically characterized as prioritizing wealth as a determinant of health status and a system in which patient outcomes are subordinated to commercial priorities.”

However, he points out the danger of the “Nirvana Fallacy,” which arises “from comparing an imperfect real-world arrangement for carrying out a specific activity to an idealized, flawless hypothetical alternative.”

In other words, the potential for for-profit hospitals to be less than perfect should not shut down the discussion at the outset.

Chris Knight is a long-time reporter/critic/editor at National Post with a special interest in science, space and movies.

stories.title: Masar Badil dismisses terrorist designation, says Toronto conference will proceed
stories.summary: Toronto police say they are aware of the event as calls grow for authorities to act on and expand anti-terrorist legislation
stories.author: Kenn Oliver
stories.content:
Organizers of a Masar Badil anti-Israel conference scheduled for Toronto this weekend issued a defiant dismissal of the terrorist entity designation given to it by Ottawa this week, insisting that their event will continue “regardless of the threats of criminalization.”

“The only force that directs us is a framework of liberation — a path that does not stop at mere self-expression, nor settle for liberal rhetoric, nor capitulate to imperialist state condemnation,” the committee behind “3 Years of Al-Aqsa Flood: Resistance & Return from the Belly of the Beast” wrote in a late Tuesday night statement.

The Toronto Police Service told National Post it’s aware of a conference at a so-far undisclosed location this Saturday and Sunday and is liaising with the RCMP-led National Security Enforcement Team, but wouldn’t comment on any related planned or potential enforcement action.

Monday - Saturday Free

NP Posted keeps you updated on the news of the day and the perspectives that define the National Post, while drawing your focus to some of the unexpected stories we like to tell. Delivered straight to your inbox Monday to Friday, with a weekend edition on Saturdays.

“That said, you are committing a criminal offence if you knowingly participate in or contribute to the activities of a terrorist group,” a spokesperson said in an email.

Richard Marceau, senior vice-president and general consul for the Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs (Cija), said the designation gives the federal government the tools to stop the event; now, “it’s a question of will.”

The former Bloc Quebecois MP also said the federal government should address some legislative gaps to help law enforcement agencies act more decisively.

“It’s time, for example, for Canada to toughen up its anti-terrorist legislation by adding a clear new section in the Criminal Code regarding willful promotion of terrorism,” he said. “It would clarify the situation, and I think it would give law enforcement sharper tools to fight those people.”

Public Safety Canada, in a press release Monday, said that evidence suggests that Masar Badil is a “faction/offshoot” of Samidoun, already a terrorist organization in Canada’s eyes, and that “the two groups are the same entity.” Both have documented links to Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine (Pflp), a listed terrorist entity in Canada, the U.S. and the EU.

Masar Badil, also known as the Palestinian Alternative Revolutionary Path Movement, was listed as a specially designated global terrorist by the U.S. this August, but remains unlisted in the EU.

According to the NGO Monitor, it describes itself as “a radical popular political movement,” operating as “a framework and a popular resistance movement confronting Zionist colonialism and the project of liquidation and surrender.”

In a statement described by Marceau as “unrepentant,” conference organizers said they “completely and absolutely reject” the designation, arguing it is an attempt to criminalize solidarity and weaken the collective “liberation” movement, even though it describes itself as a unique “internationalist movement” calling for “an alternative revolutionary path.”

The group stated that one of its founding “liberatory principles” is recognizing “armed resistance as the primary revolutionary force” and that its role abroad is “to be the steadfast internationalist front who support and amplify this legitimate resistance.”

Marceau said “resistance” is just code for achieving political goals via violence.

Other advertised sessions include “The Red-Green Alliance,” “Academia: A Demobilizing Force?” and “Building a Global Camp of Resistance” and “One Day You Too Will Be a T-rrorist.”

The organizers also describe Hamas’ Oct. 7, 2023, terrorist attack on Israel as “one of the most courageous acts of resistance in our lifetimes” in their promotional material.

For Marceau, the concern goes beyond the speakers.

“Simply participating in the conference should lead to an investigation of the participants by police,” he said.

Immediate actions he suggests authorities can take include ensuring that anyone renting space for the event is aware they’ll be complicit in an offence and liaising with the Canada Border Services Agency to deny entry to participants with links to terror groups.

Howard Fremeth, Cija’s vice-president of communications and marketing, said the designation provides a “big test” for Canada’s new national security strategy. “Threats once thought distant are now immediate and proximate,” Carney was quoted in the October announcement.

“What’s more immediate or proximate than a terrorist conference in your largest city, your economic hub,” Fremeth asked.

In response, the Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs released the… — Cija (@CIJAinfo) November 23, 2026

Cija is not the only group to express opposition to the conference and call on authorities to act.

The Simon Wiesenthal Centre Canada, in a statement, called on officials “to use the legal tools now available to address any unlawful activities associated with the event and ensure that Canada’s anti-terrorism laws are effectively enforced.”

The Alliance of Canadians Combatting Antisemitism urged the same, adding that “authorities should also ensure that potential immigration and admissibility concerns involving foreign participants are addressed.”

Chair Mark Sandler also repeated a call for people associated with Masar Badil or Samidoun, such as Barakat and Kates, to receive individual designations.

“Otherwise, those involved can simply attempt to thwart the law by continuing their activities under ever-changing organizational names,” he wrote in a statement.

The American Jewish Committee said in its statement that the group “must not be allowed to use Canadian soil as a platform to promote terrorism.”

Allied Voices for Israel also celebrated the decision and said: “Freedom of expression is fundamental. Glorifying terrorism is not.”

Glorifying terrorism is not. pic.twitter.com/wQ7KOp6lD0 — Allied Voices for Israel (@AlliedVoicesIL) November 23, 2026

York Centre MPP and Ontario Solicitor General Michael Kerzner had a message for those considering attending events, “whether in person or virtually, that inspire and foster hatred.”

“I want to be clear: this is wrong,” he said in a statement. “We in Ontario are better than that, and we know better.”

stories.title: Canadian astronaut aboard space station welcomes baby girl born on Earth
stories.summary: Couple say they feel connected despite the distance separating them as they welcome their ‘new little star’ into their lives
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The Canadian Space Agency says astronaut Joshua Kutryk and his wife, Heather, have welcomed their third child while he is aboard the International Space Station.

The agency says Kutryk announced the birth of his daughter Tuesday and that both mother and baby are doing well.

In a joint statement shared by the agency, the couple say they feel connected despite the distance separating them as they welcome their “new little star” into their lives.

The couple thanked teams at Nasa and the Canadian Space Agency for their support and said they look forward to reuniting their family of five.

Kutryk, a native of Fort Saskatchewan, Alta., launched into space on Oct. 1 as part of Nasa’s SpaceX Crew-13 mission to the International Space Station.

The former fighter pilot is the fourth Canadian to undertake a long-duration mission aboard the International Space Station and has completed two spacewalks since his arrival.

stories.title: Montreal police arrest third officer over alleged racism and misconduct
stories.summary: Police arrested two other recently fired officers on Saturday who are facing charges of assault, criminal harassment and breach of trust
stories.author: Marieke Glorieux-Stryckman
stories.content:
Montreal police have arrested a third officer who was recently fired following allegations of racism and misconduct.

The police force announced the arrest in a news release on Wednesday. Quebec’s director of public prosecutions said the officer is facing an assault charge and will appear in court at a later date.

This follows the announcement on Saturday that police arrested two other recently fired officers, who are facing charges of assault, criminal harassment and breach of trust.

The three officers have been released on a promise to appear and none of the allegations have been tested in court.

Police say they are among seven officers who were fired as part of ongoing criminal investigations into the series of scandals involving officers at two police stations.

An arrest warrant dated Nov. 19 identifies Zachary Belzil, 25, and Vincent Routhier, 24, as public servants who are facing charges of assault and breach of trust, related to alleged conduct that occurred between September 2025 and June 2026. The document also says Belzil faces an additional charge of criminal harassment.

Court documents show Belzil and Routhier are set to appear at the Montreal courthouse on Dec. 8.

Another arrest warrant dated Nov. 23 identifies a 33-year-old man who is facing an assault charge in relation to an alleged incident that occurred on or around Aug. 31, 2024.

Montreal Police Chief Fady Dagher announced the firings of seven officers on Nov. 2, describing it as an “administrative” procedure that required removing the security clearance for each of the officers involved.

In a news conference at the time, Dagher said the dismissals were unprecedented.

“To the victims of unacceptable conduct by (Montreal) police officers, I promised you truth and consequences,” he said. “You have truth, to the extent the investigation allows it, and you have consequences. In the end, we judge a police officer by the way they treat those who cannot defend themselves.”

Police also announced in late October that an officer linked to the investigation could face criminal charges after allegedly concealing evidence related to a situation involving domestic violence in 2025.

The arrested officers worked at the station in the multicultural neighbourhood of Montréal-Nord where police dismantled a patrol unit in June following allegations of racism and discrimination.

Dagher has confirmed that the allegations include claims that officers at the station in the Montréal-Nord borough cut the hair of racialized civilians to keep as trophies.

Both Montreal police and the provincial director of public prosecutions said they will not comment further because of the ongoing investigation.

Joel DeBellefeuille, founder and executive director of civil rights group the Red Coalition, said the pace at which this file was moving was “impressive.”

“Mr. Dagher is sticking to his guns, ... he’s sticking to his words. So we applaud that,” he said.

But he said the kind of behaviour the officers are accused of could have been addressed years ago.

“There’s four more (officers) to go that of course have to face criminal charges as well. And I think the community will start to be satisfied with that,” he added.

Dagher has confirmed that the allegations include claims that officers at the station in the Montréal-Nord borough cut the hair of racialized civilians to keep as trophies.
Both Montreal police and the provincial director of public prosecutions said they will not comment further because of the ongoing investigation.
Joel DeBellefeuille, founder and executive director of civil rights group the Red Coalition, said the pace at which this file was moving was “impressive.”
“Mr. Dagher is sticking to his guns, ... he’s sticking to his words. So we applaud that,” he said.
But he said the kind of behaviour the officers are accused of could have been addressed years ago.
“There’s four more (officers) to go that of course have to face criminal charges as well. And I think the community will start to be satisfied with that,” he added.

stories.title: Montreal mayor walks back ‘we’ll eat a little more Kraft Dinner’ comment in light of record tax hike
stories.summary: Soraya Martinez Ferrada addresses the backlash after 'tactless' comparison of city and personal choices
stories.author: Stewart Lewis
stories.content:
Montreal Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada is walking back her comments about people needing to eat Kraft Dinner in light of the city’s nearly 10 per cent tax increase in its 2027 budget .

Martinez Ferrada made the remarks during a recent interview on Quatre95, a division of Urbania that focuses on personal finance.

When asked how she intends to increase the city’s revenue, the mayor said she would go through each department to figure out where it could cut costs.

“It’s just like when you’re putting together your personal budget: If you know you’re going to have less money next year, well, you have to make some choices,” she added. “Let’s be honest, maybe sometimes we’ll eat a little more Kraft Dinner because we can’t afford filet mignon.”

The remark was quickly criticized online, given the steep tax increase, and picked up by the official opposition at city hall, Projet Montréal. The mayor addressed the issue in a short social media post Wednesday.

View this post on Instagram

“Let’s be honest, it was pretty tactless,” Martinez Ferrada said. “What I meant was that when a city makes choices, it’s the same as when you make personal choices. In this instance, the city has to choose between paying for new parks or filling potholes — and I’m going to choose filling potholes.”

It’s not the first time Martinez Ferrada has walked back off-the-cuff comments she’s made since her election last November.

In early September, the mayor warned the traffic brought on by the UCI Road World Championships was “going to be hell.” The remarks were met with criticism, given the importance of the event, and she sought to clarify them.

Later that month, she faced backlash for remarks made during a city council meeting after Montreal introduced a controversial bylaw barring people from insulting police officers and other municipal employees.

“If you feel like giving the middle finger to a police officer, well, go ahead and do it,” Martinez Ferrada had said while defending the bylaw.

She later took to social media to say the comment “came across poorly” and that she meant to convey people could still criticize the police under the bylaw.

The city’s 2027 budget, presented Tuesday, carries an average property tax hike of 9.8 per cent, or about $515 a household. Non-residential building owners face a 6.2 per cent average hike.

Martinez Ferrada has said she takes full responsibility for the decision , which broke a key promise of hers to keep tax increases in line with inflation.

Much of the increase is due to a new tax on infrastructure maintenance the city says is necessary after years of underinvesting in its road and water infrastructure.

Martinez Ferrada returned to the budget during Wednesday’s executive committee meeting, saying she understands she let people down with the steep tax increase.

“I know this is a major disappointment for many Montrealers who placed their trust in me,” Martinez Ferrada said. “No elected official enjoys making an unpopular decision."

The mayor, however, repeated the city has no choice but to catch up on repairing infrastructure. She also said the budget upholds her commitments on public security, cleanliness and homelessness, among other priorities.

The budget still needs to be adopted next month.

jfeith@postmedia.com

stories.title: Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk becomes father for the third time, while in space
stories.summary: The Canadian Space Agency says astronaut Joshua Kutryk and his wife, Heather, have welcomed their third child while he is aboard the International Space Station.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal — The Canadian Space Agency says astronaut Joshua Kutryk and his wife, Heather, have welcomed their third child while he is aboard the International Space Station.

The agency says Kutryk announced the birth of his daughter Tuesday and that both mother and baby are doing well.

In a joint statement shared by the agency, the couple say they feel connected despite the distance separating them as they welcome their “new little star” into their lives.

Kutryk, a native of Fort Saskatchewan, Alta., launched into space on Oct. 1 as part of Nasa’s SpaceX Crew-13 mission to the International Space Station.

The former fighter pilot is the fourth Canadian to undertake a long-duration mission aboard the International Space Station and has completed two spacewalks since his arrival.
