stories.title: ‘I kind of missed it’: Fanshawe students react to first snowfall
stories.summary: After an unusually warm autumn season, London woke up to snow on Tuesday. And Fanshawe students had mixed opin...
stories.author: Callum Contursi
stories.content:
After an unusually warm autumn season, London woke up to snow on Tuesday.

And Fanshawe students had mixed opinions on the sudden change of weather. According to Environment Canada, London received two centimetres of snow, and some welcomed the white stuff.

Chairs and trees covered in snow (Credit: Steve Young)

“Last year was the first time I’d ever seen snow,” said Mohamed Abdullahi, a second year accounting student at Fanshawe. “I recently moved from Somalia and it was my first winter, which was very brutal.

“But since it came very late this time of year, I kind of missed it in a way.”

But not everyone felt the same.

“I wish it came … later,” said student Victor Hoang, who commutes by bus to school. “I have to walk sometimes because of the winter.”

For those who have enjoyed the warmer weather, there’s good news. Experts say milder temperatures are expected to continue.

“There are no significantly cold days in the forecast. It seems to be warmer than average going forward between now and the end of the month,” said Peter Kimball, from Environment Canada.

Victor Hoang photographed at Fanshawe College on Nov, 24 Callum Contursi/XFM News

While the mild temperature continues, Monday night’s snowfall is just a tiny teaser for a delayed winter in London.

London’s first snowfall of the season (Credit: Leo Maisonville)

stories.title: Judge throws out $1-million fine against N.B. seafood company, requests new decision
stories.summary: A federal judge has thrown out a $1-million fine and foreign worker ban against a New Brunswick seafood processing company.
stories.author: Eli Ridder
stories.content:
A judge has overturned a $1-million fine and foreign worker ban imposed by the federal government on a New Brunswick seafood company — and ordered a new decision.

Federal Court Justice Love Saint-Fleur, in a two-page ruling last week, sent the matter back to the federal Temporary Foreign Worker Program for a do-over by a different government official.

Last year, Employment and Social Development Canada fined Bolero Shellfish Processing Inc. a record-setting million dollars and banned it from the foreign worker program for 10 years.

The federal government accused the company of breaking hiring laws, offering pay or working conditions that were inferior to the listed offer and not doing enough to ensure the workplace was free of abuse.

Bolero — located in northern New Brunswick — filed for a judicial review last year, arguing the federal employment ministry’s measures were procedurally unfair, unreasonable and disproportionate.

The company says it did not financially abuse any workers and that any past payroll or administrative issues were unintentional technical errors that were caused by pandemic operations.

In August, the employment ministry filed a motion calling for the federal court to send back the measures it imposed on Bolero.

It conceded the decision maker who imposed the fine and ban — an assistant deputy minister for the temporary foreign worker branch — “May have made a reviewable error”.

While the ministry said it failed to show how the heavy penalties were justified under the facts and law, it did not ask the court to dismiss the underlying labour issues of which Bolero was accused.

Saint-Fleur’s ruling, dated Nov. 17, does not specify how long federal officials have to make a “redetermination” of the punitive measures. And she does not provide reasoning for her decision beyond stating she read the material submitted by both sides.

Gabriel Elbaz, president of Bolero’s parent company Sogelco International, says he’s “flabbergasted” that the federal judge didn’t throw out the case entirely after the ministry admitted to a mistake.

He said the “discussion is done” and the case should be dropped instead of dragging it out for another review he says will continue to harm his company’s reputation.

“Either you’re pregnant or you’re not pregnant. You cannot be half pregnant,” Elbaz told The Canadian Press by phone Wednesday.

He said Sogelco International will be issuing a statement through its lawyers.

A spokesperson for the labour department did not provide a response by early Wednesday afternoon.

Syed Hussan, executive director of Migrant Workers Alliance for Change, said mistreated foreign employees at the centre of the case won’t have any justice regardless of the final outcome.

“The whole system is a public relations exercise, including these extra-large fines…it never results in any changes,” he said in an interview Wednesday.

Hussan said his organization would rather Ottawa spend time changing labour compliance rules so that fines levied against Bolero and other companies go towards the affected employees.

Last year, the alliance said workers at Bolero were given contracts in 2023 that promised them a minimum 30 hours of work a week and required them to pay rent for accommodations provided by the employer.

But working hours eventually dropped, leaving employees struggling to cover their rent payments.

The organization also described a “forced debt scheme,” where workers who worked less were paid the promised 30 hours, but were allegedly told they would have to pay back the difference later or work unpaid labour.

The application from the company says the federal government determined that Bolero had not employed the foreign workers for the minimum 30 hours a week as required by the labour impact assessments tied to the worker program.

In response, the company says eight foreign workers did not work the required hours “because of dramatic and unforeseeable changes in economic conditions.”

“Bolero paid the workers for the equivalent of 30 hours of work per week even though they did not work those hours. In other words, the temporary foreign workers were paid for work they did not perform.”

The application says Bolero was found not to have paid proper overtime to one foreign worker, and that two workers had not been covered by health insurance for a period of time.

The company blames an “unintentional administrative error” for the improper overtime pay, adding that the employee “did not suffer any financial loss and was fully compensated.”

It also blames the lack of health coverage on an “administrative error,” saying “as soon as the error was identified, the private health insurance was reinstated.”

“Bolero did not financially abuse the temporary foreign workers,” the company said in its filing.

Hussan on Wednesday said the New Brunswick government should also investigate companies like Bolero, as provinces are responsible for regulating most workplaces.

“As soon as a complaint is made — even before an investigation has happened or a decision is rendered — provinces must be informed so they can initiate their own proactive enforcement processes,” he said.

A spokesperson for New Brunswick’s labour department did not provide a response by early Wednesday afternoon.

Gabriel Elbaz, president of Bolero’s parent company Sogelco International, says he’s “flabbergasted” that the federal judge didn’t throw out the case entirely after the ministry admitted to a mistake.
He said the “discussion is done” and the case should be dropped instead of dragging it out for another review he says will continue to harm his company’s reputation.

A spokesperson for the labour department did not provide a response by early Wednesday afternoon.

The company blames an “unintentional administrative error” for the improper overtime pay, adding that the employee “did not suffer any financial loss and was fully compensated.”
It also blames the lack of health coverage on an “administrative error,” saying “as soon as the error was identified, the private health insurance was reinstated.”

Hussan on Wednesday said the New Brunswick government should also investigate companies like Bolero, as provinces are responsible for regulating most workplaces.

“As soon as a complaint is made — even before an investigation has happened or a decision is rendered — provinces must be informed so they can initiate their own proactive enforcement processes,” he said.
A spokesperson for New Brunswick’s labour department did not provide a response by early Wednesday afternoon.

stories.title: London produces more pro hockey players than most of Canada. Here’s why
stories.summary: London's reputation as a top hockey community is a direct result of community development and training opportu...
stories.author: Ryan Baynton
stories.content:
London’s reputation as a top hockey community is a direct result of community development and training opportunities, say experts.

With a thriving hockey ecosystem ranging from training programs like Snipe academy and Total Package Hockey camps to elite minor hockey and the London Knights organization, aspiring hockey players and their families have lots to choose from.

“Everyone kind of feeds off each other a little bit and makes each development company a bit better and the kids benefit in the long run,” said Karl Robb, owner of Snipe academy, which is a hockey shooting skills facility.

At the NHL’s 2025 4 Nations Face-Off, six players who were either born or played hockey in London were named to Team Canada’s roster.

The Forest City also ranks among Canada’s top 10 for producing NHL players, according to statistics site, Quant Hockey . Despite having a population of only about 500,000, it’s third in Ontario, behind only much-larger cities of Toronto and Ottawa.

Passion for the game is strong in the Forest City, which also fuels the trend, said longtime sports journalist Ryan Pyette.

“There’s a historical love for the game, and we’re far enough away from the GTA and the states which makes you a bigger center,” said Pyette, who has covered hockey for the London Free Press for nearly three decades.

The Knights have a reputation that exceeds most OHL teams reaching international heights. In fact, Pyette said he’s met people in Europe who recognize the name.

“They’re pretty much a worldwide brand in hockey,” he said. “They’ve held their own in terms of development for junior stars and NHLers.”

Former Knights who moved onto the NHL include, Nick Suzuki, Mitch Marner, Nazem Kadri and Patrick Kane.

The on-ice talent has likely contributed to community support for the Knights, who’ve averaged nearly 9,000 fans per game since 2010. With so many fans, it’s not a surprise London creates hockey players.

stories.title: Joly says she held ‘productive’ meeting with Stellantis as talks continue over future of Brampton plant
stories.summary: Ottawa is working to reverse the idled plant’s sale to armoured-car maker Roshel
stories.author: Eric Atkins
stories.content:
The future of the Stellantis Stla-N auto plant in Brampton, Ont., remains in limbo after officials from the automaker, federal and Ontario governments and the Unifor union met in Toronto and agreed to continue discussions another day.

The plant, which employed about 3,000 people when it was idled in 2023, was sold to Brampton-based armoured car maker Roshel Inc. Government and union officials are trying to reverse the transaction, announced earlier this month, and save the autoworkers’ jobs.

The parties met on Wednesday and agreed to more talks “to find the best path forward for workers, the company and Canada’s auto industry,” Unifor national president Lana Payne said in a statement. “Out of respect to the process of these negotiations, there will be no additional details at this time.”

Stellantis spokeswoman LouAnn Gosselin said the company is “committed to continuing constructive discussions.”

“The future of our Canadian operations and our employees remained the focus of today’s meeting,” Ms. Gosselin said in an e-mail. The automaker also has plants in Toronto and Windsor.

Stellantis idled the Brampton plant three years ago to retool for the Jeep Compass, but shifted production plans to Illinois in 2025, after the U.S. imposed 25-per-cent tariffs on Canadian-made cars. Since 2023, the plant hasn’t produced anything and about 2,200 workers remain on layoff benefits.

The controversy over the plant’s future comes at critical time for the industry, which has been hit hard by the tariff war with the U.S. The sale also raised the ire of the federal government which has provided funding to Stellantis.

Industry Minister Mélanie Joly has said Stellantis must repay the government “hundreds of millions” of dollars if it sells the plant, referring to aid the government gave the carmaker since 2022 for work on plants in Brampton and Windsor, as well as the Nextstar Energy EV battery plant in Windsor.

The Globe and Mail has reported the exact amount the government wants Stellantis to return is $831-million. The automaker has offered to pay $24-million, the amount it said it received for work on the Brampton plant.

Ms. Joly has said she is prepared to offer Stellantis an “aggressive package” to reverse the plant’s sale.

Ms. Joly said she had a “productive” meeting on Tuesday night with Stellantis’s chief operating officer for North America, Pablo Di Si.

“Our government is fully focused on finding a solution for the workers in Brampton,” Ms. Joly said in a statement.

The Ontario and federal governments have declared it a priority to save jobs threatened by U.S. tariffs. In October, the governments unveiled a $2.5-billion to support automakers, with the federal government contributing $1.5-billion of the total.

The governments recently each gave as much as $464-million to Ford Motor Co. to help reopen its plant, which had been closed for retooling for two years, in Oakville, Ont.

Honda this month received $313-million from Ottawa and $156-million from Ontario to retool its plant in Alliston, Ont., and reopen an adjacent engine shop.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford said last week Stellantis is spending $135-million a year to maintain the Brampton plant, and hundreds of millions of dollars more on greenhouse-gas levies. The talks with Stellantis could seek ways to mitigate these costs and find a product for the plant, said Mr. Ford, who met with Stellantis, Ms. Joly and Unifor on Friday.

The union and governments are urging Stellantis to retain ownership of the plant and keep it warm until finding a product to build there, just as General Motors did for two years ending in 2021 in Oshawa and is currently doing with an idled factory in Ingersoll, Ont.

Stellantis, which lost US$26-billion in 2025, is struggling amid weak sales and excess production capacity in North America and Europe. The company’s brands include Ram, Chrysler and Fiat.

It announced the deal with Roshel on Nov. 9 and the sale is expected to close by the end of the year.

Roshel and Stellantis have said the sale of the plant is expected to return it to productive uses in defence and automotive manufacturing. The companies said they will form a partnership in the 40-year-old plant to pursue joint manufacturing projects.

Roshel has bid to fulfill the federal government’s light-utility vehicle procurement contract, which could be worth as much as $4.9-billion. The plant could employ more than 2,000 people, Roshel said, and Stellantis workers will get first consideration for the jobs.

stories.title: Lcbo deploying police to more than 40 stores in anti-theft blitz
stories.summary: Paid duty police officers, security guards and covert agents will be present at many Lcbo stores as the liquor agency cracks down on theft.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
Paid duty police officers, security guards and covert agents will be present at many Lcbo stores going forward as the liquor agency cracks down on theft.

The Lcbo announced Wednesday its “Operation Secure Stores” initiative aims to further reduce theft while enhancing customer and employee safety.

“We’re launching ‘Operation Secure Stores’ to better protect our customers and employees and provide a safe and welcoming shopping experience for all Ontarians,” said Aaron Campbell, president and CEO of the Lcbo, in a news release.

“With expanded guarding and paid duty police presence, we will prevent thefts, disrupt organized crime networks, and drive down crime where it happens most.”

The Lcbo is partnering with police services in Toronto, Durham, Peel and York regions to deploy paid duty police officers in more than 40 stores to provide a police presence in the most high-risk areas.

Additional security guards will be placed in several of its busiest and most frequently targeted stores, and double guarding will be in effect too. Lastly, the Lcbo said it will deploy more members of its “covert security taskforce” to stores where repeat offenders are active.

“These officers can actively intervene in theft incidents occurring within stores and have the authority to make arrests onsite,” the agency said in the news release.

The Lcbo added third-party security guards will complete mandatory refresher training to deter theft, handle tense situations and assist law enforcement with evidence.

As one of Ontario’s largest retailers, with more than 690 stores carrying high-value goods, the Lcbo is a target for criminal activity, especially for organized retail crime networks.

Organized crime groups are behind approximately 70 per cent of total theft-related loss, the Lcbo said.

The Lcbo added existing anti-theft measures have led to more than 2,000 arrests in the last year.

One man dead after early morning shooting in midtown Toronto

Driver in 2025 crash that killed Ontario father of 3 expected to be sentenced

stories.title: King Toronto: A monument to new perspectives on living
stories.summary: The under-construction condo building pairs heritage facades with a mountainous glass block design
stories.author: Dave LeBlanc
stories.content:
Want to build a monument? Take your time. Mount Rushmore took 14 years. The Taj Mahal, 22. An estimated 20 to 27 years for the Great Pyramid of Giza. For Toronto’s 20th-century monument, the CN Tower, it depends on when one starts the clock, but it’s either eight or four years.

There are exceptions. Moshe Safdie’s Habitat 67 took 2½ years, and the Eiffel Tower even less, at two years, two months, both thanks to prefabrication.

Toronto’s newest monument, which pays homage to Mr. Safdie’s Montreal masterwork, currently clocks in at 11 years, three months, as Allied Properties and Westbank first announced a partnership with Copenhagen’s Bjarke Ingels Group (BIG) in August 2015. And while many months remain before the occupancy permit, King Toronto’s twin peaks of 16 storeys – the other two mountain-like peaks are 14 and 12 storeys – topped off in October of this year.

So, it’s understandable that Mr. Ingels hasn’t been seen dining at many Toronto hot spots these past few years; perhaps he’ll jet in the day residents get their keys (Elton John is one of them; he purchased a 2,600-square-foot unit).

The project is managed by Thomas Christoffersen and Andrea Zalewski out of New York. Diamond Schmitt, it should be noted, is Big’s partner office, with boots on the cold Canadian ground every day. In fact, their offices are so close, senior associate Liviu Budur can walk over to the site office on his lunch break.

Or to show wide-eyed fanboys (such as your humble Architourist) the architectural model before handing them a hard hat and guiding them into the hubbub of the multicrane construction site.

“It’s hard to say what it is,” Mr. Budur begins.

“It’s a tower, it’s a midrise … it goes against any concept that urban designers and urban planners have. It’s really a mixed-use building,” he continues as he points to the lower units, many of which incorporate heritage buildings that span from 489 to 529 King St. W. “The first three floors are all retail and commercial, and that’s roughly a third, at 200,000 square feet.”

It May be hard to define in urban planning terms, but it is a monument … of sorts. To what?

Well, just as Mr. Safdie’s building showed the world a new way of living at Expo 67, King Toronto shines a light on how we do it in the 21st century. From tiny studios to three-bedroom penthouses, all are conjoined and dependent. Some “pixels” (what the team calls each unit) are anchored so others can float. There is greenery everywhere, fed by irrigated planters. The facade May be all glass – it calls to mind the Maison de Verre in Paris – but much of it is opaque so that not only does it reflect the colour of the setting sun or blue sky, it keeps the heat in during cold winters (some portions aren’t glass block at all, but an Insulated Glass Unit that mimics the look but with much better thermal performance).

Heritage elements – the 1918 Hart Building, 1900 Conboy Carriage Company and the 1893 American Watch Case Building, to name a few – aren’t just afterthought facades, they are celebrated, living parts of the complex. There is a public courtyard/atrium that cuts through the building and links to Wellington Street; because of the rippling nature of the building above, it will be bathed in sunlight. There will be a big grocery store, small retailers and a park for the whole neighbourhood to enjoy.

Plus, the overall composition is just a joy to look at. As I walk in, I am awestruck by the glass block: there is depth and internal light. Frankly, it glows – but it wasn’t supposed to: “One of the first iterations, it was precast concrete,” Mr. Budur says. “So, it was a white building, and then it went to the Toronto Design Review Panel and it was one of the things that we were asked to change.”

As I ride the construction hoist to level 14, I almost wish exterior elevators were part of the final design; it’s wonderful to watch the building unravel and unfold as one rises. Yes, it’s a mountainscape, but with the sunlight glinting off edges, it also brings to mind a frozen tsunami (and there is a view of Lake Ontario from here).

Walking into a few unfinished units, it’s the commitment to the 45-degree angle – all pixels are made up of boxes, but rotated so the point faces out – that creates interest, despite Mr. Budur’s recollection of a Design Review panel member warning that the team might not want to be “ruled by the tyranny of the geometry.” No tyranny here, it’s liberating, literal out-of-the-box thinking that allows for light, airflow and views in a building with 435 units (as an example, Hotel X on the Exhibition Grounds has 404 rooms).

Back on the ground, it’s how the heritage buildings “guide” you from the sidewalk to the inner courtyard/atrium, right under the belly of the beast, that will be the wow moment for non-residents. And while there is much to take in with all of the intersecting angles, bridges (the atrium rises three storeys) and peek out to Wellington Street – it is all of that heritage brick (there is a heritage building on the south portion of the building as well) that keeps things grounded.

Well, somewhat grounded. My synapses are sparking as we walk inside some of the raw retail spaces, with their high ceilings and giant windows looking into the complexity and creativity of the project. “This can have more of a feeling, [be] more interesting, to give you different perspectives all the time,” Mr. Budur agrees. “I think that’s more suitable for this kind of function [rather than] the residential areas.”

Yes, that’s what King Toronto is: a monument to new perspectives on living.

content_blocks.text: It May be hard to define in urban planning terms, but it is a monument … of sorts. To what?
content_blocks.html: It may be hard to define in urban planning terms, but it is a monument … of sorts. To what?

content_blocks.text: Well, just as Mr. Safdie’s building showed the world a new way of living at Expo 67, King Toronto shines a light on how we do it in the 21st century. From tiny studios to three-bedroom penthouses, all are conjoined and dependent. Some “pixels” (what the team calls each unit) are anchored so others can float. There is greenery everywhere, fed by irrigated planters. The facade May be all glass – it calls to mind the Maison de Verre in Paris – but much of it is opaque so that not only does it reflect the colour of the setting sun or blue sky, it keeps the heat in during cold winters (some portions aren’t glass block at all, but an Insulated Glass Unit that mimics the look but with much better thermal performance).

content_blocks.text: Plus, the overall composition is just a joy to look at. As I walk in, I am awestruck by the glass block: there is depth and internal light. Frankly, it glows – but it wasn’t supposed to: “One of the first iterations, it was precast concrete,” Mr. Budur says. “So, it was a white building, and then it went to the Toronto Design Review Panel and it was one of the things that we were asked to change.”

November 25, 2026 at 8:49 a.m.

A man was fatally shot in a suspected home invasion in Toronto’s Casa Loma neighbourhood overnight on Wednesday, according to police.

Officers were called to the residence located at St. Clair Avenue W. and Poplar Plains Road just before 3 a.m. They found a man who had been shot. He was rushed to the hospital, where he was later pronounced dead.

Homicide: St Clair Avenue W & Poplar Plains Rd 2:42 am -police responded to a call for a shooting in a residential area -officers located a male victim who had been shot -victim was transported to hospital via emergency run -victim was pronounced deceased at the hospital -no… pic.twitter.com/phfeKm3enS — Toronto Police Operations (@TPSOperations) November 25, 2026

There were an “unspecified number of suspects,” police told 680 NewsRadio on Wednesday morning. When they broke into the house, the homeowner’s son — who was there with his girlfriend — encountered them.

stories.title: Lack of snow forces cancellation of World Cup giant slalom races in Quebec
stories.summary: Two women's World Cup giant slalom races scheduled in Mont-Tremblant, Que., have been cancelled due to a lack of snow, the International Ski and Snowboard Federation says.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Two women’s World Cup giant slalom races scheduled for Dec. 5 and 6 in Mont-Tremblant, Que., have been cancelled due to a lack of snow, the International Ski and Snowboard Federation (FIS) announced Wednesday.

Recent weather conditions have prevented organizers from producing enough snow to stage the races.

FIS said it is looking to reschedule the races for later in the season.

“Favourable snowmaking windows have been extremely limited over the past several weeks,” event director Nicholas Cogger said in a statement. “Despite the tremendous efforts of Tremblant’s teams and volunteers, current conditions unfortunately do not allow us to provide a course that meets the requirements for a World Cup-level competition.”

Mont-Tremblant was to be the fifth stop on the women’s alpine skiing World Cup circuit this season and the third to feature giant slalom competition following stops in Solden, Austria, in late October and Killington, Vt., this weekend.

“This is difficult news for the entire alpine skiing community,” said Alpine Canada president and CEO Andrew Baker. “I would like to recognize the outstanding work of the organizing committee, Tremblant employees and volunteers, who did everything possible to make this event happen.

“We share in the disappointment of the athletes, particularly our Canadian skiers, who were looking forward to competing in front of their home crowd.”

Organizers said ticket holders will receive automatic refunds and all festivities and musical performances associated with the event have been cancelled.

The Mont-Tremblant races were cancelled for the same reason in 2024.

Baker said organizers are looking ahead to the event’s return in December 2027.

stories.title: One man dead after shooting in midtown Toronto
stories.summary: Police say they responded to a shooting around 2:45 a.m. near St. Clair Avenue and Poplar Plains Road
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
An accomplished musician was killed during a break-in at his home in midtown Toronto early Wednesday, the second violent home invasion in the city’s affluent neighbourhoods in less than a month.

The fatal attack has heightened fear among residents, especially in wealthy areas where homeowners fed up with an increase in break-ins have gone so far as to hire their own private security guards.

“When the public feels vulnerable, they’re not going to wait for the police or anybody else to protect their family,” said City Councillor Josh Matlow, who represents the ward where Wednesday’s home invasion happened. “Those who have the means are more and more taking things into their own hands, and that’s not a burden they should have to bear, and it’s a very sad reflection on where a lot of people are at right now.”

Michael Eckert, a noted pedal steel guitarist, was killed in the home invasion.

Mr. Eckert played a solo with members of Blue Rodeo during the kick-off show for the Grey Cup earlier this month in Calgary. He was nominated for the Canadian Country Music Association’s steel guitar player of the year award in 2025 and 2023.

Police say Mr. Eckert, 39, was shot during a confrontation after an unknown number of assailants broke into his Poplar Plains Road home around 2:40 a.m. He was rushed to hospital, where he was pronounced dead.

“I understand and recognize how deeply troubling this must be, not only to the residents in that community, but to the residents of the city of Toronto as a whole,” Detective Sergeant Alan Bartlett told reporters. “It is the Toronto Police Service’s solemn commitment that we will do everything we can do and work diligently to locate, identify, apprehend and bring those responsible for this to justice.”

Though the investigation is in its early stages, Det. Sgt. Bartlett said he doesn’t believe the family was targeted. Four people were in the home at the time. None of the other residents were injured.

Mr. Eckert was shot shortly after his home was broken into, he said. “It was a relatively brief period … It’s not my understanding this was a protracted interaction.”

Investigators are poring over surveillance video to determine how many suspects were involved and whether they used a getaway vehicle, said Det. Sgt. Bartlett, who is part of the homicide and missing persons unit.

The attack happened at a home on a leafy residential street in a well-off midtown neighbourhood near Casa Loma and the intersection of St. Clair Avenue West and Avenue Road.

The home invasion occurred less than a month after a violent break-in in the city’s exclusive Bridle Path neighbourhood.

In the Oct. 29 attack, police say three masked gunmen stormed into a house and demanded money or other valuables shortly after 3 a.m.

A man and his two adult daughters sustained gunshot wounds while the mother was injured with a hammer. All four victims survived ; two were said to have “life-altering” injuries.

Home invasions are up across the city, according to Toronto Police data.

So far this year, 233 home invasions have been reported to police, compared to 170 at this time last year and 212 at this time in 2024.

However, home invasions have spiked since 2022 and 2023, when the figure at this time of year was 82 and 84, respectively.

With a report from Stephanie Chambers

stories.title: Carney Liberals haven’t fulfilled firearm commitments, advocacy groups say
stories.summary: Several voices for stronger gun control say Prime Minister Mark Carney's government has failed to live up to its commitments on firearms.
stories.author: Jim Bronskill
stories.content:
Several voices for stronger gun control say Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government has failed to live up to its commitments on firearms as the anniversary of the 1989 mass shooting in Montreal approaches.

In a report card-style assessment, PolySeSouvient and eight other advocates for tougher firearm restrictions say the government has work to do on implementing a key measure to prevent intimate partner gun violence, introducing a comprehensive ban on large-capacity magazines and ensuring the classification of new firearm models entering the market is determined by the RCMP.

The groups acknowledge the Liberals have implemented a buyback program for banned firearms the government says are fit only for the battlefield. But they point out that only half of the anticipated number of banned guns were reported by owners.

The groups also say the SKS rifle, which has been used in police killings and other high-profile shootings, remains available to purchase.

“Unfortunately, most of the Carney government’s commitments on gun control have not been delivered,” says the assessment.

PolySeSouvient was formed after a gunman killed 14 women on Dec. 6, 1989, at École Polytechnique in Montreal.

The assessment of the Liberals’ record is endorsed by PolySeSouvient, the Polytechnique Student Association, Angie’s Angels, the Canadian Femicide Observatory for Justice and Accountabilities, Danforth Families for Safer Communities, Dawson Families for Gun Control, Doctors for Protection Against Guns, the Quebec City mosque and the NOT_HERE student coalition.

Legislation that received royal assent in December 2023 opens the door to making anyone subject to a protection order — a legal order often issued in intimate partner violence cases — ineligible to hold a firearms licence while the order is in effect.

The provision is intended to quickly remove firearms from the hands of abusers at the time when they are often the most dangerous.

The government says the term “protection order” has to be defined in regulation and record-keeping and reporting requirements must be brought into force to fully implement the changes. Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree said earlier this year the government hoped to have the regulations in place by late September.

Carney’s Liberals promised in the last general election campaign to require the permanent alteration of large-capacity firearm magazines to ensure they can never hold more than five rounds again, and to prohibit the sale and transfer of magazines capable of holding more than the legally permitted number of rounds.

Last December, Anandasangaree announced an overarching review of the firearm classification system which he said would “take a broad view of the legal framework for firearms, devices, magazines and ammunition to modernize the regime.”

Carney also promised to introduce legislation creating a pre-authorization system to ensure the classification of new firearm models entering the market is determined by the RCMP — not the gun industry.

The assessment says there has been “no perceptible progress” on this element since draft regulations were published under the Trudeau Liberals in December 2024.

Since May 2020, Ottawa has outlawed approximately 2,500 types of guns on the basis they are intended for war, not hunting or sport shooting.

Conservative MPs and some gun owners have vehemently opposed the Liberals’ efforts to ban certain firearms as an attack on law-abiding citizens.

The federal firearm compensation program for individuals accepted declarations from owners of banned guns from mid-January through the end of March. Just under half of the 136,000 firearms the government budgeted to buy back were declared by owners for compensation and collection.

“Declarations are not surrenders, and the number actually collected is not known,” says the assessment by the gun control advocacy groups.

PolySeSouvient has called on the government to impose an immediate ban on new sales of the SKS, to remove from circulation modern, assault-style versions of the rifle, and to implement a voluntary buyback of older models. It calls for an exemption for Indigenous hunters who use the SKS primarily to hunt for food.

Anandasangaree has said the broad review of the firearms classification regime will involve consultations with First Nations, Inuit and Métis communities — including on the SKS — to ensure Indigenous perspectives and traditions are an active part of the process.

Public Safety Canada said in October that members of the Firearms Classification Technical Advisory Group, appointed to support the classification review, would be meeting for the first time later this fall.

The assessment by the advocacy groups says the fact the SKS is legal to own or purchase means the ban on assault-style weapons remains incomplete.

stories.title: Heavy rains, storm surge, high tides cause ‘real drama’ along B.C.’s coast
stories.summary: British Columbia's coast is getting another weather wallop as Environment Canada warns of rain of up to 225 millimetres along much of the coast before the end of the day.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
British Columbia’s coast is getting another weather wallop as Environment Canada warns of rain of up to 225 millimetres along much of the coast before the end of the day.

The storm surge comes with king tides, forced up by the full moon, and along with high winds, large waves are hammering the coast.

Geoff Johnson has lived in Ucluelet and Tofino on the west coast of Vancouver for over 20 years, and says he has never seen water levels as high as they are now in Ucluelet’s harbour.

He says he watched the waves along the coast yesterday creating “real drama,” and water was even lapping against the foundation on the homes in the harbour.

The storms prompted the District of Squamish to declare a local state of emergency and activate the local emergency operations centre due to potential coastal flooding.

It says the Sea to Sky region is expected to receive a significant amount of rainfall along with high tides over the next few days with the highest tides forecast for Thursday.

stories.title: Immigrants more likely to be overqualified for their jobs, report says
stories.summary: The Institute for Canadian Citizenship's annual report — "Selected But Neglected" — argues the government needs to do more work on foreign credential recognition.
stories.author: David Baxter
stories.content:
A new report says too many newcomers to Canada are getting stuck in jobs they are overqualified to do, undermining the federal government’s quest to recruit highly educated, highly specialized workers from abroad.

The Institute for Canadian Citizenship’s annual report — “Selected But Neglected” — argues the government needs to do more work on foreign credential recognition in key fields like health care to ensure immigrants who are courted for their qualifications can actually put them to work.

The institute projects half of the 380,000 permanent residents admitted to Canada next year will have a university education, but only 36 per cent of those people will have jobs that make use of their education and qualifications over the next 20 years.

Almost half of those with university degrees — 47 per cent — will hold jobs below their education levels, and almost one in five will leave Canada over the next 20 years, the institute says.

Census data from 2016 and 2021 shows 88 per cent of Canadian-born working-age people are in jobs that match their education levels, while just 62 per cent of immigrants can say the same.

The institute cites a 2019 RBC report that estimates closing the labour gap between immigrant and Canadian-born workers could have boosted Canada’s gross domestic product by about $50 billion at the time. The bank’s economists found immigrants were earning about 10 per cent less than their Canadian-born peers.

The report argues Canada should do more to recognize foreign credentials and professional licensing in key fields like medicine where there are persistent staff shortages.

The institute also calls on the government to do more to track how many immigrants are underemployed and how many eventually leave Canada for other opportunities.

The government does grant preferred immigration access to those with higher education and more work experience in high-demand fields like the trades, medicine and research.

The report’s methodology uses a combination of Statistics Canada, census and long-term immigration data in making projections.

stories.title: Buyer for Playter Estates home surfaces after asking price raised
stories.summary: Newly renovated three-bedroom house sells for $1.9-million
stories.author: Sydnia Yu
stories.content:
22 Pretoria Ave., Toronto

Asking price: $1,969,900 (Oct. 15)

Previous asking price: $1,849,900 (Oct. 6)

Selling price: $1.9-million (Oct. 24)

Previous selling price: $941,500 (July 2014); $720,000 (September 2009); $672,000 (September 2006); $439,900 (August 2003); $332,500 (August 1999)

Taxes: $9,898 (2026)

Days on the market: 18

Listing agent: Jenelle Cameron, Re/Max Hallmark Realty Ltd.

Agent Jenelle Cameron was concerned that the popularity of this newly renovated, three-bedroom house might be diminished by its location on a busier street near Broadview and Danforth avenues. To attract as many buyers as possible, she advised the seller to price the home below $1.85-million.

“We decided to try it and see what happens,” Ms. Cameron said. “We’ve got nothing to lose.

“It’s on a relatively busy street, which was a deterrent for some people. But over all, it’s great value for the neighbourhood. Most detached homes [there] are selling for a lot more.”

Disappointed that no one made an offer after one week, Ms. Cameron raised the home’s price to nearly $1.97-million. More buyers showed up either with appointments or unannounced at the second open house. A previous open house guest immediately negotiated a sale for $1.9-million.

“It got busier, which was weird because that doesn’t normally happen,” Ms. Cameron said.

“It was also funny because I had just been telling my client: ‘Don’t expect an offer to ever come from an open house [guest] because it hardly ever happens.’ Their offer was a nice surprise.”

The entrance to this 116-year-old house faces the side parking pad on a 32-by 66-foot lot.

It has living and dining rooms, a remodelled kitchen and a family-room addition with a gas fireplace and double doors to the yard.

Upstairs is an enlarged primary bedroom with a private bathroom.

There are two more bathrooms, and a fourth bedroom in the basement.

“The house had a traditional look at the front, but at the back it’s all very modern,” Ms. Cameron said.

“My client did the most spectacular renovation that went back and up. The whole back of the house was glass; it was stunning.”

“It was also funny because I had just been telling my client: ‘Don’t expect an offer to ever come from an open house [guest] because it hardly ever happens.’ Their offer was a nice surprise.”
The entrance to this 116-year-old house faces the side parking pad on a 32-by 66-foot lot.
It has living and dining rooms, a remodelled kitchen and a family-room addition with a gas fireplace and double doors to the yard.
Upstairs is an enlarged primary bedroom with a private bathroom.
There are two more bathrooms, and a fourth bedroom in the basement.
“The house had a traditional look at the front, but at the back it’s all very modern,” Ms. Cameron said.
“My client did the most spectacular renovation that went back and up. The whole back of the house was glass; it was stunning.”

stories.title: Avenue Road condo gets two bids after similar unit sells
stories.summary: Around 15 buyers lined up to visit the unit within days
stories.author: Sydnia Yu
stories.content:
1717 Avenue Rd., No. 303, Toronto

Asking price: $1,949,000 (September 2026)

Selling price: $2,067,000 (September 2026)

Previous selling price: $979,715 (September 2011)

Taxes: $9,959 (2026)

Days on the market: five

Listing agents: Carol Lome and Keegan Irwin, Johnston and Daniel

This 1,634-square-foot condo was gearing up for sale when a similar but more recently renovated unit in the 15-year-old building sold for $2.1-million around Labour Day. As a precaution, the seller and agent Keegan Irwin decided to set a slightly lower asking price. The strategy resonated with about 15 buyers who lined up for an in-person visit within days.

“We tend to find that if we price it right – where we think the market thinks it’s worth – we get a lot more eyes on the property,” Mr. Irwin said.

“We also had great timing at the end of the summer when people were a little more serious about looking at condos.”

Downsizing locals living in large houses nearby, around Avenue Road and Lawrence Avenue, showed the most interest in the property. It has two bedrooms and a den, plus two exit points to a 650-square-foot terrace. Two buyers made bids, with one offering $118,000 over the asking price.

“This checked a lot of boxes for downsizers,” Mr. Irwin said.

“We ended up getting two offers, pushing the price up, close to what the renovated unit had sold for.”

The unit has a den by the foyer, and two bedrooms separated by a living room with a gas fireplace.

The kitchen has granite countertops and stainless-steel appliances.

There is a laundry closet and three bathrooms, including an updated primary ensuite with heated flooring.

The unit has a storage locker and two parking spots. Monthly fees of $1,986 cover water, heating, cable, 24-hour concierge and valet parking. Recreational facilities are also on-site.

“This is a relatively new building in the area,” Mr. Irwin said.

“It’s right on Avenue Road, close to a lot of amenities and it had great outdoor space.”

stories.title: GTA home buyers, sellers in standoff as year winds down
stories.summary: Sellers are faced with slashing the asking price, pulling the listing or standing firm
stories.author: Carolyn Ireland
stories.content:
Heading into the final weeks of 2026, sellers in the Toronto area are stress-testing alternatives for riding out the fall real estate market.

“It’s a now-or-never kind of time to have conversations about changing strategy,” said broker Andre Kutyan of Harvey Kalles Real Estate.

Buyers and sellers are in a standoff, said Mr. Kutyan, who is surprised at the amount of inaction on both sides as November winds down.

The conventional options for sellers are to slash the asking price, pull the listing or stand firm.

In Mr. Kutyan’s experience, seller responses to the discussion run the gamut from obstinance to clear-eyed acquiescence.

In Deer Park, for example, Mr. Kutyan is the third listing agent for a contemporary three-bedroom townhouse at 67 Heath St. W, which the owners purchased for $3.3-million in 2017.

The property, near Avenue Road and St. Clair Avenue West, was listed in October of 2025 with an asking price of $4.895-million, then sat for months through a series of reductions until it reached $3,798,888.

Mr. Kutyan listed the property in November with an asking price of $3.495-million.

The homeowners invested heavily in landscaping the deep lot, including installing a 40-foot pool, adding an outdoor kitchen and increasing privacy, he said, but the reality today is that they will not recoup dollar-for-dollar what they spent.

The neighbourhood has some apartment buildings in addition to large, detached houses, he said, and the new price reflects that urban mix.

“It’s very important to be under $3.5-million, Mr. Kutyan advised the sellers. “If you could get more, you would have seen it by now.”

Buyers have been circling since he launched the listing with the reduced price.

“Now it makes sense to come and look at it,” he said, which in turn May prompt an offer.

The challenge during a stalemate is that buyers just hit pause.

“At least I have the opportunity to negotiate when I have an offer. Let me get them on paper and we’ll see what we can do,” he tells sellers.

At 23 Cardiff Rd. in the Davisville area, Mr. Kutyan recently reduced the asking price of a four-bedroom contemporary home to $2.695-million after listing it for $2.849-million in early November.

“After little traction in 19 days, we quickly changed gears and dropped the price $150,000,” he said, adding that the seller is pro-active.

In some cases, homeowners who are impatient to sell are the ones to suggest a price reduction, said Patrick Rocca, broker with Bosley Real Estate.

Activity in November was “eerily quiet” in the opening days, he added.

In the middle of the month, the action picked up when he tallied three deals in one week.

In the Davisville neighbourhood, for example, Mr. Rocca listed a semi-detached house with an asking price of $949,000.

He advised the seller against setting an attention-grabbing asking price and a deadline for reviewing offers because buyers have been finnicky in recent weeks.

He was surprised when four bidders vied for the property, which sold $200,000 above asking.

Another deal came together when a buyer decided to purchase a two-bedroom condo in the Yonge Street and Eglinton Avenue area for his son.

Mr. Rocca said the Bank of Canada’s interest-rate hike at the end of October May have prompted some buyers to put preapproved financing into action while they had a mortgage rate locked in by the lender.

Typically, such agreements expire after three or four months.

“That could force some people to hurry up and buy.”

Royal Bank of Canada economist Rachel Battaglia said data from the Canadian Bankers Association shows financial stress is intensifying in Ontario and British Columbia, where debt burdens are heaviest.

The share of mortgage holders behind on payments remains historically low but continues climbing, she added.

Ontario’s mortgage arrears rate reached a 15-year high in August as heavily leveraged borrowers contend with a sluggish real estate market, Ms. Battaglia said.

This leaves borrowers under financial pressure to carry mortgage payments for longer while they wait for a buyer.

Ms. Battaglia stresses that delinquency rates remain a safe distance from historical peaks nationally. Most borrowers who took on ultralow fixed-rate mortgages in the pandemic era have now renewed, she said, which limits the pool facing imminent payment shocks.

Meanwhile, Mr. Rocca said, some demoralized sellers who have seen showings slow to a trickle are wondering if they should pause the listing and relaunch in 2027.

Mr. Rocca recommends that homeowners who have spruced up the property with staging keep the for sale sign up until closer to mid-December rather than undo the preparations.

Buyers sometimes keep an eye on listings until the market winds down for the year, then submit an offer.

“We’re at the end of the cycle for the fall market but there are still some opportunities and some deals to be had,” he said.

In the second half of November, Mr. Rocca is discussing potential price reductions with sellers who decided to keep their property on the market.

Some are willing to cut the asking price now, while others choose to wait until the new year to relist with a lower number.

Some sellers are expecting a new year to bring fresh energy, he said.

“We might not be in a better place in January or February or March,” he said. “They’re willing to take that risk.”

As for buyers this fall, Mr. Kutyan said some are watching price reductions and coming to the conclusion that values are in a steep slide. But many sellers are unrealistic at the start.

“Most of those listings had no business being at those prices,” he said.

He recently worked with buyers who purchased a four-bedroom detached house after weeks of wrangling.

The property, at 34 Edgecombe Ave., was listed with an asking price of $3.189-million, then reduced to $2.988-million.

Mr. Kutyan’s clients submitted an offer, but the two sides could not reach a deal.

A few weeks later, the asking price was $2.795-million and Mr. Kutyan received notice that an offer had landed. Mr. Kutyan touched base with his clients to see if they were interested in returning to the table.

They agreed, so he advised them to submit a firm offer with no conditions. The homeowners accepted their bid of $2.65-million, which was a hefty amount below their final offer in the first round.

“We did the deal,” Mr. Kutyan said. “That hesitation cost the sellers significant money.”

Mr. Kutyan added that some sellers are not willing to budge on their asking price, even in areas flooded with inventory. Those homeowners often argue that the entire market is frozen.

In those cases, Mr. Kutyan collects data to show the transactions that have taken place in the area.

Often homeowners who do not feel pressured to sell would rather have the property languish than accept what buyers are willing to pay.

For those sellers, Mr. Kutyan jokes, his assessment can be blunt:

“Give it to one of the other 75,000 agents, or sell it yourself.”

stories.title: Cut to asking price greases sale of Lytton Park home
stories.summary: Five-bedroom house goes for $5.85-million after 13 days on market
stories.author: Sydnia Yu
stories.content:
204 Glencairn Ave., Toronto

Asking price: $6,195,000 (September 2026)

Previous asking price: $6.95-million (May 2026); $7.05-million (March 2026)*under previous agent

Selling price: $5.85-million (October 2026)

Previous selling price: not applicable

Taxes: $27,282 (2025)

Days on the market: 13

Property days on market: 79

Listing agents: Andre Kutyan, Harvey Kalles Real Estate Ltd., and James Warren, Alex Obradovich and Lindsay Whyte, Chestnut Park Real Estate Ltd.

This custom, five-bedroom house was advertised at a price of around $7-million for roughly two months this spring. This fall, it resurfaced with a light makeover and a permit for a garage on the 50-by-174-foot lot. Agent Andre Kutyan, a new addition to the sales team, advocated for a lower price, having just sold a similar home nearby for more than $5.5-million.

“There are a lot of listings currently sitting on the market anywhere from $5-million to $11-million, and a lot are sitting specifically on 50-foot lots,” Mr. Kutyan said.

“No matter what I do, if we miss the mark in terms of the asking price by 5 or 10 per cent, we’re not selling.”

Mr. Kutyan shared the new changes with a buyer he crossed paths with recently. They eventually wrote a $5.85-million deal for the 16-year-old home.

“There have only been three sales north of $5-million on 50-foot lots all year, and this is the highest one,” Mr. Kutyan said.

“It’s a classic, red-brick Georgian. That never goes out of style.”

This three-storey house has 4,648 square feet of living space, including a private office, a formal dining room off the kitchen and two entertaining areas with fireplaces.

There is a pet wash station, two laundry rooms and six bathrooms.

The basement suite has a bedroom, a gym and two recreation areas, plus a wine cellar.

Three cars can park in the driveway.

“The general preference in the area is to be closer to Avenue Road or east of Avenue Road in proximity to Yonge Street,” Mr. Kutyan said.

“It’s in the John Ross Robertson school district, which is a premier public school, and Lawrence Park Collegiate as well. It’s also close to private schools, whether Havergal or UCC.”

stories.title: Canada could face one of its warmest winters on record because of exceptionally strong El Niño
stories.summary: But a disrupted polar vortex could try to answer back with bursts of Arctic air and disruptive storms
stories.author: Jordan Omstead
stories.content:
An exceptionally strong El Niño is set to dominate Canada’s winter and possibly make it one of the warmest on record, The Weather Network’s seasonal outlook suggests, but a disrupted polar vortex could try to answer back with bursts of Arctic air and disruptive storms.

The forecast for December, January and February calls for a warmer, less snowy winter across most of Canada, marked by the potential for extended thaws and more rain than usual in some regions.

And while a record-warm winter is possible, that doesn’t mean winter is cancelled, said Doug Gillham, the network’s senior meteorologist.

“It will show up at times, and when it does, it still can be highly disruptive,” said Gillham.

Driving the outlook is El Niño, the global weather disrupter known to turn up the temperature on Canada’s winters. The last El Niño, a recurring climate cycle tied to shifting patches of warm water in the equatorial Pacific, contributed to Canada’s warmest winter starting in December 2023. This El Niño, which forecasts say could peak early this winter, is approaching the strongest ever recorded.

But the polar vortex has Gillham on alert. The band of spinning winds that normally keeps Arctic air locked near the North Pole broke down in early November, and could do so again later in the winter. While a collapse in the polar vortex is not unusual, it’s never broken down this early in November or behaved this way during a strong El Niño, a phenomenon scientists are still trying to unpack, said Gillham.

That breakdown allows cold Arctic air to spill south, where it will lower temperatures and set the stage for high-impact storms. And if that weren’t enough of a wild card, ocean temperatures are warmer than normal, allowing those winter storms to tap into abundant moisture.

It adds up to what Gillham calls “the easiest and hardest winter forecast [he’s] ever done.” He looks for a football metaphor to explain his dilemma: this historic El Niño is a hall-of-fame quarterback not to be bet against, but he’s surrounded by a cast of players unlike any he’s played with before, he said.

“So now you go on upset alert,” he said. “The cold will probably lose, but it could still raise quite a ruckus at times.”

While the forecast’s mild temperatures May be a relief for some, it could be tough on Canada’s winter tourism industry, especially for British Columbia’s low alpine regions and much of Ontario and Quebec. The possibility of big rainstorms and mid-season thaws also raises flood concerns, said Gillham.

What forecasters consider normal has shifted as climate change, driven by the burning of fossil fuels, drives up temperatures. Winters have warmed by about 3.7 degrees since the mid-20th century.

While mild conditions are set to dominate this winter, conditions still vary by region.

In B.C., dry periods are expected to be offset by some stormy stretches punctuated by atmospheric river events, which could nudge the precipitation totals above normal along the coast. The forecast calls for near-normal precipitation across most of the interior, but likely with more rain and less snow than usual. The mid- to high-alpine areas “should do fine in terms of snow” but the lower alpine ski areas May struggle, especially around the North Shore where temperatures could sit right on the margin of rain or snow, Gillham said.

Moving over the Rockies and across the Prairies, winter is expected to be “inconsistent and elusive,” said Gillham. Mild stretches could be exceptional this winter, but this is also the region where outbursts of cold Arctic air could be most impactful as well.

While it’s still early, the forecast doesn’t bode well for the coming fire season. With a drier winter expected, a thinner snowpack could translate to an early start to spring wildfires.

“There are some very concerning signals,” said Gillham. “I don’t want to be too alarmist this far in advance – I hope we’re wrong – but it is a very big cause for concern.”

In much of Ontario and Quebec, it’s shaping up to be a shorter, milder and less snowy winter than the previous two years. Periods of high impact winter weather will be more than offset by extended thaws. In southern areas, it could be a “very difficult” season for winter recreation, Gillham said.

The theme of warm, inconsistent winter continues into Atlantic Canada. An active storm track should deliver near-normal precipitation, but with more rain in the mix than usual. Cold air will try to fight at times with exceptional warmth coming from the Atlantic Ocean, setting up some high-impact storms and changeable conditions, Gillham said.

The territories can expect a gentler winter. The snowfall forecast is split from west to east: parts of Yukon and Northwest Territories are expected to see less than normal, while Nunavut could see more than normal.

That breakdown allows cold Arctic air to spill south, where it will lower temperatures and set the stage for high-impact storms. And if that weren’t enough of a wild card, ocean temperatures are warmer than normal, allowing those winter storms to tap into abundant moisture.

It adds up to what Gillham calls “the easiest and hardest winter forecast [he’s] ever done.” He looks for a football metaphor to explain his dilemma: this historic El Niño is a hall-of-fame quarterback not to be bet against, but he’s surrounded by a cast of players unlike any he’s played with before, he said.
“So now you go on upset alert,” he said. “The cold will probably lose, but it could still raise quite a ruckus at times.”

While the forecast’s mild temperatures May be a relief for some, it could be tough on Canada’s winter tourism industry, especially for British Columbia’s low alpine regions and much of Ontario and Quebec. The possibility of big rainstorms and mid-season thaws also raises flood concerns, said Gillham.
What forecasters consider normal has shifted as climate change, driven by the burning of fossil fuels, drives up temperatures. Winters have warmed by about 3.7 degrees since the mid-20th century.
While mild conditions are set to dominate this winter, conditions still vary by region.

In B.C., dry periods are expected to be offset by some stormy stretches punctuated by atmospheric river events, which could nudge the precipitation totals above normal along the coast. The forecast calls for near-normal precipitation across most of the interior, but likely with more rain and less snow than usual. The mid- to high-alpine areas “should do fine in terms of snow” but the lower alpine ski areas May struggle, especially around the North Shore where temperatures could sit right on the margin of rain or snow, Gillham said.

Moving over the Rockies and across the Prairies, winter is expected to be “inconsistent and elusive,” said Gillham. Mild stretches could be exceptional this winter, but this is also the region where outbursts of cold Arctic air could be most impactful as well.
While it’s still early, the forecast doesn’t bode well for the coming fire season. With a drier winter expected, a thinner snowpack could translate to an early start to spring wildfires.
“There are some very concerning signals,” said Gillham. “I don’t want to be too alarmist this far in advance – I hope we’re wrong – but it is a very big cause for concern.”

In much of Ontario and Quebec, it’s shaping up to be a shorter, milder and less snowy winter than the previous two years. Periods of high impact winter weather will be more than offset by extended thaws. In southern areas, it could be a “very difficult” season for winter recreation, Gillham said.

The theme of warm, inconsistent winter continues into Atlantic Canada. An active storm track should deliver near-normal precipitation, but with more rain in the mix than usual. Cold air will try to fight at times with exceptional warmth coming from the Atlantic Ocean, setting up some high-impact storms and changeable conditions, Gillham said.

The territories can expect a gentler winter. The snowfall forecast is split from west to east: parts of Yukon and Northwest Territories are expected to see less than normal, while Nunavut could see more than normal.

stories.title: Man dead after midtown residential shooting: Toronto police
stories.summary: Toronto - Police say one man is dead after an overnight shooting in a residential area of midtown Toronto.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - A 39-year-old man was fatally shot during an overnight home invasion in an affluent midtown Toronto neighbourhood on Wednesday in the latest violent break-in that has left some residents on edge.

Police have identified the victim as Michael Eckert, who was shot after a confrontation with a suspect and pronounced dead in a hospital. Multiple online tributes say Eckert was a respected local musician.

Police are seeking at least one suspect in the shooting at the home near St. Clair Avenue and Poplar Plains Road that happened shortly after 2:30 a.m.

It comes less than a month after a violent home invasion in Toronto’s exclusive Bridle Path neighbourhood, where a family of four was attacked and injured by masked intruders.

Bartlett said the latest home invasion occurred while four residents were inside the house, but no one else was injured.

“We will follow the evidence where it leads us, but at this point I have nothing to suggest that this family in particular was targeted,” he said.

No suspect description was immediately released, and Bartlett has appealed to anyone who has information about the case to come forward.

“I understand and recognize how deeply troubling this must be not only to the residents in that community but to the residents of the city of Toronto as a whole,” he said. “And it is the Toronto Police Service’s solemn commitment that we will do everything that we can do. We will work diligently to locate, identify, apprehend and bring those responsible for this to justice.”

Paramedics had told The Canadian Press earlier in the day that the shooting victim was in his 60s, but police later said he was 39.

Bartlett suggested it’s too early to draw any parallels between the Bridle Path home invasion and the latest one.

“I can tell you that we are focused on identifying the person or persons responsible for this,” he told reporters. “Oftentimes, we can’t provide the why.”

Investigators in the Bridle Path case have said that it was unclear if any belongings were stolen, or if that home was specifically targeted, suggesting the suspects May have been after “nice things” in an affluent area.

One of the victims in that case, David Morton, has said that three members of his family, which includes two adult daughters, were shot and all four were attacked with a hammer in the “horrific” ordeal.

Jennifer Dickie, who lives about a kilometre from the scene of Wednesday’s home invasion, said she immediately thought of the Bridle Path case when she heard the latest news.

“It just seems to be happening a lot more often, and in these wealthy areas,” she said.

“My apartment overlooks these mansions, and so these people that live here have private security … they’ve all pooled their money and the security guards are here 24/7.”

Dickie said it’s unnerving that no amount of private security or alarm systems seems to deter criminals.

“It’s not stopping anything,” she said. “It’s a societal issue, I believe.”

Doug Heighington, who also lives in the area, said he’s not worried about his own safety, but “I think some people in my building are.”

“It’s scary when you hear about it anywhere but, I guess, particularly when it’s this close,” he said. “It’s scary to see the increase of gun usage (that) seems to be creeping in more and more.”

Jordan Sprackman, another local resident who walked his dogs close to the scene, said he found out about the shooting after seeing a notification on a safety app.

“It’s scary, obviously, to hear about this,” he said.

Some blocks in the neighbourhood have hired private security guards to patrol the streets overnight, and Sprackman said he would be willing to chip in if people on his street decide to do so.

“I’m sure private security, more people will be interested in it, anything to make people feel safer, really, at home,” he said, adding that a greater police presence in the area would also help.

When asked about private security measures, Bartlett said people should do “what they feel is the right choice to ensure the safety of their family.”

“The Toronto Police Service is committed to providing public safety services to every single resident in the city. We do our very best to do that every single day but I think the message for all residents is that you should make decisions that are best for your family,” the detective said.

At the time of the Bridle Path shooting in late October, Toronto police said there had been 119 home invasions in the city so far this year, up more than 32 per cent from the same time last year.

Police have said that certain neighbourhoods have become “hot spots” for home invasions. That includes areas in the police force’s 32 Division, which covers multiple neighbourhoods across North York, and 53 Division, covering midtown Toronto.

The issue extends beyond the city, with violent home invasions reported across the Greater Toronto Area in recent years.

Last year, a man was fatally shot in his Vaughan home during a home invasion when he confronted the suspects. His family witnessed the shooting.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 25, 2026.

stories.title: London’s rent supplement program helping 800 families avoid homelessness paused — weeks ago
stories.summary: Near the end of Tuesday’s council meeting, city staff confirmed the program, intended to prevent precariously housed people from becoming homeless, had been paused several weeks ago.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
Coun. Sam Trosow says he would have liked to have been informed about a financial shortfall in city hall’s rent supplement program before drastic steps had to be taken.

Near the end of Tuesday’s council meeting, city staff confirmed the program, intended to prevent precariously housed people from becoming homeless, had been paused several weeks ago.

The City of London spends about $7.7 million annually on the rent supplement program, which helps about 800 families remain housed.

“At the end of October, we made a decision in conjunction with the Housing First (agencies) that administer the rent supplement program for us, that we needed to temporarily pause the issuance of rent supplements because they were projected to go well over budget,” Kevin Dickins, deputy city manager of social and health development, said in response to a question from Trosow.

Dickins attributed the shortfall to rising demand for assistance.

“Bottom line, they were housing more people than they had anticipated and budgeted. And the cost of the subsidy was growing, given the discrepancy between what people could afford and what market rents were requiring.”

Since the pause, agencies have continued case management and have been trying to find other ways to support Londoners seeking financial assistance to avoid homelessness.

Trosow believes pausing the homelessness prevention program because of a budget shortfall could ultimately cost the city more money.

“It is going to result in more hardship and more people on the streets, and it’s going to be much more expensive to deal with the situation once people are on the street,” he told CTV News after the council meeting.

Based on data from local homelessness prevention programs, including those that assist people with rent and utility arrears, Dickins estimates 1,500 to 2,000 Londoners are currently “on the cusp of homelessness.”

Mayor Josh Morgan emphasized the pause is temporary.

“When there’s actually more money in the budget, that’s when we can do this on an annual basis. We have allocated amounts in the multi-year budget.”

Morgan said council has approved expansions to some homelessness prevention programs, “but we’ve got to wait for the next fiscal year.”

The city’s fiscal year begins Jan. 1, 2027.

However, Dickins warned council that even with a previously approved increase to the rent supplement program next year, demand is expected to exceed available funding again.

“The previous council had made a budget decision that in 2027 we will see a slight increase in our rent supplements, but we are already tracking to match, or exhaust pretty much all of those,” he said.

He added that new affordable housing units will place additional pressure on the program’s budget.

The mayor said securing additional financial support from senior levels of government will be essential if homelessness prevention programs are to be adequately funded in the future.

“We’ve seen these programs, like rent supplements, go from $500,000 a year to well over $2 million when they’re open-ended and don’t have a budget cap. You know, that is completely unsustainable for municipalities.”

However, Trosow believes council can act now to prevent an increase in homelessness this winter.

“I think it’s always easy to say there’s no money in the pot and we need to step up our advocacy work and ask the provincial government,” he said. “Yes, of course, we need to do that. But we also need to be looking internally to reserve funds (and) what other programs maybe can be borrowed from.”

The next opportunity for councillors to discuss the rent supplement program will be at the community and protective services committee meeting on Nov. 30.

stories.title: Immigrants in Canada more likely to be overqualified for their jobs, report says
stories.summary: Only 36% of permanent residents with a university education admitted next year will make use of their education, qualifications
stories.author: David Baxter
stories.content:
A new report says too many newcomers to Canada are getting stuck in jobs they are overqualified to do, undermining the federal government’s quest to recruit highly educated, highly specialized workers from abroad.

The Institute for Canadian Citizenship’s annual report – Selected But Neglected – argues the government needs to do more work on foreign-credential recognition in key fields such as health care to ensure immigrants who are courted for their qualifications can actually put them to work.

The institute projects half of the 380,000 permanent residents admitted to Canada next year will have a university education, but only 36 per cent of those people will have jobs that make use of their education and qualifications over the next 20 years.

Almost half of those with university degrees – 47 per cent – will hold jobs below their education levels, and almost one in five will leave Canada over the next 20 years, the institute says.

Heather Barnabe, the institute’s chief operating officer, told a news conference in Ottawa on Wednesday the problem is particularly dire in the health care sector.

“Just 38 per cent of 2027 immigrants with health care training are projected to work in a job befitting their education by 2035,” she said.

“If these immigrants experienced the same qualification-matched employment rate as their Canadian-born peers, over 2,000 extra health professionals would be providing urgently needed care to us and our loved ones.”

Daniel Bernhard, citizenship institute CEO, said some provinces have worked out ways to recognize immigrants’ professional credentials. He pointed to a program in Nova Scotia which allows immigrant doctors to work under the supervision of a Canadian physician as their competency is assessed.

Mr. Bernhard said while it’s important to verify credentials and work experience to ensure they meet Canadian standards, some provinces and territories put up too many roadblocks.

“Colleges have ... I would call them discriminatory practices when it comes to immigrant professionals coming in. They do things like make you take a separate English or French test, then they take two years to process your paperwork. Then when it’s done, they say, ‘Your English or French test expired, you’ve got to do it all over again,’” he said.

“All Canadians expect, rightly so, that these professions be conducted by people who are qualified and who can do so safely. I don’t think anybody objects to that. But there are faster ways to do it.”

A new report says too many newcomers to Canada are getting stuck in jobs they are overqualified to do, undermining the federal government’s quest to recruit highly educated, highly s…

A Medical Council of Canada spokesperson said in an e-mailed statement the council also worries that too many internationally trained physicians are unable to practice in Canada.

The spokesperson said the council is working with regulators, governments and other parties to find ways to make licensing pathways more clear for physicians trained abroad.

The Medical Council of Canada is not a licensing body but it works to ensure national standards for verifying physician credentials and assessing their competency.

Census data from 2016 and 2021 shows 88 per cent of Canadian-born working-age people are in jobs that match their education levels, while just 62 per cent of immigrants can say the same.

The institute cites a 2019 RBC report that estimates closing the labour gap between immigrant and Canadian-born workers could have boosted Canada’s gross domestic product by about $50-billion at the time. The bank’s economists found immigrants were earning about 10 per cent less than their Canadian-born peers.

The report also calls on the government to do more to track how many immigrants are underemployed and how many eventually leave Canada for other opportunities.

This report comes at a time when the debate over Canada’s immigration policy is heating up. Claiming higher immigration will put too much pressure on health services and the housing market, the Conservative opposition tabled a motion in the House of Commons this week to block the government’s plan for permanent-resident admissions in 2027.

Mr. Bernhard said while there are real factors driving public skepticism of immigration around the world, allowing qualified people to work is a solution to pressures on public services.

“So if you’re feeling squeezed at the hospital, if you are feeling squeezed with an overcrowded classroom, and you are worried about more people coming in, then presumably we can agree that anybody who’s already here who can help to make that situation better does a service for the whole country,” he said.

The government does grant preferred immigration access to those with higher education and more work experience in high-demand fields such as the trades, medicine and research.

The report’s methodology uses a combination of Statistics Canada, census and long-term immigration data to make its projections.
