stories.title: 1 in 3 students can’t read by the time they finish Grade 3, new report says
stories.summary: An education think tank is pushing for Canadian schools to adopt a new approach to teaching children how to read, after it reported that literacy levels have plunged to an "all-time low" in Canada.
stories.author: Christl Dabu
stories.content:
An education think tank is pushing for Canadian schools to adopt a new approach to teaching children how to read, after it reported that literacy levels have plunged to an “ all-time lo w ” in Canada.

More than one in three students (38 per cent) can’t read by the time they finish Grade 3, and between 20 per cent and 56 per cent cannot read by Grade 4, according to The Aristotle Foundation for Public Policy. The numbers vary by province.

The study cited an Ontario Human Rights Commission’s Right to Read inquiry report in 2022, which called for reforms to improve Grade 3 literacy rates.

The foundation’s report noted that Alberta appeared to lead other provinces in literacy as it had rolled out “evidence-based reforms” in 2021. The province achieved 80 per cent literacy in 2021 based on Grade 4 Progress in International Reading Study (Pirls) tests.

However, the foundation said “other provincial assessments do not look any better.” The foundation called Manitoba’s Grade 3 reading results “most concerning,” citing that 44.9 per cent of students met provincial reading standards in 2024. In British Columbia, 30 per cent of Grade 4 students didn’t meet the proficiency benchmark in the Foundation Skills Assessment results. In Quebec, 31 per cent of Grade 4 students did not meet the provincial literacy standards in 2021.

The public policy think tank published two reports this month assessing the state of early grade literacy, noting that literacy in Canada is at an “all-time low.”

“Today’s Grade 10 students are two to three years behind in reading, compared to their peers 25 years ago,” the report said.

The analyses, published on Nov. 13 and Nov. 18, were based on data and reports of provinces’ assessments for Grade 3 and 4 students.

The foundation’s reports focus mainly on Grade 3 and Grade 4 students. The think tank said it targeted those grades because they mark “a critical turning point” when children “shift from learning to read to reading to learn.”

Evidence suggests that those who don’t know how to read by Grade 4 will not acquire the skill until they are adults, or they May never become literate, the analyses said.

Need for ‘evidence-based’ literacy approach: expert

David Livingstone, a senior fellow with the foundation, said his research and the Right to Read inquiry report found the need for most schools to switch from a balanced literacy approach to an “evidence-based” structured literacy method in teaching students how to read and write.

Balanced literacy assumes that learners “just catch on” based on “cueing systems,” similar to the way infants learn language, according to the report. While it places importance on books and texts, it lacks “sufficient direct instruction.”

With this approach, Livingstone said students don’t break words down into their component parts, their syllables and the sounds of words.

“What they’re doing instead, is they’re encouraged to try to guess at the whole word in its context,” Livingstone, an honorary research associate at Vancouver Island University, said in a video interview with CTVNews.CA on Tuesday.

“The research doesn’t support that as the preferred way to teach kids how to read. Instead, the structured literacy approach, sometimes just called phonics, is a better way to teach kids how to read.”

According to the foundation, structured literacy involves “explicit instruction” and “frequent evaluation” for students who need extra help.

Livingstone said a few Canadian jurisdictions have adopted the structured literacy approach recommended by the Ohrc.

“And even those that did adopt that approach, very few of them have gone far enough towards changing, for instance, the licensing requirements for teachers, or make it mandatory for teachers to be trained in how to teach this phonics structured literacy approach,” he said.

“So, there seems to be some reluctance by the school boards, by the provinces to adopt this better way of teaching children. We would just like to see them adopt what the Ohrc has strongly recommended as the preferred way to teach kids how to read,” Livingstone added.

Additionally, the foundation recommended a “knowledge-rich curriculum” for fostering success in reading, placing importance on background knowledge and vocabulary.

“A book isn’t going to explain everything to you – it expects you to come with some knowledge,” Livingstone said.

The Aristotle Foundation for Public Policy noted the challenge of learning literacy skills later in life.

“Evidence from national and international assessments shows that these gaps rarely close over time,” the foundation’s Nov. 13 report stated. “Even when many students have not acquired basic literacy skills by Grade 3, schools often shift focus in higher grades away from foundational reading instruction, leaving struggling readers behind.”

The foundation said the stakes are high if children aren’t able to read early in life.

“While the cost to Canada May be lower economic productivity and higher crime rates, the personal costs to children and their families let down by an education system that refuses to follow the evidence is incalculable,” the report added.

stories.title: Carney’s Liberals haven’t fulfilled gun control commitments, advocacy groups say
stories.summary: There’s still work to do on implementing key measure to prevent intimate partner gun violence, introducing comprehensive ban on large-capacity magazines
stories.author: Jim Bronskill
stories.content:
Several voices for stronger gun control say Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government has failed to live up to its commitments on firearms as the anniversary of the 1989 mass shooting in Montreal approaches.

In a report card-style assessment, PolySeSouvient and eight other advocates for tougher firearm restrictions say the government has work to do on implementing a key measure to prevent intimate partner gun violence, introducing a comprehensive ban on large-capacity magazines and ensuring the classification of new firearm models entering the market is determined by the RCMP.

The groups acknowledge the Liberals have implemented a buyback program for banned firearms the government says are fit only for the battlefield. But they point out that only half of the anticipated number of banned guns were reported by owners.

The groups also say the SKS rifle, which has been used in police killings and other high-profile shootings, remains available to purchase.

“Unfortunately, most of the Carney government’s commitments on gun control have not been delivered,” says the assessment.

PolySeSouvient was formed after a gunman killed 14 women on Dec. 6, 1989, at École Polytechnique in Montreal.

The assessment of the Liberals’ record is endorsed by PolySeSouvient, the Polytechnique Student Association, Angie’s Angels, the Canadian Femicide Observatory for Justice and Accountabilities, Danforth Families for Safer Communities, Dawson Families for Gun Control, Doctors for Protection Against Guns, the Quebec City mosque and the NOT_HERE student coalition.

Legislation that received royal assent in December 2023 opens the door to making anyone subject to a protection order – a legal order often issued in intimate partner violence cases – ineligible to hold a firearms licence while the order is in effect.

The provision is intended to quickly remove firearms from the hands of abusers at the time when they are often the most dangerous.

The government says the term “protection order” has to be defined in regulation and record-keeping and reporting requirements must be brought into force to fully implement the changes.

Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree said earlier this year the government hoped to have the regulations in place by late September.

Carney’s Liberals promised in the last general election campaign to require the permanent alteration of large-capacity firearm magazines to ensure they can never hold more than five rounds again, and to prohibit the sale and transfer of magazines capable of holding more than the legally permitted number of rounds.

Last December, Anandasangaree announced an overarching review of the firearm classification system which he said would “take a broad view of the legal framework for firearms, devices, magazines and ammunition to modernize the regime.”

Carney also promised to introduce legislation creating a pre-authorization system to ensure the classification of new firearm models entering the market is determined by the RCMP – not the gun industry.

The assessment says there has been “no perceptible progress” on this element since draft regulations were published under the Trudeau Liberals in December 2024.

Since May 2020, Ottawa has outlawed approximately 2,500 types of guns on the basis they are intended for war, not hunting or sport shooting.

Conservative MPs and some gun owners have vehemently opposed the Liberals’ efforts to ban certain firearms as an attack on law-abiding citizens.

The federal firearm compensation program for individuals accepted declarations from owners of banned guns from mid-January through the end of March. Just under half of the 136,000 firearms the government budgeted to buy back were declared by owners for compensation and collection.

“Declarations are not surrenders, and the number actually collected is not known,” says the assessment by the gun control advocacy groups.

PolySeSouvient has called on the government to impose an immediate ban on new sales of the SKS, to remove from circulation modern, assault-style versions of the rifle, and to implement a voluntary buyback of older models. It calls for an exemption for Indigenous hunters who use the SKS primarily to hunt for food.

Anandasangaree has said the broad review of the firearms classification regime will involve consultations with First Nations, Inuit and Métis communities – including on the SKS – to ensure Indigenous perspectives and traditions are an active part of the process.

Public Safety Canada said in October that members of the Firearms Classification Technical Advisory Group, appointed to support the classification review, would be meeting for the first time later this fall.

The assessment by the advocacy groups says the fact the SKS is legal to own or purchase means the ban on assault-style weapons remains incomplete.

stories.title: Will Navdeep Bains meet the moment?
stories.summary: The Ontario Liberal Party is welcoming Navdeep Bains as their newly-elected leader.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
The Ontario Liberal Party is welcoming Navdeep Bains as their newly-elected leader.

It was a close race, with runner-up Lee Fairclough losing by the slightest margin, signalling deep internal divide within the party.

Host Caryn Ceolin speaks to Alex Spears, former Liberal campaign manager and senior consultant at Earnscliffe, to discuss where the future of the Ontario Liberals lies with another leader missing in action from the Legislature, and whether or not Bains will meet the moment.

stories.title: Business Brief: Behind the arrears rate
stories.summary: Ontario and B.C. are faring much worse than the rest of the country in mortgage arrears
stories.author: Salmaan Farooqui
stories.content:
Good morning. Today, we’ll look at two recent reports that show Canadians are falling behind on mortgage payments at the highest rates in more than a decade. But first:

Event: Sources told The Globe that Lululemon founder Chip Wilson told a leadership conference that women are not agreeing to have as many children as men want, and made other comments about women’s reproductive choices that led some attendees to walk out.

Energy: Sources say a group of 12 northern B.C. First Nations is making a substantial investment in the TC Energy entity behind the Coastal GasLink pipeline.

Economy: The Bank of Canada is refining its approach to inflation-targeting to better navigate a world of larger and more frequent supply-side shocks.

Hi, I’m Salmaan Farooqui, The Globe’s housing and mortgages reporter. Homeowners generally pay their mortgages – it’s a type of loan that tends to have much lower delinquency rates compared with other financial products such as credit cards.

But over the past year, we’re seeing a concerning trend of homeowners failing to make mortgage payments. The problem is concentrated in Ontario and British Columbia.

A recent TD Bank analysis of industry data found the rate of Canadians missing payments in Ontario is approaching levels last seen during the 2008 financial crisis.

The current arrears rate (or the rate of homeowners behind on mortgage payments by more than 90 days) is 0.34 per cent, meaning roughly one in every 300 households is falling behind by three or more months. It’s nearly triple the prepandemic norm, and just below the peak of 0.43 per cent in the aftermath of the 2008 crash.

Different numbers from an analysis by credit-rating agency Equifax painted a similar picture this week. As my colleague Joy SpearChief-Morris wrote , that report found the arrears rate has jumped by 30 per cent in the last year.

Equifax said arrears are the worst since the credit bureau started tracking the statistic in 2013. And Ontario and B.C. accounted for 91 per cent of the year-over-year increase.

These two provinces have the highest housing costs and the largest mortgages, which means homeowners are more impacted by rising interest rates. The provinces also saw some of the biggest home-price declines, especially in the condo sector. The price drops are leaving a growing number of homeowners with properties that are worth less than than their mortgage.

The Equifax report also found that roughly 70 per cent of all Canadian mortgages with negative equity are based in Ontario, and they make up 5 per cent of mortgages in the province.

Things might get worse before they get better. TD economist Maria Solovieva, for example, told me that Ontario’s arrears rate is expected to worsen until mid-2027.

“Ontario is one of the weakest economies in Canada currently with pressure coming from U.S. tariffs, and it is seeing a higher unemployment rate,” Solovieva said.

“There is a combination of income shock and payment shock from higher interest rates.”

That financial pain is largely concentrated within specific groups in Ontario and B.C., Solovieva said, adding that the country is still holding up reasonably well as a whole.

People who purchased homes during the market peaks around 2021 and 2022 are more vulnerable, especially if they’re underwater on their loan.

Condo owners are under the most stress financially, with Equifax finding that 7.2 per cent of condominium mortgages are likely in negative equity, compared to just 2.7 per cent of freehold houses.

While arrears are expected to normalize in the coming year, Solovieva said that job losses caused by the U.S.-Canada trade war or unexpected interest-rate increases could push arrears even higher.

Financial markets expect three more hikes in 2027, and each hike will increase borrowing costs for variable-mortgage holders.

stories.title: Ford calls ads from gambling market he opened ‘out of control’
stories.summary: The proliferation of online gambling ads was sparked by the Ford government allowing non-government online gambling companies to enter the market in 2022.
stories.author: Olivia Bowden, Colin D'Mello
stories.content:
Facing scores of studies that outline the harms of Ontario opening up the province to private gambling companies, Premier Doug Ford is calling the explosion of online gambling ads “just overboard” and has directed his cabinet to look into the matter.

The Ford government made similar comments in May, when Conservative MPP Stan Cho, then the minister of tourism and gaming, said the province understood concerns around betting ads and the government was looking at stricter rules.

Also in May, the government voted down an attempt by the Ontario Liberals to ban online gambling commercials.

The proliferation of online gambling ads on television and social media was sparked by the Ford government allowing non-government online gambling companies to enter the market in 2022. They were ushered in under a system called iGaming.

Since the government opened the doors to private betting companies, health researchers have noted increases in gambling addiction rates, insolvencies and overall mental health issues related to problem gambling.

Research published in September by a health data analytics institute found emergency department visits for gambling disorders have doubled in Ontario since the 2022 expansion.

As well, a study released earlier this year by the Canadian Medical Association Journal also found people calling a betting helpline in Ontario were up 300 per cent since the government allowed private online gambling.

When asked if he would curtail betting ads, Ford said “once I receive a report back, yeah. It’s out of control in my opinion.”

“Everyone sees it. It’s not good for the people,” he said.

Gambling overall is not the problem, Ford said, clarifying his view that it’s only the commercials that seem excessive.

“Every time you pop on the TV it’s just ads, ads. It’s probably going to hurt you guys in the media, because they’re going to have to pull ads off,” he said.

stories.title: El Nino sets up warm winter, but polar vortex could answer back: Weather Network
stories.summary: An exceptionally strong El Nino is set to dominate Canada's winter and possibly make it one of the warmest on record, The Weather Network's seasonal outlook suggests, but a disrupted polar vortex could try to answer back with bursts of Arctic air and disruptive storms.
stories.author: Jordan Omstead The Canadian Press
stories.content:
An exceptionally strong El Nino is set to dominate Canada’s winter and possibly make it one of the warmest on record, The Weather Network’s seasonal outlook suggests, but a disrupted polar vortex could try to answer back with bursts of Arctic air and disruptive storms.

The forecast for December, January and February calls for a warmer, less snowy winter across most of Canada, marked by the potential for extended thaws and more rain than usual in some regions.

And while a record-warm winter is possible, that doesn’t mean winter is cancelled, said Doug Gillham, the network’s senior meteorologist.

“It will show up at times, and when it does, it still can be highly disruptive,” said Gillham.

El Niño is expected to delay winter for the city and much of the province, semi-retired Environment Canada climatologist David Phillips said.

Driving the outlook is El Nino, the global weather disrupter known to turn up the temperature on Canada’s winters. The last El Nino, a recurring climate cycle tied to shifting patches of warm water in the equatorial Pacific, contributed to Canada’s warmest winter starting in December 2023. This El Nino, which forecasts say could peak early this winter, is approaching the strongest ever recorded.

But the polar vortex has Gillham on alert. The band of spinning winds that normally keeps Arctic air locked near the North Pole broke down in early November, and could do so again later in the winter. While a collapse in the polar vortex is not unusual, it’s never broken down this early in November or behaved this way during a strong El Nino, a phenomenon scientists are still trying to unpack, said Gillham.

That breakdown allows cold Arctic air to spill south, where it will lower temperatures and set the stage for high-impact storms. And if that weren’t enough of a wild card, ocean temperatures are warmer than normal, allowing those winter storms to tap into abundant moisture.

A look at the combined rain and snow precipitation expected across Canada, as shown in this handout 2026-27 winter forecast map provided by The Weather Network.

It adds up to what Gillham calls “the easiest and hardest winter forecast (he’s) ever done.” He looks for a football metaphor to explain his dilemma: this historic El Nino is a hall-of-fame quarterback not to be bet against, but he’s surrounded by a cast of players unlike any he’s played with before, he said.

“So now you go on upset alert,” he said. “The cold will probably lose, but it could still raise quite a ruckus at times.”

While the forecast’s mild temperatures May be a relief for some, it could be tough on Canada’s winter tourism industry, especially for British Columbia’s low alpine regions and much of Ontario and Quebec. The possibility of big rainstorms and mid-season thaws also raises flood concerns, said Gillham.

What forecasters consider normal has shifted as climate change, driven by the burning of fossil fuels, drives up temperatures. Winters have warmed by about 3.7 degrees since the mid-20th century.

While mild conditions are set to dominate this winter, conditions still vary by region.

In B.C., dry periods are expected to be offset by some stormy stretches punctuated by atmospheric river events, which could nudge the precipitation totals above normal along the coast. The forecast calls for near-normal precipitation across most of the interior, but likely with more rain and less snow than usual. The mid- to high-alpine areas “should do fine in terms of snow” but the lower alpine ski areas May struggle, especially around the North Shore where temperatures could sit right on the margin of rain or snow, Gillham said.

Moving over the Rockies and across the Prairies, winter is expected to be “inconsistent and elusive,” said Gillham. Mild stretches could be exceptional this winter, but this is also the region where outbursts of cold Arctic air could be most impactful as well.

The forecast calls for less snow than normal across much of Canada, as shown in this handout 2026-27 winter forecast map provided by The Weather Network.

While it’s still early, the forecast doesn’t bode well for the coming fire season. With a drier winter expected, a thinner snowpack could translate to an early start to spring wildfires.

“There are some very concerning signals,” said Gillham. “I don’t want to be too alarmist this far in advance – I hope we’re wrong – but it is a very big cause for concern.”

In much of Ontario and Quebec, it’s shaping up to be a shorter, milder and less snowy winter than the previous two years. Periods of high impact winter weather will be more than offset by extended thaws. In southern areas, it could be a “very difficult” season for winter recreation, Gillham said.

The theme of warm, inconsistent winter continues into Atlantic Canada. An active storm track should deliver near-normal precipitation, but with more rain in the mix than usual. Cold air will try to fight at times with exceptional warmth coming from the Atlantic Ocean, setting up some high-impact storms and changeable conditions, Gillham said.

The territories can expect a gentler winter. The snowfall forecast is split from west to east: parts of Yukon and Northwest Territories are expected to see less than normal, while Nunavut could see more than normal.

paragraphs: An exceptionally strong El Nino is set to dominate Canada’s winter and possibly make it one of the warmest on record, The Weather Network’s seasonal outlook suggests, but a disrupted polar vortex could try to answer back with bursts of Arctic air and disruptive storms.
The forecast for December, January and February calls for a warmer, less snowy winter across most of Canada, marked by the potential for extended thaws and more rain than usual in some regions.
And while a record-warm winter is possible, that doesn’t mean winter is cancelled, said Doug Gillham, the network’s senior meteorologist.
“It will show up at times, and when it does, it still can be highly disruptive,” said Gillham.
El Niño is expected to delay winter for the city and much of the province, semi-retired Environment Canada climatologist David Phillips said.

Driving the outlook is El Nino, the global weather disrupter known to turn up the temperature on Canada’s winters. The last El Nino, a recurring climate cycle tied to shifting patches of warm water in the equatorial Pacific, contributed to Canada’s warmest winter starting in December 2023. This El Nino, which forecasts say could peak early this winter, is approaching the strongest ever recorded.

But the polar vortex has Gillham on alert. The band of spinning winds that normally keeps Arctic air locked near the North Pole broke down in early November, and could do so again later in the winter. While a collapse in the polar vortex is not unusual, it’s never broken down this early in November or behaved this way during a strong El Nino, a phenomenon scientists are still trying to unpack, said Gillham.

That breakdown allows cold Arctic air to spill south, where it will lower temperatures and set the stage for high-impact storms. And if that weren’t enough of a wild card, ocean temperatures are warmer than normal, allowing those winter storms to tap into abundant moisture.
A look at the combined rain and snow precipitation expected across Canada, as shown in this handout 2026-27 winter forecast map provided by The Weather Network.

It adds up to what Gillham calls “the easiest and hardest winter forecast (he’s) ever done.” He looks for a football metaphor to explain his dilemma: this historic El Nino is a hall-of-fame quarterback not to be bet against, but he’s surrounded by a cast of players unlike any he’s played with before, he said.
“So now you go on upset alert,” he said. “The cold will probably lose, but it could still raise quite a ruckus at times.”

While the forecast’s mild temperatures May be a relief for some, it could be tough on Canada’s winter tourism industry, especially for British Columbia’s low alpine regions and much of Ontario and Quebec. The possibility of big rainstorms and mid-season thaws also raises flood concerns, said Gillham.
What forecasters consider normal has shifted as climate change, driven by the burning of fossil fuels, drives up temperatures. Winters have warmed by about 3.7 degrees since the mid-20th century.
While mild conditions are set to dominate this winter, conditions still vary by region.

In B.C., dry periods are expected to be offset by some stormy stretches punctuated by atmospheric river events, which could nudge the precipitation totals above normal along the coast. The forecast calls for near-normal precipitation across most of the interior, but likely with more rain and less snow than usual. The mid- to high-alpine areas “should do fine in terms of snow” but the lower alpine ski areas May struggle, especially around the North Shore where temperatures could sit right on the margin of rain or snow, Gillham said.

Moving over the Rockies and across the Prairies, winter is expected to be “inconsistent and elusive,” said Gillham. Mild stretches could be exceptional this winter, but this is also the region where outbursts of cold Arctic air could be most impactful as well.
The forecast calls for less snow than normal across much of Canada, as shown in this handout 2026-27 winter forecast map provided by The Weather Network.
While it’s still early, the forecast doesn’t bode well for the coming fire season. With a drier winter expected, a thinner snowpack could translate to an early start to spring wildfires.
“There are some very concerning signals,” said Gillham. “I don’t want to be too alarmist this far in advance – I hope we’re wrong – but it is a very big cause for concern.”

In much of Ontario and Quebec, it’s shaping up to be a shorter, milder and less snowy winter than the previous two years. Periods of high impact winter weather will be more than offset by extended thaws. In southern areas, it could be a “very difficult” season for winter recreation, Gillham said.

Cold air will try to fight at times with exceptional warmth coming from the Atlantic Ocean, setting up some high-impact storms and changeable conditions, Gillham said.

The territories can expect a gentler winter. The snowfall forecast is split from west to east: parts of Yukon and Northwest Territories are expected to see less than normal, while Nunavut could see more than normal.

stories.title: Sunshine boosts temperatures before rain returns Thursday
stories.summary: A cold start to the day Wednesday, but temperatures recover this afternoon thanks to the sunshine.
stories.author: Fiona Robertson
stories.content:
A cold start to the day Wednesday, but temperatures recover this afternoon thanks to the sunshine.

“We have lots of sunshine and we’ll be right where we should be for this time of year. The forecast high 4 degrees,” explained CTV News London Meteorologist Julie Atchison.

However, the sun won’t stick around for long. We have a 40 per cent chance of showers Thursday.

“A big weather system moving up the eastern seaboard will bring cloud cover back into the Great Lakes basin and rainfall is expected,” said Atchison.

She adds that rain and gusty winds will likely persist into Friday.

Atchison says some lingering showers are possible this weekend, but she isn’t expecting widespread rainfall.

Here’s a look at the rest of the forecast

Wednesday: Sunny. Wind east 20 km/h gusting to 40. High plus 4. Wind chill minus 9 in the morning. UV index 2 or low.

Wednesday night: Clear. Wind east 20 km/h becoming light early in the evening. Wind becoming east 20 gusting to 40 before morning. Low minus 1.

Thursday: Cloudy with 40 per cent chance of rain. Windy. High plus 5.

Friday: Cloudy with 60 per cent chance of showers. High plus 5.

Saturday: Cloudy with 40 per cent chance of showers. High 7.

Sunday: Cloudy with 40 per cent chance of rain. High 8.

stories.title: Vancouver company says its predictive technology can reduce lightning strikes that spark wildfires
stories.summary: Skyward Wildfire Technologies reports positive field-test results but faces scrutiny over transparency
stories.author: Jesse Winter
stories.content:
A B.C.-based company developing technology aimed at reducing lightning strikes that spark devastating wildfires has done two years of field testing, with positive results.

Lightning caused 62 per cent of wildfires in British Columbia in 2026, according to the BC Wildfire Service. Nationally, lightning accounts for more than 80 per cent of the annual area burned . Across the country, wildfires have increased significantly in recent years, as climate change brings longer, hotter and drier summers.

Vancouver-based Skyward Wildfire Technologies has spent the past two years testing an AI-driven lightning-prediction platform to identify potentially dangerous storm systems, and an aircraft that can inject small amounts of aluminum-coated basalt fibres into thunderclouds.

The process is similar to cloud seeding, which is used to help shift rainfall patterns, but Skyward says that unlike traditional seeding, its own technology doesn’t trigger rain or impact precipitation. Instead, the basalt fibres are meant to disrupt and dissipate the electrical charge buildup within the storm clouds, reducing the amount of lightning that hits the earth.

Skyward says its research shows its predictive technology can accurately identify potentially troublesome thunderstorms, and its lightning-suppression flights reduced the amount of lightning generated by roughly 76 per cent compared with what would typically be expected.

To validate their research, Skyward said it partnered with lightning researchers at the New Mexico Institute of Mining and Technology, and the Applied Statistics and Data Science group, a research consulting group at the University of British Columbia.

“This is the first time ever, to our knowledge, that we now have statistical proof that cloud-to-ground lightning can be disrupted and abated,” said Nick Harterre, Skyward’s director of business development and government partnerships.

In May, the B.C. government awarded Skyward up to $1-million to test its technology in the province, and said the BC Wildfire Service would evaluate it to see whether it met the rigorous operational standards required for deployment.

The company has previously faced criticism for a lack of transparency over where it conducted testing and the potential environmental impact of spraying its material into storm clouds.

Skyward previously declined to answer questions from The Globe and Mail about where its lightning-abatement methods have been tested.

According to Environment and Climate Change Canada, Skyward filed notices of intent and subsequent reports referencing test flights in B.C. and Alberta in 2025, and said it told the ministry it planned to continue tests in both provinces in 2026.

Testing this year in Canada was unable to proceed because of an unexpected Transport Canada regulatory change that affected the aircraft the company planned to use, Mr. Harterre said.

In a statement, Transport Canada said the regulatory change did not involve Skyward’s technology, but was a broader change that limited the use of former military aircraft for civilian purposes.

Instead, Skyward tested its technology in the United States last summer, though it did not say where, citing “commercial conversations.”

Adonis Leal, a professor at New Mexico Tech who studies high-energy lightning strikes, reviewed Skyward’s work and said he found it convincing. The company’s claims are “very reasonable, and I believe in the results,” he said.

Dr. Leal’s research focuses on understanding the strongest and most intense cloud-to-ground lightning strikes, which generate intense heat and are most likely to trigger wildfires.

Introducing conductive material into thunderclouds increases the conductivity of the clouds themselves, Dr. Leal said, making it easier for electrical buildup to discharge inside the clouds, instead of building to the point that it strikes the ground.

Another New Mexico Tech professor, Richard Sonnenfeld, was more cautious. He said that Skyward’s combination of lightning detection and suppression “probably works.”

Dr. Sonnenfeld said New Mexico Tech’s role was providing highly accurate lightning-detection instruments that can be mounted on aircraft. The amount of research that the company conducted, he said, was impressive. “They really did a lot of work.”

Skyward said it conducted 58 test flights, targeting 182 storm cells across the 2025 and 2026 wildfire seasons. It also tracked the behaviour of 2,505 comparable reference storms to examine the lightning output from treated versus untreated thunderclouds.

However, Dr. Sonnenfeld also said he was broadly skeptical of geoengineering – large-scale human interventions meant to influence climate – as a solution to climate change, calling such efforts a “horrible idea.”

Skyward’s tech, he said, is “sort of focused geoengineering” and raises questions about the amount of money and time being invested in treating the symptoms of climate change, such as devastating wildfires, instead of focusing on the root causes, including the burning of fossil fuels.

Mr. Harterre said Skyward’s tech has advanced early attempts at lightning suppression from the 1960s and 70s in two key ways. First, one of the biggest challenges researchers of the past faced was figuring out which clouds had the potential to cause the most damaging lightning.

That’s where Skyward’s predictive tool Vista comes in, Mr. Harterre said.

Vista uses machine-learning to ingest weather-forecast modelling, historic lightning data and wildfire behaviour science – the same information that’s used to generate the Canadian Fire Weather Index. It produces reports that predict not just where lightning is most likely to strike, but that give a more accurate picture of the potential damage a fire could cause at a particular location and time.

The goal is not to stop all fires from occurring, Mr. Harterre said. It’s to figure out which potential fires might have the most devastating consequences, and give fire agencies another tool to prevent them.

“There’s good fire and bad fire. And we need a lot more good fire on the landscape,” Mr. Harterre said, referring to the beneficial role wildfires can play in maintaining the landscape.

Many of Canada’s ecosystems evolved to rely on wildfire and require occasional low-severity fires to remain healthy. Letting those fires burn can also help prevent larger, more devastating fires in the future by reducing the amount of forest fuel available.

The company is working on “making sure that we have all the right tools in the forecasting toolkit to go after only the highest-risk storms,” Mr. Harterre said.

“We can predict the Jaspers, we can predict the Fort McMurrays, and agencies use that to preposition aircraft, preposition resources,” he said.

Mr. Harterre said Skyward’s tech has also refined the material that lightning-abatement flights need to disperse in order to work. The material itself is about the size and feel of short human hair. By using the Vista platform to more accurately target the right storm clouds, Skyward can reduce the amount of material that it needs to spray, Mr. Harterre said.

Mr. Harterre said their research shows that at the deployment volumes necessary, the material is expected to have no measurable impact on the environment.

“Even at full scale, in the most conservative assumptions across an entire season, you’re talking about way less material than you’d use in even one drop of [fire] retardant from a plane,” he said.

Mr. Harterre said the Vista platform can also be used as a stand-alone predictive tool for agencies, without the lightning-abatement process.

The B.C. Wildfire Service said that because of the transition period between governments after last month’s provincial election, it was unable to respond to questions.

Skyward’s tech, he said, is “sort of focused geoengineering” and raises questions about the amount of money and time being invested in treating the symptoms of climate change, such as devastating wildfires, instead of focusing on the root causes, including the burning of fossil fuels.

stories.title: Sexual-misconduct reporting has changed since Galloway controversy, UBC says
stories.summary: Systemic gaps still remain in the university’s reporting process, experts and advocates say
stories.author: Mike Hager
stories.content:
Postsecondary institutions across British Columbia have improved their handling of sexual-misconduct complaints since two high-profile cases at the University of British Columbia in 2015, but systemic gaps remain, experts and advocates say.

Ubc’s actions have been at the centre of testimony in recent weeks in a defamation case brought by bestselling author Steven Galloway. He was suspended in 2015 and later fired after being accused of sexual assault and sexual harassment by a former creative writing student with whom he had a two-year relationship. Around the same time, a PhD student in the history department faced separate allegations from his fellow classmates.

A retired judge hired by UBC after Mr. Galloway’s suspension said she could not, ON a balance of probabilities, substantiate the sexual and physical assault allegations, but found he had sexually harassed his former student. He was dismissed in June 2016 for “a record of misconduct that resulted in an irreparable breach of the trust.”

Mr. Galloway was never charged with an offence. He filed the defamation lawsuit in 2018 against his accuser – known as A.B. because of a publication ban on her identity – and three other women whom he alleges went on social media to repeat her allegations. In the defamation trial, A.B. is no longer maintaining Mr. Galloway sexually and physically assaulted her – just that she reported those allegations to the university.

Janine Benedet, a UBC law professor whose research focuses on the justice system’s response to sexual violence against women, chaired an expert panel in 2016 examining how the university could improve how it handles these complaints. She says it is a gargantuan task to craft policies that respect the various workplace and privacy laws governing a host of roles with power over students: coaches, residence advisers, teaching assistants and professors.

The largest sea change from that nascent #MeToo era, many experts agree, was a provincial law passed in 2017, mandating all postsecondary institutions create standalone offices to handle sexual-misconduct complaints that involve anyone studying or working at the school.

In terms of the two cases from 2015, before the law came into effect, witnesses testified that professors in the history and creative writing programs asked grad students to gather details about the allegations from those in their classes and report back.

Since the 2019 fiscal year, Ubc’s Sexual Violence Prevention and Response Office at the school’s Vancouver campus provided support to an average of roughly 250 clients each year. Last fiscal year, it received 226 disclosures of incidents of sexual or gender-based violence, according to its annual reports posted online.

The Svpro also forwarded two “institutional reports” to the standalone Investigations Office last fiscal year. Such reports are created when more than one disclosure is made against a single person.

Ubc’s Investigations Office receives complaints from students, faculty and staff across both campuses and is also referred cases from other agencies at the school. The IO has investigated an average of 47 sexual-misconduct complaints during each of the past five fiscal years, according to its latest annual report.

The IO closed 20 cases during its last fiscal year, finding a breach of the school’s sexual-misconduct policy in 15 of them.

Ophelia Kehila, director of the Sexual Assault Support Centre funded by Ubc’s student union, said they have seen demand for the centre’s services increase significantly over the past three years, which they noted has no relationship with the university.

The centre helped 308 new people last fiscal year, with 10 per cent of all clients saying they were seeking this form of peer support after first approaching the Svpro.

Mx. Kehila said in a statement that many survivors who come to the centre would rather report to police than the university’s IO.

University spokesperson Thandi Fletcher in a statement touted the creation of the Svpro and IO as major improvements in the school’s approach to sexual violence over the past decade, noting they prioritize “procedural fairness and a trauma-informed approach.”

The statement added that UBC policy bars a professor from having sexual relationships with students they supervise if one “has influence over the student’s current or future academic activities, working conditions or career advancement.”

Someone at the university in a supervisory role or in a position of influence May have a consensual relationship with a student if it began before this power imbalance, but it must be disclosed to administrators, the statement said. Last year, UBC introduced mandatory training for faculty and staff on preventing and responding to sexual misconduct that includes a section on prohibited relationships, Ms. Fletcher said.

Ninu Kang, executive director of the Ending Violence Association of B.C., said that too often, despite reporting sexual assault through Ubc’s official channels, some students find themselves having to rearrange their lives in order to cope. The association is in the midst of crafting new investigative guidelines for the province’s 25 postsecondary institutions.

“In some instances, students are still having to make decisions about whether they drop the course or drop out of something because the alternative is that they will be facing the accused,” Ms. Kang said.

Morgyn Chandler, a Vancouver lawyer who frequently represents sexual-assault survivors in civil suits, also said that the onus is on the survivor to remove themselves from a harmful situation after they register a complaint.

She said several of her clients have reported sexual violence to the university and, from her perspective, have been disappointed.

Statistics Canada data shows only a fraction of survivors ever go a step further to make a police complaint.

Over the decade that ended last year, the University RCMP detachment reported an annual average of nearly 18 common sexual-assault cases, according to Statscan. The campus detachment solved roughly a third of these total cases by charging a suspect – slightly below the provincial RCMP average in that decade for such cases.

Dr. Benedet says the timelines of the criminal justice system often don’t line up with the lives of students, many of whom want to move on from their trauma and graduate.

stories.title: Where did that fresco come from? Nearly 20 cultural items headed back to Italy from collector, ROM, Gardiner
stories.summary: Repatriation event is ‘a major step forward in our co-operation on cultural heritage protection,’ Italy’s ambassador to Canada says
stories.author: Josh O’Kane
stories.content:
When Toronto lawyer Sara Riboldi began assessing the estate of an Italian-Canadian art collector last year, she noticed that some of the pieces didn’t have adequate documentation about their provenance.

The pieces were astounding in their age and origin. There were 15 artifacts dating back to ancient Greek and Roman times, including decorated pottery jugs and vessels, glass bottles, ceramic jars, a terracotta oil lamp. And there were two frescoes, too, that had been removed from a church. Riboldi, who practises law in both countries and was a trustee of the estate, got in touch with Italian authorities. It turned out they had significant cultural heritage and belonged back in the country, whose constitution protects its cultural property.

On Wednesday, Toronto’s Royal Ontario Museum will host an event celebrating their repatriation to Italy – alongside one item each from the ROM and the ceramics-focused Gardiner Museum. It’ll be hosted by Embassy of Italy in Canada, the Italian Cultural Institute of Toronto and Riboldi’s eponymous law firm.

“It’s good when there are these cases of international co-operation,” Riboldi said in an interview. “There’s common ground and common respect on Canada.

Repatriation discussions in Canada often centre on returning artifacts from Indigenous nations to their original communities. Italy, which has spent centuries as a global hub for art and culture, has also had its wares spread all over the globe, sometimes through illicit channels. There’s been a flurry of repatriation activity between the country and Canada in recent years.

Italian authorities helped return acclaimed photographer Yousuf Karsh’s stolen wartime portrait of Winston Churchill earlier this decade, after it was nicked from the Fairmont Château Laurier and sold to a lawyer from that country. And last year, Canadian authorities returned items related to St. Nicholas of Myra , the inspiration for the legend of Santa Claus, to Italy – including one of his bones. The two countries hosted a symposium that same month on crimes against cultural property.

The Vatican, an independent jurisdiction based in Rome, has also shown a willingness to repatriate items of cultural heritage. It handed back a historic collection of Indigenous objects last year from the Vatican Museums, including a rare Western Arctic sealskin kayak.

Italy’s ambassador to Canada, Alessandro Cattaneo, said in an interview that Wednesday’s repatriation event is “a major step forward in our co-operation on cultural heritage protection.”

Unesco established a convention fighting against the illicit trafficking of cultural property in 1970, and Canada and Italy signed toward the end of the decade. Riboldi said the collector whose estate she represents moved to Canada with the items in the seventies – but she could not determine the exact arrival date, and, as such, whether the convention would apply.

Riboldi declined to share the identity of the collector or their beneficiaries, citing a wish for privacy. But she said the collector died in Italy, which triggered its laws on cultural property. Those laws are stringent; Italy even has a special police force, the Carabinieri Command for the Protection of Cultural Heritage, that trawls the world for missing items.

After many discussions, they found that more than a dozen of the collector’s items were significant to Italy’s cultural heritage. The frescoes, for instance, were found to be from a deconsecrated church.

After discussing the items with the authorities, Riboldi said she got permission from the estate’s beneficiaries to arrange for a return. “Even though the items have been in Canada for 50 years or so, there’s a principle among countries that national property of a state should stay with the state,” she said. “There is reciprocal respect and co-operation in returning these items.”

The ROM had in its collection a terracotta antefix roof tile in the shape of a woman’s head that dated from about 530 B.C. The Gardiner Museum, meanwhile, had a majolica dish made in Castel Durante – now known as Urbania – in the 1540s. When new details about the provenance of the items began to emerge, they worked with the Italian government to prepare for their repatriation, too.

The institutions “really were very open and very pro-active in trying to find the right solution, and they wanted to be sure that those important artifacts are given back to their original proper owners,” Cattaneo said.

The Gardiner Museum said the Castel Durante dish it’s returning bears a coat of arms and was made for a dinner service. It was first donated to its collection in 1990, after its owner purchased it from Christie’s in London in 1980. But in 2021, the museum said, researchers used techniques such as an X-ray examination to confirm it was stolen from a collection in Florence in 1976.

The ROM said its returned antefix was donated to the museum in 2004, and that its team had done due diligence about its origins upon receiving it, including consulting the global Art Loss Register. But Italian authorities contacted the ROM two years ago with new information about its provenance, prompting it to review its history and prepare it for return to the country.

Both museums said they remained committed to ethical collecting practices and would continue to return objects whose acquisition histories are found to include unethical or illegal means.

stories.title: New northern B.C. berth opens, but 11-year-old exclusivity deal stops it from progressing
stories.summary: Trigon Terminals wants to build an additional liquid gas export site at the Port of Prince Rupert
stories.author: Kate Helmore
stories.content:
A new berth has opened at the Port of Prince Rupert and its owner wants to invest $800-million to upgrade it for liquid gas export, but the port authority’s 11-year-old exclusivity deal with a competitor is standing in the way.

Bulk commodity exporter Trigon Terminals has completed the structural build for its second berth at the northern B.C. port. The site doubles Trigon’s capacity, and could expand the company’s exports by $4-billion, according to corporate documents provided to The Globe and Mail.

Construction of the new berth has cost $152-million to date, $75-million of which was funded by the federal government through the National Trade Corridors Fund.

Trigon hopes the next step in the site’s development will be an open-access export facility for liquid petroleum gas, also known as propane and butane, that would cost around $800-million to construct, according to the company’s corporate documents.

LPG is a byproduct of oil and gas production increasingly used in cooking, heating and petrochemical manufacturing in Asian markets such as China, India, Japan and South Korea.

However, the proposed Trigon LPG project at Prince Rupert was rejected in 2023 because of an exclusivity deal between the port authority and a joint venture between natural gas giant AltaGas Ltd. and Dutch infrastructure developer Royal Vopak.

The port authority signed the deal with Vopak in 2015 to secure investment in a new LPG terminal. Vopak later entered into a partnership with AltaGas, which will operate the new $1.46-billion Ridley Island Energy Export Facility when it comes online early next year.

Construction began on the facility – also located at the Port of Prince Rupert – in 2024.

When operational, all LPG exported via the Port of Prince Rupert will be handled by AltaGas. The terminal will ship 55,000 barrels of LPGs per day.

The deal “enables the certainty required to advance large scale capital projects,” said a statement from port authority spokesperson James Cain, and it means the port can “secure investment in vital trade infrastructure, and fulfill Prpa’s mandate of enabling Canadian trade.”

But according to chief executive of Trigon Terminals, Craig Olley, this exclusivity deal is an “unjustified barrier to export growth.” It stands in the way of Trigon’s plans for the site, as well as Ottawa’s trade diversification ambitions, in particular its goal of doubling non-U.S. exports by 2030, he said.

“We’re encouraged by the current government’s focus on faster projects, but they need to turn aspirational conversations into a reality.”

The new Trigon berth is well-suited to a number of commodities, said Mr. Olley. Trigon currently exports mostly coal out of its first berth, and has considered solid commodities and fertilizer products such as sulphur, urea or potash for the second berth.

However, he said LPG is Trigon’s preferred option because of several factors.

The site already contains much of the infrastructure needed to safely export propane and butane, such as a liquid loading arm and rail infrastructure, according to the initial project development plan presented in the summer.

No work would need to happen within the water and no extra land cleared. The project proposal has already progressed through a number of regulatory burdens. On Nov. 4, the Impact Assessment Agency of Canada said no federal assessment would be required.

Trigon staff are also already trained on LPG handling – they unload railcars and provide ship mooring services to incoming freight on behalf of AltaGas, which sub-leases Trigon land.

This means Trigon would be able to meet a fast-growing demand for LPG from Asian markets, said Mr. Olley. The Asia-Pacific Transportation Market for LPG is forecast to grow 4.7 per cent per year to US$9.8-billion by 2034, according to market research firm Visiontavora.

The exclusivity deal should not be confused with limiting market access or competition, said AltaGas spokesperson Bryn Lukowiak, adding that the Ridley Island terminal is open-access and will be connected to more than 70 Canadian producers and aggregators with a global market.

But Mr. Olley said the deal reduces optionality for players across the marketplace. Producers must either sell to AltaGas, or they must pay more to transport their product south and export it through the U.S. Gulf. Buyers might also have to pay to use AltaGas’ vessels instead of their own, which also incurs costs.

“We’re trying to provide some optionality to the Canadian market, and we’re being thwarted as a result,” the Trigon CEO said.

Should the port be unwilling to reconsider this deal, the least it could do is provide more transparency on when the exclusivity will expire, he said. Trigon could then plan to bring its own LPG facility online for when the deal expires.

The port authority refused to make this information public. “It wouldn’t be appropriate for us to comment on the contents of our contracts with our tenants,” said a statement from Mr. Cain.

In Mr. Olley’s opinion, this lack of transparency is holding back his business and Canadian trade.

“Tell us when the end date is and we’ll build to that end date. That would really help to overcome an unjustifiable barrier to the LPG coming into the market.”

Bulk commodity exporter Trigon Terminals has completed the structural build for its second berth at the northern B.C. port. The site doubles Trigon’s capacity, and could expand the company’s exports by $4-billion, according to corporate documents provided to The Globe and Mail.
Construction of the new berth has cost $152-million to date, $75-million of which was funded by the federal government through the National Trade Corridors Fund.

Trigon hopes the next step in the site’s development will be an open-access export facility for liquid petroleum gas, also known as propane and butane, that would cost around $800-million to construct, according to the company’s corporate documents.
LPG is a byproduct of oil and gas production increasingly used in cooking, heating and petrochemical manufacturing in Asian markets such as China, India, Japan and South Korea.

However, the proposed Trigon LPG project at Prince Rupert was rejected in 2023 because of an exclusivity deal between the port authority and a joint venture between natural gas giant AltaGas Ltd. and Dutch infrastructure developer Royal Vopak.

The port authority signed the deal with Vopak in 2015 to secure investment in a new LPG terminal. Vopak later entered into a partnership with AltaGas, which will operate the new $1.46-billion Ridley Island Energy Export Facility when it comes online early next year.
Construction began on the facility – also located at the Port of Prince Rupert – in 2024.
When operational, all LPG exported via the Port of Prince Rupert will be handled by AltaGas. The terminal will ship 55,000 barrels of LPGs per day.

The new Trigon berth is well-suited to a number of commodities, said Mr. Olley. Trigon currently exports mostly coal out of its first berth, and has considered solid commodities and fertilizer products such as sulphur, urea or potash for the second berth.

stories.title: Coastal B.C. drenched with rainfall and high tides
stories.summary: Environment Canada warns of up to 225 millimetres of rain Wednesday
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
King tides combined with powerful waves destroyed part of a pier in Northern California on Wednesday, and officials warned more beachfront homes are at risk of flooding.

A video showed a massive wave tearing down a portion of the pier in the city of Pacifica and slamming it into the ocean. Officials had closed the L-shaped, 350-metre pier in the summer after finding cracks in the structure.

Beachfront homes in the city south of San Francisco began flooding this week as king tides, the highest tides of the year, arrived in the area.

North of San Francisco, Marin County officials issued an evacuation warning for residents of beachfront properties in Stinson Beach, saying large waves expected through the afternoon could send water and debris into roads and homes.

Coastal properties in the San Francisco area were battered by a king tide, amplified by the ongoing super El Niño, on Wednesday, flooding streets and sending seawater into homes. The Associated Press

The National Weather Service issued a coastal flood warning for the Pacific Coast and bay shorelines along San Francisco Bay and San Pablo Bay through 4 p.m. Wednesday. It also issued a high surf warning in the Bay Area for Wednesday, when breaking waves of six to nine metres, about two to three storeys high, could overpower swimmers and sweep people into the ocean.

“Rising tides will bring water and waves farther up the beach than normal, restricting escape from beaches and coastal area,” the weather service said.

King tides occur when the gravitational pull of the moon and sun aligns to raise water levels. Their effects this year are being amplified by the ongoing super El Niño, which has warmed the ocean, leading to an increased volume of seawater.

High tides have already flooded several communities this week along California’s coast.

In the Bay Area, some homes and streets in the coastal Marin County cities of Mill Valley, Larkspur, Sausalito and Corte Madera flooded. Farther north, in Humboldt County near the Oregon border, the sheriff’s office ordered evacuations in a small coastal community where most of the buildings flooded.

Marc Doll had been planning to use the planks of wood he watched float past his window on Tuesday to build a deck, but they’ve been put to a more urgent purpose as relentless rain swamped his property on British Columbia’s Quadra Island.

The creeks that weave around Doll’s farm run dry in the summer, but the rain that has soaked much of B.C.’s coast has turned the creeks into fast-flowing streams.

Doll said he donned shorts and Crocs to fetch the planks for his would-be deck when he saw one of the larger bridges on his 17-hectare property looking unstable.

“I noticed that the bridge was starting to float away, so I threw that wood on top of the bridge to weigh the bridge down,” he said in an interview the next day.

Rainfall and wind warnings covered Vancouver Island and the Gulf Islands, including Quadra, as the final storm in what Environment Canada called a series of “potent” weather systems hit the coast on Wednesday.

The weather office upgraded coastal flood warnings in parts of Metro Vancouver, Squamish and Gibsons, saying storm surge, large waves and very high tides could cause “moderate to significant” flooding.

The bulletin said the storm would push water levels 40 to 70 centimetres above the highest astronomical tides of the year.

Lower-level yellow warnings for coastal flooding span all of Vancouver Island and stretch along the central coast, where water levels are expected to be 30 to 50 centimetres higher. The bulletin also covers much of Haida Gwaii.

The Regional District of Nanaimo issued several evacuation alerts due to coastal flooding for communities in its jurisdiction along the east side of Vancouver Island, including Lantzville, Cedar and French Creek.

The nearby District of Lantzville also issued an alert for several properties on the waterfront, with B.C.’s emergency information system saying high water levels could lead to flooding that poses “a threat to life and safety.”

While Doll said he was able to secure his larger bridge, a smaller bridge was swept away, cutting him off from 12 pigs on the property.

He waded through thigh-deep water to reach the pigs at meal time.

“We have a mother who’s got eight little piglets, so she needs food every day otherwise there’s problems. So I couldn’t put it off,” he said.

Doll said the pigs have a covered area to stay in at the highest point in their pasture.

“My pigs usually are in 1/2 to 3/4-acre pastures. And they’re on an island at the moment, but they’re fine,” he said.

The B.C. River Forecast Centre issued an upgraded flood watch for areas between Nanaimo and Campbell River, while lower-level streamflow advisories covered the rest of Vancouver Island.

The bulletin said 60 to 120 millimetres of rain had fallen across Vancouver Island so far, with another 30 to 90 millimetres expected depending on the region.

On the mainland, high streamflow advisories were in effect for the Sunshine Coast, Sea to Sky region and Vancouver’s North Shore.

The storms also prompted the District of Squamish to declare a local state of emergency and activate its local emergency operations centre.

It said the Sea to Sky region would see a significant amount of rain along with high tides over the next few days, with the highest tides expected Thursday.

The Transportation Ministry meanwhile advised drivers to check conditions before travelling through the coastal areas due the flooding risk.

Environment Canada has said B.C.’s coast could see up to 225 millimetres of rain before the end of Wednesday.

One station on Vancouver Island had already recovered 307 millimetres in 48 hours.

The storm has also brought high winds, including gusts reaching speeds of 160 km/h off the northern tip of Vancouver Island.

stories.title: Literacy levels have plunged to an ‘all-time low’ in Canada, report shows
stories.summary: An education think tank is pushing for Canadian schools to adopt a new approach to teaching children how to read, after it reported that literacy levels have plunged to an 'all-time low' in Canada.
stories.author: Christl Dabu
stories.content:
An education think tank is pushing for Canadian schools to adopt a new approach to teaching children how to read, after it reported that literacy levels have plunged to an “ all-time lo w ” in Canada.

More than one in three students (38 per cent) can’t read by the time they finish Grade 3, and between 20 per cent and 56 per cent cannot read by Grade 4, according to The Aristotle Foundation for Public Policy. The numbers vary by province.

The study cited an Ontario Human Rights Commission’s Right to Read inquiry report in 2022, which called for reforms to improve Grade 3 literacy rates.

The foundation’s report noted that Alberta appeared to lead other provinces in literacy as it had rolled out “evidence-based reforms” in 2021. The province achieved 80 per cent literacy in 2021 based on Grade 4 Progress in International Reading Study (Pirls) tests.

However, the foundation said “other provincial assessments do not look any better.” The foundation called Manitoba’s Grade 3 reading results “most concerning,” citing that 44.9 per cent of students met provincial reading standards in 2024. In British Columbia, 30 per cent of Grade 4 students didn’t meet the proficiency benchmark in the Foundation Skills Assessment results. In Quebec, 31 per cent of Grade 4 students did not meet the provincial literacy standards in 2021.

The public policy think tank published two reports this month assessing the state of early grade literacy, noting that literacy in Canada is at an “all-time low.”

“Today’s Grade 10 students are two to three years behind in reading, compared to their peers 25 years ago,” the report said.

The analyses, published on Nov. 13 and Nov. 18, were based on data and reports of provinces’ assessments for Grade 3 and 4 students.

The foundation’s reports focus mainly on Grade 3 and Grade 4 students. The think tank said it targeted those grades because they mark “a critical turning point” when children “shift from learning to read to reading to learn.”

Evidence suggests that those who don’t know how to read by Grade 4 will not acquire the skill until they are adults, or they May never become literate, the analyses said.

Need for ‘evidence-based’ literacy approach: expert

David Livingstone, a senior fellow with the foundation, said his research and the Right to Read inquiry report found the need for most schools to switch from a balanced literacy approach to an “evidence-based” structured literacy method in teaching students how to read and write.

Balanced literacy assumes that learners “just catch on” based on “cueing systems,” similar to the way infants learn language, according to the report. While it places importance on books and texts, it lacks “sufficient direct instruction.”

With this approach, Livingstone said students don’t break words down into their component parts, their syllables and the sounds of words.

“What they’re doing instead, is they’re encouraged to try to guess at the whole word in its context,” Livingstone, an honorary research associate at Vancouver Island University, said in a video interview with CTVNews.CA on Tuesday.

“The research doesn’t support that as the preferred way to teach kids how to read. Instead, the structured literacy approach, sometimes just called phonics, is a better way to teach kids how to read.”

According to the foundation, structured literacy involves “explicit instruction” and “frequent evaluation” for students who need extra help.

Livingstone said a few Canadian jurisdictions have adopted the structured literacy approach recommended by the Ohrc.

“And even those that did adopt that approach, very few of them have gone far enough towards changing, for instance, the licensing requirements for teachers, or make it mandatory for teachers to be trained in how to teach this phonics structured literacy approach,” he said.

“So, there seems to be some reluctance by the school boards, by the provinces to adopt this better way of teaching children. We would just like to see them adopt what the Ohrc has strongly recommended as the preferred way to teach kids how to read,” Livingstone added.

Additionally, the foundation recommended a “knowledge-rich curriculum” for fostering success in reading, placing importance on background knowledge and vocabulary.

“A book isn’t going to explain everything to you – it expects you to come with some knowledge,” Livingstone said.

The Aristotle Foundation for Public Policy noted the challenge of learning literacy skills later in life.

“Evidence from national and international assessments shows that these gaps rarely close over time,” the foundation’s Nov. 13 report stated. “Even when many students have not acquired basic literacy skills by Grade 3, schools often shift focus in higher grades away from foundational reading instruction, leaving struggling readers behind.”

The foundation said the stakes are high if children aren’t able to read early in life.

“While the cost to Canada May be lower economic productivity and higher crime rates, the personal costs to children and their families let down by an education system that refuses to follow the evidence is incalculable,” the report added.

stories.title: The final Ontario Trillium Benefit payment of 2026 is coming soon. Here's what you need to know
stories.summary: The next payment is set to go out in early December. Ontarians who forgot to claim the benefit in the previous years May still be eligible to receive those payments.
stories.author: Samm Mohibuddin
stories.content:
Eligible Ontarians are set to receive their final Ontario Trillium Benefit payment of the calendar year on Dec. 10, just in time for the holiday season.

The tax-free benefit is issued by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) on behalf of the Ontario government to help residents offset the cost of energy, property and sales taxes.

Here’s what you need to know about the upcoming payment.

The Ontario Trillium Benefit (OTB) combines three provincial tax credits:

The Ontario Energy and Property Tax Credit, which helps offset property taxes and sales taxes on energy.

The Northern Ontario Energy Credit, which helps residents of northern Ontario with energy costs.

The Ontario Sales Tax Credit, which helps low- to moderate-income Ontarians offset sales taxes.

Payments for the current benefit year, which runs from July 2026 to June 2027, are based on your 2025 income tax return.

To receive the benefit, you must qualify for at least one of the three aforementioned tax credits.

The CRA determines your eligibility and how much you are entitled to based on the information you provided in your income tax return.

You must file your taxes annually to continue receiving the benefit, even if you have no income to report.

The amount you receive depends on your eligibility for each of the three credits. You can estimate your entitlement using the CRA’s child and family benefits calculator.

Ontarians entitled to more than $500 for the current benefit year could have opted to receive monthly payments beginning in July or a single lump sum in June 2027.

Those entitled to $500 or less would generally have received their benefit in a single payment in the first payment month, usually July.

To apply for the Ontario Energy and Property Tax Credit or the Northern Ontario Energy Credit, you must complete the applicable sections of Form ON-BEN when filing your income tax return.

You don’t need to apply separately for the Ontario Sales Tax Credit, as the CRA automatically determines your eligibility based on information from your tax return.

If you were previously deemed ineligible for the benefit, you can apply again in subsequent years.

If you forgot to claim any of the three tax credits in previous years, you may still be able to receive the money.

According to the CRA, taxpayers can generally request adjustments to income tax returns from the previous 10 calendar years.

Rather than filing a new tax return for those years, you can request an adjustment through your CRA My Account.

Alternatively, you can submit a tax return adjustment request form or a signed letter to your tax centre, along with any applicable forms and supporting documents.

If you already receive your income tax refund or other government benefits through direct deposit, the CRA will deposit your OTB payment into your bank account. Otherwise, you will receive your payment by cheque.

The CRA encourages recipients to sign up for direct deposit to avoid potential delivery delays.

If you owe money to the CRA or its external partners, your benefit will first be put toward those outstanding debts, with any remaining money issued to you.

Payments are typically issued on the 10th of every month, unless the date falls on a weekend or public holiday, in which case the payment is issued on the preceding business day.

The Dec. 10 payment will be the last of the calendar year, though monthly payments for the current benefit period will continue until June 2027.
