stories.title: Quebec’s Conservative Leader is doing his best to pull the province to the right
stories.summary: Éric Duhaime has remade himself several times, but his love of small government has never wavered
stories.author: Maura Forrest
stories.content:
It’s a safe bet that in 1980s Quebec , most preteens didn’t have posters of Margaret Thatcher on their bedroom walls. But then, Éric Duhaime has always been a bit of an outsider.

As a boy, he would run home from school to watch Question Period at Quebec’s National Assembly. He insisted on wearing his school uniform to supper.

The scrawny 16-year-old who wore a top hat and white gloves to his high-school prom was perhaps an unlikely candidate to become Quebec’s contrarian-in-chief. But Mr. Duhaime would transform himself from political aide to polarizing shock jock to the standard-bearer for pandemic rage.

Now he has remade himself once more as the sober head of a right-wing movement he has steered into Quebec’s political mainstream. A province that was once allergic to the Conservative brand suddenly elected 19 Tories last month, giving them the power to help decide the fate of a minority government led by the sovereigntist Parti Québécois.

Though Mr. Duhaime, 57, donned different hats before becoming leader of the Quebec Conservative Party in 2021, his politics have wavered little since he was a child gazing up at the Iron Lady. In books and on the airwaves, he has extolled the virtues of small government to a province known for its expansive bureaucracy.

It often seemed like a quixotic mission. Before this year, no Conservative had been elected to the provincial legislature in nearly a century. But amid a cost-of-living crunch and growing dissatisfaction with the state of Quebec’s public services, Mr. Duhaime has found his moment.

His success comes at an ambiguous moment for conservative politics in Canada, with the federal party faltering while Conservatives dominate provincial legislatures. Right-leaning parties now hold power in seven out of 10 provinces.

Mr. Duhaime is hoping to build an alliance with Conservatives across the country from his new perch on Quebec’s opposition benches. The long-time outsider has manoeuvred his party into the centre of provincial politics − and is doing his best to pull Quebec to the right.

“We didn’t have a Conservative force, and now we have one,” he said in a recent interview. “And I think it could change the dynamics of politics not just in Quebec, but all across Canada.”

Quebec’s first government was Conservative, elected shortly after Confederation. But the party, closely tied to its federal counterpart, won its last election in 1892.

Over time, the Conservative label was poisoned in Quebec, not least because of the federal government’s decision to invoke conscription during the First World War.

In the 1930s, then-Conservative leader Maurice Duplessis dissolved the party into the Union Nationale, a right-wing alliance that channelled growing nationalist sentiment.

Mr. Duhaime came of age more than half a century later, after the Union Nationale had run its course and successive Liberal and Parti Québécois governments had established the “ modèle québécois ” − an interventionist state that administered a suite of social programs.

At the time, Mr. Duhaime’s libertarian principles ran against the grain. “Socialist ideas were much more fashionable,” he said. “I always believed in individual freedom.”

Raised in a nationalist household, he went to work for the Bloc Québécois in Ottawa but abandoned the sovereigntist cause after the 1995 referendum. He now says he’s ready to negotiate with Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon on anything except his promised independence referendum.

Instead, Mr. Duhaime took an interest in boosting provincial autonomy within Canada. He worked on Stockwell Day’s campaign for the leadership of the Canadian Alliance in 2000, and soon became a fixture of the conservative establishment.

Today, he sees his party as a natural ally of conservatives across the country fighting “federal government intrusion.” Former Alberta premier Jason Kenney travelled to Quebec to speak to his caucus last week.

Federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre recently said he is “very pleased that there will be a party in the National Assembly that will champion our priorities.” The two parties have no official ties.

But Mr. Duhaime eventually concluded that if conservative ideals were to flourish in his own province, they would need champions outside the world of politics.

In 2009, he became a talk-show host on Quebec City’s right-leaning “trash radio,” which specializes in outrage and provocation. He quickly developed a reputation as a fiery polemicist who, in the words of one prominent TV host, appeared to be “at war with everything.”

“He had no barrier,” said former Quebec City mayor Régis Labeaume. “The more toxic they are, the more money they make.”

Mr. Duhaime routinely caused offence and was reliably unapologetic. He came out publicly in a divisive 2017 book, The End of Homosexuality and the Last Gay Man , which argued that the battle for gay rights had been won and that Lgbtq groups were part of an “industry of victimization.” (When it emerged that his latest book, published this spring, was written with the help of AI, he responded with little more than a shrug.)

But the pandemic and Quebec’s aggressive public-health measures drew the radio host back into politics. “I saw the fact that our civic rights, our individual freedom, even our democracy was at risk,” he said.

In 2021, he was elected leader of a new incarnation of the Quebec Conservative Party, which had languished ever since it was founded 12 years earlier. He railed against curfews and mandatory vaccination to his growing social-media following, tapping into a vein of discontent that helped him take nearly 13 per cent of the vote in the 2022 election.

“He really has a knack for getting his message across,” said Senator Josée Verner, a former federal Conservative minister who served as his campaign chair.

Still, those votes didn’t win him any seats, and the conspiracy theorists in his ranks made it easy to dismiss him as a fringe politician.

As the pandemic threat receded, Mr. Duhaime set about reinventing himself once more. The man who was at war with everything would now return to his roots, earnestly preaching lower taxes and more private health care.

“When you’re a radio host, you’re trying to polarize to get people’s attention,” he said. “You have to include everybody when you’re a leader of a party.”

In this fall’s election campaign, he emerged as a credible option for voters fed up with seeing their taxes rewarded with crumbling infrastructure and endless health care delays. His promise to shrink the size of government was echoed by most other parties.

“I think more and more Quebeckers are realizing that we’re not just heading toward a wall, we’ve crashed into the wall,” said Cédric Lapointe, Mr. Duhaime’s long-time right-hand man who now works in Mr. Poilievre’s office.

On Oct. 5, Quebeckers elected Mr. Duhaime and 18 other Conservatives to the National Assembly, mostly from ridings in and around Quebec City, where the federal Conservatives also hold a handful of seats. The party finished second in 32 of the province’s 127 ridings.

It was a stunning revival of a political brand that had been untouchable for so long. “The word ‘Conservative,’ he’s made it less toxic in Quebec,” said Ken Boessenkool, a senior campaign and policy adviser to former prime minister Stephen Harper and a long-time friend of Mr. Duhaime. “I think that’s an enormous feat.”

Not everyone agrees that Quebec’s political landscape is shifting to the right. Other right-leaning parties have come and gone over the years without calling themselves Conservative.

“There are people in Quebec who are angry,” Mr. Labeaume said. “People want a well-run government, but ask them if they want to lose services. The answer is no.”

Still, Mr. Duhaime believes Quebeckers are finally ready to “revisit the model” he has denounced for decades. “There’s more and more appetite,” he said. “It’s conservatism à la québécoise .”

stories.title: Faith-based university students unfairly caught up in Osap freeze, schools say
stories.summary: Students are feeling the financial pressure, even as schools defer tuition payments
stories.author: Kelly Grant
stories.content:
David Edney never expected to be caught up in the Ontario government’s freeze on financial aid to students at private career colleges.

That’s because Mr. Edney, a 36-year-old father of three and future teacher, doesn’t attend a career college. He is working toward his Bachelor of Education at Tyndale University, a degree-granting Christian postsecondary institution in Toronto.

Nonetheless, Mr. Edney and thousands of private university students like him have temporarily lost access to loan and grant payments through the Ontario Student Assistance Program, or Osap, the province’s needs-based financial aid program.

“It has changed our financial plan drastically,” Mr. Edney said from his home in Kawartha Lakes. To compensate for the lack of Osap, he is picking up shifts as a respite-care worker for children with autism while his wife works a second part-time job.

“I’m determined to finish teachers’ college, but it is a heavy burden in terms of trying to plan next steps. I’m definitely feeling the weight of that pressure.”

Tyndale University is one of seven private Christian postsecondary schools in Ontario that have banded together to urge the Progressive Conservative government to release them from an Osap pause they argue shouldn’t have included them in the first place. The province suspended Osap payments to all private postsecondary institutions and their students after a preliminary audit in the summer found suspicious – and possibly fraudulent – activity at some private, for-profit career colleges.

Members of the ad hoc group of faith-based institutions, which includes divinity schools and seminaries, say they differ from career colleges in two important ways: They already have to meet high standards to award undergraduate, master’s or doctoral degrees, and they are not profit-driven. They are only private in the sense that they aren’t subsidized by taxpayers the way better-known public universities and colleges are.

“We’re a not-for-profit,” said Ambrose Thomson, the registrar and director of student services at McMaster Divinity School in Hamilton. “The risk factors associated with the fraudulent activity that they’ve been investigating are simply not the same.”

The PC government announced in early October that it was suspending Osap payments to all private postsecondary institutions and their students while a third-party auditor investigated suspicious activity at some private, for-profit career colleges where Osap-funded enrolment in predominantly online courses had skyrocketed in recent years. Some of the issues were serious enough to be forwarded to the Ontario Provincial Police.

Nolan Quinn, Ontario’s Minister of Colleges, Universities, Research Excellence and Security, has not specified why private universities such as Tyndale and McMaster Divinity School were swept up in an action aimed at the private career college sector.

Bianca Giacoboni, a spokeswoman for the minister, declined to answer that question directly when asked by The Globe and Mail. Instead, she said by e-mail that although the ministry’s initial investigations centred on a few schools, it has recently seen evidence of systemic problems.

“At this time, we do not have assurances from the audit team that the issues are not more widespread, leaving us with no choice but to pause Osap payments to all private institutions to protect taxpayer dollars and hold bad actors accountable,” Ms. Giacoboni said.

“As the Premier and Minister have repeatedly stated, we are working as quickly as possible to get good-acting students and institutions back into the Osap system while making progress on the program criteria for third-party loans for students.”

The PC government tabled a suite of legislative changes last week aimed at protecting the integrity of student aid, including capping enrolment growth at career colleges and ending Osap for predominantly online programs offered by the sector. Mr. Quinn has said he hopes to lift the Osap freeze around the start of the new year.

In the meantime, students such as Leah Beerda, 19, are struggling.

Ms. Beerda is a second-year student working toward a Bachelor’s degree in art at Redeemer University, a private Christian postsecondary school in Hamilton. She is minoring in missions and ministry. Ms. Beerda hopes to pursue a career in interior design while working in Christian youth ministry on the side.

She hasn’t received any of the $11,000 in Osap loans she was expecting for this academic year. The loss has forced her to apply for a second job at an on-campus market on top of her work as a residence adviser, or RA. It has also left Ms. Beerda unable to afford counselling that helped her cope with anxiety and panic attacks.

“I’m an RA on campus, so I have these roles as being a mentor to younger students, and I want to be fit for that,” she said. “And without counselling, that has been an extreme struggle the past month with the whole Osap pause.”

Redeemer, Tyndale, McMaster Divinity School and others in the group of private faith-based universities are deferring tuition payments and supporting students who normally rely on Osap in other ways.

At Tyndale, where about half of approximately 1,400 students were expecting Osap this term, the institution and donors are providing transit passes to commuting students and bursaries to those grappling with bills. Tyndale has set up a free, fully stocked pantry with food and hygiene products.

“We want to do everything we can to prevent a student from feeling like they have to drop out because that’s the only option they have,” said Kevin Kirk, Tyndale’s senior vice-president of external relations.

The leaders of several private career colleges, as well as the industry association Career Colleges Ontario, say that good actors in their sector have also been unfairly hurt by the sector-wide Osap freeze. They are lobbying in private and public to have the freeze lifted sooner than the government’s previously announced timeline of the new year – just like the private Christian universities are.

Redeemer, Tyndale, McMaster Divinity School and four of their peers have engaged StrategyCorp, a government relations firm, to help make their case to the province. The other institutions are Our Lady Seat of Wisdom College in Barry’s Bay, Emmanuel Bible College in Kitchener, Master’s College and Seminary in Mississauga and Heritage College and Seminary in Cambridge.

Several of the institutions and local church congregations are taking part in a day of prayer on Sunday to pray for a speedy end to the Osap freeze.

“We produce pastors, counsellors, charity workers, community workers, teachers and other leaders who contribute substantially to the province, and we operate in this very special niche,” said Jonathan Griffiths, president of Heritage College and Seminary. “We are not career colleges. We are not businesses.”

stories.summary: The Ontario government froze Osap payments to all private career colleges in October
stories.author: The Decibel Staff, Rachel Levy-McLaughlin, Kelly Grant

A sign for the Academy of Learning career college in Brampton, Ont., last month. The Ontario government has raised concerns about potential fraud in its student financial assistance program, prompting a provincewide crackdown on private career colleges.Arlyn McAdorey/The Globe and Mail

The Ontario government has said it’s worried there’s fraud going on with the Ontario Student Assistance Program, OSAP . Earlier this fall, the government froze the financial assistance payments to all private career colleges in the province, and their students.

Kelly Grant , The Globe’s postsecondary education reporter, will explain the red flags the government found, like 400 per cent increases in enrollment in just a couple years, students using international IP addresses, and suspicious course work at some schools. And she’ll explain how the heavy crackdown from the province has rippled out to the schools and their students.

stories.title: Family hardship helped this advisor find purpose in his practice
stories.summary: After his infant son had a heart transplant, Chris Marshall started focusing on families raising children with complex medical needs
stories.author: Brenda Bouw
stories.content:
In the Behind the Advice series , Globe Advisor asks advisors about their relationship with money from a young age, the lessons they’ve learned over the years, and how those experiences shape the advice they give clients. Behind the Advice is also a podcast: You can find episodes from all five seasons here .

Chris Marshall, investment advisor at Optimize Wealth Management Inc. in Hamilton, talks about how his parents’ separation affected his relationship with money, the family medical event that brought new meaning to his career and why he thinks Chubbs Peterson of Happy Gilmore would make a good advisor.

Describe your experience with money growing up.

I was born and raised in Hamilton, the oldest of two kids. My dad was a carpenter and my mom worked in retail. Money was tight, but it got even tighter after my parents split up when I was 12 years old.

After the separation, my dad bought a home, but we lost it a couple of years later. I remember coming home from school one day with my brother and finding the locks had been changed and a note on the front door saying we weren’t allowed to enter.

My mom had a very small apartment, so my brother and I ended up sharing a room there until I moved out at the age of 18. I remember telling myself back then that I wouldn’t go through this with my family when I got older.

What did you want to be growing up and how did you get into financial services?

Initially, I wanted to be a chef. But after working late hours in restaurants while in school and having to get up early for class the next day, I changed my mind. It also didn’t seem like a good lifestyle for me if I wanted to raise a family.

I took an accounting class in high school and loved how the numbers always balanced to zero. I took accounting in college, but it didn’t turn out to be as interesting as I first thought. My now mother-in-law suggested banking, so I started as a teller at Bank of Nova Scotia in my early 20s. I then worked at a credit union, which is where I started training and working as a wealth advisor.

What’s the best move you made to date to advance your career?

Aligning my practice with a purpose. Early on as an investment advisor, I struggled a bit to find an area of expertise. Then, a couple of years ago, my son received a heart transplant at SickKids in Toronto. He was four months old. Since then, I’ve felt so indebted to that hospital. I want the next child to get the same care as we did, or better.

That led me to two recent decisions: building philanthropy planning into my practice; and focusing on families raising children with complex medical needs, helping them navigate the associated financial challenges. It’s brought a new purpose to my work. It’s what gets me to my desk every day.

What advice do you wish someone gave you earlier in your career?

Earlier in my career, I did a lot of research on stocks and presented it to prospective clients. It didn’t really help me sign on any new people. I didn’t understand what the client really wanted. Most don’t care how much you know about an individual stock. What they want is to be heard.

Clients need someone to understand their goals and family life. They want to make sure their money is growing, but the relationship and what they want their money to accomplish are much more important than the investment itself.

What advice do you have for someone who wants to do what you do?

Don’t just do it for the money. If you join the business just for money, it will show in your work with clients. Finding a purpose and partnering with people you enjoy working with will make going to work so enjoyable – it will be like seeing your friends and family every day.

How do you spend time outside of work?

I spend time with my wife, Ayla, our son, Lucas, and our dog, Gus. After everything my son has been through, we don’t take any day with him for granted. I also enjoy golf, camping, fishing and vegetable gardening.

Name a famous person or fictional character you think would make a great financial advisor and why?

Chubbs Peterson, [the golf mentor played by Carl Weathers in the 1996 comedy Happy Gilmore]. Chubbs taught Happy [played by Adam Sandler] how to play golf while also keeping his emotions in check. It’s similar to what advisors do for their clients, particularly when markets are volatile. You need to keep playing, or keep investing, to reach your goals.

This interview has been edited and condensed.

stories.title: Gun control advocacy groups say Carney Liberals haven’t fulfilled firearm commitments
stories.summary: Several voices for stronger gun control say Prime Minister Mark Carney's government has failed to live up to its commitments on firearms.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — Several voices for stronger gun control say Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government has failed to live up to its commitments on firearms as the anniversary of the 1989 mass shooting in Montreal approaches.

In a report card-style assessment, PolySeSouvient and eight other advocates for tougher firearm restrictions say the government has work to do on implementing a key measure to prevent intimate partner gun violence, introducing a comprehensive ban on large-capacity magazines and ensuring the classification of new firearm models entering the market is determined by the RCMP.

The groups acknowledge the Liberals have implemented a buyback program for banned firearms the government says are fit only for the battlefield. But they point out that only half of the anticipated number of banned guns were reported by owners.

The groups also say the SKS rifle, which has been used in police killings and other high-profile shootings, remains available to purchase.

“Unfortunately, most of the Carney government’s commitments on gun control have not been delivered,” says the assessment.

PolySeSouvient was formed after a gunman killed 14 women on Dec. 6, 1989, at École Polytechnique in Montreal.

The assessment of the Liberals’ record is endorsed by PolySeSouvient, the Polytechnique Student Association, Angie’s Angels, the Canadian Femicide Observatory for Justice and Accountabilities, Danforth Families for Safer Communities, Dawson Families for Gun Control, Doctors for Protection Against Guns, the Quebec City mosque and the NOT_HERE student coalition.

Legislation that received royal assent in December 2023 opens the door to making anyone subject to a protection order — a legal order often issued in intimate partner violence cases — ineligible to hold a firearms licence while the order is in effect.

The provision is intended to quickly remove firearms from the hands of abusers at the time when they are often the most dangerous.

The government says the term “protection order” has to be defined in regulation and record-keeping and reporting requirements must be brought into force to fully implement the changes.

Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree said earlier this year the government hoped to have the regulations in place by late September.

Carney’s Liberals promised in the last general election campaign to require the permanent alteration of large-capacity firearm magazines to ensure they can never hold more than five rounds again, and to prohibit the sale and transfer of magazines capable of holding more than the legally permitted number of rounds.

Last December, Anandasangaree announced an overarching review of the firearm classification system which he said would “take a broad view of the legal framework for firearms, devices, magazines and ammunition to modernize the regime.”

Carney also promised to introduce legislation creating a pre-authorization system to ensure the classification of new firearm models entering the market is determined by the RCMP — not the gun industry.

The assessment says there has been “no perceptible progress” on this element since draft regulations were published under the Trudeau Liberals in December 2024.

Since May 2020, Ottawa has outlawed approximately 2,500 types of guns on the basis they are intended for war, not hunting or sport shooting.

Conservative MPs and some gun owners have vehemently opposed the Liberals’ efforts to ban certain firearms as an attack on law-abiding citizens.

The federal firearm compensation program for individuals accepted declarations from owners of banned guns from mid-January through the end of March. Just under half of the 136,000 firearms the government budgeted to buy back were declared by owners for compensation and collection.

“Declarations are not surrenders, and the number actually collected is not known,” says the assessment by the gun control advocacy groups.

PolySeSouvient has called on the government to impose an immediate ban on new sales of the SKS, to remove from circulation modern, assault-style versions of the rifle, and to implement a voluntary buyback of older models. It calls for an exemption for Indigenous hunters who use the SKS primarily to hunt for food.

Anandasangaree has said the broad review of the firearms classification regime will involve consultations with First Nations, Inuit and Métis communities — including on the SKS — to ensure Indigenous perspectives and traditions are an active part of the process.

Public Safety Canada said in October that members of the Firearms Classification Technical Advisory Group, appointed to support the classification review, would be meeting for the first time later this fall.

The assessment by the advocacy groups says the fact the SKS is legal to own or purchase means the ban on assault-style weapons remains incomplete.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 25, 2026.

Jim Bronskill, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Immigrants in Canada more likely to be overqualified for their jobs: report
stories.summary: A new report says too many newcomers to Canada are getting stuck in jobs they are overqualified to do, undermining the federal government's quest to recruit highly educated, highly specialized workers from abroad.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — A new report says too many newcomers to Canada are getting stuck in jobs they are overqualified to do, undermining the federal government’s quest to recruit highly educated, highly specialized workers from abroad.

The Institute for Canadian Citizenship’s annual report — “Selected But Neglected” — argues the government needs to do more work on foreign credential recognition in key fields like health care to ensure immigrants who are courted for their qualifications can actually put them to work.

The institute projects half of the 380,000 permanent residents admitted to Canada next year will have a university education, but only 36 per cent of those people will have jobs that make use of their education and qualifications over the next 20 years.

Almost half of those with university degrees — 47 per cent — will hold jobs below their education levels, and almost one in five will leave Canada over the next 20 years, the institute says.

Heather Barnabe, the institute’s chief operating officer, told a news conference in Ottawa on Wednesday the problem is particularly dire in the health care sector.

“Just 38 per cent of 2027 immigrants with health care training are projected to work in a job befitting their education by 2035,” she said.

“If these immigrants experienced the same qualification-matched employment rate as their Canadian-born peers, over 2,000 extra health professionals would be providing urgently needed care to us and our loved ones.”

Daniel Bernhard, citizenship institute CEO, said some provinces have worked out ways to recognize immigrants’ professional credentials. He pointed to a program in Nova Scotia which allows immigrant doctors to work under the supervision of a Canadian physician as their competency is assessed.

Bernhard said while it’s important to verify credentials and work experience to ensure they meet Canadian standards, some provinces and territories put up too many roadblocks.

“Colleges have … I would call them discriminatory practices when it comes to immigrant professionals coming in. They do things like make you take a separate English or French test, then they take two years to process your paperwork. Then when it’s done, they say, ‘Your English or French test expired, you’ve got to do it all over again,'” he said.

“All Canadians expect, rightly so, that these professions be conducted by people who are qualified and who can do so safely. I don’t think anybody objects to that. But there are faster ways to do it.”

A Medical Council of Canada spokesperson said in an emailed statement the council also worries that too many internationally trained physicians are unable to practice in Canada.

The spokesperson said the council is working with regulators, governments and other parties to find ways to make licensing pathways more clear for physicians trained abroad.

The Medical Council of Canada is not a licensing body but it works to ensure national standards for verifying physician credentials and assessing their competency.

Federation of Medical Regulatory Authorities of Canada executive director Stephanie Price echoed the need for faster and clearer accreditation pathways for foreign trained physicians.

In an email, she said “regulators must be satisfied that every licensed physician has the medical knowledge and skills, language proficiency, good character, fitness to practise and current clinical experience required for practise in Canada.”

Price said work is underway involving professional groups, governments and regulators to increase the availability of practice-based assessments for internationally trained doctors and recognizing comparable foreign medical training, among other measures.

She said all of these objectives require several professional agencies, universities and governments working together in order to deliver results.

Census data from 2016 and 2021 shows 88 per cent of Canadian-born working-age people are in jobs that match their education levels, while just 62 per cent of immigrants can say the same.

The institute cites a 2019 RBC report that estimates closing the labour gap between immigrant and Canadian-born workers could have boosted Canada’s gross domestic product by about $50 billion at the time. The bank’s economists found immigrants were earning about 10 per cent less than their Canadian-born peers.

The report also calls on the government to do more to track how many immigrants are underemployed and how many eventually leave Canada for other opportunities.

This report comes at a time when the debate over Canada’s immigration policy is heating up.

Claiming higher immigration will put too much pressure on health services and the housing market, the Conservative opposition tabled a motion in the House of Commons this week to block the government’s plan for permanent resident admissions in 2027.

That motion was defeated Wednesday, with the Liberals, NDP and Green Party voting against it.

Bernhard said while there are real factors driving public skepticism of immigration around the world, allowing qualified people to work is a solution to pressures on public services.

“So if you’re feeling squeezed at the hospital, if you are feeling squeezed with an overcrowded classroom, and you are worried about more people coming in, then presumably we can agree that anybody who’s already here who can help to make that situation better does a service for the whole country,” he said.

The government does grant preferred immigration access to those with higher education and more work experience in high-demand fields like the trades, medicine and research.

The report’s methodology uses a combination of Statistics Canada, census and long-term immigration data to make its projections.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 25, 2026.

David Baxter, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Driver in 2025 crash that killed Ontario father of three expected to be sentenced
stories.summary: Newmarket - A driver in a head-on crash that killed a father of three last year is expected to be sentenced today in the case that prompted the Ontario government to introduce tougher dangerous driving penalties.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Newmarket - A driver in a head-on crash that killed a father of three last year in a case that prompted the Ontario government to introduce tougher dangerous driving penalties has been sentenced to six years and six months behind bars.

Jaiwin Kirubananthan also faces a 12-year driving ban and must provide a DNA sample to police, according to the sentence handed down by Justice Ann Marina Elias in a Newmarket, Ont., courtroom Wednesday.

Kirubananthan, who was 18 at the time of the August 2025 crash that killed 35-year-old Andrew Cristillo, had pleaded guilty to five charges, including dangerous driving causing death and failing to remain at the scene. Cristillo’s wife and three daughters were also injured in the crash in Whitchurch-Stouffville, about 50 kilometres north of Toronto.

Elias said she arrived at the sentence after weighing Kirubananthan’s young age and lack of a criminal record, with the duty of the court to “send a message” to other young people about the serious consequences of dangerous driving.

Members of Cristillo’s family were in court Wednesday, and some could be heard weeping as Elias read her reasoning for the sentence.

Cristillo’s brother Jordan told reporters outside the courthouse that Kirubananthan’s sentence “doesn’t make sense” and is evidence that the justice system “isn’t working.”

He spoke of the “egregiousness” of Kirubananthan’s driving and the fact that he fled the scene.

“We should not be treating this like an accident. We should be treating it like murder,” he said, adding that he believes Kirubananthan should spend the rest of his life behind bars.

Reading from an agreed statement of facts, Elias told the court how Kirubananthan steered his vehicle into the oncoming lane on Highway 48 and was driving nearly 60 kilometres per hour over the speed limit just seconds before he collided head-on with the Cristillo family’s SUV.

The family’s vehicle came to rest in a ditch, partially on its roof, the justice said, with Cristillo trapped in the passenger seat. The father was pronounced dead at the scene from multiple traumas and his three young daughters suffered injuries including broken bones and concussions.

Kirubananthan evaded capture for hours and was found the next morning lying in a potato field about 150 metres away after police deployed a thermal imaging drone.

Elias said Kirubananthan lied and told police he wasn’t behind the wheel.

After the crash, the Ontario government introduced a law named after Cristillo, which imposes indefinite licence suspensions for anyone convicted of dangerous driving causing death and allows police to immediately suspend a driver’s licence for 90 days and impound a driver’s vehicle if they are suspected of driving dangerously, among other measures.

At the time of Cristillo’s death, Kirubananthan was already facing another dangerous driving charge, after police alleged he hit an Ontario Provincial Police vehicle carrying Premier Doug Ford on Highway 401 in January 2025.

Cristillo’s brother said he’s pushing for a “national conversation” on dangerous driving.

“The mere fact that dangerous driving causing death doesn’t even have a minimum standard prison sentence, and the minimum is a $1,000 fine, tells us that our laws are not reflecting the egregiousness, the gravity of killing someone from behind the wheel,” he said.

Jordan Cristillo has started a petition calling on the federal government to set a minimum prison sentence for dangerous driving causing death.

With credit for time already served, Kirubananthan is set to spend another four and a half years in prison.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 25, 2026.

Note to readers:This is a corrected story. A previous version incorrectly referred to Cristillo’s brother as Andrew.

Reading from an agreed statement of facts, Elias told the court how Kirubananthan steered his vehicle into the oncoming lane on Highway 48 and was driving nearly 60 kilometres per hour over the speed limit just seconds before he collided head-on with the Cristillo family’s SUV.

The family’s vehicle came to rest in a ditch, partially on its roof, the justice said, with Cristillo trapped in the passenger seat. The father was pronounced dead at the scene from multiple traumas and his three young daughters suffered injuries including broken bones and concussions.
Kirubananthan evaded capture for hours and was found the next morning lying in a potato field about 150 metres away after police deployed a thermal imaging drone.
Elias said Kirubananthan lied and told police he wasn’t behind the wheel.

After the crash, the Ontario government introduced a law named after Cristillo, which imposes indefinite licence suspensions for anyone convicted of dangerous driving causing death and allows police to immediately suspend a driver’s licence for 90 days and impound a driver’s vehicle if they are suspected of driving dangerously, among other measures.

Cristillo’s brother said he’s pushing for a “national conversation” on dangerous driving.

“The mere fact that dangerous driving causing death doesn’t even have a minimum standard prison sentence, and the minimum is a $1,000 fine, tells us that our laws are not reflecting the egregiousness, the gravity of killing someone from behind the wheel,” he said.
Jordan Cristillo has started a petition calling on the federal government to set a minimum prison sentence for dangerous driving causing death.
With credit for time already served, Kirubananthan is set to spend another four and a half years in prison.

stories.title: Steel distributors assert they’re being stiffed on tariff rebates
stories.summary: Federal remission system is meant to provide relief when a distributor can prove an imported product isn’t made in Canada
stories.author: Niall McGee
stories.content:
Canadian steel distributor Titus Steel Co. didn’t expect any pushback after it applied for tariff relief from Ottawa on imports of specialized “oil quenched” steel.

Last year, the federal government brought in tariff rate quotas (TRQs) on imported steel to help Canadian mills win more business during the trade war with the United States. The duties are designed to encourage distributors to buy steel made in this country, but not penalize them for importing steel that isn’t manufactured in Canada. Since the TRQs are levied across the board on all steel imports, the government allows distributors to claim a rebate on the tariffs if they can prove the specific product isn’t made in Canada.

Obtaining the rebate appeared to be a slam dunk for Mississauga-based Titus, since the type of steel it imported isn’t made in Canada, and the company had the paperwork to back up its claim.

“We have e-mails and letters from every Canadian mill saying you cannot buy this in Canada, and they do not make it,” Titus president Steve Usatis said in an interview.

But Titus was turned down by the Finance Ministry, the department that oversees the remission system. Mr. Usatis was informed that even though Canadian steel maker Algoma Steel Group Inc. doesn’t make the oil-quenched steel, that “one day, possibly, they might start making it.”

Canadian steel wholesalers say that Ottawa’s tariff remission system is broken. They claim that federal and provincial governments are disproportionately favouring domestic steelmakers over distributors during the trade war. In addition to the TRQ support, distributors point to the copious amounts of direct financial aid some steelmakers have received, such as the $500-million loan Algoma got from Ottawa and Ontario last year.

Compared with the steelmakers, the rest of the industry – including distributors and the many downstream manufacturers that purchase steel products – are getting a raw deal, Mr. Usatis said.

“Our customers in automotive, manufacturing, mining, recycling will be forced to pay 50 per cent more for the specialty steels they require to stay profitable and competitive, while not saving a single job in Canadian steelmaking because none of that steel is made in Canada,” he said.

Laura Devoni, Algoma’s vice-president of human resources and corporate affairs, wrote in an e-mail to The Globe and Mail that the company can’t speak to any individual application for tariff relief and remission decisions made by Ottawa.

She added that the Sault Ste. Marie, Ont.-based steel maker provides information to the government about the products it makes, and those it is developing, “so that remission supports genuine gaps in Canadian supply, rather than displacing Canadian production.”

Titus Steel’s frustration in obtaining what it believes is legitimate tariff relief isn’t unique.

Jim Ritchie, CEO of British Columbia-based steel distributor Cascadia Metals Ltd., has been turned down repeatedly on what he said are valid remission requests.

“There’s all kinds of stuff that isn’t made in Canada that we’re paying tariffs on,” he said. “Exemptions we’ve asked for, and we’re getting crickets from them. They don’t answer at all. That’s their passive-aggressive way, like they don’t even acknowledge that they got the e-mail. That’s how bad it is.”

For this year, countries with a free-trade agreement with Canada are allowed to export 75 per cent of 2024 steel volumes tariff-free. A 50-per-cent levy applies for levels above that. (The U.S. and Mexico are excluded.)

For countries without a free-trade deal with Canada, only 20 per cent of 2024 volumes can enter the country tariff-free, before the 50 per cent tariff kicks in.

Ottawa appears to be aware that its TRQ system isn’t working the way it should, and is taking steps to address it.

John Fragos, press secretary to Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne, wrote in an e-mail to The Globe that the government is allocating additional resources to respond to the high volume of TRQ remission requests, “with a view to providing relief where circumstances warrant.”

“Canadian producers are consulted to determine whether there is domestic production capacity to supply the goods in question,” Mr. Fragos wrote in his e-mail. “Where a lack of domestic production capability is identified, remission May be granted.”

Last week, the federal government made some changes. In a Nov. 17 release, Ottawa said that it is expanding remission coverage to an additional 23 steel Chinese products where “Canadian supply is insufficient or unavailable.”

But one aspect of the TRQs that isn’t accounted for is customer preferences for specific steel products from an overseas manufacturer when there are quality concerns about using Canadian steel.

Mr. Usatis points to a type of steel plate called AR500 that Algoma makes. Even though Titus can buy this product from Algoma, Mr. Usatis said one of its OEM customers, Caterpillar Inc., has specified it will not accept the Algoma-sourced product owing to what it says are quality issues. This essentially forces Titus to buy AR500 from an alternative supplier, and potentially have to pay a TRQ with no chance of obtaining a remission.

When Algoma was asked to comment on Titus raising quality concerns about its AR500 product, Ms. Devoni didn’t respond directly but said it welcomes the opportunity “to work with any Canadian distributor or manufacturer to understand their requirements.”

Caterpillar did not respond to a request for comment.

stories.title: Even with a softening tone, Trump’s 50% tariff threat on Canada still looms
stories.summary: When talks broke down in August, the president issued a potentially devastating threat — with a deadline that is approaching
stories.author: Tracy Moran
stories.content:
Washington, D.C. — Since the U.S. midterm elections, Washington’s overall tone toward Ottawa has been a bit more conciliatory than before, with both President Donald Trump and U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer suggesting a trade deal May soon be reached.

But when talks broke down in August, the president issued a potentially devastating threat — with a deadline that now looms.

“On January First, 2027, Tariffs on all Cars, Trucks, both large and small, Automotive Parts, and Steel, will be increased to 50%. Build in the U.S. and there are Zero Tariffs. Canada will be treated like a State no longer!” Trump posted on social on August 24.

That put the clock back on, with just over four months for both sides to hammer out a trade deal by the end of the year. While no agreement has materialized, there have been comments since the Nov. 3 elections about one being close — along with a few accusations.

“We’re working on making a deal that’s fair, but (Canada has) never treated us fairly,” Trump told reporters on Friday, noting that work remains to be done. Two days later, Greer said trade negotiators were “fairly close on finding a landing zone.”

But with limited progress being made toward a signed deal — at least publicly — how realistic is Trump’s January tariff threat?

While trade analysts are loath to try predicting anything Trump might say or do, some doubt that a 50 per cent ramp-up is likely.

“The administration has been signalling that a deal with Canada is possible, desired, and close, which suggests that they would not take action to disrupt the momentum in those talks,” said Inu Manak, senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics.

Graeme Thompson, senior analyst with Eurasia Group’s Global Macro team, agrees.

“Never say never, but it has long felt unlikely to us at Eurasia Group,” he said.

A hat reading ‘Veto’ sits on the Resolute Desk as U.S. President Donald Trump speaks in the Oval Office of the White House, Washington, DC, ON Nov. 5, 2026. Mandel Ngan / AFP via Getty Images

For now, the White House has done nothing to formalize the threat of the January tariff increase, and social posts do not make policy.

“The president has issued tariff threats via social media throughout his tenure, most of which do not come to fruition. So it is important to not take them literally, but seriously instead,” said Manak, adding that she sees it as a strategic threat.

“Trump has publicly stated that he uses threats as leverage, and I don’t think there’s anything different at work here.”

Thompson also pointed to Trump’s use of threats and postponements, noting the pattern of setting deadlines “to kickstart negotiations” and then later pushing the deadlines back.

But Trump, of course, could still formalize the 50 per cent tariffs at any time.

“The president can just sign the proclamation and post it on the Federal Register,” said Alfredo Carrillo Obregon, a trade policy analyst at the Cato Institute.

Still, Washington’s softening rhetoric suggests a growing U.S. interest in reaching an agreement with Ottawa, and trade watchers point to the shifting political landscape as a possible cause.

“The change in tone … indicates that the U.S. wants a deal as much as Canada does, and that is a significant shift in the public discourse,” said Manak, noting that the recent election results May have prompted this.

“With the incoming congressional leadership speaking of repealing Canada tariffs, it is entirely possible that the administration is feeling a bit of pressure to conclude a deal before Congress votes to repeal the tariffs,” she explained, pointing to how it would reflect poorly on the president’s trade policy if Republicans crossed the floor and voted against his trade war.

“I expect a compromise if the president wants to avoid his own party turning against him publicly with a repeal of the tariffs on Canada.”

Any repeal would still be vetoed by the president, and overriding Trump’s veto would require a two-thirds majority in both chambers, so the threat is largely about political optics.

Thompson also acknowledged that congressional pressure could encourage a deal.

“There is an argument that … it would be better to do it in advance of any congressional investigations or symbolic resolutions that they May pass so that it does not appear that they were forced into it,” he said.

But that pressure could also harden Trump’s position, Thompson cautioned.

“Or do you double down and say, ‘We’re gonna fight. We’re gonna get a win’?”

Obregon also hedges, noting that the threat of the incoming Congress moving against the administration’s Section 338 authority — the part of the Tariff Act of 1930 used to impose 50 per cent tariffs on a range of Canadian goods in August — could explain the more conciliatory tone. But if no deal materializes, the president might lash out.

“This is a threat for leverage, obviously, but it could also backfire,” Obregon said.

The uncertainty of Trump’s next move makes it hard for Ottawa to know whether it’s time to make concessions and accept some level of tariffs in writing — a conclusion Prime Minister Mark Carney’s team has been trying to avoid — or if it shouldn’t budge.

“The only two countries that have been successful at navigating the trade war are the two that have maintained a tough stance towards the U.S.: China and Canada,” said Manak, and she believes Carney’s tough approach has been effective.

“Canada’s strategy is sound from a negotiator’s standpoint,” she said. “This is also not a typical negotiation where the business community has a ton of sway. Canada is negotiating with the Trump administration, and no one else. So it’s best to play the game of chicken.”

Thompson also says Ottawa’s walking away in August demonstrated that Canada would not accept a deal just for the sake of doing so, which May have helped their position. But he warns that time is on Washington’s side, given the economic asymmetry between the countries.

“This still does matter more to Canada than it does to the U.S. from an economic point of view,” he said.

The trouble, he added, is that potential damages, such as job losses, auto plant closures, and slower economic growth, May not align with the domestic political pressure needed to make a deal. The Canadian public largely favours a continued tough stance — with a November Ipsos poll showing that 53 per cent of Canadians believe Ottawa should wait until Trump’s term has ended before signing a new U.S. trade deal.

So while Trump May face domestic pressure to strike a deal rather than risk Republicans voting against his tariffs, Carney faces a conundrum of his own: how long can Canada withstand the economic pain, and what is the political cost of being seen to cave to a president many Canadians distrust?

Based in the U.S. capital region, Tracy Moran has covered Canada-U.S. relations for National Post since 2025. She previously reported on international news for DW, USA Today, Gzero Media and several online magazines. She holds a master’s degree in international affairs from George Washington University.

stories.title: Doerkson tasks new B.C. cabinet to undo key NDP policies as he sets out Conservative government’s agenda
stories.summary: Mandate letters direct ministers to reverse approaches to Indigenous rights, climate policy and substance use
stories.author: Andrea Woo
stories.content:
B.C. Premier Lorne Doerkson has tasked his new cabinet with undoing key elements of the previous NDP government’s agenda, directing ministers to reverse approaches to Indigenous rights, climate policy and substance use.

At the same time, the new Conservative government is expected to deliver on promised tax relief, strike an independent panel to review the province’s books and guarantee publicly funded health care services when medically recommended wait times are exceeded.

The directives are laid out in mandate letters that Mr. Doerkson issued to his new cabinet, which were released publicly late Tuesday. The Premier and his cabinet, which consists of 18 ministers and six ministers of state, were sworn in last Friday. The mandate letters formalize many of the promises Mr. Doerkson made on the campaign trail, committing his government to an ambitious – and costly – agenda while also vowing to rein in the province’s record $13.8-billion deficit.

“These mandate letters make clear what British Columbians expect each minister to accomplish,” the Premier said in a statement. “They are about results and accountability, and ensuring our government delivers on the priorities that matter most to British Columbians.”

Attorney-General Caroline Elliott has been directed to repeal the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act and related Interpretation Act “with a transition framework respecting constitutional obligations to First Nations,” with support from Indigenous Relations Minister Scott McInnis.

She is also to introduce legislation “to protect private property rights and uphold the validity of B.C.’s land title system,” and repeal 2022 directives on civil litigation involving Indigenous peoples that promote resolution and negotiated settlement.

Along with Mr. McInnis, she is tasked with drafting legislation to “publish information about active claims, negotiations, legal actions and agreements affecting public or private land before they become binding.”

Finance Minister Peter Milobar is to immediately appoint an independent panel to review the province’s books and report its findings publicly – something that Mr. Milobar said he expected to provide more information on in the coming days.

He’s also expected to implement the Conservatives’ campaign promise to raise the provincial basic personal tax exemption to $32,000 from $13,216 for the 2027 tax year, restore the seniors’ property tax deferral program and slash government administrative and management staffing, among other responsibilities.

Health Minister Ryan Peterson has been directed to keep rural emergency departments and maternity wards open, identify reforms from other universal public systems that improve access and implement a guarantee that publicly funded treatment will be available through “another quality provider when medically recommended wait times are exceeded.”

He is also to end the programs that offer prescribed alternatives to illicit street drugs, “stop forcing drug-friendly facilities on communities” and “reform” overdose prevention sites.

Education Minister Lynne Block has been tasked with restoring letter grades for Grades 4-9 and supervised provincial examinations, as well as the daily singing of O Canada and the display of Canadian and B.C. flags in schools.

She has also been directed to “repeal” the optional teaching resource Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity, commonly called Sogi 123.

Other ministers were also given tasks previously hinted at by Mr. Doerkson after his Conservative government was elected last month.

Environment Minister Áʼa:líya Warbus is to repeal the CleanBC program aimed at lowering emissions by 40 per cent by 2030 and introduce regulation to “remove barriers to responsible resource development.” She is also tasked with working with First Nations to ensure project assessments proceed efficiently.

Public Safety Minister Jessy Sahota has been directed to expand policing and enforcement, strengthen bail and warrant enforcement and establish a repeat-offender court stream with the Attorney-General.

Claire Rattée, Minister of Social Development, is to increase disability assistance by $100 per month and establish an annual review of assistance rates; raise the annual persons with disabilities earnings exemption to $30,000 and expand employment, skills training and employer partnerships.

Editor’s note: This article was updated to correct a quote from Attorney-General Caroline Elliott’s mandate letter, regarding the task of drafting legislation to “publish information about active claims, negotiations, legal actions and agreements affecting public or private land before they become binding.”

stories.title: Canada is bringing in 380,000 immigrants, but a new report projects their skills will be wasted
stories.summary: Institute for Canadian Citizenship projects disconnect for talents the country is recruiting, including in health care.
stories.author: Ghada Alsharif
stories.content:
As Canada prepares to welcome 380,000 new permanent residents in 2027 , with the majority selected for their economic potential and skills, a new report warns that the country is underutilizing the immigrant talent it needs and is actively recruiting.

Out of the roughly 190,000 working-age, university-educated immigrants expected to be admitted next year, just 35.9 per cent are projected to be working in occupations requiring a university degree — or jobs that make full use of their educational qualifications — even 20 years after admission, according to a report released Wednesday by the Institute for Canadian Citizenship. Of these, 17.4 per cent are projected to have left Canada entirely.

This underutilization of immigrant talent also exists in critical sectors where there are severe labour shortages and high demand for skilled labour, such as health care, the report found.

Among working-age immigrants admitted in 2027 whose highest degree is in medicine, dentistry, veterinary medicine or optometry, just half (50.9 per cent) are projected to remain in Canada and work in occupations that match their educational qualifications, even two decades after admission.

The Icc’s report uses past immigration, census data and tax records to project what might happen to immigrants admitted in 2027. It looked at immigrants’ tax-filing records to see how many newcomers eventually leave Canada — also known as “onward migration” — and census data to track whether earlier immigrants were working and if their jobs required a level of education that matched their qualifications.

For decades, Canada has positioned itself as a magnet for skilled immigrants. Over the past 25 years the country has shifted to a model where immigrants are required to study or work here as temporary residents before becoming eligible for permanent status. The aim has been to prioritize those with Canadian education and work experience in a bid to solve the “lack of Canadian experience” that earlier immigrants were penalized for.

The federal government’s immigration plan released this month emphasizes the need to “address the diverse labour market” and prioritizes “economic immigration” welcoming newcomers “who bring valuable skills and experience to strengthen our economy.”

But critics argue that Canada’s approach has become too narrow and focused on filling immediate labour needs at the expense of longer-term nation-building, without a clear plan to retain the talent it recruits or ensure they can find work that makes use of their skills and qualifications once they’re here.

The result is a bottleneck where many talented people can’t integrate into the economy, leaving jobs they were brought to Canada to do unfilled — “that is something that all Canadians suffer from and have to pay for,” said Daniel Bernhard, CEO of the Institute for Canadian Citizenship.

“Talent is here. Shame on us for turning it away.”

The loss of highly skilled workers is particularly concerning in health care, where labour shortages are affecting Canadians’ ability to access services.

Experts say the new high-wage rules can attract highly skilled migrants, but could also open a back door for others.

About one in five Canadian adults did not have a regular health-care provider in 2024, while 36 per cent of Canadians who had an initial consultation with a specialist waited three months or longer, the report notes, citing data from the Canadian Institute for Health Information and Statistics Canada.

Yet among working-age immigrants admitted in 2027 with degrees in medicine, dentistry, veterinary medicine or optometry, only 29.4 per cent are projected to be working in occupations matching their educational qualifications three years after arriving.

This gap also means that many immigrants with health-related professional degrees end up in lower-skilled health-related jobs.

The report points to several barriers that often prevent immigrants from putting their qualifications to use, including difficulties getting foreign credentials recognized, employers demanding Canadian work experience, discrimination and the high costs and complexity of obtaining Canadian credentials or professional licences. These challenges can be especially acute in regulated professions like health care, where licensing requirements vary across the country.

The system is also highly decentralized, with about 500 licensing bodies across the country.

The ICC proposes a federal Fair Licensing Act to establish national standards for recognizing foreign qualifications, alongside funding to encourage provinces and territories to improve licensing outcomes.

The report also calls for employers to move away from “discriminatory” hiring practices like Canadian-experience requirements and adopt skills-based hiring practices, and for the federal government to set measurable targets for reducing immigrant overqualification and track which groups are more likely to leave Canada.

stories.title: Ice unit investigation
stories.summary: London, ON (November 25, 2026) – A London man was arrested earlier this week by members of the LPS Internet Child Exploitation (ICE) Unit in relation to making of Child Sexual Abuse and Exploitation Material (Csaem).
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
London, ON (November 25, 2026) – A London man was arrested earlier this week by members of the LPS Internet Child Exploitation (ICE) Unit in relation to making of Child Sexual Abuse and Exploitation Material (Csaem).

On Monday, November 23, 2026, members of the London Police Service commenced an investigation after the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (Ncmec) made them aware of information involving a London man.

A search warrant was executed the same day at a residence near Dundas Street and Clarke Road.

A male suspect was arrested, and electronic devices were seized. Evidence of Child Sexual Abuse and Exploitation Material (Csaem) were located.

As a result of the investigation, Ryan Fewer, 27, of London, has been charged with one count of possess child sexual abuse and exploitation material.

The accused is scheduled to appear in London court today, in relation to the charge.

London Police Service is a member of the Provincial Strategy to Protect Children from Sexual Abuse and Exploitation on the Internet. The Strategy has been made possible by a grant from the Ministry of the Solicitor General.

Anyone with information in relation to this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670.

stories.title: Missing Person – Sarah Brazeau
stories.summary: Update - London, ON (November 25, 2026) - A previously reported missing 37 year-old London woman has been located and is safe. We would like to thank the public for sharing the information. We kindly ask that all photographs of the missing person be removed from publication.
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
Update - London, ON (November 25, 2026) - A previously reported missing 37 year-old London woman has been located and is safe. We would like to thank the public for sharing the information. We kindly ask that all photographs of the missing person be removed from publication.

London, ON (November 25, 2026) – The London Police Service is requesting the public’s assistance in locating 37-year-old, London woman.

The missing person is described as a female, White, 5’4”, approximately 120 lbs, with long red hair. The missing person was wearing a long black coat, black leggings and white shoes.

The missing person was last seen on November 25, 2026, in the area of Bancroft Road and Trafalgar Street, at approximately 12 p.m., and was reported missing November 25, 2026.

Family and police are concerned for the missing person’s welfare.

Anyone with information in relation to the missing person’s whereabouts is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670.

A person can be reported missing at any time. You do not need to wait 24 hours before you report someone missing. If you are concerned for someone’s immediate safety, call 9-1-1. Otherwise, you can report a person as missing to the London Police Service by calling the non-emergency number 519-661-5670.

stories.title: Lawyers for Galloway’s accuser say UBC caused most of the damage to author’s career
stories.summary: Former creative-writing student’s counsel argues against awarding at least $7.4-million in damages in defamation trial
stories.author: Mike Hager
stories.content:
Lawyers for the former creative-writing student who accused Steven Galloway of sexual assault say it was the University of British Columbia that caused the most damage to the bestselling author’s career.

They began their closing arguments in B.C.’s Supreme Court in Vancouver on Tuesday by stating that Mr. Galloway should not receive what would be one of the highest Canadian defamation awards from their client, who they say only disclosed her allegations to a small group of people.

Arden Beddoes, lead counsel for the accuser, who is known as A.B. because of a publication ban on her identity, told Justice Neena Sharma a direct line cannot be drawn from the defamatory statements she made to a small group to the actions of Mr. Galloway’s employer, UBC, starting with its unusual decision to publicly announce his suspension because of “serious allegations.”

“That’s the day we say this gets out of hand,” Mr. Beddoes argued.

Then, he said, seven months later, in June 2016, the school inflicted further damage to Mr. Galloway’s reputation and career by announcing his dismissal as the chair of its creative-writing program, for what it called “a record of misconduct that resulted in an irreparable breach of the trust placed in faculty members.”

During this period, he told the court, A.B. was a frightened former student desperate for UBC to investigate her claims, and not the malicious “puppet master” who, Mr. Galloway’s lawyers allege, co-ordinated a years-long push to destroy their client.

In 2018, Mr. Galloway sued A.B. for defamation over her sexual-assault allegations, along with two dozen others for repeating them online. Most of them settled, leaving only his accuser standing trial alongside her supporters Mandi Gray and Glynnis Kirchmeier, and Dana Kagis, who posted a single defamatory statement and has not participated in the legal process.

Mr. Galloway’s lawyers want a judgment of millions of dollars in damages against A.B. for embarking upon what they say was a strategic campaign to leverage criminal accusations of sexual assault and to spread these far and wide through a cast of collaborators.

Mr. Galloway’s counsel told court Tuesday their client deserves a rare award of special damages solely against A.B. amounting to $4.9-million. They are also asking she pay at least $2.5-million in general, aggravated and punitive damages, which – if granted – would total $7.4-million.

Court had previously heard that one expert’s report found the author’s lost income to date and future earnings up to the age of 70 amounted to $7.1-million, while another pegged that figure at $11.7-million.

Mr. Beddoes took issue with the higher estimate, saying that publishing expert was told only to compare Mr. Galloway’s earning potential to that of bestselling novelist and Governor-General’s Award winner Miriam Toews. The lawyer argued that was too narrow a lens.

Court has heard Mr. Galloway’s 2008 novel The Cellist of Sarajevo was an international smash hit that brought in more than a million dollars in royalties, though his follow-up work, 2014’s The Confabulist, sold a fraction of that.

The plaintiff is also seeking general, aggravated and punitive damages in the form of least $250,000 from Dr. Gray, at least $80,000 from Ms. Kirchmeier and $30,000 from Ms. Kagis.

The school is not a defendant in the lawsuit. UBC had to pay more than $240,000 in damages to Mr. Galloway following his firing after an arbitrator found the university’s actions violated his privacy rights and damaged his reputation.

In his closing statement, Mr. Beddoes argued A.B. only agreed to share her allegations with a group of creative-writing professors after they requested she do so for an emergency meeting held without Mr. Galloway. Plus, he told the court, his client’s alleged defamatory words were “spoken within the university reporting context.”

The letter A.B. sent to Ubc’s then-president Martha Piper, which Mr. Galloway’s lawyers described at trial as a “nuclear bomb,” did not mention him by name and was not alleged to have been defamatory, Mr. Beddoes said.

“The plaintiff’s case rests on a finding that a report to fewer than 10 people cost him his entire writing career,” Mr. Beddoes argued.

A.B. did not testify and, at the start of the trial, one of her lawyers told the court she was withdrawing her defences of truth and fair comment. However, she continues to deny the accusations that she spread lies about Mr. Galloway, with whom she had a two-year relationship. Her lawyers have told the court that she tried to kill herself twice this year because of the stress of the legal process.

On Tuesday, Mr. Beddoes told the court that her psychiatrist suffered a serious accident this summer, which has delayed a report into A.B.’s mental capacity.

This evidence will be central to a debate over whether A.B. can be held in contempt after Justice Sharma denied her request to be excused from testifying in pretrial discovery in June. The parties debated over whether this motion was part of the trial or whether it would be heard early next year. A resolution on this matter is expected later this week.

During closing arguments earlier this week, Mr. Galloway’s counsel took the court through various high-profile defamation cases they argue are analogous, where awards stretched into millions of dollars.

But Mr. Beddoes argued Tuesday that A.B.’s case is very different from those campaigns, which often lasted months and included defendants posting hundreds of times on social media, contacting employers and pursuing coverage in mainstream media.

A.B., Mr. Beddoes pointed out, declined media requests from a reporter right after Mr. Galloway was suspended and only ever issued a public comment at the behest of her lawyer in November 2016.

“That’s very different from our client going on social media and making every effort she can to broadcast her allegations as widely as possible,” he said, referencing other high-profile defamation judgments.

A.B.’s legal team continues its closing arguments Wednesday.

stories.title: ‘We would lose our home’: Why Alto high speed rail debate is at a ‘fever pitch’
stories.summary: Every Saturday for the past six months, Emanuele Fuldauer has stood with a small group at the corner of two rural highway roads in Crosby, Ont., bearing a sign that says “Alto” crossed out with a red circle, as well as her frustration.
stories.author: Abigail Bimman
stories.content:
Ottawa -- Every Saturday for the past six months, Emanuele Fuldauer has stood with a small group at the corner of two rural highway roads in Crosby, Ont., bearing a sign that says “Alto” crossed out with a red circle, as well as her frustration.

“I have given myself to the community and to this country, to the people in it, and to be treated with such disrespect, I find infuriating,” the retired nurse told CTV News.

She is concerned her small community of Chaffeys Locks in the Rideau Lakes would be completely cut off if one of the proposed Alto routes goes ahead. She said it is “infuriating” to hear about proposed legislative powers that would widen the government’s expropriation powers, as first reported by CBC.

Ajay Gajaria, a partner in the municipal and expropriation practice group at Aird & Berlis LLP, said property owners should be aware of two key area in the new proposal. Both expand powers granted under the government’s High-Speed Rail Network Act, passed in March.

That legislation gave the government the right of first refusal for up to eight years, which could put property owners in “purgatory”, with no one wanting to buy their land while it has yet to be expropriated. The new proposal extends the language to include lands “related” to the project, though Gajaria explained the definition of what counts as “related” is not made clear.

“So, that could be a significant increase in that power and the ability to register that right of first refusal,” he said.

A similar expansion to “related” lands involves the government’s ability to prohibit changes being made to your property for up to four years.

A third change Gajaria pointed to would send disputes over the creation of railway crossings to arbitration rather than a traditional tribunal. If the costs are less than $50,000, they are split equally by the parties. That means a landowner fighting for access to their own land via a crossing could pay up to $25,000 to push back.

“That’s significant, and it’s going to be interesting to see how that plays out with the right to claim compensation for the diminishment in value to your remaining lands,” Gajaria said.

“Taking private property is one of the most solemn things a government can do,” said professor Matti Siemiatycki, director of the Infrastructure Institute at the University of Toronto.

He told CTV News that expropriation, “when it’s critically necessary,” needs to be done fairly, with appropriate compensation for losses. Whether these new legislative changes can be done fairly depends on how they play out in practice, he said.

Siemiatycki said Alto and the government “should be much more explicit about what type of compensation they’re going to be paying,” and whether that includes compensation for first right of refusal and prohibition of work.

“If you want options in a market, that’s something you pay for, he said.”

Multiple dynamics around the project have intersected to create a “fever pitch, Siemiatycki said.”

“It’s very technical, but it has human knock-on effects, and it also clearly has political ramifications as well.”

Siemiatycki is also part of the Policy Innovation Lab, an academic advisory panel funded by Alto.

In a statement, Alto spokesperson Marlee Socket for Alto said “fair compensation will be assessed based on the circumstances of each property and farming operation.”

“The proposed measures would help us move forward responsibly toward the start of construction in 2029-2030,” Socket said.

“A more streamlined process does not mean reducing protections for affected property owners or project oversight.”

In Chaffeys Locks, Fuldauer said many of the homes are “eclectic.”

Her 88-year-old mother lives next door in a home with multiple upgrades allowing her to age in place. If her mother needs more care in a retirement home, the house was meant to serve as her nest egg - something Fuldauer worries could be tied up by the right of first refusal.

Fauldner, who lives with multiple sclerosis, has also renovated her own home so she can live on the first floor if she needs a wheelchair.

Although protesting in the cold is physically taxing, Fuldauer said she will continue to do it every Saturday for two hours – the maximum her body can handle.

“As an individual, all I can be to Alto is friction,” she said.

“And if I can get other individuals to be friction, we can be a big line of friction, and that is truly the one word that keeps going through my head.”
