stories.title: Quebec seeks expedited case as it appeals court decision on MNAs’ oath to King
stories.summary: Premier says his government is considering all options in order for the legislature to open next week
stories.author: Maura Forrest
stories.content:
The Quebec government has appealed a court ruling that declared provincial legislators must swear allegiance to King Charles III, as the Premier says he is looking for solutions to allow the National Assembly to open as planned next week.

In court documents filed Tuesday, the province argues the Quebec Superior Court decision places members of the legislature “in an unprecedented situation that could create a risk of parliamentary proceedings being brought to a standstill for an indeterminate period.”

The government has asked the Court of Appeal of Quebec to allow lawmakers to sit without taking an oath of allegiance to the Crown while the appeal proceeds. The National Assembly is scheduled to convene Dec. 1 for the first time since the Parti Québécois formed a minority government last month.

In Quebec City on Tuesday, Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon said he is hoping for a “reasonable and intelligent” remedy. He did not rule out the possibility of defying the ruling.

“We want to sit. We didn’t see this coming,” Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon told reporters.

Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon doubled down on his refusal to swear allegiance to the King after the province’s Superior Court ruled to temporarily reinstate the oath. The Canadian Press

On Monday, Justice Ian Demers granted an emergency application to suspend a 2022 law that had abolished the requirement for MNAs to swear allegiance to Canada’s monarch.

After the Oct. 5 election, the 127 members of the National Assembly swore allegiance only to the people of Quebec. But in his decision, Justice Demers wrote that they will now “be required to take an oath to the King before assuming their duties.”

Earlier in August, Ottawa lawyer Lawrence David, founder of the Public Interest Litigation Institute, launched a constitutional challenge of the 2022 law. Mr. David argued Quebec has no authority to unilaterally amend the Constitution.

In an interview Tuesday, Mr. David said he does not believe the National Assembly can sit next week if lawmakers do not swear allegiance to the King. He said the province’s request to appeal is scheduled for Friday, but a hearing on the appeal itself will not take place before Dec. 1.

Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon has said he cannot swear fealty to the monarch. “We are currently considering all options for being able to sit, without being forced by a single individual to take an action that is, frankly, quite dishonest and humiliating.”

Meanwhile, Quebec’s opposition leaders urged Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon not to delay the start of the legislative session.

Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime said he opposes the ruling but believes the session needs to start even if it means swearing allegiance to the King.

In its filing, the province argues the court “must intervene immediately, as the present case involves truly exceptional circumstances.”

The 2022 law was passed unanimously after Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon and his caucus, then in opposition, refused to take the oath and were barred from entering the National Assembly.

The substance of the case has yet to be heard, but Mr. David filed for an emergency injunction after the October election to force MNAs to take the oath before the National Assembly reconvened.

Justice Demers sided with Mr. David on Monday, ruling that if lawmakers did not swear allegiance to the Crown, “all laws passed by the National Assembly would be unconstitutional and would have to be re-enacted.”

But the province argues the judge overstepped by concluding the law is “manifestly invalid” and that the government’s defence is “doomed to failure.”

“Courts should not lightly order that laws duly enacted by a democratically elected legislature be declared inoperative before they have undergone a full constitutional review,” the filing says.

Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon also invoked the possibility of asking the president of the National Assembly to assess the matter and determine whether elected officials can sit without taking the oath.

But Patrick Taillon, a professor of constitutional law at Laval University, said such a decision would be “a form of defiance or disobedience” toward the court ruling.

“I would add that while it will be difficult for the courts to prevent members of the legislature from convening, it will be very easy for them to invalidate any laws that such a parliament might pass,” he said in an e-mail.

With a report from The Canadian Press

stories.title: Calgary budget proposes hiring more than 3,500 new staff over four years
stories.summary: The increased hiring would also require an additional $2.4 million starting in 2028 for the City of Calgary to lease more third-party office space.
stories.author: Adam MacVicar
stories.content:
As Calgary continues to grow, so too could city hall, with an influx of new hiring proposed in the four-year budget.

The budget proposal includes a requested 3,535 new full-time equivalent (FTE) positions across multiple city departments over the next four years.

The increase represents an 18.2 per cent boost to bring city staffing to 22,946 FTE positions by 2030, up from 19,411 positions this year.

According to the proposed budget, staffing would increase 1,743 positions next year, 760 new employees in 2028, 514 positions in 2029 and 518 new positions in 2030.

Calgary Transit has requested the most new positions over the next four-year budget at 648, which includes new bus and LRT operators to help increase service frequency, as well as additional mechanics for maintenance on the service’s fleet.

The Calgary Police Service is planning to hire 524 new full-time positions by 2030, according to the budget, which would add 34 officers beyond the 275 the service is able to hire next year as well as 191 civilian positions.

There’s also new hiring proposed for water services, mobility, the fire department and several other city departments.

“In some of the areas like police, fire and transit, you can’t improve service without more people,” Calgary mayor Jeromy Farkas told reporters. “There is no transit that comes more often without an additional bus driver or transit operator.”

If approved, the hiring would bring the amount of FTEs per 1,000 Calgarians from 12.26 to 13.58 in 2030.

According to the budget, Calgary currently operates with fewer (FTE) positions than many major Canadian municipalities like Toronto, Vancouver, Ottawa, Edmonton and Winnipeg.

“Calgary is on the low end when it comes to the number of full time equivalents on staff compared to other major cities,” Farkas said. “But, that said, we can always be more efficient.”

Farkas suggested there is proposed hiring requested in some city departments that could be halted or delayed as Calgarians face a proposed 15 per cent property tax increase in 2027.

Ward 13 Coun. Dan McLean agreed, and noted he wants to look internally at city hall where he said there’s “bloat” in city staffing.

“If you look at the numbers we have in communications, in HR, in IT, supply management. Every year we keep adding and adding and adding,” he said Tuesday. “I think there’s savings there for sure.”

An expanded city administration would require more space, according to the budget, with a requested $2.4 million starting in 2028 to lease more third-party spaces for operational services “due to portfolio growth.”

When asked about that spending request, Farkas noted some councillors are looking to postpone some of the “growth positions,” which could have an impact on that funding.

“If we do not grow as this budget presents, it means that we don’t need to grow as fast when it comes to office space or furnishings,” he said.

The budget proposes increases to the city’s operating budget to reach more than $8 billion by 2030, but it doesn’t include a breakdown of how much of that will be spent on salaries, wages and benefits.

According to officials, the city spent $2.7 billion on salaries, wages and benefits in 2025, which represented 51.7 per cent of the city’s operating budget that year.

When asked about the proposed hiring, Ward 6 Coun. John Pantazopoulos said he is “agnostic” to the number, and more focused on the services those positions would provide.

“If you have an outcome that makes Calgary better for a reduced amount of spending or a similar spending level, that’s a great outcome,” he told reporters. “At the end of the day, if we see a substantial increase in FTEs and the outcome and the performance of the City of Calgary degradates, that’s not a good outcome.”

Calgary city council continues a public hearing on the proposed four-year budget with more than 300 speakers registered to share their thoughts before deliberations begin.

When asked about that spending request, Farkas noted some councillors are looking to postpone some of the “growth positions,” which could have an impact on that funding.
“If we do not grow as this budget presents, it means that we don’t need to grow as fast when it comes to office space or furnishings,” he said.

The budget proposes increases to the city’s operating budget to reach more than $8 billion by 2030, but it doesn’t include a breakdown of how much of that will be spent on salaries, wages and benefits.
According to officials, the city spent $2.7 billion on salaries, wages and benefits in 2025, which represented 51.7 per cent of the city’s operating budget that year.
When asked about the proposed hiring, Ward 6 Coun. John Pantazopoulos said he is “agnostic” to the number, and more focused on the services those positions would provide.

“If you have an outcome that makes Calgary better for a reduced amount of spending or a similar spending level, that’s a great outcome,” he told reporters. “At the end of the day, if we see a substantial increase in FTEs and the outcome and the performance of the City of Calgary degradates, that’s not a good outcome.”

stories.title: ‘Fever pitch’ dynamics: Why Alto high speed train legislation is so divisive
stories.summary: Every Saturday for the past six months, Emanuele Fuldauer has stood with a small group at the corner of two rural highway roads in Crosby, Ont., bearing a sign that says “Alto” crossed out with a red circle, as well as her frustration.
stories.author: Abigail Bimman
stories.content:
Ottawa -- Every Saturday for the past six months, Emanuele Fuldauer has stood with a small group at the corner of two rural highway roads in Crosby, Ont., bearing a sign that says “Alto” crossed out with a red circle, as well as her frustration.

“I have given myself to the community and to this country, to the people in it, and to be treated with such disrespect, I find infuriating,” the retired nurse told CTV News.

She is concerned her small community of Chaffeys Locks in the Rideau Lakes would be completely cut off if one of the proposed Alto routes goes ahead. She said it is “infuriating” to hear about proposed legislative powers that would widen the government’s expropriation powers, as first reported by CBC.

Ajay Gajaria, a partner in the municipal and expropriation practice group at Aird & Berlis LLP, said property owners should be aware of two key area in the new proposal. Both expand powers granted under the government’s High-Speed Rail Network Act, passed in March.

That legislation gave the government the right of first refusal for up to eight years, which could put property owners in “purgatory”, with no one wanting to buy their land while it has yet to be expropriated. The new proposal extends the language to include lands “related” to the project, though Gajaria explained the definition of what counts as “related” is not made clear.

“So, that could be a significant increase in that power and the ability to register that right of first refusal,” he said.

A similar expansion to “related” lands involves the government’s ability to prohibit changes being made to your property for up to four years.

A third change Gajaria pointed to would send disputes over the creation of railway crossings to arbitration rather than a traditional tribunal. If the costs are less than $50,000, they are split equally by the parties. That means a landowner fighting for access to their own land via a crossing could pay up to $25,000 to push back.

“That’s significant, and it’s going to be interesting to see how that plays out with the right to claim compensation for the diminishment in value to your remaining lands,” Gajaria said.

“Taking private property is one of the most solemn things a government can do,” said professor Matti Siemiatycki, director of the Infrastructure Institute at the University of Toronto.

He told CTV News that expropriation, “when it’s critically necessary,” needs to be done fairly, with appropriate compensation for losses. Whether these new legislative changes can be done fairly depends on how they play out in practice, he said.

Siemiatycki said Alto and the government “should be much more explicit about what type of compensation they’re going to be paying,” and whether that includes compensation for first right of refusal and prohibition of work.

“If you want options in a market, that’s something you pay for, he said.”

Multiple dynamics around the project have intersected to create a “fever pitch, Siemiatycki said.”

“It’s very technical, but it has human knock-on effects, and it also clearly has political ramifications as well.”

Siemiatycki is also part of the Policy Innovation Lab, an academic advisory panel funded by Alto.

In a statement, Alto spokesperson Marlee Socket for Alto said “fair compensation will be assessed based on the circumstances of each property and farming operation.”

“The proposed measures would help us move forward responsibly toward the start of construction in 2029-2030,” Socket said.

“A more streamlined process does not mean reducing protections for affected property owners or project oversight.”

In Chaffeys Locks, Fuldauer said many of the homes are “eclectic.”

Her 88-year-old mother lives next door in a home with multiple upgrades allowing her to age in place. If her mother needs more care in a retirement home, the house was meant to serve as her nest egg - something Fuldauer worries could be tied up by the right of first refusal.

Fauldner, who lives with multiple sclerosis, has also renovated her own home so she can live on the first floor if she needs a wheelchair.

Although protesting in the cold is physically taxing, Fuldauer said she will continue to do it every Saturday for two hours – the maximum her body can handle.

“As an individual, all I can be to Alto is friction,” she said.

“And if I can get other individuals to be friction, we can be a big line of friction, and that is truly the one word that keeps going through my head.”

stories.title: Smith pushes back on hate-speech law changes, citing Alberta sovereignty act
stories.summary: Province says religious freedoms are threatened by the amendments to federal law
stories.author: Matthew Scace
stories.content:
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith is wielding her signature sovereignty act in a bid to shield her province from recent changes to Canada’s hate-speech laws that, until this year, allowed a person who quotes from a religious text to escape prosecution under the Criminal Code.

Ms. Smith’s Sovereign Alberta Within a United Canada Act is widely viewed by experts as constitutionally dubious and toothless. The motion, yet to be tabled, would not allow the government to subvert federal law, regardless of whether it is passed in the provincial legislature.

Instead, the motion asks Ms. Smith’s cabinet to “consider further lawful measures” in response to the change to federal law, Alberta Justice Minister Mickey Amery told reporters at a news conference on Tuesday.

“We do not want to create the chilling effect of dissuading people from expressing their political or religious views,” Mr. Amery said.

Ms. Smith has wielded the sovereignty act in symbolic moves to push back against Ottawa’s proposed environmental regulations, and last December, she invoked it again while directing provincial law-enforcement agencies to not enforce Ottawa’s gun buyback program.

The sovereignty act was the first piece of legislation Ms. Smith introduced as Premier in 2022 and was a key plank of her campaign for leadership of the United Conservative Party that year.

Her decision to use the act arrives almost a year since the proposed change was tabled in the House of Commons, triggering tense debate among federal legislators. It was contained in a suite of amendments to Canadian hate-speech laws that received royal assent in June.

Ms. Smith’s invocation of the sovereignty act also comes days before the UCP annual general meeting, where the Premier will look to shore up her support, even as a segment of the party refuses to heed her warnings that advocacy for an independent Alberta must be abandoned.

Separatists and free-speech absolutists in the UCP have been particularly frustrated by Ms. Smith’s demand that party leaders pledge to uphold the referendum result, in which 75 per cent of Albertans voted to remain in Canada.

The motion introduced on Tuesday targets recent changes to the Criminal Code that removed a long-standing religious exemption that allowed people quoting from religious texts to avoid prosecution for hate speech.

The change led to bitter disagreements in the House of Commons when the Bloc Québécois proposed it earlier this year.

Backers of the revised law have argued the exemption was a loophole that could be used as cover for promoting homophobia, racial abuse and antisemitism.

But the change has received significant criticism across the political spectrum and in faith communities.

The federal Conservatives vehemently opposed the move while it was being debated. At the time, Conservative MP Larry Brock said removing the religious exemption was a “direct attack on freedom of religion.”

Federal Justice Minister Sean Fraser and his colleagues with the governing federal Liberals supported the change. Last December, Mr. Fraser attempted to assuage concerns about the change, saying that it will “in no way, shape or form, prevent a religious leader from reading their religious texts.”

Joannie Fogue, spokesperson for Mr. Fraser, said in a statement to The Globe and Mail that the federal government agrees with Alberta that people should “be free to practise their faith, read scripture, and express their religious beliefs.”

Ms. Fogue said the new federal law doesn’t criminalize opinions, disagreement, criticism or religious teaching.

Consent from Alberta’s attorney-general – in this case, Mr. Amery – is required for hate-speech charges to proceed, she added.

Mr. Amery said the province isn’t planning to challenge the exemption removal in court.

He described the motion as Alberta “drawing a constitutional line.”

“The federal government, yes, has the constitutional authority to define what areas they believe should be in the Criminal Code,” he said. “We have the authority to decide which areas of priority we have for policing and which areas of priority we have for prosecution.”

Brian Dijkema, president of Christian policy think tank Cardus, said in an e-mail to The Globe and Mail that while Ottawa’s decision to remove the exemption “is ambiguous and creates uncertainty for Canadians,” he has concerns about the province attempting to override federal law.

“We need to respect the Constitution’s divisions,” said Mr. Dijkema. He added that he hasn’t reviewed the motion.

Outside of her use of the sovereignty act, Ms. Smith indicated interest in overriding federal laws in Alberta’s recent 10-question referendum , where she asked voters whether they support a constitutional amendment that would give provincial law priority over federal laws when the two conflict.

Nearly 56 per cent of Albertans rejected the idea.

stories.title: The rise of the ‘bank of grandma and grandpa’ puts retirement budgets to the test
stories.summary: Canadian grandparents are handing out more financial support to family members than they originally budgeted for in their retirement plans, according to a new survey by Embark and Angus Reid.
stories.author: Allison Bamford
stories.content:
Saskatoon - Canadian grandparents are handing out more financial support to family members than they originally budgeted for in their retirement plans, according to a new survey by Embark and Angus Reid.

The Grandparent Economy Report found 82 per cent of Canadian grandparents gave money to their children or grandchildren in the last year, while 46 per cent gave money to both.

“What we are experiencing is a bit of a living transfer of wealth,” said Michael Jesus, director of customer experience and lifecycle marketing at Embark.

“These people are very well established, and they want to give back and make sure that they are bettering their families.”

The survey found grandparents are attempting to strike a balance between supporting family and securing retirement savings.

However, 46 per cent of Canadian grandparents said they are providing more financial support than they anticipated when they planned for retirement.

“They are giving what they actually can, without jeopardizing what they need to live on,” Jesus said.

Grandparents are most likely to help cover costs for holiday or birthday gifts and education expenses, according to the report.

The survey found 51 per cent of grandparents have already helped with a grandchild’s education in some way, including 26 per cent who contributed to a Registered Education Savings Plan.

“It does not have to be $1,000 here or $1,000 there,” Jesus said. “Any little bit actually contributed can make a huge difference given some time.”

Some grandparents, about 13 per cent, say they are also likely to help cover everyday expenses such as groceries, bills and childcare.

Affordability crisis kills retirement savings

Michael Couros is a grandfather of four. He helps cover some of the cost-of-living expenses for his son and grandchildren every month.

“When my son was fortunate enough to buy a house in a small town, he never imagined the pressures of finances as difficult as they are right now,” Couros said.

“As a result, you find yourself in a situation where if there is an opportunity to help out, you help out where you can.”

Like many grandparents, Couros never planned for these additional monthly expenses at a time when he is also budgeting for his own rising cost of living.

He says the affordability crisis is chipping away at many seniors’ retirement savings.

“That money was supposed to be for your own retirement, but if you are helping (your family) every single month that just pushes back your end date,” he said.

Couros has cut back on frivolous purchases and travel. He suggests other grandparents do the same thing.

“There are a lot more people depending on you, so you do the best you can,” he said.

Embark surveyed 1,020 Canadian grandparents who are 55 or older between Oct. 8 and Oct. 14.

The margin of error is plus or minus 3.1 percentage points, 19 times out of 20.

stories.title: Canadian Forces Military Police member charged with five service offences
stories.summary: A member of the Canadian Forces Military Police has been charged with five service offences.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — A member of the Canadian Forces Military Police has been charged with five service offences.

Sgt. Harold Cubillos-Tejada is accused of being absent without leave, two counts of disobeying a lawful command of a superior officer and two counts of conduct to the prejudice of good order and discipline.

The military police did not provide details of the alleged offences.

Brig.-Gen. Vanessa Hanrahan, the commander of the military police, says Cubillos-Tejada faces a professional code of conduct investigation.

Hanrahan says the sergeant has been suspended from policing duties and functions and assigned to administrative duties.

She says that if the charges proceed to prosecution, the case will be heard in the military justice system.

stories.title: Report linking Toronto infant’s death to opioids in mother’s breast milk retracted twenty years later
stories.summary: A 2006 paper led by disgraced SickKids doctor Gideon Koren led to warnings to women worldwide about taking codeine for post-partum pain
stories.author: Sharon Kirkey
stories.content:
A pivotal report linking the death of a 12-day-old Canadian baby to opioids from his mother’s breast milk, changing pain care for millions of nursing mothers worldwide, has been retracted by one of the world’s most influential medical journals.

The “omission” of key toxicological information constitutes “fabrication,” according to the retraction issued by The Lancet02255-5/fulltext) — the latest development in a heated and long-running controversy over what came to be known as the “Toronto Case.”

The single case report suggested that newborn babies can be harmed or even killed by a mother’s use of prescription opioids while breastfeeding.

It was led by Gideon Koren, the once prominent founder of the since-dismantled Motherrisk program at Toronto’s SickKids Hospital who agreed in 2019 to permanently relinquish his licence amid an unrelated investigation by College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario into allegations of professional misconduct or incompetence.

Monday - Saturday Free

NP Posted keeps you updated on the news of the day and the perspectives that define the National Post, while drawing your focus to some of the unexpected stories we like to tell. Delivered straight to your inbox Monday to Friday, with a weekend edition on Saturdays.

Koren’s 2006 report described the unexpected death of an otherwise healthy, full-term baby in April 2005 from opioid poisoning.

The baby had occasional trouble breastfeeding and seemed listless and drowsy seven days after he was born, Koren and colleagues wrote. During a “well-baby” visit when he was 11 days old, “the pediatrician noted that the baby had regained his birthweight.”

“On day 12, however, he had grey skin and his milk intake had fallen,” the researchers wrote.

“He was found dead on day 13.”

The mother was taking Tylenol 3, which contains acetaminophen and codeine. Codeine is converted to morphine. Due to a genetic variation, the mother is an ultra-rapid metabolizer of codeine, meaning she converts codeine to morphine more efficiently than most.

The researchers said the picture was consistent with opioid toxicity, and that codeine could produce life-threateningly high amounts of morphine in breast milk if the mother is a rapid metabolizer.

“Whatever clinical approach is taken, codeine cannot be considered as a safe drug for all infants during breastfeeding,” they wrote in The Lancet.

The implications were justifying terrifying people

Dr. David Juurlink

Their report did not mention that there was white, curdled material containing codeine in the baby’s stomach, suggesting the baby had ingested it.

The case69255-6.pdf) was cited more than 600 times and led to health agencies the world over, including Health Canada and the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, cautioning nursing mothers about the “very rare but serious health risk” to breastfed babies posed by codeine.

“The implications were justifying terrifying people,” said University of Toronto pharmacologist and toxicologist Dr. David Juurlink, who worked for 16 years to have the Lancet paper pulled.

“It purported to establish definitively that that was why this baby died. And codeine was a very, very common therapy in the post-partum period,” frequently prescribed for pain from cesarean sections and other childbirth interventions.

In a 2020 paper, Juurlink argued that Koren’s conclusions were “highly implausible” and that the baby’s blood concentrations of acetaminophen and codeine were too high to have come from breast milk alone and could only be explained by ingestion of Tylenol 3, which in a 12-day-old baby would have required crushing of the tablet.

The mother refutes that and says she is disappointed with the retraction.

“It is putting mothers and babies at harm and death,” said Rani Jamieson in an interview.

The contents found in her son Tariq’s stomach were included in the official coroner’s report, Jamieson said.

“My child was breastfed. Of course that’s what’s going to happen. Milk was in his stomach and what I’m taking and passing through my breast milk into him is going to be in his stomach.”

Her doctor had prescribed Tylenol 3 because she was in severe pain after Tariq’s birth. “I was given these drugs to take and was told it was safe and so I breastfed.” The baby had a postpartum night nanny, she said.

Direct administration “didn’t happen, and I would like to know when someone says someone gave (Tylenol to the baby)…. who this mystery person might be and under what scenario.”

“It’s heartbreaking to have what I call lies and misinterpretation of facts …. take away what my son’s death has done for the world, to remind them of the risks of opioids in breastfeeding,” she said.

Dr. David Juurlink in a 2012 file photo. He has called the conclusions in the 2006 report “highly implausible.” Matthew Sherwood for Postmedia

Koren and his co-authors stand by their report.

In a paperpublished last week, two of the authors said it’s “over simplistic” to treat infant deaths attributed to morphine in breast milk as deliberate or malicious and said the baby’s high codeine levels could be a product of either ingesting more, eliminating less than expected, or both.

“We acknowledge that direct administration (i.e. poisoning) can occur but circumstances in the home are associated with clear risk factors; these risk factors were absent in the Toronto case,” they wrote.

While the case triggered alarms among obstetricians and pediatricians, concerns were raised soon after its publication in The Lancet. In 2008, the Lancet published a letter from experts with the Scottish Poisons Information Bureau who doubted Koren’s conclusions and said the presence of high amounts of morphine in the baby’s stomach should have been highlighted in the case report.

The Lancet published an “expression of concern” in February, following a year-long investigation by New Yorker journalist Ben Taub, early reporting by the Toronto Star and “new allegations of falsification of toxicological data, authorship issues and ethical concerns” brought forward by a member of the original research team.

The fresh allegations were sent to the Hospital for Sick Children’s Research Integrity Office, which conducted a new formal investigation.

“We have now received the outcome and conclusion of this investigation,” the Lancet editors wrote in their retraction.

“On the allegation of omission of material toxicological data, including the infant’s blood codeine and acetaminophen concentrations and the qualitative identification of codeine in the infant’s stomach contents, the report concluded that this omission constitutes falsification,” according to the retraction.

The missing data left readers without the full information needed to assess the report’s conclusions, they said.

But Juurlink said key information about the baby’s codeine and acetaminophen blood concentrations were in the original manuscript, which the authors shortened to one page at The Lancet’s request.

In an email to National Post, The Lancet said authors “are responsible for the accuracy and completeness of what they publish, including when a paper is shortened per submission guidelines.”

Koren and colleagues “trimmed it down,” Juurlink said. “I don’t think they were intending to conceal this stuff. I think they didn’t think critically enough about their assessment of the case.”

SickKids first investigated the case in 2020, after Juurlink called for a retraction, but concluded a retraction wasn’t warranted.

However, two Canadian journals — The Canadian Pharmacists Journal and Canadian Family Physician — issued a joint retraction of subsequent columns published by the same authors of the original case, following Juurlink’s assessment.

In a statement to the National Post, SickKids said it takes all matters of research integrity seriously and that the two inquiries examined different allegations.

“The earlier inquiry focused on questions of scientific rigour, while the most recent complaint raised a specific concern about the omission of material toxicological data from the published paper,” the hospital said.

Juurlink, who has long advocated for safer opioid prescribing, said there is “very little reason to fear that a baby is going to be poisoned by opioids dosed appropriately in the mother” and used over short periods.

“You just don’t pass that much into breast milk. It’s very, very hard to tell a story where a baby gets opioid toxicity and dies because mum is taking pain medication.

“I think guidance needs to be revised.”

The office of Ontario’s chief coroner said the investigation into the baby’s death is “active and ongoing” and, as such, no further details can be provided.

Sharon Kirkey is a national reporter with National Post focusing on health and science stories. She is also a three-time National Newspaper Awards nominee, with a win for beat reporting.

The Lancet published an “expression of concern” in February, following a year-long investigation by New Yorker journalist Ben Taub, early reporting by the Toronto Star and “new allegations of falsification of toxicological data, authorship issues and ethical concerns” brought forward by a member of the original research team.
The fresh allegations were sent to the Hospital for Sick Children’s Research Integrity Office, which conducted a new formal investigation.
“We have now received the outcome and conclusion of this investigation,” the Lancet editors wrote in their retraction.

“On the allegation of omission of material toxicological data, including the infant’s blood codeine and acetaminophen concentrations and the qualitative identification of codeine in the infant’s stomach contents, the report concluded that this omission constitutes falsification,” according to the retraction.
The missing data left readers without the full information needed to assess the report’s conclusions, they said.
But Juurlink said key information about the baby’s codeine and acetaminophen blood concentrations were in the original manuscript, which the authors shortened to one page at The Lancet’s request.
In an email to National Post, The Lancet said authors “are responsible for the accuracy and completeness of what they publish, including when a paper is shortened per submission guidelines.”
Koren and colleagues “trimmed it down,” Juurlink said. “I don’t think they were intending to conceal this stuff. I think they didn’t think critically enough about their assessment of the case.”
SickKids first investigated the case in 2020, after Juurlink called for a retraction, but concluded a retraction wasn’t warranted.

However, two Canadian journals — The Canadian Pharmacists Journal and Canadian Family Physician — issued a joint retraction of subsequent columns published by the same authors of the original case, following Juurlink’s assessment.
In a statement to the National Post, SickKids said it takes all matters of research integrity seriously and that the two inquiries examined different allegations.

“The earlier inquiry focused on questions of scientific rigour, while the most recent complaint raised a specific concern about the omission of material toxicological data from the published paper,” the hospital said.

Juurlink, who has long advocated for safer opioid prescribing, said there is “very little reason to fear that a baby is going to be poisoned by opioids dosed appropriately in the mother” and used over short periods.
“You just don’t pass that much into breast milk. It’s very, very hard to tell a story where a baby gets opioid toxicity and dies because mum is taking pain medication.
“I think guidance needs to be revised.”
The office of Ontario’s chief coroner said the investigation into the baby’s death is “active and ongoing” and, as such, no further details can be provided.

stories.title: Ontario changed out-of-country health care rules in bad faith, patients’ lawyers say
stories.summary: Two patients are appealing the rejection of their request to receive public funding for cancer therapies available in the U.S. but not in Canada
stories.author: Tu Thanh Ha
stories.content:
Ontario acted in bad faith when it retroactively changed its rule for out-of-country health care funding, breaching the constitutional rights of two cancer patients seeking life-saving treatment abroad, their lawyers told the court Tuesday.

The Ontario Superior Court of Justice was hearing an application by the two patients, Sabrina Apitz-Grossman and Kevin Nash, who are appealing the rejection of their request to receive public funding for therapies currently available in the U.S. but not in Canada.

In their court applications, lawyers for the patients said they are not trying to invalidate the province’s ability to set its funding priorities. Instead, they took a more focused approach, arguing that the government unfairly delayed the requests their clients made under an existing program, then changed the regulatory framework.

“They followed the rules. Instead of following the rules, Ontario changed them,” Thomas Conway, a lawyer representing Ms. Apitz-Grossman, told the three-judge panel.

Ms. Apitz-Grossman has synovial sarcoma, a soft-tissue cancer that was first detected in one of her legs and has now spread to her lungs. Her oncologist says she is a good candidate for afamitresgene autoleucel, a treatment where the patient’s own white cells are genetically modified to create a customized drug. It is sold under the brand name Tecelra, and she has said she can get it at a discounted cost of US$575,000.

Mr. Nash has melanoma, a type of skin cancer, which has metastasized into his lungs and pancreas. He has been seeking to be treated with lifileucel, which uses cells from the patient’s tumour to create a personalized medication. Sold under the brand name Amtagvi at a sticker price of US$515,000 in the U.S., it has been approved by Health Canada but is still being reviewed by Canada’s Drug Agency, which advises provincial and territorial governments on public funding for new drugs.

While acknowledging that Ms. Apitz-Grossman’s circumstances are “devastating and sympathetic,” the government’s lawyers said in a court filing that out-of-country funding could put pressure on health budgets. The province has maintained that such individual benefits undermine the ability of public drug plans to negotiate prices with drug manufacturers.

Speaking to reporters at the legislature, Premier Doug Ford accused pharmaceutical companies of trying to take advantage of people in need of treatment. “They’re trying to circumvent the system across the country and gouge these poor cancer patients, or ultimately try to gouge the taxpayers.”

Ms. Apitz-Grossman and Mr. Nash both applied this spring to Ontario’s program to obtain public insurance coverage for out-of-country treatments. Their applications were rejected. The government directed them to appeal to the Health Services Appeal and Review Board, but then went before the board and argued that it had no jurisdiction to order funding.

In September, the board dismissed the funding requests by Ms. Apitz-Grossman and Mr. Nash. Around the same time, ON Sept. 22, the Ontario Superior Court of Justice sided with Alex Shved , a melanoma patient challenging the province’s refusal to cover treatment in Florida.

On Oct. 6, as Ms. Apitz-Grossman and Mr. Nash applied to the court for a judicial review, the province made retroactive changes to the regulation for out-of-country treatment. Funding would only be provided if the treatment was already covered in Ontario but access was temporarily unavailable in the province.

The regulation change applied retroactively to Oct. 1. A month later, ON Nov. 3, Ms. Apitz-Grossman received records from a Freedom of Information request that she had filed with the Ontario government in July.

She discovered in those records that two clinical experts had been consulted about her funding application and had concluded that the treatment she sought in the U.S. “is very reasonable.”

The delays and lack of transparency in the case were “the essence of bad faith,” Alyssa Holland, a lawyer for Ms. Apitz-Grossman, told the court Tuesday. “Absence of good faith can be concluded and bad faith deduced.”

Government lawyer Matthew Horner said there had been a policy intent since 2011 to align out-of-country funding with services available in Ontario. Because of the Superior Court judgment in favour of Mr. Shved, the province had to change the regulation to clarify its intent, Mr. Horner said.

The government is seeking leave to appeal the Shved decision, Mr. Horner added.

Mr. Nash’s lawyer, Claire Boychuk, said her client had been told in January that there was a median life expectancy of about three to six months for his type of cancer.

She added that Ms. Apitz-Grossman was 15 months into the 12-to-18-month median survival range for her cancer.

“They do not have a day to waste.”

With files from Jeff Gray at Queen’s Park

stories.title: Salvation Army faces unprecedented demand in Okanagan as donations lag
stories.summary: The growing need is creating a double challenge for the Salvation Army, which is also struggling to find enough volunteers to help raise money.
stories.author: Klaudia Van Emmerik
stories.content:
The Salvation Army in the Central Okanagan is facing an unprecedented level of demand for Christmas assistance.

“I have never seen anything like this,” said Captain Jennifer Henson with the Salvation Army Okanagan Central. “We expected an increase. We budgeted for an increase, but we have not budgeted for the increase that we’re seeing.”

Last year, 790 families turned to the Gifts of Hope program for help.

This year, that number has already surpassed 900, with Christmas still a month away and the organization expecting demand to continue growing.

The growing need is creating a double challenge for the Salvation Army, which is also struggling to find enough volunteers to help raise money.

“Many of our volunteers are aging. They’re not able to get out as much. Many of the folks who would like to volunteer are working two jobs just to make ends meet for their family,” Henson said.

The shortage is contributing to a slow start to the annual Christmas kettle campaign.

So far, just 10 per cent of the $1-million fundraising goal has been reached.

For volunteers like Terry Kellert, helping raise money is about making sure children don’t go without on Christmas morning.

“To help kids to have Christmas,” Kellert said when asked why he volunteers. “To have a present waking up, can you imagine being two or three years old and waking up and no present under the tree?”

But for an increasing number of families, the financial pressures are making even the basics difficult to afford.

“People just can’t make ends meet,” Henson said. “They’re stretching their dollar as far as they can and they’re literally at a point where they’re choosing between, you know, paying their bills or having Christmas for their kids.”

The Salvation Army is asking the community to step up in whatever way they can–through toy donations, financial contributions, or volunteering their time to help collect donations at the kettles.

“If somebody is able to donate their time on the kettle, every two-hour shifts is about the equivalent of $150, which is one child supported at Christmas, so maybe people think about it that way,” Henson said.

New toys can be donated and dropped off at the Salvation Army Community Church location on Sutherland Avenue in Kelowna or at the Salvation Army Westbank Thrift Store on Old Okanagan Highway.

To volunteer, make a donation, or for more information, you can go to the Okanagan Central Salvation Army website.

stories.title: Anthem singer who flubbed ‘O Canada’ says she practised for a month. Then her ‘menopause brain’ hit
stories.summary: Leafs-Islanders singer, whose life changed after cancer treatment, says bright side is a chance to advocate for women.
stories.author: Kerry Gillespie
stories.content:
Sarrah Strimel Bentley spent a month practising “O Canada” ahead of Monday night’s Leafs-Islanders hockey game. She paid for vocal coaching. She drilled it in her suite at the New York arena, repeating the “glowing hearts” section that had given her trouble in the sound check.

But standing on the ice, when everyone was watching, her “menopause brain” kicked in and “we stand on guard for thee” became “we lend our hearts to thee.”

Afterwards, she made the mistake of looking at her phone, which “led to a Pandora’s box of just horrendous comments.” She held her almost three-year-old toddler and cried. “He was like, ‘Mommy, what’s wrong?’ And I’m like, I’m really sad,” she said in a phone interview Tuesday.

Strimel Bentley, 45, was thrown into menopause six years ago because of the treatment for her hormone-positive breast cancer. She’s hoping her embarrassing moment in the spotlight will at least help raise awareness and understanding about menopause. It’s a critical women’s health issue long stigmatized and dismissed , and experts say symptoms like memory loss, brain fog and insomnia take a toll.

“It’s very real,” said Dr. Sheila Wijayasinghe, the mature women’s health education co-lead at the University of Toronto’s Temerty Faculty of Medicine and staff physician at St. Michael’s Hospital.

Public conversations around menopause often focus on hot flashes and night sweats, but the symptoms that are most distressing to patients are the cognitive symptoms, she said. “The word-finding difficulties, losing your train of thought, forgetting names, all of those things are really tricky.”

Wijayasinghe said more research is needed to better understand cognitive symptoms — and find effective treatments. “It can be really scary and disconcerting to go from feeling quite capable and able to participate in normal activities to really having a struggle.”

Strimel Bentley was 38 when she was diagnosed with a hormone-positive breast cancer that led to the removal of her ovaries. That threw her into medically induced menopause overnight — and while she was fighting cancer.

In 2020, she started eight months of chemotherapy and radiation, followed by three years of oral chemotherapy.

At times, it was hard to even know what was driving her fluctuating moods and anxiety: cancer, menopause or fear of the future.

During her “menopausal chemical car crash” she worried whether the one embryo they had been able to retrieve before her cancer treatment would let her and her husband fulfil their dream of becoming parents. It did.

“I’m bald and I’m throwing Thai food — that’s like my greatest memory of menopause,” she said.

Her active cancer treatment ended, but challenging menopause symptoms continue.

“I’ve been trying for years to figure out how I’m going to address my memory issues. I don’t sleep. I wake up every night at 3, maybe 2 if it’s a bad night, and then I stay up till 5 or 6 and then my kid gets up at 7:30,” she said. “I walk out of my bedroom and I don’t remember why.”

She retired from her career on Broadway a decade ago. The New York Islanders invited her to sing on their Hockey Fights Cancer night because of her own experience with cancer. When she first said yes, she thought it was just the U.S. national anthem, something she’s been singing her whole life.

“They’re like, ‘also, can you sing the Canadian national anthem?’ And I was well, I’ve never done it, but I’d like to try because I love Canada, I’ve tried to move there,” Strimel Bentley said.

After a month of preparing for the unpaid job, she took a breath and walked out on the ice feeling excited.

“I started to sing … and I just couldn’t. My brain did not remember. My brain just went to ‘lend our hearts to thee,’” she said. “I looked around and people were yelling and they were saying you suck.”

“I’m not proud of me forgetting these lyrics,” she said. “What I can do now is to advocate for women, full stop, women’s health … this is what our hormones do to us.”

“Husbands, governments — Canadian and American — we should all take women’s health more seriously,” she said, noting women need more access to experts in menopause care.

That’s something the Menopause Foundation of Canada called for last month when it released its policy agenda asking governments across the country to tackle systemic barriers in the public health-care system that leave too many women dismissed, misdiagnosed or simply unable to find a doctor willing to treat them. Its call for action includes mandating menopause training for all physicians and nurse practitioners, investing in menopause research and strengthening the economy by supporting women in workplaces through menopause.

Dr. Lucky Sekhon, who grew up in Brampton, is an OB/GYN and reproductive endocrinologist in New York. She knows Strimel Bentley well and the “double whammy” of going through cancer and menopause.

“That’s affected her in so many different ways and one of those ways is brain fog and just having a harder time keeping track of things and remembering things,” Sekhon said. “And that’s really, from a medical standpoint, very valid.

“It’s not like you’re walking around with a sign on your head saying ‘I have brain fog,’ so I think it leads to a lot of issues,” she said.

“I’m shocked at the lack of leniency, how harsh people are and they’re not really thinking about like a person as a whole, a human being,” she said about the comments she saw online after the anthem. “Everyone needs to take it down a notch.”

But standing on the ice, when everyone was watching, her “menopause brain” kicked in and “we stand on guard for thee” became “we lend our hearts to thee.”

Afterwards, she made the mistake of looking at her phone, which “led to a Pandora’s box of just horrendous comments.” She held her almost three-year-old toddler and cried. “He was like, ‘Mommy, what’s wrong?’ And I’m like, I’m really sad,” she said in a phone interview Tuesday.

stories.title: ‘Assuredly the offender has other victims’: Cold case experts say deceased London fire captain needs to be considered in other unsolved murders
stories.summary: Experts in crime and cold cases are weighing in on the revelation Monday by London police that a deceased fire captain is responsible for the January 1968 murder of a London teen.
stories.author: Bryan Bicknell
stories.content:
Experts in crime and cold cases are weighing in on the revelation Monday by London police that a deceased fire captain is responsible for the January 1968 murder of a London teen. They say Michael Joseph Moore should be investigated and ruled out in other unsolved murders that go far beyond the London region.

Western University criminologist and author of Murder City, Mike Arntfield, says the murder of 16-year-old Jacqueline Dunleavy (Jackie) would begin a decades-long string of killings that would go unsolved. “There’s another copycat murder a month later.

And for the next 20 years, unfortunately, women and children in London were targets of predators. And Jacqueline was the first,” said Artfield. On Monday, the London Police Service identified Michael Joseph Moore, now deceased, as the person responsible for Jackie’s murder.

Investigators used preserved DNA evidence and forensic investigative genetic genealogy to solve the cold case. Moore was 25 at the time and had emigrated from Ireland one year earlier. He would go on to become a London firefighter.

Arntfield sees the resolution of this case as an opportunity for police to consider Moore in other unsolved murders. “Assuredly the offender has other victims,” exclaimed Arntfield. “What was done to her was so specific, so almost ritualistic.

Number one, we have to look at his movements in his native Ireland, and that investigation, I can tell you, also underway. But his movements, especially after he becomes a firefighter, need to be accounted for,” he said.

Former OPP Commissioner and CTV News Public Safety Analyst Chris Lewis has a similar take. “Does that happen often where someone will kill a young girl like this and then just never do it again? So, I’m sure that the investigators from a number of agencies are looking at him as a potential suspect in other cases,” Lewis said.

Moore retired from the London Fire Department as Captain in 2002 after serving for 28 years. He died in 2018. “He needs to be cross-referenced to the OPP cases where there were London victims, but they were OPP files because of where the bodies were disposed of … and certainly looked at in other cases wherever he traveled, including for training with respect to the fire department.

The Gravenhurst area where the fire college was. Toronto, where he also attended for training. Cases in those jurisdictions, open cases need to be looked at,” said Arntfield. CTV News spoke with a number of retired firefighters who knew and worked with Moore.

None wished to go on record, but some expressed disbelief, describing the “Mike Moore” they knew as a “decent man.” In the meantime, the London Professional Firefighters Association issued this statement to CTV News, in response to Moore being identified as the individual responsible for Jackie’s murder.

The London Professional Firefighters Association stands in support of victims of violent crime and their families. We are deeply saddened to hear of this tragedy and offer our sincere condolences to the family. Our Association has full confidence in our community partners at London Police Services to ensure justice is always done.

stories.title: ‘Bank of grandma and grandpa’: Canadians turn to grandparents for financial support
stories.summary: Canadian grandparents are handing out more financial support to family members than they originally budgeted for in their retirement plans, according to a new survey by Embark and Angus Reid.
stories.author: Allison Bamford
stories.content:
Saskatoon - Canadian grandparents are handing out more financial support to family members than they originally budgeted for in their retirement plans, according to a new survey by Embark and Angus Reid.

The Grandparent Economy Report found 82 per cent of Canadian grandparents gave money to their children or grandchildren in the last year, while 46 per cent gave money to both.

“What we are experiencing is a bit of a living transfer of wealth,” said Michael Jesus, director of customer experience and lifecycle marketing at Embark.

“These people are very well established, and they want to give back and make sure that they are bettering their families.”

The survey found grandparents are attempting to strike a balance between supporting family and securing retirement savings.

However, 46 per cent of Canadian grandparents said they are providing more financial support than they anticipated when they planned for retirement.

“They are giving what they actually can, without jeopardizing what they need to live on,” Jesus said.

Grandparents are most likely to help cover costs for holiday or birthday gifts and education expenses, according to the report.

The survey found 51 per cent of grandparents have already helped with a grandchild’s education in some way, including 26 per cent who contributed to a Registered Education Savings Plan.

“It does not have to be $1,000 here or $1,000 there,” Jesus said. “Any little bit actually contributed can make a huge difference given some time.”

Some grandparents, about 13 per cent, say they are also likely to help cover everyday expenses such as groceries, bills and childcare.

Affordability crisis kills retirement savings

Michael Couros is a grandfather of four. He helps cover some of the cost-of-living expenses for his son and grandchildren every month.

“When my son was fortunate enough to buy a house in a small town, he never imagined the pressures of finances as difficult as they are right now,” Couros said.

“As a result, you find yourself in a situation where if there is an opportunity to help out, you help out where you can.”

Like many grandparents, Couros never planned for these additional monthly expenses at a time when he is also budgeting for his own rising cost of living.

He says the affordability crisis is chipping away at many seniors’ retirement savings.

“That money was supposed to be for your own retirement, but if you are helping (your family) every single month that just pushes back your end date,” he said.

Couros has cut back on frivolous purchases and travel. He suggests other grandparents do the same thing.

“There are a lot more people depending on you, so you do the best you can,” he said.

Embark surveyed 1,020 Canadian grandparents who are 55 or older between Oct. 8 and Oct. 14.

The margin of error is plus or minus 3.1 percentage points, 19 times out of 20.

The Grandparent Economy Report found 82 per cent of Canadian grandparents gave money to their children or grandchildren in the last year, while 46 per cent gave money to both.
“What we are experiencing is a bit of a living transfer of wealth,” said Michael Jesus, director of customer experience and lifecycle marketing at Embark.
“These people are very well established, and they want to give back and make sure that they are bettering their families.”
The survey found grandparents are attempting to strike a balance between supporting family and securing retirement savings.
However, 46 per cent of Canadian grandparents said they are providing more financial support than they anticipated when they planned for retirement.
“They are giving what they actually can, without jeopardizing what they need to live on,” Jesus said.
Grandparents are most likely to help cover costs for holiday or birthday gifts and education expenses, according to the report.
The survey found 51 per cent of grandparents have already helped with a grandchild’s education in some way, including 26 per cent who contributed to a Registered Education Savings Plan.
“It does not have to be $1,000 here or $1,000 there,” Jesus said. “Any little bit actually contributed can make a huge difference given some time.”
Some grandparents, about 13 per cent, say they are also likely to help cover everyday expenses such as groceries, bills and childcare.

stories.title: Kelowna foster care village aims to tackle declining number of foster homes
stories.summary: A $15-million project is aiming to create a purpose-built community for foster kids, as high housing costs are making it difficult to place children.
stories.author: Cohan Sassaman
stories.content:
A $15-million project in Kelowna is aiming to create a purpose-built community for foster families, as B.C. Federation of Foster Parents say high housing costs and a shrinking number of foster homes are making it increasingly difficult to place children in care.

The Hall Family Foundation is proposing the development of 10 five-bedroom homes, along with a roughly 5,000-square-foot support hub. The project is designed to accommodate up to 40 foster children at a time, plus foster parents and support staff.

Marcy Perron, president of the B.C. Federation of Foster Parents, says the province is facing a growing need for caregivers.

“We’re seeing a big demand for caregivers. We’re down to, I think, approximately 2,000 foster homes in all of B.C., which is really, really low,” Perron adds that when she started her career that was close to 5000 care homes.

She says the cost of housing is one of the barriers preventing people from becoming foster parents.

“When you’re paying like $2,000 or $2,500 for a two-bedroom, that only allows for one child. So housing is a huge, huge problem as far as recruitment is concerned.”

The Hall Family Foundation says the proposed village is intended to address more than just the shortage of available homes.

Ed Hall, a board member of the foundation, says children in care can face frequent moves between foster homes.

“In an ideal world, a person would move into this foster village and be able to live there for their entire juvenile life and establish friends,” Hall said.

The foundation also hopes larger homes will make it easier to keep siblings together, while the support hub would provide services such as counselling and resources for foster families.

The concept is relatively uncommon, according to Hall. He says a similar model exists in California, but dedicated foster communities like the one proposed in Canada are rare. Perron says the shortage of foster homes is also being driven by an aging caregiver population, with many long-time foster parents now approaching retirement. She says the province needs to recruit younger caregivers to replace those leaving the system.

“So we need to recruit the younger caregivers, but they can’t afford the housing. So we’re in a catch-22,” Perron said.

Perron says stability can be critical for children who have experienced trauma.

“These kids have been neglected. A lot of them don’t know normal. They’ve never experienced normal.”

The proposed site is at Glenmore in Kelowna on privately owned land. The foundation says no taxpayer money is expected to be used for construction.

However, the land has not yet been secured, and the project still requires rezoning and other approvals.

The foundation hopes construction can begin in 2027, with families moving in by 2028.

stories.title: Amazon violated Ontario’s anti-discrimination laws by not hiring Iranian engineer, tribunal rules
stories.summary: Man with Canadian work permit told company’s global recruitment policy meant he couldn’t be hired because Iran was an ‘embargoed country’ and subject to U.S. export control rules
stories.author: Vanmala Subramaniam
stories.content:
Amazon Amzn-Q violated anti-discrimination laws by stopping its recruitment of an Iranian citizen for a software engineering position in Toronto because of his nationality, the Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario has ruled.

The precedent-setting decision could potentially alter the hiring landscape for immigrants from countries subject to U.S. sanctions seeking to work at large American multinationals.

Mohammadhasan Owlia, an engineering graduate from the University of Toronto, held a Canadian work permit when he applied for a software engineering position at Amazon in Toronto in late 2019. He successfully completed an initial screening and a technical assessment, but during a preinterview phone call with a recruiter, he was told that he was ineligible for employment under Amazon’s global recruitment policy because Iran was an “embargoed country” and subject to U.S. export control rules.

Mr. Owlia filed a complaint with the tribunal in 2020, alleging discrimination under Ontario’s Human Rights Code because of citizenship and country of origin. Six years later, an adjudicator ruled in his favour, ON the grounds that Amazon adopted a policy that suited its business interests, but failed to consider and comply with local human rights laws. In the Nov. 16 decision, the tribunal ordered Amazon to compensate Mr. Owlia $15,000 and amend its global recruitment policy to include language from the Human Rights Code when hiring in Ontario.

“Amazon’s export controls compliance policy was overbroad,” wrote Cyndee Todgham Cherniak, vice-chair at the commission and an international trade lawyer. “None of the arguments Amazon advanced negate the discriminatory nature of its decision to end Mr. Owlia’s advancement in the recruitment or absolve it of liability under the Code.”

In a statement, Amazon spokesperson Amy Diaz said that the company is committed to “fair and inclusive hiring and to following the laws wherever we operate, including Ontario’s Human Rights Code. Amazon will carefully review the Tribunal’s decision and will meet its obligations,” she added.

In an interview with The Globe and Mail, Mr. Owlia said he was relieved and happy at the tribunal’s decision, and hoped it would help other foreign nationals in a similar situation. He also said that it was an “open secret” in the Iranian community in Canada that getting a job with big technology companies was particularly hard because of their nationality and blanket recruitment policies that discriminate against Iranians.

“That was the most infuriating part to me. That it affected the entire [Iranian] community and that we’re just screened out of the process by big companies very early on,” he said.

The Seattle-based tech giant advises recruiters to avoid hiring potential candidates who are located in, or are nationals of “embargoed countries,” specifically Cuba, Iran, North Korea, Sudan and Syria. In an internal document about the policy, which was viewed by The Globe, Amazon justifies the existence of the policy because of the U.S. government’s trade sanctions against specific countries. Amazon also states that it updates its list of embargoed countries from time to time.

During the hearing, Amazon’s lawyers argued that the company had to comply with U.S. export control laws and the only way it could do that was to eliminate candidates from U.S.-sanctioned countries. Software engineers could come into contact with sensitive U.S. software, they argued.

But Ms. Cherniak, the adjudicator in the case, concluded that Amazon could comply with both Canadian human rights laws and U.S. export control laws. Specifically, Amazon could go through its software, categorize it, and determine which parts potential employees such as Mr. Owlia could handle and which parts needed to be safeguarded from citizens of certain countries. Alternatively, Amazon could have applied for an exemption from export control laws to handle specific pieces of software in Ontario in order to hire citizens from embargoed countries. Amazon did neither, Ms. Cherniak noted.

“In my view, having to comply with multiple laws is a cost of doing business,” she wrote, in the decision.

Mr. Owlia, who graduated with a master’s degree in industrial engineering from the University of Toronto in 2018, now has Canadian citizenship and works at a Toronto-based software startup.

Gregory Ko, Mr. Owlia’s lawyer and a partner at Kastner Ko LLP in Toronto said that his hope is the decision sets a helpful precedent and signals to other big employers that they cannot just “wave around U.S. export control laws as a defence to not hiring certain foreign nationals.”

Maarten Sangens, a Washington-based independent export compliance consultant, said that export control rules are complex and it is generally easier for companies to hire nationals from countries that are not on a sanctions list.

“Having said that, there are companies who hire embargoed nationals and there are ways to deal with it like applying for special licences or shielding software from certain employees,” he said.

Mr. Sangens also added that American multinationals regularly have to deal with the issue of complying with export control laws and human rights laws when hiring in the European Union. “This is certainly not just a Canadian issue.”

stories.title: A timeline before and after mass shooting in Tumbler Ridge, B.C.
stories.summary: Vancouver - Lawyers for the alleged co-conspirator in the mass shooting in Tumbler Ridge, B.C., are trying to have her released from jail before her expected trial next year. stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Vancouver - Lawyers for the alleged co-conspirator in the mass shooting in Tumbler Ridge, B.C., are trying to have her released from jail before her expected trial next year. A 33-page motion filed in U.S. district court says the accused, James Bryant, who goes by the name Melody, and the killer sent almost 74,000 texts between Aug. 1 last year and Feb. 10, 2026, the day of the killings.

Here is the alleged timeline set out in several court documents of the events before and after eight people were killed in the small B.C. village:

June 2025: OpenAI shuts down killer Jesse Van Rootselaar’s ChatGPT account after it was flagged for concerning behaviour. The company did not notify police.

Aug. 3, 2025: Van Rootselaar tells Bryant that she plans to “wait awhile” before executing her plan, and notes that her homicidal thoughts May “seem crazy to her in the future.”

Aug. 4, 2025: Van Rootselaar asks for small amount of money for stickers to decorate firearms she would use during the attack. That came after Bryant agreed to buy $150 shoes for Van Rootselaar’s birthday, which Van Rootselaar later said she planned to wear during the shooting.

Aug. 8, 2025: Van Rootselaar and Bryant discuss possible attack locations, as well as history of Canada’s deadliest mass shootings.

Aug. 18, 2025: Bryant agrees not to “snitch” on Van Rootselaar.

Aug. 20, 2025: Van Rootselaar asks Bryant to buy her 3D printed firearm kit.

Aug. 30, 2025: Bryant assists in testing of the quality of a livestream that Van Rootselaar wanted of the planned mass shooting.

Sept. 3, 2025: Bryant encourages Van Rootselaar to get medical help.

Oct. 9, 2025: Van Rootselaar complains to Bryant about treatment in psychiatric ward, fantasizes about killing people, threatens suicide.

Oct. 10, 2025: Bryant urges Van Rootselaar to consider how her murder/suicide would affect Bryant.

Oct. 14, 2025: Bryant agrees not to “snitch” even at the moment when Van Rootselaar initiates the livestream and it becomes clear that murders are imminent.

Nov. 21, 2025: Bryant sent Van Rootselaar $124.47 via PayPal with a message that read “Happy late birthday.”

Dec. 1, 2025: Van Rootselaar and Bryant discuss how Van Rootselaar would be remembered after she follows through with her planned attack.

Dec. 12, 2025: Van Rootselaar sends Bryant photographs of various items she planned to wear during the attack.

Dec. 15, 2025: Bryant suggests that Van Rootselaar “back off” on her plan, attempts to get her to empathize with her potential victims, saying they “could be incredibly important to someone.”

Dec. 25, 2025: Bryant and Van Rootselaar discuss whether she will have “fans” after committing murders.

Jan. 4, 2026: Van Rootselaar tells Bryant that she plans to initiate attack imminently. Bryant attempts to convince Van Rootselaar to reconsider but agrees to help conduct a test-run of livestream.

Jan. 5, 2026: Bryant talks Van Rootselaar out of killing people the next day.

Jan. 6, 2026: Van Rootselaar asks Bryant if she would “snitch” if she planned to conduct the mass shooting at her former high school. Bryant acknowledged that he had previously discouraged her from conducting the attack at a school. Bryant confirms she won’t “snitch” because “people die no matter what.”

Van Rootselaar also warns Bryant that if she reports it to police, she will “start killing everyone,” including the people she lives with and the officers.

Jan. 22 - 25, 2026: Van Rootselaar discussed plan to build explosive device to detonate during the planned attack.

Jan. 25, 2026: Bryant sends $14.33 via PayPal to Van Rootselaar to purchase lighter. Van Rootselaar sends Bryant a photograph of what the fully assembled explosive device would look like.

Feb. 4, 2026: Bryant tells Van Rootselaar she does not need to follow through with the attack and that she should “think it over properly.”

Feb. 9, 2026: Van Rootselaar emphasized to Bryant how important the livestream of the attack was. Bryant agreed to assist with the broadcast.

Feb. 10, 2026: Jesse Van Rootselaar tells Bryant she is dressed for the attack, sending photos and videos of herself including with a rifle, a satchel containing the explosive device and the shoes Bryant purchased for her.

Van Rootselaar commits the mass shooting in Tumbler Ridge, B.C. She first killed her mother and brother at their home before logging into her Twitch account an initiating a 20 second livestream that showed her sitting in a vehicle with a rifle and another long gun in her lap.

Bryant assists Van Rootselaar in starting the car. She then drove to Tumbler Ridge Secondary School where she killed five children and an education assistant, injuring 27 others before turning the gun on herself.

Feb. 12, 2026: Homeland Security Investigations Special Agents interviewed Bryant at her home in Bellingham, Wash. She told the agents that she had communicated with Van Rootselaar in the months prior to the murders and had viewed the attempted livestream of the attack.

March 3, 2026: FBI Special Agents interview Bryant again at her home, where she provided additional information about the murders. She disclosed the pair had met three years prior, and had sporadic contact until about six months before the shooting, at which point they began speaking daily.

March 13, 2026: A United States magistrate judge for the Western District of Washington issued a search warrant for Bryant’s Discord account.

March 26, 2026: FBI obtain records from Discord which contain numerous communications between Bryant and Van Rootselaar in the months before the murders.

Oct. 2, 2026: A document filed in U.S. district court by an FBI special agent sets out allegations against Bryant that are the basis for the charge of conspiracy to murder persons in a foreign country.

Oct. 6, 2026: The FBI arrest Bryant at her home.

Oct. 13, 2026: Bryant is denied bail by a Seattle court.

Oct. 14, 2026: Bryant is indicted by a federal grand jury in the Western District of Washington on a charge of conspiracy to murder persons in a foreign country.

Oct. 22, 2026: Bryant enters a plea of not guilty at her arraignment in a Seattle courthouse.

Nov. 18, 2026: Bryant’s lawyers file a 33-page application in U.S. district court in Seattle for her release from jail pending the trial, claiming the 73,858 individual texts between Bryant and the shooter are protected under the First Amendment and were misconstrued by the government as it argued for her detention.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 24, 2026.

stories.title: ‘It causes anxiety’: Guide dog handlers excited by new service-dog ID cards after having difficulties in public
stories.summary: Getting through the door of a restaurant or grocery store can still be a struggle for Canadians who rely on service dogs, but several provinces are taking steps to change that, and P.E.I. is the latest.
stories.author: Maria Sarrouh
stories.content:
Summerside, P.E.I. – Getting through the door of a restaurant or grocery store can still be a struggle for Canadians who rely on service dogs, but several provinces are taking steps to change that, and P.E.I. is the latest.

Jennifer Sanderson lives with retinitis pigmentosa, a condition that affects her peripheral vision. Her guide dog, Braden, has been by her side for a little over three years helping her navigate public places safely. But sometimes, she has to explain why he’s allowed to come along.

“You just kind of like to blend into the background and be a normal person,” Sanderson said. “Go about finding what you’re trying to find, or doing what you’re trying to do, without having to stop and explain why it’s your right to be there.”

Sanderson says she’s had business owners tell her dogs aren’t allowed. She explains that Braden is a service animal protected under P.E.I.’s Human Rights Act and can accompany her into public spaces, with some exceptions, such as commercial kitchens and operating rooms.

According to research by the Cnib Foundation, which supports Canadians who are blind or partially sighted, more than half of guide dog handlers surveyed had experienced difficulties accessing public spaces.

“It’s a shame,” said Taylor Howatt, a program lead for awareness and community outreach with the non-profit, and a guide dog handler herself.

“Having that interaction … it causes anxiety. I feel different than everybody else.”

The Service Dog Act

In hopes of reducing misunderstandings and delays, P.E.I. is joining Nova Scotia and B.C. in offering voluntary provincial certification. The Island’s program is free.

Howatt says certification gives handlers another tool to advocate for themselves, but it shouldn’t become a “key to access.”

“Having to show proof of my disability to access an establishment is not fair treatment.”

Businesses can ask to see handlers’ IDs. But the province says that shouldn’t be necessary for dogs like Braden, clearly identified by their harnesses and well-behaved.

In Ontario, police can now issue $500 tickets on the spot for illegally turning away people with guide dogs, following a regulatory change earlier this year.

Sanderson has advocated for the program and hopes it will also help educate business owners about their legal obligations.

“P.E.I. is relatively small and we don’t have a huge service dog community, so that’s great for that extra awareness,” she said.

stories.title: How well do you know the Canadian national anthem?
stories.summary: The rendition of "O Canada" at the Leafs-Islanders game was a new, inadvertent, spin. But do all Canadians know the words?
stories.author: Unknown
stories.content:
The rendition of “O Canada” at Monday’s Maple Leafs-Islanders game in New York went viral when the singer accidentally replaced a few words. Some of the initial mockery turned to sympathy when the singer, Sarrah Strimel Bentley, apologized on Instagram, saying she had entered menopause because of breast cancer treatment, leading to memory lapses. She also alluded to the challenge of performing in front of 18,000 people.

It was far from the first high-profile anthem mishap at a sports event involving Canadian teams.
