stories.title: Manitoba urged to continue work on wildfire response after devastating 2025 season
stories.summary: A new report examined how Manitoba can improve its wildfire response, after millions of hectares burned in the summer of 2025.
stories.author: Tavi Dhillon, Vasilios Bellos
stories.content:
Recommendations made in a report examining the most devastating wildfire season in Manitoba history should be implemented to improve the province’s response, those affected in 2025 said.

That 2025 wildfire season saw an estimated 2.2 million hectares of Manitoba ablaze as 445 wildfires burned, resulting in two people’s deaths in Lac du Bonnet and thousands of households being evacuated. The province declared a wildfire-related state of emergency on May 28, 2025.

An independent report, released Monday, examined Manitoba’s response to those fires and the weather conditions that preceded them. It said when fire season began in mid-May, a heatwave hit and intensified already fire-prone conditions.

The report had 22 recommendations for future wildfire responses, including bettering communication with local governments during and after incidents, improving provincial legislation and addressing staffing and operational concerns. It was prepared by Brandon University in collaboration with a team from the Alberta Management Agency and support from Manitoba Emergency Management Organization.

“For many Manitobans, the 2025 wildfire season was measured in time away from home and in uncertainty,” the report said. In total, nearly 33,000 people were evacuated from 59 communities provincewide.

Lac du Bonnet was one of the communities impacted by those evacuations two summers ago. The RM of Lac du Bonnet Reeve Loren Schinkel said the report highlighted the importance of team building among governments as they manage emergency situations.

“It seems like just yesterday that we dealt with this terrible tragedy, but really, the assistance that we received from the province was remarkable,” the reeve said, recalling his first meeting with four provincial representatives who helped the community deal with the fires. “That collaborative approach really assisted in how we moved forward.”

“Our community is resilient, and it is rebuilding and we really pulled together, both from the Town of Lac du Bonnet as well as the municipality. The loss of our two residents was devastating. And they say time heals everything, but it takes a long time for a grieving community.”

Schinkel described the fight against the fast-spreading wildfire in his community in 2025 as a “remarkable group effort,” crediting the local fire service, international firefighting teams and mutual aid who descended upon his community in its time of need.

“Without that we wouldn’t have been able to save our communities,” Schinkel continued.

Ken Pickering was the president of the Whiteshell Cottagers Association when a wildfire hit in 2025, prompting an evacuation in the eastern Manitoba community.

“(During evacuations) a lot of the information doesn’t flow as quick as people would like; however, it’s a lot of information and there were a lot of things going on,” the now-past president told Global News in an interview. “It’s difficult; you don’t know what’s going on.”

Like Schinkel, Pickering said the importance of teamwork between governmental agencies, residents and people looking to help was emphasized during the wildfire, but he said he felt that communication could have been improved.

“It was a lot of unknown, what the next steps were going to be,” he said, adding that “a rough play-by-play, as to how this would roll out, I think would help a lot of people in terms of what to expect and what’s going to come next.”

He noted the importance of also improving firefighting infrastructure and said it was a positive that the Manitoba government has taken steps to do so.

In addition to reflecting on the experiences of evacuated residents, the report called on the Manitoba government to table new, updated emergency legislation to keep it in line with modern emergency situations.

The report said the special powers in the Emergency Measures Act must be revised to consistently allow local governments decision-making powers in situations like the ones many faced two summers ago.

A news release from the Manitoba government said that the province has already taken action on some of the issues identified in the report, including its work to strengthen planning, training and coordination with local and Indigenous governments ahead of future fire seasons.

“This report will help shape our approach moving forward to ensure we are better prepared to respond whenever an emergency occurs,” Transportation and Infrastructure Minister Lisa Naylor said in the release.

Concerns regarding staffing and equipment availability were also identified in the report. It found that wildfire fighters did not have the necessary staffing or tools needed to fight all of Manitoba’s fires that season, and as a result, the response partly relied on the out-of-province teams who came to assist in the response.

“The human and material resources provided by our partners were critical in protecting communities, vital infrastructure and natural resources in Manitoba,” the report said.

More than 1,500 people were estimated to have arrived in the province that season to assist in firefighting efforts, as well as incident managers and support personnel. All of those responders faced “long shifts, limited relief coverage and demanding assignments” and continued to work despite that, according to the report.

Kyle Ross is president of the Manitoba Government and General Employees’ Union (Mgeu), which represents thousands of workers who helped in the 2025 wildfire fighting effort. He told Global News that while that fire season was unexpected, seeing the province look back and reflect on the recommendations provided “can only improve what happens in the future.”

“When we had that very difficult season where they spent the whole summer fighting fires, talking to so many of those workers, they were hard to get ahold of when the season was over. They just disappeared to take a break. Many said they don’t know if they’re coming back after a summer like that,” he said.

The Manitoba government noted that it is working to hire a total of 19 additional firefighters and 15 new emergency management staff members for future responses, a move that Ross praised.

“I think the government heard Manitobans, heard the Mgeu and has done the good work that needed to be done to be ready for an earlier firefighting season,” he said.

“They recognize that there were issues in 2025 and they’ve done a fair bit to try and rectify them. There’s always more work to do, though.”

Ross added that Mgeu workers hope to continue being part of the conversation on how the response can be improved.

stories.title: Animal protection organizations call for closure of Bruce County zoo
stories.summary: On a chilly November morning, a few animals could be seen roaming their pens at the Bervie Zoological Park.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
On a chilly November morning, a few animals could be seen roaming their pens at the Bervie Zoological Park. The roadside zoo near Kincardine has been operating for more than 30 years, but many in the animal protection industry say it’s time the zoo, one they call the worst roadside zoo in Canada, either improves or closes its doors.

“I would say the conditions are very, very poor, but it’s exactly these types of dangerous animals, lions, tigers, bears, primates that are all kept in inadequate facilities, and some even missing the basic safety infrastructure that’s called for by zoo industry standards,” said Erin Ryan, Wildlife Campaign Manager with World Animal Protection Canada.

In video shot this August, and supplied by World Animal Protection Canada, tigers, lions, bears, and other animals are seen roaming their enclosures at the Bervie Zoo. World Animal Protection says 45 animals were seized from the zoo in 2022, after the zoo owners pleaded guilty to causing animals’ distress. Animal Justice Canada reports multiple animals, including two tigers, were seized by authorities recently as well.

“Chronic neglect, inadequate housing, unsanitary conditions, deteriorating infrastructure. It really doesn’t take an expert to see that things aren’t as they should be,” said Ryan.

Ryan says the video and pictures of World Animal Protection gathered this summer suggest, in their view, that conditions haven’t improved at the Bervie Zoo. They believe animal safety and health are being compromised by small, unhealthy enclosures, and visitor safety is in jeopardy, due to sub-standard cages and pens, keeping animals and visitors separate.

“This facility has had animals seized in the past, so these previous enforcement actions haven’t meant that they need to change anything or continue operating,” said Ryan.

World Animal Protection Canada says Ontario has the weakest rules when it comes to exotic animal ownership, and roadside zoos. They say you don’t need a permit or license to open a roadside zoo in Ontario, and enforcement is not adequate.

“People assume that because they’re sort of allowed to operate, that that makes it okay, and they’re relying on their government to tell them that it’s safe. But what we’ve seen in the conditions that we’ve documented and a history of injuries, escapes, attacks is that it’s not. So, people are really trusting government to regulate something like this. And in every other province they have, but unfortunately, they’re being misled,” said Ryan.

The Ministry of Solicitor General, who oversees animal welfare in Ontario, couldn’t disagree more. They say Ontario has the strongest animal welfare protections and specifically zoo standards in Canada.

“As the first jurisdiction to introduce animal welfare legislation, Ontario is proud to have some of the strictest animal welfare rules in Canada, with the toughest penalties.

“Under the Provincial Animal Welfare Services Act (Paws Act), all animals, including those kept in zoos or used for commercial, exhibition or entertainment purposes, must be cared for in accordance with established Standards of Care.

“Animal Welfare Services (AWS) inspects zoos, including the Bervie Zoo, ON a regular basis to ensure these standards are met. When concerns are identified, AWS takes the appropriate action to remedy the situation, which May include removal of animals or issuing penalties,” said Saddam Khussaini, Senior Issues Advisor with the Ministry of the Solicitor General.

We reached out to both the owners of the Bervie Zoological Park for comment on this story. We didn’t receive a response by our deadline.

“We continue to monitor and report, and we’ve had really positive conversations with the Ministry of the Solicitor General and some of the staff in that department. But what we haven’t seen is action, or even a commitment to action. And that’s something even a commitment for action is something that we hope to see by the end of the year,” said Ryan, from World Animal Protection Canada.

stories.title: Manitoba premier says no special treatment for First Nation-backed mine proposal
stories.summary: Winnipeg - Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew says First Nation support doesn't mean a mining project will get special treatment in the permitting process.
stories.author: Ian Bickis The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Winnipeg - Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew says First Nation support doesn’t mean a mining project will get special treatment in the permitting process.

His comment comes a day after Black River First Nation Chief Sheldon Kent said he intends to go ahead with Sio Silica on a project east of Winnipeg, whether the province gives a licence or not.

stories.title: London Food Bank receives major boost as Libro Credit Union staff direct charitable funds
stories.summary: The London Food Bank is a significant beneficiary of Libro Credit Union’s innovative community investment strategy.
stories.author: Gerry Dewan
stories.content:
The London Food Bank is a significant beneficiary of Libro Credit Union’s innovative community investment strategy.

The Food Bank received a substantial $27,500 donation directly chosen by Libro employees. This contribution is part of a larger $600,000 initiative where Libro empowered its staff and board members across Ontario to direct charitable funds to organizations they believe are making a critical difference.

The London Food Bank emerged as a top London-region selection within Libro’s employee-driven program, with 55 staff members choosing it to receive their portion of the donation. Leaders at the food bank emphasize that such cash contributions are vital for bolstering their operations beyond donated goods.

Jan Roy, Co-Executive Director of the London Food Bank, explained the critical role these funds play.

“I think what it allows us to do is it helps fill in the gap,” Roy stated.

“So, it helps fill in the gaps for things like produce. Or if we’re purchasing canned goods at the times, when we know things aren’t coming in. And I think the other big thing a lot of the support that goes to other agencies.”

Libro Credit Union’s unique approach involved providing every employee and board member with $500 to donate to an eligible registered charity or not-for-profit organization of their choice. This special one-time initiative, which totals $600,000, is in addition to Libro’s budgeted community investment dollars for 2026.

The program was designed to reflect the credit union’s co-operative values and its commitment to sharing success within the communities it serves, especially following its Jan. 1 merger with Kawartha Credit Union.

“Our success in 2026 reflects the commitment of our people every day, and we wanted to find a meaningful way to share that success with the communities we serve,” said Shawn Good, President and CEO of Libro Credit Union.

“As a co-operative, we believe our success should benefit the communities where we live and work. Our people know those communities firsthand, and by putting this investment in their hands, they’ve helped direct support where it can make a real difference.”

Libro’s Purpose Integration Director, Liz Arkinstall, and Community Manager, Laura Husser, shared the positive news on Tuesday afternoon, highlighting the employee-led nature of the giving.

The London region received a total of $140,000 from the initiative, with contributions also directed to other vital agencies like the United Way, 519 Pursuit, and Anova.

Across Ontario, the $600,000 investment supported 120 organizations working on a range of causes, including Indigenous reconciliation, food and housing security, youth services, and employment. A combined $50,000 was allocated to organizations supporting Indigenous communities and reconciliation, including a $20,000 donation to the Gord Downie & Chanie Wenjack Fund.

stories.title: New P.E.I. service-dog ID cards aim to stop guide dog users from being turned away
stories.summary: Getting through the door of a restaurant or grocery store can still be a struggle for Canadians who rely on service dogs, but several provinces are taking steps to change that, and P.E.I. is the latest.
stories.author: Maria Sarrouh
stories.content:
Summerside, P.E.I. – Getting through the door of a restaurant or grocery store can still be a struggle for Canadians who rely on service dogs, but several provinces are taking steps to change that, and P.E.I. is the latest.

Jennifer Sanderson lives with retinitis pigmentosa, a condition that affects her peripheral vision. Her guide dog, Braden, has been by her side for a little over three years helping her navigate public places safely. But sometimes, she has to explain why he’s allowed to come along.

“You just kind of like to blend into the background and be a normal person,” Sanderson said. “Go about finding what you’re trying to find, or doing what you’re trying to do, without having to stop and explain why it’s your right to be there.”

Sanderson says she’s had business owners tell her dogs aren’t allowed. She explains that Braden is a service animal protected under P.E.I.’s Human Rights Act and can accompany her into public spaces, with some exceptions, such as commercial kitchens and operating rooms.

According to research by the Cnib Foundation, which supports Canadians who are blind or partially sighted, more than half of guide dog handlers surveyed had experienced difficulties accessing public spaces.

“It’s a shame,” said Taylor Howatt, a program lead for awareness and community outreach with the non-profit, and a guide dog handler herself.

“Having that interaction … it causes anxiety. I feel different than everybody else.”

The Service Dog Act

In hopes of reducing misunderstandings and delays, P.E.I. is joining Nova Scotia and B.C. in offering voluntary provincial certification. The Island’s program is free.

Howatt says certification gives handlers another tool to advocate for themselves, but it shouldn’t become a “key to access.”

“Having to show proof of my disability to access an establishment is not fair treatment.”

Businesses can ask to see handlers’ IDs. But the province says that shouldn’t be necessary for dogs like Braden, clearly identified by their harnesses and well-behaved.

In Ontario, police can now issue $500 tickets on the spot for illegally turning away people with guide dogs, following a regulatory change earlier this year.

Sanderson has advocated for the program and hopes it will also help educate business owners about their legal obligations.

“P.E.I. is relatively small and we don’t have a huge service dog community, so that’s great for that extra awareness,” she said.

stories.title: Oil money helped N.L.'s debt, but experts say the province still needs a plan
stories.summary: ST. John's - An oil windfall has helped the Newfoundland and Labrador government reduce its sizable debt, but some experts say the province still needs a long-term plan to pay off the balance.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
ST. John’s - An oil windfall has helped the Newfoundland and Labrador government reduce its sizable debt, but some experts say the province still needs a long-term plan to pay off the balance.

A comparison of budgets and financial updates across Canada shows Newfoundland and Labrador’s per-capita net debt is expected to be the highest among the provinces for the current fiscal year, which ends in March.

Economist Wade Locke said the provincial government would have to have a budget surplus of roughly $350 million a year for the next three decades to bring its per-capita net debt down to the Canadian average. That’s assuming a constant interest rate of about 3.6 per cent, he said in an interview Tuesday.

“The problem is so massive. It’s going to require a huge effort and a well laid-out plan,” said Locke, a retired professor at Memorial University. “It’s not just a matter of picking numbers off a spreadsheet.”

That plan should include changes to legislation requiring subsequent governments to follow through with it, particularly since reigning in spending and reducing debt are not popular policies, he added.

Newfoundland and Labrador’s Progressive Conservative government delivered an economic update on Monday projecting a surplus of $78 million at the end of the 2026-27 fiscal year and a reduced net debt. It was a sharp contrast to the budget tabled in April which forecast a $688 million deficit.

The province’s net debt is now expected to reach $19.3 billion by the end of March, rather than the $20.8 billion laid out in the budget.

About $1.2 billion — or just under 10 per cent of the province’s entire budget — will have to pay for debt servicing costs, including interest.

Government officials said the new numbers were driven by nearly $1.5 billion in extra revenue, most of which comes from the soaring oil prices that followed military strikes against Iran by the U.S. and Israel earlier this year. Newfoundland and Labrador is home to four offshore oil installations, and production is up at all of them, Craig Pardy, the province’s finance minister, told reporters in St. John’s on Monday.

Pardy had previously promised to deliver a debt management plan with his fall fiscal update. On Monday, he announced a $175-million investment into a new sinking fund, which officials said would mature to $750 million by 2052 and be used to pay off debt.

Locke noted the sinking fund money would only cover about four per cent of what the province currently owes.

Pardy said Monday that the province’s gross domestic product is expected to grow this fiscal year by 7.1 per cent, a number that leads the country. He also pointed to possible returns from Equinor’s proposed Bay du Nord offshore oil project and a new energy agreement with Quebec, neither of which have been finalized.

But Renaud Brossard said the anticipated economic activity May not be enough to counter some of the headwinds facing the province. One in four people in Newfoundland and Labrador are 65 or older, and seniors tend to pay fewer taxes and need more health care, said Brossard, who is the vice president of communications for the Montreal Economic Institute think tank

“There absolutely needs to be a debt management plan,” Brossard said in an interview.

In a news release Tuesday, the Canadian Taxpayers Federation applauded the Newfoundland and Labrador government’s move to squirrel away much of its oil windfall rather than spend it. Both Locke and Brossard had similar praise.

However, in an email, Devin Drover, the federation’s Atlantic director, acknowledged Pardy’s fiscal update on Monday delivered debt reduction, but not a “debt management plan per se.”

“Taxpayers still owe … over $19 billion, and that bill comes due whether oil prices co-operate or not,” Drover said.

He suggested the province introduce legislation requiring that windfall money be used to pay off debt. He also said the province needs to make clear debt-reduction targets and reign in spending.

“If the government locks that in, this year’s progress becomes a turning point instead of a one-off,” Drover said.

paragraphs: ST. John’s - An oil windfall has helped the Newfoundland and Labrador government reduce its sizable debt, but some experts say the province still needs a long-term plan to pay off the balance.

A comparison of budgets and financial updates across Canada shows Newfoundland and Labrador’s per-capita net debt is expected to be the highest among the provinces for the current fiscal year, which ends in March.

Economist Wade Locke said the provincial government would have to have a budget surplus of roughly $350 million a year for the next three decades to bring its per-capita net debt down to the Canadian average. That’s assuming a constant interest rate of about 3.6 per cent, he said in an interview Tuesday.

“The problem is so massive. It’s going to require a huge effort and a well laid-out plan,” said Locke, a retired professor at Memorial University. “It’s not just a matter of picking numbers off a spreadsheet.”

That plan should include changes to legislation requiring subsequent governments to follow through with it, particularly since reigning in spending and reducing debt are not popular policies, he added.

Newfoundland and Labrador’s Progressive Conservative government delivered an economic update on Monday projecting a surplus of $78 million at the end of the 2026-27 fiscal year and a reduced net debt. It was a sharp contrast to the budget tabled in April which forecast a $688 million deficit.
The province’s net debt is now expected to reach $19.3 billion by the end of March, rather than the $20.8 billion laid out in the budget.
About $1.2 billion — or just under 10 per cent of the province’s entire budget — will have to pay for debt servicing costs, including interest.

Government officials said the new numbers were driven by nearly $1.5 billion in extra revenue, most of which comes from the soaring oil prices that followed military strikes against Iran by the U.S. and Israel earlier this year. Newfoundland and Labrador is home to four offshore oil installations, and production is up at all of them, Craig Pardy, the province’s finance minister, told reporters in St. John’s on Monday.

Pardy had previously promised to deliver a debt management plan with his fall fiscal update. On Monday, he announced a $175-million investment into a new sinking fund, which officials said would mature to $750 million by 2052 and be used to pay off debt.
Locke noted the sinking fund money would only cover about four per cent of what the province currently owes.

Pardy said Monday that the province’s gross domestic product is expected to grow this fiscal year by 7.1 per cent, a number that leads the country. He also pointed to possible returns from Equinor’s proposed Bay du Nord offshore oil project and a new energy agreement with Quebec, neither of which have been finalized.

But Renaud Brossard said the anticipated economic activity May not be enough to counter some of the headwinds facing the province. One in four people in Newfoundland and Labrador are 65 or older, and seniors tend to pay fewer taxes and need more health care, said Brossard, who is the vice president of communications for the Montreal Economic Institute think tank
“There absolutely needs to be a debt management plan,” Brossard said in an interview.

In a news release Tuesday, the Canadian Taxpayers Federation applauded the Newfoundland and Labrador government’s move to squirrel away much of its oil windfall rather than spend it. Both Locke and Brossard had similar praise.
However, in an email, Devin Drover, the federation’s Atlantic director, acknowledged Pardy’s fiscal update on Monday delivered debt reduction, but not a “debt management plan per se.”
“Taxpayers still owe … over $19 billion, and that bill comes due whether oil prices co-operate or not,” Drover said.
He suggested the province introduce legislation requiring that windfall money be used to pay off debt. He also said the province needs to make clear debt-reduction targets and reign in spending.
“If the government locks that in, this year’s progress becomes a turning point instead of a one-off,” Drover said.

The previous Liberal government introduced a “future fund” with mandatory annual contributions to help pay off debt. The Progressive Conservatives axed the annual requirement rules earlier this year, saying it didn’t make sense to borrow more for the fund.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 24, 2026.

stories.title: Canada and Qatar sign agreement to boost investment
stories.summary: Canada and Qatar have signed a new agreement that looks to encourage increased investment, despite widespread criticism of Qatar’s human rights record.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — Canada and Qatar have signed a new agreement that looks to encourage increased investment, despite widespread criticism of Qatar’s human rights record.

Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand and her Qatari counterpart Dr. Ahmad bin Mohammed Al-Sayed signed the Canada-Qatar Foreign Investment Promotion and Protection Agreement in Ottawa on Tuesday.

International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu, who led negotiations on the agreement, said he’s proud to see the deal signed because it means more Qatari investment in Canada and more opportunities for Canadian businesses in Qatar.

Sidhu said in a media statement that Qatar’s economy is worth nearly $300 billion. He said the Qatar Investment Authority is one of the world’s largest sovereign wealth funds, with nearly US$600 billion in assets.

Canada and Qatar’s bilateral trade exceeds $350 million, said Sidhu, who added that foreign direct investment from Qatar has reached $338 million.

“With this agreement, we’re going to grow that figure,” he said. “The opportunity here is real.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney visited Doha in January, becoming the first sitting Canadian prime minister to visit Qatar. He made the trip after visiting Beijing.

Conservative MP Shuv Majumdar chided Carney on the platform X over his outreach to both China and Qatar, citing their dire human rights records and past support for Canada’s adversaries.

“They traffic in the worst elements of the world because they turn these assets they’ve built up into the indispensable dependencies,” Majumdar said. He said Canada should instead boost trade ties with Taiwan and Arab countries that have normalized relations with Israel.

Human Rights Watch still raises numerous concerns about Qatar, citing slave labour resulting in migrant work deaths, restrictions on free expression and increasing surveillance.

The country chafed at widespread criticism of its treatment of migrant workers and its human rights record in the lead-up to its 2022 hosting of the Fifa World Cup. During that event, Qatar’s officials barred the entry of articles of clothing with rainbows — including items without Lgbtq+ themes.

Sidhu was in Qatar just ahead of Carney’s visit. Sidhu said while he was in Doha, he pitched Canadian projects to the Qatar Investment Authority and the two countries agreed to launch a Canada-Qatar business council.

“The Gulf is one of the most important regions in the world as we work to attract $1 trillion in new investment to Canada and double our non-U.S. exports over the next decade,” said Sidhu. “That investment will build major projects here at home. And it will create good-paying jobs for Canadian workers.”

“We’re moving fast to diversify our trade relationships and build a stronger, more resilient Canadian economy, and this agreement is another step forward.”

Qatar has said it serves as a mediator in international talks with the Taliban. The Taliban have maintained a political office in Qatar for years, including during the period immediately prior to their takeover of Afghanistan in 2021.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 24, 2026.

-With files from Dylan Robertson, Kyle Duggan and The Associated Press

Catherine Morrison, The Canadian Press

stories.title: First Nations in B.C. to acquire stake in Coastal GasLink pipeline
stories.summary: Deal represents a stake of 11% in the TC Energy entity that partially owns the line
stories.author: Aya Dufour, Jameson Berkow
stories.content:
A group of 12 First Nations in northern B.C. is making a substantial investment in the TC Energy entity behind the Coastal GasLink pipeline, according to industry and First Nations sources.

The deal represents a stake of 11 per cent in the TC entity that holds a 35-per-cent ownership interest in the line, which carries natural gas from Dawson Creek to Kitimat in northern B.C., the two sources said.

KKR & Co. and the Alberta Investment Management Corporation hold the remaining 65-per-cent equity stake in the pipeline. They are not involved in the deal.

The Canada Indigenous Loan Guarantee Corporation (Cilgc) is providing a $168-million guarantee to the group of First Nations as part of the deal, the sources said.

First Nations are expected to announce the financial investment in Vancouver on Thursday, the sources added. Spokespeople for Finance Canada and Natural Resources Canada declined to comment on Tuesday.

The Globe and Mail is not identifying the sources as they were not authorized to discuss the matter publicly.

Ottawa’s fall budget had teased an upcoming announcement for the $10-billion Cilgc fund, stating negotiations were under way for a loan on an oil and gas project that would give multiple First Nations communities a direct stake in major energy infrastructure.

Because federal law restricts Indigenous communities from using their land as collateral, they often face barriers to borrowing. The Cilgc was set up to help bridge that gap, enabling communities to secure private-sector loans at interest rates comparable to non-Indigenous borrowers.

Last year, Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government directed the Cilgc to prioritize applications for projects referred by the Major Projects Office, which helps co-ordinate financing for projects singled out by Ottawa.

The Coastal GasLink pipeline is not under the wing of the Major Projects Office, but the planned expansion of the facility it supplies – LNG Canada – was among the first to land on the desk of the special government agency in September 2025.

Mr. Carney and Energy Minister Tim Hodgson have championed LNG expansion by setting a 2050 target of 100 million tonnes per annum in export capacity, up from the current 14 million tonnes per annum currently exported out of the LNG Canada facility in Kitimat.

That facility started shipments in 2025 and represents the first, and so far, only large-scale export terminal in the country.

In September, TC Energy unveiled a $4.9-billion plan to double the existing capacity of the 670-kilometre Coastal GasLink pipeline by adding new compressor stations and upgrading facilities.

The move was prompted by LNG Canada’s decision to expand and double production to 28 million tonnes per annum.

LNG Canada is shepherding the pipeline expansion plans, having signed commercial agreements about taking on front-end engineering and design responsibilities with TC in March.

Cost overruns have historically dogged Coastal GasLink, which cost $14.5-billion to build, compared with an earlier price tag of $6.2-billion in 2018 when construction began.

One source said the investment to be announced Thursday was set up in a way that would shield First Nations from some of the financial risks tied to the expansion of the pipeline.

This is the second First Nation consortium to announce an investment in Coastal GasLink, after TC Energy announced in October it had reached a deal with Haisla Nation, Halfway River First Nation, McLeod Lake Indian Band, Saulteau First Nations and West Moberly First Nations for a $65-million equity stake.

It announced at the time that another Indigenous transaction was well under way and was expected to close before year’s end.

In 2022, TC signed equity option agreements with 20 Indigenous communities along the project corridor.

stories.title: Civil liberties group says digital safety bill risks censorship, 'shadow banning'
stories.summary: Ottawa - The Canadian Civil Liberties Association says the Liberal government’s digital safety bill could lead to the censorship of some online content.
stories.author: Anja Karadeglija The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - The Canadian Civil Liberties Association says the Liberal government’s digital safety bill could lead to the censorship of some online content.

Association representatives told a parliamentary committee studying the bill Tuesday that includes the risk of “shadow banning,” or limiting the visibility of someone’s online content.

Anaïs Bussières McNicoll, director of the group’s fundamental freedoms program, told MPs the bill “creates a framework that leaves users of all ages vulnerable to various forms of censorship, including shadow banning.”

Bussières McNicoll said online platforms keen to avoid fines could disproportionately suppress controversial but lawful expression.

Some of the proposed definitions of harmful content in the bill are “overly broad and vague and can on their face capture nonviolent, nonthreatening expression that is unpopular, polarized, or political,” she said.

Platforms should have to assess on an ongoing basis whether their measures pose risks to charter rights, especially expression and privacy rights, Bussières McNicoll said.

“The bill creates a broad obligation for operators of regulated social media services to mitigate the risks that users will be exposed to harmful content,” she said. “While this new duty does not require operators to disproportionately limit expression, it fails to prohibit them from doing so.”

Bussières McNicoll said the bill “gives sweeping powers to a new digital safety regulator and the government, leaving it to them to determine an enormous range of substantive questions through future regulations.”

She said that makes it especially important to strengthen the regulator’s independence and require its members to have subject matter expertise in multiple areas, including “freedom of expression, privacy, and other implicated civil liberties.”

Conservative MPs have been flagging free speech concerns with Bill C-34, which would create the new digital regulator, impose new requirements on platforms and ban kids under 16 from access to social media.

Tamir Israel, director of the Canadian Civil Liberties Association’s privacy, surveillance and technology program, said the bill’s age ban puts the emphasis in the wrong place.

He said the government should focus on building an empowering digital environment for youth instead of “banishing them from the internet.”

Israel and other experts have warned the social media ban is likely to face a charter challenge.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 24, 2026.

stories.title: Fact File: Cruise line didn't cite homelessness for decision to end Halifax stops
stories.summary: A claim spread online last week that a cruise line's decision to cancel stops in Halifax resulted from passenger complaints about being confronted by people who were homeless. Online users cited a Daily Mail story about the cancellations that claimed passengers complained of encountering a "zombie apocalypse" in the port city.
stories.author: Timon Johnson The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A claim spread online last week that a cruise line’s decision to cancel stops in Halifax resulted from passenger complaints about being confronted by people who were homeless.

Online users cited a Daily Mail story about the cancellations that claimed passengers complained of encountering a “zombie apocalypse” in the port city.

Norwegian Cruise Line said its decision to add an extra night in Bermuda rather than sailing to the Nova Scotia capital was a response to “guest feedback,” but it never described the nature of the feedback. Norwegian continues to stop in Halifax on other cruise itineraries, as do other cruise operators, who say they have received positive feedback from passengers.

After the website Cruise Fever reported on Nov. 16 about the change to Norwegian Cruise Line’s Bermuda itinerary for next year, some people on X speculated that it was because passengers had unpleasant experiences in downtown Halifax.

Halifax - A Norwegian cruise line has dropped 17 stops in Halifax next year in favour of more time in Bermuda, saying the cancellations were i…

In a post the next day on the Daily Mail’s X account, the newspaper linked to its reporter’s story about the cancellations. “Norwegian Cruise Lines axes 17 Nova Scotia trips as guests complain Halifax is now ‘zombie apocalypse’ hellscape filled with vagrants,” the post said.

In the story, the reporter drew a connection between the cruise line’s cancellation of the Halifax trips and the city’s homeless population.

It included quotes from social media users described in the story as “travellers,” sharing their thoughts and experiences about the city.

“I am sure it has nothing to do with the zombie apocalypse they stumble across when they find the downtown east side,” one person quoted in the story said. Many online users later repeated the term “zombie apocalypse” in their own posts on X, Instagram, and Facebook.

“When tourists start choosing to avoid Canadian cities, it says something about the state of our country,” one user said in a post that had received over 120,000 views as of Nov. 23.

Before the change, the cruise line’s seven-night itinerary for the Norwegian Breakaway sailing from Boston included a stop in Halifax before heading to Bermuda.

In an emailed statement, a Norwegian Cruise Line spokesperson said the decision to cancel the Halifax stop was in response to unspecified “guest feedback.”

The spokesperson said Bermuda schedules have been changed next year to give passengers “more time to explore the island.” The company’s Canada and New England cruises will continue to stop in Halifax in 2027 and 2028.

In a public Facebook group for people travelling with Norwegian Cruise Line, the change received mixed reactions: most welcomed the extra time in Bermuda but others were disappointed they wouldn’t visit Halifax. None of the commenters mentioned the city’s homeless population.

Other cruise operators that stop in Halifax said they have not heard complaints. “Our guests consistently share positive feedback about their time in the city,” said Andrea Zito, CEO of Swan Hellenic Cruises.

John Waggoner, the chairman of Victory Cruise Lines, said Halifax is becoming increasingly popular among its passengers. “We are expanding our presence in Halifax with additional calls and the introduction of dedicated Halifax round-trip voyages,” he said in an emailed statement.

A search of quotes in the Daily Mail story reveals they were drawn from comments left by online users on the Cruise Fever post that first reported the itinerary change. That post referred to Norwegian cancelling visits to “a Canadian port of call.”

One example was a user who said she was based in British Columbia and wrote: “I am sure it has nothing to do with the zombie apocalypse they stumble across when they find the downtown east side.” While Halifax does not have a neighbourhood known as the downtown east side, Vancouver’s Downtown Eastside has a reputation for problems of homelessness and drug use.

Another user, who said he is from rural Saskatchewan and had recently visited Halifax on the cruise, did raise homelessness as an issue. “The touristy stops in Halifax were fine. If you got out and walked about downtown, the amount of street people was uncomfortable,” he said. “Oddly walking around downtown Boston actually felt safer.”

Other commenters quoted in the Daily Mail did not say they had been passengers on the Halifax cruise.

Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston denounced the Daily Mail story on his X account.

“Millions of visitors annually who come here to see all the wonderful things the city has to offer. I’m down enjoying the city’s waterfront often. This is a garbage story quoting random anonymous Twitter accounts to create a clickbait headline,” he said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 24, 2026.

Note to readers:This is a corrected story. The comment from Victory Cruise Lines should have been attributed to company chairman John Waggoner.

stories.title: DNA technology advancements solved the Dunleavy cold case and could help others: expert
stories.summary: Investigators have used new DNA technology and advancements to solve the 1968 cold case on Jacqueline Dunleavy...
stories.author: Owen Schuller
stories.content:
Jacqueline Bunleavy. Photo Credit: Owen Schuller

Investigators have used new DNA technology and advancements to solve the 1968 cold case on Jacqueline Dunleavy.

London police were able to solve this 58 year old homicide case by using old evidence collected at the crime scene and using new advanced DNA technologies.

Former cop, teacher and author Mike Arntfield shows great respect for those investigating the case.

“Significant respect for the fact that they continue to take this case very seriously and leverage the latest forensic technology, investigative genetic genealogy.”

Mike Arntfield. Photo Credit: https://michaelarntfield.com/

Arntfield describes how the new technology works and how it use to work.

“What this new technology does is it harvests DNA from direct to consumer home DNA kits that are shared on consent by the consumers.”

“You would need a one-to-one match but that would require that somebody got put into the databank because they got arrested. A number of these offenders eluded authorities and were never identified.”

As a result of the new DNA technologies, investigators were able to connect Michael Joseph Moore as the man who is responsible for the death of Jacqueline Dunleavy. Moore was 25 at the time of the murder, and passed away in 2018.

Michael Joseph Moore. Photo Credit: Owen Schuller

As the new advancement in technology has solved this case, Arntfield has hope for other cold cases getting solved.

“We’re really at sort of a new frontier in terms of cold case technology to the point that, certainly moving forward, I don’t see any cases really going cold anymore.”

Arntfield’s book was written 10 years ago and Jacqueline’s cold case was a part of book.

“This was a case foregrounded in that book ( Murder City ) that looks at the 25-year dark history of London as the serial killer capital of North American per capita.”

Arntfield says this case is very good for teaching purposes.

Murder City Book: Photo Credit: Amazon Selling Page

“This is a remarkable case study for teaching purposes. Students will learn how in 1968 before DNA was even on anyone’s radar and detectives exhibited tremendous crime scene work, how they preserved that sample for the future.”

At a police press conference the London police chief Thai Truong expresses that every victim matters.

“Every victim’s life matters, regardless of who they are, who their family is, or their circumstances,”

While justice for Jacqueline Dunleavy came almost six decades later, investigators hope the new advancement in DNA will help bring justice to the other cold cases in London.

stories.title: Ford defends Chow, Del Duca using strong powers as critics raise alarms
stories.summary: While Premier Doug Ford is lauding the use of strong powers, critics are concerned wielding newly expanded authority ends up circumventing democratic processes.
stories.author: Olivia Bowden
stories.content:
Newly anointed with strong mayor and chair powers handed down by the Ford government, Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow and York Region Chair Steven Del Duca have used their supercharged authority this week to restructure their leadership teams.

While Premier Doug Ford is lauding their use of the strong powers, critics are concerned wielding newly expanded authority ends up circumventing democratic processes and ultimately will serve the wants of the province. Chow’s own NDP party is among those raising concerns.

“I am very concerned about the use of strong mayor powers,” said NDP Leader Marit Stiles on Tuesday. “I absolutely think there is no excuse for using those strong mayor powers the way they are doing,” she said.

In Ontario, 216 municipalities have been granted “strong mayor powers” as of May 2025. It allows mayors to dismiss or appoint top city officials, veto or introduce some by-laws and propose the municipal budget.

Strong chair powers were introduced across eight regions in the province, including Durham, Halton and Peel, and mirror “strong mayor powers.” The Ford government appointed regional chairs in November, hand-picking those chairs when previously, they were elected.

Chow used strong mayor powers Monday to replace Toronto’s City manager and two deputy City managers.

Del Duca fired the top public servant in York Region Monday using strong chair powers. The decision, sources in the region said, was met with widespread shock.

He is also the mayor of Vaughan and has strong mayor powers at his disposal as well.

Chow told reporters Monday that she used the strong powers to align with a new mandate she’s putting forward in order to deliver better services for residents. While she’s criticized strong mayor powers in the past for being undemocratic, she defended her use of them Monday, stating she didn’t override any council decisions.

While Stiles said she has “no regrets” in endorsing Chow, who recently began her second term as Toronto’s mayor, she said she would speak to her about recently invoking strong mayor powers.

“What I’m hearing the most concern is the appointment of these regional chairs,” she said. “The government is appointing their own people, and they’re clearly doing their bidding… Doug Ford can’t stand democracy.”

Former interim Liberal Leader John Fraser also called the newly appointed regional chairs an “assault on democracy.”

“These powers and these regional chairs are just the premier creating these positions in his own image and likeness,” said Fraser.

Ford said that he’s “not surprised at all” that Chow used strong mayor powers, because “she’s in charge.”

“If she wants to do that and bring in another person, good luck to her,” he said.

It’s Chow who will be held accountable for decisions Toronto makes, not other officials, which is the “reason we put (strong mayor powers) in place,” he said.

“We continue to have a great relationship and I’ll continue working with Mayor Chow any way I can,” he said.

stories.title: Csis to ‘significantly’ increase foreign spy presence with new $6 billion funding
stories.summary: The average annual increase of roughly $600 million is a whopping 60 per cent boost from the spy agency's $1 billion budget this year.
stories.author: Christopher Nardi
stories.content:
Ottawa — Csis says it will use a historic influx of cash in the latest federal budget to significantly increase its presence abroad and in the Canadian North as the Liberals prepare to give the spy agency more foreign espionage powers.

In last month’s budget, the Liberals announced they would boost the Canadian Security Intelligence Service’s (Csis) budget by $6 billion over 10 years. The average annual increase of roughly $600 million is a whopping 60 per cent boost from the spy agency’s $1 billion budget this year.

Since then, questions have swirled among national security watchers as to what Csis will do with the new money as the Liberal government prepares a new intelligence-focused national security strategy.

Csis declined National Post’s request for an interview with Director Dan Rogers. But in a statement, spokesperson Magali Hébert provided high-level details of planned spending ahead of the strategy’s release.

Monday - Thursday (Subscriber exclusive edition Saturday) Free

First Reading is your guide to the world of Canadian politics, curated by the National Post's own Tristin Hopper. We break the news, define the issues and analyze what matters. Published Mondays through Thursdays at 6:30 p.m. (Subscriber exclusive Saturday edition, noon)

Overall, the money will be used to boost Csis’s ability to collect intelligence and counter threats, but also accelerate its hiring and update its “aging infrastructure,” she said.

Most notably, Hébert confirmed it would serve to substantially bolster the spy agency’s foreign and Northern operations.

“These improvements will be enabled by a significantly increased Csis presence abroad which will diversify and strengthen Canada’s global intelligence partnerships, as well as through an increased regional presence and capacity within Canada, including in Canada’s north,” Hébert said.

As a domestic human intelligence agency, Csis has always been coy about discussing its foreign operations. The Csis Act limits the service’s activities to curbing threats to the security of Canada, and many of its powers are limited to actions “within Canada.”

It has only publicly reported operating a few foreign stations in cities where it liaises openly with other intelligence agencies, such as Washington, D.C. and London, U.K.

But national security watchers say the agency has upped its foreign activities in recent years as it takes a more expansive view of its legal authorities to prevent terrorist and security threats against Canadians in Canada.

In recent weeks, the Liberal government has promised to go a step further. Earlier this month, a top national security official said the government was working on a bill that would give Csis more power to spy abroad as well as expand its mandate to protecting Canada’s economic security.

“There will be legislative change that is going to be needed in order to be able to provide (Csis) with an extra five, 10 per cent of what their collection can be,” top Privy Council office intelligence official Dominic Rochon said on Nov. 6.

He argued that expanding Csis’s foreign activities should start with giving the agency more incremental authorities and allow it to develop foreign human intelligence training programs.

In her statement, Hébert confirmed that Csis will also take on a bigger role in screening for economic threats. The boost comes as Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government continues wheeling and dealing with foreign countries in the hopes of weaning Canada’s export market from dependence on the United States.

Speaking to MPs on the Procedure and House Affairs committee Tuesday, Csis executive Jarrett Davis said that the agency was “quite excited” about the significant investment.

He added that the new funding would allow the agency to generate more intelligence and lessen its dependence on partner agencies, such as the Five Eyes alliance.

“These investments will allow Csis to develop a more sovereign capability and become less reliant on partner information,” Davis told MPs.

“Csis intends to translate this significant investment into capacity at a rapid pace and at a pace that is needed to match the demands of the threat environment that we’re dealing with.”

Hébert also said in her statement that Csis plans on boosting its efforts to combat foreign interference in elections as well as transnational repression.

In its latest annual report, the spy agency said China, India, Russia and Iran were the biggest threat actors in that space.

Speaking to the committee Tuesday, Public Safety’s assistant deputy minister Richard Bilodeau said the government had implemented 80 per cent of the recommendations by the 2025 Public Inquiry into Foreign Interference.

But threat actors are constantly changing how they work to influence Canada’s elections and ply its democratic institutions, he added.

“Threat actors are adapting their methods. New technologies are making influence activities faster, cheaper, and harder to attribute,” said Bilodeau.

Christopher Nardi is a senior parliamentary reporter in Ottawa. He has worked in both French and English media, speaks Italian and writes about politics, national security, justice and how things work (or don't) in government. Reach him on Signal: ChrisNardi.01 cnardi@postmedia.com

“These improvements will be enabled by a significantly increased Csis presence abroad which will diversify and strengthen Canada’s global intelligence partnerships, as well as through an increased regional presence and capacity within Canada, including in Canada’s north,” Hébert said.

As a domestic human intelligence agency, Csis has always been coy about discussing its foreign operations. The Csis Act limits the service’s activities to curbing threats to the security of Canada, and many of its powers are limited to actions “within Canada.”
It has only publicly reported operating a few foreign stations in cities where it liaises openly with other intelligence agencies, such as Washington, D.C. and London, U.K.

But national security watchers say the agency has upped its foreign activities in recent years as it takes a more expansive view of its legal authorities to prevent terrorist and security threats against Canadians in Canada.

In recent weeks, the Liberal government has promised to go a step further. Earlier this month, a top national security official said the government was working on a bill that would give Csis more power to spy abroad as well as expand its mandate to protecting Canada’s economic security.

“There will be legislative change that is going to be needed in order to be able to provide (Csis) with an extra five, 10 per cent of what their collection can be,” top Privy Council office intelligence official Dominic Rochon said on Nov. 6.
He argued that expanding Csis’s foreign activities should start with giving the agency more incremental authorities and allow it to develop foreign human intelligence training programs.

In her statement, Hébert confirmed that Csis will also take on a bigger role in screening for economic threats. The boost comes as Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government continues wheeling and dealing with foreign countries in the hopes of weaning Canada’s export market from dependence on the United States.
Speaking to MPs on the Procedure and House Affairs committee Tuesday, Csis executive Jarrett Davis said that the agency was “quite excited” about the significant investment.
He added that the new funding would allow the agency to generate more intelligence and lessen its dependence on partner agencies, such as the Five Eyes alliance.
“These investments will allow Csis to develop a more sovereign capability and become less reliant on partner information,” Davis told MPs.
“Csis intends to translate this significant investment into capacity at a rapid pace and at a pace that is needed to match the demands of the threat environment that we’re dealing with.”
Hébert also said in her statement that Csis plans on boosting its efforts to combat foreign interference in elections as well as transnational repression.
In its latest annual report, the spy agency said China, India, Russia and Iran were the biggest threat actors in that space.

Speaking to the committee Tuesday, Public Safety’s assistant deputy minister Richard Bilodeau said the government had implemented 80 per cent of the recommendations by the 2025 Public Inquiry into Foreign Interference.
But threat actors are constantly changing how they work to influence Canada’s elections and ply its democratic institutions, he added.
“Threat actors are adapting their methods. New technologies are making influence activities faster, cheaper, and harder to attribute,” said Bilodeau.

stories.title: Woman who died in Squamish boating tragedy loved life, animals, family says
stories.summary: Friends say Femke Visser, a local horse guide and dogsled guide, had gone out with neighbours to help animals and people stranded by the floodwater.
stories.author: Amy Judd, Taya Fast
stories.content:
Friends and family of a woman killed in a boating accident in Squamish are raising money to bring her body home to the Netherlands .

Femke Visser was one of three people who were killed on Nov. 12 in the Squamish Valley.

Five other people were rescued.

Friends say Visser, a local horse guide and dogsled guide, had gone out with neighbours to help animals and people stranded by the floodwater.

She leaves behind her mother Mieke, her father Henk, her sister Marieke, her dog Baloo and friends around the world.

“What really inspired her was after her schooling in high school, she wanted to travel,” Mieki Koekkoek said.

“And then she went to Curaçao and she met a lot of people… but she was always very much interested in horses.”

Friend Josh Reimer said he met Visser while working on a horse ranch in the Chilcotin region of B.C.

“What I noticed about her when she first came in was her, just, sheer excitement to be outside and out in the open where we were,” he said.

“Um, it was pretty far from anything, so it was pretty wild and she just seemed to love that feeling of being out, out in there.”

Reimer said Visser always treated every horse with kindness and worked to have a connection with them.

“Just in general, in the wildlife, that was her church, I would say, where she really felt that was her home; it was in the wild,” he said.

Maya Rose Anders met Visser in Squamish and told Global News that she wasn’t surprised to hear that Visser was trying to help animals when she died.

Reimer agreed.

“The fact that she was out there helping the animals really states of what I’ve known about her,” he said.

“She’s always had that compassion to want to help, to make things better and especially to make animals and people safe. That’s what I really took from her.”

Friends have started a GoFundMe to help bring her home to the Netherlands, cover funeral costs and care for her dog.

“I mean, you want her home,” Koekkoek said.

stories.title: Provinces waiting to see if Trump follows through on data centre tax threat
stories.summary: Canadian provinces are waiting to see if U.S. President Donald Trump will follow through on his threat to tax American companies with foreign data centres.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Canadian provinces are waiting to see if U.S. President Donald Trump will follow through on his threat to tax American companies with foreign data centres.

Trump threatened Friday to impose “a tremendous tax” on American firms that build their data centres abroad, saying the U.S. could fall behind China in the artificial intelligence race as growing political backlash threatens to put the brakes on American data centre development.

“We’re not going to allow companies to build data centres in other countries,” the president said. “If they do that, they can. But we’re going to put a tremendous tax on them.”

A recent York University report found that more than 200 data centres are in the planning stage across Canada. Almost 80 per cent of those sites are planned for Alberta which has the abundant energy resources needed to power the electricity-hungry industry.

“We are aware of the comments made by U.S President Donald Trump regarding potential taxes on data centres built outside the United States,” Premier Danielle Smith’s press secretary Ryan Fournier said in an email Tuesday.

“As there are no real details yet, we will wait to see if there are any further developments in the coming weeks. We’ll keep working with the federal government and our partners in the U.S. to make sure North America leads on AI, together.”

In July, Facebook’s U.S.-based parent company Meta announced a $13-billion, one-gigawatt AI data centre north of Edmonton which is already under construction. The province is offering what it calls a concierge service to support proponents through the regulatory approval process. More than 70 companies are working with the help of the concierge team.

Meanwhile, American AI firm Anthropic has signed a 20-year lease to occupy a planned $10-billion data centre project in Point Tupper, N.S. EverWind Fuels plans to finance, build and own the 18,600-square metre Cape Breton facility which would be Anthropic’s first Canadian data centre.

Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston’s office said in an email Tuesday that only Trump knows if his tax threat holds water. It noted that the president has made similar threats before, such as his call last year for 100 per cent tariffs on foreign films that never materialized.

“The reality is that EverWind is developing, financing, constructing and owning this (data centre) site. Preventing them from doing so would be like preventing American retailers from operating in Canadian shopping malls,” Houston’s office said in a statement.

EverWind declined to comment on U.S. politics or policies on Tuesday. Anthropic did not respond to a request for comment.

Mark Daley, chief AI officer for Western University in London, Ont., said in an email Tuesday that AI firms place their computing resources in the markets they serve. He said Trump’s taxation threats would limit their international reach and go against the White House’s existing AI policy.

He said the ability to walk away from a deal is key in any business negotiation, and if U.S. firms can’t build in foreign markets, they lose important bargaining power while talking with American utilities, states and communities.

“The irony here is that America became the world’s dominant technology power by exporting its technology everywhere. You don’t necessarily strengthen that position by ordering American companies to stay home,” said Daly.

Josh Vautour, CEO of Faster Than Light, a Fredericton-based company aiming to build a Canadian owned and operated data centre in New Brunswick, said Trump’s proposal is aimed at shoring up the United States’ massive artificial intelligence industry at home to protect its digital sovereignty.

“It’s similar to what Canada is trying to accomplish by building out its foundation for critical digital infrastructure,” he said in an interview Tuesday.

Vautour added the Canadian government should continue efforts to incentivize the growth of its fledgling domestic sector so Canada can also have protected AI infrastructure.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 24, 2026.

— With files from Eli Ridder in Fredericton and The Associated Press.

Devin Stevens, The Canadian Press

stories.title: The inspiring story of B.C.’s new Deputy Premier
stories.summary: Lorne Doerkson could have picked someone ‘safer’ than Claire Rattée – but she has an important story to tell
stories.author: Gary Mason
stories.content:
Midway through last month’s B.C. election campaign, Conservative leader Lorne Doerkson held a news conference on the border of Vancouver’s Downtown Eastside. The topic: street disorder.

He was accompanied by one of his candidates, Claire Rattée, who, although not from the area, knew it well. Soon she was standing in front of a lectern and talking about how the descriptions offered by officials of the dire conditions that existed on the nearby streets held a deep personal connection.

In the grim despair worn by those sitting on sidewalks, she could see herself.

For the next four minutes, without the slightest glimpse at a note, Ms. Rattée told her story of dependency and homelessness. “Experimenting [with drugs] became an addiction,” she said. “I moved on to harder drugs and eventually I was taking pretty much anything I could get my hands on. By 17, I was living on the streets of Vancouver.”

“I know what it is like to be unbearably cold and hungry and exhausted and somehow getting high still mattered more than finding food or somewhere warm to sleep. I stayed in shelters. I lived in an SRO [single-room occupancy hotel] and, as strange as it sounds, there were times that I actually felt safer sleeping on the street. So, I went back.”

There have been plenty of provincial politicians in B.C. who have had compelling back stories, including that of addiction. But there have been few who have overcome the odds Ms. Rattée faced as a young adult.

Forty-five days after telling her remarkable story of survival at that October news conference, the 35-year-old MLA from the northwestern B.C. riding of Skeena was named Deputy Premier and Minister of Social Development in the province’s new Conservative majority government.

The announcement of her appointment as Deputy Premier brought those sitting in a ballroom at the cabinet swearing-in ceremony at the Lieutenant-Governor’s residence on Nov. 20 in Victoria to their feet. They knew the unfathomable heights she had scaled to arrive at that moment. And there were few smiling as broadly as the Premier.

There will be lots written about the makeup of Mr. Doerkson’s cabinet and what it says about the government he will lead. But there will be few appointments he ever makes that will say as much about him as a person than the one naming Ms. Rattée his deputy.

There were certainly options that were, quote-unquote, safer. Many expected he would go with Caroline Elliott, the high-profile candidate who narrowly lost the leadership of the party to Kerry-Lynne Findlay last spring. He could have gone with someone who had more experience as an MLA – more than the two years Ms. Rattée had. But in choosing her as his deputy, he signalled that he could look beyond the tattoos on her neck and arms and see someone who had something important to contribute, someone who also had an important story to tell.

Of course, these are early days and Premier Doerkson has a mountainous task before him. The problems left by the NDP government of David Eby are immense, not the least of which is an unsustainable rate of debt. Without record rates of economic growth, the only way out of the province’s fiscal mess will be by cutting and saying no.

And when you’re doing that, it’s pretty easy to be characterized as callous and heartless. Which I’m sure this government will be at some point.

Mr. Doerkson has done himself, and the province, an enormous favour by filling the ranks of his cabinet with what can only be described as “normal” folk, eschewing any temptation there might have been to offer more than a token appointment or two to those in his caucus who supported the divisive Ms. Findlay and her far-right views.

Is that a risk? Will the overlooked become disgruntled and cause problems? Perhaps, but the Premier has a big enough majority to easily extinguish small fires of discontent that could flare up. And he has people on his side like Ms. Rattée, who has inspired a legion of supporters in Conservative ranks.

After she was sworn in as Deputy Premier and Minister of the Crown, Ms. Rattée was asked what her appointment said about Mr. Doerkson. She said it showed he believed you need people with different viewpoints around a cabinet table.

“There are many challenges British Columbians are struggling with right now, many of which I’ve experienced myself,” she said. “And he recognizes that that lived experience is useful here and relevant and hopefully I can make a difference.”

stories.title: ‘We’ve had enough’: Groups urge Nova Scotia to act on power bill costs
stories.summary: Protesters said they're being priced out and don't believe the provincial government is doing enough to help people struggling to keep up with rising energy costs.
stories.author: Mitchell Bailey, Rebecca Lau
stories.content:
Protesters in downtown Halifax Tuesday said they’re being priced out and don’t believe the provincial government is doing enough to help people struggling with rising energy costs.

“Simply put, power bills are far too high and we’ve had enough of it,” said Miriam Williams, an organizer with Acorn ‘s Halifax chapter.

“I know people, myself included, who’ve had to make choices between rent and power and groceries and the fact that bills being juggled is the normal thing.”

Advocates like Williams want the Nova Scotia government to implement several affordability measures, such as a rebate covering 50 per cent of energy costs for low-income families.

They said they would also like to see investment in energy-efficient upgrades for households, which could bring down electricity bills.

“People are already struggling and we need support, not more financial crunch,” said Tim Allenby, with Acorn’s Dartmouth chapter.

The concerns come as Nova Scotia Power bills could jump by nearly seven per cent in January. A 3.9 per cent increase will come into effect, but the utility is also awaiting a decision from the province’s energy board on an additional 2.9 per cent fee.

This has the province’s Official Opposition calling for immediate relief measures.

“That will be the highest energy increase in the country and is one of the reasons that our inflation is an outlier,” said NDP Leader Claudia Chender.

Ahead of Tuesday’s rally, Chender spoke to reporters and was joined by the co-chair of the Affordable Energy Coalition, Juli Bishwokarma.

The group is pushing the province to adopt a strategy to address energy poverty. The proposal, which was put together by the coalition, includes arrear management support, expanding funding for energy efficiency programs and a crisis management support fund.

“This program could lift 27,000 households out of energy poverty, with an investment of $35 million per year from the province,” said Bishwokarma.

In response, the province said it understands people are facing cost-of-living pressures.

In a statement, the Department of Energy said, “We have expanded energy efficiency programs through Efficiency Nova Scotia, helping households lower their power bills with home energy upgrades, heat pumps, insulation improvements, and targeted support for low- and moderate-income families.”

The department added it is working to stabilize long-term costs by reducing reliance on imported fossil fuels and focusing on locally produced renewable energy.

“Investments in wind, solar, energy storage, and modernized electricity infrastructure are designed to strengthen energy security and support a more affordable system over time,” the statement added.

But with winter around the corner, advocates believe more needs to be done to help people keep the heat on.

“People will be forced make all kinds of difficult choices about basic quality of life stuff,” said Allenby.

stories.title: Stellantis sues Unifor, alleging obstruction of environmental work at Brampton plant
stories.summary: Automaker wants Ontario court to declare that union has trespassed at the facility, which it sold to defence contractor Roshel
stories.author: Sammy Hudes
stories.content:
The dispute over the sale of Stellantis’s Stla-N Brampton, Ont., assembly plant is heading to court, as the automaker has filed a lawsuit alleging Unifor is impeding an environmental assessment necessary to the transaction.

In documents filed last Thursday in the Ontario Superior Court of Justice, Stellantis said it is seeking an injunction requiring the union, its national president Lana Payne and Unifor Local 1285 plant chairperson Ardis Snow to refrain from blocking the Brampton plant and preventing work at the site.

The company wants the court to declare that the union has trespassed at the facility and “obstructed the lawful entrance to and exit from the premises.”

A statement of claim said union officials are “physically preventing, impeding, and restricting Stellantis’ ability to provide access to the premises” to environmental consulting firm Pinchin Ltd.

Pinchin was retained by Roshel – the armoured vehicle manufacturer that agreed to buy the idled Brampton plant from Stellantis for an undisclosed amount earlier this month – to carry out environmental work starting Nov. 9, according to the documents

However, Stellantis said that morning, union representatives blockaded entrances to the plant with trucks, pylons and individuals carrying Unifor flags and that Unifor told the automaker it wouldn’t let Pinchin personnel or equipment through.

“To date, Unifor has continued to obstruct access by persons associated with the environmental work, and Pinchin has not been permitted to perform the environmental work,” the statement of claim said.

“Despite Stellantis’ reasonable efforts to obtain police assistance, those efforts have not brought the obstruction of or interference with lawful access to the premises under an acceptable degree of control, nor has Pinchin been permitted to access the premises.”

The allegations have not been tested in court.

The statement of claim said Stellantis “is suffering and will continue to suffer irreparable harm and other losses,” although the extent of those losses “are extremely difficult, if not impossible, to quantify in monetary terms.”

It added that “continued obstruction” of the environmental assessment “threatens to delay or prevent completion of a material diligence step, interfere with the timetable for the proposed transaction, and affect the responsibilities of Stellantis and Roshel following closing of the proposed transaction.”

Stellantis’s deal with Roshel is expected to close in mid-December, subject to certain conditions, according to the documents.

Payne said in a statement that the union “has been demonstrating in support of Canadian jobs at the Brampton plant throughout the past year.”

“We continue to fight for the jobs of our members and for the entire Canadian auto industry,” Payne said.

“The sale of the plant to Roshel is unacceptable to our union. And we will continue to work with all parties to try to get a different outcome.”

In addition to Unifor and its leadership, the lawsuit also lists a pair of unnamed defendants whom Stellantis alleges have participated in the demonstration.

The deal between Stellantis and Roshel has ignited a firestorm over the future of jobs at the plant, the automaker’s financial responsibilities to the federal government and Ottawa’s role throughout the process.

On Friday, Industry Minister Mélanie Joly and Ontario Premier Doug Ford met with the leadership of Stellantis and Unifor behind closed doors.

The sitdown came as Joly said the automaker could either keep the Brampton plant open rather than completing its sale to Roshel, or face a multimillion-dollar lawsuit from the federal government.

The federal government recently served Stellantis with a notice of default on its 2022 funding agreement, in which Ottawa committed up to $529-million to help Stellantis retool its Brampton and Windsor, Ont., facilities to produce electrified vehicles.

A letter from Joly said Stellantis breached conditions of the commitment by halting Jeep Compass production in Brampton, failing or refusing to identify a replacement vehicle, not maintaining any production at the facility and closing the plant.

Joly’s letter said Stellantis would have 30 days to demonstrate it will “correct these conditions” or she will declare that the company is in default of its obligations. It warned that if Stellantis remains in breach of its conditions, the company could face penalties including a requirement to repay all or part of the funding it has received, plus interest.

But Stellantis has said it intends to repay only $24-million in federal government support received for the Brampton facility’s retooling plan.

A retooling began at the Brampton plant in early 2024, but the automaker paused its plan to produce the Jeep Compass there in February 2025 – one month after U.S. President Donald Trump retook office and began issuing tariffs on imports from Canada and other countries.

Stellantis later announced it was moving Jeep Compass production to Illinois, leaving more than 2,000 workers laid off and the Brampton plant idled indefinitely.

Roshel has said its plans for the site have the potential to create more than 2,000 jobs as production ramps up, and that laid-off workers would receive first priority consideration as hiring takes place.

Joly’s letter said Stellantis would have 30 days to demonstrate it will “correct these conditions” or she will declare that the company is in default of its obligations. It warned that if Stellantis remains in breach of its conditions, the company could face penalties including a requirement to repay all or part of the funding it has received, plus interest.
But Stellantis has said it intends to repay only $24-million in federal government support received for the Brampton facility’s retooling plan.

A retooling began at the Brampton plant in early 2024, but the automaker paused its plan to produce the Jeep Compass there in February 2025 – one month after U.S. President Donald Trump retook office and began issuing tariffs on imports from Canada and other countries.
Stellantis later announced it was moving Jeep Compass production to Illinois, leaving more than 2,000 workers laid off and the Brampton plant idled indefinitely.

Roshel has said its plans for the site have the potential to create more than 2,000 jobs as production ramps up, and that laid-off workers would receive first priority consideration as hiring takes place.

stories.summary: Regina - Bus service is back in operation in Regina after the city reached a tentative deal with its transit workers amid a one-day lockout.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
REGINA - Bus service is back in operation in Regina after the city reached a tentative deal with its transit workers amid a one-day lockout.
