By The Canadian Press

Representatives from the city and Amalgamated Transit Union Local 588 returned to the bargaining table Monday, as workers gathered in the cold to protest the city-imposed lockout.

In a news release Monday night, the city said that alongside the tentative three-year deal, the two sides agreed to end the lockout and the union’s voluntary overtime ban.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Inside interior designer Nora Voon’s art-filled home

The city imposed the lockout of about 380 transit workers days after the union said employees would take job action by not working voluntary overtime.

Thousands of commuters who rely on transit in Regina were without bus service on Monday and Tuesday morning.

Transit director Nathan Luhning thanked residents and customers for their patience during the service disruption and says the city is glad to have buses back on the road quickly.

Details of the tentative deal won’t be publicly known until it’s ratified, although union brass say it addresses worker concerns and includes wage increases “closer to where our members deserve to be.”

The union previously said the sticking point in negotiations was wages and that workers were asking for a pay hike that matched inflation.

The union says a ratification vote will be held in the coming days.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 24, 2026.

stories.title: Csis engages Iranian, Jewish communities targeted by foreign interference
stories.summary: A senior Canadian intelligence official identified Canada’s Jewish and Iranian communities as being vulnerable to foreign interference.
stories.author: Alex Boutilier
stories.content:
A senior Canadian intelligence official says that the law enforcement and intelligence community are attempting to make inroads with diaspora communities vulnerable to foreign interference and transnational repression.

The Canadian Security Intelligence Service (Csis) has spent “considerable time” meeting with communities that hostile foreign powers have targeted in Canada “over the last number of years,” Jarrett Davis told a House of Commons committee Tuesday.

Davis specifically mentioned Canada’s Jewish community, which has been the target of a dramatic rise in hate crimes in recent years, and the country’s Iranian diaspora as two particularly vulnerable groups.

“The purpose of that engagement has been about listening to these groups and to better understand … the impact of foreign interference on these communities,” testified Davis, the director general of Csis’s Strategic Bureau.

“Through those trusted relationships that we’re attempting to build, (Csis conveys) threat-related information where we can, and certainly declassify information when we can, to facilitate that process … (and) build resiliency in the communities to foreign interference.”

Canada’s law enforcement and intelligence communities are starting from a significant trust deficit with the communities most likely to be targeted by transnational repression, according to a recent independent probe of foreign interference activities in Canada.

Justice Marie-Josée Hogue’s commission concluded in 2025 that community members were reluctant to report incidents to Csis or the RCMP.

“They lack trust in national security and law enforcement agencies and fear reprisals. This May deprive Csis of significant information,” Hogue’s final report stated.

“It is difficult to build trust with a community whose members feel they are over-policed, homogenized, victimized or misunderstood … Steps to reach out and build trust with affected communities have been taken. However, this work must continue and be appropriately resourced and reinforced at every level.”

Davis said Csis understands “the human nature of this threat,” and has taken considerable steps to address the issues the Hogue inquiry identified.

Davis testified before the House of Commons’ Procedure and House Affairs Committee, which has probed the ongoing issue of foreign interference intermittently for months.

Richard Bilodeau, Public Safety Canada’s assistant deputy minister for national and cyber security, told the committee Tuesday that upwards of 80 per cent of the Hogue Commission’s recommendations were either complete or in progress.

stories.title: Can’t explain thinking behind Pentagon’s Canada ‘fact sheet,’ McGuinty says
stories.summary: The Pentagon released what it called a "fact sheet" on Monday which said Canada's defence spending has limited its ability to contribute to the protection of North America.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Defence Minister David McGuinty says he can’t “divine” the thinking behind the Pentagon’s recent criticism of Canada’s defence spending.

The Pentagon released what it called a “fact sheet” on Monday which said Canada’s defence spending has limited the country’s ability to contribute to the protection of North America.

U.S. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth last week issued a classified memo imposing restrictions on military co-operation with Canada around think-tanks and socializing.

McGuinty told reporters in Ottawa Tuesday he can’t explain the messaging from Hegseth and the Pentagon.

He said Canada’s co-operation with the United States, whether directly or through Nato or Norad, has not changed.

“Canada is going to continue to execute. I have to say we’re so busy executing on plans, acquisitions, rebuilding 33 bases, improving our recruitment, our retention, fixing a cadet challenge yesterday. That’s what we’re focused on,” he said.

Last March, Prime Minister Mark Carney said Canada had met for the first time the Nato requirement to spend the equivalent of two per cent of GDP on defence. The target was set in 2014 and Canada was among the Nato members which had never hit it.

When Nato members met last year in The Hague, they agreed to increase their defence spending to the equivalent of five per cent of GDP by 2035 — 3.5 per cent on core military and defence and 1.5 per cent on broader security and defence-adjacent investments that were loosely defined.

When he was pressed by reporters on whether Canada would meet that five per cent commitment, McGuinty said Canada has a path to spending the equivalent of four per cent of GDP on defence by 2030.

“We are on track,” McGuinty said.

When he was asked how the U.S. reacted to Canada’s four-per-cent plan, McGuinty responded, “Canada is a sovereign nation. I’ll be very direct. We don’t report to the United States.”

The recent federal budget charted a course to meeting spending targets by 2030 but did not look at spending beyond that year. That plan includes spending 2.6 per cent of GDP, or about $99 billion, ON core military, including ammunition and soldiers’ salaries.

Last March, Prime Minister Mark Carney said Canada had met for the first time the Nato requirement to spend the equivalent of two per cent of GDP on defence. The target was set in 2014 and Canada was among the Nato members which had never hit it.

content_blocks.text: When Nato members met last year in The Hague, they agreed to increase their defence spending to the equivalent of five per cent of GDP by 2035 — 3.5 per cent on core military and defence and 1.5 per cent on broader security and defence-adjacent investments that were loosely defined.
When he was pressed by reporters on whether Canada would meet that five per cent commitment, McGuinty said Canada has a path to spending the equivalent of four per cent of GDP on defence by 2030.
“We are on track,” McGuinty said.
When he was asked how the U.S. reacted to Canada’s four-per-cent plan, McGuinty responded, “Canada is a sovereign nation. I’ll be very direct. We don’t report to the United States.”

The recent federal budget charted a course to meeting spending targets by 2030 but did not look at spending beyond that year. That plan includes spending 2.6 per cent of GDP, or about $99 billion, ON core military, including ammunition and soldiers’ salaries.

stories.title: Alberta takes symbolic stand against federal hate crime law, says it silences speech
stories.summary: Edmonton - Alberta Premier Danielle Smith's government is taking a symbolic stand against a federal hate crime law.
stories.author: Jack Farrell The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Edmonton - Alberta’s government is taking a symbolic stand against Ottawa’s decision to remove religious speech as a defence to hate crimes, although it acknowledges it already gets final say on whether many cases get prosecuted.

Premier Danielle Smith told a news conference Tuesday that she’s concerned the change by Ottawa, which took affect earlier this year, will have a silencing effect.

And she said she doesn’t want pastors “hauled off to jail.”

“People shouldn’t have to hide their faith to feel secure in their place in this province,” Smith said.

“I don’t think anyone wants to see their pastor, or their rabbi or their imam monitored in their sermons or arrested and prosecuted.”

Ottawa says its law captures speech made with the intention of promoting hatred or antisemitism. Sermons, scripture readings and other religious teachings delivered in good faith don’t meet the standard for potential criminal activity, says a backgrounder on the law.

A spokesperson for federal Justice Minister Sean Fraser said Tuesday that Ottawa agrees everyone must be free to practise their faith and express their religious beliefs.

The right to do so is protected under the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, the office said.

“The law strengthens the Criminal Code by giving law enforcement stronger tools to respond to hate-motivated crime and protect our communities,” it said.

Smith said her government would soon invoke her sovereignty act in the legislature and table a motion outlining Alberta’s intention to push back against the law. She provided few details on what action Alberta would be taking.

Smith’s government has already told police and Crown prosecutors that it doesn’t want to see hate crimes considered a priority.

That battle casts Alberta’s struggle as one of good versus evil, led by those who see independence as a chance to reform a nation that has lost

Mickey Amery, Alberta’s justice minister, currently has the final say on whether many hate-related cases are prosecuted in court, including wilful promotion of hatred.

Amery, speaking alongside Smith, acknowledged that authority but said the sovereignty act motion would ask cabinet ministers to come up with “further lawful measures” that Alberta could take to push back.

“It confirms to Albertans exactly where we stand on this particular issue,” Amery said of the motion.

Smith said her opposition to Ottawa’s removal of the religious speech defence doesn’t mean her United Conservative Party government supports hate-motivated crime.

“Alberta can and will protect public safety while also standing up for fundamental freedoms,” she said.

In August, the premier and her public safety minister criticized the Edmonton police for a social media post encouraging people to report hate crimes.

“We don’t believe in policing unpopular or religious-based statements even if they are controversial,” Smith said in her own social media post at the time.

Opposition NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi described the government’s motion and comments as “meaningless” theatre ahead of the Ucp’s annual gathering this weekend in Calgary.

“They need to throw some red meat to the base, so they’re trying to open yet another chapter in the culture wars,” Nenshi said.

“If you want to change the law, lobby the federal government to change the law.”

Smith said her sovereignty act motion has nothing to do with the UCP gathering and that Ottawa’s law affects everyone.

“We have probably the vast majority of Albertans who attend some kind of religious ceremony on a weekly basis. And because the federal government chose to make speech from the pulpit and scriptorial references a potential form of criminal prosecution, we had to step in,” the premier said.

“I don’t think you wait for the overzealousness in policing or prosecution on this matter, when we’ve already heard loud and clear that people don’t want that.”

Smith gave UCP members a heads-up about the sovereignty act motion during a virtual town hall on Saturday, describing the act as a mechanism for protecting provincial rights.

Beyond removing the religious speech defence from the law, Ottawa added that displaying certain symbols, including Nazi emblems and symbols connected to terrorist groups, is promoting hatred.

It’s also now an offence to intimidate someone trying to enter a place of worship or cultural centre.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 24, 2026.

— With files from Lisa Johnson

stories.title: Inside Quebec’s mad scramble to circumvent the oath to the King ahead of the start of the session
stories.summary: 'I really could have done without that judgment. We have other priorities,' said Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon.
stories.author: Catherine Lévesque
stories.content:
The ink was not yet dry on the decision of the Quebec Superior Court to force the provincial legislators to swear an oath to King Charles III before the government and opposition scrambled to find ways to circumvent the obligation.

At the heart of the issue is whether decisions from the courts or parliamentary privilege have precedence as Quebec’s national assembly is set to resume its work next week.

Speaking on Tuesday, Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon had difficulty hiding his exasperation with the court decision, which essentially suspends a provincial law passed in 2022 that declares the oath to the King optional for legislature members.

“I really could have done without that judgment. We have other priorities,” he said.

The Quebec legislature is set to resume its work next Tuesday for a short session.

Justice Ian Demers of the Quebec Superior Court made it clear in his decision on Monday that legislators cannot unilaterally change the Canadian Constitution.

All 127 members of the national assembly swore allegiance to the “people of Quebec.” As things stand, they could be in violation of the court’s order if they decide to sit next week without a new swearing-in oath that would include the monarch.

But the separatist Parti Québécois government has made it clear they have no intention of participating in what they consider to be a humiliation ritual.

There are several scenarios on the table to deal with the situation, but the government’s preferred option is to ask the Quebec Court of Appeal to remove the immediate obligation to take an oath to the King pending a decision on the merits of the case.

“Our priority is to go through the Court of Appeal and then find a legal remedy. We remain confident that we can succeed in getting things moving quickly,” explained Lucas Medernach, director of media relations for St-Pierre Plamondon.

“We’ll see how things go, but I think the court understands the urgency of the situation,” he added.

With the appeal already underway, he said the government’s ideal scenario would be to be heard in court in the next two days and that there be a decision made by Friday.

The Quebec Liberals are not waiting idly by in the meantime for the decision to drop.

Their parliamentary leader André Fortin has already reached out to the current president of the national assembly, Nathalie Roy, via a letter on Tuesday asking her to use an “exceptional procedure” to decide whether the session can start as scheduled.

“If you conclude that the judgment of the Quebec Superior Court prevents the 127 elected members from participating in the proceedings of the National Assembly, we ask that you specify the conditions required to legitimize the opening session,” it reads.

The letter goes on to ask Roy to communicate her decision in writing to all the leaders of political parties before the legislature is set to open next week.

In 2022, the president’s office had prevented PQ members from entering the chamber as they refused to take an oath to the King. But the law has since changed, and Roy will have to decide whether the will of members quashes the court order.

St-Pierre Plamondon said that, at first glance, there is nothing in the Quebec Superior Court’s decision this week that is preventing elected officials to take their seat.

But he wouldn’t guarantee that the legislature will come back next week as planned.

“My role is not to guarantee the future. My role is to find solutions,” he said.

Meanwhile, the opposition parties in Quebec agree they cannot wait any longer to start their work. They said there is simply too much to do on the cost of living and housing, among other issues, and some slammed the PQ for focusing on petty politics.

The Quebec Conservatives are so far the only party that has said it would be ready to swear an oath to the King if necessary.

“If we have to hide in a closet one by one and hold our noses or cross our fingers, we’ll do it,” Leader Éric Duhaime said, adding there is no need for a “public flogging.”

Duhaime said all former PQ governments have sworn an oath to the King in the past, and this time would be no different.

Québec solidaire’s Alexandre Leduc said he is not willing to go down that road again.

He said it is “absurd” to swear an oath to the King and called it a “fake” gesture.

However, Leduc said he does not want to postpone the session.

“I think we can think outside the box,” he said.

If things don’t work out as expected with the Court of Appeal or the president, could the Quebec government decide to further push back the start of the session or cancel it? Or could it defy the court’s orders and decide to sit in the legislature regardless?

St-Pierre Plamondon said he is currently considering all options that preserve the “dignity” of elected officials so they can start sitting next week as planned.

“There is always a solution when people are acting in good faith,” he said.

Quebec Liberal Leader Charles Milliard said that he does not want the members of his party to take their seat in the legislature illegally.

“We are not in a banana republic,” he said.

Catherine Lévesque covers federal-Quebec relations for National Post. She joined the parliamentary bureau in Ottawa in 2022, after a decade spent in French media in Montreal, Quebec City and Ottawa.

“Our priority is to go through the Court of Appeal and then find a legal remedy. We remain confident that we can succeed in getting things moving quickly,” explained Lucas Medernach, director of media relations for St-Pierre Plamondon.
“We’ll see how things go, but I think the court understands the urgency of the situation,” he added.
With the appeal already underway, he said the government’s ideal scenario would be to be heard in court in the next two days and that there be a decision made by Friday.
The Quebec Liberals are not waiting idly by in the meantime for the decision to drop.

Their parliamentary leader André Fortin has already reached out to the current president of the national assembly, Nathalie Roy, via a letter on Tuesday asking her to use an “exceptional procedure” to decide whether the session can start as scheduled.

“If you conclude that the judgment of the Quebec Superior Court prevents the 127 elected members from participating in the proceedings of the National Assembly, we ask that you specify the conditions required to legitimize the opening session,” it reads.
The letter goes on to ask Roy to communicate her decision in writing to all the leaders of political parties before the legislature is set to open next week.

In 2022, the president’s office had prevented PQ members from entering the chamber as they refused to take an oath to the King. But the law has since changed, and Roy will have to decide whether the will of members quashes the court order.
St-Pierre Plamondon said that, at first glance, there is nothing in the Quebec Superior Court’s decision this week that is preventing elected officials to take their seat.
But he wouldn’t guarantee that the legislature will come back next week as planned.
“My role is not to guarantee the future. My role is to find solutions,” he said.

Meanwhile, the opposition parties in Quebec agree they cannot wait any longer to start their work. They said there is simply too much to do on the cost of living and housing, among other issues, and some slammed the PQ for focusing on petty politics.
Editor’s Picks
The Quebec Conservatives are so far the only party that has said it would be ready to swear an oath to the King if necessary.
“If we have to hide in a closet one by one and hold our noses or cross our fingers, we’ll do it,” Leader Éric Duhaime said, adding there is no need for a “public flogging.”
Duhaime said all former PQ governments have sworn an oath to the King in the past, and this time would be no different.
Québec solidaire’s Alexandre Leduc said he is not willing to go down that road again.
He said it is “absurd” to swear an oath to the King and called it a “fake” gesture.
However, Leduc said he does not want to postpone the session.
“I think we can think outside the box,” he said.

If things don’t work out as expected with the Court of Appeal or the president, could the Quebec government decide to further push back the start of the session or cancel it? Or could it defy the court’s orders and decide to sit in the legislature regardless?
St-Pierre Plamondon said he is currently considering all options that preserve the “dignity” of elected officials so they can start sitting next week as planned.
“There is always a solution when people are acting in good faith,” he said.
Quebec Liberal Leader Charles Milliard said that he does not want the members of his party to take their seat in the legislature illegally.
“We are not in a banana republic,” he said.
Catherine Lévesque covers federal-Quebec relations for National Post. She joined the parliamentary bureau in Ottawa in 2022, after a decade spent in French media in Montreal, Quebec City and Ottawa.

stories.title: Ottawa’s plan for 100k temporary workers in provinces’ hands: minister
stories.summary: Diab said during a House of Commons debate Tuesday that the 100,000 temporary workers would be nominated by the provinces and territories.
stories.author: David Baxter
stories.content:
Immigration Minister Lena Diab says the government’s one-time plan to grant permanent residency to up to 100,000 temporary workers will be in the hands of the provinces and territories — and if they don’t use those spaces, they won’t be filled.

The headline figure in the new 2027 immigration levels plan is a target of 380,000 permanent residents. The government says about half of those people are expected to be individuals now in the country who transition from temporary to permanent residency.

The plan includes what the government calls a “one-time” addition of 200,000 permanent residents. That pool is divided between 100,000 temporary workers and 100,000 humanitarian and compassionate cases who already have applied for permanent residency.

Diab said during a House of Commons debate Tuesday that the 100,000 temporary workers would be nominated by the provinces and territories. If some slots aren’t used, they won’t be filled, she added.

“These time-limited measure admissions are real and will be reported, but a one-time maximum is not a recurring annual target. Half of these admissions will not happen unless provinces and territories agree that they want them,” Diab said.

The topic came up during debate on a Conservative motion to block the government’s permanent residency plan, which could see upwards of 662,000 people receive permanent residency in 2027.

Conservative immigration critic Michelle Rempel Garner argues Canada can’t absorb all of those people without putting additional strains on the housing and job markets and social infrastructure.

“The prime minister’s government has allowed the population to grow through immigration almost three times faster than our number of hospital beds. Too many people too fast for hospital beds, for diagnostic imaging, for doctors to keep up, means that people die. That’s the reality of this situation,” Rempel Garner said.

The government argues many people who are expected to receive permanent residency next year are already here and won’t add new pressure to the housing or labour markets.

“When someone already is living in Canada, becomes a permanent resident, that counts as an admission. They are not a new person arriving in our country,” Diab said. “This distinction is essential when we consider the effects of immigration on population growth, ON housing, ON services.”

The plan for up to 200,000 additional permanent residents involves people who have been in Canada for years. They include longtime temporary workers and about 50,000 people from Hong Kong and Ukraine who came to Canada on special programs after fleeing government persecution or Russia’s war.

There are about 45,000 humanitarian slots in the one-time plan for the family members of permanent residents, and some of these people are expected to be new arrivals to Canada.

Rempel Garner argued the former Hong Kong and Ukraine residents could have been granted permanent residency without the other increases. Conservatives have called for people who came to Canada in these cohorts to be granted permanent residency as they faced waits of more than a decade.

Ontario Conservative MP Costas Menegakis said those from Hong Kong and Ukraine should have been included in the broad 380,000 permanent resident target.

Rempel Garner accused the government of colluding with “corporate lobbyists” to use the immigration system to drive down wages and raise rents.

“We need to allow workers to have a fair deal, and we need to restore the promise to immigrants. We can have a partisan discussion on how we do those things, but today across political stripes and especially in the Liberal backbench, people need to push back on the prime minister and say too many people, too fast, it needs to stop,” Rempel Garner said.

Diab replied that the immigration plan was drafted with input from the provinces on their labour needs. She added Canada’s population is aging and immigration is necessary to maintain the working population.

“One in five Canadians is 65 or older … As more approach retirement, maintaining a strong workforce becomes increasingly important and our first priority naturally is to invest in Canadian workers through training, skills development and opportunities for young people. Immigration must complement those efforts, not replace them,” Diab said.

Statistics Canada estimated Canada’s population growth as of July 1 was 0.5 per cent year-over-year, the lowest rate since the First World War. The figure was revised after a March estimate suggested Canada’s population was declining for the first time since Confederation.

Rempel Garner argued the revised figures show the temporary resident population had been lowballed previously and the government doesn’t have a handle on the real numbers.

The Bloc Québécois says it plans to support the Conservative motion, which cannot pass without the support of some members of the Liberal majority government.

stories.title: Navdeep Bains’s Liberal leadership victory is bad news for Ontario more broadly
stories.summary: The new leader coasted to victory with few ambitious plans. He could become premier with that same paucity of ideas, too
stories.author: Robyn Urback
stories.content:
Navdeep Bains, who became Leader of the Ontario Liberal Party by the skin of his teeth on Saturday, had precisely one thing going for him during the leadership race.

It was not his professional background; he is an ex-Rogers executive and ex-Trudeau cabinet minister, both of which play negatively in today’s political environment. It was not his record in office, during which he was the face of the government’s rather silly and ineffective superclusters program. It was not his personal charisma, which – if it exists – made no appearance during the campaign. It was not a current seat in the legislature, which his predecessors, Steven Del Duca and Bonnie Crombie, also lacked when they took over the party (and never managed to acquire during their tenures). And it was not a clear platform – or really, any coherent policy – that materially distinguished his promise for Ontario from the other three candidates that made it to the end of the race.

No, the one thing that Mr. Bains had going for him was his organization: His campaign team operated a formidable machine to collect donations and sign up new members . And those new members delivered a victory to a candidate that the existing membership recognized as an unimpressive, uninspired choice.

Ontario Liberals did not use those particular descriptors for Mr. Bains, of course. Instead, its most prominent members (including former premier Kathleen Wynne) lined up to endorse Mr. Bains’s chief rival, Lee Fairclough, which is an action that largely speaks for itself.

Second to Mr. Bains’s own campaign team, the happiest people in Ontario to hear about his victory were those aligned with Premier Doug Ford. Conservative strategist Jeff Ballingall posted on X that his “conservative group chats are lighting up with delight.” The Progressive Conservatives already have attack ads in motion zeroing in on Mr. Bains’s allegiance to former prime minister Justin Trudeau and support for the federal carbon tax.

Conservatives May be overestimating Mr. Ford’s resilience, however, even against a lacklustre Liberal Leader. Mr. Ford is currently the least popular premier in Canada, and by the next scheduled provincial election, he will have been in office for nearly 12 years. That is well past the time Canadians typically decide to “kick the bums out,” and if Mr. Ford is still around by then, a houseplant might have a decent shot at taking over as Premier.

That’s why Mr. Bains’s victory is bad news for Ontario more broadly. This province desperately needs change from the status quo, which has been relatively consistent for the last 20 years, despite a change in government. Ontario is hopelessly in debt, spending an estimated $17.4-billion in 2026-27 on debt servicing alone. Our health care wait times are bad and getting worse, and our hospitals are consistently sounding the alarm about overcrowding . We’re not spending efficiently on education, with enormous duplication across four distinct school systems. We’re not building enough homes. Our productivity has stagnated .

In response to this cacophony of crises, the Ontario Liberal Party has elected a policy-less leader. And unfortunately for Ontario, that could very well be enough after more than a decade of Mr. Ford. That would mean nothing will materially change in the province, leaving everyone worse off.

Mr. Bains’s only gestures toward actual political policy has been to promise to reverse specific Doug Ford policies, such as his cuts to the Ontario Student Assistance Program (Osap), and to broadly advocate for things people tend to like, such as smaller classrooms and better health care. He has defended his position of offering no specifics by saying his “job is to highlight a vision and a path for this province and work with the Liberal Party grassroots,” and that “once you show up and you listen, then you can focus on solutions.” Mr. Bains has ostensibly been busy with other jobs for the past two decades, but surely anyone who has been present in this province for some degree of time is well aware of its deficiencies. Ontario doesn’t need another leader who vows to listen. It needs someone brave enough to make the radical changes necessary.

Nothing about Mr. Bains suggests that he is that person; he was not even brave enough to outline real plans for Ontario during his party’s leadership campaign. He was able to win by offering next to nothing of substance during the leadership race, and the sad thing about the current political outlook in Ontario is that he could very well do the same thing in a provincial election, too.

stories.title: Ending homelessness will be 'very challenging,' Ontario Premier Doug Ford says
stories.summary: Toronto - Ontario Premier Doug Ford says ending homelessness in 10 years will be "very challenging."
stories.author: Liam Casey The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - Ending homelessness in 10 years will be “very challenging,” Ontario Premier Doug Ford said Tuesday.

Earlier this month, Prime Minister Mark Carney committed to ending homelessness in Canada within the next decade.

That commitment came with the release of the 2026 federal budget, which set aside $11.2 billion to tackle homelessness over four years starting next year and $17.8 billion over 10 years.

The plan proposes Ottawa cover capital costs for supportive and transitional housing while provinces and territories cover ongoing operations and services, including training, income and health supports.

But Ford said the infrastructure costs are the least costly part of the plan and the province would need more money for operational costs.

“We’re going to do everything we can to end homelessness – that’s a big statement from the federal government – it’s very, very challenging,” Ford said.

The Association of Municipalities of Ontario has found there were about 85,000 Ontarians without a home in 2025, with more than half of those being homeless for six months or more over the previous year. There were more than 2,000 encampments across Ontario last year.

There were nearly 80,000 people living without a home the year before.

The association, which represents the province’s 444 municipalities, has for several years called for more funding to end the homelessness crisis. It said homelessness will continue to worsen over the next decade under steady economic conditions, when it projects there would be 177,000 people without a home.

Homelessness has spiked since the COVID-19 pandemic hit. Between 2016 and 2020, homelessness increased by 6.3 per cent. From 2021 to 2025, it increased by 49.1 per cent.

Municipal Affairs and Housing Minister Rob Flack said the federal government has laid out a “noble goal” to end homelessness.

“The word ‘ending’ is what concerns us,” Flack said. “We had the federal-provincial-territorial meeting a couple of weeks ago and I shared this concern with other provincial ministers. Obviously it’s a crisis, obviously we have to make changes. We have to continue to invest to try and help people get supportive housing. That’s the first step for success. That being said, the word ‘ending’ is what we’re challenged with somewhat, but it would be a noble goal and we will fight to end homelessness as best possible.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 24, 2026.

stories.title: Minister says one-time plan for permanent residents capped at 200,000 entries
stories.summary: Immigration Minister Lena Diab says the government has no intention of granting permanent residency to more than 200,000 people in its one-time plan in addition to its broad target.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — Immigration Minister Lena Diab says the government has no intention of granting permanent residency to more than 200,000 people in its one-time plan in addition to its broad target.

Diab says 100,000 permanent resident slots in the one-year plan are for workers who will be nominated by provinces and territories, and those slots will go unfilled if the provinces and territories decide they don’t need them.

The topic came up during debate in the House of Commons today on a Conservative motion to block the government’s permanent residency plan, which could see upwards of 662,000 people receive permanent residency in 2027.

Conservative immigration critic Michelle Rempel Garner argues Canada can’t absorb all of those people without putting additional strains on the housing and job markets and social infrastructure.

The government argues many people who are expected to receive permanent residency next year are already here and won’t add new pressure to the housing or labour markets.

The Bloc Québécois says it plans to support the Conservative motion, which cannot pass without the support of some members of the Liberal majority government.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 24, 2026.

David Baxter, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Full Regina Transit service will resume Tuesday afternoon, city says
stories.summary: Regina Transit service will resume Tuesday afternoon after drivers were locked out by the city Monday morning, and a tentative agreement was reached that night.
stories.author: Tavi Dhillon
stories.content:
Busses should return to Regina roads Tuesday afternoon following a day-long lockout, after the union representing transit operators reached a conditional agreement with the city.

Full transit service in Regina is expected to resume around 3 p.m. Tuesday, Nathan Luhning, the city’s director of transit, announced at a news conference that morning. Standard Regina Transit routes have been paused since 11 a.m. Monday, in accordance with the City of Regina’s lockout notice that barred union employees from working.

The Amalgamated Transit Union (ATU) Local 588, which represents the workers, claimed that the notice was delivered in response to its plan to halt voluntary overtime – which the city has previously said it needs to meet residents’ demands.

“It’s a dynamic operation,” Luhning said, referring to Regina Transit’s systems.

“Overtime is used to help supplement service when operators can’t come into work. So, service, like Agribition, puts an additional strain on the resources for Regina Transit. With not having overtime to be accessed, that would severely limit what service we could put out on the road.”

The parties reached a tentative decision to resume transit service after less than two full days of the lockout on Monday night. That agreement, which was reached with the help of a provincial mediator after almost nine hours of work, ended approximately two years of negotiations between the city and local ATU.

“With the current situation (on Monday night), there was a movement to get a deal done,” Luhning said, noting the lockout’s impacts on riders and the approximately 380 Regina Transit employees who are represented by the union.

The contract is pending ratification from local union workers and Regina city council. When asked for specific details on it, Luhning told reporters he could not comment.

The City of Regina has a pool of spare operators who can offer support if needed during times when there is an increased demand for service, such as Saskatchewan Roughriders games and concerts, Luhning said.

“When we have extra demand on that system, that pool is diminished and we don’t have as many resources to draw from,” he continued. “As a city of our size, when we have large events that come to the city, it does put a drain on our resources, but we can manage through that.”

Luhning said that the city does review the amount of overtime used in combination with the drivers who are on its standby list and is “constantly looking to improve” that ratio.

“It’s a balance between having enough operators in the pool, versus having too many. If you do have too many that are not being efficiently used, that cannot be an effective use of our resources.”

City staffers will consider that ratio and May forward a related motion to Regina city council, the transit director added.

Annual and monthly Regina Transit pass holders should see two days added to their Umo account to make up for the lockout by the end of this week .

stories.title: Global economic shocks ‘likely to be larger, more frequent,’ BoC’s Macklem says
stories.summary: The Bank of Canada is expected to announce its next and final decision of 2026 in December, but Macklem did not indicate if they would make another hike or hold it steady.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
Global economic shocks are “likely to be larger” and more frequent amid trade conflicts and war, Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem said Tuesday.

Amid these economic pressures, the central bank is committed to its two per cent inflation target to prevent consumer prices to rise to levels seen in the years following the pandemic, he added.

“We can’t prevent those shocks or their ripple effects, but monetary policy can keep them from undermining price stability,” Macklem said during a speech at the Economic Club of Canada on Tuesday.

“In uncertain waters, it’s more important than ever to have a trusted anchor.”

Macklem, who will see his term as Bank of Canada governor end in June 2027, spoke about the central bank’s decision earlier this month to renew its monetary policy framework of two per cent for five more years.

That policy has “served Canadians well,” Macklem said, pointing to the decisions made when inflation spiked following the COVID-19 pandemic and start of the Ukraine war.

The inflation rate reached about eight per cent in 2022, the highest in nearly 40 years and a number that Macklem said saw many Canadian facing their first experience with high inflation.

He also referenced the high inflation rates of the 1970s and 80s where it soared into the 10 to 13 per cent ranges where a target wasn’t in place to “anchor” policy. He said it was the severe recessions of the early 1980s and 1990s that brought that number down.

“After 25 years, the two per cent target was well understood and our record of keeping inflation close to the target had built credibility,” said Macklem.

“This meant that even when inflation rose sharply, Canadians expected us to bring it back down.”

Multiple rate hikes from 2022 to 2024 helped lower inflation below the two per cent goal, but Macklem said Canadians are now facing a rate of about three per cent.

Ongoing events like the Iran war and U.S. trade conflict are making it difficult to respond in a way that will lower rates, with the governor adding extreme weather and artificial intelligence are also adding “new layers of disruption.”

“Shocks are now likely to be larger, more frequent and more difficult to assess in real time,” Macklem said.

While demand-side shocks result in the economy, inflation and economic activity moving in the same direction, supply shocks differ.

Macklem said disruptions, such as to oil, can push prices up while slowing economic growth at the same time. This results in higher prices for households amid worse job prospects.

When this happens, the governor said the central bank has to weigh the risk of ongoing inflation with the possibility of weakening the economy with further changes to the interest rate.

“The best contribution monetary policy can make to the well-being of Canadians is to keep inflation low, stable and predictable,” he said.

Late last month, the Bank of Canada raised its key rate by a quarter point to 2.5 per cent. It was widely expected and came with notice that it might not be the last. The bank said it was forecasting inflation for 2027 to hit about 3.1 per cent, up from the two per cent predicted in July.

On Tuesday, Macklem suggested that forecast might be changing, but added that inflation could persist.

“Since October, oil prices and refinery margins have both come down, suggesting inflation May not be quite as high,” he said.

“This second-round effect of the oil shock will add to inflation persistence. At the same time, the economy has shown more resilience than we expected.”

The Bank of Canada is expected to announce its next and final decision of 2026 in December, and Macklem did not indicate if they would make another hike or hold it steady.

What he did say was he expects developments out of the Middle East and Canada’s relationship with the U.S. to evolve, while cautioning the ongoing adoption of AI could be “bumpy.” There could also been new “unforeseen shocks.”

“Our assessment of inflationary pressures will change with them, but our anchor will not,” Macklem said.

The central bank also released an inflation dashboard on its website this week to bring together all major price indicators that it monitors to assess total inflation.

“After 25 years, the two per cent target was well understood and our record of keeping inflation close to the target had built credibility,” said Macklem.
“This meant that even when inflation rose sharply, Canadians expected us to bring it back down.”
Multiple rate hikes from 2022 to 2024 helped lower inflation below the two per cent goal, but Macklem said Canadians are now facing a rate of about three per cent.

Ongoing events like the Iran war and U.S. trade conflict are making it difficult to respond in a way that will lower rates, with the governor adding extreme weather and artificial intelligence are also adding “new layers of disruption.”
“Shocks are now likely to be larger, more frequent and more difficult to assess in real time,” Macklem said.
While demand-side shocks result in the economy, inflation and economic activity moving in the same direction, supply shocks differ.
Macklem said disruptions, such as to oil, can push prices up while slowing economic growth at the same time. This results in higher prices for households amid worse job prospects.
When this happens, the governor said the central bank has to weigh the risk of ongoing inflation with the possibility of weakening the economy with further changes to the interest rate.
“The best contribution monetary policy can make to the well-being of Canadians is to keep inflation low, stable and predictable,” he said.

Late last month, the Bank of Canada raised its key rate by a quarter point to 2.5 per cent. It was widely expected and came with notice that it might not be the last. The bank said it was forecasting inflation for 2027 to hit about 3.1 per cent, up from the two per cent predicted in July.
On Tuesday, Macklem suggested that forecast might be changing, but added that inflation could persist.
“Since October, oil prices and refinery margins have both come down, suggesting inflation May not be quite as high,” he said.
“This second-round effect of the oil shock will add to inflation persistence. At the same time, the economy has shown more resilience than we expected.”
The Bank of Canada is expected to announce its next and final decision of 2026 in December, and Macklem did not indicate if they would make another hike or hold it steady.

What he did say was he expects developments out of the Middle East and Canada’s relationship with the U.S. to evolve, while cautioning the ongoing adoption of AI could be “bumpy.” There could also been new “unforeseen shocks.”
“Our assessment of inflationary pressures will change with them, but our anchor will not,” Macklem said.
The central bank also released an inflation dashboard on its website this week to bring together all major price indicators that it monitors to assess total inflation.

stories.title: How our family found an affordable vacation in an unaffordable era of travel
stories.summary: Fun can be had and memories can be made, without costing an arm and a leg
stories.author: Dan Zaiontz
stories.content:
When you’re a family of five on a budget planning a vacation, it can sometimes feel like you’re audaciously setting your sights on a moon landing during the height of the Cold War.

Tensions are high (in your suburban Toronto home).

The electorate is restless, concerned (they have their sights set on Vancouver).

Recent reports indicate rival nations have already ventured to the outer reaches (namely, your in-laws who shared lovely photos from their just-completed trip to Japan).

The CBO (Conservative Budget Office) has warned this trip could be expensive (and those fall kids’ programs aren’t going to pay for themselves), so we must carefully leverage our credit card travel points.

I’ve come to realize this decision calls for visionary leadership, inspiration and clear thinking (so I ask AI to recommend nearby family-friendly travel options that won’t break the bank).

It comes through (as if I prompted it with “Houston, we’ve had a problem”). The options are actually much closer than Houston, thankfully.

My bold, unprecedented decision requires me to rally the nation…er… my family.

Hint: It’s in Southwestern Ontario.

It’s nicknamed the Forest City.

London, England? Paris, France? New York City?

They might as well be the moon, because footing the bill for our family to reach these places, finding a place to stay in these places, feeding and keeping the kids busy in these places is truly out of this world nowadays.

Of course, I want my family to see the world, experience beauty and explore what’s out there, but at what cost, you know?

Airfare for five to [insert any notable destination] is too rich for my blood. And my wallet, I can tell you that.

What’s a commander-in-chief (my wife) and her desperate undersecretary of the treasury to do?

We do not look to the stars, no.

No, we shall go west! Southwest, to be exact.

We choose London, Ont.

“No kids, not that London.”

Uh oh. There’s some reticence among the voters.

“No, there’s no Harry Potter World there.”

“No, we’re not flying.”

“No, sorry, the hotel with the pirate-themed indoor waterpark is sold out.”

“But they do have a terrific children’s museum and Storybook Gardens!”

“…Wait! Come back! Why are you walking away?”

We do not go to London for glory. Not for social media likes or because it sounds epic. Not because of Michelin stars or bucket lists.

We choose it because it is convenient.

It is affordable.

It also doesn’t economically support disagreeable foreign powers.

It has minor league baseball (Go Majors, go!) and one of those farms with playgrounds and tractor rides, plus three-star hotels with clean rooms, friendly front desks, pullout couches, moderately sized swimming pools and free breakfasts where the kids can MTOP (make their own pancakes).

We can drive there and back on a single tank of geopolitically influenced, high-priced gas. The drive itself will be a manageable duration − just long enough for the kids to argue about violations of personal space then fall asleep, but wake up in time to catch the brown cows grazing as we drive by a farmer’s field.

We’ll find parking at a reasonable distance from that thing we planned on Saturday afternoon. Plus, they seem to have more artisanal doughnut shops per capita than any place else, so that should keep grumpiness levels in check.

It turns out that anywhere our family chooses to go, anywhere at all, fun can be had, memories can be made and enjoyment can be found.

It’s the unintended realization of trying to make a family vacation happen during inflationary times, where everything costs more. But life and unprogrammed, unstructured time are short, fleeting.

It’s a realization that teaches us the experiences that last, the ones that matter, the ones we’ll look back on with warmth and joy: they don’t need to cost an arm and a leg.

You don’t need to travel thousands of kilometres, to the moon and back, to have them.

You don’t even need a passport.

You just need the people you care about with you, an open mind and a destination.

Fun? Quality time? They can happen anywhere.

Sure, others may go further. They may even go to cooler places. Real Eat Pray Love kind of spots. But is it the distance travelled that counts? The number of pushpins on your map and where you place them? Or how you spend your time and who you spend it with?

Yes, we choose to go to London, Ont.

Not because there’s no place better.

But because a new, beautiful family adventure awaits us there.

Dan Zaiontz lives in Maple, Ont.

stories.title: Ontario vows to restore frozen Osap by New Year if fraud bill passes
stories.summary: The Ford government is under mounting criticism for freezing Osap funding, a pause that began in early October, for students at all 242 Ontario private career colleges.
stories.author: Olivia Bowden
stories.content:
Ontario Student Assistance Program (Osap) payments will be restored by the new year, according to the minister for colleges and universities, as long as new legislation that aims to tighten oversight of the troubled loan system passes.

The Ford government is under mounting criticism for freezing Osap funding, a pause that began in early October, for students at all 242 Ontario private career colleges.

For weeks, the government has said it needed to pull promised funding in order to probe allegations of student loan fraud brought forward by advocacy organizations, the federal government and a third-party audit.

But critics have decried the province’s decision to issue a blanket Osap revocation on hundreds of schools instead of a select few where the government says it’s seen evidence of alleged fraud.

“I do have confidence that by the New Year we will be returning Osap to the students,” said Nolan Quinn, Minister of Colleges and Universities, ON Tuesday.

Quinn said returning the payments is predicated on the Ford government passing new legislation, Bill 148, that would cap Osap-funded enrollment growth at private colleges and would bar predominantly online programs from being eligible for student loans.

Recovering taxpayer money that has been allegedly stolen is the government’s priority, said Quinn. “We’re talking about hundreds of millions of dollars here; we want to ensure that we recover those dollars,” he said.

The province has referred the case to the Ontario Provincial Police, which has not decided yet if it will take on the case, he said. Kpmg is currently conducting a third-party audit of Osap applications for the government.

MPP John Fraser, the former interim Liberal Party Leader, said students cannot afford to wait until January for their Osap.

“People are going to lose the place they live in; they’re going to go bankrupt,” he said. “They’re not going to be able to do the things they want to do at Christmas for their kids. Thousands and thousands of honest, hard-working people.”

Career Colleges Ontario, a non-profit that advocates for the colleges and its students, has said it’s long warned the Ford government about potential Osap fraud. It reported spikes in Osap applications at a small group of schools.

Data obtained by The Canadian Press found that one private college, the Canadian College of Business, Science and Technology, saw Osap recipients surge by 3,000 per cent. Ministry filings cited in court also allege that thousands of Osap applications at some campuses have originated from a single IP address.

But students report that paused funding has meant they not only have to drop out of their programs, they are also struggling to pay for the essentials, including housing.

Premier Doug Ford has said Kpmg will prioritize clearing lower-risk colleges first, though no exact date has been set for restoring payment. Some colleges have said they have had to fire staff and worry they will shutter without Osap being restored soon.

NDP Leader Marit Stiles said the Ford government is to blame for the fraud debacle.

“Why were they not paying attention to the flags that were raised by the associations, by the industry, by the auditor? How is it possible that they didn’t catch this?” she said.

“It’s another indication that this government and this minister in particular is not in control of this file,” she said.

The Ford government’s Osap legislation is currently on its second reading and has been referred to committee.

“I do have confidence that by the New Year we will be returning Osap to the students,” said Nolan Quinn, Minister of Colleges and Universities, ON Tuesday.

Quinn said returning the payments is predicated on the Ford government passing new legislation, Bill 148, that would cap Osap-funded enrollment growth at private colleges and would bar predominantly online programs from being eligible for student loans.

Recovering taxpayer money that has been allegedly stolen is the government’s priority, said Quinn. “We’re talking about hundreds of millions of dollars here; we want to ensure that we recover those dollars,” he said.

The province has referred the case to the Ontario Provincial Police, which has not decided yet if it will take on the case, he said. Kpmg is currently conducting a third-party audit of Osap applications for the government.
MPP John Fraser, the former interim Liberal Party Leader, said students cannot afford to wait until January for their Osap.

“People are going to lose the place they live in; they’re going to go bankrupt,” he said. “They’re not going to be able to do the things they want to do at Christmas for their kids. Thousands and thousands of honest, hard-working people.”

Career Colleges Ontario, a non-profit that advocates for the colleges and its students, has said it’s long warned the Ford government about potential Osap fraud. It reported spikes in Osap applications at a small group of schools.

Data obtained by The Canadian Press found that one private college, the Canadian College of Business, Science and Technology, saw Osap recipients surge by 3,000 per cent. Ministry filings cited in court also allege that thousands of Osap applications at some campuses have originated from a single IP address.
But students report that paused funding has meant they not only have to drop out of their programs, they are also struggling to pay for the essentials, including housing.

Premier Doug Ford has said Kpmg will prioritize clearing lower-risk colleges first, though no exact date has been set for restoring payment. Some colleges have said they have had to fire staff and worry they will shutter without Osap being restored soon.
NDP Leader Marit Stiles said the Ford government is to blame for the fraud debacle.
“Why were they not paying attention to the flags that were raised by the associations, by the industry, by the auditor? How is it possible that they didn’t catch this?” she said.
“It’s another indication that this government and this minister in particular is not in control of this file,” she said.
The Ford government’s Osap legislation is currently on its second reading and has been referred to committee.

stories.title: Constable who shot Jamal Francique offers condolences to family at inquest
stories.summary: A police officer who fatally shot a Black man nearly seven years ago offered condolences to the man's grieving family Tuesday as he began testifying at a coroner's inquest.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
A police officer who shot a Black man in the head during an attempted arrest in Mississauga, Ont., nearly seven years ago offered condolences to the man’s grieving family Tuesday as he began testifying at a coroner’s inquest.

Peel regional police Const. Milan Ivkovic told the inquest into the death of Jamal Francique that if he had a magic wand, “none of us would be here today.”

Francique, 28, was shot on Jan. 7, 2020, as a team of plainclothes officers in unmarked vehicles and on foot tried to arrest him for allegedly breaching the conditions of his bail.

He died in hospital days later.

The inquest has heard officers planned to arrest Francique before he got to his car that night, but he moved more quickly than expected, and the officer meant to block his car was late.

Ivkovic testified Tuesday that he fired four shots at the car after it began accelerating directly toward him.

The officer, who was on foot at the time, said he couldn’t see a figure in the car and just shot where a driver would be.

The car then mounted the curb, narrowly missing him, before it made a sharp turn and crashed into a garage in the townhouse complex, he said.

The officer said that based on that manoeuvre, he immediately knew the driver was most likely “not OK.”

Jurors have heard Francique did not receive medical attention until after a police tactical unit arrived and pulled him out the car about 20 minutes later.

The forensic pathologist who conducted the autopsy previously told the inquest the crash did not contribute to Francique’s death, which was caused by a gunshot wound to the head.

Dr. Ashwyn Rajagopalan said he was surprised Francique survived as long as he did, given the severity of his injury.

Ontario’s police watchdog, the Special Investigations Unit, has cleared the officers of wrongdoing in Francique’s death.

Coroner’s inquests do not assign legal responsibility, though jurors May make recommendations aimed at preventing similar deaths.

stories.title: Alberta natural gas act a potential risk to TC Energy’s Ngtl growth plans: Cibc analysts
stories.summary: Cibc analysts say in their report that provincial involvement could complicate the timing and economics of future expansions of the sprawling Nova Gas Transmission Ltd. network.
stories.author: Lauren Krugel
stories.content:
Analysts at Cibc Capital Markets say proposed Alberta legislation creates uncertainty around TC Energy Corp.’s plans to expand the vast pipeline network it has long operated in the province.

The proposed Natural Gas Infrastructure Act , if passed, would enable the provincial government to set up Crown entities to plan or build new natural gas pipelines to meet booming demand from data centres, the oilsands and other industries.

The Alberta government says such a move would be a last resort if the private sector can’t meet the pipeline capacity needs, and has raised concerns about the adequacy of TC’s expansion plans.

Cibc analysts Robert Catellier and Rogan Anantharajah say in a report that provincial involvement could complicate the timing and economics of future expansions on the Ngtl , or Nova Gas Transmission Ltd., network.

They note that Ngtl system, which spans much of Alberta and connects into neighbouring provinces, is federally regulated, raising questions over how far Alberta’s powers would extend.

Last week, TC Energy announced plans to expand Ngtl , including with a new 370-kilometre pipeline connecting gas to the oilsands region, and additional loops and compressor units.

TC also said it plans to launch 1.3 billion cubic feet per day in new service offerings as early as January, for delivery between 2030 and 2032.

“Ultimately, we view (the legislation) as creating potential risks to securing growth rather than undermining the entire Ngtl business. While the situation warrants monitoring, we believe the risk remains largely confined to headlines at this stage,” the Cibc analysts said.

TC has spent $15 billion in the last decade on expansion projects on Ngtl.

In a letter to Premier Danielle Smith obtained by The Canadian Press, TC chief executive François Poirier warned against legislation that would undermine the integrated infrastructure that TC and fellow energy shipper and distributor Atco Ltd. operate.

“Legislation that proposes overriding integration would create significant market instability. The uncertainty created by the government’s proposed measures would mean companies and customers cannot make long-term capital and contracting decisions with confidence,” Poirier wrote.

“We struggle to see how we can progress the new capacity offering of more than 1.3 billion cubic feet per day announced on Nov. 16, 2026, if legislation overrides the integrated Ngtl-Atco system. The proposed capacity offering that has been announced is premised on integration remaining intact.”

stories.title: McGuinty says he can't explain Pentagon's criticism of Canada's defence spending
stories.summary: Ottawa - Defence Minister David McGuinty says he can’t "divine" the thinking behind the Pentagon’s recent criticism of Canada’s defence spending.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - Defence Minister David McGuinty said Tuesday he can’t “divine” the thinking behind the Pentagon’s recent criticism of Canada’s defence spending — after the Trump administration took some symbolic steps to upend long-standing norms in North American continental security.

“The amount of co-operation that we are pursuing together under Norad has not changed. What we are doing together at Nato has not changed,” McGuinty told reporters in Ottawa. “Our military-to-military co-operation has not changed.”

Under U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, the Pentagon has undermined the long-standing bilateral defence relationship as Ottawa continues to review its plans for a fleet of American F-35 fighter jets.

Hegseth last week issued a classified memo imposing restrictions on military co-operation with Canada on think-tanks and socializing.

On Monday, the Pentagon released what it called a “fact sheet” which said Canada’s defence spending has limited the country’s ability to contribute to the protection of North America.

The Pentagon in May also paused the Permanent Joint Board on Defense, an advisory forum for U.S.-Canada bilateral defence co-operation that was established in 1940.

A senior U.S. Department of Defense official said the memo was intended to ensure a unified objective during engagements with Canada. It does not affect military operations.

The official from U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration briefed a small group of Canadian journalists Monday on background in order to speak more candidly about Canada-U.S. relations.

The official, who said the Pentagon is looking for Canada to commit to a realistic approach focused on military efficiency, cited the F-35 review.

The Liberal government has yet to reach a decision on its full order of F-35 fighter jets from Lockheed Martin — which Pentagon officials have cited as a source of frustration. Canada has committed to buy 16 of the aircraft, but the decision on the remainder of the planned 88-aircraft order has been the subject of a political review for more than a year.

The official claimed the Canadian Armed Forces sees the F-35 jets as superior to the alternatives but Ottawa is focusing on a middle-power strategy and prioritizing industrial policy and parochial trade issues over defence commitments.

Canada has long faced criticism over its lagging defence spending but Trump’s administration has connected it directly to larger trade issues, including the renewal of the Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement on trade.

Earlier this year, Canada announced it would purchase early warning planes from Sweden’s Saab rather than Boeing.

Last March, Prime Minister Mark Carney said Canada had met for the first time the Nato requirement to spend the equivalent of two per cent of GDP on defence. The target was set in 2014 and Canada was among the Nato members which had never hit it.

When Nato members met last year in The Hague, they agreed to increase their defence spending to the equivalent of five per cent of GDP by 2035 — 3.5 per cent for core military and defence and 1.5 per cent for broader security and defence-adjacent investments that were loosely defined.

The U.S. official said it’s good to see Canada make “modest” progress on defence spending but accused Ottawa of not having a realistic plan for the new Nato benchmark.

The U.S. official said the gap between rhetoric and reality in Ottawa is the widest among the Nato partners. They also said Canada’s readiness under Norad is well below what is expected and the military organization doesn’t have proper investment from Ottawa.

The Pentagon is exploring how to protect the United States in the event it cannot rely on Canada to meet its obligations, the official added.

McGuinty was pressed by reporters on whether Canada would meet the five per cent commitment. He said Canada has a path to spending the equivalent of four per cent of GDP on defence by 2030.

When asked how the U.S. reacted to Canada’s four-per-cent plan, McGuinty’s response was terse.

“Canada is a sovereign nation,” he said. “I’ll be very direct. We don’t report to the United States.”

The recent federal budget charted a course to meeting the spending targets by 2030 but did not look at spending beyond that year. That plan includes spending 2.6 per cent of GDP, or about $99 billion, ON core military, including ammunition and soldiers’ salaries.

“Canada has, for a long time, not lived up to our allies’ expectations,” said Jamie Tronnes of the Center for North American Prosperity and Security, a project of the Macdonald-Laurier Institute.

She added that should spur American and other allied militaries to double down on pushing Canada to increase its spending.

“A frozen relationship can only thaw with dialogue,” Tronnes said in an email.

“The (Department of Defense) strategy of disengagement in public forums says more about what the secretary of the (Department of Defense) is trying to impose on his own department, which is a one-voice-speaks-for-all policy, rather than the best way to engage with allies, especially those who May not like the messenger.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 24, 2026.

— Written by Kelly Geraldine Malone in Washington with files from Anja Karadeglija and Kyle Duggan in Ottawa

The party’s immigration critic, Michelle Rempel Garner, said the number of people coming to Canada is unsustainable.

Conservative MP Michelle Rempel Garner speaks in the foyer of the House of Commons on Parliament Hill on Nov. 24, 2026. (Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia)

November 24, 2026 at 1:35 p.m.

Ottawa — The Conservatives are using their opposition day in the House of Commons to push immigration to the top of the agenda, calling on members of Parliament to join them in rejecting the government’s new immigration levels plan.

She argued the Liberals’ plan to allow hundreds of thousands of people to become permanent residents next year will worsen the housing shortage, make it harder for young people to find work and increase wait times in hospitals.

“Here’s what Conservatives are asking for: lower immigration levels. Let the system keep up with housing, health care and jobs. Set them based on the homes (and) hospital beds that we actually have capacity for,” said immigration critic Michelle Rempel Garner.

The latest immigration plan caps the number of new permanent residents at 380,000 for each of the next three years, but it also includes a one-time plan to clear a backlog of some 200,000 people who entered Canada under permanent residency programs and who are still waiting for their cases to be processed.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said last month that those people are “effectively permanent residents” already and have been awaiting formal recognition of their status from the government.

That includes just under 19,000 people who fled Ukraine after Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, and who were already in Canada and had family in the country when they applied as part of a special program created in 2023.

The figure also includes some 32,000 people who left Hong Kong after China imposed a national security law. Canadian programs were created to allow those people to apply for permanent residency. Another 45,000 people have applied to reunite with their close family members.

Rempel Garner said she agrees that Canada should process the applications of people who came for humanitarian reasons, but said that should be folded into the existing annual target.

“For generations, Canada made a promise to the world: come here legally, work hard, play by the rules and you can build a good life,” she said.

She said Liberal governments have broken that promise.

Former prime minister Justin Trudeau acknowledged in late 2024 that the government had failed to act quickly enough to control the immigration system, after it increased the number of people entering Canada post-pandemic to help a struggling labour market.

At the time, the government had planned to allow 500,000 people to become permanent residents each year.

In a video explaining his government’s plans to reform the system, Trudeau said colleges and universities had been using foreign student admissions to boost their own bottom lines, scammers had targeted vulnerable people looking to make better lives in Canada, and the government had failed to “turn off the taps faster.”

Trudeau’s Liberals lowered the number of permanent residents to a planned 365,000 a year, and capped the number of visas for students and temporary workers.

In a September interview with the New York Times, Carney said Ottawa had regained control of the immigration system and said the government would have to start asking when to resume a “controlled increase in the population.”

On Tuesday, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said in the House of Commons that he believes the real reason Carney is increasing the levels is “to bring in more low-wage labour and more renters to profit corporate, private equity landlords and multinational corporations that want to pay less for the workers they have instead of hiring Canadians.”

A Postmedia-Leger poll earlier this month found that nearly three-quarters of respondents are worried about the government’s latest immigration levels. More than half the people who took the survey said they think Canada already allows too many immigrants into the country.

People who responded to the poll rated overcrowding in health care and pressure on the education system as a top concern, along with rising housing costs and a shortage of homes.

Sarah Ritchie joined National Post’s politics bureau after four years covering breaking news on Parliament Hill for The Canadian Press, where she worked as a reporter and editor. Before that, she was an anchor and investigative reporter at Global News in Halifax and covered the Nova Scotia legislature for CTV Atlantic.

stories.title: Transport minister defends new land seizure powers proposed for high-speed rail
stories.summary: Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon is pushing back against criticism of new land seizure powers proposed for a high-speed rail project between Toronto and Quebec City.
stories.author: Christopher Reynolds
stories.content:
Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon is pushing back against criticism of new land seizure powers proposed for a high-speed rail project between Toronto and Quebec City.

MacKinnon says the enhanced expropriation abilities detailed in draft legislation would allow Ottawa to fast-track steps that could otherwise become bogged down for years and insists that “there is no removal of due process.”

The comments comes after the federal government included in a 519-page procedural motion on Friday measures that would expand its power to lock down property rights along the corridor, such as barring sale or work on a given lot for years.

The move builds on a law passed in June that enabled the government to expropriate land without public hearings, among other reforms.

Ontario Conservative MP Michael Barrett says the latest changes would replace the existing Expropriation Act with a separate regime for high-speed rail, compounding concerns about cost and disruption to rural communities in eastern Ontario and Quebec.

The high-speed rail project would see trains running between the two provincial capitals at 300 kilometres per hour at a projected cost of between $60 billion and $90 billion, with work set to start on the Montreal-Ottawa leg by 2030.
