stories.title: Constable who shot Jamal Francique says he acted out of 'fight-or-flight' instinct
stories.summary: A police officer who shot a Black man in the head during an attempted arrest in Mississauga, Ont., nearly seven years ago told a coroner's inquest Tuesday that he did not make a conscious decision to open fire but instead acted out of a 'fight-or-flight' instinct.
stories.author: Paola Loriggio The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A police officer who shot a Black man in the head during an attempted arrest in Mississauga, Ont., nearly seven years ago told a coroner’s inquest Tuesday that he did not make a conscious decision to open fire but instead acted out of a ‘fight-or-flight’ instinct.

Peel regional police Const. Milan Ivkovic was part of a team of plainclothes officers in unmarked vehicles who sought to arrest Jamal Francique near his home on the evening of Jan. 7, 2020, over an alleged breach of bail conditions.

The inquest has heard officers planned to arrest Francique before he got to his car, but he moved more quickly than expected, and the officer meant to block his car was late.

Francique reversed out of his parking spot and briefly came to a stop, Ivkovic testified. Meanwhile, an unmarked police car pulled up, putting its nose to the vehicle’s bumper, he said.

Ivkovic got out of his car and walked toward Francique’s vehicle, which was still stationary, he said. In that time, another unmarked police car came up behind Francique’s car, and the officer could hear people shouting commands, he said.

As he stepped up onto the curb, Ivkovic saw Francique’s car suddenly reverse and lurch forward, accelerating toward him, he said. The officer said he fired his gun four times “in the area of where a driver would be,” though he couldn’t see a figure inside.

Under cross-examination, a lawyer representing Francique’s father suggested Ivkovic should have known it was “prudent” to move out of the car’s way.

Officers aren’t trained on jumping out of the way, the officer said.

“So there was no decision at that point that I made in my head, there was no moment where I had some deep thoughts and calculations about what the best course of action was. The vehicle lurched towards me and my reaction was a fight-or-flight one,” he said.

Lawyer Sabrina Shillingford noted that Peel police policies prohibit officers from shooting at people in a moving vehicle unless there is an immediate threat of death or grievous bodily harm to police or the public “by means other than the vehicle.”

“That’s information that, given your training, the public would expect you to know, fair?” she asked.

“I don’t know what the public would expect me to know — this is news to me, to be honest with you, that that is in the directive,” Ivkovic replied.

The constable rejected Shillingford’s suggestion that he drew his gun before Francique’s car moved toward him. When Shillingford pointed out that he’d previously testified he couldn’t remember when he took out his gun, Ivkovic said he knew he didn’t have it in hand when he left his car, and the rest played out in a matter of seconds.

“I’m going to suggest to you, sir, that you had other options, including staying in your car until you knew that the Acura that Mr. Francique occupied was off and all movement from the vehicle was contained. Would you agree?” the lawyer asked.

“There’s lots of options that we could have done and ... had I known this was going to transpire, I would not have gotten out of my car,” he said.

“There’s an innumerable number of what-ifs ... I thought Mr. Francique was done. He gave no indication that he was going to put that vehicle in motion until at the very end when he did.”

Francique’s car mounted the curb, narrowly missing Ivkovic, before it made a sharp turn and crashed into a garage, the officer said during his examination in chief. Based on that manoeuvre, he immediately knew the driver was most likely “not OK,” he said.

Jurors have heard Francique, 28, did not receive medical attention until after a police tactical unit arrived and pulled him out the car about 20 minutes later. He died in hospital days later.

The forensic pathologist who conducted the autopsy previously told the inquest the crash did not contribute to Francique’s death, which was caused by a gunshot wound to the head.

Dr. Ashwyn Rajagopalan said he was surprised Francique survived as long as he did, given the severity of his injury.

Ivkovic offered condolences to Francique’s grieving family Tuesday, saying that if he had a magic wand, “none of us would be here today.”

Also on Tuesday, the inquest heard a summary of the evidence of another officer, Const. Carly Houlihan, who said she jumped out of the way of Francique’s car as it drove toward her. When she heard gunshots, Houlihan believed Francique was the one firing, but she learned soon after it was her colleague, the summary said.

Police had been secretly surveilling Francique for days before they tried to arrest him, the inquest has heard. A tip had come in through Crime Stoppers that Francique had a gun and was trafficking drugs, but officers found no evidence to corroborate the tip during their surveillance, so they decided to instead arrest him for allegedly violating house arrest.

Ontario’s police watchdog, the Special Investigations Unit, later cleared the officers of criminal wrongdoing in Francique’s death.

Coroner’s inquests do not assign legal responsibility, though jurors May make recommendations aimed at preventing similar deaths.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 24, 2026.

stories.title: Ottawa defends new land seizure powers proposed for Alto’s high-speed rail project
stories.summary: Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon says it would allow Ottawa to fast-track steps that could otherwise become bogged down for years
stories.author: Christopher Reynolds
stories.content:
Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon on Tuesday defended new land seizure powers proposed for a high-speed rail project between Toronto and Quebec City.

Detailed in draft legislation, the enhanced expropriation abilities would allow Ottawa to fast-track processes that could otherwise become bogged down “for 10, 12, 15 years,” he said.

“There is no removal of due process,” he told reporters twice en route to a cabinet meeting in Ottawa.

“This is going to be a bespoke regime. It’s been used in Ontario, it’s been used in Quebec for public transit projects. It’s an extremely important component of this project and it’s one that we’re very comfortable with.”

The comments came after the federal government spelled out in a 519-page procedural motion on Friday measures that would expand its power to lock down property rights along the rail corridor.

Those rights include allowing seizure of land for transfer to a private consortium – like the one contracted to build the line – broader discretion to bar work on a given lot and sending disputes over road crossings to private arbitration, which could see farmers foot part of the bill for construction and maintenance.

The move builds on the High-Speed Rail Network Act passed earlier this year that enabled the government to sidestep purchase negotiations, expropriate land without public hearings and secure the first right to buy a property for up to eight years, without fronting the cash to the owner.

Ontario Conservative MP Michael Barrett said the latest changes would replace the existing Expropriation Act with a separate regime for high-speed rail, compounding concerns about cost and disruption to rural communities in eastern Ontario and Quebec.

“Residents are deeply concerned about the potential loss of homes and farmland, disruption to local businesses and lasting damage to our environment,” he said in a public letter to MacKinnon on Tuesday.

Barrett singled out the dispute resolution provisions, stating that farmers and municipalities could face arbitration costs of up to $25,000 on top of their own legal fees.

Locals have also voiced worries that the walled-off track will block country roads and create longer, bottleneck-prone drives for commuters and first responders, as the high train speeds rule out at-grade crossings.

NDP Leader Avi Lewis criticized the project’s public-private ownership model and said smaller communities feel excluded and “insufficiently consulted.”

“You really need the social licence for big projects because any railway – it’s got to take somebody’s land,” he said. “We need the most transparent and democratic process to do that. And when you’re in a P3, you just don’t get that.”

The high-speed rail project would see trains running between Toronto and Quebec City at a projected cost of between $60-billion and $90-billion.

Alto, the Crown corporation overseeing the project, is weighing two possible corridors for eastern Ontario. One traces a direct line between Ottawa and Peterborough and the other arcs along a more southerly path, with Kingston as a stop under consideration.

Construction of the first phase of the 1,000-kilometre rail line is set to kick off in 2029 or 2030, linking Montreal and Ottawa in an effective test case for what would be a massive infrastructure project intended to transform rail travel in Canada’s most densely populated region.

The seven stops mandated so far by the federal government are Toronto, Peterborough, Ottawa, Laval, Que., Montreal, Trois-Rivières, Que., and Quebec City.

Alto has said the benefits of the project range from greater economic output, job growth and tourism revenue to emissions reduction and safer travel. It has pledged to support local economies by hiring workers and buying materials from those areas during construction.

The proposed network would host 72 trains a day running on dedicated electric tracks at 300 km/h, slashing current travel times. It would make for a three-hour trip between Toronto and Montreal and less than one hour between Montreal and Ottawa.

Alto CEO Martin Imbleau has acknowledged that some expropriations will be necessary, though he declined to give an estimate. The Montreal-Ottawa leg would cross some 1,700 properties, including about 500 agricultural ones, he said earlier this year.

stories.title: Quebec opposition leaders urge premier not to delay session over oath to the King
stories.summary: Montreal - Quebec opposition leaders are urging Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon not to delay opening the parliamentary session over the oath to the King.
stories.author: Marieke Glorieux-Stryckman The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - The Quebec government has appealed a Superior Court judgment that temporarily reinstated the oath to the King.

The province’s justice minister, Marie-Claude Sarrazin, confirmed the appeal of Monday’s ruling that suspended the 2022 provincial law that made the oath to the King optional.

“The law (suspending the oath), adopted unanimously in 2022, confirms that the oath of allegiance to the King belongs to another era,” said Sarrazin in a press release.

While the appeal is pending, the government is asking for the ruling to be lifted and for legislature members to be allowed to sit without swearing the oath.

The ruling raised questions about whether the parliamentary session would open as planned on Dec. 1, after all 127 legislature members chose to swear an oath only to the Quebec people.

Carney has built his entire prime ministership around regard for the rule of law and institutions, Susan Delacourt writes.

In a press conference earlier on Tuesday, Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon suggested the government May be able to sit without swearing the oath to the King.

“We are currently considering all options to be able to sit without being coerced — by a single individual, really — into taking an action that is, frankly, quite dishonest and humiliating,” he said.

He did not directly say whether he would be ready to defy the court order.

“Allow me to find a solution that allows us to hold our session while preserving the dignity of the elected representatives and the dignity of our Quebec democracy,” he said.

Meanwhile, Quebec opposition leaders urged St-Pierre Plamondon not to delay opening the parliamentary session over the oath to the King.

Opposition Liberal Leader Charles Milliard asked St-Pierre Plamondon to guarantee that the session would open as planned on Dec. 1.

“It’s out of the question that we postpone the session, and it’s out of the question too that we sit illegally,” he said.

“Quebecers have waited long enough. We are paid to sit,” he added.

Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon doubled down on his refusal to swear allegiance to the King after the province’s Superior Court ruled to temporarily reinstate the oath. (Nov. 23, 2026)

Milliard said his party is waiting for the legislature president to decide whether they will need to swear the oath in order to sit.

Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime said that while he opposes the ruling, he believes the session needs to start — even if it means swearing allegiance to the King.

“If we have to hide in a closet one by one, and to cross our fingers or hold our noses, we’ll go in and take the oath,” he said, adding that the oath did not need to be a “public flogging session.”

Justice Ian Demers ruled Monday that the province’s politicians will need to swear an oath to the King in order to sit at the provincial legislature and that any law passed by legislators who did not swear the oath would be unconstitutional.

The ruling granted an emergency order requested by lawyer Lawrence David and the Consumer Law Group, who asked the court to stay the application of a 2022 law that made swearing the oath optional. The law is suspended until David’s constitutional challenge can be heard on its merits.

Speaking to The Canadian Press on Tuesday, David said the fact that the law was passed unanimously doesn’t make it constitutional.

“What we are seeing from the Parti Québécois are flagrant attacks on the rule of law that are befitting of a tinpot authoritarian autocracy,” he said.

He said the ruling bars legislature members from sitting, participating in parliamentary activities and voting on bills.

“If the MNAs attempt to start the legislature, then they will be doing so illegally,” he said. “Not to mention, they would be violating a court order.”

In Ottawa, reactions to the debate were subdued.

Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon said he would leave the matter to the Quebec government.

“I think it’s a waste of time to get bogged down in this controversy,” said Culture Minister Marc Miller.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 24, 2026.

stories.title: Unique Western lab on journey to decode addiction
stories.summary: Western University researcher Jesus Chavarria leads addiction research examining biological, psychological and social factors.
stories.author: Jacquelyn Mitchell
stories.content:
Nestled in an unassuming office at the edge of campus, Western University researcher and psychology professor Jesus “Jesse” Chavarria is building on the work of giants in the field of addictions research.

As director of the Research on Addictions and Disparities (RoAD) lab, his approach combines clinical, biological and social psychological factors to determine exactly what happens to a person when they take drugs, largely alcohol. There’s still so much we don’t know about addictions, Chavarria stressed, and much of what is considered “common knowledge” is inaccurate or incomplete.

“He is the only one in the province who is doing this exact type of research,” said second-year PhD student Karla Kovacek, part of the RoAD lab since she began her master’s degree at Western.

“The alcohol research world is very tiny. Jesse was one of the few professors I was really interested in working with.”

“I come from a family where addiction is not uncommon,” Chavarria said.

“Early in my life I lived in and around the inner city in Chicago, so it was always visible, and it was part of life. It was always something that interested me.”

Despite that, Chavarria first pursued an education in orthodontics. An elective course he described as a “crash course into substance use” proved the first serendipitous push to the path he’s on now.

Jesus Chavarria

After leaving the University of the Pacific for DePaul back home in Chicago, he got involved in community-based work studying addictions among ex-offenders. From there, he moved to Florida State University for his master’s and PhD.

“I don’t come from a family with graduate training. My dad was one of the first people to graduate from college, so I didn’t know this world, I just kind of stumbled through it and ended up here – and I’m absolutely loving what I do.”

Chavarria’s work builds on other serendipitous connections to well-known addictions researchers: Andrea King at University of Chicago, where he did a clinical psychology internship, and Christian Hendershot, with whom he worked at the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health (CAMH) before coming to Western.

King is one of the only researchers in the world doing “super-longitudinal studies” involving consumption of alcohol, which have followed participants for more than a decade so far and involves them drinking in the lab for research purposes. Hendershot, meanwhile, was the sole person in Canada doing IV administration of alcohol – which allows researchers to ensure a consistent blood alcohol level – until he moved stateside, where he is now one of only a handful of such researchers in the United States.

Chavarria’s experiences with King and Hendershot laid the foundation for his lab’s work, which studies each participant as a whole, while seeking evidence-based explanations and solutions for addiction.

While humans have been purposefully using drugs for thousands of years, Chavarria says addictions research is still in “the Dark Ages.”

“We don’t know a lot,” he said.

### “Two people can look identical in the sense that they come from very similar backgrounds, same education, participated in the same extracurriculars – one can still grow up to use substances problematically while the other doesn’t.” – Jesus Chavarria, Western psychology professor and director of RoAD lab

One misconception about alcohol use disorder is that it develops solely as a coping mechanism.

“That can be one piece of it,” said Vidhi Patel, a master’s student in the lab, “but emerging research shows people develop risky alcohol use behaviours because they’re having a lot of fun or they feel very stimulated.”

Much of the lab’s current research focuses on subjective responses to drinking, in particular the contrast between those who feel energetic and crave more while drinking – a known risk factor for developing alcohol use disorder – compared to those who report feeling sleepy or sedated.

Chavarria is working to find biological markers that can tie to those subjective responses, zeroing in on peripheral circulating inflammation to investigate its role in addiction risk.

Other research out of the lab, published earlier this year in collaboration with the kinesiology department, showed moderate exercise (such as brisk walking) can reduce alcohol cravings in the moment while a meta-analyses published last month found that subjective responses to alcohol (for example feeling energized or sedated) vary by context (such as at a bar compared to at home).

One of the major challenges in addictions research, Chavarria said, is that findings from studies with animal models don’t neatly carry over to humans.

While at CAMH working with Hendershot, just before coming to Western, Chavarria was part of a phase II medication trial that was anticipated to be groundbreaking. The results, published this year, instead found that even though the medication was extremely effective in rodents, when attached to the exact same histamine receptor in human brains, it did not improve outcomes.

People drank just as much alcohol when on the medication compared to a placebo, Chavarria said.

“It brings us back to why I do the work that I do: We need to understand how people respond to alcohol in order to understand the processes at play and eventually develop an intervention to help people stop if they want to.”

This is also why the RoAD lab’s approach goes beyond biology to include social and psychological factors in its quest to decode the contributors of addiction.

Chavarria said the purpose of the lab is “to understand addiction.”

“Once we better understand the factors that impact addictions in different people on a biological, social and psychological level, we can start targeting more specific interventions.”

Learn more about how Western is optimizing health for all.

Much of the lab’s current research focuses on subjective responses to drinking, in particular the contrast between those who feel energetic and crave more while drinking – a known risk factor for developing alcohol use disorder – compared to those who report feeling sleepy or sedated.
Chavarria is working to find biological markers that can tie to those subjective responses, zeroing in on peripheral circulating inflammation to investigate its role in addiction risk.

Other research out of the lab, published earlier this year in collaboration with the kinesiology department, showed moderate exercise (such as brisk walking) can reduce alcohol cravings in the moment while a meta-analyses published last month found that subjective responses to alcohol (for example feeling energized or sedated) vary by context (such as at a bar compared to at home).
One of the major challenges in addictions research, Chavarria said, is that findings from studies with animal models don’t neatly carry over to humans.

While at CAMH working with Hendershot, just before coming to Western, Chavarria was part of a phase II medication trial that was anticipated to be groundbreaking. The results, published this year, instead found that even though the medication was extremely effective in rodents, when attached to the exact same histamine receptor in human brains, it did not improve outcomes.
People drank just as much alcohol when on the medication compared to a placebo, Chavarria said.

“It brings us back to why I do the work that I do: We need to understand how people respond to alcohol in order to understand the processes at play and eventually develop an intervention to help people stop if they want to.”
This is also why the RoAD lab’s approach goes beyond biology to include social and psychological factors in its quest to decode the contributors of addiction.
Chavarria said the purpose of the lab is “to understand addiction.”
“Once we better understand the factors that impact addictions in different people on a biological, social and psychological level, we can start targeting more specific interventions.”

As director of the Research on Addictions and Disparities (RoAD) lab, his approach combines clinical, biological and social psychological factors to determine exactly what happens to a person when they take drugs, largely alcohol. There’s still so much we don’t know about addictions, Chavarria stressed, and much of what is considered “common knowledge” is inaccurate or incomplete.
“He is the only one in the province who is doing this exact type of research,” said second-year PhD student Karla Kovacek, part of the RoAD lab since she began her master’s degree at Western.
“The alcohol research world is very tiny. Jesse was one of the few professors I was really interested in working with.”
The road to the lab
“I come from a family where addiction is not uncommon,” Chavarria said.
“Early in my life I lived in and around the inner city in Chicago, so it was always visible, and it was part of life. It was always something that interested me.”
Despite that, Chavarria first pursued an education in orthodontics. An elective course he described as a “crash course into substance use” proved the first serendipitous push to the path he’s on now.
Jesus Chavarria

After leaving the University of the Pacific for DePaul back home in Chicago, he got involved in community-based work studying addictions among ex-offenders. From there, he moved to Florida State University for his master’s and PhD.

Chavarria’s experiences with King and Hendershot laid the foundation for his lab’s work, which studies each participant as a whole, while seeking evidence-based explanations and solutions for addiction.

While humans have been purposefully using drugs for thousands of years, Chavarria says addictions research is still in “the Dark Ages.”

stories.title: Ottawa says UN court ruling on Rohingya genocide is 'binding,' pledges no new action
stories.summary: Ottawa - The Carney government has yet to announce any actions in response to what it calls a "binding" ruling by the UN's top court last week that Myanmar perpetrated a genocide against its Rohingya minority.
stories.author: Dylan Robertson The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - The Carney government has yet to announce any actions in response to what it calls a “binding” ruling by the UN’s top court last week that Myanmar perpetrated a genocide against its Rohingya minority.

Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand wrote last Thursday that Canada welcomed the ruling by the International Court of Justice and noted that Ottawa recognized Myanmar’s actions as genocide in 2018.

“Canada welcomes today’s landmark judgment,” Anand wrote in her statement. “Canada will continue to stand with the Rohingya people and work with international partners to ensure justice and protect their rights and dignity.”

On Tuesday, Canada issued a joint statement on the ruling with multiple European countries, Australia and the Gambia, which launched the case in 2019.

“We underscore that the court’s judgment is binding upon Myanmar and call on Myanmar to comply fully with its obligations under international law, including the court’s decision,” reads the Tuesday statement.

The United Kingdom, which signed Tuesday’s statement, also expanded its sanctions on Myanmar.

“The U.K. is leading efforts to turn the historic ruling into action, with new sanctions against senior military figures, plans for legislation targeting aviation fuel supplies to Myanmar and further humanitarian assistance funding to support survivors and justice,” reads a news release from the British foreign service.

Ottawa has not indicated it will take further action as a result of the ruling.

The government of Myanmar, formerly Burma, has long denied citizenship to Rohingya people. In 2017, in response to ethnic violence by Muslim Rohingya, Buddhist groups launched brazen attacks and spread violent rhetoric on Facebook.

Rohingya Muslim men walk to offer Friday prayers at their refugee camp in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh, Friday, Nov. 20, 2026.

Myanmar’s military then launched a brutal campaign that forced roughly 700,000 Rohingya to flee the country, according to the Council on Foreign Relations.

Human rights groups say the military killed and raped Rohingya civilians and burned down entire villages.

The crisis forced families to flee to neighbouring Bangladesh, where they still languish in an overcrowded camp in the town of Cox’s Bazar.

In 2021, a military junta overthrew Myanmar’s civilian government and intensified ethnic violence, often through airstrikes.

Canada has partially maintained aid funding to help some of the nearly one million Rohingya people living in crowded camps in Bangladesh.

The Rohingya Centre of Canada is urging Ottawa to co-ordinate a diplomatic response with allies to further pressure Myanmar and provide more opportunities to refugee youth so they can one day lead the population if it is able to return home.

“Canada’s contribution should not end with supporting the judgment. It should help ensure that the judgment produces meaningful change,” the group wrote.

“Canada can play an important role in connecting international legal accountability with humanitarian protection, education, leadership development, and long-term peacebuilding.”

Legal experts are analyzing the Rohingya ruling for clues to how the top court will rule on other cases involving genocide claims made against Russia, Israel and Rwanda.

In its response to the ruling, the U.S. called for “preventing politicization of the ICJ.” Washington is attempting to disband the International Criminal Court over its rulings against Israel and fears that it might go after Americans.

Ottawa has said it will not decide whether Israel has committed a genocide against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip until there is a ruling from an international tribunal — despite having declared a genocide in the case of the Rohingya before the International Court of Justice ruled.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 24, 2026.

stories.title: Montreal mayor announces 10 per cent tax hikes to address infrastructure ‘backlog’
stories.summary: Montreal - Montrealers will see property taxes rise by about 10 per cent next year as the city struggles to maintain its aging infrastructure.
stories.author: Marieke Glorieux-Stryckman The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - Montrealers will see property taxes rise by about 10 per cent next year as the city struggles to maintain its aging infrastructure.

Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada made the announcement on Tuesday as the municipal government announced its 2027 budget.

Martinez Ferrada said she takes full responsibility for the increases that will see the residential property tax bills rise by an average of 9.8 per cent. The increase for non-residential property is 6.2 per cent.

The mayor had previously promised to limit tax hikes to the rate of inflation.

But she said she needed to break that promise in order to balance the budget and pay for $8 billion in spending.

“We had to take responsible and draconian measures to ensure the long-term viability of municipal services, protect our infrastructure, and put Montreal’s finances back on a solid footing,” she said.

The announced hike is the highest in years and follows increases of 3.8 per cent in 2026, 2.2 per cent in 2025 and 4.9 per cent in 2024.

The 2027 residential property increase includes a new 5.1 per cent infrastructure maintenance tax.

“The reality is that Montreal can no longer afford to postpone essential investments. Every time we delay necessary maintenance, the cost is bigger,” said Martinez Ferrada.

She pointed out that the city spends around 16 per cent of its annual budget on repaying its debts.

“We cannot continue to pass the bill on to future generations,” she said.

Various business and lobby groups were quick to criticize the budget and its proposed tax hikes.

François Vincent, Quebec vice-president of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, called it a “disgrace” in a press release following the announcement.

The union representing the city’s scientists and engineers, the Association des scientifiques et ingénieurs de Montréal, urged the municipal government to stop turning to external contractors for its infrastructure needs.

The union said Montreal could save money by giving consulting contracts to its own engineers.

“The infrastructure crisis must be addressed, but before reaching deeper into citizens’ pockets, the administration needs to do its homework and make better use of every dollar,” said union president Gisella Gesuale in a press release.

The Chamber of Commerce of Metropolitan Montreal said it was “disappointed” by the new budget and the fiscal burden on businesses and Montrealers. Its president, Isabelle Dessureault, said Montreal should find other ways to save money, including slashing the number of public servants.

“There should be no taboo subjects. We need to ask ourselves whether the structure established for Montreal more than twenty years ago is still suited to today’s economic, financial, and technological realities,” she said.

On Monday, Martinez Ferrada said Montreal has already eliminated jobs and will continue to do so in 2027.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 24, 2026.

stories.title: You can now pay off a parking ticket with a toy donation during Hamilton’s holiday drive
stories.summary: From Nov. 30 to Dec. 4, residents can donate toys with a value equal to or greater than their outstanding parking ticket amount to have the fine forgiven
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The City of Hamilton is kick-starting the season of giving by offering people the chance to pay off their parking tickets with toy donations.

The municipality says its Toys for Tickets program turned 99 parking tickets into over $6,000 worth of toy donations for local families last year.

From Nov. 30 to Dec. 4, residents can donate toys with a value equal to or greater than their outstanding parking ticket amount to have the fine forgiven.

The city says the donated toys will go to United Way Halton and Hamilton.

To participate in the program, the city says residents need to buy a new, unwrapped toy and bring the donation, purchase receipt and parking ticket to a City of Hamilton Municipal Service Centre.

Only city-issued parking tickets are eligible, the municipality says.

stories.title: Alberta bill poses potential risk to TC Energy growth plans, Cibc analysts say
stories.summary: Calgary - Analysts at Cibc Capital Markets say proposed Alberta legislation creates uncertainty around TC Energy Corp.'s plans to expand the vast pipeline network it has long operated in the province.
stories.author: Lauren Krugel The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Calgary - Analysts at Cibc Capital Markets say proposed Alberta legislation creates uncertainty around TC Energy Corp.‘s plans to expand the vast pipeline network it has long operated in the province.

The bill, if passed, would enable the provincial government to set up Crown entities to plan or build new natural gas pipelines to meet booming demand from data centres, the oilsands and other industries.

The Alberta government says such a move would be a last resort if the private sector can’t meet the pipeline capacity needs, and has raised concerns about the adequacy of TC’s expansion plans.

Cibc analysts Robert Catellier and Rogan Anantharajah say in a report that provincial involvement could complicate the timing and economics of future expansions on the Ngtl system.

They note that Ngtl, which spans much of Alberta and connects into neighbouring provinces, is federally regulated, raising questions over how far Alberta’s powers would extend.

Last week, TC Energy announced plans to expand Ngtl, including with a new 370-kilometre pipeline connecting gas to the oilsands region, and additional loops and compressor units.

TC also said it plans to launch 1.3 billion cubic feet per day in new service offerings as early as January, for delivery between 2030 and 2032.

“Ultimately, we view (the legislation) as creating potential risks to securing growth rather than undermining the entire Ngtl business. While the situation warrants monitoring, we believe the risk remains largely confined to headlines at this stage,” the Cibc analysts said.

TC has spent $15 billion in the last decade on expansion projects on Ngtl.

In a letter to Premier Danielle Smith obtained by The Canadian Press, TC chief executive François Poirier warned against legislation that would undermine the integrated infrastructure that TC and fellow energy shipper and distributor Atco Ltd. operate.

“Legislation that proposes overriding integration would create significant market instability. The uncertainty created by the government’s proposed measures would mean companies and customers cannot make long-term capital and contracting decisions with confidence,” Poirier wrote.

“We struggle to see how we can progress the new capacity offering of more than 1.3 billion cubic feet per day announced on Nov. 16, 2026, if legislation overrides the integrated Ngtl-Atco system. The proposed capacity offering that has been announced is premised on integration remaining intact.”

A spokesperson for Atco said its power and pipeline unit, Canadian Utilities, is reviewing the legislation.

“The integrated system was intended to maximize the use of existing infrastructure, support efficient investment, and provide reliable service for customers across the province. Canadian Utilities remains ready to invest in the infrastructure needed to meet customer demand and support Alberta’s continued growth,” the statement said.

“We will review the legislation through the lens of how it supports these outcomes for our customers. Throughout that process, our focus will remain on delivering safe, reliable, and affordable energy service for Albertans.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 24, 2026.

Companies in this story: (TSX:TRP, TSX:ACO. X, TSX:CU)

stories.title: Parfumerie review: Soulpepper’s sugar-sweet production is the ultimate holiday rom-com
stories.summary: Director Morris Panych helms a zippy production of the Hungarian play that inspired Nora Ephron’s You’ve Got Mail
stories.author: Aisling Murphy
stories.content:
Title: Parfumerie

Written by: Miklos Laszlo, adapted by Adam Pettle and Brenda Robins

Directed by: Morris Panych

Actors: Akosua Amo-Adem, Peter Fernandes, Noah Beemer, Oliver Dennis, Dan Mousseau, Jordan Pettle, Brenda Robins, Sophia Walker

Company and venue: Soulpepper Theatre

City: Toronto

Year: Runs until Dec. 27

Critic’s Pick

As a staff writer for a newspaper that regularly publishes excellent financial advice, I’m somewhat ashamed to admit the extent of my perfume addiction. I love the stuff. From the trendy Sol de Janeiro body sprays and Glossier mists to the pricier eaux de toilette that populate my nightstand, I’ve amassed a small army of fragrances (and a Sephora account with more loyalty points than I’m prepared to admit in print).

With this in mind, I feel I can say with some authority that Parfumerie , Soulpepper’s enchanting holiday rom-com, carries sugar-sweet top notes – strawberry and vanilla, maybe – atop a complex, woody base. Soulpepper’s production, directed by Morris Panych, tickles the senses and charms the heart. If it were a perfume, it might smell like Burberry’s fruity Her, or one of Jo Malone’s irresistible floral colognes.

First written in 1937 by Hungarian playwright Miklos Laszlo, Parfumerie is a play whose central story will doubtless feel familiar. The comedy, about two sales clerks unknowingly in love with one another, adheres closely to the enemies-to-lovers trope of the romance genre; what’s more, Laszlo’s script inspired the 1940 film The Shop Around the Corner , and, in 1998, Nora Ephron’s You’ve Got Mail .

In 2009, Soulpepper premiered Adam Pettle and Brenda Robins’s adaptation of the play, and the colourful production – set designer Ken MacDonald’s posy-pink retailscape is as beguiling now as then – became a tradition. Parfumerie returned to Soulpepper in 2011, 2013 and 2015, and now, 11 years later, the confection is back onstage at the Young Centre for the Performing Arts.

In the lead-up to Christmas, perfumer Michael Hammerschmidt (Oliver Dennis, who played the piece’s romantic lead in its first few outings) is all out of sorts. His wife might be having an affair with one of his employees; he suspects George Asztalos (Peter Fernandes). After a mild spat about nothing in particular, Hammerschmidt fires Asztalos, irrevocably convinced of his betrayal.

But there’s more to the story, of course. Asztalos, in addition to being innocent, loves someone else – an anonymous woman with whom he’s exchanged letters for a year and a half. He’s ready to marry her, and the loss of his job days before the winter holiday is devastating.

Almost as devastating as his rivalry with Rosanna Balaz (Akosua Amo-Adem), the gentle but disorganized co-worker with whom Asztalos can’t seem to get along. The colleagues bicker like schoolchildren, and when Hammerschmidt fires Asztalos, it seems like there could be a silver lining to come in their distance from one another.

And so on. Panych’s production unspools like a farce, zippy in its pacing and sentimental in all the best ways. When Hammerschmidt discovers his mistake – of course, Asztalos couldn’t possibly have wooed his wife – his apology is tender and heartfelt, a selfless admission of guilt and a solemn plea for forgiveness. (One gets the sense Hammerschmidt and Saturday, Sunday, Monday ’s jealous patriarch Peppino might bond over their similarly off-base accusations of infidelity.)

Indeed, while Parfumerie ’s central romance offers just the right blend of dramatic irony and feet-kicking cutesiness, its secondary conflicts are arguably the play’s richer stuff. Noah Beemer is winsome as Arpad, the bumbling apprentice trying his best to find some power in the world; Jordan Pettle’s take on Louis Sipos, the confidant burdened with a terrible secret, is similarly poignant.

Dennis, who, like Robins, has been part of the DNA of Soulpepper’s Parfumerie since its premiere close to two decades ago, is particularly enticing as Hammerschmidt. In a few moments, it seems the actor’s and the character’s memories of the perfume shop are one and the same – there’s a depth to the love we see onstage that I’m unsure anyone else could capture in all those layers of experience with the material.

But in the end, Parfumerie is Amo-Adem and Fernandes’s story to sell, and the duo couldn’t be better calibrated to the demands of the tale at hand. Amo-Adem beautifully telegraphs Rosanna’s big heart and questionable fine motor skills; Fernandes, among the funniest comic actors in the city, brings a delightful dash of slapstick to the optimistic Asztalos. In Amo-Adem and Fernandes’s care, it’s as much fun to watch the couple fight as it is to watch them fall for each other. (Asztalos’s final monologue, about Rosanna’s quirks and virtues, could easily go blow-for-blow with Harry’s New Year’s Eve speech in When Harry Met Sally. )

There’s something to be said in favour of a comfort watch – a story you’ve seen thousands of times, and whose ending you see coming from miles away, but that reminds you, for an hour or two, how it feels to be alive.

To that end, Parfumerie doesn’t reinvent the wheel of the romantic comedy – in plenty of ways, Laszlo’s play invented the wheel of the genre in the first place – but Soulpepper’s production, for all its history, feels equal parts cozy and fresh. If only I could bottle that feeling for the fragrance collection by my bedside.

Parfumerie returned to Soulpepper in 2011, 2013 and 2015, and now, 11 years later, the confection is back onstage at the Young Centre for the Performing Arts.

In the lead-up to Christmas, perfumer Michael Hammerschmidt (Oliver Dennis, who played the piece’s romantic lead in its first few outings) is all out of sorts. His wife might be having an affair with one of his employees; he suspects George Asztalos (Peter Fernandes). After a mild spat about nothing in particular, Hammerschmidt fires Asztalos, irrevocably convinced of his betrayal.

But there’s more to the story, of course. Asztalos, in addition to being innocent, loves someone else – an anonymous woman with whom he’s exchanged letters for a year and a half. He’s ready to marry her, and the loss of his job days before the winter holiday is devastating.

Almost as devastating as his rivalry with Rosanna Balaz (Akosua Amo-Adem), the gentle but disorganized co-worker with whom Asztalos can’t seem to get along. The colleagues bicker like schoolchildren, and when Hammerschmidt fires Asztalos, it seems like there could be a silver lining to come in their distance from one another.

And so on. Panych’s production unspools like a farce, zippy in its pacing and sentimental in all the best ways. When Hammerschmidt discovers his mistake – of course, Asztalos couldn’t possibly have wooed his wife – his apology is tender and heartfelt, a selfless admission of guilt and a solemn plea for forgiveness. (One gets the sense Hammerschmidt and Saturday, Sunday, Monday ’s jealous patriarch Peppino might bond over their similarly off-base accusations of infidelity.)

Indeed, while Parfumerie ’s central romance offers just the right blend of dramatic irony and feet-kicking cutesiness, its secondary conflicts are arguably the play’s richer stuff. Noah Beemer is winsome as Arpad, the bumbling apprentice trying his best to find some power in the world; Jordan Pettle’s take on Louis Sipos, the confidant burdened with a terrible secret, is similarly poignant.

Dennis, who, like Robins, has been part of the DNA of Soulpepper’s Parfumerie since its premiere close to two decades ago, is particularly enticing as Hammerschmidt. In a few moments, it seems the actor’s and the character’s memories of the perfume shop are one and the same – there’s a depth to the love we see onstage that I’m unsure anyone else could capture in all those layers of experience with the material.

But in the end, Parfumerie is Amo-Adem and Fernandes’s story to sell, and the duo couldn’t be better calibrated to the demands of the tale at hand. Amo-Adem beautifully telegraphs Rosanna’s big heart and questionable fine motor skills; Fernandes, among the funniest comic actors in the city, brings a delightful dash of slapstick to the optimistic Asztalos. In Amo-Adem and Fernandes’s care, it’s as much fun to watch the couple fight as it is to watch them fall for each other. (Asztalos’s final monologue, about Rosanna’s quirks and virtues, could easily go blow-for-blow with Harry’s New Year’s Eve speech in When Harry Met Sally. )

There’s something to be said in favour of a comfort watch – a story you’ve seen thousands of times, and whose ending you see coming from miles away, but that reminds you, for an hour or two, how it feels to be alive.

To that end, Parfumerie doesn’t reinvent the wheel of the romantic comedy – in plenty of ways, Laszlo’s play invented the wheel of the genre in the first place – but Soulpepper’s production, for all its history, feels equal parts cozy and fresh. If only I could bottle that feeling for the fragrance collection by my bedside.

From the trendy Sol de Janeiro body sprays and Glossier mists to the pricier eaux de toilette that populate my nightstand, I’ve amassed a small army of fragrances (and a Sephora account with more loyalty points than I’m prepared to admit in print).

stories.title: Mortgage delinquencies at 13-year high as Canadians fall behind on payments
stories.summary: The proportion of mortgage balances that were overdue for more than 90 days in July, August, and September rose to 0.32 per cent, a report from Equifax Canada shows.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
A growing number of Canadians are falling behind on their monthly mortgage payments with mortgage delinquencies hitting a 13-year high, a new report from Equifax Canada shows.

The proportion of mortgage balances that were overdue for more than 90 days in July, August, and September rose to 0.32 per cent – a 31 per cent increase compared to the same period in 2025.

This is the highest level that Equifax has recorded since it started tracking Canadian mortgage delinquencies in 2013.

The financial stress is concentrated in Ontario and British Columbia, with the two provinces accounting for 91 per cent of the annual growth in severely delinquent mortgage accounts.

“Mortgage delinquencies have been climbing for four years, and Ontario and B.C. continue to drive much of that increase,” said Rebecca Oakes, vice-president of advanced analytics at Equifax Canada.

Tuesday’s Equifax report also showed that Canada’s consumer debt reached $2.74 trillion in the third quarter of the year, up 4.6 per cent compared to the same period in 2025.

Many Canadians also own “negative equity” in their home, meaning they owe the bank more than their house is worth.

Ontario accounts for an estimated 70 per cent of mortgages in negative equity, representing five per cent of total mortgages in the province, compared with 1.85 per cent in British Columbia and 1.10 per cent in Quebec.

Condo owners and recent homebuyers were most at risk of negative equity, with about 7.2 per cent of condominium mortgages likely in negative equity. That risk was at 8.4 per cent for those who bought near the market peak of 2022.

In Ontario, nearly one in four mortgages held by younger Canadians between the ages of 26 and 35 are now thought to be in negative equity.

The figure is worse for auto loans, Equifax said. As of September 2026, an estimated 40 per cent of auto loans that originated in the last four years are in negative equity meaning the borrower owes more than the vehicle is worth.

The dollar value of the delinquencies is rising much faster than the actual number of delinquent mortgages, Equifax data shows.

“The data signals that borrowers with larger mortgages are increasingly struggling to keep up with their payments,” Oakes said.

The figure signals a broader financial squeeze since mortgage arrears are usually “the last domino to fall” when households struggle to make ends meet, said Joshua Harris, CEO of debt management service at Harris and Partners.

“Before someone starts missing their mortgage payments, they May already have fallen behind on credit cards, car loans or other commitments as they try to keep a roof over their heads,” Harris said.

With the Bank of Canada widely expected to deliver another rate hike on Dec. 9, some stressed homeowners could be harder hit than others, Oakes said.

“Variable-rate borrowers can feel the impact of a rate increase within weeks, while others May not experience the effect until they renew or refinance,” she said.

stories.title: Ex-London councillor Mariam Hamou receives probation for threat involving mayor
stories.summary: A former London city councillor has been sentenced after pleading guilty to uttering threats causing death, involving London Mayor Josh Morgan.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
A former London city councillor has been sentenced after pleading guilty to uttering threats causing death, involving London Mayor Josh Morgan.

During proceedings, court heard Hamou, 51, and Morgan, had once been friend but their relationship deteriorated.

The charge against Hamou stems from A September 2026 social media post, where she wrote, “When I can, I’ll be beating the sh*t out of Josh [Morgan],” and added, “He’s sitting pretty and my life is in ruins.”

A friend responding to Hamou’s post said, “Needless to say you’re clearly having a mental issue.” The friend then contact police.

Before sentencing, Hamou apologized for her actions.

“I want to apologize. I take full responsibility,” she told the court.

Defence counsel had sought a sentence of two years’ probation.

As part of the order, Hamou, who has no prior criminal record, must have no contact with Morgan or his family members, remain at least 25 metres away from city hall, participate in mental health counselling and is prohibited from possessing firearms for 10 years.

In delivering her decision, Justice Ghazala Zaman described the matter as an isolated incident while noting the expectations placed on elected officials.

“I believe this is an isolated incident,” Zaman said, adding that the public expects a higher standard from those who hold public office.

Hamou had been scheduled to stand trial next year on separate charges of extortion and criminal harassment that were laid in 2025, but those charges were dropped.

With files from CTV News London’s Nick Paparella

Yukon Energy vice-president of capital projects Paul Murchison says the utility is now focused on getting the battery-storage project “back on track.”

“We have carefully considered the challenges, the work remaining and the options available to us,” Murchison says in a separate statement.

“We believe this change provides the best path toward completing the project safely and responsibly.”

Yukon Energy says it is also pursuing “damages and other remedies” under its terminated contract with SunGrid, although it adds that doesn’t mean the utility will initiate legal proceedings against the company.

stories.title: Ontario property tax change could hike affordable housing costs: critics
stories.summary: The proposed changes would amend Ontario's Assessment Act to block charitable housing providers from getting a property tax exemption in 2027.
stories.author: Olivia Bowden, Colin D'Mello
stories.content:
Building affordable housing in Ontario could soon become far more expensive, critics warn, if the Ford government passes new regulations that would eliminate property tax exemptions for some housing providers.

The proposed changes, which were tucked into the back of the fall economic statement, would amend Ontario’s Assessment Act to block charitable housing providers and even student residences from getting a key property tax exemption in 2027.

“It doesn’t make any sense to me. We should be rolling out the red carpet to affordable housing providers, we shouldn’t be locking them out,” said MPP Jessica Bell, the Ndp’s finance critic. “That’s what this new tax change does.”

In Ontario, non-profits do not have to pay local property taxes for affordable housing units. Those breaks also apply to builders like churches and school boards.

Advocates say the organizations most affected by the changes currently build supportive and affordable housing for at-risk individuals, potentially putting homes out of reach people.

“When (housing providers) have to pay that extra cost, it puts the construction of new affordable housing at risk and it drives up the rent these affordable housing providers can charge people,” Bell said.

Several affordable housing providers, including the Hamilton is Home Coalition, which represent many non-profit housing providers in the city, are urging the Ford government to drop the proposed changes.

Steve Orsini, president and CEO of the Council of Ontario Universities, also told a Queen’s Park committee last week that post-secondary schools are also concerned about the amendment in Bill 143, as student housing comes from a mix of public and private providers.

He warned up to 12,000 existing student homes would now have to pay property tax if the law changes. Another 10,000 planned student homes could be put in jeopardy due to increased costs.

Ottawa-based lawyer Roberto Aburto said he’s representing many clients, including Indigenous housing providers, who are worried about Bill 143.

“The removal of this exemption is coming without any meaningful consultation. Not one of my clients had an opportunity to speak about it and are completely blindsided by it,” said Aburto, a partner at Dentons Ottawa’s Real Estate group.

He also said his clients will have their Build Canada Homes applications upended if Bill 143 passes. Build Canada Homes is a federal agency that requires applications to prove its budgets are financially sustainable while keeping rents affordable.

Non-profit housing providers created budgets expecting those property tax exemptions, he said, but now their funding could be at risk.

“This will cause rent to go up in existing units,” he said. “If you’re trying to build more affordable housing, making it more expensive and having less funds available. … It’s going to undermine some existing affordable housing and it’s putting future projects at risk.”

Ontario’s Ministry of Finance told Global News that due to a “recent court decision, the property tax treatment of affordable housing properties has evolved.”

The legal decision the government is referring to is a June 2025 Ontario Court of Appeal ruling that potentially made it easier for non-profit housing providers to ask for property tax exemptions. The ruling, legal experts have noted, could allow more low-income housing providers to avoid paying property tax.

In response to that decision, the “government is implementing a temporary pause on the implications of the court decisions to allow time to immediately consult directly with affordable housing providers,” said ministry spokesperson Scott Blodgett in a statement.

While the “pause” is in effect, properties that are already exempt from property taxes would “maintain their exemption to avoid impacts,” he said. Affordable housing providers can continue to seek tax relief through their municipalities, he said.

stories.title: Commuters wake up to London’s first snowfall of the season
stories.summary: An early morning snowfall covered much of London and the region on Tuesday, with sub-zero temperatures overnight hanging on into the early morning hours.
stories.author: Bailey Shakyaver
stories.content:
An early morning snowfall covered much of London and the region on Tuesday, with sub-zero temperatures overnight hanging on into the early morning hours.

Milder than usual fall temperatures had lured many across the region into a false sense of security. Snow clearance crews hit the ground running this morning, with operators within the city of London responsible for more than 3,800 kms of roads.

Daytime highs hovering around two degrees will likely thaw the worst of the snow, with chance of more flurries into the evening.

“Winter maintenance is a big job, and our crews are ready to respond,” said Joel Gillard, Division Manager, Road Operations for the city of London. “When you’re on the road, remember to slow down, be safe, and adjust your driving to the conditions. We appreciate everyone’s patience as we respond to changing conditions.”

Several minor collisions throughout the city indicated that many were caught off guard - with a collision on the 402 westbound closing a section of the highway for well over an hour.

Arterial roads throughout the region remain a top priority for snow clearance in compliance with provincial regulations, with the areas near schools, hospitals, and other high traffic routes given first pass.

Additionally, overnight street parking is restricted to help allow snow clearance to proceed as smoothly as possible.

November 24, 2026 at 11:18 a.m.

In a blunt “fact sheet” published Monday, the Pentagon says Canada needs to “get serious and focused” on defence if it wants to continue being a “credible” partner in Norad and Nato.

In the 700-word document, the renamed U.S. Department of War accuses Ottawa of “perennial and long-term under-investment,” warning that equipment shortages, low operational readiness and delayed modernization limit its capability to contribute.

“Ottawa’s prioritization of parochial economic and commercial interests over military optimization introduces further uncertainty for Norad and will further burden our Joint Force and the American taxpayer,” it reads, noting that “Canada’s defence shortfalls speak for themselves.”

The Pentagon highlights that Canada, “one of the largest and wealthiest members of the Nato alliance,” has historically spent less than 1.5 per cent of its GDP on defence, despite committing to achieving two per cent at a 2014 summit in Wales.Canada’s nominal GDP in 2024, according to the World Bank, was $3.2 trillion, 1.5 per cent of which is approximately $48 billion.

This March, Prime Minister Mark Carney announced Canada had finally reached the two per cent target.

At last year’s Nato Hague summit, Carney committed to getting Canada to invest five per cent of GDP in defence and security by 2035, including 3.5 per cent on core defence spending.

The federal budget released earlier this month projects combined defence and security spending of 4.1 per cent of GDP by 2027-28, 2.6 per cent of which is dedicated to core defense.

Regardless, the Pentagon said “decades of underinvestment” will need years of increased spending to rebuild the Canadian military. It also questioned the lack of a fully funded plan to reach the five per cent target, suggesting major spending bumps have been put off “until after the 2029 federal election.”

Canada’s own Parliamentary Budget Office has also questioned how Ottawa will fund the increases.

The document also underscores readiness problems across all three branches of the Canadian Armed Forces.

In 2025-26, “only 41.9 per cent of the Royal Canadian Air Force fleet was serviceable,” compared to 53.9 per cent of the Royal Canadian Navy fleet, and the Canadian Army’s operational readiness was listed at 48 per cent.

Figures from National Defence’s 2025-26 departmental report corroborate those figures, but they also show 61 per cent “of force elements that are ready for operations in accordance with established targets.” Its goal is to achieve 90 per cent by 2032.

The Pentagon also identified the absence of Canadian airborne early warning and control aircraft and the limited availability of the country’s four Victoria-class submarines, only one of which is “seaworthy at any given time.”

And while Canada has ordered a new fleet of up to 12 new subs made by German shipbuilder Thyssenkrupp Marine Systems, the Pentagon questions ~~its~~ Canada’s strength until those vessels “reach full operational capability.”

Canada’s fighter-jet replacement program also drew criticism.

Ottawa has been reviewing its 2023 decision to purchase 88 F-35s from the U.S., considering whether to instead acquire the Swedish-made fourth-generation Gripen, “due to perceived domestic industrial advantages.”

“Canada can maximize its limited but growing defence funds by prioritizing missions important for its homeland defence and meeting Norad and Nato obligations by committing to the best miliary (sic) platforms,” the document concludes.

The Pentagon document comes on the heels of a memo from Secretary of War Pete Hegseth that limits American general flag officer meetings “to those that advance (United States Department of Defence) objectives,” the Washington Post reported last week.

“They must request permission for Canadian think tank events or social engagements. And it is OK to attend any 9/11 events,” Republican Senator Mike Rounds of South Dakota explained at the Halifax International Security Forum.

Defence Minister David McGuinty and Gen. Jennie Carignan, Canada’s Chief of the Defence Staff, both said the memo had no bearing on the military relationship with the United States.

— With files from Chris Lambie

Kenn Oliver is a web editor and writer for National Post. He is a career journalist of more than 20 years, the bulk of which was spent as a sports writer, business reporter and web editor for the Telegram in St. John's, N.L.

The federal budget released earlier this month projects combined defence and security spending of 4.1 per cent of GDP by 2027-28, 2.6 per cent of which is dedicated to core defense.

Regardless, the Pentagon said “decades of underinvestment” will need years of increased spending to rebuild the Canadian military. It also questioned the lack of a fully funded plan to reach the five per cent target, suggesting major spending bumps have been put off “until after the 2029 federal election.”
Canada’s own Parliamentary Budget Office has also questioned how Ottawa will fund the increases.
The document also underscores readiness problems across all three branches of the Canadian Armed Forces.

In 2025-26, “only 41.9 per cent of the Royal Canadian Air Force fleet was serviceable,” compared to 53.9 per cent of the Royal Canadian Navy fleet, and the Canadian Army’s operational readiness was listed at 48 per cent.

Figures from National Defence’s 2025-26 departmental report corroborate those figures, but they also show 61 per cent “of force elements that are ready for operations in accordance with established targets.” Its goal is to achieve 90 per cent by 2032.

The Pentagon also identified the absence of Canadian airborne early warning and control aircraft and the limited availability of the country’s four Victoria-class submarines, only one of which is “seaworthy at any given time.”

And while Canada has ordered a new fleet of up to 12 new subs made by German shipbuilder Thyssenkrupp Marine Systems, the Pentagon questions ~~its~~ Canada’s strength until those vessels “reach full operational capability.”
Canada’s fighter-jet replacement program also drew criticism.

Ottawa has been reviewing its 2023 decision to purchase 88 F-35s from the U.S., considering whether to instead acquire the Swedish-made fourth-generation Gripen, “due to perceived domestic industrial advantages.”

“Canada can maximize its limited but growing defence funds by prioritizing missions important for its homeland defence and meeting Norad and Nato obligations by committing to the best miliary (sic) platforms,” the document concludes.

The Pentagon document comes on the heels of a memo from Secretary of War Pete Hegseth that limits American general flag officer meetings “to those that advance (United States Department of Defence) objectives,” the Washington Post reported last week.

“They must request permission for Canadian think tank events or social engagements. And it is OK to attend any 9/11 events,” Republican Senator Mike Rounds of South Dakota explained at the Halifax International Security Forum.
Defence Minister David McGuinty and Gen. Jennie Carignan, Canada’s Chief of the Defence Staff, both said the memo had no bearing on the military relationship with the United States.

stories.title: Two Nova Scotia seafood firms ticketed for illegal lobster processing deny claims
stories.summary: Digby - Two seafood companies facing fines following a Nova Scotia Department of Fisheries investigation into alleged illegal lobster processing deny the claims.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The department issued a statement Monday saying Oceanova Lobster Ltd. in Digby County has received five tickets with combined fines of almost $100,000.

The company is accused of selling illegally processed lobster, processing lobster without a provincial licence and failing to provide information about the source and destination of lobster.

Article continues below

Inside interior designer Nora Voon’s art-filled home

It says Shelburne County-based firm Independent Fisheries Ltd. has received a $28,872 ticket for selling illegally processed lobster.

The allegations have not been proven in court.

A spokesperson with Independent Fisheries said in an emailed statement Tuesday it denies liability and will be defending the business against the allegations.

Peter Eveleigh, a director for Oceanova, said Monday the firm denies the allegations and intends to dispute the tickets in court.

The provincial department says the investigation into both firms began after its compliance and enforcement unit learned about lobster being processed at a facility in Meteghan, N.S., without a fish processor licence.

Independent Fisheries was charged last month for allegedly buying, selling or processing lobster caught without a valid licence.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 24, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Alleged Tumbler Ridge co-conspirator seeks release from U.S. jail
stories.summary: James Bryant pleaded not guilty of conspiracy to murder persons in a foreign country in a Seattle court in October and was kept in custody
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
An American charged as a co-conspirator in the deadly mass shooting in Tumbler Ridge, B.C., has filed an application for release from jail claiming her messages with the shooter are protected under the First Amendment.

James Bryant pleaded not guilty to conspiracy to murder persons in a foreign country in a Seattle court in October and was kept in custody. The magistrate found Bryant, who uses female pronouns and goes by the name Melody, would pose a danger if allowed internet access.

The criminal complaint against Bryant, 30, alleges she colluded online with shooter Jesse Van Rootselaar, 18, and attempted to set up a livestream of the murders.

Van Rootselaar killed eight people last February, including five students and an educational assistant at the local secondary school, before fatally shooting herself as police closed in.

U.S. prosecutors allege Bryant also advised Van Rootselaar on where to carry out the attack and sent the shooter money to buy a lighter for an explosive device.

In a 33-page filing to court last week, Bryant’s lawyers argued that the 73,858 individual texts between Bryant and the shooter were misconstrued.

The lawyers said about two-thirds of the texts were from Van Rootselaar to Bryant, and that the American often discouraged the Canadian teenager’s violent urges.

The documents cite some of the texts exchanged between Bryant and Van Rootselaar – including texts in which the teenager fantasizes about killing her family, other people and herself.

Van Rootselaar also sent messages about her desire for notoriety and what it would take to surpass the deaths in the La Loche school shooting in Saskatchewan in 2016 and the École Polytechnique massacre in Quebec in 1989.

Bryant’s lawyers said that while Bryant sometimes joined in Van Rootselaar’s fantasies, “the chats also contain an extended discussion of how Van Rootselaar would commit mass murder if she grew to the size of a giant.”

The lawyers said Bryant’s jokes “May be tasteless and, in retrospect, were ill considered,” but they are protected by the First Amendment because Van Rootselaar had made it clear she had no immediate intention to commit an act of violence.

“For better or worse, the First Amendment also protects their debate about whether a school shooting or attack on a crowd would be more likely to make someone infamous, even if the government tries to recast that conversation as ‘tactical advice,’” Bryant’s application said.

The lawyers argued that Bryant also worried that reporting Van Rootselaar would lead her to act out.

The application points out that Van Rootselaar spoke about her murderous plans to other people and on ChatGPT. Bryant’s lawyers said family members and friends bought Van Rootselaar ammunition – even after her release from psychiatric hospitalization – and the RCMP returned her guns.

“Because neither Ms. Bryant, OpenAI … the many people Van Rootselaar communicated with online, Van Rootselaar’s family, nor the RCMP wanted Van Rootselaar to use her firearms to kill anyone, none are responsible as co-conspirators for her actions, even if each of these provided services that helped Van Rootselaar commit her crime,” the document said.

Bryant’s lawyers argue she would not pose a threat to society if she is released ahead of trial next year.

stories.title: Woman dies after Kipps Lane apartment fire, police investigating
stories.summary: Emergency crews were called to a working fire at a multi-unit residence in the 700 block of Kipps Lane at about 7 a.m. on Nov. 19.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
A woman critically injured in a fire at a northeast London apartment building last week has died, according to London police.

Emergency crews were called to a working fire at a multi-unit residence in the 700 block of Kipps Lane at about 7 a.m. on Nov. 19.

At the time, residents of the high-rise at 756 Kipps Ln. reported seeing heavy black smoke coming from a fourth-floor apartment. Several tenants said they were alerted to the fire by neighbours and building alarms before firefighters arrived.

One resident told CTV News smoke filled the fourth-floor hallway when she opened her apartment door. Another tenant said he managed to partially open the door of the affected unit and discovered the elderly female occupant inside.

London firefighters removed the woman from the apartment and performed lifesaving measures before she was transported to hospital with life-threatening injuries.

Officials also confirmed a second person was taken to hospital suffering from smoke inhalation.

On Tuesday, London police said the woman who was critically injured in the blaze has since died. The victim’s identity has not been released.

Members of the London Police Service Major Crime Section and the Office of the Fire Marshal are now investigating the fatal fire.

Police said the cause of the fire remains under investigation and described the investigation as being in its early stages.

The fire caused significant damage to the fourth-floor unit where it originated.

stories.title: Singer apologizes for fumbling O Canada lyrics ahead of Leafs-Islanders game
stories.summary: Sarrah Strimel Bentley sang ‘We lend our hearts to thee’ several times in place of ‘We stand on guard for thee’
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A singer and former Broadway actress issued an emotional apology to Canadians after fumbling the lyrics to O Canada ahead of Monday night’s matchup between the Toronto Maple Leafs and New York Islanders.

Sarrah Strimel Bentley sang “We lend our hearts to thee” several times in place of “We stand on guard for thee.”

She also replaced “in” with “with” when she sang “True patriot love with all of us command.”

The singer took to social media shortly after to apologize and ask people to “be kind and show grace.”

Strimel Bentley said in an Instagram video that due to breast cancer she experiences menopause, which can be induced early by cancer treatments and can cause lapses in memory.

She said she also experienced nerves singing an unfamiliar anthem in front of an audience of thousands.

“I just wish that you would be a little easier on someone who is just a human being, and I’m sorry,” Strimel Bentley said through tears. “Thank you for giving me grace. I love Canada. I stand on guard for thee.”

The Leafs referenced the lyric mishap in a post on X that shared video of defenceman Jake McCabe putting a puck in the Islanders’ net for Toronto’s first goal of the night.

“Jake McCabe, would lend my heart to thee,” the Leafs wrote.

They would go on to beat the Islanders 4-2, ending a nine-game losing streak.

Editor’s note: This story has been updated to correct Jake McCabe’s first name.

“I just wish that you would be a little easier on someone who is just a human being, and I’m sorry,” Strimel Bentley said through tears. “Thank you for giving me grace. I love Canada. I stand on guard for thee.”
The Leafs referenced the lyric mishap in a post on X that shared video of defenceman Jake McCabe putting a puck in the Islanders’ net for Toronto’s first goal of the night.
“Jake McCabe, would lend my heart to thee,” the Leafs wrote.
They would go on to beat the Islanders 4-2, ending a nine-game losing streak.

stories.title: Parole board opens online portal for cannabis possession pardons
stories.summary: The Parole Board of Canada has launched a new portal for pardon applications in a bid to streamline and simplify the application process.
stories.author: Catherine Morrison
stories.content:
The Parole Board of Canada has granted 944 pardons for pot possession — less than one tenth of the number the government was anticipating when it legalized recreational cannabis eight years ago.

The Liberals lifted a century-long prohibition on the recreational use and sale of cannabis in October 2018. Canada became just the second country in the world to legalize the drug, after Uruguay.

The following year, the government brought in legislation to offer a free and streamlined process to apply for record suspensions for simple possession of cannabis. Record suspensions effectively clear criminal records that can be a barrier to travel, employment, housing, education and volunteer work.

Ottawa estimated at the time about 10,000 Canadians would be eligible for cannabis-related record suspensions.

Parole Board of Canada spokesperson Andrea Fournier said in an email the board has received 1,477 applications for cannabis record suspensions since 2019. Of those, 526 were returned because the applicant was ineligible or the application was incomplete.

The Parole Board of Canada has launched a new portal for pardon applications in a bid to streamline and simplify the application process.

Lawyer and University of Ottawa drug policy expert Eugene Oscapella said the application process May be a deterrent for some people.

“You’ve got to get records of your conviction, you’ve got to contact courts and police departments,” he said. “It’s not that straightforward a process and some people May just sort of balk at it.

“If there is a new streamlined process, that May in itself be an acknowledgment by the government that perhaps the current process is a bit awkward.”

Oscapella also said the number of pardons granted since legalization May be lower than expected because the stigma surrounding cannabis use has faded.

“Maybe people just aren’t as worried about it anymore,” he said. “Attitudes towards cannabis have become quite normalized and maybe people don’t see there’s any real advantage.

“There was a time when if you had a cannabis conviction, it had a significant impact on your life. I don’t think that’s the case anymore, for simple possession certainly.”

Oscapella said that while most employers likely wouldn’t have a problem with a candidate who has a record for pot possession, that’s not the case for jobs that require security clearances or travel abroad.

The Parole Board of Canada says in a news release last week its new portal allows applicants and their designated representatives to submit applications for record suspensions online.

The portal allows applicants to save an incomplete application and return to it later, and permits them to track their applications.

“The secure platform reduces reliance on paper-based processes and mail delivery while giving applicants greater flexibility and visibility throughout the process,” says the news release.

“By simplifying the application process, the PBC Service Portal helps people benefit from programs that can support their successful reintegration, while maintaining the integrity of the record suspension (pardon) and cannabis record suspension processes and supporting public safety.”

stories.title: Two Nova Scotia seafood companies ticketed for alleged illegal lobster processing
stories.summary: The department issued a statement Monday saying Oceanova Lobster Ltd. in Digby County has received five tickets with combined fines of almost $100,000.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Two seafood companies are facing fines following a Nova Scotia Department of Fisheries investigation into alleged illegal lobster processing.

The department issued a statement Monday saying Oceanova Lobster Ltd. in Digby County has received five tickets with combined fines of almost $100,000.

The company is accused of selling illegally processed lobster, processing lobster without a provincial licence and failing to provide information about the source and destination of lobster.

A representative for Oceanova said the firm denies the allegations and intends to dispute the tickets in court.

The province says Shelburne County-based firm Independent Fisheries Ltd. has received a $28,872 ticket for selling illegally processed lobster.

Allegations have not been proven in court and Independent Fisheries did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The department says the investigation into both firms began after its compliance and enforcement unit learned about lobster being processed at a facility in Meteghan, N.S., without a fish processor licence.

Independent Fisheries was charged last month for allegedly buying, selling or processing lobster caught without a valid licence.
