stories.title: Three people taken to hospital after serious south London crash
stories.summary: Emergency crews responded to the crash around 8:45 a.m. in the area of Wellington Road South and Reagan Bourne.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
Three people were taken to hospital following a serious two-vehicle collision in south London on Tuesday morning.

Emergency crews responded to the crash around 8:45 a.m. in the area of Wellington Road South and Reagan Bourne.

London police said three people were transported to hospital. The extent of their injuries was not immediately known.

As a result of the collision, Wellington Road South remained closed in both directions between Reagan Bourne and Glanworth Drive late Tuesday morning.

Police said members of the Road Safety Section have taken over the investigation.

No further information was immediately available.

stories.title: Alleged Tumbler Ridge co-conspirator applies for release from jail
stories.summary: Seattle - An American charged as a co-conspirator in the deadly mass shooting in Tumbler Ridge, B.C., has filed an application for release from jail.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Seattle - The alleged co-conspirator in the Tumbler Ridge, B.C., mass shooting exchanged almost 74,000 texts with the killer but her lawyers argue that on at least three occasions she tried to talk Jesse Van Rootselaar out of killing people, U.S. court documents say.

James Bryant filed an application for release from jail last week claiming her messages with the shooter are protected under the U.S. First Amendment on the right to free speech, and she poses no risk to the community if released.

The criminal complaint against Bryant, 30, alleges she colluded online with shooter Jesse Van Rootselaar, 18, and attempted to set up a livestream of the murders.

Bryant’s lawyers say in the 33-page filing in U.S. district court in Seattle that the 73,858 individual texts between Bryant and the shooter were misconstrued by the government as it argued for her detention.

“The chats make clear that Ms. Bryant believes, at least for the bulk of their communications, that Van Rootselaar is basically a decent person who is troubled by violent thoughts she wouldn’t act on,” the document says.

Bryant pleaded not guilty to conspiracy to murder persons in a foreign country in a Seattle court in October and remains in custody. The magistrate found Bryant, who uses female pronouns and goes by the name Melody, would pose a danger if allowed internet access.

Van Rootselaar killed eight people last February, including five students and an educational assistant at the local secondary school, before fatally shooting herself as police closed in.

U.S. prosecutors allege Bryant also advised Van Rootselaar on where to carry out the attack and sent the shooter money to buy a lighter for an explosive device.

But Bryant’s court filing says that six months before the attack, the plan the two discussed over the Discord platform was fantasy because Van Rootselaar did not have access to guns.

“Ms. Bryant was not alone in initially failing to understand that Van Rootselaar was genuinely dangerous,” the document says.

It says RCMP had seized then returned one of the guns Van Rootselaar would use in the attack, which had been “altered to enable rapid firing.”

“Family members and friends bought Van Rootselaar ammunition, even after her release from psychiatric hospitalization,” the document says.

Van Rootselaar also spoke about her plans to kill “widely” with other people and with ChatGPT.

“Because neither Ms. Bryant, OpenAI … the many people Van Rootselaar communicated with online, Van Rootselaar’s family, nor the RCMP wanted Van Rootselaar to use her firearms to kill anyone, none are responsible as co-conspirators for her actions, even if each of these provided services that helped Van Rootselaar commit her crime,” the document says.

About two-thirds of the texts were from Van Rootselaar to Bryant, and that the American often discouraged the teenager’s violent and suicidal urges, the court motion says.

Van Rootselaar sent messages about her desire for notoriety and what it would take to surpass the deaths in the La Loche school shooting in Saskatchewan in 2016 and the École Polytechnique massacre in Quebec in 1989.

Bryant’s lawyers say that while Bryant sometimes joined in Van Rootselaar’s fantasies, “the chats also contain an extended discussion of how Van Rootselaar would commit mass murder if she grew to the size of a giant.”

The lawyers say Bryant’s jokes “May be tasteless and, in retrospect, were ill considered,” but they are protected by the U.S. First Amendment because Van Rootselaar had made it clear she had no immediate intention to commit an act of violence.

“For better or worse, the First Amendment also protects their debate about whether a school shooting or attack on a crowd would be more likely to make someone infamous, even if the government tries to recast that conversation as ‘tactical advice,’” Bryant’s application says.

The lawyers say that Bryant also worried that reporting Van Rootselaar “might trigger a massacre” and cautiously urged the shooter to get medical help rather than hurting herself or others.

Messages included in the application show Bryant trying to dissuade Van Rootselaar from hurting others by getting her to empathize with the potential victims, saying they “could be incredibly important to someone.”

The application noted that “because Van Rootselaar had been talking about killing people nearly every day for at least six months, Ms. Bryant did not understand when violence was imminent.”

“On at least three occasions, Van Rootselaar announces that she is going to proceed with her plan imminently, only to be talked out of killing people,” the application says.

On Feb. 10, the day of the shooting, she made a final attempt to dissuade Van Rootselaar, the motion says.

“Today doesn’t have to be the day,” she wrote.

The document argues that though it is “horrifying in retrospect” to imagine that Bryant could have prevented the killings if she had contacted police, “it is undisputed that the law provided no affirmative duty to do so.”

“In the past, Ms. Bryant had repeatedly been able talk Van Rootselaar out of committing a crime,” it says.

It also notes that though Bryant agreed to watch and screen capture the “gore scenes” during the shooting, she had stated she did not want to and “made it clear that her agreement to livestream her friend’s final moments did not indicate agreement with Van Rootselaar’s actions.”

In that exchange, Van Rootselaar also said she would commit her crimes even if Bryant was not watching or recording.

Bryant’s lawyers argue she would not pose a threat to society if she is released ahead of trial.

The evidence “of an agreement to murder people in Canada is extremely weak,” it says.

“In fact, the chats make overwhelmingly clear that Ms. Bryant did not share — and in fact opposed — Van Rootselaar’s plans to murder others,” the motion says.

“From the first chats in August 2025 until the day Van Rootselaar killed her family and attacked a school, Ms. Bryant attempted to distract and dissuade her friend from her murderous purpose.”

The application argues that Byrant co-operated with police and was arrested without incident last month.

It says the judge granted her detainment on an order that “makes several factual mistakes,” including that she suffers from a “deeply rooted” mental illness or substance abuse history that they say does not exist.

It alleges that the 41-page complaint filed by the government was “replete with distortions,” including that some texts were rearranged to make it appear that Bryant was helping Van Rootselaar build a bomb or sent her money to buy a lighter for a bomb.

“In fact, nowhere in the complete chats does Van Rootselaar say that she needs a lighter for the bomb. Nowhere does Bryant offer to provide Van Rootselaar a lighter for that purpose,” it says.

The document says that though the alleged crime is “extremely serious,” Van Rootselaar’s homicidal fantasies predate their relationship.

“The government has never contended (and there is no evidence) that Ms. Bryant recruited Van Rootselaar to commit violence or groomed her to do so,” it says.

It notes there is also no evidence that Bryant visits any chat communities that glorify violence.

“Absent any evidence of any similar relationships, there is simply no basis for concluding that Ms. Bryant poses an unmanageable risk of future danger,” it says.

It also notes the government’s willingness to leave Bryant in the community for seven months after initially reviewing the Discord chats, which it says “proves that she did not, and does not, pose any danger.”

The application asks the court to order release of Bryant with conditions, “which May include home confinement, mental health treatment if an assessment determines it is appropriate, and restrictions on her use of digital devices.”

Emily Langlie, a spokeswoman for the U.S. Attorney’s Office, said in an emailed statement that the prosecution’s response to the motion is due on Wednesday, after which the judge will rule on the filings or schedule an oral argument, “probably in early December.”

She said the trial on the charges against Bryant is expected in December next year.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 24, 2026.

— By Brieanna Charlebois in Vancouver and Kelly Geraldine Malone in Washington, D.C.

On Feb. 10, the day of the shooting, she made a final attempt to dissuade Van Rootselaar, the motion says.
“Today doesn’t have to be the day,” she wrote.

The document argues that though it is “horrifying in retrospect” to imagine that Bryant could have prevented the killings if she had contacted police, “it is undisputed that the law provided no affirmative duty to do so.”
“In the past, Ms. Bryant had repeatedly been able talk Van Rootselaar out of committing a crime,” it says.

It also notes that though Bryant agreed to watch and screen capture the “gore scenes” during the shooting, she had stated she did not want to and “made it clear that her agreement to livestream her friend’s final moments did not indicate agreement with Van Rootselaar’s actions.”
In that exchange, Van Rootselaar also said she would commit her crimes even if Bryant was not watching or recording.
Bryant’s lawyers argue she would not pose a threat to society if she is released ahead of trial.
The evidence “of an agreement to murder people in Canada is extremely weak,” it says.
“In fact, the chats make overwhelmingly clear that Ms. Bryant did not share — and in fact opposed — Van Rootselaar’s plans to murder others,” the motion says.
“From the first chats in August 2025 until the day Van Rootselaar killed her family and attacked a school, Ms. Bryant attempted to distract and dissuade her friend from her murderous purpose.”
The application argues that Byrant co-operated with police and was arrested without incident last month.

It says the judge granted her detainment on an order that “makes several factual mistakes,” including that she suffers from a “deeply rooted” mental illness or substance abuse history that they say does not exist.

It alleges that the 41-page complaint filed by the government was “replete with distortions,” including that some texts were rearranged to make it appear that Bryant was helping Van Rootselaar build a bomb or sent her money to buy a lighter for a bomb.
“In fact, nowhere in the complete chats does Van Rootselaar say that she needs a lighter for the bomb. Nowhere does Bryant offer to provide Van Rootselaar a lighter for that purpose,” it says.
The document says that though the alleged crime is “extremely serious,” Van Rootselaar’s homicidal fantasies predate their relationship.
“The government has never contended (and there is no evidence) that Ms. Bryant recruited Van Rootselaar to commit violence or groomed her to do so,” it says.
It notes there is also no evidence that Bryant visits any chat communities that glorify violence.
“Absent any evidence of any similar relationships, there is simply no basis for concluding that Ms. Bryant poses an unmanageable risk of future danger,” it says.

It also notes the government’s willingness to leave Bryant in the community for seven months after initially reviewing the Discord chats, which it says “proves that she did not, and does not, pose any danger.”

The application asks the court to order release of Bryant with conditions, “which May include home confinement, mental health treatment if an assessment determines it is appropriate, and restrictions on her use of digital devices.”

Emily Langlie, a spokeswoman for the U.S. Attorney’s Office, said in an emailed statement that the prosecution’s response to the motion is due on Wednesday, after which the judge will rule on the filings or schedule an oral argument, “probably in early December.”
She said the trial on the charges against Bryant is expected in December next year.

stories.title: Alleged Tumbler Ridge co-conspirator from the U.S. applies for release before trial
stories.summary: An American charged as a co-conspirator in the deadly mass shooting in Tumbler Ridge, B.C., has filed an application for release from jail.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Seattle — The alleged co-conspirator in the Tumbler Ridge, B.C., mass shooting exchanged almost 74,000 texts with the killer but her lawyers argue that on at least three occasions she tried to talk Jesse Van Rootselaar out of killing people, U.S. court documents say.

James Bryant filed an application for release from jail last week claiming her messages with the shooter are protected under the U.S. First Amendment on the right to free speech, and she poses no risk to the community if released.

The criminal complaint against Bryant, 30, alleges she colluded online with shooter Jesse Van Rootselaar, 18, and attempted to set up a livestream of the murders.

Bryant’s lawyers say in the 33-page filing in U.S. district court in Seattle that the 73,858 individual texts between Bryant and the shooter were misconstrued by the government as it argued for her detention.

“The chats make clear that Ms. Bryant believes, at least for the bulk of their communications, that Van Rootselaar is basically a decent person who is troubled by violent thoughts she wouldn’t act on,” the document says.

Bryant pleaded not guilty to conspiracy to murder persons in a foreign country in a Seattle court in October and remains in custody. The magistrate found Bryant, who uses female pronouns and goes by the name Melody, would pose a danger if allowed internet access.

Van Rootselaar killed eight people last February, including five students and an educational assistant at the local secondary school, before fatally shooting herself as police closed in.

U.S. prosecutors allege Bryant also advised Van Rootselaar on where to carry out the attack and sent the shooter money to buy a lighter for an explosive device.

But Bryant’s court filing says that six months before the attack, the plan the two discussed over the Discord platform was fantasy because Van Rootselaar did not have access to guns.

“Ms. Bryant was not alone in initially failing to understand that Van Rootselaar was genuinely dangerous,” the document says.

It says RCMP had seized then returned one of the guns Van Rootselaar would use in the attack, which had been “altered to enable rapid firing.”

“Family members and friends bought Van Rootselaar ammunition, even after her release from psychiatric hospitalization,” the document says.

Van Rootselaar also spoke about her plans to kill “widely” with other people and with ChatGPT.

“Because neither Ms. Bryant, OpenAI … the many people Van Rootselaar communicated with online, Van Rootselaar’s family, nor the RCMP wanted Van Rootselaar to use her firearms to kill anyone, none are responsible as co-conspirators for her actions, even if each of these provided services that helped Van Rootselaar commit her crime,” the document says.

About two-thirds of the texts were from Van Rootselaar to Bryant, and that the American often discouraged the teenager’s violent and suicidal urges, the court motion says.

Van Rootselaar sent messages about her desire for notoriety and what it would take to surpass the deaths in the La Loche school shooting in Saskatchewan in 2016 and the École Polytechnique massacre in Quebec in 1989.

Bryant’s lawyers say that while Bryant sometimes joined in Van Rootselaar’s fantasies, “the chats also contain an extended discussion of how Van Rootselaar would commit mass murder if she grew to the size of a giant.”

The lawyers say Bryant’s jokes “May be tasteless and, in retrospect, were ill considered,” but they are protected by the U.S. First Amendment because Van Rootselaar had made it clear she had no immediate intention to commit an act of violence.

“For better or worse, the First Amendment also protects their debate about whether a school shooting or attack on a crowd would be more likely to make someone infamous, even if the government tries to recast that conversation as ‘tactical advice,'” Bryant’s application says.

The lawyers say that Bryant also worried that reporting Van Rootselaar “might trigger a massacre” and cautiously urged the shooter to get medical help rather than hurting herself or others.

Messages included in the application show Bryant trying to dissuade Van Rootselaar from hurting others by getting her to empathize with the potential victims, saying they “could be incredibly important to someone.”

The application noted that “because Van Rootselaar had been talking about killing people nearly every day for at least six months, Ms. Bryant did not understand when violence was imminent.”

“On at least three occasions, Van Rootselaar announces that she is going to proceed with her plan imminently, only to be talked out of killing people,” the application says.

On Feb. 10, the day of the shooting, she made a final attempt to dissuade Van Rootselaar, the motion says.

“Today doesn’t have to be the day,” she wrote.

The document argues that though it is “horrifying in retrospect” to imagine that Bryant could have prevented the killings if she had contacted police, “it is undisputed that the law provided no affirmative duty to do so.”

“In the past, Ms. Bryant had repeatedly been able talk Van Rootselaar out of committing a crime,” it says.

It also notes that though Bryant agreed to watch and screen capture the “gore scenes” during the shooting, she had stated she did not want to and “made it clear that her agreement to livestream her friend’s final moments did not indicate agreement with Van Rootselaar’s actions.”

In that exchange, Van Rootselaar also said she would commit her crimes even if Bryant was not watching or recording.

Bryant’s lawyers argue she would not pose a threat to society if she is released ahead of trial.

The evidence “of an agreement to murder people in Canada is extremely weak,” it says.

“In fact, the chats make overwhelmingly clear that Ms. Bryant did not share — and in fact opposed — Van Rootselaar’s plans to murder others,” the motion says.

“From the first chats in August 2025 until the day Van Rootselaar killed her family and attacked a school, Ms. Bryant attempted to distract and dissuade her friend from her murderous purpose.”

The application argues that Byrant co-operated with police and was arrested without incident last month.

It says the judge granted her detainment on an order that “makes several factual mistakes,” including that she suffers from a “deeply rooted” mental illness or substance abuse history that they say does not exist.

It alleges that the 41-page complaint filed by the government was “replete with distortions,” including that some texts were rearranged to make it appear that Bryant was helping Van Rootselaar build a bomb or sent her money to buy a lighter for a bomb.

“In fact, nowhere in the complete chats does Van Rootselaar say that she needs a lighter for the bomb. Nowhere does Bryant offer to provide Van Rootselaar a lighter for that purpose,” it says.

The document says that though the alleged crime is “extremely serious,” Van Rootselaar’s homicidal fantasies predate their relationship.

“The government has never contended (and there is no evidence) that Ms. Bryant recruited Van Rootselaar to commit violence or groomed her to do so,” it says.

It notes there is also no evidence that Bryant visits any chat communities that glorify violence.

“Absent any evidence of any similar relationships, there is simply no basis for concluding that Ms. Bryant poses an unmanageable risk of future danger,” it says.

It also notes the government’s willingness to leave Bryant in the community for seven months after initially reviewing the Discord chats, which it says “proves that she did not, and does not, pose any danger.”

The application asks the court to order release of Bryant with conditions, “which May include home confinement, mental health treatment if an assessment determines it is appropriate, and restrictions on her use of digital devices.”

Emily Langlie, a spokeswoman for the U.S. Attorney’s Office, said in an emailed statement that the prosecution’s response to the motion is due on Wednesday, after which the judge will rule on the filings or schedule an oral argument, “probably in early December.”

She said the trial on the charges against Bryant is expected in December next year.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 24, 2026.

Van Rootselaar sent messages about her desire for notoriety and what it would take to surpass the deaths in the La Loche school shooting in Saskatchewan in 2016 and the École Polytechnique massacre in Quebec in 1989.

Bryant’s lawyers say that while Bryant sometimes joined in Van Rootselaar’s fantasies, “the chats also contain an extended discussion of how Van Rootselaar would commit mass murder if she grew to the size of a giant.”

The lawyers say Bryant’s jokes “May be tasteless and, in retrospect, were ill considered,” but they are protected by the U.S. First Amendment because Van Rootselaar had made it clear she had no immediate intention to commit an act of violence.

“For better or worse, the First Amendment also protects their debate about whether a school shooting or attack on a crowd would be more likely to make someone infamous, even if the government tries to recast that conversation as ‘tactical advice,'” Bryant’s application says.
The lawyers say that Bryant also worried that reporting Van Rootselaar “might trigger a massacre” and cautiously urged the shooter to get medical help rather than hurting herself or others.

Messages included in the application show Bryant trying to dissuade Van Rootselaar from hurting others by getting her to empathize with the potential victims, saying they “could be incredibly important to someone.”
The application noted that “because Van Rootselaar had been talking about killing people nearly every day for at least six months, Ms. Bryant did not understand when violence was imminent.”
“On at least three occasions, Van Rootselaar announces that she is going to proceed with her plan imminently, only to be talked out of killing people,” the application says.
On Feb. 10, the day of the shooting, she made a final attempt to dissuade Van Rootselaar, the motion says.
“Today doesn’t have to be the day,” she wrote.

The document argues that though it is “horrifying in retrospect” to imagine that Bryant could have prevented the killings if she had contacted police, “it is undisputed that the law provided no affirmative duty to do so.”
“In the past, Ms. Bryant had repeatedly been able talk Van Rootselaar out of committing a crime,” it says.

It also notes that though Bryant agreed to watch and screen capture the “gore scenes” during the shooting, she had stated she did not want to and “made it clear that her agreement to livestream her friend’s final moments did not indicate agreement with Van Rootselaar’s actions.”
In that exchange, Van Rootselaar also said she would commit her crimes even if Bryant was not watching or recording.
Bryant’s lawyers argue she would not pose a threat to society if she is released ahead of trial.
The evidence “of an agreement to murder people in Canada is extremely weak,” it says.
“In fact, the chats make overwhelmingly clear that Ms. Bryant did not share — and in fact opposed — Van Rootselaar’s plans to murder others,” the motion says.
“From the first chats in August 2025 until the day Van Rootselaar killed her family and attacked a school, Ms. Bryant attempted to distract and dissuade her friend from her murderous purpose.”
The application argues that Byrant co-operated with police and was arrested without incident last month.

It says the judge granted her detainment on an order that “makes several factual mistakes,” including that she suffers from a “deeply rooted” mental illness or substance abuse history that they say does not exist.

It alleges that the 41-page complaint filed by the government was “replete with distortions,” including that some texts were rearranged to make it appear that Bryant was helping Van Rootselaar build a bomb or sent her money to buy a lighter for a bomb.
“In fact, nowhere in the complete chats does Van Rootselaar say that she needs a lighter for the bomb. Nowhere does Bryant offer to provide Van Rootselaar a lighter for that purpose,” it says.
The document says that though the alleged crime is “extremely serious,” Van Rootselaar’s homicidal fantasies predate their relationship.
“The government has never contended (and there is no evidence) that Ms. Bryant recruited Van Rootselaar to commit violence or groomed her to do so,” it says.
It notes there is also no evidence that Bryant visits any chat communities that glorify violence.
“Absent any evidence of any similar relationships, there is simply no basis for concluding that Ms. Bryant poses an unmanageable risk of future danger,” it says.

It also notes the government’s willingness to leave Bryant in the community for seven months after initially reviewing the Discord chats, which it says “proves that she did not, and does not, pose any danger.”

The application asks the court to order release of Bryant with conditions, “which May include home confinement, mental health treatment if an assessment determines it is appropriate, and restrictions on her use of digital devices.”

Emily Langlie, a spokeswoman for the U.S. Attorney’s Office, said in an emailed statement that the prosecution’s response to the motion is due on Wednesday, after which the judge will rule on the filings or schedule an oral argument, “probably in early December.”
She said the trial on the charges against Bryant is expected in December next year.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 24, 2026.
— By Brieanna Charlebois in Vancouver and Kelly Geraldine Malone in Washington, D.C.

stories.summary: A singer and former Broadway actress issued an emotional apology to Canadians after fumbling the lyrics to O Canada ahead of Monday night's matchup between the Toronto Maple Leafs and New York Islanders.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A singer and former Broadway actress issued an emotional apology to Canadians after fumbling the lyrics to O Canada ahead of Monday night’s matchup between the Toronto Maple Leafs and New York Islanders.

Nov. 24, 2026

New subscriber benefit!

Copied to clipboard

A gifted article has been claimed.

Out of gifts for the month

Unfortunately you've used all of your gifts this month. Your counter will reset on the first day of next month.

FF[](https://www.thestar.com/news/ontario/singer-offers-tearful-apology-for-o-canada-flub-at-leafs-islanders-game-in-new-york/article_c86aad45-7074-5320-ab6a-a871c9a4d1cb.html)

By The Canadian Press

Sarrah Strimel Bentley sang “We lend our hearts to thee” several times in place of “We stand on guard for thee.”

She also replaced “in” with “with” when she sang “True patriot love with all of us command.”

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Inside interior designer Nora Voon’s art-filled home

The singer took to social media shortly after to apologize and ask people to “be kind and show grace.”

Strimel Bentley said in an Instagram video that due to breast cancer she experiences menopause, which can be induced early by cancer treatments and can cause lapses in memory.

She said she also experienced nerves singing an unfamiliar anthem in front of an audience of thousands.

“I just wish that you would be a little easier on someone who is just a human being, and I’m sorry,” Strimel Bentley said through tears. “Thank you for giving me grace. I love Canada. I stand on guard for thee.”

The Leafs referenced the lyric mishap in a post on X that shared video of defenceman Jack McCabe putting a puck in the Islanders’ net for Toronto’s first goal of the night.

“Jack McCabe, would lend my heart to thee,” the Leafs wrote.

They would go on to beat the Islanders 4-2, ending a nine-game losing streak.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 24, 2026.

The Canadian Press

She said this after messing up the national anthem at a Maple Leafs game in New York Monday night, switching out “We lend our hearts to thee” in place of the song’s final line, “We stand on guard for thee.”

Bentley also swapped out words in other lines, singing “True patriot love with all of us command.” The correct line is “True patriot love in all of us command.” She switched “A” for “The” in “The true north strong and free.”

Fans were upset with the gaffe, with multiple videos on social media suggesting Leafs captain Auston Matthews looked puzzled as he stood at attention on the ice.

Leafs centre John Tavares told The New York Times: “I thought something sounded different, but sometimes as you’re listening to the anthem, you get in your own world a little bit, just preparing for the game.”

However, Bentley took to social media directly afterwards to apologize for the mixup.

“I just wanted to apologize to all of my Canadians,” the Pittsburgh-born singer said in a post on Instagram, “because I practiced the s— out of O Canada, and getting up in front of 18,000 people, singing an anthem that you haven’t heard for your whole life is scary, and I botched the lyrics, and I’m really sorry.”

Choking back tears, she added: “I got put in menopause because I had breast cancer, and tonight is about hockey fighting cancer, and menopause makes you forget things. So, I just wish that you’d be a little easier on someone who’s just a human being. And I’m sorry.”

She concluded: Thank you for giving me grace. I love Canada. I stand on guard for thee.”

View this post on Instagram

The Islanders put out their own statement in support of Bentley, noting that she had been invited by the team as part of Hockey Fights Cancer Night, founded in 1998 by the NHL and the NHL Players’ Association as a way to raise money and awareness of cancer.

“For Hockey Fights Cancer Night, the Islanders invited Broadway performer Sarrah Strimel Bentley to sing on this emotional evening,” the statement read. “During her performance of ‘O Canada,’ she stumbled on the lyrics. Bentley knows the fight against cancer firsthand. After a double mastectomy, eight rounds of chemotherapy, and 28 rounds of radiation, she rang the bell as cancer-free.”

Tavares further told NYT: “It’s incredible what she’s gone through and those difficulties, so obviously, a great moment for her to sing the anthem.”

Unrattled by the mistakes, the Leafs went on to score four consecutive goals and beat the Islanders 4-2, snapping a nine-game losing streak.

“Oh, it felt good,” coach Jim Hiller said after the game. “I felt extremely happy for them because they battled. They have been battling for the most part, making some mistakes. They battled straight through, didn’t make as many mistakes, and they got rewarded. So I’m really happy for them.”

stories.title: The casino that never closes: Inside Canada’s online gambling epidemic
stories.summary: Problem gambling in Ontario has tripled since 2018
stories.author: Unknown
stories.content:
For decades, legal gambling in Canada usually meant a trip to the corner store for a lottery ticket or a night out at a casino. But over the past five years, the landscape has shifted dramatically. A wave of digital betting platforms has brought the casino to our pockets, transforming how, when and how much Canadians wager.

That convenience has come at a steep price. New research suggests that the number of people experiencing problem gambling in Ontario has tripled since 2018. Behind these figures are real people facing profound financial strain and mental health challenges, caught in an ecosystem designed to keep them engaged around the clock.

Today’s episode of Stress Test examines how easy access to digital gambling can become a financial trap. We hear from a 21-year-old whose rapidly escalating gambling addiction cost him his financial security and relationships. Then Roma speaks with Dr. Nigel Turner of the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health (CAMH) about the forces driving gambling-related harm in Canada, how technology and game design influence players’ behaviour, and why the odds of winning are worse than you might think.

stories.title: Astronomers spot record-setting quasar in the early universe
stories.summary: A quasar is a bright galactic core powered by a black hole
stories.author: Will Dunham
stories.content:
A quasar, one of the universe’s most energetic and luminous objects, is the enormously bright core of a galaxy, powered by a central supermassive black hole. Astronomers have now found the oldest-known quasar, one that formed so early in cosmic history that they are still trying to decipher how it happened.

They identified a quasar dating to more than 13.1 billion years ago when the cosmos was less than 5 per cent of its current age, some 630 million years after the Big Bang event that initiated the universe. The quasar dates to 40 million years earlier than the previous record holder, disclosed in July.

“I think it adds to the evidence that some objects in the early universe developed remarkably quickly. Just 630 million years after the Big Bang, this black hole had already grown to about 360 million times the mass of the sun and was shining as a quasar,” said astronomer Julien Wolf of the European Southern Observatory in Germany, lead author of the research published in the journal Astronomy and Astrophysics.

Black holes are extraordinarily dense objects with gravity so strong that not even light can escape.

The quasar was first detected by the European Space Agency’s Euclid orbiting telescope and then further characterized using a combination of ground- and space-based telescopes.

The researchers gave the quasar the nickname Dún Aonghasa, the name of an ancient stone fort in Ireland that is perched atop a cliff overlooking the vast expanse of the Atlantic Ocean.

A supermassive black hole that powers a quasar is typically billions of times more massive than the sun.

“As enormous amounts of gas, dust and matter fall toward the black hole, they form a swirling accretion disk that heats up to extreme temperatures and radiates tremendous amounts of energy, outshining the entire rest of the galaxy by factors of hundreds or even thousands,” said astronomer and study co-author Silvia Belladitta of the Max Planck Institute for Astronomy in Germany and the Inaf Bologna Observatory of Astrophysics and Space Science in Italy.

“This makes quasars visible across billions of light-years, allowing us to observe them from the very early universe. Studying quasars helps astronomers understand how the first galaxies formed and evolved, and how the supermassive black holes at their hearts grew to such enormous sizes,” Belladitta said.

The Dún Aonghasa supermassive black hole is about 90 times more massive than the one at the centre of our Milky Way.

It dates to one of the universe’s most dramatic and transformative epochs. After the Big Bang, the cosmos cooled into a dark and neutral fog of hydrogen gas. The first stars and galaxies then began to ignite, and their intense radiation slowly burned through the fog, making the universe transparent to light for the first time.

“This process was still unfolding at the time this quasar and its host galaxy were forming. It is a remarkable epoch to find such an object. The supermassive black hole powering this quasar had already grown to an enormous mass in an extremely short time, which challenges our understanding of how black holes can grow so large so quickly in the early universe,” Belladitta said.

One possibility is that this black hole started out small after the demise of a star that was part of the first stellar generation, but the observations indicated it was consuming material at a rate too slow to have achieved its great mass so quickly. Another possibility is that it May have been born big in a formation scenario called direct collapse.

“Normally, a large cloud of gas cools and breaks up into smaller clumps that form stars. Under the right conditions, the gas could stay warm enough to limit that fragmentation, allowing much of it to flow towards the centre. That gas can build up a single enormous star that quickly collapses into a black hole. That black hole would start out far more massive than the remnant of a typical first-generation star,” Wolf said.

The researchers said Euclid May yet spot quasars at farther distances – meaning older – than Dún Aonghasa, with theoretical models suggesting that the first quasars could potentially date to 270 million to 470 million years post-Big Bang.

“So in short: this is the furthest quasar we have ever seen, but maybe not the furthest there is to find,” Belladitta said.

stories.title: George Weston profit rises, boosted by Loblaw’s sale of PC Financial
stories.summary: Company holds large stakes in Loblaw and Choice Properties Reit
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
George Weston Ltd. WN-T reported a profit available to common shareholders of $1.27-billion for its third quarter, boosted by Loblaw’s sale of its PC Financial business.

The company, which holds large stakes in Loblaw Cos. Ltd. L-T and Choice Properties Real Estate Investment Trust CHP-UN-T , says the profit amounted to $3.37 per diluted share for the quarter ended Oct. 10.

The result was up from a profit of $477-million or $1.23 per diluted share a year earlier.

On an adjusted basis, George Weston says it earned $1.44 per diluted share in its latest quarter, up from an adjusted profit of $1.33 per diluted share in the same quarter last year.

Revenue in the quarter totalled $20.01-billion, up from $19.31-billion a year earlier.

Chair and CEO Galen Weston says the company delivered another quarter of earnings growth, with solid operational and financial performance from Loblaw and Choice Properties.

stories.title: 1968 murder of teen girl in London, Ont. solved
stories.summary: Police in London, Ont., say they have identified the suspect in the murder of a 16-year-old girl nearly six decades ago using advanced genetic technology. They say Jacqueline “Jackie” Dunleavy was last seen after finishing her shift at a variety store in the evening of Jan. 9, 1968. Police say three youths found Dunleavy dead […]
stories.author: Natasha O'Neill
stories.content:
By Sharif Hassan, The Canadian Press

Posted November 24, 2026 9:39 am.

Police in London, Ont., say they have identified the suspect in the murder of a 16-year-old girl nearly six decades ago using advanced genetic technology.

They say Jacqueline “Jackie” Dunleavy was last seen after finishing her shift at a variety store in the evening of Jan. 9, 1968.

Police say three youths found Dunleavy dead on the grounds of a school, now known as Matthews Hall, at around 8 p.m. that evening.

They say while she had a head injury, the investigation revealed she had died of strangulation.

Investigators say they identified Michael Joseph Moore, who was 25 years old at the time, as the person responsible for the girl’s murder after re-examination of carefully persevered evidence and additional DNA testing.

They say no criminal charges will be laid because Moore died in 2018.

Police said while the case has been thoroughly reviewed by generations of investigators over the years, the use of modern genetic genealogy made it possible to “construct family trees and narrow the investigation toward a potential suspect.”

“Our investigators conducted additional interviews, gathered new evidence, and obtained DNA samples for comparison. Those samples were submitted to the Centre of Forensic Sciences for analysis,” Det. Mike Budzyn, who is leading the investigation, said in a news release.

“Based on the evidence obtained through this investigation, we are confident that the evidentiary threshold to support criminal charges was met. Had Moore been alive today, he would have been arrested and charged in relation to Jackie’s murder.”

Identifying the suspect answers questions that the victim’s family and community had for decades, police said.

Investigators are now asking people who knew Moore to come forward.

“Information that May not have seemed significant at the time could have meaning today,” police said in a statement.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 23, 2026.

stories.title: Conservatives want Parks Canada officials, union to answer questions on cuts
stories.summary: In the latest federal budget, Ottawa said it plans to bring back the Canada Strong pass next year, which gave free admission to national parks.
stories.author: Nick Murray
stories.content:
Conservative MPs are looking for answers about planned cuts to Parks Canada.

The organization has signalled upwards of 700 positions could be eliminated, along with Banff’s dog search and rescue program.

Manitoba Conservative MP Branden Leslie said he’s hoping to invite senior Parks Canada officials and union representatives to the House of Commons environment committee.

He told The Canadian Press he wants to look into the consequences of the cuts, particularly as Parks Canada saw a 13 per cent increase in visitors last year.

In the latest federal budget, Ottawa said it plans to bring back the Canada Strong pass next year, which gave free admission to national parks.

Leslie said he plans to have his motion addressed when the committee meets Tuesday afternoon.

stories.title: Bonus payments for trades workers going out early next month
stories.summary: Tradespeople who completed an apprenticeship and earned Red Seal trade certification on or after April 1, 2025, are eligible for a $5,000 bonus
stories.author: Catherine Morrison
stories.content:
Bonuses for Red Seal trades workers are set to be delivered starting early next month.

Since last week, tradespeople who completed an apprenticeship and earned their certification in a Red Seal trade on or after April 1, 2025, have been able to apply for a $5,000 completion bonus .

Jobs Minister Patty Hajdu says more than 16,000 applications have been received and the first payments will go out to eligible people starting the first week of December.

Starting in July, “trade qualifiers” who haven’t completed an apprenticeship but have enough practical work experience and are certified in a Red Seal trade, can apply for the bonus as well.

Red Seal trades are skilled jobs with national standards, including for training, such as electricians, plumbers and welders.

The Liberals have announced billions of dollars in spending to train up to 100,000 new skilled workers over the next half decade to support the government’s ambitious infrastructure agenda.

stories.title: Can my employer track my location when I’m working?
stories.summary: You do not have an absolute expectation of privacy at work. The key consideration is whether the monitoring is reasonable in both its purpose and the manner in which it is carried out
stories.author: Andrea Yu
stories.content:
Interested in more careers-related content? Check out our new weekly Work Life newsletter . Sent every Monday afternoon.

My role was recently changed from being a nine-to-five desk job to doing some regular travel to clients’ offices for meetings and presentations. My boss told me that I had to download a tracking app and turn it on whenever I leave the office for a meeting. This seems invasive and unnecessary. I know he’s just paranoid I’ll be purposely trying to waste time outside of the office or do personal errands. He said some BS about it being for my safety but I know it’s a lie. Is this legal for my employer to track my location outside of the office during working hours?

Shibil Siddiqi , employment lawyer, Progressive Barristers , Toronto

Your privacy concern is understandable. The answer depends partly on where you work.

British Columbia, Alberta and Quebec have private-sector privacy laws and federal legislation covers federally regulated employers such as banks and airlines. These laws require monitoring to be reasonable for its purpose and limited in scope.

Ontario lacks comprehensive employee privacy legislation. For most provincially regulated private-sector employees there, the answer is a qualified yes: an employer May lawfully track location during work-related travel.

Location tracking is common in mobile work, such as package delivery, and privacy commissioners and arbitrators have accepted it for legitimate purposes, including safety, dispatching and accountability for working time. But tracking your phone can reveal more than tracking a company vehicle, particularly if it follows you beyond the work trip.

Ontario employers with at least 25 employees must have a written electronic-monitoring policy explaining how monitoring occurs and how the information May be used. These rules require transparency but do not restrict monitoring.

Employment contracts and collective agreements May provide protection and serious, unjustified intrusions into private affairs can attract civil liability.

You May wish to raise your concerns with your employer in a polite, direct manner, perhaps alongside other affected employees. Ask for the policy and details of the app’s permissions. Does tracking stop during breaks and after work? Who can access the information, how long is it retained and can it be used for discipline?

If this is your personal phone, consider requesting a company device. If safety is the stated purpose, ask how tracking helps in an emergency and whether scheduled check-ins would suffice.

Get legal advice before refusing to comply with your employer’s instruction, because refusing a lawful workplace direction could put your employment at risk.

Alexandra Monkhouse , partner, Monkhouse Law Employment Lawyers , Toronto

In Ontario, the Employment Standards Act requires employers with 25 or more employees to maintain a written electronic-monitoring policy and to provide a copy of it to every employee. That obligation, however, is purely about disclosure: it requires the employer to tell you whether, how and why it monitors, but it does not give you any right to refuse the monitoring or limit how the information is used.

You do not have an absolute expectation of privacy at work. The key consideration is whether the monitoring is reasonable in both its purpose and the manner in which it is carried out. Purpose is decisive. Monitoring tied to a genuine safety or security need is given considerable latitude, while monitoring aimed at assessing your performance or conduct attracts much closer scrutiny and generally requires real evidence of a problem. If the true purpose is to measure your productivity rather than to protect your safety, you May well have grounds to object.

Taking the matter further depends on your situation. There is no provincial privacy regulator to whom a private-sector Ontario employee can complain. If you are unionized, you would challenge the monitoring through a grievance. If you are not, your practical recourse is a civil claim in court for intrusion upon seclusion, available where monitoring is covert or unreasonable.

In the meantime, you cannot simply refuse to comply with the policy. Doing so would be treated as insubordination and could expose you to discipline, so any challenge should proceed through the proper channel.

My boss told me that I had to download a tracking app and turn it on whenever I leave the office for a meeting. This seems invasive and unnecessary. I know he’s just paranoid I’ll be purposely trying to waste time outside of the office or do personal errands. He said some BS about it being for my safety but I know it’s a lie. Is this legal for my employer to track my location outside of the office during working hours?
Shibil Siddiqi , employment lawyer, Progressive Barristers , Toronto
Your privacy concern is understandable. The answer depends partly on where you work.

British Columbia, Alberta and Quebec have private-sector privacy laws and federal legislation covers federally regulated employers such as banks and airlines. These laws require monitoring to be reasonable for its purpose and limited in scope.

Ontario lacks comprehensive employee privacy legislation. For most provincially regulated private-sector employees there, the answer is a qualified yes: an employer May lawfully track location during work-related travel.

Location tracking is common in mobile work, such as package delivery, and privacy commissioners and arbitrators have accepted it for legitimate purposes, including safety, dispatching and accountability for working time. But tracking your phone can reveal more than tracking a company vehicle, particularly if it follows you beyond the work trip.

Ontario employers with at least 25 employees must have a written electronic-monitoring policy explaining how monitoring occurs and how the information May be used. These rules require transparency but do not restrict monitoring.
Employment contracts and collective agreements May provide protection and serious, unjustified intrusions into private affairs can attract civil liability.

You May wish to raise your concerns with your employer in a polite, direct manner, perhaps alongside other affected employees. Ask for the policy and details of the app’s permissions. Does tracking stop during breaks and after work? Who can access the information, how long is it retained and can it be used for discipline?
If this is your personal phone, consider requesting a company device. If safety is the stated purpose, ask how tracking helps in an emergency and whether scheduled check-ins would suffice.
Get legal advice before refusing to comply with your employer’s instruction, because refusing a lawful workplace direction could put your employment at risk.

stories.title: Final paving underway for Wellington Road stretch near White Oaks
stories.summary: The City of London says paving between Harlech Gate and the Wellington Commons entrance is expected to start Nov. 23 and continue through Nov. 26, weather permitting.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
Final paving on a section of Wellington Road is underway this week as work on the latest phase of the Wellington Gateway project nears completion.

The City of London says paving between Harlech Gate and the Wellington Commons entrance is expected to start Nov. 23 and continue through Nov. 26, weather permitting.

The work marks one of the final stages of Wellington Gateway Phase 4. City officials say motorists will see significant improvements to the roadway once paving is complete.

Construction crews will work during daytime hours over the four-day paving operation. Traffic will be maintained through the area, but drivers should expect delays and temporary disruptions.

Local businesses and shopping destinations, including White Oaks Mall and Wellington Commons, will remain open throughout the work. Access to business entrances, parking lots and driveways will be maintained when possible, although brief interruptions May occur as paving equipment passes through driveway and plaza entrances.

Pedestrian access to nearby businesses and shopping areas will also be maintained, though temporary route adjustments May be required. Residents are being asked to follow posted signage and use designated pedestrian pathways.

London Transit Commission buses will detour around the construction zone. Transit riders can check the LTC website for updated schedules and detour information.

Following the paving operation, crews are expected to return in 2027 to complete the remaining Phase 4 work, including installing transit shelters, permanent traffic signals, landscaping and other finishing touches. The city says that work is expected to cause minimal traffic disruption.

stories.title: Storm surge, king tides converge to raise flooding risk on B.C. coast
stories.summary: Another frontal system is washing over coastal B.C., bringing heavy rains and strong winds, swelling waterways just as king tides peak this week.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Another frontal system is washing over coastal B.C ., bringing heavy rains and strong winds, swelling waterways just as king tides peak this week.

Environment Canada has posted rainfall warnings for Vancouver Island, the central coast and Haida Gwaii, while coastal flood warnings are up for Metro Vancouver, the Sunshine and central coasts and Western sides of Vancouver Island and Haida Gwaii.

The weather agency says a strong frontal system will persist through Tuesday night, bringing a prolonged period of heavy rain as well as heavy winds with rainfall amounts from 100 to 200 millimetres, depending on the location.

The flood warnings come with the storm surge from the rain, very high tides and blustery winds, setting off large waves for the next several days.

Environment Canada says the king tides will lift water levels an extra 20 to 50 centimetres higher than the highest astronomical tides.

The B.C . River Forecast Centre has also issued a high streamflow advisory for most of Vancouver Island, saying heavy rain and already saturated soils will bring sharp increases in river levels, while the king tides will exacerbate water levels at the mouths of rivers.

The centre says an evacuation alert has been issued for some shoreline properties of the Tla-o-qui-aht First Nation due to flooding.

It says anyone in the affected area must be ready to leave on short notice.

stories.title: Author Galloway’s lawyer asks B.C. court for millions in defamation award
stories.summary: The lawyer for author and former UBC professor Steven Galloway says his client's accuser started rape allegations and encouraged others to spread the claims.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
The lawyer for author and former University of British Columbia professor Steven Galloway said in closing arguments that his client’s accuser started rape allegations then poured gasoline on them by encouraging others to spread the claims.

Galloway alleges defamation against the woman, identified only as A.B., and three others who are alleged to have spread the allegations in 2015.

His lawyer Daniel Burnett told a B.C. Supreme Court judge in Vancouver that A.B. knew she was going to cause “massive wreckage” to the reputation of Galloway, who is the author of the bestselling novel “The Cellist of Sarajevo.”

Burnett said general, aggravated and punitive damages should be awarded to Galloway in the range of $3 million to $4 million, minus 25 per cent to account for the several other defendants who already settled with Galloway.

He said there was recklessness in knowingly spreading false allegations, which clearly establishes malice and opens the door to aggravated and punitive damages.

Final submissions in the trial are scheduled through the week more than 10 years after unproven allegations were made against Galloway, prompting his firing as a professor at the University of B.C. and what the court heard was the loss of his writing career.

stories.title: Conservatives want answers on planned Parks Canada cuts, layoffs
stories.summary: Ottawa - Conservative MPs are looking for answers about planned cuts to Parks Canada.
stories.author: Nick Murray The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - Opposition MPs are looking for answers about planned cuts to Parks Canada, and one says Ottawa shouldn’t proceed with its plan to continue free admission to parks through 2027.

Parks Canada sent a notice last month to almost 3,000 employees stating that it was planning layoffs.

In a Nov. 10 memo sent to Parks Canada staff, obtained by The Canadian Press, interim president and CEO Andrew Campbell said there could be a reduction of 700 to 750 people, taking into account the seasonal workforce.

“I know these numbers are large and May cause worry,” said Campbell. “I want to be clear: Being identified as affected does NOT mean you will lose your job.

“Some jobs will stay the same. Some others May change. Some employees May find different positions within Parks Canada. Some jobs May be eliminated.”

Campbell said senior staff had shared updates with their teams, adding that Parks Canada would continue to look at how these changes May affect each employee.

“I know waiting for answers is hard. We are working as quickly as we can to give staff more details. Our goal is to confirm the status of as many employees as possible early in the new year,” he said.

In the latest federal budget, Ottawa said it plans to bring back next year the Canada Strong pass, which offers free admission to national parks. Parks Canada saw a 13 per cent increase in visitors in the summer of 2025 after the special pass was introduced.

Manitoba Conservative MP Branden Leslie said Tuesday he’s hoping to invite senior Parks Canada officials and union representatives to the House of Commons environment committee.

“Step one is knowing, right? Like right now, all we know is that half of the workforce on the ground got noticed as saying that your job might be cut,” Leslie told reporters Tuesday on Parliament Hill.

“There’s nothing wrong with finding efficiencies in government. There is plenty of efficiency to be found. I will certainly have questions as to how top-heavy Parks Canada is.”

Alberta Conservative MP William Stevenson, whose riding encompasses Jasper and Banff national parks, said if Ottawa is proceeding with the planned cuts, it should cancel the Canada Strong Pass for 2027.

“I’ve got a lot of constituents, including Liberal supporters, that have written to me … saying they cannot accept having the Canada Strong Pass while they’re also doing cuts. The two don’t coincide,” Stevenson said.

“But if they don’t want to do that, they need to look at adjusting the program so that it actually works within the off-peak seasons. Have it operate now until the May long weekend. Don’t add the problems to the peak seasons of travellers.”

In a letter to Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin, NDP MP Gord Johns said attracting more visitors to national parks with the Canada Strong Pass while also cutting staff “makes little sense.”

“Employees have also raised concerns that Pacific Rim wardens could be required to assume enforcement responsibilities at Gulf Islands National Park Reserve,” Johns wrote on Monday.

“While unconfirmed, this possibility raises serious questions about response times and adequate enforcement coverage at Pacific Rim.”

Conservative MPs also took aim Tuesday at the amount of money Ottawa is sending to other countries, arguing that money could be spent to fund jobs within Parks Canada.

In its departmental report, Parks Canada forecasts cutting $24 million in spending this coming fiscal year, $45 million in 2027-28, and $75 million in 2028-29.

“In that time we have money to go to China, to Brazil $560 million no problem, Senegal for electric vehicles. Vietnam, Fiji, Peru, Mozambique, $40 million we’ve given,” said Quebec Conservative MP Gabriel Hardy in French. paragraphs: Ottawa - Opposition MPs are looking for answers about planned cuts to Parks Canada, and one says Ottawa shouldn’t proceed with its plan to continue free admission to parks through 2027.
Parks Canada sent a notice last month to almost 3,000 employees stating that it was planning layoffs.

In a Nov. 10 memo sent to Parks Canada staff, obtained by The Canadian Press, interim president and CEO Andrew Campbell said there could be a reduction of 700 to 750 people, taking into account the seasonal workforce.
“I know these numbers are large and May cause worry,” said Campbell. “I want to be clear: Being identified as affected does NOT mean you will lose your job.
“Some jobs will stay the same. Some others May change. Some employees May find different positions within Parks Canada. Some jobs May be eliminated.”
Campbell said senior staff had shared updates with their teams, adding that Parks Canada would continue to look at how these changes May affect each employee.

“I know waiting for answers is hard. We are working as quickly as we can to give staff more details. Our goal is to confirm the status of as many employees as possible early in the new year,” he said.

In the latest federal budget, Ottawa said it plans to bring back next year the Canada Strong pass, which offers free admission to national parks. Parks Canada saw a 13 per cent increase in visitors in the summer of 2025 after the special pass was introduced.
Manitoba Conservative MP Branden Leslie said Tuesday he’s hoping to invite senior Parks Canada officials and union representatives to the House of Commons environment committee.

“Step one is knowing, right? Like right now, all we know is that half of the workforce on the ground got noticed as saying that your job might be cut,” Leslie told reporters Tuesday on Parliament Hill.
“There’s nothing wrong with finding efficiencies in government. There is plenty of efficiency to be found. I will certainly have questions as to how top-heavy Parks Canada is.”

Alberta Conservative MP William Stevenson, whose riding encompasses Jasper and Banff national parks, said if Ottawa is proceeding with the planned cuts, it should cancel the Canada Strong Pass for 2027.

“I’ve got a lot of constituents, including Liberal supporters, that have written to me … saying they cannot accept having the Canada Strong Pass while they’re also doing cuts. The two don’t coincide,” Stevenson said.

“But if they don’t want to do that, they need to look at adjusting the program so that it actually works within the off-peak seasons. Have it operate now until the May long weekend. Don’t add the problems to the peak seasons of travellers.”

“Employees have also raised concerns that Pacific Rim wardens could be required to assume enforcement responsibilities at Gulf Islands National Park Reserve,” Johns wrote on Monday.
“While unconfirmed, this possibility raises serious questions about response times and adequate enforcement coverage at Pacific Rim.”
Conservative MPs also took aim Tuesday at the amount of money Ottawa is sending to other countries, arguing that money could be spent to fund jobs within Parks Canada.
In its departmental report, Parks Canada forecasts cutting $24 million in spending this coming fiscal year, $45 million in 2027-28, and $75 million in 2028-29.

The goal is to protect more than one billion hectares of tropical forests annually across more than 70 countries.

stories.title: Mortgage delinquency rate up 31% in Q3, driven by Ontario and B.C.: Equifax report
stories.summary: A new report suggests there's growing stress among homeowners, with some struggling to keep up with monthly mortgage payments as interest rates rise again.
stories.author: Ritika Dubey
stories.content:
A new report suggests there’s growing stress among homeowners, with some struggling to keep up with monthly mortgage payments as interest rates rise again.

Equifax Canada’s third-quarter consumer credit trends report says the national 90-plus day mortgage delinquency rate — defined as missed payments three months in a row — reached 0.32 per cent, the highest since the credit agency started tracking the metric in 2013.

That’s up 31.1 per cent year-over-year, mainly pushed higher by missed mortgage payments in Ontario and British Columbia.

“That’s the highest we’ve seen, particularly for Ontario. And it’s still going up,” said Rebecca Oakes, Equifax Canada’s vice-president of advanced analytics, said in an interview.

“That’s the biggest concern for us.”

The Equifax data echoes the findings of a recent a TD report, which showed Ontario’s mortgage arrears have nearly tripled from pre-pandemic levels to approach their 2008 financial crisis peak.

“This reflects elevated mortgage balances and greater sensitivity to borrowing costs,” wrote TD economist Maria Solovieva in the report published last week.

Growing pressure on households comes as the Bank of Canada raised its policy interest rate by a quarter of a percentage point to 2.5 per cent last month for the first time in more than three years, amid concerns that higher energy prices could spill into broader inflation.

The move prompted the big banks to raise their prime rates, which is used to set interest rates on a range of loans including variable-rate mortgages.

Equifax estimates about 1.4 million Canadians have a variable-rate mortgage out of a total 9.1 million homeowners. Another 1.3 million consumers also have a home equity line of credit, or Heloc, balance of more than $50,000.

Every quarter-point rate hike adds roughly $860 million a year in interest on variable-rate mortgages, the company estimates.

Oakes suspects mortgage delinquencies will continue to rise in the coming months, depending on changes to interest rates.

“If interest rates stay relatively flat from this point on, I’d expect to see it ease off in the middle of next year,” she said.

But if more hikes come in, “it’s just going to put additional pressure.”

The central bank is expected to make its last rate decision of the year on Dec. 9.

Financial market odds for a quarter-point rate hike was 63 per cent as of Monday afternoon, according to Lseg Data & Analytics.

Oakes said first-time homebuyers and younger Canadians May bear the brunt of rising rates because they tend to carry a higher-balance mortgage.

Still, she said mortgage delinquencies overall are less than one per cent.

“It’s quite small, you know, from that standpoint, but of course it knocks on to other types of credit, like credit cards, auto loans,” Oakes said.

“That’s where those individuals miss the payments first rather than on the mortgage itself.”

Credit card balances reached $136.2 billion in the third quarter, up 4.82 per cent from a year earlier, the Equifax data showed.

Overall, total Canadian consumer debt was $2.74 trillion in the third quarter, up 4.68 per cent from a year ago.

stories.title: Largest emissions spike in decade further sets back climate goals in Toronto area
stories.summary: A more polluting energy grid and rising demand for gas heating during a cold winter drove the largest annual spike in planet-warming emissions in at least a decade across the Gtha.
stories.author: Jordan Omstead
stories.content:
A more polluting energy grid and rising demand for gas heating during a colder winter drove the largest annual spike in planet-warming emissions in at least a decade across the Greater Toronto and Hamilton Area, a new report found, putting the region further off track to its climate goals.

The findings paint a bleak picture of the region’s trajectory. Emissions rose for a fifth straight year and increased by eight per cent from 2024 to 2025, the biggest annual jump since tracking began in 2015, said the report from The Atmospheric Fund, a regional climate agency.

The Gtha, responsible for a major share of Ontario’s emissions, now faces a steep climb to meet local climate commitments. If Toronto’s 2030 target were used as a regional benchmark, emissions would need to be slashed by about 16 per cent each year.

“This increase really brings us way off track from reaching any of the climate targets we’ve set out and really highlights the urgent need to take strong action to bend the curve and bring emissions back onto a downward trajectory,” said Bryan Purcell, the agency’s vice president of policy and programs.

The report released Tuesday offers some bright spots: Toronto recently removed local barriers to installing heat pumps and electric vehicle chargers; Ontario procured a record amount of battery storage this year, beating out gas on cost; and the federal government recently announced a $2-billion investment in building retrofits, including rebates for heat pumps.

But the report says government policy rollbacks are threatening to overshadow that progress as climate change fuels more intense wildfires, flooding and extreme heat.

The findings, Purcell said, challenge a common political argument that climate action must take a back seat to affordability concerns. Many of the measures needed to cut emissions, such as building retrofits, switching to heat pumps and improving public transit, will also help alleviate those pocketbook pressures, he said.

“We know what works, we have the technology, and it’s really about the political will to put policies and programs in place to consistently move emissions downward. And that’s really the missing ingredient right now,” Purcell said.

Buildings, which account for nearly half of the region’s emissions, were among the biggest drivers of the annual increase. Building-sector emissions — mostly from burning gas for heat and, to a smaller extent, from electricity — rose by 15 per cent annually.

Electricity-related building emissions were up 26 per cent, due to what the report says is the province’s increasingly carbon-intensive grid. Nearly a fifth of Ontario’s electricity was generated by fossil fuels last year, the most since the coal phaseout, as the province turns to gas to help fill the gap left by nuclear reactors turned off-line for refurbishment.

Heating-related emissions were up by 14 per cent over the previous year, largely due to the colder winter, the report found. But even when researchers adjusted for weather, those emissions were still up three per cent, pointing to what the report suggests is an underlying problem with the region’s aging, inefficient housing stock.

Those emissions are increasing at a time when municipalities have lost a key tool to bring them down. Premier Doug Ford’s government has blocked Toronto and other municipalities from enforcing green building standards, siding with some developers who argued the requirements added costs and complexity to construction.

The change set Toronto back “about 10 years in terms of the efficiency and technology going into new buildings,” Purcell said.

With limits on what cities can require of new construction, Purcell said there’s still headway to be made with existing homes and businesses. He pointed to Toronto’s proposed building emissions performance standards as one of the most significant local climate policies under consideration in the region.

“Existing buildings are the largest source of emissions for most of our cities. And we really need policy tools that will help to control and reverse that growth over time,” he said.

Transportation, the next-largest source after buildings, saw emissions increase by between one and three per cent across most of the region. Most of that was driven by increasing number of cars on the road and an ongoing preference for larger vehicles that tend to be less fuel efficient, Purcell said.

The number of registered battery-electric and plug-in hybrid vehicles continued to rise but Purcell said policy uncertainty had created new headwinds. Ottawa cancelled an EV sales mandate earlier this year and its promise to enhance tailpipe emissions regulations to help offset the environmental blow has yet to materialize. Municipal support for charging networks could help give car buyers more confidence to make the switch, he said.

While investments in public transit expansion were promising, Purcell said cities needed to place a focus on day-to-day service improvements to encourage some residents to switch toA more polluting energy grid and rising demand for gas heating during a colder winter drove the largest annual spike in planet-warming emissions in at least a decade across the Greater Toronto and Hamilton Area, a new report found, putting the region further off track to its climate goals. buses and trains. Ridership across the region was down by about 1.5 per cent annually, and remains well below pre-pandemic levels.

“It’s those basic nuts and bolts issues that drive ridership growth more than the mega projects,” he said.

Industrial emitters, mostly steel and cement manufacturers, showed no signs of progress as the decarbonization plans “stalled,” the report said. It comes as Ford is pressuring the federal government to abandon the industrial carbon price as part of an effort to keep automaker Stellantis from selling its idled Brampton plant.

stories.title: Changes to inspection rules at food plants putting safety at risk: union
stories.summary: The daily inspection program is continuing in plants where food is bound for the U.S. The agency said that's because of U.S. equivalency and market access requirements.
stories.author: Catherine Morrison
stories.content:
A federal union is warning about risks to food safety as the government cuts back on inspections at meat plants.

Canadian Food Inspection Agency documents, obtained by The Canadian Press, show that as of Oct. 1, daily inspections are no longer being conducted in domestic-only meat plants. They are also no longer being conducted in plants that export exclusively to non-U.S. markets.

The daily inspection program is continuing in plants where food is bound for the U.S. The agency said that’s because of U.S. equivalency and market access requirements.

“This reflects trade requirements and should not be interpreted as a difference in food safety standards,” said a Canadian Food Inspection Agency document. “Products destined for domestic and export markets remain subject to the same regulatory requirements and food safety expectations.”

The agency called the changes to inspection rules a “reallocation” of inspection activities and “not a reduction.”

The agency said it will continue to deliver inspection and oversight activities using a “risk-based approach” that considers food safety risks, compliance history, regulatory requirements and trade requirements.

It said establishments with higher-risk activities or unsatisfactory inspection outcomes will continue to see a heightened inspection presence, whether they serve domestic or international markets.

Milton Dyck, national president of the Agriculture Union, said inspectors on the plant floor are the “last line of defence” between Canadians and a deadly outbreak.

“A drop in inspection can be the difference between a routine day and another Maple Leaf 2008 tragedy,” he said.

In 2008, a listeria outbreak at a Maple Leaf Foods meat plant in Ontario led to dozens of illnesses and 22 deaths.

The union is raising concerns about the planned “risk-based” approach replacing daily inspection presence. It said it’s not clear what “risk” means and that there is no information on how often an inspector will now walk a domestic plant floor.

“They’ve replaced a written, transparent standard with a black box and called it modernization,” said Dyck. “The Carney government is rolling back protections to your health under the guise of cuts to red tape. We’re calling on the government to stop the cuts and to consult the people who do this work before it’s too late.”

Federal government data shows there were 6,207 employees working at the Canadian Food Inspection Agency as of the end of March. That’s down from 6,380 in 2025, and 6,833 the year before.

A Canadian Food Inspection Agency document said it’s reallocating approximately $30 million from existing resources to modernize how its inspection workforce is deployed and direct resources to “areas of greatest impact.” It said the funds will allow for around 250 new inspection and oversight positions.

It said the agency is creating a national food inspection team to support risk-based activities in the areas of food fraud, consumer protection and import oversight.

“The team will also provide surge capacity during large-scale food-related incidents and emergencies, helping to ensure a co-ordinated and effective operational response across the country,” said the document. “The Cfia’s mandate and regulatory responsibilities remain unchanged.”

stories.title: Seller of updated semi lists at realistic price to find buyer
stories.summary: Wychwood
stories.author: Sydnia Yu
stories.content:
92 Winona Dr., Toronto

Asking price: $1,325,000 (September 2026)

Selling price: $1.31-million (October 2026)

Previous selling price: $727,000 (July 2013); $161,000 (November 1994)

Taxes: $6,836 (2026)

Days on the market: 13

Listing agent: Christopher Bibby, Re/Max Hallmark Bibby Group Realty

The long-time owners of this semi-detached house near the Wychwood Barns art space knew that some nearby homes for sale were setting their asking prices low in hopes of generating multiple offers. But they decided to price their home closer to what they thought was a reasonable take-home price.

“In that area, some agents were opting to price low with an offer date,” agent Christopher Bibby said. “But I didn’t feel the need to take that risk.

“We didn’t want to put all our faith or hope in one night, and if it didn’t work out, then we’d be in a position to increase the price or relist it.”

By October, there were no other comparable homes for sale nearby, and the three-bedroom home across from two schools had 17 visitors. One of those negotiated a purchase at $15,000 below the asking price prior to Thanksgiving.

“There was nothing quite like this, and that’s where the timing was perfect,” Mr. Bibby said.

“The location is unbeatable and great for families, with great schools in the neighbourhood.

“It’s in proximity to St. Clair [Avenue] restaurants and shopping and has easy access to Wychwood Barns.”

This two-storey house has living and dining areas with hardwood floors, and a kitchen with tile flooring and stainless-steel appliances.

Three bedrooms and an updated four-piece bathroom are upstairs.

Another full bathroom is in the basement. It also has a rear entrance to the patio and a carport facing a laneway behind the 17-by-151-foot lot.

“The house was really turnkey with big, open-concept living and dining rooms,” Mr. Bibby said.

“There was an extra enclosed bedroom downstairs, which was great for family or guests, and a big recreation room.”
