stories.title: Only 944 pardons granted for cannabis possession since legalization
stories.summary: It is less than one tenth of the number the government was anticipating when it legalized recreational cannabis eight years ago
stories.author: Catherine Morrison
stories.content:
The Parole Board of Canada has granted 944 pardons for pot possession – less than one tenth of the number the government was anticipating when it legalized recreational cannabis eight years ago.

The Liberals lifted a century-long prohibition on the recreational use and sale of cannabis in October 2018. Canada became just the second country in the world to legalize the drug, after Uruguay.

The following year, the government brought in legislation to offer a free and streamlined process to apply for record suspensions for simple possession of cannabis. Record suspensions effectively clear criminal records that can be a barrier to travel, employment, housing, education and volunteer work.

Ottawa estimated at the time about 10,000 Canadians would be eligible for cannabis-related record suspensions.

Parole Board of Canada spokesperson Andrea Fournier said in an e-mail the board has received 1,477 applications for cannabis record suspensions since 2019. Of those, 526 were returned because the applicant was ineligible or the application was incomplete.

The Parole Board of Canada has launched a new portal for pardon applications in a bid to streamline and simplify the application process.

Lawyer and University of Ottawa drug policy expert Eugene Oscapella said the application process May be a deterrent for some people.

“You’ve got to get records of your conviction, you’ve got to contact courts and police departments,” he said. “It’s not that straightforward a process and some people May just sort of balk at it.

“If there is a new streamlined process, that May in itself be an acknowledgment by the government that perhaps the current process is a bit awkward.”

Oscapella also said the number of pardons granted since legalization May be lower than expected because the stigma surrounding cannabis use has faded.

“Maybe people just aren’t as worried about it anymore,” he said. “Attitudes towards cannabis have become quite normalized and maybe people don’t see there’s any real advantage.

“There was a time when if you had a cannabis conviction, it had a significant impact on your life. I don’t think that’s the case anymore, for simple possession certainly.”

Oscapella said that while most employers likely wouldn’t have a problem with a candidate who has a record for pot possession, that’s not the case for jobs that require security clearances or travel abroad.

The Parole Board of Canada says in a news release last week its new portal allows applicants and their designated representatives to submit applications for record suspensions online.

The portal allows applicants to save an incomplete application and return to it later, and permits them to track their applications.

“The secure platform reduces reliance on paper-based processes and mail delivery while giving applicants greater flexibility and visibility throughout the process,” says the news release.

“By simplifying the application process, the PBC Service Portal helps people benefit from programs that can support their successful reintegration, while maintaining the integrity of the record suspension [pardon] and cannabis record suspension processes and supporting public safety.”

stories.title: Fire quickly extinguished at Dundas Street business; no injuries reported
stories.summary: A fire at a commercial building on Dundas Street was quickly extinguished after crews responding to reports of smoke discovered flames inside the structure.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
A fire at a commercial building on Dundas Street was quickly extinguished after crews responding to reports of smoke discovered flames inside the structure.

Firefighters were called to the 1000 block of Dundas Street, where crews investigating smoke in the area located a fire involving one of the businesses.

Crews advanced a hose line to the second floor and were able to knock down the fire. Primary searches of both the main floor and second floor were completed, with no occupants inside.

The blaze extended into the attic, requiring firefighters to access the space and extinguish remaining hot spots.

Officials later reported the fire had been fully extinguished and ventilation efforts successfully cleared smoke from the building.

Fire prevention investigators are expected to attend the scene to determine the cause of the fire.

Crews remained at the scene Monday night clearing equipment and hose lines. Dundas Street was temporarily closed at Edgerton Street during the response.

No injuries were reported, and the cause of the fire remains under investigation.

stories.title: Food safety at risk after cut back on inspections at meat plants, union warns
stories.summary: Canadian Food Inspection Agency documents show that as of Oct. 1, daily inspections are no longer being conducted in domestic-only meat plants
stories.author: Catherine Morrison
stories.content:
A federal union is warning about risks to food safety as the government cuts back on inspections at meat plants.

Canadian Food Inspection Agency documents, obtained by The Canadian Press, show that as of Oct. 1, daily inspections are no longer being conducted in domestic-only meat plants. They are also no longer being conducted in plants that export exclusively to non-U.S. markets.

The daily inspection program is continuing in plants where food is bound for the U.S. The agency said that’s because of U.S. equivalency and market access requirements.

“This reflects trade requirements and should not be interpreted as a difference in food safety standards,” said a Canadian Food Inspection Agency document. “Products destined for domestic and export markets remain subject to the same regulatory requirements and food safety expectations.”

The agency called the changes to inspection rules a “reallocation” of inspection activities and “not a reduction.”

The agency said it will continue to deliver inspection and oversight activities using a “risk-based approach” that considers food safety risks, compliance history, regulatory requirements and trade requirements.

It said establishments with higher-risk activities or unsatisfactory inspection outcomes will continue to see a heightened inspection presence, whether they serve domestic or international markets.

Milton Dyck, national president of the Agriculture Union, said inspectors on the plant floor are the “last line of defence” between Canadians and a deadly outbreak.

“A drop in inspection can be the difference between a routine day and another Maple Leaf 2008 tragedy,” he said.

In 2008, a listeria outbreak at a Maple Leaf Foods meat plant in Ontario led to dozens of illnesses and 22 deaths.

The union is raising concerns about the planned “risk-based” approach replacing daily inspection presence. It said it’s not clear what “risk” means and that there is no information on how often an inspector will now walk a domestic plant floor.

“They’ve replaced a written, transparent standard with a black box and called it modernization,” said Dyck. “The Carney government is rolling back protections to your health under the guise of cuts to red tape. We’re calling on the government to stop the cuts and to consult the people who do this work before it’s too late.”

Federal government data shows there were 6,207 employees working at the Canadian Food Inspection Agency as of the end of March. That’s down from 6,380 in 2025, and 6,833 the year before.

A Canadian Food Inspection Agency document said it’s reallocating approximately $30-million from existing resources to modernize how its inspection workforce is deployed and direct resources to “areas of greatest impact.” It said the funds will allow for around 250 new inspection and oversight positions.

It said the agency is creating a national food inspection team to support risk-based activities in the areas of food fraud, consumer protection and import oversight.

“The team will also provide surge capacity during large-scale food-related incidents and emergencies, helping to ensure a co-ordinated and effective operational response across the country,” said the document. “The Cfia’s mandate and regulatory responsibilities remain unchanged.”

stories.title: Toronto-area emissions see largest rise in decade, setting back climate goals
stories.summary: If Toronto’s 2030 target were used as a regional benchmark, emissions would need to be cut by about 16% each year to meet local climate commitments
stories.author: Jordan Omstead
stories.content:
A more polluting energy grid and rising demand for gas heating during a colder winter drove the largest annual spike in planet-warming emissions in at least a decade across the Greater Toronto and Hamilton Area, a new report found, putting the region further off track to its climate goals.

The findings paint a bleak picture of the region’s trajectory. Emissions rose for a fifth straight year and increased by eight per cent from 2024 to 2025, the biggest annual jump since tracking began in 2015, said the report from The Atmospheric Fund, a regional climate agency.

The Gtha, responsible for a major share of Ontario’s emissions, now faces a steep climb to meet local climate commitments. If Toronto’s 2030 target were used as a regional benchmark, emissions would need to be slashed by about 16 per cent each year.

“This increase really brings us way off track from reaching any of the climate targets we’ve set out and really highlights the urgent need to take strong action to bend the curve and bring emissions back onto a downward trajectory,” said Bryan Purcell, the agency’s vice president of policy and programs.

The report released Tuesday offers some bright spots: Toronto recently removed local barriers to installing heat pumps and electric vehicle chargers; Ontario procured a record amount of battery storage this year, beating out gas on cost; and the federal government recently announced a $2-billion investment in building retrofits, including rebates for heat pumps.

But the report says government policy rollbacks are threatening to overshadow that progress as climate change fuels more intense wildfires, flooding and extreme heat.

The findings, Purcell said, challenge a common political argument that climate action must take a back seat to affordability concerns. Many of the measures needed to cut emissions, such as building retrofits, switching to heat pumps and improving public transit, will also help alleviate those pocketbook pressures, he said.

“We know what works, we have the technology, and it’s really about the political will to put policies and programs in place to consistently move emissions downward. And that’s really the missing ingredient right now,” Purcell said.

Buildings, which account for nearly half of the region’s emissions, were among the biggest drivers of the annual increase. Building-sector emissions – mostly from burning gas for heat and, to a smaller extent, from electricity – rose by 15 per cent annually.

Electricity-related building emissions were up 26 per cent, due to what the report says is the province’s increasingly carbon-intensive grid. Nearly a fifth of Ontario’s electricity was generated by fossil fuels last year, the most since the coal phaseout, as the province turns to gas to help fill the gap left by nuclear reactors turned off-line for refurbishment.

Heating-related emissions were up by 14 per cent over the previous year, largely due to the colder winter, the report found. But even when researchers adjusted for weather, those emissions were still up three per cent, pointing to what the report suggests is an underlying problem with the region’s aging, inefficient housing stock.

Those emissions are increasing at a time when municipalities have lost a key tool to bring them down. Premier Doug Ford’s government has blocked Toronto and other municipalities from enforcing green building standards, siding with some developers who argued the requirements added costs and complexity to construction.

The change set Toronto back “about 10 years in terms of the efficiency and technology going into new buildings,” Purcell said.

With limits on what cities can require of new construction, Purcell said there’s still headway to be made with existing homes and businesses. He pointed to Toronto’s proposed building emissions performance standards as one of the most significant local climate policies under consideration in the region.

“Existing buildings are the largest source of emissions for most of our cities. And we really need policy tools that will help to control and reverse that growth over time,” he said.

Transportation, the next-largest source after buildings, saw emissions increase by between one and three per cent across most of the region. Most of that was driven by increasing number of cars on the road and an ongoing preference for larger vehicles that tend to be less fuel efficient, Purcell said.

The number of registered battery-electric and plug-in hybrid vehicles continued to rise but Purcell said policy uncertainty had created new headwinds. Ottawa cancelled an EV sales mandate earlier this year and its promise to enhance tailpipe emissions regulations to help offset the environmental blow has yet to materialize. Municipal support for charging networks could help give car buyers more confidence to make the switch, he said.

While investments in public transit expansion were promising, Purcell said cities needed to place a focus on day-to-day service improvements to encourage some residents to switch to buses and trains. Ridership across the region was down by about 1.5 per cent annually, and remains well below pre-pandemic levels.

“It’s those basic nuts and bolts issues that drive ridership growth more than the mega projects,” he said.

Industrial emitters, mostly steel and cement manufacturers, showed no signs of progress as the decarbonization plans “stalled,” the report said. It comes as Ford is pressuring the federal government to abandon the industrial carbon price as part of an effort to keep automaker Stellantis from selling its idled Brampton plant.

stories.title: Why it costs so much to build energy pipelines: Benchmark Canada
stories.summary: Just look at Tmx's skyrocketing pricetag: 'We start from a high base cost and then go up from there,' says one infrastructure expert
stories.author: Jared Lindzon
stories.content:
Countries don’t typically get report cards, but there are hard facts that can be collated, assessed and compared. Enter Benchmark Canada, a new project from the Macdonald-Laurier Institute that brings togethermore than 40 different metrics that measure this nation’s performance. This fall, the National Post is examining many of those findings.

As the world grapples with oil supply challenges and rising fuel costs, Canada is proving to be one of the most expensive places to build pipelines.

According to a comparative analysis published by Benchmark Canada, the per-kilometre capital construction cost of Canada’s Trans Mountain Expansion (TMX) came to $34.2 million. That’s 6.3 times the original 2013 estimates and well above the price tag of pipeline projects in the United States, Europe, Australia and the UAE.

Monday - Saturday Free

NP Posted keeps you updated on the news of the day and the perspectives that define the National Post, while drawing your focus to some of the unexpected stories we like to tell. Delivered straight to your inbox Monday to Friday, with a weekend edition on Saturdays.

The Mountain Valley Pipeline in Virginia and West Virginia placed second at $22.2 million per kilometre, followed by British Columbia’s Coastal GasLink at $21.6 million. Among major pipelines in Canada, Alberta’s Ngtl System Expansion and Enbridge’s Line 3 replacement — which crosses the Canada-U.S. border — landed near the middle of the pack at $6.7 million and $4.8 million per kilometre, respectively.

On the other end of the spectrum, northern Europe’s Baltic Pipe cost $3.4 million per kilometre, the United States’ Dakota Access Pipeline cost $2.8 million, and Australia’s Northern Gas Pipeline cost just $1.2 million per kilometre. (All figures in Canadian dollars and are not adjusted for inflation.)

“Our baseline of what we expect to pay per kilometre of pipeline or per kilometre of transit is already typically more than our peers, and that should be concerning,” says Matti Siemiatycki, director of the Infrastructure Institute at the University of Toronto.

While TMX stands out for its extraordinary cost and delays, it also faced a series of extraordinary challenges. The project that was approved in 2016 was halted by its original owner, Kinder Morgan, in the spring of 2018. Just as Ottawa was finalizing its purchase of TMX that summer, the Federal Court of Appeal quashed its approval over inadequate environmental review and Indigenous consultation.

Workers lay pipe for the Trans Mountain Expansion project near Popukum in B.C.’s Fraser Valley in May 2021. The per-kilometre capital construction cost of the project was 6.3 times the original 2013 estimates, according to a Benchmark Canada analysis. Trans Mountain Corporation

Once the project was re-approved and construction resumed in 2019, TMX faced new challenges ranging from the pandemic in 2020 to B.C.’s 2021 floods to supply-chain issues and labour shortages in 2022. It was finally completed in 2024.

“They encountered productivity issues related to pandemic measures that had to be implemented, like social distancing and testing,” says TD economist Likeleli Seitlheko. “When there’s a delay, you still need to pay the contractors, and the same thing happened with the 2021 floods, which caused disruptions to construction activities.”

As Canada plows ahead with its next major pipeline project, Pacific Link — which will follow the same corridor and be managed by the same Crown corporation, Trans Mountain Corp. — the industry hopes it can avoid the same delays and cost overruns.

Siemiatycki says Canada’s climate, terrain, regulatory environment and access to labour all push starting costs above those of peer nations. “The vast majority of the big infrastructure projects we’re building also have troubling cost overruns and are often significantly delayed, so we start from a high base cost and then go up from there.”

The causes of those delays and cost overruns, according to Siemiatycki, are many, ranging from an “optimism bias” that pins estimates to best-case scenarios to unexpected technical challenges to more human issues like deal structure and leadership shortfalls.

“Don’t get me wrong; you’re not going anywhere if you don’t have people managing the bad soil or the high water table or inclement weather — all of those things are real,” Siemiatycki says. “But what you see when you look at these over and over again is the challenges that they face between corporations — the contracting models that lead these folks to be frequently suing each other when things go wrong, and sometimes even before they start to go wrong.”

That common outcome, according to Siemiatycki, is a function of how a major project like a pipeline comes together. Often a small prep team spends years developing proposals and pursuing permitting and approvals before quickly scaling up to a multi-billion-dollar project. “Think of it like a company that went from zero to Fortune 500 in the span of three months: that takes a very specific type of project leadership,” Siemiatycki says.

The Benchmark Canada study notes that in the last decade four major pipelines in Canada were held up by regulatory and political challenges for four to 14 years before being cancelled.

A series of open letters signed by Canadian energy executives in late 2025 noted that “Canada still lacks the clear, competitive and durable fiscal and regulatory policies” required to advance major projects “with significant emissions reductions, expanded market access and material upstream production growth.” Now members of the industry seem optimistic that, if passed, Bill C-39 — also known as the Building Canada Strong Act — will help fast-track project approvals in the future.

During TC Energy’s third-quarter financial update, for example, president and CEO François Poirier said the legislation “could offer greater certainty and reduce project timelines by one to two years, while also offering improved cost efficiency and without compromising the rigour of the process.”

“Progress has been made on simplifying regulations, accelerating project approvals and expanding Indigenous investment opportunities,” says Enbridge spokesperson Gina Sutherland, whose CEO, Greg Ebel, signed the letters. “These are significant steps, and we look forward to continued work that enables Canada to realize its potential as an energy superpower.”

Given the challenges encountered by TMX, TD’s Seitlheko is hopeful that using the same Crown corporation and following the same path will help the Pacific Link project avoid the same fate.

“I hope that the experience from TMX has informed the cost estimates,” she says. “And since Pacific Link will follow a similar corridor, the company already knows what kind of terrain to expect, what sort of challenges to expect, so hopefully there won’t be too many surprises.”

stories.title: The cost of Ontario’s nuclear plan spirals. When will the province get serious?
stories.summary: Ontario does have options for its electricity system other than a massive and enormously risky nuclear construction program – it just refuses to consider them
stories.author: Mark Winfield
stories.content:
Mark Winfield is a professor in the faculty of Environmental and Urban Change at York University. He is co-chair of the Sustainable Energy Initiative, and co-editor of Sustainable Energy Transitions in Canada (UBC Press 2023).

There are growing concerns over the costs of Ontario’s expensive and questionable nuclear strategy. With only one of the new-build projects under way – the small (300MW) reactor at Darlington – the province is already spending between $7-billion and $8-billion a year subsidizing the electricity rates that help pay for them. In effect, the province is hiding the actual costs of its plans from consumers.

This cost amounts to nearly half of the provincial deficit, and exceeds annual capital expenditures in areas such as education and health care by wide margins. The current arrangements likely represent the fiscal limits of this strategy. Last month the government began to modify its subsidy arrangements to reduce costs to the provincial treasury, particularly by reducing support to high electricity consumers.

In Depth: Ontario spent nearly $13-billion and 20 years refurbishing the Darlington nuclear station. Why has it struggled?

Into this mix has come further bad news. Ontario Power Generation is now reporting that the Darlington New Nuclear Reactor, ON which construction has barely begun, is already behind schedule and now projected to come in at more than its original $7.7-billion budget.

Although consistent with the track record of previous nuclear projects, this cannot bode well for the likely costs of the much larger Wesleyville and Bruce C projects. And, as a first-of-its-kind small reactor, whose construction was authorized by the Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission on the basis of an incomplete design , there remains the risk that even when completed, the new Darlington reactor May not work as planned, or at all. That is what happened with the last new-build reactor project in Canada, the Maple isotope reactors , in 2008.

Moreover, the refurbishment of the existing Darlington facility, which was announced in February 2026 as being completed “on time and on budget” has been followed by a series of shutdowns and requirements for additional work. The implications for the refurbishment of the much older Pickering B station – whose estimated costs at more than $26-billion would already be double those of the Darlington refurbishment – cannot give any comfort to Ontario electricity ratepayers or taxpayers.

In the meantime, the province’s reliance on fossil fuel-fired generation has been accelerating. Fossil gas-fired generation – and by implication the associated emissions of greenhouse gases and smog precursors – has quintupled, to at least 20 per cent of supply, since 2017, and is expected to continue to increase through the 2030s. The province has also announced that it has contracted fossil fuel-fired electricity (likely made using oil) from the United States over the winter of 2026-27. The growth in emissions from the Ontario electricity system has been so significant that it’s emerging as a key factor in driving the overall increase now being observed in Canada’s national emissions trajectory . That overall growth is being principally attributed to the electricity sector.

Beyond the dramatic growth in emissions, the costs associated with the province’s nuclear ambitions seem likely to undermine competitiveness, affordability and electrification itself, as electricity prices are driven upward. Worse, Ontario’s model is having national effects, as the same nuclear- and gas-centric focus seems to underlie much of the federal government’s Powering Canada Strong electricity strategy.

Ontario does have options for its electricity system other than a massive and enormously risky nuclear construction program – it just refuses to consider them. Ontario has been the subject of more efforts to develop and model alternative pathways for its electricity system, and the broader decarbonization of its energy system, than any other province in Canada.

Those options emphasize energy efficiency and productivity, renewable energy, energy storage and microgrids, options offering the potential to avoid the need for new-build nuclear projects and the high-risk, high-cost Pickering B and additional fossil-fired generation. But there is no public and independent regulatory process to assess whether the directions set by the provincial government represent the best options for the province in economic, environmental and energy security terms relative to the alternative pathways that have been identified.

That situation needs to change rapidly. The province needs to engage in a serious, objective assessment of its options for meeting future energy needs in the context of high levels of uncertainty. It needs to adopt a strategy to control energy costs, decarbonize the province’s electricity system, ensure energy security, and advance economic and environmental sustainability before it’s too late.
paragraphs: Mark Winfield is a professor in the faculty of Environmental and Urban Change at York University. He is co-chair of the Sustainable Energy Initiative, and co-editor of Sustainable Energy Transitions in Canada (UBC Press 2023).

There are growing concerns over the costs of Ontario’s expensive and questionable nuclear strategy. With only one of the new-build projects under way – the small (300MW) reactor at Darlington – the province is already spending between $7-billion and $8-billion a year subsidizing the electricity rates that help pay for them. In effect, the province is hiding the actual costs of its plans from consumers.

This cost amounts to nearly half of the provincial deficit, and exceeds annual capital expenditures in areas such as education and health care by wide margins. The current arrangements likely represent the fiscal limits of this strategy. Last month the government began to modify its subsidy arrangements to reduce costs to the provincial treasury, particularly by reducing support to high electricity consumers.
In Depth: Ontario spent nearly $13-billion and 20 years refurbishing the Darlington nuclear station. Why has it struggled?

Into this mix has come further bad news. Ontario Power Generation is now reporting that the Darlington New Nuclear Reactor, ON which construction has barely begun, is already behind schedule and now projected to come in at more than its original $7.7-billion budget.

Although consistent with the track record of previous nuclear projects, this cannot bode well for the likely costs of the much larger Wesleyville and Bruce C projects. And, as a first-of-its-kind small reactor, whose construction was authorized by the Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission on the basis of an incomplete design , there remains the risk that even when completed, the new Darlington reactor May not work as planned, or at all. That is what happened with the last new-build reactor project in Canada, the Maple isotope reactors , in 2008.

Moreover, the refurbishment of the existing Darlington facility, which was announced in February 2026 as being completed “on time and on budget” has been followed by a series of shutdowns and requirements for additional work. The implications for the refurbishment of the much older Pickering B station – whose estimated costs at more than $26-billion would already be double those of the Darlington refurbishment – cannot give any comfort to Ontario electricity ratepayers or taxpayers.

In the meantime, the province’s reliance on fossil fuel-fired generation has been accelerating. Fossil gas-fired generation – and by implication the associated emissions of greenhouse gases and smog precursors – has quintupled, to at least 20 per cent of supply, since 2017, and is expected to continue to increase through the 2030s. The province has also announced that it has contracted fossil fuel-fired electricity (likely made using oil) from the United States over the winter of 2026-27. The growth in emissions from the Ontario electricity system has been so significant that it’s emerging as a key factor in driving the overall increase now being observed in Canada’s national emissions trajectory . That overall growth is being principally attributed to the electricity sector.

Beyond the dramatic growth in emissions, the costs associated with the province’s nuclear ambitions seem likely to undermine competitiveness, affordability and electrification itself, as electricity prices are driven upward. Worse, Ontario’s model is having national effects, as the same nuclear- and gas-centric focus seems to underlie much of the federal government’s Powering Canada Strong electricity strategy.

Ontario does have options for its electricity system other than a massive and enormously risky nuclear construction program – it just refuses to consider them. Ontario has been the subject of more efforts to develop and model alternative pathways for its electricity system, and the broader decarbonization of its energy system, than any other province in Canada.

Those options emphasize energy efficiency and productivity, renewable energy, energy storage and microgrids, options offering the potential to avoid the need for new-build nuclear projects and the high-risk, high-cost Pickering B and additional fossil-fired generation. But there is no public and independent regulatory process to assess whether the directions set by the provincial government represent the best options for the province in economic, environmental and energy security terms relative to the alternative pathways that have been identified.

That situation needs to change rapidly. The province needs to engage in a serious, objective assessment of its options for meeting future energy needs in the context of high levels of uncertainty. It needs to adopt a strategy to control energy costs, decarbonize the province’s electricity system, ensure energy security, and advance economic and environmental sustainability before it’s too late.

stories.title: Ontario rec centre includes Canada’s first known glass floor for sport events
stories.summary: The court at the Kitchener facility can be configured based on the sport being played
stories.author: David McPherson
stories.content:
A new community centre in Kitchener, Ont., boasts a couple of firsts – it is Canada’s first known facility with a glass floor that can accommodate different types of sports games and is the City of Kitchener’s first net-zero building.

The 227,000-square-foot Cowan Recreation Centre , located at 1664 Huron Rd. within RBJ Schlegel Park, opened on Nov. 14 and offers free and low-cost programs such as children’s swimming lessons, fitness classes, drop-in basketball, pickleball and soccer.

“We estimate the Cowan Recreation Centre will serve 500,000 users annually,” Kitchener Mayor Berry Vrbanovic says. “It was designed to meet the needs of multiple generations, multiple interests and skill sets, and to make sure all members of our community – regardless of age or ability – have a place where they feel they belong.”

Community stakeholders discussed the prospect of a new recreation facility for decades before construction began in June 2024. Construction company Multiplex managed the project, working with the City of Kitchener and lead architect Unity Design Studio .

The Cowan Recreation Centre is part of a renewed interest in community facilities across Canada. In August, a once-in-a-generation sports complex opened in Whitby, Ont. And earlier this month, Toronto and Whitechurch-Souffville, Ont., announced new recreation facilities, while a sports multiplex, dubbed the Arbec Wellness Centre , is set to open in New Brunswick in 2027.

The centre was built with the diversity of Kitchener’s population in mind and with the goal of fostering an inclusive space that supports community and connection. This cohesion is felt the moment visitors enter the facility, with swimmers doing laps at the left-side aquatic centre, a local volleyball team practising on a right-side court and a drop-in basketball game taking place on another court to the right.

While the $174-million recreation centre received part of its funding from the federal and provincial governments, it also relied on private donors and naming-rights sponsors. The name of the new centre recognizes a $2.5-million donation from the Cowan Foundation, which was established in 1995 to honour Frank Cowan, the founder of Cambridge-based Cowan Insurance Group.

When designing the facility, the City of Kitchener gathered input from more than 30 local sports organizations to make sure it met both the current and future needs of the community.

“It’s a generational investment for sport, recreation and community infrastructure that will impact the lives of residents for decades,” Mr. Vrbanovic says.

For Kitchener parents, securing swimming lessons for their children can be as challenging as buying highly coveted concert tickets. To help reduce the city’s waiting lists for swimming lessons, the Cowan Recreation Centre introduces two new public pools: a 25-metre eight-lane pool for competitive and recreational swimming, as well as a leisure pool for aquatic fitness classes and swimming lessons.

These are Waterloo Region’s first public pools that have been built with stainless steel, which requires less maintenance than traditional concrete.

Less upkeep means less water is used over the pools’ lifespans, with annual drainings no longer required to retile their bases and fix the grout.

The centre’s showpiece is a glass floor in the 30,000-square-foot quad gymnasium, which is believed to be a first of its kind in Canada. Powered by LED lighting underneath the glass panels, the technology displays digital sports lines directly onto the playing ground surface.

Designed and installed by ASB GlassFloor , the technology allows the facility to host multiple sports games with minimal effort. Rather than relying on permanent painted lines or temporary taped boundaries, the centre can tailor and transform the lines by sport with the touch of a button.

The centre also prioritizes accessibility and inclusion in its design through the installation of accessible viewing areas, ramps leading to the pools, gender-neutral changerooms and multifaith rooms.

The glass floor in the gymnasium is also more durable than traditional hardwood floors, making it more inclusive for wheelchair basketball, volleyball and pickleball.

In addition to traditional sports, the Cowan Recreation Centre provides visitors with spaces to play cricket and futsal, a fast-paced indoor alternative to traditional soccer. This aligns with cricket’s popularity in Waterloo, with a 2025 survey finding that 70 per cent of respondents played the sport multiple times a week. To meet demand, the Cowan centre includes two dedicated practice nets for cricket enthusiasts to train year-round.

Additionally, the new centre includes an indoor-turf fieldhouse that can be divided into four stand-alone fields, with a 366-metre walking track overlooking it above.

To reduce the Cowan Recreation Centre’s embodied carbon, the total amount of greenhouse gases emitted throughout the building’s entire life cycle, the architect used prefabricated cross-laminated timber (CLT) panels on the walls of the aquatic centre, gym and fieldhouse.

Also located 350 feet underneath the centre’s street-level parking lot, 120 geothermal wells and 13 kilometres of piping tap into the earth’s natural temperatures to heat and cool the facility.

The building’s roof, which includes a patio for staff and patrons, is lined with 1,709 solar panels that provide about one megawatt of renewable energy to help offset nearly half of the facility’s annual energy consumption and reduce its yearly emissions by approximately 43 tonnes.

In addition to being a community landmark, the Cowan Recreation Centre was built to attract visitors from outside Waterloo Region and promote tourism revenue.

“The facility will no doubt host many outside tournaments and sporting events that will bring athletes, coaches and their families to our community, potentially bringing millions into the local economy from a sports tourism perspective – money that’ll get spent at area hotels, restaurants and other businesses,” Mr. Vrbanovic says.

stories.title: Transparency goes off the rails at Ontario’s transit agency
stories.summary: Metrolinx is wrong to aim to save money by cutting back on public board meetings
stories.author: The Editorial Board
stories.content:
Metrolinx wants you to know it’s all about fiscal prudence. The regional transit agency for Toronto and much of Southern Ontario is becoming less transparent by axing half of its board’s public meetings, granted, but doing so will result in savings.

So how much will be saved? Not much. While $50,000 is a substantial sum for most Canadians – it’s enough to buy a car – for Metrolinx it’s a piddling amount.

Consider that the agency is presiding over the construction of a massively expensive transit project. The Ontario Line is currently expected to cost $34-billion, though that price-tag will rise again with one more big contract to come.

Or consider that the agency has 127 vice-presidents , and about 4,700 staff earning more than $100,000. The number of Metrolinx workers on the Sunshine List has more than tripled since 2021.

While it’s always good for public agencies to watch their spending, transparency is not the place to find savings.

On the contrary, transparency is an important way to shine a light on problems. Scrutiny can force change. Accountability engenders public confidence.

Which is why it was self-defeating for the agency to cut the annual number of public board meetings from four to two. These board meetings typically began behind closed doors – and the agency is legitimately criticized for handling important decisions during that part of the session – but then moved into open view.

Members of the public, including the media, can keep an eye on the public sessions. And journalists have had the chance afterward to ask questions of senior executives. Restricting access to these meetings limits accountability. The agency needs more of that, rather than less.

Public faith in Metrolinx is, rightly, limited. The agency presided over the debacle of the Eglinton Crosstown, a project that took years longer and billions of dollars more than predicted. And then it said it would do better with the Ontario Line which is – wait for it – going up in cost and expected to take longer than promised. The project does not currently have a target for opening, which is one way to avoid missing a deadline.

Metrolinx is a public agency that builds and runs public transit, but doesn’t really answer to the public at all. It has, as a former chair was fond of saying, one shareholder – at the legislature. Ontario Premier Doug Ford is the ultimate boss, which has led to reflexive caution at the agency about saying anything that could cause political embarrassment.

While this instinct for self-preservation May seem pragmatic, doing so corrodes public confidence. And Metrolinx has not done a good job of informing the public.

In one surreal moment, Metrolinx’s then-chief executive Phil Verster called the media together in 2023 to offer an update on the Eglinton Crosstown, then limping toward completion. That day, Mr. Verster said that he had a pretty good idea of when the Crosstown would open, but that he wasn’t going to reveal it. Instead, he told bemused reporters that he would hold another news conference every two months until he could announce the date. That pledge was soon abandoned.

By the time the Crosstown opened, Mr. Verster had left the agency. But his successor, Michael Lindsay, is no more forthcoming. A reporter from this newspaper once spent months trying to get an interview with Mr. Lindsay, to no avail.

Mr. Lindsay is presumably a busy man. His agency runs regional transit and also builds transit, including the 15.6-kilometre Ontario Line.

The Ontario Line cost has surged such that it is among the most expensive transit projects – per kilometre – in the world. It is to be hoped that Mr. Lindsay is working tirelessly to finish that project as quickly and cheaply as possible.

However, he should find time to talk to the media about the agency’s work. And Metrolinx should be more candid about what it does too.

When it comes to major infrastructure, projects that finish quickly and on budget can be used to make the case for further investment. But when the work drags on and the bills mount, those failures will be used to argue against building more transit. It would be devastating to Toronto’s future if the latter view takes root.

Owning up to problems is a way to keep the public onside. By hiding behind closed doors, Metrolinx can’t make the case that it is still on track.

stories.title: Storm surge, king tides prompt flood warnings for coastal B.C.
stories.summary: Environment Canada says the king tides will lift water levels an extra 20 to 50 centimetres higher than the highest astronomical tides
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The risk of flooding is elevated across British Columbian’s coast as drenching rain and blustery winds coincide with king tides, setting off widespread warnings.

Environment Canada said water levels in coastal regions May rise to 50 centimetres above the highest astronomical tides from now through Thursday, accompanied by a storm surge and large waves.

King tides are the highest tides of the year, pulled by the gravitational force of the moon, which was full on Tuesday.

The District of Squamish declared a local state of emergency on Tuesday due to incoming high tides and potential flood risk.

The district says in a statement that the declaration will ensure it has legal authority from the province to complete the flood mitigation work through B.C.’s Emergency and Disaster Management Act.

“The Sea to Sky region is expected to receive a significant amount of rainfall and high tides over the next few days. Highest tides are forecast for Thursday morning,” it said in the statement.

King tides and an approaching weather system are combining to create coastal flooding risks across British Columbia. The Canadian Press

Coastal flood warnings or statements cover Metro Vancouver, Vancouver Island, Haida Gwaii, the central and Sunshine coasts and much of the northern coast.

Warnings also remain up for most of Vancouver Island for up to 225 millimetres of rain expected through to Thursday, while wind warnings cover Greater Victoria, calling for gusts reaching 90 kilometres an hour.

The B.C. River Forecast Centre has issued high streamflow advisories for waterways on most of Vancouver Island, the South Coast, Howe Sound, Sunshine Coast and Sea to Sky region, saying rivers are expected to rise rapidly following the rainfall.

The centre says previous periods of heavy rain and already saturated soils will bring sharp increases in river levels, while the king tides will exacerbate water levels at the mouths of rivers.

“Peak levels are forecasted to potentially reach up to two-year to five-year return period flows, however some weather model scenarios indicate that higher flows could be possible,” said the statement from the forecast centre.

The B.C. Ministry of Transportation says in a news release that motorists along the South Coast should use caution due to “possible fallen debris and flooding” potentially leading to sudden road closures.

Drivers on the Malahat Highway and other routes on Western Vancouver Island are also being urged to be vigilant, and the ministry said it is increasing highway patrols and is ready to respond if needed.

Meteorologist Chloe Katsademas said residents should also “keep an eye out” for weather updates, as the arriving low-pressure system May trigger upgrades in warnings for coastal flooding, wind and rain.

“When there’s (a) low pressure (system), things move toward it,” said Katsademas.

She said the system creates high winds and storm surges.

“It’s coinciding with this run of king tides, which elevates water levels at high tide in general,” she said.

“And by having those two things together, the water levels at high tide could be 20 to 50 centimetres higher than the highest astronomical tide.”

The arrival of the supersized tide along B.C.’s Coast has created a spectacular show of pounding surf and tall, foaming waves, drawing photographers, citizen scientists and the curious to the shorelines.

Photographer and filmmaker Geoff Heith from Port Hardy, ON northeastern Vancouver Island, said he’s been going out at least once a day to capture photos on the beach, and he is fond of storms when they roll up on the northern Island.

Heith said the king tide, and rain and wind warnings have created their own “perfect storm.”

He said when he was out at Thomas Point on northern Vancouver Island on Monday, the high tides reached more than five meters tall, which created “massive” waves.

“The cliff I was standing on … is probably 40, 50 feet up over the water, and those waves splashing was easily coming over top of that.”

Another video taken by Heith shows large logs moved easily by waves.

“Usually we’ll get king tides, but not with a very big storm. So, this is the first time I’ve seen a king tide with a big storm.”

Tim Carver from Colwood, B.C., visited Esquimalt Lagoon on Tuesday, to watch the stormy waters.

Carver said the ocean was “angry” as it tossed large logs around in the surf.

“The beach is being rearranged. It’ll be a brand new beach when the storm is over,” said Carver.

“We have a very old wooden bridge down there, and the water is coming up so high, it’s brought all the logs up to the bridge and it’s pushing on the bridge,” said Carver.

The city of Colwood said its team was monitoring “very high tides” at the Lagoon.

The Tla-o-qui-aht First Nation in Tofino has issued an evacuation alert for some shoreline properties, saying residents need to be ready to leave.

The nation said in a public notice that tides could reach more than four metres on Wednesday, and there has also been concern about the weather phenomenon combining with the effects of a “Kelvin wave,” a slow-moving underwater wave connected to this year’s El Nino weather pattern.

“While conditions May ultimately remain manageable and no significant impacts are currently anticipated, we are encouraging residents to take reasonable precautions out of an abundance of caution,” the notice says.

Katsademas said the B.C. coast is not expected to see a break from wet and windy weather until the weekend, before another low-pressure system potentially moves through next week.

stories.title: Elderly couple fears financial burden if city council imposes heritage designation on home
stories.summary: A looming provincial deadline has put an elderly couple’s home at the centre of a debate about the financial consequences of heritage designations.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
A looming provincial deadline has put an elderly couple’s home at the centre of a debate about the financial consequences of heritage designations.

For the past 12 years, Alex and Anna Porzecanski have lovingly maintained their small one-storey mid-century modern home in south London.

“Our attitude has been to keep it original, to keep it as beautiful as it was when it was done,” said Alex.

But the retirees oppose a recommendation from city staff to assign a heritage designation to their property.

“This will impose an enormous financial cost to us at this time in our life,” Alex told CTV News. “We are retired. We are over 80 years old, and our finances are limited.”

The provincial government set a Jan. 1, 2027, deadline for municipalities to remove buildings that have not been designated from their heritage registries.

In London, that meant narrowing a list of more than 2,000 potential heritage buildings to 13 prioritized for designation — including the Porzecanskis’ home that was inspired by the work of famed architect Frank Lloyd Wright.

“The heritage designation will mean that changes to the outside will have to be done according to the original design of the house. Every material has to be copied exactly,” Alex explained.

The couple fears higher insurance and maintenance costs.

They also worry a designation could shrink the pool of potential buyers if they eventually need to sell their home to finance a move to a supportive care facility.

“The financial cost May actually make us sell it at an earlier time than we should, and it will really put us in hard difficulties to live because we were counting on selling this house in the future to somebody who cares and who will love it as much as we do,” Alex said.

“It’s just the thought that your property is not your property anymore because you don’t have a say in what the municipality is going to do. Whether you want to, or not, your house can be made heritage,” Anna added.

To qualify for heritage designation, a building must meet at least two of nine provincial criteria in a Cultural Heritage Evaluation.

Without the couple’s knowledge, city staff prepared a 30-page report that concluded it met five of the nine criteria.

Other property owners have successfully opposed the recent spree of designations.

In July, council rejected a staff recommendation to pursue designation of the six-storey former Hunt Bros. Flour Mill at 471 Nightingale Ave. in east London amid questions about the cultural evaluation and the owner’s concerns about significantly higher maintenance and insurance costs.

Subsequently, the same community advisory committee that generated the list of 13 priorities properties for designation acknowledged the sudden financial impact on owners.

Council approved a motion by Deputy Mayor Shawn Lewis that directed staff to report back with options including a property tax credit for Part Four heritage properties (those not in heritage districts) that meet certain maintenance expectations.

However, no decision has yet been made, and offsetting the costs would have to be considered during future budget deliberations.

In the meantime, the Porzecanskis are preparing to oppose the designation of their home at the Planning and Environment Committee (PEC) on Dec. 1.

“It has been very stressful. We’ve had other health issues that have occupied most of our time, and it’s meant we couldn’t dedicate a lot of energies into fighting this,” explained Anna.

Council will make a final decision on Dec. 15, just two weeks before the provincial deadline.

“I will have to fight my own battle. I don’t know how it’ll end, but I have good arguments to put forward, and I’ll try my best to make my point,” said Alex.

stories.title: Inside Operation Niagara, a week-long blitz to halt cryptocurrency scams
stories.summary: Canadian and U.S. law enforcement agencies work with private sector to uncover nearly 1,500 compromised wallets
stories.author: Alexandra Posadzki
stories.content:
Inside a large room on the 22nd floor of an office tower in downtown Toronto, several dozen people huddled around tables last week in a co-ordinated effort to stop criminals from siphoning cryptocurrency out of compromised wallets in real time.

Among them were staff from the Ontario Securities Commission, the United States Secret Service, the Ontario Provincial Police and several other law-enforcement agencies and securities watchdogs.

Representatives from blockchain tracing platforms Chainalysis and TRM Labs and several cryptocurrency exchanges, including Crypto.com and Coinbase, were present as well.

On one side of the room’s retractable partition, investigators hunted for wallets that had been compromised through what’s known as approval phishing, a scam in which a victim is tricked into granting a fraudster permission to transfer funds out of their digital wallet.

On the other side sat police officers and OSC personnel tasked with contacting the victims, taking their statements and helping them regain control over their wallets by revoking the permissions they’d inadvertently granted to fraudsters.

Over the course of the week, some 50 participants passed through the blue double doors bearing a sign for Operation Niagara, as the blitz was dubbed. They hunkered down with their laptops in small groups. Coffee and pastries were arranged on a long white table along one side of the room, fuel for the fight against fraud. Another team gathered in Washington, and others joined virtually.

Fraud has surged in recent years, with victims reporting $535-million in losses to the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre in the first nine months of the year. The centre estimates that only 5 per cent to 10 per cent of fraud is reported.

Cryptocurrency is often targeted by fraudsters because of how difficult it is to recover stolen funds. While banks May be able to reverse electronic funds transfers or freeze accounts, recovering cryptocurrency requires intercepting the money when the fraudster tries to swap it for another form of currency at an exchange.

“Crypto fraud moves incredibly quickly, and no single organization has all the information, expertise or tools needed to tackle it effectively,” said Cosmin Cazan, manager of intelligence, analytics and research in the Osc’s enforcement division.

Sprints like the one hosted at the offices of the Ontario Securities Commission for five days last week aim to address that problem by tackling fraud in real time. In some cases, victims are able to regain control over their digital wallets, preventing the loss of funds. Where tokens have already been transferred out, police officers work with exchanges to try to freeze them.

“This type of online harm crosses international boundaries ... so it’s really important that we work with our partners,” Bonnie Lysyk, executive vice-president of enforcement at the Ontario Securities Commission, said in an interview.

It’s the fourth such sprint that the Canadian authorities have participated in. Earlier this year, during another initiative known as Operation Atlantic, Canadian, American and British law-enforcement agencies froze more than US$12-million of fraudulently obtained funds.

This time around, investigators uncovered nearly 1,500 compromised wallets. Approximately $5.7-million in wallet holdings were protected from theft, although the OSC said that number May increase over the coming weeks as the work is finalized.

“We’ve seen values in excess of a million dollars potentially vulnerable to fraud in this sprint,” OPP Inspector Dan Dusto said in an interview.

“Most commonly it’s less than that, but there are some significant losses that have already happened, and some significant losses prevented through what we’re doing,” he added.

The process starts with identifying leads, using a tool built by the Osc’s senior crypto and open-source intelligence specialist, Chris Sutton. The tool identifies patterns that can indicate a particular crypto wallet has been compromised.

Someone who has sworn an affidavit then writes production orders, which are taken to the courthouse at 10 Armoury St., less than a kilometre away, for a judge to review. If approved, the orders are then delivered virtually to the relevant exchanges, asking them to provide information about the individuals sending funds to or from compromised wallets. In some cases, the orders aim to identify victims; in others, the perpetrators of the thefts.

A whiteboard tracks the dollar amount of fraud prevented each day, to keep the participants motivated.

“There’s an emotional toll that it takes, speaking with victims all day, every day, particularly when those victims are challenging you and arguing with you,” said Insp. Dusto, the OPP’s case manager for the operation.

Often, victims don’t believe that the callers are who they say they are – unsurprising given that police officers, including at the OPP, have been impersonated in the past, said Detective Sergeant Lynn Danis, with the OPP’s Anti-Rackets Branch. There have even been instances in which criminals have leveraged the names of operations such as Niagara in an attempt to defraud victims.

The officers calling victims take steps to verify their identities, for instance pointing victims to the operation’s landing page and encouraging them to call the contact centre using the number listed on the official website.

For the officers, the work doesn’t end with the sprint. Information gathered during the course of the week can lead to future investigations and, potentially, charges against the fraudsters, Insp. Dusto said.

The sprints are a lot of work, he said, but they provide an opportunity to do something that he described as unusual in law-enforcement work.

“So often in our careers, we’re called after the fact and we investigate and perhaps lay a charge, perhaps hold an offender accountable,” he said.

“It’s rare that we can get ahead of crime, and these sprints provide us an opportunity to do that.”

stories.title: Parole board launches online portal for pot pardons — only 944 granted so far
stories.summary: The Parole Board of Canada has granted 944 pardons for pot possession — less than one tenth of the number the government was anticipating when it legalized recreational cannabis eight years ago.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — The Parole Board of Canada has granted 944 pardons for pot possession — less than one tenth of the number the government was anticipating when it legalized recreational cannabis eight years ago.

The Liberals lifted a century-long prohibition on the recreational use and sale of cannabis in October 2018. Canada became just the second country in the world to legalize the drug, after Uruguay.

The following year, the government brought in legislation to offer a free and streamlined process to apply for record suspensions for simple possession of cannabis. Record suspensions effectively clear criminal records that can be a barrier to travel, employment, housing, education and volunteer work.

Ottawa estimated at the time about 10,000 Canadians would be eligible for cannabis-related record suspensions.

Parole Board of Canada spokesperson Andrea Fournier said in an email the board has received 1,477 applications for cannabis record suspensions since 2019. Of those, 526 were returned because the applicant was ineligible or the application was incomplete.

The Parole Board of Canada has launched a new portal for pardon applications in a bid to streamline and simplify the application process.

Lawyer and University of Ottawa drug policy expert Eugene Oscapella said the application process May be a deterrent for some people.

“You’ve got to get records of your conviction, you’ve got to contact courts and police departments,” he said. “It’s not that straightforward a process and some people May just sort of balk at it.

“If there is a new streamlined process, that May in itself be an acknowledgment by the government that perhaps the current process is a bit awkward.”

Oscapella also said the number of pardons granted since legalization May be lower than expected because the stigma surrounding cannabis use has faded.

“Maybe people just aren’t as worried about it anymore,” he said. “Attitudes towards cannabis have become quite normalized and maybe people don’t see there’s any real advantage.

“There was a time when if you had a cannabis conviction, it had a significant impact on your life. I don’t think that’s the case anymore, for simple possession certainly.”

Oscapella said that while most employers likely wouldn’t have a problem with a candidate who has a record for pot possession, that’s not the case for jobs that require security clearances or travel abroad.

The Parole Board of Canada says in a news release last week its new portal allows applicants and their designated representatives to submit applications for record suspensions online.

The portal allows applicants to save an incomplete application and return to it later, and permits them to track their applications.

“The secure platform reduces reliance on paper-based processes and mail delivery while giving applicants greater flexibility and visibility throughout the process,” says the news release.

“By simplifying the application process, the PBC Service Portal helps people benefit from programs that can support their successful reintegration, while maintaining the integrity of the record suspension (pardon) and cannabis record suspension processes and supporting public safety.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 24, 2026.

Catherine Morrison, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Montreal touts aerospace, AI in bid to host Nato defence bank
stories.summary: The Defence, Security and Resilience Bank is expected to launch next year with about 50 employees, growing to as many as 700 within a decade.
stories.author: Alessia Simona Maratta, Amanda Jelowicki
stories.content:
Montreal is officially in the running to become the Canadian home of a new international defence bank , with city and provincial leaders pitching its aerospace, finance and artificial intelligence sectors as key advantages.

Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada and Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon joined business leaders at Montreal city hall to launch the city’s bid to host the Defence, Security and Resilience Bank.

It was announced in April that Canada would host the multinational bank, which would provide “long-term, low-cost financing” for defence projects by Nato members and allies, according to a statement from the federal government.

Nine countries, including Canada, signed an agreement this year to launch the financial institution.

Martinez Ferrada thanked the premier for backing Montreal’s bid and argued the city has what it takes to support the bank.

“I think we have the population, the ecosystem you see in the room here today, that will support the success of a bank that can come to Montreal,” she said.

St-Pierre Plamondon also expressed confidence in the city’s chances.

“When you look at the criteria applicable to that project, we have all the arguments to win this,” he said.

Melissa Denis, interim CEO of Montreal International, pointed to the city’s bilingual workforce and its strength in several industries.

“Montreal is the best place because we bring together finance, aerospace, defence, AI, also international diplomacy,” Denis said. “We have also a qualified bilingual talent pool.

“It makes Montreal the better place for the bank.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "It makes Montreal the better place for the bank."

Michael Nault, general manager of Bell Textron Canada, said Montreal’s established aerospace sector could also work in its favour.

“The bank is there to serve the industry — so you can have the bank where a lot of banks are, or you can have a bank where the industry is that will benefit from the bank,” Nault said.

“The aerospace industry is here in Montreal, and so it will definitely benefit from this.”

The bank is expected to launch next year with about 50 employees, growing to as many as 700 within a decade.

Toronto, Ottawa, Vancouver and Montreal are competing to host the bank, with the contract yet to be awarded.

Applications are due Dec. 3, after which the federal government will make the final decision.

stories.title: German submarine CEO says Canadian business will benefit from tighter European ties
stories.summary: Halifax - The CEO of a German company in talks to build Canada’s new submarine fleet says tighter ties with Europe offer Canadian defence firms a great opportunity to expand their businesses.
stories.author: Devin Stevens The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Halifax - The CEO of a German company in talks to build Canada’s new submarine fleet says tighter ties with Europe offer Canadian defence firms a great opportunity to expand their businesses.

Oliver Burkhard, CEO of German defence manufacturer Tkms, said the company has agreements with more than 40 Canadian companies who could supply parts and material for the estimated $24-billion submarine project Prime Minister Mark Carney has described as the largest procurement project in Canadian history.

The cost of operating, maintaining and repairing the replacements for Canada’s aging Victoria-class submarines is expected to eclipse $100 billion over two decades.

Oliver Burkhard, CEO of German submarine maker ThyssenKrupp Marine Systems (Tkms), visits Ottawa on Monday, March 2, 2026.

The Canadian suppliers involved, including Seaspan, CAE, Magellan Aerospace and Irving Shipbuilding, could also supply materials to build submarines for other countries as North Atlantic Treaty Organization members bolster their defence spending, said the CEO.

“The demand for our submarines at the moment, conventional submarines that size (which) Canada is also seeking, is very high,” Burkhard said in a recent interview at the Halifax International Security Forum.

“So I expect that a new supply chain for us will also be generated, which is a benefit for us, but it’s also a benefit for Canada.”

Carney announced in July that Canada had selected Tkms as the preferred partner to deliver up to 12 submarines, ahead of South Korea’s Hanwha.

The prime minister spoke of the Tkms 212CD submarine’s stealth and Arctic capabilities, and emphasized that it can operate alongside Nato allies Norway and Germany, which are buying the same vessels.

“The Type 212CD sub will operate seamlessly alongside our Nato partners, sharing training, maintenance, parts, technology and even crews throughout their service lives,” Carney said at the time.

Burkhard said having three allied nations involved in building and operating the same vessels is a great sales pitch when he speaks to other potential submarine customers. He said Canadian firms will be in the supply chain if and when they sign up. A larger international partnership also increases efficiency and lowers costs for all involved, he said.

“Canada gets not only 12 submarines,” he said. “It also gets infrastructure, an ecosystem which is then available for the rest of the world to buy things here for other (submarine) units outside Canada.”

Now that the bidding is over, it’s time we turned to some unanswered questions about our forthcoming fleet.

Burkhard said both sides of the Atlantic recognize the increasing threats coming from Russia, and that relationships in the Western alliance, especially with a more aggressive U.S., have changed as well.

He said he agrees with Carney’s contention that so-called middle powers have to stick together.

Canada’s bonds with Europe are growing stronger, having signed a partnership in June 2025 to work together on security and defence. That included Canada’s participation in the continent’s 150-billion-euro defence procurement program, known as ReArm Europe.

In the months since Tkms was selected for the submarine project, Ottawa and Brussels have started exploring tighter connections, including a possible “associate membership” for Canada in the EU.

Defence Minister David McGuinty announced Saturday in Halifax that Canada is formally becoming the 25th member of Nato’s Innovation Fund with a $100-million contribution. The deal allows the 1.1-billion-euro venture capital fund to invest in Canadian startups in fields like artificial intelligence, quantum technologies, biotech, space and communications.

“For Canadian innovators, that means new investment, new partnerships and access to international markets,” McGuinty told reporters at the defence conference Saturday. “For Canadian workers, it means good jobs in a growing industry. And for our armed forces, it means access to cutting-edge technologies and capabilities faster.”

Canada is also planning to gather its partners to sign onto a new Defence, Security and Resilience Bank at the end of the month. The bank will have headquarters in both Canada and Luxembourg with Belgium, Greece, Turkey and Ukraine among the eight countries supporting the plan.

Burkhard said he doesn’t think Canada will ever officially join the European Union, but he’s in favour of tighter bonds.

“I expect even more to come because Canada has a lot to offer to Europe,” he said.

“It’s a different topology. It’s a different country. It has different resources which Europe has not.”

Meanwhile, Canada’s negotiations with Tkms continue with a goal of having all submarine contracts signed by the end of 2027.

CBC recently reported Canada May pursue breaking the submarine order into two batches with an initial order of eight vessels and four more at a later date. Delivery of the first boats is not expected until the mid-2030s.

Burkhard said Germany and Norway put a lot of effort into the submarine bid, and if Canada ends up with a smaller order, that will increase the price per unit and scale back the economic benefits as well.

If Canada buys the full order of 12 submarines, Tkms has committed to more than $80 billion in commercial benefits that Burkhard said will be spread to suppliers across the entire country.

“If it’s now less than 12, then maybe this will also have a reduction on that,” he said. “But if it’s at the end, the 12 they’re aiming for, then everything will be good, but maybe in two steps, let’s say.”

stories.title: Sean Fraser says mental illness was never meant to be criteria for Maid
stories.summary: 'It wasn't a response to an individual case; it was systemic in nature,' the justice minister said
stories.author: Sarah Ritchie
stories.content:
Ottawa — The federal justice minister says changes he’s proposed to the country’s medical assistance in dying laws are meant to return the controversial policy to the government’s original intent.

Thelegislation, which is being studied by a House of Commons committee, will ensure people cannot qualify for Maid on the basis of a mental illness. Some advocates worry, though, that broadening the exclusion of people with mental illness could have a chilling effect.

Justice Minister Sean Fraser said his department recommended the change after reviewing the law.

‘There was a potential for people to have access to the system that were not intended to have access to medical assistance in dying,” Fraser said in an interview.

“It wasn’t a response to an individual case; it was systemic in nature.”

At issue is whether a mental illness can be deemed to cause the kind of intolerable suffering or irreversible decline that would make a person eligible for an assisted death.

NP Posted keeps you updated on the news of the day and the perspectives that define the National Post, while drawing your focus to some of the unexpected stories we like to tell. Delivered straight to your inbox Monday to Friday, with a weekend edition on Saturdays.

Justice Minister and Attorney General of Canada Sean Fraser speaks at the Marine Renewables Canada Conference in Ottawa Nov. 18, 2026. Blair Gable / Postmedia

The Maid regime was expanded in 2021 to include people whose natural deaths were not “reasonably foreseeable.” People whose sole underlying condition was a mental illness were temporarily excluded from accessing Maid. That is now being made permanent in Fraser’s bill.

But that has not meant that people with a mental illness cannot get Maid.

Eligibility is determined based on several criteria, including that the person asking for Maid has a “grievous and irremediable medical condition.”

The law says this requires a diagnosis of a serious and incurable illness, disease or disability that is not a mental illness. The person must be in an advanced state of irreversible decline, and they must be suffering intolerably.

Jocelyn Downie, a professor emeritus in the faculties of law and medicine at Dalhousie University, wrote a paper arguing that a person who’s experiencing intolerable suffering or an irreversible decline as a result of a mental illness (for example, severe bipolar disorder), and who also has a diagnosis of a serious and incurable condition (for example, early stage Parkinson’s disease), should be deemed eligible for Maid based on both conditions taken together.

“Our intent from the beginning was not to include a person in those circumstances,” Fraser said.

Downie said the changes Fraser is proposing will mean people who are eligible today will not be allowed to access Maid once the bill becomes law. She also said it could put a chill on Maid assessments, with health-care providers worried about possible criminal charges.

“I think some (eligible people) won’t get access because clinicians will be scared that they’re getting it wrong,” she said.

Trudo Lemmens, a professor in the faculty of law and the school of public health at the University of Toronto, agrees with Fraser’s interpretation of the current law.

“The law was intended to deal with irremediable medical conditions, where there is no hope of recovery, where there is no expectation that the person will get better, and to relieve intolerable suffering in those specific circumstances,” he said.

That question of whether a person can get better is at the heart of why people with mental illness are being indefinitely excluded from Maid, Fraser said. The government heard through its own consultations and through a parliamentary committee last spring that there’s a “lack of a clear consensus from the medical community on the irremediable nature of mental illness,” he said.

Lemmens said on an individual basis it is impossible to predict whether a person with mental illness will recover.

Dr. Mona Gupta, a psychiatrist and clinical professor in the department of psychiatry and addictions at Université de Montréal, said throughout the debate there has been a broad failure to recognize that some mental disorders can be severe, chronic and refractory to treatment.

“There are individuals who continue to suffer, despite our best efforts to help them and their best efforts to feel better,” she said.

Gupta called the proposed change to the law “regressive” and said the government risks further stigmatizing mental illness. She worries how that will affect patients.

“Patients who are thinking about requesting Maid, or who are requesting Maid, will inevitably come to realize that the easiest way not to create difficulties for themselves in the Maid process is simply to not talk about their psychiatric history,” she said.

Sarah Ritchie joined National Post’s politics bureau after four years covering breaking news on Parliament Hill for The Canadian Press, where she worked as a reporter and editor. Before that, she was an anchor and investigative reporter at Global News in Halifax and covered the Nova Scotia legislature for CTV Atlantic.

Lemmens said on an individual basis it is impossible to predict whether a person with mental illness will recover.

Dr. Mona Gupta, a psychiatrist and clinical professor in the department of psychiatry and addictions at Université de Montréal, said throughout the debate there has been a broad failure to recognize that some mental disorders can be severe, chronic and refractory to treatment.
“There are individuals who continue to suffer, despite our best efforts to help them and their best efforts to feel better,” she said.
Gupta called the proposed change to the law “regressive” and said the government risks further stigmatizing mental illness. She worries how that will affect patients.

“Patients who are thinking about requesting Maid, or who are requesting Maid, will inevitably come to realize that the easiest way not to create difficulties for themselves in the Maid process is simply to not talk about their psychiatric history,” she said.

Sarah Ritchie joined National Post’s politics bureau after four years covering breaking news on Parliament Hill for The Canadian Press, where she worked as a reporter and editor. Before that, she was an anchor and investigative reporter at Global News in Halifax and covered the Nova Scotia legislature for CTV Atlantic.
