stories.title: Canadian mortgage delinquency rate reaches 13 year high, report shows
stories.summary: More recent homeowners or those who purchased condos and cars in the past four years are now in negative equity
stories.author: Joy SpearChief-Morris
stories.content:
The number of Canadians behind on mortgage payments by more than 90 days has increased over 30 per cent year-over-year, according to a new report by Equifax Canada.

The report, released Tuesday, showed the national mortgage delinquency rate reached 0.32 per cent, its highest since Equifax began tracking it in 2013, with homeowners in Ontario and British Columbia accounting for 91 per cent of the 12 month increase.

The report also showed that more Canadians who are recent homeowners, or who purchased condos and cars in the past four years, are now in negative equity, with more at risk of going underwater as interest rates continue to climb.

Total Canadian consumer debt reached $2.74-trillion in the third quarter of 2026, up 4.86 per cent year-over-year. Canadians aged 46 to 55 had the highest average of non-mortgage debt, such as debt accumulated on credit cards or other loans, at $36,151, a 2.16 per cent increase.

Rebecca Oakes, vice-president of advanced analytics at Equifax, said Ontario and British Columbia contributed the most to the increase in mortgage delinquency rates. Ontario’s rate was up 44 per cent in the last 12 months and B.C. was up 30 per cent, in comparison with a nearly 5-per-cent increase across the rest of Canada.

“It’s very concentrated. It’s not like everybody in Canada is seeing a big challenge with making payments on their credit cards and things right now,” she said.

Ms. Oakes said Ontario and B.C. homeowners took advantage of low interest rates post-pandemic when housing prices were higher, but are now seeing the fallout as interest rates have gone up. This trend is set to continue through 2027, she said.

According to Equifax’s report, of the 9.1 million mortgage holders in Canada, about 1.4 million have variable rate mortgages, and another 1.3 million carry a home equity line of credit (Heloc) over $50,000.

These homeowners are most exposed to interest rate hikes on monthly payments. Every quarter-point hike adds about $860-million a year in interest to variable rate mortgages and $419-million on HELOCs.

The Bank of Canada increased its benchmark interest rate by a quarter-point to 2.5 per cent last month, the first hike since 2023. The central bank is scheduled to make its next rate decision on Dec. 9.

Some non-homeowners are seeing relief. Those without mortgages did see a 3.4-per-cent improvement in delinquency rates, while homeowners still saw a 9.8-per-cent year-over-year increase on non-mortgaged debt.

“There’s just more people starting to miss payments in certain parts of the population. In other areas, they’re actually coping very well and actually improving a little bit,” Ms. Oakes said.

On top of delinquencies, Equifax’s report showed a growing number of Canadians are now experiencing negative equity, particularly new homebuyers and recent condo and car owners.

Ontario homebuyers accounted for an estimated 70 per cent of all mortgages in negative equity across Canada, and made up 5 per cent of all mortgages in the province. In comparison, only 1.85 per cent of homeowners in B.C. were underwater, as were 1.1 per cent in Quebec.

Condo owners were at the highest risk, with 7.2 per cent of condo mortgages likely in negative equity compared with 2.7 per cent of freehold house mortgages.

Condo owners who bought in 2022 – when inflation and housing prices were at their peak – had the highest rate of negative equity risk at 8.4 per cent.

Car owners were facing the same challenges, with Equifax’s report showing an estimated 40 per cent of auto loans in the last four years were in negative equity.

Ms. Oakes said this is because more buyers have locked themselves into longer-term loans to make monthly payments more affordable, with 54 per cent of car loans carrying terms 84 months or longer.

“They’re paying more interest over time,” she said.

“It just kind of highlights that it’s still not very affordable right now for consumers with the auto side.”

While not all home or car owners in negative equity are delinquent or are at risk of delinquency, Ms. Oakes said the problem is when these owners want to renew their loans or sell those assets, which are now worth less than the debt they owe.

“If you’re in negative equity, well, it’s almost impossible to switch lender, and if you do switch lender or you do manage to, then you May now be looking at insured versus an uninsured,” Ms. Oakes said.

“They might be managing their payments, but it starts to reduce their options of what they could do.”

Ms. Oakes said debtors need to be aware when looking to renew their loans and seek financial advice if their assets are at greater risk.

stories.title: Years after making promise, Ottawa finally moving to form Milgaard Law’s wrongful convictions commission
stories.summary: The ‘Miscarriage of Justice Review Commission’ is intended to review claims from people seeking exoneration for crimes they didn’t commit.
stories.author: Kevin Donovan
stories.content:
Three years after the federal government promised an independent commission to review miscarriage of justice claims, they have opened applications for commissioners.

“Wrongful convictions can have lasting consequences,” Justice Minister Sean Fraser said Monday.

“As we begin recruiting its first commissioners, I encourage qualified candidates to apply and help build a team,” Fraser said in a news release.

How candidates should apply is not mentioned in Fraser’s release, and as of Monday there was no portal on the government’s website inviting applications.

The Justice Department has refused to grant an interview with the Star to explain the delay in creating the new Miscarriage of Justice Review

This proposed independent body has long been lobbied for by groups representing people exonerated and awaiting review of their cases under the current in-house system at the Justice Department. The legislation behind the new body is the David and Joyce Milgaard Law , named for the late David Milgaard and his mother Joyce. David was wrongfully convicted of rape and murder and served 23 years in prison before being released and exonerated.

Since announcing it in 2023, the government has made no moves, other than to say repeatedly to the Star that they are seeking a commissioner to preside over what will be called the “Miscarriage of Justice Review Commission.” How they are doing that remains a mystery, as there has been no public appeal other than press releases.

The Star’s request to the Justice Department for explanation and more details on Friday was not answered.

Still, the main group lobbying for the commission, Innocence Canada, is pleased that there has been some movement, but cautions that there should be no dragging of feet. “To fulfil its mandate, the commission must be brought into operation without further delay, be adequately funded, maintain true institutional independence from government, and significantly reduce the lengthy wait times that innocent Canadians currently face while seeking justice,” the advocacy group said in a statement.

One man in prison who is hoping for a new day in court is Chris Sheriffe, a one-time soccer star whom the Star profiled in its Murder on Mount Olive series and podcast . Sheriffe was convicted in 2012 of first-degree murder for a crime he said he had nothing to do with. He told the jury at his trial that he was in the wrong place at the wrong time. Nineteen at the time, he said an acquaintance he was driving home with asked him to stop near Mount Olive Drive on a hot summer afternoon in 2009. The man, Awet Asfaha, returned to Sheriffe's car shortly after. Both Sheriffe and Asfaha were arrested later that day and convicted of first-degree murder in the killing of furniture maker Bishen Golaub, with no chance of parole for 25 years. Asfaha has recently admitted to the shooting, and at a "faint hope" hearing this year had one year knocked off his 25-year wait for parole.

Kevin Donovan sits down with Chris Sheriffe in prison at Collins Bay.

In Murder on Mount Olive, Chief Investigative Reporter Kevin Donovan investigates a crime the courts closed the book on in 2012.

You can also listen to the podcast series for more at: https://www.thestar.com/murderonmountolive

Sheriffe maintains his innocence. His lawyers, Samara Sector and Rebecca Amoah of the Addario Law Group, working pro bono, are preparing an appeal to the existing federal system, but are hopeful they will be able to make their case to an independent body. They plan to argue that “hearsay” gang evidence put forward by a junior police officer quoting confidential sources should never have been heard by the jury. There was no forensic or eyewitness evidence linking Sheriffe to the shooting of Golaub, who was a guest at a neighbourhood barbecue. Currently, the federal justice department, staffed by federal lawyers, reviews applications and determines if a case should be sent back for a new trial. Critics of this system say it is unfair that government lawyers make these decisions.

“Please do not allow the man who murdered our father to experience the freedom he so cruelly stole from him and from all of us.”

Fraser recognized this issue in his statement Monday, noting that “the Commission will operate at arm’s length from government and independently of police, prosecutors and the courts.”

Lawyer James Lockyer, who has devoted his career to advocating on this issue, estimates that between two and three per cent of people convicted are innocent. Lockyer, who worked on Milgaard’s case and is a founding director of Innocence Canada, told the Star that the criminal justice system is “a human system, so it’s fallible.”

Lawyer James Lockyer, seen here in a Jan. 22, 2025, file photo.

Sheriffe has told the Star he remains hopeful his case will be reviewed. He has been told over the years that if he had pleaded guilty years ago, he would have had a significantly lighter sentence — “The problem is, I can’t take accountability for something I didn’t do.”

During his 14 years in prison, Sheriffe has worked on construction projects behind bars, mentored troubled youth brought in for prison visits, and acted as a liaison between corrections staff and inmates. He has completed dozens of educational modules and public speaking sessions through Toastmasters.

content_blocks.text: One man in prison who is hoping for a new day in court is Chris Sheriffe, a one-time soccer star whom the Star profiled in its Murder on Mount Olive series and podcast . Sheriffe was convicted in 2012 of first-degree murder for a crime he said he had nothing to do with. He told the jury at his trial that he was in the wrong place at the wrong time. Nineteen at the time, he said an acquaintance he was driving home with asked him to stop near Mount Olive Drive on a hot summer afternoon in 2009. The man, Awet Asfaha, returned to Sheriffe's car shortly after. Both Sheriffe and Asfaha were arrested later that day and convicted of first-degree murder in the killing of furniture maker Bishen Golaub, with no chance of parole for 25 years. Asfaha has recently admitted to the shooting, and at a "faint hope" hearing this year had one year knocked off his 25-year wait for parole.

stories.title: Ontario faces proposed class action over strip searches of children in custody
stories.summary: The Ontario government says in court filings it is not liable for the actions of contracted organizations operating youth detention centres.
stories.author: Jennifer Pagliaro
stories.content:
Two young people on behalf of potentially thousands of former detainees are challenging the Ontario government over what they say was the unconstitutional strip searching they experienced while in youth custody — an experience that left them feeling “dehumanized.”

Lawyers will argue this week whether a proposed class action should be certified, allowing the case to move ahead in Superior Court. The legal battle comes after the high profile case against eight teenage girls in the murder of Kenneth Lee publicly revealed the troubling practice of routine strip searching in Ontario detention facilities for kids as young as 12.

The hearing, which begins Tuesday, will decide whether the claims of nearly 33,000 former youth detainees can proceed as a single class action, and whether Ontario can be held responsible for strip searches that are legally permitted but not required, and mostly carried out by third-party operators.

“The searches all involve the nudity and exposure to adult strangers of every part of the child’s body,” the court filing on behalf of the young people says.

“A twelve-year-old girl entering a facility for the first time, a thirteen-year-old boy returning from a court hearing, a seventeen-year-old youth on his first detention, and countless other children have been made to remove all of their clothing, spread their bodies open to view for adult strangers, and submit to being watched in the most intrusive fashion, again and again, as a matter of course.”

Two teens, identified only as A.A. and D.D., have been made lead plaintiffs in the case — both young people who were subjected to strip searches at different facilities despite no specific suspicions they were concealing contraband like drugs or weapons.

The largest youth detention centre in Ontario is still routinely strip searching boys in their

A.A., court documents allege, spent a year in a facility called Sundance, operated by the St. Lawrence Youth Association in Kingston, Ont., whose detention services are paid for by the Ministry of Children, Community and Social Services.

Upon entry to the facility, A.A. was made to strip completely naked, “shake out her hair, open her mouth, lift her arms, and spin so that staff could view every part of her body” before squatting and coughing, the documents filed by Sotos LLP, Emily Lam Law and Ruffo Law allege.

“The thing that has struck me the most as a lawyer, having spoken to many such youth, is how they consistently report being made to feel subhuman while undergoing these graphic, routine strip searches,” said Sotos LLP lawyer Mohsen Seddigh.

“This class action, if certified by the court, is the only way for the thousands of affected children to get their day in court at a trial and seek answers about how they have been treated by the state.”

While in an hospital for medical treatment, A.A., the documents say, opted to have a Sundance staff member observe a colonoscopy rather than face another routine search.

“Staff strip searched her anyway upon her return, while she was still partially sedated,” the documents allege.

D.D., who was detained at both the Brookside Youth Centre, operated by the province, and at Murray McKinnon House in Oshawa, which is run by the Murray McKinnon Foundation, is alleged to have experienced similar treatment.

“Routine strip searches were also imposed as discipline and punishment for failing a bathroom-cleaning inspection,” the court documents allege.

“Any contact with the outside world, family visits, court, outside health care, triggered a search. And there was ‘no real option to say no’: refusal meant being locked in his cell until he yielded to being strip searched.”

The Crown on behalf of the provincial government argued in responding legal filings that the proposed class action was “doomed to fail” and certification should be dismissed, saying that Ontario law permitted but did not require strip searching across facilities, saying it can be “an appropriate and reasonable” tool to address safety and security concerns. The implementation of those practices varied by organization, the Crown said.

The Crown wrote that of 153 youth facilities across the province, 136 of them were operated by what the province calls “third-party transfer payment recipients,” organizations contracted by the government to operate youth detention centres.

The province argues they are not legally liable for any potential charter violations at the facilities that are operated on behalf of and paid for by the province.

Despite the fact they operate under Ontario laws governing youth detention, the Crown argues that “does not make Ontario ultimately responsible for their actions.”

Provincially-operated facilities, like the Roy McMurtry Youth Centre in Brampton — the province’s largest youth jail — have also, the courts have previously heard, continued to conduct routine strip searches despite judicial comments and rulings finding the practice unconstitutional.

stories.title: Dropped by Amazon over his citizenship, a Toronto engineer just won an Ontario human rights case
stories.summary: The Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario issues a fine, and orders the company to amend its hiring practices.
stories.author: Ghada Alsharif
stories.content:
The Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario has ruled that Amazon discriminated against a software engineer in Toronto when it cancelled his recruitment process because of his Iranian citizenship.

In a decision last week, the tribunal ordered Amazon to pay $15,000 in compensation to Mohammad Owlia “for injury to his dignity, feelings and self-respect.” It also ordered the company to amend its discriminatory hiring policies and to require Amazon’s Ontario-based human resources department to complete human rights training.

“Amazon is committed to fair and inclusive hiring and to following the laws wherever we operate, including Ontario’s Human Rights Code,” the company said in an emailed statement. “We’re carefully reviewing the tribunal’s decision and will meet our obligations under it.”

The decision comes six years after Owlia filed a human rights application with the tribunal challenging what he sees as discrimination against Iranians facing hiring barriers because of their country of origin, despite having valid Canadian work permits.

“It means a great deal to have the tribunal recognize that what happened to me was discrimination,” Owlia said in a statement. “I’m proud that I stood up for my right to be judged on my ability to do the work, instead of where my birth certificate was issued.” Owlia, who is now a Canadian citizen, has been working at software startups in Toronto and is currently working as an engineering manager.

The company says its hiring policies comply with U.S. law, and apply to its Canadian operations.

Owlia — who had moved from Iran to Canada and completed his master’s degree in engineering at the University of Toronto — applied for a software engineering position at Amazon after being approached by a recruiter in 2019, while holding a valid open work permit. He had kicked off 2020 with what seemed like a successful round of job interviews at the company.

That was, he says, until Amazon informed him of an apparent deal-breaker: his citizenship.

According to his submissions to the Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario, he had passed a technical assessment that tested his programming skills in January 2020. But when he showed up for an in-person interview later that month, Owlia said things took a sudden turn. Reading through his resumé, the recruiter noticed he did his undergraduate degree at the University of Tehran — and then asked about his citizenship.

Owlia says he was surprised by the question, because the position did not require travel outside Canada and his open work permit allowed him to live and work here.

But the recruiter then “indicated that she could not proceed with Mr. Owlia’s application because there was a company-wide policy not to employ Iranian citizens who do not have permanent residency or citizenship in Canada, because of United States law,” according to Owlia’s submission to the tribunal.

Amazon argued that its policy was justified by U.S. export control laws. The recruiter had “determined that (Owlia) was ineligible for employment under Amazon’s internal export controls compliance policy that prohibited hiring individuals based on citizenship from certain embargoed countries, including Iran,” according to the tribunal’s decision.

Amazon’s internal safety records show mounting injury rates across Canadian warehouses. But in

Owlia walked away from the interview stunned. Even worse, he said, was the reaction when he messaged a group chat of Iranians living in Canada, who told him the experience was commonplace for Iranian job seekers and that he would have to “endure it until you get your permanent residency or your citizenship.”

“It’s not a lot to ask to be judged based on merits and merits only,” Owlia said in an interview with the Star. “Everybody in my community is used to being discriminated against so much from the visa process to kind of immigration ... I hope this will help level the playing field.”

The tribunal found that “Amazon’s export controls compliance policy was overbroad.”

“Amazon failed to establish that applicable Canadian or U.S. export or re-export control laws required the exclusion of Owlia from Amazon’s recruitment process,” according to the tribunal’s decision. “None of the arguments Amazon advanced negate the discriminatory nature of its decision to end Owlia’s advancement in the recruitment process or absolve it of liability under the Code.”

Owlia’s lawyer Gregory Ko of Toronto-based law firm Kastner Ko said dropping a qualified candidate’s job application because of their nationality is “blatantly discriminatory.”

“This decision confirms that employers cannot exclude candidates by simply invoking U.S. export control laws,” Ko said.

“Every year, hundreds of thousands of Iranian citizens come to Canada, graduate from post-graduate or graduate programs and are eligible to work here,” he added. “People legally entitled to work in Canada deserve to be judged on their qualifications, and not on their place of birth.”

In 2017, an online poll of 600 Iranian-Canadians conducted by the Iranian Canadian Congress revealed that 65 per cent of respondents reported experiencing discrimination; half said they had faced discrimination in employment-related matters.

paragraphs: The Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario has ruled that Amazon discriminated against a software engineer in Toronto when it cancelled his recruitment process because of his Iranian citizenship.

In a decision last week, the tribunal ordered Amazon to pay $15,000 in compensation to Mohammad Owlia “for injury to his dignity, feelings and self-respect.” It also ordered the company to amend its discriminatory hiring policies and to require Amazon’s Ontario-based human resources department to complete human rights training.

“Amazon is committed to fair and inclusive hiring and to following the laws wherever we operate, including Ontario’s Human Rights Code,” the company said in an emailed statement. “We’re carefully reviewing the tribunal’s decision and will meet our obligations under it.”

The decision comes six years after Owlia filed a human rights application with the tribunal challenging what he sees as discrimination against Iranians facing hiring barriers because of their country of origin, despite having valid Canadian work permits.

“It means a great deal to have the tribunal recognize that what happened to me was discrimination,” Owlia said in a statement. “I’m proud that I stood up for my right to be judged on my ability to do the work, instead of where my birth certificate was issued.” Owlia, who is now a Canadian citizen, has been working at software startups in Toronto and is currently working as an engineering manager.
The company says its hiring policies comply with U.S. law, and apply to its Canadian operations.

Owlia — who had moved from Iran to Canada and completed his master’s degree in engineering at the University of Toronto — applied for a software engineering position at Amazon after being approached by a recruiter in 2019, while holding a valid open work permit. He had kicked off 2020 with what seemed like a successful round of job interviews at the company.
That was, he says, until Amazon informed him of an apparent deal-breaker: his citizenship.

According to his submissions to the Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario, he had passed a technical assessment that tested his programming skills in January 2020. But when he showed up for an in-person interview later that month, Owlia said things took a sudden turn. Reading through his resumé, the recruiter noticed he did his undergraduate degree at the University of Tehran — and then asked about his citizenship.
Owlia says he was surprised by the question, because the position did not require travel outside Canada and his open work permit allowed him to live and work here.

But the recruiter then “indicated that she could not proceed with Mr. Owlia’s application because there was a company-wide policy not to employ Iranian citizens who do not have permanent residency or citizenship in Canada, because of United States law,” according to Owlia’s submission to the tribunal.

Amazon argued that its policy was justified by U.S. export control laws. The recruiter had “determined that (Owlia) was ineligible for employment under Amazon’s internal export controls compliance policy that prohibited hiring individuals based on citizenship from certain embargoed countries, including Iran,” according to the tribunal’s decision.

Owlia walked away from the interview stunned. Even worse, he said, was the reaction when he messaged a group chat of Iranians living in Canada, who told him the experience was commonplace for Iranian job seekers and that he would have to “endure it until you get your permanent residency or your citizenship.”

“It’s not a lot to ask to be judged based on merits and merits only,” Owlia said in an interview with the Star. “Everybody in my community is used to being discriminated against so much from the visa process to kind of immigration ... I hope this will help level the playing field.”
The tribunal found that “Amazon’s export controls compliance policy was overbroad.”

“Amazon failed to establish that applicable Canadian or U.S. export or re-export control laws required the exclusion of Owlia from Amazon’s recruitment process,” according to the tribunal’s decision. “None of the arguments Amazon advanced negate the discriminatory nature of its decision to end Owlia’s advancement in the recruitment process or absolve it of liability under the Code.”
Owlia’s lawyer Gregory Ko of Toronto-based law firm Kastner Ko said dropping a qualified candidate’s job application because of their nationality is “blatantly discriminatory.”

stories.title: Ontario watchdog orders Metrolinx to reveal internal records on long-delayed Mimico GO station upgrades
stories.summary: Ontario’s privacy commissioner orders Metrolinx to disclose internal timeline for Mimico GO station accessibility upgrades delayed by a decade.
stories.author: Sheila Wang
stories.content:
Ontario’s transparency watchdog has ordered Metrolinx to release project schedule details for a GO station accessibility upgrade that was supposed to be finished a decade ago.

The provincial transit agency had planned to make the Mimico GO Station on the Lakeshore West Line barrier-free by 2016, but to date no construction work has been done.

Through freedom-of-information legislation, a local resident asked for a document that spells out the agency’s project timelines, but it was sent with heavy redactions.

The decision, issued on Nov. 12 , comes as Metrolinx faces criticism for a lack of transparency into significant delays and cost overruns on multiple infrastructure projects. For the Ontario Line and other delayed projects, Metrolinx has refused to release specific opening dates.

In the case of Mimico GO, after a resident requested the information in January 2025, Metrolinx said the redactions to the scheduling record were necessary, in part, to protect the agency’s economic interest.

The Premier’s office said the new route, chosen by Metrolinx, is “the best option” to serve the needs of the growing region.

But the Information and Privacy Commissioner (IPC) decision said Metrolinx failed to provide sufficient evidence to show that the release of the information could cause financial harm , and ordered it to disclose the responsive records.

“Metrolinx’s submissions on harm are highly speculative and do not satisfy the threshold to establish the harms it alleges,” Steven Faughnan, an adjudicator at the IPC, wrote in the decision.

David Lepofsky, chair of the Accessibility for Ontarians with Disabilities Act (Aoda) Alliance, applauded the decision but said he was concerned that Metrolinx staff, paid by the public purse, are trying to “block public accountability.”

“They are not telling the public anything who has a right to know. At the same time they’re covering up their internal plans and they are foot dragging, and putting a member of the public to the ridiculous burden of having to fight and appeal to the Information and Privacy Commissioner to win,” Lepofsky said.

Metrolinx faced criticism after it recently announced that it will reduce the number of its board meetings, when staff often provide project updates, from four times a year to two, the CBC reported.

In response to questions from the Star, Metrolinx did not address the commissioner’s ruling or the transparency concerns, stating that its priority “is improving accessibility at Mimico station and providing customers with a seamless, integrated and barrier-free experience.”

Built in 1967, Mimico GO has long been identified by Metrolinx as a station that needs to be rehabilitated to meet its standards for accessibility.

The initial 2016 completion deadline for an accessibility upgrade was pushed to 2017.

At Mimico GO station, long due for an upgrade, passengers must use the stairs and existing underground tunnels to reach the platforms.

Then the project suffered multiple additional delays and alterations over the next decade, with the completion date pushed to 2023, then to 2025. Metrolinx won’t disclose its current targeted completion date. Over the years, the original design has changed from a new pedestrian bridge over the tracks, to new underground tunnels with elevators, and then back to a pedestrian bridge.

The upgrade had also been considered as part of a broader effort by the provincial government to develop the area as a Transit-Oriented Community (TOC), though that plan was abandoned.

The station work has still not broken ground. Passengers must use the old stairs in the existing underground tunnels to reach the platforms.

“Someone really has to be there (at the station) to assist me … and someone has to carry my walker,” said Katelyn Eathorne, who uses a rollator walker — a four-wheeled mobility aid — after she suffered a stroke six years ago.

Without automatic doors, elevators and ramped platforms for level boarding at the Mimico station, it’s impossible for her to use the GO Line on her own, she said.

As part of Metrolinx’s most recent plan, Mimico GO’s upgrades will include a pedestrian bridge with elevator and a new building entrance, according to the agency.

Eathorne said that between the grand promises touted in public meetings and the quietly missed deadlines, Metrolinx has not kept the public well informed about what is actually happening.

During mediation of the dispute over access to the project timeline, Metrolinx handed over a version of the document that revealed some information, which was obtained by the Star and offers a glimpse into what has been happening behind the scenes.

It took half a year for Metrolinx to procure design services for the station upgrades and nearly another year to hire a construction manager.

Metrolinx told the Star that a contract for design and construction management services was awarded in May 2025, and the contract for major construction is expected to be awarded in 2027.

Metrolinx argued to the IPC that a fully-disclosed record could be “misconstrued or lead to further confusion and frustration by the public,” noting that several separate issues at Mimico GO have been conflated within the media, leading to “negative public sentiment.”

The adjudicator ruled that FOI exemptions are not meant to “insulate institutions” from public disappointment.

Metrolinx is required to release the record by Dec. 21, almost two years after the agency first received the public-record request.

“Justice delayed is justice denied,” said Duff Conacher, co-founder of Democracy Watch. “This is a victory at the end, but two years later than it should have happened. You can take that as encouraging that they finally won, or discouraging that the government was legally able to delay disclosure by two years.”

The transit agency did not say whether it will appeal the IPC decision.

content_blocks.text: Why is Mimico GO still not accessible?
content_blocks.html: Why is Mimico GO still not accessible?

content_blocks.text: Built in 1967, Mimico GO has long been identified by Metrolinx as a station that needs to be rehabilitated to meet its standards for accessibility.
content_blocks.html: Built in 1967, Mimico GO has long been identified by Metrolinx as a station that needs to be rehabilitated to meet its standards for accessibility.

content_blocks.text: The initial 2016 completion deadline for an accessibility upgrade was pushed to 2017.

content_blocks.alt: GO Mimico 2.JPG

content_blocks.text: At Mimico GO station, long due for an upgrade, passengers must use the stairs and existing underground tunnels to reach the platforms.

content_blocks.text: Then the project suffered multiple additional delays and alterations over the next decade, with the completion date pushed to 2023, then to 2025. Metrolinx won’t disclose its current targeted completion date. Over the years, the original design has changed from a new pedestrian bridge over the tracks, to new underground tunnels with elevators, and then back to a pedestrian bridge.

content_blocks.text: The upgrade had also been considered as part of a broader effort by the provincial government to develop the area as a Transit-Oriented Community (TOC), though that plan was abandoned.

content_blocks.text: Living with an inaccessible station
content_blocks.html: Living with an inaccessible station

content_blocks.text: “Someone really has to be there (at the station) to assist me … and someone has to carry my walker,” said Katelyn Eathorne, who uses a rollator walker — a four-wheeled mobility aid — after she suffered a stroke six years ago.
content_blocks.html: “Someone really has to be there (at the station) to assist me … and someone has to carry my walker,” said Katelyn Eathorne, who uses a rollator walker — a four-wheeled mobility aid — after she suffered a stroke six years ago.

content_blocks.text: Without automatic doors, elevators and ramped platforms for level boarding at the Mimico station, it’s impossible for her to use the GO Line on her own, she said.

content_blocks.text: As part of Metrolinx’s most recent plan, Mimico GO’s upgrades will include a pedestrian bridge with elevator and a new building entrance, according to the agency.
content_blocks.html: As part of Metrolinx’s most recent plan, Mimico GO’s upgrades will include a pedestrian bridge with elevator and a new building entrance, according to the agency.

content_blocks.text: Eathorne said that between the grand promises touted in public meetings and the quietly missed deadlines, Metrolinx has not kept the public well informed about what is actually happening.

content_blocks.text: During mediation of the dispute over access to the project timeline, Metrolinx handed over a version of the document that revealed some information, which was obtained by the Star and offers a glimpse into what has been happening behind the scenes.

content_blocks.text: It took half a year for Metrolinx to procure design services for the station upgrades and nearly another year to hire a construction manager.

content_blocks.text: Metrolinx told the Star that a contract for design and construction management services was awarded in May 2025, and the contract for major construction is expected to be awarded in 2027.

content_blocks.text: Metrolinx argued to the IPC that a fully-disclosed record could be “misconstrued or lead to further confusion and frustration by the public,” noting that several separate issues at Mimico GO have been conflated within the media, leading to “negative public sentiment.”

content_blocks.text: The adjudicator ruled that FOI exemptions are not meant to “insulate institutions” from public disappointment.

content_blocks.text: “Justice delayed is justice denied,” said Duff Conacher, co-founder of Democracy Watch. “This is a victory at the end, but two years later than it should have happened. You can take that as encouraging that they finally won, or discouraging that the government was legally able to delay disclosure by two years.”

stories.title: Fatal fire investigation
stories.summary: London, ON (November 24, 2026) - Members of the London Police Service Major Crime Section, along with the Ontario Fire Marshall’s Office, are investigating a residential fire that took place last week on Kipps Lane.
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
London, ON (November 24, 2026) - Members of the London Police Service Major Crime Section, along with the Ontario Fire Marshall’s Office, are investigating a residential fire that took place last week on Kipps Lane.

On Thursday, November 19, 2026, at approximately 7 a.m., emergency crews responded to the 700 block of Kipps Lane for a working fire at a multi-unit residence.

One person was transported to hospital by paramedic services with critical injuries and has since died.

The cause of the fire remains under investigation.

The investigation is in its early stages. More information will be released as appropriate.

Anyone with information in relation to this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670.

Tuesday, November 24, 2026

Its that time of year again, and we’re ready for another busy winter season.Last year, lake-effect snow and extreme cold tested our patience, but we never backed down.

Through blizzards, squalls, and freezing rain, our snowplow operators keep London safe by maintaining:

3,800+ kmof roads. That’s a lot of ground to cover whenever winter decides to show off!

1,600+ kmof sidewalks. We’re not just talking the talk, we’re clearing the walk.

2,100+bus stops.A stop for the bus doesn’t mean a stop for our crews.

720+ cul-de-sacs We’re not turning a blind eye to these dead ends!

Plus bridges, bike lanes and pedestrian crossings,because there’s more than one way to get around the city.

“Winter maintenance is a big job, and our crews are ready to respond,” said Joel Gillard, Division Manager, Road Operations. “From roads and sidewalks to bus stops and bike lanes, we’re committed to keeping London moving this winter. Before heading out, visit london.ca/snow for updates from our teams, and when you’re on the road, remember to slow down, be safe, and adjust your driving to the conditions. We appreciate everyone’s patience as we respond to changing conditions.”

What to expect after a major snowfall

Following Provincial regulation, we focus on major roads and bus routes first. This includes clearing snow on roads around hospitals, schools, and high-traffic routes that let you travel in and out of the city. Once these areas are clear and safe, we move on to neighbourhood streets, sidewalks, and bus stops.

You can learn more about our levels of service online here.

Let’s talk about salt

We know keeping roads and sidewalks safe in winter is important, but so is protecting our environment. That’s why we’re mindful of how and where we use road salt. Using too much salt can affect our waterways, soil and surrounding vegetation, so we aim to use it only where it’s needed most.

Salt is primarily used on main roads, bus routes and core pedestrian areas to help prevent snow and ice from sticking. On neighbourhood streets, we use sand at intersections, curves and hills to keep things grippy.

We have a good supply of salt this winter and will continue to balance winter safety with responsible salt use

Walkin’ in a winter wonderland

The Thames Valley Parkway and select park paths are cleared to a recreational standard after 8 cm of snow over a 48-hour period. We leave them snow-packed, so bundle up and check the forecast before heading out for your dose of fresh winter air.

Skating and swimming during a storm

Community centres, arenas, and pools may stay open, open late, or close early depending on the weather. During a snow event, visit london.ca/snow for the latest updates about our community centres, arenas, and pools before heading out for a skate or swim.

On street parking

From November 15 to March 31, overnight street parking is restricted. A maximum of 15 free overnight parking passes can be requested per vehicle licence plate, valid on most city streets. Vehicles parked on city streets without a valid pass may receive a parking fine.

Additional passes beyond the free limit are available for $5 each on the HONK website or mobile app.

At times, we may issue a parking ban to clear the roads for our snowplows. If you’ve registered for a parking pass, we’ll give you a heads-up by phone or email, and update london.ca/snow.

Stay off stormwater ponds

Stormwater management ponds may appear frozen, but they’re not safe. Beneath the ice, water continues to flow, making the surface unstable and unsafe for skating, hockey, or any recreation.

These ponds collect rain, snowmelt, and surface runoff to prevent flooring and erosion, and improve water quality.

Watch this video to learn more about stormwater ponds. Stay safe, and stay off the ice this winter!

Did we miss something?

After the snow stops falling, and our crews have had a chance to respond, let us know through the Service London Portal if you come across snow not plowed. After a snowfall, we continue plowing roads, sidewalks, and pathways, and your reports help us keep things moving!

We’ve got you, London! This winter, be kind, be safe, and be ready. We’re in this together!

Tuesday, November 24, 2026
Its that time of year again, and we’re ready for another busy winter season.Last year, lake-effect snow and extreme cold tested our patience, but we never backed down.
Through blizzards, squalls, and freezing rain, our snowplow operators keep London safe by maintaining:

items: 3,800+ kmof roads. That’s a lot of ground to cover whenever winter decides to show off!
1,600+ kmof sidewalks. We’re not just talking the talk, we’re clearing the walk.
2,100+bus stops.A stop for the bus doesn’t mean a stop for our crews.
720+ cul-de-sacs We’re not turning a blind eye to these dead ends!
Plus bridges, bike lanes and pedestrian crossings,because there’s more than one way to get around the city.

content_blocks.text: “Winter maintenance is a big job, and our crews are ready to respond,” said Joel Gillard, Division Manager, Road Operations. “From roads and sidewalks to bus stops and bike lanes, we’re committed to keeping London moving this winter. Before heading out, visit london.ca/snow for updates from our teams, and when you’re on the road, remember to slow down, be safe, and adjust your driving to the conditions. We appreciate everyone’s patience as we respond to changing conditions.”
What to expect after a major snowfall

Following Provincial regulation, we focus on major roads and bus routes first. This includes clearing snow on roads around hospitals, schools, and high-traffic routes that let you travel in and out of the city. Once these areas are clear and safe, we move on to neighbourhood streets, sidewalks, and bus stops.
You can learn more about our levels of service online here.
Let’s talk about salt

We know keeping roads and sidewalks safe in winter is important, but so is protecting our environment. That’s why we’re mindful of how and where we use road salt. Using too much salt can affect our waterways, soil and surrounding vegetation, so we aim to use it only where it’s needed most.

Salt is primarily used on main roads, bus routes and core pedestrian areas to help prevent snow and ice from sticking. On neighbourhood streets, we use sand at intersections, curves and hills to keep things grippy.
We have a good supply of salt this winter and will continue to balance winter safety with responsible salt use
Walkin’ in a winter wonderland

The Thames Valley Parkway and select park paths are cleared to a recreational standard after 8 cm of snow over a 48-hour period. We leave them snow-packed, so bundle up and check the forecast before heading out for your dose of fresh winter air.
Skating and swimming during a storm

Community centres, arenas, and pools may stay open, open late, or close early depending on the weather. During a snow event, visit london.ca/snow for the latest updates about our community centres, arenas, and pools before heading out for a skate or swim.
On street parking

From November 15 to March 31, overnight street parking is restricted. A maximum of 15 free overnight parking passes can be requested per vehicle licence plate, valid on most city streets. Vehicles parked on city streets without a valid pass may receive a parking fine.
Additional passes beyond the free limit are available for $5 each on the HONK website or mobile app.
At times, we may issue a parking ban to clear the roads for our snowplows. If you’ve registered for a parking pass, we’ll give you a heads-up by phone or email, and update london.ca/snow.
Stay off stormwater ponds
Stormwater management ponds may appear frozen, but they’re not safe. Beneath the ice, water continues to flow, making the surface unstable and unsafe for skating, hockey, or any recreation.
These ponds collect rain, snowmelt, and surface runoff to prevent flooring and erosion, and improve water quality.
Watch this video to learn more about stormwater ponds. Stay safe, and stay off the ice this winter!
Did we miss something?

After the snow stops falling, and our crews have had a chance to respond, let us know through the Service London Portal if you come across snow not plowed. After a snowfall, we continue plowing roads, sidewalks, and pathways, and your reports help us keep things moving!
We’ve got you, London! This winter, be kind, be safe, and be ready. We’re in this together!

stories.title: Galloway’s lawyers say he deserves one of Canada’s largest defamation awards
stories.summary: Legal team argues sexual assault allegations cost the bestselling author millions in past and future earnings
stories.author: Mike Hager
stories.content:
Bestselling author Steven Galloway ’s legal team says he deserves one of the biggest defamation awards in Canadian history, asking a B.C. Supreme Court justice to award their client millions in total damages from four defendants they allege ruined his career by spreading sexual assault allegations.

Mr. Galloway’s two lawyers began their closing arguments Monday by asking Justice Neena Sharma to punish the author’s former creative writing student – known as A.B. because of a publication ban on her identity – with at least $2.5-million in general, aggravated and punitive damages linked to her 2015 allegations.

His counsel will continue Tuesday morning by arguing for an additional rare award of special damages solely against A.B. The claim for these special damages is expected to be millions more to represent what they argue was Mr. Galloway’s lost income over the past decade as well as his nullified future earning potential – all a result of her alleged defamations.

“She orchestrated lies to support the lies and she knew, she was tactical and it was to ensure maximum damage,” his lead counsel Daniel Burnett told the court of A.B.’s actions. “That conduct caused wreckage to every aspect of Mr. Galloway’s life – years of suffering – it’s really quite unprecedented and the award should reflect that.”

Daniel Coles, Mr. Galloway’s other lawyer, told the court that one expert’s report found his client’s lost income to date and future earnings up to the age of 70 amounted to $7.1-million, while another pegged that figure at $11.7-million.

Mr. Burnett argued the other three co-defendants should also be ordered to pay general, aggravated and punitive damages to Mr. Galloway, the former chair of the University of British Columbia’s creative writing department, in the form of least $250,000 from Mandi Gray, at least $80,000 from Glynnis Kirchmeier and $30,000 from Dana Kagis.

That trio posted on social media allegedly repeating the claims Mr. Galloway sexually assaulted A.B.

A.B. did not testify and, at the start of the trial, one of her lawyers told the court she was withdrawing her defences of truth and fair comment – but she denies the accusations that she spread lies about Mr. Galloway, with whom she had a two-year relationship. Her lawyers have told the court that she tried to kill herself twice this year because of the stress of the legal process.

Mr. Galloway was never charged with a crime but was suspended by UBC when the allegations surfaced in November 2015 and created a media maelstrom. In 2016, a former Supreme Court justice hired by UBC found that, ON a balance of probabilities, it could not be established that he committed sexual assault or assault. She did find that he had sexually harassed her and committed other misconduct, which led to his dismissal that year.

Mr. Galloway launched a lawsuit against almost two dozen defendants in 2018.

On Monday, Mr. Burnett argued that Justice Sharma should make a ruling that A.B.’s allegations are false, which would help toward restoring his client’s reputation. Such a determination would also help his client recover any damages from Ms. Kirchmeier, who Mr. Burnett explained lives in the United States and, as such, is not typically liable for a foreign ruling unless a defamatory claim was proven to be false.

Mr. Burnett also argued A.B. embarked upon a strategic campaign to leverage criminal accusations of sexual assault “through as many others as she could, to spread them as far as she could.”

He noted that, in correspondence with other creative writing professors, A.B. said CBC News had reviewed her evidence and was intent on covering her story, which Mr. Burnett said she has admitted was not the case in earlier litigation.

He also singled out how a producer for CBC’s fifth estate was copied on A.B.’s e-mail to the university president alleging sexual assault, because she “wanted the publicity to be out there,” damaging his client.

Mr. Burnett argued A.B. clearly acted out of malice, as did Dr. Gray, whom he said posted repeatedly about his client as if he were “roadkill,” and Ms. Kirchmeier, who he said should be penalized for blurting out in court the description of “other bad acts” alleged by a different former creative writing student who settled with Mr. Galloway on the eve of the trial.

Closing arguments will continue this week, with arguments from A.B.’s counsel, Dr. Gray’s lawyer and Ms. Kirchmeier, who is attending law school and representing herself remotely. Ms. Kagis has not participated in the trial and has no representation.

Some time in the new year, the court will hear whether A.B. can be held in contempt after Justice Sharma denied her request for an excusal from testifying in pre-trial discovery last June.

On Monday, court heard a number of a number of high-profile defamation decisions Mr. Galloway’s counsel said are analogous to their client’s loss of reputation and income, including a 1995 Supreme Court of Canada decision in favour of a Crown prosecutor who sued the Church of Scientology.

In that case, the court dismissed an appeal by the organization and affirmed that attorney S. Casey Hill be awarded $1.6-million after allegations the group had made were found to be false. Mr. Hill had been accused of misleading a judge and breaching court orders sealing documents.

“Without minimizing that, he still continued in his profession, he became a judge – the suffering on Steven Galloway is an entirely more devastating category,” Mr. Burnett said.

stories.title: Liberals agree to limited parliamentary oversight of minister’s power to end strikes
stories.summary: The Bill C-39 legislative committee has held marathon meetings this past week, as its members work through clause-by-clause consideration of the bill
stories.author: Jordan Gowling
stories.content:
Ottawa — Liberal members on the Bill C-39 committee have accepted a Conservative amendment to provide some parliamentary oversight on the government’s use of Section 107 under the Canada Labour Code.

The amendment, presented Monday evening at committee, requires that within three sitting days following the invocation of Section 107, which allows a labour minister to end a strike or lockout, the government must designate a committee of the House of Commons to review and study the order.

The committee will also allow affected parties to testify and then must prepare a report within seven sitting days and table it in the House of Commons.

The modification to the bill is a diluted version of Conservative labour critic Kyle Seeback’s original amendment, which would have allowed members of Parliament to revoke the labour minister’s use of Section 107.

Bloc Québécois MP Gabriel Ste-Marie took issue with the watered-down version of the Conservative amendment and voted against it, noting that committees already have the right to conduct studies and deliver reports. Ste-Marie also lamented the extent to which the Liberal government has become anti-union.

In response to Ste-Marie, Seeback said the amendment allows for a mandatory process.

“In a Liberal majority government, the chance of putting forward a motion to review a Section 107 order and getting that passed at committee to get a study, I think I have a better chance of winning the lottery on Friday night with the Lotto Max,” he said.

Conservative MP Kyle Seeback attends a House of Commons standing committee studying Bill C-39 in Ottawa on Nov. 23, 2026. Blair Gable / Postmedia

The Bill C-39 legislative committee has held marathon meetings this past week, as its members work through clause-by-clause consideration of the bill, also known as the Building Canada Strong Act.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has called the bill one of the most consequential bills of this Parliament, which attempts to fast-track the regulatory process around the approval of major projects and makes consequential amendments to the labour code.

Unions in Canada have been adamant that the bill infringes on workers’ fundamental right to strike, by codifying what they see as the misuse of Section 107 into the labour code. The Liberal government’s repeated use of Section 107 on strikes and lockouts since 2024, is the subject of several court challenges.

On Monday, the Liberals rejected most of the amendments from the Conservatives, NDP and the Bloc Québécois, which would have provided safeguards to protect the right to strike.

The other Conservative amendment that Liberal members agreed to was to give the special mediator more powers to determine the procedure of bringing two conflicting parties together during bargaining and allow the special mediator to require those parties to participate in those meetings.

Other amendments rejected by the Liberals were in relation to providing changes to the geographic certification process that was laid out in the bill.

The bill allows for employers to send in an application to Canada Industrial Relations Board to group multiple bargaining units into a single bargaining unit. Whether this applies to just the longshore industry or across other industries was a subject of debate between members of the committee.

NDP MP Heather McPherson introduced an amendment to get the consent of the impacted unions through a vote, which was rejected by the Liberal members of the committee.

Conservative MP Dan Albas said the geographic certification process will be litigated in the courts, as it directly impacts freedom of association under Section 2(d) of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

In a statement Monday, Canadian Labour Congress vice-president Siobhan Vipond said the Liberal government’s rejection of the proposed amendments to the bill is “a betrayal of workers across Canada.”

“Workers won these rights through decades of struggle; we won’t give them up without a fight,” she said. “And we’ll never forget who stood with us and who torpedoed our fundamental rights.”

“Karma never forgets and she’s a union sister,” Vipond added.

Jordan Gowling joined National Post's parliamentary bureau in 2026 after two years as Financial Post's economics reporter on Parliament Hill. She previously worked as a producer at CTV News in Ottawa.

stories.title: Montrealers could face nearly 10% property tax hike in 2027
stories.summary: The city says the increase is largely tied to new investments in aging infrastructure, including maintenance and Montreal's water systems.
stories.author: Alessia Simona Maratta
stories.content:
Montreal property owners could be facing a sharp increase in municipal taxes next year, with the average property tax rate potentially rising by 9.8 per cent.

A summary of the city’s 2027 budget was briefly posted on its website before being removed Monday. The document suggests the average tax bill could increase by 9.8 per cent. This would represent the highest residential property tax rate hike in 20 years.

The city says the increase is tied largely to new investments in aging infrastructure, including the creation of a reserve fund for maintenance, as well as additional spending on Montreal’s water systems.

Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada said difficult decisions are needed to protect city services and avoid passing infrastructure costs on to future generations.

“We need to have the means to deliver on housing, ON homelessness issues, ON infrastructure, having a city that hopefully will never have potholes again and having a city that is a metropolis at the highest level of efficiency and agility,” Martinez Ferrada told reporters Monday.

She said the city made the decision with an eye toward delivering on its priorities over the next several years.

“That’s why we took the decision and I assume that decision plainly because I know that we’ll be able to deliver on what we need to deliver in the next few years,” she said.

The city is set to officially table its 2027 budget Tuesday.

stories.title: Google says 'lawful access' bill creates 'attractive' opportunities for bad actors
stories.summary: A provision in the federal 'lawful access' bill requiring companies to keep months of people’s metadata gives criminals a new avenue of attack, a senior Google official told senators Monday.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — A provision in the federal “lawful access” bill requiring companies to keep months of people’s metadata gives criminals a new avenue of attack, a senior Google official told senators Monday.

The Liberal government bill would require service providers to retain metadata — digital traces of a communication, but not the email or text itself — for up to six months.

The government agreed to shorten the period, which was originally up to one year, after a wave of concern.

The measure still forces companies to stockpile sensitive logs about the digital activity of millions of law-abiding Canadians suspected of no crime, said Jeanette Patell, Google Canada’s director of government affairs and public policy.

“This overrides Canadians’ own privacy choices and creates attractive new attack surfaces for bad actors,” Patell told members of a Senate committee studying the bill.

The government says the legislation will ensure law enforcement has the tools to prevent, investigate and respond to modern crime and protect Canadians in a manner consistent with the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

Opponents argue the legislation unnecessarily expands the powers of police and intelligence agencies, endangering the privacy of Canadians, flouting the Charter and placing unreasonable demands on companies.

The bill would require electronic service providers to develop and maintain the technical capabilities necessary to enable police and the Canadian Security Intelligence Service to effectively obtain communications and information for investigations.

Critics of the legislation say it could allow the government to force companies to break encryption by inserting backdoors into their products.

John Hultquist, chief analyst with Google’s Threat Intelligence Group, pointed to the dangers of creating such vulnerabilities.

In the Salt Typhoon campaign, Chinese state-sponsored actors breached major telecommunications carriers and targeted the systems they had built to handle court-authorized wiretaps, Hultquist said at the committee Monday.

“Mechanisms designed for lawful access become an open door for foreign espionage against citizens and senior government officials alike,” he said.

While a secret order forcing a tech company to push spyware to a single suspect’s phone May seem like targeted law enforcement, modern software engineering makes a localized backdoor impossible to build safely, he added.

A provider would have to build targeting mechanisms directly into their core infrastructure, and if adversaries discover these weaknesses, they can and will reverse engineer them, threatening billions of people globally, he said.

“In a threat landscape where adversaries use advanced technologies and automation to rapidly identify and exploit weaknesses, there is no such thing as a back door only the good guys can use.”

Earlier this month, Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree told the Senate committee the bill “is not about weakening privacy protections. It is not about surveillance. It is not about creating backdoors to Canadians’ private communications.”

Erik Neuenschwander, senior director of user privacy and child safety at Apple, touted the benefits of end-to-end encryption, which prevents a message from being read by a third party while in transit.

He said that despite amendments to the bill in the House of Commons, it would still allow the government to “force companies to stop offering end-to-end encrypted products or to build backdoors into their new encrypted products — something Apple will never do.”

“We are committed to supporting law enforcement’s work to keep Canadians safe, and we’re committed to encryption for the same reason: it keeps Canadians safe,” he said.

“Speaking as an engineer, we do not know of a way to provide access to encrypted information only for the good guys, or only in extenuating circumstances, without creating new ways for the bad guys to break in.”

Google and Apple each suggested specific changes to the bill to the committee.

A senior Australian official told the senators his country’s system to help police and spies access online communications relies heavily on co-operation between law enforcement agencies and technology companies.

Andrew Warnes of Australia’s Department of Home Affairs said 99 per cent of notices issued under the framework have been voluntary, meaning agencies have worked collaboratively with companies to successfully obtain needed assistance.

Communications data obtained under the Australian framework has helped identify previously unknown child victims of alleged sexual offences and uncover corrupt relationships involving elected officials, he said.

Australia has never issued what it calls a technical capability notice, a demand that a company build a new means of accessing someone’s digital information, he added.

Senators plan to begin clause-by-clause review of the legislation Tuesday.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 23, 2026.

Jim Bronskill, The Canadian Press

The bill would require electronic service providers to develop and maintain the technical capabilities necessary to enable police and the Canadian Security Intelligence Service to effectively obtain communications and information for investigations.
Critics of the legislation say it could allow the government to force companies to break encryption by inserting backdoors into their products.
John Hultquist, chief analyst with Google’s Threat Intelligence Group, pointed to the dangers of creating such vulnerabilities.

In the Salt Typhoon campaign, Chinese state-sponsored actors breached major telecommunications carriers and targeted the systems they had built to handle court-authorized wiretaps, Hultquist said at the committee Monday.
“Mechanisms designed for lawful access become an open door for foreign espionage against citizens and senior government officials alike,” he said.

While a secret order forcing a tech company to push spyware to a single suspect’s phone May seem like targeted law enforcement, modern software engineering makes a localized backdoor impossible to build safely, he added.

A provider would have to build targeting mechanisms directly into their core infrastructure, and if adversaries discover these weaknesses, they can and will reverse engineer them, threatening billions of people globally, he said.
“In a threat landscape where adversaries use advanced technologies and automation to rapidly identify and exploit weaknesses, there is no such thing as a back door only the good guys can use.”

Earlier this month, Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree told the Senate committee the bill “is not about weakening privacy protections. It is not about surveillance. It is not about creating backdoors to Canadians’ private communications.”

Erik Neuenschwander, senior director of user privacy and child safety at Apple, touted the benefits of end-to-end encryption, which prevents a message from being read by a third party while in transit.

He said that despite amendments to the bill in the House of Commons, it would still allow the government to “force companies to stop offering end-to-end encrypted products or to build backdoors into their new encrypted products — something Apple will never do.”
“We are committed to supporting law enforcement’s work to keep Canadians safe, and we’re committed to encryption for the same reason: it keeps Canadians safe,” he said.

“Speaking as an engineer, we do not know of a way to provide access to encrypted information only for the good guys, or only in extenuating circumstances, without creating new ways for the bad guys to break in.”
Google and Apple each suggested specific changes to the bill to the committee.

A senior Australian official told the senators his country’s system to help police and spies access online communications relies heavily on co-operation between law enforcement agencies and technology companies.

Andrew Warnes of Australia’s Department of Home Affairs said 99 per cent of notices issued under the framework have been voluntary, meaning agencies have worked collaboratively with companies to successfully obtain needed assistance.

Communications data obtained under the Australian framework has helped identify previously unknown child victims of alleged sexual offences and uncover corrupt relationships involving elected officials, he said.
Australia has never issued what it calls a technical capability notice, a demand that a company build a new means of accessing someone’s digital information, he added.
Senators plan to begin clause-by-clause review of the legislation Tuesday.

stories.title: What if Quebec’s premier refuses to swear allegiance to the King?
stories.summary: Members of the National Assembly (MNA) unanimously declined to swear allegiance to the King when they were sworn in after this fall’s provincial election.
stories.author: Genevieve Beauchemin
stories.content:
Montreal – Members of the National Assembly (MNA) unanimously declined to swear allegiance to the King when they were sworn in after this fall’s provincial election.

But now a court ruling says they are required to. Refusing to do it, could plunge the institution into a constitutional crisis and Quebec’s next move is now at the centre of political and legal wrangling.

Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon says the province will seek an appeal in the case and is looking at all legal and political options, but the clock is ticking until the upcoming session of the legislative assembly set for Dec. 1.

“I cannot take an oath to the King of England. And I think we are dozens and maybe more than 100 elected members of Parliament, duly elected through a democratic process, who think it’s a disgrace,” said Plamondon. “If you look at the polls, we also have huge popular support.”

Public Interest Litigation Institute founder Lawrence David filed the application to suspend the 2022 Quebec law stating that the oath was optional. The Ottawa-based lawyer says the Quebec government May seek an appeal, but one will not be granted automatically. And that it will take time before a judgement is rendered.

“It is necessarily the case that the National Assembly will not reconvene on Dec. 1,” he says. “That is, unless the politicians take the oath of allegiance. They’ve said that they will not do that. As a result, they are not lawfully entitled to sit in the National Assembly to participate in any parliamentary activities, including proposing or voting bills. And so, they are left with a quandary entirely of their own making.”

Lawrence also points out that in his ruling, Justice Ian Demers spells out that the judgement is immediately applicable and that it cannot be suspended while an appeal process is underway. The Superior Court explained that if Mna’s vote in laws, for instance, those could be declared annulled later if the appeal fails.

“There would be a very important prejudice if that happens,” says Université de Montréal constitutional law professor Karine Millaire. “It would mean that everything that the National Assembly did, like adopting laws would be invalid, and so the prejudice would be significant. The courts want to avoid that.”

She says that leaves the Quebec government little room to manoeuvre.

“They said they would appeal, which is absolutely legitimate. They can seek an appeal. But they will have to take the oath if they want to be sitting at the National Assembly on Dec. 1,” she says.

Constitutional lawyer Frédéric Bérard says there is a possibility the Court of Appeal could expedite a decision on some part of the ruling and decide not to interfere with the opening of a session. But he says no matter the timing, the courts have to take a clear stand against the erosion of the rule of law.

“I don’t like the oath to the King myself,” says Bérard. “But I hate the violations of the rule of law even more. There is a way to get rid of the oath under the Constitution and that includes getting unanimity agreement from provincial parliaments across Canada. Maybe they could be okay with the fact that Quebec wants to get rid of the oath itself, even if they decide they want the oath for themselves. So, there is a way, and that is why we have amendment formulas within the Constitution.”

During the election campaign, Plamondon pledged to go even further and abolish “whatever monarchy exists in Quebec.”

In its ruling, the Superior Court says nothing prevents the province from setting up a republic but that it must follow the rules laid out in the Constitution, including agreement from all provinces, the House of Commons and the Senate.

stories.title: Calgary budget talks begin as hundreds sign up for public hearing
stories.summary: Calgary has proposed a 15 per cent property tax increase for 2027, which is expected to cost in an extra $53 monthly when combined with waste, recycling and water fee increases.
stories.author: Adam MacVicar
stories.content:
Hundreds of Calgarians descended upon city hall Monday for a public hearing on city council’s proposed four-year budget, with deliberations on a potential 15 per cent property tax increase expected to last well into next week.

City officials confirmed more than 260 people were signed up to speak as of Monday afternoon to share their thoughts with city council on the proposed spending plan.

Among them was Merle Terleski, a former council candidate and current Bankview resident who said he is concerned with affordability and the potential impact a significant property tax increase could have on monthly expenses.

“Just because you own a house doesn’t mean you’re a multi-millionaire,” he told Global News. “A lot of people are scraping by, barely making their mortgages, so to give them another increase is just going to hurt families more in the city of Calgary.”

City administration has proposed a 15 per cent property tax increase in the budget’s first year, followed by increases of 10 per cent in 2028, 7.7 per cent in 2029 and 6 per cent in the budget’s final year in 2030.

As proposed, the budget would result in an extra $53 cost per month for the typical residential property assessed at the median of $688,000 in 2027, which includes an additional $16 monthly due to a proposed increase in waste and recycling fees as well as water bills.

Arthur Gallant, another Calgarian who spoke to city council Monday, said council needs to find efficiencies to lower the potential increases.

“I think there is a lot of good things in this budget,” he told Global News. “But at the same time, I think council is going to need to make some difficult decisions and prioritize what it is that Calgarians truly need.”

The property tax hike is set to help increase proposed city operational spending to nearly $6 billion in 2027, as well as a $21 billion four-year capital budget for city infrastructure.

City council will need to consider requests for funding boosts including more than $130 million over the next four years for the Calgary Police Service and $62 million next year for Calgary Transit to improve service.

The proposed budget also includes $284 million for recreation projects through the GamePLAN strategy, $420.2 million for road rehabilitation and close to $6.5 billion in water infrastructure projects.

“If council is serious about supporting public safety and serious about supporting essential infrastructure, some level of property tax increase will be required,” Calgary Mayor Jeromy Farkas said Monday. “That said, we need to strike the balance right. We need to make sure Calgary is affordable and competitive.”

Some councillors have already indicated they plan to bring forward amendments to find cuts throughout the budget, including Ward 1 Coun. Kim Tyers, who told reporters she will ask administration what reductions would be required to achieve a zero per cent tax increase next year.

“I think what we do is ask administration to go back to the drawing board,” she said. “They think it’s egregious to ask for zero per cent but I think Calgarians would appreciate showing what that would look like.”

Ward 7 Coun. Myke Atkinson, however, said that would be “irresponsible,” and noted the move would contribute to a trend of underinvestment in city infrastructure and services.

“Picking any random number and not thinking about the outcomes that delivers for Calgarians is a reckless way to budget,” he told reporters.

A contingent from the Calgary Alliance for the Common Good was also on hand Monday to urge council to keep social funding off the chopping block as well as increase funding for mental health supports and affordable housing.

According to the advocacy group, the proposed budget would only fund 10 per cent of the city’s annual target of 3,000 new affordable housing units.

“The people who are most vulnerable, we can’t have the budget cut on their backs,” said Kersi Bird, the group’s co-chair.

The public hearing is expected to last throughout the week, and then city councillors will ask questions of each city department.

Nearly 70 amendments to the budget have been drafted so far, city officials said, with more expected as the week continues.
