stories.title: Two cancer patients taking Ontario to court after requests for treatment in the U.S. denied
stories.summary: Government delays slowed down their requests at a critical time, patients say
stories.author: Tu Thanh Ha
stories.content:
Two cancer patients in dire need of treatment not available in Ontario alleged in court filings that the province misdirected their funding requests for novel out-of-country treatment, sending them into months of time-wasting administrative roadblocks.

Sabrina Apitz-Grossman and Kevin Nash, who have been told they have months to live, are challenging the province’s refusal to pay for therapies available in the United States that are not currently covered by public health insurance in Canada.

Their judicial applications will be heard jointly Tuesday morning at Toronto’s Osgoode Hall courthouse.

Ms. Apitz-Grossman has synovial sarcoma, a soft-tissue cancer that was first detected in her right leg which has spread to her lungs. In September 2025, she was told the median survival for her cancer ranges from 12 to 18 months.

Mr. Nash has melanoma, a skin cancer that has metastasized into his lungs and pancreas. He learned in January that the median life expectancy for people with his type of cancer is 2.75 to six months.

In their filings to the Ontario Superior Court, Ms. Apitz-Grossman and Mr. Nash said the letters rejecting their funding requests advised them they could appeal to the Health Services Appeal and Review Board.

However, earlier this year when they brought their cases before Hsarb, the government argued, successfully, that the board had no jurisdiction to order funding for a drug without a recommendation from Patrick Dicerni, the executive officer of the Ontario Public Drug Programs.

Ms. Apitz-Grossman and Mr. Nash applied to the court for a judicial review after Hsarb ruled in September that it couldn’t order funding for their treatments.

“Being misdirected to the Hsarb cost me months that I simply do not have to spare,” Ms. Apitz-Grossman, 31, of Toronto, said in a court affidavit.

Mr. Nash’s lawyers said a written legal argument that he was also misdirected and endured “a repeated pattern of delay, dead-ends, and disregard from Ontario.”

Their cases are the latest instances where Canadians who haven’t responded to conventional oncology seek access to the new personalized treatments that use drugs customized to each patients’ genetic profiles and tumours.

In September, the Ontario Superior Court of Justice sided with Alex Shved , a melanoma patient challenging the province’s refusal to cover treatment abroad.

However two weeks later, the government amended its regulation so that out-of-country drug funding would only be available if a medication is already insured in Ontario, but temporarily unavailable.

The regulation change was necessary to close “a back door for global pharmaceutical companies to avoid negotiating directly with the province to achieve more competitive pricing,” the government said in an October press release.

Questioned on Monday by the NDP, Health Minister Sylvia Jones told the legislature that she couldn’t comment on specific cases. She said funding denials are not political decisions but are “based on expert advice.”

Mr. Nash and Ms. Apitz-Grossman have said in their court filings that during the review of their funding applications, independent clinical experts were consulted and said the out-of-country therapy could help them. Their requests were ultimately turned down by Mr. Dicerni, the provincial drug program’s executive officer.

The two cancer patients were present at the legislature Monday. Sabrina Apitz-Grossman and Kevin Nash, who have been told they have months to live, are challenging the province’s refusal to pay for therapies available in the United States that are not currently covered by public health insurance in Canada.
Their judicial applications will be heard jointly Tuesday morning at Toronto’s Osgoode Hall courthouse.

Ms. Apitz-Grossman has synovial sarcoma, a soft-tissue cancer that was first detected in her right leg which has spread to her lungs. In September 2025, she was told the median survival for her cancer ranges from 12 to 18 months.

stories.title: Regina transit suspension leaves commuters stranded in freezing weather
stories.summary: Thousands of people were forced to find alternative transportation around the city after Regina transit workers were locked out Monday morning.
stories.author: Allison Bamford
stories.content:
Regina - Thousands of people were forced to find alternative transportation around the city after Regina transit workers were locked out Monday morning.

The city issued the lockout and shut down transit operations in response to escalating job action over the weekend.

“I was shocked because I felt like we had been bargaining in good faith,” said Pat Nichol, vice-president of Amalgamated Transit Union (ATU) Local 588.

The Union represents more than 380 transit workers who have been without a contract since December 2024.

On Friday, the transit union issued notice of an overtime ban that would prevent employees from working voluntary overtime.

The City of Regina determined transit would not be able to operate safely and reliably as a result of the ban.

“The decision to lock out the union was not taken lightly and is based on safety and service reliability concerns,” the city said in a statement.

“Regina Transit relies on a combination of regularly scheduled hours and voluntary overtime worked by bus operators to provide the full range of services to residents.”

The lockout comes at a crucial time for passengers as temperatures drop below zero. Patricia Prefontaine relies on the bus every day.

She has health issues with one of her feet and walking great distances is not an option. “This is affecting me greatly,” she told CTV News at a bus stop.

“There is no bus, so I am stuck downtown.”

‘A critical system’

Regina Transit averages roughly 25,000 passenger trips every day, according to Statistics Canada data. Like thousands of university students, Ethan Wiechert relies on the bus to get to and from campus.

“Buses are a crucial and critical system for our students to get to campus,” said Wiechert, president of the University of Regina Students’ Association.

As winter temperatures settle in, walking to class is not an ideal or feasible alternative, especially for those who live across the city.

Wiechert said many will not be able to afford ride-hailing and taxis long term.

“For those students who are not privileged enough to be able to use Uber or a taxi, what are the options for them?” he said.

Wiechert hitched a ride with a friend to campus on Monday and hopes to continue doing that until transit resumes.

Both sides were back at the bargaining table Monday afternoon.

Paratransit services are unaffected during the lockout. Standard routes, including high school routes, are suspended.

stories.title: Pentagon criticizes Canada in 'fact sheet' after Hegseth memo
stories.summary: The Pentagon has released a document that criticizes Canada’s defence spending, pointing to operational readiness deficits in air, land and sea operations.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Washington — The Pentagon has released what it calls a “fact sheet” criticizing Canada’s defence spending in the latest symbolic push from the Trump administration to upend long-standing norms in North American continental security.

“Unfortunately, Canada has yet to make the hard decisions and tradeoffs needed to put it on track to fulfill its Nato Defense Investment Pledge and become a credible partner in the defense of our shared continent,” said the document released publicly on Monday and first reported by Axios the day prior.

“Canada’s defense shortfalls speak for themselves.”

The document points to operational readiness deficits in air, land and sea operations. It denounces Canadian political leadership for pursuing “parochial economic and commercial interests over military optimization.”

It was released after U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth last week issued a classified memo imposing restrictions on military co-operation with Canada on think tanks and socializing.

Sen. Mike Rounds, a Republican, told reporters at the Halifax International Security Forum on Saturday that the move would not affect military operations.

Defence Minister David McGuinty’s office has not yet responded to a request for comment about the fact sheet. On Saturday at the security conference, McGuinty said it was “business as usual” between the Canadian and U.S. militaries.

He assured Canadians that co-operation between the two countries on defence, security and intelligence was continuing.

In response to Hegseth’s memo, chief Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said the defence department is “taking steps to ensure its engagements with Canada advance tangible U.S. defense objectives and ultimately support a reinvigorated defense relationship.”

The memo and Monday’s fact sheet are the latest moves the Pentagon has taken under the Trump administration to break norms with Canada.

In May, Elbridge Colby, U.S. undersecretary of defence for policy, said his department was pausing the Permanent Joint Board on Defense “to reassess how this forum benefits shared North American defence.”

The board was established in 1940 and is an advisory forum for U.S.-Canada bilateral defence co-operation.

At that time, a high-ranking U.S. defence official said the Pentagon gave Ottawa a classified paper laying out priorities for a collective North American defence pact with Canada, but that Ottawa did not deliver a “credible” response.

That same month, Canada announced it would purchase early warning planes from Sweden’s Saab rather than a competing option from Boeing.

This criticism of Canada’s defence readiness is not happening in a vacuum. Experts have said it’s likely connected to a planned purchase of F-35 fighter jets and ongoing tensions between the two countries.

The Liberal government has yet to reach a decision on its order of F-35 fighter jets from Lockheed Martin — which Pentagon officials have cited as a source of frustration. The fighter jet purchase has been the subject of a political review for more than a year.

“It is a major issue for them and a leverage point for us,” said former Conservative leader Erin O’Toole, who is also a distinguished fellow at the Washington-based Hudson Institute.

Canada has long faced criticism about its lagging defence spending, but with U.S. President Donald Trump’s return to the White House it was directly connected to larger trade issues, including the renewal of the Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement on trade, known as Cusma.

O’Toole said he was not surprised by the content of the fact sheet but, in a text message, he added that it “ignores everything in the last year.”

“This is like someone was asked to prepare a one-sided, negative summary without acknowledging any of the changes made in the last 18 months,” O’Toole said.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has made historic defence investments as Trump rattled the bilateral relationship with tariffs and threats of annexation.

Canada spent $63.4 billion on national defence in 2025, meeting its Nato commitment to spend two per cent of gross domestic product on defence for the first time.

Nato members met last year in The Hague and agreed to up defence spending to the equivalent of five per cent of GDP by 2035.

Ottawa has said Canada continues to accelerate its path to Nato’s new target of 3.5 per cent on core defence and is optimizing an additional 1.5 per cent of GDP spending on defence and security-related investments.

November’s federal budget laid out a plan to spend around four per cent of Canada’s gross domestic product on defence per year by the end of the decade — which includes the purchase of submarines, early warning jets and other capabilities.

But Carney has also faced domestic pressure about the lack of transparency around defence spending moving forward.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 23, 2026.

Kelly Geraldine Malone, The Canadian Press

He assured Canadians that co-operation between the two countries on defence, security and intelligence was continuing.

At that time, a high-ranking U.S. defence official said the Pentagon gave Ottawa a classified paper laying out priorities for a collective North American defence pact with Canada, but that Ottawa did not deliver a “credible” response.
That same month, Canada announced it would purchase early warning planes from Sweden’s Saab rather than a competing option from Boeing.

Canada spent $63.4 billion on national defence in 2025, meeting its Nato commitment to spend two per cent of gross domestic product on defence for the first time.
Nato members met last year in The Hague and agreed to up defence spending to the equivalent of five per cent of GDP by 2035.

Ottawa has said Canada continues to accelerate its path to Nato’s new target of 3.5 per cent on core defence and is optimizing an additional 1.5 per cent of GDP spending on defence and security-related investments.

November’s federal budget laid out a plan to spend around four per cent of Canada’s gross domestic product on defence per year by the end of the decade — which includes the purchase of submarines, early warning jets and other capabilities.

stories.title: Okanagan MLAs secure prominent positions in B.C. cabinet
stories.summary: Political science lecturer at the University of British Columbia Stewart Prest said having not one but two Okanagan voices in cabinet, where big decisions are made, is significant.
stories.author: Klaudia Van Emmerik
stories.content:
The Okanagan will have a significant presence around the B.C. cabinet table with a pair of Okanagan MLAs appointed to key ministerial portfolios in the province’s new Conservative government.

Among them is Kelowna-Mission MLA Gavin Dew , who has been named Minister of Economic Development and Tourism.

Dew says bringing the two areas together under one ministry creates an opportunity to support economic growth.

“Tourism is a really important economic driver. It’s a really important area of growth potential for us as a province, so having economic development and tourism tied together in one ministry is going to work very effectively,” Dew said.

He says one of his top priorities will be rebuilding confidence in B.C.’s economy by connecting directly with those who make investment decisions.

“Talking to people who are building businesses, talking to people who are creating jobs and giving them confidence that they have a government that is listening to them,” Dew said.

Also joining him at the cabinet table is Kelowna-Centre MLA Kristina Loewen, appointed as minister of Children and Family Development.

The appointments have drawn mixed reactions from local residents.

“I don’t know their background enough to know that they have the experience to cover that portfolio,” said one Kelowna resident.

While another welcomes the strong Okanagan representation.

I think it’s good… to have local representation at that level is a positive thing,” said another Kelowna resident.

Political science lecturer at the University of British Columbia Stewart Prest said having not one, but two Okanagan voices in cabinet, where big decisions are made, is significant.

“That’s a significant achievement for Kelowna and ensures that the interests of the Okanagan are going to be front and center for any debate,” Prest said. “If something matters to the Okanagan and those MLAs hear about it, it’s going to find its way to cabinet, so there is an automatic conduit for information.”

Prest added that the interests of the Okanagan will go beyond just the two portfolios.

“Somebody is there thinking about the Okanagan, saying, “How is this policy, how is this initiative, how is it going to matter to Kelowna, to the region and so that brings that lens to every issue that comes in front of government,” Prest said.

Loewen’s appointment comes as the results of the Kelowna-Centre riding remain subject to a judicial recount.

The recount got underway Monday morning behind closed doors at the Ramada Hotel.

It marks a repeat of the process following the 2024 election, when Loewen and NDP candidate Loyal Wooldridge were involved in a judicial recount.

Loewen ultimately retained her seat following that recount and has expressed confidence on social media that the outcome will be the same this time around.

“So a judicial recount will be ordered but, last time, it changed Nothing at all. I feel confident that that will hold once again,” Loewen posted on X on November 8.

Loewen and Wooldridge were only 43 votes apart in the latest election, 4o votes apart in 2024.

stories.author: Kelly Geraldine Malone
stories.content:

stories.title: Regina residents left without bus service as city locks out transit workers
stories.summary: Thousands of commuters left without bus service as city imposes lockout of about 380 transit workers
stories.author: Jeremy Simes
stories.content:
Thousands of commuters who rely on transit in Regina were without bus service Monday as workers and the city hit an impasse over a new contract.

The city imposed a lockout of about 380 transit workers days after the Amalgamated Transit Union Local 588 said employees would take job action by not working voluntary overtime.

The city says the lockout is a matter of public safety and ensuring timely service, because it doesn’t want to risk residents waiting in the cold for a bus that might not come.

But the union says the city could have readjusted schedules to keep buses running.

“I think this is absolutely appalling that the city took these draconian measures while leaving (commuters) stranded,” John Di Nino, the union’s national president, told reporters.

“This is not the respect that transit workers deserve, not in this city or not in any city across the nation.”

More than 150 workers gathered outside the city’s transit operations centre Monday to protest the lockout. They held signs urging a fair contract and waved flags while trucks and cars driving by honked their horns.

“When do we want it?” shouted John Callahan, an international vice-president with the union, while members gathered around him.

“Now!” workers shouted back.

Thousands of commuters who rely on transit in Regina were without bus service Monday as workers and the city hit an impasse over a new contract. The city’s imposed a lockout of about…

Di Nino said the union was scheduled to meet with the city later in the afternoon for negotiations.

“If they come to the table with a reasonable offer, we’re prepared to go back and provide the service, as long as they open up the gates and let us go and do our work,” he said.

Pat Nichol, the vice-president with the local union, said the sticking point in negotiations is wages. Workers are asking for a top-up in pay that matches the rate of inflation, she said.

“It’s a sad thing when we have members that have to go use the food bank to feed their families,” she said.

“This used to be a job that somebody would be able to have and raise a family on, and now that’s not the case any more.”

The city said in a statement that it wants to negotiate a fair contract with the union.

“The decision to lock out the union was not taken lightly and is based on safety and service reliability concerns,” it said.

“Even if the city had taken no further action, the (union’s) withdrawal of voluntary overtime would have had significant impacts on transit service.”

Had drivers not worked overtime, it said, the city would have had to cancel 25 per cent of routes, including high school services and a special shuttle for Canadian Western Agribition, a cattle show.

“The city would not be able to let residents know which routes were impacted in advance,” it said.

The city added that maintenance would also have been affected. Without overtime, the city couldn’t have guaranteed buses were safe and reliable to operate, it said.

Nichol said the city could have kept buses running without overtime, citing schedule changes it made during the COVID-19 pandemic, including shorter routes.

“We didn’t have to be locked out,” she said.

Di Nino took aim at Mayor Chad Bachynski and city council for not stepping in.

“(Council) should be giving them the directive to get this issue resolved, put our members back onto the job and get transit running in this city,” he said.

Bachynski said in a statement the union and the city need to come to the bargaining table before service can restart and that council won’t interfere in labour negotiations.

“We all want service restored as soon as possible,” he said.

Meanwhile, some residents have taken it into their own hands to help people who rely on the bus.

Thom Hamilton has created a website, called No Fare!, to connect people with free rides. Hamilton said he’s heard concerns from business owners worried their staff won’t be able to make it into work without the bus.

“I put together a site with no real intention other than to try and help people out that might be struggling while this disruption happens,” he said.

“If they come to their senses and they’re able to come to an agreement, I’d love it if it never had to be used .”

At the protest Monday, Di Nino said workers picked up people from bus stops earlier in the day to give them rides at no cost.

Workers at the protest also said the lockout came at an ironic time, as the city had originally scheduled a pancake breakfast for employee appreciation.

“Where’s my pancakes?” one worker shouted, in jest, at the gathering.

stories.title: Mississauga family spent just over $1,000 to power home and two electric cars in 2025
stories.summary: With heating costs expected to peak during Canada’s coldest months, one Mississauga family says it managed to cover its home and transportation energy costs for approximately $1,100 in 2025.
stories.author: Joseph Ryan
stories.content:
By Loveen Gill, Omni News

Posted November 23, 2026 6:10 pm.

Mississauga, Ont. — With heating costs expected to peak during Canada’s coldest months, one Mississauga family says it managed to cover its home and transportation energy costs for approximately $1,100 in 2025.

Harminder Dhillon and Jyoti Grewal have gone to considerable lengths to reduce their reliance on conventional energy sources. They have installed rooftop solar panels, disconnected their natural gas service, replaced conventional heating and cooling equipment with heat pumps, switched to an induction stove and replaced gasoline-powered vehicles with two electric cars.

The couple says solar generation helps offset their electricity costs, bringing their reported annual energy spending to about $92 a month. Canadian households spent an average of $4,943 on energy in 2023, according to Natural Resources Canada’s Energy Fact Book 2025–2026 . That included approximately $2,376 for residential energy and $2,567 for fuels used in vehicles and other equipment.

Dhillon and Grewal’s reported $1,100 expenditure is approximately 78 per cent lower than that national average — a difference of about $3,843 annually.

The figures are from different years and are not a direct comparison between equivalent households. Energy costs vary depending on the size of a home, driving distances, local rates and individual consumption. The couple’s figure also excludes the upfront cost of purchasing electric vehicles and installing solar panels and other equipment.

Still, their experience illustrates how household energy bills can change when a family combines energy-efficient technology with its own electricity generation.

For Dhillon, an engineer who later became a criminal lawyer, the transformation began with concerns about climate change rather than an effort to reduce household expenses.

“For me, it was purely a climate-change perspective,” Dhillon said. “Our entire house is electrified.”

He says his interest in climate change began about 25 years ago, when he started reading about international climate agreements and the environmental consequences of burning fossil fuels.

Over time, he began examining how much his family depended on fossil fuels, from heating their home and preparing meals to everyday transportation.

About three years ago, the couple made some of their biggest changes, installing solar panels and disconnecting their natural gas service.

The transformation required an initial financial investment, but Dhillon argues that homeowners should consider the long-term operating costs of the equipment they purchase.

He says his heat pump cost approximately $10,000, an amount he considers comparable to what he would have spent replacing both a conventional furnace and an air conditioner.

Ontario’s Home Renovation Savings program offers rebates for qualifying heat pump installations, although eligibility and rebate amounts depend on factors including the home’s existing heating system and the equipment installed.

Dhillon encourages homeowners to explore heat pumps when their heating or cooling systems need replacing, rather than automatically purchasing another conventional system.

He offers similar advice to drivers considering their next vehicle, suggesting they compare electric options with gasoline-powered models.

The family’s changes extend beyond energy bills.

For Grewal, who enjoys cooking, switching from gas to induction meant challenging a common belief about preparing traditional Indian meals.

“I am fond of cooking, and I cook a lot,” she said. “I used to hear Indian cooking can’t be done well on an electric stove, which is not true.”

She also buys locally grown produce during Ontario’s growing season and freezes it for use throughout the winter.

“We have the best garlic here, and saag (rapini), tomatoes, and I have all of that produce saved up to use in winter,” she said.

The family also uses cloth napkins and reusable utensils instead of disposable alternatives.

“To use something once and throw it away just for a little convenience creates so much garbage,” Grewal said. “It is disrespectful to the Earth.”

“Sustainability is modern,” she added.

Their household choices come at a time when both the cost of living and the financial consequences of climate change are concerns for Canadians. Dhillon worries that increasingly severe weather could add further pressure to food prices, home insurance, and household expenses.

For Dhillon and Grewal, the goal is not to suggest that every family must make all these changes at once. They hope their experience encourages others to consider practical alternatives when replacing appliances, heating equipment, or vehicles.

And while their energy bills have become a remarkable part of their story, Dhillon says his greatest motivation remains the world he will leave to his children.

“My living should not ruin the only planet we have,” he said. “I shouldn’t leave the planet in a worse shape for my children than what I got from my parents.”

stories.title: B.C. man charged with murder in actor Stewart McLean’s death
stories.summary: Nathan Neima, 35, of New Westminster, B.C., was arrested on Saturday and charged with second-degree murder
stories.author: Nono Shen
stories.content:
News that a Metro Vancouver man has been charged with second-degree murder in the death of British Columbia actor Stewart McLean is a “big relief” to everyone in the entertainment industry, said actor and acting coach Jeff Seymour.

Seymour said he was anxious to follow information released on the case on Monday.

“But at this point, I’m just pleased that he wasn’t forgotten that they pursued this, that they had due diligence. They did their work, and I have all the respect in the world for these people that did this,” Seymour said, referring to police, in an interview from Los Angeles on Monday.

Nathan Neima, 35, of New Westminster, B.C., was arrested Saturday and appeared in provincial court in North Vancouver on Monday and another court appearance on a procedural matter was set for Jan. 6.

Seymour said he met Stewart through one of his acting classes a decade ago and they became friends.

McLean was someone that he could call any time to share joys and sorrows, and now he finds himself thinking about picking up the phone to call his friend to share some news, Seymour said.

He said McLean’s death had been “eating away” at him.

“There was nothing nefarious about Stew’s life. He was adored. He didn’t cross lines. He wasn’t involved in shady dealings or people,” said Seymour, “When someone who just has a pristine life is suddenly murdered, it’s just so confounding.”

McLean, 45, who appeared on series such as Virgin River and Murder in a Small Town , was reported missing on May 18 after he was last seen at his home in Lions Bay, north of Vancouver.

Cpl. Esther Tupper of the Integrated Homicide Investigation Team said Monday that officers believe the death was targeted.

While the men weren’t strangers, she wouldn’t say how they knew each other.

“However, the details of their exact relationship is going to form part of the evidence in court and so those details will emerge at that time,” said Tupper.

Neima does not have a criminal record, she said.

Seymour said Neima’s arrest also raised more questions, including why his friend was killed.

Word of the criminal charge travelled quickly through the acting community, but no one in Stewart’s circle of friends in Vancouver has ever heard about the accused before, Seymour said.

Squamish RCMP said in May that the homicide team took over the case after officers found evidence that McLean was killed.

His remains were found days later in the Lions Bay area.

Tupper said investigators want to extend their gratitude to residents of Lions Bay for assisting them with the investigation.

“I know that it did take several months, however, these homicide files are very lengthy,” said Tupper.

“I hope that this brings some measure of peace that we’ve located and charged an individual with this really tragic and senseless act of violence.”

She said the investigation also included speaking with people within the film community, “and everyone who they did speak to was very helpful.”

Tributes flooded social media after the news of his death broke in May.

Jennifer Lee, an agent with Vancouver’s Lucas Talent Inc., said after the death that she had the pleasure of working with McLean starting in 2014, and he was “the most positive, kind, funny, chill” person you could ever know.

McLean’s credits also included CW’s Arrow and Netflix’s Travelers .

Seymour said the fondest memories were of McLean flying out to visit him in Los Angeles.

“Good friends are hard to find these days,” said Seymour, “And he is sorely missed.”

McLean was someone that he could call any time to share joys and sorrows, and now he finds himself thinking about picking up the phone to call his friend to share some news, Seymour said.
He said McLean’s death had been “eating away” at him.

“There was nothing nefarious about Stew’s life. He was adored. He didn’t cross lines. He wasn’t involved in shady dealings or people,” said Seymour, “When someone who just has a pristine life is suddenly murdered, it’s just so confounding.”
McLean, 45, who appeared on series such as Virgin River and Murder in a Small Town , was reported missing on May 18 after he was last seen at his home in Lions Bay, north of Vancouver.
Cpl. Esther Tupper of the Integrated Homicide Investigation Team said Monday that officers believe the death was targeted.
While the men weren’t strangers, she wouldn’t say how they knew each other.
“However, the details of their exact relationship is going to form part of the evidence in court and so those details will emerge at that time,” said Tupper.
Neima does not have a criminal record, she said.
Seymour said Neima’s arrest also raised more questions, including why his friend was killed.
Word of the criminal charge travelled quickly through the acting community, but no one in Stewart’s circle of friends in Vancouver has ever heard about the accused before, Seymour said.
Squamish RCMP said in May that the homicide team took over the case after officers found evidence that McLean was killed.
His remains were found days later in the Lions Bay area.
Tupper said investigators want to extend their gratitude to residents of Lions Bay for assisting them with the investigation.
“I know that it did take several months, however, these homicide files are very lengthy,” said Tupper.
“I hope that this brings some measure of peace that we’ve located and charged an individual with this really tragic and senseless act of violence.”
She said the investigation also included speaking with people within the film community, “and everyone who they did speak to was very helpful.”
Tributes flooded social media after the news of his death broke in May.

Jennifer Lee, an agent with Vancouver’s Lucas Talent Inc., said after the death that she had the pleasure of working with McLean starting in 2014, and he was “the most positive, kind, funny, chill” person you could ever know.
McLean’s credits also included CW’s Arrow and Netflix’s Travelers .
Seymour said the fondest memories were of McLean flying out to visit him in Los Angeles.
“Good friends are hard to find these days,” said Seymour, “And he is sorely missed.”

stories.title: Doug Ford, Danielle Smith tout potential pipeline partnership but point fingers on interprovincial trade
stories.summary: Alberta Premier chides Ontario counterpart for barely stocking any booze from her province at joint Q&A in Toronto
stories.author: Jeff Gray
stories.content:
Ontario Premier Doug Ford and Alberta Premier Danielle Smith mostly presented a united front on Monday as the two leaders touted the still-embryonic concept of a new cross-country pipeline but pointed fingers over foot-dragging on interprovincial trade barriers.

The pair appeared together at a downtown Toronto business luncheon organized by the Toronto Region Board of Trade and the Calgary Chamber of Commerce, where they were questioned onstage by CTV chief financial correspondent Amanda Lang.

The two premiers shared a stage at a similar event in Calgary in September, and are usually eager to show unity and talk pipelines. But in the face of tariffs and annexation threats from U.S. President Donald Trump, they have often taken different approaches. Some have dubbed Mr. Ford “Captain Canada” for his confrontational tack, while Ms. Smith has urged a more conciliatory tone. The U.S. tariffs have targeted Ontario’s key auto and steel sectors, while recent rising oil prices have benefited Alberta.

On Monday, Ms. Smith praised Mr. Ford for his “outspoken support” for Alberta’s oil and gas sector and for his “visionary” idea for a “Northern Shield” pipeline that would run from Alberta to Ontario. Mr. Ford said his proposed pipeline, which he has in the past suggested could be funded by Ontario taxpayers, would provide energy security and allow for larger oil and gas reserves.

The initiative, which is undergoing a feasibility study, has buy-in from Alberta and Saskatchewan but not Manitoba. Mr. Ford said he recently spoke to Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew, who told him he was “very, very close” on the pipeline idea, but was focused on a proposal to upgrade the Arctic Port of Churchill .

Mr. Ford and Ms. Smith briefly aired differences on measures to lower interprovincial trade barriers, something governments and business leaders have focused on as a counterweight to the tariffs imposed by Mr. Trump.

Some economic studies have said these barriers – which include differing rules for doctors and divergent standards for everything from food to trucks – cost Canada’s economy as much as $200-billion a year. While provinces and the federal government have all pledged to lower them, actual progress has been slow.

Asked by Ms. Lang why Alberta was insisting on various exemptions to interprovincial trade rules, Ms. Smith responded with a shot at Ontario – and said the gritty details of actually lowering barriers are complicated.

She said Alberta has a “free enterprise” system for stocking alcohol shelves that allows in more than 1,000 Ontario products. Meanwhile, Ontario, she added, has a “monopoly system” that stocks just 53 products from Alberta.

“So we can say all we want, ‘Yeah, we want to have free trade.’ But you have to get down to the purchasing decisions of the individual agency and how much shelf space they have,” Ms. Smith said.

Mr. Ford did not directly address Ms. Smith’s criticism of the Liquor Control Board of Ontario’s purchasing monopoly, but pointed to his changes that have allowed alcohol sales in corner stores.

He boasted that Ontario was the only province to drop all of its exceptions to interprovincial trade rules and said other provinces were insisting on maintaining some of them, including Quebec.

The Ontario Premier also repeated his calls, made in recent months, for an end to the federal requirement for provinces to have industrial carbon pricing systems, saying that Ontario’s steel and auto industries face an existential threat from U.S. tariffs.

Ms. Smith would not go so far as Mr. Ford on the industrial levy. She said Alberta’s system has been in place since 2007 and is applied differently than in other provinces. She said provincial governments should make their own deals with Ottawa.

Mr. Ford has previously said he wanted Ottawa to allow exemptions for “tariff-impacted sectors.” In a letter to Prime Minister Mark Carney in August, Mr. Ford said Ontario was considering such a move and called on Mr. Carney to “accelerate these efforts.” Any changes to Ontario’s system must align with Ottawa’s rules.

These industrial pricing systems are separate from the former consumer carbon price, which was imposed by the government of Justin Trudeau and repealed by Mr. Carney.

stories.title: Pentagon releases ‘fact sheet’ criticizing Canada’s defence spending
stories.summary: Ottawa’s decisions limit ability to contribute to protection of North America, Pentagon claims
stories.author: Kelly Geraldine Malone
stories.content:
The Trump administration is cranking up the pressure on Ottawa to increase defence spending and complete a deal to buy U.S.-made fighter jets by issuing a new “fact sheet” deriding the Canadian military’s lack of operational readiness.

The Pentagon posted the document online Monday, two weeks after U.S. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth wrote a memo that reportedly puts restrictions on American military personnel attending Canadian conferences and social events.

The missive accuses Canada of having no concrete plan to increase defence spending to 5 per cent of GDP by 2035, as the country agreed to at last year’s Nato summit in The Hague. It also slams Ottawa for taking nearly two decades to reach the previous Nato target of 2 per cent of GDP and highlights the capability shortfalls of Canada’s Army, Navy and Air Force.

“Underinvestment in defense has atrophied the Canadian Armed Forces and limited Canada’s ability to contribute to the defense of North America,” the document says.

It cites the impending retirement of Canada’s fleet of CF-18 fighter jets and Ottawa’s decision last year to review a plan to buy 88 F-35s from Lockheed Martin.

Prime Minister Mark Carney put the brakes on the purchase when U.S. President Donald Trump launched a trade war on Canada, hammering the country with tariffs and threatening to annex it as the “51st state.”

“Ottawa’s prioritization of parochial economic and commercial interests over military optimization introduces further uncertainty for Norad and will further burden our Joint Force and the American taxpayer,” the Pentagon’s missive says.

The office of Defence Minister David McGuinty did not respond to a request for comment on the fact sheet late Monday.

The document also cites Canada’s lack of airborne early warning and control aircraft and says just one of Canada’s four Victoria-class submarines is seaworthy at any time.

The Washington Post reported Friday that Mr. Hegseth had written the memo the week before last, placing new “restrictions” on the U.S.-Canada defence relationship. But The Globe and Mail reported that neither the Canadian government nor military had been told anything about it.

This past weekend, at the Halifax International Security Forum, Republican Senator Mike Rounds said the memo just required U.S. military personnel to receive approval from their bosses before taking part in events with their Canadian counterparts. He said it did not change anything about actual military co-operation.

“They’re basically limiting some social engagements and they’re asking people to get permission before they come in and do think tanks and so forth,” he said. “We don’t expect any real changes over the way it has been going for the last year or a year and a half.”

The Trump administration had already been blocking officials from attending the Halifax confab since last year.

Earlier this year, the U.S. suspended its participation in the Permanent Joint Board on Defense, an advisory body that it has run with Canada since the Second World War to make recommendations on military planning.

The dispute over military spending has long pitted the U.S. against its Nato allies and has become a central grievance during the Trump administration. In Canada’s case, it has also become bound up with the trade war and bilateral negotiations, which have included discussions of national security as well as commerce.

Canada and other Nato countries signed the 2-per-cent pledge in 2006 and again in 2014. But Ottawa was slow to meet the target. In 2024, then-prime minister Justin Trudeau dismissed it as a “crass mathematical calculation” that wouldn’t “actually make us automatically safer.”

When Mr. Carney took over last year, he boosted funding by more than $80-billion over five years and, this past March, Nato reported that Canada had finally hit the promised spending number. The Prime Minister and every other Nato country but Spain also agreed to Mr. Trump’s new 5-per-cent-by-2035 figure.

So far, however, Mr. Carney’s government has not explained how it will reach that goal, which would entail devoting 3.5 per cent of GDP to core military spending and another 1.5 per cent to security- and defence-related infrastructure.

The 2026 budget released in early November offered few details. It said Canada’s core defence spending will climb to 2.2 per cent this fiscal year, then remain at 2.6 per cent for four years.

The government has played down questions about the imperative to boost defence spending, saying it has plenty of years left before the Nato deadline to increase military expenditure.

With a report from The Associated Press

The office of Defence Minister David McGuinty did not respond to a request for comment on the fact sheet late Monday.
The document also cites Canada’s lack of airborne early warning and control aircraft and says just one of Canada’s four Victoria-class submarines is seaworthy at any time.

The Washington Post reported Friday that Mr. Hegseth had written the memo the week before last, placing new “restrictions” on the U.S.-Canada defence relationship. But The Globe and Mail reported that neither the Canadian government nor military had been told anything about it.

This past weekend, at the Halifax International Security Forum, Republican Senator Mike Rounds said the memo just required U.S. military personnel to receive approval from their bosses before taking part in events with their Canadian counterparts. He said it did not change anything about actual military co-operation.

“They’re basically limiting some social engagements and they’re asking people to get permission before they come in and do think tanks and so forth,” he said. “We don’t expect any real changes over the way it has been going for the last year or a year and a half.”
The Trump administration had already been blocking officials from attending the Halifax confab since last year.

Earlier this year, the U.S. suspended its participation in the Permanent Joint Board on Defense, an advisory body that it has run with Canada since the Second World War to make recommendations on military planning.

The dispute over military spending has long pitted the U.S. against its Nato allies and has become a central grievance during the Trump administration. In Canada’s case, it has also become bound up with the trade war and bilateral negotiations, which have included discussions of national security as well as commerce.

Canada and other Nato countries signed the 2-per-cent pledge in 2006 and again in 2014. But Ottawa was slow to meet the target. In 2024, then-prime minister Justin Trudeau dismissed it as a “crass mathematical calculation” that wouldn’t “actually make us automatically safer.”

When Mr. Carney took over last year, he boosted funding by more than $80-billion over five years and, this past March, Nato reported that Canada had finally hit the promised spending number. The Prime Minister and every other Nato country but Spain also agreed to Mr. Trump’s new 5-per-cent-by-2035 figure.

So far, however, Mr. Carney’s government has not explained how it will reach that goal, which would entail devoting 3.5 per cent of GDP to core military spending and another 1.5 per cent to security- and defence-related infrastructure.
The 2026 budget released in early November offered few details. It said Canada’s core defence spending will climb to 2.2 per cent this fiscal year, then remain at 2.6 per cent for four years.
The government has played down questions about the imperative to boost defence spending, saying it has plenty of years left before the Nato deadline to increase military expenditure.

stories.title: New act allows Alberta step in on natural gas pipelines — if private sector falls short
stories.summary: The proposed Natural Gas Infrastructure Act does not in itself create new Crown entities to plan or invest in pipelines — but gives the province the ability to do so, if necessary.
stories.author: Lauren Krugel
stories.content:
The Alberta government has introduced legislation that would enable it to take a greater role in pushing forward new natural gas pipelines — as a last resort, if the private sector fails to do so — setting the scene for a potential showdown with the industry’s dominant player.

Brian Jean, the minister of energy and minerals, says Alberta has an “unbelievable” amount of natural gas in the ground, but pipeline capacity to get that gas to customers is increasingly becoming a “constraint to growth” amid booming demand from data centres, the oilsands and other industries in the province.

The backbone of Alberta’s existing natural gas system is TC Energy’s Ngtl , or Nova Gas Transmission Ltd., network, which has been in operation for almost 70 years and started out as a government entity.

TC Energy plans to grow the network that’s the backbone of Alberta’s existing natural gas system, but the province is preparing in case

The company recently announced expansion plans for that system , but Jean says it’s fully subscribed until 2029 and there is uncertainty around capacity additions beyond 2030.

In a letter dated Saturday and obtained by The Canadian Press, TC Energy CEO François Poirier warns Alberta Premier Danielle Smith that the proposed legislation could undermine the company’s planned investments, “create significant market instability” and lead to duplication.

The proposed Natural Gas Infrastructure Act does not in itself create new Crown entities to plan or invest in natural gas pipelines, but gives the province the ability to do so if necessary.

Jean called the it “proactive legislation.”

“It gives Alberta the ability to plan for tomorrow instead of waiting for private industry to completely determine all of our opportunities,” he told reporters Monday.

Jean said he’s encouraged by TC Energy’s announcement on Nov. 16 that it’s planning to expand the Ngtl system, including with a new 370-kilometre pipeline connecting gas to the oilsands region.

Poirier wrote in his letter that representatives from TC met with government officials Nov. 19 to walk them through the company’s expansion plans, and were told the province intended to go ahead with the proposed legislative changes, details of which were leaked to media in November.

The Alberta cabinet report, first reported on by The Narwhal and later viewed by The Canadian Press, said TC’s dominant position as a natural gas shipper in Alberta has led to a “market failure” that has left key growth regions unable to access gas.

The report included a recommendation that the province create two Crown corporations to spur new natural gas transmission lines.

It flagged court challenges from TC and potentially Atco Gas and Pipelines Ltd. as “legal considerations.”

“We are concerned the government’s proposed policy direction could have significant, material and negative consequences for Albertans,” Poirier wrote in the letter.

“As the government’s own analysis acknowledged in the now-public cabinet brief, it could result, among other things, in increased costs for Alberta families and businesses and expose taxpayers to significant financial risk.”

Jean said TC should not take the legislation as a threat or an ultimatum, but that the government’s goal is to act in the best interests of Albertans.

stories.title: Station 20 West appeals Saskatoon order to dismantle encampment
stories.summary: Station 20 West has appealed the City of Saskatoon's order to clean up an encampment on its property by the end of this month, according to its director.
stories.author: Tavi Dhillon
stories.content:
The group behind a tent encampment in Saskatoon that was ordered to come down is refusing to dismantle the encampment until long-term housing for residents can be secured.

Station 20 West was handed an Order to Remedy Contravention from the City of Saskatoon earlier this month . That notice, dated Oct. 30, told the organization it must clear the encampment from its 20th Street property by Nov. 30.

In response to that letter, Wanda Martin, director of Station 20 West, said the encampment would not be removed without a conversation with the city that results in a long-term solution for those living on the property.

On Monday, Martin told reporters she stands by those comments.

“We have appealed. We are complying to the very best of our ability in terms of fire, in terms of cleanliness, in terms of drug use, we are working with the people,” she said.

If Station 20 West’s appeal is denied, the city will be allowed to move in and take down the encampment. Martin noted that she hopes that will not be the case after she speaks with City of Saskatoon officials about finding appropriate housing.

“We don’t see the benefit of moving these tents. We don’t know where they would go, except to some other private property,” she continued. “These aren’t just tents. We’re talking about real people here.”

Station 20 West had not heard back on the status of its appeal of the city order as of Monday morning, Martin said.

In a statement to Global News, the City of Saskatoon said it is the responsibility of Station 20 West to comply with all relevant bylaws.

“The City’s approach to encampments has consistently focused on connecting individuals with available supports and services while addressing significant health and safety concerns for people staying in encampments, for neighbouring residents, businesses and the broader community,” the city said.

“The City remains committed to working with community partners to support vulnerable individuals and to uphold its responsibility to maintain safe public spaces.”

It added that the Saskatoon Fire Department does not publicly discuss operations that May require bylaw enforcement.

stories.title: Bains defends record as PCs prepare attack ads linking him to Trudeau
stories.summary: New Ontario Liberal leader calls it ‘a huge honour’ to have served in Justin Trudeau’s cabinet
stories.author: Laura Stone
stories.content:
Navdeep Bains says he’s proud of his record as a former federal cabinet minister, as Doug Ford’s Progressive Conservatives prepare attack ads linking the new Ontario Liberal Leader to ex-prime minister Justin Trudeau.

Mr. Ford criticized Mr. Bains, who served as industry minister, accusing him of supporting the federal carbon price that the Premier said hurt working people.

“You were the right-hand person to Justin Trudeau under the ministry of industry, and you wanted to slap on the carbon tax. You wanted to hurt the hard-working people of Ontario, you wanted to hurt companies, drive investment out of the country,” Mr. Ford told CTV News on Monday.

Mr. Bains, who was narrowly chosen as party leader over the weekend, appeared at the provincial legislature on Monday alongside his 14-member caucus. He is the third party leader elected since 2020 who doesn’t have a seat.

The former five-term MP from Mississauga worked as a senior executive at Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce and Rogers Communications before resigning from the telecommunications company to run for the provincial leadership earlier this spring.

Mr. Bains said Monday his focus is on creating opportunities for those in the province who are struggling, and that his team is united.

“The ultimate goal is to replace this out-of-touch and corrupt Conservative government, and this Premier who just is so preoccupied by his friends and his donors,” he said.

The PCs, however, wasted no time linking Mr. Bains to the previous Liberal government and Mr. Trudeau’s consumer carbon price, which was repealed by Prime Minister Mark Carney on his first day in office in March 2025 after Mr. Trudeau resigned.

The PC Party is preparing to launch a digital ad campaign in the coming weeks, followed by an increase in traditional television and radio ads in the new year, according to a senior party source. The Globe and Mail is not naming the source as they are not authorized to speak publicly about internal discussions.

The source declined to say how much the party planned to spend. The PC Party did not respond to a request for comment.

Mr. Bains has already said he expects the PCs to go after him: “Look, they’re going to attack me. They’re going to go negative. That’s not a surprise. They would do that with whoever won,” he told reporters Saturday after he clinched the leadership.

The PC party also spent millions on pre-election ads targeting former Ontario Liberal leader Bonnie Crombie in the lead-up to the February 2025 campaign.

Energy Minister Stephen Lecce on Monday called Mr. Bains “the architect of the carbon tax.”

“We don’t need to reimpose the Trudeau legacy on the people of Ontario,” Mr. Lecce told reporters.

Mr. Bains, however, said he’s proud of his record as industry minister, a portfolio then called innovation, which he held for six years until 2021.

“It was a huge honour and privilege to serve in cabinet as industry minister, fighting for jobs, fighting for economic growth. I’m so proud of the track record that we put forward that made Canada one of the fastest-growing countries in the G7 in terms of economic growth,” he said on Monday.

He added that he hadn’t heard from Mr. Carney since he won the leadership, but that the Prime Minister’s chief of staff and others on his team had been in touch. He said that Mr. Trudeau sent him a “nice message” about his victory.

Jonathan Rose, a political studies professor at Queen’s University, said it’s a standard move for political parties to attempt to define a new opponent.

He said the link with Mr. Trudeau could have an impact. “I think it could be effective, but of course the problem with this is it’s about timelines. The election’s not going to be held for years,” he said.

“What it does do, I think effectively, is plant the seed about who this guy is.”

The Ontario Liberals released their own digital ad on Monday, which features Mr. Bains as well as citizens voicing concerns about the provincial government.

Ontario NDP Leader Marit Stiles, who released her own digital ad about affordability last week, told reporters Monday she was “not beholden to any corporate interests,” a reference to Mr. Bains’s time as a Rogers executive.

Mr. Ford called Mr. Bains the “king lobbyist” at Rogers, referring to his time as chief corporate affairs officer.

Two of Mr. Bains’s fellow leadership contenders, MPPs Lee Fairclough and Stephanie Bowman, were at the legislature on Monday and took turns asking questions of the government. Both received a standing ovation from all parties.

stories.title: Thamesford Man Charged in Thames Centre
stories.summary: The Middlesex OPP conducted a Ride Program and caught a driver trying to avoid the checkpoint.
stories.author: Kyle Freel
stories.content:
News Home

Monday, 23 November 2026 at 17:20

By Kyle Freel X @KFreelHeartFM

Share on Facebook

Share on Messenger

Share on Messenger

The Middlesex OPP conducted a RIDE Program and caught a driver trying to avoid the checkpoint.

THAMES CENTRE - A Thamesford man is facing charges in Thames Centre.

Yesterday, just after midnight, the Middlesex OPP conducted a RIDE program, and a vehicle tried to avoid the checkpoint.

A traffic stop was conducted, and the OPP cruiser sustained minor damage. As a result, a 44-year-old was charged with operation while impaired by alcohol, operation while impaired with a blood alcohol concentration of 80 plus, and dangerous operation.

He is set to appear in a London Courtroom next month.

WPS Briefs - Nov. 23rd, 2026 The Woodstock Police are looking for a vehicle from a hit-and-run and have also recovered a stolen vehicle.

PJHL Recap - Nov 20th to Nov 22nd The Tavistock Braves are no longer on top of the Doherty Division standings.

Navy Vets Recap - Nov 20th to Nov 22nd The Navy Vets lost to the Vipers 2-1 on Friday and fell to the Cyclones 5-4 in overtime on Sunday.

Theatre Woodstock Presents: A Christmas Story The classic holiday film from 1983 will be brought to life on stage.

Home Stretch for United Way Ultimate Burger Battle You have until November 30th to try one of the unique burgers and support United Way Oxford.

2026 Sharing Guide Released United Way Oxford has released the Sharing Guide as the holiday season is upon us.

Woodstock City Council Recap - Nov. 20th, 2026 Two topics dominated the first City Council meeting of the new term.

PJHL Preview - Nov 20th to Nov 22nd The Braves and the Merchants have one game scheduled for this weekend, while the Trojans have two.

Navy Vets Preview - Nov 20th to Nov 22nd Woodstock will host LaSalle tonight and visit Listowel on Sunday.

Woodstonian Shines a Light on Pancreatic Cancer Awareness Bernadette Hewitt was diagnosed with pancreatic cancer in June 2022, three weeks after he father received the same diagnosis.

Fatal Crash Investigation in Woodstock An 87-year-old has died after a vehicle left the roadway and rolled over Tuesday afternoon.

Festive RIDE Campaign Begins! Police officers across the province will be on the lookout for impaired drivers this holiday season.

RRT Shows Appreciation to Woodingford Lodge Staff Eight volunteers served 200 lunches to Woodingford Lodge staff members on November 5th.

Ingersoll Christmas Parade Celebrates 29 Years! The holiday tradition will get underway at 11:00 a.m. on Saturday.

Christmas Place Returns this Holiday Season The Christmas Place gives families in need the opportunity to shop through donated gifts for significantly reduced prices.

Oxford Youth Invitational Robotics Challenge Today Each team had to build an autonomous collection and sorting robot using a VEX IQ robotics kit.

Winter Carnival Hosted by Local School Winchester Public School will be hosting a winter carnival to help raise funds for playground equipment.

Information Session Happening in Tillsonburg If you have thought about joining the Oxford OPP Auxiliary Unit, you have the opportunity to hear what it is all about.

Human Trafficking Case Tied to Oxford County The London Police are searching for a Thamesford man who is accused of being involved in a case of human trafficking.

Holiday Season Begins in Woodstock! The city will be hosting three of it's most popular holiday events this weekend.

stories.title: Minister defends not initially banning college with surging Osap usage
stories.summary: Universities Minister Nolan Quinn this spring made six career colleges ineligible for Osap due to what the ministry called concerns with "high-risk" admissions practices.
stories.author: Allison Jones
stories.content:
A career college with student financial aid usage that grew thousands of per cent in a few years was not one of six the Ontario government cut off in May because of the “evolving” nature of the data, the minister in charge said Monday.

Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn this spring made six career colleges ineligible for the Ontario Student Assistance Program due to what the ministry called concerns with “high-risk” admissions practices.

Data obtained by The Canadian Press through a freedom-of-information request shows that those schools saw the number of students receiving Osap increase between about 650 per cent and 1,375 per cent from 2021-22 to 2024-25.

Not among those schools was the Canadian College of Business, Science and Technology, where the data shows an overall increase of 3,000 per cent during that time — at one of its four campuses it was nearly 6,000 per cent.

Quinn said Monday that the data the ministry was receiving was “evolving.”

“Once we had that data that showed that they were worse than what we initially thought, that’s when we put a pause,” Quinn said, referring to when he stopped Osap payments to all private post-secondary institutions last month.

“We put a pause across the whole system because we wanted to understand just the impact it’s having on all of the institutions, and make sure that there’s no other institutions like them that could have fallen through the cracks.”

Liberal critic Tyler Watt said that at the end of the day, the ministry did not stop the skyrocketing growth at that school until late this year, as part of a system-wide Osap pause.

“So either you didn’t catch it, despite all these all these inspections you’re bragging about, or you did catch it and you chose to do nothing about it,” Watt said.

“Both are not great choices.”

The Canadian College of Business, Science and Technology has not responded to multiple requests for comment.

It has four campuses in the Greater Toronto Area, and in 2021-22 it had 562 students accessing Osap, and three years later that number was 17,157. One campus went from 74 students on Osap in 2021-22 to 4,481 in 2024-25, an increase of 5,955 per cent. The amount of provincial grants for students at that one campus rose by more than 8,000 per cent in that time frame, to $39 million.

The students at four campuses in total in that latter year accounted for about $151 million in provincial grants.

The six schools cut off earlier in the year are ones the federal government warned the province about a year prior.

They are fighting the decision in court and deny any wrongdoing. Allegations made by the government have not been proven in court.

stories.title: Canadians should be warned when targeted by surveillance pricing: commissioner
stories.summary: Philippe Dufresne told a parliamentary committee Monday he will be developing formal guidance about how Canada's current privacy law applies to surveillance pricing.
stories.author: Anja Karadeglija
stories.content:
Canada’s privacy commissioner says people should be warned when they are being targeted by surveillance pricing.

Philippe Dufresne told a parliamentary committee Monday he will be developing formal guidance about how Canada’s current privacy law applies to surveillance pricing.

He said the privacy commissioner’s office wants Canadians to know why they’re paying what they’re paying.

“We have requirements for meaningful consent in the current law. And so our guidance is going to set out what we want to see in that. We want Canadians to know what’s happening, why they’re getting the prices,” he said.

Dufresne said it’s one thing for prices to rise because of market conditions — like a big conference taking place in town — but another to charge people more for a drug because they’re sick.

Even if people are getting a discount because of surveillance pricing, they should be made aware of it, he added.

Dufresne said his office hasn’t received any complaints about surveillance pricing and he hopes the practice is not happening in Canada, or is not prevalent.

The privacy commissioner’s office will launch a consultation with stakeholders and experts in the coming weeks, with the aim of issuing formal guidance in the coming months, Dufresne said.

That guidance, he said, will set out how current privacy law applies and “key expectations so that Canadians’ privacy is protected in this context.”

The House of Commons ethics committee is studying the use of artificial intelligence in algorithmic pricing, also referred to as surveillance pricing.

It heard last week that surveillance pricing is a black box for customers because they’re not told when they’re seeing a price other consumers don’t see, or why they’re seeing it.

Dufresne said Monday people “May have little awareness that their personal information is influencing the prices that they’re offered, which would limit their ability to recognize or challenge differential treatment.”

He said surveillance pricing raises privacy risks and could negatively affect vulnerable groups.

NDP MP Jenny Kwan is set to introduce a private member’s bill to ban surveillance pricing Monday.

stories.title: CP NewsAlert: Pentagon criticizes Canada in 'fact sheet' after Hegseth memo
stories.summary: Washington - The Pentagon has released what it calls a "fact sheet" criticizing Canada's defence spending, saying it has limited the country's ability to contribute to the defence of North America.
stories.author: Kelly Geraldine Malone The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Washington - The Pentagon has released what it calls a “fact sheet” criticizing Canada’s defence spending in the latest symbolic push from the Trump administration to upend long-standing norms in North American continental security.

“Unfortunately, Canada has yet to make the hard decisions and tradeoffs needed to put it on track to fulfill its Nato Defense Investment Pledge and become a credible partner in the defense of our shared continent,” said the document released publicly on Monday and first reported by Axios the day prior.

“Canada’s defense shortfalls speak for themselves.”

The document points to operational readiness deficits in air, land and sea operations. It denounces Canadian political leadership for pursuing “parochial economic and commercial interests over military optimization.”

In July, Carney announced that Canada had selected German defence manufacturer Tkms as the preferred partner to deliver up to 12 submarines, ahead

It was released after U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth last week issued a classified memo imposing restrictions on military co-operation with Canada on think tanks and socializing.

Sen. Mike Rounds, a Republican, told reporters at the Halifax International Security Forum on Saturday that the move would not affect military operations.

Defence Minister David McGuinty’s office has not yet responded to a request for comment about the fact sheet. On Saturday at the security conference, McGuinty said it was “business as usual” between the Canadian and U.S. militaries.

He assured Canadians that co-operation between the two countries on defence, security and intelligence was continuing.

In response to Hegseth’s memo, chief Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said the defence department is “taking steps to ensure its engagements with Canada advance tangible U.S. defense objectives and ultimately support a reinvigorated defense relationship.”

The memo and Monday’s fact sheet are the latest moves the Pentagon has taken under the Trump administration to break norms with Canada.

In May, Elbridge Colby, U.S. undersecretary of defence for policy, said his department was pausing the Permanent Joint Board on Defense “to reassess how this forum benefits shared North American defence.”

The board was established in 1940 and is an advisory forum for U.S.-Canada bilateral defence co-operation.

At that time, a high-ranking U.S. defence official said the Pentagon gave Ottawa a classified paper laying out priorities for a collective North American defence pact with Canada, but that Ottawa did not deliver a “credible” response.

That same month, Canada announced it would purchase early warning planes from Sweden’s Saab rather than a competing option from Boeing.

This criticism of Canada’s defence readiness is not happening in a vacuum. Experts have said it’s likely connected to a planned purchase of F-35 fighter jets and ongoing tensions between the two countries.

The Liberal government has yet to reach a decision on its order of F-35 fighter jets from Lockheed Martin — which Pentagon officials have cited as a source of frustration. The fighter jet purchase has been the subject of a political review for more than a year.

“It is a major issue for them and a leverage point for us,” said former Conservative leader Erin O’Toole, who is also a distinguished fellow at the Washington-based Hudson Institute.

Canada has long faced criticism about its lagging defence spending, but with U.S. President Donald Trump’s return to the White House it was directly connected to larger trade issues, including the renewal of the Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement on trade, known as Cusma.

O’Toole said he was not surprised by the content of the fact sheet but, in a text message, he added that it “ignores everything in the last year.”

“This is like someone was asked to prepare a one-sided, negative summary without acknowledging any of the changes made in the last 18 months,” O’Toole said.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has made historic defence investments as Trump rattled the bilateral relationship with tariffs and threats of annexation.

Canada spent $63.4 billion on national defence in 2025, meeting its Nato commitment to spend two per cent of gross domestic product on defence for the first time.

Nato members met last year in The Hague and agreed to up defence spending to the equivalent of five per cent of GDP by 2035.

Ottawa has said Canada continues to accelerate its path to Nato’s new target of 3.5 per cent on core defence and is optimizing an additional 1.5 per cent of GDP spending on defence and security-related investments.

November’s federal budget laid out a plan to spend around four per cent of Canada’s gross domestic product on defence per year by the end of the decade — which includes the purchase of submarines, early warning jets and other capabilities.

But Carney has also faced domestic pressure about the lack of transparency around defence spending moving forward.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 23, 2026.

stories.title: Newfoundland and Labrador forecasts budget surplus due to oil windfall
stories.summary: Province benefits from $1-billion in extra oil revenue as war in Iran sends crude prices soaring
stories.author: Sarah Smellie
stories.content:
Newfoundland and Labrador is forecasting a modest budget surplus, thanks in part to more than $1-billion in extra oil revenue after the war in Iran sent crude prices soaring.

Craig Pardy, the province’s finance minister, said there are sectors beyond oil — mining, for example — that are driving production and economic growth. But he admitted Monday that without the surge in oil prices, the indebted province would be having a very different year.

And even with a good year, Newfoundland and Labrador still faces grave financial challenges and a towering debt to overcome, he said.

“Let me be clear: that is one good year. It does not mean that the problem is fixed,” Pardy told reporters in St. John’s, N.L., on Monday. “So we will not manage the province’s finances as if one good year will last forever.”

Newfoundland and Labrador is forecasting a modest budget surplus, thanks in part to more than $1 billion in extra oil revenue after the war in Iran sent crude prices soaring. Finance…

In April, Pardy delivered a budget for the current 2026-27 fiscal year forecasting a deficit of $688-million and a net debt of $20.8-billion. But as of Monday’s fiscal update, those numbers have changed. The Progressive Conservative government is now expecting nearly $1.5-billion more revenue than forecast in the budget, much of which comes from nearly $1.1-billion in additional oil revenues.

Pardy’s update forecasted a $78-million surplus and a $19.3-billion net debt. The government will still have to borrow about $3.9-billion this fiscal year, which ends in March 2027, and it will pay about $1.2-billion in debt servicing fees, including interest.

Newfoundland and Labrador is expecting to take in more than $3-billion in oil royalties this fiscal year, accounting for roughly 25 per cent of the province’s entire revenue, officials said.

Pardy insisted his government is looking beyond the temporary surge in revenue from high oil prices, pointing to anticipated benefits from Equinor’s proposed Bay du Nord offshore oil project, and an agreement between Crown utilities in Newfoundland and Labrador and Quebec to expand the hydroelectric output of the Churchill River in Labrador.

Equinor is expected early next year to decide whether to proceed with Bay du Nord. Officials are still hammering out final contracts for the Churchill River deal.

Spending in Newfoundland and Labrador is also higher than was anticipated in April’s budget, by about $704-million. More than half of that is due to health-care costs, Pardy said. The rest he largely attributed to inflation and a recently announced suite of measures to offset the high cost of living.

The province is investing $175-million into a new sinking fund, which officials said would mature to $750-million by 2052. That money will be used to pay off debt.

Sheilagh O’Leary, who represents the St. John’s East-Quidi Vidi district for the NDP, said the government needs to come up with a better plan to manage its debt.

“We can’t rely on oil revenues that are being made on an illegal war,” O’Leary told reporters after Pardy’s announcement. “It’s unsustainable.”

Officials with the United Nations have said that U.S. and Israeli airstrikes on Iran this year violated international law, including the UN Charter. However, the Trump administration has insisted the military campaign is a lawful measure to ensure Tehran does not build nuclear weapons.

Newfoundland and Labrador’s population sat at about 552,000 as of July, according to the provincial government. Its gross domestic product is expected to grow by 7.1 per cent this year, which officials said was the highest anticipated growth in the country.

In October, the Montreal Economic Institute think tank released a report showing Newfoundland and Labrador’s net debt-to-GDP grew by 14 per cent between 2015 and 2024, which was the largest growth among the provinces. The report blamed much of the increase on what it called economic fundamentals, such as slow economic growth.

With files from The Associated Press

stories.title: Cadet weekend activities to resume until end of March: minister
stories.summary: McGuinty did not say how much funding is being provided in addition to the operating budget of about $265 million for cadet programs this year.
stories.author: David Baxter
stories.content:
The cadet program will receive more funding so weekend and supplemental activities can continue as planned until the end of March, Defence Minister David McGuinty said Monday.

McGuinty did not say how much funding is being provided in addition to the operating budget of about $265 million for cadet programs this year.

The minister said much of the program spending for cadets happens during the summer months — when cadets take part in things like camping and sailing — and costs this year ticked up faster than anticipated.

Cadet chapters across the county were notified last week that all extra activities — including weekend training, hiking, camping, sailing and glider flights — were being cancelled or suspended until the end of the fiscal year.

McGuinty said last week core programming would continue as cadet program leadership reviews the funding following a 59 per cent increase in enrolment in the last three years.

He said Monday the cadets program is unlike many other recreational programs because it allows people to join up at any time of the year.

“So it’s difficult for us to know in so many locations around the country, just in time, what the numbers are. Now when we look back and we see what the growth has been, it’s been considerable,” McGuinty said.

The Defence Department’s 2025-26 results report says the cadet program had more than 61,000 participants in that fiscal year.

A petition launched on Change.org last week calling on the government to restore the extra programming quickly collected more than 52,000 signatures.

Kelowna, B.C. resident Dustin Siewert is the person behind the petition and said he was “shocked’ to hear more funding is heading the cadets to keep all parts of the program going.

“This is the last thing I expected to happen. I didn’t even know what to respect when I started it,” he said.

Siewert said he took part in cadets when he was growing up and now his two children, aged 15 and 13, are in sea cadets and the Navy league respectively.

“I’m glad he’s decided to reverse the funding and put some back. I hope that that’s enough to fulfil all the corps across Canada and maybe next year look at funding more,” Siewert said.

“Just because 20,000 kids joined, it shouldn’t end the program. It wouldn’t be any different if 20, 000 military servicemen joined. Would they cut the funding?”

Both Conservative and Bloc Québécois MPs made the cadet funding a focus of question period in the House of Commons on Friday.

Saskatchewan Conservative MP Fraser Tolmie said the funding is being restored thanks to pressure from opposition MPs and parents across the country.

McGuinty said the Defence Department will do its best to ensure the cadet program has the fiscal resources it needs from April onward.
