stories.title: Csis plans ‘significant’ increase to foreign posts after $6b budget boost
stories.summary: The Canadian Security Intelligence Service is currently limited in what information it can collect outside of the country, but there are signs that’s about to change.
stories.author: Alex Boutilier
stories.content:
Canada’s spy agency is planning to increase its international presence “significantly” after a recent $6 billion budget boost from the Liberal government.

In a statement to Global News, the Canadian Security Intelligence Service (Csis) said that a bigger footprint abroad will “diversify and strengthen” intelligence-sharing arrangements with foreign governments.

A Csis spokesperson said the agency’s increased foreign operations will help bolster efforts across their mandate — including counter-terrorism and counterespionage.

The Carney government’s “investment” in the spy service will allow Csis “to both address the greatest pressures it faces today and to build the sovereign capacity, global partnerships, and domestic presence it will need to address the more complex environment of tomorrow,” the statement read.

Canada does not have a foreign intelligence service, and Csis is limited in what information it can collect abroad. The agency only publicly acknowledges stations in a handful of allied capitals, including Washington, D.C., London and Paris.

There are signs that could soon change. Prime Minister Mark Carney recently stressed the need for “sovereign” intelligence gathering and his government’s budget, while giving Csis $6 billion over ten years, talked about reducing Canada’s reliance on allies.

Both developments have led national security observers to speculate that Csis May soon get a foreign espionage mandate — similar to the U.K.’s MI6 or the U.S.’s CIA.

Wesley Wark, a senior fellow with the Centre for International Governance Innovation (Cigi) and longtime national security researcher, said in an interview that he expects Csis will be looking to both expand its number of overseas stations as well as expand operations in under-served regions.

That could include a presence in “Nordic countries and the Baltics,” where Csis has not typically had a presence, Wark said, as well as in Japan and South Korea, giving Canada a closer eye on developments in the Indo-Pacific.

“Many of the other (Csis) stations in the Middle East (and) Africa are very small, and I suspect Csis would love to be able to expand their footprint in both infrastructure and people in some key regions,” Wark said in an interview.

“They’ll be looking at areas where it makes sense to have a permanent presence in terms of securing intelligence partnerships, in terms of areas of concern.”

Csis’s statement, the agency’s first public comments on the proposed new funding, also made reference to “economic security” — a top-of-mind concern for the current government as it attempts to navigate new international trading relationships and Donald Trump’s trade war.

Also on the agency’s wishlist is an increased “regional presence” in Canada, including in Canada’s North. The region is increasingly being looked at with a lens of economic opportunity — particularly for mining and critical minerals — but which also presents unique national security vulnerabilities.

While Csis works with authorities in the north, the agency does not have a permanent presence in a region that includes a permanent American presence, increased Chinese interest and proximity to Russia.

In October, the Carney government released an updated National Security Strategy — the first major overhaul of Canada’s approach to the intelligence world since 2004.

In the document, Carney stressed the need for “sovereign” capabilities to reduce Canada’s reliance on intelligence collected by allies and doled out to Ottawa. It’s clear the government no longer sees the security partnership with the United States as sufficient to Canada’s foreign intelligence needs.

“The long-held belief that the combination of our geography, interconnectedness, and a rules-based international order could substitute for Canadian sovereign capacity to protect ourselves is no longer tenable,” Carney’s introduction to the strategy reads

“Once distant threats are now proximate and immediate. The global order that long protected our sovereignty has ruptured. We are prepared to protect Canada’s sovereignty, and when it is threatened, we will act.”

stories.title: Oil and gas drillers optimistic heading into 2027, but warn of labour shortages
stories.summary: Oil and gas service firms say improving market conditions and a more supportive political climate are expected to bolster Canadian drilling activity next year.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Calgary — Oil and gas service firms say improving market conditions and a more supportive political climate are expected to bolster Canadian drilling activity next year, but labour shortfalls could threaten that momentum.

Industry advocacy group Enserva has released its annual state of the industry report, which calls for an increase in the number of wells drilled in 2027 versus this year.

But it flags competition for workers as a major challenge at a time when artificial intelligence data centres and major infrastructure projects draw from the same talent pool.

Latest updates on company news here

Bradley Fedora, president and CEO of Trican Well Service Ltd. , says the prospect of “hyperinflation” in the cost of labour and materials is what scares him most.

Thomas Alford, president of completion and production services at Precision Drilling , told reporters at the event that it can take up to eight years to train up a competent drill rig staffer, and the industry has been so unstable in recent years that it’s been hard for those workers to get that consistent job experience.

Gurpreet Lail, Enserva’s president and CEO, says the sector needs to work hard to attract and keep talent as data centre developments offer big paycheques to tradespeople and perks that have until now been “unheard of.”

Lauren Krugel, The Canadian Press

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 23, 2026.

stories.title: Non-profits fear housing halt as Ontario bill targets tax exemption
stories.summary: A legislative proposal introduced by the Ontario government as part of its Fall Economic Update is sparking alarm among non-profit housing agencies across the province.
stories.author: Gerry Dewan
stories.content:
A legislative proposal introduced by the Ontario government as part of its Fall Economic Update is sparking alarm among non-profit housing agencies across the province.

Agencies fear a critical property tax exemption could be revoked, potentially halting the development of much-needed affordable housing projects.

The bill, identified as Bill 143, the “Plan to Protect Ontario Act (Budget Measures), 2026 (No. 2),” contains an amendment to the Assessment Act that critics argue will suspend a crucial property tax exemption for rental housing properties starting in 2027.

While the government states the change is a temporary pause related to court decisions, many non-profit housing providers feel “exposed” rather than protected.

Katelyn Schoffer, a lawyer specializing in multi-residential housing law with the London-based firm Cohen Highley LLP, warned that the impact of the proposed change will be “widespread.”

“The result is we are going to see a stoppage in the development of affordable housing in Ontario. If this is pushed through and is extended beyond 2027,” Schoffer stated.

Schoffer explained that the proposed change could remove a property tax exemption that many non-profit agencies have relied upon for project budgeting and financial projections.

“If they remove this property tax exemption, they’re jeopardizing projects currently underway. They’re operating on narrow margins, and there’s very little room in the budget for unaccounted expenses,” she noted.

According to a joint submission by Cohen Highley LLP to the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs, property taxes can represent “approximately one-third of an affordable housing provider’s operating costs.”

Agencies that have already been granted the exemption are grandfathered in and will not be affected. However, Schoffer highlighted that numerous projects currently in development, with contracts signed and preliminary work underway, stand to lose this vital tax relief.

“Having to face a new bill that accounts for many organizations up to one third of their operating budgets per year. It would be financially devastating,” she added.

The Ministry of Finance, in a statement attributed to Senior Media Relations Advisor Scott Blodgett, indicated that the government is implementing a “temporary pause on the implications of the court decisions” to allow for consultations with affordable housing providers and municipalities.

“While the pause is in effect, properties already exempt from property taxes would maintain their exemption to avoid impacts at the property level,” the statement read, adding that providers can “continue to seek other tax relief options through their municipality.”

The ministry also reiterated the government’s commitment to building more housing, citing an “Affordable Rental Housing Subclass” that offers municipalities the option to reduce property taxes on these developments by up to 35 per cent.

The bill has already passed second reading and is currently before the Standing Committee, leaving a narrow window for potential amendments.

In response to the proposed changes, 24 non-profit housing agencies have collectively voiced their opposition through Cohen Highley, including prominent organizations such as the United Way Elgin Middlesex, Indwell, and the Canadian Mental Health Association Thames Valley.

In their letter to the Standing Committee, dated Nov. 17, 2026, Cohen Highley LLP, representing the non-profit organizations, urged the committee to reject or revise the proposed amendment.

“Removing the exemption for affordable rental units will have devastating consequences,” the letter states, emphasizing that the exemption has been relied upon for project budgeting and financial projections.

The firm warned that the proposed restriction “will reduce Ontario’s supply of affordable rental housing” and divert funds needed for operations, capital, and resident services.

stories.title: Hope for restart grows as Nackawic, N.B. feels effects of mill shutdown
stories.summary: Nearly three weeks after the Nackawic pulp mill shut down in New Brunswick, putting 350 workers out of work, the ripple effects are now reaching local businesses.
stories.author: Rebecca Lau, Reeti Rohilla
stories.content:
Nearly three weeks after the Nackawic pulp mill shut down in New Brunswick, putting 350 workers out of work, the ripple effects are now reaching local businesses.

AV Group NB Inc., a subsidiary of the India-based Aditya Birla Group, announced in September it would idle its AV Nackawic facility west of Fredericton and attributed the decision to “prevailing market conditions” and other challenges.

While a Quebec company explores giving the site a second life, there’s a lot of uncertainty in the area.

Logger Joe Blaney hasn’t delivered to Nackawic, N.B., since August. He says he’s found American buyers, but they’re about 100 kilometres further away and require more than $100 in extra costs per load.

“As long as we’re moving wood, it’s a reduced negative impact, but it’s still 15 to 20 per cent hit,” he said.

He says he’s been able to keep his crew working, but finding buyers for local poplar remains a concern.

The New Brunswick Federation of Woodlot Owners says private woodlot sales in Carleton-Victoria County are down about 60 per cent from a year ago.

“There always seems to be a lack of concern about how these things are impacting private woodlot owners and specifically private wood producers. They’re always the last thought in every crisis, it seems,” said Rick Doucett, the group’s president.

Other businesses outside of the lumber industry are also feeling the effects of the shutdown.

Crystal King, the manager of the local Robin’s Donuts, says the truckers and shift workers are sorely missed.

“We’ve had to cut the employees’ hours a little to compensate for the sales,” she said.

The municipality has money at stake too, with its sustainability at risk if the closure continues.

“The mill represents about 10 per cent of the municipal tax revenue and it’s 14 per cent of municipal utility, so water and sewer charges,” said Tim Fox, mayor of Nackawic-Millville Rural Community.

There’s also the risk of those workers leaving the community entirely.

But news that the New Brunswick government is in talks with a Quebec-based forest products company about restarting the mill is bringing about a sense of optimism.

“I think in the short term we can hope that, you know, the optimism of having somebody in looking at the plant might change some of the decisions that people would make normally and we’ll keep folks in the community,” said Fox.

Provincial Natural Resources Minister John Herron issued a statement last week saying government officials were talking to Arbec Forest Products Inc., based in Saint-Léonard, Que.

Adam Stone, the vice-president of operations for Arbec Forest Products, told Global News the company is still in the early stages of an assessment.

“Nackawic has long been an important part of New Brunswick’s forest sector. What attracted our attention is the opportunity to evaluate whether the site could support future industrial activity that aligns with our expertise and our business,” Stone wrote in an email.

“As with any evaluation, we’re looking at a range of factors, including the site’s infrastructure, its location, available workforce, and the broader forest resource base.”

Prior to the mill’s shutdown, the union representing the workers called for the mill to be heated through the winter in order to preserve the possibility of reopening.

The New Brunswick government says AV Group is responsible for key equipment but hasn’t confirmed if the mill will stay heated.

“They have indicated that they intend to take care of the key equipment and preserve it for potential future use,” the province’s Department of Natural Resources said in a statement.

“The Province is continuing its discussions with AV Group to ensure the mill is placed in a position that could support future opportunities.”

The mill faced a similar situation in 2004, closing its doors for over a year before a different operator took over.

Other businesses outside of the lumber industry are also feeling the effects of the shutdown.
Crystal King, the manager of the local Robin’s Donuts, says the truckers and shift workers are sorely missed.
“We’ve had to cut the employees’ hours a little to compensate for the sales,” she said.
The municipality has money at stake too, with its sustainability at risk if the closure continues.
“The mill represents about 10 per cent of the municipal tax revenue and it’s 14 per cent of municipal utility, so water and sewer charges,” said Tim Fox, mayor of Nackawic-Millville Rural Community.
There’s also the risk of those workers leaving the community entirely.
But news that the New Brunswick government is in talks with a Quebec-based forest products company about restarting the mill is bringing about a sense of optimism.

“I think in the short term we can hope that, you know, the optimism of having somebody in looking at the plant might change some of the decisions that people would make normally and we’ll keep folks in the community,” said Fox.
Provincial Natural Resources Minister John Herron issued a statement last week saying government officials were talking to Arbec Forest Products Inc., based in Saint-Léonard, Que.
Adam Stone, the vice-president of operations for Arbec Forest Products, told Global News the company is still in the early stages of an assessment.

“Nackawic has long been an important part of New Brunswick’s forest sector. What attracted our attention is the opportunity to evaluate whether the site could support future industrial activity that aligns with our expertise and our business,” Stone wrote in an email.
“As with any evaluation, we’re looking at a range of factors, including the site’s infrastructure, its location, available workforce, and the broader forest resource base.”
Prior to the mill’s shutdown, the union representing the workers called for the mill to be heated through the winter in order to preserve the possibility of reopening.
The New Brunswick government says AV Group is responsible for key equipment but hasn’t confirmed if the mill will stay heated.
“They have indicated that they intend to take care of the key equipment and preserve it for potential future use,” the province’s Department of Natural Resources said in a statement.
“The Province is continuing its discussions with AV Group to ensure the mill is placed in a position that could support future opportunities.”
The mill faced a similar situation in 2004, closing its doors for over a year before a different operator took over.

stories.title: Alberta to restrict upstart political parties from accessing provincial voter list
stories.summary: Justice Minister says tabled legislation is ‘exactly in response’ to alleged leak of province’s list of electors
stories.author: Carrie Tait
stories.content:
Alberta will restrict upstart or straggling political parties from accessing the province’s voter list, giving the United Conservative Party and provincial New Democratic Party an advantage in the next election, as part of a package of reforms the government said will help protect personal data.

Justice Minister Mickey Amery, in legislation tabled Monday, also proposed stripping voting rights from those convicted of failing to protect, or unauthorized use of, Alberta’s list of electors, according to a summary of the proposed amendments.

Alberta’s list of electors, which contains a trove of sensitive personal information for the province’s three million eligible voters, allegedly leaked in April, sparking widespread backlash and safety concerns. Elections Alberta, in court documents, alleges a copy of the list of electors it legally provided to the Republican Party of Alberta ended up in the hands of the Centurion Project, a separatist organization that made some of the contents available to its members through an online tool.

“This is exactly in response to the data breach,” Mr. Amery told reporters Monday before he tabled the legislation.

Currently, all registered political parties in Alberta are permitted access to the list of electors without providing a bond. Elections Alberta counts 13 registered political parties.

Mr. Amery’s proposed restrictions would make Alberta an outlier compared with its provincial peers. Elections BC and Elections Ontario both permit registered political parties to access their respective voter lists.

Elections Alberta and the RCMP are investigating the alleged mishandling of the province’s list of electors this spring. None of Elections Alberta’s allegations have been tested in court, and the government’s proposed punishments for mishandling the voter list are not retroactive.

But privacy concerns run deep. The Centurion Project’s founder, David Parker, worked with Michigan’s 10X Votes when pitching his get-out-the-vote tool.

The Globe and Mail found a loophole in the Centurion Project’s online security measures in April. Using login credentials supplied by the organization, The Globe accessed the database powering the Centurion Project’s basic search tool. It contained personal information for roughly 2.9 million voters, including unique elector identification numbers, addresses, legal names and 2,083,175 phone numbers.

Now, Alberta wants to restrict access to the provincial voter list to political parties that clear at least one hurdle, according to the government’s summary of the amendments. To access the provincewide list, political parties must have backed at least one candidate elected to the legislative assembly in the most recent election or by-election; or supported candidates in at least half the electoral divisions in the most recent election; or, after the writs are issued, endorse candidates in at least half the electoral divisions.

Under the proposed rules, only the governing UCP and the Alberta NDP would be eligible for access to the province’s list of electors. Parties that qualify must pay a deposit of $100,000, Mr. Amery said.

The government’s adversaries argue Mr. Amery’s proposals are designed to stifle democracy and shield the UCP from challengers. The next provincial election is scheduled for October 2027.

“It is obviously very limiting and intended to tip the scale in favour of the government,” said Peter Guthrie, the leader of the Progressive Tory Party of Alberta.

Mr. Guthrie, elected under the UCP banner in the last election, revived the Tory brand last summer. He said his party’s request for the provincewide list has not been fulfilled.

Under the proposed changes, Mr. Guthrie’s Tory party would not be eligible for access to the full voter list, unless it has candidates in 50 per cent of the ridings when the writs are issued.

The changes also prevent new parties, such as a breakaway conservative faction, or those that might plot a comeback, such as the Alberta Liberal Party, from accessing the provincewide list. The Republican Party of Alberta, which does not have a seat in the legislature but ran candidates in three by-elections last year, would also be iced out.

Stephen Carter, a political strategist, said the UCP is limiting competition and curbing the ability for new and dormant parties to connect with constituents.

New parties are not unusual in Alberta. For example, the UCP formed in 2017, when the Progressive Conservative Association of Alberta merged with the Wildrose Party, which years earlier splintered from the PCs.

“This is protectionism,” Mr. Carter said. “It is a democratic responsibility for parties to communicate with the electorate. They are constraining that ability.”

Independent candidates could access the list of electors for their respective riding should they post a bond of $2,000, Mr. Amery said. New parties running a small slate of candidates could also access the lists for the relevant constituencies after posting a bond of $2,000 a riding, he said.

Alberta also plans to disenfranchise people convicted of mishandling the lists. It will “disqualify a person from voting, running for or holding public office, or (if other amendments pass) registering as a third party advertiser for eight years if they are convicted of unauthorized use or failure to protect the list of electors,” according to the government’s summary sheet.

Heather Jenkins, a spokeswoman for Mr. Amery, in a statement defended the province’s plan to suspend voting rights as a form of punishment. “Alberta has long imposed serious consequences for corrupt electoral practices, and BC’s election law similarly disqualifies convicted offenders from voting.”

The amendments would increase the maximum penalty for mishandling the list of electors to a $1-million fine, up to two years in prison, or both. The existing penalty for unauthorized use or failure to protect the list of electors is a maximum fine of $100,000, up to a year in prison, or both.

Further, Alberta intends to “make a person or party liable for damages in cases of unauthorized disclosure of the list of electors that result from negligence, recklessness, willful blindness, intentional conduct or that contravene the Election Act in relation to the list of electors.”

The proposed amendments would also prevent Elections Alberta from distributing the list of electors to people or political parties “charged with or under investigation for unauthorized use or failure to protect the list of electors.”

Mr. Amery’s new rules also prohibit storing the list of electors outside Alberta, including digital copies.

stories.title: ‘Violated’: Seaforth seniors find homeless encampment in bush lot
stories.summary: Gene Baynham couldn’t believe her eyes when she first found out that people were living in her bush lot on the edge of Seaforth for at least the last two years.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
Gene Baynham couldn’t believe her eyes when she first found out that people were living in her bush lot on the edge of Seaforth for at least the last two years.

“It’s a big shock to find that you’ve been, I would call it violated,” said the 85-year-old Baynham.

Baynham says her husband decided to check on their bush lot last Thursday when he saw a well-worn path along the field’s edge headed towards the woods.

The path wound its way into the heart of the forest, where he found two structures with wooden floors and structured walls.

“We called the OPP to see what we should do. And they said, ‘Well, we’ve known that’s been there for a couple of years. So do you want to charge them with trespassing?’ And I said, ‘Yeah, we want them out of there.’ So, the next day, another OPP officer came in here and told them they had 24 hours to leave. And so in 24 hours, we were able to come in and begin the cleanup,” said Baynham.

“There was a structure in here half as big as our home,” she said.

stories.title: More Canadians are turning to weed than booze every day, and youngsters are leading the pack: study
stories.summary: Daily cannabis use edges out that of alcohol in Canada, but in young adults the gap is much wider
stories.author: Chris Knight
stories.content:
A wide-ranging study published Monday in the Canadian Medical Association Journal (Cmaj) found that 5.7 per cent of Canadians report using cannabis every day or nearly every day, compared with 5.2 per cent who say the same thing about alcohol. This amounts to about 1.8 million Canadians using cannabis daily, and 1.65 million using alcohol.

The study, Daily Cannabis, Alcohol, and Cigarette Use in the Canadian Provinces: Results From the 2023 to 2024 Canadian Community Health Survey, drew from almost 100,000 respondents aged 18 and older. Overall, it noted that cigarette use was the highest number, with 8.5 per cent of respondents (2.7 million) saying they smoked daily or almost daily.

Among younger demographics, however, the split between one substance and another was much wider. Among females aged 18 to 24, for instance, daily cannabis use was 6.6 per cent whereas daily drinking was just 0.4 per cent, meaning more than 17 times as many young women are using cannabis than drinking regularly.

Daily cigarette smoking among young women was also relatively low at just 2 per cent, or less than a third the rate of cannabis use.

Meanwhile, men aged 25 to 34 had the highest rate of daily cannabis use of any age group (10.8 per cent). They reported daily alcohol use at 2.9 per cent, and daily cigarette use at 8 per cent.

Daily cannabis use was also high among people who identified as transgender or gender-diverse (22.6 per cent said they used it daily) and people who reported having mood disorders (14.7 per cent) or anxiety disorders (12.2 per cent).

Daily alcohol use was much higher among older Canadians, however. Among those aged 65 years or older, daily cannabis use was just 3.3 per cent among males and 2.3 per cent among females, compared with much higher numbers for alcohol use — 13 per cent and 6.7 per cent, respectively.

“Over the past two decades, cannabis use has increased in many high-income countries alongside liberalization of cannabis policy and greater social acceptance, while tobacco use has declined and alcohol use has remained stable or decreased in some populations,” the study noted.

“Globally, alcohol and tobacco use remain the leading modifiable risk factors for cardiovascular disease, cancer, and premature death,” it added. However, “growing evidence suggests that cannabis use May confer important cardiovascular and chronic respiratory risks.”

Canada legalized non-medical cannabis use for adults in 2018, becoming the first country to do so at the federal level. The legal age to purchase cannabis is 18 in Alberta, 21 in Quebec, and 19 years in all other provinces and territories.

Overall, 41 per cent of adults who reported daily cannabis use started after legalization in 2018, although more females than males fell into this group.

“Post-legalization initiation was most common among younger adults aged 18 to 24 years who were aged 12 to 19 in 2018, a developmental stage when most individual cannabis use is typically initiated, independent of legalization,” the study found.

“Our findings highlight a generational shift in substance exposure, with potential long-term implications for cardiorespiratory and mental health,” wrote André McDonald of the Peter Boris Centre for Addictions Research at McMaster University in Hamilton, Ont., lead author of the study.

Canada is not alone in this shift. Similar studies in the United States found that cannabis has outstripped alcohol as the drug of choice there, with figures from 2022 showing 17.7 million Americans used marijuana daily or near-daily, compared to 14.7 million for alcohol. The use of marijuana grew 15-fold between 1992 and 2022, one study found.

The Canadian study noted that its responses were self-reported, and “cannabis use May have been under-reported because of residual stigma even after legalization.”

It also did not quantify whether people were using cannabis for medical or non-medical purposes, nor the number of times each substance was used per day. It also did not study vaping, which it noted is more common among younger people.

“Nonetheless, a strength of our study is that comparisons between cannabis, alcohol and cigarettes were measured within the same sample,” it added.

“These findings … suggest a shift in the epidemiology of substance use, with implications for public health policy and clinical practice,” the report concluded. “Screening and treatment in clinical practice and broader policies to reduce substance-related harms should place greater priority on regular cannabis use, particularly among younger adults, people experiencing social and structural inequities, and people with mental health problems.”

Chris Knight is a long-time reporter/critic/editor at National Post with a special interest in science, space and movies.

stories.title: Alberta proposes ending mandatory public inquiries for deaths in police or prison custody
stories.summary: Bill tabled on the same day as three Calgary officers were charged with manslaughter after man’s death
stories.author: Matthew Scace
stories.content:
The Alberta government is proposing changes to provincial law that would eliminate mandatory public fatality inquiries for people who die in prison or police custody, a move the province says aims to clear a backlog of investigations.

The bill, tabled Monday afternoon in the Alberta Legislature, proposes establishing new criteria that would determine whether a death is sent for public inquiry, a change provincial Justice Minister Mickey Amery said would allow “remarkable efficiencies” to help grieving families get answers into the circumstances of their loved ones’ deaths.

“What this is suggesting is that we narrow the mandatory wide net that is currently cast,” Mr. Amery told reporters at a news conference.

The new legislation was tabled on the same day that Alberta’s police watchdog announced that manslaughter charges have been laid against three officers with the Calgary Police Service after a 42-year-old Indigenous man died after an encounter with police in a hotel lobby.

A fatality inquiry has not been called in that case.

The changes Mr. Amery unveiled on Monday were included with an unrelated set of proposed amendments to other Alberta legislation, including new restrictions on which political parties can access the provincial voters list.

The proposed updates to the province’s Fatality Inquiries Act would give the Chief Medical Examiner more information to help reach conclusions about an individual’s death and narrow the circumstances under which deaths would be investigated by a judge, Mr. Amery said.

Fatality inquiries are non-criminal court proceedings that are investigated by a judge, most commonly after a death in custody, in child welfare or in a workplace. They are intended to provide insight into how similar deaths can be prevented. Earlier this year, for example, the Alberta government ordered a public inquiry into the death of Prashant Sreekumar, a 44-year-old father of three who died while waiting for eight hours in an Edmonton emergency room.

Currently, public inquiries are mandatory when a person dies in jail or in police custody, regardless of whether an investigation would yield new death-prevention recommendations.

If the new amendments pass, the province would instead require public inquiries only where “they would best serve the public interest.”

Certain deaths are often explained without needing a public inquiry, Mr. Amery said, but they are nevertheless subject to a lengthy investigation that can take longer than a decade to complete. He pointed to a person’s history of terminal illness or addiction as examples of circumstances that May not require a public inquiry.

“Oftentimes the feedback that we’re receiving is that some of these are so obvious, despite the recommendation that they proceed – that there are no conclusions because they already know what the conclusions are going to be.”

The proposed legislation says the Chief Medical Examiner would be equipped with more personal and health information to guide their decision whether to initiate a public inquiry.

“We think that that change alone is going to be able to achieve remarkable efficiencies in how they make their conclusions and how they report to families,” Mr. Amery said.

Separately, ON Monday, the Alberta Serious Incident Response Team (Asirt), the independent police-oversight agency, said three Calgary officers had been arrested and charged with manslaughter in the case of a man who died in 2024 after hotel staff called police asking to remove him from the lobby.

The 42-year-old man, Jon Wells, was tackled to the ground after he resisted an officer trying to grab him, Asirt said. He was then punched in the head, restrained and sedated, the watchdog said. Emergency crews found him unresponsive and he was declared dead a short while later.

Asirt, in a statement to The Globe and Mail, said it’s not involved in convening a fatality inquiry. It said that decision rests with the Justice Minister.

In Ontario, Premier Doug Ford’s government is proposing to scrap the requirement for an inquest into the cases of any inmate who dies from non-natural causes.

His government, also managing a backlog of cases, has argued that annual reviews of correctional facilities would avoid retraumatizing families while better identifying systemic issues and providing more timely recommendations.

But the Ontario government has faced substantial pushback on the proposed rule change, partly after facing criticism for not consulting people whose loved ones had died in jail. Critics have also panned the idea as a broader attempt to erode scrutiny of correctional institutions that could lead to more deaths.

The number of inmates who’ve died in provincial custody in Ontario has been increasing over the past 15 years, rising to 41 in 2025 from 16 in 2010, according to the coroner’s officer. (The numbers include natural deaths, drug overdoses and suicides. Most people in provincial custody are awaiting trial.)

Ontario hasn’t moved forward with the proposal yet. On Monday, a spokesperson for the Office of the Chief Coroner said it’s still exploring methods to review non-natural deaths that occur while a person is in custody, but it doesn’t have a timeline on when the province plans to introduce proposed amendments to its legislation.

With files from Jill Mahoney

stories.title: Bringing the magic of Christmas to Children’s Hospital
stories.summary: Patients staying at Children’s Hospital in London, Ont. this holiday season are receiving an extra special package.
stories.author: Lauren Stallone
stories.content:
Patients staying at Children’s Hospital in London, Ont. this holiday season are receiving an extra special package.

“Our Santa packages were created by an amazing group of volunteers and individuals that put their heart and souls into these packages,” said Jennifer Baxter, director with Children’s Hospital.

Each child will be given a festive red envelope to write their letter to Santa, with express delivery straight to the North Pole.

“No one wants to be in the hospital over the holiday season,” said Baxter. “If we can make it even remotely a little bit better for them by bringing letters to Santa, having our toy drive, doing things that make it normal for them, it’s just making their lives a lot better and happier.”

The initiative was started by Kayla O’Conell; her son was once a patient at Children’s.

“Back in October of 2024 I took my son to emerge at Children’s Hospital,” said O’Connell. “They found he had a tumour growing on his left kidney.”

She said the doctors were successfully able to remove the tumour, and her son would not need chemotherapy.

“The Children’s Hospital has a special place in our heart because of all the support and care that we’ve received,” said O’Connell.

Now O’Connell is spreading joy to families in need.

“I felt like it was the perfect fit,” she said. “I get to be crafty but also create some of the magic that people get to experience over Christmas.”

“Anything that can make kids and families smile, take away some of those daunting thoughts of what’s going on in their life at that moment I’m all for that,” said O’Connell. “I think it’s so important that we do that as a community, anything we can do to brighten the days of children in the hospital over the holidays.”

stories.title: Alberta bill could give province greater role in gas pipelines as 'last resort'
stories.summary: Calgary - The Alberta government has introduced legislation that would enable it to create Crown entities to push forward new natural gas pipelines — as a last resort, if the private sector fails to do so — setting the scene for a potential showdown with the industry's dominant player.
stories.author: Lauren Krugel The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Calgary - The Alberta government has introduced legislation that would enable it to create Crown entities to push forward new natural gas pipelines — as a last resort, if the private sector fails to do so — setting the scene for a potential showdown with the industry’s dominant player.

Brian Jean, the minister of energy and minerals, says Alberta has an “unbelievable” amount of natural gas in the ground, but pipeline capacity to get that gas to customers is increasingly becoming a “constraint to growth” amid booming demand from data centres, the oilsands and other industries in the province.

stories.title: Taiwan envoy says proposed deal could help shield Canada from Chinese trade coercion
stories.summary: Ottawa - Taiwan's deputy foreign minister says a trade agreement with Canada that has gone unsigned for months could yield deeper co-operation in high-tech fields like AI and help shield Canada from coercion by Beijing.
stories.author: Dylan Robertson The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - Taiwan’s deputy foreign minister says a trade agreement with Canada that has gone unsigned for months could yield deeper co-operation in high-tech fields like AI and help shield Canada from coercion by Beijing.

Chen Ming-chi told The Canadian Press Taiwan fears Beijing might move to weaponize Canada’s new trade ties with China and suggested Ottawa spread out its trade.

“China is going to leverage its ties (and) weaponize this interdependence to their advantage,” he said Monday

“That’s the part that we worry (about), that we all have to be very clear-eyed and set the guardrails when it comes to building a relationship with China.”

Chen is visiting Ottawa this week, shortly after Prime Minister Mark Carney concluded his second trip to China this year. While the prime minister was in Shenzhen this month, China announced a deal to drop some restrictions on Canadian pork imports in exchange for more steel market access.

During a visit to Beijing in January, Carney announced a renewed strategic partnership with China — one that shifted away from a 2022 federal policy document describing China as an increasingly disruptive power that challenges Canadian interests.

That 2022 policy document, introduced under the Trudeau government, called for “multi-faceted engagement with Taiwan” while respecting the long-standing “One China” policy, which officially recognizes the government in Beijing as the sole government of China.

Taiwan is a self-governing island that China considers to be a breakaway province and Beijing has never ruled out reuniting Taiwan with the mainland by force. Chinese nationalist forces fled to Taiwan after losing the civil war to the communists in 1949.

As part of Canada’s Indo-Pacific strategy, Ottawa negotiated a Canada-Taiwan Trade Cooperation Framework Arrangement. Parliamentary documents tabled in September show Canada and Taiwan concluded talks in March 2025 and the federal government consulted the provinces on the agreement two months later.

While in China recently, Carney was asked about the Taiwan deal sitting unsigned for months. The prime minister pushed back and said he hoped the deal would be signed soon.

His office has not explained why the deal has not been signed.

China’s embassy in Ottawa argued the deal goes against the One China principle.

“China consistently and firmly opposes countries that have diplomatic relations with China engaging in any form of official exchanges with the Taiwan region of China, or signing any agreement with the Taiwan region that carries implications of sovereignty or has an official nature,” the embassy wrote in a statement Monday.

Chen said Taiwan is glad to hear the deal will be concluded but added Canada hasn’t raised it with Taiwan since spring 2025.

“Last year before your big election, we had reached a conclusion,” Chen said. “It’s been sitting there.”

He said there have been talks with Canada on technology, students and deeper economic ties but “not on this specific issue” of the framework agreement.

“We do have a very good channel of communication,” he added.

Chen said Taipei wants to connect Canadian minerals, research and automotive know-how with Taiwan’s prowess in advanced manufacturing and military drones.

He said Taiwan has strong trade ties with mainland China but is careful about maintaining diverse supply chains.

“We have learned it the hard way,” he said. “I would like to share our experience, how closer economic ties get in the way for us to make … political decisions, who we want to be friends with, how are we going to participate in the international community.”

China has restricted trade with various partners over political disputes; it limited U.S. access to certain rare earths last year in response to American restrictions on U.S. technology. China also has imposed restrictions on Canadian canola — in one instance, immediately after the house arrest of a Chinese tech leader.

“That is never a free market. It’s a market controlled by a Leninist state,” Chen said. “Even Taiwan will not abandon the Chinese market entirely. But how to manage the risk, I think especially, is about security issues.”

Chen addressed a panel hosted Monday by the Macdonald-Laurier Institute think tank. Just before the panel discussion, Macdonald-Laurier Institute founder Brian Lee Crowley urged Ottawa not to turn its back on the United States despite the tensions with President Donald Trump.

He argued Canadians need to look beyond “the parochial and the immediate” sources of friction with the U.S. and see the larger picture.

“Authoritarian powers are challenging international norms. Coercion is becoming a routine instrument of statecraft. And economic relationships are increasingly being used to exercise strategic leverage,” Crowley said.

“If Canadians view the world principally through the lens of our disagreements with Washington, we risk overlooking developments that could have much more profound consequences for our security, prosperity and sovereignty.”

Chen said Taiwan undertook “painful” negotiations to land a trade deal with Washington this February, after a year of negotiations and concerns about Trump’s rapprochement with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Despite Trump’s rhetoric, Taipei has shifted a large chunk of its outbound investment from China to the United States, a move Chen argued is strategically smart.

“A one-sided strategy is never a good idea. And we also need to have multiple markets and multiple partners,” he said.

Chen warned that the world’s democracies probably only have three or four years to prevent “very dire consequences” coming from China and other authoritarian states which are building up their militaries.

“We have to build an effective mechanism for collective deterrence by denial,” he said. “I urge all democracies in the world to face the reality. We have the opportunity but the time is very limited.”

Chen added that China is working more closely with Russia, Iran and North Korea to promote authoritarian responses to the challenges facing the world.

“Dictatorships are making inroads, and especially spreading their ideas in the global south. That’s because … we let down our guard,” he said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 23, 2026.

stories.title: Calgary ski hill gets exemption for snow-making during water restrictions
stories.summary: Calgary - Calgary has granted a special exemption to allow snow-making at Canada Olympic Park while the city remains under water use restrictions.
stories.author: Bill Graveland The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Calgary - Calgary has granted a special exemption to allow snow-making at Canada Olympic Park while the city remains under water use restrictions.

The ski hill would normally be open to the public by now, but work continues on repairs to a major water main in the city.

WinSport, which operates the park, is being allowed to make up to 15 per cent of its normal amount of snow, said spokesperson Dale Oviatt.

He said that after Dec. 4, when water restrictions are to be lifted, WinSport would still be limited to 40 per cent of its snow-making for about two additional weeks.

“The good news is we’re allowed a limited exemption for us to proceed with overnight snow-making. And then kind of on the bad news side is we found out there’s going to be a localized system restraint that’s going to impact us after the citywide restrictions are lifted,” he said.

There’s still no official opening date for the ski hill, he added.

The city brought back water restrictions earlier this month in order to complete work on the Bearspaw South Feeder Main, which provides 60 per cent of Calgary’s treated water.

The problematic water main has burst twice in the last two years.

Residents have been asked to take shorter showers, make fewer toilet flushes and run only full loads in the washing machine and dishwasher.

In an update Monday, the city said the repair work is on schedule to be completed by Dec. 4. It acknowledged the impact that the water restrictions have on WinSport.

“WinSport, a not-for-profit organization, relies heavily on early-season snow-making to build their snow base that will carry it through the winter,” the city said in a release.

“This work has been delayed due to weather and water restrictions, impacting staff waiting to start work, community and school programming, and the athletes and sport organizations that rely on the facility.”

The city said it would be monitoring the system and water supply very carefully and that WinSport could be affected further.

“If overall water demand rises too high, there are issues in the system, or any other significant changes, the permission will be withdrawn. This could happen at any time.”

Oviatt said WinSport’s school program had to turn away 3,500 children because of the water restrictions.

He said it’s costing money, although the organization doesn’t yet have an exact amount.

“Making snow is one of our largest expenses every winter and … as every day goes by, obviously, we can’t get the revenue to offset that expense.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 23, 2026.

stories.title: Strathroy’s Santa Claus Parade sees no Krampus
stories.summary: It's not every year that an annual Santa Claus Parade fractures a community. But when the Strathroy Lions Club...
stories.author: Samantha Luis
stories.content:
Strathroy Lions Club’s Santa Claus (Credit: Sam Luis/ XFM News)

It’s not every year that an annual Santa Claus Parade fractures a community.

But when the Strathroy Lions Club dismisssed a local business float due to its controversial “Krampus” theme, the news led to a town divided in social media outrage.

On Nov. 16, Tanya Griffin, owner of Coven House Tattoos announced the exclusion of the Krampus float, that previously won second place for the ‘best costumes’ category.

2025 Santa Claus Parade Award won by Coven House (Credit: Sam Luis)

“Despite our efforts to communicate, compromise, educate, and address concerns, we have been informed that the Lions Club will not be allowing our float to participate,” she wrote on Facebook.

On Nov. 17, In ‘The Official Strathroy Rants’ group on Facebook Rachael Jenner started a thread.

“Why are there grown adults in town whining they can’t have a krampus float to scare children in a Santa parade,” Jenner wrote. “… get off the drugs it’s a Santa parade for kids and families.”

The replies were animated.

“You clearly don’t know what Krampus is,” one person replied, leading another to answer: “I know what it is and it has no place in the parade.”

Krampus is a horned half-goat, half-demon figure from Central European folklore. According to the lore, he is Santa’s opposite counterpart, responsible for punishing misbehaving children.

While many online accused the parade organizers of banning Krampus due to religious beliefs, the club denied that, saying the decision was based on the parade’s young audience.

“We did not remove the Krampus display because of the folklore or any religious objection,” the Lions Club posted on Facebook Thursday. “We have received many concerns from parents of young children who were scared of the Krampus costume last year. Adding even more characters with scary costumes, rattling chains and beating sticks changes the environment for all attendees”

Posters that were handed out by Coven House (Credit: Sam Luis/ XFM News)

Although dismissed from the parade, Coven House invited the town to stop by for pictures with Krampus, asking for food donations for the Strathroy Police ‘Cram a Cruiser’ event.

Hundreds of residents piled in to show their support to the local shop owner, some left with ‘#Freekrampus’ posters taped to their backs.

In a Facebook post Saturday, Coven House owner Griffin thanked the Strathroy Lions Club “for the work they put into bringing our community’s Santa Claus Parade to life year after year.

“Regardless of the challenges surrounding this year’s festivities,” she said. “I know how much work goes into making these events happen, and that deserves recognition,” she said.

Griffin said Krampus will be back for Krampusnacht (Krampus day) on Dec. 5.

stories.title: ‘Resistance’ group hosting Toronto conference added to Canada’s terrorist list
stories.summary: Masar Badil had been planning to host its North American conference in Toronto later this month.
stories.author: Stewart Bell
stories.content:
A “resistance” group that was planning to host its North American conference in Toronto later this month was added to Canada’s list of terrorist organizations on Monday.

Masar Badil had invited “militants” to mark the third anniversary of what it called the “glorious” and “courageous” Oct. 7, 2023 Hamas attack that killed hundreds of Israelis.

But following complaints from Canadian Jewish leaders, the government announced it had blacklisted Masar Badil on the grounds it was a faction of terror group Samidoun.

Also known as the Palestinian Alternative Revolutionary Path Movement, Masar Badil advances the interests of Hamas and Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine, the government said.

The listing gives law enforcement tools to “disrupt their financing, dismantle their networks, hold their members accountable, and to protect all people in Canada from terrorism and organized violence,” said Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree.

Canada’s national security agencies have prevented a half-dozen terrorist plots targeting the Jewish community since the Hamas attack that triggered an Israeli military response that killed tens of thousands in Gaza.

Amid spiking antisemitism, Jewish schools, synagogues, centres, businesses and community members have faced violence including shootings, arsons and vandalism.

“At a time when antisemitism is rising across Canada, decisive action against organizations linked to terrorism is more important than ever,” said Michael Levitt, President and CEO of Wiesenthal Canada.

“It sends a clear message that Canada will not be a safe haven for terrorists or agents of the Islamic regime,” Cija said, while also calling on the government to do more.

B’nai Brith Canada, which had also complained about Masar Badil, similarly applauded the decision, saying the group was “inextricably linked” to other terror factions.

“Listing Masar Badil as a terrorist entity is an important step towards protecting Canada’s democracy, but more must be done to prevent transnational terrorist organizations from abusing our country’s freedoms to inculcate hate, violence, and extremism,” it said.

Meanwhile, the Simon Wiesenthal Centre Canada commended the move, noting Masar Badil was already sanctioned by the U.S. as a front for the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine.

“The group has promoted a conference in Toronto on November 28 and 29, with promotional materials celebrating Hamas’s October 7, 2023 massacre in Israel,” it said.

“Advertised speakers included individuals connected to terrorist organizations, some with documented ties to the Iranian regime.”

The listing makes it a crime to “knowingly deal with property owned or controlled” by the group. Financial institutions must also freeze the group’s assets.

Stewart.Bell@globalnews.CA

stories.title: Detective says police did not plan to arrest Francique, inquest hears
stories.summary: A coroner's inquest into the death of a Black man who was shot by police is hearing that officers did not plan to arrest the man the night of the fatal incident.
stories.author: Sadeen Mohsen The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A coroner’s inquest into the death of a Black man who was shot by police in Mississauga, Ont., heard Monday that officers did not necessarily plan to arrest him that night nearly seven years ago.

Peel regional police Det. Mani Sharifi said that changed when officers surveilling Jamal Francique saw him breaching his bail conditions by leaving his home on Jan. 7, 2020.

Sharifi said the plan was for police to continue surveillance on Francique, which they had been doing for roughly three or four days, when the opportunity for an arrest came up. Had Francique not left the house that evening, officers observing him would have eventually left, he said under questioning from counsel for the police force.

Francique, 28, was fatally shot by police when they attempted to arrest him as he started to drive away from the Mississauga townhouse complex.

The inquest has heard that he did not receive medical care until a tactical unit arrived about 20 minutes later and removed him from the vehicle, which had smashed into the pillar of a nearby garage. Francique died in hospital days later.

Jurors have heard that police were observing Francique for days after receiving a tip that he May have a gun and was involved in drug trafficking. However, police did not find any evidence to corroborate those allegations. The inquest has heard that officers instead determined they would arrest Francique for breaching the conditions of his bail, which included house arrest.

Asked by a juror why Francique was not arrested earlier in the week when police first observed him breaching his bail, Sharifi said his unit was focused on investigating if the man had a firearm or was involved in any drug activity.

Peel regional police Const. Ryan Andrews, who was also on scene in an unmarked police vehicle, testified that he could see Francique entering a car.

He said he attempted to let the other officers know over a police radio but another officer was using their device at the same time.

“I wasn’t sure if my transmission was fully heard by other members of the team,” he said. “The issues with the radios that we have is that there’s only one person that can speak at a time.”

He maintained that the plan was to arrest Francique before he entered his vehicle.

Andrews said Francique’s vehicle had made contact with Sharifi’s vehicle, which jurors previously heard had damage to the front passenger side bumper.

The inquest also heard on Monday that Andrews had been involved in a 2017 shooting case in which Francique was a victim. He said he was unaware of the connection to Francique until the inquest counsel brought it to his attention.

Andrews said he had responded to reports of a man who walked into a hospital with gunshot wounds.

He said he did not recall speaking with members of Francique’s family at the time but noted that multiple people had shown up at the hospital and refused to provide identification.

“Because of the nature of the shooting and we didn’t have any information on who potential shooters were, I refused them access to Mr. Francique in order to protect him,” he said.

“Apart from your attendance on that day, did you have any further involvement in respect of that investigation into the shooting of Mr. Francique back in 2017?” asked inquest counsel Roger Shallow.

“No sir,” said Andrews.

Asked if he would have disclosed the connection to his supervisor at the time of the fatal attempt to arrest Francique in 2020, Andrews said he would.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 23, 2026.

stories.title: Premiers Ford, Smith say interprovincial trade remains complicated despite efforts
stories.summary: Ford says Ontario is the only province that eradicated every trade exemption, but he agrees that internal free trade has been challenging to implement.
stories.author: Liam Casey
stories.content:
The leaders of Ontario and Alberta say internal trade barriers remain across the country despite moves to open up interprovincial free trade.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith says problems exist in the bureaucracy that underpins things like selling alcohol to the Liquor Control Board of Ontario.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford says Ontario is the only province that eradicated every trade exemption in an effort to spur the movement of goods and services between provinces, but he agrees that internal free trade has been challenging to implement.

The two spoke Monday at a fireside chat held by the Toronto Region Board of Trade.

Ontario and Alberta signed a memorandum of understanding in 2025 to open up trade, just a few months after U.S. President Donald Trump launched the trade war with Canada.

The two provinces have also agreed to recognize each other’s regulated professions, including doctors, nurses and many skilled trades.

Smith said there are more than 1,000 different types of Ontario alcohol being sold in Alberta while the Lcbo only stocks 53 Alberta alcohol products.

“Every single issue that we face as a trade barrier is exactly that, that we as premiers can make a decision that, yes, we want to open up free trade, but we have mountains and mountains of legislation, regulation and agency directives that act as individual barriers,” Smith said. “And it’s not easy to rewrite that.”

She said the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Alberta, which regulates the practice of medicine, had limited out-of-province doctors to treating 12 patients in Alberta. Smith said the province wanted to use doctors from anywhere in Canada for virtual appointments, but ran into the barrier created by the college, which is run by an independent board.

That rule was eliminated in April, Smith said.

“I just want to use those two things as a way of explaining how complicated it is,” she said.

Smith admitted that Alberta needs to further reduce the number of trade exemptions

Ford said if doctors, nurses and skilled trade workers are good enough for Alberta, they are good enough for Ontario.

“The only difference is we’re the only province, the largest province, that has zero exceptions,” Ford said.

“We got rid of everything. We said, ‘welcome.’ Now we’re seeing provinces all of a sudden starting to put up barriers.”

Ford said Ontario has signed 10 memorandums of understanding with other provinces and territories, but Quebec still has plenty of exemptions that he’d like them to get rid of.

“We were at the table and everything is: ‘no, no, no,” Ford said. “I love Quebec, I love the Quebecers — I still have to learn a little more French but I love the Quebecers — you know, it’s costing our country $200 billion to our economy.”

Ford remained frustrated at the state of interprovincial trade.

“It’s pretty sad that it’s easier to trade with other countries in the world and we can’t even get rid of these barriers within Canada,” he said.

Ford pointed to his government’s moves to open up the wine, beer and spirits market in Ontario, where grocery stores and some 8,000 convenience stores can now sell booze.

The Lcbo, however, remains in control of purchasing and selling spirits.

“Protectionism does not work, no matter if it’s in our country or across North America,” Ford said.

The two premiers are also on the same page on expanding the energy trade within the country – both want a pipeline carrying crude oil from Alberta to refineries in southern Ontario, a project they’ve dubbed the Northern Shield Energy Corridor.

stories.title: Steven Del Duca fires top civil servant using ‘strong chair’ powers
stories.summary: One source in the region, granted confidentiality to speak freely, said staff felt “blindsided” and that the decision feels “ruthless and mean.”
stories.author: Colin D'Mello
stories.content:
Days into his tenure as the Chair of York Region, Steven Del Duca has fired the top civil servant and directed staff to begin working on next year’s budget, Global News has learned, in his first use of the strong chair powers granted by the Ford government.

Shortly after he was re-elected as Mayor of Vaughan, Del Duca was appointed by the province to lead York Region council, affording him extraordinary powers to overrule both the municipal and the regional councils and control over a $5.2 billion regional budget.

On Friday, Del Duca used his “strong chair” powers for the first time, dismissing the region’s Chief Administrative Officer (CAO) who had served in the role since 2023.

“I’m writing to inform you that, following a mutual agreement, Erin Mahoney is departing as York Region’s Chief Administrative Officer. Erin’s last day is today,” Del Duca said in an internal “message from the regional chair.”

stories.title: Premier Ford won’t agree to trade deal without auto, steel and manufacturing approval
stories.summary: Ottawa is seeking what it says is an “interim deal” that would provide tariff relief for Canadian businesses and resolve core trade irritants.
stories.author: Mackenzie Gray
stories.content:
Ontario Premier Doug Ford says he will not support a trade deal between Canada and the US without approval from his province’s auto, steel, and manufacturing sectors.

“Only if the auto sector, the steel sector and manufacturing sector come to me after they see a proposal and say, we’re good with this, we can grow and survive, and then I’m all in,” Ford told the Toronto Region Board of Trade and the Calgary Chamber of Commerce on Monday.

While Ottawa and Washington would negotiate any trade deal, premiers could still skuttle an agreement. Any deal with the US is expected to include provinces putting American alcohol back on liquor store shelves and ending bans on US companies bidding on provincial procurement contracts.

Before the previous round of trade talks fell apart in August, Prime Minister Mark Carney asked provinces to put US alcohol back in liquor stores as a sign of good faith to the Americans, a move Premiers did not agree to.

US tariffs on Canadian autos were also a core sticking point during the talks, and multiple sources with knowledge of the negotiations have told Global News they remain an issue.

The US proposed in August reducing tariffs on Canadian-made autos and parts from 25% to 15%, but with no carve-out for Cusma-compliant goods, according to multiple sources.

While the Carney government tried to sell the proposal privately, key Canadian stakeholders resisted.

Automakers, labour leaders, and auto parts manufacturers told the Liberal government that a 15% tariff with no Cusma carve-out would pose substantial challenges for Canada’s auto industry, according to multiple sources familiar with the trade talks.

While US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told Fox News on Sunday that a deal between Canada and the US is “fairly close”, the Canadian side has been slightly less optimistic.

On Thursday, Canada’s chief negotiator, Janice Charette, told the Prime Minister’s Advisory Committee on Canada–U.S. Economic Relations that several trade issues remain unresolved, three sources in the meeting told Global News.

Ottawa is seeking what it says is an “interim deal” that would provide tariff relief for Canadian businesses and resolve core trade irritants ahead of Canada-U.S.-Mexico free trade renegotiation talks, according to individuals briefed by Ottawa.

This strategy has been employed by the Liberals since the Carney government took office, as part of a three-pronged approach, according to government sources.

The first step is to deal with outstanding trade issues with the Americans. Step two is to partner with the Americans in key areas, such as defence and energy, before finalizing a new free trade agreement.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith is supporting the Liberal government’s approach to negotiations.

“I think if there’s going to be a deal, there’s a very high chance it would be before the end of the year because just knowing the type of personality that we have in the White House, I don’t think he wants to be perceived to having been pushed into a deal by the Democrats,” Smith said, alongside Ford in Toronto.

“ It seems to me that this is the window for (US President Donald Trump) to say that whatever strategy he was employing with Canada, that it worked and here’s a big, beautiful deal that works for America and so that’s what I’m hoping for.”

stories.title: Privacy commissioner says transparency on surveillance pricing needed
stories.summary: Canada’s privacy commissioner says people should be warned when they are being targeted by surveillance pricing.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — Canada’s privacy commissioner says people should be warned when they are being targeted by surveillance pricing.

Philippe Dufresne says he will be developing formal guidance on how Canada’s current privacy law applies to surveillance pricing.

He says the privacy commissioner’s office wants Canadians to know why they’re paying what they’re paying.

Dufresne says it’s one thing for prices to rise because of market conditions, like a big conference taking place in town, but another to charge people more for a drug because they are sick.

Dufresne says even if people are getting a discount because of surveillance pricing, they should be made aware of it.

He says he hopes surveillance pricing is not happening in Canada or that it is not prevalent.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 23, 2026.

Anja Karadeglija, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Cadet weekend activities to be restored, Defence Minister says
stories.summary: More funding will allow weekend and supplemental activities to continue for remainder of fiscal year, says David McGuinty
stories.author: David Baxter
stories.content:
The cadet program will receive more funding so weekend and supplemental activities can continue as planned until the end of March, Defence Minister David McGuinty said Monday.

McGuinty did not say how much funding is being provided in addition to the operating budget of about $265-million for cadet programs this year.

The minister said much of the program spending for cadets happens during the summer months – when cadets take part in things like camping and sailing – and costs this year ticked up faster than anticipated.

“That was drawn down at a faster rate than we had predicted, given the size of the cadet group across the country. And so we’ve decided to basically … increase the funding to give them the support they need to pursue their activities from now [until] March 31,” McGuinty told a news conference in Ottawa on Monday.

Defence Minister David McGuinty says more funding is coming for cadet programs so that weekend and supplemental activities can continue as planned until the end of March. The Canadian Press

Cadet chapters across the county were notified last week that all extra activities – including weekend training, hiking, camping, sailing and glider flights – were being cancelled or suspended until the end of the fiscal year.

McGuinty said last week core programming would continue as cadet program leadership reviews the funding following a 59 per cent increase in enrolment in the last three years.

He said Monday the cadets program is unlike many other recreational programs because it allows people to join up at any time of the year.

“So it’s difficult for us to know in so many locations around the country, just in time, what the numbers are. Now when we look back and we see what the growth has been, it’s been considerable,” McGuinty said.

The Defence Department’s 2025-26 results report says the cadet program had more than 61,000 participants in that fiscal year.

A petition launched on Change.org last week calling on the government to restore the extra programming quickly collected more than 52,000 signatures.

Kelowna, B.C. resident Dustin Siewert is the person behind the petition and said he was “shocked’ to hear more funding is heading to the cadets to keep all parts of the program going.

“This is the last thing I expected to happen. I didn’t even know what to expect when I started it,” he said.

Siewert said he took part in cadets when he was growing up and now his two children, aged 15 and 13, are in sea cadets and the Navy league respectively.

“I’m glad he’s decided to reverse the funding and put some back. I hope that that’s enough to fulfill all the corps across Canada and maybe next year look at funding more,” Siewert said.

“Just because 20,000 kids joined, it shouldn’t end the program. It wouldn’t be any different if 20, 000 military servicemen joined. Would they cut the funding?”

Both Conservative and Bloc Québécois MPs made the cadet funding a focus of question period in the House of Commons on Friday.

Saskatchewan Conservative MP Fraser Tolmie said the funding is being restored thanks to pressure from opposition MPs and parents across the country.

McGuinty said the Defence Department will do its best to ensure the cadet program has the fiscal resources it needs from April onward.

Ottawa — The cadet program will receive more funding so weekend and supplemental activities can continue as planned until the end of March, Defence Minister David McGuinty said Monday.

McGuinty did not say how much funding is being provided in addition to the operating budget of about $265 million for cadet programs this year.

The minister said much of the program spending for cadets happens during the summer months — when cadets take part in things like camping and sailing — and costs this year ticked up faster than anticipated.

“That was drawn down at a faster rate than we had predicted, given the size of the cadet group across the country. And so we’ve decided to basically … increase the funding to give them the support they need to pursue their activities from now [until] March 31,” McGuinty told a press conference in Ottawa on Monday.

Cadet chapters across the county were notified last week that all extra activities — including weekend training, hiking, camping, sailing and glider flights — were being cancelled or suspended until the end of the fiscal year.

McGuinty said last week core programming would continue as cadet program leadership reviews the funding following a 59 per cent increase in enrolment in the last three years.

He said Monday the cadets program is unlike many other recreational programs because it allows people to join up at any time of the year.

“So it’s difficult for us to know in so many locations around the country, just in time, what the numbers are. Now when we look back and we see what the growth has been, it’s been considerable,” McGuinty said.

The Defence Department’s 2025-26 results report says the cadet program had more than 61,000 participants in that fiscal year.

A petition launched on Change.org last week calling on the government to restore the extra programming quickly collected more than 52,000 signatures.

Kelowna, B.C. resident Dustin Siewert is the person behind the petition and said he was “shocked’ to hear more funding is heading the cadets to keep all parts of the program going.

“This is the last thing I expected to happen. I didn’t even know what to respect when I started it,” he said.

Siewert said he took part in cadets when he was growing up and now his two children, aged 15 and 13, are in sea cadets and the Navy league respectively.

“I’m glad he’s decided to reverse the funding and put some back. I hope that that’s enough to fulfil all the corps across Canada and maybe next year look at funding more,” Siewert said.

“Just because 20,000 kids joined, it shouldn’t end the program. It wouldn’t be any different if 20, 000 military servicemen joined. Would they cut the funding?”

Both Conservative and Bloc Québécois MPs made the cadet funding a focus of question period in the House of Commons on Friday.

Saskatchewan Conservative MP Fraser Tolmie said the funding is being restored thanks to pressure from opposition MPs and parents across the country.

McGuinty said the Defence Department will do its best to ensure the cadet program has the fiscal resources it needs from April onward.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 23, 2026.

David Baxter, The Canadian Press
