stories.title: Former London fire captain identified in 1968 killing of Jacqueline Dunleavy
stories.summary: London police say a historical homicide investigation has been solved through the use of modern DNA technology and investigative techniques.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
Nearly 59 years after the killing of 16-year-old Jacqueline “Jackie” Dunleavy, police in London, Ont., say they have identified the man responsible for her death through new DNA testing and forensic investigative genetic genealogy.

The London Police Service announced Monday that investigators have identified Michael Joseph Moore, a former London firefighter who retired as a captain, as the person responsible for Dunleavy’s murder.

Police say Moore, who was 25 at the time of the murder, died on March 3, 2018, before he was identified through the investigation. As a result, no criminal charges can be laid.

Dunleavy, a Grade 10 student at Westminster Secondary School, was working at Stanley Variety Store on Stanley Street near Wharncliffe Road on Jan. 9, 1968. Police say she finished her shift at approximately 6:30 p.m. and was last seen leaving the store on foot.

At about 8 p.m., three youths found Dunleavy on the grounds of Katherine Harley School, now the site of Matthews Hall on Oxford Street. Emergency responders attended the scene, and she was pronounced dead.

Gallery: Jackie Dunleavy cold case photos

Investigators determined Dunleavy had been murdered. While she suffered a head injury, police say the cause of death was strangulation.

‘A daughter, a sister, a friend’

The case remained unsolved for decades despite an extensive investigation that included witness interviews, the pursuit of numerous leads and the collection and preservation of forensic evidence.

“For nearly six decades, Jackie’s family has lived with a loss that no passage of time could ever erase, and with unanswered questions about who was responsible for her death,” Thai Truong, London’s police chief, said during a press conference Monday.

“A daughter, a sister, a friend and a young girl who had her entire life ahead of her. Jackie was also the daughter of a London police officer. As chief of police, I recognize the particular significance of that connection to our profession.”

According to police, the case was reviewed repeatedly over the years, including through Project Angel, a joint initiative involving the London Police Service and the Ontario Provincial Police between 1997 and 2001.

More recently, members of the Major Crime Section conducted a comprehensive review of the investigation, re-examining historical evidence and taking advantage of advances in forensic science.

Police say additional DNA testing was conducted on preserved evidence. Investigators worked with forensic laboratory Othram, the Toronto Police Service, the Ontario Provincial Police and the Centre of Forensic Sciences to identify distant genetic relatives linked to an unknown DNA profile and narrow the investigation to a suspect.

According to police, investigators conducted further interviews, gathered additional evidence and obtained DNA samples for comparison. Based on the evidence collected, police say they determined the threshold for criminal charges had been met had Moore still been alive.

What we know about Michael Moore

According to police, Michael Joseph Moore was born in Ireland in 1942 and immigrated to Canda in January 1967.

At the time of Dunleavy’s murder, police said Moore was living in an apartment on Sprinbank Drive. He had been living in the city for less than a year when Dunleavy was killed.

He was described as being about 6′ tall, had dark hair, was typically clean shaven and spoke with an Irish accent and it’s believed the vehicle he drove was a 1964 Ford Galaxy 500, four-door sedan.

Det. Mike Budzyn with London police said, “Based on the evidence obtained through this investigation, we are confident that the evidentiary threshold to support criminal charges was met. Had Moore been alive today, he would have been arrested and charge with Jackie’s murder.”

At the time of the murder in January 1968, police said Moore was not a firefighter, but that he joined after and served for approximately 28 years, retiring as a captain.

“We recognize that this information May be significant to individuals who knew Moore personally, worked alongside him, or had contact with him during his years of servie,” said Budzyn.

He went on to say, “the investigative findings we are announcing today are based on forensic evidence and the totality of the investigation, not on Moore’s subsequent profession or standing in the community.”

Budzyn acknowledged the impact the findings have had on Moore’s family.

“They were understandably shocked by the results of this investigation and asked that their privacy be respected. They also expressed their hope that these findings will provide long awaited answers for Jackie’s family.”

According to an obituary, Moore passed away in 2018 after a long illness.

Statement from London fire

The London Fire Department offered condolences to the family of Jacqueline Dunleavy following the announcement that police had identified a suspect in her 1968 killing.

“Today’s news has been deeply troubling for many within the London Fire Department,” the department said in a statement. “Our focus at this time is on supporting our staff and acknowledging the impact of this news on our community.”

The department noted that Moore was not a firefighter at the time of Dunleavy’s murder, adding that he retired from the fire service in 2012.

The department said it remains committed to maintaining the trust of the community and will continue to cooperate with London police as needed.

Information still sought

Police say they have chosen to publicly identify Moore to provide clarity in a case that remained unresolved for nearly six decades and to give answers to Dunleavy’s family and the community.

Investigators are still encouraging anyone with historical information about Moore or the case to come forward, saying details that May have seemed insignificant at the time could still be relevant today.

This is a developing story.

stories.title: To live longer, you’ll not only need to move to a big city, but to the right neighbourhood
stories.summary: In wealth and health, the increasing gap between the haves and have-nots should concern us all
stories.author: Mike Moffatt
stories.content:
Where you live in Canada will determine how long you’ll live. And if you want to live longer, you’ll not only need to move to a big city but to the right part of that city – the richer part.

Recent Statistics Canada data shows kids born in or near Montreal, Vancouver or Toronto can expect to have the greatest longevity. However, a second study by St. Michael’s Hospital in Toronto finds that simply moving to the city is not enough, since kids growing up in one Toronto neighbourhood could, ON average, live a decade or more longer than those just a few blocks away.

The recent Statscan data on life expectancy at birth is mostly good news, showing that the expected lifespan of a newborn has increased by almost a full year since 2008, to 81.7 years from 80.8. Advancements in health care and reductions in smoking rates are helping Canadians lead longer, healthier lives.

Unfortunately, a rising health tide is not lifting all boats. In 2008, babies born in the top 20 per cent of the 93 Canadian regions in the dataset were expected to live, ON average, five years longer than those born in the bottom 20 per cent.

Examining those same regions today, the top regions of 2008 have seen their life expectancy rise by more than a year, while those at the bottom have seen theirs fall by more than a year, widening that gap to nearly eight full years.

It appears that the key to living a long life, ON average, is living in a city. The regions in the top 20 per cent are almost entirely urban, with York Region, Peel Region and Vancouver in the top three. The bottom 20 per cent are almost entirely remote rural regions, with Northern Manitoba, Nunavut and Nunavik rounding out the bottom three.

This rise in life expectancy inequality mirrors rising inequality in other aspects of Canadian life. Both the length and quality of someone’s life are shaped by income security and access to health care.

Canada continues to urbanize, creating regions that are being left behind both in terms of economic opportunity and the critical population mass needed to keep health care and other social services viable.

Appearances, however, can be misleading; simply moving to a city is not enough to extend your life, as health outcomes vary substantially within a city, even at the neighbourhood level.

According to research from St. Michael’s Hospital in Toronto, kids who grow up in wealthier neighbourhoods such as Yonge-Doris, East Willowdale and Hillcrest Village can expect to live more than a decade longer than those who are raised in Moss Park.

Lower-income Canadians might live close to a hospital or a family doctor, but that does not guarantee equal access to these resources. The poor often lack the resources to navigate a complex system, making it less likely they will have a family doctor or be referred to a specialist.

Lack of access to a family doctor or specialist leads to poorer outcomes for both poorer families and poorer communities. A 2024 study found that lower-income Canadians have less access to cancer screening and diagnosis and higher rates of mortality than those living in higher-income areas.

Opinion: Do children need to grow up in a detached home with a yard to thrive?

Whether we are thinking about wealth or health, the increasing gap between the haves and have-nots should concern us all. It has always been true that one of the most important things we can do is to choose our parents carefully.

But a successful country is one where someone can rise from humble beginnings, and with a bit of talent, hard work and luck, a person can overcome early-life challenges.

Economists have been sounding the alarm about the decline in economic mobility in Canada and the growing power of “poverty traps.” A growing cohort of young people is being denied both wealth and health, simply by being born to the wrong parents in the wrong neighbourhood, a trend that threatens social cohesion. The rise of far-right parties in left-behind regions, like the AfD in Saxony in eastern Germany, highlights the risks.

Smart public policy, from regional economic development policies to health care reforms, can make it less risky to grow up in the wrong neighbourhood or the wrong part of Canada.

But this will require acknowledging the depth of inequality in Canada and that, despite our public health care system, the wealthy still have better access to care than the poor.

Mike Moffatt is the founding director of the Missing Middle Initiative and co-host of the Missing Middle podcast .
paragraphs: Where you live in Canada will determine how long you’ll live. And if you want to live longer, you’ll not only need to move to a big city but to the right part of that city – the richer part.

Recent Statistics Canada data shows kids born in or near Montreal, Vancouver or Toronto can expect to have the greatest longevity. However, a second study by St. Michael’s Hospital in Toronto finds that simply moving to the city is not enough, since kids growing up in one Toronto neighbourhood could, ON average, live a decade or more longer than those just a few blocks away.

The recent Statscan data on life expectancy at birth is mostly good news, showing that the expected lifespan of a newborn has increased by almost a full year since 2008, to 81.7 years from 80.8. Advancements in health care and reductions in smoking rates are helping Canadians lead longer, healthier lives.

Unfortunately, a rising health tide is not lifting all boats. In 2008, babies born in the top 20 per cent of the 93 Canadian regions in the dataset were expected to live, ON average, five years longer than those born in the bottom 20 per cent.

Examining those same regions today, the top regions of 2008 have seen their life expectancy rise by more than a year, while those at the bottom have seen theirs fall by more than a year, widening that gap to nearly eight full years.

It appears that the key to living a long life, ON average, is living in a city. The regions in the top 20 per cent are almost entirely urban, with York Region, Peel Region and Vancouver in the top three. The bottom 20 per cent are almost entirely remote rural regions, with Northern Manitoba, Nunavut and Nunavik rounding out the bottom three.

This rise in life expectancy inequality mirrors rising inequality in other aspects of Canadian life. Both the length and quality of someone’s life are shaped by income security and access to health care.

Canada continues to urbanize, creating regions that are being left behind both in terms of economic opportunity and the critical population mass needed to keep health care and other social services viable.
Appearances, however, can be misleading; simply moving to a city is not enough to extend your life, as health outcomes vary substantially within a city, even at the neighbourhood level.

According to research from St. Michael’s Hospital in Toronto, kids who grow up in wealthier neighbourhoods such as Yonge-Doris, East Willowdale and Hillcrest Village can expect to live more than a decade longer than those who are raised in Moss Park.

Lower-income Canadians might live close to a hospital or a family doctor, but that does not guarantee equal access to these resources. The poor often lack the resources to navigate a complex system, making it less likely they will have a family doctor or be referred to a specialist.

Lack of access to a family doctor or specialist leads to poorer outcomes for both poorer families and poorer communities. A 2024 study found that lower-income Canadians have less access to cancer screening and diagnosis and higher rates of mortality than those living in higher-income areas.

stories.title: Temperatures plunge to seasonal levels as snow, strong winds move in
stories.summary: Southwestern Ontario is in for a return to more seasonal weather this week, with colder temperatures, strong winds and the possibility of snow, freezing rain and icy conditions.
stories.content:
Southwestern Ontario is in for a return to more seasonal weather this week, with colder temperatures, strong winds and the possibility of snow, freezing rain and icy conditions.

“We’ve been spoiled of late,” CTV News meteorologist Gary Archibald said. “Now we’re looking at temperatures that will be seasonal, if not slightly below seasonal.”

London is expected to reach 6 C on Monday before temperatures fall to the freezing mark overnight. Rain is forecast to change to snow, while northwesterly winds could gust up to 55 km/h Tuesday morning.

“There’s even a chance of some ice pellets or freezing rain,” Archibald said.

London could see between two and five centimetres of snow, with daytime highs remaining between 2 C and 5 C for much of the week.

“Be prepared for the precipitation, colder temperatures and some icy surfaces for this week,” Archibald said.

stories.title: Locked out Regina Transit union says ‘status quo is not going to be acceptable’
stories.summary: Almost two years after their last contract expired, the City of Regina has locked out Regina Transit workers, instructing them not to come into work.
stories.author: Tavi Dhillon
stories.content:
Regina Transit employees are experiencing a “pivotal movement” after being locked out by the city during contract negotiations, according to the union’s president.

The contract between the Amalgamated Transit Union (ATU) Local 588, which represents Regina Transit employees, and the City of Regina expired at the end of 2024.

“This is a pivotal moment for transit and for negotiations. We have been at the bargaining table for almost two years in this city. We have been bargaining in good faith,” John Di Nino, national president of ATU Canada told reporters and transit workers.

They were gathered at the Regina Transit Operations Centre on Winnipeg Street Monday morning at 11 a.m., when the City of Regina’s lockout notice, instructing employees not to work, was set to go into effect. The city locked employees out after the union said Friday it would take job action by suspending voluntary overtime.

“Our members showed up to work today in uniform, prepared to continue to provide the valuable service that our riders need. And the gates were locked, and our members were refused entry,” Di Nino said, adding that this is first lockout notice he has dealt with in his decades working in transit.

ATU Canada represents approximately 40,000 transit workers across the country, including roughly 380 in Regina.

Speaking to striking workers and the media, local ATU vice-president Pat Nichol said Regina Transit union members deserve fair compensation for their work. She said she could not speak to exact figures on what that general wage increase would look like.

“We have come to work every day. We have done our jobs every day. We come, we work. We make sure that the citizens of Regina are taken care of,” Nichol said. “It’s just so frustrating that all of a sudden, they can just knock us off like that.”

“When COVID happened, we were heroes. And right now, we’re being locked out. It’s crazy.”

Nichol said some Regina Transit employees have been using the food bank to make ends meet.

She and Di Nino both said the union is ready to go back to the table, but only if the city is ready to present a fair deal.

“We are only prepared to go back to the bargaining table if the company is willing to come and sit down and have fruitful discussions and resolve this contract. Status quo is not going to be acceptable,” Di Nino said.

Regina Mayor Chad Bachynski noted in a Monday morning statement that city council is not responsible for union negotiations, saying that it’s the responsibility of city administration.

“This situation arose after negotiations reached an impasse, a stage in the process where Saskatchewan labour law allows legal job action by either party,” Bachynski wrote.

The mayor said that the decision to halt service was “not taken lightly and was based on safety and reliability concerns.” He pointed to the transit schedule, which varies daily, and the expected effect that disrupted staffing would have on riders.

“The City determined that without sufficient staffing and maintenance coverage, it could not guarantee safe, dependable service for riders, employees and the public. For example, impacted service would vary each day and would not be able to be communicated in advance to customers as Administration May only get 30 minutes of notice,” Bachynski said.

“As a result, customers May be waiting extended periods of time for a bus and when one arrives, it May be overcrowded and unable to accept more passengers. We want all service restored as soon as possible.”

In response to the mayor’s comments, Di Nino said, “although (city council is) not at the bargaining table, it is city council that has to mandate what those contracts look like, they have to approve them.

“They’re the ones who hire the city managers and transit managers. They should be giving them the directive to get this issue resolved Asap. Put our members back onto the job and get transit running in this city,” Di Nino added.

To reach that resolution, Regina’s mayor and Di Nino both said the city and union must be willing to return to the table and negotiate a fair agreement. The parties are set to meet with a provincial negotiator on Monday afternoon, according to the ATU president.

Ottawa — The federal government added anti-Israel group Masar Badil to its terrorist entity list on Monday, days before the organization was set to host a conference in Toronto.

In a release, Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree said Masar Badil is effectively an alias for Samidoun, another anti-Israel group that is already listed as a terrorist group in Canada.

The listing comes after weeks of pressure from various Jewish and Israeli groups, including the Israeli government, to have Masar Badil listed due to its open ties to other terrorist groups, such as Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine (Pflp) and Samidoun.

“There is evidence that the two groups are the same entity and that Masar Badil is acting as a faction/offshoot of Samidoun,” reads a release by the minister. It also confirmed the group’s close ties to the Pflp, Samidoun and Hamas.

On Monday, National Post reported that Amichai Chikli, Israel’s Minister of Diaspora Affairs and Combating Antisemitism, wrote to Prime Minister Mark Carney calling for “an urgent interagency security assessment” of a Nov. 28-29 conference organized by Masar Badil in Toronto.

In the letter, Chikli also called for an examination of its organizers’ “financing and logistical support,” and a review of “the admissibility of foreign participants.”

The conference program includes discussions on international coalition-building, campus activism, diaspora organizing and opposition to counterterrorism politics. Other advertised sessions include “The Red-Green Alliance,” “Academia: A Demobilizing Force?” and “Building a Global Camp of Resistance.”

The organizers also describe Hamas’s Oct. 7, 2023, attack on Israel as “one of the most courageous acts of resistance in our lifetimes” in their promotional material.

The Israeli minister alleged the advertised conference name and program represent an effort to celebrate the Hamas-led attack rather than discuss Palestinian political issues.

Being listed as a terrorist organization will likely halt Masar Badil from hosting any event in Canada.

Under the Criminal Code, it is prohibited from providing any form of support to a listed terrorist organization. That means it’s illegal to financially aid the group or even allow it to use property in Canada, according to Public Safety Canada.

stories.title: Police solve 1968 murder of teen girl in London, Ont., thanks to genetic genealogy
stories.summary: Police in London, Ont., say they have identified the suspect in the murder of a 16-year-old girl nearly six decades ago using advanced genetic technology.
stories.author: Sharif Hassan The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Police in London, Ont., say they have identified the suspect in the murder of a 16-year-old girl nearly six decades ago using advanced genetic technology.

Nov. 23, 2026

By Sharif Hassan The Canadian Press

They say Jacqueline “Jackie” Dunleavy was last seen after finishing her shift at a variety store in the evening of Jan. 9, 1968.

Police say three youths found Dunleavy dead on the grounds of a school, now known as Matthews Hall, at around 8 p.m. that evening.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Inside interior designer Nora Voon’s art-filled home

Image 10Image 11

They say while she had a head injury, the investigation revealed she had died of strangulation.

Investigators say they identified Michael Joseph Moore, who was 25 years old at the time, as the person responsible for the girl’s murder after re-examination of carefully persevered evidence and additional DNA testing.

They say no criminal charges will be laid because Moore died in 2018.

Police said while the case has been thoroughly reviewed by generations of investigators over the years, the use of modern genetic genealogy made it possible to “construct family trees and narrow the investigation toward a potential suspect.”

“Our investigators conducted additional interviews, gathered new evidence, and obtained DNA samples for comparison. Those samples were submitted to the Centre of Forensic Sciences for analysis,” Det. Mike Budzyn, who is leading the investigation, said in a news release.

“Based on the evidence obtained through this investigation, we are confident that the evidentiary threshold to support criminal charges was met. Had Moore been alive today, he would have been arrested and charged in relation to Jackie’s murder.”

Identifying the suspect answers questions that the victim’s family and community had for decades, police said.

Investigators are now asking people who knew Moore to come forward.

“Information that may not have seemed significant at the time could have meaning today,” police said in a statement.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 23, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.summary: Toronto - Ontario's minister of colleges and universities says a career college with student financial aid usage that grew thousands of per cent in a few years was not one of six he cut off in May because of the "evolving nature of the data."
stories.author: Allison Jones The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - A career college with student financial aid usage that grew thousands of per cent in a few years was not one of six the Ontario government cut off in May because of the “evolving” nature of the data, the minister in charge said Monday.

Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn this spring made six career colleges ineligible for the Ontario Student Assistance Program due to what the ministry called concerns with “high-risk” admissions practices.

stories.title: Three Calgary police officers charged with manslaughter
stories.summary: Charges are in relation to the death of a 42-year-old man at a hotel in southern Calgary in September 2024
stories.author: Bill Graveland
stories.content:
Three Calgary officers were arrested Monday and charged with manslaughter in the death of a man who was allegedly punched in the head, put in restraints and sedated in a hotel lobby.

The Alberta Serious Incident Response Team, the province’s police watchdog, said the 42-year-old man died at the hotel in 2024. Staff had called police to ask for help removing the man, as he was loitering near a check-in desk.

Constables Roy Braun, Filip Poskovic and Vincent Washington were also charged with assault causing bodily harm.

“Asirt’s investigation found reasonable grounds to believe offences were committed,” the watchdog said in a news release.

“Following a review of the investigation and further review and advice from the Alberta Crown Prosecution Service that charges be laid, Asirt executive director Matthew Block determined that the involved officers should be charged.”

The accused officers were released on an undertaking. They are set to appear in court Jan. 6.

In a video posted on social media, Calgary police Chief Katie McLellan said the officers have been relieved from their duties with pay.

“These are very serious charges and we recognize the significant impact this incident has had and continues to have on everyone involved. This is a very difficult time for all of the families involved,” Mr. McLellan said.

“This is not the time to make assumptions about what happened. There are real people and families behind this … many whose lives have and will be impacted forever.”

Mr. McLellan said the police service works hard to build meaningful relationships with all communities that it serves.

“As we move forward in the days, weeks and months, I want to be clear that our commitment to providing fair, transparent and respectful policing remains as steadfast as it has ever been,” she said.

“We have every confidence in the criminal justice system and its ability to address this matter fairly and thoroughly.”

At the time of the man’s death, the chief of the Blood Tribe identified him as Jon Wells.

He appeared dazed when he was told to leave the Carriage House Hotel and Conference Centre by police on Sept. 17, 2024, Asirt said in a statement at the time.

It said the man raised his hands and started to walk out, telling officers, “I don’t want to die.”

Mr. Wells was tackled to the ground after he resisted an officer trying to grab him and was then punched in the head. At this point, Asirt said, officers fought the man for 3 1/2 minutes with “various uses of force.”

The man was put in handcuffs and leg restraints, and a spit mask was placed on his mouth, said Asirt. He was then “noted to be bleeding from the mouth and vomits.”

Seven minutes later, the agency said the man was sedated by emergency crews and left lying face down. After three more minutes, he was found unresponsive.

Mr. Wells was declared dead a short while later.

“At no point during the interaction had the male been identified, nor was he ever told he was being detained or under arrest,” Asirt said.

Defence lawyer Cory Wilson, who represents Const. Poskovic, said his client denies the allegations.

“He is presumed innocent and plans to vigorously defend himself at trial,” said Mr. Wilson.

Defence lawyer Shamsher Kothari said his client, Const. Braun, also denies the allegations and is presumed innocent.

“We look forward to challenging the evidence in court and having him exonerated,” Kothari said.

Defence lawyer Don MacLeod, who represents Washington, said his client also maintains he did nothing wrong.

“My client maintains his innocence and intends to mount a vigorous defence,” MacLeod said in an interview Monday evening.

stories.title: Canadian-resident return trips from U.S. in September up again
stories.summary: Statistics Canada says the number of Canadian-resident return trips from the United States in September was up compared with a year ago, continuing a trend that began earlier this year.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — Statistics Canada says the number of Canadian-resident return trips from the United States in September was up compared with a year ago, continuing a trend that began earlier this year.

The agency says it was the sixth consecutive month the number of Canadian residents returning from the United States was up year-over-year, following 15 consecutive months of year-over-year decreases.

The shift reverses a trend of Canadians shunning travel to the United States in the face of President Donald Trump’s tariffs and talk of making Canada the 51st state.

The number of Canadian-resident return trips from the United States in September totalled 2.5 million, up 8.7 per cent compared with a year earlier. However, Statistics Canada said that even with the increase, the number of Canadian-resident return trips from the United States in September were down 24.9 per cent compared with September 2024.

U.S.-resident trips to Canada in September numbered 2.5 million, up 16.7 per cent from a year earlier, the eighth consecutive month of year-over-year increases.

Canadian resident return trips from overseas countries totalled one million in September, up 3.2 per cent from the same month a year earlier.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 23, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Tardy Carney teases Trump, via surrogates, at press gallery dinner
stories.summary: The PM, who was late to arrive and left early, invited impersonators of the U.S. president and himself to deliver part of his speech
stories.author: Kenn Oliver
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney arrived late and left early at Saturday’s 2026 Parliamentary Press Gallery Dinner, but stayed long enough to land a few well-placed, mostly collegial jabs at his political counterparts, the media, and U.S. President Donald Trump, mostly via comic surrogate.

He even borrowed a page from Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre’s 2025 dinner playbook, bringing on This Hour has 22 Minutes cast to deliver part of his speech.

Carney made his “long-awaited” appearance about 30 minutes into the event in downtown Ottawa, weaving through tables on his way to the stage, the applause waning before he stepped to the microphone.

“God, I couldn’t even sustain the applause to get up to this stage,” he said.

“Look, I thought I should show up when I heard I was on the menu.”

He first remarked on the night’s “amazing meal,” which he appeared not to partake of, but said it was “nothing compared to” what’s served on official prime ministerial flights aboard Canada One, a subject routinely highlighted by the Canadian Taxpayers Federation and media outlets.

“But then again, what are those media subsidies really for,” he joked.

In the time since last year’s press gallery soiree, Carney said he’s learned that the biggest challenge “isn’t managing the economy… it’s managing relationships with difficult, antagonistic, unpredictable leaders.”

“Look, I am all for taking the world as it is,” he continued. “So I will work with anyone — ideologues, tyrants, dictators. I call it cooperative federalism.”

The prime minister often invokes the term when publicly discussing working with provinces, territories, and Indigenous partners on major projects, economic growth, and national unity.

Carney welcomed federal NDP Leader Avi Lewis to his first press gallery dinner, working in a dig at Poilievre in the process.

“Hope you’re enjoying your seat. Pierre and I know they’re hard, right? They’re hard to come by,” he said. “But if you can get a seat, and then you can stick around long enough trying to tear Canada down, you too can have a taxpayer-funded pension.”

Carney only alluded to U.S. President Trump once in his speech.

“Damn. This is a tough room. And I’ve been in the Oval Office. Alone. With its new interior decorator,” he said, drawing perhaps his biggest laughs.

U.S. President Donald Trump, right, shakes hands with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney during a meeting in the Oval Office of the White House on Oct. 7, 2025, in Washington, D.C. Anna Moneymaker / Getty Images

Shortly after, though, Carney turned a chunk of his time over to Canadian actor Mark McKinney, who regularly impersonates him on 22 Minutes, often portraying him as a taciturn elitist.

Poilievre did the same in 2025, getting 22 Minutes’ Chris Wilson to reprise his oft-used impersonation.

Faux-Carney brought breaking news about Canada’s decision over which fighter jet it will purchase, the American F-35 or the Swedish-made Gripen.

“The American ambassador, naturally, is doing everything he can to make sure it’s the Gripen,” he said, referencing Canada’s sometimes prickly relationship with U.S. ambassador Pete Hoekstra.

“But we are going with a made-in-Canada option that will terrify our enemies and it’s called Air Canada Rouge.”

The Carneys were soon joined on stage by 22 Minutes mainstay Mark Critch, doing his Trump impersonation and promising the actual prime minister that they’re going to soon settle a trade deal.

“We’re going to have a deal, aren’t we? Mark, we’re going to have an incredible deal,” Critch’s Trump said. “I call him Mark. I don’t call him the governor to his face because I’m a coward.”

He went on to say his real reason for attending is to scalp a member of Canada’s press gallery to become his new press secretary and he wanted Carney’s opinion.

“Mr. President, if I May, the press gallery is very different than a press secretary. The press secretary argues with the press. They don’t answer questions. They accuse the media of fake news. No one here would do that,” Carney said.

“Although, Pierre, I think I May have found your next gig. Jamil (Jivani), are you willing to put in a good word with JD?”

The Conservative MP is a former college classmate and personal friend of U.S. Vice-President JD Vance.

After a few more light quips, including a few at Postmedia’s expense, Carney left the stage and appeared to make his way for the exit, prompting emcees to question aloud whether he was staying. He eventually settled on the sidelines, but was shown on Cpac standing throughout Poilievre’s follow-up address.

Poilievre delivered a few remarks in French before switching to English for the rest of the way at what he described as a “God-awful event.”

“This year I was planning to have a temporary foreign worker come and give my speech. But for the first time in history, the immigration minister refused the permit. I should have just said it was for Tim Hortons,” he joked.

He then turned on Carney, remarking on the prime minister’s seemingly routine absence from Canada and suggesting he only showed up because he was told it was a “foreign correspondents’ dinner.”

Governor-General Louise Arbour, who spoke before any of the politicians, made a similar joke before Carney arrived.

“Do you know the difference between God and Mark Carney,” she asked. “God is everywhere and Mark Carney is everywhere except in Ottawa where he’s supposed to be.”

Poilievre drew his biggest laughs from a self-deprecating joke.

“Some say that Mark has a controlling leadership style. There’s been reports that he yells and micromanages his staff. He acts like a miserable p—k to journalists. And when I hear things like that, I say, once again, he’s stealing all my ideas.”

His biggest swing at Carney came right after, while talking about efforts to secure a trade deal with the U.S.

“Imagine having to sit across the table from that guy. We’re talking about a New York-based, tax-dodging wheeler-and-dealer who insults female journalists, uses his office to enrich himself and his friends and has been photographed with the Epstein circle many times,” he said as it became clear where the punchline was heading.

“And on the other side of the table, you’ve got Donald Trump.”

Carney’s name appears in passing across dozens of U.S. Department of Justice documents related to the late Jeffrey Epstein, disgraced financier and child sex offender, though none point to any direct involvement between the men.

Poilievre ended his speech by tossing fake $20 bills out to media outlets he accused of being “dependent on money from politicians and from government.”

“But let me assure you, it is not spending; it is an investment.”

Lewis followed, arguing that he is more than an “overeducated purity tester, a latte-swilling downtown dilettante, an ivory tower, job-killing environmental zealot.” He’s also serious about tackling “Carney-mania.”

“What consultant would ever have predicted that a central banker quoting Thucydides would make the whole world go weak in the knees,” he pondered.

Before turning the microphone over to the new Green Party Leader Mike Morris, with whom he decided to share his time, Lewis thanked Poilievre for standing up for the working class by “showing up everywhere in a hard hat, looking like one of the Village People.”

He concluded by saying the NDP, which has but five seats in the House of Commons, was facing an uphill battle in the years ahead. But the future of the party, he said, is not in his hands.

“It’s up to (Manitoba Premier) Wab Kinew when he finally decides to return to Ottawa.”

“We’re going to have a deal, aren’t we? Mark, we’re going to have an incredible deal,” Critch’s Trump said. “I call him Mark. I don’t call him the governor to his face because I’m a coward.”
He went on to say his real reason for attending is to scalp a member of Canada’s press gallery to become his new press secretary and he wanted Carney’s opinion.

“Mr. President, if I May, the press gallery is very different than a press secretary. The press secretary argues with the press. They don’t answer questions. They accuse the media of fake news. No one here would do that,” Carney said.
“Although, Pierre, I think I May have found your next gig. Jamil (Jivani), are you willing to put in a good word with JD?”
The Conservative MP is a former college classmate and personal friend of U.S. Vice-President JD Vance.

After a few more light quips, including a few at Postmedia’s expense, Carney left the stage and appeared to make his way for the exit, prompting emcees to question aloud whether he was staying. He eventually settled on the sidelines, but was shown on Cpac standing throughout Poilievre’s follow-up address.
Poilievre delivered a few remarks in French before switching to English for the rest of the way at what he described as a “God-awful event.”

“This year I was planning to have a temporary foreign worker come and give my speech. But for the first time in history, the immigration minister refused the permit. I should have just said it was for Tim Hortons,” he joked.
He then turned on Carney, remarking on the prime minister’s seemingly routine absence from Canada and suggesting he only showed up because he was told it was a “foreign correspondents’ dinner.”
Governor-General Louise Arbour, who spoke before any of the politicians, made a similar joke before Carney arrived.
“Do you know the difference between God and Mark Carney,” she asked. “God is everywhere and Mark Carney is everywhere except in Ottawa where he’s supposed to be.”
Poilievre drew his biggest laughs from a self-deprecating joke.

“Some say that Mark has a controlling leadership style. There’s been reports that he yells and micromanages his staff. He acts like a miserable p—k to journalists. And when I hear things like that, I say, once again, he’s stealing all my ideas.”
His biggest swing at Carney came right after, while talking about efforts to secure a trade deal with the U.S.

“Imagine having to sit across the table from that guy. We’re talking about a New York-based, tax-dodging wheeler-and-dealer who insults female journalists, uses his office to enrich himself and his friends and has been photographed with the Epstein circle many times,” he said as it became clear where the punchline was heading.
“And on the other side of the table, you’ve got Donald Trump.”

Carney’s name appears in passing across dozens of U.S. Department of Justice documents related to the late Jeffrey Epstein, disgraced financier and child sex offender, though none point to any direct involvement between the men.
Poilievre ended his speech by tossing fake $20 bills out to media outlets he accused of being “dependent on money from politicians and from government.”
“But let me assure you, it is not spending; it is an investment.”
Editor’s Picks

Lewis followed, arguing that he is more than an “overeducated purity tester, a latte-swilling downtown dilettante, an ivory tower, job-killing environmental zealot.” He’s also serious about tackling “Carney-mania.”
“What consultant would ever have predicted that a central banker quoting Thucydides would make the whole world go weak in the knees,” he pondered.

Before turning the microphone over to the new Green Party Leader Mike Morris, with whom he decided to share his time, Lewis thanked Poilievre for standing up for the working class by “showing up everywhere in a hard hat, looking like one of the Village People.”
He concluded by saying the NDP, which has but five seats in the House of Commons, was facing an uphill battle in the years ahead. But the future of the party, he said, is not in his hands.
“It’s up to (Manitoba Premier) Wab Kinew when he finally decides to return to Ottawa.”

stories.title: Olivia Chow uses strong mayor powers to replace Toronto's city manager
stories.summary: Toronto - Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow is using her strong mayor powers to replace the city's top bureaucrat with an interim hire and shake up the city's organizational structure.
stories.author: Kathryn Mannie The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow is using her strong mayor powers to replace the city’s top bureaucrat with an interim hire and shake up the city’s organizational structure.

City manager Paul Johnson is exiting the role after four years and Toronto’s chief financial officer, Stephen Conforti, will take over the job temporarily starting this Friday.

stories.title: Child killed in crash involving SUV, semi-truck on Regina Bypass
stories.summary: RCMP in Saskatchewan say a young child has died after a two-vehicle collision involving an SUV and a semi-truck.
stories.author: Rebecca Lau
stories.content:
RCMP in Saskatchewan say a young child has died after a two-vehicle collision involving an SUV and a semi-truck.

Officers with White Butte RCMP responded to the crash on Nov. 20 at around 5 p.m. on the Regina Bypass, just south of Highway 1.

According to police, a child under the age of five who was a passenger in the SUV was declared deceased at the scene.

The driver and another passenger in the SUV were taken to hospital with injuries described as serious.

Police say the driver of the semi did not report any injuries.

White Butte RCMP continue to investigate the incident, along with a Saskatchewan RCMP collision reconstructionist.

Police note that as of Nov. 23, there have been 84 fatal collisions with 100 deaths on roadways policed by the Saskatchewan RCMP in 2026.

stories.title: Remains of N.B. sailor recovered nearly 80 years after plane crash
stories.summary: Nearly 80 years after a two-seat naval fighter crashed in Northern Ireland, the remains of a young man from New Brunswick have been recovered and identified.
stories.author: Rebecca Lau
stories.content:
Nearly 80 years after a two-seat naval fighter crashed in Northern Ireland, the remains of a young man from New Brunswick have been recovered, and he will be laid to rest in the presence of his family.

Steward James (Jimmy) Willard MacDonald died in the plane crash in 1947. Recovery efforts at the time were unsuccessful.

But in June 2025, two Northern Ireland aviation archaeologists became interested in investigating the site.

After multiple ground penetrating radar surveys, a recovery operation began in July 2026 by the Casualty Identification Program with the support of various Canadian and Commonwealth military units and archaeologists.

Just this month, the remains recovered were identified after careful analysis using historical, anthropological and dental records.

“The identification of Steward MacDonald reminds us of the dedication of generations of Canadians who gave everything for their country,” said National Defence Minister David McGuinty in a new release.

“We thank all those who contributed to this effort, and to the ongoing work to remember and honour those who made the ultimate sacrifice in service to Canada. To Steward MacDonald’s family: know that we will remember and honour him always.”

MacDonald was 25 years old and serving with the 803 Naval Air Squadron at Royal Naval Air Service Eglinton at the time of his death.

He was born in Newcastle, N.B., and joined the Royal Canadian Naval Volunteer Reserve in April 1942 during the Second World War.

According to the Department of National Defence, MacDonald began as a probationary steward on Hmcs Brunswicker. Stewards had various duties, including serving meals, tending officers’ quarters and caring for the officers’ uniforms.

Records showed MacDonald worked his way up, and was posted to Hmcs Stadacona in Halifax in 1944, and served the remainder of the war on both sides of the Atlantic.

“When the fighting in Europe ended in May 1945, Steward MacDonald was part of the ship’s company of Hmcs Warrior, a light aircraft carrier commissioned into the RCN in January 1946,” his biography on the Department of National Defence’s website reads.

“With the end of hostilities, Steward MacDonald extended his service for two additional years. On 22 July 1946, he signed on with the RCN, re-engaging as a member of the permanent navy for five years of continuous service.”

He was assigned to Hmcs Warrior and was based in Northern Ireland while the Canadian naval air squadrons re-equipped with new aircraft.

On Nov. 4, 1947, MacDonald was a passenger in a Fairey Firefly (TW 736) when the pilot lost control of the aircraft and it crashed at Mayoghill, near Garvagh, County Londonderry.

While the pilot was able to safely eject from the plane, MacDonald died in the crash.

According to the Department of National Defence, the crash took place in boggy ground and it was determined only a “major operation” would be able to recover the aircraft and MacDonald’s remains. Official recovery efforts ended on Nov. 20, 1947.

“On 20 February 1949, in a letter to Steward MacDonald’s brother, the commanding officer of the 19th Carrier Air Group wrote, ‘The death of your brother James was a shock and a very sad blow to me, for I had formed a very high opinion of him in the years that I had known him,'” the biography said.

MacDonald was presumed dead and his name is commemorated on the Halifax Memorial in Point Pleasant Park.

The local community in Mayoghill also placed a monument near the crash site.

The Casualty Identification Program was established by the Department of National Defence in 2007 and works to identify newly-found skeletal remains and pre-existing unknown graves of Canadian service members.

MacDonald is the first identification of a member from the Royal Canadian Navy, and the first time in 10 years the program has been directly involved in the recovery of a fallen member.

The Canadian Armed Forces says members of MacDonald’s family have been notified of the identification. He will be buried in Northern Ireland, “in the presence of his family, at the earliest possible opportunity.”

stories.title: Police identify suspect in 1968 murder of London teen Jackie Dunleavy
stories.summary: London police say they have solved one of the city's oldest cold cases: the 1968 murder of 16-year-old Jacquel...
stories.author: Owen Schuller
stories.content:
London police say they have solved one of the city’s oldest cold cases: the 1968 murder of 16-year-old Jacqueline Dunleavy.

Jackie Bunleavy. Photo Credit: Owen Schuller

DNA technology, including genetic genealogy helped police identify a former London firefighter as a suspect in the killing of Dunleavy, whose body was found in the snow shortly after she left her part-time job at a London variety store, police said Monday.

“For nearly six decades, Jackie’s family has lived with a loss that no passage of time could ever erase and with unanswered questions about who was responsible for her death,” Police Chief Thai Truong said at a news conference. “Today we are in a position to provide answers.”

Truong said the case marked “the first time the London police service has successfully used forensic, investigative, genetic genealogy to identify an individual response for a homicide.”

The suspect, former London fire Capt. Michael Joseph Moore, died in 2018 and cannot be charged.

Then 25 and not yet working as a firefighter in London, Moore had moved to Canada from Ireland in 1967. He was living in an apartment on Springbank Drive at the time of the murder, police said.

Photos of evidence. Photo Credit: Owen Schuller

“Based on evidence obtained through this investigation, we are confident that the evidentiary threshold to support criminal charges was met,” said Det. Mike Budzyn. “Had Moore been alive today, he would have been arrested and charged in the connection of Jackie’s murder.”

Dunleavy was the daughter of a London police officer and a Grade 10 student at Westminster Secondary School. She she was killed Jan. 9, 1968, shortly after leaving her shift at Stanley Variety near the intersection of Stanley St. and Wharncliffe Rd., where she worked part time.

“She finished her shift at approximately 6:30 p.m. and was last seen leaving the store on foot. At approximately 8 p.m. that evening, three youths found Jackie on the grounds of Katherine Harley School, now known as the location of Matthews Hall, ON Oxford Street. Emergency responders attended, and Jackie was pronounced deceased,” police said in a statement.

London investigators have reviewed Dunleavy’s case repeatedly over the decades “as new investigative opportunities emerged,” police said, including through a joint project with the Ontario Provincial Police called Project Angel, which ran from 1997 to 2001.

More recently, major crime officers used advances in technology and forensic science to re-examine historical evidence, police said in a statement that also recognized contributions from the Centre of Forensic Sciences, Othram Laboratories, the Toronto Police Service and the Ontario Provincial Police. The DNA profile that led to identifying Moore was connected to earlier work completed through Project Angel, the statement said.

Who was Michael Joseph Moore

Michael Joseph Moore. Photo Credit: Owen Schuller

According to an obituary, Moore died in 2018 after a long illness. He’d been married with children and grandchildren and had worked as a firefighter for 28 years in both London and Ireland, it said.

Fire Chief Lori Hamer said in a statement that Moore had retired from the service in 2012, and that Monday’s news was “deeply troubling,” to many employees there.

“Our thoughts are with Jacqueline Dunleavy’s family at this time, and we offer them our heartfelt condolences.”

Dunleavy’s brother was at the news conference, but did not want to speak publicly, said police who asked journalists to respect the family’s privacy.

Former chief, authors welcome the news

Dunleavy’s murder has long been one London’s most troubling unsolved murders.

For decades, investigators, journalists and, more recently, true-crime authors have explored the circumstances of Dunleavy’s case. Among those who attended Monday’s news conference were former Chief Brad Duncan and two London authors who had written about the murder.

“For me to be here today, six decades later and that sample size was still viable, that’s pretty incredible,” said Duncan, speaking to reporters after the event.

Forest City Killer author Vanessa Brown called the news an “incredibly important moment.” Her true-crime book suggested London at least one serial killer was responsible for a slew of murders, including Dunleavy’s, in the 1960s.

“Jackie Dunleavy’s case was the first one that really resonated with me and it is sort of the first in the series,” Brown said.

“I’m hoping that’s this will lead to resolution in the other cases as well and motivate law enforcement to really invest in cold case research.”

-With files from Ryan Baynton, Callum Contursi and Sam Luis

stories.title: Canada Ireland Foundation presents a bleak Endgame – and a gleaming new waterfront performance venue
stories.summary: Druid’s production of Samuel Beckett’s tragicomedy – among the first to play at the brand-new Corleck – is as desolate as you’d expect
stories.author: Aisling Murphy
stories.content:
Title: Endgame

Written by: Samuel Beckett

Directed by: Garry Hynes

Actors: Bosco Hogan, Aaron Monaghan, Marie Mullen, Rory Nolan

Company: Druid, presented by Canada Ireland Foundation

Venue: The Corleck

City: Toronto

Year: Runs until Nov. 28

Endgame , Samuel Beckett’s treatise on death – and the stories we tell ourselves to dampen its inevitability – is famously bleak. Wars wage just out of view from the play’s derelict setting; elderly parents waste away in metal dustbins. Even the work’s fleeting moments of intergenerational tenderness feel like accidental by-products of a world soon to be snuffed out.

Druid Theatre’s evocative production, directed by Garry Hynes, lives up to the play’s dreary promise. Set and costume designer Francis O’Connor conjures a drab room that suggests some sort of submarine or bunker; lighting designer James F. Ingalls thumbs the scale of the play’s pessimism with barely perceptible changes to the production’s smoky atmosphere.

But at the Corleck, Canada Ireland Foundation’s brand-new arts and culture venue on Toronto’s waterfront, Endgame feels less like a meditation on what’s lost and more like a sign of what’s possible.

Snuggled into the ribs of Billy Bishop Toronto City Airport – the Uber drop-off lines for the theatre and the airport’s departures lounge are one and the same – the recently completed space still carries the faint smell of paint and drywall. Listen close, and you’ll hear airplanes taxiing down the runway in the distance.

It’s a strange spot for a performance venue, and there remain logistics to iron out around signage and the like, lest audiences accidentally find themselves on a flight to Ottawa. But the Corleck, a malleable black box space somewhere between Coal Mine and Crow’s theatres in size, suggests a promising future for small-scale theatre along Toronto’s waterfront – and not just gems of the Irish canon such as Endgame.

To that end, Beckett is a playwright not unlike the humble beet: Either you love him, dirt-taste and all, and you’re proud to wear the red stain of his brilliance across your teeth, or you can hardly stand him. Druid offers an Endgame unlikely to appeal to the latter camp. Under Hynes’s direction, Beckett’s tragicomedy hovers in its script’s repetitions – if you’re looking for action-packed narrative, you won’t find it here.

Instead, Endgame offers a subtler story – or, at least, a story’s end. Four people share a single room: Hamm (Rory Nolan, mesmerizing in the role), blind and vociferous, occupies a tattered recliner that might once have looked like a throne. His parents Nell (Marie Mullen) and Nagg (Bosco Hogan) rest in metal trash cans to his left, floating busts mere inches from death, nearly numb to their son’s belligerence.

It’s a wonder any of them have survived this long – Nell and Nagg, ancient in their bickering and sunken in their cheeks, subsist solely on withered biscuits. But somehow, ambulatory youngster Clov (Aaron Monaghan) has kept the crew alive, drawing the curtains of the room’s strange portholes and indulging each of Hamm’s booming whims.

Hamm might be confined to his lounge chair, but his tyranny is absolute; so too is Clov’s subservience. Perhaps it’s their codependence that’s kept the motley group tethered earthside. Even as they torture each other, Monaghan’s Clov rough with resentment, the future of their companionship feels just as certain as its past: They’ve survived thousands of airless days in each other’s blistering company. Why not one more?

Indeed, Endgame is gloomy stuff. Its banter is repetitive and meandering; its sense of brutality weighs heavily on even the play’s lighter moments of cross-generational compassion. Hynes’s cast finds gentleness and humour where they can – Mullen’s fragile Nell is as heartbreaking as Nolan’s Hamm is despotic – but even the occasional chuckle soon gives way to the same desolation as before. ( Endgame is, after all, about the unforgiving cycles of life.)

In Endgame ’s final moments, however, something shifts. A tear streaks down Clov’s stubbled cheek; the portholes allow tiny threads of yellow sunlight to illuminate that awful room.

Hynes’s meticulous staging isn’t so foolish as to conclude Endgame with the fantasy of hope – there’s enough of that from the production’s surrounding venue, shiny and plump with the possibilities of all the theatre still to be produced at the Corleck.

But for a bracing second, Clov glimpses a future defined not by its ending, but by its uncertainty. And hey: Isn’t that something?

stories.title: Canada and Qatar to sign investment deal on Tuesday, source says
stories.summary: Deal sets legally binding rules to protect Canadian and Qatari investors and make it easier for companies from the two countries to do business in both jurisdictions
stories.author: Andrew Mills and Promit Mukherjee
stories.content:
Canada and Qatar are set to sign a foreign investment promotion and protection deal on Tuesday, a source familiar with the process said, a key step toward unlocking investment which the Gulf Arab state pledged in January but has yet to deliver.

The deal, the finalization of which has not been previously reported, sets legally binding rules to protect Canadian and Qatari investors and make it easier for companies from the two countries to do business in both jurisdictions.

It is the latest example of Prime Minister Mark Carney’s pursuit of new investment and trade opportunities because he says Canada can no longer rely on the United States.

Carney and Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani are expected to sign the agreement during the countries’ first strategic dialogue, a formal channel for regular talks between Ottawa and Doha.

Carney’s office and Qatar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne, who is in Qatar and the United Arab Emirates this week with investment funds and banks from the North American country, signalled on Sunday that an announcement was coming.

“I think there’ll be good news, and I think it’s going to be well received on both sides,” Champagne said in an interview with Reuters in Doha, adding it would come this year.

Talks began in 2018, according to a post on the Government of Canada’s website, but have picked up since Carney visited Qatar in January, when the countries said in a joint statement they would conclude “in a timely fashion” and aimed to sign by summer.

Qatar committed to making “significant strategic investments in Canada’s nation-building projects.” Qatar has not put a figure on its pledge, and no significant Qatari investments in Canada have been announced since Carney’s visit.

Champagne said the agreement would help prepare the ground for investors and lead to investment. “The foreign investment and protection agreement is one additional level of providing stability and predictability in our relationship,” he said.

“We need to build the foundational aspects to make sure that those who want to invest would find, for example, the banking facilities, the professional services,” he said.

The Qatar deal appears narrower than the Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement that Canada signed with the UAE last month. That deal will reduce or eliminate tariffs on over 99 per cent of current Canadian exports to the UAE and is expected to take effect in 2027. The UAE also committed up to US$50-billion in investment in Canada last year.

Asked how much Qatar had committed, Champagne said: “We’re looking at opportunities. Beyond the figure itself, it’s the opportunities we need to create.”

Champagne was due to meet the Qatar Investment Authority, the Gulf Arab state’s sovereign wealth fund, which has estimated assets under management of US$580-billion.

Asked whether any money had arrived, Champagne urged patience. “Obviously, it takes a bit of time,” he said. “But this is a region which is looking long-term.”

While conflict in the region and disruption in the Strait of Hormuz had strained Gulf economies, investors were now seeking safe places for their money, Champagne said.

stories.title: New report reveals Intimate Partner Violence hits record high, but police reports tell only part of the story
stories.summary: For southern Ontario woman Tracy Belle, experiencing intimate partner violence across two relationships meant losing her home. Her experience comes amid new Statistics Canada figures that show police-reported intimate partner violence reached its highest rate since comparable data became available in 2009.
stories.author: Myron Mayne, CJF Black Journalism Fellow
stories.content:
For southern Ontario woman Tracy Belle, experiencing intimate partner violence across two relationships over the past decade meant sleepless nights, financial insecurity, and losing the stability of having a home.

“I couldn’t sleep for about two months,” The mother of four told CTVNews.CA on Monday. “I was pregnant, and I didn’t even know that until a couple weeks after I had been attacked.”

Her experience comes amid new Statistics Canada figures that show police-reported intimate partner violence reached its highest rate since comparable data became available in 2009.

The report, released earlier in November, recorded 133,256 victims in 2025, with the rate rising 1.9 per cent from 2024.

Statistics Canada defines intimate partner violence as psychological, physical or sexual abuse committed by a current or former partner, including spouses and dating partners.

Mitzie Hunter, president and CEO of the Canadian Women’s Foundation, said broader societal challenges can worsen violence against women.

“No matter what the stresses are that are affecting society, it could be a pandemic, it could be affordability crisis, it could be environmental disasters. But in every situation, violence against women increases,” Hunter said.

‘Significant public concern’

A separate Statistics Canada report released Wednesday also looked at intimate partner violence in 2025, including experiences that never reached police.

“Intimate partner violence (IPV) is a significant public concern in Canada and internationally,” analyst Adam Cotter wrote in a statement posted on the StatCan website.

“Its impacts and consequences are numerous, including the immediate consequences for victims such as poor mental and psychological health and well-being, trauma, physical injury, economic hardship, and significant disruptions to daily life.”

Key findings from the report include:

Nearly half of women (45 per cent) and more than one-third of men (35 per cent) have experienced some form of intimate partner violence since age 15.

About one in seven women (14 per cent) and one in eight men (12 per cent) experienced it in the past year. Those numbers were not significantly different from 2018.

Only nine per cent of women and four per cent of men who experienced it in the past year reported it to the police.

More than one-third of girls and young women aged 15 to 24 (37 per cent) experienced it in the past year, compared with 12 per cent of women aged 25 and older.

About one in six women (16 per cent) and one in eight men (13 per cent) who experienced intimate partner violence left a shared home with their partner because of the abuse.

The survey also found differences among racialized women, with 42 per cent Latin American women, 38 per cent of West Asian women, and 36 per cent of Black women reporting intimate partner violence at some point since age 15.

The findings are based on Statistics Canada’s 2025 Survey of Safety in Public and Private Spaces, which gathered responses from 48,547 people aged 15 and older across all 10 provinces and three territories.

“When it displaces you, when it removes you from security, like you not having a home and things like that, it changes you. You can’t be the same.” Belle said.

University of Calgary Prof. Lana Wells, who researches domestic violence prevention, said the record-high figures require careful interpretation.

“An increase in police-reported intimate partner violence does not necessarily mean that violence itself is increasing at the same rate,” Wells said.

She explained that greater public awareness could encourage more survivors to report abuse, while changes in police practices could affect how incidents are recorded. An actual increase in violence could also be contributing to the higher figures, she said.

System is ‘broken’

Belle, who runs a catering business called Magic Munch, said she experienced years of abuse in a relationship without reporting it to police.

After experiencing violence in a subsequent relationship, she contacted police.

“I made up my mind that I was going to reach out to the authorities, and I didn’t care how that affected my partner because you are affecting the livelihood of myself and children,” she said.

But seeking help brought its own challenges.

Belle said she struggled to find housing and navigate social services while pregnant.

“There’s a system in place, but that system is flawed. It’s broken,” she said.

She said survivors need more than temporary assistance. She said they also need practical help rebuilding their lives and encouragement to regain their confidence and independence.

The report found that among women who left a shared home because of intimate partner violence, 72 per cent stayed with friends or family, while six per cent stayed in a shelter.

Wells said financial dependence, housing insecurity, fear of retaliation and concerns for children can make seeking help difficult or unsafe.

“We should be asking what makes it so difficult or unsafe for survivors to seek help,” she said.

Shelter demands outpaced available space

Those housing challenges were also echoed in the growing demand reported by Harmony House, Ottawa’s only second-stage shelter, which provides longer-term transitional housing and support to women and children fleeing abuse.

Francesca Davila, its development and communications director, said the waiting list had grown from approximately 25 families to 130 over five years, with 280 children and youth awaiting support.

Harmony House operates 16 apartments, providing housing, counselling and other services while families work toward independent living.

Davila said a shortage of affordable housing prevented some families from moving out, limiting space for others seeking safety.

“If the woman, when they stay with us…they cannot find the next stage that is affordable housing, they have to stay with us,” she said.

‘It’s really not easy’

Wells said addressing intimate partner violence requires more than police, shelters and the justice system.

She called for engaging men and boys, challenging harmful attitudes about masculinity and strengthening prevention efforts in schools, workplaces and communities.

“We cannot expect police, shelters and the justice system to solve this problem on their own,” she said.

Despite the challenges, Belle said experience has given her a renewed sense of purpose.

“I feel like it’s my purpose to help other people that go through those things,” she said.“

It’s really not easy. It’s not easy. It needs to be talked about more.”

stories.title: Man charged with second-degree murder in killing of B.C. actor Stewart McLean
stories.summary: Squamish - A 35-year-old Metro Vancouver man has been charged with second-degree murder in the killing of British Columbia actor Stewart McLean.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
News that a Metro Vancouver man has been charged with second-degree murder in the death of British Columbia actor Stewart McLean is a “big relief” to everyone in the entertainment industry, said actor and acting coach Jeff Seymour.

Seymour said he was anxious to follow information released on the case on Monday.

“But at this point, I’m just pleased that he wasn’t forgotten that they pursued this, that they had due diligence. They did their work, and I have all the respect in the world for these people that did this,” Seymour said, referring to police, in an interview from Los Angeles on Monday.

Nathan Neima, 35, of New Westminster, B.C., was arrested Saturday and appeared in provincial court in North Vancouver on Monday and another court appearance on a procedural matter was set for Jan. 6.

Seymour said he met Stewart through one of his acting classes a decade ago and they became friends.

McLean was someone that he could call any time to share joys and sorrows, and now he finds himself thinking about picking up the phone to call his friend to share some news, Seymour said.

He said McLean’s death had been “eating away” at him.

“There was nothing nefarious about Stew’s life. He was adored. He didn’t cross lines. He wasn’t involved in shady dealings or people,” said Seymour, “When someone who just has a pristine life is suddenly murdered, it’s just so confounding.”

McLean, 45, who appeared on series such as “Virgin River” and “Murder in a Small Town,” was reported missing on May 18 after he was last seen at his home in Lions Bay, north of Vancouver.

Cpl. Esther Tupper of the Integrated Homicide Investigation Team said Monday that officers believe the death was targeted.

While the men weren’t strangers, she wouldn’t say how they knew each other.

“However, the details of their exact relationship is going to form part of the evidence in court and so those details will emerge at that time,” said Tupper.

Neima does not have a criminal record, she said.

Seymour said Neima’s arrest also raised more questions, including why his friend was killed.

Word of the criminal charge travelled quickly through the acting community, but no one in Stewart’s circle of friends in Vancouver has ever heard about the accused before, Seymour said.

Squamish RCMP said in May that the homicide team took over the case after officers found evidence that McLean was killed.

His remains were found days later in the Lions Bay area.

Tupper said investigators want to extend their gratitude to residents of Lions Bay for assisting them with the investigation.

“I know that it did take several months, however, these homicide files are very lengthy,” said Tupper.

“I hope that this brings some measure of peace that we’ve located and charged an individual with this really tragic and senseless act of violence.”

She said the investigation also included speaking with people within the film community, “and everyone who they did speak to was very helpful.”

Tributes flooded social media after the news of his death broke in May.

Jennifer Lee, an agent with Vancouver’s Lucas Talent Inc., said after the death that she had the pleasure of working with McLean starting in 2014, and he was “the most positive, kind, funny, chill” person you could ever know.

McLean’s credits also included CW’s “Arrow” and Netflix’s “Travelers.”

Seymour said the fondest memories were of McLean flying out to visit him in Los Angeles.

paragraphs: News that a Metro Vancouver man has been charged with second-degree murder in the death of British Columbia actor Stewart McLean is a “big relief” to everyone in the entertainment industry, said actor and acting coach Jeff Seymour.
Seymour said he was anxious to follow information released on the case on Monday.

“But at this point, I’m just pleased that he wasn’t forgotten that they pursued this, that they had due diligence. They did their work, and I have all the respect in the world for these people that did this,” Seymour said, referring to police, in an interview from Los Angeles on Monday.
Nathan Neima, 35, of New Westminster, B.C., was arrested Saturday and appeared in provincial court in North Vancouver on Monday and another court appearance on a procedural matter was set for Jan. 6.
Seymour said he met Stewart through one of his acting classes a decade ago and they became friends.
McLean was someone that he could call any time to share joys and sorrows, and now he finds himself thinking about picking up the phone to call his friend to share some news, Seymour said.
He said McLean’s death had been “eating away” at him.

“There was nothing nefarious about Stew’s life. He was adored. He didn’t cross lines. He wasn’t involved in shady dealings or people,” said Seymour, “When someone who just has a pristine life is suddenly murdered, it’s just so confounding.”
McLean, 45, who appeared on series such as “Virgin River” and “Murder in a Small Town,” was reported missing on May 18 after he was last seen at his home in Lions Bay, north of Vancouver.
Cpl. Esther Tupper of the Integrated Homicide Investigation Team said Monday that officers believe the death was targeted.
While the men weren’t strangers, she wouldn’t say how they knew each other.
“However, the details of their exact relationship is going to form part of the evidence in court and so those details will emerge at that time,” said Tupper.
Neima does not have a criminal record, she said.
Seymour said Neima’s arrest also raised more questions, including why his friend was killed.
Word of the criminal charge travelled quickly through the acting community, but no one in Stewart’s circle of friends in Vancouver has ever heard about the accused before, Seymour said.
Squamish RCMP said in May that the homicide team took over the case after officers found evidence that McLean was killed.
His remains were found days later in the Lions Bay area.
Tupper said investigators want to extend their gratitude to residents of Lions Bay for assisting them with the investigation.
“I know that it did take several months, however, these homicide files are very lengthy,” said Tupper.
“I hope that this brings some measure of peace that we’ve located and charged an individual with this really tragic and senseless act of violence.”
She said the investigation also included speaking with people within the film community, “and everyone who they did speak to was very helpful.”
Tributes flooded social media after the news of his death broke in May.

McLean’s credits also included CW’s “Arrow” and Netflix’s “Travelers.”
Seymour said the fondest memories were of McLean flying out to visit him in Los Angeles.
“Good friends are hard to find these days,” said Seymour, “And he is sorely missed.”
