stories.title: COP31 outcome not what Ottawa had 'hoped' for: environment minister
stories.summary: Ottawa - Federal Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin says the outcome of the recent annual United Nations climate conference was not what her government had "hoped" for.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - The outcome of the recent annual United Nations climate conference was not what her government had “hoped for,” Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin said.

In a statement issued Sunday afternoon, Dabrusin called on all parties to achieve “tangible outcomes” over the next year to move the world toward net-zero emissions.

“We have one year until COP32. It is incumbent on all parties to use that time to reflect on this process and make sure we can have achievable tangible outcomes that move us forwards,” Dabrusin wrote.

For the first time since 2009, a U.N. climate summit has ended without an overarching agreement. COP31 talks in Antalya, Turkey, collapsed over disagreements on fossil fuels, leaving countries without a new collective plan to tackle global warming. Here’s what the failure to reach a deal means for the planet and the fight against climate change. (Nov. 23, 2026)

She thanked Canada’s negotiators for what she called “real outcomes on key issues like methane, electrification and the oceans-climate nexus.”

After two weeks of meetings in Antalya, Turkey, delegates to the COP31 climate conference ended their deliberations Sunday without reaching an overall agreement.

The draft agreement up for debate at COP31, which was rejected by the European Union and other delegates, failed to mention the phrase “fossil fuels.”

It’s the first time a UN climate conference has failed to come up with a final, non-binding agreement since 2009.

At the COP28 conference in Dubai in 2023, the world agreed to “transition away” from fossil fuels.

Expectations for COP31 were low heading in, but disagreements emerged among nations over the scale of the crisis and over explicitly calling out the role of fossil fuels in climate change. Many negotiators, activists and even organizers used the word “disappointing” to describe the discussions.

While the talks failed to reach a main agreement, also known as a cover decision, they did make progress on smaller issues. The two-week session ended Sunday night after running more than 50 hours overtime.

Climate change is accelerating and driving heat waves, floods, storms and droughts, while a stronger El Niño system this year is expected to amply severe weather events. The UN says it’s now inevitable that the world will blow past the temperature threshold established by the 2015 Paris climate agreement.

“I am deeply disappointed that COP31 has ended without consensus on an overarching outcome,” United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said. “Temperatures keep shattering records. Climate extremes keep intensifying. Emissions remain far too high. And every delay makes our task harder and more costly.”

Any pact approved at the talks requires near-unanimous consensus. Several countries and the 27-nation European Union said they could not accept the final proposal from the joint Turkish-Australian leadership at COP31, which didn’t mention fossil fuels.

A considerably larger number of nations accepted the decision — in some cases reluctantly — in the interest of consensus. Russia and Saudi Arabia sought to keep fossil fuels out of the document.

“It’s unconscionable that we would have a climate act that makes no reference to fossil fuels,” Darragh O’Brien, Ireland’s climate minister, said on behalf of the EU at the climate talks.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 23, 2026.

— With files from The Associated Press

stories.title: Western PhD candidate studies trans experiences in higher education
stories.summary: Malcolm Macdonald’s lived experience led to impactful research on trans student experiences, especially related to belonging, support systems
stories.author: Shana Dalby Althaus
stories.content:
When Malcolm Macdonald, MA’24, began his master’s degree at Western in 2022, he was also navigating questions about his gender identity. That experience would go on to shape his research.

As he was beginning his transition later that year, rising media attention and political discourse focused on trans people caused mounting pressure and stress.

“I kept coming back to this question: am I the only trans graduate student feeling the walls push in on me in this way?” he said.

Now a PhD student in the Faculty of Education, a member of its critical policy, equity and leadership studies academic research cluster, Macdonald studies how trans and non-binary students navigate belonging, institutional systems and access to support in higher education. He focuses on how faculty and staff support transgender equity in university classrooms, including the ways they balance commitments to equity, diversity, and inclusion (EDI) with academic freedom and freedom of expression policies.

Before coming to Western, Macdonald became interested in the role belonging plays in student success. Conversations with peers who felt disconnected and unsure of their place on campus, coupled with his own experiences, ignited a passion for understanding student belonging. Eventually, it led him to study the experiences of trans students in higher education.

What began as a broader interest in belonging evolved into a closer look at how trans and non-binary students experience Canadian university spaces, both socially and structurally.

Macdonald’s work shows students experience campus not as a single environment, but as a series of distinct spaces with different pressures and supports. A student might feel supported in a classroom but encounter challenges when navigating administrative offices or campus service centres.

“A campus is really a collection of microclimates,” he said. “Students might feel supported in one space, but not in another.”

Understanding the differences between campus spaces led Macdonald to a renewed focus on learning environments, especially the ways trans people are presented within classroom group discussions.

Malcolm Macdonald gives a presentation at Weldon Library for Trans Day of Visibility. (Christopher Kindratsky/Western Communications)

Macdonald points to moments of support that have made a difference for him at Western, particularly through student health services and peers and faculty who affirm his identity. Access to trans-informed care and visible signs of that safety, such as trained staff and inclusive spaces, can make a measurable difference in how students feel, he said.

“Seeing there were doctors trained in trans health care made it easier to reach out,” he said of seeking care through Health and Wellness Services at Western. “Even small things, like staff asking for my preferred name so I didn’t have to hear my legal name in a waiting room, made a difference.”

He sees these efforts as part of a meaningful shift toward inclusion but says there is still more work to do across everyday systems.

While filling out paperwork to update his information, Macdonald encountered a form that didn’t include an option to update gender information. He ended up writing it in the margins. Though the update was made, for Macdonald, the experience demonstrated how small improvements in communication and awareness can make existing supports more accessible.

He said it’s an example of a broader reality – supports for trans or non-binary students May exist, but when they aren’t aware of those options, it can still be difficult to access.

“It’s not supportive unless you know it’s there,” he said.

For many students, accessing support requires self-advocacy, which can be especially difficult in an unfamiliar and often overwhelming environment, Macdonald said. Institutions can play a key role by not only offering support, but also making it visible and accessible.

Macdonald’s work emphasizes the importance of centring lived experience in research. Trans and non-binary people bring essential perspectives on gender, identity and campus life because they can identify gaps that might otherwise go unnoticed, he noted.

“Trans people, whether they’re academically trained or not, are experts in their own lived experience.”

He hopes his research will inform how universities can design more inclusive systems and better support trans and non-binary students.

Conversations, particularly with non-binary students, highlighted how experiences of visibility, safety and self-advocacy can differ widely, even within the same community, he said. For Macdonald, that awareness has become central to both his research and personal growth.

Seeing student-led advocacy at Western, including the Society of Graduate Students’ efforts to expand gender-affirming care, reinforced for Macdonald that progress was already underway and others shared his commitment to inclusion. That shared desire to drive change ultimately drew him to continue his work at Western.

“Being able to do this work means contributing to change,” he said. “It’s about making sure other students don’t feel like they’re navigating these systems alone.”

Learn more about how Western is preparing future leaders and global citizens.

Now a PhD student in the Faculty of Education, a member of its critical policy, equity and leadership studies academic research cluster, Macdonald studies how trans and non-binary students navigate belonging, institutional systems and access to support in higher education. He focuses on how faculty and staff support transgender equity in university classrooms, including the ways they balance commitments to equity, diversity, and inclusion (EDI) with academic freedom and freedom of expression policies.

Before coming to Western, Macdonald became interested in the role belonging plays in student success. Conversations with peers who felt disconnected and unsure of their place on campus, coupled with his own experiences, ignited a passion for understanding student belonging. Eventually, it led him to study the experiences of trans students in higher education.
What began as a broader interest in belonging evolved into a closer look at how trans and non-binary students experience Canadian university spaces, both socially and structurally.

Macdonald’s work shows students experience campus not as a single environment, but as a series of distinct spaces with different pressures and supports. A student might feel supported in a classroom but encounter challenges when navigating administrative offices or campus service centres.
“A campus is really a collection of microclimates,” he said. “Students might feel supported in one space, but not in another.”
Understanding the differences between campus spaces led Macdonald to a renewed focus on learning environments, especially the ways trans people are presented within classroom group discussions.
Malcolm Macdonald gives a presentation at Weldon Library for Trans Day of Visibility. (Christopher Kindratsky/Western Communications)

Macdonald points to moments of support that have made a difference for him at Western, particularly through student health services and peers and faculty who affirm his identity. Access to trans-informed care and visible signs of that safety, such as trained staff and inclusive spaces, can make a measurable difference in how students feel, he said.

“Seeing there were doctors trained in trans health care made it easier to reach out,” he said of seeking care through Health and Wellness Services at Western. “Even small things, like staff asking for my preferred name so I didn’t have to hear my legal name in a waiting room, made a difference.”
He sees these efforts as part of a meaningful shift toward inclusion but says there is still more work to do across everyday systems.

While filling out paperwork to update his information, Macdonald encountered a form that didn’t include an option to update gender information. He ended up writing it in the margins. Though the update was made, for Macdonald, the experience demonstrated how small improvements in communication and awareness can make existing supports more accessible.
He said it’s an example of a broader reality – supports for trans or non-binary students May exist, but when they aren’t aware of those options, it can still be difficult to access.
“It’s not supportive unless you know it’s there,” he said.

For many students, accessing support requires self-advocacy, which can be especially difficult in an unfamiliar and often overwhelming environment, Macdonald said. Institutions can play a key role by not only offering support, but also making it visible and accessible.

Macdonald’s work emphasizes the importance of centring lived experience in research. Trans and non-binary people bring essential perspectives on gender, identity and campus life because they can identify gaps that might otherwise go unnoticed, he noted.
“Trans people, whether they’re academically trained or not, are experts in their own lived experience.”
He hopes his research will inform how universities can design more inclusive systems and better support trans and non-binary students.

Conversations, particularly with non-binary students, highlighted how experiences of visibility, safety and self-advocacy can differ widely, even within the same community, he said. For Macdonald, that awareness has become central to both his research and personal growth.

Seeing student-led advocacy at Western, including the Society of Graduate Students’ efforts to expand gender-affirming care, reinforced for Macdonald that progress was already underway and others shared his commitment to inclusion. That shared desire to drive change ultimately drew him to continue his work at Western.
“Being able to do this work means contributing to change,” he said. “It’s about making sure other students don’t feel like they’re navigating these systems alone.”

stories.title: Newfoundland and Labrador expects oil windfall, balanced budget after soaring prices
stories.summary: ST. John's - The Newfoundland and Labrador government is expecting more than $1 billion in extra oil revenue this year after the war in Iran sent crude prices soaring.
stories.author: Sarah Smellie The Canadian Press
stories.content:
ST. John’s - Newfoundland and Labrador is forecasting a modest budget surplus, thanks in part to more than $1 billion in extra oil revenue after the war in Iran sent crude prices soaring.

Craig Pardy, the province’s finance minister, said there are sectors beyond oil — mining, for example — that are driving production and economic growth. But he admitted Monday that without the surge in oil prices, the indebted province would be having a very different year.

And even with a good year, Newfoundland and Labrador still faces grave financial challenges and a towering debt to overcome, he said.

Newfoundland and Labrador is forecasting a modest budget surplus, thanks in part to more than $1 billion in extra oil revenue after the war in Iran sent crude prices soaring. Finance Minister Craig Pardy says the province’s net debt shrank slightly, but it still faces steep financial challenges. (Nov. 23, 2026)

“Let me be clear: that is one good year. It does not mean that the problem is fixed,” Pardy told reporters in St. John’s, N.L., ON Monday. “So we will not manage the province’s finances as if one good year will last forever.”

In April, Pardy delivered a budget for the current 2026-27 fiscal year forecasting a deficit of $688 million and a net debt of $20.8 billion. But as of Monday’s fiscal update, those numbers have changed. The Progressive Conservative government is now expecting nearly $1.5 billion more revenue than forecast in the budget, much of which comes from nearly $1.1 billion in additional oil revenues.

Pardy’s update forecasted a $78-million surplus and a $19.3-billion net debt. The government will still have to borrow about $3.9 billion this fiscal year, which ends in March 2027, and it will pay about $1.2 billion in debt servicing fees, including interest.

Newfoundland and Labrador is expecting to take in more than $3 billion in oil royalties this fiscal year, accounting for roughly 25 per cent of the province’s entire revenue, officials said.

Pardy insisted his government is looking beyond the temporary surge in revenue from high oil prices, pointing to anticipated benefits from Equinor’s proposed Bay du Nord offshore oil project, and an agreement between Crown utilities in Newfoundland and Labrador and Quebec to expand the hydroelectric output of the Churchill River in Labrador.

Equinor is expected early next year to decide whether to proceed with Bay du Nord. Officials are still hammering out final contracts for the Churchill River deal.

Spending in Newfoundland and Labrador is also higher than was anticipated in April’s budget, by about $704 million. More than half of that is due to health-care costs, Pardy said. The rest he largely attributed to inflation and a recently announced suite of measures to offset the high cost of living.

The province is investing $175 million into a new sinking fund, which officials said would mature to $750 million by 2052. That money will be used to pay off debt.

Sheilagh O’Leary, who represents the St. John’s East-Quidi Vidi district for the NDP, said the government needs to come up with a better plan to manage its debt.

“We can’t rely on oil revenues that are being made on an illegal war,” O’Leary told reporters after Pardy’s announcement. “It’s unsustainable.”

Officials with the United Nations have said that U.S. and Israeli airstrikes on Iran this year violated international law, including the UN Charter. However, the Trump administration has insisted the military campaign is a lawful measure to ensure Tehran does not build nuclear weapons.

Newfoundland and Labrador’s population sat at about 552,000 as of July, according to the provincial government. Its gross domestic product is expected to grow by 7.1 per cent this year, which officials said was the highest anticipated growth in the country.

In October, the Montreal Economic Institute think tank released a report showing Newfoundland and Labrador’s net debt-to-GDP grew by 14 per cent between 2015 and 2024, which was the largest growth among the provinces. The report blamed much of the increase on what it called economic fundamentals, such as slow economic growth.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 23, 2026.

— With files from The Associated Press

stories.title: Two Americans sentenced to life in prison for murder of Quebec entrepreneur, partner
stories.summary: Jonathan Lehrer and Robert Thomas Snyder Jr. were found guilty in July of killing the couple in 2023
stories.author: Marieke Glorieux-Stryckman
stories.content:
The two Americans convicted of murdering Quebec entrepreneur Daniel Langlois and his partner Dominique Marchand in Dominica have been sentenced to life in prison without parole.

Jonathan Lehrer and Robert Thomas Snyder Jr. were found guilty in July of killing the couple in late 2023.

The victims’ bodies were discovered in a burned-out vehicle near a luxury eco-resort they owned on the Caribbean island.

“We are satisfied that due process took its course,” the prosecutor in the case, Keith Scotland, told The Canadian Press after the sentence was announced.

Lehrer and Snyder have appealed the verdict. Ravi Rajcoomar, their lead counsel, said they also intend to appeal the sentence.

“My clients’ position is that they are not guilty and wrongly convicted,” he wrote in an e-mail to The Canadian Press.

“It’s not over for either party,” said Scotland.

In a statement shared last week, family spokesperson Sylvie Deslauriers said the ashes of both victims had recently been returned to Canada. She also shared the families’ thanks to the people who supported them in Quebec, Dominica and internationally.

“It is still very difficult for me to believe that my son is gone,” reads a statement attributed to Langlois’s mother, “but the fact that the criminals were found guilty and that the ashes have just been repatriated will finally allow me to bury my son with dignity.”

Deslauriers said the families would not comment on the sentence.

Born in 1957 in Jonquière, Que., Langlois was a pioneer in digital animation who founded Montreal-based Softimage, whose technology was used to create special effects for major Hollywood films including Jurassic Park, Titanic and The Lord of the Rings .

He later started a foundation in his name to support arts and technology, and was involved in charitable endeavours in Dominica.

He and Marchand had lived for years on the island, where they opened the resort Coulibri Ridge in 2022.

The couple were found dead inside their burned vehicle in December 2023. An autopsy determined Langlois died from multiple gunshot wounds.

Lehrer, an American property owner and chocolate producer, had been involved in a years-long legal dispute with Langlois over access to a public road crossing his property and leading to the couple’s resort.

Court documents show the prosecutors alleged Lehrer hired Snyder to kill Langlois and Marchand.

On July 28, a jury found Lehrer and Snyder guilty after about two hours of deliberations.

stories.title: St. Catharines cheerleading coach charged with sexual exploitation
stories.summary: A cheerleading coach from St. Catharines, Ont., is facing a sexual exploitation charge a month after he was charged with sexual assault offences.
stories.author: Maan Alhmidi The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Niagara regional police say detectives received information about a sexual assault dating back to a period between 2011 and 2012.

Police say the female victim, who was 16 years old at the time, reported being sexually assaulted by a cheerleading coach.

Article continues below

Inside interior designer Nora Voon’s art-filled home

They say a 42-year-old man has been arrested and charged with sexual exploitation.

Police had charged the man last month with sexual assault, sexual interference and four counts of sexual exploitation after two women reported being sexually assaulted on several occasions between 2009 and 2012.

Police say the suspect was a volunteer cheerleading coach at high schools in St. Catharines within the District School Board of Niagara before opening his own cheerleading gym called Cheer Empire Eagles.

Detectives believe there May be additional sexual assault victims and they are asking anyone with information to contact them.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 23, 2026.

stories.title: Former firefighter responsible for Ontario teen’s death in 1968, police say
stories.summary: Jacqueline Dunleavy, 16, died on Jan. 9, 1968. The Grade 10 student at Westminster Secondary School was working at the Stanley Variety Store that evening.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
Police in London, Ont., say a former firefighter is responsible for the 1968 death of a teenager in the Ontario city.

Michael Joseph Moore was named Monday as the suspect behind Jacqueline Dunleavy’s killing.

Dunleavy, 16, died on Jan. 9, 1968. The Grade 10 student at Westminster Secondary School was working at the Stanley Variety Store that evening.

She finished work at 6:35 p.m. and was last seen walking out the front of the store, police said.

At 8:10 p.m., three youths found Jacqueline at the Katherine Harley School, now Matthews Hall. She was later pronounced dead.

Although she had suffered a head injury, police determined the cause of death was strangulation.

Moore was not a firefighter at the time of the killing, Det. Mike Budzyn told reporters Monday. He later joined the London Fire Department and served as a firefighter for approximately 28 years.

Born in Ireland, Moore was 25 at the time of Jacqueline’s death. He has since died, Budzyn said.

Investigators used genetic genealogy to link Moore to the homicide. He was never considered a suspect before.

“Based on the evidence obtained through this investigation, we are confident that the evidentiary threshold to support criminal charges was met,” Budzyn said.

“We recognize that this information May be significant to individuals who knew Moore personally, worked alongside him, or had contact with him during his years of service.”

Budzyn said Moore’s family was “understandably shocked” when they were told and have asked for their privacy to be respected.

“I want to acknowledge Jackie’s family. While the criminal justice process cannot proceed because Moore is deceased, we recognize the importance of being able to provide answers that were not available for nearly six decades,” Budzyn said.

“It has been a privilege to contribute to this investigation and to the effort to establish who was responsible for Jackie’s death . ”

stories.title: Navdeep Bains vows united front at Queen’s Park after narrow Liberal leadership win
stories.summary: Bains has a long road ahead of him if he wants to challenge the Ford government in the next election, which could be as far away as 2030.
stories.author: Olivia Bowden
stories.content:
Newly elected Ontario Liberal Party Leader Navdeep Bains made his debut at Queen’s Park Monday, promising the entire party is united behind him despite narrowly claiming victory in Saturday’s leadership election.

“We had thousands and thousands of people that joined the Liberal Party because they wanted to be part of the team that could take on this Conservative government,” Bains told reporters. “And that’s the exciting part, that everyone is coming together.”

On Saturday’s election, Bains received 50.3 per cent of the vote on the third and final ballot at the party’s leadership convention. The recently minted leader is a former federal cabinet minister from the Justin Trudeau era and a former executive at Rogers.

But Bains has a long road ahead of him if he wants to challenge the Ford government in the next election, which could be as far away as 2030.

He is likely to face sharp critiques from the NDP and the Ford government on his commitment to fighting the affordability crisis and his affiliation with the Trudeau regime, as the former prime minister experienced deep unpopularity in his final months in office.

While he said he hasn’t heard from Prime Minister Mark Carney on his leadership win, he has heard from Trudeau who sent him a “nice message.”

Bains conceded Saturday that rebuilding the party to be in striking position for the next election will be a challenge.

“It’s going to be hard,” he said. “It’s going to be really, really hard. But we’re in it together.”

The frequently rudderless Ontario Liberal Party has now elected three new leaders since 2018, undergirding several shaky years marked by internal divisions and ideological challenges over where on the political spectrum that party should even fall.

Bains was flanked by MPPs Lee Fairclough and Stephanie Bowman at Monday’s press conference, who were two of his central competitors in the Liberal leadership race.

He just inched out Fairclough by a few points in the final vote tally.

“The fact that we’re united sets the tone for the entire party,” he told reporters.

“We have an incredible team here,” Bains said. “And now we realize the ultimate goal is to replace this out of touch and corrupt Conservative government.”

Another challenge facing Bains is that he does not hold a seat in the Ontario legislature. Neither did the previous two leaders of the party, an issue that Liberal party members brought up during the race.

Bains has said he will run for a seat, but he has not yet revealed which riding he’s looking at.

He’s also bracing for what could be a slew of attack ads from the Progressive Conservatives, as the Conservative party previously spent millions on an advertising blitz against former Liberal leader Bonnie Crombe in 2024.

The Conservatives are “going to go negative,” he said at a news conference following his victory Saturday.

He’s also likely to face criticism from the NDP as it sets its sights on Bain’s career at Rogers.

“All of these experiences taught me how important it is to build great teams and focus on solutions,” Bains told reporters when discussing his work history.

“I can tell you right now the number one issue is affordability,” he said. “That’s what we’re focusing on.”

stories.title: Regina buses not running as city locks out workers following labour impasse
stories.summary: Regina - Thousands of commuters who rely on transit in Regina are without bus service today as workers and the city remain at an impasse over a new contract.
stories.author: Jeremy Simes The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Regina - Thousands of commuters who rely on transit in Regina were without bus service Monday as workers and the city hit an impasse over a new contract.

The city imposed a lockout of about 380 transit workers days after the Amalgamated Transit Union Local 588 said employees would take job action by not working voluntary overtime.

The city says the lockout is a matter of public safety and ensuring timely service, because it doesn’t want to risk residents waiting in the cold for a bus that might not come.

Thousands of commuters who rely on transit in Regina were without bus service Monday as workers and the city hit an impasse over a new contract. The city’s imposed a lockout of about 380 transit workers days after the Amalgamated Transit Union Local 588 said employees would take job action by not working voluntary overtime. (Nov. 23, 2026)

But the union says the city could have readjusted schedules to keep buses running.

“I think this is absolutely appalling that the city took these draconian measures while leaving (commuters) stranded,” John Di Nino, the union’s national president, told reporters.

“This is not the respect that transit workers deserve, not in this city or not in any city across the nation.”

More than 150 workers gathered outside the city’s transit operations centre Monday to protest the lockout. They held signs urging a fair contract and waved flags while trucks and cars driving by honked their horns.

“When do we want it?” shouted John Callahan, an international vice-president with the union, while members gathered around him.

“Now!” workers shouted back.

Di Nino said the union was scheduled to meet with the city later in the afternoon for negotiations.

“If they come to the table with a reasonable offer, we’re prepared to go back and provide the service, as long as they open up the gates and let us go and do our work,” he said.

Pat Nichol, the vice-president with the local union, said the sticking point in negotiations is wages. Workers are asking for a top-up in pay that matches the rate of inflation, she said.

“It’s a sad thing when we have members that have to go use the food bank to feed their families,” she said.

“This used to be a job that somebody would be able to have and raise a family on, and now that’s not the case anymore.”

The city said in a statement that it wants to negotiate a fair contract with the union.

“The decision to lock out the union was not taken lightly and is based on safety and service reliability concerns,” it said.

“Even if the city had taken no further action, the (union’s) withdrawal of voluntary overtime would have had significant impacts on transit service.”

Had drivers not worked overtime, it said, the city would have had to cancel 25 per cent of routes, including high school services and a special shuttle for Canadian Western Agribition, a cattle show.

“The city would not be able to let residents know which routes were impacted in advance,” it said.

The city added that maintenance would also have been affected. Without overtime, the city couldn’t have guaranteed buses were safe and reliable to operate, it said.

Nichol said the city could have kept buses running without overtime, citing schedule changes it made during the COVID-19 pandemic, including shorter routes.

“We didn’t have to be locked out,” she said.

Di Nino took aim at Mayor Chad Bachynski and city council for not stepping in.

”(Council) should be giving them the directive to get this issue resolved, put our members back onto the job and get transit running in this city,” he said.

Bachynski said in a statement the union and the city need to come to the bargaining table before service can restart and that council won’t interfere in labour negotiations.

“We all want service restored as soon as possible,” he said.

Meanwhile, some residents have taken it into their own hands to help people who rely on the bus.

Thom Hamilton has created a website, called No Fare!, to connect people with free rides. Hamilton said he’s heard concerns from business owners worried their staff won’t be able to make it into work without the bus.

“I put together a site with no real intention other than to try and help people out that might be struggling while this disruption happens,” he said.

“If they come to their senses and they’re able to come to an agreement, I’d love it if it never had to be used.”

At the protest Monday, Di Nino said workers picked up people from bus stops earlier in the day to give them rides at no cost.

Workers at the protest also said the lockout came at an ironic time, as the city had originally scheduled a pancake breakfast for employee appreciation.

“Where’s my pancakes?” one worker shouted, in jest, at the gathering.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 23, 2026.

“This used to be a job that somebody would be able to have and raise a family on, and now that’s not the case anymore.”
The city said in a statement that it wants to negotiate a fair contract with the union.
“The decision to lock out the union was not taken lightly and is based on safety and service reliability concerns,” it said.
“Even if the city had taken no further action, the (union’s) withdrawal of voluntary overtime would have had significant impacts on transit service.”
Had drivers not worked overtime, it said, the city would have had to cancel 25 per cent of routes, including high school services and a special shuttle for Canadian Western Agribition, a cattle show.
“The city would not be able to let residents know which routes were impacted in advance,” it said.
The city added that maintenance would also have been affected. Without overtime, the city couldn’t have guaranteed buses were safe and reliable to operate, it said.
Nichol said the city could have kept buses running without overtime, citing schedule changes it made during the COVID-19 pandemic, including shorter routes.
“We didn’t have to be locked out,” she said.
Di Nino took aim at Mayor Chad Bachynski and city council for not stepping in.
”(Council) should be giving them the directive to get this issue resolved, put our members back onto the job and get transit running in this city,” he said.
Bachynski said in a statement the union and the city need to come to the bargaining table before service can restart and that council won’t interfere in labour negotiations.
“We all want service restored as soon as possible,” he said.
Meanwhile, some residents have taken it into their own hands to help people who rely on the bus.

Thom Hamilton has created a website, called No Fare!, to connect people with free rides. Hamilton said he’s heard concerns from business owners worried their staff won’t be able to make it into work without the bus.
“I put together a site with no real intention other than to try and help people out that might be struggling while this disruption happens,” he said.
“If they come to their senses and they’re able to come to an agreement, I’d love it if it never had to be used.”
At the protest Monday, Di Nino said workers picked up people from bus stops earlier in the day to give them rides at no cost.
Workers at the protest also said the lockout came at an ironic time, as the city had originally scheduled a pancake breakfast for employee appreciation.
“Where’s my pancakes?” one worker shouted, in jest, at the gathering.

‘The Constitution is not an à la carte menu from which one May choose to follow only those parts that suit one’s preferences,’ reads the decision.

Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon talks to reporters as BQ leader Yves-François Blanchet looks on in Quebec City on Nov. 10, 2026. (Francis Vachon / Postmedia)

Catherine Lévesque

November 23, 2026 at 11:16 a.m.

Ottawa — The Quebec Superior Court has agreed to suspend a Quebec law, that made the oath to the king optional since 2022, with the suspension taking immediate effect.

“The 127 members of the current legislature, who have only taken the oath to the National Assembly, will also be required to swear an oath to the King before assuming their duties,” reads the judgment rendered Monday by Justice Ian Demers.

The decision is casting doubt on whether the legislature will be able to open on Dec. 1, as expected. Quebec elected officials will either have to be sworn-in again before that date or decide to violate a court order.

The law, known as Bill 4, added a clause to the Constitution Act of 1867 stating that the oath to the monarch no longer applies to Quebec legislators.

It was adopted unanimously in the provincial legislature after the current premier of Quebec, Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, and the two other members of his caucus in 2022 refused to take an oath to the King and were therefore barred from taking their seats.

In his decision, delivered solely in French, Demers wrote that it matters little that Bill 4 was adopted unanimously, or that the lieutenant-governor granted it royal assent.

“Strong support does not validate such a law, nor does royal assent endorse it: the Lieutenant Governor grants it as a matter of course, without debate,” he wrote.

Demers insisted that legislators cannot unilaterally change the Constitution.

“The Constitution is not an à la carte menu from which one May choose to follow only those parts that suit one’s preferences,” he wrote.

Demers added that while nothing prevents Quebec, another province, or even the federal government from establishing a republican system, it requires unanimity.

He also pushed back against suggestions that the oath to the King forces elected officials to take a political stance.

“Taking the oath does not require one to be a monarchist, but rather to commit to abiding by the Constitution, which the sovereign personifies,” he wrote.

Monday’s decision is a victory for Lawrence David, a professor at the University of Ottawa’s faculty of law and founder of the Public Interest Litigation Institute, who initiated the legal challenge leading to the suspension.

In August, the Public Interest Litigation Institute filed a constitutional challenge against the Attorney General of Quebec and the Attorney General of Canada about Bill 4, but David admitted it could take years before a judgement is rendered.

That is why, the day after the Quebec election, the Institute filed an application in the Quebec Superior Court to essentially freeze the application of Bill 4.

That request was granted, meaning that the Quebec law is suspended pending the adjudication of the constitutional challenge to that law on its merits.

Bloc Québécois Leader Yves-François Blanchet said while it would be unfortunate for Quebec legislators to have to “humiliate” themselves in having to swear an oath to the King, he called for calm and moderation in finding a solution moving forward.

“I am convinced that the National Assembly and all the parties will work together toward a solution,” he said.

The Quebec government is expected to appeal this judgment to the Quebec Court of Appeal.

Catherine Lévesque covers federal-Quebec relations for National Post. She joined the parliamentary bureau in Ottawa in 2022, after a decade spent in French media in Montreal, Quebec City and Ottawa.

stories.title: Some Bell customers’ information accessed in cybersecurity incident
stories.summary: It's the latest in a series of cybersecurity incidents across Canada and globally in recent days, with some seeing personal data accessed.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
Bell says it’s investigating a cybersecurity incident after some customers’ personal information May have been accessed last week.

According to the company , an “unknown party” gained unauthorized access on Nov. 17 to an internal Bell system.

Personal information, including names, mailing addresses, phone numbers, email addresses and account details, May have been affected. Account details accessed could include the date and amount of last payment, account number and business name where applicable, Bell added.

“Upon discovering the incident, Bell immediately removed the threat actor and initiated emergency protocols,” a statement released by Bell said.

After becoming aware of the incident last Tuesday, Bell said it started notifying customers as soon as it confirmed some data May have been affected.

The company did not say how many customers were affected.

Bell added that no highly sensitive personal information, such as credit card or bank account information, was accessed.

It’s the latest in a series of cybersecurity incidents across Canada and globally in recent days, with some seeing personal data accessed.

Last Wednesday, Kpmg Canada said some client tax documents were accessed in a breach. The company said it was confident the accessed data was not available online or being misused for any purpose, though it is reaching out to affected clients.

The International Ice Hockey Federation said on Nov. 17 it had been hit by a cyberattack that took down its website for a period of time. It did not identify any information that was accessed, saying it was confident their platforms were secure.

Several Ontario police forces suspended their use of Crime Stoppers last month after a cybersecurity breach potentially exposed identifying information included in some anonymous tips.

The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security said in an alert in October that multiple firms had been targeted by people impersonating internal IT support and directing employees to fake sign-in pages.

The RCMP’s cyber crime unit has been contacted, Bell said. It will also be working with other regulatory authorities.

Customers are advised to stay wary of unsolicited requests from actors posing as Bell that ask for personal information or direct them to a website to enter it. They should also regularly review accounts for suspicious activity and avoid clicking links or downloading attachments from suspicious emails or text messages.

stories.title: Quebec court rules provincial legislators must swear oath to King
stories.summary: Judge rules law passed by legislature abolishing requirement was unconstitutional
stories.author: Maura Forrest
stories.content:
A Quebec Superior Court judge has ruled that members of the provincial legislature will have to take an oath of allegiance to King Charles III before they can assume their duties in the National Assembly.

In a decision released Monday, Justice Ian Demers granted an emergency application to suspend a 2022 law that had abolished the requirement for provincial MNAs to swear fealty to the British monarch.

“Contrary to what it May seem, the oath does in fact play a vital role in our democracy,” he wrote, adding that the oath “acknowledges the primacy of the Constitution, personified by the King.”

After the Oct. 5 Quebec election, the province’s 127 legislators swore allegiance only to the people of Quebec. The National Assembly is set to resume next week.

But Justice Demers ruled that if lawmakers do not take the oath of allegiance to the Crown, “all laws passed by the National Assembly would be unconstitutional and would have to be re-enacted.”

“The paralysis that would inevitably result is an irreparable harm to the public interest,” he wrote.

The 2022 law was passed unanimously after then-Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon and his caucus refused to take an oath to the King and were not permitted to enter the National Assembly.

Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon doubled down on his refusal to swear allegiance to the King after the province’s Superior Court ruled to temporarily reinstate the oath. The Canadian Press

Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon, who became premier in October, has promised to go further, saying he will eliminate the office of lieutenant-governor in Quebec. The province’s lieutenant-governor did not attend the government’s swearing-in last month.

But his promises have raised the prospect of a constitutional battle. A legal group called the Public Interest Litigation Group filed a legal challenge of the 2022 law in August, and requested an emergency injunction in October.

In granting the injunction on Monday, Justice Demers cast doubt on Quebec’s ability to make unilateral changes to the Constitution.

“If the amendment is made unilaterally when it should have been adopted through a different process, it is invalid,” he wrote.

His decision suspends the law pending the outcome of the legal challenge.

stories.title: Toronto police identify two teens killed in shooting at Scarborough gas station
stories.summary: Police have identified the teens who died as Ezekiel Tarrance Joseph-Jeffrey and Jakson Robin Clifford Persaud
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto police have identified two teenagers killed in a shooting at a Scarborough gas station that also left a third boy with serious injuries.

Police say officers responded early Sunday morning to reports of a shooting in the area of Ellesmere Road and Brimley Road, where three 16-year-old boys were found with gunshot wounds.

They say two of the boys died in hospital, while the third had serious injuries.

Police have identified the teens who died as Ezekiel Tarrance Joseph-Jeffrey and Jakson Robin Clifford Persaud, both from Toronto.

Toronto police Det. Sgt. Trevor Grieve told a news conference on Sunday that a confrontation had broken out between two different groups following a private event at a nearby venue.

Grieve said investigators believe the shooting initially began along Ellesmere Road before the victims eventually made their way to the Petro-Canada gas station.

He said all victims were at the private event and it’s unclear if the assailants were also present or in the area for separate reasons.

stories.title: Quebec court suspends law making it optional to swear oath to King
stories.summary: Quebec Superior Court has ruled that the province's politicians will need to swear an oath to the King in order to sit at the provincial legislature.
stories.author: Marieke Glorieux-Stryckman
stories.content:
Quebec Superior Court has ruled that the province’s politicians will need to swear an oath to the King in order to sit at the provincial legislature.

Justice Ian Demers ruled that any law passed by legislators who did not swear the oath would be unconstitutional.

He adds in his ruling that all 127 current legislature members have yet to swear allegiance to the King.

The ruling grants an emergency order requested by lawyer Lawrence David and the Consumer Law Group who were asking court to stay the application of a 2022 law that made swearing the oath optional.

The Quebec legislature adopted the law after Parti Québécois members were temporarily barred from taking their seats after they refused to swear allegiance to the King.

David says he expects Quebec to appeal the decision.

stories.title: London police solve 1968 homicide of 16-year-old Jacqueline Dunleavy
stories.summary: London police say a historical homicide investigation has been solved through the use of modern DNA technology and investigative techniques.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
London police have announced the 1968 homicide of Jacqueline Dunleavy has been solved.

Dunleavy, 16, died on Jan. 9, 1968.

She had been working at Stanley Variety Store on Stanley Street at Wharncliffe Road and finished her shift at 6:30 p.m. Investigators said she was last seen leaving the store.

Gallery: Jackie Dunleavy cold case photos

At about 8 p.m., three youths found Dunleavy at Katherine Harley School, now Matthews Hall, ON Oxford Street west of Sanatorium Road. She was pronounced dead when officers arrived.

The investigation determined Dunleavy died from asphyxiation.

At the time of her death, Dunleavy was a Grade 10 student at Westminster Secondary School.

This is a developing story.

stories.title: Children’s Place, Gymboree liquidating all Canadian stores
stories.summary: 56 outlets set to sell off inventory as parent company seeks buyer
stories.author: Tara Deschamps
stories.content:
The Children’s Place and Gymboree are liquidating all of their Canadian stores while the brands’ parent company hunts for a buyer.

The two children’s apparel retailers have 56 stores across nine Canadian provinces, documents filed with an Ontario court by The Children’s Place Inc. Plce-Q and its affiliates earlier this month show.

The locations are due to sell off their inventory by Feb. 28 at the latest – an effort meant to help the company pay off the mountain of debt that led to its insolvency proceedings.

All sales are final, except for purchases made between Oct. 23 and Nov. 6. Both brands’ websites said they will continue accepting gift cards for a “limited time” but will soon share a cutoff date for using the vouchers.

However, if a buyer is found for some of the Canadian stores, the court filings say those locations could be removed from the liquidation sales and perhaps run by a new owner. Bids for the company and its assets are due by Dec. 9 with an auction scheduled for Dec. 11, but any transaction would be subject to court approval.

The sell-off comes as the retailers, known for offering affordable kids clothing, are simultaneously liquidating U.S. stores. An Ontario court has previously recognized the U.S. bankruptcy protection proceedings for the stores’ owner.

The Secaucus, N.J., company founded in 1969 blamed its need for court protection on declining consumer demand for value-oriented children’s apparel, persistent inflation, tariffs on imported goods and intense competition and promotions from retailers and e-commerce brands.

Court documents show the company recorded a net loss of $84.1-million for the first half of its fiscal 2026. Sales for the 26 weeks leading up to Aug. 1 declined by 15.4 per cent to $457-million.

In fiscal 2025, Canadian sales were $92.5-million, making up 7.7 per cent of the company’s consolidated net sales, the documents say. Some $52-million of that cash was generated through brick-and-mortar locations, while the rest came from e-commerce.

The company had been trying to stave off creditor protection for a few years. In its court filings, it said it refinanced over the last two years and reviewed its store footprint and inventory to uncover savings.

Court documents say these efforts generated “meaningful liquidity,” but ultimately, “did not offset the magnitude of the revenue decline and operating losses.”

As of Nov. 6, court records show the company owed $381.6-million through various loans and credit facilities to Wells Fargo, Crystal Financial and Mithaq Capital SPC.

Mithaq Capital, an investment company for Saudi Arabia’s Al Rajhi family, has a 61.1 per cent equity stake in The Children’s Place and Gymboree’s parent company, court records show. Mithaq initially purchased a 50 per cent stake in 2024 and later increased its holdings.

The Children’s Place and Gymboree empire includes 512 stores in North America and 323 international distribution points. They are serviced by a distribution centre in Fort Payne, Ala., and a third-party facility in Mississauga, Ont.

Court records also say the company had 749 employees in Canada at the end of October. Most of them had part-time roles at Children’s Place and Gymboree stores.

stories.title: Live: London police solve 1968 homicide of 16-year-old Jacqueline Dunleavy
stories.summary: London police say a historical homicide investigation has been solved through the use of modern DNA technology and investigative techniques.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
London police have announced the 1968 homicide of Jacqueline Dunleavy has been solved.

Dunleavy, 16, died on Jan. 9, 1968.

She had been working at Stanley Variety Store on Stanley Street at Wharncliffe Road and finished her shift at 6:30 p.m. Investigators said she was last seen leaving the store.

At about 8 p.m., three youths found Dunleavy at Katherine Harley School, now Matthews Hall, ON Oxford Street west of Sanatorium Road. She was pronounced dead when officers arrived.

The investigation determined Dunleavy died from asphyxiation.

At the time of her death, Dunleavy was a Grade 10 student at Westminster Secondary School.

This is a developing story.

stories.title: Conservatives want MPs to vote on government’s plan for permanent residents
stories.summary: The Conservatives plan to introduce a motion Monday calling on the House of Commons to reject the increase in permanent residents
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — The Conservatives plan to introduce a motion Monday calling on the House of Commons to reject the increase in permanent residents outlined in the government’s immigration plan, with a vote expected later this week.

Immigration critic Michelle Rempel Garner told a Sunday news conference the plan to admit about 662,000 permanent residents next year is not sustainable due to unemployment, the cost of housing and availability of health care.

“We would love to see the Liberal backbench vote in favour of this motion. We need to take a pause. We need to bring down immigration levels and address these serious social infrastructure deficits so that everybody can succeed,” Rempel Garner said.

The government’s plan includes a broad target of 380,000 new permanent residents next year, plus a “one-time” plan to grant permanent residency to up to 200,000 additional people.

That 200,000 figure is split between 100,000 new permanent residents selected through provincial input and 100,000 people chosen from humanitarian and compassionate immigration streams — including about 50,000 Ukrainians and former Hong Kong residents who are already in Canada under special programs.

Rempel Garner says the government could still grant permanent residency to people from Ukraine and Hong Kong without increasing the overall number.

The government also plans to introduce 82,000 more permanent residents through a separate one-time program that started this year for protected individuals already in Canada and some temporary workers. This two-year plan includes 115,000 protected persons and around 33,000 temporary workers.

The government says the addition of 380,000 permanent residents through 2029 makes the system more predictable. It also says about half of the annual admissions are expected to be people already here on temporary visas.

Immigration Minister Lena Diab has defended the one-time plan for 200,000 additional permanent residents. She said the new permanent residents are largely people who are already here, so they won’t be imposing any new strains on the housing market or social infrastructure.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 23, 2026.

David Baxter, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Feds’ wrongful-conviction review body begins commissioner recruitment
stories.summary: The Liberal government passed a bill to allow for the creation of the commission in December 2024, but the organization is still not set up.
stories.author: Anja Karadeglija
stories.content:
The federal government is beginning recruitment for its independent Miscarriage of Justice Review Commission.

It says in a news release that recruitment of commissioners is the next step in building a team to examine potentially wrongful convictions.

The government says the commission will review applications from people who believe they have been wrongly convicted.

The Liberal government passed a bill to allow for the creation of the commission in December 2024, but the organization is still not set up.

Currently, wrongful convictions are dealt with through a ministerial review process, which has been criticized for taking too much time to review too few cases.

The commission won’t be able to overturn a conviction but will have the power to order a new trial or appeal.

stories.title: B.C. trial in author Stephen Galloway’s defamation lawsuit enters final week
stories.summary: Final submissions in the trial of author and former UBC professor Stephen Galloway's defamation lawsuit are set to begin in B.C. Supreme Court in Vancouver Monday.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Final submissions in the trial of author and former UBC professor Stephen Galloway’s defamation lawsuit are set to begin in B.C. Supreme Court in Vancouver Monday.

Galloway’s lawsuit, originally filed in 2018, alleges that he was falsely accused of rape and assault by a former student, whose unproven allegations spread widely online after they became public in November 2015.

Several people originally named as defendants in the case settled before the trial and issued apologies to the author of the bestselling novel “The Cellist of Sarajevo.”

There are four remaining defendants, including a former creative writing student only identified as A.B., who alleged Galloway sexually assaulted her, though the trial heard that she was no longer asserting that Galloway assaulted her, rather that she reported he had done so.

The defamation trial has heard that Galloway’s writing career was destroyed, and his public suspension and firing by the University of B.C. was set off by the allegations, which he denies and were found unsubstantiated by a retired judge hired to investigate.

Galloway was awarded $167,000 in 2018 by an arbitrator who found the university, which was not a party in the lawsuit, violated his privacy rights and harmed his reputation.

stories.title: B.C. Greens take the oath of office as Leader Lowan laments failed climate conference
stories.summary: Green Party Leader Emily Lowan and her caucus colleague Jeremy Valeriote will be sworn into office today at the legislature and Lowan has already set the tone for her tenure.
stories.author: Wolfgang Depner
stories.content:
Green Party Leader Emily Lowan and her caucus colleague Jeremy Valeriote will be sworn into office today at the legislature and Lowan has already set the tone for her tenure.

She says in a release that British Columbians “shouldn’t have to keep bracing for the next climate disaster” after a global climate conference concluded without a deal.

The United Nations Climate Change Conference wrapped up Sunday in Turkey, without agreement among the almost 200 participating countries, after some from Europe and the developing world rejected language that would have weakened commitments to phase out fossil fuels.

Lowan says “countries on the front lines of the climate crisis were right to reject the deal” because an agreement that “ignores the cause of the crisis isn’t a deal worth signing.”

Lowan says the lack of a deal represents failure for those living with the consequences of the climate crisis, and the new provincial Conservative government is moving in the wrong direction by promising to double natural gas production and triple liquefied natural gas exports.

Lowan and Valeriote will be sworn in at 2 p.m., while New Democrats will be sworn in Thursday morning.

‘We are close,’ to deal with Canada, Trump’s trade representative says

stories.title: Winnipeg police required to note race in use-of-force reports
stories.summary: The Winnipeg Police Service has historically kept track of some race information but, as of last month, officers must include it in reports when force has been used in a case.
stories.author: Brittany Hobson
stories.content:
Police in Winnipeg are now required to collect race-based data in their use-of-force interactions to address systemic racism in policing and advance reconciliation with racialized and other communities.

The Winnipeg Police Service has historically kept track of some race information but, as of last month, officers must include it in reports when force has been used in a case.

David Bowman, the service’s director of organizational support and development, said it will help address significant gaps in data collection and eventually lead to reform.

“It’s going to help drive potential policy creation updates, as well as training, if there’s culturally appropriate training that stems from any of this,” he said.

The move follows years of consultations with groups, including the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police, Statistics Canada and the Winnipeg Police Board.

At the national level, there are no laws requiring police to collect race-based data. But many advocacy groups have called for the move, saying it’s important to addressing systemic racism.

Several police departments are already collecting such data in use of force, arrests and routine checks.

Calgary police made a commitment to collect and report race-based data in 2020. Findings in 2024 showed Indigenous women and men, along with Black men, were overrepresented in use-of-force cases.

The Ontario government’s Anti-Racism Act requires several public sectors to collect race information. A 2022 report from Toronto police showed Black and racialized residents faced disproportionate use of force.

RCMP also launched a pilot project with some detachments collecting race-based data in 2024, after former commissioner Brenda Lucki acknowledged that systemic racism exists in the ranks.

While some police agencies have taken the steps to integrate the data in their reporting, there isn’t a national standard on how it should be collected.

“The absence of those national standards in many ways prevented us from moving forward on this,” said Bowman.

The Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police doesn’t collect race-based data but says it supports it. Some member organizations also share such data with Statistics Canada.

A committee with the association has documents outlining the collection and reporting of Indigenous and racialized identity information.

Bowman, who’s on the committee, said that guidance helped Winnipeg police create its road map. What happens next will largely be determined in consultation with the Winnipeg Police Board and the community.

Data collection will be based on an officer’s perceptions, said Bowman. “How an individual is perceived by an officer is the relevant data point.”

Data from last year shows Winnipeg police were dispatched to just over 254,000 calls for service, with 780 resulting in use of force. That can include the use of a stun gun, pointing a firearm or using a firearm.

Bowman said it’s too soon to release its race data from the past month, but the service May make it available to the public later.

Advocates and policing experts say collecting the data is a fundamentally good premise but must be done with transparency.

“Collecting that data is going to help with oversight and trust,” said Meaghan Daniel, a lawyer for the Coalition of Families Affected by Police Violence.

“But we have to say, who is collecting it? How are they going to collect it? How is it going to be shared? There are so many underlying questions.”

The way data is tracked can either obscure or inform, said Daniel.

“It’s really popular right now to say, we’re going to be tough on crime. But it’s not that popular to say that we’re going to be tough on police,” she said.

“People are missing the very circular connection here. Because to the extent that we are tough on the police, we can be more tough on crime, because you will have the communities buy in their trust. And effective policing depends on trust.”

The Winnipeg Police Service has historically kept track of some race information but, as of last month, officers must include it in reports when force has been used in a case.
David Bowman, the service’s director of organizational support and development, said it will help address significant gaps in data collection and eventually lead to reform.
“It’s going to help drive potential policy creation updates, as well as training, if there’s culturally appropriate training that stems from any of this,” he said.
The move follows years of consultations with groups, including the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police, Statistics Canada and the Winnipeg Police Board.
At the national level, there are no laws requiring police to collect race-based data. But many advocacy groups have called for the move, saying it’s important to addressing systemic racism.
Several police departments are already collecting such data in use of force, arrests and routine checks.
Calgary police made a commitment to collect and report race-based data in 2020. Findings in 2024 showed Indigenous women and men, along with Black men, were overrepresented in use-of-force cases.

The Ontario government’s Anti-Racism Act requires several public sectors to collect race information. A 2022 report from Toronto police showed Black and racialized residents faced disproportionate use of force.
RCMP also launched a pilot project with some detachments collecting race-based data in 2024, after former commissioner Brenda Lucki acknowledged that systemic racism exists in the ranks.
While some police agencies have taken the steps to integrate the data in their reporting, there isn’t a national standard on how it should be collected.
“The absence of those national standards in many ways prevented us from moving forward on this,” said Bowman.
The Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police doesn’t collect race-based data but says it supports it. Some member organizations also share such data with Statistics Canada.
A committee with the association has documents outlining the collection and reporting of Indigenous and racialized identity information.

Bowman, who’s on the committee, said that guidance helped Winnipeg police create its road map. What happens next will largely be determined in consultation with the Winnipeg Police Board and the community.
Data collection will be based on an officer’s perceptions, said Bowman. “How an individual is perceived by an officer is the relevant data point.”

Data from last year shows Winnipeg police were dispatched to just over 254,000 calls for service, with 780 resulting in use of force. That can include the use of a stun gun, pointing a firearm or using a firearm.
Bowman said it’s too soon to release its race data from the past month, but the service May make it available to the public later.

“Collecting that data is going to help with oversight and trust,” said Meaghan Daniel, a lawyer for the Coalition of Families Affected by Police Violence.

stories.title: Petes blank Knights, hand London sixth loss in seven games
stories.summary: The Peterborough Petes shut out the London Knights 5-0 in Ontario Hockey League action on Sunday night.
stories.content:
The Peterborough Petes shut out the London Knights 5-0 in Ontario Hockey League action on Sunday night.

Matthew Koprowski turned aside all 20 shots he faced for his third career shutout as Peterborough outshot London 34-20.

Braydon McCallum led the Petes’ offence with two goals, including one on the power play, while Yanis Lutz chipped in with a goal and an assist.

Adam Novotny added an empty-net marker as Peterborough improved to 14-11-0-0, winning for the sixth time in its last seven games.

London goaltender Brian Cooke stopped 29 of 32 shots in the loss.

The defeat continued a difficult stretch for the Knights, who have dropped six of their last seven games and fell to 12-8-1-2 on the season.

stories.title: London police to provide update on cold case homicide investigation
stories.summary: London police say a historical homicide investigation has been solved through the use of modern DNA technology and investigative techniques.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
London police say a historical homicide investigation has been solved through the use of modern DNA technology and investigative techniques.

The London Police Service has scheduled a news conference Monday morning to announce the resolution of the cold case investigation and provide details about the identification of the believed to be person responsible.

Police said members of the Major Crime Section used advances in DNA technology and modern investigative methods to identify a suspect in the homicide.

Police Chief Thai Truong will be joined by Det.-Sgt. Micah Bourdeau and Det. Mike Budzyn of the Major Crime Section at the briefing.

Investigators are expected to discuss the findings of the cold case investigation, as well as the role advancements in DNA analysis played in identifying the suspect.

The news conference is scheduled for 10 a.m. and can be livestreamed on the CTV News London website.

Police have not released additional information about the homicide investigation ahead of the announcement.

stories.title: Tailscale, one of Canada’s fastest-growing tech companies, set to accelerate on AI demand
stories.summary: Company aiming to win big contracts from governments, multinationals for its networking software with new ‘sovereign’ strategy
stories.author: Sean Silcoff
stories.content:
Tailscale Inc. isn’t an artificial intelligence company, but it has been growing like one – and has AI to thank for it.

Now, the Toronto company is preparing to capitalize even further on mushrooming demand for its secure virtual private network and connectivity software. That’s a shift in how its fiscally prudent chief executive officer Avery Pennarun has managed the seven-year-old company, and includes a play to win big contracts from government and multinationals with a new “sovereign” offering.

“This is the year where some jets will get stepped on, based on the huge demand we’ve been fighting off,” he said. “We just need to get over ourselves and deliver what the market has been asking for. We should be spending a lot of money to make a lot of money in a short time, especially in this current AI tornado.”

Tailscale has benefitted as rapidly proliferating AI startups have turned to its products to build out their digital infrastructure. This year it got a boost as AI search engines automatically recommended its product to those looking for networking tools. Other infrastructure players such as Supabase and Vercel have experienced similar spikes.

Meanwhile, personal AI tools and agent platforms, including Meta’s Muse and OpenAI’s Codex Cloud, have integrated Tailscale’s open-source networking layer into their products – often “without talking to us first,” said Mr. Pennarun.

With so many customers coming to its front door on their own, Tailscale has spent little to attract new business. As AI agents spring up everywhere and need security and connectivity to underpin them, “Tailscale just got elected, almost despite ourselves, as the standard way to do that,” he said.

Tailscale board member Amit Kumar, a partner with Silicon Valley venture capital firm Accel, said, “We’re benefitting from being in the right place at the right time, having built the right product for that.”

Widespread adoption of Tailscale’s free product has increased uptake of its revenue-generating version: It has 60,000 paying business customers, up sixfold since January 2025, and 3.5 million individual monthly users. Its top-line growth has quickened: Annualized revenues doubled to US$40-million during its fiscal year ended Feb. 1, then doubled again to US$80-million in the next nine months. Net dollar retention, a measure of how much customers spend compared to the previous year, is 140 per cent.

Until now, Montreal-based Mr. Pennarun, a serial entrepreneur who previously worked at Google as a software engineer, has resisted calls from U.S. venture capitalists on his board to spend more and grow Tailscale even faster.

That’s changing. Tailscale is investing more in sales efforts and other initiatives to fuel global expansion, and plans to double its roughly 400-person head count in the next year. That includes building out a team to land government deals, led by former Google executive Patricia Prewitt, who joined the company this fall. The company will also be more proactive in pursuing strategic acquisitions.

Tailscale is planning to raise hundreds of millions of dollars of fresh capital in the coming months, said Mr. Pennarun. It only this fall started dipping into the US$230-million it raised early last year in a financing that valued the company at US$2-billion, after previously raising US$115-million.

The company is leaning into another big opportunity by adopting a sovereign AI strategy run by Ms. Prewitt. That’s in response to growing demand from large corporations and governments for a version of its product that would let customers completely self-host their data.

To turn its offering into a sovereign play, Tailscale needs to “enable anyone who wants to have every aspect of what we do for their data controlled within the space that they define,” said Ms. Prewitt, whether that’s in a customer’s country or on their premises.

At the moment, Tailscale’s “control plane,” or data-routing system for connecting the secured endpoints of specific customers within their networks, is located in Germany. To become more sovereign, Tailscale will need to set up relay points in each country where clients are located, which Mr. Pennarun said wasn’t a significant technological change.

Tailscale expects to launch the offering this year, and Mr. Pennarun said individual contracts for the sovereign offering should grow into the tens of millions of dollars a year per customer from multinational businesses and governments.

Newly hired chief financial officer Kunal Mehta, who’s based in the San Francisco Bay area, said, “The return on investment on every dollar is so high that it behooves us to accelerate our growth.”

“Avery and I would be very disappointed if we just doubled” revenues next year, he added.

stories.title: Israel urges Carney to act on Toronto conference linked to designated terrorist groups
stories.summary: Upcoming event's ‘explicit purpose is to glorify Hamas’ October 7, 2023’ attack, Israeli minister says in letter to PM
stories.author: Kenn Oliver
stories.content:
The Israeli government is urging Canada to take action against a conference slated for Toronto next weekend, citing what it describes as significant organizational leadership ties to groups designated as terrorist entities in Canada and the U.S.

In a Nov. 19 letter to Prime Minister Mark Carney, Amichai Chikli, Israel’s Minister of Diaspora Affairs and Combating Antisemitism, called for “an urgent interagency security assessment” of the Nov. 28-29 conference, an examination of its organizers’ “financing and logistical support,” and a review of “the admissibility of foreign participants.’

He also urged Canada to consider formally listing Masar Badil, organizers of “3 Years of Al-Aqsa Flood: Resistance & Return from the Belly of the Beast,” as a terrorist entity.

Chikli said the conference’s “explicit purpose is to glorify Hamas’ October 7, 2023 brutal and barbaric onslaught on Israel and to expand international networks of radical mobilization.

“For example, one of the published panels is called ‘One Day You Too Will Be a T-rrorist’ and the session is aimed at normalizing terrorism.”

That panel discussion, according to the ministry’s special report on Masar Badil and the conference, will feature Charlotte Kates, a co-founder of Vancouver-based Samidoun, which has been declared a terrorist entity by the Canadian government.

Masar Badil, also known as the Palestinian Alternative Revolutionary Path Movement, is also associated with the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine (Pflp), a group listed by Canada as a terrorist entity since 2003.

“There is a direct, undeniable link between the hate speech and violent incitement promoted by groups like Masar Badil and the physical threats, shootings, and arson targeting Jewish Canadians and their institutions,” Chikli wrote to Carney.

The conference’s connection with Samidoun is one of two areas of chief concern for Israel. The other is the involvement of advertised speakers with alleged connections to other designated organizations.

The U.S. Department of the Treasury sanctioned Masar Badil in August under counterterrorism authorities, citing shared leadership and fundraising with Samidoun.

Masar Badil has rejected the U.S. sanctions, portraying them as politically motivated attempts to suppress Palestinian resistance. In a September statement, organizers said the event would proceed regardless.

The report says the conference website identifies Samidoun as a member of Masar Badil. It also highlights overlapping leadership between the groups, including Khaled Barakat and Kates as co-founders of both movements.

Barakat, advertised as the event’s keynote speaker, was designated by the U.S. Treasury in October 2024 for allegedly acting on behalf of the Pflp and for being a member of its leadership abroad.

Another advertised participant, Mohammed Khatib, is identified in the report as a Samidoun official designated by the U.S. Treasury in May 2026.

The conference program includes discussions on international coalition-building, campus activism, diaspora organizing and opposition to counterterrorism politics. Other advertised sessions include “The Red-Green Alliance,” “Academia: A Demobilizing Force?” and “Building a Global Camp of Resistance.”

The organizers also describe Oct. 7, 2023 as “one of the most courageous acts of resistance in our lifetimes” in their promotional material. The Israeli minister alleged the advertised conference name and program represent an effort to celebrate the Hamas-led attack rather than discuss Palestinian political issues.

There is no publicly released date or location for the two-day event.

“Canada and Israel share a fundamental duty to confront violent extremism and protect our communities,” Chikli concluded. “Allowing an event tied to a Canadian-designated terrorist group to proceed unchecked undermines counterterrorism efforts and endangers Canadian citizens.”

The Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs (Cija) called on Ottawa to prevent the conference from occurring, investigate its organizers and examine whether foreign speakers should be allowed into Canada.

“An Iranian-backed, pro-terror conference in the heart of our country’s largest city is a clear threat not only to our national security, but our democratic way of life,” Max Robert, vice president of policy at the Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs, told National Post last week.

“Canada’s new National Security Strategy, the first in 20 years, warns that ‘threats once thought distant are now immediate and proximate.’”

Cija also wrote to Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree earlier this month, urging government intervention. A spokesperson for his office told National Post the minister was concerned and that any “relevant evidence” about possible criminal violations should be handed over to law enforcement agencies to investigate.

Other groups to voice concerns and ask Ottawa to intervene include B’Nai Brith Canada, Tafsik and the Association of Canadian Families of Victims of Oct. 7.

“Every official who has the power to stop it and does nothing needs to look our families in the eye and explain that choice,” said Raquel Look, whose son, Alex, was murdered by Hamas terrorists in Israel on Oct. 7, 2023.

— With files from Courtney Greenberg.
