stories.title: Two U.S. men sentenced to life in Dominica for murders of Canadian animation pioneer and his partner
stories.summary: Americans Jonathan Lehrer, 60 and Robert Snyder Jr., 66, were both found guilty of murder by a jury in the High Court of Justice in Roseau, the capital city of
stories.author: Jason Miller
stories.content:
Two men convicted in the 2023 murders of Canadian animation pioneer Daniel Langlois and his partner , Dominique Marchand, ON the Caribbean island nation of Dominica were sentenced to spend the remainder of their lives in prison by a judge Monday.

Justice Sejilla McDowall said even though the case meets the mark of the “worst of the worst” killings in Dominica, she opted not to impose the death penalty, the maximum available punishment, noting that the two men have no previous convictions, showed redeemable traits and displayed prospects for rehabilitation.

“This court finds that it is not a fitting case to impose a death penalty (by hanging), and that the decision is by no means diminishing the significance of the loss,” McDowall told the High Court of Justice in the island’s capital Roseau.

Langlois, 66, and Marchand, 58, were found dead with gunshot wounds in a burnt-out SUV not far from the off-grid mountaintop resort they owned on the island on Dec. 1, 2023.

She said the “unprovoked attack” on two respected people had a “chilling community impact.” Evidence called at trial showed that Langlois and Marchand were ambushed on a remote trail near Soufriere, a village in the southern part of the island, as they returned to their upscale resort.

Four days later, Americans Jonathan Lehrer, 60, an entrepreneur, and Robert Snyder Jr., 66, who was purportedly working for Lehrer as a mechanic, were arrested.

Both were found guilty of murder by a jury in July.

“It is a double murder of two entrepreneurs who are both killed under gunfire with attempts to dispose their bodies by incineration and steering a burning vehicle down a steep precipice,” the judge said.

“I’m satisfied in this case that the whole life sentence is appropriate,” she said, adding that “incarceration rather than death can meet the objectives of sentencing.”

The prosecution had asked the courts to imprison the men for the rest of their lives, but the final say on punishment was with justice McDowall, who ultimately ruled in favour of that outcome based on the features of the case and court rulings from previous murder cases.

While the island nation maintains capital punishment within its criminal code, executions have not occurred for the past four decades.

Court documents revealed that both victims were known for their charitable work in their adopted home and, just a month before the murder, Langlois had received a meritorious service award from the president of Dominica.

“The death of the couple is deeply felt,” McDowall said. “Their pleasant manner, enterprising, infrastructure building and philanthropy made a tremendous impact on their staff and surrounding communities.”

Langlois made his fortune in the 1990s selling his Montreal-based company, Softimage, which produced software used in Hollywood blockbusters such as “Jurassic Park,” the “Harry Potter” franchise and “Titanic.” He and Marchand moved to Dominica in 1997.

Daniel Langlois, 66, and his partner Dominique Marchand, 58.

The state’s case against the two Americans was based on the allegation that it was a “contract killing,” and that Lehrer hired Snyder to kill them, according to court filings.

Snyder was said to be a hit man who, armed with a licensed firearm belonging to Lehrer, shot Langlois and Marchand as they returned to their home.

The judge said the case involved a substantial degree of “premeditation and planning,” and that “the bodies retrieved from the vehicle were so burned beyond recognition that DNA analysis was critical for identification.”

A statement from the families of the victims said they are relieved by the guilty verdict and thanked those who “showed their support throughout this heartbreaking tragedy.”

“It is still very difficult for me to believe that my son is gone, but the fact that the criminals were found guilty and that the ashes have just been repatriated, will finally allow me to bury my son with dignity,” Langlois’ mother said in the statement released Friday.

McDowall said there was “a long-standing dispute over land,” and there were “aggressive tendencies displayed by Lehrer,” that diminished arguments supporting his good character.

Langlois and Marchand built a 285-acre, 14-suite eco-resort that opened in 2022; Lehrer oversaw Bois Cotlette Estate, a historic cocoa plantation next door.

Prior to the killings, Langlois and Lehrer had been locked in a protracted legal battle over the use of a road, known as the Morne Rouge Public Road, that connects their properties, the judge said.

The road crossed through the Lehrer estate, sparking the conflict. There was a civil trial and judgment in the case was pending at the time of the offence, the court heard Monday.

McDowall explained that the prosecution did not seek the death penalty because of a commitment to French authorities.

An agreement was made with the French government to get access to Norville Williams, a key witness in the case, Keith Scotland, the prosecutor, previously said, adding that Williams was in France seeking treatment at the time of the trial. In exchange for the co-operation of the French government to facilitate his testimony, the prosecutor agreed that it wouldn’t seek the death penalty.

stories.title: Cold case homicide solved using DNA evidence
stories.summary: London, ON (November 23, 2026) – Members of the London Police Service Major Crime Section have solved the 1968 homicide of 16-year-old Jacqueline “Jackie” Dunleavy following an extensive review of historical evidence and the use of modern forensic DNA technology and Forensic Investigative Genetic Genealogy.
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
London, ON (November 23, 2026) – Members of the London Police Service Major Crime Section have solved the 1968 homicide of 16-year-old Jacqueline “Jackie” Dunleavy following an extensive review of historical evidence and the use of modern forensic DNA technology and Forensic Investigative Genetic Genealogy.

Through the careful preservation and re-examination of evidence collected nearly six decades ago, investigators have identified Michael Joseph Moore, who was 25 years old at the time, as the individual responsible for Jackie’s murder.

Moore died on March 3, 2018, before he was identified through this investigation. As a result, no criminal charges can be laid.

At the time of Jackie’s murder, Moore had been living in London for less than a year. He was born in Ireland in 1942 and emigrated to Canada in January 1967. He moved into an apartment on Springbank Drive in May 1967. He was white, around six feet tall and had dark hair. Typically, he was clean shaven, but he would sometimes grow out a beard when he was on vacation.

“I want to acknowledge the tremendous work of our Major Crime Section and the investigators, forensic specialists, and partner agencies, the Ontario Provincial Police and Toronto Police Service, who contributed to this outcome.,” said Chief Thai Truong of the London Police Service. “Their collective efforts reflect the professionalism, persistence, and commitment that serious investigations demand.”

On Tuesday, January 9, 1968, Jackie was working at the Stanley Variety Store on Stanley Street near Wharncliffe Road. She finished her shift at approximately 6:30 p.m. and was last seen leaving the store on foot.

At approximately 8 p.m. that evening, three youths found Jackie on the grounds of Katherine Harley School, now known as the location of Matthews Hall, ON Oxford Street. Emergency responders attended, and Jackie was pronounced deceased.

The investigation determined that Jackie had been murdered. While she had suffered a head injury, the cause of death was determined to be strangulation.

Jackie was 16 years old and a Grade 10 student at Westminster Secondary School.

At the time, investigators conducted an extensive homicide investigation. Numerous leads were pursued, witnesses were interviewed, and forensic evidence, including biological material, was collected and carefully preserved. Despite those efforts, the person responsible was not identified, and the case remained unsolved.

Over the years, generations of investigators continued to review the case as new investigative opportunities emerged. This included being part of Project Angel, a joint London Police Service and Ontario Provincial Police project that ran from 1997 to 2001. More recently, members of the Major Crime Section undertook a comprehensive review of the investigation, re-examining historical evidence and exploring advances in forensic science.

“The investigators who worked on Jackie’s homicide in 1968 did everything they could with the investigative and forensic tools available to them at the time,” said Detective Sergeant Micah Bourdeau of the London Police Service Major Crime Section. “The evidence they carefully collected and preserved ultimately allowed investigators decades later to continue that work. This investigation shows the importance of preserving evidence and continuing to revisit historical cases as new technology becomes available.”

Using modern forensic techniques, additional DNA testing and analysis was conducted on preserved evidence.

“Through specialized forensic testing conducted by Othram, investigators were able to identify distant genetic relatives associated with the unknown suspect's DNA profile," said Detective Mike Budzyn of the London Police Service Major Crime Section and the current lead investigator. "Working with our partners at the Toronto Police Service, genealogical research was then used to construct family trees and narrow the investigation toward a potential suspect. Our investigators conducted additional interviews, gathered new evidence, and obtained DNA samples for comparison. Those samples were submitted to the Centre of Forensic Sciences for analysis. Based on the evidence obtained through this investigation, we are confident that the evidentiary threshold to support criminal charges was met. Had Moore been alive today, he would have been arrested and charged in relation to Jackie’s murder.”

The decision to publicly identify Moore was not made lightly. It followed careful consideration of the evidence, the public interest and the responsibility of the London Police Service to be transparent about the outcome of an investigation that had remained unresolved for nearly six decades.

While criminal proceedings are no longer possible due to Moore’s death, that does not diminish the strength of the evidence or the confidence investigators have in the conclusion reached through this investigation. Publicly identifying Moore provides an accurate historical record and answers that Jackie’s family and the community have sought for decades.

The London Police Service recognizes the important contributions of the Centre of Forensic Sciences, Othram Laboratories, the Toronto Police Service and the Ontario Provincial Police. The DNA profile that ultimately assisted investigators was also connected to earlier work completed through Project Angel. These partnerships, along with advances in forensic science and the work of generations of investigators, played an important role in moving the investigation forward.

While the investigation has identified the person responsible for Jackie’s murder, investigators recognize there May still be people with historical information. Hearing the name Michael Joseph Moore, or learning information about him today, May bring back memories for people who knew him, had contact with him or were familiar with him during that time. Information that May not have seemed significant at the time could have meaning today.

Anyone with information related to this investigation, or who believes they May have relevant historical information, is encouraged to contact the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670.

stories.title: Understanding Canada’s commitment to the $100 million Nato Innovation Fund
stories.summary: The Nato Innovation Fund is a multi-sovereign venture capital fund that invests in technology, industries and start up businesses connected to security and defense.
stories.author: Paul Hollingsworth
stories.content:
Halifax - The Nato Innovation Fund is a multi-sovereign venture capital fund that invests in technology, industries and start up businesses connected to security and defense.

Canada is contributing more than $100 million and is now one of 25 Nato-allied nations that form the fund’s membership.

“Opening new opportunities for investment in Canadian startups and innovation funds,” said Defence Minister David McGuinty, when describing the fund while speaking the at the Halifax International Security Forum. McGuinty also announced defence businesses in Canada will have access to more than €1 billion, more than $1.5 billion which is managed by the fund.

“We have the talent, we have the technology and partnerships to lead,” said McGuinty. “And today we are giving Canadian innovators greater access to the capital and the opportunities they need to succeed.”

McGuinty also suggested, Canada joining the Nato Innovation Fund is designed to diversity and strengthen its defence partnerships with European allies.

“And that should be significant,” said retired navy commander and defence analyst Ken Hansen.

Hansen said as Canada’s relationship with the U.S. continues to be strained, the federal government is shifting its focus to overseas partnerships, beyond its existing transactions and agreements with south of the border.

“The Prime Minister has been plain about how he sees the Canada-U.S. relationship, especially when it comes to defense,” said Hansen. “He does not want to be limited, and he does not want to be sandwiched.”

The U.S. is not a part of the Nato Innovation Fund -- in fact Canada is the only North American member of the fund

Democratic Virginia Sen. Andy Kim suggested this as another example of the gap widening between the countries.

“We don’t want partners to be working around us,” said Kim. “We want them to be working with us.”

Hansen predicted the fund will eventually support a multitude of Canadian businesses, entrepreneurs and defence contractors.

“This should be seed money for more good things,” Hansen said, and added it is a move aimed at enhancing Canada’s security, while pivoting away from the U.S. and building new defence partnerships.

November 22, 2026 at 6:43 p.m.

The U.S. and Canada are “fairly close” to signing a trade deal, Washington’s chief trade negotiator has said.

In an interview with Fox News on Sunday morning, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said both sides have made “a lot of progress” toward “finding a landing zone.”

Greer’s comments followed what he called a “bipartisan” consensus that Canada seeking deeper economic ties with China was a “concern.”

Canada is “actually having a little bit of a rapprochement on trade with China,” he said, citing Canada’s decision to lower tariffs on Chinese vehicles, steel and aluminum. In January, Prime Minister Mark Carney announced that Canada would allow domestic imports of up to 49,000 Chinese electric vehicles at a reduced tariff rate of 6.1 percent, down from 100.

“Our view is this: this goes a little bit backwards,” Greer said, explaining that the differences came down to policy.

“We’re trying to manage North American trade in auto steel and aluminum; they’ve always been more inclined to free trade and open trade,” he said.

“We’re more inclined to fixing the challenges of globalization,” while Canada is more interested in “doubling down,” he added.

“I think it’s a philosophical difference, and we’re trying to square the circle between their economy and ours, because we are close — we are integrated.”

Greer had neared a trade deal with Canada in August on a swath of goods, including steel, aluminum and autos. But the deal was scuppered after a last-minute intervention by U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, whose department oversees Section 232 national security tariffs imposed on those three imports.

U.S. tariffs on Canadian vehicles are set to double from 25 to 50 per cent in January, putting thousands of jobs at risk. As National Post previously reported, Carney has suggested Canada could seek investment from Chinese automakers to protect the sector.

Still, Greer noted in the interview that talks were “constructive” and that Canada remains a close trade partner.

“The vast majority of goods going back and forth between Canada and the United States still are duty-free, still supporting a lot of jobs on both sides of the border,” he said. “So it’s a more positive story, I think, than people realize.”

Greer concluded that the U.S. wants “to make sure that we’re protecting the North American economy while also landing at a deal that’s good for the United States and good for Canada.”

stories.title: Trump impersonator joins Prime Minister Mark Carney at Ottawa press dinner
stories.summary: An impersonator of U.S. President Donald Trump joined Prime Minister Mark Carney last night for his comedic address at the annual Parliamentary Press Gallery Dinner in Ottawa.
stories.author: Elianna Lev
stories.content:
An impersonator of U.S. President Donald Trump joined Prime Minister Mark Carney last night at the annual Parliamentary Press Gallery Dinner in Ottawa.

Throughout his nearly 17-minute set, Carney took aim at journalists and journalism, the leaders of the other Canadian political parties, Ontario Premier Doug Ford, and even himself.

At one point, he remarked: “Damn, this is a tough room, and I’ve been in the Oval Office... alone... with its new interior decorator.”

He was joined onstage by comedian Mark McKinney, who played his “comedy Carney” lookalike, and then by the Trump impersonator, who pointed out the PM’s “great” posterior.

The faux Trump joked about Canada’s version of the “blue wave” – a reference to the Democratic comeuppance after the U.S. midterm election – as “when a Conservative crosses the floor.”

“So many people are leaving Pierre Poilievre’s office that we’re going to have to build a wall and Canada’s going to pay for it,” he quipped.

Poilievre also got some time at the mic. He started by saying how much he didn’t want to be there, and how last year he wanted to have an impersonator replace him.

“This year, I was planning to have a temporary foreign worker come and give my speech,” Poilievre said. “But for the first time in history the immigration minister refused the permit. I should have just said it was for Tim Hortons.”

The opposition leader also poked fun at NDP leader Avi Lewis, the Canadian Green party, former prime minister Justin Trudeau, and his girlfriend Katy Perry.

At the end of his set, Poilievre critiqued Carney’s spending and brought out a bag filled with money, which he flung at the media outlets sitting in the crowd.

“Let me reassure you, it is not spending, it is an investment,” he said.

Bloc Québécois Leader Yves-François Blanchet took a serious approach to his speech, which focused on the importance of journalism.

stories.title: Carney, federal party leaders bust out comedic chops at press gallery dinner
stories.summary: Ottawa — Two Mark Carneys and a Donald Trump shared the stage at the Parliamentary Press Gallery dinner Saturday, when the prime minister got a little help from This Hour Has 22 Minutes impersonators to give the traditional comedic speech.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — Two Mark Carneys and a Donald Trump shared the stage at the Parliamentary Press Gallery dinner Saturday, when the prime minister got a little help from “This Hour has 22 Minutes” impersonators to give the traditional comedic speech.

“I am pressing the emergency comedy button,” Carney said as comedian Mark McKinney came out to perform his Carney impression on stage, before comedian Mark Critch joined with his Trump impersonation.

But Carney delivered plenty of zingers of his own in his speech, taking aim at Canadian media, his fellow party leaders, Ontario Premier Doug Ford and Trump.

“This is a tough room. And I’ve been in the Oval Office. Alone. With its new interior decorator,” he said.

The dinner is an annual event organized by the Parliamentary Press Gallery and is attended by journalists, politicians and lobbyists. Party leaders try their hand at comedy, giving self-deprecating speeches at which they also poke fun at each other.

Carney made fun of his remarks from last week in which he was asked about Quebecor’s proposal to acquire Telus. He’d answered that under certain circumstances and depending on the market structure, an oligopoly situation can lead to more competition.

“My staff are going to hate me for this, but this reminds me of a good oligopoly joke that I heard the other day. All the telcos told it to me at the same time,” he said. “Look, there are market structures in which that actually would be funny.”

This year, Gov. Gen. Louise Arbour also gave a speech that garnered many laughs and applause. The speech included a joke about Carney’s extensive international travel.

“Our prime minister is already getting a lot of attention. Actually, I heard a guy the other day compare him to God. Now seriously, do you know the difference between God and Mark Carney? God is everywhere, and Mark Carney is everywhere except in Ottawa where he’s supposed to be,” she said.

Arbour also said Carney “should continue to do the wonderful job he’s doing on homelessness, particularly his inspiring initiative on 24 Sussex.”

She added: “And of course, he should continue the very impactful work he’s doing on the environment, especially in Alberta.”

The party leaders often stay for the full duration of the dinner event, but this year Carney arrived in time for his speech and headed for the door right afterward. After the journalist emcees called him out on stage for leaving, Carney watched Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre’s speech from the back of the room before exiting. Poilievre, who only attended for part of the evening last year, stayed for the whole event Saturday.

“Some say that Mark has a controlling leadership style. There’s been reports that he yells and micromanages his staff. He acts like a miserable prick to journalists. And when I hear things like that, I say once again, he’s stealing all my ideas,” Poilievre said.

Poilievre ended his speech by taking aim at Liberal government funding to support journalism, bringing a bag of money on stage and pretending to hand out cash to journalists.

“I’m taking the Liberal approach. I have a special gift to help with my new media strategy. I’ve got a media bailout for you all. Here we go. Here’s some for the Globe and Mail. Here’s some for the CBC,” he said.

Bloc Québécois Leader Yves-François Blanchet used part of his speech to strike a serious tone and recognize journalists’ work, saying that without independent journalism there is no democracy.

NDP Leader Avi Lewis took aim at Carney’s early exit. “I do not have a seat in the House of Commons, but when I am given one at dinner, I stay there all night long,” he said.

He also harkened back to his previous career as a CBC host. “Back then, I was a member of the media class on the outside, looking in at the powerful. Now I’m the leader of the NDP. On the outside, looking in at the powerful,” he said.

Lewis had a big act to follow, after then-interim NDP leader Don Davies gave a self-deprecating speech last year that was widely viewed as the funniest of the night.

Newly-elected Green Party Leader Mike Morrice closed out the evening, poking at Lewis and Poilievre, who lost his Carleton riding in the last federal election.

“I’m now the leader of a federal political party, having not won my own riding in 2025. But I’ve heard that’s not a problem, right, Pierre? Avi? We’re good,” he joked.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 22, 2026.

Anja Karadeglija, The Canadian Press

By The Canadian Press

In an interview with Fox News, Greer said the two countries are having constructive discussions and are “fairly close on finding a landing zone.”

But he criticized Canada’s decision to allow more Chinese electric vehicles into the country and expand tariff relief for certain Chinese steel and aluminum products.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Inside interior designer Nora Voon’s art-filled home

Greer said the Trump administration wants to protect the North American economy as it manages trade in the auto, steel and aluminum sectors.

He described differences between the two governments as philosophical, saying Canada favours freer trade while the United States is focused on addressing the problems of globalization.

Greer also emphasized that most goods traded between Canada and the United States remain duty-free, supporting jobs on both sides of the border.

“It’s a more positive story, I think, than people realize,” he said, adding that Washington wants an agreement that benefits both countries.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 22, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: New Ontario Liberal Leader to appear with caucus Monday at Queen’s Park – without a seat
stories.summary: Navdeep Bains, who narrowly won the leadership this weekend, says he’ll run for office, but won’t specify where or when
stories.author: Laura Stone
stories.content:
New Ontario Liberal Leader Navdeep Bains will appear alongside his 14-member caucus at the provincial legislature on Monday – but he doesn’t have a seat in the chamber, so he won’t yet be able to face Premier Doug Ford .

Mr. Bains narrowly won the party’s leadership on Saturday, beating Toronto MPP Lee Fairclough, a former hospital executive, with 50.3 per cent support on the third ballot, compared with 49.7 per cent for Ms. Fairclough.

Mr. Bains, who was previously elected five times as a federal MP in Mississauga and Brampton, said he’ll be seeking elected office, but wouldn’t say where or when.

“I will run after I engage with the party. I want to make sure I speak to the executive, speak to caucus as well,” he told reporters Saturday after he won.

It is the third time since 2020 that Liberal party members have chosen a leader without a seat in the Ontario Legislature. Mr. Bains said he would not ask one of the current 14 MPPs to resign so he can run in a by-election.

The other contenders in the contest were Stephanie Bowman, a former finance executive and two-term MPP from Toronto, and Dylan Marando, a former senior adviser in federal and provincial Liberal governments.

The debate over whether the new Liberal leader should have a seat was prominent during the leadership race, with Ms. Fairclough and Ms. Bowman, the only contenders who currently sit in the legislature, arguing it is necessary to take on Mr. Ford immediately.

The past two leaders, Steven Del Duca and Bonnie Crombie, also didn’t hold seats when they were chosen. They resigned their posts after the party placed third in the 2022 and 2025 provincial elections, and after they failed to win their bids for a seat.

The Ontario Liberals, currently in third place in the legislature, have struggled to regain prominence since losing government to Mr. Ford’s Progressive Conservatives in 2018.

Mr. Bains told reporters that his focus is on uniting the party and beating Mr. Ford’s PCs in the next provincial election, calling the government “corrupt” and out of touch with everyday people.

“This may be the end of a leadership race, ladies and gentlemen, but this is just the beginning of our campaign to replace Doug Ford and the Conservative Party of Ontario,” Mr. Bains said during his victory speech Saturday after the results were announced to a room of about 1,000 Liberals at the Metro Toronto Convention Centre in the city’s downtown.

A one-time federal industry minister in Justin Trudeau’s government who was one of the former prime minister’s key organizers in the Greater Toronto Area, Mr. Bains left Parliament in 2021. He held senior roles at CIBC and Rogers Communications, but he resigned from the telecommunications company last spring to run for provincial leader.

Mr. Bains said his top priorities as leader will be tackling affordability and cost-of-living concerns.

The son of immigrants from a small village in India, Mr. Bains said he wants to restore the opportunities afforded to him as a young boy growing up in Canada.

“One in four people in my community of Mississauga visit the food bank, who have a job, who have multiple jobs, who play by the rules and are falling further and further behind,” he said during his victory speech.

“And the reason why that is, is because Doug Ford and the Conservatives have abandoned the fight. They are not in it for the people; they are in it for their buddies.”

The provincial Tories wasted no time linking Mr. Bains to the former prime minister.

Graham McGregor, Ontario’s Minister of Citizenship and Multiculturalism, said Mr. Bains was “one of the biggest supporters of Justin Trudeau, not only as Prime Minister, but when he was running for Liberal leader in the first place.”

“So, we know that connection very well,” Mr. McGregor told reporters Saturday, as he took aim at the now-repealed federal consumer carbon tax.

In a post on X, Mr. Ford congratulated Mr. Bains, and said families want parties to work collaboratively “and put province over party so we can stand up to tariffs, protect workers and make life more affordable.”

Ontario NDP Leader Marit Stiles also congratulated Mr. Bains and said her focus is on affordability, mentioning high cellphone bills – an apparent reference to his time at Rogers.

“From rising grocery costs to growing health care wait times to expensive cellphone and internet bills, Ontarians are looking for solutions to make their life better, and that’s exactly what the Ontario NDP is focused on,” she said on X.

stories.title: Craigwiel Gardens opens new long-term care home
stories.summary: Craigwiel Gardens is celebrating the grand opening of its new Craigholme Long-Term Care home.
stories.author: Melanie Kentner
stories.content:
Craigwiel Gardens is celebrating the grand opening of its new Craigholme Long-Term Care home.

Natalia Kusendova-Bashta, Minister of Long-Term Care, alongside over 100 guests, including residents, donors, staff, community partners, and dignitaries attended a ribbon-cutting ceremony on Nov. 13.

The new $39.7 million, two-storey facility is a state-of-the-art, 96-bed long-term care home. The project was completed on time and on budget, creating 320 construction jobs and adding 40 new staff members, bringing the total workforce to 163.

Elaine Shantz, president and CEO, said that the building represents more than just construction; it’s the outcome of a rural community and extraordinary partners working together to ensure nearly eight decades of senior care legacy continues.

Kusendova-Bashta toured the new home and Craigwiel Gardens’ “Connections” program. This program is part of a pilot initiative by the Ministry of Long-Term Care aimed at providing enhanced supports for healthy living, maintaining independence, assisting families, and reducing the need for emergency medical care.

The Connections program supports individuals awaiting long-term care placement, those deemed eligible by Ontario Health atHome, or those soon to be eligible.

Craigwiel Gardens’ program includes memory care through its Mint Memory Clinic and is situated in the Community Connections Centre, which also houses the Adult Day Program and Seniors Active Living Centre.

stories.title: Ottawa unlikely to meet 2030 emissions target, despite official statements
stories.summary: Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin criticized for insisting Canada is committed to its Paris commitments
stories.author: Nick Murray
stories.content:
In June, Prime Minister Mark Carney told Canadians that the country’s emissions would be higher “in the next few years” than previously projected. Those projections already said Canada would miss its 2030 emissions target under the Paris climate accord .

The government’s own projections – published in its emissions reductions progress report a year ago – showed a best-case scenario of a 28 per cent reduction in emissions from 2005 levels in 2030.

And that was before the Carney government introduced a suite of climate policy rollbacks over the past year, including a delay to the introduction of more stringent tailpipe emissions. That measure was supposed to take the place of the now-scrapped electric vehicle sales mandate; it won’t come into effect now until at least 2029.

Canada’s commitment under the Paris agreement was to cut emissions by between 40 to 45 per cent of 2005 levels. The government of Stephen Harper set a target of 30 per cent.

This week, Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin insisted Canada is committed to its Paris commitments. That claim earned her some public criticism from two of her predecessors while she attended the United Nations climate conference in Turkey last week.

Dabrusin wouldn’t answer when asked whether that commitment includes the 2030 target. In its public statements, the government has leaned on the target of achieving net-zero by 2050.

All the studies suggest Canada won’t meet its target. The government’s own projections say it will miss it. The prime minister himself acknowledged emissions are on the rise. So why hasn’t the federal government said it is no longer committed to the 2030 target?

“I think they’re afraid to come out and say it because it’s putting in people’s faces that they’re making a choice to make wildfires worse, to make flooding worse, to actually leave a worse world for our children,” said Keith Stewart, senior energy strategist with Greenpeace Canada.

“Julie Dabrusin seems like a very nice person. But she’s going to go down in history as the worst environment minister in Canada’s history because it’s been on her watch that Canada has rolled back environment and climate policies in a way that not even Stephen Harper attempted.”

Asked whether Dabrusin has been put in the job to defend Carney’s policy choices, Stewart said nobody is under the impression that she is “calling the shots.”

“This is clearly coming from the prime minister. But she’s at that cabinet table and she’s standing behind those decisions. And as someone who has said she’s committed to action on climate change, her other option is to resign in protest to make it clear that this is unacceptable,” Stewart said.

“If being at a cabinet table is more important to you than having the right decisions come out of the cabinet table, that’s a choice a politician can make.”

In a statement, Dabrusin’s office said Canada is “committed to its Paris agreement of achieving net-zero by 2050.” The statement did not address a direct question of whether Canada is still committed to its 2030 target.

“We cannot achieve our climate goals when we are divided,” wrote Amy Falkner, Dabrusin’s press secretary.

“Our focus is on results that unite Canadians: building major clean energy projects across the country, driving mass electrification, making significant investments in the low-carbon economy, and working in co-operation with provinces, territories and Indigenous Peoples.”

Falkner added that Canada is still committed to reporting its progress under the Net-Zero Accountability Act as required in December 2027, and will report on its 2030 target next month to the United Nations Climate Change Secretariat – as required under the Paris Agreement.

But whether the Net-Zero Accountability Act even has any teeth was the subject of debate on Parliament Hill this week. The act doesn’t set out any fines or penalties for Canada missing or abandoning its climate targets.

At Thursday’s meeting of the House of Commons environment committee, B.C. Conservative MP Ellis Ross grilled Canada’s interim environment commissioner on what purpose the act even serves.

“It seems like everybody agrees, except government, that they’re not going to meet their targets. So when the government is clearly falling short of emissions targets, and in actuality intends to expand its emissions, what exactly does the Net-Zero Accountability Act do?” Ellis asked.

“We’ve been talking about (emissions) for the better part of 20 years. But in terms of the 2030 commitments and 2050 commitments, we’re not going to meet it. So does the Net-Zero Accountability Act mean anything today?”

Elsa Da Costa, the interim environment commissioner, replied that the act was an “important tool” for her office to hold the government to account.

The Angus Reid Institute released an online poll of 1,770 Canadians in July which suggested climate was the top issue for 21 per cent of respondents.

The poll also suggested the Liberals’ track record on climate might be driving one in six Liberal voters to the NDP. The poll found climate was the top concern for half of NDP supporters.

The Canadian Research Insights Council, an industry organization that promotes polling standards, says online surveys cannot be assigned a margin of error because they do not randomly sample the population

Aside from the political repercussions of publicly abandoning its commitment to the 2030 emission targets, Stewart said there are also legal implications.

The federal government is fighting a lawsuit brought by a group of climate advocates over Canada’s trajectory on emission commitments. The lawsuit is asking the Federal Court to order Ottawa to bring its 2030 emissions reductions plan into compliance with the Net-Zero Accountability Act.

“The courts can order the government to do something,” said Julia Levin, the associate director of national climate with Environmental Defence, one of the organizations behind the lawsuit.

“There is a clear consequence to that. But it is mostly political.”

Levin said climate change has become a point of political vulnerability for the Liberals.

“The prime minister knows this, and that’s why he’s done everything to dismantle the 2030 target. But I think it’s the reason that they won’t actually admit that they’ve abandoned this target,” Levin said.

“Internationally, this is a prime minister who cares deeply about his international reputation. And it’s hard to claim middle-power status and moral authority when you’ve abandoned a target that your peers are way more committed to.”

An analysis last year by the think tank 440 Megatonnes found Canada was the worst performer among G7 countries at reducing emissions compared to 2005 levels. All other G7 countries had an average reduction of 32 per cent by 2023, while Canada had only achieved 8.5 per cent.

“It seems like everybody agrees, except government, that they’re not going to meet their targets. So when the government is clearly falling short of emissions targets, and in actuality intends to expand its emissions, what exactly does the Net-Zero Accountability Act do?” Ellis asked.

“We’ve been talking about (emissions) for the better part of 20 years. But in terms of the 2030 commitments and 2050 commitments, we’re not going to meet it. So does the Net-Zero Accountability Act mean anything today?”
Elsa Da Costa, the interim environment commissioner, replied that the act was an “important tool” for her office to hold the government to account.
The Angus Reid Institute released an online poll of 1,770 Canadians in July which suggested climate was the top issue for 21 per cent of respondents.
The poll also suggested the Liberals’ track record on climate might be driving one in six Liberal voters to the NDP. The poll found climate was the top concern for half of NDP supporters.

Aside from the political repercussions of publicly abandoning its commitment to the 2030 emission targets, Stewart said there are also legal implications.

The federal government is fighting a lawsuit brought by a group of climate advocates over Canada’s trajectory on emission commitments. The lawsuit is asking the Federal Court to order Ottawa to bring its 2030 emissions reductions plan into compliance with the Net-Zero Accountability Act.
“The courts can order the government to do something,” said Julia Levin, the associate director of national climate with Environmental Defence, one of the organizations behind the lawsuit.
“There is a clear consequence to that. But it is mostly political.”
Levin said climate change has become a point of political vulnerability for the Liberals.

“The prime minister knows this, and that’s why he’s done everything to dismantle the 2030 target. But I think it’s the reason that they won’t actually admit that they’ve abandoned this target,” Levin said.

“Internationally, this is a prime minister who cares deeply about his international reputation. And it’s hard to claim middle-power status and moral authority when you’ve abandoned a target that your peers are way more committed to.”

stories.title: Magic of Lights returns to London for sixth season
stories.summary: The Magic of Lights has returned to London for its sixth holiday season, promising millions of lights, magical memories, and affordable family fun.
stories.author: Melanie Kentner
stories.content:
The Magic of Lights has returned to London for its sixth holiday season, promising millions of lights, magical memories, and affordable family fun.

The event runs from Nov. 20, 2026, to Jan. 2, 2027.

The drive-through experience, powered by Liuna Local 1059, transformed Fanshawe Conservation Area into a dazzling winter wonderland.

Produced by Woodlo Productions Inc. and Family Entertainment Holdings, LLC., this year’s event boasts over two million lights, four “Insta-worthy” tunnels, and dozens of illuminated displays. Highlights include Candy Cane Lane, Prehistoric Christmas dinosaurs, Christmas on Wheels, Fairy Tales, a 50-foot mega tree, and a giant monster truck.

New this year is “Pedal the Lights,” offering a unique sneak peek for cyclists on Thursday, November 19, from 6:30 to 8:30 p.m. This exclusive opportunity allows riders to experience the 3km show on two wheels before it opens to cars, encouraging festive decorations and offering prizes and refreshments.

Magic of Lights London also proudly gives back to the community through its partnership with the Children’s Health Foundation. Since its 2021 debut, the event has supported local charities, providing meaningful aid to children and families across Southwestern Ontario.

Scott Fortnum, President & CEO of Children’s Health Foundation, expressed gratitude, noting the event’s impact extends beyond holiday memories. He explained that support funds exceptional care, equipment, research, and programs at Children’s Hospital, LHSC, turning holiday joy into hope for children facing difficult times.

There are approximately 2+ million lights bulbs in the show.

It takes about 16 km of steel and 16 km of LED lighting to build the displays.

A crew of 6-8 staff work approximately 3,750 hours to set up the event.

There are 10 different colors of LED bulbs used in the show.

Scenes are as high as 32-feet tall and as long as several hundred feet.

Since its inception five years ago, Magic of Lights London has donated $80,000 to local charities.

stories.title: Two teens killed in Scarborough triple shooting, Toronto police say
stories.summary: Confrontation between two different groups followed private event at nearby venue, police say
stories.author: Sadeen Mohsen
stories.content:
Toronto police say two teenagers are dead following a triple shooting at a Scarborough gas station.

Officers responded to calls of a shooting in the area of Ellesmere Road and Brimley Road at around 12:30 a.m. on Sunday.

When they arrived, officers found three 16-year-old boys who had been shot, and they were taken to the hospital.

Toronto police Det. Sgt. Trevor Grieve told a news conference Sunday a confrontation had broken out between two different groups following a private event at a nearby venue.

Grieve says investigators believe the shooting initially began along Ellesmere Road before the victims eventually made their way to the Petro-Canada gas station.

He says all victims were at the private event and it’s unclear if the assailants were also present or in the area for separate reasons.

Police say two of the victims were pronounced dead at the hospital, while the third suffered serious but non-life-threatening injuries. He was expected to be released from hospital on Sunday.

The Homicide and Missing Persons Unit has taken over the investigation.

Police say this is an ongoing investigation and are asking anyone with information or camera footage to come forward.

Investigators have not identified any suspects.

stories.title: London property owners can now apply for the 2027 tree program
stories.summary: Londoners interested in a tree for their property can apply now.
stories.author: Melanie Kentner
stories.content:
Londoners interested in a tree for their property can apply now.

The City of London is inviting property owners to apply for the 2027 Tree Canopy Conservation Program , which provides financial assistance to help care for and preserve mature trees on private property.

City officials say mature trees play an important role in London’s urban forest. They provide shade, support wildlife, improve air quality and help make neighbourhoods more livable.

“Protecting London’s mature trees is just as important as planting new ones. These trees are a valuable part of our neighbourhoods, and caring for them helps ensure they can continue providing benefits for generations to come,” says Shawna Chambers, director of Climate, Forestry and Waste Services. “As the 2026-2027 Forest Capital of Canada, we are committed to protecting, maintaining, and growing our urban forest.”

The City’s Urban Forest Strategy sets a target of achieving 34 per cent tree canopy cover by 2065.

Eligible property owners can receive financial assistance for the care and management of qualifying mature trees. To be eligible, trees must be at least 50 centimetres in diameter, and all work must be undertaken in consultation with a qualified arborist to help ensure the health of the tree and the safety of the property.

Property owners do not need to live at the property to apply.

stories.title: Museum London showcases three new exhibitions at Fall Launch Party
stories.summary: Museum London held its Fall Launch Party on Thursday. Hundreds attended the event, which featured multiple exh...
stories.author: Callum Contursi
stories.content:
Museum London held its Fall Launch Party on Thursday. Hundreds attended the event, which featured multiple exhibitions and its first musician-in-residence program.

The new program brings on London-born rapper Shad who will work with the museum to make new music with local artists and create visual art about his story alongside frequent collaborator Justin Broadbent . Museum London/Facebook

Artwork the Museum unveiled Thursday included Kim Neudorf’s real_real, Erika DeFreitas’ I am not tragically coloured and an beadwork exhibit called Bingo, by Anishinaabe artist Nico Williams, who gave a guided tour during the event.

“So these are the beads that would have been used during the trade for the country. And each pattern has been taken from a book called Ojibwa Crafts , that was documenting our practice when it was during a period when we weren’t allowed to practice being Indigenous, Anishinaabe, or our nations” said Williams, who is from Aamjiwaang First Nation and attended H.B. Beal Secondary School in London.

Nico Williams, “ Red Bandana “, 2025. Callum Contursi/XFM News

Apart of the Bingo exhibition, Williams also drew inspiration from everyday objects and pop culture for Pawn Stars.

Pawn Stars draws inspiration from VHS tapes to clothing found in pawn shops.

Williams’ beaded version of video games, VHS tapes and films photographed on Nov, 19 Callum Contursi/XFM News

Neudorf’s: real_real exhibit consists of a loosely autobiographical archive. From Museum London’s website, the title real_real describes “openness rather than a single fixed idea or meaning.” Museum London/Neudorf

The exhibit contains several untitled pieces. Neudorf is currently an instructor in the Department of Visual Arts at Western University.

The new program brings on London-born rapper Shad who will work with the museum to make new music with local artists and create visual art about his story alongside frequent collaborator Justin Broadbent . Museum London/Facebook

“So these are the beads that would have been used during the trade for the country. And each pattern has been taken from a book called Ojibwa Crafts , that was documenting our practice when it was during a period when we weren’t allowed to practice being Indigenous, Anishinaabe, or our nations” said Williams, who is from Aamjiwaang First Nation and attended H.B. Beal Secondary School in London.

stories.title: Tumbler Ridge begins consultation on design for new school building
stories.summary: Six people were killed in Tumbler Ridge when 18-year-old Jesse Van Rootselaar opened fire at the northeastern B.C. school on Feb. 10.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
Residents of Tumbler Ridge , where a mass shooting at a school shook the community in February, are being asked for feedback on designs for a new secondary school.

Six people were killed when 18-year-old Jesse Van Rootselaar opened fire at the northeastern B.C. school on Feb. 10. Before the school shooting, Rootselaar killed her mother and half-brother at their home. Rootselaar died at the school from a self-inflicted gunshot injury.

In July, School District 59 officials began the demolition of the school after then-Premier David Eby said the students can’t return to the school where such a devastating event happened.

Now, the district is turning a new page.

“We’re now at the stage of taking design concepts to the community for consultation on the next steps towards a permanent new school build,” said Chad Anderson, the board chair for School District 59, Peace River South.

So far, the board has narrowed down to two options, he added. One is a design for a pre-fabricated school building, while the other is a site-built design.

A pre-fabricated building, as opposed to traditional construction methods where the building is constructed on-site, is largely constructed off-site in a facility and assembled on-site.

“Hopefully, we can choose from the best features available to create a really beautiful new facility that students and staff will feel both safe and comfortable in for the long term in Tumbler Ridge,” Anderson said.

The school board will decide the mode of construction after a two-week consultation period, in which officials will conduct a survey of Tumbler Ridge residents. The board expects to make a decision by late this winter, Anderson said.

“If all goes well, let’s hope that construction can begin in the summer of 2027. It just depends on what mode of construction is chosen and the specifics in terms of the timeline after that,” he added.

stories.title: Alberta to introduce citizen voter ID law, Smith says
stories.summary: Critics say the policy will make voting more difficult and open door to racial or ethnic bias at voting booths
stories.author: Lisa Johnson
stories.content:
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith is telling her United Conservative Party members to get their documents in order to ensure they can vote in next year’s election.

She said Saturday her government will likely introduce a law in the spring enacting a referendum proposal that individuals provide proof of citizenship to vote.

“I’ll let you know, because people need to get their papers in order, we will probably be acting on that one in the spring session,” she said at a virtual town hall meeting reserved for UCP members.

Smith told rank and file members that last month’s referendum vote gave her government a mandate, offering a sneak peak at the spring sitting of the legislature.

Her comments come days before more than 7,000 members are set to meet for the Ucp’s annual general meeting in Calgary beginning Friday.

About three million Albertans will be able to vote in the provincial general election, scheduled for Oct.18, 2027.

Smith said when they go to cast a ballot, they will need to bring their passport, birth certificate or one of the province’s updated driver’s licences, which have space for a citizenship marker.

She said it’s about enforcing the integrity of the voter system.

“You’ll have to prove that you have the right to vote as a Canadian citizen.”

Critics say the policy will only make voting more difficult and time-consuming for residents, and will open the door to racial or ethnic bias at the voting booth.

The premier’s office said Sunday it stands by the premier’s statements, pointing to the referendum results.

October’s ballot had 10 questions, including one that saw three-quarters of voters saying they want to stay in Canada rather than hold a second, binding referendum on separation.

But on the proof of citizenship question, about 58 per cent of voters said yes to the proposal.

It was the highest voter turnout among all ten questions, and saw the highest approval except for the separation question.

Overall, referendum turnout was the highest in roughly five decades.

Voting is already restricted to Canadian citizens and both Elections Canada and Elections Alberta have reported very few cases of ineligible voting.

In July, Alberta’s introduction of new identification cards and their new requirements sparked an avalanche of complaints.

The redesigned provincial IDs, which include health care numbers, have space to include a Maple Leaf marker of citizenship.

But the new IDs came with hurdles for thousands of Canadian citizens living in the province, with some concerned they would be unable to legally drive, including as required for work.

Some reported their historical documents were being rejected by registries, and they faced a long line up to replace them, including through federal agencies.

That prompted Smith’s government to provide temporary exemptions, announced last week.

Service Alberta Minister Dale Nally blamed the federal government for processing delays.

On Saturday, Smith also claimed that voter verification has been operating under an “honour system.”

Voters must be registered and provide proof of residence at polling stations.

Smith suggested that the current mail-in voting process, instituted by her government, will need further changes to make for in-person verification.

“It May mean that there has to be some more restrictions on those who can order special (ballots),” she said.

More than half-a-million Albertans voted through a special, mail-in ballot in the October referendum.

By slim margins, Albertans signed off on the province pursuing other changes to immigration policies, and to reject proposals to push for change on Canada’s Constitution.

The government has hinted that it could introduce legislation tackling immigration issues in the spring, but has not offered details.

UCP president Rob Smith, who is not related to the premier, signed off from Saturday’s virtual members’ call by telling attendees that the board candidates forum would likely be shared online.

The premier’s hour-long question and answer period, however, would not be shared.

“We don’t generally make those public for, you know, for obvious reasons, but I don’t think that our candidates have said anything that is a problem,” he said.

stories.summary: Victoria - A British Columbia First Nations leader says he will try to work with Premier Lorne Doerkson, but warns of "dire" consequences if Conservatives follow through on their promise to repeal the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act.
stories.author: Wolfgang Depner The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Victoria - British Columbia’s new Conservative government could face “dire” consequences if they repeal the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act as promised, a First Nations leader said, adding that he’s willing to work with new Premier Lorne Doerkson.

First Nations Summit Political Executive Robert Phillips said Doerkson has built many “really good relationships” with First Nations during his time as an opposition legislator and Phillips hopes that continues after becoming premier.

stories.title: ‘Woefully inadequate’: Tech analyst criticizes Staples Canada’s response to data breach
stories.summary: A tech analyst whose personal information was exposed in data breach on a Staples Canada’s website says the company’s response has been “woefully inadequate.”
stories.author: Elianna Lev
stories.content:
A tech analyst whose personal information was exposed in a data breach on a Staples Canada website says the company’s response has been “woefully inadequate.”

In an interview with CTV News Channel on Saturday, tech analyst Carmi Levy said he received an email from Staples on Friday saying he was identified as one of the customers impacted by the breach. The email recommended that he change his password on the site, use safe password protocol and keep an eye out for suspicious emails. However, he said he found the company’s response significantly lacking when it came to concrete protection.

“What I find interesting is (there was) no offer for identity theft protection or credit monitoring, which is often standard in cases of this,” he said.

A Staples spokesperson said its Staples Print website was breached during the first week of November. Hackers accessed data including contact information, order summaries and encrypted passwords, though no financial data was exposed.

Levy said he was alarmed by how long it took the company to inform impacted customers of the breach. The site was hacked between Nov. 1 and Nov. 5 but customers were notified almost two weeks later, ON Nov. 20.

That delay leaves “lots of questions and not as many answers as we’d like,” he said.

“Has this data showed up anywhere? Exactly what are you doing to address it and who are you working with to ensure it won’t happen again?” he said. “Woefully inadequate response.”

Once breached data is exposed, Levy said “it’s not coming back,” and for the company to downplay the impact is “disingenuous.”

The stolen data will likely be sold on the dark web, where it will be bought and sold within the cybercriminal community, he added.

“It will be used to craft customized, personalized identity theft attacks and other forms of attacks, and phishing messages…in the days, weeks, months to come, ” Levy said. “You can’t sugarcoat this. It’s as bad as it seems.”

Training employees, not technology, can help

Cyberattacks and data breaches have been a frequent occurrence in recent weeks, including targets such as the Fbi’s job portal , an Alberta charity , Kpmg Canada , and on a key European Union institution.

Levy said many organizations aren’t sufficiently training their employees. As a result, employees will click on meeting requests, or download files, which then compromises their computers, allowing threat actors to gain access to internal systems.

“The answer to this…isn’t really a technology that will solve this, it’s to train your people,” he said. “Make sure you create a cybersecurity-first culture so that your human frontline is as robustly protected against these kinds of outreaches as possible.”

CTV News reached out to Staples for comment.

With files from The Canadian Press

stories.title: St. Thomas Chamber of Commerce creates Hallmark-style film featuring local businesses and actors
stories.summary: The St. Thomas and District Chamber of Commerce (Stdcc) has created a Hallmark-style film, and the first of the six episodes is now online.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
I must admit I’m hooked.

I can’t wait for the next episode of “Our Favourite Things”.

Maybe it’s because I know the local business owners who are starring as the actors, or because it’s focused on my hometown, but this holiday romantic comedy is so much fun.

The St. Thomas and District Chamber of Commerce (Stdcc) has created a Hallmark-style film, and the first of the six episodes is now online.

“It’s supposed to be the love story that the big city lawyer, she is from the small town, moves to the big city, comes back, falls in love, and then falls back in love with the city that she grew up with because it’s changed,” said lead actor Adam Beverley, who plays “Nick”.

Julia Margetts, co-owner of Our Place Respite was cast alongside Beverley as “Holly”.

“The Chamber (of Commerce) has seen all of our, Our Place Respite funny videos,” said Margetts.

“They asked (co-owner) Sam (Daniel) and I to be in it and we thought, as long as it’s funny, we’re doing it.”

The film is being written by the cast and producers, and it came together quickly.

“We were shooting basically the next day and then like the next week, we’re up in Toronto to do cut scenes between Toronto and Saint Thomas to take the AGO (Art Gallery of Ontario) and pair it next to the (St. Thomas) Public Art Centre,” said Grayden Laing - who is directing and producing the film through his production company, Establish Media, in collaboration with Brandon Dietz from Obsidian AI Labs."

“We have three episodes that are mostly shot… and we still have sponsors coming on board. If anyone wants to be a part of it, whether they’re getting a placement or they like, we’re going into their business with the stars of the show or whatever it is, just give the chamber a call. We’ll make it as big and as great as we can.”

The Stdcc is always trying to promote their local businesses. In previous years, they’ve done a shopping catalogue, but this year they have decided to tackle this enormous project.

“We want to keep it as local of a Christmas as possible,” said Lindsey Massecar, event and experience manager for the Stdcc.

“It’s just not as fun to hire actors and actresses. Of course, we reached out to (Hollywood star) Rachel McAdams to see if she was available, but Julia is basically the same thing, so it’s great.”

The first episode is about seven minutes long and features some cameos by MPP Rob Flack and former politician Tim Hudak.

Everyone involved says the reaction has been overwhelming.

Laing believes it’s possible the entire project could be an hour-long film.The first episode dropped last week on the Stdcc Facebook page.

“We’re also going to be putting it on YouTube,” said Laing.

“We’re going to do a feature length version at the end, and then we’ll share that out. We’re going to do a screening and invite the community out to see the whole film all together at the end when everything’s put together. It’s a moving target right now, and we’re going to figure it out. We have deadlines for releasing each episode every Tuesday.”

Beverley – who owns Total Plumbing Solutions – is not originally from St. Thomas but fell in love with the city when he moved here 12 years ago.

“I felt at home here and I love the business community,” said Beverley.

“Everybody is very supportive of each other and to be honest, yeah, if we can help any business out by doing this production. I’m happy about that.”

stories.title: Group calls on people to give coyote space following Edward Gardens incident
stories.summary: Toronto - A non-profit wildlife organization is calling on people to give coyotes space following a confrontation last week in a Toronto neighbourhood.
stories.author: Sadeen Mohsen The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Coyote Watch Canada says in a Facebook post that they have received reports of people purposefully approaching the coyote involved in the incident, including photographers luring the animal closer with food.

They say engaging with coyotes using items such as toys or food teaches the animal to approach humans.

Article continues below

Inside interior designer Nora Voon’s art-filled home

Toronto police have said a child was attacked by a coyote at Edward Gardens, a park located in northeast Toronto, ON Thursday morning.

They said bystanders scared off the coyote, but the child was dragged by the animal and suffered minor injuries.

Coyote Watch Canada says their thoughts are with the family, but claims in the post that while a coyote made contact with the child, the child was neither bitten or nor dragged.

They also said comments on social media have unfairly blamed the child’s caregivers, who were present and responded immediately.

The organization said the coyote was “failed by human behaviour.”

Police are urging people to call 911 if a person or pet is being attacked by a coyote. The non-profit says to never feed, approach or lure a coyote and back away slowly if a coyote approaches you.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 22, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: ‘We are close,’ to deal with Canada, Trump’s trade representative says
stories.summary: Trade talks collapsed between Canada and the United States in August after Ottawa walked away from the negotiating table in response to last-minute terms.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
Canada and the United States are “fairly close” to finalizing a trade deal, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said on Sunday.

Trade talks collapsed between Canada and the United States in August after Ottawa walked away from the negotiating table in response to last-minute terms that Prime Minister Mark Carney said the U.S. demanded, including restrictions on Canada entering into new trade deals with other countries.

“We’ve made a lot of progress. I think we’re fairly close on finding a landing zone,” Greer told Fox News in an interview Sunday.

Both sides have renewed their efforts this month after U.S. President Donald Trump’s Republican Party received a drubbing in the U.S. midterms elections, which saw several Democratic candidates blame Trump’s trade war on Canada for the high cost of living.

Ottawa resetting its trade relationship with Beijing has given Washington some “concern,” Greer said, particularly the decision to allow 49,000 Chinese EVs a year into the Canadian market at a lower tariff rate.

“We’re trying to manage North American trade in auto steel and aluminum. We’re still having constructive conversations with our Canadian counterparts,” Greer said.

“We’re trying to square the circle between their economy and ours because we are close,” he said.

However, overall, trade between Canada and the U.S. was still “a more positive story, I think, than people realize,” Greer added.

“We want to make sure that we’re protecting the North American economy while also landing on a deal that’s good for the United States and good for Canada,” he said.

Carney and Trump were in Shenzhen, China last week, where the two had a discussion on trade ties.

“The leaders discussed the work underway to reach a mutually beneficial trade agreement that would create good jobs, boost affordability, and fully respect Canada’s languages, culture, and sovereignty. They agreed to continue the work and to stay in close contact,” Carney’s office said in a statement.

Canada’s chief trade negotiator, Janice Charette, told a federal advisory committee that “multiple trade issues” remain outstanding with the United States and are preventing a deal, several sources who were briefed by the federal government have told Global News .

The biggest issue still outstanding is the 25 per cent U.S. tariff on Canadian automobiles, according to sources in the meeting. Negotiations around auto tariffs were a core reason trade talks between the Carney government and Trump administration fell apart in August.

Canada’s chief trade negotiator, Janice Charette, told a federal advisory committee that “multiple trade issues” remain outstanding with the United States and are preventing a deal, several sources who were briefed by the federal government have told Global News .

The biggest issue still outstanding is the 25 per cent U.S. tariff on Canadian automobiles, according to sources in the meeting. Negotiations around auto tariffs were a core reason trade talks between the Carney government and Trump administration fell apart in August.

stories.title: Seven vehicles impounded in London traffic blitz
stories.summary: Seven vehicles were taken off the road after a traffic enforcement blitz in the south end of the city by the London Police Service Road Safety Section.
stories.author: Melanie Kentner
stories.content:
Seven vehicles were taken off the road after a traffic enforcement blitz in the south end of the city by the London Police Service Road Safety Section.

On Monday, Nov. 16, officers conducted traffic enforcement along Colonel Talbot Road between Orr Road and the 401.

As a result of the enforcement, eight people were charged with a combined total of 15 Highway Traffic Act and vehicle-related offences, and two of the individuals were additionally charged with impaired driving-related charges.

All eight vehicles were impounded and towed as part of the enforcement action.

The charges related to stunt driving, unsafe vehicle operation, various vehicle equipment offences, and impaired driving. Speeds ranged between 101km/hr to 121 km/hr in a posted 60 km/hr zone.

“Stunt driving and impaired driving puts everyone at risk, including drivers, pedestrians and anyone just trying to get home safely,” said Sgt. Chis Andrews of the Road Safety Section. “Our message is simple: slow down, drive sober and look out for one another. Everyone deserves to arrive safely to their destination, and our officers are out there working to make that happen.”

Police said they will continue proactive traffic enforcement in areas where community members have raised concerns, working to keep roads safe for everyone who uses them.

stories.title: Community groups blindsided as Ottawa pauses refugee sponsorship program
stories.summary: The federal government has quietly pressed pause on a program that helped community groups sponsor and support refugees come to Canada.
stories.author: Rebecca Lau, Heidi Petracek
stories.content:
The federal government has quietly put on hold a refugee sponsorship program that helped community groups support newcomers coming to Canada.

It was a small program, but at one time helped Syrian refugees like Tareq Hadhad start a new life in Canada.

“Canadians are born everywhere. It just takes them a little bit to get here,” said Hadhad.

Hadhad, his parents, and his siblings came to Nova Scotia in 2015 after the Syrian civil war broke out.

They were sponsored by a community group in Antigonish, N.S. through the federal government’s Blended Visa Office-Referred (Bvor) program. It divides the financial cost of supporting refugees for a year between private organizations and the federal government, and is focused on refugees identified by the United Nations.

After arriving in the small community of Antigonish, Hadhad’s father, who had previously been a chocolate-maker in Damascus, began making and selling sweet treats.

The family received a loan from the community, raised money through crowdfunding, and eventually opened their business, Peace by Chocolate.

More than a decade after arriving, Hadhad is a Canadian citizen and a successful entrepreneur. He has won awards, speaks to international audiences routinely, and had a movie made about his experience.

“(The Bvor program) meant everything, it (is) the reason why I’m standing right here right now and behind me is a beautiful flagship boutique on the Halifax waterfront,” Hadhad told Global News outside the Peace by Chocolate store on Lower Water Street.

“Without it, we would be still struggling as refugees somewhere, whether in Lebanon or in Turkey or in Egypt, Jordan, somewhere where we would not have been able to get a resettlement in any country, would not be able to start a new life, would have not been able get anything done over the past 10 years.”

The federal government reduced the initiative’s target immigration numbers from up to 1,000 people a decade ago, to just 50 this past year.

Now, community groups that have used the program say they’ve discovered that Bvor has been put on hold by Ottawa.

A spokesperson for Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada said that although the program is closed, “all remaining applications will continue to be processed, and individuals already matched with sponsors will continue to arrive in Canada and receive support as intended.”

“The program required significant resources to support a small number of admissions. In 2025, it admitted 82 people against a target of 100. The 2026 target was 50, and final figures are not yet available,” Ircc told Global News in a statement.

Halifax’s Open Harbour Refugee Association has used the program for 11 years. Its volunteer members have dedicated their time to arranging housing, medical care, skills training, and education for new arrivals.

Now, they say they feel blindsided.

“There’s no announcement. We had to read between the lines and access anonymous sources,” said Marie Thompson, volunteer director with the group. “We really need them to reconsider.”

Thompson says the group managed to match with a young woman from Kenya last September, who volunteers hope will arrive in Canada in December. The group has been busy raising money and collecting furniture to help her, and future arrivals.

“We wanted to sponsor another family in 2027. And then within the last two weeks, we found out that that won’t happen,” she said.

Thompson adds that the group does more than provide financial assistance. Their dedication involves helping newcomers adjust to life in Canada.

“We try really hard to make their integration into Canadian society successful. And I don’t mean cultural integration. I mean finding jobs, getting extra education, babysitting, for example, when their parents have to go for job interviews. That’s what we do,” she said.

“We become their new extended family. Our obligation is for one year, but we stay friends with them for years afterwards.”

Gauri Sreenivasa, co-director of the Canadian Council for Refugees, says it feels like a “systematic closing” of opportunities for Canadians who want to help resettle refugees.

“ And that is a very concerning thing we have seen in the past few years: generally, private sponsorship opportunities reduced dramatically despite there being a huge demand and capacity and an interest among Canadians to bring and sponsor refugees,” she said.

“Having these restrictions on private sponsorship effectively doesn’t allow Canadians to be as generous and welcoming as they want to and the overall patterns show a concerning reduction of Canadian government’s commitment to this (history of welcoming refugees), which is a core part of Canada’s identity.”

In a world where the subject of immigration has become politically charged, Hadhad says he wants people to know the program works — and represents what Canada believes in.

“I became a father this February and it has changed my life in very immense ways. And I would not have imagined that my son would have been born anywhere else except this country,” he said.

“This program has had a tremendous effect on many families like mine and I hope it’s going to continue into the future of changing lives and changing communities for the better.”

stories.title: Guelph Storm hand London Knights fifth loss in six games
stories.summary: The OHL’s Western Conference is so tight, a few losses and you can find yourself near the bottom of the playoff picture.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
The OHL’s Western Conference is so tight, a few losses and you can find yourself near the bottom of the playoff picture.

The London Knights lost 4-2 to Guelph Saturday, their fifth loss in their last six games, and have fallen to seventh in the conference.

Londoner Ryan Roobroeck had a goal and two assists for the Storm who jumped out to a 3-0 lead before Thomas Zocco and Ryan Brown answered for the Knights in a five-goal opening period.

Arvin Jaswal made his second start in goal for the Knights after Brian Cooke got the call Friday.

Jaswal missed the beginning of the year after an injury he suffered with the Barrie Colts before being acquired by London.

London will play Sunday night at Canada Life Place against the Peterborough Petes.

It will mark the return of goalie Aleksei Medvedev who was traded by London to Peterborough weeks ago.

Medvedev is 4-1 with a 2.01 Goals Against Average with the Petes.
