stories.title: The man who says AI is a big, scary hoax … for now
stories.summary: 'Sometime true AI will come,' says one Canadian pioneer, 'and that will be a really big deal. But that’s not what’s happening right now'
stories.author: Donna Kennedy-Glans
stories.content:
The world is freaking out about AI, but Rich Sutton is here with a Valium.

Sutton, the Edmonton-based pioneer of reinforcement learning and AI (more on that later), insists that these are early days, that “true” AI isn’t here yet, and we’ll all be better off if we take a deep breath.

“The public is deciding, ‘How do they feel about the existence of machines that have abilities like ours,’” says Sutton. “It’s like a first contact thing, meeting a strange new people, and you have to deal with it.”

Data-centre fights are splitting communities. Artificial intelligence is propping up (and potentially tanking) stock markets. Governments are racing for “sovereign AI” as a matter of defence and security. Canada’s first AI minister, Evan Solomon, has just announced a plan to put up to $1.6 billion in public money into Cohere, the Toronto LLM (large-language-models) AI company.

NP Posted keeps you updated on the news of the day and the perspectives that define the National Post, while drawing your focus to some of the unexpected stories we like to tell. Delivered straight to your inbox Monday to Friday, with a weekend edition on Saturdays.

Meanwhile, Geoffrey Hinton — the “Godfather of AI” — has been hosting a lecture series in Toronto where top researchers warn that governments need to slam the brakes before the machines end human self-determination. And when things go wrong, AI is the convenient scapegoat: officials insist last Friday’s nationwide U.S. ground stop had nothing to do with the Faa’s newly rolled-out AI airspace tool, but that didn’t stop the speculation.

Sutton, speaking by phone, doesn’t dismiss the worries — data centres, job losses, the fear that AI is “somehow going to kill us all.” He understands the economics: these companies are worth trillions, and a collapse would hurt. But the people claiming “we’re going to lose control, the machines will take over” are, he argues, incentivized to exaggerate.

“All that stuff about deception is just hyped,” he says. “It’s made up in the sense the people who create these sandboxes to test (AI) abilities, they make them so they can escape, and then they’ll say, ‘Oh look, we were trying to keep them under control and they get away, even from us.’ Really, the whole point of the exercise was to be able to say that… The big companies are in a strange situation. They want people to be worried their AI is so strong, so they should invest in the system, and powerful technology.”

> All that stuff about deception is just hyped

I last interviewed Sutton a few years ago, after Google closed the DeepMind lab he ran in Edmonton. In 2024 he shared the Turing Award — the Nobel of computing — for foundational work on reinforcement learning. He still teaches and mentors at the University of Alberta, serves as chief scientific adviser to the Alberta Machine Intelligence Institute (Amii), and runs Openmind Research Institute on a pro-bono basis.

In July, he launched Oak Lab with one of his protégés, Khurram Javed, to push further on reinforcement learning. Through Openmind he is also working with Tashan Technology and other Chinese robotics firms on a “robot kindergarten” in Beijing — a dedicated space where robots can learn by trial and error. “It’s always been a dream,” he says, “but robots have always been too fragile.” Now Tashan has set aside two floors of a lab for this research.

Reinforcement learning — “figuring out the learning algorithms” — rarely gets the money or attention lavished on large-language models and the data centres that feed them. That May be shifting.

Last month, while Liberals campaigned in Alberta, both Sutton and Amii received a public shout-out from the prime minister. And reinforcement learning research is starting to attract capital: David Silver, another of Sutton’s former doctoral students, launched Ineffable in the U.K. and has raised over a billion dollars in initial funding. Sutton and Javed set out to raise $10 million for Oak Lab — “small potatoes,” he says with a chuckle. “I didn’t want to have to run a billion-dollar thing or a $4-billion thing like my poor student, David Silver.”

Sutton isn’t opposed to people making money and he is not anti-LLM. But, he quips, “they’re really not AI. They’re not minds.” Figuring out the learning algorithms, in his view, is the actual route to true AI — systems that learn from their own experiences rather than frozen internet scrapes.

Large-language models, he explains, are “a great interface to the body of knowledge that we have — human knowledge — but they can’t make any new knowledge. They’re frozen.” If they produce something new, “we call it a hallucination.” They “ignore all their experience. They’re not even trying to learn from experience. They’re trying to learn from the internet.” Recursive self-improvement is the latest buzzword, he laughs, “but it means very little… you’re still going to be frozen.”

Then, he sketches a cartoon: LLMs scrape the internet and freeze the result. “People crawl all over it, they fine-tune it, and make it a little bit better, a little bit more polite… more deliberative and goal-directed.” LLMs will remain useful — a better way to search the internet — “but they won’t be what we consider AI.

“Sometime true AI will come,” he predicts, “and that will be a really big deal. But that’s not what’s happening right now.” Companies are “pretending this is happening right now — that AI is like a PhD scientist already,” when it is not. “That time will eventually come, but it’s not now. What is happening now is the public is coming face-to-face with the possibility that it will happen someday.”

Right now, the public is deciding how they feel about the possibility that machines — or machine-augmented people — will be the smartest thing around. Sutton’s bet is that treating them as first-contact rather than existential threat is the better way to avoid setting the whole enterprise back for years. The rest of us get to decide whether we agree.

stories.title: When patients attack: Canadian doctors say they don't get much help in the face of violence
stories.summary: More than 51 per cent of polled physicians have been involved in, or impacted by, a safety incident at work, according to professional association.
stories.author: Dr. Kimberly Williams
stories.content:
Dr. Maryna Mammoliti was in her first year of practice in Southwestern Ontario and pregnant when she was punched in the head by a patient so hard she suffered a concussion. A psychiatrist and former chair of the Ontario Medical Association psychiatry section, Mammoliti says the attack led her to leave the hospital where she worked and turn away from patients there that she would have cared for.

Violence from patients, she says, is “violating on several levels” — for her, it was a violation of her humanity, a violation of her belief in systemic support and a violation of her confidence that police would help. Instead, she says, they told her that she should put up with this as part of her job.

Mammoliti’s experience is far from unique. Doctors of BC , which represents more than 20,000 doctors in British Columbia, reports on its website that more than 51 per cent of polled physicians have been involved in, or impacted by, a physical or psychological safety incident at work — 72 per cent of them perpetrated by patients.

“Physicians and other health-care providers cannot deliver quality, timely care to patients when their own safety is at risk,” it says.

Dr. Maryna Mammoliti recalls being punched in the head by a patient so hard she suffered a concussion.

Like Mammoliti, many doctors also feel their workplaces do not support them sufficiently. Dr. Adam Thompson, a family physician and president of Doctors of BC, says two-thirds of polled doctors “told us they don’t feel their workplace effectively addresses situations that May threaten or harm employees, such as harassment, discrimination or violence.”

Incidents described on the Doctors of BC website show why. Anonymous physicians reported that “a patient threatened to kill me and clinic staff in response to cancelling his driver’s licence,” that “a patient pulled out a machete and threatened people,” and that the doctor saw “a triage nurse punched in the face by a patient.” Mammoliti says “nowadays people expect that violence against physicians and nurses is just part of the job.”

A psychiatrist in Ontario who fears being identified publicly says he was assaulted by a patient at work. The patient was “yelling he was going to kill me, tackled me and then strangled me.” The psychiatrist required medical attention for bruising on his neck and worried that he might “get in trouble for exercising my rights.” He says he feared that reporting the assault to police would be seen as a breach of his patient’s privacy.

He says it was strange to wonder “Am I going to get in trouble because I was attacked and almost died?” — a thought he suggests other professionals would not think about if this occurred at their workplace.

He says he doesn’t want his name used to protect his patient’s confidentiality and because he doesn’t want to be identified online as a doctor who was assaulted by a patient.

The violence can be deadly. The United States Bureau of Labor Statistics reported 23 murders of health-care workers by patients from 2011 to 2018. This has happened in Canada too. For example, Dr. Walter Reynolds was attacked with a machete and hammer by a former patient and later died in hospital in Red Deer, Alta., in 2020.

Doctors who spoke to the Star say they’re frustrated by a system preventing them from delivering the care patients need.

Doctors understand some of what drives these incidents. Thompson says “doctors and other health-care workers regularly care for people in very difficult circumstances. Patients and families May be experiencing pain, fear, frustration or crisis, and pressures (in the health system) such as long wait times, overcrowding, staffing shortages and insufficient mental-health and addictions resources can add to those tensions. Those pressures help us understand the environment in which incidents can occur.”

However, he says, understanding does “not make abusive or violent behaviour acceptable.”

Frustration can also come from a gap between what patients expect and what physicians can deliver. Doctors cite patients struggling with housing and finances, and doctors cannot fix these problems, says Mammoliti.

“We can’t provide for systemic issues,” she says. Patients May not realize that “it is not because we are choosing not to or we don’t care,” but because it is outside of the scope of what a physician can do.

“The doctor is the face in front of you, and they are bearing the brunt of frustrations,” she says.

The consequences affect patients directly. In addition to leaving the hospital where she was attacked, Mammoliti reduced the size of her practice for a while after she was assaulted. Doctors of BC says the pattern is widespread: “We have heard from doctors that unsafe working conditions have caused them and their colleagues to change how and where they practice, including leaving the hospital or community.

“In a health-care system already facing workforce and access pressures, losing doctors or having them reduce or change their practices can significantly impact local health-care capacity.”

And the problem is growing. Mammoliti says “physicians and nurses face completely different work environments than they did … five years ago.” The Workers’ Compensation Board of Alberta reported that health-care workers filed 1,108 workplace violence claims in 2025, the largest number in the past 10 years, according to the CBC.

Physical protections in hospitals and clinics vary from place to place in Canada. Most hospitals have contract or in-house security guards, and call police when required. Some provinces, like Alberta, have community peace officers who have more legislated power than security guards. Hospitals often have duress alarms, electronic access control systems for doorways and video surveillance. Some in Saskatchewan have reportedly added metal detectors.

Still, there can only be so many guards, and doctors must be alone with patients sometimes.

Nor is this only a North American problem. In a study on workplace violence published in Eclinicalmedicine, an open access clinical journal published by The Lancet, researcher Connor O’Brien of the University of Queensland reported that workplace violence against health-care workers is a growing global problem, with incidents rising in both severity and number.

Several countries have responded with tougher laws. In 2020, Sweden introduced stricter penalties to deter harassment and physical aggression toward health-care workers, and Italy enacted a law that same year making violence against health-care professionals an aggravated offence warranting sentences of up to five years in prison. In Canada, Bill C-3, which came into effect on Jan. 16, 2022, criminalizes intimidation threats and violent conduct directed at health-care workers, with convictions punishable by up to 10 years in prison.

Even so, safety concerns remain, and some doctors say no single change will resolve them. “We need both stronger protections when incidents occur and action on the underlying pressures that can contribute to unsafe environments,” says Thompson. Doctors of BC is calling for increased hospital security, better real-time incident reporting, stronger responses when incidents occur and additional preventive measures.

Mammoliti says doctors also need to be “working with police and law enforcement to educate them that this is a serious issue” and “working with the government to change the laws.”

Despite everything, she says, “I care about my patients, I like what I do, despite what happened.” She just wants to feel safe at work, just like everyone else.

Dr. Kimberly Williams is a journalism fellow at the Dalla Lana School of Public Health and a neuropsychiatrist at the University of Calgary’s Cumming School of Medicine with an interest in physician wellness.

stories.title: 'Such hard work:' professor and Métis builder team up on 13-foot birch-bark canoe
stories.summary: Winnipeg - A canoe crafted out of birch, oak and cedar bark May be Brian Rice's swansong.
stories.author: Brittany Hobson The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Winnipeg - A canoe crafted out of birch, oak and cedar bark May be Brian Rice’s swansong.

The Mohawk professor’s academic career has spanned nearly 35 years in classrooms across the globe, eventually planting him in the faculty of kinesiology and recreation management at the University of Manitoba.

With retirement on his mind, Rice knew he wanted to leave something behind for Manitoba’s largest university, where he teaches land-based learning.

Two Indigenous men teamed up to construct a 13-foot Eastern Woodland-style handcrafted birch-bark canoe that is now on display at the University of Manitoba. The arduous process took about 350 hours to complete over a four-and-a-half month period from research to construction. (Nov. 22, 2026)

So he turned to his ancestors. The result: a 13-foot Eastern Woodland-style handcrafted birch-bark canoe.

“You do something for many years and we often walk away ... sometimes we’re forgotten or we forget where we were. I didn’t want that to happen this time,” Rice said at an event unveiling the finished product in early November.

“I wanted that memory to (always) be there.”

Birch-bark canoes were the primary mode of transportation for First Nations in eastern and central Canada, especially during the fur-trade era.

It is considered a cultural mainstay in Canada.

Rice enlisted Métis historian and craftsman Denis Gendron to complete the project, which brought Indigenous land-based learning, traditional knowledge and hands-on craftsmanship together.

The arduous process took about 350 hours to complete over a four-and-a-half month period from research to construction.

2 min readtruct the vessel.

Under the warmth of the summer sun, the two men, with the help of volunteers, used shovels, gardening tools and their gloved hands to coax stubborn spruce roots from forest beds that would later be used to secure portions of the canoe.

“It took two weeks for my hands to recover,” said Gendron.

That same summer, heat took longer to pierce through the winter frost that coated trees until June. Once the men were able to cut through the bark, they sliced a strip down the side of each trunk and then peeled the bark off in sheets.

They were careful to only take what they needed, never more. Whenever they took something from the forest, they laid down tobacco and offered a prayer, a customary practice for some Indigenous nations when harvesting from the land.

For Gendron, there was a steep learning curve going from his experience building furniture to constructing a fully functional canoe.

“You have to travel into the woods. Not only that, you have to know where to look, and what to look for. Birch bark is a cantankerous material to work with, but it’s extremely strong. It’s got a lot of resilience to it,” said Gendron.

“It took a lot and it was a hot summer. So it brought a lot of determination. I lost about 25 pounds. It was great exercise.”

The challenges didn’t end there.

When it came to building the canoe, timing was everything.

Cedar ribs, strips of wood used to form the skeletal shape of the vessel, were shaped by pouring boiling water over them to make them flexible.

“It’s so exhaustive. It’s such hard work and it’s litres and litres of hot water. I had dreams about water,” said Gendron.

Throughout the build, Gendron would put the canoe in the water to take care of kinks and leaks, eventually taking it for a spin but not going very far because in his own words, he’s no “expert canoeist.”

The finished craft now greets students, staff and visitors as they enter the university’s active living centre.

Gendron already has plans to build a bigger canoe that can be used in the classroom and on the land.

While newer materials have changed the way canoes are made, Indigenous craftsmen and women continue to carry on the traditional artform. And, in the case of Rice and Gendron, bringing two people from different nations together with the common goal of exploring a shared history.

“We’re tied to this now, probably for the rest of our lives,” said Rice.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 22, 2026.

stories.title: 'Happy, exercise, help others': The secrets behind Raymond Cho's 90 years on Earth
stories.summary: Toronto - On a recent Friday in the far eastern reaches of Toronto, Raymond Cho deftly serves a table tennis ball against a new rival, a reporter about half his age from The Canadian Press.
stories.author: Liam Casey The Canadian Press
stories.content:
TORONTO - On a recent Friday in the far eastern reaches of Toronto, Raymond Cho deftly serves a table tennis ball against a new rival, a reporter about half his age from The Canadian Press.

The ball crosses the net in the basement of a community centre and takes a 90-degree turn, spinning furiously. The reporter, surprised at the ball movement, stretches far to the side of the table and makes a miraculous return before an unrepentant Cho smashes the ball to the opposite corner to win the point. The reporter tweaks a hamstring in the process.

Cho, Ontario’s minister for seniors and accessibility, turned 90 earlier this week. With each passing day he sets a new record as the oldest Ontario provincial politician in history. He intends to keep breaking records. Will he run in the 2030 Ontario election?

“Definitely,” Cho says without skipping a beat. “As long as I can make contributions, I keep running.”

On a recent Friday at the Chinese Cultural Centre of Greater Toronto in Scarborough, an institution he helped build and expand over the last several decades, Cho reveals the secrets of his 90 years on Earth.

They often come in threes, but one dominates all others: his mother.

“The most important person in my life is my mother,” Cho says.

Boon Young Kah raised Cho and his seven siblings in Korea with little help. His father, whom he says he has “no respect for,” left to start a new family when Cho was young.

She was born in rural Korea to farmers in 1900 and was not allowed to attend school.

“She didn’t have any contact with learned people, but she was full of wisdom,” Cho says.

She taught him three lessons he holds to this day.

The first: “Greet people warmly and respectfully.”

Later in life when he was studying counselling in a doctoral program at the University of Toronto, he learned that’s the first step to establishing a personal relationship with a patient.

“The second thing she advised me, when somebody come and ask your help, please help them,” he says.

She instructed her boy to thank everyone who helps, even in small ways.

The third: “Don’t argue over small things,” he recalls. “If you keep arguing over small things, you become small yourself.”

He also learned lessons from his childhood nemesis, Johnny. In Grade 1, Cho says Johnny was relentless: Poking him, throwing water on him, and making fun of him. One day, Cho had enough.

“Johnny, you bug me so much, let’s have a fight,” he recalls telling his bully.

Students gathered to watch. Cho let loose a flurry of punches to Johnny’s face.

“I’m not a strong boy, but I really mustered all the power to keep punching him in the face,” Cho says, adding Johnny never bothered him again.

“When you’re strong, people respect you.”

In Grade 7, he caught tuberculosis, often a death sentence in those days. He focused on eating better as he tried to recover. He spent a lot of time at the beach in Incheon, swimming and walking and digging out oysters at low tide.

“After one year, I overcame tuberculosis,” he says.

Cho saw firsthand the ravages of the Korean War. He can still picture North Korean tanks and soldiers rolling into Incheon as a teenager in the 1950s.

“I dug trenches with North Korean soldiers, communist soldiers, and only then did they give a ticket to get rice from the ration station,” Cho says.

He was there for the Battle of Incheon, where Allied forces bombed the city. He can still see the American B-29 Superfortress bombers as they pummeled North Korean forces in and around the coastal city he grew up in.

“Every time I hear the sound of the airplane, I follow the airplane to see how the bomb exploded,” he says. “I was really stupid — good thing I didn’t get killed.”

He’d later survive several other near misses.

By the end of high school, Cho hoped to attend Seoul National University — “like Harvard in the USA,” he says — but he failed the entrance exam.

That brought him great shame.

“I said to myself, I’m going to make my mother the happiest person,” he says. “How I can make her happy? Only if I become successful.”

A year later, he got into Hankuk University of Foreign Studies in Seoul. He set a strict studying schedule where he slept from 10 p.m. to midnight, woke up and studied until 5 a.m., slept for a few more hours then went to class for the day.

After graduating, he got a job at the American embassy in Seoul, which was like “catching a star in the sky.”

One day in the 1960s, he got a call from his stepbrother, who was just discharged from the Republic of Korea Navy, who wanted to go to Canada. Cho helped arrange an interview for him with a Canadian immigrant officer and stepped in to be his brother’s interpreter.

They both filled out applications. Cho got in, his stepbrother didn’t.

“If I didn’t come to Canada, I could never become a minister in Korea and probably by now I’m a dead man because those days, Korea, they just drink too much and if I get a job then I have to drink a lot for the company to make business,” he says.

His younger and older brothers died of liver cancer related to their drinking, he says. Consequently, Cho does not drink alcohol.

In 1967, at 30 years old, Cho left for Vancouver.

On the plane trip over, somewhere in the middle of the Pacific Ocean, Cho envisioned his future. He had big dreams for a big life with a big job in Canada.

“I’m going to be a big hunter,” he thought. “I will catch polar bears, grizzly bears, moose, and big animals and I will become a millionaire and then go back to Korea.”

He worked as a dishwasher at his first job in Canada. He worked at an asbestos mine, as a waiter and a janitor, all while attempting to complete an MBA at the University of British Columbia.

He also bought a Bible, the New Testament, and began reading it as a way to learn English. That sparked his love of Jesus Christ.

“That was a major turning point in my life,” he says. He soon became Christian.

It would help him when the dark moments came.

It was in his early days in Canada, while he was cleaning dishes at a restaurant, that he decided to marry the love of his life, SoonOk, who was a teaching assistant at the Ewha Womans University in Seoul.

“I proposed to her to marry me as a dishwasher and she folded her dream to be president of the university and she came over to Canada to marry me,” he says.

Cho struggled at UBC, largely because of the frenetic pace he kept between work and class.

“I was scared,” he said. “And I said, ‘I don’t think I could finish.’”

He thought about a trip around the world before returning to Korea. But friends he met in Vancouver who moved to Toronto encouraged him to come east where they said he’d find better work.

So he ditched school and boarded a train. Three days later he arrived in Toronto.

“I started out way at the bottom of life,” Cho says.

He found work as a janitor at the Toronto General Hospital, but he couldn’t get thoughts of going to university out of his mind. So he got another job to save money as a worm picker.

He lived through discrimination when he came to Canada, first in Vancouver and then again in Toronto.

But he soon grew to make his way in Toronto, becoming tight with the Korean Christian community.

He also went back to school and completed a masters of social work and education and then went on to complete his doctorate in counselling psychology at the University of Toronto.

That would lead to a career as a social worker with several organizations, including the Toronto Board of Education and the Catholic Children’s Aid Society.

By the 1980s, Cho morphed into a community activist for Korean human rights.

Back then, Japan had a law that required Koreans 14 years or older who lived there to be fingerprinted.

Koreans around the world rose up — along with some non-Koreans. Cho took up the cause and organized rallies against the Consulate General of Japan, taking up the mantle as a community leader.

Then he found his way to Japan alongside Rev. Jesse Jackson, the famous African-American civil rights activist, who joined the fight in Japan. It came with risks as violent riots broke out. Despite having three young boys at home, he forged ahead to Japan.

The pair were vocal in their critiques of the Japanese government, especially after Koreans were being arrested for refusing to be fingerprinted.

“This is nonsense,” he recalls Jackson saying over lunch, “we cannot let it happen.”

Cho was impressed with Jackson.

“He’s not even Korean, but he was fighting for Koreans, he was fighting for human rights and principles,” Cho says.

Cho worked for years as a social worker, but the federal NDP came calling in the late 1980s.

He wasn’t interested initially, but eventually gave in to run for Ed Broadbent’s party in 1988.

But he worked hard during the campaign and began to make a name for himself. The NDP pushed him to run for Metropolitan Toronto Council.

“I said I will run, but I’m not going to run as NDP, NDP is least popular, I will run my own campaign,” Cho says.

He ran and won as an independent in 1991, but soon became a member of the federal Liberal party.

His reign as a Scarborough councillor lasted until 2016, though there were a few attempts at federal and provincial politics in between.

He had long championed immigrants and was stepping up his activism to help the Korean community, which had dominated convenience stores, particularly in Toronto. They were suffering after American giants like Walmart, Costco and Amazon came to Canada.

The Korean Business Association said one way to survive is to allow convenience stores to sell booze. Former Progressive Conservative leader Tim Hudak told Cho he would do just that if they formed government.

So Cho told Hudak to appoint him — Cho says he did not want to waste time and money to go through a nomination process. So he was on the ballot, now as a Progressive Conservative.

“Then Tim Hudak made a terrible mistake, like political suicide,” Cho says.

Hudak announced late in the 2014 provincial campaign he’d lay off 100,000 civil servants. Throngs of locals who were set to support Cho pivoted.

Cho lost. As did the Conservatives.

After Patrick Brown took over as leader, he sought out Cho to run again. A byelection was coming up in 2016 and Brown believed Cho could win the Liberal stronghold of Scarborough North.

Brown was relentless, but Cho was unsure of another run. He was 80 years old, but still full of energy.

Cho had also become friends with Rob and Doug Ford during his time on Toronto’s city council. The current premier managed Cho’s campaign in the 2016 byelection and he won.

When Ford became leader of the Conservatives, he pledged, like Hudak, to bring booze to convenience stores, a promise he would fulfil in 2024.

After Ford won the 2018 election, he made Cho the minister for seniors and accessibility.

But before that, Cho had a scare. Shortly after winning, Cho was out driving to churches to thank them for their help and support during his campaign.

His voice became slow, his speech unclear. His assistant called his wife, who rushed over and then called an ambulance once she saw him. Paramedics rushed him to Sunnybrook hospital.

Ford rushed over, the first visitor. He leaned in, hugged him and said, “Raymond, don’t worry, you’ll be fine.”

“I’ll never forget,” Cho says, “and I was fine.”

The stroke did leave him with hearing and balance troubles, though that has not slowed him down.

At Cho’s birthday bash last week with 650 friends, Ford praised his minister.

“You’ll have that job forever,” Ford said. “And you’ll outlive everyone in this room anyways. We’ll be here celebrating your 100th birthday.”

Ford and Cho are close friends, Cho being in many ways the party’s conscience.

“I love you more than anything in the world and I appreciate you,” Ford said.

Cho says he also nearly died last year on a family vacation in the Dominican Republic. He waded into the ocean, but soon found himself sucked out to deeper water, where he was flailing. He managed to get out, but was disoriented after choking down a bunch of water.

He spent three days in a Dominican intensive care unit, his three sons — “two doctors and a teacher!” — by his side.

“Somebody up there really loves me,” he says.

‘EVERYBODY LOVES RAYMOND’

He also has lots of love inside cabinet.

Finance Minister Peter Bethlenfalvy has long called Cho his “best friend forever.” He connects with Cho because he is the son of two Hungarian immigrants who fought for a better life in Canada.

“You come with nothing but the shirt on your back, like my parents, and you can build a career and you can give back, you can succeed,” he says. “And he’s just a perfect example of that.”

The reason the two are BFFs, Bethlenfalvy explains, comes from a cabinet meeting. The finance minister put forward an idea to cabinet — he won’t say what in order not to betray cabinet confidence — and the idea fell flat.

No one liked it, he says, except Cho. Bethlenfalvy appreciated the backing and told him they were now BFFs.

“I did see him a few other times going out and saying to another one, ‘you’re my favourite cabinet minister,’” Bethlenfalvy says with a big laugh.

“I’m sitting right here, Raymond! I thought I was your favourite cabinet minister. He is so charming, he is smart, and he’s got so much wisdom.”

Energy and Mines Minister Stephen Lecce says Cho is an elder statesmen who provides sage advice to younger colleagues. Lecce turned to him a decade ago when he was weighing whether to run for public office.

Cho’s advice: just do it.

“His story, for me, is inspiring,” Lecce says. “Like many immigrants to Canada, he left persecution, he survived the Korean War, understands the consequences of authoritarianism and communism and came here to make our country and our democracy better and stronger.”

“Quite literally, everybody loves Raymond,” says Economic Development Minister Vic Fedeli. It’s an oft-running line within the caucus and an ode to an old sitcom. He helped him knock on doors back in 2016.

“He would run from door to door and I’m thinking, holy crackers, I’ve knocked on doors for 20 years … You chat a little bit and you walk along with the staff and the volunteers.”

Not Cho, he said. “He ran.”

Fedeli had a hard time keeping up.

But the love isn’t universal.

He has critics among seniors and disability advocates who say he has not done nearly enough, especially on accessibility issues.

Cho says progress has been slow in some areas, but he says he will keep working to improve life for “those who built this country.”

He also apologized during the 2018 campaign after getting into a physical altercation with a Grade 7 student who ripped up campaign literature while Cho handed out pamphlets at a school. He said he “lightly touched” the student’s head after telling him to pick up the litter.

He says his Chinese doctor has told him he’ll live to be 105 years old. He told Cho his reasoning, in three parts.

First, he is happy. Cho agreed.

Second, he is fit and active. Cho agreed.

“I love golf and have had two holes in one!” he says with a smile.

“Happy, exercise, help others,” he says. “That’s the secret of my long, strong, happy life.”

Every day he wakes up, Raymond Cho thanks the Lord for three things: “My mother, Canada, and my beautiful wife.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 22, 2026.

Note to readers: This is a corrected story. A previous version stated Raymond Cho served as city councillor for Scarborough until 2014. In fact, he served until 2016.

He also apologized during the 2018 campaign after getting into a physical altercation with a Grade 7 student who ripped up campaign literature while Cho handed out pamphlets at a school. He said he “lightly touched” the student’s head after telling him to pick up the litter.
He says his Chinese doctor has told him he’ll live to be 105 years old. He told Cho his reasoning, in three parts.
First, he is happy. Cho agreed.
Second, he is fit and active. Cho agreed.
“I love golf and have had two holes in one!” he says with a smile.
“Happy, exercise, help others,” he says. “That’s the secret of my long, strong, happy life.”
Every day he wakes up, Raymond Cho thanks the Lord for three things: “My mother, Canada, and my beautiful wife.”

stories.title: All signs show Canada can’t meet its Paris target — here’s why Ottawa won’t admit it
stories.summary: Ottawa - In June, Prime Minister Mark Carney told Canadians that the country's emissions would be higher “in the next few years” than previously projected. Those projections already said Canada would miss its 2030 emissions target under the Paris climate accord.
stories.author: Nick Murray The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - In June, Prime Minister Mark Carney told Canadians that the country’s emissions would be higher “in the next few years” than previously projected. Those projections already said Canada would miss its 2030 emissions target under the Paris climate accord.

The government’s own projections — published in its emissions reductions progress report a year ago — showed a best-case scenario of a 28 per cent reduction in emissions from 2005 levels in 2030.

And that was before the Carney government introduced a suite of climate policy rollbacks over the past year, including a delay to the introduction of more stringent tailpipe emissions. That measure was supposed to take the place of the now-scrapped electric vehicle sales mandate; it won’t come into effect now until at least 2029.

Canada’s commitment under the Paris agreement was to cut emissions by between 40 to 45 per cent of 2005 levels. The government of Stephen Harper set a target of 30 per cent.

This week, Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin insisted Canada is committed to its Paris commitments. That claim earned her some public criticism from two of her predecessors while she attended the United Nations climate conference in Turkey last week.

Dabrusin wouldn’t answer when asked whether that commitment includes the 2030 target. In its public statements, the government has leaned on the target of achieving net-zero by 2050.

All the studies suggest Canada won’t meet its target. The government’s own projections say it will miss it. The prime minister himself acknowledged emissions are on the rise. So why hasn’t the federal government said it is no longer committed to the 2030 target?

“I think they’re afraid to come out and say it because it’s putting in people’s faces that they’re making a choice to make wildfires worse, to make flooding worse, to actually leave a worse world for our children,” said Keith Stewart, senior energy strategist with Greenpeace Canada.

“Julie Dabrusin seems like a very nice person. But she’s going to go down in history as the worst environment minister in Canada’s history because it’s been on her watch that Canada has rolled back environment and climate policies in a way that not even Stephen Harper attempted.”

Asked whether Dabrusin has been put in the job to defend Carney’s policy choices, Stewart said nobody is under the impression that she is “calling the shots.”

“This is clearly coming from the prime minister. But she’s at that cabinet table and she’s standing behind those decisions. And as someone who has said she’s committed to action on climate change, her other option is to resign in protest to make it clear that this is unacceptable,” Stewart said.

“If being at a cabinet table is more important to you than having the right decisions come out of the cabinet table, that’s a choice a politician can make.”

In a statement, Dabrusin’s office said Canada is “committed to its Paris agreement of achieving net-zero by 2050.” The statement did not address a direct question of whether Canada is still committed to its 2030 target.

“We cannot achieve our climate goals when we are divided,” wrote Amy Falkner, Dabrusin’s press secretary.

“Our focus is on results that unite Canadians: building major clean energy projects across the country, driving mass electrification, making significant investments in the low-carbon economy, and working in co-operation with provinces, territories and Indigenous Peoples.”

Falkner added that Canada is still committed to reporting its progress under the Net-Zero Accountability Act as required in December 2027, and will report on its 2030 target next month to the United Nations Climate Change Secretariat — as required under the Paris Agreement.

But whether the Net-Zero Accountability Act even has any teeth was the subject of debate on Parliament Hill this week. The act doesn’t set out any fines or penalties for Canada missing or abandoning its climate targets.

At Thursday’s meeting of the House of Commons environment committee, B.C. Conservative MP Ellis Ross grilled Canada’s interim environment commissioner on what purpose the act even serves.

“It seems like everybody agrees, except government, that they’re not going to meet their targets. So when the government is clearly falling short of emissions targets, and in actuality intends to expand its emissions, what exactly does the Net-Zero Accountability Act do?” Ellis asked.

“We’ve been talking about (emissions) for the better part of 20 years. But in terms of the 2030 commitments and 2050 commitments, we’re not going to meet it. So does the Net-Zero Accountability Act mean anything today?”

Elsa Da Costa, the interim environment commissioner, replied that the act was an “important tool” for her office to hold the government to account.

The Angus Reid Institute released an online poll of 1,770 Canadians in July which suggested climate was the top issue for 21 per cent of respondents.

The poll also suggested the Liberals’ track record on climate might be driving one in six Liberal voters to the NDP. The poll found climate was the top concern for half of NDP supporters.

The Canadian Research Insights Council, an industry organization that promotes polling standards, says online surveys cannot be assigned a margin of error because they do not randomly sample the population

Aside from the political repercussions of publicly abandoning its commitment to the 2030 emission targets, Stewart said there are also legal implications.

The federal government is fighting a lawsuit brought by a group of climate advocates over Canada’s trajectory on emission commitments. The lawsuit is asking the Federal Court to order Ottawa to bring its 2030 emissions reductions plan into compliance with the Net-Zero Accountability Act.

“The courts can order the government to do something,” said Julia Levin, the associate director of national climate with Environmental Defence, one of the organizations behind the lawsuit.

“There is a clear consequence to that. But it is mostly political.”

Levin said climate change has become a point of political vulnerability for the Liberals.

“The prime minister knows this, and that’s why he’s done everything to dismantle the 2030 target. But I think it’s the reason that they won’t actually admit that they’ve abandoned this target,” Levin said.

“Internationally, this is a prime minister who cares deeply about his international reputation. And it’s hard to claim middle-power status and moral authority when you’ve abandoned a target that your peers are way more committed to.”

An analysis last year by the think tank 440 Megatonnes found Canada was the worst performer among G7 countries at reducing emissions compared to 2005 levels. All other G7 countries had an average reduction of 32 per cent by 2023, while Canada had only achieved 8.5 per cent.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 21, 2026.

stories.title: Can a drone really replace a million-dollar farm sprayer in Canada?
stories.summary: Potato farmers, blueberry growers and researchers gathered at a meeting this week to learn whether drones could make their work easier, as Ottawa expands their use for crop spraying.
stories.author: Maria Sarrouh
stories.content:
ST. Peters BAY, P.E.I. – Potato farmers, blueberry growers and researchers gathered at a meeting this week to learn whether drones could make their work easier, as Ottawa expands their use for crop spraying.

Under a new federal policy introduced this summer, pesticides already approved for spraying by planes and helicopters can now be applied by drones, too. Previously, those products needed specific authorization for drone use, a barrier because relatively few had received approval.

In P.E.I., where conventional aerial pesticide spraying remains prohibited, eligible drones offer another way to treat crops from above.

“Anywhere we can kind of save money and increase yield, we’ll usually take a risk on something like that as farmers,” said Chad Mooney, a potato farmer and the founder of AgronomAI, a company specializing in agricultural drone technology.

The equipment could be helpful when fields are too wet for heavy machinery. Drones can also spray tall or delicate crops without risking damage from wheels and reach harder-to-access areas or rough terrain.

Perhaps the biggest benefit is the ability to target specific parts of a field rather than spraying the whole thing.

“That’s cost savings to the producer. And it’s less pesticide use, which is good for the environment,” said Ryan Barrett, research and agronomy specialist with the P.E.I. Potato Board.

In late July, Barrett and other researchers ran a trial comparing a conventional ground sprayer with a drone applying insecticide against Colorado potato beetles in a field in Huntley, P.E.I.

Both treatments proved effective. Six days later, beetle populations had dropped by 100 per cent in the area treated by the ground sprayer and 96 per cent where the drone was used. Neither area needed another insecticide application for the rest of the growing season.

The findings suggest farmers could significantly reduce pesticide use and costs by treating isolated problem areas. Colorado potato beetles tend to start at the edges of fields before moving inward, so farmers could first spray the circumference.

For example, researchers calculated that if a 500-acre potato farm needed to treat just 75 acres, it could save $12,750 in insecticide costs, assuming a product cost of $30 per acre. That doesn’t include potential savings on labour and fuel.

Manitoba researchers are developing AI-powered farm machinery that could transform agriculture and expand the technology far beyond the field. Alex Karpa report

But the technology comes with its own costs and limitations.

A drone can cost between $20,000 and $50,000, according to Mooney, with another $20,000 to $40,000 needed for supporting equipment. That brings the total investment to less than$100,000.

While that might sound steep, it’s far less expensive than a new wheeled sprayer, with a price tag of around $1 million.

“When it comes to cost-benefit analysis and ROI, it’s there if the tool can start to replace this,” Mooney said.

Barrett says drones could also make more sense for farmers who don’t need to spray very often. A corn grower, for example, might only need to spray once or twice a year, making it difficult to justify buying an expensive conventional sprayer.

But a ground sprayer could be more efficient on a very large field that needs to be treated in full. There are regulatory hurdles, too. Some products, including certain herbicides, have yet to be approved for drone use.

Mooney sees another reason to embrace drones: getting younger generations interested in agriculture.

“The drones, an exciting thing for young people that want to farm and learn,” he said.

stories.title: Jacobs' foursome advances to final at Gsoc National in Sydney
stories.summary: Sydney - Brad Jacobs and his Calgary squad scored a deuce in the sixth end and stole two more in the seventh en route to a 7-3 victory over Oskar Eriksson of Sweden in the men's semifinals of the Grand Slam of Curling National event on Saturday night.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Sydney - Brad Jacobs and his Calgary squad scored a deuce in the sixth end and stole two more in the seventh en route to a 7-3 victory over Oskar Eriksson of Sweden in the men’s semifinals of the Grand Slam of Curling National event on Saturday night.

Jacobs, with third Marc Kennedy, second Brett Gallant and lead Ben Hebert, punched their ticket to Sunday’s final against Yannick Schwaller of Switzerland, who beat Matt Dunstone’s Winnipeg-based team 6-2 in the other men’s semifinal on Saturday.

stories.title: Nova Scotia Liberals elect Becky Druhan to lead party
stories.summary: Former Tory minister is the first woman to lead the party
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A former provincial Progressive Conservative cabinet minister has been elected as leader of Nova Scotia’s opposition Liberals, becoming the first woman to lead the party.

Becky Druhan won the leadership Saturday at a convention in Halifax, defeating lone rival Amanda Mombourquette.

Druhan is the party’s first permanent leader since the Liberals were steamrolled in the 2024 provincial election, dropping from 14 seats to just two and losing their role as official Opposition to the New Democratic Party, led by Claudia Chender.

The Liberals gained a third seat in the legislature in May after Druhan, the Independent member for Lunenburg West, announced she would join the Liberals and contest the party’s leadership.

Druhan, a lawyer, was first elected to the legislature in 2021 when Tim Houston led the Progressive Conservatives to a surprise majority win. She served as the education minister and later as justice minister during Houston’s second term in office.

Last fall, she was dumped from cabinet and, less than a week later, left the Conservatives to sit as an Independent. At the time, she cited differences with the government’s leadership. Druhan has taken aim at the Houston government’s budget cuts, as well as its push for more natural resource extraction, and what she has described as its lack of transparency.

When she joined the Liberals this spring, she said her values have always been aligned with the Liberal team.

During the leadership race, Druhan said that if the Liberals are elected to govern, she would lead an open and fair government focused on strengthening communities and promoting sustainable growth.

For now, the priority for the party should be rebuilding public trust, she said.

As for Mombourquette, the municipal councillor from Cape Breton ran on a platform that called for implementing recommendations from a 2022 report that concluded the party was in need of an overhaul.

The Liberals relinquished their hold on government in 2021, when the party dropped 10 seats to 17, losing to Houston’s Progressive Conservatives. Former Liberal premier Stephen McNeil had led the Liberals to back-to-back majority governments before stepping down in 2021.

stories.title: Western Mustangs blow out St. Mary’s to advance to Vanier Cup
stories.summary: The Western Mustangs scored three first quarter touchdowns and added two more in the second quarter en route to a 64-14 over the St. Mary’s Huskies in the Mitchell Bowl at Alumni Stadium in London, Ont.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
This time it was Goliath who defeated David.

The Western Mustangs scored three first quarter touchdowns and added two more in the second quarter en route to a 64-14 over the St. Mary’s Huskies in the Mitchell Bowl at Alumni Stadium in London, Ont.

The Mustangs are off to their first Vanier Cup game since winning the National Championship in 2021. They will face the Uteck Bowl champion in Quebec City on Saturday Nov. 28.

“It hasn’t really sunk in yet,” said Faulds of going to the Vanier Cup in his first year as Mustangs head coach.

“In that opening training camp meeting, you talk about wanting to play Saturday, November 28th and we get to do that. It’s easier said than done. There’s a lot of hard work. It’s going to be our 13th straight football game, so it just couldn’t be more proud of our coaches and our players.”

The undefeated Huskies looked like they could open the scoring after an impressive opening drive. However, Western linebacker Eliot Blake picked off a Justin Shibley pass deep in Mustangs territory which thwarted the scoring drive.

First-year linebacker Nathan Summers was named the defensive player of the game after racking up nine total tackles and an interception.

“That really changed the momentum,” said Summers when asked about Blake’s interception.

“We came out, the kickoff wasn’t great and they got a few big runs. We stood strong and made a play and then the rest of the game it started rolling from there.”

Faulds agreed that interception changed the game.

“That kind of woke us up a little bit and then we went down and scored and took care of business after that,” said Faulds.

Quarterback Ben Casselman went 15-19 through the air for 173 yards and four touchdowns. The offensive game “

The Mustangs running backs went wild on the ground, rushing for 407 total yards.

Ethan Dolby ran for 116 yards and a touchdown on 11 carries on the ground in front of a home crowd of around 4,000.

Jack Kelly had 78 yards and two scores which included a 59-yard run for a score to start the third quarter, while Geoff Clubine had 120 and a score to lead the Mustangs in rushing with the game in doubt. Jevaughn Roberts broke free on a 42-yard TD run in the final quarter to give all four backs a score.

“Our O-line basically had to play the whole game when unfortunately we had fresh backs and fresh wide receivers,” said Dolby.

“We all got in the end zone which is you know a good thing for the running backs.”

Western moved the ball all day, scoring nine touchdowns with Nik Shewchuk catching two receiving scores. Jackson Taylor and Dasani McIntosh hauled in the others.

“We made a decision that, you know, we’re not losing another game,” he said.

Prior to this season, Faulds left Wilfrid Laurier University to return to his alma mater.

“I haven’t got one (Vanier Cup title). Numerous coaches, numerous players have gotten them. Our program is rich with eight Vanier Cup championships, but it’s something I haven’t ever had. I’ve got to taste it as a player. I got to taste it as a coach a few years ago at Laurier but have never finished the journey, so our guys will be pretty pumped up to have a great week of practice.”

I’ve got to taste it as a player. I got to taste it as a coach a few years ago at Laurier but have never finished the journey, so our guys will be pretty pumped up to have a great week of practice.”

stories.title: Ontario Liberals choose Navdeep Bains as new leader
stories.summary: Former federal cabinet minister fends off a stiff challenge from Lee Fairclough as party looks to rebuild after three consecutive election losses
stories.author: Laura Stone
stories.content:
Former Trudeau-era federal cabinet minister Navdeep Bains has been chosen as the new Ontario Liberal leader, narrowly defeating Toronto MPP Lee Fairclough in the contest.

Mr. Bains won on the third ballot with 50.3 per cent support, compared with Ms. Fairclough who had 49.7 per cent.

“This May be the end of a leadership race, ladies and gentleman, but this is just the beginning of our campaign to replace Doug Ford and the Conservative Party of Ontario,” Mr. Bains said Saturday after the results were announced to a room of about 1,000 Liberals at the Metro Toronto Convention Centre in downtown Toronto.

The party is hoping to rebuild after three consecutive election losses with the goal of presenting a serious alternative to Mr. Ford’s Progressive Conservatives in the next election.

It is the third time since 2020 that party members have chosen a leader without a seat in the Ontario legislature. Mr. Bains told reporters after the results that he’ll be seeking a seat, but offered no details about where or when. He said he wouldn’t ask one of the current 14 MPPs to resign so he can run.

A former industry minister in Justin Trudeau’s government, Mr. Bains faced a stiff challenge from Ms. Fairclough, a first-term MPP who represents Etobicoke-Lakeshore in west-end Toronto.

Mr. Bains, who was elected five times federally in the Greater Toronto areas of Mississauga and Brampton, left his high-profile position as chief corporate affairs officer at Rogers Communications earlier this spring to return to politics. Ms. Fairclough is a former hospital executive and national women’s rugby player. She first ran provincially in 2022 and was narrowly defeated, but was elected in the 2025 election.

The other contenders were Stephanie Bowman, a former finance executive and two-term MPP from Toronto, and Dylan Marando, a former senior adviser in federal and provincial Liberal governments.

Ms. Bowman finished third, followed by Mr. Marando.

In his victory speech, Mr. Bains said people in the province have fallen behind economically and face challenges such as the inability to find a family doctor.

“The reason why that is, is because Doug Ford and the Conservatives have abandoned the fight. They are not in it for the people; they are in it for their buddies. And so this is why the Liberal Party matters, because are the party with the incredible legacy,” he said.

He cited the previous ruling party’s achievements throughout the years, including the creation of the Greenbelt, an environmentally protected area around the Greater Toronto Area. The RCMP has for three years been investigating the Ford government’s decision to open up the more than 800,000-hectare region to development, a move since reversed. Mr. Ford has consistently denied wrongdoing.

“We are the party of full-day kindergarten. We are the party that created and protected the Greenbelt,” Mr. Bains said. “We are the party that reduced class sizes.”

He also took aim at the ongoing controversy around the Ontario Student Assistance Program, which the government scaled back this year. Mr. Ford’s party is now facing questions about alleged abuse of Osap by private career colleges.

“We’re going to reverse Osap, Asap,” Mr. Bains said.

Mr. Bains is the first racialized person to lead any major party in the province. Asked about this on Saturday, he said it’s important that people across the province feel they belong. “Doesn’t matter where you live, where you come from, you want to make sure you have a chance to succeed, and that’s what my campaign’s been about,” he said, adding that he’s met a few “mean-spirited people,” but most are generous, kind and thoughtful.

The PCs took no time criticizing Mr. Bains, who they said, will now preside over a divided party, and his ties to Mr. Trudeau, who formally resigned as federal Liberal leader in March 2025.

Graham McGregor, Ontario’s minister of citizenship and multiculturalism in Mr. Ford’s government, said Mr. Bains was “one of the biggest supporters of Justin Trudeau, not only as Prime Minister, but when he was running for Liberal leader in the first place.”

“So we know that connection very well,” Mr. McGregor told reporters Saturday, as he took aim at the now-repealed federal consumer carbon tax.

In a post on social media, Mr. Ford congratulated Mr. Bains, and said families want parties to work collaboratively “and put province over party so we can stand up to tariffs, protect workers and make life more affordable.”

NDP strategist Erin Morrison, vice-president at Texture Communications, said Mr. Bains’ platform lacked concrete policy and that the party has work to do to figure out what it stands for. She also criticized his past role at Rogers, calling it “a contrast with Marit Stiles and the NDP,” who recently launched an ad campaign focused on affordability.

In the lead-up to the results, candidates gave speeches and stressed the need for unity regardless of the results.

“I’m asking you to keep showing up, keep working for our party and our province. No grudges. No one takes their marbles and goes home,” Ms. Bowman said.

According to the party, turnout was about 37 per cent. Out of 55,000 registered members, 20,510 members cast ballots in the contest. Liberals voted online using a ranked-ballot system, with all ridings weighted equally by points.

The Ontario Liberals, currently in third place in the legislature, have struggled to regain prominence since losing government to Mr. Ford’s PCs in 2018. The new leader will be the party’s third since 2020. Interim Leader John Fraser has held the temporary job three times.

Previous Liberal leaders Steven Del Duca and Bonnie Crombie resigned their posts after the party lost the 2022 and 2025 provincial elections. Neither held a seat when they were named leader.

The debate over whether the new Liberal leader should have a seat also dominated the discussion, with Ms. Fairclough and Ms. Bowman, the only contenders who currently in the legislature, arguing it is necessary to take on Mr. Ford immediately.

stories.title: From Trudeau cabinet minister to Ontario Liberal leader: Who is Navdeep Bains?
stories.summary: The former MP takes the helm of a provincial party that desperately needs a rebuild after losing badly to Premier Doug Ford's Progressive Conservatives in the last three elections.
stories.author: Rob Ferguson
stories.content:
It was a good lesson for the new Ontario Liberal leader to learn on a seminal election night early in his political life.

Navdeep Bains settled down to write a victory speech, expecting to land a third term as MP of Mississauga—Brampton South. But the accountant saw his Conservative challenger Eve Adams piling up votes and put his pen aside.

This was 2011, when prime minister Stephen Harper’s minority government vaulted to a majority. The Liberals fell to a humbling third place in the House of Commons behind the New Democrats, who suddenly — and for the first time — became the Official Opposition.

“The party might be in trouble, but you’ve got a safe seat,” Bains, now 49, recalls a Liberal senator reassuring him before the campaign and the jolting defeat.

“It was a wake-up call. There’s no such thing as a safe seat,” said Bains, who would make his return to Parliament four years later in Mississauga—Malton in the Justin Trudeau wave, serving as industry, innovation and economic development minister until taking a break from politics in 2021.

“The old adage of take nothing for granted? That was forever etched and embedded in my head. You’ve got to roll up your sleeves, work hard, and just not assume the outcome,” added the married father of two girls.

Now Bains is back again, making the switch to provincial politics with another third-place Liberal party — one that desperately needs a rebuild after losing badly to Premier Doug Ford’s Progressive Conservatives in the last three elections.

Ontario Liberals have selected Navdeep Bains as their new leader, emerging as victor less than one percentage point ahead of his next closest competitor, provincial caucus member Lee Fairclough. After receiving 50.3 per cent of the vote on the third and final ballot at the party’s leadership convention, Bains took to the stage and thanked his fellow contestants. (Nov. 21, 2026)

Bains credits the lesson from voters 15 years ago for serving him well in this year’s leadership race against three challengers, two of whom held the advantage of being current MPPs.

“I started from scratch. I was in the private sector for six years. I didn’t have a provincial Liberal riding association. I didn’t have a seat,” said the former Cibc and Rogers Communications executive, sipping from an iced mocha at his favourite coffee shop in Erin Mills.

“We had over 2,000 volunteers. We’ve been very successful with fundraising. We’ve been able to recruit members in all 124 ridings. So that’s what the rebuild looks like.”

On that front, there is plenty more work to be done for a party whose last two leaders also did not have seats in the legislature, leaving them unable to take on Ford face to face in daily question periods.

Bains says he is up to the challenges, having won five elections, having been on the receiving end of questions in Parliament and working on the federal Liberal rebuild in his four years out of elected politics leading up to Trudeau’s surprise 2015 majority.

That win marked the first time in Canadian history a federal party leapfrogged from third place to first.

“What we basically did was we just rebuilt the party one person at a time … it was focused very much on building the team, recruiting great candidates. I was responsible for that, and also updating our database, our systems, changing the culture,” Bains told the Star.

“What was exciting, too, is that no one was really paying attention, and we were so underestimated.”

It is now up to Bains to solve the Ontario Liberal conundrum.

Even without a permanent leader, the party has regularly placed second in public opinion polls behind Ford’s Tories and ahead of the NDP. But it has been unable to convince enough voters in enough ridings to elect more than 14 Liberals to the legislature, just two over the threshold for official party status at Queen’s Park.

Born in Toronto, Bains was raised in the Jane-Finch area before moving to Brampton for high school. Then it was on to York University — where he met his future wife — for a business degree before heading to the University of Windsor and a co-op MBA.

During a work term as a financial analyst at Ford Motor Co. in Oakville, he was offered a full-time job upon graduation. Bains and his wife lived with his parents for a year to save for a house, a purchase he describes as an “incredibly empowering” accomplishment he is worried too many young adults are unable to achieve now.

For Bains, the journey into politics began with volunteer work at local soup kitchens and after-school clubs, helping kids who were “falling through the cracks” with their homework. By 2004, he was ready to run for office.

“I wasn’t the preferred candidate,” he noted, speaking of internal party machinations. And while he got the nomination, “I had no expectation of winning.”

But he did, at 26 becoming the youngest Liberal MP in the House of Commons. Soon afterwards he was named parliamentary secretary to then-prime minister Paul Martin.

After three terms in Mississauga—Brampton South and his equally unexpected 2011 loss, the suddenly unemployed 33-year-old father turned to teaching, at the University of Waterloo and the Ted Rogers School of Management at what is now Toronto Metropolitan University.

It was quite a change in pace.

“I asked my wife a few weeks after the loss, ‘Can you call me? Because I think there’s something wrong with my phone.’ She said, ‘Nothing’s wrong with your phone. People have moved on.’”

That quiet left spare time for family, the party rebuild and meeting with voters.

“In those conversations, you learn what people are thinking, what concerns they have. And they’re real stories. They’re not a briefing note … you can read their body language. You can see on their faces what they’re looking for.”

Having won two more elections in 2015 and 2019 in Mississauga—Malton, Bains is not worried about not having a seat in the legislature now, saying that will come “when the opportunity presents itself.”

“When I talk to Liberals and the Liberal membership in particular, their primary concern is who can replace Doug Ford and the Conservatives … who has the ability, the experience, the know-how,” he said.

“The fact I’ve won five times, that I was a national campaign co-chair here federally, that I also was a provincial co-chair and had my name on the ballot more than anyone else running in the leadership race, it just underscores I have the political experience.”

Bains says he will present a clear alternative to Ford, who can be bombastic and insulting of political rivals at times.

“People look for thoughtful and serious leadership. Doing politics the right way is important. I don’t have to disrespect people to make my point,” he added, noting political discourse has taken a dive in the Trump era.

“People want civility and respect, and that’s always been part of my DNA.”

He added, grinning in a thinly veiled shot at Ford, who is removing bike lanes in the province’s capital city, “I have no intention of being the mayor of Toronto.”

“The party might be in trouble, but you’ve got a safe seat,” Bains, now 49, recalls a Liberal senator reassuring him before the campaign and the jolting defeat.

“It was a wake-up call. There’s no such thing as a safe seat,” said Bains, who would make his return to Parliament four years later in Mississauga—Malton in the Justin Trudeau wave, serving as industry, innovation and economic development minister until taking a break from politics in 2021.

“The old adage of take nothing for granted? That was forever etched and embedded in my head. You’ve got to roll up your sleeves, work hard, and just not assume the outcome,” added the married father of two girls.

Now Bains is back again, making the switch to provincial politics with another third-place Liberal party — one that desperately needs a rebuild after losing badly to Premier Doug Ford’s Progressive Conservatives in the last three elections.

Ontario Liberals have selected Navdeep Bains as their new leader, emerging as victor less than one percentage point ahead of his next closest competitor, provincial caucus member Lee Fairclough. After receiving 50.3 per cent of the vote on the third and final ballot at the party’s leadership convention, Bains took to the stage and thanked his fellow contestants. (Nov. 21, 2026)
Bains credits the lesson from voters 15 years ago for serving him well in this year’s leadership race against three challengers, two of whom held the advantage of being current MPPs.

“I started from scratch. I was in the private sector for six years. I didn’t have a provincial Liberal riding association. I didn’t have a seat,” said the former Cibc and Rogers Communications executive, sipping from an iced mocha at his favourite coffee shop in Erin Mills.
“We had over 2,000 volunteers. We’ve been very successful with fundraising. We’ve been able to recruit members in all 124 ridings. So that’s what the rebuild looks like.”

On that front, there is plenty more work to be done for a party whose last two leaders also did not have seats in the legislature, leaving them unable to take on Ford face to face in daily question periods.

Bains says he is up to the challenges, having won five elections, having been on the receiving end of questions in Parliament and working on the federal Liberal rebuild in his four years out of elected politics leading up to Trudeau’s surprise 2015 majority.
That win marked the first time in Canadian history a federal party leapfrogged from third place to first.

“What we basically did was we just rebuilt the party one person at a time … it was focused very much on building the team, recruiting great candidates. I was responsible for that, and also updating our database, our systems, changing the culture,” Bains told the Star.
“What was exciting, too, is that no one was really paying attention, and we were so underestimated.”
It is now up to Bains to solve the Ontario Liberal conundrum.

Even without a permanent leader, the party has regularly placed second in public opinion polls behind Ford’s Tories and ahead of the NDP. But it has been unable to convince enough voters in enough ridings to elect more than 14 Liberals to the legislature, just two over the threshold for official party status at Queen’s Park.

Born in Toronto, Bains was raised in the Jane-Finch area before moving to Brampton for high school. Then it was on to York University — where he met his future wife — for a business degree before heading to the University of Windsor and a co-op MBA.

During a work term as a financial analyst at Ford Motor Co. in Oakville, he was offered a full-time job upon graduation. Bains and his wife lived with his parents for a year to save for a house, a purchase he describes as an “incredibly empowering” accomplishment he is worried too many young adults are unable to achieve now.

For Bains, the journey into politics began with volunteer work at local soup kitchens and after-school clubs, helping kids who were “falling through the cracks” with their homework. By 2004, he was ready to run for office.
“I wasn’t the preferred candidate,” he noted, speaking of internal party machinations. And while he got the nomination, “I had no expectation of winning.”
But he did, at 26 becoming the youngest Liberal MP in the House of Commons. Soon afterwards he was named parliamentary secretary to then-prime minister Paul Martin.

After three terms in Mississauga—Brampton South and his equally unexpected 2011 loss, the suddenly unemployed 33-year-old father turned to teaching, at the University of Waterloo and the Ted Rogers School of Management at what is now Toronto Metropolitan University.
It was quite a change in pace.
“I asked my wife a few weeks after the loss, ‘Can you call me? Because I think there’s something wrong with my phone.’ She said, ‘Nothing’s wrong with your phone. People have moved on.’”
That quiet left spare time for family, the party rebuild and meeting with voters.

“In those conversations, you learn what people are thinking, what concerns they have. And they’re real stories. They’re not a briefing note … you can read their body language. You can see on their faces what they’re looking for.”

Having won two more elections in 2015 and 2019 in Mississauga—Malton, Bains is not worried about not having a seat in the legislature now, saying that will come “when the opportunity presents itself.”

“When I talk to Liberals and the Liberal membership in particular, their primary concern is who can replace Doug Ford and the Conservatives … who has the ability, the experience, the know-how,” he said.

“The fact I’ve won five times, that I was a national campaign co-chair here federally, that I also was a provincial co-chair and had my name on the ballot more than anyone else running in the leadership race, it just underscores I have the political experience.”
Bains says he will present a clear alternative to Ford, who can be bombastic and insulting of political rivals at times.

“People look for thoughtful and serious leadership. Doing politics the right way is important. I don’t have to disrespect people to make my point,” he added, noting political discourse has taken a dive in the Trump era.
“People want civility and respect, and that’s always been part of my DNA.”
He added, grinning in a thinly veiled shot at Ford, who is removing bike lanes in the province’s capital city, “I have no intention of being the mayor of Toronto.”

stories.title: U.S. senator says Hegseth memo does not change military co-operation with Canada
stories.summary: A Republican senator says a U.S. defence department’s memo that reportedly placed restrictions on co-operation with Canada applies to things such as participating in think-tank conferences, not military operations.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Halifax -- A Republican senator says a U.S. defence department’s memo that reportedly placed restrictions on co-operation with Canada applies to things such as participating in think-tank conferences, not military operations.

Sen. Mike Rounds was responding to a Washington Post report on Friday that said Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth penned the classified memo putting restrictions on military co-operation with Canada last week. The paper reportedly said it had not seen the memo and offered no detail on its contents.

The senator said the memo does not affect any U.S. defence personnel in Canada today and does not impact the North American Aerospace Defence Command, North Atlantic Treaty Organization operations or the Five Eyes security alliance.

“It does limit general flag officer meetings to those that advance (defence department) objectives,” Rounds told reporters at the Halifax International Security Forum on Saturday. “(U.S. defence officials) must request permission for Canadian think-tank events or social engagements. And it is OK to attend any 9/11 events.”

Rounds said he and a delegation of U.S. senators attending the Halifax conference had just attended a meeting with Canadian officials and shared the information with them. Defence Minister David McGuinty told reporters hours earlier he was unaware of the memo’s contents.

“After listening to this, (Canadian officials) said it sounds like it’s nothing new, nothing different than what they’ve been really practising under for the last year-and-a-half,” said the South Dakota senator.

McGuinty said earlier in the day that it was “business as usual” between the Canadian and U.S. militaries and assured Canadians that co-operation between the two countries on defence, security and intelligence was continuing.

“I’ve seen no evidence of (a change). I’ve checked with our top military folks, they’ve seen no evidence of change. We continue to co-operate. We continue to work together,” McGuinty told reporters.

Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said in a response to the story about the memo that the defence department is “taking steps to ensure its engagements with Canada advance tangible U.S. defense objectives and ultimately support a reinvigorated defense relationship.”

The statement, made late Friday, added that the department is prioritizing bilateral co-operation that strengthens the defence of the U.S. and “shared hemisphere” while also supporting Canada’s ability to meet Nato obligations.

“This guidance does not impact defense intelligence co-operation, our binational Norad command, or our co-operation through Nato,” Parnell said.

Several U.S. senators at the Halifax event acknowledged their country’s standing around the world has been impacted by the aggressive policies of U.S. President Donald Trump.

Senator Tim Kaine, a Democrat, said the memo doesn’t help relations with Canada. He said he’s hopeful things will change when the new U.S. Congress takes office in January. Democrats took control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives in this month’s midterm election.

“The tone is bad and it’s unnecessary,” said Kaine. “And we understand this actually goes back a ways and it is just the formalization of something that is now months and months old. I do think the new Congress is going to change the tone dramatically. ”

McGuinty also announced Saturday that Canada is formally becoming the 25th member of Nato’s Innovation Fund. Canada is contributing more than $100 million to the fund, enabling it to invest in Canadian startups.

Launched in 2022, the venture capital fund is designed to strengthen Nato by investing in cutting edge technologies such as artificial intelligence, quantum technologies, biotech, space and communications.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 21, 2026.

Devin Stevens, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Quebec students are considering a general strike to protest affordability crisis
stories.summary: Montreal - College and university students are gathering in Montreal on Saturday to discuss and vote on the possibility of launching an indefinite general strike during their winter semester.
stories.author: Audrey Sanikopoulos The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - College and university students gathered in Montreal on Saturday to discuss and vote on the possibility of launching an indefinite general strike during their winter semester.

A general assembly started in the early afternoon at the Université du Québec à Montréal. The results of the vote will be announced at a press conference on Monday morning, said members of the student union coalition organizing the strike, the Coalition de résistance pour l’unité étudiante syndicale.
