stories.title: Ottawa says it lost $2M from emergency drug stockpile after freezer malfunction
stories.summary: The Public Health Agency of Canada has reported losing another $2 million in pharmaceuticals from the national emergency stockpile because of the mechanical failure of a freezer.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — The Public Health Agency of Canada has reported losing another $2 million in pharmaceuticals from the national emergency stockpile because of the mechanical failure of a freezer.

The figure is in the annual federal public accounts published earlier this fall, and comes after the agency had to write off $20 million in pharmaceuticals from the stockpile a year earlier after another freezer malfunction.

The agency says the second loss involved a small portion of a specific drug treatment for responding to a biological threat.

“A mechanical failure prevented a freezer from maintaining its required temperature, which led to a small portion of a stockpiled drug treatment being exposed to temperatures outside the required storage requirements,” said Health Canada spokesperson Hélène-Annie Lavoie. “The affected products had to be disposed of as a result.”

Lavoie said the agency immediately launched an internal investigation and identified the cause of the problem.

She said the incident did not compromise Canada’s ability to respond to that potential threat, since the stockpile still had another treatment.

The official said she could not disclose the lost drug inventory for national security reasons. She said sharing that information could “expose sensitive operational details about how Canada prepares for and responds to chemical, biological, radiological, nuclear or other public health threats.”

The agency says it has put in place new measures to prevent a recurrence.

The Canadian Press reported last year that an open freezer door caused the loss of medication worth $20 million at the national emergency stockpile in December 2024.

While officials again would not say exactly what was destroyed or how much, the agency said at the time it affected one type of therapeutic drug as a result of temperature fluctuations “caused by several factors.”

The Office of the Auditor General issued a report on the emergency stockpile in October which said the agency had written off more than $331 million in expired or damaged medical supplies. A spokesperson for the office confirmed both the $20 million loss and the $2 million loss, from the malfunctioning freezers, were included in that figure.

The national stockpile is a network of warehouses across the country where the government stores medical supplies, vaccines and emergency response equipment.

First established during the Cold War, the stockpile was initially intended to respond to a nuclear emergency.

Since then, it has been adapted to respond to outbreaks of diseases — including Sars and COVID-19 — natural disasters like hurricanes and floods, bioterror attacks and other emergencies.

Kyle Duggan and Catherine Morrison, The Canadian Press

stories.title: London Knights snap losing streak with home win over Soo Greyhounds
stories.summary: The London Knights losing streak is over.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
The London Knights losing streak is over.

After four straight defeats, the Knights beat the Soo Greyhounds 4-3 at Canada Life Place (CLP) on Friday Nov. 20, 2026.

The Knights got goals from Jaxon Cover, Caleb Mitchell, Cooper McAslan and Evan Van Gorp and held off a late charge by the Greyhounds in the third meeting between the clubs in 20 days.

The game featured the return of Knights 6’8 defenceman Maxim Sokolovskii who had been out of the lineup with a lower body injury since Sept. 25.His return pushed fellow defender Caleb Mitchell to centre and it paid off with Mitchell scoring a goal in the second period.Mitchell had never played forward in his life.

The Knights will look for a second straight win Saturday afternoon when they travel to Guelph for a 4 p.m. start.

They will return back to CLP Sunday to face the Peterborough Petes.

stories.title: B.C. business groups are praising plans by Conservative government to cut red tape
stories.summary: Victoria - Various business group are praising plans by Conservative Premier Lorne Doerkson to cut red tape and speed up approvals through the creation of a dedicated cabinet post.
stories.author: Wolfgang Depner The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Victoria - Various business group are praising plans by Conservative Premier Lorne Doerkson to cut red tape and speed up approvals through the creation of a dedicated cabinet post.

The Canadian Federation of Independent Business says the appointment of Carson Binda as minister of state responsible for cutting red tape sends a “clear signal” that speeding up approvals is a “real priority” for the new government.

Ryan Mitton, director of legislative affairs for B.C., says in a statement that cutting red tape represents a “low-cost measure” for government to improve the business climate in British Columbia, which currently finds itself in an “entrepreneurial drought.”

Cfib says it estimates that red tape cost B.C. businesses more than $8.3 billion in 2024, up 26 per cent from 2017, when the NDP assumed power, and that small business owners lost the equivalent of 32 business days while dealing with red tape.

Joslyn Young, chief executive officer of the Surrey and White Rock Board of Trade, says reducing unnecessary regulations, streamlining approvals and making government easier to navigate “are essential” to improving business confidence and strengthening economic competitiveness.

She says in a statement that businesses continue to face complex regulations, administrative delays and unnecessary barriers that can impact investment, expansion and job creation.

Conservatives campaigned on the promise to cut red tape back to 2017 levels by the end of their first term and speed up permitting and approvals with fixed timelines and a one-approach-one-review process.

Other promises around speeding up approvals include the introduction of legislation to permit projects over $250 million in 120 days, as part of Doerkson’s larger goal to “supercharge” the provincial economy.

Doerkson said at his first news conference after Friday’s swearing-in ceremony that Conservatives are committed to growing the economy.

“There is no other way forward for us in British Columbia,” he said. “We cannot continue to tax our residents at the rate that they have, and there are so many residents, my mom included, that are pretty close to the bone with respect to their financial situation, and we can’t continue to go to that well for support.”

Finance Minister Peter Milobar said cutting red tape and charging the economy go hand in hand.

“That will be critical for my ministry to see that we can actually get the economy moving once again, so that we can actually get that growth, and hit those target numbers that we are aggressively going after to make sure that we do have the funds to fund things like healthcare and education and all those critical services people rely on,” he said.

The Conservative platform says that the provincial Gross Domestic Product could grow by 2.5 per cent in 2027/28, 2.8 per cent in 2028/29 and 3.2 per cent by 2029/30 under a pro-growth agenda.

If B.C.‘s economy grows by those rates, the province collects $2.62 billion more over three years than the forecast of the previous government without raising a single tax.

“By 2029, growth is back to the pace B.C. achieved from 2014 to 2017,” it reads. “Getting there means approving projects in months, not years, putting the Crown harvest back to work, doubling natural gas production and repealing CleanBC.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 21, 2026.

stories.title: Canada unaware of U.S. changes to military cooperation policy, McGuinty says
stories.summary: The Department of War is “taking steps to ensure its engagements with Canada advance tangible U.S. defense objectives, the Chief Pentagon spokesperson told Global News.
stories.author: Rachel Morgan
stories.content:
Defence Minister David McGuinty said Canada is moving forward “business as usual” despite reports of an internal memo from U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth that imposes new restrictions on the two countries’ defence relationship.

“It’s clear that there’s some sort of document we haven’t seen. I’m not aware of the contents of it, but I can assure Canadians and I can assure anybody who’s interested that the Canadian-American cooperation on defence, security and intelligence continues,” McGuinty told reporters Saturday.

The Washington Post reported Friday, citing a U.S. official, that the new restrictions would be a “slap in the face” to Canadians and raise questions about how interactions between the two militaries will be curtailed.

Global News has not seen the classified memo.

The Department of War is “taking steps to ensure its engagements with Canada advance tangible U.S. defense objectives and ultimately support a reinvigorated defense relationship,” Sean Parnell, Chief Pentagon spokesperson, told Global News in a statement.

He said the department is “prioritizing opportunities for bilateral cooperation that strengthens the defense of our Homelands and shared hemisphere, while supporting Canada’s ability to meet Nato obligations.”

Hegseth’s directive would not impact defence intelligence cooperation, the bilateral Norad common, or cooperation through Nato, Parnell said.

McGuinty said he has seen “no evidence of a change” amongst the two countries’ defence relationship.

“I’ve checked with our top military officials. They’ve seen no evidence of change,” he said.

The news comes as Canada announced it was officially joining the Nato Innovation Fund, which could help secure investment into new technologies and capabilities for the Canadian Armed Forces.

When asked whether the state of its relationship with the U.S. has impacted Canada’s decision to look elsewhere for military partnerships, McGuinty said, “not exactly.”

He said Canadian officials have had their “heads down” working on a domestic, continental and international defence plan.

“If something else evolves, we’ll deal with it,” he said.

stories.title: Barred from Santa Claus Parade, Strathroy, Ont. tattoo shop offers photos with Krampus
stories.summary: Barred from taking part in the Strathroy Santa Claus Parade by the local Lions Club, Tanya Griffin decided to turn a negative into a positive.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
Barred from taking part in the Strathroy Santa Claus Parade by the local Lions Club, Tanya Griffin decided to turn a negative into a positive.

Her Krampus-themed entry was excluded this year , after finishing with a runner-up award in 2025.

She decided on the day of the parade to open her store for photos with the horned figure who, in the Central and Eastern Alpine folkloric tradition is said to accompany Saint Nicolas.

“ We did one post and next thing you know, we hit Germany and Austria and the New York Times, it’s been insane,” said Griffin, who owns Coven House Tattoos & Piercings.

Saturday morning, the shop was busy with supporters coming in to get photos with Krampus. They were asked to bring a non-perishable food donation towards the Strathroy Police Cram a Cruiser event.

“The community asked for it and they’ve been asking for him everywhere,” said Griffin.

“We just thought if we’re not allowed to be on the street, my shop is right on the route anyways. We’ll bring them out there for the parade and he’ll be in here all day. We’re getting to take pictures for anyone who wants to show their support.”

Griffin says she’s been asked to bring Krampus to a local hockey game for a ceremonial faceoff and also to an upcoming concert.

“It’s been a great reaction,” she added.

“There are some people that aren’t going to the parade but they’re here for this. We’re getting lots of donations for the cruiser. It’s a win-win when you look at it this way. Like, everyone still gets their chance with him.”

Griffin is predicting a massive turnout on Saturday and has been thrilled with the support.

By Sadeen Mohsen The Canadian Press

Beloved nine-year-old Fiona died from complications after ingesting a visitor’s knit hat that was accidentally flung into her enclosure at the Cincinnati Zoo.

She had become a social media darling after being born prematurely and surviving against all odds.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Toronto Marlies reflect on the meaning behind their Calder Cup Championship

The Toronto Zoo says it conducted the review to determine whether any additional measures were needed to prevent a similar fate to its animals, including at the river hippo habitat.

While the zoo said it found no structural or infrastructure changes that were required, it will be taking additional steps to remind visitors to refrain from throwing items into animal habitats.

The Toronto Zoo is home to one river hippopotamus, Perky II. It euthanized 39-year-old Petal back in October 2025 due to health issues.

The zoo also cares for three pygmy hippos, Kindia, Harvey and a calf named Maple that was born in August 2026.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 21, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: McGuinty not aware U.S. has changed military co-operation policy with Canada
stories.summary: Canada’s defence minister says he has not seen a memo from the U.S. secretary of war that reportedly restricts American defence co-operation with Canada.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Halifax — Canada’s defence minister says he has not seen a memo from the U.S. secretary of war that reportedly restricts American defence co-operation with Canada.

David McGuinty said while speaking at the Halifax International Security Forum on Saturday that it’s “business as usual” between the Canadian and U.S. militaries.

McGuinty was asked about the memo after the Washington Post reported U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth wrote the classified directive last week.

The Post reported it had not seen the memo and did not include further details on its contents.

McGuinty said he can assure Canadians that co-operation between the two countries on defence, security and intelligence continues.

The minister said he has met with several different U.S. defence officials in the last week and has not been advised of a change.

“I’ve seen no evidence of (a change). I’ve checked with our top military folks, they’ve seen no evidence of change. We continue to cooperate. We continue work together,” McGuinty said during a news conference Saturday.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 21, 2026.

Devin Stevens, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Montreal police arrest two officers recently fired over misconduct allegations
stories.summary: They face charges of assault, criminal harassment and breach of trust
stories.author: Marieke Glorieux-Stryckman
stories.content:
Montreal police have arrested two former officers who were recently fired following allegations of discriminatory and racist conduct.

The Montreal police force announced the arrests in a press release on Saturday morning.

The provincial Crown prosecutor’s office announced a few minutes earlier it had filed charges of assault, criminal harassment and breach of trust against the former officers following a review of the Montreal force’s investigation into the allegations.

The two former officers have been released on a promise to appear, added Montreal police.

The former officers worked at the station in the multicultural neighbourhood of Montréal-Nord where police dismantled a patrol unit in June following allegations of racism and discrimination.

Police Chief Fady Dagher confirmed earlier this year that the allegations include claims that officers at the station in the Montréal-Nord borough cut the hair of racialized civilians to keep as trophies.

In a written statement on Saturday, Montreal mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada applauded the arrests.

“Today’s arrests send a clear signal regarding the authorities’ commitment to see this through to the end. Those who come forward must be heard and taken seriously. I would like to thank, once again, the police officers who had the courage to break the code of silence. The work continues, and justice must now take its course,” read the statement.

Both Montreal police and the provincial Crown prosecutor’s office said they would not comment further because of the ongoing investigation.

“We will continue to keep the public informed about the progress of the related criminal investigations, which, it should be noted, are being conducted with the oversight of an independent observer appointed by the internal security ministry,” said Montreal police.

In an e-mail to The Canadian Press, the union representing Montreal police officers acknowledged the prosecutor’s announcement but did not respond to further questions.

Joel DeBellefeuille, founder and executive director of civil rights group the Red Coalition, said his group was “pleased” with the arrests, but that he believed they should have happened a long time ago.

He said advocacy groups and residents have been speaking out about these issues for decades, without seeing any action.

“Why did they only trust these allegations when it comes from police officers internally and they’re not believing their own public? That’s a major problem,” he said.

He said he expects allegations against police officers to multiply in the near future.

“I think this is the tip of the iceberg, where everybody will start to see things like this occurring quite regularly, because we do feel that it’s a major problem, not only in the [Montreal police], but in the provinces as a whole,” he said.

The arrested officers were among the seven officers who were fired as part of ongoing criminal investigations into the series of scandals involving officers at two police stations.

In a news conference announcing the firings on Nov. 2, Dagher said the dismissals were unprecedented.

“To the victims of unacceptable conduct by [Montreal] police officers, I promised you truth and consequences,” he said.

Police also announced in late October that an officer linked to the investigation could face criminal charges after allegedly concealing evidence related to a situation involving domestic violence in 2025.

stories.title: Conservative Premier Doerkson gets ready to tear housing plans: NDP interim leader
stories.summary: Victoria - British Columbia's official Opposition says the new Conservative cabinet is getting ready to tear down existing housing plans after eliminating the Ministry of Housing and Municipal Affairs as a separate office.
stories.author: Wolfgang Depner The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Victoria - British Columbia’s official Opposition says the new Conservative cabinet is getting ready to tear down existing housing plans after eliminating the Ministry of Housing and Municipal Affairs as a separate office.

NDP interim leader Jennifer Whiteside says it is “deeply disappointing” to see the housing portfolio become part of the new Ministry of Local Government, Housing, Sport and Culture.

stories.title: Poll finds most Canadians think Americans share our values. But it gets complicated from there
stories.summary: The respondents most attached to Canada are less likely to trust Americans
stories.author: Stewart Lewis
stories.content:
A new survey reveals over one in three Canadians do not respect Americans and a similar number don’t think they respect us.

That’s despite almost 60% believing we share values with Americans and three in four often or sometimes being in contact with Americans, says Jack Jedwab, president of the Association for Canadian Studies.

“For much of the twentieth century, protecting Canada’s identity meant resisting American cultural and economic influence,” he says. The ACS decided to revisit this question in a new poll conducted by Ekos Research.

Jedwab says that in the many surveys ACS has commissioned in the last 20 years asking Canadians how attached they feel to the country, it is left to the respondents to rely on “their own understanding of what that connection means.”

He notes that of 1,232 people surveyed, 59 per cent stated they are “very attached,” 28 per cent “somewhat attached,” while 8 per cent said they were “not very attached” and 4 per cent “not at all.” A slim 1 per cent “didn’t know.”

According to the survey, Canadians most attached to the country are “somewhat” less likely to say they “very much” or “somewhat” respect Americans, 59 per cent versus 66 per cent of respondents who said they are not attached to Canada.

Meanwhile, those more attached to Canada are less likely to agree that Americans respect us. For those who very much or somewhat perceive respect coming from Americans, the numbers show 55% among respondents are attached to Canada and 58% for those who are not.

Those most attached to Canada are also less likely to trust Americans, according to the survey. That sits at 50% for those are attached, versus 57% who are not.

The numbers are similarly split when it comes to perception of shared values. Fifty-nine per cent of respondents attached to the country believe Americans very much or somewhat share our values, as opposed to 65% among respondents not attached to Canada.

Among Canadians who have less respect for Americans, the two top sets of issues were Trump, Maga and electoral accountability (36 per cent) and political leadership, democracy and authoritarianism (20 per cent). These issues also resonated among those who believe Americans don’t respect us.

Prairie and Western Canadians showed themselves to be more respectful of Americans than Eastern Canadians. For example 62% of British Columbians very much or somewhat expressed respect for our southern neighbours. That’s opposed to 56% of Quebecers and 32% of Atlantic Canadians. Prairie and Western folk are also more likely to think Americans respect us.

Jedwab suspects political outlook accounts for some of the difference between Canadian regions. “Conservative views are more common in parts of the Prairies, and that May shape how people there respond to U.S. politics.”

He notes, however, that on the east coast, where there have been long-held historic ties to New England, “Atlantic Canadians were nearly as likely as Prairie respondents to say they respected Americans very much. The wider gap shows up among those who said they respected Americans somewhat. Close ties with New England can coexist with more mixed views of Americans generally.”

British Columbians were shown to have the most contact with Americans, 21% often and 55% sometimes. Quebecers had the least contact with only 15% expressing often and 36% saying sometimes.

A narrow majority of Quebecers believe Americans share our values even though they are least likely in Canada to think so. Jedwab, a Montrealer, explains the attitude of Quebeckers by pointing to the language difference.

“A shared border makes visits easier, and a shared language makes it easier to build and maintain the kinds of relationships that lead to regular contact. The survey asked about contact generally, which can include work, friendships and everyday conversations as well as travel. I’d expect language to matter more for some of those interactions than it does for a trip across the border.”

Contrary to the above trends, the number of Canadians who have a lot of respect for Americans (24%) almost matches those who have frequent contact with them (23%). Moreover, nearly 60% believe we share values with Americans (18% very much, 42% somewhat).

Jedwab explains this distinction by saying, “Canadians have a lot in common with Americans but still feel the respect goes only one way. The perception that Canada and Canadians are being treated with disrespect explains the broader survey results.”

Ekos Research conducted this survey for ACS on Oct. 15-20, 2026, surveying 1,232 respondents nationally. The survey mode, weighting variables and precision estimates were not supplied.

Stewart Lewis is a writer and editor with National Post. A journalist and lawyer, he has worked in newspapers, radio and TV, and served a legal stint with Global Affairs Canada at the United Nations in New York City.

stories.title: Cadbury Dairy Milk Oreo treats hit under new recall
stories.summary: This is the second time Cadbury’s Dairy Milk Oreo candy bar has been recalled this year due to undeclared pistachio.
stories.author: Rachel Morgan
stories.content:
Cadbury’s parent company has issued a recall for its Dairy Milk Oreo candy bar which it says May contain pistachios, the Canadian Food Inspection Agency (Cfia) said.

Mondelez Canada Inc. issued the recall following a consumer complaint.

The Cfia said there has been one reported reaction associated with the consumption of the product.

The recall affects the treat size candy bar, sold individually, or as part of Cadbury Favourites 45 and 90 packs.

The Cfia said it is conducting a safety investigation which could lead to the recall of other products.

“The Cfia is verifying that industry is removing recalled products from the marketplace,” it said.

This is the second time Cadbury’s Dairy Milk Oreo candy bar has been recalled this year due to undeclared pistachio.

In July, the snack food and confectionary manufacturer issued a recall for the full size candy bar product after multiple reactions were reported.

stories.title: London’s homeless numbers hit new high as shelters prepare for winter
stories.summary: London’s revamped Winter Response to Homelessness is preparing to open more overnight spaces, but amid a growing crisis there’s uncertainty about whether everyone who needs a warm space will get one.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
London’s revamped Winter Response to Homelessness is preparing to open more overnight spaces, but amid a growing crisis there’s uncertainty about whether everyone who needs a warm space will get one. “I am very pleased that the city announced it early, and (shelters) plan to be fully open across the city Dec.

1, and there is a coordinated approach with service providers so that it is an every night approach, largely,” explained Sarah Campbell, executive director of Ark Aid Street Mission. When city council approved the winter response in the summer, the scale of London’s homelessness crisis had been relatively stable, but the previous two months saw numbers hit highs never before experienced in London.

According to the city’s online dashboard, roughly 2,200 to 2,300 unique individuals interacted with frontline services each month from January to August. That number climbed to 2,388 in September and 2,534 in October—a net increase of 146 people in a single month.

A question from CTV News asking city hall to explain what might be causing the record-setting surge was not specifically answered in an emailed response Friday afternoon. Campbell acknowledges it could put additional pressure on shelters, “We could be looking at more people coming to us (this winter), and we May find ourselves tight on space.” Unlike last winter, the Boyle Community Centre will not be utilized as a cold weather emergency shelter.

Instead, council allocated $5.8 million for existing shelters to provide an additional 238 spaces every night between Dec. 1 and March 31, plus another 29 spaces will open when temperatures fall below -15 C or the wind chill drops below -20 C.

Ark Aid plans to use its two existing locations and is now unlikely to temporarily rent a third. The 20 to 40 beds initially envisioned for that third shelter will instead be divided between The Ark and Cronyn-Warner House, as well as other frontline shelters.

“The truth is we had a hard time securing a third location this year,” admitted Campbell. ”That’s the first time in six-years, but it’s happened. We were being specific to an area of the city, and we’re continuing to be in talks with some churches just in case we need some of that expansion space.” Peak demand experienced last winter was 240 individuals at the Winter Response to Homelessness emergency shelters.

This year shelters will create a total of 267 additional overnight spaces, 27 more than last winter’s peak demand, but London’s Unique Client Count has risen by more than 300 people since last winter. “I think when we see these new numbers about homelessness, this is an important number to track, because when people are new to homelessness they have some resources initially, maybe they can stay with a friend for a little while, maybe they can manage in various ways, but over time this is when the crisis becomes really intense for people,” Campbell said.

City staff commit to track the situation as the winter progresses. “The City will monitor demand and availability with local providers throughout the winter. If demand exceeds available spaces, we’ll work with providers to assess options and keep City Council informed,” wrote Jonathan John, the City of London’s director of Housing Stability Services.

Campbell says the municipal funding will only provide nighttime spaces this winter, participating shelters and frontline agencies will still depend on the generosity of Londoners for everything else. “One thing is, if you’ve cleaned out your closet and you have any winter gear at all, please donate to the organization of your choice.

At Ark Aid if we have more, (then) we share with others. But the truth is, we always run out,” she said. “The second thing is come and volunteer with us. You know, get your hands involved. We need people on the ground,” Campbell added.

“The third thing would be make a donation to one of these organizations. There’s always gaps to be filled.” The City of London’s full statement: “Last winter, many warming spaces opened only during extreme cold conditions.

On the busiest night, 240 people used those spaces, exceeding planned capacity. This year, 238 Winter Response spaces will be available every night from December 1 to March 31, with 29 more opening during extreme cold conditions.

That gives people more reliable options for coming indoors throughout the entire duration of the winter season. In addition, 419 year-round emergency shelter beds, respite beds and transitional housing spaces will continue to operate throughout the winter months.

Together, year-round shelters, respite programs, transitional housing and seasonal services will provide 657 spaces this winter and 686 during extreme cold conditions. The City and its partners will continue helping people move from shelters into housing this winter, which can free up shelter spaces for others who need them.

In addition, the Canada-Ontario Housing Benefit and other rent supplements will help people find or keep housing. Federal reimbursement through the Unsheltered Homelessness and Encampments Initiative also allowed Council to reinvest $350,000 in outreach, daytime drop-ins and access to showers and other basic needs.

If demand exceeds available spaces, we’ll work with providers to assess options and keep City Council informed. This year’s Winter Response represents an investment of $5,784,775, including $3,632,500 in municipal funding and $2,152,275 in federal funding.

Like other major cities across Canada, London continues to face a shortage of deeply affordable and attainable housing. The City is working closely with federal and provincial partners on long-term solutions to expand access to housing.”

This year shelters will create a total of 267 additional overnight spaces, 27 more than last winter’s peak demand, but London’s Unique Client Count has risen by more than 300 people since last winter. “I think when we see these new numbers about homelessness, this is an important number to track, because when people are new to homelessness they have some resources initially, maybe they can stay with a friend for a little while, maybe they can manage in various ways, but over time this is when the crisis becomes really intense for people,” Campbell said.

City staff commit to track the situation as the winter progresses. “The City will monitor demand and availability with local providers throughout the winter. If demand exceeds available spaces, we’ll work with providers to assess options and keep City Council informed,” wrote Jonathan John, the City of London’s director of Housing Stability Services.

Campbell says the municipal funding will only provide nighttime spaces this winter, participating shelters and frontline agencies will still depend on the generosity of Londoners for everything else. “One thing is, if you’ve cleaned out your closet and you have any winter gear at all, please donate to the organization of your choice.

At Ark Aid if we have more, (then) we share with others. But the truth is, we always run out,” she said. “The second thing is come and volunteer with us. You know, get your hands involved. We need people on the ground,” Campbell added.

“The third thing would be make a donation to one of these organizations. There’s always gaps to be filled.” The City of London’s full statement: “Last winter, many warming spaces opened only during extreme cold conditions.

On the busiest night, 240 people used those spaces, exceeding planned capacity. This year, 238 Winter Response spaces will be available every night from December 1 to March 31, with 29 more opening during extreme cold conditions.

That gives people more reliable options for coming indoors throughout the entire duration of the winter season. In addition, 419 year-round emergency shelter beds, respite beds and transitional housing spaces will continue to operate throughout the winter months.

Together, year-round shelters, respite programs, transitional housing and seasonal services will provide 657 spaces this winter and 686 during extreme cold conditions. The City and its partners will continue helping people move from shelters into housing this winter, which can free up shelter spaces for others who need them.

In addition, the Canada-Ontario Housing Benefit and other rent supplements will help people find or keep housing. Federal reimbursement through the Unsheltered Homelessness and Encampments Initiative also allowed Council to reinvest $350,000 in outreach, daytime drop-ins and access to showers and other basic needs.

If demand exceeds available spaces, we’ll work with providers to assess options and keep City Council informed. This year’s Winter Response represents an investment of $5,784,775, including $3,632,500 in municipal funding and $2,152,275 in federal funding.

Like other major cities across Canada, London continues to face a shortage of deeply affordable and attainable housing. The City is working closely with federal and provincial partners on long-term solutions to expand access to housing.”

stories.title: ‘No change’: Top Canadian officials deny U.S. is restricting military co-operation
stories.summary: McGuinty, Carignan react to Washington Post report of classified Hegseth memo limiting two countries' relationship
stories.author: Chris Lambie
stories.content:
'Getting back to basics ... means fostering pride in our province and country by bringing back the singing of O Canada.' — B.C. premier-designate

Canada's Defence Minister David McGuinty looks on prior to at a defence summit in Berlin on Nov. 19. He said on Saturday at the Halifax Security Forum that he is not aware of "any restrictions" in Canada-U.S. military co-operation. (Kenzo Tribouillard / AFP via Getty Images)

November 21, 2026 at 10:38 a.m.

Halifax – Canada’s top soldier and defence minister both insisted Saturday that nothing has changed in the country’s military relationship with the United States, downplaying a report that U.S. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has restricted co-operation.

The Washington Post reported late Friday that Hegseth has issued a classified memo that one unnamed U.S. official indicated was sure to be seen as a “slap in the face” to the Canadian military.

“We’re not aware of any restrictions,” Defence Minister David McGuinty said Saturday morning in Halifax for the international Halifax Security Forum.

“In fact, the 70-year plus relationship we’ve had, for example, under the umbrella of Norad – the only binational command in the world – served us well, kept us safe and continues to keep us safe. That work continues.”

The Canadian military is also working with the U.S. military on interdicting drug smugglers in the Caribbean, McGuinty said.

“We’ve been working together since the arrival of (President Donald Trump) and his administration in lock-step,” he said. “I haven’t seen any daylight between them.”

Canada is currently negotiating with the U.S. on an integrated air missile defence system, McGuinty said. “We are looking at … establishing our own over-the-horizon radar system and how that would connect with an American version.”

The two militaries are also collaborating on border protection, he said.

“From our perspective, we’re moving forward, and we continue to do so together,” McGuinty said.

According to the Washington Post, the memo outlining Hegseth’s restrictions “raise questions about how the two militaries’ interaction will be curtailed.”

Gen. Jennie Carignan, Canada’s Chief of the Defence Staff, said Saturday that “from my perspective, in terms of my interactions with U.S. colleagues, there is no change to what we are doing. We are really much focused on the business of continental defence, whether it’s in Nato or via Norad.”

The two militaries “figure out how to best implement each other’s policy while maintaining the focus on defence,” Carignan said.

Indeed, the Washington Post report quoted Hegseth spokesman Sean Parnell as saying that the Pentagon is “taking steps to ensure its engagement with Canada advance tangible U.S. defence objectives and ultimately support a reinvigorated defence relationship.”

It goes on to say Hegesth’s new directive “will not affect defence intelligence sharing or how the U.S. and Canadian militaries collaborate through the Nato military alliance, which also includes European allies, and the bilateral North American Aerospace Defence Command.”

TORONTO - Toronto police say they have arrested a man in a homicide investigation, one day after he was placed at No. 9 on Canada’s most wanted list of fugitives.

Nov. 21, 2026

They arrested the 25-year-old in Toronto on Friday, alongside a 26-year-old woman who has been charged with accessory.

In September 2026, officers responded to a report of a vehicle on fire in a field near the Steeles Avenue East and Reesor Road area, where they found a 32-year-old man dead inside.

Investigators later identified three suspects in the death and arrested two people, while the man arrested Friday remained an outstanding suspect.

The accused is charged with first-degree murder.

Police say the investigation remains ongoing and ask anyone with information to come forward.

stories.title: The CCH Crusaders win 3rd straight city football title in ‘Fog Bowl’
stories.summary: The Catholic Central (CCH) Crusaders won their third straight Tvra high school football title in a game which nearly had to be postponed due to fog.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
The Catholic Central (CCH) Crusaders won their third straight Tvra high school football title in a game which nearly had to be postponed due to fog.

The heavily favoured Crusaders beat upstart Oakridge 37-3 to head to Ofsaa.

“It feels amazing because this was the end goal we worked for,” said CCH quarterback Morgan Gleason who threw for three touchdowns.

“Our goal is to get a three-peat and God we I’m just so happy for our boys and we ended up doing it. But I’m at a loss for words right now.”

The Crusaders jumped out to a 16-0 lead at halftime on a pair of touchdown catches by Alek Hodgeson and Harper Asuncion. The Oaks conceded a safety in the second quarter to round out the first half scoring.

In what was the warmest championship game in years, the fog was above field level at 1Password Park in St. Thomas, Ont. for the first half.

As half-time approached, the fog reached field level and nearly unplayable conditions.

“Starting the second half of the game, we had some really heavy fog,” said Crusaders running back Nathan Sims, who scored two touchdowns.

“I’ve never seen it in like 11 years of playing football. I’ve never had a game like that.”

The referees had discussions with both coaches and decided to continue.

“It shut down all the passing plays, which means our offensive line time to pick up the pace and run the ball down the field. And that’s what happened,” said Sims.

“We got the touchdown and the side people in the side, the fans of the sidelines cheering we got we knew we got the touchdown but on our sideline on the bench nobody knew what happened. So, I was told that the ref (referee) came through the fog with his hands up and that’s when they started celebrating.”

The conditions – which lasted into the fourth quarter before the fog lifted – altered the play calling for the coaching staff.

“It was a bit difficult because we had to change some of the stuff we do procedurally for how we signaled plays in,” said Alex Kurowski, Crusaders head coach.

“We sort of have to run players in, and it made that complicated. I’ve never seen that. The only time I’ve seen that is on NFL films, and I think it was the bears and the Eagles (1988 at Solider Field in Chicago).”

Despite the conditions, the Crusaders picked up right where they left off in the first half. They scored three more touchdowns, two by Sims and a receiving touchdown by AJ Davis.Davis – a defensive end and tight end - was named game MVP for his play on both sides of the ball.

“It’s just great, five years I love all these boys and can’t do without them,” said Davis of his MVP award.

Gleason was quick to praise the Oaks who reached their first city final since 1980.

That game will be played in Kingston, Ont. on November 30 at 5 p.m vs the York Region champions.

“We are continuing that momentum into next week,” said Sims.

So, I was told that the ref (referee) came through the fog with his hands up and that’s when they started celebrating.”
The conditions – which lasted into the fourth quarter before the fog lifted – altered the play calling for the coaching staff.
“It was a bit difficult because we had to change some of the stuff we do procedurally for how we signaled plays in,” said Alex Kurowski, Crusaders head coach.

“We sort of have to run players in, and it made that complicated. I’ve never seen that. The only time I’ve seen that is on NFL films, and I think it was the bears and the Eagles (1988 at Solider Field in Chicago).”

Despite the conditions, the Crusaders picked up right where they left off in the first half. They scored three more touchdowns, two by Sims and a receiving touchdown by AJ Davis.Davis – a defensive end and tight end - was named game MVP for his play on both sides of the ball.
“It’s just great, five years I love all these boys and can’t do without them,” said Davis of his MVP award.
Gleason was quick to praise the Oaks who reached their first city final since 1980.
That game will be played in Kingston, Ont. on November 30 at 5 p.m vs the York Region champions.
“We are continuing that momentum into next week,” said Sims.

stories.title: $2M from emergency drug stockpile lost after freezer malfunction, Ottawa says
stories.summary: The agency says the loss involved a small portion of a specific drug treatment for responding to a biological threat.
stories.author: Kyle Duggan and Catherine Morrison
stories.content:
The Public Health Agency of Canada has reported losing another $2 million in pharmaceuticals from the national emergency stockpile because of the mechanical failure of a freezer.

The figure is in the annual federal public accounts published earlier this fall, and comes after the agency had to write off $20 million in pharmaceuticals from the stockpile a year earlier after another freezer malfunction.

The agency says the second loss involved a small portion of a specific drug treatment for responding to a biological threat.

“A mechanical failure prevented a freezer from maintaining its required temperature, which led to a small portion of a stockpiled drug treatment being exposed to temperatures outside the required storage requirements,” said Health Canada spokesperson Hélène-Annie Lavoie. “The affected products had to be disposed of as a result.”

Lavoie said the agency immediately launched an internal investigation and identified the cause of the problem.

She said the incident did not compromise Canada’s ability to respond to that potential threat, since the stockpile still had another treatment.

The official said she could not disclose the lost drug inventory for national security reasons. She said sharing that information could “expose sensitive operational details about how Canada prepares for and responds to chemical, biological, radiological, nuclear or other public health threats.”

The agency says it has put in place new measures to prevent a recurrence.

The Canadian Press reported last year that an open freezer door caused the loss of medication worth $20 million at the national emergency stockpile in December 2024.

While officials again would not say exactly what was destroyed or how much, the agency said at the time it affected one type of therapeutic drug as a result of temperature fluctuations “caused by several factors.”

The Office of the Auditor General issued a report on the emergency stockpile in October which said the agency had written off more than $331 million in expired or damaged medical supplies. A spokesperson for the office confirmed both the $20 million loss and the $2 million loss, from the malfunctioning freezers, were included in that figure.

The national stockpile is a network of warehouses across the country where the government stores medical supplies, vaccines and emergency response equipment.

First established during the Cold War, the stockpile was initially intended to respond to a nuclear emergency.

Since then, it has been adapted to respond to outbreaks of diseases — including Sars and COVID-19 — natural disasters like hurricanes and floods, bioterror attacks and other emergencies.

stories.title: Quebecor’s bid for Telus, Anthropic’s IPO debut and Ford’s Oakville assembly plant reopens: Must-read business and investing stories for the week of Nov. 14
stories.summary: Plus, search for new Bank of Canada governor begins as Macklem confirms he won’t seek second term
stories.author: Abigale Subdhan
stories.content:
Getting caught up on a week that got away? Here’s your weekly digest of The Globe’s most essential business and investing stories, with insights and analysis on the biggest headlines, stock tips, personal finance strategies and more.

Earlier this week, Quebecor Inc. made public a proposal to buy Telus Corp. for about $31-billion in cash and shares. Essentially, the No. 4 competitor in the country’s telecom industry is proposing to buy the No. 3 player – and the deal, if it succeeds, would remake the entire industry.

The deal carries significant regulatory, financial and governance risks. A successful merger would reduce the country’s four major telecom players to just three. So it would require approval from Canada’s competition watchdog, several government agencies and federal Industry Minister Mélanie Joly – who will be the final arbiter .

Business reporters Irene Galea and Andrew Willis met the two CEOs Monday and pressed for details on key issues. Here’s what they told us .

Meanwhile, Bell Canada parent company BCE Inc. has held preliminary discussions with Telus and hired financial and legal advisers as it explores its options following Quebecor’s takeover proposal. BCE would weigh what concessions Ottawa might demand before making a formal offer.

Anthropic PBC made its debut on the stock market on Thursday, becoming one of the world’s most valuable public companies. It raised a record US$81.3-billion in its initial public offering, plus a further US$26-billion in a private placement of shares. It is the first major AI lab to tap public markets to help fund vast capital expenditures to build, train and run advanced models.

The public offering has been treated as a bellwether for the health of the AI sector, especially after investors were rattled by Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang’s resignation last week.

Meanwhile, two of Canada’s largest pension funds could stand to reap large gains on investments in Anthropic. The country’s largest pension fund, the Canada Pension Plan Investment Board, earlier this year disclosed a US$50-million investment in Anthropic. Ontario Teachers’ Pension Plan also invested in the same fundraising round. Anthropic’s Nasdaq trading debut will also usher in a parade of new investment offerings for Canadian investors.

As of Friday, the S&P 500 and the Dow were on track for a correction as Anthropic shares retreated after a blockbuster debut, dashing hopes that the listing would stabilize an AI ⁠trade already ​shaken by valuation concerns.

On Monday, Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem confirmed that he will not be seeking a second term when his seven-year appointment ends next June.

The field of candidates to replace him is expected to include the top economist at BlackRock Inc., several current and former central bankers, and at least two chief economists at the Big Six banks. The odds-on favourite is Jean Boivin, head of the BlackRock Investment Institute, the macroeconomic arm of the world’s largest asset manager.

The central bank’s board of directors has formed a search committee to select the next governor and the recruitment process is expected to be completed by spring 2027, the Bank of Canada said on Monday. While the governor is technically chosen by the board, in practice the final decision will rest with Prime Minister Mark Carney and Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne.

Ford Motor Co. has reopened its assembly plant in Oakville, Ont. to make heavy-duty pickup trucks, after more than two years. About 2,000 people have returned to work at the plant, which makes Ford’s F-Series Super range of large pickups for Canadian, U.S. and global markets.

The plant, which used to make the Ford Edge, closed in 2024 to be retooled for an electric car . Ford scrapped that plan amid slowing demand for EVs and began work to make the trucks, including the F-250, F-350 and F-450, trucks that are used in construction, agriculture and other commercial uses. The plant’s reopening is a rare bit of good news for parts suppliers that have been rocked by financial crises, market shocks, a pandemic and now trade war.

Canadian businesses have spent much of the last 18 months racing to adopt AI into their operations, all while the technology itself continues to rapidly develop. The Carney government too, is pushing employers to embrace the technology. The official goal, laid out in Ottawa’s AI for All strategy, is that AI adoption across businesses will rise from 12 per cent to 60 per cent by 2034.

But integrating AI into workplaces with different departments, personalities and hierarchies has not been smooth sailing, according to conversations with numerous employers, managers and workers in Canada. While use of the technology is accelerating, major chokepoints are emerging, threatening to derail the pace of adoption and upend goals companies have set for themselves.

In some workplaces, the AI rollout has been chaotic, with the push to use the technology exhausting workers and frustrating managers. Future of Work reporter Vanmala Subramaniam reports on the AI bottleneck , the challenges of adoption, and the stumbling blocks companies find themselves having to navigate.

stories.title: A funny — and not funny — SNL ‘Sister’ skit on elder care went viral. Here’s why
stories.summary: Viewed millions of times since its airing, the three-minute Saturday Night Live parody cuts close to home
stories.author: Sharon Kirkey
stories.content:
It got funnier the more she watched it, but what first struck social scientist Allison Williams about Saturday Night Live’s viral, infomercial-like spoof of elder care was how uncannily it mirrored her own research.

Viewed millions of times on social media since it aired on Nov. 14, the “Sister” parody opens with comedian John Mulaney’s character, dripping with false sincerity, worried about an elderly father who, he claims, “means the world to me.”

“So, when I noticed him start to slow down, I knew I needed to get him the best care possible.”

After nixing a nursing home or thousands-of-dollars-a-week private home care, “I didn’t know where to turn.

“That’s when I heard about Sister,” a live-in, round-the-clock “completely free” care provider, Mulaney narrates. “Now I don’t have to worry about dad getting the care and attention he needs, because my sister will do it, and I can get back to my life and the stuff I like to do.”

Monday - Saturday Free

NP Posted keeps you updated on the news of the day and the perspectives that define the National Post, while drawing your focus to some of the unexpected stories we like to tell. Delivered straight to your inbox Monday to Friday, with a weekend edition on Saturdays.

The three-minute sketch is a razor-sharp take on the visible and invisible loads women carry when they assume, and are expected to assume, the role of elder caregiver, said Williams, a professor in McMaster University’s faculty of science.

What resonated most was “Sister’s” conscientiousness and dutifulness, quitting everything — job, lease — and rushing back home to care for her father. It reflects “that kind of exasperation that, ‘This is my role; this is what I must do,’” Williams said.

“I’ve seen it so many times in my own research. Women don’t even stop to think, ‘Maybe there’s another way.’”

In the skit, “Dr. Grant” describes how “years of internalized sexism warps Sister’s brain into thinking caretaking is her responsibility and somehow, not yours.”

“Next, your text (“dad fell”) arrives, instantly activating her. And that’s it! You’re done for life. See you at the funeral.” A cartoonish graphic shows a man speeding off on a Jet Ski.

Screengrab from skit viewed millions of times on social media since it aired on Nov. 14, 2026, the Saturday Night Live “Sister” parody. Saturday Night Live/NBC

The skit was crafted by men, including American comedian and writer Streeter Seidell, who dedicated it to his sister on X.

It had social media and group chats buzzing with a mixture of humour and exasperation. “Thank you for giving me the gift of guilting my brothers this holiday season,” Jamie Steinberg, managing editor at Starry Constellation Magazine, responded to Seidell’s post. “Bravo! It was hilarious and not at the same time,” remarked another. Other commentators called it a brutal and uncomfortable takedown of gendered roles.

Granted, men are stepping up: According to StatCan, in 2022, almost one-quarter (23 per cent) of women provided unpaid care to adults with long-term conditions or disabilities. So, too, did 19 per cent of men.

Family sizes are decreasing, and in cases where the only child is male, he May be the only one available to take care of aging parents, Williams said. If he still has a full-time job, he might pull in his wife, or private care. “Men are generally better with logistical, problem-solving tasks, where care can be delegated,” she said.

Women (seven per cent) were slightly more likely to be “sandwich caregivers,” providing dual, unpaid care to both children and adults, than men (five per cent), according to the StatCan report.

Men are more likely to do home maintenance and outdoor work. Women, ON the other hand, Williams said, are more likely to assist with the daily activities of life, feeding, bathing, dressing, emotional support, scheduling and coordinating appointments and helping with medications.

In the SNL spoof, “Sister,” played by Jane Wickline, juggles phone calls with doctors, insurance companies, pharmacists, at one point yelling in frustration into her phone, “Speak to human. Speak to human.”

Women are more likely to go in, elbows up, and try to get all the work done themselves, Williams said: “The martyr syndrome.”

Elder care often grows more intense over time. Dementia and other chronic conditions make it more so.

Most families can’t afford private care, public support is limited and most aging parents want to remain in their own home, leaving families, more often women, to carry the burden.

Many “carer-workers” are in their peak career years (45 to 65), said Williams, who advocates for more “caregiver-friendly” workplaces and employers. Leaving a job not only affects a paycheque and benefits, “it affects our sense of purpose and meaning.”

“There’s not only an ethical imperative for employers to support them; there’s also a really strong business case,” Williams said.

Like a TV pharmaceutical ad, the SNL skit ends with a disclaimer: “Quantities are limited. Sister May break down without warning. Offer void if Sister has good therapist.”

“She will ultimately burn out, because that’s what the data show,” Williams said.

Therapy might make her more aware of stereotypical gender expectations and how women are expected to be “caring and warm and communal,” said Christy Zhou Koval, an assistant professor of organizational behaviour at Queen’s University’s Smith School of Business.

“A lot of women grow up with that kind of expectation, and they kind of grow into it,” she said.

“If you are aware of these psychological processes, you might be more likely to speak up for yourself, or propose an alternative division of labour: ‘Hey, why don’t you take on an aspect of care taking?’”

What struck Koval was “Sister’s” invisible, mental load — remembering appointments, anticipating her father’s needs, monitoring his blood pressure and salt intake. The toll of “just to be constantly thinking about all these things.”

“Even when you’re trying to relax, even when you’re trying to do work, even when you’re trying to sleep, this is still going on in your mind,” Koval said. “When you ruminate, you never get a true recovery from this engaging and taxing mental work.”

What also resonated with viewers was the father’s grumbling over his daughter’s monitoring of his salt intake. “She’s a b–ch,” he says across the kitchen table to his son, who gives his dad a “you got it” salute.

It’s more emotional cargo, Koval said: “Anytime they say no, or are being assertive, there is this unwelcome response.”

The burden shouldn’t be on women to speak up or ask for help, she said, though they can get help learning to do so through groups like the Ontario Caregivers Organizationor the Family Caregivers of British Columbia.

But the skit pokes at that family dynamic as well.

Another brother describes feeling overwhelmed by his dad’s medications. “Not Sister. She doesn’t get confused by that stuff at all. Or if she does, she hasn’t brought it up to me,” he said.

Because he hadn’t bothered asking.

Sharon Kirkey is a national reporter with National Post focusing on health and science stories. She is also a three-time National Newspaper Awards nominee, with a win for beat reporting.

stories.title: Tech outages show we’re too reliant on the U.S., experts say. Here’s how Canadians can prepare
stories.summary: The bigger issue, is that Canada doesn't own the technology it depends on, one analyst said.
stories.author: Beatriz Baleeiro
stories.content:
A string of recent technology outages has exposed how heavily Canada relies on U.S.-based tech companies, and experts say the disruptions are likely to keep happening.

Analysts say there’s no sign of a coordinated or malicious cyberattack and the Microsoft 365 outage appears to have been a server problem. The bigger issue, is that Canada doesn’t own the technology it depends on, one analyst said.

“I get people’s concern,” said Ritesh Kotak, a cybersecurity and technology analyst. “There is nothing tying all of these issues together and there’s nothing to suggest that it’s a co-ordinated cyber attack. We can only go on the information that’s been provided to us by authorities.”

He said the Microsoft 365 outage on Nov. 12 which took down platforms like Outlook and caused delays and disruptions, was a server issue and seems to be an isolated incident.

“The Microsoft outage definitely caused some heartburn for us,” said David Shipley, the CEO of New Brunswick cybersecurity firm Beauceron Security. “This thing (technology) that we think is magic is way more breakable than anybody ever appreciated.”

Kotak said there are “multiple” reasons some of the outages occurred and Canadians should trust what authorities are saying over online theories, but he added there’s a larger problem.

“The underlying theme here is that Canada doesn’t own the technology and we are subjected to what happens to our partners around the world,” said Kotak.

Routine updates, security patches and other malfunctions appear to have caused problems at Microsoft, JPMorgan Chase and Apple, and even the U.S. government’s FAA and NSA.

Unity Health Toronto, a hospital network, was affected by the global outage for most of Nov. 12 and Nov. 13. It declared a Code Grey, which is called when a hospital experiences an infrastructure failure. Other GTA hospitals also reported disruptions.

Traveller by complimentary phones at Pearson International Airport following lifted FAA ground stop.

On Nov. 13, passengers at Pea rson , Canada’s busiest airport, faced delays and cancellations as it worked to restore normal operations after the FAA grounded planes across the U.S. late that afternoon.

Monday brought a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase that left thousands of customers unable to reach online accounts at several major U.S. banks and the Zelle money transfer service.

On Tuesday, A pple said on its system status page that some its services were also affected. That same day, Marriott reported a technical issue that disrupted sign-ins on its website and app. The National Security Agency in the U.S. also appeared on the growing list.

“It’s been a hell of an unprecedented week, and it feels really bad because we’re getting it everywhere all at once,” said Shipley. “And it’s not going to stop.”

Questions about Canada’s reliance on U.S. technology come as Washington replaced its cyber chief on Thursday. The White House named Kirsten Davies, the Defense Department’s chief information officer, as national cyber director, replacing Sean Cairncross.

Kotak said Canada “isn’t immune to outages” and that the bigger issue is “digital sovereignty.” Most tech Canadians use daily is “heavily reliant” on U.S. companies, where much of the data is also stored. “If there is an extreme situation, sanctions or anything like that, it’s very clear that Canada would be cut off from certain digital systems,” he said.

Canada “is prepared for outages from a mission-critical and an infrastructure standpoint,” particularly in banking, he added.

“I feel confident in the sense that Canada is prepared in some ways, but in other ways, we have long way to go,” he said.

Shipley said upgrading Canada’s network infrastructure and building “a secure, nationwide, sovereign, and resilient internet is going to be expensive.”

For small businesses without IT departments, Kotak recommended listing all the technology they rely on, including inventory and payment systems, internet, communication and email. Individuals should do the same, focusing on email and any banking apps they use every day.

Kotak also suggested writing down connected devices, such as smart thermostats and smart locks, and planning for what to do if systems go down. That includes keeping key phone numbers somewhere other than your phone, such as on paper.

“You’ll be better prepared for these (outages), when the inevitable happens,” he said.

Phishing is another risk, Kotak added, such as emails with links that claim to come from IT, Microsoft or a bank, especially those asking to reset passwords due to the outage.

“Just be cognizant of those emails, hit the pause button, validate and verify and go directly to the source,” said Kotak. “Hackers and fraudsters are definitely going to take full advantage of this unprecedented time that we’re going through.”

About 72 hours of monetary preparedness to cover basic expenses is ideal, said Shipley.

Kotak says he’s “confident” in the Canadian banking system, which is “investing heavily” in cybersecurity, but people shouldn’t put all their eggs in one basket.

“Make sure you have cash on hand just in case systems go down,” he said. “What is that number? It really depends from individual to individual, family to family.”

Kotak suggested having enough for a few days of groceries, food, unexpected expenses and gas. He also recommends keeping a list of your account information, using two separate banks and two credit cards from different institutions and automating payments where possible.

“And the reason for that is if one temporarily goes down, at least you can still have access to funds. There could always be glitches and issues, so you need to protect yourself first,” he said.

Files from Matthew Daldalian and The Associated Press

stories.title: Discover ‘the anti-Whistler’ on the ski hills of the Kootenay Rockies
stories.summary: Along Southeastern B.C.’s Powder Highway, the slow-living ethos extends to the skiing itself
stories.author: Haley Steinberg
stories.content:
One thing is clear when you arrive in the Kootenay Rockies: These aren’t your big box store-loving, development-obsessed, corporate-owned mountain towns. Anchored by ski centres such as Nelson, Fernie, Golden and Revelstoke, the region in southeastern British Columbia is dotted with old mining towns and settlements – places with evocative names such as Risk and Hope Ranch, Deadwood Junction and Dun Roamin’ Ranch.

Arriving at the one-room airport in Trail, B.C. (coffee and tea are by donation), I waited as all 30 or so passengers picked up their bags from the luggage rack. Mine never showed up. When we phoned the number on the remaining suitcase’s ID tag, the owner, who we deduced had mistakenly taken my bag, said, “You know this means we’re relatives now.”

Bag in hand and one relation richer, I set out to tour two mountains along B.C.’s Powder Highway. This circuitous path connects eight alpine ski resorts, 20 backcountry lodges and several helicopter and cat-skiing experiences.

Nelson’s Whitewater Mountain Resort , in the Selkirk Mountains, is a roughly 20-minute drive from town. Somewhere along the route, cell service disappears. There’s no WiFi on the property, including in the rustic day lodge (and its fabulously named Coal Oil Johnny’s Pub), which has resisted the kinds of enlargements and upgrades that slowly degrade a place’s character. Inside, it’s all warm wood beams, picnic tables and snug, elbow-to-elbow seating.

These quirks May seem backward to some, but they’re all intentional and part of the resort’s old-school charm. The emphasis, both here and at Red Mountain , is on slowing down and speaking to other people. I am embarrassed to admit I couldn’t remember the last time I’d gone an entire day without cell service – or seen so many kids without phones sticking to their faces – and I was taken aback by how much I relished it.

The slow-living ethos extends to the skiing itself. There are no high-speed lifts at Whitewater and, with a yearly average of 40 feet of powder, there’s no need for snowmaking. When I visited in early February, after weeks of unseasonably warm temperatures, every person I spoke to, from our mountain hosts to servers in town, was deeply apologetic about the lack of “fresh pow.” Although I could sympathize, I assured them that apologies were not necessary. As an Ontarian, I found the conditions irreproachable, and I suspect this only made them feel sorry for me.

The resort is nestled in Ymir bowl, making it easy to navigate, with runs of varying difficulty – as well as cat tracks – leading to the base. One chair, Glory, provides access to the back of the mountain, doubling the resort’s terrain when it opened in 2010. Whitewater also offers plenty of exhilaration for backcountry skiers, such as traversing Ymir Peak, the area’s highest point at 2,400 metres.

Now for the food: It is the best ski hill fare I have come across in North America. The antithesis of the typical assortment of fried beige food, the menu originated with the previous co-owner Shelley Adams, a trained chef who is known locally for her Whitewater Cooks cookbooks. The Glory Bowl – a Whitewater staple of marinated tofu, veggies and basmati rice anointed in an addictive tahini sauce – is the pinnacle of what all ski hill food should be.

It’s perhaps unsurprising then that Nelson’s claim to fame is its dining scene. I ate everything from Mexican to Japanese to Italian. Marzano, located along the town’s main street, is a cozy modern Italian restaurant with a nice B.C. wine list. The roasted lingcod and Osoyoos pinot noir were superb.

Our visit coincided with the Kootenay Coldsmoke Powderfest, an annual event that features competitions as well as arts and culture programming. One night, we made our way to the United church for the Stellar Film Competition, where several hundred townspeople crammed into the pews to watch a slate of short films shot by locals. The People’s Choice award winner follows a self-described ski bum’s misadventures around town, which include challenging a local snowboarding hero to do a backflip while eating a meat pie (spoiler: he succeeds ).

The Josie Hotel offers a ski valet service, hillside barrel saunas and a restaurant with mountain views. Mitch Winton/Supplied

From Nelson, we drove an hour south to Rossland, 10 kilometres from the U.S. border. With a population of 4,000, the one-stoplight former mining town might be tiny, but it offers everything a visitor could need: A brewery (Rossland Beer Company), a supermarket known for its prepared foods (Ferraro’s), a liquor store and an Italian restaurant serving fresh pasta and seafood (Gabriella’s). Minutes away are Red Mountain Resort and the Josie Hotel , a swish Marriott property that, as I heard more than once, arrived about five years too early. Now, its high-end amenities – a ski valet service, hillside barrel saunas and an elegant restaurant with mountain views – are a main draw.

At 3,850 skiable acres, Red Mountain Resort is the oldest resort in Western Canada and significantly larger than Whitewater. One of its unique features is the 1940s-built, ON-mountain cabins that skiers can visit, many currently inhabited by descendants of the original owners. Some residents May raise a sheet to let passersby know when they’re in. There are also warming huts on the mountain, some with wood-burning stoves. With so much varied terrain – moguls, glades, groomed and ungroomed runs – I blissfully skied from the first chair to the last. Afterward, it was on to the lively Rafters Bar for après-ski, where shotskis are tipped and Caesars and nachos are downed to the stomping sounds of a live band.

But the true spirit of Red Mountain is best captured by the sentiment, “Fight the Man. Own the Mountain,” a message that’s plastered across the skis of many locals. It refers to a campaign to keep the resort independent (the hill has never been owned by a chain, bank or big corporation) and avoid the trend of megaresort mergers and acquisitions through crowdfunding.

In other words, it is the anti-Whistler. One mountain guide told me that when Red solicited feedback on adding a high-speed chairlift, they found that locals didn’t want one – they liked being able to spend the time talking to their kids.

Nelson is about a one-hour drive from Trail Regional Airport (YZZ), or 30 minutes from the West Kootenay Regional Airport in Castlegar (YCG). Rent a car or book a shuttle from either airport to get to Nelson (a public transit option is also available).

Lift tickets at Whitewater are $154 for adults and cheaper when booked online. At RED Mountain , peak-season adult tickets are $209 and cheaper when booked online.

Skiers take note: flights out of Trail are susceptible to weather delays. On the day we were flying out, conditions were touch-and-go, so we decided to fly through Kelowna airport (a 3½-hour drive away) to avoid any delays. Pacific Coastal Airlines says they will shuttle passengers to Penticton airport in the case of inclement weather, but it’s unclear how effectively this works in practice when many travellers have connections in Vancouver.

The writer was a guest of Destination British Columbia, which did not review or approve this article. Stories are based on merit; The Globe does not guarantee coverage.

Editor’s note: A previous version of this article incorrectly stated that Red Mountain Resort has 4,200 skiable acres; that is its total acreage. The resort has 3,850 skiable acres.

When I visited in early February, after weeks of unseasonably warm temperatures, every person I spoke to, from our mountain hosts to servers in town, was deeply apologetic about the lack of “fresh pow.” Although I could sympathize, I assured them that apologies were not necessary. As an Ontarian, I found the conditions irreproachable, and I suspect this only made them feel sorry for me.

content_blocks.text: The resort is nestled in Ymir bowl, making it easy to navigate, with runs of varying difficulty – as well as cat tracks – leading to the base. One chair, Glory, provides access to the back of the mountain, doubling the resort’s terrain when it opened in 2010. Whitewater also offers plenty of exhilaration for backcountry skiers, such as traversing Ymir Peak, the area’s highest point at 2,400 metres.

content_blocks.text: Now for the food: It is the best ski hill fare I have come across in North America. The Glory Bowl – a Whitewater staple of marinated tofu, veggies and basmati rice anointed in an addictive tahini sauce – is the pinnacle of what all ski hill food should be.

content_blocks.text: Our visit coincided with the Kootenay Coldsmoke Powderfest, an annual event that features competitions as well as arts and culture programming. One night, we made our way to the United church for the Stellar Film Competition, where several hundred townspeople crammed into the pews to watch a slate of short films shot by locals. The People’s Choice award winner follows a self-described ski bum’s misadventures around town, which include challenging a local snowboarding hero to do a backflip while eating a meat pie (spoiler: he succeeds ).

content_blocks.text: From Nelson, we drove an hour south to Rossland, 10 kilometres from the U.S. border. With a population of 4,000, the one-stoplight former mining town might be tiny, but it offers everything a visitor could need: A brewery (Rossland Beer Company), a supermarket known for its prepared foods (Ferraro’s), a liquor store and an Italian restaurant serving fresh pasta and seafood (Gabriella’s). Minutes away are Red Mountain Resort and the Josie Hotel , a swish Marriott property that, as I heard more than once, arrived about five years too early. Now, its high-end amenities – a ski valet service, hillside barrel saunas and an elegant restaurant with mountain views – are a main draw.

content_blocks.text: At 3,850 skiable acres, Red Mountain Resort is the oldest resort in Western Canada and significantly larger than Whitewater. One of its unique features is the 1940s-built, ON-mountain cabins that skiers can visit, many currently inhabited by descendants of the original owners. Some residents May raise a sheet to let passersby know when they’re in. There are also warming huts on the mountain, some with wood-burning stoves. With so much varied terrain – moguls, glades, groomed and ungroomed runs – I blissfully skied from the first chair to the last. Afterward, it was on to the lively Rafters Bar for après-ski, where shotskis are tipped and Caesars and nachos are downed to the stomping sounds of a live band.

content_blocks.text: But the true spirit of Red Mountain is best captured by the sentiment, “Fight the Man. Own the Mountain,” a message that’s plastered across the skis of many locals. It refers to a campaign to keep the resort independent (the hill has never been owned by a chain, bank or big corporation) and avoid the trend of megaresort mergers and acquisitions through crowdfunding.

On the day we were flying out, conditions were touch-and-go, so we decided to fly through Kelowna airport (a 3½-hour drive away) to avoid any delays. Pacific Coastal Airlines says they will shuttle passengers to Penticton airport in the case of inclement weather, but it’s unclear how effectively this works in practice when many travellers have connections in Vancouver.
