stories.title: A new heli-ski outfit in B.C. brings you where no one has skied before
stories.summary: With Gold Rush Heli Skiing in Atlin, the views are pristine, the powder is perfect, and the personalities are just as delightful
stories.author: John Briley
stories.content:
In a land once legendary for its fierce weather, intimidating landscapes and feisty characters, life as a ski tourist is downright cushy. I’m thinking this as I descend through thigh-deep powder high in the Boundary Range of British Columbia, a realm of colossal alpine faces, couloirs and spires by the Alaska and Yukon borders.

I’ve just stepped off a helicopter – with two other visitors and two guides – and onto a summit rendered sparkling white by the previous day’s storm. It’s March 2026, and we’re the first-ever client group with Gold Rush Heli Skiing, based in the lakeside town of Atlin, in northern B.C. The outfit explores a vast area – 262,236 hectares – so we couldn’t possibly see, let alone ski, it all in four days.

This region funnels storms off the Gulf of Alaska but is far enough inland that most of the snow falls as feathery powder. Gold Rush takes only eight skiers a week, lending credence to the claim it advertises: “Fresh tracks aren’t a hope; they’re a promise.”

On Day 1, the promise delivers, with an asterisk. As our group, led by guide Johnny Mellis , arcs 1,000 metres down a mountain face, we find mostly wind-packed snow. It’s indeed untracked, but not the nearly weightless fluff I’d come for. And because almost all this land we’re skiing sits above the tree line, and a blistering wind strafed these mountains the week before, even Mellis, who guided for Canadian Mountain Holidays for 35 years, cannot find consistently soft snow.

But this adds to our collective sense of discovery as we chopper among steeples of cretaceous-era rock, land on narrow ridges and ski, occasionally where it’s unlikely anyone has ever skied before.

The lodge offers six deluxe loft cabins with a hot tub and sauna. Andrew Strain/Supplied

The Taku River Tlingit lived here for millennia before prospectors discovered gold in Atlin, B.C., in 1898. The town boomed, burned and was rebuilt twice before transforming into a destination that drew adventure tourists avoiding Europe during the Second World War. They were attracted to Atlin in part because of how hard it was to reach.

Today, with a population of 220 and a quaint cluster of buildings with early 19th-century architecture, Atlin remains at the frontier of adventure, which Gold Rush Heli Skiing founder Brian McCutcheon found irresistible.

With climate change, he says, these northern latitudes represent the future of heli-skiing, although he acknowledges working in such a remote area makes it hard to get things done sometimes.

McCutcheon, a jocular, industrious Canadian, changed contractors to finish building six luxury cabins that were supposed to be ready for our arrival. As a result of the delay, he instead puts us up in a motel in Atlin, a five-minute drive from the Gold Rush Lodge.

That night as we dine on seared tuna, overlooking views of frozen Lake Atlin, a storm pulses in. We awake to 25 centimetres of fresh snow but, with the maelstrom raging, we must wait to fly. No problem, says McCutcheon.

“You can snowmobile, cross-country ski, snowshoe or go ice fishing until the weather breaks,” he tells us over breakfast. “The sun doesn’t set until 8 p.m., so we have time.” I stare out at the lake, an infinite canvas of white, and I want to be out there.

Minutes later, I’m kicking and gliding on cross-country skis through spruce forest, past the town’s Victorian homes and onto the lake, which spans 775 square kilometres, the largest natural lake in B.C. I circle an island and angle back toward shore, where I meet local resident Rosa Brown walking her Aussie Shepherd mix. Brown tells me why she moved to Atlin after 25 years in the Yukon.

“This,” she says, gesturing at the nature enveloping us. “When there’s so much beauty around, it does something to you inside.” I’m nodding in agreement when I notice blue sky over the mountains, a promising sign for our heli-skiing fortunes, and excuse myself to sprint back to the lodge.

The ensuing days are a powder skier’s fantasy – long, sustained sequences of snow blasting up from our skis and billowing into our faces. The views are astounding: We see slivers of frozen lake, peaks stacked to the horizon and, after one run, the terminus of a short-distance, narrow-gauge rail line that brought tourists here 100 years ago.

A couple of caveats: If you, like me, love to ski in the trees, Gold Rush’s massive alpine terrain might leave you pining for pines. Also, the lodge, while delightful, lacks a singular great room where guests can recline together around a roaring fire, although the adjacent cabins – which are now ready for guests – will no doubt serve as their own sanctuaries.

Gold Rush has some of the nicest staff you’ll ever meet. By the end of my stay, we’re all sharing inside jokes, gourmet meals and acoustic guitar jams in the lodge bar.

On our final night, we hang out at the local Atlin saloon with miners, Tinglit fishing guides and grad students from Whitehorse. A trio of dogs wander the room, Moosehead draught flows and the other heli guests hug newfound friends, vowing to return for someone’s engagement party and again for more skiing.

When it’s this easy, why not?

Gold Rush Heliskiing is located in Atlin, B.C., two hours south of Whitehorse, Yukon. Guests will be picked up in Whitehorse. Four-day, five-night heli-ski trips start at US$13,500 and include meals, alcohol, accommodation, equipment and permit fees. goldrushheliskiing.com

Special to The Globe and Mail

The writer was a guest of Gold Rush Heli Skiing, which did not review or approve this article. Stories are based on merit; The Globe does not guarantee coverage.

I circle an island and angle back toward shore, where I meet local resident Rosa Brown walking her Aussie Shepherd mix. Brown tells me why she moved to Atlin after 25 years in the Yukon.

'It’s possible to change,' Steve Patry says about his latest film, Un Souffle à la fois. 'I believe in rehabilitation'

Filmmaker Steve Patry's documentary Un Souffle à la fois (A Breath at a Time) follows men who are seeking help to confront their violent behaviour toward women in relationships. (Evan Buhler / Montreal Gazette)

November 21, 2026 at 6:55 a.m.

Steve Patry makes films about people in difficult situations, often on the margins of society. The Quebec director profiled ex-convicts adapting to life on the outside in Prisons to Prisons (2014); Indigenous inmates at a Correctional Service of Canada healing lodge in Waseskun (2016); people experiencing homelessness in I Might Be Dead By Tomorrow (2020); and a forest-dwelling hermit and his feline entourage in These Wild Cats (2024).

His latest film, Un Souffle à la fois (A Breath at a Time), which screens Tuesday at 5:30 p.m. at Maison Théâtre and Thursday at 3:30 p.m. at the Cinémathèque québécoise as part of the Rencontres internationales du documentaire de Montréal (Ridm) film festival, is no different. In fact, the idea took root nearly a decade ago at a screening for Waseskun.

A counsellor at a Gatineau centre that helps men with a history of conjugal violence who are struggling with emotional regulation came up to talk to him after the film. By the end of their conversation, Patry sensed he had the makings of a future project.

“I didn’t know anything about this type of accompaniment or the existence of these centres, which have existed for at least 20 years,” he told The Gazette. “What grabbed me was the thought that it might be possible to talk about the prevention of violence from a point of view I had never seen or heard — the side of the authors of violence.”

The National Film Board of Canada production takes us inside the above noted help centre, called Donne-toi une chance. We sit in on difficult, tense and intimate conversations — both one-on-one and group sessions, in French and English — between men and the counsellors who attempt to provide them with the tools to think and act differently in response to their anger.

“It was a film that was challenging, ON many levels,” Patry said. “There was a personal process I had to go through. In documentary, they say you have to love the subject to devote yourself to a film. Here, it wasn’t a question of liking or not liking the men who appeared in front of the camera. Rather, it was about giving myself the right to have a certain empathy for these men, so that I could listen to them and be interested in them — empathy without condoning their actions.

“I couldn’t be complacent. Some of them had serious violent behaviours. I couldn’t make them into victims, but I had to have empathy for their distress and their lives in order to be interested in them. When I had that realization, it changed everything.”

Viewers May be surprised to find themselves having similar feelings as they witness these men wrestle with their pent-up emotions, their actions and their past, and try to find a new way forward. They are heard, assisted and challenged by the counsellors at the centre, whom Patry calls “the heroes of this whole process. I was going there for a few days in a row, every two weeks. They’re there every day. They have to confront difficult realities, heavy cases like femicide, and suicidal people.”

He doesn’t gloss things over in the film. There are small successes, and there are setbacks. The real results of what we see on-screen May take years to reveal themselves.

“It’s micro-changes,” Patry said. “That’s what interested me, to see if it’s possible to change — and we see that it is, but it takes time and it’s not a straight line. We don’t follow someone for three years; it wasn’t that kind of film.”

Though his documentary doesn’t provide easy answers, Patry hopes by revealing the difficult, but necessary work being done at these centres, it May provide food for thought.

“My wish is to show men it’s possible to ask for help,” he said. “It’s possible to change. That May be a bit naive, but I think if it can participate in the debate and shed light on the many initiatives to prevent conjugal violence and models of toxic masculinity, this is one part of the solution.

“It’s a bit taboo to talk about help for men, but it’s something that has to be put forward. I believe in rehabilitation. It’s not easy, but I would like people to understand that each person can change and abandoning them won’t fix the situation. If you want to help the victims, you have to help the perpetrators. It all goes together.”

AT A Glance: Un Souffle à la fois (A Breath at a Time)screens Tuesday at 5:30 p.m. at Maison Théâtre and Thursday at 3:30 p.m. at the Cinémathèque québécoise as part of the Rencontres internationales du documentaire de Montréal (Ridm) film festival. There will be French and English subtitles for both screenings. For tickets and information, visit ridm.CA tdunlevy@postmedia.com

stories.title: The curious persistence of the medical fax
stories.summary: The continuing screech of the antiquated technology underscores the lack of modern data sharing in Canadian health care
stories.author: The Editorial Board
stories.content:
When was the last time you sent a fax? If you work in a doctor’s office, the answer is: probably today. Most people haven’t relied on the antiquated workplace technology since the 1980s or ’90s, yet it remains oddly ubiquitous in health care settings. In an age of precision medicine and digital everything, it’s time to box up the screeching machines for good.

For starters, doctors themselves don’t like being tethered to the things. The issue snuck up recently when Ontario’s doctors flagged long patient wait times for specialist care, after a survey found 22 per cent of respondents with a chronic condition waited six months or longer for an appointment.

To improve access, the Ontario Medical Association urged the province to adopt a team-based model of specialist care, with physicians working alongside other health professionals to deliver treatment more quickly. It also advocated for a central intake system, noting that currently, doctors often rely on word-of-mouth or social media group chats to find out where to fax patient referrals.

The proposals – including the call to scrap the fax in favour of e-referrals – are sensible. The tyranny of the fax machine is a persistent symptom of a larger malady: outdated data sharing across Canada’s health sector.

According to the Canadian Medical Association, the health-care system still relies on faxes because they are seen as a secure way to share confidential patient information, despite the significant risk of misdirected faxes leading to privacy breaches. Health providers in Ontario alone send an estimated 152 million faxes a year.

Although hospitals and clinics have their own digital systems to store patient records, there is no way to exchange this information between systems.

The CMA says 78 per cent of doctors can’t share patient information with doctors outside their own practice, not to mention hospitals, labs or pharmacies. Relying on faxes rather than integrated electronic medical records adds to doctors’ paperwork and burnout, delays patient care and means patients can’t easily access their own clinical files, it says.

Welcome to 2026, when tech giants have managed to build advanced AI systems researchers warn could pose an existential threat to humanity , but no one has figured out how to seamlessly get the X-ray results from one’s trip to the emergency department (along with the medical notes transcribed by an AI scribe) to the family doctor drowning in paperwork, or to the specialist who can help.

There are some faint signs of progress, including Ontario’s creation of a centralized electronic medical record system for family doctors intended to make it easier to share patient information.

When the plan was announced in March, Dr. Jane Philpott, chair of the government’s primary care action team, said the system will help family doctors deliver more co-ordinated care and reduce administrative burdens. However, the system is voluntary and does not include specialists. The fax machine screeches on.

The federal government has also taken notice of the problem of information silos. Bill S-5, the Connected Care for Canadians Act , is winding its way through the House of Commons. It would compel tech companies to make it easier to share digital health information safely between different health data systems, to improve patient and provider access to medical records.

The bill would help rid doctors’ offices of the dreaded fax, a throwback so comical it made a cameo in an episode of The Pitt , the one where a cyberattack threw Dr. Robby’s ER back to an era of handwritten charts and dry-erase boards, and young staffers had to learn how to use (and unjam) one.

This is where the fax machine belongs: in the collective memory and inside jokes of people of a certain age, reminiscing about a time when things were both simpler and more complex.

It has no place in the health-care system of the future, the one Canadians will increasingly rely on as a rapidly aging population demands ever more sophisticated, well co-ordinated and timely health care.

Canada’s health-care system has had decades to catch up to the administrative norms of the rest of society. Governments should help it take one final step – stat – by replacing its warbling faxes with comprehensive and compatible digital systems. Patients, and their records, are waiting.

The bill would help rid doctors’ offices of the dreaded fax, a throwback so comical it made a cameo in an episode of The Pitt , the one where a cyberattack threw Dr. Robby’s ER back to an era of handwritten charts and dry-erase boards, and young staffers had to learn how to use (and unjam) one.
This is where the fax machine belongs: in the collective memory and inside jokes of people of a certain age, reminiscing about a time when things were both simpler and more complex.

It has no place in the health-care system of the future, the one Canadians will increasingly rely on as a rapidly aging population demands ever more sophisticated, well co-ordinated and timely health care.

Canada’s health-care system has had decades to catch up to the administrative norms of the rest of society. Governments should help it take one final step – stat – by replacing its warbling faxes with comprehensive and compatible digital systems. Patients, and their records, are waiting.

Most people haven’t relied on the antiquated workplace technology since the 1980s or ’90s, yet it remains oddly ubiquitous in health care settings. In an age of precision medicine and digital everything, it’s time to box up the screeching machines for good.

stories.title: Windsor bed-building competition raises money for program helping local children
stories.summary: A friendly competition among Windsor-Essex home-building and real estate professionals is helping put beds within reach for local children in need.
stories.author: Chris Campbell
stories.content:
A friendly competition among Windsor-Essex home-building and real estate professionals is helping put beds within reach for local children in need.

The event was held on World Children’s Day, with proceeds supporting the organization’s Kids Building Beds for Kids program.

The initiative gives high school skilled trades students an opportunity to develop leadership skills while building beds for children in financially insecure families.

Brian Cyncora of Sleep in Heavenly Peace Windsor says the program has been running for five years and has involved close to 350 students.

He says it gives young people an opportunity to put their skills to work for a meaningful cause while preparing for careers in the skilled trades.

Sleep in Heavenly Peace builds and delivers beds to children who do not have a proper place to sleep. Cyncora says the organization works with families to identify genuine needs and help parents who cannot afford to provide beds for their children.

He says the opportunity to make a difference firsthand is also meaningful for the volunteers involved.

“She said, I came back to the shop, and I cried for half an hour. And it has such a sense of meaning to every one of our people in a different way.”

Sleep in Heavenly Peace Windsor is part of a volunteer-driven organization dedicated to ensuring no child has to sleep on the floor.

stories.title: Mmfa celebrates its signature fundraiser, ROM Immortal Gala spotlights climate change
stories.summary: Montreal Museum of Fine Arts raises more than $2 million, while Royal Ontario Museum celebrates climate change initiative
stories.author: Nolan Bryant
stories.content:
The evening of Nov. 7 saw more than $2-million raised in Montreal for the city’s Museum of Fine Art. The Museum Ball is the institution’s signature annual fundraiser, having raised many millions for the 166-year-old organization over more than six decades. This year’s event, titled “Returning to Love,” was a nod to the museum’s current exhibition Chiharu Shiota: The Soul Trembles . It’s the largest solo show to date of the Berlin-based Japanese artist, whose handwoven webs of red, black and white thread, all site-specific, are on view through February.

Cocktails and an after-hours look at the exhibit were the first orders of business, followed by dinner. The 800 guests in attendance trickled into various galleries that were set up as individual dining rooms, each with their own mood linked to the theme. Sculptor and installation artist Karilee Fuglem, one of the evening’s scenographic artists, installed strips of reflective material that were suspended to create what she called an “air-light-shadow drawing” in one gallery. Back this year were the couple of hundred members of the museum’s Young Philanthropists’ Circle, who filed in after dinner for the Museum After-Ball, which kept the celebration going well into the night thanks to the band Broken Nails and DJ Dr. MaD. This year’s ball was presented by IG Private Wealth Management and co-chaired by Rana Ghorayeb, executive vice-president, head of real estate at La Caisse; Yves Lalumière, president and CEO of Tourisme Montréal; and Annamaria Testani, head of strategy, advisor and client experience at IG Wealth Management.

On the evening of Nov. 2, the Royal Ontario Museum held the second edition of its Immortal Gala, a black-tie fundraiser in support of the Rom’s exhibitions, research and educational programming. Central this year was the Rom’s climate change initiative. The museum was reportedly the first in North America to appoint a curator of climate change, Dr. Soren Brothers, who leads the organization’s climate strategy and works to integrate climate science and sustainability into the Rom’s existing and new collections.

Honoured at the event were renowned photographer Edward Burtynsky and John Bianchini, chair and CEO of engineering, project management and professional services firm Hatch. The pair, who are longtime friends and collaborators, were celebrated for their extraordinary contributions to environmental stewardship, public awareness and innovation in their respective fields. Instead of the usual sit-down dinner, the night featured a cocktail-style format: food stations inspired by Canada’s landscape (think wild salmon on a “rock” of dehydrated grains) bordered the Samuel Hall Currelly Gallery. In the centre were lounges set up for each of the evening’s main sponsors and supporters including Prestige Sponsor The Hennick Family Foundation, The Browning Watt Foundation (Roly Browning Watt is set to co-chair next year’s gala) and W. Bruce. C. Bailey. Guests, of which there were several hundred, had after-hours access to a number of galleries, where curators were on-hand to share insights into their research. Helen Burstyn and her daughter Amy Burstyn Fritz served as co-chairs, and author Margaret Atwood served as honorary chair.

stories.title: Ontario Liberals to name new leader after weeks of voting, months of campaigning
stories.summary: Toronto - Ontario Liberals are getting ready to name their new party leader, with results from members' ranked ballots set to be revealed later today.
stories.author: Allison Jones and Liam Casey The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - Former MP Navdeep Bains eked out a narrow victory Saturday to become the next Ontario Liberal leader, pledging to focus now on uniting the party and getting it in fighting shape for the next election.

Bains received 50.3 per cent of the vote on the third and final ballot at the party’s leadership convention, just a few points ahead of his next closest competitor, provincial caucus member and former hospital executive Lee Fairclough, who received 49.7 per cent of the vote.

After the results were announced in front of a crowd of more than 1,000 Liberals gathered in downtown Toronto, Bains took to the stage thanking his fellow contestants.

Ontario Liberals have selected Navdeep Bains as their new leader, emerging as victor less than one percentage point ahead of his next closest competitor, provincial caucus member Lee Fairclough. After receiving 50.3 per cent of the vote on the third and final ballot at the party’s leadership convention, Bains took to the stage and thanked his fellow contestants. (Nov. 21, 2026)

“This May be the end of a leadership race, ladies and gentlemen, but this is just the beginning of our campaign to replace Doug Ford and the (Progressive) Conservative Party of Ontario,” he said.

Bains is likely to face several hurdles on that road, including not having a seat in the legislature. His two predecessors were also without a seat and some party members had suggested during this race that it was time to select a leader who already has a voice in Queen’s Park.

He suggested at a media availability later in the day that he does want to seek a seat, but does not yet have a plan for when and where.

“I’ll definitely be running, and the determination around the exact location will be made at the appropriate time,” he said.

From outside the party, Bains is likely to face opposition attacks based on his past with the Justin Trudeau federal government. Progressive Conservative cabinet minister Graham McGregor, speaking at the leadership event as an observer, congratulated Bains but gave a preview of the narrative critics are looking to build.

“Certainly, in my region in Peel, we remember well when he was one of the biggest supporters of Justin Trudeau, not only as prime minister but when he was running for Liberal leader in the first place,” McGregor said.

“So we know that connection very well. I think Ontarians know that well.”

Bains conceded that the next several years before an election that May happen as late as 2030 won’t be easy.

“It’s going to be hard,” he said. “It’s going to be really, really hard. But we’re in it together.”

Bains is new to provincial elected office, but previously represented Mississauga ridings federally as a Liberal MP for 13 years, and served as federal minister of innovation, science and industry.

Before entering politics he was a senior financial analyst at Ford Motor Company, and after leaving Parliament in 2021, he worked as an executive at Cibc and later at Rogers Communications.

He spoke in his victory speech about his family, in particular his parents, who moved to Ontario 50 years ago from a small village in Rajasthan in India. His dad learned cabinet-making as a trade and his mother worked the night shift at a factory, he said.

This province provided opportunities for his parents and for himself, Bains said, and he worries that those same opportunities are no longer available.

“One in four people in my community of Mississauga visit the food bank, who have a job, who have multiple jobs, who play by the rules and are falling further and further behind,” he said. “The reason why that is, is because Doug Ford and the Conservatives have abandoned the fight, they are not in it for the people.”

Bains becomes the party’s third leader since former premier Kathleen Wynne resigned following the party’s sweeping defeat in the 2018 election.

Steven Del Duca was chosen as leader in 2020 but resigned two years later after a disappointing election result, and Bonnie Crombie served as leader from late 2023 until early this year, when she left following a weak leadership vote at an annual general meeting.

This leadership race started with five contestants and ended with four, as housing advocate Eric Lombardi dropped out partway through. Former government staffer Dylan Marando finished last, with 9.3 per cent of the vote on the first ballot.

He was dropped for the second ballot, ON which provincial caucus member and former bank executive Stephanie Bowman finished last, with 15.7 per cent.

In a speech before the results were announced, Bowman said that at the end of the day, some people in the room would be disappointed.

“Of course they will, but I’m asking you to keep showing up, keep working for our party and our province,” she said. “We came into this room as four teams. We must leave as one.”

paragraphs: Toronto - Former MP Navdeep Bains eked out a narrow victory Saturday to become the next Ontario Liberal leader, pledging to focus now on uniting the party and getting it in fighting shape for the next election.

Bains received 50.3 per cent of the vote on the third and final ballot at the party’s leadership convention, just a few points ahead of his next closest competitor, provincial caucus member and former hospital executive Lee Fairclough, who received 49.7 per cent of the vote.
After the results were announced in front of a crowd of more than 1,000 Liberals gathered in downtown Toronto, Bains took to the stage thanking his fellow contestants.

Ontario Liberals have selected Navdeep Bains as their new leader, emerging as victor less than one percentage point ahead of his next closest competitor, provincial caucus member Lee Fairclough. After receiving 50.3 per cent of the vote on the third and final ballot at the party’s leadership convention, Bains took to the stage and thanked his fellow contestants. (Nov. 21, 2026)
“This May be the end of a leadership race, ladies and gentlemen, but this is just the beginning of our campaign to replace Doug Ford and the (Progressive) Conservative Party of Ontario,” he said.

Bains is likely to face several hurdles on that road, including not having a seat in the legislature. His two predecessors were also without a seat and some party members had suggested during this race that it was time to select a leader who already has a voice in Queen’s Park.
He suggested at a media availability later in the day that he does want to seek a seat, but does not yet have a plan for when and where.
“I’ll definitely be running, and the determination around the exact location will be made at the appropriate time,” he said.

From outside the party, Bains is likely to face opposition attacks based on his past with the Justin Trudeau federal government. Progressive Conservative cabinet minister Graham McGregor, speaking at the leadership event as an observer, congratulated Bains but gave a preview of the narrative critics are looking to build.

“Certainly, in my region in Peel, we remember well when he was one of the biggest supporters of Justin Trudeau, not only as prime minister but when he was running for Liberal leader in the first place,” McGregor said.
“So we know that connection very well. I think Ontarians know that well.”
Bains conceded that the next several years before an election that May happen as late as 2030 won’t be easy.
“It’s going to be hard,” he said. “It’s going to be really, really hard. But we’re in it together.”
Bains is new to provincial elected office, but previously represented Mississauga ridings federally as a Liberal MP for 13 years, and served as federal minister of innovation, science and industry.
Before entering politics he was a senior financial analyst at Ford Motor Company, and after leaving Parliament in 2021, he worked as an executive at Cibc and later at Rogers Communications.

He spoke in his victory speech about his family, in particular his parents, who moved to Ontario 50 years ago from a small village in Rajasthan in India. His dad learned cabinet-making as a trade and his mother worked the night shift at a factory, he said.
This province provided opportunities for his parents and for himself, Bains said, and he worries that those same opportunities are no longer available.

“One in four people in my community of Mississauga visit the food bank, who have a job, who have multiple jobs, who play by the rules and are falling further and further behind,” he said. “The reason why that is, is because Doug Ford and the Conservatives have abandoned the fight, they are not in it for the people.”
Bains becomes the party’s third leader since former premier Kathleen Wynne resigned following the party’s sweeping defeat in the 2018 election.

Steven Del Duca was chosen as leader in 2020 but resigned two years later after a disappointing election result, and Bonnie Crombie served as leader from late 2023 until early this year, when she left following a weak leadership vote at an annual general meeting.

This leadership race started with five contestants and ended with four, as housing advocate Eric Lombardi dropped out partway through. Former government staffer Dylan Marando finished last, with 9.3 per cent of the vote on the first ballot.
He was dropped for the second ballot, ON which provincial caucus member and former bank executive Stephanie Bowman finished last, with 15.7 per cent.

“Of course they will, but I’m asking you to keep showing up, keep working for our party and our province,” she said. “We came into this room as four teams. We must leave as one.”

stories.title: B.C.’s new government must make the province an easier place to grow a modern economy
stories.summary: Too many of the province’s best and brightest are moving elsewhere to build their companies
stories.author: Dan Burgar
stories.content:
Dan Burgar is the founder and CEO of Frontier Collective.

David Eby’s own-goal election call has given British Columbians a new government and a chance for bold action to fix B.C.’s economy.

In Vancouver, voters also opted for change in electing Pete Fry as mayor.

Premier Lorne Doerkson, a B.C. Conservative sworn in on Friday, deserves credit for his focus on economic issues. He will now have serious work to do.

Decades of bipartisan neglect has led to a budget deficit of $13.3-billion atop ever-increasing debt. We are years behind in implementing a real innovation agenda to build an economy that will dig us out of the hole.

The province had been coasting on its worthy foundations of resources, real estate and a very talented population. But we cannot count on major federal projects to carry the entire resource sector, property is in a downturn and the population growth that papered over economic cracks is finished.

I’ve spent the last decade building innovation ecosystems with Frontier Collective, and I’m seeing an accelerating number of very talented workers and company founders leaving for places that make it easier to start a business and attract the risk capital they need to scale up.

If we don’t invest now in growth and keeping our best companies and people here, amid one of the biggest technological revolutions ever, we risk becoming a place where great companies are born but create wealth somewhere else.

B.C. should be backing our best people, leading at the technological frontier and creating conditions for companies to make long-term bets.

A successful innovation economy will require, above all, a new approach. What’s holding us back? Let’s begin in Vancouver.

Municipal decisions are more important than we think. Mr. Fry should speed up and liberalize permitting and zoning for innovation, lab and advanced manufacturing space. Delays mean lost opportunities.

Vancouver city council has already debated reviving and accelerating a central technology and innovation hub to serve as the centre of gravity for its ecosystem. This is a kind of “third space” where deal-making happens, people collaborate on prototypes in shared labs, and teams from different industries create new product and service crossovers to mutual benefit.

Newlab in Brooklyn and Station F in Paris are great entrepreneur-run (not government-run) examples to look to. It’s the kind of engine and flywheel setup that’s powered by in-person collaboration that just can’t happen over Zoom. The next council should move beyond debate and create the conditions for it to happen, while encouraging a pro-business environment everywhere.

Our inability to build enough affordable housing drives high costs that ripple throughout the economy, one of the main reasons for top talent and founders leaving (or not even considering) B.C.

Much municipal funding for day-to-day spending on infrastructure comes from development charges and permit fees that, together, can add many thousands of dollars to the cost of each new housing unit. Do new leaders (and voters) have the courage to reform municipal taxation, unlock much-needed new housing and bring down housing costs?

City and provincial procurement should also give local startups the “anchor” customer they May need to go from zero to one, powering local jobs and economies instead of giant foreign vendors. We must make municipal and provincial procurement a legitimate first-customer pathway for B.C. startups. City-owned land is another growth lever that can be powered up for mixed-use leases and development with little upfront spending.

On the provincial side, continuing to delay more serious investment will cost us talent, companies and capital deployed elsewhere. Retaining and scaling B.C.-founded companies must be an explicit economic development goal with measurable outcomes.

Voters should ask our new provincial government what they will do to work with municipalities to drive down the cost and complexity that gets in the way of people finding or building places to live and work.

A new government cannot turn B.C. into Silicon Valley overnight, nor should it, but it can turn B.C. into an easier place to start and grow the companies of the future.

Key questions: How fast can a company start? Can it hire the best people from anywhere? Can it access capital? And can it scale up without moving to Seattle, San Jose or Toronto?

The new Conservative government also has an opportunity to link our resource, energy and innovation sectors thanks to B.C.’s clean power advantage for AI and computer centres. Innovation need not happen in silos; better connecting B.C. tech companies with the resource sector and its wealth of experience will lead to more profitable and greener resource projects.

The window of opportunity to put our economy on firmer footing is only a few years, not decades, and every cycle we wait costs us the founders and companies we most want to keep.

British Columbians have voted for change. It is now up to our new leaders to deliver and be bold in this existential moment for B.C.

stories.title: Ucp’s direction is a battleground as Smith fails to purge separatists from party
stories.summary: The party’s future is expected to be a major focus at next week’s annual meeting – the first post-referendum
stories.author: Matthew Scace, Carrie Tait
stories.content:
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith has failed to purge separatists from the United Conservative Party’s leadership ranks, a month after decreeing that officials within her organization must be committed to federalism.

Further, Ms. Smith’s demand that all local party presidents stop advocating for Alberta’s secession has aggravated independence advocates and free-speech absolutists ahead of the Ucp’s annual meeting next weekend in Calgary.

“We are bitterly divided,” Vince Byfield, once one of Ms. Smith’s most reliable supporters, said at a UCP forum this week.

Ms. Smith has begged her fellow conservatives to focus on winning the 2027 provincial election, which she said will require abandoning the quest for secession given that 75 per cent of Albertans rejected the idea in a referendum last month.

She first encouraged Albertans to drop the issue in a televised address after the vote, and again the next day when she told UCP members that separatist agitators were no longer welcome in the party. In late October, her party asked all candidates in the Ucp’s coming board elections to sign a pledge committing to respect the referendum results. It has recently expanded that request to its 87 constituency association presidents.

But many of the movement’s leaders are prominent players in the UCP and believe most party members want the organization to continue pushing for separation.

The Premier’s inability to quell dissent means UCP members will, once again, battle over the party’s direction and focus at what is expected to be a raucous annual meeting. The organization has sold roughly 7,000 tickets to the event, where members will elect eight people to the party’s provincial board, which influences the Ucp’s strategy, policies and politics.

While the candidates are largely split between two slates, their histories reveal deeper divisions within the party. Mr. Byfield is challenging incumbent Patrick Malkin, a senior official in the Premier’s office, for a vice-president position. Both men first won spots on the provincial board in the fall of 2022, as part of a populist wave that just weeks prior had helped Ms. Smith become party leader.

Now, Mr. Malkin is on the Team Unity slate backing Ms. Smith, and Mr. Byfield is informally aligned with the separatist cluster of candidates.

Dozens of UCP members gathered on Wednesday evening at a private Christian academy in south Calgary for an event dubbed the “Cowtown Showdown,” to hear board candidates make their pitch.

TJ Schmidt, who is running against a Team Unity candidate for a vice-president position, compared the party’s proclivity for infighting to an Olympian with an immune system prone to illness.

“It pits about half the cells in the body against the other half,” he told the crowd. “That strength is still there for that athlete, but it’s turned inwards to fight itself.”

At the end of October, the UCP stripped boisterous independence leader Jeffrey Rath of his membership. At the Ucp’s annual meeting last year, Mr. Rath whipped up the crowd in support of secession; the audience booed Ms. Smith when she responded by touting Alberta’s renewed relationship with Ottawa.

Mr. Rath’s removal gave credibility to Ms. Smith’s post-referendum promise to focus on the 2027 election. Party members, including separatist sympathizers, cheered his removal.

However, large pockets within the party have rejected Ms. Smith’s broader housecleaning effort.

Earlier this month, the UCP demanded its 87 constituency association presidents respect and abide by the results of October’s referendum question on separation, effectively ordering them to stop publicly pushing for independence. The deadline elapsed without full compliance.

Fifteen presidents openly defied Ms. Smith by releasing a letter stating the dictate exceeded the party’s power. The signatories include Mitch Sylvestre, a key separatist organizer who fiercely supported the Premier in the past.

Ms. Smith has yet to specify – let alone mete out – consequences for refusing to comply. Instead, she said last week that she would continue her persuasion campaign.

The party brass has not yet discussed repercussions, according to UCP president Rob Smith, who defended the organization’s decree. “Is it not reasonable to actually expect those individuals to recognize, respect and abide by a decision that was made by 75 per cent of Albertans?”

Mr. Smith, who is not up for re-election this year and is not related to the Premier, declined to share his position on separation, but said he is “satisfied that the issue has been laid to rest.”

Asked whether he believes the secession conversation is over within the UCP, Mr. Smith said: “In the short term, it is.”

UCP spokesman Dave Prisco backed the Premier’s diplomatic approach to dissent.

“We’re going to work with people respectfully,” he said in an e-mailed statement.

The outcome of October’s referendum question on separation raised the stakes in the fight for control over the Ucp’s provincial board and the makeup of its constituency associations. Ms. Smith could face a leadership review if two-thirds of the provincial directors vote in favour of a special general meeting, or if 22 of 87 constituency associations call for one.

Board candidates running with the Team Unity slate launched an e-mail blitz this week.

“We must stand united behind our party’s leader, Danielle Smith and her call to respect the results of the recent referendum and, as a party, commit to a strong Alberta within a United Canada,” Ken Engler, a candidate for the party’s chief financial officer, said in an e-mail.

Mr. Engler, who did not acknowledge an interview request, was first elected treasurer in 2022, after serving as Ms. Smith’s CFO during her leadership campaign. He does not currently sit on the board.

While the UCP expects record crowds at its annual meeting, and the voting booths will only be open for five hours, Mr. Engler encouraged prospective attendees to be in the main convention hall for Saturday’s keynote address.

“Hear Premier Smith speak and cheer her on.”

stories.title: London, Ont., police officer charged with assault in off-duty incident
stories.summary: London - Police in London, Ont., say one of their own officers has been charged with assault and forcible confinement in an off-duty incident earlier this month.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
LONDON - Police in London, Ont., say one of their own officers has been charged with assault and forcible confinement in an off-duty incident earlier this month.

Nov. 27, 2026

Spencer Colby/The Canadian Press[](https://www.thestar.com/news/ontario/london-ont-police-officer-charged-with-assault-in-off-duty-incident/article_0e2af0ea-3747-5b54-ad49-c4837ae0e90a.html)

By The Canadian Press

The force says it referred the investigation to the Strathroy-Caradoc Police Service to ensure impartiality after receiving the initial report, and that led to charges against the officer.

Investigators say the officer’s name and identifying details will not be released to protect the victim’s privacy.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Inside interior designer Nora Voon’s art-filled home

Police say the officer has been reassigned to administrative duties.

They say the matter is also subject to an internal conduct review in accordance with the Community Safety and Policing Act.

The force says in a statement that it takes the allegations seriously.

“As police officers, we are entrusted with significant responsibilities and are held to high standards of conduct, both on and off-duty,” it said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 27, 2026.

stories.title: The engineering feat at the heart of Canada’s next big Arctic build
stories.summary: Kugluktuk - Nobody lives at Grays Bay.
stories.author: Jeremy Simes, Be Giant and The Canadian Press The Canadian Press
stories.content:
KUGLUKTUK - Nobody lives at Grays Bay.

The deepwater inlet on Nunavut’s northwestern Arctic coast is ringed by treeless tundra, threaded with lakes, ponds and streams and scattered with boulders and the odd hunting cabin. There is no all-season road in. Everything needed to build one – fuel, steel, heavy equipment and people – would have to arrive by barge in the few ice-free months, or by truck over a road made of ice.

West Kitikmeot Resources Corp (WKR) plans to change that by building an all-season gravel road, a deepwater port and an airfield in a megaproject that would be a first step in connecting Nunavut by road to the rest of the country. The company says it would also provide Canada with its first deepwater seaport on the western Arctic coast, bolstering security in the North and making Grays Bay one of Canada’s major economic gateways.

The goal, says Brendan Bell, WKR’s CEO, is to kickstart copper and zinc mining in the area, spurring development that would ultimately funnel hundreds of millions of dollars into the economy by enabling the movement of critical minerals to international markets. “There are a number of very high-grade copper and zinc deposits that are landlocked,” Bell says. “You can’t fly this material out of here – you need infrastructure to get to tidewater.”

Starting close to the Nunavut-Northwest Territories border and stretching 230 kilometres north along several mining deposits, Grays Bay Road and Port (GBRP) would take an estimated five years to build and cost upward of $1 billion. The project is currently before the Nunavut Impact Review Board for assessment, and Prime Minister Mark Carney has referred it to the federal major projects office, which could fast-track its construction through the federal regulatory process.

“I think Canada must do it, needs to do it,” Bell says.

The more difficult question is how.

Ed Grozic has been down this road before. As director of Arctic engineering with Tetra Tech, he worked on the 138-kilometre Inuvik-Tuktoyaktuk Highway (ITH), which his firm helped plan, design and build before it opened in 2017.

“It’s a big deal and a big challenge to complete,” he says of the GBRP. It takes what he calls “alignments” – of labour, resources and equipment, but also of the people of Nunavut, governments, landowners, regulators and the environment.

Consider just the resources. The proposed road needs 15 million cubic metres of rock – enough to build the Great Pyramid of Giza six times over – and nearly all of it has to come from land it is planned to cross. In total, crews will open up to 40 new quarries along the route, blasting rock into pieces less than a metre across and crushing it into gravel. Blasting would be timed to avoid sensitive periods for wildlife, fish and migratory birds, according to WKR’s filings with the review board.

Then there’s the route. The road – about 10 metres wide to carry traffic in both directions – will traverse low-lying tundra and wind through a maze of lakes, ponds and streams, requiring about 230 bridges and culverts. Those components would need to be prefabricated in the south and brought in by sealift or over a winter road, then installed when the ground and water are frozen.

And there are the workers – they’ll need hundreds of them. With no existing communities along the proposed route, the biggest challenges are likely to be staffing and accommodations. In the first year, the company plans to set up a temporary work camp with supplies delivered by ship at the Grays Bay port site.

At the coastal end of the project, about a metre of sediment and loose rock will need to be dredged from the ocean floor. Crews also need to build a harbour breakwater and a boat launch to allow for the transportation of goods during the open-water season, from June to October. Due to sea ice, marine construction season is naturally shorter, says Elliot Holland, WKR’s chief operating officer. “We have to account for the force of the ice pushing on the in-water wharf structures.”

Once winter arrives, crews would build a temporary airstrip and a pad for a permanent camp, a fuel station, the first quarries and a vital winter road. Rebuilt each year over ice and snow, the road would connect Jericho Station, a dormant diamond mine site at the south end of the Grays Bay road, to the Tibbitt to Contwoyto Winter Road in the Northwest Territories. About 1,000 trucks would haul materials and equipment along the route each winter.

Construction would then start at both ends of the route, with crews working towards each other until they meet in the middle. As the road advances, crews would move the camps every three months.

Beneath it all is melting permafrost – ground that’s at or below 0 C and held together by ice. When permafrost thaws, the ground shifts and sinks, buckling roads and tilting buildings; that’s why many homes in the North are built on pilings drilled deep into the ground. Designed to last 75 years, Grays Bay road needs to remain stable well into the 2100s, in a region warming several times faster than the global average.

WKR plans to use fill-only construction where possible, adding gravel or other materials on top of the existing ground to minimize disruption, rather than using conventional cut-and-fill techniques. As much as possible, the road would be routed on top of stable bedrock. Where that’s not practical, it would sit on a base of large rocks, preferably non-acid-generating granite. In either case, gravel goes on top.

The road’s embankment would be thicker, with coarse materials such as sand and gravel acting as a blanket. The company says this limits heat seeping into the ground, keeping the permafrost frozen. Where the ground is most sensitive, the base would be laid in winter.

In the Arctic, says Holland, time is everything. “If you don’t plan or execute properly, a construction season could definitely be lost,” he says. “A delay of a month can imply a delay of a year in the Arctic.”

There are two precedents for this kind of ambitious road construction in Canada’s Arctic, and both carry hard-won lessons.

The 740-kilometre Dempster Highway, which runs from near Dawson City, Yukon, to Inuvik, N.W.T., opened in 1979 after 20 years of construction. The project was slowed in part by a funding dispute between Yukon and Ottawa, as well as a shortage of gravel. The ITH faced the same problem decades later: it was built with poorer-quality soil, all that was available in the region, says Grozic.

“The ITH’s road embankment was placed right on the tundra’s surface. That translates to a fair bit of settlement.” To keep embankments level, he says, crews must continually top up the gravel. During ITH’s first spring, muddy, slippery conditions forced the road to close.

Grays Bay has an advantage here: much of its route crosses bedrock, and Grozic expects crews to use higher-quality quarried rock.

On the ITH, most heavy construction happened in winter, often in darkness and at temperatures below -30 C, because the thawed summer ground couldn’t support heavy equipment. Crews placed more than three million cubic metres of fill and installed more than 300 culverts; Grays Bay will need roughly five times as much gravel.

Monitoring has shown that the thickest sections of the ITH’s embankment perform best. Its designers modelled how ground temperatures would change over the road’s lifetime and set the embankment thickness to ensure the permafrost would stay frozen as the Arctic warms.

The Yukon stretch of the Dempster was built entirely on permafrost, and climate-related maintenance costs have risen since the 1990s as thawing ground triggers landslides, washouts and slumping. Water flowing through culverts carries heat into the frozen ground around them, and the Dempster has seen multiple culvert failures attributed to permafrost thaw – a warning for a road like Grays Bay, with so many water crossings of its own.

It has already taken decades for the idea of a road to get this far. In 1970, the mining company Texasgulf found a rich zinc and copper deposit at Izok Lake, inland from the Arctic coast. Getting the metal out was the problem. In 1992, other interested parties asked Ottawa to help pay for a road and port on Bathurst Inlet, to the east of Grays Bay. Brian Mulroney’s government said no.

Versions of plans for an all-season road have surfaced ever since. An Inuit-backed Bathurst Inlet port and road went before the review board in 2003, then stalled as its estimated cost more than doubled. In 2012, the mining company MMG proposed a route to Grays Bay, then shelved it the following year over cost.

In 2016, the Kitikmeot Inuit Association, which represents Inuit in the region, partnered with the Nunavut government on the current GBRP project, but the territory pulled out two years later, saying it couldn’t afford its quarter of the cost.

WKR took over in 2023, with Kitikmeot Inuit Association as a major shareholder, and Calgary-based Atco. invested with a 40 per cent stake. This time, the company expects to raise 25 per cent of its initial funds to get started from the private sector, while the remaining 75 per cent could come from Ottawa.

Bell believes the timing is finally right. “I feel better than ever before,” he says. “We were toiling away in obscurity before the prime minister was elected and stood up the major projects office.

“This project has real traction now, and we need to take advantage of that. I’ve never seen the environment so conducive to getting investments in Arctic infrastructure as I do now.”

Regulatory approvals are still to come. The Nunavut Impact Review Board received WKR’s revised impact statement in May, with community meetings scheduled for this fall. Bell says he hopes the board can make a recommendation in early 2027, with a federal decision later that year.

A shortlist of three international construction consortiums has been selected, and WKR plans to choose one in March. It hopes to start construction in 2030, with operations beginning in 2035.

The road before the road is a long one, but its supporters are resolute. Caroline Wawzonek, strategic infrastructure minister for the Northwest Territories, counts herself among them.

“If we’re saying that we want to get to a place where we’re going to actually connect this country and build it into a truly Arctic and northern nation,” Wawzonek says, “then let’s do that.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 27, 2026.

stories.title: Ontario calls for Criminal Code changes to give home invasion victims more protection
stories.summary: Ontario is calling on Ottawa to amend federal law to give Canadians stronger protections to confront attackers in their homes after a spate of violent home invasions in Toronto.
stories.author: Kathryn Mannie
stories.content:
The Ontario government is calling on Ottawa to amend federal law to give Canadians stronger legal protections to confront attackers in their homes after a spate of violent home invasions in Toronto.

The request was made by Ontario’s Attorney General Doug Downey and Solicitor General Michael Kerzner in a letter to the federal justice and public safety ministers, asking for more clarity on when people can resort to self-defence to fend off attackers on their property.

They ask that the Criminal Code of Canada be changed to explicitly guarantee that residents do not need to first retreat from their home before relying on self-defence to confront a home invader.

They also call for the Criminal Code to include a list of considerations to help determine if self-defence was reasonable during a home invasion, including whether children were in the home, if someone forced their way in and the time the residents had to respond to the situation.

The requests come after a 39-year-old musician was killed in a home invasion in an affluent Toronto neighbourhood, not long after a family of four was injured in another home invasion in the wealthy Bridle Path area of the city.

Federal law already allows Canadians to – when reasonable – defend themselves from attacks and threats of force and to defend their property.

Downey and Kerzner write that the changes they’re calling for will “provide greater certainty about how those protections apply during a home invasion.”

The Canadian Press has reached out to the offices of federal justice and public safety ministers for comment.

The Ontario lawmakers also ask that Ottawa work with provinces and territories to lay out best practices around claims of self-defence in home invasion cases.

After the fatal Toronto home invasion, Ontario Premier Doug Ford drew headlines and criticism from opposition leaders by encouraging people to use any means necessary to defend their families, including using weapons like guns, knives and baseball bats.

Ford also called on the federal government to strengthen bail laws and increase mandatory jail time for violent offenders.

Toronto police say there have been 111 home invasions in the city so far this year, up from 93 last year. In 2024 the city saw 149 home invasions.

stories.title: A road through Nunavut: The monumental billion-dollar plan to connect Canada's Arctic
stories.summary: Kugluktuk - Amanda Dumond lifts the lid of a large freezer chest in Kugluktuk, Nunavut's westernmost community, where the Arctic Ocean feeds into Coronation Gulf.
stories.author: Jeremy Simes, Be Giant and The Canadian Press The Canadian Press
stories.content:
KUGLUKTUK - Amanda Dumond lifts the lid of a large freezer chest in Kugluktuk, Nunavut’s westernmost community, where the Arctic Ocean feeds into Coronation Gulf.

The Inuk woman pulls out several bags: there’s a deep-red caribou leg, then a package of the animal’s stomach fat, followed by a hoof and an entire goose. She gasps when she finds a piece of maktaaq, a traditional food of whale skin and blubber.

“This is the last piece I have,” she says, showing off the fatty, marbled tissue.

Dumond, manager of the hamlet’s hunters and trappers organization, goes hunting with her family every year, taking all-terrain vehicles onto the landscape largely untouched by development.

There are no roads in the surrounding treeless tundra, just an expanse of land stretching to the horizon.

West Kitikmeot Resources Corp., an Inuit-owned and -led company, is planning to build the Grays Bay Road and Port, east of Kugluktuk.

The mega project, which could cost upward of $1 billion, is currently before the Nunavut Impact Review Board for assessment. Prime Minister Mark Carney has referred it to the federal major projects office, which could fast-track its construction by overriding certain federal regulations.

The all-season gravel road would be the first to run across the territory, starting at the Nunavut-Northwest Territories boundary and stretching 230 kilometres north along several mining deposits to Grays Bay. There, Canada would have its first deepsea port on the western Arctic coast.

It would also be a first step in connecting Nunavut by road to the rest of the country.

The major projects office is also considering a 400-kilometre road called the Arctic Economic Security Corridor, stretching north of Yellowknife to where Grays Bay Road would begin.

Both roads would become part of Canada’s national highway system, and Canadians would be able to drive to Nunavut for the very first time.

The benefits are many, says the company. Besides being able to truck minerals to the port, the project would create jobs, lower housing and food costs, and provide Canada with Arctic security.

But there are worries, too — impacts to caribou herds and marine life.

Dumond says hunting is integral for her family and others in the community. “It’s what I live for. It’s a part of me.”

Kugluktuk Mayor Ryan Nivingalok says he understands the concerns, but his hamlet could benefit from the project.

“As a community leader, you’re looking for the best solution and opportunities to help your people,” Nivingalok says.

“You want to see growth.”

The region and its people

The tiny inlet in the frigid Coronation Gulf is surrounded by low-lying tundra with a network of lakes, ponds and streams. Boulders scatter the region, along with the odd hunting cabin.

Kugluktuk, 180 kilometres to the west, is the closest community. It wouldn’t be connected to Grays Bay Road, but residents often take their ATVs out to the area or zip across the water by boat.

In early September, the tundra’s fall colours have set in. Willows and grasses have turned dark yellow and deep red. Orange lichens and green moss are splotched on exposed bedrock, and ravens make throaty caws in the overcast sky above. The air is cool and fresh.

In Kugluktuk, people bounce on rumbling quads from one point to the next. Some homes are painted in bright yellow, green and blue. Animal furs are draped over porch railings, and some roofs are adorned with caribou or muskox skulls.

Christmas lights are still up from last year on the sides of some homes, in shapes of stars and trees. Each holiday season, residents travel roughly 60 kilometres south to cut down and haul back a tree.

New mothers walk around the hamlet’s two grocery stores carrying babies in pouches on their backs. After school, children jump on their bikes, climb in the playground and kick balls on the soccer field, squealing with laughter.

Unemployment and poverty in the hamlet of 1,380 is high. Those who have jobs mostly work for mining companies or in public administration.

Groceries are more expensive than in Southern Canada, and many rely on food hampers. Some sell sealskin garments to help make ends meet.

The Grays Bay project would make it easier to get goods to the community and others in the territory, says West Kitikmeot. People currently rely on planes to get products year-round or, in the warmer months, infrequent ships from Montreal.

Simon Kuliktana, a member of Nunavut’s legislative assembly who represents the hamlet, hasn’t thrown his support behind the Grays Bay project. He says he’s speaking with residents and groups before taking a position.

“Our caribou herd is so delicate that it’s a fine line,” Kuliktana says. “We need to ensure that they are around for many centuries to come.”

Nunavut Premier John Main, however, is on board.

“It will bolster Arctic connection into the Arctic Ocean, open mining opportunities and meet Canada’s growing need for responsibly sourced rare earth elements and battery metals, which are essential for clean energy and defence applications,” he says in a statement.

Likewise, the N.W.T. government has thrown its support behind both the Grays Bay and Arctic Economic Security Corridor projects.

Caroline Wawzonek, the territory’s strategic infrastructure minister, says the corridor could cost a lot more, up to $7 billion.

But both projects are tied, she says. And if Canada wants to connect the country and the Arctic, it needs it.

“Let’s do it in a way that involves Indigenous nations so that they are involved from Day 1.”

Building the road and port

The Grays Bay project has been in the works for decades, says Brendan Bell, West Kitikmeot’s CEO.

It has been reimagined several times, Bell says, including changing routes to address concerns about caribou. The port site was selected because the tidewater is naturally deep.

In 2016, the Kitikmeot Inuit Association and Nunavut’s government signed an agreement to partner on the project, but the territory later pulled out. In 2025, West Kitikmeot took over. The Kitikmeot Inuit Association, which represents Inuit in the region, is a major shareholder of the company. Calgary-based Atco Ltd. also has a 40 per cent stake.

The company expects it will need to raise 25 per cent of funds from the private sector, while the rest could come from Ottawa.

Bell says Canada needs the project.

Its goal is to kick-start mining copper and zinc in the area, spurring development that would ultimately funnel hundreds of millions of dollars into the economy.

The project would take five years to build.

Several reports from West Kitikmeot detail the massive construction process. The company would hire hundreds of workers, bring equipment in on barges, and build a winter road to bring in more equipment and materials.

Construction on the permanent road would start at the same time from both ends and eventually meet in the middle.

The road has to be gravel, not asphalt or concrete, because of finicky permafrost, ground that’s at or below 0 C and held together by ice.

When it thaws, the ground shifts and can cause roads or structures to distort. That’s why many homes in the North are built on elevated foundations with pilings drilled deep into the ground.

Building a road on permafrost isn’t a new challenge, says Bell.

The 740-kilometre Dempster Highway, cited as Canada’s longest gravel road, stretches from near Dawson City, Yukon, to Inuvik, N.W.T.

“Even if we had the money, I think you probably wouldn’t pave roads in this part of the world,” Bell says.

Carney has argued the Grays Bay project would also bolster the country’s security.

Ottawa is planning to spend an extra $32 billion on the Armed Forces to beef up operations in the North, and it says the Grays Bay Port could assist the military.

Bell says it could host military ships and submarines. The coast guard, for example, could dock and fuel up.

“We need to send a message to not just our allies that we will do our part, but our adversaries that we’re here, we’re present and will match their intensity in the Arctic.”

The port could also support the coast guard’s search and rescue missions, Bell adds.

The Forces have various operations in the Arctic.

There’s a training centre in Resolute, Nvt., along with an alert station on Ellesmere Island – the most northern continuously inhabited location in the world.

The Forces also have three other sites in the region that can support fighter jets: Inuvik, Iqaluit and Yellowknife. Ottawa’s $32-billion plan aims to enhance aircraft operations at these locations as well as a base in Newfoundland and Labrador.

Kuliktana, the legislature member for Kugluktuk, says it makes sense to beef up security in the region.

“With declining ice on the Northwest Passage, we have other countries like China and Russia very interested in using the Northwest Passage.”

Improving the economy, housing and food prices

Back in Kugluktuk, 18-year-old Deagan Miyok plays basketball outside with a friend.

The Grays Bay project is “not bad,” he says.

Miyok graduated high school this year and hopes to get a job at a mine.

Others in the community looking for work also say Grays Bay could help them get jobs and put food on the table.

West Kitikmeot says it would hire 250 to 400 people for construction on the project over the five years. The port could also support up to 80 permanent employees with West Kitikmeot and other companies.

West Kitikmeot also estimates the project would add about $750 million each year to Nunavut’s economy by 2040.

There would be new businesses, including mines shipping out copper and zinc, and barging companies bringing in food and supplies. The project could also spur tourism and excursion operators.

On the outskirts of Kugluktuk, a new 12-unit housing complex is going up, but there’s no timeline on when it might be finished. An additional 10 modular units were set to arrive on a sealift in late September.

The federal government has said it plans to build 750 housing units in Nunavut by March 2031.

“You have big waiting lists for new people applying for units in town,” Nivingalok says. “There’s still not enough units to go around.”

A dozen people sometimes squeeze into a two-bedroom house in the hamlet, the mayor adds. In many cases, large multi-generational families live together, or singles and couples stay with friends or relatives.

The Grays Bay project could speed up more housing, as infrequent shipments and high costs make it difficult to build homes quickly.

West Kitikmeot promises the port could help communities get goods more reliably, frequently and at a lower cost. It would have an area where supplies could be unloaded, stored and later shipped out to communities by boat.

Bell says the company could also build ice roads — or permanent ones – linking communities to the port, if people support it.

Northeast of Kugluktuk, across the sea, is Cambridge Bay. The community of 1,750 is the centre of government for Nunavut’s Kitikmeot region.

Fred Pederson, the legislature member representing Cambridge Bay, supports the Grays Bay project not only for the jobs it would create, but for getting food and supplies to communities more easily.

In September, Cambridge Bay found itself in a bit of a food crisis.

Grocery store shelves were empty, with fresh vegetables, bread, flour and some frozen goods out of stock for weeks, due to timing issues with the sealift. Residents were panic buying when items became available again.

In Kugluktuk, Joey Kunana bags his full cart of groceries at a store checkout. He’s buying toilet paper, eggs, margarine, yogurt cups, frozen pizzas, cereal and canned goods. The trip comes to about $800.

“These prices, it’s like, holy smokes,” he says, adding he pays that amount twice a month to feed his four children. Their mother recently died.

A two-kilogram, family-size jar of peanut butter costs $21. Oranges are $10 per kilogram, and bananas are $4 per kilogram.

Statistics Canada figures show the monthly average price for food items in Nunavut is about double the provincial average. The average in September was $11 for the same jar of peanut butter, $4.50 per kilogram for oranges and $2 per kilogram for bananas.

Asked about the Grays Bay project, Kunana says he’s never heard of it.

West Kitikmeot says in a report that by enhancing supply chains, the Grays Bay project would make store-bought food more accessible.

Bell says he expects non-perishable bulk goods would become cheaper, but items that need to be flown in, such as milk, may not see prices change.

Organizers at the elders centre in Kugluktuk serve lunch three times a week. On the menu one afternoon is bannock and hamburger soup. The room is packed with people talking and joking.

Doris Elatiak, who works at the centre, says many who stop in don’t have much food at home or are out of work.

Some worry about what the Grays Bay project could do to caribou and other animals that are sources of food, she says.

“Most of the elders, they really don’t want it to go ahead.”

Most of Canada’s barren-ground caribou give birth and raise their calves in Nunavut.

Herd populations in the territory’s western region have sharply fallen over the last few decades.

Figures from the Global Initiative on Ungulate Migration show the Bathurst herd fell from 400,000 animals in the 1980s to fewer than 4,000 in 2025. The Dolphin-Union and Bluenose-East herds have also diminished, although the Beverly herd has increased in recent years.

Researchers and hunters have said warming temperatures, predation and hunting have contributed to declines.

The Dolphin-Union herd, for example, crosses sea ice every spring to give birth on Victoria Island, north of Nunavut’s mainland, before returning in the fall. On weak ice, they can fall into the sea and drown.

Hunters say industrial development has also played a role.

Leah Kadlun started an online petition opposing the Grays Bay project. As of early October, nearly 180 people had signed it.

She says she’s not only concerned about caribou, but also fish, seals, whales and other ocean animals in the region.

“It’s going to affect our water, especially along the Coronation Gulf, if they have a lot of ships, tankers and haulers passing by.”

Kadlun sits in Kugluktuk’s visitor centre, surrounded by cultural exhibits, artwork and artifacts. The building is in the shape on an ulu knife, a crescent-shaped blade used by Inuit for centuries.

On display is a large kayak made with caribou skin. Kadlun says her grandmother taught her how to soften such skins when she was little.

“We don’t have a road in or out, but I’m not complaining,” she says. “Of course we’re going to have problems with housing. We’re going to have problems with food.

“This is how I choose to live, this is what we have. We have our fresh food we get off the land.”

West Kitikmeot says it expects the project won’t change fish populations and that marine habitat is not expected to be significantly affected.

It also doesn’t anticipate significant adverse effects on caribou.

The company plans to reduce disturbances to the animals, including building the road with smaller slopes so the animals can cross easily.

The road, running straight through traditional hunting areas, would give more access points for hunting. But the company says the road would close during times of mass migration, and hunting would be controlled by the Kitikmeot Inuit Association.

“It really is a vast, wide-open area with lots of room for caribou,” says Bell. “Our largest shareholder is the Inuit people of the region, so we have a mandate in making sure this project facilitates future investments.”

In an October 2024 submission to the Nunavut Impact Review Board, the Inuit association said it supports the project but also raised concerns of significant effects to caribou and other wildlife.

The association recently said it’s aware of ongoing discussions and that people can have their voices heard through the review board’s assessment process.

If the Grays Bay project goes ahead, Dumond says she’s not confident the caribou can be properly managed.

She has been eating what locals call country foods since she was little. She sees the caribou numbers in decline, even without the Grays Bay project.

During a hunting trip this past summer, she says her family harvested only one caribou.

“It’s what our people have lived on for thousands of years.”
