paragraphs: KUGLUKTUK - Amanda Dumond lifts the lid of a large freezer chest in Kugluktuk, Nunavut’s westernmost community, where the Arctic Ocean feeds into Coronation Gulf.

The Inuk woman pulls out several bags: there’s a deep-red caribou leg, then a package of the animal’s stomach fat, followed by a hoof and an entire goose. She gasps when she finds a piece of maktaaq, a traditional food of whale skin and blubber.
“This is the last piece I have,” she says, showing off the fatty, marbled tissue.
Dumond, manager of the hamlet’s hunters and trappers organization, goes hunting with her family every year, taking all-terrain vehicles onto the landscape largely untouched by development.
There are no roads in the surrounding treeless tundra, just an expanse of land stretching to the horizon.
West Kitikmeot Resources Corp., an Inuit-owned and -led company, is planning to build the Grays Bay Road and Port, east of Kugluktuk.

The mega project, which could cost upward of $1 billion, is currently before the Nunavut Impact Review Board for assessment. Prime Minister Mark Carney has referred it to the federal major projects office, which could fast-track its construction by overriding certain federal regulations.

The all-season gravel road would be the first to run across the territory, starting at the Nunavut-Northwest Territories boundary and stretching 230 kilometres north along several mining deposits to Grays Bay. There, Canada would have its first deepsea port on the western Arctic coast.
It would also be a first step in connecting Nunavut by road to the rest of the country.
The major projects office is also considering a 400-kilometre road called the Arctic Economic Security Corridor, stretching north of Yellowknife to where Grays Bay Road would begin.
Both roads would become part of Canada’s national highway system, and Canadians would be able to drive to Nunavut for the very first time.
The benefits are many, says the company. Besides being able to truck minerals to the port, the project would create jobs, lower housing and food costs, and provide Canada with Arctic security.
But there are worries, too — impacts to caribou herds and marine life.
Dumond says hunting is integral for her family and others in the community. “It’s what I live for. It’s a part of me.”
Kugluktuk Mayor Ryan Nivingalok says he understands the concerns, but his hamlet could benefit from the project.
“As a community leader, you’re looking for the best solution and opportunities to help your people,” Nivingalok says.
“You want to see growth.”
The region and its people
The tiny inlet in the frigid Coronation Gulf is surrounded by low-lying tundra with a network of lakes, ponds and streams. Boulders scatter the region, along with the odd hunting cabin.
Kugluktuk, 180 kilometres to the west, is the closest community. It wouldn’t be connected to Grays Bay Road, but residents often take their ATVs out to the area or zip across the water by boat.

In early September, the tundra’s fall colours have set in. Willows and grasses have turned dark yellow and deep red. Orange lichens and green moss are splotched on exposed bedrock, and ravens make throaty caws in the overcast sky above. The air is cool and fresh.

In Kugluktuk, people bounce on rumbling quads from one point to the next. Some homes are painted in bright yellow, green and blue. Animal furs are draped over porch railings, and some roofs are adorned with caribou or muskox skulls.

Christmas lights are still up from last year on the sides of some homes, in shapes of stars and trees. Each holiday season, residents travel roughly 60 kilometres south to cut down and haul back a tree.

New mothers walk around the hamlet’s two grocery stores carrying babies in pouches on their backs. After school, children jump on their bikes, climb in the playground and kick balls on the soccer field, squealing with laughter.
Unemployment and poverty in the hamlet of 1,380 is high. Those who have jobs mostly work for mining companies or in public administration.
Groceries are more expensive than in Southern Canada, and many rely on food hampers. Some sell sealskin garments to help make ends meet.

The Grays Bay project would make it easier to get goods to the community and others in the territory, says West Kitikmeot. People currently rely on planes to get products year-round or, in the warmer months, infrequent ships from Montreal.

Simon Kuliktana, a member of Nunavut’s legislative assembly who represents the hamlet, hasn’t thrown his support behind the Grays Bay project. He says he’s speaking with residents and groups before taking a position.
“Our caribou herd is so delicate that it’s a fine line,” Kuliktana says. “We need to ensure that they are around for many centuries to come.”
Nunavut Premier John Main, however, is on board.

“It will bolster Arctic connection into the Arctic Ocean, open mining opportunities and meet Canada’s growing need for responsibly sourced rare earth elements and battery metals, which are essential for clean energy and defence applications,” he says in a statement.
Likewise, the N.W.T. government has thrown its support behind both the Grays Bay and Arctic Economic Security Corridor projects.
Caroline Wawzonek, the territory’s strategic infrastructure minister, says the corridor could cost a lot more, up to $7 billion.
But both projects are tied, she says. And if Canada wants to connect the country and the Arctic, it needs it.
“Let’s do it in a way that involves Indigenous nations so that they are involved from Day 1.”
Building the road and port
The Grays Bay project has been in the works for decades, says Brendan Bell, West Kitikmeot’s CEO.
It has been reimagined several times, Bell says, including changing routes to address concerns about caribou. The port site was selected because the tidewater is naturally deep.

In 2016, the Kitikmeot Inuit Association and Nunavut’s government signed an agreement to partner on the project, but the territory later pulled out. In 2025, West Kitikmeot took over. The Kitikmeot Inuit Association, which represents Inuit in the region, is a major shareholder of the company. Calgary-based Atco Ltd. also has a 40 per cent stake.
The company expects it will need to raise 25 per cent of funds from the private sector, while the rest could come from Ottawa.
Bell says Canada needs the project.
Its goal is to kick-start mining copper and zinc in the area, spurring development that would ultimately funnel hundreds of millions of dollars into the economy.
The project would take five years to build.

Several reports from West Kitikmeot detail the massive construction process. The company would hire hundreds of workers, bring equipment in on barges, and build a winter road to bring in more equipment and materials.
Construction on the permanent road would start at the same time from both ends and eventually meet in the middle.
The road has to be gravel, not asphalt or concrete, because of finicky permafrost, ground that’s at or below 0 C and held together by ice.
When it thaws, the ground shifts and can cause roads or structures to distort. That’s why many homes in the North are built on elevated foundations with pilings drilled deep into the ground.
Building a road on permafrost isn’t a new challenge, says Bell.
The 740-kilometre Dempster Highway, cited as Canada’s longest gravel road, stretches from near Dawson City, Yukon, to Inuvik, N.W.T.
“Even if we had the money, I think you probably wouldn’t pave roads in this part of the world,” Bell says.
Carney has argued the Grays Bay project would also bolster the country’s security.
Ottawa is planning to spend an extra $32 billion on the Armed Forces to beef up operations in the North, and it says the Grays Bay Port could assist the military.
Bell says it could host military ships and submarines. The coast guard, for example, could dock and fuel up.
“We need to send a message to not just our allies that we will do our part, but our adversaries that we’re here, we’re present and will match their intensity in the Arctic.”
The port could also support the coast guard’s search and rescue missions, Bell adds.
The Forces have various operations in the Arctic.
There’s a training centre in Resolute, Nvt., along with an alert station on Ellesmere Island – the most northern continuously inhabited location in the world.

The Forces also have three other sites in the region that can support fighter jets: Inuvik, Iqaluit and Yellowknife. Ottawa’s $32-billion plan aims to enhance aircraft operations at these locations as well as a base in Newfoundland and Labrador.
Kuliktana, the legislature member for Kugluktuk, says it makes sense to beef up security in the region.
“With declining ice on the Northwest Passage, we have other countries like China and Russia very interested in using the Northwest Passage.”
Improving the economy, housing and food prices
Back in Kugluktuk, 18-year-old Deagan Miyok plays basketball outside with a friend.
The Grays Bay project is “not bad,” he says.
Miyok graduated high school this year and hopes to get a job at a mine.
Others in the community looking for work also say Grays Bay could help them get jobs and put food on the table.

West Kitikmeot says it would hire 250 to 400 people for construction on the project over the five years. The port could also support up to 80 permanent employees with West Kitikmeot and other companies.
West Kitikmeot also estimates the project would add about $750 million each year to Nunavut’s economy by 2040.
There would be new businesses, including mines shipping out copper and zinc, and barging companies bringing in food and supplies. The project could also spur tourism and excursion operators.

On the outskirts of Kugluktuk, a new 12-unit housing complex is going up, but there’s no timeline on when it might be finished. An additional 10 modular units were set to arrive on a sealift in late September.
The federal government has said it plans to build 750 housing units in Nunavut by March 2031.
“You have big waiting lists for new people applying for units in town,” Nivingalok says. “There’s still not enough units to go around.”

A dozen people sometimes squeeze into a two-bedroom house in the hamlet, the mayor adds. In many cases, large multi-generational families live together, or singles and couples stay with friends or relatives.
The Grays Bay project could speed up more housing, as infrequent shipments and high costs make it difficult to build homes quickly.

West Kitikmeot promises the port could help communities get goods more reliably, frequently and at a lower cost. It would have an area where supplies could be unloaded, stored and later shipped out to communities by boat.
Bell says the company could also build ice roads — or permanent ones – linking communities to the port, if people support it.
Northeast of Kugluktuk, across the sea, is Cambridge Bay. The community of 1,750 is the centre of government for Nunavut’s Kitikmeot region.
Fred Pederson, the legislature member representing Cambridge Bay, supports the Grays Bay project not only for the jobs it would create, but for getting food and supplies to communities more easily.
In September, Cambridge Bay found itself in a bit of a food crisis.

Grocery store shelves were empty, with fresh vegetables, bread, flour and some frozen goods out of stock for weeks, due to timing issues with the sealift. Residents were panic buying when items became available again.

In Kugluktuk, Joey Kunana bags his full cart of groceries at a store checkout. He’s buying toilet paper, eggs, margarine, yogurt cups, frozen pizzas, cereal and canned goods. The trip comes to about $800.
“These prices, it’s like, holy smokes,” he says, adding he pays that amount twice a month to feed his four children. Their mother recently died.
A two-kilogram, family-size jar of peanut butter costs $21. Oranges are $10 per kilogram, and bananas are $4 per kilogram.

Statistics Canada figures show the monthly average price for food items in Nunavut is about double the provincial average. The average in September was $11 for the same jar of peanut butter, $4.50 per kilogram for oranges and $2 per kilogram for bananas.
Asked about the Grays Bay project, Kunana says he’s never heard of it.
West Kitikmeot says in a report that by enhancing supply chains, the Grays Bay project would make store-bought food more accessible.
Bell says he expects non-perishable bulk goods would become cheaper, but items that need to be flown in, such as milk, may not see prices change.
Organizers at the elders centre in Kugluktuk serve lunch three times a week. On the menu one afternoon is bannock and hamburger soup. The room is packed with people talking and joking.
Doris Elatiak, who works at the centre, says many who stop in don’t have much food at home or are out of work.
Some worry about what the Grays Bay project could do to caribou and other animals that are sources of food, she says.
“Most of the elders, they really don’t want it to go ahead.”

stories.title: Cause of plane crash that killed a teen near Toronto undetermined: TSB
stories.summary: The investigation into the death of a 16-year-old boy after a float plane crash northeast of Toronto provided more answers but it's still not clear what caused the accident.
stories.author: Sadeen Mohsen
stories.content:
The investigation into the death of a 16-year-old boy after a float plane crash northeast of Toronto provided more answers but it’s still not clear what caused the accident.

The teenager was standing on a dock on Lake Scugog at the time of the crash, near the community of Caesarea, north of Oshawa, Ont., ON July 18, 2025.

The boy was killed while the pilot and a passenger suffered minor injuries.

The Transportation Safety Board of Canada said in a report released Thursday the pilot was attempting to land the float plane when it bounced off the water at least twice upon touchdown.

It was the pilot’s third flight that day and he was flying with a potential buyer for the Ultravia Pelican aircraft.

The report said the pilot then used “full engine power” to lift the plane up and try another landing approach.

This is when the plane veered sharply to the left and into one boat dock. It struck another dock before coming to a rest upside-down on top of a boat.

The report said the pilot was following the recommended landing procedures for the water conditions that day, which bystanders say was “glassy with no visible ripples.”

He made contact with the water about 200 feet from the shore.

The report noted that the pilot was experienced and had regularly flown Ultravia Pelican aircraft, although this particular float plane had different features from what he was used to, such as a different engine, propeller, floats and wings.

Transportation Canada recommends pilots fly parallel to and as close to the shoreline as possible to “aid height perception” since glassy water conditions can present a hazard for pilots trying to land.

Pilots should also factor in “whether safety margins can be maintained” and consider if they’re landing near docks, boats and people, which could reduce safety margins and “whether another landing area would provide a safer option.”

The report couldn’t determine what exactly caused the crash.

stories.title: Jury in Jamal Francique inquest deliberating recommendations
stories.summary: The jury heard police secretly surveilled 28-year-old Jamal Francique for days, after receiving a tip that he was trafficking drugs and had a gun.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
A coroner’s jury is deliberating recommendations after hearing evidence in an inquest into the death of a Black man who was shot during an attempted arrest in Mississauga, Ont., nearly seven years ago.

The inquest into Jamal Francique’s death has heard from multiple witnesses, including officers who were at the scene and Francique’s mother, who told the jury she believes anti-Black racism played a role in her son’s death.

The jury heard police secretly surveilled 28-year-old Francique for days, after receiving a tip that he was trafficking drugs and had a gun.

Officers did not find anything to corroborate those allegations but decided to instead arrest him on Jan. 7, 2020, for an alleged breach of his bail conditions as he left a townhouse complex.

Jurors heard that Francique was shot by one of the police officers as he attempted to drive away, and that officer told the inquest that he acted out of “fight-or-flight” instinct when he saw the car accelerate toward him.

Inquest counsel and most of the parties presented a total of 40 proposed recommendations to the jury on Thursday, but the jury is not required to adopt them.

Many of the proposed recommendations were aimed at Peel regional police and the lawyer for the force opposed at least a dozen of them, arguing they were not feasible, not supported by evidence or overlapped with existing efforts.

Ontario’s police watchdog, the Special Investigations Unit, cleared the officers of criminal wrongdoing in Francique’s death about a year after the shooting.

Coroner’s inquests do not assign legal responsibility, though jurors May make recommendations aimed at preventing similar deaths.

stories.title: Ontario calls for Criminal Code changes to give home invasion victims more protection
stories.summary: Toronto - The Ontario government is calling on Ottawa to amend federal law to give Canadians stronger legal protections to confront attackers in their homes after a spate of violent home invasions in Toronto.
stories.author: Kathryn Mannie The Canadian Press
stories.content:
TORONTO - The Ontario government has called on Ottawa to amend federal law to give Canadians stronger legal protections to confront attackers in their homes after a spate of violent home invasions in Toronto.

The request was made by Ontario’s Attorney General Doug Downey and Solicitor General Michael Kerzner in a letter to the federal justice and public safety ministers, asking for more clarity on when people can resort to self-defence to fend off attackers on their property.

They asked that the Criminal Code of Canada be changed to explicitly guarantee that residents do not need to first retreat from their home before relying on self-defence to confront a home invader.

They also called for the Criminal Code to include a list of considerations to help determine if self-defence was reasonable during a home invasion, including whether children were in the home, if someone forced their way in and the time the residents had to respond to the situation.

The requests come after a 39-year-old musician was killed in a home invasion in an affluent Toronto neighbourhood, not long after a family of four was injured in another home invasion in the wealthy Bridle Path area of the city.

Federal law already allows Canadians to – when reasonable – defend themselves from attacks and threats of force and to defend their property.

Downey and Kerzner wrote that the changes they’re calling for will “provide greater certainty about how those protections apply during a home invasion.” Premier Doug Ford called them “common-sense changes” that would protect people who defend their homes from criminals.

In a statement to The Canadian Press, a spokesperson for Justice Minister Sean Fraser reaffirmed the right to self-defence already exists and said the federal government has introduced stricter laws to keep violent offenders in prison longer under the Bail and Sentencing Reform Act, which came into force this July.

Joannie Fogue wrote in an email that Ottawa is committed to keeping Canadians safe, but provincial governments are responsible for key parts of the justice system, including policing.

“As threats evolve, our government will keep working with law enforcement and provinces, move with urgency to strengthen Canada’s laws, and keep Canadians safe,” Fogue wrote.

Downey and Kerzner have also asked that Ottawa work with provinces and territories to lay out best practices around claims of self-defence in home invasion cases.

Asked about Ontario’s requests, Prime Minister Mark Carney pointed to the recently introduced tougher bail and sentencing standards for violent crimes.

“What needs to happen is that those changes move quickly through the system ... so that they are fully applied,” he said Friday at a press conference in Yellowknife.

“We have just made arguably the tightest, the most significant tightening of the Criminal Code in many years, in decades. So we need that to settle first,” he said.

After the fatal Toronto home invasion, Ford drew headlines and criticism from opposition leaders by encouraging people to use any means necessary to defend their families, including using weapons like guns, knives and baseball bats.

The premier also called on the federal government on Thursday to strengthen bail laws and increase mandatory jail time for violent offenders.

Toronto police say there have been 111 home invasions in the city so far this year, up from 93 last year. In 2024 the city saw 149 home invasions.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 27, 2026.

stories.title: Crown seeks 25-year sentence for Kenneth Law, who admitted to aiding suicide
stories.summary: Kenneth Law pleaded guilty earlier this year to 14 counts of aiding suicide in the deaths of 14 people in Ontario.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
WARNING: Details of this story may be disturbing to some readers. Discretion is advised.

Money was the motivation for an Ontario man who sold potentially deadly substances and equipment online to people knowing they would likely use the products to take their own lives, prosecutors argued Friday as they sought a 25-year sentence for Kenneth Law in what they called an unprecedented case.

Law’s lawyers, meanwhile, argued the 61-year-old was not a “mercenary predator” but rather a misguided man committed to his belief in the right to die and whose actions did not warrant a “de facto life sentence.”

Law’s reasons for selling his wares over nearly 2 1/2 years were a focal point as the Crown and the defence laid out what they believe would be an appropriate sentence for Law, who pleaded guilty earlier this year to 14 counts of aiding suicide in the deaths of 14 people in Ontario.

The former chef has been linked to dozens of deaths worldwide, including 79 in the United Kingdom that are being considered as part of the sentencing process.

Scores of grieving family members and friends told the court about the lasting impact of Law’s crimes over two days in September as his sentencing hearing got underway. Some delivered the message in person, others did so by video and others in written statements read by prosecutors.

Law spoke on the final day of the sentencing hearing, saying to the court and the victims’ familes that he would never commit these actions again.

“My past behavior was not only illegal, it was also categorically wrong,” Law said in court. “Going through this process has changed me, and I am committed to continuing my rehabilitation while in custody by taking part in available programming and in counseling, I will continue to better myself, so that I may return to being a contributing member of society.”

Both sides noted the unique nature of the case and the resulting absence of meaningful jurisprudence as they made their arguments in a Newmarket, Ont., court.

“No case such as this has come before this court, and hopefully it never will again,” said Crown attorney Katie Doherty.

“Part of ensuring that that happens is to denounce and deter the offender’s conduct with a sentence that is fit and proportionate in all the circumstances.”

The scale of Law’s operations should be counted as an aggravating factor, as should the fact that his actions “actually caused death,” she argued.

Ninety-three people died because they used the products purchased from Law, including 12 teenagers, she said.

“These were vulnerable people … What they needed was help, but what they found was Mr. Law and his products for death,” Doherty said.

Law’s actions run contrary to his claim of an altruistic purpose, the prosecutor argued. The only factor that determined whom he sold to was whether they paid upfront, she said.

“If people could pay, he sold it to them. There’s no discussion or inquiries or anything going on whereby Mr. Law would have any ability to appreciate the circumstances of the individual he was dealing with,” she said.

Law’s guilty plea, which spared grieving families a lengthy trial, and his lack of a prior criminal record count as mitigating factors, she said.

The maximum sentence for aiding suicide is 14 years and Doherty argued Law should face 12 1/2 years for each count, with two to be served back to back and the rest at the same time.

After subtracting credit for the time Law has spent in custody since his arrest in May 2023, he would be left with 19 years and 7 1/2 months to serve.

Defence lawyer Matthew Gourlay argued that while Law sold the victims the tools they used to end their lives, he was not “the cause of the struggles and hardships that caused all of these victims to seek out his products in the first place,” nor did he play a role in their decision to use the products in the way they did.

“In short, Mr. Law did not kill anyone,” he said.

Law’s actions and sentence should also be considered in the context of the ongoing, unresolved debate in Canadian society over assisted dying, Gourlay argued.

“To be very clear, the context in no way justifies Mr. Law’s choice to act outside of lawful bounds,” he said.

“But in my submission, you do need to look at that social context in order to evaluate what a proportionate sentence for Mr. Law might look like, and you have to do that especially because of the relative dearth of meaningful sentencing jurisprudence in this area.”

An appropriate sentence under the circumstances would be 12 years — nine for the cases involving sodium nitrite and three for those involving other equipment, to be served one after the other — minus credit for the time he’s already served, the defence lawyer argued.

Law should also receive enhanced credit for his time in detention due to the particularly harsh conditions he faced, which included lockdowns, triple bunking and “a life-threatening case” of flesh-eating disease he contracted at the Maplehurst Correctional Complex, he argued.

Law’s plea deal in May came soon after he was set to stand trial on the aiding suicide charges and another 14 counts of first-degree murder related to the same victims.

Prosecutors are expected to withdraw the murder charges after Law is sentenced.

An agreed statement of fact presented after his plea said Law ran several websites that were used to sell sodium nitrite and other products that can be used for self-harm.

He shipped products to people in more than 40 countries, knowing his customers were likely to use them for suicide, the document said.

Law also went on a forum where people talked about using certain substances to take their own life, at times leaving comments and referring people to his websites, it said.

The judge is expected to make a ruling on Feb. 26, 2027.

If you or someone you know is thinking about suicide, support is available 24/7 by calling or texting 988, Canada’s national suicide prevention helpline.

stories.title: Jury in Jamal Francique inquest deliberating recommendations
stories.summary: A coroner's jury is deliberating recommendations after hearing evidence in an inquest into the death of a Black man who was shot during an attempted arrest in Mississauga, Ont., nearly seven years ago.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A coroner’s jury has deemed the death of Jamal Francique after an attempted arrest a homicide as it made more than 20 recommendations aimed at preventing similar deaths in the future, most of them directed at Peel regional police.

Inquest jurors are required to make a finding on the manner of death, but the homicide designation carries no legal liability. The officer who fatally shot Francique in Mississauga, Ont., nearly seven years ago was cleared of wrongdoing by Ontario’s police watchdog.

Jurors made 21 recommendations on Friday after hearing evidence about the death of the 28-year-old Black man who was shot as he attempted to drive away from a townhouse complex on Jan. 7, 2020. He died in hospital days later.

The inquest heard from multiple witnesses, including officers who were at the scene and Francique’s mother, who told the jury she believes anti-Black racism played a role in her son’s death.

The jurors made 16 recommendations directed at the Peel police force. They include reviewing policies and procedures around arrests based on anonymous tips, arrests by plainclothes officers in which the suspect is expected to use a vehicle, and considering foreseeable risks in such arrests.

The jury also recommended that Peel police require all officers to complete mandatory scenario and competency-based anti-Black racism training by Dec. 31, 2028, as part of its use-of-force and firearms training.

“Use-of-force training should also teach officers about specific anti-Black stereotypes and how they may affect their perceptions of danger, decisions about force, and responses to medical distress,” another recommendation reads.

The jury had heard that police secretly surveilled Francique for days, after receiving a tip that he was trafficking drugs and had a gun. Officers did not find anything to corroborate those allegations but decided to instead arrest him for an alleged breach of his bail conditions as he left his home.

Jurors heard that Francique was shot by one of the police officers as he attempted to drive away, and his car crashed into a garage moments later. He did not receive medical care until after the Peel police tactical unit arrived at the scene roughly 20 minutes later and removed him from the car, the inquest has heard.

The officer who shot Francique, Milan Ivkovic, told the inquest that he acted out of “fight-or-flight” instinct when he saw the car accelerate toward him.

Francique’s mother, Ann-Marie White, told the jury she was “deeply troubled” by the delay in medical care her son received after being shot and that she doesn’t understand why police resorted to such an “elaborate and botched plan” to arrest Francique on the basis of unconfirmed allegations.

She said she believes Peel regional police saw her son for the colour of his skin rather than as a human being.

One of the jury’s recommendations is that Peel police review, “and where necessary, enhance” the force’s emergency casualty care course to ensure that it “incorporates education concerning the potential influence of implicit racial bias on the assessment of injured persons and the provision of emergency medical assistance.”

Another recommendation says officers who may be part of planned vehicle arrests should receive scenario-based training about the risks of approaching and apprehending a driver.

“The training should include the risk of sudden vehicle movement, the positioning of officers on foot, the protection of members of the public and officer safety, including removing themselves from the path of threat and disengaging without use of force,” the recommendation read.

Inquest counsel and most of the parties presented a total of 40 proposed recommendations to the jury on Thursday, but the jury was not required to adopt all of them.

The jury made one recommendation directed at the chief coroner’s office: that inquests “shall be scheduled as soon as practicable from the date of death.”

Coroner’s inquests do not assign legal responsibility, and the recommendations are not binding.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 27, 2026.

stories.title: Stolen smart glasses saved video of suspect's face on paired device: Police
stories.summary: Police north of Toronto are asking the public for help in identifying a suspect who allegedly stole a pair of smart glasses that saved video footage of him trying the eyewear on in front of a mirror before leaving the store.
stories.author: Maan Alhmidi The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Police north of Toronto are asking the public for help in identifying a suspect who allegedly stole a pair of smart glasses that saved video footage of him trying the eyewear on in front of a mirror before leaving the store.

South Simcoe Police say a man walked into an eyewear store in Cookstown, Ont., on Nov. 11 at around 7:30 p.m. and asked to try on a pair of Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses.

stories.title: Cause of plane crash that killed a teen near Toronto undetermined: TSB
stories.summary: The investigation into the death of a 16-year-old boy after a float plane crash northeast of Toronto provided more answers but it's still not clear what caused the accident.
stories.author: Sadeen Mohsen The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The investigation into the death of a 16-year-old boy after a float plane crash northeast of Toronto provided more answers but it’s still not clear what caused the accident.

The teenager was standing on a dock on Lake Scugog at the time of the crash, near the community of Caesarea, north of Oshawa, Ont., on July 18, 2025.

stories.title: Navy Vets Preview - Nov. 27th to Nov. 29th
stories.summary: Here is a look at when the Woodstock Navy Vets take to the ice in the Gohl.
stories.author: Kyle Freel
stories.content:
News Home

Friday, 27 November 2026 at 07:38

By Kyle Freel X @KFreelHeartFM

Share on Facebook

Share on Messenger

Share on Messenger

Here is a look at when the Woodstock Navy Vets take to the ice in the GOHL.

WOODSTOCK - There are two games on the schedule for the Woodstock Navy Vets in the Greater Ontario Hockey League.

They are off tonight, but will hit the road tomorrow to Strathroy and take on the Rockets. The Navy Vets have faced the Rockets twice already this season, and not fared well. stories.title: District of Squamish asks residents to limit indoor water use after wet B.C. weather
stories.summary: Squamish - The rain and wind warnings have been dropped across British Columbia's coast, but flooding is still a risk as other communities manage the aftermath.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
VANCOUVER - Nicalena Chidley’s dock was swept away this week as a storm surge, king tides and strong winds pounded it into bits on her oceanfront property on northwestern Vancouver Island.

She lives in the small community of Kyuquot, a remote settlement that has no roads and is accessible only by boat or plane.

With no dock, she’s been stranded since Tuesday.

November has “kicked our butts,” Chidley said, referring to back-to-back storms and long stretches of power outages and being marooned.

Video taken by Chidley shows her son in an orange waterproof suit standing on the shoreline, assessing the destruction.

The walkway to the dock is gone, the front section has also disappeared, but two boats, bucking in the strong waves, are still attached to the end of the stranded structure.

“God sakes, what a frikin’ disaster,” she said behind the camera.

Wood debris and other building material are scattered along the waterfront.

“It pulled out our whole platform and our first ramp that goes down to our bigger ramp to our dock. So, we were stranded on the island,” Chidley said, describing the damage.

“It was just incredibly rough in there.”

Her family is one of many cleaning up after days of relentless rain along coastal B.C., made worse by strong winds and king tides that prevented storm surges from washing out.

Environment Canada dropped its rain and wind warnings late Thursday, while alerts from the B.C. River Forecast Centre were lifted Friday for all but central Vancouver Island where a high-streamflow advisory remains posted.

The weather agency has also lifted all coastal flood warnings and statements, which at the peak covered almost the whole B.C. coast.

Residents of Parksville, on the east coast of Vancouver Island, who live on low-lying or coastal properties were put on evacuation alert earlier this week due to rising water levels. Those have since been rescinded and a spokesman for the city said “minimal cleanup has been identified.”

“The only part from the storm that needs monitoring is waiting for the fields and parks to begin drying up, as there’s a lot of sitting water in those areas,” the statement said.

“There might be some work required to move debris and logs from some beach areas, but that’s done in partnership with (fisheries departments) on the provincial and federal government side of things.”

The weather agency said the storms between Monday and Thursday dropped 734 millimetres of rain on Effingham Island off western Vancouver Island, which is about 160 kilometres south of Chidley’s home.

Chidley said she has been living in Kyuquot since 1988 — her parents were long-serving lightkeepers on B.C.‘s coast, so the area is “in her DNA.” While she has seen storms before, this has “been quite a week.”

The sound of the storm made itself known on Tuesday.

“I was taking a nap and I woke up to a huge thud of water against my window side. Scared the daylights out of me,” said Chidley.

The B.C. River Forecast Centre said the king tides coinciding with the full moon made the coastal flooding situation worse, but that influence was also diminishing.

The District of Squamish, which declared a state of local emergency over high tides and flood risk earlier this week, has asked residents to limit indoor water use until further notice to help manage sewer flows, adding that more rainfall will impact the system.

The district said flood protection measures it took have succeeded in mitigating the effects of localized flooding.

Environment Canada said Squamish received 147 millimetres of rain since Monday, among the highest totals recorded on B.C.‘s mainland in the weather event.

Peak winds were recorded in Comox at 89 km/h and Tofino at 82 km/h.

While it’s been a difficult time, Chidley said she has been overwhelmed with the support from people in her tight-knit community.

“I’ve done a lot of crying the last couple of days, everybody’s been pitching in and helping in any way they can. So, that’s fantastic and amazing. I’m very proud of our community on the receiving end instead of being the giving end.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 27, 2026.

stories.title: Premier Ford, Unifor leader call on Ottawa to scrap greenhouse gas rules for Canadian automakers
stories.summary: Statement follows politicians’ attempts to reverse the sale of the Stellantis assembly plant in Brampton, Ont., to armoured-car maker Roshel
stories.author: Laura Stone
stories.content:
Ontario Premier Doug Ford and Unifor national president Lana Payne are calling on the federal government to exempt Canadian automakers from tailpipe emissions rules and other greenhouse gas regulations, arguing they threaten the viability of operations in this country.

The unusual joint statement from the Progressive Conservative Premier and the union leader was issued as federal and provincial politicians are attempting to reverse the sale of the Stellantis assembly plant in Brampton, Ont., to armoured-car maker Roshel Inc.

In the statement, Mr. Ford and Ms. Payne say Canada’s environmental regulations are hurting the domestic auto sector, calling them an “own goal” that helps Mr. Trump achieve his aim of seeing every Canadian auto worker out of a job.

“In response to President Trump’s direct attacks on Canadian auto workers, the federal government must address the significant costs that its own greenhouse gas emission regulations impose on domestic auto manufacturers that, along with U.S. tariffs, threaten the jobs of Canadian auto workers and the viability of Canadian automaker operations,” the statement says.

“Together, we are calling on the federal government to exempt non-compliance penalties for passenger automobile greenhouse gas emission regulations for Canadian automakers.”

Polluters in Canada face a web of regulations and taxes aimed at reducing the emissions that cause climate change. The leaders are seeking breaks for automakers on the carbon tax and tailpipe emissions rules.

Canada’s tailpipe emissions system requires companies whose cars don’t meet federal emissions standards to buy credits from those whose automobiles do. It is designed to encourage the sale of low-emissions vehicles and to make it expensive to sell gas guzzlers.

Stellantis’s most popular vehicles in Canada include Ram trucks and Jeeps.

In the letter, Mr. Ford and Ms. Payne say the system rewards companies that do not manufacture in Canada.

The two leaders said the penalties will force companies that build in Canada to pay out billions in non-compliance costs, adding that an exemption for Canadian automakers must come with “a firm commitment that automotive production will be preserved in Canada, including a full reversal of the sale of the Stellantis Brampton Assembly Plant.”

Hannah Jensen, a spokeswoman for Mr. Ford, said the non-compliance regulations are costing Stellantis $300-million a year. Stellantis declined to comment.

On Wednesday, officials from Stellantis, the federal and Ontario governments and Unifor met in Toronto and agreed to continue discussions another day.

A spokesperson for federal Industry Minister Mélanie Joly did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Brian Kingston, head of the Canadian Vehicle Manufacturers’ Association, which represents Stellantis, Ford and General Motors, said the tailpipe rules can be costly for car companies.

There are a variety of ways car companies can make their overall fleets more efficient, he explained, including using lighter materials, installing smaller engines or offering fewer trucks for sale.

“But at the end of the day, if you can’t meet it with your fleets, you have to purchase credits,” he said. “If you can’t purchase credits, you have to restrict sales. So it’s a quite impactful regulation that can have real cost consequences on manufacturers.”

The credit sales are private and prices are not disclosed. Tesla is the main seller in Canada, followed by Honda and Toyota, Mr. Kingston said.

Joanna Kyriazis, director of policy and strategy at Clean Energy Canada, a think tank at Simon Fraser University, said Canada is already offering many incentives to retain auto manufacturing, including billions of dollars in grants and subsidies, plus tariff remissions for manufacturing here.

“If the idea is that it costs too much to produce vehicles in Canada, then removing a policy that applies to the vehicles sold in Canada is not helping Stellantis’s Brampton plant that only sells 10 per cent of its vehicles here,” she said. “It’s actually disproportionately going to help Stellantis’s American plants that sell more of its vehicles into the Canadian market.”

Vic Fedeli, Ontario’s Minister of Economic Development, told reporters on Thursday that giving Stellantis a break on tailpipe emissions would help defray some of the expense of keeping the Brampton plant warm.

The emissions costs “don’t make us competitive with the United States,” Mr. Fedeli said. “They’re costs that Canadian companies, Canadian manufacturers bear that are not available in the States. We’re not aligned with the cost structure in the United States, and it makes it very difficult for companies to be here.”

Stellantis announced it had sold the plant, which employed about 3,000 people when it was idled in 2023, to Brampton-based Roshel earlier this month. Government and union officials are trying to reverse the transaction and save the auto workers’ jobs.

Ms. Joly has said Stellantis must repay the government “hundreds of millions” of dollars if it sells the plant, referring to aid the government has given the company since 2022 for work on car plants in Brampton and Windsor, Ont., plus the NextStar Energy EV battery plant in Windsor.

The Globe and Mail has reported the exact amount the government wants Stellantis to return is $831-million. The automaker has offered to pay $24-million, the amount it said it received for work on the Brampton plant. Ms. Joly has said she is prepared to offer Stellantis an “aggressive package” to reverse the plant’s sale.

Speaking to reporters in Ottawa on Thursday, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre called the government’s tailpipe emissions rules a “backdoor” electric vehicle mandate. He said the regulations benefit American-made Teslas while putting Canadian vehicle manufacturing under water.

The agency says several hours of freezing will bring two to five millimetres of ice-build up, with possible utility outages.

stories.title: Alberta health officials to give update on soldiers injured in CFB Wainwright fire
stories.summary: Edmonton - Alberta health officials are expected to provide an update today on the recovery of soldiers injured during a deadly fire at a military base.
stories.author: Daniela Germano The Canadian Press
stories.content:
EDMONTON - Soldiers being treated in hospital for burns from a deadly fire at an Alberta military base have a long psychological recovery ahead of them, says an Edmonton surgeon treating some of the injured.

Dr. Josh Wong, the interim medical director of the Edmonton Firefighters Burn Treatment Unit at the University of Alberta Hospital, says recovering from such severe burns can take months or years.

“For patients who experience severe burns, recovery is often a long and challenging journey. Their care doesn’t end when they leave the ICU or even the hospital,” Wong said Thursday at a news conference at the hospital.

“Many will require ongoing treatment and rehabilitation.”

Wong, who is a plastic and reconstructive surgeon specializing in burn cases, said the mental impact from even small burns can become more intense over time.

“I have mentioned to the families that the psychological effect actually comes up stronger as they recover and become more aware later on as well,” he said.

The Armed Forces had said that a windstorm on Oct. 17 pushed flames from a grass fire onto troops in a training exercise at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, southeast of Edmonton.

Prime Minister Mark Carney called the fire one of the worst tragedies for the Armed Forces on home soil during peacetime.

Four were killed in the fire. They have been identified as: Pte. Shaun Farrell, 23, of Prince Albert, Sask.; Pte. Aidan Goulding, 23, of North Vancouver, B.C.; Pte. Hayden Lykkemark, 19, of Langley, B.C.; and Sgt. Morgan Wong, 26, of Edmonton.

A fifth soldier, Pte. William Douglas Dal Bianco, died of his injuries earlier this month while in an Ontario hospital.

About three dozen soldiers were initially injured.

Acute Care Alberta said 19 were still being cared for in provincial hospitals, with seven listed in critical condition.

The military said Saturday that two others remained in hospitals in British Columbia and Ontario, where they were transferred to be closer to their families.

Michael Suddes, interim chief operating officer for the Alberta Health Services’ Edmonton area, said officials could not provide specifics about the recovering soldiers due to patient confidentiality.

“But there is a spectrum,” he said. “Several patients, while they may be in critical condition, several (other) patients have already been discharged home.”

Dr. Sayeh Zielke, interim chief executive officer of Acute Care Alberta, said the fire put a huge stress on the province’s health-care system.

“We passed it,” she said. “We were able to manage the capacity and co-ordinate the response to provide the care, not only for the injured soldiers, but also the rest of our version that needed care.”

Zielke said health-care providers are still in the thick of treating the injured soldiers, but soon there will be a debriefing process to see if improvements can be made.

“We’re trying to do our best by every single day. So for us, it very much feels like a marathon,” she said.

“There’s always lessons to be learned, and we can always do better and aim for perfection.”

Wong said patients with severe burns require complex, intensive treatment that involves multiple procedures and surgeries, extensive rehabilitation, psychological support and ongoing followup care.

He said the Wainwright fire presented an extraordinary challenge for his team, who admitted 20 critically injured patients in a short period of time — about five times the specialized burn critical care capacity.

He added that there were already 15 other burn patients in care at the time.

“Our teams moved quickly to mobilize the physicians, the nurses, other health-care professionals with specialized training and experience needed to provide this level of care,” Wong said.

He also recognized that many health-care workers may start to feel the effects of their hard work and trauma they have witnessed, and his team is preparing for that.

“When you’re in the midst of all the work and the adrenalin rushing and trying to help these patients, that’s where our focus is going to,” he said.

“But we know very well that as the weeks and the months go on, there will be some effects, there will be some fatigue, there’ll be some psychological effects of these injuries.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 26, 2026.

“But there is a spectrum,” he said. “Several patients, while they may be in critical condition, several (other) patients have already been discharged home.”
Dr. Sayeh Zielke, interim chief executive officer of Acute Care Alberta, said the fire put a huge stress on the province’s health-care system.
“We passed it,” she said. “We were able to manage the capacity and co-ordinate the response to provide the care, not only for the injured soldiers, but also the rest of our version that needed care.”
Zielke said health-care providers are still in the thick of treating the injured soldiers, but soon there will be a debriefing process to see if improvements can be made.
“We’re trying to do our best by every single day. So for us, it very much feels like a marathon,” she said.
“There’s always lessons to be learned, and we can always do better and aim for perfection.”
Wong said patients with severe burns require complex, intensive treatment that involves multiple procedures and surgeries, extensive rehabilitation, psychological support and ongoing followup care.

He said the Wainwright fire presented an extraordinary challenge for his team, who admitted 20 critically injured patients in a short period of time — about five times the specialized burn critical care capacity.
He added that there were already 15 other burn patients in care at the time.
“Our teams moved quickly to mobilize the physicians, the nurses, other health-care professionals with specialized training and experience needed to provide this level of care,” Wong said.
He also recognized that many health-care workers may start to feel the effects of their hard work and trauma they have witnessed, and his team is preparing for that.
“When you’re in the midst of all the work and the adrenalin rushing and trying to help these patients, that’s where our focus is going to,” he said.
“But we know very well that as the weeks and the months go on, there will be some effects, there will be some fatigue, there’ll be some psychological effects of these injuries.”

stories.title: Heavy rains, storm surge, high tides cause 'real drama' along B.C.'s coast
stories.summary: Vancouver - British Columbia's coast is getting another weather wallop as Environment Canada warns of rain of up to 225 millimetres along much of the coast before the end of the day.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
VANCOUVER - Marc Doll had been planning to use the planks of wood he watched float past his window on Tuesday to build a deck, but they’ve been put to a more urgent purpose as relentless rain swamped his property on British Columbia’s Quadra Island.

The creeks that weave around Doll’s farm run dry in the summer, but the rain that has soaked much of B.C.‘s coast has turned the creeks into fast-flowing streams.

Doll said he donned shorts and Crocs to fetch the planks for his would-be deck when he saw one of the larger bridges on his 17-hectare property looking unstable.

“I noticed that the bridge was starting to float away, so I threw that wood on top of the bridge to weigh the bridge down,” he said in an interview the next day.

Rainfall and wind warnings covered Vancouver Island and the Gulf Islands, including Quadra, as the final storm in what Environment Canada called a series of “potent” weather systems hit the coast on Wednesday.

The weather office upgraded coastal flood warnings in parts of Metro Vancouver, Squamish and Gibsons, saying storm surge, large waves and very high tides could cause “moderate to significant” flooding.

The bulletin said the storm would push water levels 40 to 70 centimetres above the highest astronomical tides of the year.

Lower-level yellow warnings for coastal flooding spanned all of Vancouver Island and stretched along the central coast, where water levels were expected to be 30 to 50 centimetres higher. The bulletin also covers much of Haida Gwaii.

Wednesday evening, around 8:30 p.m. local time, the Comox Valley Regional District issued a State of Local Emergency to support its emergency response to current flood conditions, including rising waters, flooding, and risk to property. Officials are warning residents to stay away from the water’s edge and follow any official emergency orders or directions.

Earlier, the Regional District of Nanaimo issued several evacuation alerts due to coastal flooding for communities in its jurisdiction along the east side of Vancouver Island, including Lantzville, Cedar and French Creek.

The nearby District of Lantzville also issued an alert for several properties on the waterfront, with B.C.‘s emergency information system saying high water levels could lead to flooding that poses “a threat to life and safety.”

While Doll said he was able to secure his larger bridge, a smaller bridge was swept away, cutting him off from 12 pigs on the property.

He waded through thigh-deep water to reach the pigs at mealtime.

“We have a mother who’s got eight little piglets, so she needs food every day otherwise there’s problems. So I couldn’t put it off,” he said.

Doll said the pigs have a covered area to stay in at the highest point in their pasture.

“My pigs usually are in half- to three-quarter-acre pastures. And they’re on an island at the moment, but they’re fine,” he said.

John Clague, professor emeritus at Simon Fraser University’s earth sciences department, said B.C.‘s wet week is the result of a combination of heavy rains, strong winds and the highest tides of the year, known as king tides.

“I hate to use the phrase, (but) it’s a perfect storm, both figuratively and actually,” he said in an interview.

Clague said the king tides, caused by the gravitational pulls of the sun and the moon, are expected to diminish toward the end of the week.

The B.C. River Forecast Centre issued an upgraded flood watch for areas between Nanaimo and Campbell River on Wednesday, while lower-level streamflow advisories covered the rest of Vancouver Island.

Environment Canada figures show one station on Vancouver Island had already recorded 469 millimetres between 11 a.m. on Monday and 1 p.m. on Wednesday.

The storm has also brought high winds, even reaching speeds of nearly 160 km/h off the northern tip of Vancouver Island.

On the mainland, high streamflow advisories were in effect for the Sunshine Coast, Sea to Sky region and Vancouver’s North Shore.

The storms also prompted the District of Squamish to declare a local state of emergency and activate its local emergency operations centre.

It said the Sea to Sky region would see a significant amount of rain along with high tides over the next few days, with the highest tides expected Thursday.

The Transportation Ministry, meanwhile, advised drivers to check conditions before travelling through coastal areas due to the risk of flooding.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 25, 2026.

— With files from Chuck Chiang

stories.title: Canada and Qatar sign agreement to boost investment
stories.summary: Ottawa - Canada and Qatar have signed a new agreement that looks to encourage increased investment, despite widespread criticism of Qatar's human rights record.
stories.author: Catherine Morrison The Canadian Press
stories.content:
OTTAWA - Canada and Qatar have signed a new agreement that looks to encourage increased investment, despite widespread criticism of Qatar’s human rights record.

Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand and her Qatari counterpart Dr. Ahmad bin Mohammed Al-Sayed signed the Canada-Qatar Foreign Investment Promotion and Protection Agreement in Ottawa on Tuesday.

International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu, who led negotiations on the agreement, said he’s proud to see the deal signed because it means more Qatari investment in Canada and more opportunities for Canadian businesses in Qatar.

Sidhu said in a media statement that Qatar’s economy is worth nearly $300 billion. He said the Qatar Investment Authority is one of the world’s largest sovereign wealth funds, with nearly US$600 billion in assets.

Canada and Qatar’s bilateral trade exceeds $350 million, said Sidhu, who added that foreign direct investment from Qatar has reached $338 million.

“With this agreement, we’re going to grow that figure,” he said. “The opportunity here is real.”

Conservative MP Shuv Majumdar chided Carney on the platform X over his outreach to both China and Qatar, citing their dire human rights records and past support for Canada’s adversaries.

“They traffic in the worst elements of the world because they turn these assets they’ve built up into the indispensable dependencies,” Majumdar said. He said Canada should instead boost trade ties with Taiwan and Arab countries that have normalized relations with Israel.

stories.title: Provinces waiting to see if Trump follows through on data centre tax threat
stories.summary: Premier Tim Houston’s office said that Trump has made similar threats before, such as his call last year for 100 per cent tariffs on foreign films that never materialized.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Canadian provinces are waiting to see if U.S. President Donald Trump will follow through on his threat to tax American companies with foreign data centres.

Trump threatened Friday to impose “a tremendous tax” on American firms that build their data centres abroad.

Meanwhile American artificial intelligence firm Anthropic has signed a 20-year lease to occupy a planned $10-billion data centre project in Cape Breton.

EverWind fuels plans to finance, build and own the 18,600-square metre facility in Point Tupper, N.S., which would be Anthropic’s first Canadian data centre.

Premier Tim Houston’s office said in an email Tuesday that Trump has made similar threats before, such as his call last year for 100 per cent tariffs on foreign films that never materialized.

U.S. firm Meta is building a $13-billion data centre in Alberta and a spokesperson for Premier Danielle Smith said Tuesday that her government will wait to see if there are further details from the White House in the coming weeks.

“The reality is that EverWind is developing, financing, constructing and owning this (data centre) site. Preventing them from doing so would be like preventing American retailers from operating in Canadian shopping malls,” Houston’s office said in a statement.

stories.title: London Police solve 1968 murder of Jackie Dunleavy killing with new DNA technology
stories.summary: London police have identified a former city firefighter as a suspect in one of London's oldest cold cases: the...
stories.author: Owen Schuller
stories.content:
London police have identified a former city firefighter as a suspect in one of London’s oldest cold cases: the 1968 murder of London teenager, Jacqueline Dunleavy.

Genetic geniology technology helped identify a suspect in the killing of 16-year-old Jacqueline Dunleavy, whose body was found in the snow shortly after she left her part time job at a London variety store police said at a news conference Monday.

“For nearly six decades, Jackie’s family has lived with a loss that no passage of time could ever erase,” said London Police Chief Thai Truong. “This is…the first time the London police service has successfully used forensic, investigative, genetic genealogy to identify an individual response for a homicide.”

Police identified the suspect as Michael Joseph Moore, who died in 2018 and cannot be charged.

Then 25 and not yet working as a firefighter in London, Moore had moved to Canada from Ireland in 1967. He was living in an apartment on Springbank Drive at the time of the murder, police said.

Dunleavy’s brother was at the news conference but police ask to respect the family’s privacy.

Investigators said they are confident in the DNA technology results.

“Based on evidence obtained through this investigation, we are confident that the evidentiary threshold to support criminal charges was met,” said Det. Mike Budzyn. “Had Moore been alive today, he would have been arrested and charged in the connection of Jackie’s murderer,”

Dunleavy was a Grade 10 student at Westminster Secondary school and the daughter of a London police officer when she was killed after her shift at the Stanley Variety store where she worked part time.

“She finished her shift at approximately 6:30 p.m. and was last seen leaving the store on foot. At approximately 8 p.m. that evening, three youths found Jackie on the grounds of Katherine Harley School, now known as the location of Matthews Hall, ON Oxford Street. Emergency responders attended, and Jackie was pronounced deceased,” said the London Police news release.

Dunleavy’s murder has long been one London’s most troubling unsolved murders.

More to come . . .

stories.title: $5K bonus payments for trades workers going out early next month, government says
stories.summary: Ottawa - Bonuses for Red Seal trades workers are set to be delivered starting early next month.
stories.author: Catherine Morrison The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Since last week, tradespeople who completed an apprenticeship and earned their certification in a Red Seal trade on or after April 1, 2025, have been able to apply for a $5,000 completion bonus.

Jobs Minister Patty Hajdu says more than 16,000 applications have been received and the first payments will go out to eligible people starting the first week of December.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Inside interior designer Nora Voon’s art-filled home

Starting in July, “trade qualifiers” who haven’t completed an apprenticeship but have enough practical work experience and are certified in a Red Seal trade, can apply for the bonus as well.

Red Seal trades are skilled jobs with national standards, including for training, such as electricians, plumbers and welders.

The Liberals have announced billions of dollars in spending to train up to 100,000 new skilled workers over the next half decade to support the government’s ambitious infrastructure agenda.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 24, 2026.

stories.title: Author Galloway's lawyer asks B.C. court for millions in defamation award
stories.summary: Vancouver - The lawyer for author and former University of British Columbia professor Steven Galloway said in closing arguments that his client's accuser started rape allegations then poured gasoline on them by encouraging others to spread the claims.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
VANCOUVER - A lawyer for the woman who accused author Steven Galloway of rape says she shared her allegations with a small circle of people and can’t be held legally responsible for all the harms done to his reputation.

Arden Beddoes, a lawyer for the woman known as A.B, who can’t be named under a publication ban, said there were “intervening” causes that harmed the former creative writing professor’s career.

Beddoes began his final submissions in B.C. Supreme Court on Tuesday after Galloway’s lawyers concluded their closing arguments, asking the court to award several million dollars in damages for defamation.

They asked the court to make an explicit finding that the rape allegations against Galloway are false.

Beddoes said Galloway is seeking one of the largest defamation awards in Canadian history, but his client can’t be liable for the actions of others, including the University of British Columbia’s statements about Galloway’s suspension and firing.

He said the university’s public statements about Galloway being suspended due to “serious allegations” and terminated for a “record of misconduct, resulting in an irreparable breach of trust” were key factors driving the controversy that ensued.

Beddoes told the court that other defamation cases have involved sustained public campaigns where allegations are spread widely, which his client did not do.

She had refused to participate in a CBC documentary about sexual assault, Beddoes said, and had only confided in people over emails and in conversations, sharing details only when asked to do so by others.

“That pales in comparison to other cases where there have been malicious campaigns involving hundreds of posts and extensive public efforts,” to spread defamatory allegations, he said.

Later Tuesday, the judge asked about the testimony of A.B.‘s husband, who told the court that she had expressed a desire to “destroy” Galloway.

“Is that not evidence of malice?,” Justice Neena Sharma asked Beddoes.

“It is evidence of animus at that point in time,” Beddoes said.

Final submissions in the defamation trial began this week, and the court heard that Galloway is seeking nearly $5 million in rarely-awarded special damages in his defamation lawsuit against the woman who accused him of rape.

Galloway’s lawyer Dan Coles told the judge that special damages would include financial losses — both past and future — stemming from the loss of Galloway’s writing career.

Coles said on Tuesday that Galloway is also seeking almost $4 million in general, aggravated and punitive damages against A.B. and three other defendants for defamation, minus 25 per cent to account for defendants who settled the case before the trial.

The other defendants, Mandi Gray and Glynnis Kirchmeier should be on the hook for six-figure sums in damages and Dana Kagis around $30,000 in damages, Galloway’s lawyer told the court on Monday.

Beddoes said on Tuesday that the fire analogy “falls apart,” because Galloway is asking the court for the woman to be “answerable for far more than the words she uttered.”

“In November 2015, she reported her allegations in confidence to fewer than 10 people, professors to whom she reported, a friend and a small circle of support persons,” Beddoes said. “Her alleged defamatory words were spoken within a university reporting context.”

Correspondence, Beddoes said, showed she had sought to go through the complaint process and none of that shows evidence of a “malicious campaign” of defamation.

“We say she sought a process and not publicity,” Beddoes said. “She did not use social media to accuse the plaintiff by name. She did not go to the media.”

Beddoes told the judge that Galloway’s lawyers tried to cast A.B. as a “hidden hand behind the conduct of others.”

“We say that the evidence does not support that theory.”

A.B. did not testify in the trial, and she did not attend a court-ordered discovery for the case.

The court heard that the woman is not defending her allegations as true, but has not conceded them to be false.

“A.B. accepts that she is answerable for what she herself said and wrote to her own audience,” Beddoes said.

But he said the court should “confine her liability,” and not “attribute the consequences of UBC’s conduct and the independent acts of third parties, and of the plaintiff’s own decisions, to those responsible for them.”

The final submissions bring an end to the trial more than 10 years after the allegations were made against Galloway, paving the way to his suspension and eventual firing as a professor from the University of B.C.

The trial continues on Wednesday, and the court will still have to deal with issues of costs and an application to hold A.B. in contempt for failing to attend a court-ordered discovery.

stories.title: Storm surge, king tides converge to raise flooding risk on B.C. coast
stories.summary: Vancouver - Another frontal system is washing over coastal B.C., bringing heavy rains and strong winds, swelling waterways just as king tides peak this week.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
VANCOUVER - The risk of flooding is elevated across British Columbia’s coast as drenching rain and blustery winds coincide with king tides, setting off widespread warnings.

Environment Canada said water levels in coastal regions may rise to 50 centimetres above the highest astronomical tides from now through Thursday, accompanied by a storm surge and large waves.

King tides are the highest tides of the year, pulled by the gravitational force of the moon, which was full on Tuesday.

The District of Squamish declared a local state of emergency on Tuesday due to incoming high tides and potential flood risk.

The district says in a statement that the declaration will ensure it has legal authority from the province to complete the flood mitigation work through B.C.’s Emergency and Disaster Management Act.

“The Sea to Sky region is expected to receive a significant amount of rainfall and high tides over the next few days. Highest tides are forecast for Thursday morning,” it said in the statement.

Coastal flood warnings or statements cover Metro Vancouver, Vancouver Island, Haida Gwaii, the central and Sunshine coasts and much of the northern coast.

Warnings also remain up for most of Vancouver Island for up to 225 millimetres of rain expected through to Thursday, while wind warnings cover Greater Victoria, calling for gusts reaching 90 kilometres an hour.

The B.C. River Forecast Centre has issued high streamflow advisories for waterways on most of Vancouver Island, the South Coast, Howe Sound, Sunshine Coast and Sea to Sky region, saying rivers are expected to rise rapidly following the rainfall.

The centre says previous periods of heavy rain and already saturated soils will bring sharp increases in river levels, while the king tides will exacerbate water levels at the mouths of rivers.

“Peak levels are forecasted to potentially reach up to two-year to five-year return period flows, however some weather model scenarios indicate that higher flows could be possible,” said the statement from the forecast centre.

The B.C. Ministry of Transportation says in a news release that motorists along the South Coast should use caution due to “possible fallen debris and flooding” potentially leading to sudden road closures.

Drivers on the Malahat Highway and other routes on western Vancouver Island are also being urged to be vigilant, and the ministry said it is increasing highway patrols and is ready to respond if needed.

Meteorologist Chloe Katsademas said residents should also “keep an eye out” for weather updates, as the arriving low-pressure system may trigger upgrades in warnings for coastal flooding, wind and rain.

“When there’s (a) low pressure (system), things move toward it,” said Katsademas.

She said the system creates high winds and storm surges.

“It’s coinciding with this run of king tides, which elevates water levels at high tide in general,” she said.

“And by having those two things together, the water levels at high tide could be 20 to 50 centimetres higher than the highest astronomical tide.”

The arrival of the supersized tide along B.C.‘s coast has created a spectacular show of pounding surf and tall, foaming waves, drawing photographers, citizen scientists and the curious to the shorelines.

Photographer and filmmaker Geoff Heith from Port Hardy, on northeastern Vancouver Island, said he’s been going out at least once a day to capture photos on the beach, and he is fond of storms when they roll up on the northern Island.

Heith said the king tide, and rain and wind warnings have created their own “perfect storm.”

He said when he was out at Thomas Point on northern Vancouver Island on Monday, the high tides reached more than five metres tall, which created “massive” waves.

“The cliff I was standing on … is probably 40, 50 feet up over the water, and those waves splashing was easily coming over top of that.”

Another video taken by Heith shows large logs moved easily by waves.

“Usually we’ll get king tides, but not with a very big storm. So, this is the first time I’ve seen a king tide with a big storm.”

Tim Carver from Colwood, B.C., visited Esquimalt Lagoon on Tuesday, to watch the stormy waters.

Carver said the ocean was “angry” as it tossed large logs around in the surf.

“The beach is being rearranged. It’ll be a brand new beach when the storm is over,” said Carver.

“We have a very old wooden bridge down there, and the water is coming up so high, it’s brought all the logs up to the bridge and it’s pushing on the bridge,” said Carver.

The City of Colwood said its team was monitoring “very high tides” at the lagoon.

The Tla-o-qui-aht First Nation in Tofino has issued an evacuation alert for some shoreline properties, saying residents need to be ready to leave.

The nation said in a public notice that tides could reach more than four metres on Wednesday, and there has also been concern about the weather phenomenon combining with the effects of a “Kelvin wave,” a slow-moving underwater wave connected to this year’s El Nino weather pattern.

“While conditions may ultimately remain manageable and no significant impacts are currently anticipated, we are encouraging residents to take reasonable precautions out of an abundance of caution,” the notice says.

Katsademas said the B.C. coast is not expected to see a break from wet and windy weather until the weekend, before another low-pressure system potentially moves through next week.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 24, 2026.

— With files from Chuck Chiang
