stories.title: Largest emissions spike in decade further sets back climate goals in Toronto area
stories.summary: A more polluting energy grid and rising demand for gas heating during a colder winter drove the largest annual spike in planet-warming emissions.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
By Jordan Omstead, The Canadian Press

Posted November 24, 2026 6:15 am.

A more polluting energy grid and rising demand for gas heating during a colder winter drove the largest annual spike in planet-warming emissions in at least a decade across the Greater Toronto and Hamilton Area, a new report found, putting the region further off track to its climate goals.

The findings paint a bleak picture of the region’s trajectory. Emissions rose for a fifth straight year and increased by eight per cent from 2024 to 2025, the biggest annual jump since tracking began in 2015, said the report from The Atmospheric Fund, a regional climate agency.

The Gtha, responsible for a major share of Ontario’s emissions, now faces a steep climb to meet local climate commitments. If Toronto’s 2030 target were used as a regional benchmark, emissions would need to be slashed by about 16 per cent each year.

“This increase really brings us way off track from reaching any of the climate targets we’ve set out and really highlights the urgent need to take strong action to bend the curve and bring emissions back onto a downward trajectory,” said Bryan Purcell, the agency’s vice president of policy and programs.

The report released Tuesday offers some bright spots: Toronto recently removed local barriers to installing heat pumps and electric vehicle chargers; Ontario procured a record amount of battery storage this year, beating out gas on cost; and the federal government recently announced a $2-billion investment in building retrofits, including rebates for heat pumps.

But the report says government policy rollbacks are threatening to overshadow that progress as climate change fuels more intense wildfires, flooding and extreme heat.

The findings, Purcell said, challenge a common political argument that climate action must take a back seat to affordability concerns. Many of the measures needed to cut emissions, such as building retrofits, switching to heat pumps and improving public transit, will also help alleviate those pocketbook pressures, he said.

“We know what works, we have the technology, and it’s really about the political will to put policies and programs in place to consistently move emissions downward. And that’s really the missing ingredient right now,” Purcell said.

Buildings, which account for nearly half of the region’s emissions, were among the biggest drivers of the annual increase. Building-sector emissions — mostly from burning gas for heat and, to a smaller extent, from electricity — rose by 15 per cent annually.

Electricity-related building emissions were up 26 per cent, due to what the report says is the province’s increasingly carbon-intensive grid. Nearly a fifth of Ontario’s electricity was generated by fossil fuels last year, the most since the coal phaseout, as the province turns to gas to help fill the gap left by nuclear reactors turned off-line for refurbishment.

Heating-related emissions were up by 14 per cent over the previous year, largely due to the colder winter, the report found. But even when researchers adjusted for weather, those emissions were still up three per cent, pointing to what the report suggests is an underlying problem with the region’s aging, inefficient housing stock.

Those emissions are increasing at a time when municipalities have lost a key tool to bring them down. Premier Doug Ford’s government has blocked Toronto and other municipalities from enforcing green building standards, siding with some developers who argued the requirements added costs and complexity to construction.

The change set Toronto back “about 10 years in terms of the efficiency and technology going into new buildings,” Purcell said.

With limits on what cities can require of new construction, Purcell said there’s still headway to be made with existing homes and businesses. He pointed to Toronto’s proposed building emissions performance standards as one of the most significant local climate policies under consideration in the region.

“Existing buildings are the largest source of emissions for most of our cities. And we really need policy tools that will help to control and reverse that growth over time,” he said.

Transportation, the next-largest source after buildings, saw emissions increase by between one and three per cent across most of the region. Most of that was driven by increasing number of cars on the road and an ongoing preference for larger vehicles that tend to be less fuel efficient, Purcell said.

The number of registered battery-electric and plug-in hybrid vehicles continued to rise but Purcell said policy uncertainty had created new headwinds. Ottawa cancelled an EV sales mandate earlier this year and its promise to enhance tailpipe emissions regulations to help offset the environmental blow has yet to materialize. Municipal support for charging networks could help give car buyers more confidence to make the switch, he said.

While investments in public transit expansion were promising, Purcell said cities needed to place a focus on day-to-day service improvements to encourage some residents to switch to buses and trains. Ridership across the region was down by about 1.5 per cent annually, and remains well below pre-pandemic levels.

“It’s those basic nuts and bolts issues that drive ridership growth more than the mega projects,” he said.

Industrial emitters, mostly steel and cement manufacturers, showed no signs of progress as the decarbonization plans “stalled,” the report said. It comes as Ford is pressuring the federal government to abandon the industrial carbon price as part of an effort to keep automaker Stellantis from selling its idled Brampton plant.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 24, 2026.

stories.title: Mortgage delinquency rate up 31% in Q3, driven by Ontario and B.C.: Equifax report
stories.summary: Toronto - A new report suggests there's growing stress among homeowners, with some struggling to keep up with monthly mortgage payments as interest rates rise again.
stories.author: Ritika Dubey The Canadian Press
stories.content:
TORONTO - A new report suggests there’s growing stress among homeowners, with some struggling to keep up with monthly mortgage payments as interest rates rise again.

Equifax Canada’s third-quarter consumer credit trends report says the national 90-plus day mortgage delinquency rate — defined as missed payments three months in a row — reached 0.32 per cent, the highest since the credit agency started tracking the metric in 2013.

That’s up 31.1 per cent year-over-year, mainly pushed higher by missed mortgage payments in Ontario and British Columbia.

“That’s the highest we’ve seen, particularly for Ontario. And it’s still going up,” said Rebecca Oakes, Equifax Canada’s vice-president of advanced analytics, said in an interview.

“That’s the biggest concern for us.”

The Equifax data echoes the findings of a recent a TD report, which showed Ontario’s mortgage arrears have nearly tripled from pre-pandemic levels to approach their 2008 financial crisis peak.

“This reflects elevated mortgage balances and greater sensitivity to borrowing costs,” wrote TD economist Maria Solovieva in the report published last week.

Growing pressure on households comes as the Bank of Canada raised its policy interest rate by a quarter of a percentage point to 2.5 per cent last month for the first time in more than three years, amid concerns that higher energy prices could spill into broader inflation.

The move prompted the big banks to raise their prime rates, which is used to set interest rates on a range of loans including variable-rate mortgages.

Equifax estimates about 1.4 million Canadians have a variable-rate mortgage out of a total 9.1 million homeowners. Another 1.3 million consumers also have a home equity line of credit, or HELOC, balance of more than $50,000.

Every quarter-point rate hike adds roughly $860 million a year in interest on variable-rate mortgages, the company estimates.

Oakes suspects mortgage delinquencies will continue to rise in the coming months, depending on changes to interest rates.

“If interest rates stay relatively flat from this point on, I’d expect to see it ease off in the middle of next year,” she said.

But if more hikes come in, “it’s just going to put additional pressure.”

The central bank is expected to make its last rate decision of the year on Dec. 9.

Financial market odds for a quarter-point rate hike was 63 per cent as of Monday afternoon, according to LSEG Data & Analytics.

Oakes said first-time homebuyers and younger Canadians may bear the brunt of rising rates because they tend to carry a higher-balance mortgage.

paragraphs: TORONTO - A new report suggests there’s growing stress among homeowners, with some struggling to keep up with monthly mortgage payments as interest rates rise again.

Equifax Canada’s third-quarter consumer credit trends report says the national 90-plus day mortgage delinquency rate — defined as missed payments three months in a row — reached 0.32 per cent, the highest since the credit agency started tracking the metric in 2013.
That’s up 31.1 per cent year-over-year, mainly pushed higher by missed mortgage payments in Ontario and British Columbia.
“That’s the highest we’ve seen, particularly for Ontario. And it’s still going up,” said Rebecca Oakes, Equifax Canada’s vice-president of advanced analytics, said in an interview.
“That’s the biggest concern for us.”
The Equifax data echoes the findings of a recent a TD report, which showed Ontario’s mortgage arrears have nearly tripled from pre-pandemic levels to approach their 2008 financial crisis peak.
“This reflects elevated mortgage balances and greater sensitivity to borrowing costs,” wrote TD economist Maria Solovieva in the report published last week.

Growing pressure on households comes as the Bank of Canada raised its policy interest rate by a quarter of a percentage point to 2.5 per cent last month for the first time in more than three years, amid concerns that higher energy prices could spill into broader inflation.
The move prompted the big banks to raise their prime rates, which is used to set interest rates on a range of loans including variable-rate mortgages.

Equifax estimates about 1.4 million Canadians have a variable-rate mortgage out of a total 9.1 million homeowners. Another 1.3 million consumers also have a home equity line of credit, or HELOC, balance of more than $50,000.
Every quarter-point rate hike adds roughly $860 million a year in interest on variable-rate mortgages, the company estimates.
Oakes suspects mortgage delinquencies will continue to rise in the coming months, depending on changes to interest rates.
“If interest rates stay relatively flat from this point on, I’d expect to see it ease off in the middle of next year,” she said.
But if more hikes come in, “it’s just going to put additional pressure.”
The central bank is expected to make its last rate decision of the year on Dec. 9.

stories.title: Changes to inspection rules at food plants putting safety at risk: union
stories.summary: A federal union is warning about risks to food safety as the government cuts back on inspections at meat plants.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
OTTAWA — A federal union is warning about risks to food safety as the government cuts back on inspections at meat plants.

Canadian Food Inspection Agency documents, obtained by The Canadian Press, show that as of Oct. 1, daily inspections are no longer being conducted in domestic-only meat plants. They are also no longer being conducted in plants that export exclusively to non-U.S. markets.

The daily inspection program is continuing in plants where food is bound for the United States. The agency said that’s because of U.S. equivalency and market access requirements.

“This reflects trade requirements and should not be interpreted as a difference in food safety standards,” said a Canadian Food Inspection Agency document. “Products destined for domestic and export markets remain subject to the same regulatory requirements and food safety expectations.”

The agency called the changes to inspection rules a “reallocation” of inspection activities and not a reduction.

The agency said it will continue to deliver inspection and oversight activities using a “risk-based approach” that considers food safety risks, compliance history, regulatory requirements and trade requirements.

It said establishments with higher-risk activities or unsatisfactory inspection outcomes will continue to see a heightened inspection presence, whether they serve domestic or international markets.

Milton Dyck, national president of the Agriculture Union, said inspectors on the plant floor are the “last line of defence” between Canadians and a deadly outbreak.

“A drop in inspection can be the difference between a routine day and another Maple Leaf 2008 tragedy,” he said.

In 2008, a listeria outbreak at a Maple Leaf Foods meat plant in Ontario led to dozens of illnesses and 22 deaths.

The union is raising concerns about the planned “risk-based” approach replacing daily inspection presence. It said it’s not clear what “risk” means and that there is no information on how often an inspector will now walk a domestic plant floor.

“They’ve replaced a written, transparent standard with a black box and called it modernization,” said Dyck. “The Carney government is rolling back protections to your health under the guise of cuts to red tape. We’re calling on the government to stop the cuts and to consult the people who do this work before it’s too late.”

A Canadian Food Inspection Agency spokesperson said that while inspectors are no longer required to be present during every 12-hour production shift, that requirement was separate from regular food safety inspection activities. The spokesperson said inspectors continue to be present during slaughter at all federally regulated facilities.

“The frequency and rigour of food safety inspections remain unchanged,” said the spokesperson. “Establishments carrying out higher-risk activities or demonstrating unsatisfactory compliance will continue to receive heightened inspection presence.”

The spokesperson said the requirement for daily shift inspection presence at establishments exporting to the United States remains in place because it is a condition of U.S. import requirements.

“It is a trade requirement, not an indication that meat produced for Canadians is subject to lower food safety standards,” said the spokesperson. “Meat produced for the Canadian market and meat produced for export must meet the same federal food safety requirements.”

The spokesperson said Canada’s federally regulated meat sector continues to demonstrate strong compliance with food safety requirements, with compliance rates typically ranging between 95 and 97 per cent.

The spokesperson said the change to daily presence “modernizes” how inspection resources are allocated, allowing the agency to direct additional capacity toward higher-priority food safety activities and emerging risks, while maintaining strong regulatory, food safety, animal welfare and trade outcomes.

Federal government data shows there were 6,207 employees working at the Canadian Food Inspection Agency as of the end of March. That’s down from 6,380 in 2025, and 6,833 the year before.

A Canadian Food Inspection Agency document said it’s reallocating approximately $30 million from existing resources to modernize how its inspection workforce is deployed and direct resources to “areas of greatest impact.” It said the funds will allow for around 250 new inspection and oversight positions.

It said the agency is creating a national food inspection team to support risk-based activities in the areas of food fraud, consumer protection and import oversight.

“The team will also provide surge capacity during large-scale food-related incidents and emergencies, helping to ensure a co-ordinated and effective operational response across the country,” said the document. “The CFIA’s mandate and regulatory responsibilities remain unchanged.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 24, 2026.

Catherine Morrison, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Largest emissions spike in decade further sets back climate goals in Toronto area
stories.summary: Toronto - A more polluting energy grid and rising demand for gas heating during a colder winter drove the largest annual spike in planet-warming emissions in at least a decade across the Greater Toronto and Hamilton Area, a new report found, putting the region further off track to its climate goals.
stories.author: Jordan Omstead The Canadian Press
stories.content:
TORONTO - A more polluting energy grid and rising demand for gas heating during a colder winter drove the largest annual spike in planet-warming emissions in at least a decade across the Greater Toronto and Hamilton Area, a new report found, putting the region further off track to its climate goals.

The findings paint a bleak picture of the region’s trajectory. Emissions rose for a fifth straight year and increased by eight per cent from 2024 to 2025, the biggest annual jump since tracking began in 2015, said the report from The Atmospheric Fund, a regional climate agency.

The GTHA, responsible for a major share of Ontario’s emissions, now faces a steep climb to meet local climate commitments. If Toronto’s 2030 target were used as a regional benchmark, emissions would need to be slashed by about 16 per cent each year.

“This increase really brings us way off track from reaching any of the climate targets we’ve set out and really highlights the urgent need to take strong action to bend the curve and bring emissions back onto a downward trajectory,” said Bryan Purcell, the agency’s vice president of policy and programs.

The report released Tuesday offers some bright spots: Toronto recently removed local barriers to installing heat pumps and electric vehicle chargers; Ontario procured a record amount of battery storage this year, beating out gas on cost; and the federal government recently announced a $2-billion investment in building retrofits, including rebates for heat pumps.

But the report says government policy rollbacks are threatening to overshadow that progress as climate change fuels more intense wildfires, flooding and extreme heat.

The findings, Purcell said, challenge a common political argument that climate action must take a back seat to affordability concerns. Many of the measures needed to cut emissions, such as building retrofits, switching to heat pumps and improving public transit, will also help alleviate those pocketbook pressures, he said.

“We know what works, we have the technology, and it’s really about the political will to put policies and programs in place to consistently move emissions downward. And that’s really the missing ingredient right now,” Purcell said.

Buildings, which account for nearly half of the region’s emissions, were among the biggest drivers of the annual increase. Building-sector emissions — mostly from burning gas for heat and, to a smaller extent, from electricity — rose by 15 per cent annually.

Electricity-related building emissions were up 26 per cent, due to what the report says is the province’s increasingly carbon-intensive grid. Nearly a fifth of Ontario’s electricity was generated by fossil fuels last year, the most since the coal phaseout, as the province turns to gas to help fill the gap left by nuclear reactors turned off-line for refurbishment.

Heating-related emissions were up by 14 per cent over the previous year, largely due to the colder winter, the report found. But even when researchers adjusted for weather, those emissions were still up three per cent, pointing to what the report suggests is an underlying problem with the region’s aging, inefficient housing stock.

Those emissions are increasing at a time when municipalities have lost a key tool to bring them down. Premier Doug Ford’s government has blocked Toronto and other municipalities from enforcing green building standards, siding with some developers who argued the requirements added costs and complexity to construction.

The change set Toronto back “about 10 years in terms of the efficiency and technology going into new buildings,” Purcell said.

With limits on what cities can require of new construction, Purcell said there’s still headway to be made with existing homes and businesses. He pointed to Toronto’s proposed building emissions performance standards as one of the most significant local climate policies under consideration in the region.

“Existing buildings are the largest source of emissions for most of our cities. And we really need policy tools that will help to control and reverse that growth over time,” he said.

Transportation, the next-largest source after buildings, saw emissions increase by between one and three per cent across most of the region. Most of that was driven by increasing number of cars on the road and an ongoing preference for larger vehicles that tend to be less fuel efficient, Purcell said.

The number of registered battery-electric and plug-in hybrid vehicles continued to rise but Purcell said policy uncertainty had created new headwinds. Ottawa cancelled an EV sales mandate earlier this year and its promise to enhance tailpipe emissions regulations to help offset the environmental blow has yet to materialize. Municipal support for charging networks could help give car buyers more confidence to make the switch, he said.

While investments in public transit expansion were promising, Purcell said cities needed to place a focus on day-to-day service improvements to encourage some residents to switch to buses and trains. Ridership across the region was down by about 1.5 per cent annually, and remains well below pre-pandemic levels.

“It’s those basic nuts and bolts issues that drive ridership growth more than the mega projects,” he said.

Industrial emitters, mostly steel and cement manufacturers, showed no signs of progress as the decarbonization plans “stalled,” the report said. It comes as Ford is pressuring the federal government to abandon the industrial carbon price as part of an effort to keep automaker Stellantis from selling its idled Brampton plant.

stories.title: Pentagon criticizes Canada in ‘fact sheet’ after Hegseth memo
stories.summary: Washington — The Pentagon has released what it calls a "fact sheet" criticizing Canada's defence spending and saying it has limited the country's ability to contribute to the protection of North America.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
WASHINGTON — The Pentagon has released what it calls a “fact sheet” criticizing Canada’s defence spending in the latest symbolic push from the Trump administration to upend long-standing norms in North American continental security.

“Unfortunately, Canada has yet to make the hard decisions and tradeoffs needed to put it on track to fulfill its NATO Defense Investment Pledge and become a credible partner in the defense of our shared continent,” said the document released publicly on Monday and first reported by Axios the day prior.

“Canada’s defense shortfalls speak for themselves.”

The document points to operational readiness deficits in air, land and sea operations. It denounces Canadian political leadership for pursuing “parochial economic and commercial interests over military optimization.”

It was released after U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth last week issued a classified memo imposing restrictions on military co-operation with Canada on think tanks and socializing.

Sen. Mike Rounds, a Republican, told reporters at the Halifax International Security Forum on Saturday that the move would not affect military operations.

Defence Minister David McGuinty’s office has not yet responded to a request for comment about the fact sheet. On Saturday at the security conference, McGuinty said it was “business as usual” between the Canadian and U.S. militaries.

He assured Canadians that co-operation between the two countries on defence, security and intelligence was continuing.

In response to Hegseth’s memo, chief Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said the defence department is “taking steps to ensure its engagements with Canada advance tangible U.S. defense objectives and ultimately support a reinvigorated defense relationship.”

The memo and Monday’s fact sheet are the latest moves the Pentagon has taken under the Trump administration to break norms with Canada.

In May, Elbridge Colby, U.S. undersecretary of defence for policy, said his department was pausing the Permanent Joint Board on Defense “to reassess how this forum benefits shared North American defence.”

The board was established in 1940 and is an advisory forum for U.S.-Canada bilateral defence co-operation.

At that time, a high-ranking U.S. defence official said the Pentagon gave Ottawa a classified paper laying out priorities for a collective North American defence pact with Canada, but that Ottawa did not deliver a “credible” response.

That same month, Canada announced it would purchase early warning planes from Sweden’s Saab rather than a competing option from Boeing.

This criticism of Canada’s defence readiness is not happening in a vacuum. Experts have said it’s likely connected to a planned purchase of F-35 fighter jets and ongoing tensions between the two countries.

The Liberal government has yet to reach a decision on its order of F-35 fighter jets from Lockheed Martin — which Pentagon officials have cited as a source of frustration. The fighter jet purchase has been the subject of a political review for more than a year.

“It is a major issue for them and a leverage point for us,” said former Conservative leader Erin O’Toole, who is also a distinguished fellow at the Washington-based Hudson Institute.

Canada has long faced criticism about its lagging defence spending, but with U.S. President Donald Trump’s return to the White House it was directly connected to larger trade issues, including the renewal of the Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement on trade, known as CUSMA.

O’Toole said he was not surprised by the content of the fact sheet but, in a text message, he added that it “ignores everything in the last year.”

“This is like someone was asked to prepare a one-sided, negative summary without acknowledging any of the changes made in the last 18 months,” O’Toole said.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has made historic defence investments as Trump rattled the bilateral relationship with tariffs and threats of annexation.

Canada spent $63.4 billion on national defence in 2025, meeting its NATO commitment to spend two per cent of gross domestic product on defence for the first time.

NATO members met last year in The Hague and agreed to up defence spending to the equivalent of five per cent of GDP by 2035.

Ottawa has said Canada continues to accelerate its path to NATO’s new target of 3.5 per cent on core defence and is optimizing an additional 1.5 per cent of GDP spending on defence and security-related investments.

November’s federal budget laid out a plan to spend around four per cent of Canada’s gross domestic product on defence per year by the end of the decade — which includes the purchase of submarines, early warning jets and other capabilities.

But Carney has also faced domestic pressure about the lack of transparency around defence spending moving forward.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 23, 2026.

Kelly Geraldine Malone, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Quebec court suspends law making it optional to swear oath to King
stories.summary: Montreal - Quebec Superior Court has ruled that the province's politicians will need to swear an oath to the King in order to sit at the provincial legislature.
stories.author: Marieke Glorieux-Stryckman The Canadian Press
stories.content:
MONTREAL - Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon doubled down on his refusal to swear allegiance to the King after the province’s Superior Court ruled to temporarily reinstate the oath.

“I do not, and I cannot, take an oath to the King of England,” he said in a press conference at Montreal City Hall on Monday.

Earlier in the day, Quebec Superior Court Justice Ian Demers ruled that the province’s politicians will need to swear an oath to the King in order to sit at the provincial legislature and that any law passed by legislators who did not swear the oath would be unconstitutional.

Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon doubled down on his refusal to swear allegiance to the King after the province’s Superior Court ruled to temporarily reinstate the oath. (Nov. 23, 2026)

“The Constitution is not an à la carte menu from which an individual subject to its provisions can choose to respect only what suits them,” wrote Demers in his decision.

Monday’s ruling grants an emergency order requested by lawyer Lawrence David and the Consumer Law Group, who asked the court to stay the application of a 2022 law that made swearing the oath optional. The law is suspended until David’s constitutional challenge can be heard on its merits.

The suspension of the law raises questions about whether the parliamentary session will open as planned on Dec. 1.

St-Pierre Plamondon questioned the democratic value of the Canadian constitution, which Quebec never signed.

“I’m sorry, but a constitution that was never accepted by the population and that comes from military conquest and colonialism is nothing in terms of democracy compared to 127 members of Parliament, duly elected, that make a law and say, ‘that’s what we want,’” he said.

He said the government intends to appeal Monday’s stay order, adding that he expects the issue will eventually end up in front of the Supreme Court of Canada.

The 1867 Constitution Act orders legislators to swear allegiance to the monarch in order to take their seat.

The Quebec legislature adopted a law in 2022 to amended a section of the Act and exempt Quebec from the section that requires the oath. The change came after Parti Québécois members were temporarily barred from taking their seats because they refused to swear allegiance to the King.

The 127 Quebec legislature members who were elected on Oct. 5 chose not to swear allegiance to the King, opting instead for an oath to the people of Quebec. For the first time in the province’s history, Quebec’s lieutenant-governor, Manon Jeannotte, was not present at the swearing-in ceremony, at St-Pierre Plamondon’s request.

Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime and interim Coalition Avenir Québec Leader Mathieu Lévesque both took to social media and called on the government to appeal the judge’s decision.

“As members of the National Assembly, our primary loyalty is to the people of Quebec. Period,” wrote Duhaime on X.

He added that the legal battle should not delay the opening of the parliamentary session, a request echoed by Liberal Leader Charles Milliard.

“Let’s be pragmatic and get to work,” wrote Milliard on X.

The Parti Québécois won a minority mandate in October. St-Pierre Plamondon has previously said he was seeking legal advice on how to further cut ties with the monarchy, including stripping the lieutenant-governor of her roles and funding.

“There’s something abnormal about a foreign king coming to tell us what to do right at the start of a legislative term, a mandate,” he told reporters after the elections. “People might say it’s symbolic, but I would reply that it’s still totally abnormal.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 23, 2026.

stories.title: B.C. trial in author Stephen Galloway's defamation lawsuit enters final week
stories.summary: Vancouver - Final submissions in the trial of author and former UBC professor Stephen Galloway's defamation lawsuit are set to begin in B.C. Supreme Court in Vancouver today.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
VANCOUVER - There is “overwhelming evidence” that rape allegations against author and former University of British Columbia professor Steven Galloway are false, and he has waited years for “vindication” and a return to normal life, his lawyer said Monday.

Daniel Burnett began his final submissions in the trial where Galloway alleges defamation against a former student with whom he had an extramarital affair, and three other defendants who repeated the rape allegations online and elsewhere.

Burnett said the allegations spread at the behest of the woman known as A.B., who can’t be named under a publication ban, and were repeated by numerous people, many of whom settled and apologized to Galloway before the trial began.

Burnett said A.B.’s allegations were like a fire on which she poured “gasoline” by encouraging others to spread them.

“She knew she was setting a fire, and she knew that it was going to cause massive wreckage,” he said.

Burnett said general, aggravated and punitive damages should be awarded to Galloway in the range of $3 million to $4 million, minus 25 per cent to account for the defendants who already settled with Galloway.

He told the court that recklessness and knowingly spreading false allegations “clearly establishes malice and opens the door to aggravated and punitive damages.”

Burnett told B.C. Supreme Court Justice Neena Sharma that Galloway was a credible witness who “acknowledged his own failings” and was “emphatic” in his denials of the allegations of rape, sexual assault and physical assault.

“In a defamation case as severe as this one, it serves the underlying purpose of defamation law, which has to do with vindicating reputation.

“There’s been a horrific stain on his name for a decade,” Burnett said.

Burnett said the allegations caused Galloway “suffering and loss” and vindicating his reputation through a favourable ruling could allow him to “return to some semblance of the life that he and his family had before November 2015.”

Final submissions in the trial are scheduled through this week in the Vancouver court, where Galloway’s lawsuit was originally filed in 2018 over the spread of unproven allegations that surfaced in November 2015.

“This case has awaited trial for eight years on account of an inordinate number of motions and appeals, each one inflicting more delay on the vindication of Mr. Galloway’s reputation,” Burnett said.

“The suffering and loss that he’s endured since then is something no person should wish for another. Hopefully, the outcome of this case will, as far as a court decision can, enable him to recover some of that and have a better future.”

The court heard later on Monday from Dan Coles, another lawyer for Galloway, who said special damages in defamation cases involve “loss of income, profits, and other financial benefits, past and future,” caused by the defamatory expressions.

He said the court heard that Galloway is estimated to have lost more than $11 million in potential earnings over his lifetime, if not for the allegations derailing his career.

Coles noted the court has heard evidence that cast Galloway as a literary star at the height of his career in 2015, but book sales, pending deals, speaking engagements and festival initiations dried up after the accusation of rape.

“His future looked very bright,” Coles said.

Justice Neena Sharma said it was “noteworthy evidence” from Galloway who testified earlier that he can no longer write, and that he no longer reads much anymore.

Galloway is the author of the bestselling novel “The Cellist of Sarajevo.”

He was suspended by the University of B.C. over the allegations and later fired, though a former judge hired to investigate the claims found them unsubstantiated.

Galloway was awarded $167,000 in 2018 by an arbitrator who found the university — which was not a party in the lawsuit — violated his privacy rights and harmed his reputation.

Burnett told the court there was “pretty overwhelming evidence of falsehood” in the allegations that left Galloway “twisting in the wind” as an accused rapist for a decade.

“The defamations here convey that Mr. Galloway was guilty of such depravity that he would be despised even in a criminal population,” the lawyer said.

Burnett said there was “wave after wave” of pushback after information came out in favour of Galloway, including the report of retired Justice Mary Ellen Boyd, who was hired by the university to investigate and found the rape claims unsubstantiated.

“It could have been the end of it,” Burnett said of Boyd’s report.

Burnett said the court will have to consider the role each defendant in Galloway’s lawsuit allegedly played in keeping the story of the assault claims alive.

He said the allegations by A.B. “started it all” and the other defendants, Mandi Gray and Glynnis Kirchmeier, repeated and republished the alleged defamatory statements, along with Dana Kagis, who hasn’t participated in the trial.

Burnett said Gray was A.B.‘s most aggressive supporter, and “there’s no person who did more to keep the defamatory message alive.”

He said Kirchmeier, who is attending the trial remotely and defending herself, was “fanning the flames” of the allegations, though only one of her statements on the social media platform X, then Twitter, is at issue.

The court has also heard that A.B., who did not testify or attend the courtroom during the trial, violated a court order compelling her to sit for a discovery, which is the subject of a contempt of court application.

Galloway’s lawyers are expected to conclude their final submissions on Tuesday, with final submissions from the defendants expected afterwards.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 23, 2026.

stories.title: B.C. Greens take the oath of office as Leader Lowan laments failed climate conference
stories.summary: Victoria - Green Party Leader Emily Lowan and her caucus colleague Jeremy Valeriote will be sworn into office today at the legislature and Lowan has already set the tone for her tenure.
stories.author: Wolfgang Depner The Canadian Press
stories.content:
VICTORIA - British Columbia Greens see areas of agreement with Premier Lorne Doerkson’s government, but will hold the Conservatives and their “corporate lobbyists” accountable, Leader Emily Lowan said.

She said her two-member party in the provincial legislature will have a “historic opportunity” to be very clear about the inconsistencies and the hypocrisies that the new Conservative government represents.

“I think there’s also areas of common ground,” she said.

She made the comments after she and caucus colleague Jeremy Valeriote were sworn in as legislators on Monday in a ceremony attended by former federal Green Party leader Elizabeth May and former provincial Green legislator Adam Olsen.

“We need to see real affordability measures and lasting change, and I’m very concerned that we’re not seeing that in the mandate that has been set out so far,” she said.

Conservatives are already sliding toward “culture war issues” such as their promises to repeal sexual orientation and gender identity programming and restore the daily singing of O Canada in public schools, she said.

Lowan said the culture war issues are “distractions” from the “failing economic system” that the Conservatives are advancing.

“I meet British Columbians every day who are absolutely crushed by the status quo and don’t think that the best use of public dollars is to empty out the purse for foreign-owned LNG and subsidize extractive corporations that, more often than not, rip-and-ship those profits overseas,” she said.

Lowan, who is 26 years old and newly elected to the legislature, said areas of agreement with the Conservatives include health care.

She said Greens shared “common ground” with Conservatives when they were the Official Opposition around emergency room closures, foreign ownership of farmland and concerns around B.C.‘s “crumbling” infrastructure.

“So, I’m excited to hold them to account on their record that they’ve laid out … in the last years,” Lowan said.

Valeriote said Greens will also focus on the issue of climate change, even as others may crowd it out.

“It is an existential threat that we can’t delay on,” he said.

Valeriote is returning to the legislature as the incumbent of West Vancouver-Sea to Sky and Lowan takes her seat in the legislature little more than a year after winning her party’s leadership.

A climate activist and organizer, Lowan won a three-way race with a campaign that centred on recruiting young voters and criticizing corporate control of the provincial economy.

During last month’s provincial snap election, she ran in Saanich North and the Islands, after Green MLA Rob Botterell said he would not run again.

Lowan said during her victory speech on Oct. 24 that her party will hold the Conservatives accountable.

Lowan said the Greens’ job over the next four years is to be a “voice for the many people who will be harmed” by Conservative policies.

“That is going to require some serious movement building,” she said on election night.

She said the Greens will stand with marginalized people, workers, and with everyone who depends on strong public services.

“We may have a small caucus, but tonight we have inherited an enormous responsibility, and that is to hold a Conservative majority government to account,” she said. “That is our job. We are the only party who is equipped to stand against the Conservatives and their existence.”

Asked Monday what she meant by the phrase ‘existence,’ Lowan said the word she was looking for was Conservative ‘agenda’ and “the corporate lobbyists that really run their party.”

Doerkson congratulated Lowan and Valeriote on social media.

“I look forward to working together in the (legislature), building a constructive relationship and finding common ground, where we can deliver results for British Columbians.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 23, 2026.

stories.title: U.S. senator says Hegseth memo does not change military co-operation with Canada
stories.summary: Canada’s defence minister says he has not seen a memo from the U.S. secretary of war that reportedly restricts American defence co-operation with Canada.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
HALIFAX — A Republican senator says a U.S. defence department’s memo that reportedly placed restrictions on co-operation with Canada applies to things such as participating in think-tank conferences, not military operations.

Sen. Mike Rounds was responding to a Washington Post report on Friday that said Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth penned the classified memo putting restrictions on military co-operation with Canada last week. The paper reportedly said it had not seen the memo and offered no detail on its contents.

The senator said the memo does not affect any U.S. defence personnel in Canada today and does not impact the North American Aerospace Defence Command, North Atlantic Treaty Organization operations or the Five Eyes security alliance.

“It does limit general flag officer meetings to those that advance (defence department) objectives,” Rounds told reporters at the Halifax International Security Forum on Saturday. “(U.S. defence officials) must request permission for Canadian think-tank events or social engagements. And it is OK to attend any 9/11 events.”

Rounds said he and a delegation of U.S. senators attending the Halifax conference had just attended a meeting with Canadian officials and shared the information with them. Defence Minister David McGuinty told reporters hours earlier he was unaware of the memo’s contents.

“After listening to this, (Canadian officials) said it sounds like it’s nothing new, nothing different than what they’ve been really practising under for the last year-and-a-half,” said the South Dakota senator.

McGuinty said earlier in the day that it was “business as usual” between the Canadian and U.S. militaries and assured Canadians that co-operation between the two countries on defence, security and intelligence was continuing.

“I’ve seen no evidence of (a change). I’ve checked with our top military folks, they’ve seen no evidence of change. We continue to co-operate. We continue to work together,” McGuinty told reporters.

Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said in a response to the story about the memo that the defence department is “taking steps to ensure its engagements with Canada advance tangible U.S. defense objectives and ultimately support a reinvigorated defense relationship.”

The statement, made late Friday, added that the department is prioritizing bilateral co-operation that strengthens the defence of the U.S. and “shared hemisphere” while also supporting Canada’s ability to meet NATO obligations.

“This guidance does not impact defense intelligence co-operation, our binational NORAD command, or our co-operation through NATO,” Parnell said.

Several U.S. senators at the Halifax event acknowledged their country’s standing around the world has been impacted by the aggressive policies of U.S. President Donald Trump.

Senator Tim Kaine, a Democrat, said the memo doesn’t help relations with Canada. He said he’s hopeful things will change when the new U.S. Congress takes office in January. Democrats took control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives in this month’s midterm election.

“The tone is bad and it’s unnecessary,” said Kaine. “And we understand this actually goes back a ways and it is just the formalization of something that is now months and months old. I do think the new Congress is going to change the tone dramatically. ”

McGuinty also announced Saturday that Canada is formally becoming the 25th member of NATO’s Innovation Fund. Canada is contributing more than $100 million to the fund, enabling it to invest in Canadian startups.

Launched in 2022, the venture capital fund is designed to strengthen NATO by investing in cutting edge technologies such as artificial intelligence, quantum technologies, biotech, space and communications.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 21, 2026.

Devin Stevens, The Canadian Press

“It does limit general flag officer meetings to those that advance (defence department) objectives,” Rounds told reporters at the Halifax International Security Forum on Saturday. “(U.S. defence officials) must request permission for Canadian think-tank events or social engagements. And it is OK to attend any 9/11 events.”

Rounds said he and a delegation of U.S. senators attending the Halifax conference had just attended a meeting with Canadian officials and shared the information with them. Defence Minister David McGuinty told reporters hours earlier he was unaware of the memo’s contents.

“After listening to this, (Canadian officials) said it sounds like it’s nothing new, nothing different than what they’ve been really practising under for the last year-and-a-half,” said the South Dakota senator.

McGuinty said earlier in the day that it was “business as usual” between the Canadian and U.S. militaries and assured Canadians that co-operation between the two countries on defence, security and intelligence was continuing.
“I’ve seen no evidence of (a change). I’ve checked with our top military folks, they’ve seen no evidence of change. We continue to co-operate. We continue to work together,” McGuinty told reporters.

Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said in a response to the story about the memo that the defence department is “taking steps to ensure its engagements with Canada advance tangible U.S. defense objectives and ultimately support a reinvigorated defense relationship.”

The statement, made late Friday, added that the department is prioritizing bilateral co-operation that strengthens the defence of the U.S. and “shared hemisphere” while also supporting Canada’s ability to meet NATO obligations.
“This guidance does not impact defense intelligence co-operation, our binational NORAD command, or our co-operation through NATO,” Parnell said.
Several U.S. senators at the Halifax event acknowledged their country’s standing around the world has been impacted by the aggressive policies of U.S. President Donald Trump.

Senator Tim Kaine, a Democrat, said the memo doesn’t help relations with Canada. He said he’s hopeful things will change when the new U.S. Congress takes office in January. Democrats took control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives in this month’s midterm election.

“The tone is bad and it’s unnecessary,” said Kaine. “And we understand this actually goes back a ways and it is just the formalization of something that is now months and months old. I do think the new Congress is going to change the tone dramatically. ”

McGuinty also announced Saturday that Canada is formally becoming the 25th member of NATO’s Innovation Fund. Canada is contributing more than $100 million to the fund, enabling it to invest in Canadian startups.

Launched in 2022, the venture capital fund is designed to strengthen NATO by investing in cutting edge technologies such as artificial intelligence, quantum technologies, biotech, space and communications.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 21, 2026.
Devin Stevens, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Ottawa says it lost $2M from emergency drug stockpile after freezer malfunction
stories.summary: Ottawa - The Public Health Agency of Canada has reported losing another $2 million in pharmaceuticals from the national emergency stockpile because of the mechanical failure of a freezer.
stories.author: Kyle Duggan and Catherine Morrison The Canadian Press
stories.content:
OTTAWA - The Public Health Agency of Canada has reported losing another $2 million in pharmaceuticals from the national emergency stockpile because of the mechanical failure of a freezer.

The figure is in the annual federal public accounts published earlier this fall, and comes after the agency had to write off $20 million in pharmaceuticals from the stockpile a year earlier after another freezer malfunction.

stories.title: McGuinty not aware U.S. has changed military co-operation policy with Canada
stories.summary: Halifax - Canada’s defence minister says he has not seen a memo from the U.S. secretary of war that reportedly restricts American defence co-operation with Canada.
stories.author: Devin Stevens The Canadian Press
stories.content:
HALIFAX - A Republican senator says a U.S. defence department’s memo that reportedly placed restrictions on co-operation with Canada applies to things such as participating in think-tank conferences, not military operations.

Sen. Mike Rounds was responding to a Washington Post report on Friday that said Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth penned the classified memo putting restrictions on military co-operation with Canada last week. The paper reportedly said it had not seen the memo and offered no detail on its contents.

The senator said the memo does not affect any U.S. defence personnel in Canada today and does not impact the North American Aerospace Defence Command, North Atlantic Treaty Organization operations or the Five Eyes security alliance.

U.S. Sen. Mike Rounds says a classified memo from Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth does not change the department’s co-operation with the Canadian military. Rounds was responding to a media report that said the memo placed restrictions on military co-operation between the two countries. (Nov. 21, 2026)

“It does limit general flag officer meetings to those that advance (defence department) objectives,” Rounds told reporters at the Halifax International Security Forum on Saturday. “(U.S. defence officials) must request permission for Canadian think-tank events or social engagements. And it is OK to attend any 9/11 events.”

Rounds said he and a delegation of U.S. senators attending the Halifax conference had just attended a meeting with Canadian officials and shared the information with them. Defence Minister David McGuinty told reporters hours earlier he was unaware of the memo’s contents.

“After listening to this, (Canadian officials) said it sounds like it’s nothing new, nothing different than what they’ve been really practising under for the last year-and-a-half,” said the South Dakota senator.

McGuinty said earlier in the day that it was “business as usual” between the Canadian and U.S. militaries and assured Canadians that co-operation between the two countries on defence, security and intelligence was continuing.

“I’ve seen no evidence of (a change). I’ve checked with our top military folks, they’ve seen no evidence of change. We continue to co-operate. We continue to work together,” McGuinty told reporters.

Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said in a response to the story about the memo that the defence department is “taking steps to ensure its engagements with Canada advance tangible U.S. defense objectives and ultimately support a reinvigorated defense relationship.”

The statement, made late Friday, added that the department is prioritizing bilateral co-operation that strengthens the defence of the U.S. and “shared hemisphere” while also supporting Canada’s ability to meet NATO obligations.

“This guidance does not impact defense intelligence co-operation, our binational NORAD command, or our co-operation through NATO,” Parnell said.

Several U.S. senators at the Halifax event acknowledged their country’s standing around the world has been impacted by the aggressive policies of U.S. President Donald Trump.

Senator Tim Kaine, a Democrat, said the memo doesn’t help relations with Canada. He said he’s hopeful things will change when the new U.S. Congress takes office in January. Democrats took control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives in this month’s midterm election.

“The tone is bad and it’s unnecessary,” said Kaine. “And we understand this actually goes back a ways and it is just the formalization of something that is now months and months old. I do think the new Congress is going to change the tone dramatically.”

McGuinty also announced Saturday that Canada is formally becoming the 25th member of NATO’s Innovation Fund. Canada is contributing more than $100 million to the fund, enabling it to invest in Canadian startups.

Launched in 2022, the venture capital fund is designed to strengthen NATO by investing in cutting edge technologies such as artificial intelligence, quantum technologies, biotech, space and communications.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 21, 2026.
